questions.explanation: Physical health is about your body, while mental health is about your mind and emotions. Sharing feelings helps keep your mind healthy.

questions.title: Mediums of Expression
questions.prompt: If you want to express how it feels to be in a windy storm using only paper and glue, which technique is most creative?

options.A: Cutting out a perfect square.
options.B: Tearing the paper into jagged, swirling shapes.
options.C: Drawing a straight line with a ruler.
options.D: Keeping the paper completely flat.

questions.explanation: The 'texture' and shape of the paper can reflect the feeling of the subject, like messy wind.

questions.title: Morning First
questions.prompt: Which event usually happens first in the day?

options.A: Bedtime
options.B: Dreaming after midnight
options.C: Watching sunset
options.D: Breakfast

questions.explanation: Breakfast usually comes earlier than bedtime or sunset.

questions.title: Beach Care
questions.prompt: What should you do if you finish a snack at the beach?

options.A: Leave it in the sand
options.B: Bury it by the water
options.C: Throw it at the waves
options.D: Put the wrapper in a bin

questions.explanation: Putting trash in a bin keeps beaches cleaner.

questions.title: Math Masterminds: Better Inquiry Question
questions.prompt: Which question would best guide an investigation about modeling situations with mathematical reasoning under the constraint of incomplete data? Focus on valid evidence, fair comparison, and strong reasoning.

options.A: How does changing one important factor affect support strong evidence-based decisions?
options.B: Which option is easiest to complete quickly?
options.C: Who should be blamed if results are poor?
options.D: Can we skip data collection and trust first impressions?

questions.explanation: Good inquiry questions are testable and focused on relationships between variables, not blame or convenience.

questions.title: Science Tools
questions.prompt: Why does a class have rules for using scissors and glue?

options.A: To make the room colder
options.B: To stop art forever
options.C: To keep everyone safe
options.D: To turn glue into music

questions.explanation: Safety rules help people use shared tools carefully.

questions.title: Systems & Societies: Perspective Taking
questions.prompt: A proposal about analyzing governance and social systems affects different public institutions. Which approach best shows perspective taking? Choose the option that is fair, clear, and based on real evidence.

options.A: Accept only the perspective of the loudest group.
options.B: Avoid asking stakeholders to prevent disagreement.
options.C: Compare viewpoints from multiple public institutions and explain trade-offs before deciding.
options.D: Keep the original plan unchanged, even after new feedback.

questions.explanation: Perspective taking means examining different viewpoints and making justified decisions that acknowledge trade-offs.

questions.title: Longer Ribbon
questions.prompt: Which is likely longer?

options.A: A paper clip
options.B: A jump rope
options.C: A coin
options.D: A button

questions.explanation: A jump rope is much longer than the other objects.

questions.title: Global Perspectives: Better Inquiry Question
questions.prompt: Which question would best guide an investigation about understanding local issues in a global context under the constraint of different cultural norms? Choose the option that is fair, clear, and based on real evidence.

options.A: How does changing one important factor affect build fair cooperation across regions?
options.B: Which option is easiest to complete quickly?
options.C: Who should be blamed if results are poor?
options.D: Can we skip data collection and trust first impressions?

questions.explanation: Good inquiry questions are testable and focused on relationships between variables, not blame or convenience.

questions.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: The 'Tragedy of the Commons' occurs when individuals acting in their own self-interest deplete a shared resource. Which is an example of this?

options.A: A person buying a private car.
options.B: Overfishing in international waters where no single country has control.
options.C: A farmer planting corn on their own land.
options.D: A city building a public library.

questions.explanation: When a resource is open to all (like the ocean), individuals take as much as possible, eventually destroying the resource for everyone.

questions.title: Music From Away
questions.prompt: What can music from another place teach us?

options.A: How people celebrate or feel
options.B: That only one style matters
options.C: Nothing at all
options.D: How to bake a brick

questions.explanation: Music can share feelings and traditions from a place.

questions.title: Color and Mood
questions.prompt: Why might an artist use mostly dark blues and purples in a painting of a quiet forest?

options.A: They ran out of other colors.
options.B: To make the viewer feel calm or perhaps a little mysterious.
options.C: Because the sun is always purple in forests.
options.D: To make the painting look like a fire.

questions.explanation: Artists use 'cool colors' like blue and purple to communicate feelings of peace, sadness, or nighttime.

questions.title: Rainy Song
questions.prompt: Which sound would fit a quiet rainy-day song best?

options.A: Soft taps on a drum
options.B: A car horn
options.C: A fire alarm
options.D: A loud shout

questions.explanation: Soft sounds match a calm rainy song best.

questions.title: States of Matter
questions.prompt: What happens to the molecules of a substance during 'Sublimation'?

options.A: They slow down and turn into a liquid.
options.B: They speed up and turn directly from a solid into a gas.
options.C: They stop moving entirely.
options.D: They turn into a solid from a gas.

questions.explanation: Sublimation is the phase transition where a solid becomes a gas without passing through the liquid phase (e.g., dry ice).

questions.title: Sleepy Music
questions.prompt: Which sound would fit a sleepy scene best?

options.A: A racing drum solo
options.B: A whistle blast
options.C: A trumpet alarm
options.D: A soft lullaby hum

questions.explanation: Soft gentle music fits a sleepy scene.

questions.title: Global Landmarks
questions.prompt: Which of these is a famous 'Human-made' landmark rather than a 'Natural' one?

options.A: The Grand Canyon
options.B: The Eiffel Tower
options.C: Mount Everest
options.D: The Amazon River

questions.explanation: Human-made landmarks are built by people. Natural landmarks are created by Earth over millions of years.

questions.title: Alphabet Order
questions.prompt: Which of these words would come FIRST if you put them in alphabetical order: Zebra, Apple, Monkey, Dog?

options.A: Zebra
options.B: Monkey
options.C: Apple
options.D: Dog

questions.explanation: Apple starts with 'A', which is the very first letter of the alphabet.

questions.title: Ocean Scene
questions.prompt: Which prop would fit an ocean puppet show best?

options.A: A snow shovel
options.B: A traffic cone
options.C: A blue cloth wave
options.D: A toothbrush

questions.explanation: A blue cloth can look like a wave in an ocean scene.

questions.title: Language & Craft: Ethical Decision
questions.prompt: Your class notices a risk: manipulating readers with misleading wording. What is the most ethical next step? Choose the option that is fair, clear, and based on real evidence.

options.A: Set clear consent and fairness rules, then review impacts on different groups before implementation.
options.B: Proceed quickly and discuss ethics only if someone complains.
options.C: Hide uncertain results so the project seems successful.
options.D: Exclude groups that are harder to consult.

questions.explanation: Ethical decisions require proactive consent, fairness checks, and attention to who might be helped or harmed.

questions.title: Different Homes
questions.prompt: Why might homes look different in different places?

options.A: Places have different weather and needs
options.B: People forgot how to build
options.C: All homes should look the same
options.D: The moon picks the shape

questions.explanation: Weather and local needs can change how homes are built.

questions.title: Language & Craft: Better Inquiry Question
questions.prompt: Which question would best guide an investigation about crafting precise meaning through language choices under the constraint of strict word limit? Prioritize methodological rigor, ethical implications, and long-term impact.

options.A: How does changing one important factor affect communicate with clarity and integrity?
options.B: Which option is easiest to complete quickly?
options.C: Who should be blamed if results are poor?
options.D: Can we skip data collection and trust first impressions?

questions.explanation: Good inquiry questions are testable and focused on relationships between variables, not blame or convenience.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: If 'Ice cream sales rise at the same time as drowning incidents', which logical error is made by concluding 'Ice cream causes drowning'?

options.A: False Dilemma
options.B: Confusing correlation with causation.
options.C: Ad hominem attack.
options.D: Circular reasoning.

questions.explanation: Both variables are likely caused by a third factor: hot weather. Correlation does not equal causation.

questions.title: Need Space
questions.prompt: What is a clear way to tell a friend you need quiet time?

options.A: I will hide and never talk
options.B: I need a few quiet minutes
options.C: You are the worst
options.D: I am going to throw this

questions.explanation: Clear calm words help others understand what you need.

questions.title: Cafeteria Choice
questions.prompt: At lunch, one tray of apples is left. What is a fair choice?

options.A: Take the whole tray
options.B: Hide the apples
options.C: Take one apple only
options.D: Throw them

questions.explanation: Taking one helps leave some for others.

questions.title: Globe vs. Map
questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a 'Globe' and a 'Wall Map'?

options.A: A globe is flat and a map is round.
options.B: A globe is a 3D model of Earth, while a map is 2D and flat.
options.C: Globes only show water, maps only show land.
options.D: There is no difference.

questions.explanation: Because Earth is a sphere, a globe is more accurate, but a map is easier to carry and see all at once.

questions.title: Creative Expression: Evidence Quality
questions.prompt: A team claims their creative performance improves outcomes in communicating mood and meaning through the arts. Which action gives the strongest evidence? Prioritize methodological rigor, ethical implications, and long-term impact.

options.A: Ask one audience member if they liked it.
options.B: Collect data from different audience members, compare it against a clear success criterion, and look for patterns.
options.C: Choose whichever option was finished first.
options.D: Keep the original idea without testing because it feels right.

questions.explanation: Strong evidence comes from multiple data points, clear criteria, and comparison. A single opinion or speed alone does not validate a claim.

questions.title: Kind Reply
questions.prompt: A friend says, 'I worked hard on this.' What is a kind reply?

options.A: That is silly
options.B: I do not care
options.C: Go away
options.D: I can see your effort

questions.explanation: Kind words can encourage and support a friend.

questions.title: Where We Are in Place and Time: Perspective Taking
questions.prompt: A proposal about understanding continuity and change across history and geography affects different community historians. Which approach best shows perspective taking? Focus on valid evidence, fair comparison, and strong reasoning.

options.A: Accept only the perspective of the loudest group.
options.B: Avoid asking stakeholders to prevent disagreement.
options.C: Compare viewpoints from multiple community historians and explain trade-offs before deciding.
options.D: Keep the original plan unchanged, even after new feedback.

questions.explanation: Perspective taking means examining different viewpoints and making justified decisions that acknowledge trade-offs.

questions.title: Homework Folder
questions.prompt: Why do many students use one folder just for homework?

options.A: To keep homework together
options.B: To hide cookies
options.C: To store water
options.D: To grow flowers

questions.explanation: One folder makes homework easier to find and return.

questions.title: Valuation Logic
questions.prompt: Why might an investment banker favor a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) valuation over Precedent Transactions for a highly unique startup?

options.A: DCF is easier to calculate manually.
options.B: Precedent Transactions rely on finding similar past deals, which may not exist for a unique company.
options.C: DCF ignore future growth, making it safer.
options.D: Precedent Transactions are only used for government agencies.

questions.explanation: DCF provides an intrinsic value based on future cash flows, whereas Precedent Transactions are relative and require comparable market data.

questions.title: Night and Day
questions.prompt: If it is daytime where you live, what is happening on the exact opposite side of the world?

options.A: It is also daytime.
options.B: It is nighttime.
options.C: The sun is just rising.
options.D: There is no sun there.

questions.explanation: Earth is always spinning. Only one half can face the sun at a time, so the other half is in shadow (night).

questions.title: Interconnected Civilizations
questions.prompt: How did the 'Silk Road' influence the development of cultures in both Europe and Asia?

options.A: It was only used for selling silk, having no other impact.
options.B: It facilitated the exchange of goods, religions, technologies, and even diseases across continents.
options.C: It was a wall that kept people apart.
options.D: It was an underwater tunnel for ships.

questions.explanation: The Silk Road was a network of trans-continental trade routes that acted as a primary conduit for cultural diffusion.

questions.title: Day And Night
questions.prompt: Why does it become night where you live?

options.A: The sun falls asleep under your bed
options.B: Clouds eat the light
options.C: The moon switches it off
options.D: Earth turns away from the sun

questions.explanation: Night happens when your part of Earth turns away from the sun.

questions.title: Creative Expression: Perspective Taking
questions.prompt: A proposal about communicating mood and meaning through the arts affects different audience members. Which approach best shows perspective taking? Focus on valid evidence, fair comparison, and strong reasoning.

options.A: Accept only the perspective of the loudest group.
options.B: Avoid asking stakeholders to prevent disagreement.
options.C: Compare viewpoints from multiple audience members and explain trade-offs before deciding.
options.D: Keep the original plan unchanged, even after new feedback.

questions.explanation: Perspective taking means examining different viewpoints and making justified decisions that acknowledge trade-offs.

questions.title: Emotions and Body Signals
questions.prompt: When you feel nervous before a big event, your heart beats faster and your hands might sweat. What does this tell us about emotions?

options.A: Emotions only exist in your imagination and do not affect your body
options.B: Emotions can cause real physical changes in your body
options.C: Only adults experience physical signs of nervousness
options.D: Physical signs like a fast heartbeat mean you are getting sick

questions.explanation: Emotions are connected to the body — nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and activates sweat glands. Option D is a strong distractor, but a fast heartbeat caused by emotion is not the same as illness; it stops once the stressful moment passes.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Every student has the right to learn in a safe classroom. What is the matching responsibility that comes with this right?

options.A: Choosing which lessons you want to attend each day
options.B: Helping to keep the classroom safe for everyone else too
options.C: Asking the teacher to remove students who bother you
options.D: Spending extra time on the activities you enjoy most

questions.explanation: Rights and responsibilities are paired — if you have the right to a safe space, you also have the responsibility to help create that safety for others. Option A is wrong because rights do not include unlimited personal choice over shared resources like lesson time.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Thinking
questions.prompt: A student tries to solve a maths puzzle and gets it wrong. She says, 'I can't do this yet.' Which mindset does the word 'yet' show?

options.A: A fixed mindset, because she admits she cannot solve it
options.B: A creative mindset, because she is thinking of new ideas
options.C: A growth mindset, because she believes she can improve with effort
options.D: A reflective mindset, because she is looking back at her mistake

questions.explanation: The word 'yet' is a key marker of a growth mindset — it shows the belief that abilities can be developed through practice and effort. Option A is wrong because acknowledging a current struggle is not the same as believing the ability is fixed forever.

questions.title: Cultural Identity and Belonging
questions.prompt: Two children in the same class celebrate different new year festivals. What does this best show about identity?

options.A: One child's tradition is correct and the other is mistaken
options.B: Cultural backgrounds can shape different parts of who we are
options.C: Festivals are only important when shared with the whole school
options.D: Children should all follow the same celebrations to feel included

questions.explanation: Cultural background is a key part of identity — the festivals, languages, and customs a family practices help shape a child's sense of self and belonging. Option D is wrong because sharing the same traditions is not required for inclusion; diversity of culture enriches a community.

questions.title: Identifying Feelings Accurately
questions.prompt: Omar finishes a long project and feels relieved it is done, but also a little sad it is over. Which statement is true about feelings?

options.A: You can only feel one emotion at a time
options.B: Feeling sad after finishing something means the project was too hard
options.C: A person can experience two different emotions at the same moment
options.D: Relief and sadness together mean something is wrong with your thinking

questions.explanation: It is completely normal to feel two emotions at once — this is called having mixed feelings, and it happens when a situation has more than one meaning for us. Option A is wrong because humans regularly experience blended emotions simultaneously.

questions.title: Healthy Relationships
questions.prompt: A friend always tells you what games to play and gets angry when you choose something different. Identify the problem in this friendship.

options.A: The friend is showing strong leadership skills
options.B: The friendship does not include fairness or respect for both people's choices
options.C: The problem is that you are choosing the wrong games to suggest
options.D: This is a healthy friendship because one person organises activities

questions.explanation: Healthy friendships are built on mutual respect, which includes taking turns making decisions and accepting each other's choices. Option A is wrong because leadership is not the same as controlling others — real leadership involves listening and sharing power.

questions.title: Personal Beliefs and Values
questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a personal 'value'?

options.A: A favourite food that makes you feel happy
options.B: A rule written in a school handbook
options.C: Something you believe is important and that guides how you act
options.D: A skill you have practised and become good at

questions.explanation: A value is an inner belief about what matters — such as honesty or kindness — that influences the choices a person makes. Option B is wrong because a school rule is an external instruction, not a personal belief that comes from within the individual.

questions.title: Social Health and Friendship
questions.prompt: Why is having at least one trusted person to talk to considered part of being socially healthy?

options.A: Because talking uses more energy and keeps your brain active
options.B: Because sharing feelings with a trusted person helps manage stress and feel supported
options.C: Because it means you do not have to solve any problems by yourself ever
options.D: Because social health is only measured by how many friends you have

questions.explanation: Social health includes having supportive connections — being able to share worries with a trusted person reduces stress and strengthens wellbeing. Option D is wrong because quality of relationships matters far more than the number of friends.

questions.title: Understanding Empathy
questions.prompt: Empathy means trying to understand how another person feels. Which action best shows empathy?

options.A: Telling a upset friend that your own day was harder than theirs
options.B: Listening carefully and saying 'That sounds really difficult for you'
options.C: Quickly solving your friend's problem so they stop being sad
options.D: Reminding your friend of all the good things they have

questions.explanation: Empathy involves listening and acknowledging another person's feelings without immediately trying to fix or compare — saying 'That sounds really difficult' shows you understand their experience. Option C focuses on solving rather than understanding, which is sympathy in action, not empathy.

questions.title: Brain and Learning
questions.prompt: Scientists have found that practising a skill over and over actually changes the brain. What does this tell us about our ability to learn?

options.A: Only some children are born with brains that can change and grow
options.B: The brain reaches its limit by age seven and stops changing
options.C: The brain can grow stronger connections when we practise and make effort
options.D: Changing the brain requires special medical treatment, not everyday practice

questions.explanation: Neuroscience shows that the brain has 'neuroplasticity' — repeated practice strengthens the neural pathways connected to a skill, making it easier over time. Option A is wrong because all healthy brains have the capacity for neuroplasticity, not just some children's.

questions.title: Responsibility for Self
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'It is my teacher's job to make sure I learn, so I don't need to try hard myself.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because teachers are trained to manage all learning
options.B: The claim is partly right because effort only matters in hard subjects
options.C: The claim is wrong because learners share responsibility for their own learning
options.D: The claim is correct because the teacher chooses what students practise

questions.explanation: Learning is a shared responsibility — teachers create opportunities, but the learner's own effort, attention, and practice are equally essential. Option A is wrong because even the best teacher cannot learn on behalf of the student.

questions.title: What Makes Us Similar
questions.prompt: Even though people around the world look different and speak different languages, which experience do all humans share?

options.A: Celebrating the same holidays and traditions each year
options.B: Feeling basic emotions such as joy, fear, sadness, and surprise
options.C: Living in communities that follow the same rules
options.D: Eating the same types of food for energy and health

questions.explanation: Research shows that basic emotions — like happiness, fear, sadness, and surprise — are universal across all human cultures. Option A is wrong because holidays and traditions are shaped by culture and vary widely across the world.

questions.title: Making Fair Choices
questions.prompt: There is only one extra turn on the computer. Two students both want it. What is the fairest way to decide who goes first?

options.A: The student who arrived at school first should always get priority
options.B: Use an agreed method like taking turns or drawing lots so both have an equal chance
options.C: The student with the better grades deserves the reward
options.D: The teacher should decide without asking the students

questions.explanation: Fairness means each person has an equal chance — using a neutral method like taking turns or a random draw respects both students equally. Option C is wrong because academic performance is unrelated to who deserves a fair turn at a shared activity.

questions.title: Physical and Emotional Wellbeing
questions.prompt: Why might a child who feels very worried find it hard to concentrate on a maths lesson?

options.A: Worry lowers the body's temperature, making thinking slower
options.B: Emotional feelings and thinking happen in completely separate parts of life
options.C: Strong emotions can take up mental energy that is needed for focusing
options.D: Maths is always difficult when done in the afternoon

questions.explanation: Emotional wellbeing and thinking are linked — when the brain is busy processing worry, fewer mental resources are available for tasks like concentration and problem-solving. Option B is wrong because emotions and thinking are deeply connected, not separate.

questions.title: Expressing Identity Through Art
questions.prompt: A class is asked to create self-portraits that show 'who they are inside, not just what they look like.' What does this activity explore?

options.A: How to improve drawing and painting techniques
options.B: The parts of identity that go beyond physical appearance, like interests and values
options.C: The history of self-portrait painting in different countries
options.D: How to compare your looks to other students in the class

questions.explanation: Identity includes inner qualities — such as values, interests, feelings, and beliefs — not just how a person looks. Option A is wrong because the instruction says the focus is on what is 'inside', making it an identity inquiry, not a technical art lesson.

questions.title: Handling Conflict Peacefully
questions.prompt: Two friends disagree about which game to play at break time and both start raising their voices. What is the best first step toward a peaceful solution?

options.A: Each person should walk away and not speak to the other until tomorrow
options.B: Each person should take turns explaining their feelings calmly and listen to the other
options.C: One person should give up immediately so there is no more conflict
options.D: Find a teacher to choose the game for them straight away

questions.explanation: Peaceful conflict resolution begins with each person feeling heard — taking turns to speak and listening builds understanding and opens the door to a solution both can accept. Option A is wrong because avoiding the conversation delays rather than solves the conflict.

questions.title: Understanding Stereotypes
questions.prompt: A stereotype is a fixed idea that all people in a group are the same. Why can stereotypes be harmful?

options.A: They are harmful because people should never talk about groups of people
options.B: They ignore the unique qualities and differences of individual people
options.C: They are only harmful when used to describe children, not adults
options.D: They make conversations about culture too complicated for young children

questions.explanation: Stereotypes are harmful because they treat everyone in a group as identical, which ignores each person's individual identity, experiences, and talents. Option A is wrong because discussing different groups of people can be done respectfully — the problem is assuming all members are the same.

questions.title: Self-Care and Boundaries
questions.prompt: Laila feels tired after school and wants quiet time before helping her brother. Which statement best explains why this is a healthy choice?

options.A: It is healthy because helping family members is never a child's responsibility
options.B: Taking care of your own needs first sometimes helps you support others better
options.C: It is healthy because rest is more important than relationships with family
options.D: Quiet time is only necessary when you have been ill during the week

questions.explanation: Self-care helps refill your energy so you can be more present and helpful to others — resting before helping means Laila can support her brother more effectively. Option C is wrong because it sets up a false choice; rest and relationships are both important parts of wellbeing.

questions.title: Beliefs Shaping Behaviour
questions.prompt: If a child believes that 'mistakes help me learn', how is she likely to react when she gets an answer wrong?

options.A: She will avoid trying again so she does not make another mistake
options.B: She will feel curious about what went wrong and try to improve
options.C: She will ask the teacher to give her an easier question instead
options.D: She will feel embarrassed and try to hide her answer from classmates

questions.explanation: When someone believes mistakes are learning opportunities, they respond with curiosity rather than shame — this belief motivates reflection and effort rather than avoidance. Option A describes the behaviour of someone with the opposite belief — that mistakes are bad and should be avoided.

questions.title: Belonging in a Community
questions.prompt: What does it mean to feel a sense of 'belonging' in a group or community?

options.A: Everyone in the group agrees on all the same things
options.B: You live in the same neighbourhood as the other group members
options.C: You feel accepted and valued as part of the group
options.D: You have been a member of the group for a very long time

questions.explanation: Belonging is an emotional experience — feeling accepted and valued by others, regardless of how long you have been part of the group or where you live. Option D is wrong because time in a group does not guarantee that a person feels accepted and valued.

questions.title: Understanding Strengths
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this statement: 'If something is easy for you, that means it is one of your strengths.'

options.A: There is no error — things that are easy are always strengths
options.B: The error is that a strength also needs to be something that energises and engages you, not just something easy
options.C: The error is that strengths must be physical skills, not thinking skills
options.D: The error is that only teachers can identify a student's true strengths

questions.explanation: A strength is not just something easy — researchers like Martin Seligman describe strengths as skills that also feel energising and meaningful when you use them. Option A is wrong because a task can be easy yet feel boring or draining, which means it may not be a true personal strength.

questions.title: Influence of Family on Identity
questions.prompt: In what way does a child's family most strongly shape their sense of who they are?

options.A: By deciding exactly which career the child will have when they grow up
options.B: By passing on languages, traditions, values, and stories that form part of identity
options.C: By controlling all of the friendships the child is allowed to have
options.D: By making sure the child looks similar to other members of the family

questions.explanation: Families are one of the earliest and most powerful shapers of identity — through shared language, traditions, values, and stories, children build their first understanding of who they are and where they come from. Option A is wrong because while family may influence aspirations, they do not determine a child's future career.

questions.title: Asking for Help
questions.prompt: A student always tries to figure out problems completely alone and refuses to ask for help. What might this show about her understanding of learning?

options.A: She understands that independence is the most important learning skill
options.B: She may not yet understand that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness
options.C: She shows she has a very strong growth mindset
options.D: She demonstrates that she is more capable than students who ask questions

questions.explanation: Asking for help is a sign of self-awareness and courage — learners who seek support often progress faster than those who struggle silently. Option D is wrong because seeking help when needed reflects intelligence about one's own learning needs, not a lack of capability.

questions.title: Comparing Feelings and Facts
questions.prompt: Mia says, 'I feel like nobody likes me.' Her teacher says, 'Let's check — did your friends play with you at break today?' Why does the teacher ask this question?

options.A: Because feelings are never true and should be ignored
options.B: To help Mia see whether the feeling matches what actually happened
options.C: Because the teacher does not believe Mia is telling the truth
options.D: To prove that Mia's emotions are less important than the facts

questions.explanation: Sometimes strong feelings can seem more absolute than the facts — checking what actually happened helps a person understand their emotion more clearly and respond thoughtfully. Option A is wrong because feelings are real and important, even when they do not accurately reflect events.

questions.title: Wellbeing Across Three Dimensions
questions.prompt: Which example shows a child taking care of all three dimensions of health at once — physical, mental, and social?

options.A: Reading a book alone in a quiet room for two hours
options.B: Playing a team sport outside while enjoying the game with friends
options.C: Doing twenty minutes of exercise before eating dinner alone
options.D: Spending the evening talking with family without any physical activity

questions.explanation: Playing a team sport covers physical health (exercise), social health (connecting with friends), and mental health (enjoyment and stress relief) simultaneously. Option C covers physical and possibly mental health, but lacks the social dimension that team sport provides.

questions.title: Emotions and Decision Making
questions.prompt: Maya feels very angry after losing a game. She wants to shout at her friend. Which part of her wellbeing is most affecting her choice right now?

options.A: Her physical health, because her body is tired from playing
options.B: Her social health, because she is thinking about what others will say
options.C: Her mental and emotional health, because her feelings are guiding her actions
options.D: Her spiritual health, because she is questioning what is fair

questions.explanation: Mental and emotional health refers to how our feelings and thoughts influence our behaviour — Maya's anger is an emotion that is directly shaping the choice she is about to make. Physical health (option A) relates to the body's fitness and rest, not to the emotional trigger driving her reaction.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Every child has the right to go to school. A student says, 'Because I have the right to education, I can do whatever I want in class.' Identify the error in this thinking.

options.A: The student is wrong because not every child actually has the right to education
options.B: The student is wrong because rights always come paired with responsibilities, such as letting others learn too
options.C: The student is wrong because only teachers have rights inside a classroom
options.D: The student is wrong because rights only apply outside of school buildings

questions.explanation: In the IB PYP, students learn that rights and responsibilities are connected — having a right does not remove the duty to respect the rights of others, so a student's right to learn does not allow behaviour that stops classmates from learning. Option A is incorrect because the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child does establish education as a universal right for every child.

questions.title: Beliefs and Identity
questions.prompt: Two children grow up in the same neighbourhood but celebrate different festivals and eat different foods at home. What does this best show about identity?

options.A: Identity is shaped mainly by where you live, so neighbours always share the same identity
options.B: Identity is fixed from birth and cannot be influenced by family customs
options.C: Identity is partly shaped by family beliefs, cultural practices, and traditions, even within the same community
options.D: Identity is determined by the language spoken at school rather than practices at home

questions.explanation: Wait — the correct answer is C. Family beliefs, cultural practices, and traditions are key components of identity; the scenario shows that shared geography does not create identical identities because each family's customs differ. Option A contradicts this by claiming location alone determines identity, ignoring the powerful role of family culture and belief systems.

questions.title: Emotions and Decision Making
questions.prompt: Mia feels very angry after losing a game. She wants to shout at her friend. Which reason best explains why pausing before she acts is a good idea?

options.A: Pausing helps her brain move from reacting quickly to thinking carefully about what to do
options.B: Pausing means she will forget why she was angry
options.C: Pausing always makes the other person feel sorry
options.D: Pausing helps her win the next game

questions.explanation: When we pause, the thinking part of our brain (the prefrontal cortex) can take over from the fast-reacting emotional part, helping us choose a kinder response. Pausing does not make us forget our feelings — it gives us time to understand and manage them instead.

questions.title: Beliefs Shaping Behaviour
questions.prompt: Two children both fall off their bikes. Sam thinks 'I'll never be able to ride — I'm just bad at this.' Jordan thinks 'I need more practice.' Which idea best explains why Jordan is more likely to keep trying?

options.A: Jordan's bike is probably better quality
options.B: Jordan believes that effort can improve ability, so failure feels like useful information
options.C: Jordan is naturally more athletic than Sam
options.D: Jordan does not feel pain as much as Sam does

questions.explanation: A growth mindset — the belief that ability can be developed through effort — makes challenges feel like opportunities rather than proof of failure. Sam's belief is a fixed mindset, which treats ability as unchangeable, making it harder to persist after a setback.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Every child has the right to an education. A student claims this means schools must teach every child, but children do not need to do anything in return. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct — rights exist without any matching responsibilities
options.B: The claim is partly wrong — rights and responsibilities are connected, so learners also have responsibilities like attending and respecting others
options.C: The claim is correct — only teachers have responsibilities in a school
options.D: The claim is partly wrong — children have no rights, only responsibilities

questions.explanation: In the IB framework, rights and responsibilities are linked — having a right to education also means taking responsibility for engaging respectfully and attending. Option A is a common misconception that separates rights entirely from responsibilities.

questions.title: Cultural Identity and Belonging
questions.prompt: Amara celebrates two different New Year festivals because her parents come from two different cultures. A classmate says Amara must choose just one culture as her 'real' identity. What is wrong with this thinking?

options.A: Amara should celebrate only the culture of the country she lives in now
options.B: Identity can include multiple cultural influences at the same time, so both cultures are genuinely hers
options.C: Celebrating two festivals is too confusing for a child to manage
options.D: Amara's parents should have agreed on one culture before she was born

questions.explanation: Identity is not a single fixed box — people can genuinely belong to more than one cultural group at the same time, and this enriches rather than confuses their sense of self. The idea that only one culture can be 'real' ignores how identity is shaped by many overlapping experiences and relationships.

questions.title: Empathy vs Sympathy
questions.prompt: Leo's friend is upset because his dog died. Leo says 'I know exactly how you feel — I once lost my favourite toy.' Compare what Leo did with what empathy actually involves.

options.A: Leo showed perfect empathy by sharing a personal loss
options.B: Leo tried to connect but compared different kinds of loss, which may not truly show he understands his friend's specific feeling
options.C: Leo showed sympathy correctly by feeling sorry for his friend
options.D: Leo was being unkind by talking about himself

questions.explanation: Empathy means trying to understand another person's specific feeling from their perspective, not just matching it to your own experience. Losing a toy and losing a pet are very different kinds of grief, so Leo's comparison may not fully capture his friend's pain, even though his intention was kind.

questions.title: Social Health and Conflict
questions.prompt: Two friends disagree about which game to play at break time. What is the most important first step toward resolving this disagreement fairly?

options.A: Let the louder person decide so the argument ends quickly
options.B: Each person listens to understand what the other wants and why
options.C: Ask a teacher to make the decision for them
options.D: Play alone to avoid any disagreement

questions.explanation: Fair conflict resolution begins with each person genuinely listening to understand the other's perspective and reasons, not just waiting for their turn to speak. Letting the louder person decide rewards forcefulness over fairness and does not help both children feel heard.

questions.title: Brain and Learning
questions.prompt: Scientists have found that every time you practise a skill, connections in your brain grow stronger. What does this tell us about intelligence?

options.A: Intelligence is fixed at birth and does not change no matter how much you practise
options.B: Only certain subjects like maths can make brain connections stronger
options.C: Intelligence can be developed because the brain physically changes when we learn and practise
options.D: Practising too much can make brain connections weaker

questions.explanation: Neuroscience shows that the brain is neuroplastic — it physically changes by forming stronger connections (synapses) each time a skill is practised. The idea that intelligence is fixed at birth is a fixed-mindset misconception contradicted by this evidence.

questions.title: Personal Values and Choices
questions.prompt: Priya values honesty. Her friend asks her to say she was present at a party she never went to. Priya refuses even though it would help her friend. Which idea best explains Priya's choice?

options.A: Priya does not care about her friend's feelings
options.B: Priya is acting according to her personal values even when it is difficult
options.C: Priya is following a school rule about lying
options.D: Priya knows she will be caught if she lies

questions.explanation: Values are the deep beliefs that guide our choices — when someone acts on a value like honesty even when it is uncomfortable or costly, that shows character. Option D mistakes acting from fear of punishment for acting from genuine values.

questions.title: Physical and Mental Health Link
questions.prompt: A student notices that on days when she exercises, she feels less worried about things. What is the most likely explanation for this connection?

options.A: Exercise makes her too tired to remember her worries
options.B: Exercise releases chemicals in the brain that improve mood and reduce feelings of anxiety
options.C: Worrying burns more energy, so exercise replaces it
options.D: She only worries about physical things, and exercise fixes those directly

questions.explanation: Physical exercise causes the brain to release chemicals called endorphins and other mood-boosting substances that genuinely reduce anxiety and improve wellbeing. Option A is a misconception — tiredness alone does not explain the mood benefit, and the effect happens even with mild exercise.

questions.title: Stereotypes and Identity
questions.prompt: Some people assume that all boys like football and all girls like dancing. Identify the error in this kind of thinking.

options.A: It is only an error if most boys and girls in your school disagree with it
options.B: It treats all people in a group as the same, ignoring each person's individual identity and interests
options.C: It is an error because sports and dance are not school subjects
options.D: It is only wrong if the children involved feel upset about it

questions.explanation: Stereotypes apply a single trait to every member of a group, which ignores individual identity — the fact that each person has their own unique interests, experiences, and characteristics. Option D is a misconception because stereotypes are flawed regardless of whether they cause visible upset.

questions.title: Wellbeing and Basic Needs
questions.prompt: Maslow's idea says people need to feel safe before they can focus on learning and friendship. What would happen if a child came to school hungry and worried about where she would sleep that night?

options.A: She would likely find it harder to concentrate on learning because basic needs are not yet met
options.B: She would focus better because she would want to distract herself from her worries
options.C: Her learning would not be affected because the brain separates feelings from thinking
options.D: She would feel motivated to work harder so her situation improves

questions.explanation: When basic physical and safety needs are unmet, the brain stays in a survival-focused state, making it genuinely harder to concentrate, remember, and connect with others. Option D is a common but overly optimistic misconception — stress from unmet needs usually reduces, not increases, academic performance.

questions.title: Fairness and Equity
questions.prompt: Three children need to see the stage at a concert. One is tall, one is average height, and one uses a wheelchair. Giving each child the exact same box to stand on would be equal. Would it be fair? Why or why not?

options.A: Yes, because equal treatment always means fair treatment
options.B: No, because the child in the wheelchair cannot use a box, so the same solution does not give everyone the same outcome
options.C: No, because the tall child should not receive any box
options.D: Yes, because rules must be the same for everyone to be respected

questions.explanation: Fairness (equity) means giving people what they each need to reach the same outcome, which is different from equality, which gives everyone the identical thing. A box does not help a wheelchair user see the stage, so identical treatment produces an unequal result.

questions.title: Self-Awareness and Feelings
questions.prompt: Before an important spelling test, Kai's heart beats fast and his hands feel sweaty. He thinks this means he is not ready. Could these same body signals mean something different? Which answer best explains this?

options.A: No — a racing heart always means you are unprepared
options.B: Yes — these body signals can also mean excitement or readiness, and how we label them affects how we feel
options.C: Yes — but only athletes learn to use these signals positively
options.D: No — body signals are facts, not interpretations

questions.explanation: The same physical sensations — fast heartbeat, sweaty hands — can be labelled as anxiety or excitement, and research shows that calling it 'excitement' can actually improve performance. Option A is a misconception because the body's stress response is context-dependent and open to reinterpretation.

questions.title: Responsibility to Community
questions.prompt: A student claims that keeping her classroom tidy is only important because the teacher will give out stickers. What does this reasoning miss about responsibility?

options.A: Nothing — rewards are the only real reason to behave responsibly
options.B: It misses that responsibility also means acting for the good of the group even without a reward
options.C: It misses that tidiness is only the teacher's job
options.D: It misses that stickers are not a good enough reward

questions.explanation: Genuine responsibility means understanding that your actions affect others in the community and choosing to contribute even when no reward is offered. Relying entirely on external rewards means the responsible behaviour may stop the moment the reward disappears.

questions.title: Friendship and Trust
questions.prompt: What makes trust an important part of a healthy friendship, compared to simply liking the same things?

options.A: Trust is less important than shared interests because friendships are built on fun
options.B: Trust allows friends to feel safe being honest and vulnerable, which shared interests alone cannot provide
options.C: Trust only matters in adult relationships, not children's friendships
options.D: Liking the same things automatically creates trust between people

questions.explanation: Trust means knowing that a friend will keep your secrets, tell you the truth, and support you even when it is hard — this sense of safety goes much deeper than enjoying the same activities. Shared interests can bring people together, but trust is what makes the friendship feel secure and meaningful.

questions.title: Recognising Peer Pressure
questions.prompt: A group of children tells Zara she must take an extra biscuit from the lunch trolley or they will not play with her. Zara knows this is against the rules. Which best describes what Zara is experiencing?

options.A: A test of her physical courage
options.B: Peer pressure, where belonging is used to push her into breaking her own values
options.C: A normal part of making friends at school
options.D: A conflict between two school rules she must follow

questions.explanation: Peer pressure occurs when the desire to belong or be accepted is used to push someone into acting against their own values or rules. Option C is a misconception — healthy friendship-making does not involve threats of exclusion to force rule-breaking.

questions.title: Language and Identity
questions.prompt: Carlos speaks Spanish at home and English at school. He sometimes mixes words from both languages in one sentence. A student says Carlos is confused about his identity. Is this correct?

options.A: Yes, because using two languages at once shows he has not fully learned either one
options.B: No, because speaking more than one language is a sign of language confusion, not identity confusion
options.C: No, because the languages Carlos speaks are part of his identity, and mixing them is a natural part of being bilingual
options.D: Yes, because people should keep languages separate to respect each culture

questions.explanation: Mixing languages (code-switching) is a natural, skilled behaviour among bilingual speakers — it reflects a rich identity that includes multiple cultural and linguistic influences, not confusion. Knowing two languages is a cognitive strength, not a sign of incomplete learning.

questions.title: Healthy Boundaries
questions.prompt: Your friend keeps hugging you even after you have asked her to stop. She says she is just being friendly. Which idea best explains why this situation is still a problem?

options.A: It is not a problem if the friend means well
options.B: Personal boundaries must be respected even if the other person has good intentions
options.C: It only becomes a problem if an adult sees it happening
options.D: You should just accept it because hugging is a normal part of friendship

questions.explanation: Personal boundaries are about your right to decide what happens to your own body, and a good intention does not remove another person's responsibility to respect a clear boundary. Option A is a common misconception — intent does not override the impact on the person whose boundary was crossed.

questions.title: Asking for Help
questions.prompt: Yusuf struggles with reading but never asks for help because he worries it will make him look less intelligent. What misunderstanding is Yusuf making about asking for help?

options.A: He is right — asking for help in reading shows a fixed weakness
options.B: He is confusing needing support with being unable to grow, when asking for help is actually a strategy that leads to learning
options.C: He is right that others may judge him, so he should find all answers independently
options.D: He misunderstands that only maths help is acceptable to ask for

questions.explanation: Asking for help is a learning strategy — it allows the brain to receive new information and practise, which is how skills develop. Believing that needing help proves permanent inability is a fixed-mindset error that gets in the way of growth.

questions.title: Comparing Past and Present Self
questions.prompt: Nina looks at a drawing she made when she was five and compares it to one she made last week. She notices many differences. Which idea does this comparison best illustrate?

options.A: That she has a natural talent for art that was always there
options.B: That identity and ability stay the same throughout childhood
options.C: That people change and develop over time through experience and practice
options.D: That younger children are less creative than older ones

questions.explanation: Comparing earlier and later work shows that we are not fixed — our skills, thinking, and even how we see ourselves change and grow over time through experience, practice, and learning. Option B is the opposite of what the comparison shows.

questions.title: Kindness and Wellbeing
questions.prompt: Research shows that doing something kind for someone else can also make the person doing it feel happier. Why might this be true?

options.A: Because people feel proud of themselves only when others notice what they did
options.B: Because kindness activates feelings of connection and meaning in the brain, which improves wellbeing
options.C: Because helping others means you expect them to help you back, which is reassuring
options.D: Because doing kind things keeps you busy so you have no time to feel unhappy

questions.explanation: Acts of kindness trigger the release of oxytocin and other wellbeing chemicals in the brain, creating a genuine sense of connection and purpose that boosts the giver's mood. Option A is a misconception because research shows the positive effect occurs even when acts of kindness are done anonymously.

questions.title: Making and Breaking Rules
questions.prompt: A class agrees on a rule that everyone must take turns speaking. One day, a student breaks the rule because she says her idea is very important. What does this show about why rules matter in a community?

options.A: It shows that rules should only apply when someone's idea is not important
options.B: It shows that community rules protect everyone's right to participate, and breaking them — even for good reasons — affects fairness for all
options.C: It shows that the rule about turn-taking was a bad rule and should be removed
options.D: It shows that important ideas should always be allowed to interrupt the normal order

questions.explanation: Community rules are agreements that protect equal participation — when one person decides their reason is important enough to break the rule, it undermines the fairness the rule was designed to create. Option D is a common student misconception that judges the importance of an idea as a justification for ignoring agreed norms.

questions.title: Media and Self-Image
questions.prompt: Many children see images in advertisements where all the people look similar — tall, slim, and with particular features. What effect might seeing only these images have on how children feel about themselves?

options.A: No effect — children understand that advertisements are not real life
options.B: It might lead some children to believe there is only one way to look, making them feel less valued if they look different
options.C: It would help children set healthy goals for how to look as they grow
options.D: It would only affect children who already had low confidence before seeing the images

questions.explanation: When media repeatedly shows a narrow range of body types and features, it can create the impression that this is the 'correct' way to look, which may lower self-esteem in children who do not match that image. Option A overestimates young children's ability to critically analyse advertising, which is a skill that develops over time.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Beliefs
questions.prompt: A student fails a math test and thinks, 'I'm just not a math person.' Which response best shows a growth mindset?

options.A: Accept that some people are naturally better at math and focus on other subjects.
options.B: Ask the teacher to make the next test easier so you can feel more confident.
options.C: Recognise that the brain can strengthen with practice and try different study strategies.
options.D: Compare your score with classmates to see whether you are really behind.

questions.explanation: A growth mindset, defined by psychologist Carol Dweck, means believing that ability develops through effort and effective strategies — exactly what option C describes. Option A reflects a fixed mindset, mistaking current performance for permanent, unchangeable ability.

questions.title: Brain and Emotions
questions.prompt: Which part of the brain is most responsible for processing strong emotions like fear and anger?

options.A: Cerebellum
options.B: Amygdala
options.C: Prefrontal cortex
options.D: Hippocampus

questions.explanation: The amygdala is an almond-shaped structure in the limbic system that detects threats and triggers emotional responses such as fear and anger. The prefrontal cortex is a common distractor because it regulates emotional responses, but it processes reasoning rather than generating the raw emotion.

questions.title: Cultural Identity Formation
questions.prompt: A student moves from Japan to Brazil at age nine and starts adopting new local customs while keeping Japanese traditions at home. Which term best describes this process?

options.A: Assimilation
options.B: Isolation
options.C: Acculturation
options.D: Stereotyping

questions.explanation: Acculturation describes adapting elements of a new culture while maintaining aspects of one's original culture — precisely what the student is doing. Assimilation is a strong distractor but means fully adopting the new culture and losing the original one, which is not what the student is doing.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child states that children have the right to education. What is the matching responsibility that comes with this right?

options.A: Choosing which subjects you personally prefer to study.
options.B: Engaging seriously with learning and respecting others' right to learn too.
options.C: Requiring the school to provide every resource you request.
options.D: Deciding your own school timetable independently.

questions.explanation: Rights and responsibilities are paired: the right to education comes with the responsibility to engage genuinely and allow others the same opportunity. Option A confuses personal preference with civic responsibility, making it a plausible but incorrect choice.

questions.title: Social Health Relationships
questions.prompt: Why is having at least one trusted person to talk to considered important for a child's social health?

options.A: It guarantees that you will never feel sad or anxious.
options.B: It reduces the need to develop your own problem-solving skills.
options.C: It provides emotional support that helps regulate stress and builds resilience.
options.D: It means your thoughts and decisions are always validated.

questions.explanation: Research in social psychology shows that secure, trusting relationships activate support systems that buffer stress hormones and build resilience over time. Option A is the top distractor because trusted relationships genuinely help with difficult emotions, but they cannot guarantee freedom from sadness or anxiety.

questions.title: Perspective and Empathy
questions.prompt: A classmate argues loudly during a group project. Instead of getting angry, you pause and consider what pressures they might be dealing with at home. Which IB PYP key concept are you applying?

options.A: Function
options.B: Causation
options.C: Perspective
options.D: Form

questions.explanation: Perspective as a PYP key concept involves understanding that different viewpoints, values, and experiences shape how people think and behave — which is exactly what you do by considering your classmate's situation. Causation is a strong distractor because thinking about 'pressures at home' involves cause-and-effect, but the deliberate act of adopting another's viewpoint is specifically the concept of perspective.

questions.title: Wellbeing Frameworks
questions.prompt: In wellbeing models often used in schools, which of the following is considered a dimension of wellbeing SEPARATE from physical health?

options.A: Nutritional intake
options.B: Cardiovascular fitness
options.C: Spiritual or purposeful wellbeing
options.D: Bone density

questions.explanation: Wellbeing frameworks such as the WHO definition and CASEL models identify spiritual, emotional, social, and cognitive dimensions alongside physical health. Nutritional intake and cardiovascular fitness are strong distractors but both fall under physical health rather than representing a separate dimension.

questions.title: Identity and Stereotypes
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this statement: 'Because Marcus is from a country where football is popular, he must love football himself.'

options.A: The statement correctly links national culture to individual preferences.
options.B: The statement applies a group generalisation to predict an individual's personal identity.
options.C: The statement is only wrong because football is not actually popular in that country.
options.D: The statement makes an error only if Marcus has never seen a football match.

questions.explanation: The error is stereotyping — assuming an individual shares all traits of their cultural group, which ignores personal identity. Option A is the top distractor because culture does influence individuals, but it does not determine every individual preference, making a blanket assumption a logical error.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning Basics
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'An action is right if it follows a rule that everyone agreed on, regardless of the outcome.' Which ethical approach does this best describe?

options.A: Consequentialism
options.B: Virtue ethics
options.C: Deontological ethics
options.D: Relativism

questions.explanation: Deontological ethics, associated with philosopher Immanuel Kant, holds that actions are right or wrong based on rules or duties, not on their consequences. Consequentialism is the top distractor because it is a well-known ethical theory, but it judges actions by outcomes rather than rules — the opposite of what the statement describes.

questions.title: Reflection and Metacognition
questions.prompt: What is the difference between thinking about a topic and metacognition?

options.A: Metacognition only happens when you are studying science or mathematics.
options.B: Metacognition means thinking about your own thinking processes and how you learn.
options.C: Thinking about a topic and metacognition are exactly the same thing.
options.D: Metacognition refers exclusively to memorising facts more efficiently.

questions.explanation: Metacognition literally means 'thinking about thinking' — it involves monitoring your own understanding, strategies, and learning processes rather than just engaging with content. Option C is a common distractor because both involve thinking, but metacognition specifically turns attention inward to the process of thought itself.

questions.title: Physical and Mental Health Link
questions.prompt: Research shows that regular physical exercise can improve mood. Which biological mechanism best explains this connection?

options.A: Exercise lowers body temperature, which directly silences anxious thoughts.
options.B: Exercise releases endorphins, which are chemicals that reduce pain and boost positive feelings.
options.C: Exercise increases the amount of sleep hormones circulating during the day.
options.D: Exercise strengthens bones, which sends positive signals directly to the brain.

questions.explanation: During and after exercise, the brain releases endorphins — natural chemicals that bind to receptors in the nervous system to reduce pain perception and create feelings of wellbeing, sometimes called a 'runner's high.' Option D is a distractor because exercise does strengthen bones, but bone density does not directly influence mood through neural signalling.

questions.title: Personal Values and Decisions
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen if a person's actions consistently contradicted their own stated values?

options.A: They would feel a sense of internal conflict, sometimes called cognitive dissonance.
options.B: Their values would automatically update to match their actions.
options.C: Other people would immediately trust them less with no inner effect on the person.
options.D: They would become more decisive because their values become clearer through contrast.

questions.explanation: Psychologist Leon Festinger identified cognitive dissonance as the mental discomfort felt when one's actions conflict with one's beliefs or values. Option B is a plausible distractor because over time values can shift, but this is a gradual social process, not an automatic update that resolves the conflict immediately.

questions.title: Healthy Human Relationships
questions.prompt: Compare a relationship built on mutual respect with one built on fear. Which statement accurately identifies a key difference?

options.A: Fear-based relationships are more stable over time because rules are clearly enforced.
options.B: Mutual-respect relationships allow people to express disagreement safely, while fear-based ones discourage honest communication.
options.C: Both types of relationship produce equally positive mental health outcomes for all involved.
options.D: Respect-based relationships only work among people with the same cultural background.

questions.explanation: In mutual-respect relationships, people feel psychologically safe to voice concerns without punishment, which promotes honest dialogue and problem-solving. Fear-based relationships suppress authentic communication because people worry about negative consequences, which is a key structural difference identified in relationship psychology. Option A is a distractor because enforced rules may create short-term compliance but long-term instability due to resentment.

questions.title: Responsibility and Community
questions.prompt: A student notices litter in the school garden but did not drop it. Should they pick it up? Which reasoning best supports the idea that they should?

options.A: Responsibility only applies to actions you personally caused.
options.B: Picking it up earns reward points from the school.
options.C: Community responsibility extends beyond personal causation to shared care of shared spaces.
options.D: They should only act if a teacher specifically instructs them to.

questions.explanation: Community responsibility is a concept that holds members of a shared space accountable for its wellbeing, not just for their own direct actions. Option A is the top distractor because it represents a common and logically coherent alternative view, but it reflects a narrow personal-causation model that does not account for civic responsibility.

questions.title: Self-Concept Development
questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the term 'self-concept'?

options.A: The score you receive on a personality test taken at school.
options.B: The collection of beliefs a person holds about who they are, including roles, traits, and values.
options.C: The way other people describe your behaviour in social situations.
options.D: Your genetic traits inherited from your biological parents.

questions.explanation: Self-concept refers to the cognitive and evaluative beliefs an individual holds about themselves — encompassing personal identity, roles, values, and characteristics. Option C is a plausible distractor because others' perceptions can influence self-concept, but self-concept itself is internal, not the external description itself.

questions.title: Conflict Resolution Skills
questions.prompt: Two friends disagree about how to divide a group project fairly. Which strategy is most likely to result in both friends feeling heard and the conflict being resolved?

options.A: One friend gives in completely to keep the peace.
options.B: They each present their reasoning and try to find a solution that addresses both perspectives.
options.C: They ask the teacher to decide for them without discussing it first.
options.D: They work in separate groups so there is no need to agree.

questions.explanation: Collaborative problem-solving, where each party articulates their needs and works toward mutual accommodation, is the most effective conflict resolution strategy for maintaining relationships and reaching fair outcomes. Option A is a distractor because giving in may end the immediate conflict, but it does not make the person feel heard and may cause future resentment.

questions.title: Beliefs and Behaviour
questions.prompt: Why might a person's deeply held beliefs affect the decisions they make every day?

options.A: Beliefs are stored in long-term memory and act as filters through which people interpret situations and choose actions.
options.B: Beliefs are only relevant during major life decisions like choosing a career.
options.C: Beliefs affect decisions only when a person consciously thinks about them.
options.D: Beliefs influence decisions solely in religious or cultural ceremonies.

questions.explanation: Cognitive psychology shows that beliefs function as mental schemas — stored frameworks that automatically shape how individuals interpret events and evaluate options in everyday situations, not just major decisions. Option C is a strong distractor because it seems reasonable, but research shows that unconscious beliefs guide routine decision-making even without deliberate reflection.

questions.title: Emotional Regulation Strategies
questions.prompt: A student feels overwhelmed before a big presentation. Which strategy uses the connection between breathing and the nervous system to reduce anxiety?

options.A: Reviewing all the things that could go wrong in order to prepare mentally.
options.B: Slow, deep diaphragmatic breathing to activate the parasympathetic nervous system.
options.C: Drinking a caffeinated drink to increase alertness and focus.
options.D: Avoiding eye contact with the audience to reduce sensory input.

questions.explanation: Slow, deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system — sometimes called 'rest and digest' — which counteracts the stress response driven by the sympathetic nervous system, lowering heart rate and reducing anxiety. Option D is a distractor because reducing eye contact may feel soothing momentarily, but it does not change the physiological stress response.

questions.title: Human Rights in Practice
questions.prompt: Article 12 of the UNCRC states that children have the right to express their views freely in matters that affect them. Which school practice best reflects this right?

options.A: Teachers deciding all classroom rules without student input.
options.B: Students completing anonymous surveys on school improvements that are then reviewed by leadership.
options.C: Holding a school assembly where attendance is mandatory but speaking is not permitted.
options.D: Allowing students to express views only outside of school hours.

questions.explanation: Article 12 requires that children's views be genuinely sought and given due weight in decisions affecting them — an anonymous survey reviewed by leadership is a structured mechanism that satisfies both expression and consideration. Option A is the top distractor because it involves teachers making decisions about students, but it excludes student voice entirely, directly contradicting Article 12.

questions.title: Connection Between Identities
questions.prompt: A student identifies as both a competitive swimmer and a creative writer. Why is it important to recognise that one person can hold multiple identities at once?

options.A: Because only one identity can be authentic at a time.
options.B: Because recognising multiple identities prevents people from having any single strong interest.
options.C: Because identity is complex and reducing a person to one label leads to incomplete and sometimes harmful understanding.
options.D: Because schools legally require students to list all their identities officially.

questions.explanation: Identity is multidimensional — social scientists use the term 'intersectionality' to describe how overlapping identities interact. Reducing a person to a single identity produces stereotyping and misses the richness of individual experience. Option A is a common misconception and a plausible distractor, but authenticity does not require exclusivity among identities.

questions.title: Mindfulness and Attention
questions.prompt: What does the practice of mindfulness primarily train a person to do?

options.A: To suppress all negative thoughts permanently.
options.B: To focus attention on the present moment without judging what is noticed.
options.C: To plan future goals while ignoring current distractions.
options.D: To recall past events accurately through structured memory exercises.

questions.explanation: Mindfulness, rooted in contemplative traditions and validated by neuroscience research (including work by Jon Kabat-Zinn), trains attention to rest on present-moment experience with non-judgmental awareness. Option A is a strong distractor because mindfulness does address negative thoughts, but the goal is to observe them without judgment rather than suppress them.

questions.title: Cause of Peer Pressure
questions.prompt: Why does peer pressure tend to be stronger during the pre-teenage and teenage years than in early childhood?

options.A: Younger children have stronger memories and are less easily influenced.
options.B: Social belonging becomes increasingly important to identity formation as children develop, making peer approval more significant.
options.C: Peer pressure is actually equal across all age groups but is reported more by teenagers.
options.D: The brain fully matures by age seven, so younger children make more independent choices.

questions.explanation: Developmental psychology shows that as children move toward adolescence, peer relationships become a primary source of identity and self-evaluation, increasing sensitivity to social approval and group norms. Option D is a distractor because it contains a factual error — the brain, especially the prefrontal cortex, continues developing into the mid-twenties.

questions.title: Form of Cultural Expression
questions.prompt: Language, art, food, and ceremony are all examples of what aspect of cultural identity?

options.A: Genetic heritage passed through family bloodlines.
options.B: Legal nationality as recorded on official documents.
options.C: Cultural practices and expressions that shape and transmit shared identity.
options.D: Economic status indicators within a community.

questions.explanation: Language, art, food, and ceremony are forms of cultural expression — the practices and symbols through which communities construct, communicate, and transmit their shared identity across generations. Option A is a distractor because genetics can be related to heritage, but cultural practices are learned and transmitted socially, not biologically.

questions.title: Responsibility Toward Self
questions.prompt: A student stays up until midnight gaming on a school night, knowing they have an important test the next morning. Which IB PYP key concept is most relevant to evaluating this choice?

options.A: Form
options.B: Connection
options.C: Responsibility
options.D: Function

questions.explanation: The PYP key concept of Responsibility includes taking ownership of one's own actions and their consequences — in this case, choosing short-term enjoyment over the self-care needed for academic performance. Connection is a plausible distractor because one could argue the choice connects gaming habits to test results, but the primary evaluative lens for personal decision-making and self-care is Responsibility.

questions.title: Sink or Float Forces
questions.prompt: A wooden block and a small metal bolt are both dropped into a tank of water. The bolt sinks but the wooden block floats. What is the BEST explanation for this difference?

options.A: The wooden block is larger, so water cannot touch all of it
options.B: The wooden block is less dense than water, so water pushes it up more than gravity pulls it down
options.C: The metal bolt is heavier in total weight, so all metal objects always sink
options.D: Wood repels water while metal attracts water

questions.explanation: An object floats when its density is lower than the density of water; wood typically has a density less than 1 g/cm³ while most metals are far denser, so the upward push from water (buoyancy) is enough to keep wood at the surface. Option C is tempting but incorrect — a large, hollow metal ship floats because its overall density (including the air inside) is less than water, so total weight alone does not determine sinking or floating.

questions.title: Plant Food Making
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Plants get all their food from the soil through their roots.' Evaluate this claim. What is missing from this explanation?

options.A: Plants also need sunlight and carbon dioxide from the air to make their own food through photosynthesis
options.B: Plants do not use their roots at all — they absorb everything through their leaves
options.C: Plants only need water and warmth to produce food, not anything from the air
options.D: The claim is correct; roots provide minerals and sugars that count as all the food a plant needs

questions.explanation: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis, which requires sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide — the carbon dioxide comes from the air through tiny pores called stomata, not from the soil.
