questions.prompt: A poet writes: 'The bees buzzed busily between blooms.' Which sound device is the poet using in this line?

options.A: Rhyme
options.B: Simile
options.C: Alliteration
options.D: Metaphor

questions.explanation: Alliteration is the repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of nearby words — here the 'b' sound repeats in 'bees,' 'buzzed,' 'busily,' 'between,' and 'blooms.' Rhyme is the top distractor because it is also a sound device in poetry, but rhyme involves matching sounds at the end of words or lines, not repeated initial consonants.

questions.title: Architecture as Expression
questions.prompt: Many ancient temples and cathedrals were built to be extremely tall and grand. What were architects most likely trying to express through this design choice?

options.A: The need to house as many people as possible inside
options.B: A sense of awe, spiritual power, and the importance of the institution
options.C: The availability of cheap building materials in the region
options.D: A desire to block sunlight from the surrounding streets

questions.explanation: Throughout history, architects used height and grandeur in religious buildings — such as Gothic cathedrals like Notre-Dame de Paris — to inspire awe in visitors and communicate the spiritual authority and importance of the institution. Practical capacity is the top distractor because large buildings do hold more people, but ancient temples and cathedrals were deliberately designed to overwhelm the senses, not primarily to maximise occupancy.

questions.title: Photography and Framing
questions.prompt: A photographer takes a picture of a child by crouching down to the child's eye level instead of shooting from above. How does this choice change what the photograph expresses?

options.A: It makes the child appear less important than the background
options.B: It creates an equal and empathetic view of the child's world
options.C: It causes the image to be blurry and out of focus
options.D: It shows the photographer does not know basic camera skills

questions.explanation: Shooting at a subject's eye level is a deliberate compositional choice that communicates equality and invites the viewer into the subject's perspective — photographers like Henri Cartier-Bresson used this technique to create empathy. Shooting from above is the top distractor because it would make the child appear smaller or less powerful, but the question describes the opposite angle.

questions.title: Oral Storytelling Traditions
questions.prompt: Many Indigenous cultures pass knowledge and history from one generation to the next through spoken stories rather than written texts. What is a key advantage of this oral tradition?

options.A: It means the stories never change and are perfectly preserved forever
options.B: It allows stories to be shared within communities that may not use written language, keeping culture alive
options.C: It is faster to produce than any form of written communication
options.D: It prevents outsiders from ever learning about the culture

questions.explanation: Oral traditions are particularly valuable for communities where literacy rates are low or where writing was historically unavailable, allowing culture, values, and history to survive across generations through performance and memory. The idea that stories never change is the top distractor because oral stories actually do evolve with each telling — this flexibility is both a feature and a limitation of oral tradition.

questions.title: Semiotics and Signs
questions.prompt: Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols. A red octagon on a road is recognised as meaning 'Stop' by drivers in many countries. What type of sign is this, according to semiotic theory?

options.A: An iconic sign, because it looks exactly like what it represents
options.B: An indexical sign, because it points to a natural cause
options.C: A symbolic sign, because the meaning is agreed upon by society rather than looking like the thing it represents
options.D: A decorative sign, because its main purpose is aesthetic

questions.explanation: According to semiotician Charles Sanders Peirce, a symbolic sign is one where the connection between sign and meaning is arbitrary — agreed upon by social convention rather than resemblance. A red octagon does not look like 'stopping,' so its meaning must be learned culturally. An iconic sign is the top distractor because people often think visual signs must look like what they represent, but the stop sign's shape and colour carry no natural resemblance to the act of stopping.

questions.title: Costume and Character
questions.prompt: In a school play, a student is cast as a villain. The costume designer gives the character all-black clothing and a long dark cloak. What does this costume choice rely on?

options.A: The audience's ability to read cultural colour symbolism to understand the character's role
options.B: The cheapest available fabric in the costume store
options.C: The actor's personal preference for dark colours
options.D: A scientific rule that dark colours absorb more stage light

questions.explanation: In many Western theatrical traditions, black is culturally associated with danger, evil, and mystery — a convention audiences recognise from fairy tales and films, making it an effective shorthand for villainy without dialogue. The cost of fabric is the top distractor because practical constraints do affect costume choices in some productions, but the question asks what the choice 'relies on,' pointing to its communicative function.

questions.title: Graffiti as Art
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Graffiti painted without permission is not real art because it is illegal.' Evaluate this claim. Which response most accurately addresses the relationship between legality and artistic value?

options.A: The claim is correct — something illegal cannot have artistic value
options.B: The claim confuses legal status with artistic merit; many recognised artworks were created illegally or challenged social rules
options.C: The claim is correct because museums only accept legal artworks
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because all graffiti is eventually made legal by city councils

questions.explanation: Legal status and artistic value are separate judgements — artist Banksy, whose unauthorised street art now sells for millions at major auction houses, is a well-known example of illegally produced work with significant recognised artistic value. The idea that museums only accept legal artworks is the top distractor, but museums frequently display works with complicated legal histories, and artistic merit is judged independently of legality.

questions.title: Metaphor in Language
questions.prompt: A writer describes a fierce argument using the sentence: 'The debate was a battlefield, with words flying like bullets.' What literary device is used here?

options.A: Personification
options.B: Extended metaphor
options.C: Onomatopoeia
options.D: Hyperbole

questions.explanation: An extended metaphor applies a single comparison — in this case comparing debate to warfare — across multiple connected images ('battlefield,' 'words flying like bullets'), sustaining the comparison beyond a single phrase. Hyperbole is the top distractor because the language does feel exaggerated, but hyperbole means deliberate overstatement for effect, while this sentence builds a consistent warfare comparison throughout rather than simply exaggerating one fact.

questions.title: Film and Cause-Effect
questions.prompt: In a suspense film, the director plays eerie, slow violin music just before a surprise moment. What effect does this musical choice most likely have on the audience, and why?

options.A: It relaxes the audience so they are more comfortable in their seats
options.B: It builds tension and signals danger, preparing the audience emotionally before the shock arrives
options.C: It distracts the audience from noticing poor acting
options.D: It tells the audience the film is about to end

questions.explanation: Film composers deliberately use dissonant, slow string music to trigger a physiological sense of unease — this is a well-documented technique in horror and thriller scoring, used by composers like Bernard Herrmann in Psycho. Relaxing the audience is the top distractor because music does affect comfort, but slow eerie violin music is specifically calibrated to increase anxiety, not reduce it.

questions.title: Mask Traditions Globally
questions.prompt: Masks are used in ceremonies and performances across many different cultures — from Japanese Noh theatre to West African Yoruba festivals. What shared function do masks most commonly serve in these contexts?

options.A: They protect the wearer's face from physical harm
options.B: They allow the wearer to take on a different identity or spiritual role
options.C: They are used only to frighten children during festivals
options.D: They indicate how wealthy the wearer's family is

questions.explanation: Across cultures, masks serve as transformative objects that allow wearers to embody ancestral spirits, deities, or fictional characters — in Japanese Noh theatre masks represent specific character types, while in Yoruba Egungun ceremonies masks represent ancestral presences. Physical protection is the top distractor because modern safety equipment includes masks, but ceremonial masks across these cultures have a symbolic, identity-transforming purpose rather than a protective one.

questions.title: Change in Art Movements
questions.prompt: In the late 19th century, Impressionist painters like Claude Monet began painting loose, blurry brushstrokes instead of the precise, detailed style that was expected at the time. What does this change in style suggest about the function of art?

options.A: Art styles never change because beauty is the same in every century
options.B: Artists intentionally broke rules to express a new way of seeing and capture feeling rather than exact detail
options.C: Monet could not afford high-quality paintbrushes, so his work was imprecise
options.D: Blurry painting is technically easier, so artists chose it to save time

questions.explanation: The Impressionist movement was a deliberate artistic rebellion against the precise academic style required by institutions like the French Salon — Monet and his peers wanted to capture fleeting moments of light and atmosphere rather than photographic accuracy, representing a philosophical shift in what art was for. The idea that Monet lacked quality materials is the top distractor, but Impressionists were established professional artists who chose their technique deliberately.

questions.title: Audience and Purpose
questions.prompt: A children's picture book and a newspaper editorial are both about the same environmental issue — deforestation. Identify the most important difference in how each text would express its message.

options.A: The picture book would contain more accurate scientific data than the editorial
options.B: The editorial would use persuasive argument and evidence, while the picture book would use simple narrative and illustrations to build empathy
options.C: Both texts would use identical language because they are about the same topic
options.D: The editorial would avoid opinions, presenting only neutral facts

questions.explanation: Texts are shaped by their audience and purpose — an editorial targets adult readers and aims to persuade through logical argument and evidence, while a picture book targets young children and uses storytelling and images to build emotional connection rather than political argument. The idea that both texts would use identical language is the top distractor because the topic is the same, but audience awareness means form and language must differ significantly.

questions.title: Reflection in Creative Process
questions.prompt: After finishing a painting, an art teacher asks students to write about what worked well and what they would change. What is the primary reason for this reflection step in the creative process?

options.A: To give the teacher extra work to mark at the end of term
options.B: To help students develop self-awareness and improve their creative decision-making for future work
options.C: To prove to parents that the student spent time on the project
options.D: To make the painting look more complete by adding written notes beside it

questions.explanation: Reflection is a core IB PYP concept and a recognised stage in inquiry-based and design cycles — by evaluating their own choices, students build metacognitive skills and learn to apply improved thinking in future creative work. Providing evidence for parents is the top distractor because documentation does communicate effort, but the educational purpose of reflection is internal growth and self-directed improvement, not external proof.

questions.title: Fairness in Shared Resources
questions.prompt: A village has one well that everyone uses for water. Some families start taking much more water than they need each day. What is most likely to happen to the other families in the village?

options.A: The other families will automatically get more water from the well.
options.B: The other families may not have enough water for their own needs.
options.C: The well will refill faster because more people are using it.
options.D: The other families will find a different well nearby without any trouble.

questions.explanation: When some people take more than their fair share of a shared resource like a well, less is left for others — this is why sharing resources fairly matters for the whole community. Option D is tempting but wrong because finding a new well is not always possible and does not solve the unfairness of the original problem.

questions.title: Animal Habitats and Human Needs
questions.prompt: Farmers want to cut down a forest to grow more food. Scientists warn that many animals live only in that forest. Which statement best explains why this decision is difficult to make fairly?

options.A: Forests are always more important than food, so farming should never happen near trees.
options.B: Animals can easily move to a new forest, so cutting trees causes no lasting harm.
options.C: Both humans and animals have needs, and meeting one group's needs can harm the other.
options.D: Farmers only need a small amount of land, so the problem will solve itself over time.

questions.explanation: This is a real tension in environmental stewardship — humans need food and space, but animals depend on specific habitats to survive, so decisions must consider both sets of needs carefully. Option B is a common misconception; many forest animals are specialists that cannot survive outside their particular habitat and would not simply relocate.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities Outdoors
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Parks are free and open to everyone, so people can do whatever they like there.' Identify the error in this thinking.

options.A: Parks are not actually free — everyone must pay an entry fee before entering.
options.B: Having the right to use a shared space also comes with the responsibility to care for it.
options.C: Only adults are allowed to make decisions about how parks are used.
options.D: Parks belong to the government, so only government workers can use them freely.

questions.explanation: Having rights to use a shared space like a park always comes with responsibilities — for example, not littering or damaging plants — so the space remains enjoyable for all. Option A is a plausible-sounding correction but misses the real error; many public parks are genuinely free to enter, so that is not what is wrong with the student's claim.

questions.title: Reducing Waste Choices
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to the amount of rubbish a school produces if students started choosing drinks in reusable bottles instead of single-use plastic ones every day?

options.A: The amount of rubbish would stay the same because bottles are small items.
options.B: The amount of rubbish would increase because reusable bottles need to be washed.
options.C: The amount of rubbish would decrease because fewer plastic bottles would be thrown away.
options.D: The amount of rubbish would decrease only if teachers also changed their habits.

questions.explanation: Each reusable bottle replaces a new single-use plastic bottle every day, so over a school year hundreds of plastic bottles per student are kept out of the bin — a significant reduction. Option A is wrong because even though individual bottles seem small, multiplied across all students every day they add up to a large portion of school waste.

questions.title: Peace and Conflict Resolution
questions.prompt: Two neighbouring towns both want to use the same river — one for drinking water and one for a new factory. Which approach would most fairly help both towns meet their needs?

options.A: The larger town should get priority because it has more people who need water.
options.B: Both towns should talk together, share information, and agree on rules for how the river is used.
options.C: The factory should be built first because it will create jobs that help everyone eventually.
options.D: A judge should decide immediately without asking either town for their opinion.

questions.explanation: Peaceful conflict resolution over shared resources works best when all parties communicate, share their perspectives, and create agreed rules — this is a core IB idea about how communities manage common resources fairly. Option A is tempting because population size feels logical, but it ignores the rights and needs of the smaller town and does not result in a fair agreement.

questions.title: Sharing Water Fairly
questions.prompt: Two villages share the same river. Village A is upstream and uses a lot of water for farming. Village B is downstream and is running out of water. Who has the responsibility to change their behavior, and why?

options.A: Village B, because they should find a different river to use.
options.B: Village A, because using shared water upstream affects everyone downstream.
options.C: Neither village, because rivers belong to nature and not to people.
options.D: Village A, but only if Village B pays them to use less water.

questions.explanation: When a shared resource like a river is used upstream, it directly reduces what is available downstream, so the upstream user has a responsibility to use only their fair share. Option A is wrong because moving to another river does not solve the shared responsibility — it just avoids it.

questions.title: Rainforest and Medicines
questions.prompt: Scientists say about half of our medicines come from plants found in rainforests. A student says, 'We should cut down rainforests to build farms so more people can eat.' What is the strongest reason to question this idea?

options.A: Rainforests are too wet and muddy to build good farms anyway.
options.B: Cutting rainforests could destroy plants we have never studied that might cure future diseases.
options.C: Farms already grow enough food for every person on Earth right now.
options.D: Rainforests are only important for animals, not for people.

questions.explanation: Many rainforest plant species have not yet been studied by scientists, meaning destroying them could eliminate potential medicines before we even discover them — this is a real concern called 'bioprospecting loss.' Option C is a common misconception; food is actually produced in large amounts globally but distribution is unequal, so claiming farms already feed everyone misses the real issue.

questions.title: Ocean Fishing Rights
questions.prompt: Many countries share the same ocean. A fishing company catches as many fish as possible to make money. After a few years, there are very few fish left. What does this situation teach us about shared resources?

options.A: Shared resources need agreed rules so no one takes too much.
options.B: The fishing company should own the entire ocean so they can manage it.
options.C: Fish populations will always recover on their own if people wait long enough.
options.D: Countries should each fish as much as they can before other countries do.

questions.explanation: When a shared resource has no rules, individuals acting in self-interest can destroy it for everyone — this is why international fishing agreements like catch limits exist. Option C is a misconception because some fish species, once reduced below a critical population level, may not recover without human intervention.

questions.title: Circular Economy Choices
questions.prompt: A shoe company makes shoes that cannot be repaired or recycled. A second company makes shoes that can be fully taken apart and remade into new shoes. Which company is practicing circular economy thinking, and what is the key reason?

options.A: The first company, because making new shoes means more jobs for people.
options.B: The second company, because it keeps materials in use and reduces waste.
options.C: The first company, because brand-new shoes are always better quality.
options.D: The second company, because recycled shoes cost less money to buy.

questions.explanation: A circular economy is designed so that materials are kept in use as long as possible and waste is minimized — the second company's design directly achieves this goal. Option A is a misconception because creating jobs does not define circular economy thinking; the defining feature is keeping resources cycling rather than being thrown away.

questions.title: Animal Habitats and Farms
questions.prompt: When forests are cleared to grow food, wild animals lose their homes. A student says the best solution is to simply stop all farming near forests. Identify the error in this thinking.

options.A: Forests do not actually provide homes for many animals.
options.B: Stopping all farming ignores that people also need food to survive.
options.C: Farmers already use methods that never harm any forests.
options.D: Animals can easily move to cities when their forest homes are removed.

questions.explanation: The error is that the solution ignores the human need for food — a good solution must balance both protecting habitats and ensuring people can eat, which is the essence of sustainable land use. Option D is a common misconception; most wild species cannot adapt to urban environments and lose essential food sources, shelter, and conditions they need to survive.

questions.title: Clean Air Belongs to All
questions.prompt: A factory in Country A releases smoke that causes acid rain in Country B. Country B's forests and lakes are being damaged. What does this situation show about environmental problems?

options.A: Environmental damage only affects the country that causes it.
options.B: Pollution can cross borders, so countries must cooperate to solve it.
options.C: Country B should build a wall to stop the smoke from entering.
options.D: Country A has the right to run its factories however it chooses.

questions.explanation: Air pollution does not stop at national borders — acid rain from factories in one country has historically damaged ecosystems in neighboring countries, as seen in the US-Canada and UK-Scandinavia disputes, making international cooperation essential. Option A is a common misconception because many students assume pollution only harms where it is created, not realizing wind and weather carry pollutants far away.

questions.title: Bees and Food Supply
questions.prompt: Bees pollinate many of the plants that humans eat. If bees disappeared, what would most likely happen to our food supply?

options.A: Food supply would stay the same because machines can do all the farming.
options.B: Only sweet foods like honey would become rare.
options.C: Many fruits, vegetables, and nuts would become much harder to grow.
options.D: Other insects would immediately replace bees with no problems.

questions.explanation: About one-third of the world's food crops depend on bee pollination, including apples, almonds, and tomatoes — without bees, yields of these foods would drop dramatically. Option D is a misconception because while some other insects do pollinate, they are far less efficient and do not exist in large enough numbers to fully replace bees' role.

questions.title: Fairness in Resource Use
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Richer countries use much more energy per person than poorer countries, so richer countries should cut their energy use first when fighting climate change.' Do you agree with the reasoning?

options.A: No, because all countries should make exactly equal cuts regardless of how much they use.
options.B: Yes, because countries that have used more resources have a greater responsibility to reduce use.
options.C: No, because poorer countries cause more pollution than richer ones.
options.D: Yes, but only if richer countries are paid by poorer countries to make those cuts.

questions.explanation: This reflects the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' used in real climate agreements — countries that have historically consumed more resources and emitted more greenhouse gases bear greater responsibility for reducing emissions first. Option A sounds fair on the surface but ignores that a country using ten times more energy cutting the same amount as a low-energy country creates a very unequal burden.

questions.title: Mangrove Forests and Coasts
questions.prompt: Mangrove trees grow along coastlines and protect villages from storm waves. A developer wants to cut them down to build a beach resort. What would be the most important consequence to consider?

options.A: The resort would block the view of the ocean for local people.
options.B: Removing mangroves would leave coastal villages more vulnerable to flooding and storm damage.
options.C: Mangrove wood could be used to build the resort, making it eco-friendly.
options.D: Tourists might not enjoy visiting a beach that previously had trees.

questions.explanation: Mangrove forests act as natural barriers that reduce wave energy and protect coastlines — studies show areas with mangroves experienced significantly less damage during storms like the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Option C is a misconception because using mangrove wood to build the resort still means the living forest is destroyed, eliminating its protective function permanently.

questions.title: Conflict Over Land Use
questions.prompt: Farmers and a local indigenous community both claim the right to use the same piece of land. The farmers want to grow crops; the community uses the land for traditional food and ceremonies. What is the fairest first step toward resolving this conflict?

options.A: Let the government decide immediately without asking either group.
options.B: Give the land to whoever can produce more food from it.
options.C: Have both groups share their needs and listen to each other before deciding.
options.D: Divide the land in half automatically so both groups get equal area.

questions.explanation: Genuine conflict resolution requires that all parties have a voice and understand each other's needs before decisions are made — this is the foundation of negotiation and peacebuilding. Option D seems fair but dividing land in half ignores whether half the land actually meets either group's needs, which may require specific locations or seasonal access patterns.

questions.title: Plastic in the Ocean
questions.prompt: Most ocean plastic comes from rivers that carry plastic waste from inland cities to the sea. A student says we should only clean up plastic already in the ocean. What is the limitation of this plan?

options.A: Ocean cleanup is illegal in most countries.
options.B: It treats the symptom but not the cause, so more plastic will keep arriving.
options.C: Cleaning ocean plastic always harms the sea animals living nearby.
options.D: Oceans are too big for any cleanup effort to make any difference at all.

questions.explanation: Addressing only the plastic already in the ocean without stopping the flow from rivers is like bailing water from a sinking boat without fixing the hole — the problem continues. Option D is a misconception because ocean cleanup projects like The Ocean Cleanup have successfully removed significant amounts of plastic, showing effort does make a real difference even if the problem is large.

questions.title: SDG Goals and Trade-offs
questions.prompt: SDG 8 wants good jobs and economic growth. SDG 15 wants to protect life on land. Sometimes these goals seem to conflict. Which situation best shows this tension?

options.A: A country builds a library in a city centre.
options.B: A mining company creates jobs by digging for minerals in a protected forest.
options.C: A school teaches children about endangered animals.
options.D: A farmer grows vegetables using rainwater collected from the roof.

questions.explanation: Mining in a protected forest directly illustrates the conflict between creating economic jobs (SDG 8) and protecting land ecosystems (SDG 15) because the same activity advances one goal while harming the other. Option D actually shows harmony between goals rather than tension, since rooftop rainwater collection supports sustainable livelihoods without damaging land ecosystems.

questions.title: Water Scarcity Solutions
questions.prompt: In a dry region, farmers use flood irrigation, which soaks the ground with much more water than crops need. A water expert suggests switching to drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to plant roots. Why would this change help the whole community?

options.A: Drip irrigation makes crops grow faster because they receive warmer water.
options.B: Less water wasted by farmers means more water remains for everyone in the region.
options.C: Drip irrigation eliminates the need for rain, solving drought permanently.
options.D: Flood irrigation is already the most efficient method, so no change is needed.

questions.explanation: Drip irrigation uses up to 50% less water than flood irrigation by targeting plant roots directly, meaning the saved water stays in aquifers and rivers for other community members to use. Option D is a misconception — flood irrigation is actually one of the least efficient methods, losing significant water to evaporation and runoff.

questions.title: Endangered Species Protection
questions.prompt: A rare frog lives only in one small wetland. A company wants to drain the wetland to build a shopping centre. The company says it will create a small pond nearby for the frogs. Why might scientists say this replacement pond is not a good solution?

options.A: Frogs do not need water to survive.
options.B: A new pond would be too cold for tropical frog species.
options.C: A replacement pond may lack the specific plants, insects, and conditions the frogs depend on.
options.D: Building ponds is always more expensive than protecting existing wetlands.

questions.explanation: Ecosystems are complex — a wetland that evolved over thousands of years contains specific food webs, plant communities, and microorganisms that a newly built pond cannot instantly replicate, making survival for specialist species very unlikely. Option B is a plausible-sounding distractor but is incorrect because pond temperature is not the defining problem; the ecological complexity is.

questions.title: Refugee Rights and Resources
questions.prompt: When many refugees move to a new region quickly, local water and food supplies can become strained. What does this situation show about the connection between human rights and shared resources?

options.A: Refugees should not have access to the same resources as local people.
options.B: Meeting human rights for all people requires careful management of shared resources.
options.C: Shared resources are only limited in very poor countries.
options.D: Local people always have more rights to resources than newcomers do.

questions.explanation: Human rights include access to safe water and food, but fulfilling these rights for a growing population requires thoughtful resource planning — this is why international organizations work on both rights protection and resource management together. Option A directly contradicts international human rights law, which states all people, regardless of status, have the right to food and water.

questions.title: Solar Energy and Equity
questions.prompt: Solar panels help create clean energy, but they are expensive to buy. A student says: 'If only rich families can afford solar panels, then switching to solar energy might not be fair for everyone.' Is this reasoning correct?

options.A: No, because solar energy automatically becomes free for everyone once enough panels are built.
options.B: Yes, because a solution that only benefits wealthy people does not equally share the planet's resources.
options.C: No, because clean energy only matters in countries that are already wealthy.
options.D: Yes, but only if the solar panels are made in the same country where they are used.

questions.explanation: Environmental solutions that are only accessible to wealthy people can increase inequality — this is why many governments create subsidy programs to help lower-income families access solar energy too. Option A is a misconception because solar infrastructure still requires payment, maintenance, and grid access that do not automatically extend to those who cannot afford panels.

questions.title: Comparing Forest Uses
questions.prompt: Compare two ways of using a forest: cutting all the trees down for timber, or using the forest for eco-tourism while keeping the trees standing. Which approach is more sustainable, and what is the key reason?

options.A: Cutting all trees, because timber is worth more money in one year than tourism over many years.
options.B: Eco-tourism, because the forest keeps providing value year after year without being destroyed.
options.C: Cutting all trees, because new trees can always be planted and will grow back quickly.
options.D: Eco-tourism, because tourists always pay governments more money than timber companies do.

questions.explanation: Eco-tourism allows a forest to generate income continuously for decades while maintaining its biodiversity, carbon storage, and water regulation — in contrast, clear-cutting provides income once and destroys all those ongoing benefits. Option C is a misconception because replanted forests, called plantations, take decades to mature and rarely replicate the biodiversity of an original old-growth forest.

questions.title: Food Waste and Sharing
questions.prompt: A supermarket throws away large amounts of unsold food each day while many people nearby do not have enough to eat. What does this situation best illustrate about how resources are shared?

options.A: There is not enough food produced in the world to feed everyone.
options.B: Food scarcity is only a problem in countries that do not have supermarkets.
options.C: Resources can exist in large amounts but still be distributed unfairly.
options.D: Supermarkets should stop selling food and give it all away for free.

questions.explanation: The world produces enough food to feed every person, yet hunger persists because of unequal distribution — food waste by retailers while neighbors go hungry perfectly illustrates this distribution problem. Option A is a common misconception; the global food production system produces roughly 1.5 times what is needed for the current world population, but access and distribution are unequal.

questions.title: Soil Health and Future Farming
questions.prompt: A farmer grows the same crop in the same field every year without resting the soil or rotating crops. After many years, the soil becomes weak and produces less food. What would happen if all farmers worldwide did this?

options.A: Soil would gradually become richer as the same plant returns its nutrients each year.
options.B: Future generations would have less fertile land to grow food on.
options.C: Rainfall would increase to compensate for the weaker soil.
options.D: Only the crops planted in that soil would be affected, not other foods.

questions.explanation: Continuous single-crop farming depletes specific soil nutrients and destroys soil structure over time — this is already a global problem, with scientists estimating that poor soil management threatens the long-term food security of future generations. Option A is a misconception because the same plant removes the same nutrients from soil each year without replacing them, causing nutrient depletion rather than enrichment.

questions.title: Nature Reserves and Local People
questions.prompt: A government creates a nature reserve to protect endangered animals, but the new rules stop local farmers from grazing their animals on land they have used for generations. A student says this is completely fair because animals need protection. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is fully correct because protecting animals is always more important than farming.
options.B: The student is fully correct because local farmers can simply find other land nearby.
options.C: The student is partly right, but the plan is only truly fair if local farmers are also supported with alternative ways to earn a living.
options.D: The student is wrong because nature reserves never successfully protect endangered animals.

questions.explanation: Conservation is most effective and ethical when it considers the rights and livelihoods of local communities — programs that combine habitat protection with support for affected farmers are more sustainable and just. Option A is a misconception because protecting nature at the expense of people who depend on that land for survival creates conflict and often leads to communities resisting conservation efforts.

questions.title: Renewable vs Non-Renewable
questions.prompt: A student says, 'We should switch to solar energy because it is renewable.' What is the best explanation for why solar energy is considered renewable?

options.A: It produces no pollution of any kind during its entire lifecycle
options.B: The Sun continuously releases energy and will not be used up by human activity
options.C: Solar panels can be recycled after use, reducing waste
options.D: It is cheaper to install than coal or gas power plants in most countries

questions.explanation: Solar energy is renewable because the Sun is a practically inexhaustible source of energy on human timescales — it will continue fusing hydrogen for about 5 billion more years. Option A is a common distractor: manufacturing solar panels does produce some pollution, so 'no pollution of any kind' is incorrect.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystems
questions.prompt: In a forest ecosystem, bees suddenly disappear. Which chain of effects is most likely to follow?

options.A: Soil nutrients increase, causing faster tree growth across the forest
options.B: Flowering plants reproduce less, reducing food for animals that eat fruit and seeds
options.C: Rainfall patterns change, making the forest drier within one season
options.D: Predators at the top of the food chain immediately increase in number

questions.explanation: Bees are key pollinators; without them, flowering plants produce fewer fruits and seeds. Animals that depend on those fruits and seeds then have less food, showing a multi-step cause-and-effect chain. Rainfall patterns (Option C) are influenced by large-scale deforestation, not by the loss of one pollinator species in the short term.

questions.title: Rights and Shared Resources
questions.prompt: A river flows through three different countries. Country A builds a large dam that reduces the water reaching Countries B and C. Which principle of international environmental responsibility is MOST relevant here?

options.A: Sovereign nations may use all natural resources within their borders without restriction
options.B: Shared water resources should be managed cooperatively so all countries receive fair access
options.C: Downstream countries should build their own dams to store whatever water remains
options.D: International courts automatically control all rivers that cross national borders

questions.explanation: Transboundary water resources fall under international agreements such as the UN Watercourses Convention, which promotes equitable and reasonable use so all nations sharing a river can meet their needs. Option A is incorrect because international law recognises that actions on shared resources can harm other states, limiting absolute sovereignty.

questions.title: Circular Economy Basics
questions.prompt: A company redesigns its product so that all parts can be disassembled and used to make new products after the original is worn out. Which economic concept does this BEST represent?

options.A: Linear economy, because the product still ends its life as waste eventually
options.B: Subsistence economy, because the company is meeting only basic needs
options.C: Circular economy, because materials are kept in use rather than discarded
options.D: Command economy, because a central authority controls what the company produces

questions.explanation: A circular economy aims to eliminate waste by keeping materials in use for as long as possible — designing products for disassembly and reuse is a core strategy. Option A is wrong because a linear economy follows a 'take-make-dispose' pattern; designing for reuse specifically breaks that pattern.

questions.title: Sustainable Development Goals
questions.prompt: SDG 14 is called 'Life Below Water.' Identify the error in this student's statement: 'SDG 14 is only relevant to countries that border an ocean, so landlocked countries do not need to care about it.'

options.A: The statement is correct; landlocked countries have no rivers or lakes to protect
options.B: The error is that rivers and lakes in landlocked countries eventually drain into oceans, so pollution anywhere affects ocean health
options.C: The error is that SDG 14 covers freshwater only, not oceans at all
options.D: The statement is correct; the SDGs were designed so each country only follows the goals matching its geography

questions.explanation: Waterways are interconnected: rivers in landlocked countries carry nutrients, plastic, and chemicals downstream until they reach the sea, making ocean health a shared global responsibility. Option C is wrong because SDG 14 explicitly focuses on marine (ocean and sea) ecosystems, not freshwater, which is covered by SDG 6.

questions.title: Carbon Footprint
questions.prompt: Why does eating less beef tend to lower a person's carbon footprint compared to eating less chicken?

options.A: Beef farming uses far more water and produces more methane per kilogram of food than chicken farming
options.B: Chickens are kept indoors, so they use more electricity than cattle kept outdoors
options.C: Beef is transported longer distances to shops than chicken in most countries
options.D: Cattle require less land per animal than chickens, but produce more packaging waste

questions.explanation: Cattle are ruminants that produce large amounts of methane through digestion, and beef production requires significantly more land and water per kilogram than poultry — studies estimate beef produces roughly 20 times more greenhouse gas than chicken per kilogram. Option B is incorrect because the main source of cattle emissions is methane from digestion, not electricity use for housing.

questions.title: Resource Scarcity
questions.prompt: Fresh water covers less than 3% of Earth's total water, and most of that is frozen in ice caps. What is the MAIN reason that access to fresh water is described as a growing global challenge?

options.A: Oceans are slowly absorbing all available fresh water through evaporation
options.B: Population growth and pollution reduce available fresh water while demand for it increases
options.C: Fresh water is only found in wealthy countries, making trade the only solution
options.D: Underground aquifers naturally refill faster than humans can use them

questions.explanation: Global population growth increases agricultural, industrial, and domestic water demand, while pollution and climate change reduce the supply of safe fresh water — a classic scarcity problem. Option D is the top distractor and is wrong: many aquifers, like the Ogallala in the USA, are being drawn down far faster than they naturally recharge.

questions.title: Environmental Stewardship
questions.prompt: A coastal community relies on fishing for food and income. Scientists warn that current fishing rates will cause fish populations to collapse in ten years. What does environmental stewardship suggest the community should do?

options.A: Fish as much as possible now to maximise income before stocks run out
options.B: Agree on catch limits that allow fish populations to recover while still meeting community needs
options.C: Stop all fishing immediately and permanently to protect the ecosystem
options.D: Replace fish in the diet entirely with farmed land animals to avoid the issue

questions.explanation: Environmental stewardship means caring responsibly for shared resources so they remain healthy for future generations — setting science-based catch limits allows fish stocks to recover while sustaining livelihoods, as shown by successful management in places like Iceland. Option C is incorrect because stewardship seeks a balance between human needs and ecosystem health, not a complete halt to resource use.

questions.title: Peace and Conflict Over Resources
questions.prompt: Historians have noted that conflicts sometimes break out between communities when a shared resource becomes scarce. Which scenario BEST illustrates this connection between resource scarcity and conflict?

options.A: Two neighbouring villages argue over grazing land as a long drought reduces available grass
options.B: A city builds a new library, causing debate about which neighbourhood it should be placed in
options.C: Two countries compete to host the Olympic Games for tourism benefits
options.D: A school reduces its budget, leading teachers to disagree about curriculum priorities

questions.explanation: When drought reduces grazing land, communities that depend on livestock face direct competition for a shrinking essential resource — a documented driver of conflict in regions like the Sahel in Africa. Options B, C, and D involve disagreements but not the scarcity of a survival resource, making them weaker examples of resource-driven conflict.

questions.title: Biodiversity Economics
questions.prompt: A government is deciding whether to protect a rainforest or allow logging companies to clear it. An economist argues that protecting the forest has hidden economic value. Which hidden value is the economist MOST likely referring to?

options.A: The forest makes the country look more attractive on maps used in geography textbooks
options.B: Ecosystem services such as water purification, carbon storage, and pollination support agriculture worth billions
options.C: Logging companies will eventually replant the same species they remove, so there is no real loss
options.D: Rainforest timber is actually worth less per cubic metre than timber from managed plantations

questions.explanation: Ecosystem services — including carbon sequestration, flood regulation, clean water provision, and pollination of nearby crops — have been estimated to be worth trillions of dollars globally each year, often far exceeding the one-time value of logging. Option C is the top distractor and is wrong: replanted monoculture plantations do not replicate the biodiversity or ecosystem functions of primary rainforest.

questions.title: Climate Change and Responsibility
questions.prompt: Country X has historically released most of the world's greenhouse gases but is now reducing emissions. Country Y is a developing nation that currently releases very little but wants to industrialise. A student claims both countries have exactly equal responsibility to limit future emissions. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because all countries share the same atmosphere and must make identical cuts
options.B: The claim is partly wrong; the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' means historical emitters bear greater obligation
options.C: The claim is correct because future emissions matter more than past emissions in international law
options.D: The claim is wrong because only the largest current emitters have any legal duty to act

questions.explanation: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) established 'common but differentiated responsibilities,' recognising that wealthy nations that industrialised earlier contributed most to current CO₂ levels and therefore have a greater obligation to lead in reducing emissions. Option A ignores historical contribution and is therefore an oversimplification rejected by international climate agreements.

questions.title: Deforestation Causes
questions.prompt: Which combination of factors MOST directly drives large-scale tropical deforestation in countries like Brazil and Indonesia?

options.A: Tourism development and the construction of new airports near forest areas
options.B: Agricultural expansion for cattle ranching and palm oil plantations, plus logging for timber
options.C: Rapid urbanisation as people move from farms into cities, abandoning rural land
options.D: Mining for gemstones and the building of hydroelectric dams on small rivers

questions.explanation: Studies by organisations like Global Forest Watch show that cattle ranching and commodity agriculture (especially soy and palm oil) account for the majority of tropical forest loss, with commercial logging also a significant driver. Option C is the top distractor and is actually wrong in this context — urbanisation can sometimes reduce pressure on forests as fewer people farm subsistence plots.

questions.title: Plastic Pollution Pathways
questions.prompt: A plastic bottle dropped on a street in a city far from the coast eventually ends up in the ocean. Which sequence of events BEST explains how this happens?

options.A: Rain washes the bottle into storm drains → drains flow into rivers → rivers carry it to the sea
options.B: Wind carries the lightweight bottle directly from land across the ocean surface
options.C: Microorganisms break the bottle into particles that travel through soil to the water table and then to the sea
options.D: City waste trucks accidentally drop bottles on roads near ports, where they fall into the water

questions.explanation: Surface runoff from rain carries litter into storm drains, which connect to river systems; rivers then transport plastic to the coast and into the ocean — this is the primary documented pathway for inland plastic pollution reaching the sea. Option B is partially possible for very light items but is not the main pathway for a plastic bottle.

questions.title: Endangered Species Protection
questions.prompt: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) bans the commercial trade of products from certain animals. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this international agreement?

options.A: To ensure that wealthy countries can buy exotic animals for zoos at regulated prices
options.B: To prevent trade-driven hunting and poaching from pushing vulnerable species toward extinction
options.C: To create a global list of animals that may be used freely in scientific experiments
options.D: To allow governments to sell permits for limited hunting as a way to raise conservation funds

questions.explanation: CITES was established in 1963 specifically to ensure that international trade does not threaten the survival of wild animal and plant species; it currently protects over 38,000 species by regulating or banning trade. Option D describes trophy hunting permit systems used in some national laws, which is different from CITES' primary international trade-restriction purpose.

questions.title: Environmental Policy Perspectives
questions.prompt: A factory owner and an environmental scientist both look at the same river pollution data. Why might they reach different conclusions about whether action is needed immediately?

options.A: The factory owner has access to different scientific instruments and therefore sees different data
options.B: Their different roles mean they prioritise different values: the owner weighs economic costs while the scientist weighs ecological risk
options.C: Scientists are trained to ignore economic issues, so they always recommend stopping all industrial activity
options.D: Factory owners are not allowed to read scientific reports under international business law

questions.explanation: Perspective in the IB PYP context means recognising that different stakeholders have different values, needs, and priorities — a factory owner may prioritise jobs and profit while a scientist prioritises measurable harm to ecosystems, leading to different conclusions from the same data. Option C is an exaggeration; scientists do consider socioeconomic factors in environmental policy recommendations.

questions.title: Soil Degradation
questions.prompt: Farmers who plant the same crop in the same field every year often find that yields decrease over time. What is the MOST likely scientific explanation for this?

options.A: The crop species evolves to become smaller each generation, producing less food
options.B: Repeated planting of the same crop depletes specific soil nutrients and encourages pest populations that target that crop
options.C: Rain gradually washes the seeds deeper into the soil so they cannot sprout as easily
options.D: Sunlight weakens as more crops absorb it over the years, leaving less energy for plant growth

questions.explanation: Monoculture farming depletes the specific nutrients that one crop type heavily uses and creates ideal conditions for specialist pests and diseases, reducing yields — this is why crop rotation replenishes different nutrients and breaks pest cycles. Option A is incorrect because agricultural crop species do not evolve on such short timescales under normal growing conditions.

questions.title: Energy Choices and Change
questions.prompt: What would happen to a country's greenhouse gas emissions if it replaced all its coal-fired power plants with wind turbines, assuming electricity demand stayed the same?

options.A: Emissions would increase because wind turbines require more electricity to operate than they generate
options.B: Emissions from electricity generation would drop sharply because wind turbines produce no CO₂ while generating power
options.C: Emissions would remain the same because the country still needs the same amount of energy
options.D: Emissions would decrease slightly, but wind turbines release water vapour which is a stronger greenhouse gas

questions.explanation: Wind turbines generate electricity through the movement of air turning blades and a generator — they release no CO₂ during operation, unlike coal plants which burn carbon-based fuel. Option C confuses the amount of energy with the source; the same quantity of electricity can be generated with very different levels of emissions depending on the energy source.

questions.title: Coral Reef Threats
questions.prompt: Coral reefs are described as the 'rainforests of the sea.' A student claims that warmer ocean temperatures harm coral reefs by causing coral bleaching. Which explanation BEST supports this claim?

options.A: Warm water causes coral skeletons to dissolve, leaving only the soft tissue behind
options.B: Heat stress causes corals to expel the algae living inside them; without algae they lose colour and their main food source
options.C: Warmer water increases the speed of ocean currents, physically breaking coral structures apart
options.D: Higher temperatures cause coral to absorb too much sunlight, turning their surface permanently black

questions.explanation: Corals live in a symbiotic relationship with photosynthetic algae called zooxanthellae, which provide up to 90% of the coral's energy; when water temperature rises even 1–2°C above normal for several weeks, corals expel this algae, turning white (bleaching) and eventually dying if conditions do not improve. Option A is incorrect — coral bleaching is a biological stress response, not a chemical dissolution of the skeleton.

questions.title: Fairness in Resource Use
questions.prompt: Compare the water use of a person in a high-income country with that of a person in a low-income country. What does this comparison reveal about global fairness in resource use?

options.A: People in low-income countries use more water per person because they rely on manual irrigation for farming
options.B: Water use is roughly equal globally because everyone needs the same amount to survive
options.C: People in high-income countries typically use far more water per person, raising questions about equitable resource distribution
options.D: Water use depends entirely on climate, so desert countries always use the most regardless of income level

questions.explanation: Data from the UN show that people in high-income countries can use 300–500 litres of water per day while many people in low-income countries survive on fewer than 20 litres, highlighting a significant inequality in access to and consumption of a shared resource. Option D is incorrect because income and infrastructure (pipes, irrigation systems, industry) are stronger predictors of per-capita water use than climate alone.

questions.title: Invasive Species Impact
questions.prompt: When a species from one region is introduced to a new ecosystem where it has no natural predators, what is the MOST likely outcome for native species?

options.A: Native species quickly adapt their behaviour to avoid the newcomer within one generation
options.B: The introduced species may outcompete or prey on native species, reducing their populations or driving them extinct
options.C: Native species always increase in number because the new species adds variety to the ecosystem
options.D: The introduced species typically dies out quickly because the local climate is unsuitable for it

questions.explanation: Without natural predators or competitors to keep its population in check, an invasive species can multiply rapidly and outcompete or consume native species — the brown tree snake introduced to Guam caused the extinction of 12 native bird species. Option A is incorrect because evolutionary adaptation takes many generations, far too slow to respond to a rapidly multiplying invasive species.

questions.title: Responsibility and Reflection
questions.prompt: After learning about ocean plastic pollution, a student reflects: 'I buy products in plastic packaging every week. Even though I recycle, am I still part of the problem?' Which response BEST shows genuine critical reflection about personal responsibility?

options.A: No, because recycling completely eliminates the impact of buying plastic packaging
options.B: Yes, because demand for plastic products drives their production; reducing purchases and choosing alternatives matters alongside recycling
options.C: No, because individual choices have no effect on large-scale industrial pollution
options.D: Yes, but only if the student lives within 50 kilometres of an ocean coastline

questions.explanation: Recycling helps but does not capture all plastic — globally, only about 9% of plastic ever produced has been recycled; reducing demand by buying less plastic and choosing alternatives addresses the problem at its source. Option A is the top distractor and is incorrect because recycling rates are far from 100% and do not eliminate production emissions or the risk of plastic escaping into the environment.

questions.title: Sustainable Cities
questions.prompt: A city planner wants to reduce both traffic congestion and air pollution at the same time. Which single change to city infrastructure would BEST address both problems simultaneously?

options.A: Build wider roads so more private cars can travel at the same time
options.B: Expand reliable public transport so more people travel together in fewer vehicles
options.C: Increase parking fees in the city centre to encourage people to park farther away
options.D: Plant more trees along existing roads to absorb carbon dioxide produced by traffic

questions.explanation: Expanding public transport moves more people in fewer vehicles, directly reducing the number of cars on roads (cutting congestion) and lowering total exhaust emissions (reducing air pollution) — cities like Singapore and Zurich demonstrate this with low congestion and good air quality. Option A makes congestion worse long-term by inducing more car trips through 'induced demand,' a well-documented urban planning phenomenon.

questions.title: Map Keys and Symbols
questions.prompt: A map shows a small picture of a tree repeated across a large area. A student says this means the area has many forests. What part of the map helped the student figure this out?

options.A: The compass rose
options.B: The map scale
options.C: The map key (legend)
options.D: The map title

questions.explanation: A map key, also called a legend, explains what each symbol or picture on a map stands for — so a tree symbol meaning 'forest' would be listed there. The compass rose only shows directions like north and south, and would not explain what symbols mean.

questions.title: Heritage and Traditions
questions.prompt: Why do communities often celebrate the same festivals year after year, even when the world around them has changed a lot?

options.A: Because new celebrations are against the law in most countries
options.B: To keep their history and shared identity alive for future generations
options.C: Because modern technology has made old festivals easier to film
options.D: To make sure children learn the same songs as adults

questions.explanation: Repeating festivals across generations is a way communities preserve their heritage — the stories, values, and identity passed down through time. Option D is partly true in a narrow sense, but learning songs is a detail, not the main reason communities continue traditions across changing times.

questions.title: Why Civilisations Near Rivers
questions.prompt: Many of the world's earliest civilisations, like ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, grew up beside large rivers. What is the BEST reason this happened?

options.A: Rivers made it easy to build tall stone monuments
options.B: Rivers kept wild animals away from villages
options.C: Rivers provided fresh water and rich soil for growing food
options.D: Rivers were used to send messages to faraway lands

questions.explanation: Rivers like the Nile and the Tigris-Euphrates flooded each year, leaving behind rich, fertile soil that made farming possible, and they provided a reliable source of fresh water — both essential for a growing civilisation. While rivers were sometimes used for trade and travel, keeping animals away was not a key reason early people settled near them.

questions.title: Primary Sources
questions.prompt: A student wants to find out what life was like for children 100 years ago. Which of these would be a PRIMARY source?

options.A: A history textbook written last year about childhood in the past
options.B: A diary written by a ten-year-old child in 1924
options.C: A documentary film made in 2010 about old-fashioned schools
options.D: A website explaining how children lived 100 years ago

questions.explanation: A primary source is created at the time being studied, by someone who was actually there — a diary written by a child in 1924 is a direct, first-hand record from that period. A textbook, documentary, or website made long after the events are secondary sources because they describe the past from a distance.

questions.title: Reasons People Migrate
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's statement: 'People only move from one place to another when they want to find exciting new adventures.'

options.A: The statement is correct — adventure is always the main reason people move
options.B: The error is that people also move because of push factors like danger, drought, or poverty
options.C: The error is that people only move within the same country, never to a new one
options.D: The statement is correct because moving always leads to a better life

questions.explanation: Migration is driven by both push factors — things that force people to leave, such as war, famine, or natural disasters — and pull factors, like better jobs or safety. The student's statement ignores push factors entirely, which are often the most powerful reasons people migrate throughout history.

questions.title: Timelines and Chronology
questions.prompt: A class is making a timeline of important events in their school's history. They place 'School building opened' AFTER 'First students graduated.' What is wrong with this timeline?

options.A: Nothing is wrong — timelines can be arranged in any order
options.B: Timelines should only show events that happened within the last ten years
options.C: The events are in the wrong order — a building must open before students can graduate from it
options.D: The timeline should show the events side by side, not one after the other

questions.explanation: A timeline must show events in chronological order — the sequence in which they actually happened. A school building must open before any students can attend and eventually graduate, so placing 'building opened' after 'first students graduated' breaks the correct sequence of cause and effect.

questions.title: Comparing Past and Present
questions.prompt: Compare how people got news long ago with how people get news today. Which statement describes the BIGGEST change?

options.A: Long ago, people read newspapers; today, news can reach millions of people instantly through the internet
options.B: Long ago, people talked to neighbours; today, people still talk to neighbours
options.C: Long ago, news came by ship; today, news still arrives slowly by post
options.D: Long ago, only kings received news; today, only scientists receive news

questions.explanation: The invention of the internet created an enormous change in how fast and how widely news travels — something that was impossible in the era of printed newspapers, which took hours or days to reach readers. Option C is inaccurate because modern news does not travel slowly by post; it reaches people almost instantly through digital technology.

questions.title: Maps and Real Places
questions.prompt: A map of a town shows a small blue square for every building that has a swimming pool. A student says this map tells us which buildings are the tallest. Is the student correct, and why?

options.A: Yes, because blue usually means tall buildings on maps
options.B: No, because the map's symbols only show where swimming pools are, not height
options.C: Yes, because buildings with pools are always the biggest buildings
options.D: No, because maps can never show buildings at all

questions.explanation: A map symbol only represents the specific feature it is designed to show — in this case, swimming pools. A symbol's colour or shape tells us what the map-maker chose to record, not other features like height. Option A is a common misconception because students sometimes assume colour always carries the same meaning across all maps, but map legends define symbols differently for each map.

questions.title: Primary vs Secondary Sources
questions.prompt: Maria wants to find out what life was like for children 100 years ago. She finds an old diary written by a child in 1924 and also a book written last year about children in the 1920s. Which source is a PRIMARY source, and what makes it primary?

options.A: The book from last year, because it has more information gathered together
options.B: The diary from 1924, because it was created by someone who lived at that time
options.C: The diary from 1924, because diaries are always more accurate than books
options.D: Both are primary sources because they both contain facts about the 1920s

questions.explanation: A primary source is created by someone who lived through or witnessed the events being described — the 1924 diary was written by a real child at that time, making it a firsthand account. Option A is a common misconception because students often think that having more information makes a source better or more 'primary', but a secondary source summarises or analyses primary sources rather than being a direct record from the time.

questions.title: Why Civilisations Grew Near Rivers
questions.prompt: Many of the world's earliest civilisations, like ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, started beside large rivers. Which explanation BEST connects two reasons why rivers helped civilisations grow?

options.A: Rivers kept people cool in summer and gave them somewhere to swim for fun
options.B: Rivers provided water for farming and also made it easier to travel and trade
options.C: Rivers gave people fish to eat and made it impossible for enemies to cross
options.D: Rivers created flat land for building cities and scared away dangerous animals

questions.explanation: Early civilisations like ancient Egypt depended on the Nile River both to irrigate their crops and to transport goods by boat, helping trade networks grow. Option C is tempting because rivers did provide fish, but the idea that rivers made it 'impossible' for enemies to cross is an overstatement — many armies crossed rivers — and this option misses the crucial farming and trade connections.

questions.title: Understanding Heritage Objects
questions.prompt: A museum displays an old clay pot found in the ground. A student claims: 'This pot tells us nothing useful because it is broken and has no writing on it.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct — only written records can tell us about the past
options.B: The student is correct — broken objects cannot be studied by historians
options.C: The student is incorrect — the pot's shape, material, and decoration can show how people lived and what they made
options.D: The student is incorrect — all pots automatically tell us what language people spoke

questions.explanation: Artefacts like clay pots reveal information about how people cooked, stored food, and created art even without writing — archaeologists study their shape, clay type, and patterns to learn about a civilisation's technology and daily life. Option A is a very common misconception because many students believe written sources are the only valid historical evidence, but artefacts provide rich information about cultures that had no writing system.

questions.title: Continuity and Change Over Time
questions.prompt: In a village 200 years ago, people travelled by horse and cart. Today, people in the same village travel by car. Which statement BEST describes both continuity AND change in this situation?

options.A: Everything has changed — the village is completely different now
options.B: The need to travel between places has stayed the same, but the method of travel has changed
options.C: Nothing has changed because people still need to move from place to place the same way
options.D: The roads have stayed the same but the people who live there have completely changed

questions.explanation: Continuity means some things stay the same across time — here, the human need to move between places continues — while change refers to what is different, which is the technology used to travel. Option A represents a common student error of seeing history as either all-change or all-continuity rather than recognising that both happen simultaneously.

questions.title: Reasons People Migrate
questions.prompt: Long ago, a group of people left their homeland and moved to a distant land. They left because there was very little rain and crops were failing. What type of reason caused this migration?

options.A: A pull factor, because they were attracted by better weather in the new land
options.B: A push factor, because difficult conditions in their homeland forced them to leave
options.C: A push factor, because they wanted to explore and discover new places
options.D: A pull factor, because the new land offered them more farmland to buy

questions.explanation: A push factor is something that drives people away from a place, such as drought or crop failure making it impossible to survive — the group was forced to leave rather than attracted somewhere else. Option A is a strong distractor because students often confuse push and pull factors, and might assume that any mention of weather is about being attracted to a better climate elsewhere rather than being driven away by a bad one.

questions.title: Reading a Simple Timeline
questions.prompt: A timeline shows four events in a city's history: a market was built, then a school, then a bridge, then a hospital. If the bridge was built 60 years ago and the school was built 20 years before the bridge, how long ago was the school built?

options.A: 40 years ago
options.B: 20 years ago
options.C: 80 years ago
options.D: 60 years ago

questions.explanation: If the bridge was built 60 years ago, and the school was built 20 years BEFORE the bridge, you add 20 to 60, giving 80 years ago. Option A is the most tempting wrong answer because students often subtract 20 from 60 instead of adding, confusing 'before' with 'after' when working on timelines.

questions.title: Ancient Trade and Cultural Exchange
questions.prompt: When traders from one ancient civilisation visited another, they often brought more than just goods. They also brought ideas, stories, and beliefs. What does this suggest about how ancient cultures changed over time?

options.A: Ancient cultures only changed when they were invaded by armies
options.B: Trade could cause cultures to share and mix ideas even without conflict
options.C: Traders always tried to make other cultures copy their own customs exactly
options.D: Ancient peoples refused to accept new ideas from outside their civilisation

questions.explanation: Historical evidence from civilisations like ancient India, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean shows that trade routes allowed the peaceful spread of writing systems, religious ideas, foods, and technologies between cultures. Option A is a misconception because many students learn about conquests and assume that is the main way cultures changed, overlooking how much peaceful contact through trade shaped civilisations.

questions.title: Comparing Past and Present Homes
questions.prompt: Houses built 150 years ago in cold countries often had very thick stone walls and small windows. Modern houses in the same cold countries usually have thinner walls but special glass and insulation inside. What BEST explains why both designs try to solve the same problem in different ways?

options.A: People in the past liked small windows because they thought they were more beautiful
options.B: Both designs try to keep warmth inside, but they use the materials and technology available in their time
options.C: Modern houses are always better because people today are smarter than people in the past
options.D: Old houses had thick walls to protect people from wild animals rather than to keep warm

questions.explanation: Both thick stone walls and modern insulated walls serve the same purpose — trapping heat — but the methods reflect what materials and knowledge were available at each point in history; this shows how human needs stay constant while solutions change with technology. Option C is a tempting but incorrect claim that imposes a bias that 'newer is smarter', which historians and IB students are taught to challenge.

questions.title: Choosing the Right Map
questions.prompt: A family wants to drive from one city to another. They have two maps: one shows where forests and mountains are, the other shows roads and distances between towns. Which map should they use, and why?

options.A: The forest and mountain map, because it shows whether the journey will be safe
options.B: The road and distance map, because it shows the routes they can actually drive on
options.C: The forest and mountain map, because all maps show roads in their corners
options.D: Either map would work equally well because both show the same land area

questions.explanation: Different maps are made for different purposes — a road map is specifically designed to show driveable routes and distances, making it the correct tool for planning a car journey. Option A is plausible because knowing about mountains might seem relevant to safety, but a physical geography map does not show driveable roads, so it cannot actually help the family plan their route.

questions.title: Landmarks and Local History
questions.prompt: A very old building in a town has been used as a market, then a school, and now a community centre. A student says: 'This building is part of the town's heritage.' What does the word 'heritage' mean in this sentence?

options.A: Heritage means the building is very expensive and worth a lot of money
options.B: Heritage means the building belongs to the government and cannot be changed
options.C: Heritage means the building is part of the history and identity passed down through a community over time
options.D: Heritage means the building was constructed using traditional methods that nobody uses today

questions.explanation: Heritage refers to the traditions, buildings, and stories from the past that a community values and passes on to future generations as part of its shared identity — the building's long history of community use makes it part of local heritage. Option D is a plausible distractor because students may connect heritage with old construction methods, but heritage is about the building's meaning and history within a community, not only how it was built.

questions.title: Cause of Historical Change
questions.prompt: After a new railway line was built through a small town 100 years ago, the town grew much larger very quickly. What is the MOST likely reason the town grew after the railway arrived?

options.A: The railway made the town famous and people wanted to see the trains
options.B: The railway allowed people and goods to move more easily, bringing new businesses and workers to the town
options.C: The town's leaders built more houses because they knew the railway would arrive soon
options.D: The railway replaced all the old roads so people had to live closer to the station

questions.explanation: Railways historically caused towns to grow by making it faster and cheaper to transport goods and people — merchants set up shops, factories were built near stations, and workers moved to find jobs, causing rapid population growth. Option C is a plausible distractor because planning by leaders might seem logical, but the historical evidence shows growth was primarily driven by economic opportunity created by improved transport, not by pre-emptive housing construction.

questions.title: Perspectives in History
questions.prompt: Two children from different countries both read about the same explorer from 500 years ago. One child's book calls the explorer a 'brave discoverer.' The other child's book calls the same person an 'unwelcome invader.' Why might the same person be described so differently?

options.A: One book must contain mistakes because there can only be one true description of any historical person
options.B: The books were written at different times, so only the newer one is accurate
