questions.prompt: A graphic designer wants viewers to look at one specific part of a poster immediately. Which design strategy would most effectively create a focal point?

options.A: Using the same size and colour for all elements across the whole poster
options.B: Making every element a different bright colour so nothing is missed
options.C: Using a contrasting colour and larger size for the key element against a simpler background
options.D: Placing text and images only along the very edges of the poster

questions.explanation: Emphasis and focal point are created through contrast — size difference, colour contrast, or isolation against a simpler background draws the eye. Using the same size and colour for everything (option A) creates unity but eliminates any focal point, which is the most common misunderstanding.

questions.title: Art History: Pop Art
questions.prompt: Pop Art emerged in the 1950s and 1960s. What was a defining characteristic of this movement that connected it to the society of its time?

options.A: It used only natural materials gathered from forests and rivers.
options.B: It drew inspiration from religious icons and sacred imagery.
options.C: It incorporated imagery from mass consumer culture, advertising, and popular media.
options.D: It rejected all colour in favour of black-and-white compositions.

questions.explanation: Pop Art, associated with artists such as Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein, deliberately used imagery from commercial products, advertisements, comic books, and celebrity culture to comment on consumerism in post-war society. Religious imagery (option B) is more characteristic of Renaissance or Byzantine art, making it the strongest distractor.

questions.title: Drama: Empathy and Character
questions.prompt: Why is it important for an actor to understand a character's motivations before performing, rather than simply memorising the lines?

options.A: Knowing motivations helps the actor memorise lines more quickly.
options.B: Understanding motivation allows the actor to make believable physical and vocal choices that reflect why the character acts.
options.C: Motivation is only important for the director, not the actor.
options.D: Memorising motivations replaces the need to memorise lines at all.

questions.explanation: Understanding a character's internal motivation enables an actor to make authentic physical, vocal, and emotional choices that bring consistent believability to the performance — a core principle of performance theory. Option A is a tempting distractor but confuses a minor side effect with the main purpose of motivation study.

questions.title: Music: Timbre
questions.prompt: Two musicians play the exact same note at the same volume and tempo — one on a flute and one on a violin. What musical quality makes their sounds different from each other?

options.A: Pitch
options.B: Duration
options.C: Timbre
options.D: Tempo

questions.explanation: Timbre (also called tone colour) is the quality that distinguishes the sound of one instrument from another even when pitch, duration, and dynamics are identical — it results from differences in overtones and resonance. Pitch (option A) is the same for both instruments in this scenario, making it the most tempting but incorrect answer.

questions.title: Visual Arts: Sculpture Form
questions.prompt: A student is asked to describe the 'form' of a sculpture. Which answer correctly applies this concept?

options.A: Form refers to the material cost of creating the sculpture.
options.B: Form refers to the three-dimensional quality and volume of the sculpture — its height, width, and depth.
options.C: Form refers only to the colour applied to the surface of the sculpture.
options.D: Form refers to the location where the sculpture is displayed.

questions.explanation: In visual arts, form is the element that describes a three-dimensional object with height, width, and depth — distinguishing it from a flat two-dimensional shape. Colour (option C) is a separate element of design and does not define form, making it the most plausible distractor.

questions.title: Aesthetics: Purpose of Art
questions.prompt: A student claims that art can only have value if it is beautiful. Which argument best challenges this claim?

options.A: Art without beauty is illegal in most countries.
options.B: Art can communicate important ideas, provoke thought, or document history even when it is deliberately disturbing or uncomfortable.
options.C: Only trained artists can decide whether art is valuable.
options.D: Beauty is the same for everyone, so all art that is well made is automatically beautiful.

questions.explanation: Aesthetics philosophy recognises that art serves many purposes beyond beauty — including social commentary, emotional provocation, and historical record — a view supported by movements such as Expressionism and Dada that deliberately rejected traditional beauty. Option D incorrectly assumes beauty is universal and objective, which is itself a debated philosophical claim.

questions.title: Music: Time Signature
questions.prompt: A piece of music has a time signature of 3/4. What does the top number tell the performer?

options.A: There are three beats in each measure.
options.B: The piece should be played three times.
options.C: The note value is three beats long.
options.D: There are three instruments playing.

questions.explanation: In a time signature, the top number indicates how many beats are contained in each measure (bar); 3/4 means three beats per bar, which is characteristic of a waltz. The bottom number (4) tells the performer which note value equals one beat — a crotchet (quarter note) — not the top number, making option C the most tempting distractor.

questions.title: Drama: Proxemics on Stage
questions.prompt: Two characters in a play are in conflict. A director asks them to stand very close together and face each other. How does this use of space (proxemics) affect the audience's experience?

options.A: It signals friendship and trust between the characters.
options.B: It creates tension and intensity, signalling confrontation or strong emotion.
options.C: It shows that the characters cannot hear each other well.
options.D: It indicates that neither character has any power in the scene.

questions.explanation: Proxemics — the deliberate use of physical distance between performers — communicates relationship and emotion; close proximity combined with direct facing heightens tension and signals confrontation or charged emotion to the audience. Option A is the most plausible distractor because closeness can also signal intimacy, but when paired with conflict context it signals confrontation.

questions.title: Visual Art: Pattern and Repetition
questions.prompt: An artist creates a design by repeating the same leaf motif at regular intervals across a fabric. Which principle of design is most clearly demonstrated?

options.A: Contrast
options.B: Proportion
options.C: Pattern
options.D: Emphasis

questions.explanation: Pattern is created through the consistent repetition of a motif, shape, or element at regular intervals — exactly what is described with the repeating leaf design. Contrast (option A) involves difference rather than repetition and is a common distractor for students who confuse principles of design.

questions.title: Art: Socio-Political Context
questions.prompt: An artist living during a war paints images of broken cities and suffering civilians. How does understanding the historical context change the way a viewer analyses this artwork?

options.A: It makes no difference — a formal analysis of line and colour is always sufficient.
options.B: It reveals possible reasons behind the artist's choices and adds layers of meaning connected to real human experience.
options.C: It proves that the artist was not skilled enough to paint pleasant subjects.
options.D: It means the artwork can only be understood by people who lived through that war.

questions.explanation: Contextual analysis in IB Visual Arts considers how historical, cultural, and socio-political circumstances shape an artist's intentions and an artwork's meaning — giving viewers richer understanding beyond what formal analysis alone provides. Option A is a direct challenge to contextual analysis and the most common misconception to address.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Empathise
questions.prompt: A designer wants to make a better school bag for young children. Which action is the BEST first step in the design thinking process?

options.A: Draw ten different bag designs on paper
options.B: Watch and talk to children about how they use their current bags
options.C: Choose the fabric colour for the new bag
options.D: Build a cardboard model of the bag straight away

questions.explanation: The first stage of design thinking is 'empathise,' which means observing and listening to the people you are designing for so you understand their real needs. Drawing designs or building models comes later; choosing colours is not a needs-finding activity.

questions.title: Materials and Properties
questions.prompt: A student is building a small bridge from craft materials. The bridge must hold ten small blocks without bending. Which property of a material is MOST important for this task?

options.A: Colour
options.B: Flexibility
options.C: Strength
options.D: Transparency

questions.explanation: Strength is a material's ability to hold a load without breaking or bending, which is exactly what a bridge carrying blocks needs. Flexibility means the material bends easily, which would cause the bridge to sag under weight.

questions.title: Prototyping Purpose
questions.prompt: Why do designers make a prototype before creating the final product? Choose the BEST reason.

options.A: To show the finished product in a museum
options.B: To test and improve ideas before spending lots of money on the real thing
options.C: To make a perfect copy that never needs changing
options.D: To decide what colour to paint the final product

questions.explanation: A prototype is an early model used to test ideas cheaply and find problems before the final version is made, saving time and resources. A prototype is not meant to be perfect or final — it is expected to be changed after testing.

questions.title: Sustainability in Design
questions.prompt: A class is designing a new pencil case. Which choice is MOST sustainable?

options.A: Making it from single-use plastic that cannot be recycled
options.B: Using recycled fabric so less new material is needed
options.C: Designing it to look very colourful using many different dyes
options.D: Making it as large as possible so it holds more items

questions.explanation: Using recycled fabric reduces the need to produce new raw materials, which saves energy and reduces waste — key ideas in sustainable design. Single-use plastic that cannot be recycled creates long-lasting waste, which is harmful to the environment.

questions.title: Ergonomics Basics
questions.prompt: Ergonomics means designing objects so they are comfortable and safe for people to use. Which chair feature is the BEST example of ergonomic design for a young child?

options.A: A seat height that matches the child's leg length so feet touch the floor
options.B: A bright red colour so the chair is easy to spot in the classroom
options.C: A very heavy base so the chair does not slide
options.D: A curved back that points forward to encourage leaning ahead

questions.explanation: Ergonomic design fits the human body — a seat height that lets a child's feet rest flat on the floor supports posture and reduces discomfort. Colour and weight are not ergonomic features because they do not relate to how the body fits the object.

questions.title: Defining a Design Problem
questions.prompt: In design thinking, the 'define' step means writing a clear problem statement. A student says: 'I want to make something cool.' Why is this NOT a good design problem statement?

options.A: It is too long and has too many words
options.B: It does not name a user or explain a real need to be solved
options.C: It uses the word 'cool,' which is not a design word
options.D: It should mention a specific material to use

questions.explanation: A good design problem statement names WHO has the problem and WHAT the problem is, so the designer knows exactly what to solve. The statement 'make something cool' has no user and no clear need, making it impossible to design toward a specific goal.

questions.title: Ideation Techniques
questions.prompt: During the 'ideate' stage, a design team wants to come up with as many ideas as possible. Which rule is MOST important during this stage?

options.A: Only share ideas that already work perfectly
options.B: Let one person decide all the ideas to save time
options.C: Welcome all ideas without judging them straight away
options.D: Only use ideas that have been used before

questions.explanation: In ideation, the goal is to generate many ideas freely — judging too early stops people from sharing creative possibilities. Brainstorming rules specifically say to defer judgement so that even unusual ideas can spark better solutions.

questions.title: Testing a Design
questions.prompt: A student makes a paper boat and wants to test if it floats well. What should she do AFTER the test to improve her design?

options.A: Throw away the boat and start a completely different project
options.B: Look at what went wrong and change one thing, then test again
options.C: Keep the boat exactly the same because testing is finished
options.D: Ask a friend to test a totally different boat instead

questions.explanation: After testing, designers analyse results and make one change at a time so they know which change made the difference — this is the iterative design process. Changing everything at once makes it impossible to know which change improved the design.

questions.title: User Needs Research
questions.prompt: A team is designing a water bottle for children who play sport. Which research method would give them the MOST useful information about real user needs?

options.A: Looking at pictures of water bottles in a magazine
options.B: Asking sporty children what problems they have with their current bottles
options.C: Counting how many water bottles are sold in a shop
options.D: Measuring how tall different water bottles are

questions.explanation: Interviewing the target users directly gives first-hand information about their real problems and needs, which is the goal of user research in design. Magazine pictures and bottle measurements tell you about existing products but not what problems users actually experience.

questions.title: Reducing, Reusing, Recycling
questions.prompt: A school wants to reduce the waste it creates when making art projects. Which action is an example of REUSING materials rather than recycling them?

options.A: Putting used paper into a recycling bin
options.B: Using the back of printed paper to draw new pictures
options.C: Buying new art supplies every week
options.D: Melting old crayons into new crayon shapes

questions.explanation: Reusing means using a material again in its current form without processing it — flipping paper over to draw on the blank side is a direct reuse. Melting crayons is closer to recycling because the material is changed into a new form before being used again.

questions.title: Innovation vs. Invention
questions.prompt: An inventor creates something completely new that has never existed before. An innovator improves something that already exists. Which example is an INNOVATION rather than an invention?

options.A: Designing the very first wheel
options.B: Creating the first ever pencil
options.C: Making a pencil that also has an eraser attached to the end
options.D: Discovering that wood can be used to write marks

questions.explanation: Adding an eraser to an existing pencil is an innovation — it improves a product that already existed to make it more useful. Inventing the first wheel or the first pencil are inventions because nothing like them existed before.

questions.title: Purpose of a System
questions.prompt: A system is a group of parts that work together to do a job. Which of these is the BEST example of a system?

options.A: A single nail sitting on a table
options.B: A bicycle, where wheels, pedals, chain, and brakes all work together
options.C: A piece of blank paper on a desk
options.D: A single colour of paint in a jar

questions.explanation: A system has multiple parts that interact and depend on each other to achieve a goal — a bicycle's wheels, chain, pedals, and brakes all work together to make it move and stop safely. A single object like a nail or paper has no interacting parts working toward a shared function.

questions.title: Function vs. Aesthetics
questions.prompt: A student designs a stool. She spends all her time painting beautiful patterns on it but forgets to check if it is strong enough to sit on. What design principle did she forget?

options.A: The stool should have more legs than usual
options.B: Function — the product must actually do its job safely
options.C: Aesthetics — the colours she chose were not bright enough
options.D: Sustainability — she should have used recycled paint

questions.explanation: Function means a product must safely and reliably do what it is designed to do — a stool must hold a person's weight. Aesthetics (appearance) is also important in design but cannot replace function; a beautiful stool that breaks when you sit is a design failure.

questions.title: Design Constraints
questions.prompt: A design constraint is a rule or limit that a designer must follow. A student is told: 'Your model must cost less than five dollars and be finished in one class.' What are the TWO constraints she must work within?

options.A: Colour and shape
options.B: Budget and time
options.C: Weight and height
options.D: Material type and number of parts

questions.explanation: Constraints limit what a designer can do — in this case the cost (under five dollars) is a budget constraint and 'one class' is a time constraint. Colour, shape, weight, and number of parts were not mentioned as limits in the brief.

questions.title: Feedback and Improvement
questions.prompt: After showing their prototype to classmates, a design team hears: 'The handle is hard to grip.' What should the team do with this feedback?

options.A: Ignore it because classmates are not real designers
options.B: Use it to redesign the handle so it is easier to hold
options.C: Change the colour of the handle instead
options.D: Add more information to their poster about the handle

questions.explanation: Feedback from users identifies real problems with a prototype, and the design team should use that specific feedback to improve the part that is not working — in this case, the handle grip. Changing the colour does not address the gripping problem the users reported.

questions.title: Natural vs. Manufactured Materials
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a NATURAL material — one that comes directly from nature without being made in a factory?

options.A: Plastic
options.B: Cotton
options.C: Nylon
options.D: Steel

questions.explanation: Cotton is a natural material that comes from the cotton plant and can be harvested directly from nature. Plastic, nylon, and steel are all manufactured — they are made through industrial processes using chemicals or by combining and heating raw materials.

questions.title: Safety in Design
questions.prompt: A designer is making a toy for children aged 3–5 years. She wants to add small decorative beads. Why is this a safety concern?

options.A: Beads are too expensive to use in toys
options.B: Young children might put small beads in their mouths and choke
options.C: Beads make the toy heavier than it should be
options.D: Beads are difficult to attach and will fall off in rain

questions.explanation: Small parts like beads are a choking hazard for young children, who often explore objects by putting them in their mouths — this is why toy safety standards set minimum size limits for parts on toys for under-3s. Cost and weight are not the primary safety concern here.

questions.title: Waterproof vs. Absorbent
questions.prompt: A student is choosing a material for the outside of a raincoat. She is deciding between wool and nylon. Which property makes nylon a better choice for this purpose?

options.A: Nylon is softer than wool against skin
options.B: Nylon is waterproof and does not soak up water easily
options.C: Nylon is a natural material grown on plants
options.D: Nylon is heavier than wool so it hangs better

questions.explanation: Nylon is a synthetic material with waterproof properties, meaning water runs off it rather than soaking through — exactly what is needed for a raincoat. Wool is absorbent and soaks up water, making it a poor choice for the outer layer of a raincoat.

questions.title: Design Brief Components
questions.prompt: A design brief tells a designer what problem to solve and what rules to follow. Which piece of information belongs in a design brief?

options.A: The name of the designer's favourite colour
options.B: A description of who the product is for and what it must do
options.C: A list of all the tools in the school workshop
options.D: The history of how similar products were made long ago

questions.explanation: A design brief always includes who the user is and what the product must achieve, because these guide every design decision the designer makes. The designer's personal preferences and workshop tool lists are not part of a brief because they do not describe the problem to solve.

questions.title: Why We Evaluate Designs
questions.prompt: At the end of a design project, a student compares her finished product to her original design brief. Why is this evaluation step important?

options.A: To find out how long the project took compared to other projects
options.B: To check whether the product actually meets the needs and goals set at the start
options.C: To decide which colours look best in the final display
options.D: To make sure the product looks the same as a classmate's product

questions.explanation: Evaluation checks whether the solution genuinely solves the problem stated in the design brief — it measures success against the original goals. Timing comparisons and colour choices are not the purpose of design evaluation.

questions.title: Thinking About Users
questions.prompt: A student designs a storybook app for grandparents to share with their grandchildren. Which feature shows she has thought carefully about BOTH users?

options.A: Using very small text to fit more words on each screen
options.B: Including large text for easy reading and colourful pictures for children to enjoy
options.C: Making the app only available in one language
options.D: Adding a complicated password system to keep the app secure

questions.explanation: Large text helps older users who may find small text hard to read, while colourful pictures engage young children — this shows empathy for both user groups at once. Very small text would make the app difficult for grandparents, and complicated passwords would frustrate both users.

questions.title: Structures and Stability
questions.prompt: A student notices that a tall, thin tower of blocks falls over easily, but a wide, short tower stays standing. What design idea does this show?

options.A: Taller structures always hold more weight
options.B: A wider base gives a structure more stability
options.C: Short structures are always lighter than tall ones
options.D: Using more blocks always makes a structure weaker

questions.explanation: A wider base lowers a structure's centre of gravity and spreads its weight over a larger area, making it more stable and harder to tip over — this is a key principle in structural design and engineering. A wider base does not necessarily make a structure lighter; stability is about weight distribution, not total weight.

questions.title: Design for the Environment
questions.prompt: A company says its new toy is 'eco-friendly.' Which feature gives the STRONGEST evidence that this claim is true?

options.A: The toy is packaged in a bright green box
options.B: The toy is made from wood grown in a managed forest and uses non-toxic paint
options.C: The toy has been tested by many children
options.D: The toy comes in five different colours

questions.explanation: Using wood from a managed forest (where trees are replanted) and non-toxic paint reduces environmental harm during production and disposal — these are measurable eco-friendly features. A green box is a colour choice and says nothing about environmental impact.

questions.title: Communicating Design Ideas
questions.prompt: A designer wants to show her classmates exactly how her new lunchbox will look and what size it will be. Which method communicates this MOST clearly?

options.A: Writing a long paragraph describing the box
options.B: Telling classmates about it during circle time
options.C: Drawing a labelled diagram with measurements
options.D: Choosing a name for the product

questions.explanation: A labelled diagram with measurements gives exact visual and numerical information that others can understand clearly — this is why technical drawing is a standard tool in design. A written paragraph or spoken description leaves room for misunderstanding because it cannot show shape and size precisely.

questions.title: Problem-Solving Steps Order
questions.prompt: A student is going through the design thinking stages. She has already empathised and defined the problem. What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Build the final product immediately
options.B: Show the finished product to parents
options.C: Ideate — brainstorm many possible solutions
options.D: Test whether the product works with real users

questions.explanation: The design thinking process follows the order: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test — so after defining the problem, the next step is ideation (generating many possible ideas). Building the final product or testing come later in the process, after prototyping.

questions.title: Design Thinking Steps
questions.prompt: A student wants to design a better backpack for classmates. She talks to them, watches how they carry their bags, and writes down what is hard for them. Which step of the design thinking process is she doing?

options.A: Ideate — she is thinking of new ideas to solve the problem
options.B: Prototype — she is building a first version to test
options.C: Empathise — she is learning about users' feelings and needs
options.D: Define — she is writing a clear problem statement

questions.explanation: Empathising means observing and listening to users to understand their real needs before deciding on a solution — this is exactly what she is doing by watching and interviewing classmates. Defining comes after empathising, when you turn those discoveries into a clear problem statement, so D is the next step, not this one.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.prompt: A designer needs to choose a material for a school water bottle. She wants something that will not break if dropped and will not let water leak out. Which property is MOST important to check first?

options.A: Transparency — so you can see how much water is inside
options.B: Flexibility — so it bends without cracking when dropped
options.C: Colour — so it looks appealing to children
options.D: Texture — so it feels comfortable in the hand

questions.explanation: Flexibility is the key structural property here because a flexible material can absorb the energy of a drop without cracking, keeping the bottle waterproof and intact. Transparency is useful but does not prevent leaking or breaking, making it a secondary rather than primary consideration.

questions.title: Sustainable Choices
questions.prompt: Why would a designer choose to make a toy from wood rather than plastic, even if the wood toy costs a little more to produce?

options.A: Wood is always lighter than plastic, making the toy easier to carry
options.B: Wood comes from a renewable source and can break down naturally at end of life
options.C: Wood toys are always stronger than plastic toys of the same shape
options.D: Wood is easier to paint in bright colours that children prefer

questions.explanation: Wood is a renewable resource — trees can be replanted — and it is biodegradable, meaning it breaks down naturally instead of polluting the environment for hundreds of years like most plastics. Wood is not always lighter or stronger than plastic; those properties depend on the specific type of wood and plastic being compared.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Users
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'If a chair is comfortable for a grown-up teacher, it will also be comfortable for a six-year-old student.' Evaluate this claim. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes — comfort depends only on the chair's padding, not its size
options.B: Yes — both users sit the same way, so the same chair works for both
options.C: No — ergonomics means designing for the measurements of the actual user, and children's bodies are much smaller
options.D: No — children always prefer softer chairs, so the material must change

questions.explanation: Ergonomics is the science of matching a design to the physical size and needs of the specific user. A chair sized for an adult will leave a young child's feet dangling and may cause poor posture and discomfort, because their body proportions are very different. The distractor about padding is wrong because seat height and depth matter far more than softness for proper support.

questions.title: Prototyping Purpose
questions.prompt: After ideating, a design team builds a quick model of their new pencil case using cardboard and tape. What is the MAIN reason designers build this kind of early model?

options.A: To show clients a finished product that is ready to sell
options.B: To find problems with the idea cheaply before making the real version
options.C: To practise using expensive tools and real materials safely
options.D: To keep the idea secret so no one else can copy it

questions.explanation: A prototype is a low-cost early model built specifically to discover faults and test ideas before spending money on real materials — this is why cardboard is often used. It is definitely not a finished product ready to sell; the whole point is that it will probably need changes after testing.

questions.title: Identifying the User's Need
questions.prompt: Compare these two design questions: (1) 'How can we make a louder school bell?' and (2) 'How can we help students know when class starts, even if they are far from the building?' Which question is better for a designer and why?

options.A: Question 1 — it is more specific, so it is easier to test
options.B: Question 1 — louder bells are always the simplest and cheapest solution
options.C: Question 2 — it costs less money to answer than question 1
options.D: Question 2 — it focuses on the user's real need and leaves room for many creative solutions

questions.explanation: Good design questions focus on the user's actual need rather than jumping straight to one solution. Question 2 opens up many possible answers — an app, a light signal, a vibration alert — whereas Question 1 locks the team into only one idea (a louder bell) before any research. Question 1 is not more specific in a helpful way; specificity at the solution stage too early actually limits creativity.

questions.title: Testing Fairly
questions.prompt: A class made two different book bag designs and wants to test which one holds more weight before the strap breaks. What must they do to make the test fair?

options.A: Use heavier weights in the bag they think will win
options.B: Let different people hold each bag, because different people are stronger
options.C: Use the same type and amount of weight added each time for both bags
options.D: Test each bag on a different day so the team has time to rest

questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one variable at a time — in this case the bag design — while keeping everything else the same, including the weight used. If different amounts of weight are used for each bag, the result cannot tell you which design is stronger because two things changed at once. Testing on different days or with different people introduces extra variables that could affect the result unfairly.

questions.title: Innovation and Improvement
questions.prompt: What is the difference between an invention and an innovation? A classmate says they are exactly the same thing. Is your classmate right?

options.A: Yes — both words mean creating something that has never existed before
options.B: No — an invention is a brand-new idea, while an innovation improves or finds a new use for something that already exists
options.C: No — an innovation is always digital, while an invention can be any physical object
options.D: Yes — both require a patent before the creator can share the idea

questions.explanation: An invention creates something completely new that did not exist before, while an innovation takes an existing idea and improves it or applies it in a new way — for example, adding a camera to a mobile phone was an innovation because phones already existed. Not all innovations are digital; a redesigned bicycle seat is an innovation too, so option C is incorrect.

questions.title: Lifecycle Thinking
questions.prompt: A designer thinks about what happens to a product from the moment its materials are collected all the way until it is thrown away or recycled. What is this way of thinking called?

options.A: Ergonomic analysis — checking if the product fits the user's body
options.B: Lifecycle thinking — considering every stage of a product's life and its impact
options.C: Prototype testing — building and trying out an early version of the product
options.D: Market research — finding out how many people would buy the product

questions.explanation: Lifecycle thinking (or lifecycle assessment) means examining every stage a product goes through — gathering raw materials, manufacturing, using, and disposing of it — to understand its full environmental and social impact. Ergonomic analysis focuses on body fit and comfort, not the product's environmental journey, making it a plausible but incorrect answer here.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: A student wants to design a better backpack for first graders. She already has lots of ideas. Which step should she do BEFORE she starts sketching solutions?

options.A: Build a quick prototype using cardboard and tape
options.B: Watch and talk to first graders about how they use their current backpacks
options.C: Choose the colours that most children say they like in a survey
options.D: Look at what backpacks are already sold in shops

questions.explanation: In design thinking, the empathise stage means observing and listening to real users before generating solutions, so the designer understands actual problems rather than assumed ones. Choosing colours (option C) addresses preference but skips the deeper 'what is the real problem?' investigation that empathy uncovers.

questions.title: Defining the Problem
questions.prompt: After talking to users, a design team writes this problem statement: 'We need to make something cool.' Why is this a weak problem statement?

options.A: It does not mention which materials will be used
options.B: It does not include the cost of the product
options.C: It does not say who has the problem or what the problem actually is
options.D: It does not list how many ideas the team will create

questions.explanation: A strong problem statement names the specific user and describes their real need or difficulty, giving the team a clear target to design toward. Mentioning materials (option A) comes much later in the design process and is not what a problem statement needs to include.

questions.title: Ideation Strategies
questions.prompt: During the ideate stage, a teacher says, 'Write down every idea, even ones that seem silly.' Why is this rule helpful for the design process?

options.A: It means the team never has to test their ideas later
options.B: Unusual ideas can spark connections that lead to a better final solution
options.C: Having more ideas always means the product will cost less money
options.D: It stops the team from needing to talk to users again

questions.explanation: Ideation encourages quantity and wild thinking because unexpected ideas often combine with practical ones to create genuinely novel solutions — a principle called 'creative collision.' Having more ideas does not automatically reduce cost (option C); cost depends on materials and manufacturing choices made later.

questions.title: Prototype Purpose
questions.prompt: A design team spends three weeks making a perfectly painted, finished model of their new water bottle before any user has tried it. What is the main risk of this approach?

options.A: The bottle might be the wrong colour for the market
options.B: If users find problems, a lot of time and effort will have been wasted before changes can be made
options.C: The team will have learned too much about their design too quickly
options.D: A finished model is too heavy to carry to user testing sessions

questions.explanation: Prototypes in design thinking are meant to be quick and low-cost so that failures are cheap to fix; building a polished version first means any redesign wastes the investment already made. Option A (wrong colour) is a real but comparatively minor risk and can be fixed without rebuilding the whole structure.

questions.title: Testing and Evidence
questions.prompt: Two children test their new bookmark design. Mia says, 'I think it looks great!' Luca says, 'Five out of eight classmates could find their page in under ten seconds.' Which response gives better evidence that the design works well, and why?

options.A: Mia's, because personal opinion shows the designer cares about the product
options.B: Luca's, because a number measured by real users is harder to argue with than one person's feeling
options.C: Mia's, because the way something looks is the most important design goal
options.D: Luca's, because eight is always a large enough group to prove any design works

questions.explanation: Measurable data from real users (how many succeeded, how fast) is objective evidence, while personal opinion is subjective and reflects only one perspective. Option D is incorrect because eight users is a useful early test but is not automatically large enough to prove a design works in every situation.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.prompt: A student is choosing a material for the hinge of a lunchbox lid. She needs it to bend many times without breaking. Which property is MOST important to look for?

options.A: Transparency, so she can see inside the box
options.B: Flexibility and durability, so it can bend repeatedly without snapping
options.C: Absorbency, so any spills are soaked up quickly
options.D: Hardness, so it cannot be scratched by other objects

questions.explanation: A hinge must flex repeatedly, so a material that is both flexible (bends without cracking) and durable (keeps its strength over many uses) is the right match for this function. Hardness (option D) is actually the opposite of what a hinge needs — a very hard, rigid material would snap rather than bend.

questions.title: Ergonomics for Children
questions.prompt: A designer is making a pencil grip for 7-year-olds. She discovers that the grip works perfectly for adults but causes hand cramps for children after five minutes. What does this tell her about her design process?

options.A: She should test the grip with adults first and then add more padding
options.B: The grip's colour scheme needs to be changed to be more appealing
options.C: She did not design for the actual body size and strength of her real users
options.D: Children should practise more so the grip eventually feels comfortable

questions.explanation: Ergonomics means designing tools that fit the physical measurements and abilities of the specific user group; a child's hand is smaller and has less grip strength than an adult's, so testing only on adults misses critical data. Option D blames the user rather than the design, which is the opposite of user-centred design thinking.

questions.title: Sustainability in Materials
questions.prompt: A school wants to make name tags for students. Option 1 is plastic that lasts five years. Option 2 is cardboard that lasts two months but is made from recycled paper. Which factor is MOST important when deciding which is more sustainable?

options.A: Which option is cheaper to buy at the start
options.B: Which option looks nicer on a student's shirt
options.C: How much total waste and resources each option creates over the same period of time
options.D: Which option the teachers find easier to write names on

questions.explanation: Sustainability compares total environmental impact over time — plastic may create less frequent waste but involves oil-based production, while recycled cardboard requires more replacements but uses fewer new resources; only comparing both across the same time period gives a fair picture. Initial cost (option A) is an economic factor, not a sustainability measure.

questions.title: Iteration in Design
questions.prompt: After testing version 1 of a bird feeder, a team finds that seeds fall out too easily in the wind. They fix only that problem before testing version 2. A classmate says they should have changed everything at once to save time. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The classmate, because more changes at once means fewer testing rounds overall
options.B: The team, because changing one thing at a time helps them know exactly what caused any improvement
options.C: The classmate, because designers should always finalise all features before the first test
options.D: The team, because rules require exactly one change per design round in all projects

questions.explanation: Changing one variable at a time is a fair-test principle: if multiple things change at once and the result improves, you cannot tell which change caused the improvement. Option A seems efficient but actually produces confusing results that may force even more testing rounds later.

questions.title: User Research Methods
questions.prompt: A student wants to find out why classmates dislike the school's water fountain. She could observe them using it or ask them to fill in a written survey. When would observing be MORE useful than a survey?

options.A: When she wants to collect opinions from students who are absent that day
options.B: When users may not be able to explain in words what makes the experience uncomfortable
options.C: When she needs students to rank their preferences in a numbered list
options.D: When she wants to compare answers easily across a large group

questions.explanation: Observation captures behaviours and physical reactions that users themselves might not notice or be able to describe — for example, a child might not realise they are straining to reach the spout. Ranking preferences in a numbered list (option C) is precisely what surveys are designed for, not observation.

questions.title: Function vs. Aesthetics
questions.prompt: Two chair designs are presented. Chair A is beautifully decorated and wins a design award, but children find it uncomfortable after ten minutes. Chair B looks plain but children sit in it happily for an hour. For a classroom, which chair is the better design choice, and what does this reveal?

options.A: Chair A, because award-winning designs always meet user needs best
options.B: Chair A, because children will be more motivated to sit in a beautiful chair
options.C: Chair B, because a design that fulfils its main function for the intended user is more successful
options.D: Chair B, because plain objects are always cheaper and easier to clean

questions.explanation: In user-centred design, the primary measure of success is whether the product fulfils its intended function for its specific users; comfort over extended use directly matches the classroom purpose. Option B is a common misconception — motivation to sit is not improved by appearance alone if the chair causes physical discomfort.

questions.title: Systems Thinking in Design
questions.prompt: A school replaces its paper lunch trays with reusable plastic ones to cut waste. Surprisingly, the school's water bill goes up significantly. What is the most likely reason this happened?

options.A: Plastic trays are heavier, so students drink more water to stay hydrated
options.B: Reusable trays must be washed after every use, which uses water that disposable trays did not require
options.C: The school accidentally ordered the wrong size trays, causing food spills that needed cleaning
options.D: Plastic attracts more dirt than paper, so extra rinses are needed before the trays can be used

questions.explanation: This is a systems-thinking example: solving one problem (paper waste) created a new demand in another part of the system (washing water). It shows that designers must consider the full lifecycle and connected systems, not just the immediate change. Option C is a possible but highly specific accident, not a predictable systemic consequence of the switch.

questions.title: Identifying Design Constraints
questions.prompt: A team wants to design a new playground slide. Their teacher gives them these rules: it must cost under $200, fit in a 3-metre space, and be safe for children aged 5–8. What are these rules called in design, and why do they matter?

options.A: Criteria, because they describe what the design must achieve
options.B: Constraints, because they set the limits within which the design must work
options.C: Prototypes, because they show an early version of the final product
options.D: Specifications, because they list every single part needed to build the slide

questions.explanation: Constraints are the fixed boundaries that a design cannot exceed — budget, size, and safety rules are all limits, not goals. Criteria (option A) describe what success looks like (e.g., 'children enjoy using it'), whereas constraints describe what the design must not go beyond.

questions.title: Innovation vs. Invention
questions.prompt: A student says, 'The smartphone was an invention, but adding a fingerprint scanner to unlock it was just an innovation.' Is she correct, and what is the key difference?

options.A: No — both are inventions because they use new technology
options.B: Yes — an invention creates something completely new, while an innovation improves or adds to something that already exists
options.C: No — an innovation is always bigger and more important than an invention
options.D: Yes — an innovation only counts if it makes a product cheaper than before

questions.explanation: Invention refers to creating something that did not exist before, while innovation means improving an existing product, process, or idea in a meaningful way; the fingerprint scanner improved an existing device. Option C reverses the relationship — inventions are typically the original breakthrough, while innovations build on them.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment
questions.prompt: A company says its new plastic toy is eco-friendly because the factory uses solar power. A designer says this claim is incomplete. What important part of the toy's life is the company ignoring?

options.A: The colour of the packaging used in shops
options.B: What happens to the toy after children stop playing with it and throw it away
options.C: Whether the factory workers enjoy their jobs
options.D: How long it takes to ship the toy from the factory to the shop

questions.explanation: A lifecycle assessment looks at every stage — raw materials, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life disposal; a plastic toy that cannot be recycled may still end up in landfill even if its factory runs on solar power. Shipping time (option D) is part of the lifecycle but relates more to carbon from transport, which is a separate concern from whether the toy itself is eco-friendly after disposal.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Basics
questions.prompt: A 7-year-old invents a new way to fold paper to make stronger boxes and draws her design in a notebook. Her friend copies the exact design and sells the boxes at the school fair without asking. What important idea about creators does this situation raise?

options.A: Ideas written in notebooks are free for anyone to use because they are not sold in shops
options.B: Creators have rights over their original ideas and designs, and using them without permission is unfair
options.C: Only adults can own ideas because children cannot register inventions officially
options.D: Once an idea is shared at school, it belongs to the school community

questions.explanation: Intellectual property principles protect creators' original work — even children — because the effort and creativity belong to them; using someone's design without permission violates that right. Option A is incorrect: writing an idea down is actually one way to establish when it was created, and it does not make the idea free for others to use.

questions.title: Tech Ethics in Design
questions.prompt: A new app is designed to help children track their reading. It also quietly collects data about which websites the child visits and shares this with advertisers. A student claims this is fine because the app is free. What is the strongest argument against this claim?

options.A: Free apps always have lower quality features than paid apps
options.B: Collecting and sharing personal data without clear permission is unfair, even if the app costs nothing
options.C: Advertisers should only be allowed to target adults, not children
options.D: Children should not use apps that track any activity, paid or free

questions.explanation: Technology ethics requires that data collection be transparent and consensual regardless of price; 'free' does not mean users give up the right to know how their information is used. Option C is a reasonable concern but is narrower than option B — the core problem is secret data collection, not only who the ads target.

questions.title: UX and Inclusive Design
questions.prompt: A designer creates a new library app where all instructions appear only as written text. A classmate who has difficulty reading finds the app impossible to use. What design principle did the designer fail to consider?

options.A: The app should have been tested only by adult librarians before launch
options.B: Designing for all likely users, including those with different abilities, so no one is excluded
options.C: Every app must include a video tutorial as required by international design rules
options.D: Text-only interfaces are always cheaper and should be avoided for that reason

questions.explanation: Inclusive design (sometimes called universal design) means considering the full range of users from the start — including those with reading difficulties — so that the solution works for as many people as possible. Option C is incorrect: there is no universal rule requiring video tutorials; the issue is about inclusion, not a checklist requirement.

questions.title: Design Thinking Stages
questions.prompt: A student is designing a new backpack for classmates. She interviews five students about what bothers them about their current bags. Which stage of the design thinking process is she in?

options.A: Prototype
options.B: Ideate
options.C: Empathise
options.D: Test

questions.explanation: The empathise stage involves gathering information directly from users to understand their needs and frustrations — interviewing classmates fits this exactly. Ideation comes later, when you generate possible solutions after you have already understood the problem.

questions.title: Defining the Problem
questions.prompt: After collecting lots of user research, a design team writes this statement: 'Students aged 9–11 need a way to carry heavy textbooks without hurting their shoulders.' What is this statement called in the design thinking process?

options.A: A design brief
options.B: A point of view statement
options.C: A prototype description
options.D: A lifecycle assessment

questions.explanation: A point of view (POV) statement captures who the user is, what they need, and why — matching the example exactly. A design brief is broader and includes constraints and success criteria, not just the user need.

questions.title: Prototype Purpose
questions.prompt: Why does a designer build a prototype before making the final product? Choose the most accurate reason.

options.A: To create the finished product that will be sold to customers
options.B: To test ideas quickly and find problems before spending lots of money
options.C: To skip the testing stage and go straight to manufacturing
options.D: To replace the need to interview users

questions.explanation: Prototypes are intentionally rough and quick to make so designers can discover faults early, before expensive manufacturing begins. A prototype is never the finished product — it is a learning tool that leads back into testing and refinement.

questions.title: Material Properties
questions.prompt: A student wants to make a reusable water bottle. She needs a material that is waterproof, lightweight, and does not break easily when dropped. Which property description best matches what she needs?

options.A: High density, brittle, and transparent
options.B: Absorbent, rigid, and heavy
options.C: Impermeable, low density, and tough
options.D: Magnetic, flexible, and opaque

questions.explanation: Impermeable means waterproof, low density means lightweight, and tough means it resists breaking on impact — all three match the requirements. Option A includes 'brittle,' meaning it would crack when dropped, which directly fails one requirement.

questions.title: Ergonomics Basics
questions.prompt: Ergonomics is the study of designing products to fit the human body. Which of the following is the best example of an ergonomic design feature on a school chair?

options.A: Painting the chair a bright colour to look attractive
options.B: Adding a curved back rest that supports the lower spine
options.C: Making the chair out of the cheapest available wood
options.D: Increasing the seat height so the chair looks taller

questions.explanation: A curved backrest that supports the lumbar (lower spine) region reduces strain and fits the natural shape of the human back — a classic ergonomic feature. Bright colours relate to aesthetics, not body fit, and an arbitrary increase in seat height could actually harm posture.

questions.title: Sustainability in Design
questions.prompt: A toy company wants to make its packaging more sustainable. Which change would have the greatest positive impact on the environment?

options.A: Switching from cardboard to single-use plastic wrapping
options.B: Printing the logo in a different colour
options.C: Replacing plastic packaging with recycled cardboard
options.D: Making the packaging slightly smaller but still plastic

questions.explanation: Recycled cardboard is biodegradable and uses fewer virgin resources than plastic, significantly reducing waste and carbon footprint. Making plastic packaging slightly smaller still leaves it as plastic, which does not biodegrade easily and harms ecosystems.

questions.title: Ideation Techniques
questions.prompt: During the ideation stage, a design team wants to generate as many ideas as possible without judging them. Which technique are they using?

options.A: Lifecycle assessment
options.B: Brainstorming
options.C: User testing
options.D: Specification writing

questions.explanation: Brainstorming is a classic ideation technique where participants produce many ideas freely without immediate criticism, to encourage creative thinking. User testing happens after a prototype exists and focuses on evaluating ideas, not generating them.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment (LCA) looks at a product's impact on the environment from start to finish. Which of the following stages would be included in an LCA of a plastic ruler?

options.A: Only the manufacturing stage
options.B: Only the disposal stage
options.C: Raw material extraction, manufacturing, use, and disposal
options.D: The design stage and the advertising stage only

questions.explanation: A full lifecycle assessment covers every stage: extracting raw materials (e.g., oil for plastic), manufacturing, the use phase, and end-of-life disposal or recycling. Examining only one stage, like manufacturing, misses significant environmental impacts that occur before and after.

questions.title: User Research Methods
questions.prompt: A designer wants to find out how 10-year-olds actually use their pencil cases during a school day. Which research method would give her the most realistic information?

options.A: Asking students to fill in a questionnaire about how they think they use their pencil cases
options.B: Reading a book about general stationery design
options.C: Observing students in class while they actually use their pencil cases
options.D: Asking the school principal what students need

questions.explanation: Direct observation captures real behaviour — what users actually do — rather than what they think or say they do, which is often different. Questionnaires rely on self-reporting, which can be inaccurate because people do not always remember or accurately describe their own habits.

questions.title: Function vs Form
questions.prompt: In design, 'form' refers to how something looks, and 'function' refers to how it works. A student designs a lamp shaped like a flower that gives very little light. Which statement best evaluates this design?

options.A: The design succeeds because its form is creative and attractive
options.B: The design fails because its function does not meet the primary purpose of a lamp
options.C: The design succeeds because function is always more important than form
options.D: The design fails because flower shapes are not allowed in design

questions.explanation: A lamp's primary function is to provide adequate light; if it gives very little light it fails its core purpose, regardless of attractive form. Option C is incorrect because good design balances both form and function — neither always overrides the other.

questions.title: Intellectual Property
questions.prompt: Mia invents a new type of foldable water bottle and registers it so no one else can copy and sell her invention without permission. What is the name of this legal protection?

options.A: Copyright
options.B: Trademark
options.C: Patent
options.D: Creative Commons licence

questions.explanation: A patent protects a new invention or technical process, giving the inventor exclusive rights to make, use, or sell it for a set period (usually 20 years). Copyright protects creative works like books and music, not inventions, so it would not apply here.

questions.title: Iterative Design Process
questions.prompt: A student tests her prototype, finds two problems, fixes them, and then tests again. She repeats this three times. What design principle is she demonstrating?

options.A: Mass production
options.B: Iterative design
options.C: Lifecycle assessment
options.D: Outsourcing

questions.explanation: Iterative design involves repeatedly cycling through designing, testing, and improving — each cycle (iteration) uses feedback to make the product better. Mass production means making many identical items quickly and does not involve repeated testing cycles.

questions.title: Technology Ethics
questions.prompt: A company creates an app that collects location data from children aged 8–12 without telling their parents. Which ethical concern does this raise most directly?

options.A: The app uses too much battery power
options.B: The app's colour scheme is unappealing
options.C: Children's private data is being collected without informed consent
options.D: The app lacks a sufficient number of features

questions.explanation: Collecting personal data from children without parental consent violates privacy rights and laws like COPPA and GDPR, making it a serious ethical and legal issue. Battery usage and colour scheme are usability concerns, not ethical violations involving safety or rights.

questions.title: Design Constraints
questions.prompt: A design specification states: 'The product must cost less than $5 to make and fit inside a standard school bag.' What are these requirements called in design?

options.A: Design constraints
options.B: Ergonomic guidelines
options.C: Lifecycle stages
options.D: Brainstorming rules

questions.explanation: Design constraints are the limits and boundaries a solution must stay within, such as cost, size, and materials — exactly what the specification describes. Ergonomic guidelines relate specifically to human body fit and comfort, not cost or dimensions.

questions.title: Renewable vs Non-Renewable
questions.prompt: A designer chooses bamboo instead of aluminium for a phone stand. Bamboo is considered more sustainable partly because it is renewable. What does 'renewable' mean in this context?

options.A: It can be charged using solar power
options.B: It can be regrown naturally within a human lifetime
options.C: It never needs to be replaced once used in a product
options.D: It is produced in a factory using recycled materials

questions.explanation: Renewable materials come from sources that can be naturally replenished relatively quickly — bamboo can grow to full size in just a few years. Aluminium comes from bauxite ore, a finite mineral that takes millions of years to form and is therefore non-renewable.

questions.title: Systems Thinking
questions.prompt: In a school's heating system, the thermostat detects when the room gets too cold and switches the heater on. When the room is warm enough, it switches the heater off. What type of system feature does the thermostat provide?

options.A: Open-loop control
options.B: Feedback loop
options.C: Lifecycle assessment
options.D: Ergonomic adjustment

questions.explanation: A feedback loop is when the output of a system (room temperature) is measured and fed back to control the input (heater on/off), keeping the system stable. An open-loop control system would have no such automatic adjustment based on actual conditions.

questions.title: Innovation vs Invention
questions.prompt: The wheel was invented thousands of years ago. Adding rubber tyres to wheels on bicycles is best described as which of the following?

options.A: An invention, because rubber tyres had never existed before
options.B: An innovation, because it improves an existing idea to better meet a need
options.C: A prototype, because rubber tyres were tested before being sold
options.D: A patent, because the design was legally registered

questions.explanation: Innovation means improving or adapting an existing product or idea to create added value — rubber tyres improved the wheel by adding grip, cushioning, and durability. Invention refers to creating something completely new for the first time, which the wheel itself was, not the tyre improvement.

questions.title: UX and Usability
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'My app is easy to use because I think it looks simple.' A design teacher says this is not enough evidence. What should the student do to properly test usability?

options.A: Add more colours to make the app look more exciting
options.B: Ask real target users to complete tasks on the app and observe where they struggle
options.C: Write a longer description of why the app is simple
options.D: Show the app to the school principal for approval

questions.explanation: Usability testing requires observing real users attempting actual tasks so problems can be identified objectively — the designer's own opinion is biased and unreliable. A school principal is not the target user and cannot provide evidence about whether the intended audience finds it easy to use.

questions.title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
questions.prompt: In the '3 Rs' hierarchy of sustainability, which action is considered the most effective way to reduce environmental impact — and why?

options.A: Recycle, because materials can be turned into new products
options.B: Reuse, because items last longer before becoming waste
options.C: Reduce, because using fewer resources in the first place creates the least waste and energy use
options.D: Recycle, because it is the easiest action for individuals to take

questions.explanation: Reducing consumption is ranked first because it prevents waste and resource use from occurring at all — recycling still requires energy and processing. Recycling, while valuable, is ranked last in the hierarchy because it only recovers some material value after the product has already been used.

questions.title: Target User Identification
questions.prompt: Before designing a new classroom reading chair, which piece of information about the target users would be MOST useful to a designer?

options.A: The favourite subjects of the students who will use the chair
options.B: The average height and sitting measurements of children aged 9–11
options.C: The school's annual technology budget
options.D: The number of books in the school library

questions.explanation: Anthropometric data — measurements of the human body such as height and sitting dimensions — directly informs ergonomic decisions about seat height, depth, and backrest position. Favourite subjects and library book counts have no direct connection to the physical design of a chair.

questions.title: Copyright in Design
questions.prompt: Leo copies a famous graphic designer's poster artwork, changes the colours slightly, and sells it as his own. Which statement is most accurate about what Leo has done?

options.A: Leo has legally innovated on the original work
options.B: Leo has violated copyright because the original artwork is protected
options.C: Leo is allowed to sell the work as long as he changed the colours
options.D: Leo needs only a trademark, not copyright permission, for visual artwork

questions.explanation: Copyright automatically protects original creative works, including graphic design, as soon as they are created — minor changes like colour alteration do not make a copy legally original. A trademark protects brand names and logos for commercial identity, not artistic works.

questions.title: Input, Process, Output
questions.prompt: In systems engineering, a blender takes fruit and ice (input), spins blades at high speed (process), and produces a smoothie (output). What part of the system is the spinning blades?

options.A: The output
options.B: The feedback
options.C: The input
options.D: The process

questions.explanation: In an input-process-output model, the process is the transformation step that converts inputs into outputs — the spinning blades transform the fruit and ice into a smoothie. The output is the smoothie itself, which is the result after the transformation has occurred.

questions.title: Biomimicry in Design
questions.prompt: Engineers designed a high-speed train's nose to be shaped like a kingfisher bird's beak, which helped the train move through air tunnels without a loud boom. This approach — copying solutions found in nature — is called what?

options.A: Ergonomics
options.B: Biomimicry
options.C: Rapid prototyping
options.D: Open-source design

questions.explanation: Biomimicry is the practice of designing products and systems by imitating structures and strategies found in nature — the Shinkansen bullet train's beak-shaped nose is one of the most famous real examples. Ergonomics focuses on fitting designs to human bodies, not on copying nature.

questions.title: Design for Inclusion
questions.prompt: A student claims that designing a product for people with disabilities makes it less appealing to everyone else. Evaluate this claim. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: The claim is correct — features for disabled users always reduce appeal for other users
options.B: The claim is correct — designers should make two separate versions of every product
options.C: The claim is incorrect — inclusive design often produces features that benefit all users
options.D: The claim is correct — inclusive design is only required by law, not by good design practice

questions.explanation: Inclusive design frequently benefits everyone — for example, kerb cuts on pavements were designed for wheelchair users but are also used by cyclists, parents with prams, and delivery workers. This 'curb-cut effect' shows that designing for edge cases usually improves products for the majority.

questions.title: Evaluating Against Criteria
questions.prompt: A design specification states a water bottle must hold at least 500 ml and be crush-proof. A student's prototype holds 480 ml and crumples when squeezed. How many design criteria has the prototype failed?

options.A: None — the prototype is close enough to the specification
options.B: One — only the volume criterion is not met
options.C: Both criteria — volume and crush-resistance are both not met
options.D: It is impossible to judge without testing the prototype again

questions.explanation: 480 ml is below the minimum 500 ml requirement, and crumpling when squeezed means it is not crush-proof — both stated criteria have been failed. In design evaluation, criteria are objective benchmarks, and 'close enough' is not an acceptable outcome unless the specification states a tolerance range.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: During the 'empathise' stage of design thinking, a student wants to understand why elderly users struggle with a medicine bottle cap. Which method would give the most useful firsthand information?

options.A: Search online for reviews of medicine bottles
options.B: Observe and interview elderly users while they open the bottle
options.C: Sketch five different cap designs immediately
options.D: Build a prototype cap using cardboard

questions.explanation: Empathising means gathering direct insight from real users; observing and interviewing users reveals specific pain points that secondary sources miss. Searching online reviews (option A) provides secondhand data and skips the direct human connection that defines the empathise stage.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A design team has gathered lots of information about users. The 'define' stage asks them to do one key thing with that information. What is it?

options.A: Choose the cheapest materials available
options.B: Build the first working model of their solution
options.C: Create a clear problem statement focused on user needs
options.D: Decide which team member will present the final product

questions.explanation: The 'define' stage synthesises research into a focused problem statement (sometimes called a 'point of view') that guides all later design work. Building a working model (option B) belongs to the prototype stage, not the define stage.

questions.title: Ideation Techniques
questions.prompt: During ideation, a class uses brainstorming rules. Which rule is MOST important for making sure all ideas are captured without judgment?

options.A: Only write down ideas that are already possible to build
options.B: Defer judgment so no idea is criticised during the session
options.C: Let only the team leader suggest ideas
options.D: Focus on a single idea until it is fully developed

questions.explanation: Deferring judgment is a core brainstorming rule because criticism early on stops people from sharing creative ideas; quantity and openness are valued first. Allowing only the team leader to suggest ideas (option C) would reduce diversity of thinking and contradicts collaborative ideation principles.

questions.title: Prototype Purpose
questions.prompt: A student says, 'Our prototype must be perfect before we show anyone.' A classmate disagrees. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The first student is correct; a polished prototype avoids wasting feedback time
options.B: The classmate is correct; prototypes are meant to be rough so feedback improves them early
options.C: Both are correct; it depends on the material cost of the prototype
options.D: Neither is correct; prototypes should only be shown to the teacher, not to users

questions.explanation: Prototypes in design thinking are intentionally rough and low-fidelity so that designers can fail fast, learn quickly, and improve before investing in expensive final versions. A polished prototype (option A) wastes time and resources before the design has been validated by real user feedback.

questions.title: Material Properties: Conductivity
questions.prompt: A student is choosing a material for the handle of a cooking pot. They want the handle to stay cool when the pot is on the stove. Which property should the handle material have?

options.A: High thermal conductivity
options.B: High electrical conductivity
options.C: Low thermal conductivity
options.D: High density

questions.explanation: Low thermal conductivity means the material transfers heat slowly, keeping the handle safe to touch; wood and many plastics have this property and are commonly used for pot handles. High thermal conductivity (option A) would cause the handle to heat up quickly, creating a burn risk.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Fit
questions.prompt: Ergonomics is the science of designing products to fit the people who use them. Which of these is the BEST example of an ergonomic design decision?

options.A: Making a school chair seat the same height for all students from age 6 to 16
options.B: Designing a computer keyboard with a slight curve to match the natural arc of the hands
options.C: Choosing bright colours for a classroom wall to match the school logo
options.D: Using the heaviest wood available so the furniture lasts longer

questions.explanation: A curved keyboard is shaped around the natural resting position of human hands and wrists, reducing strain — a textbook ergonomic adaptation. Using one seat height for all ages (option A) is the opposite of ergonomic thinking because it ignores variation in human body size.

questions.title: Sustainability: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
questions.prompt: A toy company wants to make its packaging more sustainable. Rank these options from MOST to LEAST sustainable: (1) using recycled cardboard, (2) reducing packaging size, (3) making packaging reusable as a storage box. Which ranking is correct?

options.A: Recycle, then reuse, then reduce
options.B: Reduce, then reuse, then recycle
options.C: Reuse, then reduce, then recycle
options.D: Recycle, then reduce, then reuse

questions.explanation: The waste hierarchy places 'reduce' first because using fewer materials is better than managing waste later; 'reuse' comes second, and 'recycle' is third because it still requires energy for reprocessing. Recycling first (options A and D) overlooks the higher priority of using less material in the first place.

questions.title: Testing Stage: Fair Tests
questions.prompt: A design team built two versions of a water-resistant school bag. What does a fair test of both bags require?

options.A: Testing each bag in a different rainstorm on different days
options.B: Exposing both bags to the same amount of water under the same conditions
options.C: Choosing the bag that looks more waterproof before testing begins
options.D: Asking users to guess which bag is better without getting them wet

questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one variable (the bag design) while keeping all other conditions — amount of water, duration, angle — identical so results can be compared accurately. Testing in different rainstorms (option A) introduces uncontrolled variables that make results unreliable.

questions.title: Iterative Design Process
questions.prompt: After testing their prototype, a team finds that users cannot read the labels on their product. According to the iterative design process, what should the team do next?

options.A: Abandon the project and start a completely new one
options.B: Present the product as finished because testing is complete
options.C: Return to ideating and prototyping with larger, clearer labels
options.D: Ask the users to try harder to read the labels

questions.explanation: Iterative design means using test results to loop back and improve the design; finding a problem leads to redesigning and building a new prototype with the fix applied. Presenting the flawed product as finished (option B) ignores the purpose of testing and produces a poor user experience.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Basics
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment (LCA) looks at the environmental impact of a product. Which stages does an LCA include?

options.A: Only the manufacturing stage, because that uses the most energy
options.B: Only the use and disposal stages
options.C: From raw material extraction through to disposal or recycling
options.D: Only the transport stage, because that creates the most pollution

questions.explanation: An LCA tracks environmental impact across the entire life of a product — extraction, manufacturing, transport, use, and end-of-life — to identify where improvements can be made. Looking only at manufacturing (option A) misses significant impacts in other stages, such as energy used during the product's lifespan.

questions.title: User Experience (UX) Research
questions.prompt: A designer wants to find out whether children find a new app confusing. Which UX research method would give the richest qualitative information?

options.A: Counting how many downloads the app receives in the first week
options.B: Watching children use the app and asking them to think aloud
options.C: Reading comments on the app store after launch
options.D: Calculating the average screen time per session

questions.explanation: The 'think-aloud' observation method captures real-time thoughts and confusion as users interact with the product, providing rich qualitative insight into usability problems. Download counts and screen time (options A and D) are quantitative metrics that show popularity but not why users find something confusing.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright
questions.prompt: A student finds a photograph online and uses it in their design project without asking permission or crediting the creator. What is this an example of?

options.A: Fair use, because the image was used for education
options.B: Copyright infringement, because the creator's rights were not respected
options.C: Open-source sharing, because the image was available on the internet
options.D: Plagiarism only, because images cannot have copyright

questions.explanation: Copyright protects creative works including photographs; using them without permission or credit is infringement regardless of the purpose. Fair use (option A) is a specific legal exception with strict conditions — educational use alone does not automatically qualify as fair use.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Inputs and Outputs
questions.prompt: In systems engineering, a simple system takes inputs and produces outputs. For a water filtration system, which correctly identifies the input, process, and output?

options.A: Input: clean water; Process: pumping; Output: dirty water
options.B: Input: dirty water; Process: filtering; Output: clean water
options.C: Input: electricity; Process: heating; Output: dirty water
