options.D: Input: clean water; Process: filtering; Output: electricity

questions.explanation: A water filtration system takes dirty water (input), passes it through a filter medium (process), and produces clean water (output) — a classic input–process–output model. Option A reverses the logical flow, claiming clean water enters and dirty water exits, which contradicts the purpose of the system.

questions.title: Innovation vs. Invention
questions.prompt: A company takes an existing bicycle and adds a small electric motor so riders can pedal more easily up hills. Is this best described as an invention or an innovation, and why?

options.A: Invention, because the electric motor had never existed before
options.B: Innovation, because it improves an existing product in a new way
options.C: Invention, because adding anything new to a product counts as inventing
options.D: Neither; it is only a modification and has no economic value

questions.explanation: Innovation means applying new ideas to improve or adapt existing products or processes; the electric bicycle builds on two already-existing technologies (bicycles and electric motors) to create added value. An invention (option A) refers specifically to something created for the first time — the electric motor itself was already invented long before e-bikes.

questions.title: Material Properties: Flexibility vs. Rigidity
questions.prompt: A designer is creating a protective phone case. She wants it to absorb impact but still hold its shape over time. Which combination of material properties should she look for?

options.A: Brittle and rigid
options.B: Flexible enough to absorb shock and durable enough to resist permanent deformation
options.C: Highly transparent and rigid
options.D: Soft enough to melt at room temperature

questions.explanation: A good phone case needs elasticity (to absorb impact energy without cracking) combined with durability (to return to shape and resist wear); thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) is commonly used for exactly this balance. A brittle and rigid material (option A) would crack on impact rather than absorbing the shock.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Data Privacy
questions.prompt: A student designs a health-tracking app for children. A classmate says the app should store users' location data permanently to improve its suggestions. Identify the ethical concern with this idea.

options.A: Storing location data uses too much battery power
options.B: Permanently storing children's location data risks privacy and could expose them to harm if the data is breached
options.C: Location data is not useful for health tracking, so there is no point storing it
options.D: The app would become too expensive to build if it stores extra data

questions.explanation: Wait — re-reading: option A says battery power, which is not the ethical concern. The correct answer is B: permanently storing children's location data creates serious privacy risks; if the data is accessed by unauthorised parties, children's safety could be compromised. Option C is factually incorrect — location can relate to activity levels — but the primary issue here is ethical, not practical usefulness.

questions.title: Design Brief Components
questions.prompt: A design brief is a written document that guides a design project. Which element is MOST important to include so the designer knows exactly what success looks like?

options.A: A list of the team members' favourite colours
options.B: Clear design specifications and success criteria
options.C: A schedule of when each team member will take breaks
options.D: A list of every tool available in the workshop

questions.explanation: Design specifications and success criteria define measurable targets — size, weight, cost, performance — that the final product must meet, giving the team an objective way to evaluate their solution. Listing favourite colours (option A) has no functional relevance to guiding design decisions.

questions.title: Cause and Effect: Material Choice
questions.prompt: A school decides to replace all its plastic water bottles with glass ones. What is the most likely NEGATIVE consequence of this change?

options.A: Glass bottles are more transparent than plastic, making drinks look different
options.B: Glass is heavier and breakable, increasing injury risk and carrying weight for students
options.C: Glass cannot be cleaned as thoroughly as plastic
options.D: Glass bottles will make drinks taste worse than plastic bottles

questions.explanation: Glass is denser than most plastics and shatters when dropped, creating both a weight burden for children carrying bags and a safety hazard if bottles break. Claiming glass cannot be cleaned as well as plastic (option C) is incorrect — glass is non-porous and often considered easier to clean thoroughly.

questions.title: Feedback Loops in Design
questions.prompt: In design thinking, what is the PURPOSE of collecting user feedback after testing a prototype?

options.A: To prove to the teacher that the design process was followed
options.B: To identify what works and what needs improvement before finalising the design
options.C: To decide which team member deserves the most credit
options.D: To show that the prototype was built correctly from the start

questions.explanation: User feedback after testing reveals real-world strengths and weaknesses of the prototype, giving designers evidence to guide targeted improvements in the next iteration. Collecting feedback to prove process compliance (option A) misunderstands the purpose — feedback should drive design decisions, not just satisfy documentation requirements.

questions.title: Sustainability: Circular Economy
questions.prompt: In a circular economy model, what happens to a product at the end of its useful life, instead of being thrown in a landfill?

options.A: It is exported to another country for disposal
options.B: Its materials are returned to the production cycle through reuse, repair, or recycling
options.C: It is stored in a warehouse indefinitely
options.D: It is burned to generate electricity as the only alternative to landfill

questions.explanation: A circular economy aims to keep materials in use as long as possible by designing for reuse, repair, remanufacturing, or recycling so that waste is minimised and resources are preserved. Burning for electricity (option D) is a linear end-of-life strategy called 'energy recovery' and is considered a last resort, not a circular approach.

questions.title: Perspective in Design
questions.prompt: A student designs a playground slide. She tests it only with her friends from her class. Why might this give an incomplete picture of how well the design works?

options.A: Friends are always too positive and will only say good things
options.B: The slide might be used by children of different ages, sizes, or abilities whose needs were not tested
options.C: Testing with friends is not allowed under IB design rules
options.D: Playground equipment can only be tested by professional engineers

questions.explanation: Testing with only one group of similar users limits perspective; a playground slide may also be used by younger children, larger children, or those with physical disabilities — groups with very different needs that the narrow test group cannot represent. While friends may be encouraging (option A), bias is a separate issue from the core problem of limited diversity in the test group.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Patents
questions.prompt: A designer invents a new type of solar panel that generates 40% more electricity than existing panels. To stop other companies from copying and selling her invention without permission, she should apply for:

options.A: A trademark, to protect the brand name of her panel
options.B: A patent, to protect the technical invention itself
options.C: A copyright, to protect her design drawings
options.D: A trade secret, by simply never telling anyone how it works

questions.explanation: A patent grants an inventor exclusive rights to make, use, and sell a new technical invention for a set period (typically 20 years), directly protecting the functional innovation from being copied. A trademark (option A) only protects brand names and logos, not the underlying technology.

questions.title: States of Matter
questions.prompt: A student heats a solid chocolate bar and it slowly turns into a liquid. What is happening to the particles inside the chocolate as it melts?

options.A: The particles break apart into smaller particles
options.B: The particles move faster and spread further apart
options.C: The particles stop moving completely
options.D: The particles shrink in size

questions.explanation: When a solid is heated, its particles gain energy and vibrate faster until they can move past each other, forming a liquid — the particles spread further apart and move more freely. The particles do not break apart or change size; those are chemical changes, not the physical process of melting.

questions.title: Food Chains and Energy
questions.prompt: In a food chain, grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk, which organism is the primary producer?

options.A: Grasshopper
options.B: Frog
options.C: Grass
options.D: Hawk

questions.explanation: Grass is the primary producer because it makes its own food using sunlight through photosynthesis, forming the base of the food chain. The grasshopper is a primary consumer, not a producer, because it must eat the grass to get energy.

questions.title: Water Cycle
questions.prompt: When the sun heats a puddle and the water slowly disappears on a warm day, what process is taking place?

options.A: Condensation
options.B: Precipitation
options.C: Evaporation
options.D: Infiltration

questions.explanation: Evaporation is the process by which liquid water absorbs heat energy and changes into water vapour, rising into the atmosphere — this is why puddles disappear on warm days. Condensation is the opposite process, where water vapour cools and becomes liquid, such as clouds forming.

questions.title: Living vs Non-Living
questions.prompt: A student lists these characteristics: grows, responds to the environment, reproduces, and needs energy. A flame grows, responds to wind, and needs oxygen for energy, but cannot reproduce. What does this tell us about a flame?

options.A: A flame is a living thing because it grows and uses energy
options.B: A flame is non-living because it cannot reproduce on its own
options.C: A flame is a living thing because it responds to the environment
options.D: A flame is non-living because it does not need oxygen

questions.explanation: All living things must carry out all the life processes, including reproduction; since a flame cannot reproduce on its own, it is classified as non-living. Options A and C are incorrect because meeting some life characteristics but not all is not enough to classify something as living.

questions.title: Photosynthesis Basics
questions.prompt: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for several days. Which statement best describes what will happen to its ability to make food?

options.A: It will make more food because it is resting
options.B: It will make the same amount of food using heat instead
options.C: It will stop making food because light is needed for photosynthesis
options.D: It will make food from the soil water alone

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires light as an energy source to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose; without light, the process stops and the plant cannot produce its own food. Plants cannot substitute heat or soil water alone for sunlight in photosynthesis.

questions.title: Gravity and Weight
questions.prompt: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. Her mass stays the same, but her weight changes. Why does her weight decrease on the Moon?

options.A: The Moon has weaker gravity than Earth
options.B: The Moon has no atmosphere to push her down
options.C: She loses some of her body mass during the journey
options.D: The Moon is further from the Sun, so there is less energy

questions.explanation: Weight is the force of gravity acting on a mass; the Moon's gravity is about one-sixth that of Earth's because the Moon is less massive, so the astronaut weighs less there even though her mass is unchanged. Atmosphere does not determine weight — weight depends on gravitational pull, not air pressure.

questions.title: Solids Liquids Gases
questions.prompt: Which property is shared by both liquids and gases, but is NOT a property of solids?

options.A: They have a fixed shape
options.B: They can flow
options.C: They have a fixed volume
options.D: Their particles cannot move

questions.explanation: Both liquids and gases are fluids — their particles can move past one another, allowing them to flow and take the shape of their container, unlike solids whose particles are held in fixed positions. Solids have a fixed shape precisely because their particles cannot flow freely.

questions.title: Light and Shadows
questions.prompt: A student moves a torch closer to an opaque ball. What happens to the shadow cast on the wall behind the ball?

options.A: The shadow gets smaller
options.B: The shadow gets larger
options.C: The shadow disappears
options.D: The shadow stays exactly the same size

questions.explanation: When a light source moves closer to an opaque object, more light rays are blocked at wider angles, creating a larger shadow on the surface behind. The shadow does not disappear or shrink — those would only happen if the light moved further away or if the object became transparent.

questions.title: Habitats and Adaptation
questions.prompt: A desert plant has very small leaves, a thick waxy coating, and stores water in its stem. What is the main advantage of having very small leaves in a hot, dry habitat?

options.A: Small leaves absorb more sunlight for photosynthesis
options.B: Small leaves reduce the surface area through which water is lost
options.C: Small leaves make the plant lighter so roots grow deeper
options.D: Small leaves help the plant attract fewer insects

questions.explanation: Plants lose water through tiny pores called stomata on their leaves; smaller leaves have less surface area, which reduces the total amount of water lost through transpiration in a hot, dry environment. Larger leaves would actually absorb more sunlight, so small leaves are a trade-off that prioritises water conservation.

questions.title: Electricity and Circuits
questions.prompt: A student builds a circuit with a battery, a switch, and a bulb. When the switch is open, the bulb is off. What does an open switch do to the circuit?

options.A: It creates a complete path for electricity to flow
options.B: It breaks the circuit so electricity cannot flow
options.C: It increases the voltage from the battery
options.D: It stores electricity for later use

questions.explanation: An open switch creates a gap in the circuit, breaking the conducting path so electric current cannot flow and the bulb stays off; current only flows in a complete, unbroken circuit. A closed switch is what creates a complete path — open and closed switches have opposite effects.

questions.title: Seasons and Earth's Tilt
questions.prompt: Why does the Northern Hemisphere experience summer while the Southern Hemisphere experiences winter at the same time of year?

options.A: The Northern Hemisphere is closer to the Sun during summer
options.B: Earth's axis is tilted, so each hemisphere leans toward the Sun at different times
options.C: The Sun moves in a circle and heats different parts of Earth at different times
options.D: Earth speeds up in its orbit during summer, gaining more heat

questions.explanation: Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees, so as Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere takes turns being tilted toward the Sun — receiving more direct sunlight and experiencing summer — while the other tilts away and experiences winter. The two hemispheres are not at different distances from the Sun; it is the angle of sunlight, not distance, that drives the seasons.

questions.title: Magnets and Forces
questions.prompt: A student holds the north pole of one magnet close to the north pole of another. What will happen, and why?

options.A: They attract, because opposite poles always attract
options.B: They repel, because like poles push each other away
options.C: Nothing happens, because magnets only affect iron objects
options.D: They attract, because north poles are always the stronger pole

questions.explanation: Like poles of magnets — north-north or south-south — always repel each other; only unlike poles (north-south) attract. Option A is incorrect because attraction only occurs between opposite poles, not matching ones.

questions.title: Sound and Vibration
questions.prompt: A student stretches a rubber band across a box and plucks it. She then plucks a thinner, tighter rubber band. How will the sound change?

options.A: The sound will be louder
options.B: The sound will be lower in pitch
options.C: The sound will be higher in pitch
options.D: The sound will travel slower through the air

questions.explanation: A thinner, tighter rubber band vibrates at a higher frequency, which produces a higher pitch sound; frequency and pitch are directly related. A thicker or looser band vibrates more slowly, giving a lower pitch — the opposite of what happens with the tighter band.

questions.title: Human Body — Skeleton
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's statement: 'The skeleton's only job is to give the body its shape and hold it upright.'

options.A: The statement is correct; the skeleton does only provide shape
options.B: The skeleton also protects organs and allows movement, not just shape
options.C: The skeleton has no role in shape; it only protects organs
options.D: The error is that the skeleton is made of cartilage, not bone

questions.explanation: The skeleton has multiple functions: it gives the body shape, supports it upright, protects vital organs (such as the skull protecting the brain), and works with muscles to allow movement. The statement is incomplete because it ignores protection and movement as key skeletal functions.

questions.title: Rocks and Soil
questions.prompt: A gardener notices that plants grow better in soil that contains small pieces of broken rock mixed with decayed plant material. What does the decayed plant material add to the soil that helps plants grow?

options.A: Sunlight stored inside the decayed material
options.B: Nutrients that plants can absorb through their roots
options.C: Water that the decayed material has produced
options.D: Carbon dioxide that plants use for photosynthesis

questions.explanation: Decayed plant material, called humus, releases nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus into the soil; plant roots absorb these dissolved nutrients and use them for growth. Sunlight cannot be stored in soil, and plants take in carbon dioxide through their leaves, not roots.

questions.title: Fair Testing
questions.prompt: Two students want to find out whether plants grow taller in sand or in potting soil. Student A uses big pots for sand and small pots for soil. A student claims this is a fair test. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because only the soil type needs to change
options.B: The claim is incorrect because the pot size is different, making it unfair
options.C: The claim is correct because pot size does not affect plant growth
options.D: The claim is incorrect because both pots should be filled with sand

questions.explanation: In a fair test, only one variable — the type of soil — should change; all other conditions, including pot size, must stay the same. Using different pot sizes introduces another variable that could affect the results, making it impossible to know if growth differences are due to soil type or pot size.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Decomposers
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to a forest ecosystem if all the decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, suddenly disappeared?

options.A: Plants would grow faster because there would be less competition
options.B: Dead material would build up and nutrients would not return to the soil
options.C: Animals would eat more plants to replace lost nutrients
options.D: Rain would replace the nutrients that decomposers usually provide

questions.explanation: Decomposers break down dead plants and animals, releasing essential nutrients back into the soil for plants to reuse; without them, dead material would pile up and nutrients would become locked away, eventually reducing soil fertility and harming the whole ecosystem. Rain carries some minerals but cannot substitute for the chemical breakdown that decomposers perform.

questions.title: Heat Transfer — Conduction
questions.prompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon are both left in a hot bowl of soup for the same amount of time. Which spoon's handle will feel hotter, and why?

options.A: The wooden spoon, because wood absorbs heat more quickly
options.B: Both spoons will feel equally hot after the same amount of time
options.C: The metal spoon, because metal conducts heat better than wood
options.D: The wooden spoon, because wood is denser and holds more heat

questions.explanation: Metal is a good conductor of heat, meaning energy passes quickly through its particles from the hot end to the cooler handle; wood is a poor conductor (an insulator) so heat travels through it much more slowly. Wood's density has little to do with how quickly heat travels through it — thermal conductivity, not density, determines this.

questions.title: Air and Atmosphere
questions.prompt: A student claims that air is 'nothing' because we cannot see it. Which piece of evidence best proves that air is matter and takes up space?

options.A: Air makes sounds when it blows through trees
options.B: An inflated balloon expands and pushes back when squeezed
options.C: We feel cold when the wind blows on us
options.D: Clouds form in the air on humid days

questions.explanation: An inflated balloon expands because air particles fill the space inside and exert pressure on the walls; when squeezed, the air pushes back, proving it occupies space and has mass — two defining properties of matter. Feeling cold from wind demonstrates air movement but does not directly prove air takes up space.

questions.title: Plant Parts and Functions
questions.prompt: Which part of a flowering plant is most responsible for absorbing water and minerals from the soil?

options.A: The stem
options.B: The leaves
options.C: The roots
options.D: The petals

questions.explanation: Roots anchor the plant in the soil and are covered in tiny root hair cells that increase surface area, enabling them to absorb water and dissolved minerals efficiently. The stem transports these substances upward to the leaves but does not absorb them from the soil.

questions.title: Simple Machines — Ramps
questions.prompt: A worker uses a ramp to push a heavy box onto a platform. What advantage does the ramp give her compared with lifting the box straight up?

options.A: The ramp reduces the total amount of work needed to raise the box
options.B: The ramp means she needs less force, but pushes over a longer distance
options.C: The ramp reduces the weight of the box by spreading it over more surface
options.D: The ramp stores energy that it releases to help push the box

questions.explanation: A ramp is an inclined plane — a simple machine that reduces the force required to move an object by spreading the effort over a longer distance; the trade-off is that you push further but with less force. The total work done is actually the same or slightly more (due to friction), not less, so option A is incorrect.

questions.title: Weather and Climate
questions.prompt: A student says that weather and climate are the same thing. What is the most important difference between them?

options.A: Weather is measured in the ocean; climate is measured on land
options.B: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term patterns
options.C: Climate changes every day; weather stays the same for years
options.D: Weather only refers to temperature; climate includes wind and rain too

questions.explanation: Weather refers to the day-to-day atmospheric conditions such as rain or sunshine in a specific place, while climate describes the average weather patterns over a long period of time — typically 30 years or more — for a region. Option C reverses the definitions; it is weather that changes daily, not climate.

questions.title: Animal Classification
questions.prompt: A dolphin breathes air, gives birth to live young, and feeds its babies milk. A fish breathes through gills and lays eggs. Why is a dolphin classified as a mammal rather than a fish, even though it lives in the ocean?

options.A: Because dolphins are larger than most fish
options.B: Because dolphins have a streamlined body shape like other mammals
options.C: Because dolphins breathe air, are warm-blooded, and feed young with milk
options.D: Because dolphins live in salt water, which is where mammals evolved

questions.explanation: Classification is based on shared characteristics, not habitat; dolphins breathe air using lungs, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young, and nurse them with milk — all defining mammal traits. Body size and streamlined shape are not classification criteria, and many fish also live in salt water.

questions.title: Natural Resources
questions.prompt: Coal, oil, and natural gas are called non-renewable resources. What does 'non-renewable' mean in this context?

options.A: They cannot be used to generate electricity
options.B: They take millions of years to form, so they cannot be replaced at the rate we use them
options.C: They are only found in certain countries and cannot be shared
options.D: They produce energy that cannot be renewed once it is used

questions.explanation: Fossil fuels like coal and oil form over millions of years from compressed ancient organisms; humans use them far faster than they can ever be replaced, making them effectively non-renewable. Option D confuses the energy produced with the resource itself — the resource being irreplaceable is the key idea.

questions.title: Forces — Friction
questions.prompt: A student slides the same wooden block across a smooth tile floor and then across a rough carpet. On which surface does the block travel further before stopping, and why?

options.A: The carpet, because rough surfaces push the block forward
options.B: The tile, because smooth surfaces create less friction
options.C: Both surfaces, because the block's mass stays the same
options.D: The carpet, because rough surfaces grip the block and keep it moving

questions.explanation: Friction is a force that opposes motion; a smooth tile floor has less friction than rough carpet, so less force acts to slow the block down, allowing it to travel further. Rough surfaces create more friction, which slows objects down faster — they do not push or propel the block forward.

questions.title: Roles in Community Systems
questions.prompt: In most organised communities — such as schools, towns, or countries — different people are assigned specific roles like lawmaker, enforcer, and judge. Why is it considered important that the same person does NOT perform all three roles at once?

options.A: It ensures that laws are written more quickly because specialists focus only on their own task
options.B: It prevents any one person from having unchecked power, reducing the chance of unfair decisions
options.C: It guarantees that every citizen will agree with the rules that are created and enforced
options.D: It makes government less expensive by spreading the workload across more people

questions.explanation: Separating roles like making, enforcing, and judging laws is the principle of separation of powers — it creates checks and balances so no single person can abuse authority, as famously described by Montesquieu in the 18th century. Option A is incorrect because specialisation may speed up some tasks, but that efficiency is not the reason roles are separated — the core purpose is preventing abuse of power, not saving time.

questions.title: Fair Trade and Farmers
questions.prompt: A cocoa farmer in Ghana earns very little money even though chocolate made from cocoa is sold at high prices in shops across Europe. Which idea from fairness and development best explains this gap?

options.A: The farmer chooses to grow less cocoa than buyers need, so the price stays low at the farm.
options.B: Most of the profit goes to companies that process, package, and sell the chocolate, not to the farmer who grows the cocoa.
options.C: European governments set the price of cocoa very high to help farmers earn more money.
options.D: Ghana produces too much cocoa compared to other crops, which automatically raises farm incomes.

questions.explanation: In global supply chains, the largest share of profit is typically captured by processors, brands, and retailers in wealthier countries, while primary producers like cocoa farmers receive only a small fraction — a core concern of Fairness and Development. Option A is wrong because the gap between farm-gate price and shop price is not caused by farmers deliberately limiting supply; it reflects how value is distributed unequally along the supply chain.

questions.title: Market Failure and Public Goods
questions.prompt: A city park is open to all residents regardless of whether they contributed taxes to build it. A private company argues there is no profit in maintaining it. Which TWO characteristics of public goods best explain why markets tend to underprovide them?

options.A: Non-excludability and non-rivalry — no one can be stopped from using it and one person's use does not reduce availability for others
options.B: Scarcity and rivalry — the park becomes less valuable when too many people use it simultaneously
options.C: High production cost and government monopoly — only the state can afford to build large spaces
options.D: Inelastic demand and price controls — residents would pay any price, so companies still avoid it

questions.explanation: Public goods are defined by non-excludability (you cannot stop free-riders from benefiting) and non-rivalry (one person's enjoyment does not deplete it for others), making private profit impossible and causing market underprovision. Option B confuses public goods with common-pool resources, where congestion does reduce availability — a genuine but distinct concept.

questions.title: Authoritarian Control Methods
questions.prompt: Examine the following scenario: a government controls all television and newspaper content, requires citizens to carry identity papers at all times, and jails opposition party leaders before elections. Which concept from political science best describes the combination of these three strategies?

options.A: Federalism — distributing power to regional governments to maintain order
options.B: Totalitarian authoritarianism — the state seeks to control political, social, and information spaces simultaneously
options.C: Constitutional monarchy — a hereditary ruler uses traditional authority to limit opposition
options.D: Technocracy — rule by qualified experts who restrict participation to prevent uninformed decisions

questions.explanation: Totalitarian authoritarianism is characterised by the state's attempt to dominate all spheres of life including media, movement, and political competition — all three measures in the scenario match this definition. Technocracy describes rule by experts based on competence, not suppression of opposition, making it a tempting but incorrect distractor.

questions.title: Locke vs Rousseau on Society
questions.prompt: John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau both wrote social contract theories, but they disagreed on a key point. A student claims: 'Both philosophers believed that individuals should always keep their full personal rights when joining society.' Identify the error in this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — both Locke and Rousseau agreed that natural rights are completely preserved in civil society
options.B: The claim is wrong about both — neither philosopher believed individuals retain any rights once a government is formed
options.C: The claim misrepresents Rousseau, who argued individuals surrender all rights to the collective general will, receiving civil liberty in return rather than keeping natural rights intact
options.D: The claim misrepresents Locke, who believed governments could freely override natural rights whenever the majority demanded it

questions.explanation: Rousseau argued that individuals surrender their natural freedom entirely to the community, gaining civil liberty defined by the general will — a fundamentally different position from Locke, who held that natural rights (life, liberty, property) are retained and protected by government. Option D is wrong because Locke specifically argued majority rule cannot override fundamental natural rights, which is why revolution is justified when it does.

questions.title: Planned Economy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, the government sets prices and decides what goods are produced. A student argues this system eliminates inequality because everyone receives what they need. Evaluate this claim by identifying its strongest weakness.

options.A: Planned economies always produce more military goods than consumer goods, causing civilian poverty
options.B: Central planners lack the price signals that markets generate, making it extremely difficult to match supply to millions of individual consumer preferences efficiently
options.C: Planned economies cannot reduce inequality because tax systems are the only tool for redistribution
options.D: The claim is correct — historical planned economies successfully eliminated all economic inequality

questions.explanation: The 'knowledge problem,' identified by economist Friedrich Hayek, explains that no central authority can gather and process the vast decentralised information that price signals provide, leading to chronic shortages and surpluses — as seen in the Soviet Union. Option A describes a tendency in some planned economies but is not a structural flaw of planning itself, making it a plausible but imprecise distractor.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitary Systems
questions.prompt: Country X has one central government that can change any regional policy without regional approval. Country Y requires both the national parliament and regional assemblies to agree before certain laws pass. Which statement best compares these two systems?

options.A: Country X is federal and Country Y is unitary, because X has stronger central control
options.B: Both countries are democracies because they both have parliaments and regional assemblies
options.C: Country X is a unitary state and Country Y is a federal state, because Y constitutionally divides sovereignty between levels of government
options.D: Country Y is a confederation because regional governments hold more power than the national government

questions.explanation: A unitary state concentrates sovereign power in the central government, which can override or abolish regional bodies — matching Country X. A federal state constitutionally divides power so regional governments have guaranteed authority the centre cannot unilaterally remove — matching Country Y. Option A reverses the labels, a common student error because 'stronger central control' is mistakenly linked to federalism.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: John Rawls used the 'original position' thought experiment to argue for a just society. Which type of inequality would Rawls most likely justify as acceptable under his 'difference principle'?

options.A: A surgeon earns significantly more than a shop worker because higher pay attracts skilled doctors, improving healthcare for the poorest patients
options.B: A monarch's family inherits wealth because tradition and stability benefit the whole society
options.C: Wealthy families pay lower tax rates because their investment creates jobs for lower-income workers
options.D: A corporation pays executives high bonuses because shareholder profit eventually trickles down to employees

questions.explanation: Rawls's difference principle states that social and economic inequalities are only just if they benefit the least advantaged members of society — higher surgeon pay that improves healthcare access for the poorest directly meets this test. Option C is tempting because it mentions economic benefit, but lower tax rates for the wealthy primarily advantage the already-well-off rather than specifically benefiting the least advantaged.

questions.title: Legitimacy and Revolution
questions.prompt: A government was democratically elected ten years ago but has since cancelled future elections, imprisoned journalists, and rewritten the constitution to keep the ruling party in power permanently. Using Locke's political theory, what would be the most justified response by citizens?

options.A: Citizens must continue to obey because the government was originally elected by a democratic majority
options.B: Citizens are justified in withdrawing consent and resisting the government, because it has broken the social contract by removing the mechanisms of accountability
options.C: Citizens should appeal to international courts, since Locke believed only external authorities could judge whether a contract was broken
options.D: Citizens should form a new political party and wait for the next election, as changing constitutions is a normal government function

questions.explanation: Locke argued in the Second Treatise of Government that when a government breaks the social contract — particularly by removing citizens' ability to replace it — the people's right of revolution is activated and withdrawal of consent is justified. Option A is the strongest distractor because initial democratic election seems to confer permanent legitimacy, but Locke's theory ties legitimacy to ongoing protection of rights, not a single vote.

questions.title: Market Economy Limitations
questions.prompt: In a purely free-market economy, a life-saving medicine is priced so high that only wealthy patients can afford it. Which TWO market economy features most directly explain why this outcome can occur?

options.A: Prices are set by supply and demand, and profit motive drives producers to maximise revenue regardless of social need
options.B: Governments in market economies always set medicine prices, so high costs reflect deliberate policy choices
options.C: Market economies produce too many goods overall, causing prices to fall and making medicine unaffordable
options.D: Free markets eliminate competition in healthcare, ensuring medicines are always scarce and expensive

questions.explanation: In a market economy, price is determined by supply and demand rather than need, and the profit motive encourages firms to charge what consumers will bear — especially with inelastic demand for life-saving drugs. Option D is a distractor because free markets are actually associated with competition, not its elimination; students often confuse market outcomes with monopoly outcomes.

questions.title: Social Stratification and Mobility
questions.prompt: In Society A, a person's job and income are almost entirely determined by the family they are born into. In Society B, individuals can move between economic classes based on education and effort. Which sociological concepts best describe Society A and Society B respectively?

options.A: Society A shows meritocracy; Society B shows a caste system
options.B: Society A shows a closed stratification system (e.g., caste); Society B shows an open stratification system with social mobility
options.C: Society A is an authoritarian state; Society B is a democracy, because only democracies allow social mobility
options.D: Both societies show the same level of inequality — they simply use different methods to distribute resources

questions.explanation: Closed stratification systems, like caste systems, fix social position at birth with little possibility of movement, while open systems theoretically allow upward or downward mobility based on individual achievement — this is the defining sociological distinction. Option A reverses the concepts, a common error since students sometimes confuse which term means fixed versus flexible status.

questions.title: International Law Compliance
questions.prompt: A powerful nation violates an international treaty it signed, but no global police force arrests its leaders. A student concludes: 'This proves international law is not really law at all.' Evaluate this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is fully correct — without physical enforcement, rules cannot function as genuine law
options.B: The conclusion oversimplifies: international law operates through consent, reputation, diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions, and institutions like the ICC, even without a central enforcer
options.C: The conclusion is wrong because the United Nations has a standing army that enforces all international treaties automatically
options.D: The conclusion is correct only for powerful nations; smaller countries are always forced to comply with international law

questions.explanation: International law uses compliance mechanisms including treaty obligations, international courts (e.g., the International Court of Justice), economic sanctions, and reputational costs rather than a centralised enforcement body — it functions differently from domestic law but still constitutes a legal order. Option A is the top distractor because students naturally associate 'law' with police enforcement, overlooking alternative compliance mechanisms.

questions.title: Power, Authority, and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A military general seizes control of a country by force and rules through fear. Five years later, citizens widely accept his rule as normal and natural. Which concept explains the shift in citizens' attitudes, and which type of authority does his rule eventually represent?

options.A: The shift reflects growing legitimacy; his rule transitions toward traditional authority as it becomes habitual and accepted over time
options.B: The shift reflects declining power; his rule becomes rational-legal authority because citizens start voting for him
options.C: There is no meaningful shift — coercive power and legitimate authority are identical concepts in political science
options.D: The shift reflects false consciousness; citizens accept his rule only because they have been economically bribed

questions.explanation: Sociologist Max Weber distinguished power (forcing compliance) from authority (accepted right to rule); when citizens habitually accept a ruler's commands as normal over time, coercive power can evolve into traditional authority through a process of legitimation. Option B is wrong because rational-legal authority specifically derives from established laws and procedures, not mere citizen acceptance of a ruler who bypassed legal processes.

questions.title: Comparing Democratic Models
questions.prompt: Country A uses proportional representation, where parties win seats matching their share of votes. Country B uses a first-past-the-post system, where only the candidate with the most votes in each district wins a seat. Which statement best analyses a key difference in political outcomes between these systems?

options.A: Country A tends to produce stronger single-party majority governments because all votes are converted directly into power
options.B: Country B is more democratic because citizens vote directly for a local representative they personally know
options.C: Country A tends to produce multi-party coalition governments, while Country B tends to favour two dominant parties and may leave smaller parties underrepresented
options.D: Both systems produce identical political outcomes because the total number of votes cast is the same

questions.explanation: Proportional representation translates vote shares into seat shares, encouraging multiple parties and coalition-building (as seen in Germany or the Netherlands), while first-past-the-post concentrates power by wasting votes cast for losing candidates, systematically disadvantaging smaller parties (as seen in the UK and USA). Option A is a common misconception — proportional systems actually make single-party majorities harder to achieve, not easier.

questions.title: Causes of Social Revolution
questions.prompt: Historians studying the French Revolution (1789) note that the bourgeoisie (middle class) had gained economic power but was excluded from political power by the aristocracy. Which theoretical framework best explains why this group became key drivers of revolution?

options.A: Status inconsistency — when economic and social status are mismatched, groups are motivated to change the system to align them
options.B: Elite circulation theory — revolutions happen only when the existing elite voluntarily agrees to share power
options.C: Dependency theory — the bourgeoisie revolted because France was economically exploited by foreign colonial powers
options.D: Modernisation theory — revolutions inevitably occur in all countries once they reach a certain level of industrial development

questions.explanation: Status inconsistency — where a group holds high economic status but low political status — creates resentment and motivation to change political structures, which closely matches the French bourgeoisie's position before 1789. Option D is a plausible distractor because France was industrialising, but modernisation theory predicts revolution as inevitable at an economic threshold, not because of a specific political exclusion gap.

questions.title: Government and Information Control
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to political decision-making in a democracy if a single corporation owned all major newspapers, television stations, and social media platforms in that country?

options.A: Democracy would function better because consistent messaging reduces public confusion and speeds up decision-making
options.B: The corporation would lose money because citizens in democracies always seek out independent sources of information
options.C: Citizens' ability to form independent political opinions would be weakened, distorting informed consent and undermining the foundations of democratic participation
options.D: Political outcomes would be unchanged because citizens in democracies vote based on personal experience, not media exposure

questions.explanation: Democracy depends on citizens being able to access diverse, independent information to make informed choices; media monopoly enables agenda-setting and selective framing that can systematically skew public opinion, undermining genuine informed consent. Option A is a genuine distractor because efficiency and clarity are real values, but consistency in the hands of one owner serves that owner's interests rather than democratic deliberation.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Government Role
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'In a mixed economy, the government's only role is to correct market failures — it should never intervene for any other reason.' Identify the most significant flaw in this argument.

options.A: The argument is correct — mixed economies are defined solely by government responses to externalities and public goods failures
options.B: The argument ignores that governments in mixed economies also intervene to redistribute income, provide merit goods like education, and pursue macroeconomic goals such as full employment
options.C: The argument is flawed because governments in mixed economies should not intervene even in cases of market failure, leaving all correction to consumers
options.D: The argument is only wrong because governments in mixed economies must also control all prices to prevent inflation

questions.explanation: Mixed economies involve government intervention for multiple reasons beyond market failure correction: redistribution through taxation and welfare, provision of merit goods (education, healthcare), and macroeconomic management (e.g., fiscal and monetary policy to address unemployment and inflation). Option A is the strongest distractor because it accurately captures one legitimate reason for intervention but falsely presents it as the only one.

questions.title: Comparative Constitutions
questions.prompt: Country A has a constitution that can be changed by a simple majority vote in parliament. Country B requires a two-thirds majority in parliament plus approval by regional governments to amend its constitution. Which statement best evaluates the significance of this difference?

options.A: Country A has a more rigid constitution than Country B because simple majority decisions are harder to reverse
options.B: Country B's higher amendment threshold better protects fundamental rights from being eroded by temporary political majorities, but may make needed reforms harder to achieve
options.C: Country A's constitution is superior because democratic governments should always be able to respond quickly to majority public opinion
options.D: Both constitutions offer equal protection because the content of rights matters more than the amendment procedure

questions.explanation: A rigid amendment process, like Country B's supermajority plus regional approval requirement, protects constitutional rights from being changed by a temporary ruling majority — a core purpose of constitutional democracy — but can also entrench outdated provisions. Option C is a thoughtful distractor because democratic responsiveness is a genuine value, but it ignores the risk that simple majority amendments can be used to undermine minority rights.

questions.title: Non-State Actors in Global Politics
questions.prompt: Multinational corporations, international NGOs, and terrorist networks are all examples of non-state actors in global politics. Which statement most accurately analyses their significance for the international system?

options.A: Non-state actors have no real influence because international law only recognises nation-states as legitimate actors
options.B: Non-state actors challenge the traditional state-centred model of international relations by exercising power across borders without territorial sovereignty
options.C: Non-state actors are only significant in economic matters; political power remains exclusively with national governments
options.D: Non-state actors are simply extensions of powerful states, meaning they do not represent genuinely independent sources of global influence

questions.explanation: Non-state actors like Amnesty International, the Red Cross, or multinational corporations exercise real political, economic, and normative influence across borders without holding territory or formal sovereignty, challenging realist assumptions that states are the only meaningful actors in international relations. Option A is a common misconception because while international law traditionally centres on states, organisations like the ICC and UN give non-state actors increasing formal recognition.

questions.title: Gender and Political Representation
questions.prompt: Country Z introduces a law requiring that at least 40% of parliamentary candidates from each party must be women. Critics argue this violates the principle of equal treatment. Supporters argue it corrects a structural inequality. Which argument best justifies the policy from a political philosophy perspective?

options.A: The policy is unjustified because any form of preferential treatment based on identity violates individual rights regardless of historical context
options.B: The policy is justified because women are biologically better suited to political decision-making than men
options.C: The policy can be justified as corrective justice — addressing historical structural barriers that produced underrepresentation, rather than simply creating unfair preference
options.D: The policy is justified only if it also guarantees that women candidates will win their elections, otherwise it achieves nothing

questions.explanation: Corrective or substantive justice distinguishes between formal equality (treating everyone the same) and substantive equality (accounting for structural disadvantages to achieve genuine equal opportunity) — gender quotas are typically defended on the latter grounds. Option A is the strongest distractor because it correctly identifies a real tension in liberal political philosophy between individual rights and group-based remedies, making it a genuinely competing argument.

questions.title: Economic Sanctions as Foreign Policy
questions.prompt: When Country A imposes economic sanctions on Country B — blocking trade and freezing financial assets — it hopes to change Country B's government behaviour. Analyse why sanctions sometimes fail to achieve their intended political goals.

options.A: Sanctions always work eventually — they simply need enough time to cause economic damage before governments comply
options.B: Sanctions can fail when the targeted government redirects economic hardship onto ordinary citizens rather than the elite decision-makers, or when other countries continue trading and undermine the sanctions' effect
options.C: Sanctions fail because they only affect international trade, leaving a country's domestic economy completely unaffected
options.D: Sanctions inevitably fail because international law prohibits one country from interfering in another's economy

questions.explanation: Historical cases such as sanctions on Russia (post-2014), Cuba, or North Korea show that authoritarian governments can insulate their elites while ordinary citizens bear the costs, reducing pressure on decision-makers; additionally, sanctions leak when third countries continue trading, as seen with North Korea's trade through intermediaries. Option A is a tempting distractor because sustained pressure can eventually work in some cases, but it falsely implies sanctions always succeed with enough time.

questions.title: Nationalism and State Formation
questions.prompt: A region within a larger country shares a distinct language, history, and culture and its people begin demanding their own independent state. Which concept from political science best describes this movement, and what tension does it create within the existing state?

options.A: Imperialism — the region is attempting to colonise neighbouring territories, threatening international stability
options.B: Federalism — the region is simply requesting more local government powers within the existing constitutional framework
options.C: Nationalist self-determination — the belief that a people sharing identity have the right to govern themselves, creating tension between that principle and the existing state's territorial integrity and unity
options.D: Authoritarianism — regional identity movements always indicate a desire for stricter centralised control over a cultural minority

questions.explanation: National self-determination — the principle that distinct peoples have the right to their own state — is recognised in the UN Charter but directly conflicts with the principle of territorial integrity, which protects existing states from fragmentation; this tension has driven conflicts from Kosovo to Catalonia. Option B is a significant distractor because federalism is sometimes offered as a compromise solution, but it describes a different concept from full independence movements.

questions.title: Fraction Division Logic
questions.prompt: A student claims that 3/4 ÷ 1/2 equals 3/8, because you simply multiply the denominators. Identify the error in this reasoning and choose the correct answer.

options.A: 3/8, the student is correct
options.B: 1 1/2, because you multiply by the reciprocal of 1/2
options.C: 3/2, because you add the numerators instead
options.D: 6/4, because you multiply both numerators by 2

questions.explanation: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2/1 = 6/4 = 1 1/2. The student incorrectly multiplied denominators instead of flipping the second fraction and multiplying.

questions.title: Properties of Negative Exponents
questions.prompt: What is the value of 2⁻³? Choose the correct answer and think carefully about what a negative exponent means.
questions.explanation: A negative exponent means taking the reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. The answer is positive 1/8, not negative — a negative exponent does not make the result negative.

questions.title: Perimeter vs Area Change
questions.prompt: A square has a side length of 4 cm. If the side length is doubled to 8 cm, what happens to its area?

options.A: It doubles, from 16 cm² to 32 cm²
options.B: It triples, from 16 cm² to 48 cm²
options.C: It quadruples, from 16 cm² to 64 cm²
options.D: It increases by 16 cm², from 16 cm² to 32 cm²

questions.explanation: Area of a square = side². When side doubles, area = (2s)² = 4s², so area quadruples: 4² = 16 cm² and 8² = 64 cm². Doubling the side length does not double the area because area depends on the square of the side.

questions.title: Mean vs Median Comparison
questions.prompt: A dataset has the values: 2, 3, 3, 4, 100. A student says the mean best represents the typical value. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; the mean always represents data most accurately
options.B: The student is incorrect; the median of 3 is more representative because the outlier 100 skews the mean
options.C: The student is incorrect; the mode of 3 is always the best measure for any dataset
options.D: The student is correct; the mean of 22.4 reflects the spread of the data well

questions.explanation: The mean is (2+3+3+4+100)/5 = 22.4, which is far above most values due to the outlier 100. The median is 3, which better represents the typical value in a skewed dataset. The mode can also be useful but is not always the best choice.

questions.title: Coordinate Geometry Reflection
questions.prompt: Point P is at (3, −2). It is reflected across the x-axis. What are the coordinates of its image P'?
questions.explanation: Reflecting across the x-axis keeps the x-coordinate the same and negates the y-coordinate: (3, −2) becomes (3, 2). Option A reflects across the y-axis instead, which would negate the x-coordinate, not the y-coordinate.

questions.title: Arithmetic Sequences Pattern
questions.prompt: The first term of an arithmetic sequence is 7 and the common difference is 5. What is the 8th term of this sequence?
questions.explanation: The nth term of an arithmetic sequence is a + (n−1)d. For the 8th term: 7 + (8−1)×5 = 7 + 35 = 42. A common mistake is computing 7 + 8×5 = 47, which incorrectly uses n instead of (n−1).

questions.title: Probability Complementary Events
questions.prompt: The probability that it rains on any given day is 0.35. What is the probability that it does NOT rain?
questions.explanation: Complementary events always sum to 1. P(no rain) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. Option B (0.55) is a common arithmetic error from subtracting 0.35 from 0.9 instead of from 1.

questions.title: Identifying Linear Functions
questions.prompt: Which of the following equations represents a linear function when graphed on a coordinate plane?

options.A: y = x²+ 3
options.C: y = 1/x
options.D: y = x³

questions.explanation: A linear function has the form y = mx + c, where the highest power of x is 1, producing a straight-line graph. y = x² + 3 is a parabola (quadratic), not linear, making it the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.title: Percentage Increase Calculation
questions.prompt: A school library had 250 books last year. This year it has 310 books. What is the percentage increase in the number of books, to the nearest whole percent?
questions.explanation: Percentage increase = (change/original) × 100 = (60/250) × 100 = 24%. Option A (19%) results from incorrectly dividing by the new value 310 instead of the original 250.

questions.title: Order of Operations
questions.prompt: Evaluate: 18 ÷ (2 + 1) × 3 − 4. A student gets 50. What error did they most likely make?

options.A: The student forgot to subtract 4 at the end; the correct answer is 54
options.B: The student ignored the brackets; dividing 18 by 2 first gives the wrong result
options.C: The correct answer is 14; the student multiplied before dividing
options.D: The correct answer is 14; the student ignored the brackets, computing 18 ÷ 2 = 9 first, then 9 + 1 = 10

questions.explanation: Following BODMAS: (2+1) = 3, then 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then 6 × 3 = 18, then 18 − 4 = 14. The student likely ignored the brackets and computed 18 ÷ 2 = 9 first, leading to a much larger answer like 50.

questions.title: Properties of Parallel Lines
questions.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle formed is 65°. What is the size of the co-interior (same-side interior) angle?
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary, meaning they add up to 180°. So the co-interior angle = 180° − 65° = 115°. Alternate angles are equal (65°), which is a common mix-up — those are not co-interior angles.

questions.title: Simplifying Algebraic Expressions
questions.prompt: Simplify: 3a + 2b − a + 5b. Which expression is equivalent?

options.A: 2a + 7b
options.B: 4a + 7b
options.C: 2a + 3b
options.D: 3a + 7b

questions.explanation: Collecting like terms: (3a − a) = 2a and (2b + 5b) = 7b, giving 2a + 7b. Option B (4a + 7b) is wrong because it adds instead of subtracts the 'a' terms.

questions.title: Volume of Cylinder Concept
questions.prompt: A cylinder has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 10 cm. Which formula correctly gives its volume, and what is the approximate value using π ≈ 3.14?
questions.explanation: Volume of a cylinder = πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.6 cm³. Option C uses the diameter (6) instead of the radius (3), a very common error when applying the formula.

questions.title: Solving Two-Step Equations
questions.prompt: Solve for n: 2n + 9 = 3. Which value of n is correct?
questions.explanation: Subtract 9 from both sides: 2n = 3 − 9 = −6. Then divide by 2: n = −3. A common error is computing 3 + 9 = 12 then dividing, giving n = 6, because the student adds instead of subtracts.

questions.title: Factors and Divisibility
questions.prompt: What is the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of 36 and 48?
questions.explanation: Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Factors of 48: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48. The highest common factor is 12. Option A (6) is a common factor but not the highest; students sometimes stop searching too early.

questions.title: Reading Pie Charts
questions.prompt: A pie chart shows how 120 students travel to school. The 'bus' sector covers 90°. How many students travel by bus?
questions.explanation: A full circle is 360°, so 90° represents 90/360 = 1/4 of the students. 1/4 × 120 = 30 students. Option D is correct. Option D might seem surprising, making option B or C tempting, but 90° is exactly one quarter of 360°.

questions.title: Pythagorean Theorem Application
questions.prompt: A right-angled triangle has legs of length 6 cm and 8 cm. What is the length of the hypotenuse?

options.A: 14 cm
options.B: 12 cm
options.C: 10 cm
options.D: 100 cm

questions.explanation: Using Pythagoras' theorem: hypotenuse² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, so hypotenuse = √100 = 10 cm. Option A (14) results from simply adding 6 + 8, forgetting to use the theorem.

questions.title: Comparing Fractions Efficiently
questions.prompt: Which of the following fractions is the largest? Compare carefully before choosing.
questions.explanation: Converting to decimals: 5/8 = 0.625, 3/5 = 0.6, 7/10 = 0.7, 2/3 ≈ 0.667. The largest is 7/10 = 0.7. Students often choose 2/3 incorrectly because it appears 'close to 1' or confuse it with having a small denominator.

questions.title: Place Value in Decimals
questions.prompt: What is the value of the digit 7 in the number 3.0748?

options.A: 7 tenths
options.B: 7 hundredths
options.C: 7 thousandths
options.D: 7 ten-thousandths

questions.explanation: In 3.0748, the digits after the decimal point are: 0 (tenths), 7 (hundredths), 4 (thousandths), 8 (ten-thousandths). So the 7 is in the hundredths place. Students often miscount the positions and pick 'tenths' or 'thousandths'.

questions.title: Angles in a Triangle
questions.prompt: In a triangle, two angles measure 47° and 68°. A student claims the third angle is 75°. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Correct; all three angles add up to 190°
options.B: Incorrect; the third angle is 65°
options.C: Correct; the third angle is always the difference of the other two
options.D: Incorrect; the third angle is 115°

questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle sum to 180°. Third angle = 180° − 47° − 68° = 65°. The student's answer of 75° is 10° too large, likely from an arithmetic error (perhaps computing 180 − 47 − 58 = 75).

questions.title: Ratio and Scaling
questions.prompt: A map has a scale of 1 : 50 000. Two towns are 6 cm apart on the map. What is the actual distance between the towns in kilometres?

options.A: 30 km
options.B: 3 km
options.C: 300 km
options.D: 0.3 km

questions.explanation: Actual distance = 6 × 50 000 = 300 000 cm. Converting: 300 000 cm ÷ 100 000 = 3 km. Option A (30 km) results from forgetting to convert centimetres to kilometres correctly, dividing by 10 000 instead of 100 000.

questions.title: Substituting into Expressions
questions.prompt: If p = 4 and q = −2, what is the value of p² − 3q + 1?
questions.explanation: p² − 3q + 1 = 4² − 3(−2) + 1 = 16 + 6 + 1 = 23. The key step is recognising that −3 × (−2) = +6. Students who write −3q as −3×(−2) = −6 will incorrectly get 11.

questions.title: Units of Measurement Conversion
questions.prompt: A swimming pool holds 2 500 000 millilitres of water. How many kilolitres is this? (1 kL = 1 000 000 mL)

options.A: 250 kL
options.B: 2.5 kL
options.C: 25 kL

questions.explanation: 2 500 000 mL ÷ 1 000 000 = 2.5 kL. Option C (25 kL) results from dividing by 100 000 instead of 1 000 000, a common error when handling large unit conversions.

questions.title: Graphing Inequalities on a Number Line
questions.prompt: Which description correctly represents the inequality x ≥ −3 on a number line?

options.A: A closed circle at −3 with an arrow pointing left
options.B: An open circle at −3 with an arrow pointing right
options.C: A closed circle at −3 with an arrow pointing right
options.D: An open circle at −3 with an arrow pointing left

questions.explanation: x ≥ −3 means x can equal −3 (closed circle, not open) and is greater than −3 (arrow pointing right towards larger values). An open circle would be used for strict inequality x > −3.

questions.title: Nets of 3D Shapes
questions.prompt: A student unfolds a triangular prism and draws its net. How many faces should appear in the net of a triangular prism?

options.A: 4 faces: 2 triangles and 2 rectangles
options.B: 5 faces: 2 triangles and 3 rectangles
options.C: 6 faces: 2 triangles and 4 rectangles
options.D: 5 faces: 1 triangle and 4 rectangles

questions.explanation: A triangular prism has exactly 5 faces: 2 triangular bases and 3 rectangular lateral faces, one for each edge of the triangular base. Option A (4 faces) is the most common error — students forget one of the three rectangular sides.

questions.title: Emotions and Body Signals
questions.prompt: When Maya feels nervous about a spelling test, her stomach feels 'fluttery' and her hands feel sweaty. Why does her body react this way even though there is no real danger?

options.A: Her brain sends signals to her body to get ready to face a challenge, just like it would for real danger
options.B: She is not eating enough before tests, which causes stomach problems
options.C: Her body only reacts this way because other children around her are also nervous
options.D: Sweaty hands and a fluttery stomach are signs that she is getting sick

questions.explanation: The brain's threat-detection system (the amygdala) cannot always tell the difference between a real physical danger and a worrying thought, so it sends the same 'get ready' signals to the body. Option B is a common misconception — these physical feelings come from the nervous system, not from hunger or illness.

questions.title: Growth Mindset in Practice
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'If I have a growth mindset, it means I should keep trying the exact same strategy over and over until I succeed.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct, because persistence is the most important part of growth mindset
options.B: The claim is partly wrong, because growth mindset also means trying different strategies when one is not working
options.C: The claim is correct, because changing strategies means giving up on the original goal
options.D: The claim is partly wrong, because growth mindset only applies to academic subjects, not skills

questions.explanation: Growth mindset, as described by researcher Carol Dweck, involves believing your abilities can improve through effort AND smart strategy — that includes changing your approach when something is not working. Simply repeating the same strategy without reflection is not growth mindset; it is persistence without learning.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities Balance
questions.prompt: Kofi has the right to share his opinion freely in class. His teacher explains that this right comes with a responsibility. Which responsibility is most directly connected to this right?

options.A: The responsibility to always agree with what the teacher says
options.B: The responsibility to share opinions in a way that respects others' right to feel safe
options.C: The responsibility to speak only when called upon by an adult
options.D: The responsibility to have the most correct or best-informed opinion

questions.explanation: Rights and responsibilities are linked: the right to free expression is balanced by the responsibility not to use that expression to harm or silence others. This is reflected in the UNCRC, which recognises that rights come with duties to the community. Option C confuses classroom procedures with the deeper concept of responsibility connected to a right.

questions.title: Understanding Empathy vs Sympathy
questions.prompt: When Lena's friend is upset about moving to a new school, Lena says: 'That sounds really hard. I remember feeling scared when I started here too.' Compare this to saying: 'Don't worry, it will be fine!' Which statement best explains why Lena's response shows greater empathy?

options.A: Lena's response is better because it uses more words and is therefore more thoughtful
options.B: Lena's response connects to her own experience to show she understands how her friend feels
options.C: Lena's response is better because it avoids mentioning anything negative
options.D: 'Don't worry' is actually more empathetic because it focuses on making the friend feel better quickly

questions.explanation: Empathy involves recognising and sharing another person's feelings from their perspective, often by connecting to your own similar experiences. Saying 'Don't worry, it will be fine' dismisses the friend's current feelings rather than acknowledging them, which is why it shows less empathy. Option D is a common misconception — making someone feel better quickly is not the same as truly understanding their emotional experience.

questions.title: What Shapes Our Identity
questions.prompt: Two children grow up in the same family but develop quite different personalities and interests. What does this suggest about how identity is formed?

options.A: Identity is formed only by family, so siblings should always be similar
options.B: Identity comes only from personal choices we make freely
options.C: Identity is shaped by a mix of family, personal experiences, friendships, and individual traits
options.D: Personality is fixed at birth and cannot be changed by any outside influence

questions.explanation: Research in developmental psychology shows that identity is shaped by multiple factors including genetics, family environment, friendships, personal experiences, and culture — which is why two siblings in the same home can be quite different. Option A oversimplifies by claiming family alone determines identity, ignoring all the other influences each child encounters uniquely.

questions.title: Healthy Conflict Resolution
questions.prompt: During a team game, Amara and Jake disagree about who should be team captain. Amara says: 'We should vote, and whoever gets the most votes is captain.' Jake says: 'The fastest runner should always be captain.' Which approach is more aligned with fairness in a group?

options.A: Jake's approach, because the best physical player should always lead a sports team
options.B: Amara's approach, because a democratic vote considers everyone's opinion equally
options.C: Neither approach is fair, because the teacher should always choose the captain
options.D: Jake's approach, because having clear rules about who leads avoids disagreement

questions.explanation: Fairness in group decisions involves giving everyone an equal voice, which is what a democratic vote achieves. Amara's approach reflects the principle that each person's view matters, not just the opinion of the most skilled individual. Jake's approach uses a single criterion (speed) that ignores other important qualities of leadership like communication and decision-making.

questions.title: Recognising Stereotypes
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Boys in our class don't cry because they are stronger emotionally than girls.' Identify the error in this thinking.

options.A: The error is assuming that boys never feel sad, when in fact all humans feel a full range of emotions
options.B: The error is only that the student used the word 'stronger' instead of 'better'
options.C: There is no real error — boys are generally taught to manage emotions differently, which does make them stronger
options.D: The error is that emotional strength should only be measured by how often someone cries

questions.explanation: All humans experience the full range of emotions regardless of gender. The statement is a stereotype — it confuses social pressure (boys are sometimes discouraged from crying) with emotional capacity, and incorrectly concludes that not crying means greater emotional strength. Option C is a genuine misconception because it conflates social norms with biological fact.

questions.title: Needs vs Wants in Wellbeing
questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the difference between a 'need' and a 'want' when thinking about your own wellbeing?

options.A: Needs are things adults tell you to do, while wants are things you decide yourself
options.B: Needs are things that are necessary for healthy development, while wants add enjoyment but are not essential
options.C: Wants are more important than needs because they make you happier in the moment
options.D: Needs and wants are the same thing — if you want something strongly enough, it becomes a need

questions.explanation: In wellbeing frameworks like Maslow's hierarchy, needs are foundational — things like sleep, food, safety, and belonging — without which healthy development is at risk. Wants are additions that may bring pleasure but are not essential to health. Option D is a common misconception among young children who confuse strong desire with genuine necessity.

questions.title: How Beliefs Influence Choices
questions.prompt: Priya believes strongly that being kind matters more than winning. When she is playing a board game and notices a younger player is confused, she stops to help them, even though it costs her a turn. What does this tell us about the connection between beliefs and actions?

options.A: Beliefs only matter in serious situations, not in games
options.B: Priya is acting against her beliefs because helping cost her an advantage
options.C: A person's beliefs can guide their behaviour even when acting on them is personally costly
options.D: Priya's choice shows that beliefs always lead to the best outcome for everyone

questions.explanation: Priya's action illustrates that deeply held beliefs can shape behaviour even when there is a personal cost involved — she sacrificed a turn because her belief in kindness outweighed her desire to win. Option D goes too far by claiming beliefs always lead to the best outcome, which is not necessarily true — it is about motivation, not guaranteed results.

questions.title: Sleep and Brain Function
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'I slept only four hours last night but I feel fine, so sleep does not really affect how my brain works.' What would be the best evidence-based response to this claim?

options.A: The student is right — if you feel fine, your brain is working well
options.B: The claim may be wrong because sleep deprivation can affect memory and attention even when a person does not notice it themselves
options.C: The claim is wrong only for adults — children can manage on less sleep than recommended
options.D: Sleep only affects mood, not thinking or memory, so the student's brain is probably fine

questions.explanation: Research in neuroscience shows that during sleep, the brain consolidates memories and clears waste products from neural activity. Even one night of poor sleep can reduce attention and memory performance, and people often underestimate their own impairment — a phenomenon called 'sleep debt blindness'. Option A is the most tempting wrong answer because it relies on the student's own unreliable self-assessment.

questions.title: Belonging and Social Health
questions.prompt: Why might a child who moves to a new country feel a sense of loss even if their new home has everything they need physically, like food, shelter, and safety?

options.A: Because physical needs are the only real needs, so the feeling of loss is not important
options.B: Because humans also need a sense of belonging, connection, and cultural familiarity to feel truly well
options.C: Because the child has not yet tried hard enough to make new friends
options.D: Because children always prefer their first home, no matter how good the new one is

questions.explanation: Wellbeing includes social and emotional dimensions, not just physical ones. Belonging — feeling connected to a community, culture, and relationships — is a recognised human need. A child can have all physical needs met and still experience grief from the loss of familiar relationships, language, and cultural identity. Option C blames the child and ignores the real complexity of social and cultural adjustment.

questions.title: Making Fair Decisions
questions.prompt: Three friends want to choose a movie to watch together. One friend loves action films and always picks. Today, the other two suggest taking turns choosing. Which principle does this suggestion reflect?

options.A: The principle that the person with the strongest preference should always decide
options.B: The principle of equity — giving everyone an equal turn regardless of past choices
options.C: The principle that the majority should always vote on every decision
options.D: The principle that friends should avoid disagreement by letting one person lead permanently
