questions.explanation: Taking turns ensures that each person has an equal opportunity to influence group decisions over time, which reflects the principle of equity and fairness in relationships. Option C describes majority voting, which is a different fair process — but taking turns is not a vote, it is a rotation of decision-making authority.

questions.title: Self-Awareness and Reflection
questions.prompt: Before handing in her drawing, Sasha looks at it carefully and thinks: 'I worked hard on the colours, but I want to improve my lines next time.' What skill is Sasha practising?

options.A: Memorisation, because she is remembering what she did
options.B: Self-assessment, because she is evaluating both her strengths and areas for growth
options.C: Perfectionism, because she is not satisfied with her own work
options.D: Critical thinking, because she is comparing her drawing to others in the class

questions.explanation: Self-assessment involves looking at your own work, identifying what went well and what could improve — both of which Sasha does. This is a key IB learner profile skill linked to being reflective. Option C is a misconception: noticing areas for growth is healthy self-reflection, not perfectionism, which would involve distressing dissatisfaction rather than balanced evaluation.

questions.title: Courage and Emotional Health
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to a child's emotional health if they never felt safe enough to express difficult feelings like sadness, fear, or anger?

options.A: Their emotional health would improve because they would not focus on negative feelings
options.B: Nothing would change — emotions that are not expressed simply disappear on their own
options.C: Their emotional health might suffer because unexpressed emotions can build up and affect behaviour and relationships
options.D: They would become better at controlling emotions, which is always a sign of good emotional health

questions.explanation: Emotional health research shows that suppressing difficult feelings does not make them disappear — unexpressed emotions can accumulate and affect physical health, relationships, and behaviour over time. Expressing emotions in safe, constructive ways is a key part of wellbeing. Option D confuses suppression of emotion with healthy emotional regulation, which actually involves acknowledging and processing feelings.

questions.title: Family Structures and Identity
questions.prompt: A student says: 'A real family must have a mother, a father, and children living together.' Identify what is problematic about this definition.

options.A: It is problematic only because some families are very large and do not fit the description
options.B: It excludes the many valid family structures that exist, such as single-parent, grandparent-led, or same-sex parent families
options.C: It is not problematic — this definition matches how families are described in most school textbooks
options.D: It is only problematic if the child using this definition has a different kind of family themselves

questions.explanation: Family structures vary enormously across cultures and communities, and all of these structures can provide children with love, stability, and belonging. Defining 'real family' narrowly excludes and invalidates the lived experience of many children. Option D is a misconception because a definition is either accurate or inaccurate regardless of who is using it — the problem is with the definition itself, not who holds it.

questions.title: Responsibility for Personal Health
questions.prompt: Describe what it means to take responsibility for your own physical health at age 7. Which of the following is the best example of this?

options.A: Telling a friend to eat vegetables even though you do not eat them yourself
options.B: Waiting for an adult to remind you to wash your hands before meals
options.C: Choosing to drink water instead of a sugary drink when you are thirsty, without being told
options.D: Following all health rules only when a teacher is watching

questions.explanation: Taking personal responsibility for health means making health-supporting choices independently, not only when prompted by others. Choosing water without being told shows self-directed healthy behaviour. Options B and D both describe reactive behaviour that depends on an adult's instruction or supervision, which is not the same as personal responsibility.

questions.title: Kindness vs People-Pleasing
questions.prompt: Theo always agrees with everything his friends say because he does not want them to be upset with him. His teacher points out that this is different from being kind. Why might the teacher be right?

options.A: The teacher is wrong — agreeing with friends is always an act of kindness
options.B: True kindness sometimes means sharing an honest opinion, while always agreeing is about avoiding conflict for oneself
options.C: The teacher is right because kindness means never agreeing with others
options.D: Theo should agree with friends in class but disagree at home — context decides what kindness means

questions.explanation: Kindness is about genuine care for others' wellbeing, which sometimes requires honest, respectful disagreement. Always agreeing to avoid conflict is driven by a desire to feel safe or liked, not primarily by care for the other person. Option A is the most common misconception because agreement can feel kind, but it may actually prevent friends from hearing useful perspectives or growing.

questions.title: Role of Rules in Communities
questions.prompt: Why do communities create shared rules, even for people who would behave well without them?

options.A: Rules are only useful for people who misbehave — good people do not need them
options.B: Rules create a shared and predictable framework that makes living together safer and fairer for everyone
options.C: Communities create rules mainly to give adults power over children
options.D: Rules replace the need for individuals to make personal decisions about right and wrong

questions.explanation: Shared rules create consistency and predictability in a community — everyone knows what to expect, which makes cooperation safer and more equitable. Even people who would act well without rules benefit from knowing others are held to the same standard. Option D is a genuine misconception: rules guide but do not replace personal ethical reasoning — people still make choices within and sometimes about rules.

questions.title: Noticing Change Over Time
questions.prompt: A student looks at a photograph of herself from three years ago and notices she has changed in many ways. Which type of change is LEAST visible in a photograph but is still a real part of how she has grown?

options.A: Her height
options.B: Her hair length
options.C: Her beliefs about what is right and fair
options.D: Her clothing style

questions.explanation: Physical changes like height, hair, and clothing are visible in a photograph, but internal growth — such as developing beliefs, values, and understanding of fairness — cannot be captured in an image. This kind of invisible growth is just as important as physical development and is central to the concept of identity in the IB PYP. Options A, B, and D are all things a photograph can show directly.

questions.title: Handling Disappointment Healthily
questions.prompt: Raj's team loses an important sports competition. He feels disappointed. Which response shows the healthiest way to handle this feeling?

options.A: Pretending he is not disappointed so his teammates do not feel bad
options.B: Blaming the referee so the feeling of disappointment goes away faster
options.C: Acknowledging the disappointment, letting himself feel it, and then thinking about what the team can improve
options.D: Deciding never to play competitive sports again to avoid the feeling in the future

questions.explanation: Healthy emotional regulation involves acknowledging feelings honestly and then moving toward constructive action — not suppressing, avoiding, or misdirecting the emotion. Recognising disappointment and using it as information for future improvement is a sign of emotional maturity and resilience. Option A is a common misconception because appearing fine to protect others actually involves emotional suppression, which is not healthy long-term.

questions.title: What Makes a Good Friend
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A good friend always makes you feel happy.' What is the most important limitation of this idea?

options.A: It is too limited — a good friend sometimes tells you something difficult but honest that helps you grow
options.B: It is correct — if a friend ever makes you feel unhappy, they are not a true friend
options.C: It is too limited — a good friend should also buy you things to show they care
options.D: It is only partly wrong because good friends should make you happy at least half the time

questions.explanation: A good friendship is built on honesty, trust, and genuine care — not just on consistently producing positive feelings. Sometimes a caring friend will share an uncomfortable truth or disagree with you, which may feel uncomfortable but serves your wellbeing. Option B reflects the common misconception that any negative feeling in a friendship signals that it is unhealthy, when in fact some discomfort is a normal part of meaningful relationships.

questions.title: Celebrating Differences
questions.prompt: Why might having classmates who come from different cultural backgrounds make a classroom a richer place to learn?

options.A: Because it means the class will always agree on everything, since everyone brings the same values
options.B: Because different backgrounds bring different perspectives, stories, and ways of thinking that expand everyone's understanding
options.C: Because children from other cultures are usually better at solving problems than children from one culture
options.D: Because cultural diversity only benefits social activities, not academic learning

questions.explanation: Diverse cultural backgrounds bring different lived experiences, perspectives, and knowledge systems into a shared learning space, which gives all learners access to a wider range of ideas and ways of seeing the world. This is a core value in the IB's international-mindedness framework. Option A is incorrect because diversity typically introduces more varied perspectives, not agreement — and the value lies in that productive difference.

questions.title: Asking for Help as a Strength
questions.prompt: Some children think asking for help means they are not smart or capable. What would an IB learner say to challenge this idea?

options.A: Asking for help is a weakness — capable people should always solve problems independently
options.B: Asking for help shows self-awareness and the courage to recognise the limits of your current knowledge
options.C: Asking for help is only acceptable in maths and science, not in personal or social situations
options.D: Asking for help is fine, but only if you have tried and failed at least three times first

questions.explanation: In the IB learner profile, being 'open-minded' and 'reflective' includes recognising when you need support and seeking it — this is a sign of metacognitive awareness and courage, not weakness. Research in education shows that students who seek help strategically tend to learn more effectively. Option A is the central misconception the question challenges — it confuses independence with competence.

questions.title: Actions and Consequences
questions.prompt: Before acting, an IB student asks herself: 'How will this affect me AND the people around me?' Which thinking habit does this question reflect?

options.A: Memorisation, because she is trying to remember what adults have told her to do
options.B: Consequentialist thinking, because she is considering the likely outcomes of her action for herself and others
options.C: Perfectionism, because she is trying to find the action with zero negative consequences
options.D: Rule-following, because she is checking her action against a specific school rule

questions.explanation: Thinking about how an action will affect oneself and others before acting is a core feature of consequentialist ethical reasoning — evaluating choices based on their likely outcomes. This is also reflected in the IB PYP's focus on responsible action. Option D describes a different ethical approach — following rules (deontological thinking) — which does not focus on outcomes but on whether an action follows a stated rule.

questions.title: Balancing Independence and Interdependence
questions.prompt: Even very capable and independent people still rely on others in many ways every day. Which of the following best explains why independence and interdependence are BOTH important parts of a healthy identity?

options.A: Because truly independent people never need to rely on anyone — relying on others is a sign of weakness
options.B: Because being fully dependent on others means you can never develop your own identity
options.C: Because a healthy person can make their own decisions while also recognising that human beings grow and thrive through connection with others
options.D: Because independence is more important when you are young, and interdependence only matters when you are an adult

questions.explanation: Healthy development involves both developing personal agency — the ability to make your own choices — and recognising that humans are fundamentally social beings who grow through relationships, cooperation, and community. These are not opposites but complementary aspects of a full identity. Option A is a misconception that equates dependence with weakness, ignoring the social nature of human wellbeing across the lifespan.

questions.title: Emotions and Brain Signals
questions.prompt: When you feel sudden fear, your heart beats faster and your hands might sweat. Which part of the brain sends the first signal that causes these body changes?

options.A: The cerebellum, which controls balance and movement
options.B: The amygdala, which detects threats and triggers the stress response
options.C: The prefrontal cortex, which plans and makes decisions
options.D: The hippocampus, which stores and retrieves memories

questions.explanation: The amygdala is the brain's alarm system — it detects potential threats and immediately triggers the 'fight or flight' response, causing the heart to beat faster and sweat to form. The prefrontal cortex is involved in calm, reasoned thinking rather than the instant fear reaction, so it acts too slowly to be the first signal.

questions.title: Rights vs. Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Layla has the right to free expression at school, but she uses it to share information she knows is untrue about a classmate. A student claims: 'Since it is her right, her action is fully acceptable.' What is the most precise reason this claim is flawed?

options.A: Rights only apply to adults, so Layla cannot use this argument
options.B: Rights come with responsibilities, and using expression to harm others exceeds the limit of that right
options.C: Free expression is not actually listed in the UNCRC
options.D: A right is only valid if the majority of people in the school agree with it

questions.explanation: Under the UNCRC and most rights frameworks, every right is balanced by a responsibility not to use that right in ways that harm others — so free expression does not protect deliberate misinformation that damages someone. Option A is wrong because the UNCRC explicitly grants children rights, including free expression under Article 13.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Nuance
questions.prompt: A student studies hard for a maths test and still scores poorly. She says: 'I just need to try harder next time.' Her teacher suggests this response is only partly a growth mindset. Why might the teacher be right?

options.A: A true growth mindset means accepting that some people are naturally better at maths
options.B: Growth mindset only applies to creative subjects, not mathematics
options.C: Trying harder without changing strategy may not lead to improvement; growth mindset also includes reflecting on and adjusting methods
options.D: The student should focus on her strengths instead of continuing with maths

questions.explanation: Carol Dweck's research on growth mindset emphasises that effort alone is not enough — learners must also reflect on what went wrong and try different strategies. Simply repeating the same effort without reflection is sometimes called 'false growth mindset.' Option A contradicts the core idea of growth mindset, which holds that ability can be developed by anyone.

questions.title: Cultural Identity and Change
questions.prompt: Tomás moved from Mexico to Canada when he was five. Now at age seven he celebrates both Día de los Muertos and Thanksgiving. Which statement best explains what this shows about cultural identity?

options.A: Tomás has lost his original culture and replaced it with a new one
options.B: Cultural identity is fixed at birth and cannot be influenced by where a person lives
options.C: Cultural identity can be layered and added to over time through new experiences and environments
options.D: Celebrating two cultures means Tomás belongs fully to neither culture

questions.explanation: Cultural identity is understood in IB frameworks as dynamic and cumulative — people can hold and blend multiple cultural influences rather than having to choose one. Option A is incorrect because maintaining Día de los Muertos shows his original culture has not been lost or replaced.

questions.title: Beliefs Shaping Behaviour
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this reasoning: 'Nina recycles because she was told to, so she must believe that protecting the environment is important.'

options.A: Recycling has no connection to environmental beliefs at all
options.B: The error is assuming that an action caused by instruction necessarily reflects a personal belief
options.C: The error is that children Nina's age are not yet capable of forming beliefs
options.D: The error is that only adults who volunteer to recycle can have environmental beliefs

questions.explanation: Actions can be driven by rules, rewards, or habit rather than deeply held personal beliefs — a distinction central to understanding authentic values. Option A is wrong because there is a well-documented link between environmental beliefs and recycling behaviour; the logical flaw is specifically about assuming the direction of that link.

questions.title: Social Health and Loneliness
questions.prompt: A student has many online followers but says she often feels lonely. Which statement most accurately explains how this is possible?

options.A: She cannot really be lonely because she has people paying attention to her
options.B: Loneliness depends on the number of contacts a person has, so more followers should reduce it
options.C: Social health requires connections that feel meaningful and mutual, which online follower counts do not guarantee
options.D: Loneliness is only a physical health issue caused by not spending time outdoors

questions.explanation: Wellbeing researchers distinguish between the quantity of social connections and their quality — a large audience does not provide the reciprocal, emotionally supportive relationships that protect against loneliness. Option B incorrectly treats all social contact as equally meaningful, ignoring the depth dimension of social health.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Sympathy
questions.prompt: When a friend is upset about losing a competition, Priya says: 'I know exactly what it feels like to be disappointed — I felt the same way last month.' Omar says: 'That's too bad for you.' Which response shows more empathy, and why?

options.A: Omar, because he acknowledges the loss without making it about himself
options.B: Priya, because she connects to her own similar emotion and shows she understands the feeling from the inside
options.C: Both equally, because any response to a friend's sadness counts as empathy
options.D: Neither, because true empathy requires giving practical advice about how to win next time

questions.explanation: Empathy involves perspective-taking and connecting to another's emotional experience from the inside — Priya does this by drawing on her own parallel feeling of disappointment. Omar's response acknowledges the event but does not engage with the feeling, which is closer to indifference than to either empathy or sympathy.

questions.title: Self-Image and Media
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Seeing edited photos of people online cannot affect how I feel about my own body because I know the photos are not real.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — knowing images are edited completely removes any negative effect on self-image
options.B: The claim is partly wrong because research shows repeated exposure can still influence self-perception even when a person knows the images are edited
options.C: The claim is partly wrong because edited photos always make viewers feel better about themselves by showing what is possible
options.D: The claim is fully wrong because children cannot tell the difference between real and edited photos

questions.explanation: Psychological research shows that repeated exposure to idealised images creates a 'social comparison' effect that can lower body satisfaction even when people consciously know the images are digitally altered. Option A overstates the protective power of media literacy knowledge alone.

questions.title: Personal Values Conflicts
questions.prompt: Ben values both honesty and kindness. His friend shows him a drawing and asks, 'Is it good?' Ben privately thinks it needs a lot of improvement. These two values are pulling him in different directions. What does this situation demonstrate about personal values?

options.A: A person should only hold one value at a time to avoid confusion
options.B: Values never conflict with each other in real life
options.C: Personal values can conflict, and navigating that tension is part of ethical decision-making
options.D: Kindness is always more important than honesty, so Ben should simply say the drawing is excellent

questions.explanation: One of the core ideas in ethical reasoning is that genuinely held values can pull in opposite directions in real situations, requiring careful judgment rather than a simple rule. Option D incorrectly claims a fixed hierarchy between kindness and honesty, which IB ethical frameworks do not support.

questions.title: Mental Health vs. Happiness
questions.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between mental health and happiness?

options.A: Good mental health means feeling happy all the time
options.B: Mental health and happiness are exactly the same thing
options.C: Good mental health includes being able to cope with difficult emotions, not just feeling happy
options.D: Happiness is a physical health matter, while mental health only relates to thinking and learning

questions.explanation: Mental health frameworks, including the WHO definition, describe it as a state of wellbeing in which a person can manage stress, work productively, and cope with normal life challenges — it explicitly includes negative emotions handled constructively, not just happiness. Option A is a common misconception: expecting constant happiness is itself linked to poorer mental health outcomes.

questions.title: Fairness and Equal Treatment
questions.prompt: In a relay race, one runner uses a wheelchair. The teacher gives that student a shorter track distance so all runners finish at roughly the same time. A classmate says this is unfair because the rules should be identical for everyone. Who has the stronger argument?

options.A: The classmate, because identical rules always produce the fairest outcomes
options.B: The teacher, because fairness sometimes means adjusting conditions so everyone has an equal opportunity to participate
options.C: The classmate, because modifying rules always gives an unfair advantage to one person
options.D: The teacher, because physical education rules should never be the same for any two students

questions.explanation: This illustrates the distinction between equality (same treatment) and equity (adjusted treatment to reach equal opportunity) — a central idea in IB rights and responsibilities thinking. Option A is incorrect because identical rules applied to people in very different circumstances often produce unequal outcomes rather than fair ones.

questions.title: Stereotypes and Identity
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Stereotypes are always harmful.' Another student responds: 'Some stereotypes are positive, like saying a group is good at maths, so those are fine.' Evaluate the second student's response.

options.A: The second student is fully correct — positive stereotypes build confidence and cause no problems
options.B: The second student is wrong because even positive stereotypes can create unfair pressure and ignore individual differences
options.C: The second student is correct because only stereotypes based on physical appearance are harmful
options.D: Both students are wrong because stereotypes have no real effect on how people feel about themselves

questions.explanation: Research on 'stereotype threat' and related effects shows that positive group stereotypes can cause stress and reduce performance in individuals who do not fit the expectation, and erase individual identity. Option A ignores the documented negative psychological effects of positive stereotyping on individuals within the labelled group.

questions.title: Trust and Healthy Relationships
questions.prompt: What is the most accurate reason why trust is considered the foundation of a healthy relationship, rather than just one feature among many?

options.A: Trust makes relationships more fun and entertaining
options.B: Without trust, other positive features like kindness and communication cannot function effectively because people cannot rely on them being genuine
options.C: Trust is only important in relationships between adults, not children
options.D: Trust matters mainly in professional relationships, such as between a doctor and patient

questions.explanation: Relationship researchers describe trust as foundational because it is the condition that makes other positive behaviours — like honest communication and kindness — reliable and meaningful rather than unpredictable. Option A reduces trust to entertainment value, which misses its structural role in relationships.

questions.title: Courage and Speaking Up
questions.prompt: Amir sees a friend being left out at lunch but says nothing because he worries his other friends will exclude him too. Which IB learner profile attribute is Amir most struggling to demonstrate, and why?

options.A: Inquirer, because he has not asked enough questions about the situation
options.B: Knowledgeable, because he does not know enough about the school's rules
options.C: Risk-taker, because acting to defend his friend requires accepting the possibility of a social consequence
options.D: Reflective, because he has not yet thought about what happened

questions.explanation: The IB learner profile describes 'risk-taker' as approaching uncertainty with courage and defending beliefs and values — Amir understands the situation but is held back by fear of social risk. Option A is less accurate because inquiry is about seeking knowledge, not about acting on moral conviction under pressure.

questions.title: Sleep and Learning
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'I can replace sleep with extra study time and still learn just as well.' Which specific fact about sleep and the brain most directly contradicts this claim?

options.A: The brain stops all activity during sleep, so nothing useful happens
options.B: During sleep, the brain transfers information from short-term to long-term memory, which cannot happen as effectively while awake
options.C: Sleep only affects physical growth, not thinking or memory
options.D: Extra study always compensates for reduced sleep because repetition is the only factor in memory

questions.explanation: During sleep — particularly during slow-wave and REM stages — the hippocampus replays and consolidates newly learned information into long-term memory, a process that cannot be fully replicated during wakefulness. Option C is incorrect because sleep's role in cognitive function and memory consolidation is well-established alongside its physical growth effects.

questions.title: Resilience and Setbacks
questions.prompt: Two students both fail a spelling test. Student A thinks: 'I am bad at spelling and always will be.' Student B thinks: 'I made mistakes this time; I wonder which words tripped me up.' Which student is showing resilience, and what specifically makes it resilience rather than just optimism?

options.A: Student A, because accepting limitations honestly shows self-awareness
options.B: Student B, because resilience means never admitting you made mistakes
options.C: Student B, because resilience involves bouncing back by analysing what went wrong and planning to improve, not just feeling positive
options.D: Both equally, because resilience simply means continuing to try regardless of how you think about the setback

questions.explanation: Resilience is defined not as blind optimism but as the ability to recover from setbacks through active coping strategies — in Student B's case, analysing errors and planning corrective action. Option D is too broad and misses the key element of constructive analysis that distinguishes resilience from mere persistence.

questions.title: Consent and Personal Boundaries
questions.prompt: A younger student does not want to be hugged by a relative, but the relative says, 'Come on, I'm family!' Which principle about personal boundaries does this scenario most clearly highlight?

options.A: Family relationships are exceptions where personal boundaries do not apply
options.B: A person's right to set boundaries over their own body applies regardless of the relationship
options.C: Younger children should always follow the wishes of older relatives out of respect
options.D: Physical boundaries are only important in relationships between strangers

questions.explanation: Body autonomy and the right to set physical boundaries are principles taught in child safeguarding and UNCRC-aligned education — they apply to all relationships, not just those with strangers. Option A is incorrect and directly contradicts child protection guidelines, which specifically address boundary-crossing by family members.

questions.title: Identity and Language
questions.prompt: Research suggests that the language a person speaks can influence how they think about time, colour, and relationships. What does this finding suggest about the connection between language and identity?

options.A: Language is only a tool for communication and has no connection to how a person sees themselves or the world
options.B: Language shapes the way people perceive and organise their experience, making it part of their cognitive and cultural identity
options.C: Only written languages influence identity; spoken languages do not
options.D: Language affects identity only in people who speak more than two languages

questions.explanation: Linguistic relativity research (associated with Sapir and Whorf) shows that language influences cognition — for example, languages with more colour terms lead speakers to distinguish colours more finely — meaning language is woven into how people experience and understand themselves and their world. Option A ignores this well-documented cognitive connection.

questions.title: Conflict Resolution Strategies
questions.prompt: During a disagreement, one student immediately gives in to stop the argument. This is called 'accommodating.' Why might accommodating repeatedly be harmful to a person's wellbeing, even though it ends conflicts quickly?

options.A: Accommodating is always the most respectful strategy, so there is no harm in using it repeatedly
options.B: It is harmful because it means the person never gets to share their perspective or have their needs met over time
options.C: It is harmful only when the disagreement involves rules, not personal matters
options.D: Accommodating is harmful because it always makes the other person feel guilty

questions.explanation: Conflict resolution frameworks identify accommodating as useful occasionally but harmful as a habit because consistently suppressing one's own needs and views can erode self-worth and allow unresolved issues to build up. Option A incorrectly treats accommodation as always respectful, ignoring the cost to the accommodating person's own needs and voice.

questions.title: Recognising Hidden Feelings
questions.prompt: Sometimes when a person feels afraid, they show anger instead. Psychologists call this 'masking.' Which statement best explains why understanding masking is important for healthy relationships?

options.A: It explains that anger and fear are the same emotion with different names
options.B: It shows that responding only to the visible emotion can miss the real need, making it harder to help
options.C: It proves that people cannot control which emotions they display
options.D: It means that fear is always a more serious emotion than anger

questions.explanation: When a person masks fear with anger, responding to the anger directly (such as punishing it) misses the underlying fear that is driving the behaviour — so addressing the root emotion leads to more effective support and healthier interaction. Option A is incorrect: fear and anger are distinct emotions that can appear in combination, but they are not the same.

questions.title: Responsibility for Community
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'I only have responsibilities toward people I have chosen to be friends with, not toward everyone in my school community.' Which idea from the IB PYP most directly challenges this view?

options.A: The idea that responsibilities only arise from formal agreements
options.B: The idea that being part of a community creates shared responsibilities toward all members of that community
options.C: The idea that children do not yet have the same responsibilities as adults in a community
options.D: The idea that responsibility depends entirely on whether you caused a problem

questions.explanation: The IB PYP's 'Who We Are' strand and its central ideas around belonging and community emphasise that membership in a group — not just personal friendship — generates responsibilities toward other members. Option D is too narrow: responsibility frameworks extend beyond causal responsibility to include care for others in shared spaces.

questions.title: Self-Regulation Strategies
questions.prompt: Before responding to an upsetting comment, Cleo counts slowly to ten in her head. Which explanation most accurately describes why this strategy can help her respond more thoughtfully?

options.A: Counting distracts the amygdala permanently so it stops producing emotional responses
options.B: The pause gives the prefrontal cortex time to become more involved, allowing reasoned thinking to moderate the initial emotional reaction
options.C: Counting to ten signals to others that she is angry, which makes them treat her more carefully
options.D: The strategy works because any physical action automatically cancels an emotional response

questions.explanation: When the amygdala triggers a strong emotion, the prefrontal cortex — the reasoning part of the brain — can take a moment to 'catch up.' Introducing a deliberate pause gives this regulatory process time to engage, reducing impulsive reaction. Option A overstates the effect: the amygdala is not permanently silenced; it still functions but is moderated.

questions.title: Belonging and Exclusion
questions.prompt: Research shows that social exclusion activates the same brain regions as physical pain. What is the most important implication of this finding for how schools should treat social exclusion?

options.A: Schools should focus only on preventing physical injury because emotional pain is not as serious
options.B: Social exclusion should be treated as seriously as physical harm because the distress it causes is neurologically comparable
options.C: Because physical pain and social pain feel the same, the same medicines used for pain should be used for loneliness
options.D: Social exclusion is unavoidable in schools, so teaching children to ignore it is the most practical approach

questions.explanation: Naomi Eisenberger's neuroimaging research found that social exclusion activates the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex — the same region involved in physical pain — suggesting exclusion is a genuine and serious form of harm. Option A contradicts this evidence by treating emotional distress as categorically less important than physical harm.

questions.title: Philosophy of Self
questions.prompt: The ancient question 'Who am I?' is considered difficult partly because the answer can change over time. Which of the following observations best supports the idea that identity is not completely fixed?

options.A: A person's fingerprints remain the same throughout their life
options.B: A person's name is usually given at birth and does not change
options.C: A person who once feared public speaking becomes a confident presenter after practice and experience
options.D: A person's blood type is determined by genetics and does not change

questions.explanation: Identity includes qualities, beliefs, and characteristics — all of which can shift with experience, growth, and context — so a change from fearfulness to confidence illustrates identity's dynamic nature. Options A, B, and D all describe fixed biological or administrative facts, not the psychological and social dimensions of identity that are known to change.

questions.title: Nutrition and Brain Function
questions.prompt: A student skips breakfast before a test, saying it will not matter because thinking only uses the brain, not the body. Identify the most important flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: The brain does not need energy to function, so skipping breakfast is actually fine
options.B: The flaw is that the brain is part of the body and requires a steady supply of glucose to concentrate and process information effectively
options.C: The flaw is that skipping breakfast only affects physical performance like running, not thinking
options.D: The flaw is that all students should eat the same breakfast to perform equally on tests

questions.explanation: The brain consumes approximately 20% of the body's energy and relies on glucose as its primary fuel — low blood glucose from skipping breakfast is associated with reduced concentration, slower processing speed, and poorer memory performance. Option C perpetuates the false mind-body split that the student's reasoning also relies on.

questions.title: Emotions and Brain Signals
questions.prompt: When you feel scared, your body releases a chemical called adrenaline. What is the MAIN job of adrenaline in that moment?

options.A: It helps your body get ready to act quickly by speeding up your heart and muscles
options.B: It sends a signal to your brain to feel happy so you calm down faster
options.C: It slows your breathing so you can think more carefully about what scared you
options.D: It tells your stomach to digest food faster so you have more energy

questions.explanation: Adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands and prepares the body for 'fight or flight' — speeding up the heart, tensing muscles, and sharpening senses so you can react fast. Option C is wrong because adrenaline actually quickens breathing rather than slowing it; slowing breath is a calming strategy that works against the adrenaline response.

questions.title: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset
questions.prompt: Layla says, 'I got a low score on my maths quiz, so I must not be a maths person.' Which statement best explains the error in Layla's thinking?

options.A: She should compare herself to other students before drawing any conclusion
options.B: One low score tells us about effort or strategy on that day, not about fixed ability
options.C: Maths ability is decided only by the teacher, not by quiz results
options.D: She should wait until the end of the year before judging her maths skills

questions.explanation: A growth mindset recognises that a single result reflects effort, strategy, or preparation on a particular occasion — not a permanent, fixed ability. Option D is plausible but misses the key point: the error is not about timing but about confusing one result with fixed identity.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities Balance
questions.prompt: You have the right to express your opinion freely. A classmate says this means you can say anything at any time in any way. Which response best challenges this claim?

options.A: Rights are always unlimited as long as you believe what you are saying is true
options.B: Every right comes with a responsibility to exercise it in a way that respects others' rights and dignity
options.C: You can say anything you want, but only outside school hours and school buildings
options.D: The right to free expression only applies to adults, not to children in class

questions.explanation: The UNCRC and IB frameworks both emphasise that rights are balanced by responsibilities — expressing yourself freely must still respect others' dignity and rights. Option C is wrong because the responsibility to respect others does not simply disappear off school grounds; it is a universal principle.

questions.title: Understanding Empathy Types
questions.prompt: There are two kinds of empathy: feeling what someone else feels (affective empathy) and understanding what someone else thinks without necessarily feeling it yourself (cognitive empathy). Which example below shows COGNITIVE empathy?

options.A: You start crying when you see your friend cry at a sad movie
options.B: You realise your friend is nervous about speaking in class even though you feel calm yourself
options.C: You feel excited along with your friend when they open a birthday present
options.D: You feel your stomach tighten when you watch someone fall off their bike

questions.explanation: Cognitive empathy means understanding another person's perspective or feelings through reasoning, even without sharing the emotion yourself — exactly what happens when you recognise a friend's nervousness while feeling calm. Options A, C, and D all describe shared or mirrored feelings, which is affective empathy.

questions.title: Identity and Belonging
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'If you move to a new country, you must give up your old identity to truly belong.' Evaluate this claim. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: The claim is correct because fitting in requires matching the customs of the new country completely
options.B: The claim is partly right — language must change, but traditions can be kept privately
options.C: The claim is incorrect because identity is layered and people can add new aspects without losing existing ones
options.D: The claim is incorrect because belonging is only about where you were born, not what you do

questions.explanation: Research on cultural identity shows that people can hold multiple, layered identities simultaneously — adopting new cultural practices while maintaining existing ones. Option B is a common misconception: it concedes too much by suggesting language must fully change, which is not supported by models of bicultural identity.

questions.title: Fairness vs Equality
questions.prompt: Three children need to reach books on a high shelf. The teacher gives each child one same-sized step stool. The tallest child can now reach easily, but the shortest still cannot. What concept explains why this situation is NOT yet fair?

options.A: Equality — the children were given equal resources, which always produces fair outcomes
options.B: Equity — fairness sometimes requires giving different support based on individual need
options.C: Responsibility — the shortest child should have asked for more help earlier
options.D: Rights — the tallest child is breaking the shorter child's right to read

questions.explanation: Equity means adjusting support so that everyone reaches the same outcome, even if that requires giving different amounts of help. This is distinct from equality, which gives the same resource to everyone regardless of starting point. Option A is wrong precisely because it confuses equal treatment with fair outcomes.

questions.title: Beliefs Shaping Behaviour
questions.prompt: Two students both see a classmate sitting alone at lunch. Student A believes 'strangers are usually unfriendly,' and Student B believes 'most people welcome kindness.' Which outcome is most likely, and why?

options.A: Both students will act the same way because the situation is identical for both of them
options.B: Student A is more likely to sit with the classmate because cautious people observe first
options.C: Student B is more likely to approach the classmate because beliefs shape what actions feel possible
options.D: Neither student will approach because children do not act on beliefs at this age

questions.explanation: Beliefs act as internal lenses that influence whether an action feels worthwhile or safe — Student B's belief makes approaching feel likely to succeed, so action follows. Option A is wrong because the same external situation produces different responses when people hold different internal beliefs.

questions.title: Physical Health and Sleep
questions.prompt: A child regularly gets only five hours of sleep each night. Which effect is MOST directly linked to too little sleep, according to health research?

options.A: Stronger immune system because the body spends less time resting and more time fighting germs
options.B: Reduced ability to pay attention and regulate emotions the following day
options.C: Faster physical growth because growth hormones increase when the body is awake longer
options.D: Improved memory because the brain stays active and practises what it learned

questions.explanation: During sleep, the brain consolidates memory and restores emotional regulation systems; insufficient sleep impairs attention and makes emotional responses harder to control. Option C is a common misconception — growth hormone is actually released during deep sleep, so less sleep means less growth hormone, not more.

questions.title: Conflict and Communication
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this statement: 'The best way to resolve any disagreement is to avoid talking about it until both people have completely calmed down and feel no emotion at all.'

options.A: The error is suggesting both people must calm down — only one person needs to be calm
options.B: The error is that avoiding discussion indefinitely can allow misunderstandings to grow, and some emotion during conversation is normal and useful
options.C: The error is recommending talking at all — written notes are always better for resolving conflict
options.D: The error is that only a teacher or adult can decide when it is safe to have the conversation

questions.explanation: Conflict resolution research shows that completely suppressing emotion before talking is unnecessary and often impossible; moderate emotion can actually help people communicate what truly matters to them. Option A is wrong because it still accepts the flawed idea that emotions must be eliminated — it only changes how many people need to reach that state.

questions.title: Stereotypes and Assumptions
questions.prompt: A student says: 'I always know how someone is feeling just by looking at their face.' Which reasoning best explains why this claim is problematic?

options.A: Facial expressions are completely random and carry no information about feelings
options.B: Only trained adults can correctly read facial expressions; children never can
options.C: Facial expressions can be influenced by culture, context, and personal habit, so they are not always a reliable guide to inner feelings
options.D: It is problematic only if the student uses this belief to judge strangers rather than friends

questions.explanation: Research shows that while some facial expressions are recognised across cultures, many are shaped by cultural norms, context, and individual differences — making assumptions based solely on appearance unreliable. Option A goes too far in the opposite direction; expressions do carry some information, but the claim of always knowing is the error.

questions.title: Responsibility to Community
questions.prompt: A student helps clean up the classroom even though it was other students who made the mess. Which principle BEST explains why this is still the right thing to do?

options.A: Shared spaces belong to everyone, so maintaining them is a collective responsibility regardless of who caused the problem
options.B: It is always fair to do extra work because it builds strong character in yourself
options.C: Helping only matters when the teacher is watching and can give recognition for it
options.D: Only the people who made the mess have any duty to clean it up, so helping is optional kindness only

questions.explanation: IB PYP emphasises that communities thrive when members take collective responsibility for shared spaces, not just personal actions. Option D is a plausible counter-argument, but it confuses legal/personal blame with broader civic responsibility — being blameless does not remove a person's stake in the shared environment.

questions.title: Mental Health Stigma
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Asking for help when you feel very sad is a sign of weakness.' Which response most precisely challenges this belief?

options.A: Sadness is not real, so there is nothing to ask for help about
options.B: Only people who have no friends need to ask for help with their feelings
options.C: Recognising when you need support and seeking it requires self-awareness and courage, which are signs of strength
options.D: It is weakness if adults ask for help, but acceptable for children because they are still learning

questions.explanation: Mental health frameworks recognise that self-awareness — knowing when you are struggling — and the courage to seek help are sophisticated skills linked to emotional intelligence and resilience. Option D is a common double-standard that still frames help-seeking negatively for adults, which is also incorrect.

questions.title: Values and Personal Identity
questions.prompt: Suppose two children both say honesty is their top value, but one tells the truth even when it is hard, while the other only tells the truth when it is easy. What does this difference MOST reveal about values?

options.A: Values are meaningless because everyone claims to have them but no one practises them
options.B: A value is only truly held when it guides behaviour even under difficult conditions
options.C: The second child has a stronger value of honesty because avoiding hard situations is wise
options.D: Both children hold honesty equally because they both said it was important

questions.explanation: In ethics and character education, a value is demonstrated through consistent action, especially when it is costly or difficult — otherwise it remains a stated preference rather than a guiding principle. Option D is wrong because stating a value and acting on it in difficult situations are two different things.

questions.title: Human Relationships and Trust
questions.prompt: What would MOST LIKELY happen to a friendship if one person repeatedly shared the other's secrets with other people?

options.A: The friendship would grow stronger because sharing information increases closeness between groups
options.B: Trust would erode, making the person whose secrets were shared less willing to be open in the future
options.C: Nothing would change if the secrets were not very important ones
options.D: The friendship would only suffer if the person found out, so the impact depends entirely on discovery

questions.explanation: Trust is built through consistent reliability and confidentiality; repeated breaches signal that the relationship is not safe, reducing openness over time. Option D is plausible but misses the point: trust is also eroded by the act itself, and relationships built on secrets-kept-by-luck are inherently fragile.

questions.title: Wellbeing: Multiple Dimensions
questions.prompt: A child eats healthily and exercises every day but feels lonely and anxious most of the time. According to multi-dimensional wellbeing models, what does this situation show?

options.A: Physical health automatically creates emotional and social health if maintained long enough
options.B: Wellbeing has several separate dimensions, and strength in one area does not guarantee wellbeing in others
options.C: Anxiety and loneliness are just physical problems that will disappear once the child's diet is improved
options.D: The child's wellbeing is mostly fine because physical health is the most important dimension

questions.explanation: Wellbeing frameworks such as CASEL and WHO distinguish physical, emotional, and social dimensions as separate but interconnected — excelling in one does not compensate for deficits in others. Option A is a common but incorrect assumption that physical health automatically produces overall wellbeing.

questions.title: Responsibility and Choices
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'I cannot be responsible for my choices if other people influenced me to make them.' Evaluate this claim. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: The claim is fully correct because influence from others always removes personal responsibility
options.B: The claim is fully correct only when the influence comes from an adult authority figure
options.C: The claim is incorrect because influence is one factor among many, but the person making the choice still bears responsibility for their action
options.D: The claim is correct because responsibility is decided entirely by whoever has the most power in the situation

questions.explanation: Ethical reasoning recognises that while external influence is real and matters, individuals retain moral agency — the capacity to evaluate and choose — which means responsibility is shared rather than erased. Option A is a tempting but flawed escape from accountability; it would mean no one is ever responsible for anything.

questions.title: Cultural Practices and Respect
questions.prompt: Two families celebrate the new year on different dates using very different traditions. A child says one family's celebration must be wrong because it is different from their own. What kind of thinking error is this?

options.A: Ethnocentrism — using one's own culture as the standard to judge all others
options.B: Growth mindset — assuming only one approach to a task can be correct
options.C: Confirmation bias — only remembering evidence that supports what you already believe
options.D: Overgeneralisation — applying one example of a group to all members of that group

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism is the specific error of treating one's own cultural norms as the universal standard for judging other cultures. Option D describes a different thinking error — applying a characteristic of some members to all — which is not what is happening in this scenario.

questions.title: Self-Regulation Strategies
questions.prompt: Before responding to something that makes her angry, Priya pauses, names the feeling silently, and then decides how to respond. Which skill is Priya practising?

options.A: Suppression — pushing down emotions so they do not interfere with behaviour
options.B: Self-regulation — managing emotional responses by creating space between feeling and action
options.C: Metacognition — thinking about how she learned the skill of pausing
options.D: Avoidance — choosing not to engage with situations that cause strong feelings

questions.explanation: Self-regulation involves noticing an emotion and intentionally choosing a response rather than reacting automatically — Priya's pause and naming are exactly this process. Option A is wrong because suppression means hiding or denying the emotion, while Priya is acknowledging it and using it to inform a deliberate choice.

questions.title: Understanding Bias in Thinking
questions.prompt: A student remembers every time a classmate was late to school but forgets the many times that same classmate arrived on time. Which thinking pattern is this an example of?

options.A: Empathy — focusing on another person's challenges to understand their perspective
options.B: Selective attention bias — noticing and remembering information that confirms an existing belief
options.C: Overgeneralisation — applying one observed behaviour to all students in the class
options.D: Attribution error — deciding the classmate's lateness is caused by laziness rather than circumstance

questions.explanation: Selective attention bias (related to confirmation bias) means we more readily notice and store information that fits a belief we already hold — here, the lateness stands out while on-time arrivals are forgotten. Option D describes a different error (attribution error) which concerns the reason assigned to behaviour, not the pattern of what information is remembered.

questions.title: Healthy Relationships: Boundaries
questions.prompt: A friend keeps asking you to share answers on a test even though you have said no twice. Which statement BEST explains why saying no a third time is the right choice?

options.A: Saying no means you do not care about the friendship and should expect it to end
options.B: A boundary that is dropped under pressure was never a real boundary and teaches others it can be ignored
options.C: You should say yes on the third time because persistence shows the friend really needs the help
options.D: Saying no is only right the first time; after that, social rules require compromise

questions.explanation: Healthy boundaries require consistency — if a boundary is abandoned under repeated pressure, it signals that the boundary is negotiable, which can lead others to keep pushing. Option C confuses persistence with genuine need and rewards pressure rather than respecting personal limits.

questions.title: Perspective and Empathy in Action
questions.prompt: A new student joins the class and seems very quiet. One classmate says, 'She must be unfriendly.' Another says, 'She might be nervous in a new place.' Which IB Learner Profile attribute best describes the second classmate's response?

options.A: Principled — because the classmate is following the school rule of being kind to newcomers
options.B: Open-minded — because the classmate is considering an alternative explanation before judging
options.C: Knowledgeable — because the classmate knows facts about what it feels like to be new
options.D: Reflective — because the classmate is thinking carefully about their own past experiences

questions.explanation: Being open-minded in the IB Learner Profile means considering multiple perspectives and withholding judgement — the second classmate does this by offering an alternative explanation instead of assuming. Option D is plausible but describes looking inward at one's own experience, not the outward consideration of another person's possible perspective.

questions.title: Causes of Emotion vs. Emotion Itself
questions.prompt: Two students both feel nervous before a class presentation. One finds nerves helpful; the other finds them unhelpful. What does this BEST suggest about emotions?

options.A: The two students must be feeling different emotions even though they both call it nervousness
options.B: The same emotion can have different effects depending on how a person interprets and responds to it
options.C: Nervousness is always harmful and should be eliminated through better preparation
options.D: Whether an emotion is useful depends only on the difficulty of the task, not on the person

questions.explanation: Emotional regulation research shows that the appraisal of an emotion — how we interpret and frame it — strongly influences its effect on performance. Nervousness interpreted as 'I'm ready to focus' can enhance performance, while the same feeling interpreted as threat can hinder it. Option A assumes different labels are needed, but both students correctly identify the feeling as nervousness.

questions.title: Inquiry into Personal Strengths
questions.prompt: A student is very good at helping others solve problems but struggles with writing long answers. She says, 'I am not smart.' Which is the most precise error in her conclusion?

options.A: She is wrong to focus on writing; all school subjects are equally easy for smart people
options.B: She is treating 'smart' as a single fixed trait rather than recognising intelligence has many different forms
options.C: She is wrong because a student who helps others must already know they are smart
options.D: She is correct that she is not smart but wrong to feel bad about it

questions.explanation: Theories of multiple intelligences and a growth mindset both recognise that capability is multi-dimensional — strength in interpersonal skills is a form of intelligence just as valid as written expression. Option C is wrong because it makes a logical leap: helping others demonstrates one type of ability but does not prove a single comprehensive 'smartness.'

questions.title: Social Health: Inclusion
questions.prompt: During free play, a group of children always forms and leaves one child outside the game. If this pattern continues every day, what is the MOST significant harm according to social health research?

options.A: The excluded child will miss out on fun but will have no lasting effects once they make new friends
options.B: The group misses out on the excluded child's ideas, so their games become less creative
options.C: Repeated exclusion damages the child's sense of belonging and can harm both emotional wellbeing and self-worth over time
options.D: Exclusion is only harmful if the child's parents find out and complain to the school

questions.explanation: Chronic social exclusion triggers the same neural pathways as physical pain and consistently predicts reduced self-esteem, anxiety, and wellbeing in children. Option A underestimates the cumulative harm: repeated daily exclusion is not easily offset by later friendships and can create lasting negative effects on self-concept.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning: Consequences vs Rules
questions.prompt: A student finds a lost purse with money inside. She could keep it, and no one would ever know. She returns it because she believes 'taking something that is not yours is always wrong, no matter what.' Which approach to ethics does her reasoning follow?

options.A: Consequentialist — she is thinking about the outcome of getting caught if she keeps it
options.B: Virtue ethics — she is acting the way a person with good character would act
options.C: Duty-based ethics — she believes certain actions are right or wrong regardless of the outcome
options.D: Social contract ethics — she is following a rule that her community agreed on together

questions.explanation: Duty-based (deontological) ethics holds that some actions are inherently right or wrong independent of consequences — 'always wrong, no matter what' is the key phrase signalling this approach. Option B is a tempting alternative because returning the purse does reflect good character, but the student's reasoning focuses on rules, not on what a virtuous person would do.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Basics
questions.prompt: A student receives a low score on a maths test and thinks, 'I am just not a maths person.' Which type of mindset does this thought best represent, and what is its main problem?

options.A: A growth mindset, because the student is reflecting on their performance
options.B: A fixed mindset, because it assumes ability cannot change with effort
options.C: A resilient mindset, because the student is being honest about a weakness
options.D: A strategic mindset, because the student is identifying an area to avoid

questions.explanation: Psychologist Carol Dweck defines a fixed mindset as the belief that intelligence and talent are static traits you either have or do not have — exactly what 'I am just not a maths person' expresses. A growth mindset, the top distractor, is actually the opposite belief: that ability develops through practice and effort, so option A misidentifies the mindset entirely.

questions.title: Brain Neuroplasticity
questions.prompt: Scientists have discovered that the brain can form new connections throughout a person's life in response to learning and experience. What is the correct term for this ability?

options.A: Homeostasis
options.B: Neuroplasticity
options.C: Synaptic pruning
options.D: Cognitive load

questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity is the brain's documented ability to reorganise itself by forming new neural connections throughout life, which is why practice genuinely changes the brain's structure. Synaptic pruning, the top distractor, is a related but different process where unused connections are eliminated — it describes reduction, not formation, of new pathways.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Evaluate this student's claim: 'Because I have the right to free expression, I can say anything I want about anyone, anywhere, with no limits.' What is the key flaw in this reasoning?

options.A: Free expression is not a recognised right in international law
options.B: Rights always come paired with responsibilities and do not override others' rights to dignity and safety
options.C: Children under 18 do not yet hold the right to free expression
options.D: Free expression only applies in formal government settings, not schools

questions.explanation: The UNCRC and most rights frameworks explicitly state that exercising a right must not violate the rights and freedoms of others — every right carries a corresponding responsibility. Option A is wrong because free expression is enshrined in Article 13 of the UNCRC, making it very much a recognised right.

questions.title: Emotions and the Body
questions.prompt: When a person feels sudden fear, their heart beats faster, their muscles tense, and their breathing quickens. What name is given to this automatic physical response?

options.A: The relaxation response
options.B: Cognitive dissonance
options.C: The fight-or-flight response
options.D: Emotional regulation

questions.explanation: The fight-or-flight response is triggered by the release of adrenaline from the adrenal glands, preparing the body to confront or escape a threat — hence the rapid heartbeat, muscle tension, and fast breathing. The relaxation response, the top distractor, is actually the opposite: a calming state activated by techniques like slow breathing.

questions.title: Cultural Identity Formation
questions.prompt: A student moves from Japan to Brazil at age ten and gradually adopts some Brazilian customs while keeping Japanese traditions at home. Which term best describes the process of adapting to a new culture without completely abandoning one's original culture?

options.A: Assimilation
options.B: Stereotyping
options.C: Acculturation
options.D: Socialisation

questions.explanation: Acculturation describes the process of adapting elements of a new culture while retaining aspects of one's heritage culture — a two-way blending rather than full replacement. Assimilation, the top distractor, specifically means fully adopting the new culture and abandoning the original one, which is the opposite of what the student in the scenario does.

questions.title: Empathy vs Sympathy
questions.prompt: Your friend is upset after losing a school competition. You say, 'I can imagine how disappointed you feel — I felt something similar when I didn't make the team last year.' Which skill are you demonstrating?

options.A: Sympathy, because you are feeling sorry for your friend
options.B: Empathy, because you are connecting to their feeling from your own experience
options.C: Active listening, because you are paying attention to what they say
options.D: Conflict resolution, because you are trying to fix the situation

questions.explanation: Empathy involves taking another person's perspective and connecting emotionally to their experience, often by drawing on similar feelings of your own — exactly what the student does by referencing their own past disappointment. Sympathy, the top distractor, is feeling pity or sorrow for someone from a distance, without stepping into their emotional experience.

questions.title: Sleep and Wellbeing
questions.prompt: Why do health researchers consistently recommend that children aged 9–11 get between 9 and 11 hours of sleep per night, rather than the 7–9 hours recommended for adults?

options.A: Children's bodies are smaller, so they need more time for digestion during sleep
options.B: Children's brains and bodies are still developing rapidly, requiring more restorative sleep
options.C: Children have less stressful lives than adults, making it easier to sleep longer
options.D: Children's body clocks run faster, consuming energy more quickly overnight

questions.explanation: During sleep, the brain consolidates memories, processes emotions, and releases growth hormone — processes that are especially intense during childhood when development is rapid. Option C is plausible but wrong: the amount of sleep needed is determined by biological development needs, not by stress levels.

questions.title: Stereotypes and Bias
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this statement: 'All introverted people are shy and dislike being around others.'

options.A: The statement is correct because introversion is defined as disliking social interaction
options.B: It treats introversion as a temporary mood rather than a personality trait
options.C: It conflates introversion, which is about where people gain energy, with shyness, which is about social anxiety
options.D: It incorrectly assumes that all people fit neatly into either introvert or extrovert categories

questions.explanation: Introversion describes a preference for less stimulating environments and a tendency to recharge alone — not a fear of or dislike of people; many introverts are confident in social settings but simply find them draining. Option D is also a genuine critique of personality categories, but it does not address the specific error the statement makes about equating introversion with shyness.

questions.title: Responsibility and Agency
questions.prompt: What does it mean for a person to have 'agency' in making decisions about their own life?

options.A: The person always makes the right choices without making mistakes
options.B: The person has the capacity and freedom to make genuine choices and act on them
options.C: The person is told by a trusted adult what the best decision is
options.D: The person is old enough to be held legally responsible for their actions

questions.explanation: Agency refers to the ability and freedom to make deliberate choices and take actions that reflect one's own values and intentions — it is about capacity, not perfection. Option D describes legal accountability, which is a related but distinct concept from agency as used in psychology and philosophy.

questions.title: Mental Health Basics
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Mental health is only relevant when a person has a diagnosed mental illness.' What is wrong with this claim?

options.A: Mental health is actually a physical condition, not a mental one
options.B: Mental health exists on a continuum and everyone has it, whether they have a diagnosis or not
options.C: Mental illness affects so many people that the student's claim is statistically unlikely
options.D: Only medical professionals are qualified to make claims about mental health

questions.explanation: The World Health Organization defines mental health as a state of wellbeing in which every individual realises their potential — it is a continuum everyone exists on, not a binary 'ill or not ill' state. Option C is a statistical argument that does not address the conceptual error in treating mental health as exclusively illness-focused.

questions.title: Values and Behaviour
questions.prompt: Compare a person who values honesty with a person who values loyalty above all else. If a close friend lies on an exam, which statement best explains why the two people might respond very differently?

options.A: The person valuing honesty may feel compelled to report it, while the loyalty-focused person may feel compelled to protect the friend
options.B: Both would respond the same way because friendship always overrides personal values
options.C: The loyalty-focused person would definitely report the friend to demonstrate responsibility
options.D: Personal values are too abstract to have any real effect on everyday decisions

questions.explanation: Core values act as internal guides that directly shape how a person interprets and responds to situations — someone who prioritises honesty sees deception as a wrong to be corrected, while someone who prioritises loyalty sees protecting the friend as the right thing to do. Option B is wrong because when values conflict with social bonds, the conflict is precisely what makes the situation ethically interesting and unresolved.

questions.title: Self-Esteem vs Self-Efficacy
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between self-esteem and self-efficacy?

options.A: Self-esteem is about feeling capable at a specific task; self-efficacy is a general sense of worth
options.B: Self-esteem is a general sense of self-worth; self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task
options.C: Self-esteem applies only to academic performance; self-efficacy applies to sports and hobbies
options.D: Self-esteem and self-efficacy describe the same psychological concept using different terms

questions.explanation: Psychologist Albert Bandura defined self-efficacy as a task-specific belief — 'I can solve this type of maths problem' — while self-esteem refers to a broader overall evaluation of one's worth as a person. Option A reverses the two definitions, making it the most dangerous distractor.

questions.title: Social Health and Belonging
questions.prompt: Why do psychologists describe a sense of belonging as a fundamental human need, rather than simply a preference or luxury?

options.A: Because belonging makes people more productive at work and school
options.B: Because humans evolved as social creatures whose survival depended on group membership, making connection a core need
options.C: Because children who feel they belong tend to score higher on standardised tests
options.D: Because belonging reduces the number of rules a person needs to follow

questions.explanation: Abraham Maslow placed belonging in the middle tier of his hierarchy of needs, and evolutionary psychology explains this by noting that early humans who were excluded from groups faced drastically reduced survival odds — making social connection a genuine biological need, not merely nice to have. Option A describes a benefit of belonging but not why it qualifies as a fundamental need rather than a preference.

questions.title: Perspective and Conflict
questions.prompt: Two students both witnessed the same argument in the playground but described it completely differently afterwards. Which IB PYP key concept best explains why their accounts can both be sincere yet still differ?

options.A: Function, because each student has a different role in the school
options.B: Causation, because the argument was caused by different factors for each student
options.C: Perspective, because each person's viewpoint is shaped by their own experiences and position
options.D: Reflection, because the students are thinking back on a past event

questions.explanation: The PYP key concept of perspective explicitly addresses how different people can observe the same event and arrive at genuinely different, sincerely held interpretations based on their backgrounds, prior experiences, and physical vantage points. Reflection describes looking back on an experience to learn from it, which is a thinking process, not an explanation for why accounts differ.

questions.title: Healthy Boundaries
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen if a person never set any personal boundaries in their relationships with others?

options.A: They would develop very deep and trusting friendships more quickly
options.B: They would be seen as especially generous and kind by everyone around them
options.C: They might experience burnout, resentment, and difficulty maintaining a clear sense of identity
options.D: They would have more time for their own needs because others would appreciate them more

questions.explanation: Psychologists identify personal boundaries as essential for protecting mental energy and maintaining a coherent sense of self; without them, people often overextend themselves, leading to emotional exhaustion and resentment when their needs are repeatedly unmet. Option A sounds positive but is misleading — a lack of boundaries often leads to relationships that are unbalanced and ultimately less trusting, not more.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning Consequentialism
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'It was right for me to lie to my friend because telling the truth would have made them very sad and no real harm was done.' Which ethical framework is this student using?

options.A: Virtue ethics, because the student is trying to be a good friend
options.B: Consequentialism, because the student judges the action by its outcomes
options.C: Deontological ethics, because the student is following a duty to protect others
options.D: Relativism, because the student believes truth is different for everyone

questions.explanation: Consequentialism, most famously associated with utilitarian philosophers like John Stuart Mill, holds that the morality of an action is determined entirely by its consequences — if the outcome is good (or at least not harmful), the action is justified. Virtue ethics, the top distractor, focuses on the character of the person acting rather than on outcomes, so it does not match the student's outcome-based reasoning.

questions.title: Physical Health and Function
questions.prompt: Why do nutritionists describe breakfast as particularly important for children's cognitive performance during the school morning, compared with adults?

options.A: Children's stomachs are smaller, so they digest breakfast faster and need fuel sooner
options.B: Children's developing brains consume a proportionally higher share of the body's glucose, making steady fuel supply critical
options.C: Children are more active than adults in the morning and therefore burn more calories walking to school
options.D: Breakfast helps children socialise, which indirectly improves their ability to focus in class

questions.explanation: Research shows that the developing brain uses up to 50% of the body's glucose supply in young children, so gaps in fuel supply after an overnight fast have a proportionally greater impact on their concentration and memory than on adult brains. Option C describes physical activity rather than the cognitive mechanism, making it the most plausible but incorrect distractor.
