Option D is plausible because dependency and loss of autonomy can occur in adolescence, but Erikson specifically names 'role confusion' as the crisis outcome, not authority-dependence, which relates more to his earlier stage of Autonomy vs Shame.

questions.title: Physical and Mental Health Connection
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Mental health and physical health are separate systems — fixing one does not affect the other.' What is the most precise reason this claim is incorrect?

options.A: It is incorrect because mental health problems are always caused by physical illnesses, making physical health the root of all wellbeing.
options.B: It is incorrect because the mind and body interact bidirectionally — mental states affect physical health (e.g., chronic stress raises cortisol) and physical health affects mental states (e.g., poor sleep worsens mood).
options.C: It is incorrect because the World Health Organization defines health as the absence of both physical and mental disease in the same policy document.
options.D: It is incorrect because every mental health treatment requires a physical component, such as medication, to be effective.

questions.explanation: The mind-body connection is bidirectional: chronic psychological stress elevates cortisol levels, which can impair immune function and increase risk of cardiovascular disease, while physical conditions like chronic pain reliably increase rates of depression. Option C is a tempting distractor because the WHO definition of health is real and relevant, but it defines health as a state of complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing — not merely absence of disease — and citing a policy document is a weaker scientific explanation than the bidirectional mechanism.

questions.title: Moral Responsibility and Bystander Effect
questions.prompt: In a well-known social psychology finding, people are less likely to help someone in an emergency when many other bystanders are present than when they are alone with the person. Which concept explains this, and what does it reveal about moral responsibility?

options.A: Social facilitation — the presence of others improves performance, so bystanders become overconfident that someone else will respond better.
options.B: Diffusion of responsibility — when many people are present, each individual feels less personally obligated to act, revealing that our sense of moral duty can be weakened by the size of the group.
options.C: Conformity pressure — people in crowds follow the behaviour of the majority, and if no one else acts, individuals assume action is wrong.
options.D: Deindividuation — being in a crowd causes people to lose their personal identity and therefore lose their sense of ethical judgement.

questions.explanation: The bystander effect operates primarily through 'diffusion of responsibility' — each person assumes shared responsibility means reduced personal obligation, so the larger the crowd, the less any one person feels they must act. Option C is a strong distractor because conformity is also present (people look to others for cues), but the core mechanism identified by Darley and Latané's original research is specifically diffusion of responsibility, not conformity.

questions.title: Stereotypes and Prejudice Distinction
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this argument: 'Prejudice is simply having a stereotype about a group. If we eliminate all stereotypes, prejudice will automatically disappear.'

options.A: The error is that stereotypes are always positive generalisations, so eliminating them would increase prejudice, not reduce it.
options.B: The error is that prejudice also involves an emotional attitude (usually negative feelings) toward a group, which can persist even when stereotypes are removed or are not present.
options.C: The error is that prejudice is purely behavioural — it only exists when discrimination occurs — so stereotypes are completely unrelated.
options.D: There is no error; psychologists universally agree that prejudice is identical to stereotyping.

questions.explanation: Psychologists distinguish stereotypes (cognitive beliefs about a group), prejudice (emotional attitudes, often negative, toward a group), and discrimination (behaviour). Prejudice includes an affective component that can exist independently of specific stereotypes and may be triggered by group membership alone. Option C is plausible because discrimination is the behavioural outcome, but defining prejudice as purely behavioural is incorrect — prejudice is specifically the attitudinal/emotional component, separate from the action of discrimination.

questions.title: Sleep and Cognitive Function
questions.prompt: Why does sleep deprivation specifically impair tasks requiring creativity and decision-making more severely than it impairs well-practised automatic tasks such as typing familiar words?

options.A: Because sleep deprivation reduces blood flow equally to all brain areas, but creative tasks require more blood overall.
options.B: Because automatic tasks are stored in long-term procedural memory and require minimal prefrontal cortex activity, while creativity and decision-making depend heavily on the prefrontal cortex, which is disproportionately affected by lack of sleep.
options.C: Because familiar tasks are processed in the right hemisphere while creative tasks use only the left hemisphere, and sleep loss damages only the left hemisphere.
options.D: Because sleep deprivation lowers IQ scores permanently, and creativity is a higher-IQ function than automaticity.

questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation particularly impairs the prefrontal cortex — the region governing complex reasoning, creativity, impulse control, and decision-making — while well-practised, automatic procedural tasks rely on basal ganglia and cerebellum pathways that are more resilient to sleep loss. Option A is tempting because blood flow and oxygenation are genuinely affected by sleep loss, but the effect is not uniform across all areas; the prefrontal cortex is disproportionately impacted.

questions.title: Perspective and Conflict Resolution
questions.prompt: Two students disagree about a school rule banning mobile phones in class. Student A says the rule protects learning. Student B says it ignores students' right to communicate. Which approach to resolving the disagreement best reflects the IB PYP concept of 'perspective'?

options.A: Finding the rule that the majority of students prefer through a vote, then enforcing it consistently.
options.B: Each student researching evidence to prove the other wrong so the debate can be settled definitively.
options.C: Each student articulating why the other's view makes sense given their values and experiences, then exploring whether both concerns can be partially addressed.
options.D: Asking a teacher to decide which student is correct, since adults have more experience with school rules.

questions.explanation: The PYP key concept of 'perspective' asks learners to consider that different viewpoints arise from different values, knowledge, and experiences — genuinely understanding another's perspective is the first step toward solutions that honour multiple concerns. Option A is plausible because democratic decision-making is fair, but a majority vote does not require either student to understand the other's perspective; it simply overrides the minority view, which is not the same as applying the concept of perspective.

questions.title: Wellbeing Dimensions — PERMA Model
questions.prompt: Martin Seligman's PERMA model of wellbeing includes five elements. A student has strong friendships, regularly achieves goals, and finds meaning in helping others — yet still reports feeling unhappy. According to PERMA, which element is most likely missing?

options.A: Relationships (R), because even though the student has friends, they may not be communicating enough.
options.B: Positive Emotion (P), because having meaning and achievement does not guarantee regularly experiencing positive feelings such as joy or gratitude.
options.C: Accomplishment (A), because achieving goals is not the same as feeling accomplished without external recognition.
options.D: Meaning (M), because helping others only counts as meaningful if it is connected to a formal cause or organisation.

questions.explanation: In PERMA, Positive Emotion (P) is distinct from the other elements — a person can have Relationships, Engagement, Meaning, and Accomplishment yet still lack sufficient positive emotional experiences (joy, gratitude, love) in daily life, which are necessary for wellbeing. Option C is a strong distractor because the idea that achievement without recognition feels hollow is psychologically real, but PERMA defines Accomplishment as the subjective sense of achievement, not external validation, so this does not identify the missing element.

questions.title: Form of Beliefs and Behaviour
questions.prompt: A student notices that two classmates hold the same religious belief but behave very differently in how they treat others. What does this best illustrate about the relationship between beliefs and behaviour?

options.A: Beliefs have no meaningful influence on behaviour — only personality determines how people act.
options.B: The same belief can be interpreted and applied differently depending on a person's upbringing, values, and the specific context they face.
options.C: One of the classmates must not truly hold the belief, since genuine belief always produces consistent behaviour.
options.D: Religious beliefs are unique in that they create contradictory behaviours, unlike secular beliefs which produce predictable actions.

questions.explanation: Beliefs function as frameworks for interpreting the world, but how a belief is applied depends on factors like personal upbringing, cultural context, and situational pressures — meaning two people with the same belief may derive different behavioural conclusions from it. Option C is the most tempting distractor because it sounds like a reasonable philosophical stance, but it is contradicted by evidence: people can hold sincere beliefs while interpreting their obligations very differently.

questions.title: Change in Identity Over Time
questions.prompt: Ten-year-old Sam strongly identifies as shy and avoids speaking in class. By age 20, Sam is a confident public speaker. Which statement best explains how this change is possible, using both psychological and IB reasoning?

options.A: It is not truly possible; personality traits like shyness are determined by genetics and remain constant throughout life.
options.B: Sam must have received a medical treatment that altered their brain chemistry, since character traits cannot change through experience alone.
options.C: Identity is not fixed — new experiences, deliberate practice, social environments, and how we interpret our own story can all reshape the traits and roles we identify with.
options.D: Sam's original identity as 'shy' was always incorrect; they were actually confident but suppressing it, and adulthood simply revealed their true self.

questions.explanation: Both developmental psychology and the IB concept of 'change' support the idea that identity is dynamic: personality research (including work on the 'Big Five') shows traits can shift significantly across the lifespan, especially through major experiences and intentional self-development. Option A is a strong distractor because genetics do influence temperament, but the claim that traits remain constant is refuted by longitudinal studies showing meaningful personality change from childhood to adulthood.

questions.title: Connection Between Nutrition and Brain Function
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'What I eat only affects my body, not how well I can concentrate or remember things at school.' Which finding from nutrition science most directly contradicts this claim?

options.A: Research shows that overweight students perform worse academically, proving diet affects grades.
options.B: The brain consumes approximately 20% of the body's energy and relies on a steady supply of glucose and micronutrients like omega-3 fatty acids for neurotransmitter production and focus.
options.C: Eating breakfast has been proven to raise IQ scores by an average of 10 points in primary school children.
options.D: Sugar consumption directly causes hyperactivity, which distracts from learning in classroom settings.

questions.explanation: The brain is one of the most metabolically demanding organs — it uses roughly 20% of the body's total energy and requires specific nutrients (glucose for energy, omega-3s for membrane function, amino acids for neurotransmitter synthesis) to maintain attention, memory consolidation, and mood regulation. Option D is a tempting distractor because the idea that sugar causes hyperactivity is widely believed, but controlled studies have found no causal link between sugar and hyperactivity — it is largely a myth.

questions.title: Evaluating Fairness Frameworks
questions.prompt: A teacher gives extra time on a test to a student with dyslexia. A classmate argues: 'That is unfair — everyone should get exactly the same conditions.' Evaluate which concept of fairness the teacher is applying.

options.A: The teacher is applying equity — giving each person what they specifically need to have an equal opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge.
options.B: The teacher is applying equality — ensuring every student has identical test durations regardless of ability.
options.C: The teacher is applying a consequentialist rule — calculating that the student with dyslexia will produce better outcomes for the class as a whole.
options.D: The teacher is applying favouritism, which may feel unfair to some students but is legally required in most countries.

questions.explanation: Equity involves adjusting support based on individual need so that all students have a genuinely fair chance — giving more to those who need more, not the same to everyone. Option B is the key distractor because students often confuse equality (identical treatment) with equity (need-based treatment); the classmate's complaint reflects an equality framework, but the teacher is deliberately applying equity.

questions.title: Social Media and Self-Image
questions.prompt: Research finds that teenagers who spend more time passively viewing idealised images on social media report lower self-esteem than those who use social media to actively communicate with friends. Which psychological mechanism best explains this difference?

options.A: Classical conditioning — passive viewing repeatedly pairs social media with negative emotions, training users to feel bad.
options.B: Upward social comparison — passively viewing curated, idealised content leads people to compare themselves unfavourably to unrealistic standards, whereas active communication focuses on connection rather than comparison.
options.C: Cognitive dissonance — active users experience more discomfort because they must decide what to say, which builds self-awareness.
options.D: The mere exposure effect — seeing idealised images more frequently makes them seem like an achievable norm, increasing dissatisfaction when reality differs.

questions.explanation: Social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954) predicts that comparing oneself to those perceived as superior (upward comparison) reduces self-esteem; passive consumption of curated, highlight-reel content maximises these upward comparisons, while active communication shifts focus to relationships rather than rankings. Option D is a plausible distractor because the mere exposure effect is a real phenomenon, but it predicts increased liking and familiarity with repeated exposure — not necessarily increased dissatisfaction, making it a less precise explanation.

questions.title: Cause-Effect in Stress Response
questions.prompt: When the body activates its 'fight-or-flight' response due to stress, which sequence of events correctly describes what happens in the first few seconds?

options.A: The prefrontal cortex detects threat → signals the heart to speed up → cortisol is released → digestion slows.
options.B: The amygdala detects threat → signals the adrenal glands → adrenaline is released → heart rate, breathing, and alertness increase rapidly.
options.C: The hippocampus detects threat → releases serotonin → muscles tense → the body prepares to fight or flee.
options.D: The hypothalamus detects threat → signals the pancreas → insulin is released → blood sugar spikes to fuel the muscles.

questions.explanation: The fight-or-flight response begins in the amygdala (threat detection), which signals the hypothalamus, which in turn activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline (epinephrine) — rapidly increasing heart rate, breathing rate, and muscle readiness within seconds. Option A is a strong distractor because it places the prefrontal cortex as the starting point, but under acute stress the amygdala can bypass the prefrontal cortex, triggering the response before conscious analysis occurs.

questions.title: Reflective Journalling and Self-Awareness
questions.prompt: A student keeps a daily journal, writing about mistakes made and what could be done differently. Over time, which outcome is most strongly supported by research on reflective practice?

options.A: The student will become more self-critical and develop higher levels of anxiety because they are constantly reviewing failures.
options.B: The student will develop greater self-awareness, a more accurate self-concept, and improved ability to regulate future behaviour by spotting recurring patterns.
options.C: The student's academic performance will automatically improve because writing about problems transfers understanding to all subjects.
options.D: The student will develop a stronger fixed mindset because repeatedly documenting mistakes reinforces the belief that errors define ability.

questions.explanation: Reflective practice research, including work by John Dewey and Donald Schön, shows that deliberate structured reflection helps learners identify patterns in their thinking and behaviour, leading to more accurate self-concept and better self-regulation over time. Option A is plausible because rumination (passive, repetitive negative thinking) does increase anxiety — but structured reflection with a forward-looking focus ('what could be done differently') is distinct from rumination and associated with positive outcomes.

questions.title: Responsibility to Future Generations
questions.prompt: A school decides to plant trees that will provide shade primarily for students 20 years from now. A student argues: 'We should spend the money on things that benefit us now, not future students we will never meet.' Which ethical reasoning BEST challenges this argument?

options.A: The student's argument is correct under consequentialist ethics because benefits to existing people outweigh uncertain future benefits.
options.B: The student's argument fails because future people have interests and rights that exist independently of whether we will personally meet them, giving us obligations to consider their wellbeing.
options.C: The student's argument is undermined by the fact that trees also benefit the current generation through oxygen production, making the distinction irrelevant.
options.D: The student's argument is flawed only if the trees are mandated by a government law, since legal obligations override personal preferences.

questions.explanation: Intergenerational ethics holds that future persons have morally relevant interests even though they do not yet exist — philosophers like Hans Jonas argue we have a 'duty of care' to future generations because our actions shape the world they will inherit. Option C is tempting because trees do provide present benefits, but this response sidesteps the deeper ethical question about obligations to people we will never meet — it does not actually challenge the argument, it just removes its premise.

questions.title: Language and Identity Connection
questions.prompt: Research on bilingual individuals suggests that people sometimes feel like 'a slightly different person' when speaking their second language compared to their first. Which explanation best accounts for this phenomenon?

options.A: Each language activates a physically separate brain and therefore produces completely different thought processes.
options.B: Languages are neutral tools and cannot affect identity; the feeling is purely a side effect of concentration required when using a less-practised language.
options.C: Different languages carry different cultural norms, emotional associations, and social roles, so switching languages can shift which cultural frameworks and self-schemas a person draws on.
options.D: The phenomenon occurs only in people who learned their second language after age 10, because early language acquisition prevents identity separation.

questions.explanation: Psycholinguistic research, including work by Michele Koven and others, shows that languages are embedded in specific cultural contexts, relationships, and emotional memories — switching languages can therefore activate different cultural identities, social roles, and even emotional responses, producing a genuine shift in how one experiences and expresses oneself. Option B is the most confident-sounding distractor, but it contradicts research demonstrating that language is deeply intertwined with culture and emotion, not simply a neutral tool.

questions.title: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset
questions.prompt: A student receives a low score on a maths test and thinks: 'I'm just not a maths person — there's no point trying harder.' Which of the following most accurately explains why this thinking pattern is likely to limit their development?

options.A: It prevents the student from choosing easier tasks where they would naturally succeed.
options.B: It treats ability as fixed, which discourages the effort and strategies that actually build skills.
options.C: It causes the student to compare themselves to others, which is always harmful to learning.
options.D: It shows the student lacks intrinsic motivation, which cannot be developed once lost.

questions.explanation: A fixed mindset treats intelligence and talent as unchangeable traits, so the student stops investing effort — but neuroscience shows that practising skills actually strengthens neural pathways, making ability genuinely improvable. Option C is a distractor because comparing oneself to others is not always harmful; it can sometimes provide useful benchmarks, so the blanket claim is incorrect.

questions.title: Neuroscience of Emotions
questions.prompt: When a person feels sudden fear, a small almond-shaped brain structure triggers a rapid physical response before the thinking part of the brain has fully processed what is happening. What is this structure called, and why does it act so quickly?

options.A: The hippocampus; it stores emotional memories and replays them faster than conscious thought.
options.B: The prefrontal cortex; it prioritises survival signals over logical reasoning.
options.C: The amygdala; it processes threat signals and triggers the fight-or-flight response before slower cortical thinking occurs.
options.D: The cerebellum; it coordinates automatic body responses including emotional reactions.

questions.explanation: The amygdala is the brain's rapid threat-detection centre; it sends alarm signals along a 'low road' pathway to the body before the prefrontal cortex has finished analysing the situation, which is why fear reactions feel automatic. The hippocampus (option A) is primarily involved in forming and retrieving memories rather than triggering immediate fear responses.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning — Consequences vs Rules
questions.prompt: Priya tells a small lie to prevent her friend from feeling hurt by honest feedback. A classmate argues this is wrong because lying is always wrong, no matter what. Another student says it is right because it produced a good outcome. Which ethical framework does each student's argument represent, in order?

options.A: Virtue ethics, then consequentialism
options.B: Deontological ethics, then consequentialism
options.C: Consequentialism, then deontological ethics
options.D: Deontological ethics, then virtue ethics

questions.explanation: Deontological ethics (associated with Kant) holds that actions are right or wrong based on rules or duties — lying is always wrong regardless of outcome. Consequentialism judges actions by their results — the lie is justified because it produced a good outcome (less hurt). Option A is tempting because virtue ethics asks 'what would a virtuous person do?' but neither argument is framed around character traits.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities Balance
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'I have the right to freedom of expression, so I can say anything I want at school without consequences.' Identify the flaw in this reasoning about rights and responsibilities.

options.A: Freedom of expression is not a recognised right for children under the UNCRC.
options.B: Rights exist within a social framework; exercising a right still carries the responsibility not to harm others' rights and wellbeing.
options.C: Schools are private spaces where national rights do not apply, so the student has no legal protection.
options.D: The student is correct — freedom of expression is absolute and overrides all other considerations in educational settings.

questions.explanation: The UNCRC and broader human rights frameworks recognise that rights are not absolute; Article 13 explicitly states that freedom of expression may be restricted to protect others' rights or reputations. Option A is wrong because Article 13 of the UNCRC does grant children the right to freedom of expression, making it a well-recognised right.

questions.title: Cultural Identity and Stereotyping
questions.prompt: Two students are debating identity. Student A says cultural identity is something you are born into and cannot change. Student B says cultural identity is dynamic and can shift over a lifetime. Which statement most accurately evaluates their claims?

options.A: Student A is correct because culture is passed down genetically and therefore fixed.
options.B: Student B is correct because people choose their culture entirely through personal preference.
options.C: Student B is more accurate; cultural identity is shaped by birth context but also evolves through migration, education, and personal experience.
options.D: Both students are equally correct because cultural identity is different for every individual and no general claim can be made.

questions.explanation: Research in cultural psychology shows that while people are born into a cultural context that shapes early identity, experiences such as immigration, intermarriage, education, and globalisation can significantly reshape cultural identity over time — making it dynamic rather than fixed. Student B's claim is partially right but option B overstates personal choice, ignoring the powerful influence of one's birth context and community.

questions.title: Self-Regulation and Impulse Control
questions.prompt: In a famous psychology experiment, young children were left alone with one marshmallow and told they could eat it immediately or wait and receive two marshmallows. Later research suggested children who waited tended to have better outcomes in several life areas. What does this experiment most specifically measure?

options.A: General intelligence, because planning ahead requires higher cognitive ability.
options.B: Delayed gratification, which is the ability to resist an immediate reward in order to gain a larger future reward.
options.C: Intrinsic motivation, because children who waited were motivated by internal rewards rather than external ones.
options.D: Emotional resilience, because enduring discomfort without reacting is the definition of resilience.

questions.explanation: The Stanford Marshmallow Experiment, conducted by Walter Mischel, was specifically designed to measure delayed gratification — the capacity to forgo an immediate reward for a greater future benefit — which is a core component of self-regulation. While intelligence may correlate with this ability, the experiment was not designed to measure IQ, making option A an inaccurate characterisation of what it tests.

questions.title: Mental Health Stigma
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Mental health problems are a sign of weakness, so people should just try harder to feel better.' Which of the following most effectively challenges this claim using evidence-based reasoning?

options.A: Mental health problems are entirely caused by difficult life events, so willpower is irrelevant.
options.B: Conditions such as depression involve measurable changes in brain chemistry, meaning effort alone is often insufficient as a treatment.
options.C: People with mental health problems should not be told to try harder because that makes them feel guilty.
options.D: Mental health is too complex to measure, so no evidence can support or refute this claim.

questions.explanation: Depression and anxiety involve biological factors such as altered levels of neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine, which are not simply corrected by willpower — this is why clinical approaches often include therapy and sometimes medication. Option A is a tempting distractor but is also incorrect; mental health conditions have biological, psychological, and social causes, not exclusively life events.

questions.title: Perspective-Taking and Empathy
questions.prompt: Empathy and sympathy are often confused. A friend is upset about failing a test. You feel sad on their behalf and say 'That must be really difficult for you — I can imagine how that feels.' Which of the following best describes what you are practising, and why it differs from the alternative?

options.A: Sympathy, because you are feeling emotion on behalf of another person rather than with them.
options.B: Empathy, because you are trying to understand their experience from their perspective, not just pitying them.
options.C: Compassion, because you are moved to help them through their difficulty.
options.D: Emotional contagion, because their sadness has caused you to feel the same emotion automatically.

questions.explanation: Empathy involves perspective-taking — actively trying to imagine another's inner experience — which is exactly what the phrase 'I can imagine how that feels' demonstrates. Sympathy (option A) involves feeling for someone from your own perspective, often with pity, without necessarily entering their viewpoint — the distinction hinges on whether you step into their experience or observe it from outside.

questions.title: Beliefs Shaping Identity
questions.prompt: A student notices that two of their friends hold very different religious beliefs yet both describe their faith as central to who they are. What does this observation most strongly suggest about the relationship between beliefs and identity?

options.A: Beliefs only form part of identity when they are shared by a wider community.
options.B: The content of a belief matters more than the role it plays in a person's sense of self.
options.C: Beliefs can be a core component of identity regardless of their specific content, because it is their significance to the person that matters.
options.D: Holding different beliefs means two people cannot have similarly constructed identities.

questions.explanation: Identity theorists note that a belief's role in organising a person's values, choices, and community connections is what makes it identity-central — not the particular content of the belief itself. Option B reverses this logic by claiming content matters more than role, which misrepresents how beliefs function in identity formation.

questions.title: Cause and Effect in Social Health
questions.prompt: Research consistently finds that children with strong, supportive friendships recover from stressful events more quickly than those who are socially isolated. Which chain of causation most accurately explains this finding?

options.A: Friendly children are naturally happier, which makes stress feel less intense regardless of social support.
options.B: Supportive relationships provide emotional validation and practical help, which buffer the physiological stress response and speed recovery.
options.C: Isolated children experience more stressful events, so they have less practice at recovering.
options.D: Having friends increases self-esteem, which is the only factor that determines how quickly stress fades.

questions.explanation: Studies in social neuroscience show that perceived social support actually reduces cortisol levels (the primary stress hormone), directly buffering the body's stress response and enabling faster emotional and physical recovery. Option A is a distractor because it attributes recovery speed to personality rather than the mechanism of social support, reversing cause and effect.

questions.title: Wellbeing Frameworks — PERMA
questions.prompt: Martin Seligman proposed the PERMA model to describe human flourishing. A school redesigns its programme to include more student choice, creative projects, and community service. Which combination of PERMA elements is this redesign most directly targeting?

options.A: Positive Emotions and Relationships only
options.B: Engagement, Meaning, and Accomplishment
options.C: Positive Emotions, Meaning, and Relationships
options.D: Relationships, Accomplishment, and Positive Emotions

questions.explanation: Student choice promotes Engagement (deep involvement in tasks), creative projects and community service cultivate Meaning (sense of purpose), and completing these challenges builds Accomplishment (achievement of goals) — three distinct PERMA elements. Option C is tempting but community service primarily targets Meaning and Relationships more than Positive Emotions directly, and creative projects align more with Engagement than Positive Emotions.

questions.title: Responsibility and Collective Action
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'One individual's actions are too small to matter when solving big problems like inequality or environmental damage, so personal responsibility is not really meaningful.' Which response most effectively refutes this using the concept of collective action?

options.A: Personal actions do not matter individually, but governments can force enough people to act together to create change.
options.B: Individual actions create norms and demonstrate possibilities, and when many individuals act, the combined effect is substantial — collective change begins with personal choices.
options.C: The student is correct that individual action is ineffective, which is why only large institutions carry real responsibility.
options.D: Personal responsibility only applies to actions that directly harm another individual, not to large systemic problems.

questions.explanation: Collective action theory and social norm research show that individual behaviours signal what is acceptable, inspire others, and aggregate into large-scale change — for example, recycling habits spread through communities partly because individuals model the behaviour for peers. Option A is incorrect because it dismisses individual agency entirely, whereas research shows individual action is a catalyst for collective momentum.

questions.title: Physical Health and Chronic Stress
questions.prompt: A student is under constant pressure from exams, family conflict, and social difficulties. A doctor explains that long-term stress, unlike short-term stress, can weaken the immune system. Which explanation best accounts for this specific effect?

options.A: Chronic stress causes people to sleep less, and poor sleep is the sole reason immunity weakens.
options.B: Prolonged release of cortisol suppresses the activity of immune cells, making the body less able to fight infection.
options.C: Stress causes people to eat unhealthily, and poor nutrition is the only pathway linking stress to immune weakness.
options.D: The nervous system directly destroys immune cells when a person feels anxious for long periods.

questions.explanation: Psychoneuroimmunology research shows that sustained high cortisol levels directly suppress lymphocyte function — white blood cells needed to fight infection — making chronic stress a biological risk factor for illness independent of sleep or diet. Options A and C each identify one contributing pathway but wrongly claim it is the only mechanism, whereas the cortisol–immune link is the most direct and well-documented connection.

questions.title: Evaluating Personal Values
questions.prompt: Consider this scenario: Layla values both honesty and kindness. A friend shows her a drawing they are proud of, but Layla thinks it is not very good. These two values appear to conflict. Which reasoning process should Layla use to decide how to respond?

options.A: Always prioritise honesty over kindness, as truth-telling is an objectively higher moral value.
options.B: Reflect on the context and purpose: honest feedback can be kind if delivered thoughtfully, so the values may not be as opposed as they first appear.
options.C: Choose kindness in all social situations because preserving relationships is more important than truth.
options.D: Avoid responding at all so that neither value is compromised.

questions.explanation: Ethical reasoning recognises that apparent conflicts between values can often be resolved by examining context and manner — constructive, sensitive honesty is itself a form of kindness and respects the friend's growth. Option A applies a rigid hierarchy to values, but ethical philosophy does not universally rank honesty above kindness; the appropriate balance is context-dependent.

questions.title: Identity — Nature vs Nurture
questions.prompt: Identical twins raised in different countries often share some personality traits but develop different cultural values, languages, and social habits. What does this most precisely illustrate about the formation of identity?

options.A: Genetics determines personality completely, while environment only affects superficial preferences.
options.B: Environment determines identity entirely because twins with the same genes become different people.
options.C: Identity is shaped by an interaction between inherited traits and environmental experiences, with neither alone being sufficient.
options.D: Cultural identity is biologically inherited and cannot be influenced by where a person grows up.

questions.explanation: Twin studies consistently show that identical twins share a genetic baseline for traits like temperament (supporting a nature component), yet diverge significantly in language, cultural practices, and values when environments differ (supporting a nurture component) — demonstrating that identity emerges from the interplay of both. Option B overstates the environmental argument by ignoring the documented shared traits, and option A overstates genetics.

questions.title: Philosophy of Self — Continuity
questions.prompt: A philosopher poses this puzzle: if every single cell in your body is replaced over several years, and your memories and personality also change, in what sense are you the same person you were as a toddler? Which answer best represents the concept of psychological continuity?

options.A: You are the same person because your physical body, though changed, has never been completely replaced at one moment.
options.B: You are the same person because there is an overlapping chain of memories, intentions, and experiences that links your past self to your present self.
options.C: You are not the same person at all; identity is entirely reset when cells and memories change.
options.D: You are the same person only if other people who knew you as a toddler still recognise you.

questions.explanation: Psychological continuity theory, developed by philosophers like John Locke and later Derek Parfit, proposes that personal identity persists through an overlapping chain of connected memories and mental states rather than physical matter. Option A describes physical or biological continuity, which is a separate (and weaker) argument that does not address the philosophical puzzle about cell replacement directly.

questions.title: Conflict Resolution Strategies
questions.prompt: A student claims that the fairest way to resolve any disagreement is to split every disputed resource exactly in half, regardless of circumstances. Identify the flaw in this 'equality means identical shares' reasoning.

options.A: Equal shares are always unfair because people's needs are always different.
options.B: Identical shares ignore differing needs and contexts; fairness sometimes requires proportional or needs-based distribution rather than equal division.
options.C: Splitting resources equally is only fair when both people contributed the same amount of work.
options.D: Fairness cannot be defined objectively, so any division is equally valid.

questions.explanation: The distinction between equality (same for everyone) and equity (adjusted to need) is central to justice frameworks; for example, giving the same amount of food to a hungry person and a well-fed person treats an unequal situation as if it were equal. Option A goes too far by claiming equal shares are always unfair — there are situations where identical shares are genuinely the most equitable solution.

questions.title: Social Norms and Behaviour
questions.prompt: When students move to a new school, they often quickly adopt the behavioural norms of their peer group, sometimes abandoning habits from their previous school. Which concept from social psychology best explains this pattern?

options.A: Confirmation bias, because students seek information that confirms their existing habits.
options.B: Normative social influence, where people conform to group behaviour to gain acceptance and avoid rejection.
options.C: Informational social influence, where students assume the new group's behaviour must be the correct way to act.
options.D: Cognitive dissonance, where students change behaviour to reduce internal conflict between old and new habits.

questions.explanation: Normative social influence explains conformity driven by the desire to belong and be accepted by a group — the motivation is social approval rather than a belief that the group is necessarily correct. Option C (informational social influence) is also plausible and partially overlapping, but it specifically applies when a person is uncertain and uses others as a guide to truth — new students adopting norms for belonging fits the normative pathway more precisely.

questions.title: Reflection and Self-Improvement
questions.prompt: After a failed group project, a teacher asks students to reflect on what went wrong. Student X writes only about what other team members did poorly. Student Y analyses her own decisions, identifies one specific change she would make, and considers why she made those choices. Whose reflection demonstrates the deeper IB approach, and why?

options.A: Student X, because identifying others' errors gives a more complete picture of what went wrong.
options.B: Student Y, because genuine reflection requires examining one's own reasoning and actions to enable future growth.
options.C: Both equally, because effective reflection must always include both self-analysis and evaluation of others.
options.D: Student X, because blaming the team shows higher critical thinking about external factors.

questions.explanation: The IB PYP concept of reflection specifically involves looking inward at one's own thinking and choices — metacognitive reflection — because only by understanding your own decisions can you make different ones in the future. Student X's approach focuses on others, which may have some analytical value but does not constitute the self-directed inquiry that meaningful reflection requires.

questions.title: Form of Human Relationships
questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the same action — for example, offering advice — can strengthen one friendship but damage another?

options.A: The quality of advice determines its impact; only accurate advice strengthens relationships.
options.B: Relationships have different norms, histories, and power dynamics, so the same action carries different meaning depending on the relationship's form.
options.C: People's emotional states at the time are the only variable that determines whether an action helps or harms a relationship.
options.D: Actions always have a fixed social meaning that is interpreted the same way across all friendships.

questions.explanation: The IB PYP key concept of 'form' applies here — relationships have particular structures, expectations, and histories that shape how any action is interpreted; in a trusting long-term friendship, advice may feel supportive, while in a new or unequal relationship it may feel intrusive or critical. Option C oversimplifies by reducing all variation to momentary emotional state, ignoring the structural features of the relationship itself.

questions.title: Change and Personal Development
questions.prompt: A student reflects: 'I used to be terrified of speaking in front of the class. Now I enjoy it. But I still feel like the same person.' Which of the following most accurately accounts for how significant personal change and a stable sense of self can coexist?

options.A: The student's core identity has actually changed entirely; they are simply not aware of it.
options.B: Core values and the narrative thread connecting past and present experiences remain stable even as specific skills, fears, and traits evolve.
options.C: Personality is fixed at birth, so any perceived change in behaviour is only superficial and temporary.
options.D: The student feels the same because their physical appearance has not changed, which anchors identity.

questions.explanation: Narrative identity theory (developed by psychologist Dan McAdams) proposes that people maintain a coherent sense of self by constructing a life story that integrates change and continuity — specific characteristics can develop dramatically while core values and the connecting narrative remain stable. Option A is incorrect because it denies the felt continuity the student experiences, which is itself a psychologically real and meaningful phenomenon.

questions.title: Cognitive Biases and Decision-Making
questions.prompt: A student always trusts the first piece of information they hear about a topic, even when later evidence suggests something different. For example, they heard that a classmate was 'difficult' before meeting them, and despite many positive interactions, still views them negatively. Which cognitive bias does this most precisely describe?

options.A: Confirmation bias, because the student only seeks evidence that confirms their existing negative view.
options.B: The halo effect, because one negative trait is causing the student to rate all traits negatively.
options.C: Anchoring bias, because the first piece of information (the label 'difficult') is disproportionately influencing all later judgements.
options.D: Attribution error, because the student is blaming the classmate's character rather than considering situational factors.

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias specifically describes the tendency to rely heavily on the first information received as a reference point for all subsequent judgements — here, the initial label 'difficult' acts as an anchor that distorts evaluation of later positive evidence. Confirmation bias (option A) is a strong distractor but technically refers to actively seeking confirming evidence, whereas anchoring is about the disproportionate weight given to first information even passively.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Basics
questions.prompt: A student receives a low grade and thinks, 'I am just not a maths person.' Which response would best reflect a growth mindset approach to this situation?

options.A: Accept the grade and avoid maths tasks in the future to protect self-esteem
options.B: Ask the teacher for extra feedback and practise the specific skills that caused errors
options.C: Compare results with classmates to judge whether the grade was fair
options.D: Conclude that the test was poorly designed and therefore not meaningful

questions.explanation: A growth mindset, developed by Carol Dweck, holds that ability can be improved through effort and targeted strategy; seeking feedback and practising weak areas directly applies this belief. Option A reflects a fixed mindset — avoiding challenge to protect self-image — which is the opposite of growth mindset thinking.

questions.title: Neuroscience of Stress
questions.prompt: When the brain detects a threat, the amygdala sends an alarm signal. Which part of the brain is most responsible for regulating this alarm and helping a person think calmly before reacting?

options.A: The cerebellum, which coordinates physical movement and balance
options.B: The hippocampus, which stores and retrieves long-term memories
options.C: The prefrontal cortex, which manages reasoning and impulse control
options.D: The brain stem, which controls automatic functions like heartbeat

questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is associated with executive functions including emotional regulation, decision-making, and impulse control; it can dampen the amygdala's alarm response when fully engaged. The hippocampus (option B) is a strong distractor because it interacts with the amygdala in memory formation, but it does not regulate emotional reactions in the same way.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Having the right to free expression means I can say anything I want, anywhere, with no consequences.' Identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Free expression is not recognised in the UNCRC, so the claim has no legal basis at all
options.B: Rights always come paired with responsibilities, and expression that harms others can be legitimately limited
options.C: Only adults are granted free expression rights; children must wait until they turn 18
options.D: Free expression applies only to written communication, not to spoken words

questions.explanation: The UNCRC Article 13 grants children the right to free expression but explicitly notes that this right carries responsibilities and may be restricted to protect the rights or reputations of others; rights and responsibilities are interdependent. Option A is wrong because free expression is indeed recognised in the UNCRC, making it a plausible but factually incorrect distractor.

questions.title: Philosophical Self-Concept
questions.prompt: The philosopher John Locke argued that personal identity over time is based on continuity of memory rather than continuity of the physical body. Which scenario would most directly challenge Locke's view?

options.A: A person changes their career goals after moving to a new country
options.B: A person with severe amnesia cannot recall their past yet others still recognise them as the same individual
options.C: A person's body changes significantly between childhood and adulthood
options.D: A person adopts a new cultural identity after living abroad for several years

questions.explanation: If identity depends on memory continuity, then someone with severe amnesia who has lost their memories should no longer be the 'same person' — yet we still legally and socially treat them as the same individual, which challenges Locke's memory theory. Option C is a distractor because Locke's theory was specifically designed to move identity away from bodily continuity, so physical change actually supports rather than challenges his view.

questions.title: Ethical Frameworks Compared
questions.prompt: A consequentialist and a virtue ethicist both observe a student cheating on a test. Compare their likely responses: which statement most accurately describes the key difference in how each would evaluate the act?

options.A: The consequentialist focuses on what kind of person the student is becoming; the virtue ethicist focuses on the outcomes for others
options.B: The consequentialist evaluates the act by its results; the virtue ethicist evaluates it by the character trait it expresses
options.C: Both agree the act is wrong, so there is no meaningful difference between the two frameworks here
options.D: The consequentialist uses religious scripture to judge the act; the virtue ethicist uses social agreements

questions.explanation: Consequentialism judges actions by their outcomes (e.g., unfair advantage gained, trust broken in the class), while virtue ethics asks whether the action reflects a virtuous character trait — cheating expresses dishonesty, a vice. Option A reverses the frameworks, making it the most tempting distractor for students who confuse the two theories.

questions.title: Cultural Identity Formation
questions.prompt: Examine this statement: 'Cultural identity is fixed at birth and does not change throughout a person's lifetime.' Which piece of evidence most directly refutes this claim?

options.A: People inherit physical traits from their parents that remain largely stable over time
options.B: Many immigrants adopt elements of a new culture while retaining aspects of their heritage, showing identity evolving over time
options.C: Governments officially record a person's nationality at birth in legal documents
options.D: Historical records show that cultural traditions are often passed down across many generations unchanged

questions.explanation: The experience of immigrants who blend two cultures — known as acculturation or bicultural identity — directly demonstrates that cultural identity is fluid and can shift in response to new environments and experiences. Option D is a plausible distractor because tradition-preservation might seem to support fixed identity, but it describes cultural practices rather than an individual's personal cultural identity.

questions.title: Mental Health Stigma
questions.prompt: Why does stigma surrounding mental health conditions make it harder for people to seek help, even when effective treatments are available?

options.A: Stigma increases the financial cost of therapy, making it unaffordable for most people
options.B: Stigma causes people to fear social judgement or rejection, so they hide symptoms rather than seek support
options.C: Stigma legally prevents doctors from diagnosing mental health conditions in minors
options.D: Stigma reduces the number of medical researchers who study mental health treatments

questions.explanation: Social stigma creates shame and fear of being labelled 'weak' or 'dangerous,' which leads individuals to conceal their struggles rather than risk social exclusion — a well-documented barrier in public health research. Option A is plausible because cost is a real barrier to mental health care, but it describes a structural barrier rather than the specific mechanism of stigma itself.

questions.title: Adolescent Brain Development
questions.prompt: Neuroscientists note that the prefrontal cortex is not fully developed until the mid-20s. Which behaviour pattern in teenagers is most directly explained by this fact?

options.A: Teenagers tend to need more sleep than adults because their circadian rhythms shift later
options.B: Teenagers often show stronger language acquisition skills than adults learning a second language
options.C: Teenagers are more likely to take risks without fully weighing long-term consequences
options.D: Teenagers typically have faster physical reaction times than older adults

questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex governs impulse control, risk assessment, and long-term planning; its incomplete development means the emotional limbic system often overrides careful reasoning, increasing risk-taking behaviour in adolescents. Options A and D are both true adolescent characteristics but are explained by different biological mechanisms — circadian rhythm shifts and motor development — not PFC maturation.

questions.title: Maslow's Hierarchy Needs
questions.prompt: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, a student who arrives at school hungry and worried about her family's housing situation is unlikely to engage fully in learning. Which level of the hierarchy best explains this?

options.A: Esteem needs — the student lacks recognition from teachers and peers
options.B: Physiological and safety needs — basic survival and security must be met before higher needs can be addressed
options.C: Self-actualisation needs — the student has not yet discovered her personal potential
options.D: Love and belonging needs — the student is missing meaningful social connections at school

questions.explanation: Maslow's model places physiological needs (food, shelter) and safety needs at the base of the hierarchy; until these are sufficiently met, attention and energy cannot effectively be directed toward learning or esteem. Option D is a strong distractor because social connection is also a lower-level need in Maslow's model, but the scenario specifically names hunger and housing insecurity, which map to the two most foundational levels.

questions.title: Cognitive Dissonance
questions.prompt: A student strongly believes in environmental sustainability but regularly takes long, unnecessary car journeys when she could walk. The discomfort she feels about this contradiction is known as what?

options.A: Confirmation bias
options.B: Cognitive dissonance
options.C: Attribution error
options.D: Emotional dysregulation

questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance, described by Leon Festinger, is the psychological discomfort that arises when a person holds two contradictory beliefs or when their actions conflict with their stated beliefs — exactly what the student experiences. Confirmation bias (option A) is a plausible distractor because it also involves beliefs, but it refers to selectively seeking information that confirms existing views, not the discomfort of internal contradiction.

questions.title: Empathy vs Sympathy
questions.prompt: A friend tells you she failed an audition she worked hard for. You respond, 'That sounds really painful — I remember how crushed I felt when I didn't make the team.' Which concept does your response best demonstrate?

options.A: Sympathy, because you are feeling sorry for your friend from a distance
options.B: Projection, because you are placing your own feelings onto your friend's experience
options.C: Empathy, because you are connecting emotionally by drawing on a similar personal experience
options.D: Active listening, because you are paraphrasing exactly what your friend said

questions.explanation: Empathy involves stepping into another person's emotional experience and connecting with it, often by drawing on one's own similar feelings — which is exactly what the response does by referencing a comparable disappointment. Sympathy (option A) is a common distractor but involves feeling for someone from the outside rather than genuinely connecting with their inner emotional state.

questions.title: Social Identity Theory
questions.prompt: Psychologist Henri Tajfel found that simply placing people into arbitrary groups caused them to favour their own group over others. What does this suggest about the origins of in-group bias?

options.A: In-group bias only develops when groups have genuinely competed for resources over a long period
options.B: In-group bias is rooted in deep cultural traditions that are passed down through generations
options.C: In-group bias can emerge from group membership alone, even without real differences or conflict
options.D: In-group bias is primarily caused by media representations of different social groups

questions.explanation: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm experiments showed that even random, meaningless group assignments (e.g., preferring one painting style over another) were enough to trigger favouritism, demonstrating that group membership itself — not history or competition — can generate bias. Option A is a strong distractor because realistic conflict theory (Sherif) does link bias to resource competition, but Tajfel's work specifically refutes the idea that competition is necessary.

questions.title: Autonomy and Decision-Making
questions.prompt: Evaluate this claim: 'Teenagers should always follow adult advice because adults have more experience and therefore always know what is best.' Which response best identifies a limitation of this view?

options.A: The claim is correct because adult brain development is complete, making their judgement always superior
options.B: The claim ignores that developing autonomy and practising decision-making is itself essential to adolescent growth
options.C: The claim is wrong because teenagers always have better access to current information than adults
options.D: The claim overlooks the fact that adults are legally required to consult teenagers before making any decisions

questions.explanation: Developmental psychology emphasises that adolescents need opportunities to make their own choices — including mistakes — in order to build identity, self-efficacy, and decision-making skills; always deferring to adults prevents this growth. Option A is a plausible distractor because adult cognitive development is more complete, but 'more experience' does not equate to knowing what is best in every specific, personal context for a particular teenager.

questions.title: Stereotype Threat
questions.prompt: Research by Claude Steele shows that reminding students of a negative stereotype about their group just before a test can lower their performance, even if they personally reject the stereotype. What is this phenomenon called?

options.A: Self-fulfilling prophecy
options.B: Implicit bias
options.C: Stereotype threat
options.D: Learned helplessness

questions.explanation: Stereotype threat, coined by Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson, describes the anxiety of confirming a negative group stereotype that can consume cognitive resources and depress test performance, even among high-achieving individuals who do not personally believe the stereotype. Self-fulfilling prophecy (option A) is a strong distractor because it also involves expectations affecting outcomes, but it operates through changed behaviour over time, not the acute anxiety of stereotype activation immediately before a task.

questions.title: Positive Psychology PERMA
questions.prompt: Martin Seligman's PERMA model proposes five elements of wellbeing. A student who regularly achieves goals she sets for herself is benefiting from which element of the model?

options.A: Positive Emotion — she feels happy when goals are achieved
options.B: Relationships — her goals are connected to supporting others
options.C: Accomplishment — she gains wellbeing from achieving and mastering goals
options.D: Engagement — she is fully absorbed in the process of goal-setting

questions.explanation: In Seligman's PERMA model, Accomplishment (or Achievement) refers specifically to pursuing and reaching goals for their own sake, which contributes independently to wellbeing and flourishing. Option A is a strong distractor because achieving goals does produce positive emotion, but Positive Emotion in PERMA refers to the broader experience of pleasant feelings, not specifically the satisfaction of goal attainment.

questions.title: Moral Development Stages
questions.prompt: A 13-year-old says, 'I won't cheat because cheating is against the rules and I could get in trouble.' According to Kohlberg's stages of moral development, which level of reasoning does this reflect?

options.A: Post-conventional — the student is reasoning from universal ethical principles
options.B: Pre-conventional — the student is motivated by avoiding punishment
options.C: Conventional — the student is motivated by maintaining social order and following rules
options.D: Pre-moral — the student has not yet developed any genuine ethical reasoning

questions.explanation: In Kohlberg's framework, pre-conventional reasoning is driven by personal consequences — specifically obedience and punishment avoidance at Stage 1; the student's focus on getting in trouble places her squarely here. Option C is a strong distractor because rule-following sounds like conventional morality, but conventional reasoning is motivated by maintaining relationships and social systems, not by personal punishment avoidance.

questions.title: Intersectionality of Identity
questions.prompt: The concept of intersectionality, developed by Kimberlé Crenshaw, argues that a person's experience of discrimination cannot be understood by looking at each aspect of their identity separately. Why is this important when analysing inequality?

options.A: It shows that discrimination only affects people who belong to more than three minority groups at once
options.B: It demonstrates that multiple aspects of identity can interact to create unique and compounded experiences of disadvantage
options.C: It proves that economic class is the most important factor in determining a person's life outcomes
options.D: It suggests that individuals should focus on one aspect of their identity to avoid confusion

questions.explanation: Crenshaw developed intersectionality to show that categories like race, gender, and class do not operate independently — their combination creates distinct patterns of disadvantage that cannot be understood by examining each category alone. Option C is a plausible distractor because class is a significant factor in inequality, but intersectionality explicitly argues against prioritising any single identity category over others.

questions.title: Active Listening Skills
questions.prompt: During a conversation, a student nods, maintains eye contact, avoids interrupting, and then paraphrases what the speaker said before responding. Which communication skill is this student demonstrating?

options.A: Assertiveness, because the student is clearly expressing their own position
options.B: Persuasion, because paraphrasing helps convince the speaker to change their view
options.C: Active listening, because the student demonstrates attention and checks understanding before responding
options.D: Negotiation, because the student is working toward a shared agreement with the speaker

questions.explanation: Active listening involves physical signals of attention (eye contact, nodding), restraint from interruption, and comprehension checks such as paraphrasing — all of which the student demonstrates. Assertiveness (option A) is a distractor because confident communication skills share some surface features, but assertiveness specifically concerns expressing one's own needs and views, not demonstrating attention to another's.

questions.title: Locus of Control
questions.prompt: Student A believes her exam results depend mostly on how hard she studies. Student B believes his results depend mostly on luck and how strict the marker is. Which psychological concept best describes the difference between these two students?

options.A: Self-efficacy — Student A has higher confidence in her abilities than Student B
options.B: Locus of control — Student A has an internal locus while Student B has an external locus
options.C: Attribution style — Student A makes global attributions and Student B makes specific ones
options.D: Resilience — Student A bounces back from failure more effectively than Student B

questions.explanation: Locus of control, developed by Julian Rotter, describes whether people attribute outcomes to their own actions (internal) or to outside forces like luck and others (external) — Student A is internal and Student B is external. Self-efficacy (option A) is a strong distractor because both concepts relate to belief in one's ability to succeed, but self-efficacy specifically concerns confidence in performing a particular task, not the broader belief about where control resides.

questions.title: Conflict Resolution Styles
questions.prompt: In the Thomas-Kilmann conflict model, a person who consistently gives in to others' preferences to avoid disagreement, even at personal cost, is using which conflict style?

options.A: Compromising — both parties give up something to reach a middle ground
options.B: Collaborating — both parties work together to find a solution that satisfies everyone
options.C: Accommodating — one person prioritises the other's needs over their own
options.D: Avoiding — the person withdraws from the conflict entirely without engaging

questions.explanation: In the Thomas-Kilmann model, accommodating means being cooperative but unassertive — consistently placing the other person's interests first, often to preserve the relationship at one's own expense. Avoiding (option D) is a common distractor because both styles can appear passive, but avoiding involves withdrawing from conflict altogether rather than actively yielding to the other person's preferences.

questions.title: Biological Basis of Emotion
questions.prompt: The James-Lange theory of emotion proposes that emotions arise from our interpretation of bodily changes. According to this theory, what is the correct sequence of events when you see a dangerous dog and feel afraid?

options.A: You see the dog → you feel afraid → your heart races as a result of the fear
options.B: You see the dog → your heart races → you interpret this physical response as fear
options.C: You feel afraid → your brain signals danger → your body prepares to run
options.D: Your heart races → the environment triggers the sensation → the brain labels it as excitement

questions.explanation: The James-Lange theory reverses the common assumption: the physical response (racing heart, tense muscles) comes first, and the conscious emotion is the brain's interpretation of those bodily changes — we feel afraid because we notice our heart racing. Option A reflects the intuitive but opposite sequence (emotion causes physical reaction), which is exactly what James and Lange argued against.

questions.title: Child Rights and Participation
questions.prompt: A school decides to redesign the playground without consulting students. A student argues this violates her rights. Which UNCRC article most directly supports her argument?

options.A: Article 28 — the right to education in a safe environment
options.B: Article 31 — the right to rest, leisure, play, and participation in cultural life
options.C: Article 12 — the right to have views heard in decisions that affect them
options.D: Article 19 — the right to protection from all forms of violence

questions.explanation: UNCRC Article 12 specifically grants children the right to express their views freely on all matters affecting them, and states that those views must be given due weight — playground redesign directly affects students, making Article 12 the most relevant article. Article 31 (option B) is a plausible distractor because it protects the right to play and recreation, but it does not address participation in decision-making processes.

questions.title: Belonging and Social Exclusion
questions.prompt: Research by Roy Baumeister suggests that social exclusion can impair cognitive performance and increase aggressive behaviour. What does this finding imply about the role of belonging in human wellbeing?

options.A: Belonging is a luxury need that only matters once physical and safety needs are fully satisfied
options.B: The need to belong is a fundamental human motivation with measurable effects on behaviour and cognition
options.C: Social exclusion only affects people who already have low self-esteem before the exclusion occurs
options.D: Humans can adapt fully to social exclusion over time with no lasting negative effects

questions.explanation: Baumeister's research on the 'need to belong' demonstrates that social exclusion has concrete, measurable consequences including reduced cognitive function and increased aggression, indicating that belonging is a core psychological need, not merely a preference. Option A is a tempting distractor because Maslow's hierarchy places belonging above physiological and safety needs, but Baumeister's evidence shows the need operates powerfully regardless of whether 'lower' needs are fully met.

questions.title: Nature vs Nurture in Identity
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Who I am is entirely determined by my genes — environment plays no real role.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from developmental psychology.

options.A: The claim is correct because identical twins always develop identical personalities regardless of where they grow up
options.B: The claim is partially supported because genes determine intelligence completely, though environment shapes personality
options.C: The claim is an oversimplification because identical twins raised apart often show differences, demonstrating environmental influence
options.D: The claim is correct because epigenetics proves that genes entirely override environmental factors in shaping identity

questions.explanation: Studies of identical twins raised in different environments show that while they share many traits due to identical genes, they also develop measurable differences in personality, values, and behaviour — directly demonstrating environmental influence on identity. Option A is factually wrong and serves as a distractor by misrepresenting twin study findings; identical twins raised apart do not always have identical personalities.

questions.title: Resilience and Adversity
questions.prompt: Psychologists distinguish between resilience and simply avoiding difficulty. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates genuine resilience?

options.A: A student chooses only subjects she already excels at to maintain a high grade point average
options.B: A student withdraws from the school play after a difficult rehearsal to avoid further stress
options.C: A student experiences a serious setback in a competition, reflects on it, and returns with adjusted strategies
options.D: A student asks a parent to solve every difficult problem she faces so she can focus on enjoying school

questions.explanation: Resilience is defined as the capacity to adapt positively and recover after adversity; it requires experiencing difficulty, processing it, and continuing forward — which the student in option C demonstrates through reflection and strategy adjustment. Options A and D both avoid adversity altogether rather than demonstrating adaptation in the face of it, making them opposite to the definition of resilience.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Foundations
questions.prompt: A student receives a low mark on a maths test and thinks, 'I'm just not a maths person.' Which response best demonstrates a growth mindset approach to this situation?

options.A: Accept the mark and move to subjects that feel more natural
options.B: Analyse which specific strategies failed and adjust study methods for the next attempt
options.C: Ask the teacher to grade more leniently on future assessments
options.D: Compare the result with classmates to judge whether the mark was fair

questions.explanation: Growth mindset, developed by Carol Dweck, holds that ability can be expanded through deliberate effort and strategy adjustment — identifying which strategies failed directly applies this belief. Option A reflects a fixed mindset by treating ability as permanent and redirecting away from challenge rather than toward it.

questions.title: Neuroscience of Stress Response
questions.prompt: During a stressful event, the brain's amygdala triggers a release of cortisol and adrenaline. What is the primary short-term effect of this response on a person's ability to think through complex problems?

options.A: It enhances long-term memory formation so the event is remembered clearly
options.B: It sharpens creative thinking by increasing dopamine in the prefrontal cortex
options.C: It reduces activity in the prefrontal cortex, making careful reasoning harder
options.D: It strengthens empathy by activating mirror neurons more intensely

questions.explanation: High cortisol levels temporarily suppress prefrontal cortex function — the region responsible for rational decision-making and complex problem-solving — which is why people often 'freeze' or react impulsively under stress. Option A is a distractor because while emotional events can be memorable, acute stress often impairs the consolidation of precise factual details.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities Balance
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'I have the right to post whatever I want online because freedom of expression is a human right.' Evaluate this claim. Which response most accurately identifies its limitation?

options.A: Freedom of expression is not recognised as a human right by the UNCRC
options.B: Rights are always absolute and cannot be limited under any circumstances
options.C: Rights exist alongside responsibilities, and expression that harms others can be legitimately restricted
options.D: Online spaces are not covered by human rights frameworks because they are privately owned

questions.explanation: Article 13 of the UNCRC grants freedom of expression but explicitly states it may be restricted to protect the rights and reputations of others — rights and responsibilities are interdependent, not absolute. Option A is incorrect because freedom of expression is specifically recognised in Article 13 of the UNCRC.

questions.title: Cultural Identity Formation
questions.prompt: A student raised in Japan moves to Brazil at age 13 and begins adopting new cultural practices while still maintaining Japanese traditions. What term best describes the process of adapting to a new culture without losing one's original cultural identity?

options.A: Assimilation
options.B: Acculturation
options.C: Socialisation
options.D: Enculturation

questions.explanation: Acculturation refers to the process by which an individual adopts elements of a new culture while retaining aspects of their original culture — it is a two-way adaptation. Assimilation (Option A) describes a more complete absorption into the new culture, where the original cultural identity is largely replaced, which does not match the scenario described.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning Frameworks
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Lying is wrong because it treats other people as a means to an end rather than as ends in themselves.' Which ethical framework is this student applying?

options.A: Utilitarianism
options.B: Virtue ethics
options.C: Kantian deontology
options.D: Social contract theory

questions.explanation: The phrase 'means to an end rather than ends in themselves' is Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative — specifically his Formula of Humanity, which holds that people must always be treated as having intrinsic worth. Utilitarianism (Option A) would evaluate lying based on whether it maximises overall happiness, not on the inherent dignity of persons.

questions.title: Self-Esteem vs Self-Efficacy
questions.prompt: Compare self-esteem and self-efficacy. Which statement correctly identifies the key difference between these two psychological concepts?

options.A: Self-esteem refers to confidence in completing a specific task, while self-efficacy is a general sense of overall worth
options.B: Self-esteem is how a person judges their overall worth, while self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task
