questions.explanation: SDT identifies autonomy (feeling volitional control over one's actions), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (feeling connected to others) as the three innate psychological needs whose satisfaction supports intrinsic motivation and wellbeing. Option B lists Maslow-related terms, which is the most common confusion for students who have studied both theories.

questions.title: Implicit Bias and Self-Awareness
questions.prompt: What would a student most likely discover if they completed an Implicit Association Test (IAT) honestly?

options.A: That their explicit beliefs and implicit associations are always identical
options.B: That implicit associations can exist independently of consciously held beliefs
options.C: That implicit bias only affects people who have been exposed to prejudiced upbringings
options.D: That unconscious bias disappears once a person becomes aware of it

questions.explanation: IAT research consistently shows that individuals can hold implicit associations that contradict their explicit, conscious values — for instance, someone who consciously endorses racial equality may still show an implicit preference for one group. Option D is wrong because awareness of bias does not automatically eliminate it; deliberate and sustained effort is required.

questions.title: Philosophical Self: Hume's Bundle Theory
questions.prompt: David Hume argued that when he looked inward, he never discovered a persistent 'self' — only a bundle of perceptions. Which view of personal identity does this most directly challenge?

options.A: The social constructivist view that identity is shaped by culture
options.B: The Cartesian view that there is a unified, enduring thinking substance
options.C: The behaviourist view that the self is defined entirely by observable actions
options.D: The existentialist view that identity is created through choices

questions.explanation: Hume's bundle theory directly challenges Descartes' view of a continuous, unified thinking substance (the cogito) — Hume denied that introspection reveals any such permanent self, finding only fleeting perceptions. Option D is plausible because existentialism also questions fixed identity, but existentialists like Sartre still affirm a choosing subject, which Hume's theory undermines most directly.

questions.title: Positive Psychology PERMA Model
questions.prompt: Martin Seligman's PERMA model identifies five elements of wellbeing. Which of the following correctly lists all five?

options.A: Positivity, Empathy, Resilience, Mindfulness, Achievement
options.B: Positive emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment
options.C: Pleasure, Esteem, Relatedness, Motivation, Autonomy
options.D: Positive emotions, Empathy, Resilience, Meaning, Achievement

questions.explanation: Seligman's PERMA acronym stands for Positive emotions, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment — five measurable elements he argues together constitute flourishing. Option D substitutes 'Empathy' and 'Resilience' for 'Engagement' and 'Relationships,' which are plausible-sounding but incorrect terms that trip up students who know parts of the model.

questions.title: Social Learning Theory
questions.prompt: Albert Bandura's Bobo Doll experiments were designed to test which hypothesis about how children acquire behaviour?

options.A: Children acquire aggressive behaviour only through direct reinforcement
options.B: Children can learn new behaviours by observing and imitating models, without direct reinforcement
options.C: Children imitate behaviour only when the model is a parent or primary caregiver
options.D: Aggressive behaviour in children is primarily determined by genetic factors

questions.explanation: Bandura's experiments showed that children who watched an adult model act aggressively toward the Bobo Doll replicated those behaviours without being rewarded — demonstrating observational learning. Option A represents the behaviourist position that Bandura was specifically challenging, making it a meaningful distractor for students who confuse social learning theory with classical or operant conditioning.

questions.title: Mental Health Stigma
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Stigma around mental illness exists mainly because people don't want to admit weakness.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from social psychology.

options.A: Fully accurate, because research confirms personal fear of weakness is the single cause of stigma
options.B: Partially inaccurate, because stigma also arises from structural factors such as media portrayals and cultural norms
options.C: Fully inaccurate, because stigma has been completely eliminated in educated communities
options.D: Fully accurate, because admitting mental illness is universally perceived as weakness across all cultures

questions.explanation: Social psychology identifies multiple drivers of mental health stigma, including media misrepresentation (e.g., associating mental illness with violence), cultural norms, and institutional practices — not merely individual fear of appearing weak. Option D is wrong because cross-cultural research shows wide variation in how mental health is perceived and stigmatised.

questions.title: Locus of Control
questions.prompt: Julian Rotter's concept of 'locus of control' divides individuals into two broad orientations. Which pair of descriptions correctly contrasts internal and external locus of control?

options.A: Internal: outcomes are controlled by luck; External: outcomes are controlled by effort
options.B: Internal: believes personal actions determine outcomes; External: believes fate or others control outcomes
options.C: Internal: motivated by extrinsic rewards; External: motivated by intrinsic values
options.D: Internal: focuses on others' needs; External: focuses on self-interest

questions.explanation: Rotter defined internal locus of control as the belief that one's own behaviour and choices drive outcomes, while external locus of control reflects the belief that outside forces such as luck, powerful others, or fate determine what happens. Option A inverts the definitions — a common error students make when they confuse 'internal' with 'inside information' rather than the source of perceived control.

questions.title: Emotional Intelligence Components
questions.prompt: Daniel Goleman popularised emotional intelligence (EI). Which of the following is NOT one of the five core domains in Goleman's model?

options.A: Self-regulation
options.B: Empathy
options.C: Abstract reasoning
options.D: Social skills

questions.explanation: Goleman's five domains are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills — none of which is abstract reasoning, which belongs to traditional IQ frameworks rather than EI. Options A, B, and D are genuine components of Goleman's model, making them strong distractors for students who partially remember the framework.

questions.title: Bioethics and Personal Identity
questions.prompt: If a person's entire set of memories could be erased and replaced with new ones, which philosophical question about personal identity would this most directly raise?

options.A: Whether genetic continuity is sufficient for personal identity
options.B: Whether psychological continuity — particularly memory — is necessary for being the same person over time
options.C: Whether social relationships alone define who a person is
options.D: Whether the soul is a biological or metaphysical concept

questions.explanation: Locke's memory theory of personal identity argues that what makes you the same person over time is psychological continuity, especially memory connecting past and present experiences. This thought experiment directly tests that claim. Option A concerns a different debate — biological continuity — which would not be disrupted by memory replacement.

questions.title: Adolescent Social Identity
questions.prompt: Henri Tajfel's Social Identity Theory (SIT) predicts that people tend to favour the groups they belong to. What term describes the tendency to view one's own group more positively than out-groups?

options.A: Outgroup homogeneity effect
options.B: Ingroup bias
options.C: Social loafing
options.D: Attribution error

questions.explanation: Tajfel and Turner's SIT identifies ingroup bias — the tendency to evaluate members of one's own group more favourably — as a core mechanism by which people maintain positive social identity. Option A (outgroup homogeneity) is related but describes a different phenomenon: perceiving out-group members as more similar to each other than in-group members are.

questions.title: Wellbeing and Eudaimonia
questions.prompt: Aristotle distinguished between two conceptions of happiness: hedonia and eudaimonia. Which statement correctly contrasts them in the context of wellbeing?

options.A: Hedonia refers to long-term flourishing through virtue; eudaimonia refers to immediate pleasure
options.B: Hedonia refers to the pursuit of pleasure and avoidance of pain; eudaimonia refers to flourishing through living in accordance with one's highest potential
options.C: Both terms describe the same concept — sustained positive emotion over a lifetime
options.D: Eudaimonia refers to physical wellbeing; hedonia refers to spiritual wellbeing

questions.explanation: Aristotle valued eudaimonia — a life of virtuous activity and realising one's potential — over hedonia, which simply seeks pleasure and avoids pain. Option A inverts the two concepts, which is the most frequent error among students who have encountered both terms but not memorised their exact definitions.

questions.title: Growth Mindset Foundations
questions.prompt: Carol Dweck's research distinguishes between a fixed mindset and a growth mindset. Which statement most accurately captures the core difference between the two?

options.A: A fixed mindset focuses on effort over talent, while a growth mindset focuses on innate ability.
options.B: A growth mindset holds that intelligence and abilities can be developed through dedication and learning, while a fixed mindset treats them as static traits.
options.C: A fixed mindset is associated with high achievement, while a growth mindset is associated with lower academic standards.
options.D: A growth mindset means believing all people are equally talented if they try hard enough.

questions.explanation: Dweck's research shows that individuals with a growth mindset believe abilities are malleable and improve with effort, leading to greater resilience and achievement. The fixed mindset, by contrast, treats intelligence as a set trait — not, as option A inverts, the other way around.

questions.title: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
questions.prompt: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is frequently referenced in wellbeing frameworks. According to the original model, which level of need must generally be satisfied before 'esteem needs' can be meaningfully pursued?

options.A: Self-actualisation
options.B: Cognitive needs
options.C: Belongingness and love needs
options.D: Aesthetic needs

questions.explanation: In Maslow's original five-level hierarchy, belongingness and love needs (social connection, friendship, intimacy) sit directly below esteem needs, and must be substantially met before esteem — achievement, status, respect — becomes the primary motivator. Self-actualisation is above esteem, not below it, making option A incorrect.

questions.title: Neuroscience of Stress Response
questions.prompt: When a person perceives a threat, the amygdala triggers the release of adrenaline and cortisol. What is the primary physiological purpose of this acute stress response?

options.A: To suppress the immune system permanently so energy is redirected to digestion.
options.B: To increase long-term memory consolidation in the hippocampus.
options.C: To prepare the body for rapid physical action by increasing heart rate, blood flow to muscles, and alertness.
options.D: To activate the parasympathetic nervous system and promote relaxation.

questions.explanation: The fight-or-flight response evolved to mobilise the body for immediate physical action: adrenaline raises heart rate, dilates airways, and redirects blood to skeletal muscles. Option D describes the opposite — parasympathetic activation, which is the rest-and-digest state that stress hormones actively suppress.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge — Knower's Perspective
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, the 'knower's perspective' is identified as a factor that shapes how we acquire and interpret knowledge. Which of the following best illustrates how a knower's perspective can act as a limitation on knowledge?

options.A: A researcher uses a double-blind trial to remove experimenter bias from drug testing results.
options.B: A historian raised in one country interprets the same treaty differently from a historian raised in the opposing nation.
options.C: A mathematician checks a proof by deriving it independently using a different method.
options.D: A scientist publishes data that contradicts their own hypothesis.

questions.explanation: The knower's perspective encompasses cultural background, personal experience, and values — all of which can bias interpretation of the same evidence. Two historians interpreting the same treaty differently based on national upbringing is a classic illustration. Options A, C, and D all describe methods that reduce or overcome bias rather than illustrate it as a limitation.

questions.title: Erikson's Stages of Development
questions.prompt: Erik Erikson proposed eight psychosocial stages of development. Which stage is most directly associated with the central challenge faced by most adolescents aged 12–18?

options.A: Autonomy vs. shame and doubt
options.B: Industry vs. inferiority
options.C: Identity vs. role confusion
options.D: Intimacy vs. isolation

questions.explanation: Erikson placed 'Identity vs. role confusion' in adolescence (approximately ages 12–18), during which young people explore who they are — their values, beliefs, and future roles. 'Intimacy vs. isolation' comes next in young adulthood, and 'Industry vs. inferiority' occurs in middle childhood — both common distractors for this stage.

questions.title: Utilitarian Ethical Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'We should adopt the school policy that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number of students, even if a small minority are significantly disadvantaged.' Evaluate which ethical framework this position most closely reflects.

options.A: Virtue ethics, because it focuses on developing good character within the school community.
options.B: Utilitarianism, because it judges actions by their consequences and aims to maximise overall welfare.
options.C: Kantian deontology, because it applies a universal principle that everyone should follow.
options.D: Social contract theory, because it references what the majority of people have agreed upon.

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism, associated with Bentham and Mill, holds that the morally correct action maximises aggregate well-being — precisely what the student describes. Kantian deontology is often confused here because it also uses universalisability, but Kant explicitly rejected outcomes as the basis for moral duty, making option C incorrect.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias and Self-Identity
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following reasoning: 'I have always believed I am bad at mathematics, so when I scored well on a test, I assumed it was just luck — confirming that ability is not really there.'

options.A: The student is applying inductive reasoning correctly by updating their belief based on new evidence.
options.B: The student is committing confirmation bias by reinterpreting contradictory evidence to fit a pre-existing belief.
options.C: The student is using the availability heuristic by recalling only memorable past failures.
options.D: The student is engaging in self-serving bias by attributing failure to external causes.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to interpret new information in a way that confirms existing beliefs rather than challenging them. The student discounts a positive result (high test score) to preserve the belief of being bad at maths — a textbook example. The availability heuristic (option C) relates to overweighting memorable events, which is a separate cognitive error not demonstrated here.

questions.title: Rights vs. Responsibilities Balance
questions.prompt: The UNCRC outlines children's rights, but IB frameworks also emphasise corresponding responsibilities. A student claims: 'My right to freedom of expression means I can say anything I want without consequence.' To what extent is this claim philosophically defensible?

options.A: It is fully defensible because Article 13 of the UNCRC guarantees children freedom of expression with no stated conditions.
options.B: It is partially defensible because rights are absolute within democratic societies, though social norms may limit them in practice.
options.C: It is not defensible, because Article 13 itself specifies that freedom of expression may be restricted to protect the rights or reputations of others.
options.D: It is not defensible because the UNCRC only applies to adults, not to children in educational settings.

questions.explanation: Article 13 of the UNCRC explicitly states that the right to freedom of expression carries restrictions, including those necessary for 'respect of the rights or reputations of others.' The claim is therefore indefensible as stated. Option A is a common misconception — students often overlook the limitation clauses present in the very article they cite.

questions.title: Prefrontal Cortex Development
questions.prompt: Neuroscience research indicates that the prefrontal cortex is not fully developed until the mid-twenties. What specific implication does this have for adolescent decision-making?

options.A: Adolescents process emotional information more slowly than adults due to underdeveloped limbic systems.
options.B: Adolescents may show relatively stronger emotional reactivity and weaker impulse control compared to adults, because the region governing planning and risk assessment is still maturing.
options.C: Adolescents are incapable of rational thought until the prefrontal cortex is fully developed at age 25.
options.D: The prefrontal cortex controls memory formation, so adolescents struggle to retain new information until adulthood.

questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex governs executive functions including impulse control, risk assessment, and long-term planning. Its incomplete myelination in adolescence means emotional signals from the limbic system are less effectively regulated. Option C is a damaging overgeneralisation — adolescents are entirely capable of rational thought; the difference is one of degree, not absence.

questions.title: Social Identity Theory
questions.prompt: Henri Tajfel's Social Identity Theory proposes that people derive part of their self-concept from group membership. Which psychological process does the theory identify as a key driver of in-group favouritism?

options.A: Cognitive dissonance, which motivates people to align their behaviour with group norms to reduce internal conflict.
options.B: The need to maintain or enhance a positive social identity by favourably comparing one's group to others.
options.C: Operant conditioning, whereby group members are rewarded for displaying loyalty to the in-group.
options.D: Attachment theory, in which early bonds with caregivers transfer to group identification in adulthood.

questions.explanation: Tajfel and Turner's Social Identity Theory holds that people are motivated to maintain a positive self-concept, which includes their group memberships. When a group is perceived positively relative to others (social comparison), it enhances self-esteem, driving in-group favouritism. Cognitive dissonance (option A) is a separate theory about resolving conflicting beliefs and behaviours.

questions.title: Philosophical Self — Personal Identity
questions.prompt: The philosopher Derek Parfit argued that personal identity over time is not what matters — what matters is psychological continuity. Which scenario best supports his view?

options.A: A person who has lost all memories and personality traits due to severe brain injury may not be the same 'person' in the morally relevant sense, even if their body is continuous.
options.B: A person is the same individual over time as long as their body remains biologically alive.
options.C: A person's identity is fixed at birth and remains constant throughout life regardless of experience.
options.D: A person's identity is defined solely by their social roles and the community in which they live.

questions.explanation: Parfit argued that what makes someone the 'same person' over time is psychological continuity — overlapping chains of memories, beliefs, desires, and intentions. A person whose psychology is entirely severed (e.g., through severe amnesia) represents a disruption of this continuity, supporting his claim. Option B represents the biological or bodily criterion of identity, which Parfit explicitly challenged.

questions.title: Cognitive Dissonance in Values
questions.prompt: A student who strongly believes in environmental responsibility continues to take long daily showers. According to Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance, what is the most likely psychological response?

options.A: The student will experience no discomfort because beliefs and behaviours are processed in separate parts of the brain.
options.B: The student will experience psychological discomfort and be motivated to reduce it — either by changing behaviour, changing beliefs, or rationalising the inconsistency.
options.C: The student will automatically change their behaviour to align with their beliefs through unconscious conditioning.
options.D: The student will experience increased motivation to advocate publicly for environmental causes to compensate.

questions.explanation: Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory (1957) states that holding conflicting cognitions produces psychological discomfort, and individuals are motivated to reduce this tension. They may change behaviour, alter the belief, or rationalise (e.g., 'my showers save water elsewhere'). Option D describes a possible but specific rationalisation strategy — it is not the general principle the theory predicts.

questions.title: Cultural Relativism vs. Universalism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Human rights cannot be truly universal because what counts as a right is determined by each culture.' Which philosophical position does this statement most closely represent?

options.A: Moral universalism, because the statement appeals to cross-cultural reasoning.
options.B: Cultural relativism, because it holds that moral standards are culture-dependent and not universally binding.
options.C: Ethical egoism, because the student is prioritising their own cultural perspective.
options.D: Natural law theory, because it implies rights arise from cultural practices rather than divine or rational sources.

questions.explanation: Cultural relativism is the meta-ethical position that moral judgements — including those about rights — are only valid relative to a particular cultural framework, with no cross-cultural standard of correctness. This directly opposes moral universalism, which holds that certain rights apply to all humans regardless of culture. Option A is the opposite position to what the student argues.

questions.title: Self-Determination Theory
questions.prompt: Deci and Ryan's Self-Determination Theory identifies three basic psychological needs essential for intrinsic motivation and wellbeing. Which set correctly identifies all three?

options.A: Competence, autonomy, and relatedness
options.B: Mastery, purpose, and recognition
options.C: Safety, esteem, and self-actualisation
options.D: Autonomy, achievement, and affiliation

questions.explanation: Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 1985) specifies three innate psychological needs: competence (feeling effective), autonomy (feeling self-directed), and relatedness (feeling connected to others). Option B is drawn from Daniel Pink's 'Drive' framework, which is related but distinct — and 'recognition' is not one of SDT's core constructs.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Sympathy
questions.prompt: Compare empathy and sympathy as responses to another person's distress. Which statement most accurately distinguishes the two concepts in a psychological context?

options.A: Empathy involves feeling sorry for someone from a distance, while sympathy involves sharing their emotional experience fully.
options.B: Empathy involves perspective-taking and sharing another's emotional state, while sympathy involves acknowledging another's feelings without necessarily experiencing them oneself.
options.C: Sympathy is a cognitive process, while empathy is purely physiological and linked to mirror neuron activation.
options.D: Empathy and sympathy are interchangeable terms in psychological literature, differing only in formality of language.

questions.explanation: In psychological usage, empathy involves affective sharing — taking another's perspective and experiencing a resonant emotion — while sympathy involves recognising and caring about another's situation without necessarily feeling the same emotion. Option A reverses the definitions, a very common error among students who conflate the everyday uses of these terms.

questions.title: Stereotype Threat and Performance
questions.prompt: Claude Steele's research on stereotype threat found that members of a negatively stereotyped group can underperform on relevant tasks when the stereotype is made salient. What is the primary psychological mechanism proposed to explain this effect?

options.A: Classical conditioning causes individuals to associate testing environments with negative group stereotypes.
options.B: The anxiety of potentially confirming the stereotype consumes cognitive resources, impairing performance.
options.C: Individuals deliberately perform worse to avoid the social stigma of outperforming their group.
options.D: Negative stereotypes reduce long-term memory capacity in the hippocampus through chronic stress.

questions.explanation: Steele proposed that the apprehension of confirming a negative stereotype creates intrusive thoughts and anxiety that consume working memory resources, directly reducing available cognitive capacity for the task. This is supported by studies showing that when the stereotype is not made salient, the performance gap largely disappears. Option C misrepresents the mechanism as deliberate — the effect is largely involuntary.

questions.title: Locus of Control
questions.prompt: Julian Rotter introduced the concept of 'locus of control.' A student who consistently attributes their academic results — both successes and failures — to luck, fate, or their teachers' marking demonstrates which orientation?

options.A: An internal locus of control, because they are actively evaluating external feedback.
options.B: A growth mindset orientation, because they are open to external influences on their learning.
options.C: An external locus of control, because they believe outcomes are determined by forces outside themselves.
options.D: Defensive attribution, because they are protecting their self-esteem by blaming others for failures only.

questions.explanation: An external locus of control describes the belief that outcomes are controlled by external factors — luck, powerful others, or chance — rather than by one's own actions. The student attributes both successes and failures externally, which is the defining characteristic. Option D (defensive attribution) would apply only if successes were attributed internally and failures externally — that asymmetry is absent here.

questions.title: Bioethics — Autonomy Principle
questions.prompt: In bioethics, the principle of autonomy is considered foundational to medical and psychological practice. Which of the following most accurately defines this principle in a health context?

options.A: Health professionals must always act in the best interest of the patient, even if the patient disagrees.
options.B: Patients have the right to make informed decisions about their own healthcare free from coercion.
options.C: The state has the authority to override individual health decisions when public welfare is at risk.
options.D: Doctors must distribute healthcare resources equally across all patients regardless of need.

questions.explanation: Autonomy in bioethics — as articulated by Beauchamp and Childress — is the principle that competent individuals have the right to make their own informed healthcare decisions without undue influence or coercion. Option A describes the beneficence principle, which can conflict with autonomy when a patient refuses recommended treatment.

questions.title: Intersectionality in Identity
questions.prompt: The concept of intersectionality, introduced by Kimberlé Crenshaw, is used in sociology and gender studies. Which of the following best captures its core claim about identity and social experience?

options.A: Social identity is determined primarily by the single most dominant characteristic a person possesses, such as race or gender.
options.B: All forms of discrimination are equally severe and should be addressed with identical policy responses.
options.C: Multiple dimensions of identity — such as race, gender, class, and disability — interact to create overlapping systems of advantage and disadvantage that cannot be understood in isolation.
options.D: Intersectionality describes the process by which different cultures blend over time to form hybrid identities.

questions.explanation: Crenshaw coined intersectionality in 1989 to describe how overlapping social identities create compounded forms of discrimination that are qualitatively different from each category considered alone. A Black woman, for example, may face discrimination not reducible to racism alone or sexism alone. Option D confuses intersectionality with cultural syncretism or hybridity, a frequent misconception.

questions.title: Seligman's PERMA Model
questions.prompt: Martin Seligman's PERMA model outlines five pillars of wellbeing. A school counsellor notes that a student has strong friendships, a sense of purpose, and regular achievements but reports feeling emotionally flat and uninvolved in activities. Which PERMA element is most clearly lacking?

options.A: Relationships (R), because the student lacks deep social bonds.
options.B: Positive emotion (P), because the student reports emotional flatness and low engagement.
options.C: Meaning (M), because the student has not found a clear sense of purpose.
options.D: Accomplishment (A), because the student is not achieving sufficiently in academic settings.

questions.explanation: In PERMA, 'Positive Emotion' refers to the experience of joy, gratitude, hope, and similar states — distinct from relationships or meaning. The student explicitly reports feeling emotionally flat, which points directly to a deficit in positive emotion. The stem specifies that relationships, meaning, and accomplishment are present, ruling out options A, C, and D.

questions.title: Attribution Theory — Fundamental Error
questions.prompt: The Fundamental Attribution Error (FAE) describes a systematic bias in how people explain others' behaviour. A student who sees a classmate trip and immediately concludes 'she's so clumsy' without considering the wet floor is demonstrating which aspect of the FAE?

options.A: Over-weighting situational factors while under-weighting dispositional factors when explaining others' behaviour.
options.B: Over-weighting dispositional factors while under-weighting situational factors when explaining others' behaviour.
options.C: Attributing positive outcomes to internal causes and negative outcomes to external causes for oneself.
options.D: Assuming that others share the same attitudes and behaviours as oneself in similar situations.

questions.explanation: The Fundamental Attribution Error, described by Ross (1977), is the tendency to over-attribute others' behaviour to stable internal dispositions ('she's clumsy') while neglecting situational factors (the wet floor). Option A describes the reverse — actually the actor-observer bias pattern — and option C describes self-serving attribution bias, a separate phenomenon.

questions.title: Virtue Ethics and Character
questions.prompt: According to Aristotle's virtue ethics, moral virtue is best understood as which of the following?

options.A: An innate quality present from birth that determines a person's moral worth.
options.B: A disposition to follow universal moral rules derived from reason alone.
options.C: A habituated disposition to feel and act in a way that represents the mean between excess and deficiency.
options.D: A commitment to maximising good outcomes for the community through consistent rule-following.

questions.explanation: Aristotle defined virtue as a stable character disposition (hexis) lying at the mean (mesotes) between two vicious extremes — for example, courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Crucially, Aristotle argued virtue is acquired through habituation, not innate (ruling out A). Option B describes Kantian deontology, not Aristotelian ethics.

questions.title: Neuroplasticity and Learning
questions.prompt: What does the neuroscientific concept of neuroplasticity most directly imply about human identity and capacity for change?

options.A: Neural pathways formed in childhood are permanent and cannot be significantly altered by later experience.
options.B: The brain's structure and function can be modified by experience and learning throughout a person's lifetime, not only during critical developmental windows.
options.C: Neuroplasticity applies only to physical skills such as music or sport, not to personality or beliefs.
options.D: The brain compensates for injury by transferring functions to genetically predetermined backup regions.

questions.explanation: Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's ability to reorganise synaptic connections in response to learning, experience, and environment across the lifespan. This directly contradicts fixed-mindset assumptions and supports the view that identity and ability are not static. Option A is the misconception neuroplasticity research specifically overturns — critical period theories once suggested fixed windows, but adult plasticity is now well-documented.

questions.title: Informed Consent and Adolescent Rights
questions.prompt: In many legal systems, adolescents below the age of majority may still give valid consent to certain medical treatments without parental involvement. Which principle from rights-based frameworks most strongly supports this practice?

options.A: The principle of non-maleficence, which prohibits any action that could harm the adolescent.
options.B: The principle of Gillick competence, which holds that a sufficiently mature minor can consent if they demonstrate adequate understanding.
options.C: The principle of parens patriae, which grants the state authority to override both parental and individual decisions.
options.D: The principle of justice, which requires equal treatment of all patients regardless of age.

questions.explanation: The Gillick competence principle, established in the 1985 UK House of Lords case Gillick v West Norfolk, holds that minors who demonstrate sufficient maturity and understanding to appreciate the nature and implications of a medical decision can give valid consent independently of parents. Option C (parens patriae) is a doctrine that allows courts to act for incapacitated individuals — it does not support adolescent autonomy.

questions.title: Altruism and Reciprocal Behaviour
questions.prompt: Evolutionary psychologists debate whether true altruism — helping others at a cost to oneself with no expected return — exists. Robert Trivers proposed 'reciprocal altruism' as an alternative explanation. What does this theory claim?

options.A: Helping behaviour evolved because individuals who help kin directly increase the survival of shared genes.
options.B: Apparent altruism can evolve when individuals help non-relatives because future reciprocation makes it evolutionarily advantageous over time.
options.C: Altruistic behaviour is exclusively the result of cultural conditioning rather than any evolutionary pressure.
options.D: Organisms help others only when the cost to themselves is zero, making all altruism a form of selfish interest.

questions.explanation: Trivers (1971) proposed that non-kin helping can evolve if individuals are likely to interact again and reciprocate help — making the behaviour evolutionarily stable despite short-term costs. Option A describes kin selection (Hamilton's inclusive fitness), which is a related but distinct mechanism explaining help given to genetic relatives rather than non-relatives.

questions.title: Resilience and Protective Factors
questions.prompt: Research on psychological resilience identifies several protective factors that help individuals recover from adversity. Which of the following is most consistently identified in the empirical literature as a key protective factor for adolescent resilience?

options.A: The complete avoidance of stressful experiences during childhood and adolescence.
options.B: A high socioeconomic background that removes financial stressors entirely.
options.C: The presence of at least one stable, caring relationship with a competent adult.
options.D: An IQ above the population average, which predicts superior problem-solving under stress.

questions.explanation: Decades of resilience research — including longitudinal studies by Werner and Smith on Kauai — consistently identify a stable, supportive relationship with a competent and caring adult as the single most reliable protective factor for resilience. Option A is actually counterproductive; exposure to manageable adversity (not avoidance of it) builds coping skills through what researchers call 'stress inoculation.'

questions.title: Cognitive Dissonance and Belief
questions.prompt: A student publicly advocates for environmental sustainability but regularly takes long-haul flights for leisure without reflecting on the contradiction. Leon Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance predicts which of the following responses is most likely when the inconsistency is pointed out to them?

options.A: They will immediately and permanently change their behaviour to align with their stated values.
options.B: They will rationalise the behaviour — for example, arguing that their individual flights have negligible global impact — to reduce psychological discomfort.
options.C: They will experience no discomfort because beliefs and actions are stored in separate cognitive systems.
options.D: They will abandon their environmental values entirely to achieve internal consistency.

questions.explanation: Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory holds that people are motivated to reduce the tension between conflicting cognitions, most commonly through rationalisation or reframing rather than wholesale behaviour change. Option A is a common misconception — research shows behaviour change is the least likely and most effortful resolution; rationalisation ('my contribution is negligible') requires far less psychological effort and is statistically the dominant response.

questions.title: Neuroplasticity and Growth Mindset
questions.prompt: A DP Psychology teacher claims: 'Carol Dweck's growth mindset concept is simply a motivational idea with no basis in neuroscience.' Evaluate this claim. Which response most accurately synthesises the psychological and neurological evidence?

options.A: The teacher is correct; growth mindset is a purely philosophical construct that neuroscience has neither confirmed nor contradicted.
options.B: The teacher is partially correct; neuroplasticity exists, but it only applies to motor skills, not academic or intellectual abilities.
options.C: The teacher is incorrect; neuroimaging studies show that people with a growth mindset display greater error-related neural activity in the anterior cingulate cortex, suggesting deeper engagement with mistakes.
options.D: The teacher is incorrect; the hippocampus physically doubles in size when students adopt a growth mindset, providing the neurological foundation for the theory.

questions.explanation: Research by Moser et al. (2011) used EEG to show that individuals with a growth mindset exhibited larger error-positivity (Pe) signals in the anterior cingulate cortex after making mistakes, reflecting greater attention to and processing of errors — a genuine neurological correlate. Option D is a compelling distractor but is factually wrong; the hippocampus does show experience-dependent growth (as in London taxi driver studies) but no research shows it doubles in size through mindset adoption alone.

questions.title: Erikson's Identity Development
questions.prompt: According to Erik Erikson's psychosocial theory, adolescence is characterised by the conflict of 'Identity vs. Role Confusion.' Which of the following student behaviours is the BEST example of successfully navigating this stage?

options.A: A student experiments with different social groups, values, and career ideas before committing to a set of personal beliefs that feel authentically their own.
options.B: A student adopts their parents' career path and political views without questioning them, feeling settled and secure.
options.C: A student avoids all social experimentation to focus entirely on academic achievement, forming a stable identity around scholarship.
options.D: A student changes their personality entirely depending on who they are with, demonstrating flexible identity across contexts.

questions.explanation: Erikson described healthy identity formation as an active process of exploration (a 'moratorium') followed by commitment — trying on roles before settling into an authentic self. Option B describes what James Marcia later termed 'identity foreclosure,' where commitment occurs without prior exploration, which Erikson considered an incomplete resolution of the crisis rather than a success.

questions.title: Utilitarianism vs Deontology
questions.prompt: A doctor can save five patients by harvesting the organs of one healthy, non-consenting patient. A utilitarian would endorse this action; a Kantian deontologist would not. Which statement most accurately identifies WHY the deontologist rejects it, even when the outcome saves more lives?

options.A: The deontologist rejects it because the long-term social consequences of distrust in medicine would outweigh the benefit of saving five lives.
options.B: The deontologist rejects it because killing the one patient violates a categorical duty never to use a person merely as a means to an end, regardless of outcomes.
options.C: The deontologist rejects it because five lives are not mathematically worth more than one life under any rational framework.
options.D: The deontologist rejects it because the doctor cannot be certain the five patients will survive even after receiving the organs.

questions.explanation: Kant's categorical imperative — specifically the 'Formula of Humanity' — holds that rational beings must never be treated merely as means but always also as ends in themselves. Using the healthy patient as an organ source reduces them to a tool, violating a duty-based constraint that is independent of outcomes. Option A actually describes a rule-utilitarian or indirect-consequentialist argument, not a deontological one, and is the most common misconception among students who conflate the two frameworks.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge and Self
questions.prompt: In TOK, a student argues: 'I can know my own mind better than anyone else can, because I have direct, private access to my own thoughts.' To what extent is this claim justified? Which response best identifies a significant limitation of this position?

options.A: The claim is fully justified; introspection is the most reliable form of self-knowledge because it requires no external validation.
options.B: The claim is limited because psychological research on implicit bias and unconscious motivation demonstrates that much of what drives our behaviour lies below the level of conscious introspective access.
options.C: The claim is limited only in cases of mental illness; for neurotypical individuals, introspection accurately captures all mental states.
options.D: The claim is fully unjustified; neuroscience has proven that self-reports are always less accurate than brain scans for understanding one's own mind.

questions.explanation: Research by Nisbett and Wilson (1977) showed that people frequently confabulate — they construct plausible but inaccurate explanations for their own choices, suggesting conscious introspection often does not access actual cognitive processes. Studies on implicit association (e.g., the IAT) further show that attitudes operate below conscious awareness. Option C is the most seductive distractor but is wrong because unconscious bias affects neurotypical individuals systematically, not only those with mental illness.

questions.title: Cultural Identity and Acculturation
questions.prompt: Berry's acculturation framework identifies four strategies used by migrants navigating a new culture. A student who maintains their heritage culture while also fully engaging with the new culture is best described as using which strategy?

options.A: Assimilation
options.B: Separation
options.C: Integration
options.D: Marginalisation

questions.explanation: In Berry's model, integration (also called biculturalism) describes maintaining one's heritage identity while simultaneously adopting aspects of the host culture — it is associated with the best psychological outcomes in most research. Assimilation (Option A) involves giving up the heritage culture in favour of the new one, which is the most common misconception because students conflate blending in with integration.

questions.title: Maslow's Hierarchy Applied
questions.prompt: A 16-year-old refugee student arrives at a new school. She is highly academically motivated but is living in temporary shelter with inconsistent food access. Applying Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which prediction is most strongly supported by the theory?

options.A: Her academic motivation will compensate for unmet physiological needs because intrinsic goals override basic deficits.
options.B: Unmet physiological and safety needs are likely to impair her capacity to pursue the esteem and self-actualisation needs associated with academic achievement.
options.C: She will self-actualise through academic success, which will in turn resolve her physiological needs by earning scholarships.
options.D: Because she is intrinsically motivated, Maslow's hierarchy does not apply; it only predicts behaviour for extrinsically motivated individuals.

questions.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy proposes that lower-order deficiency needs (physiological, safety) must be sufficiently met before higher-order growth needs (esteem, self-actualisation) can be consistently pursued. Chronic food and shelter insecurity directs cognitive and emotional resources toward survival, reducing bandwidth for academic engagement. Option A is the top distractor — students often assume intrinsic motivation is a sufficient override, but the theory explicitly positions physiological needs as foundational prerequisites.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities Tension
questions.prompt: Article 17 of the UNCRC gives children the right to access information from the media. A government proposes filtering all internet content for under-18s to protect mental health. Critically assess this proposal: which argument most effectively identifies the core ethical tension?

options.A: The proposal is straightforwardly justified because protection rights always override participation rights for minors.
options.B: The proposal creates no ethical tension because governments have an absolute duty to protect children's wellbeing.
options.C: The proposal highlights a tension within the UNCRC itself, where the right to information (Article 17) conflicts with the right to protection from harm (Article 36), requiring proportionality analysis rather than an absolute rule.
options.D: The proposal is straightforwardly unjustified because any restriction on information is a violation of international law.

questions.explanation: The UNCRC does not establish a strict hierarchy among rights; when Articles conflict, international human rights law requires proportionality — the restriction must be necessary, suitable, and not excessive relative to the protective aim. Option A is the most common misconception: students are often taught that protection rights are paramount, but the UNCRC's General Comment No. 20 explicitly recognises adolescents' evolving autonomy and participation rights as equally valid.

questions.title: Social Identity Theory
questions.prompt: Henri Tajfel's Social Identity Theory proposes that people derive part of their self-esteem from their membership in social groups. Which of the following phenomena is MOST directly predicted by this theory?

options.A: People will rate members of their own group more favourably than out-group members, even when group membership is based on something arbitrary like a coin flip.
options.B: People will always prefer individualistic goals over group goals because personal identity is more psychologically fundamental than social identity.
options.C: People with high self-esteem are immune to in-group bias because they do not need external validation from group membership.
options.D: Intergroup conflict only arises when groups are competing for scarce material resources, not from group membership itself.

questions.explanation: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm experiments demonstrated that even arbitrary group assignments (based on trivial criteria such as aesthetic preference or a coin flip) led participants to favour in-group members in resource allocation — showing that group membership alone, independent of shared history or material competition, generates bias. Option D reflects Realistic Conflict Theory (Sherif), a competing explanation that Tajfel's work was specifically designed to challenge.

questions.title: Philosophical Concept of Personal Identity
questions.prompt: The philosopher Derek Parfit argued that personal identity over time is not what matters — what matters is psychological continuity of memories, beliefs, and intentions. Identify the error in the following student response to Parfit: 'Parfit is wrong because your body remains the same throughout your life, which is sufficient to make you the same person.'

options.A: The student is correct; bodily continuity is the standard philosophical account of personal identity and Parfit's view is widely rejected.
options.B: The error is that the student ignores that almost all cells in the human body are replaced over years, undermining the premise that the body remains physically identical over time.
options.C: The error is that the student conflates Parfit's view with Locke's memory theory; Parfit actually agreed that bodily continuity is sufficient for identity.
options.D: The error is purely logical; the student uses a circular argument by defining 'same person' to mean 'same body.'

questions.explanation: The student's counter-argument relies on physical continuity, but this is undermined by the biological fact that most human cells are replaced within years (though neurons persist longer, reinforcing Parfit's emphasis on psychological continuity). Parfit explicitly addressed physical continuity arguments and noted they face the 'ship of Theseus' problem. Option D contains a real logical observation but is not the primary error Parfit would identify — the more devastating challenge is the empirical fragility of the bodily-continuity premise.

questions.title: Stress Response and HPA Axis
questions.prompt: During a high-stakes exam, a student experiences a rapid heartbeat, heightened alertness, and sweaty palms. Which sequence most accurately describes the neuroendocrine pathway responsible for these symptoms?

options.A: The hippocampus detects threat → releases cortisol directly into the bloodstream → activates the sympathetic nervous system.
options.B: The amygdala signals the hypothalamus → the hypothalamus activates the sympathetic nervous system and the HPA axis → the adrenal glands release adrenaline and cortisol.
options.C: The prefrontal cortex detects the stressor → activates the parasympathetic nervous system → the pancreas releases glucagon to fuel the stress response.
options.D: The thalamus releases cortisol → the pituitary gland amplifies the signal → the thyroid gland produces adrenaline.

questions.explanation: The stress response begins when the amygdala perceives a threat and signals the hypothalamus, which simultaneously activates the sympathetic nervous system (producing rapid adrenaline release from the adrenal medulla) and the HPA axis (hypothalamus → pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex cortisol). Option A is the most common student error: students know cortisol and the hippocampus are involved in stress but confuse the hippocampus's role (it actually downregulates the HPA axis via negative feedback) with the amygdala's role in initiating the response.

questions.title: Evaluating Conformity Research
questions.prompt: Solomon Asch's conformity experiments (1951) showed that 75% of participants conformed to an obviously incorrect group answer at least once. A student claims: 'This proves that humans are fundamentally irrational and incapable of independent judgment.' Evaluate this interpretation.

options.A: The interpretation is correct; Asch's results definitively show that social pressure overrides rational thinking in all humans.
options.B: The interpretation is overstated; 25% of participants never conformed, and most conformity was likely driven by normative social influence — a desire to be accepted — rather than a failure of rational cognition.
options.C: The interpretation is correct, but only applies to collectivist cultures; individualist participants were unaffected by group pressure in Asch's study.
options.D: The interpretation is overstated because Asch's sample was too small to draw any conclusions about human nature.

questions.explanation: Asch himself distinguished between informational influence (genuinely updating beliefs based on others) and normative influence (conforming to avoid social rejection while privately disagreeing). The fact that 25% never conformed, and that private answers showed far less conformity, suggests the issue is social motivation rather than cognitive incapacity. Option C is a plausible distractor because cultural variations in conformity exist (Bond & Smith, 1996 meta-analysis), but Asch's original sample was American — he did not compare cultures.

questions.title: Mental Health Stigma
questions.prompt: Research consistently shows that mental health stigma has two components: social stigma (public attitudes) and self-stigma (internalised shame). Which intervention strategy has the strongest empirical support for reducing SELF-stigma specifically?

options.A: Large-scale public awareness campaigns that correct factual misconceptions about mental illness in the general population.
options.B: Self-compassion and mindfulness-based approaches that help individuals separate their identity from their diagnosis and challenge self-critical thought patterns.
options.C: Strict laws penalising discriminatory language about mental illness in media and public discourse.
options.D: Encouraging people with mental health conditions to keep their diagnosis private to avoid triggering stigmatising responses from others.

questions.explanation: Self-stigma arises from internalising public stigma — applying negative stereotypes to oneself — so interventions targeting self-compassion, psychological flexibility, and cognitive restructuring show the strongest evidence for reducing self-stigma (Lucksted et al.; Corrigan's group). Option A addresses social stigma effectively but does not reliably translate to reduced self-stigma; a person can know public attitudes are wrong while still internalising them, making this the most tempting but incorrect distractor.

questions.title: Gender Identity and Biology
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Gender identity is purely a social construction with no biological component, because identical twins don't always share the same gender identity.' To what extent does current scientific evidence support or challenge this claim?

options.A: The claim is fully supported; concordance rates of 0% in identical twins prove there is no genetic influence on gender identity.
options.B: The claim is overstated; twin studies show concordance rates significantly above zero for identical twins (approximately 28–39%), suggesting a genetic contribution, even though social and developmental factors also play a role.
options.C: The claim is fully refuted; genetics entirely determines gender identity, and discordance in twins is due to measurement error.
options.D: Twin studies are irrelevant to this question because identical twins share environments, not just genes, making it impossible to separate nature from nurture.

questions.explanation: Research, including Heylens et al. (2012), found concordance rates for gender identity disorder of approximately 39% in monozygotic twins versus 0% in dizygotic twins, indicating a heritable component while confirming that genetics is not deterministic — social and developmental influences clearly also matter. Option A is factually wrong about the concordance rates. Option D raises a real methodological concern (the equal environments assumption) but does not make twin studies entirely irrelevant; they remain the primary tool for heritability estimation.

questions.title: Autonomy and Paternalism
questions.prompt: A 17-year-old competent student refuses a blood transfusion for religious reasons, despite doctors saying it is medically necessary. Which philosophical principle is MOST directly in conflict with respecting their decision?

options.A: The principle of justice, which requires equal treatment for all patients regardless of religious belief.
options.B: The principle of beneficence, which obliges medical professionals to act in the patient's best interest, potentially overriding their stated wishes.
options.C: The principle of non-maleficence, which only concerns avoiding active harm rather than failing to provide treatment.
options.D: The principle of veracity, which requires doctors to tell the truth even when patients prefer not to know their prognosis.

questions.explanation: Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of biomedical ethics include beneficence (acting in the patient's best interest) as the principle most directly in tension with respecting the patient's autonomous refusal. When a patient refuses life-saving treatment, beneficence pulls physicians toward overriding that refusal (paternalism). Option C is a common student error: non-maleficence (do no harm) could be argued to support non-intervention, so students mistake it for the principle in conflict, when it is actually beneficence that most directly contradicts autonomy here.

questions.title: Locus of Control and Wellbeing
questions.prompt: Julian Rotter's concept of 'locus of control' distinguishes between internal and external orientations. Research consistently finds that an internal locus of control is associated with better mental health outcomes. Which explanation BEST accounts for this relationship?

options.A: People with an internal locus of control have objectively more control over their lives, so they face fewer actual stressors.
options.B: Believing that outcomes are influenced by one's own actions promotes active coping strategies and greater persistence, reducing learned helplessness.
options.C: People with an internal locus of control are more intelligent, which independently improves both their problem-solving and their mental health.
options.D: An internal locus of control is genetically linked to lower cortisol production, directly reducing physiological stress responses.

questions.explanation: The relationship between internal locus of control and wellbeing is mediated by coping style: internal individuals are more likely to engage in problem-focused coping and persist through adversity, reducing the onset of learned helplessness (Seligman). Option A is the most seductive distractor — students confuse the perception of control with actual control; the research controls for objective circumstances and still finds the internal orientation is protective.

questions.title: Virtue Ethics and Character
questions.prompt: Aristotle argued that virtues are developed through habituation, not innate talent. A student responds: 'This means that being courageous just requires practising courageous acts, so any action called courageous is a virtue.' Identify the flaw in this student's interpretation of Aristotle's eudaimonia framework.

options.A: Aristotle did not believe virtues could be developed; he argued they were entirely determined by one's upbringing and social class.
options.B: The student ignores that Aristotle's doctrine of the mean requires virtuous action to avoid both excess and deficiency — recklessness is not courage, it is the excess of confidence; true courage lies between cowardice and recklessness.
options.C: The student is correct; in Aristotelian ethics, the repeated performance of an act is both necessary and sufficient for that act to constitute a virtue.
options.D: The flaw is that Aristotle believed only intellectual virtues, not moral virtues like courage, could be taught through practice.

questions.explanation: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean holds that each virtue represents the appropriate midpoint between two vices — for courage, the deficiency is cowardice and the excess is recklessness. Merely performing an act labelled 'courageous' does not make it virtuous if it is actually reckless or context-inappropriate. Option C is wrong because Aristotle explicitly required that virtuous action be accompanied by the right motivation, at the right time, toward the right person — practice is necessary but not sufficient without practical wisdom (phronesis).

questions.title: Implicit Bias in Self-Perception
questions.prompt: Research using the Implicit Association Test (IAT) repeatedly shows that people often hold implicit biases inconsistent with their explicitly stated egalitarian values. What does this finding most directly imply about the relationship between self-knowledge and behaviour?

options.A: Explicit self-reports are always more accurate than implicit measures, because people know their own minds better than any test can reveal.
options.B: Implicit attitudes are more predictive of spontaneous behaviours than explicit attitudes, suggesting that conscious self-concept does not fully capture the cognitive processes shaping action.
options.C: Implicit bias results are invalid because the IAT measures reaction speed, which is confounded by typing ability and individual differences in motor skills.
options.D: Because implicit biases are unconscious, they cannot be changed and should not be considered a matter of personal responsibility.

questions.explanation: Meta-analyses (e.g., Greenwald et al.) show that implicit measures predict spontaneous, uncontrolled behaviours (e.g., non-verbal cues in interactions) better than explicit measures, while explicit attitudes better predict deliberate, controlled behaviours. This dual-process finding challenges the naive view that people have transparent self-knowledge. Option D is tempting because it contains a partial truth (biases are unconscious) but is wrong because research shows implicit biases can be reduced through deliberate counter-conditioning, accountability, and structural interventions.

questions.title: Attachment Theory in Adolescence
questions.prompt: Bowlby's attachment theory was originally applied to infants and caregivers. A student claims it becomes irrelevant after childhood because adolescents transfer their primary attachment bonds from parents to peers. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; Bowlby's own research showed that parental attachment bonds dissolve at puberty and are fully replaced by peer bonds.
options.B: The claim is partially correct; peer bonds become increasingly important in adolescence, but research shows parental attachment continues to function as a 'secure base' for risk-taking and exploration and predicts adult relationship quality.
options.C: The claim is incorrect; attachment theory shows that peer relationships are irrelevant to psychological development beyond early childhood.
options.D: The claim is correct because adolescence is defined neurologically by a shift in the brain's reward system that makes peer approval intrinsically more valuable than parental approval.

questions.explanation: Hazan and Zeifman's research showed that attachment functions are gradually transferred to peers across adolescence, but parental attachment remains a significant predictor of mental health, romantic relationship quality, and identity development well into adulthood. Secure parental attachment enables healthy autonomy. Option D contains a genuine neuroscientific observation about the adolescent reward system (the striatum becomes more sensitive to peer feedback) but incorrectly uses this to support the claim that parental attachment becomes irrelevant.

questions.title: Intersectionality and Identity
questions.prompt: Kimberlé Crenshaw introduced the concept of intersectionality to describe how overlapping social identities create unique, compounded experiences of discrimination. Which of the following scenarios BEST illustrates an intersectional analysis, as opposed to a single-axis analysis?

options.A: Documenting that women earn less than men on average in a given company, controlling for job type.
options.B: Recognising that Black women in a workplace may face discrimination that is not predicted by adding the experiences of Black men and white women together, because their combined identity creates a distinct form of marginalisation.
options.C: Arguing that class is the most important identity category and that racial and gender inequalities are secondary effects of economic inequality.
options.D: Measuring discrimination by comparing the experiences of the most marginalised group (e.g., disabled transgender women of colour) to those of the most privileged group (white able-bodied men).

questions.explanation: Crenshaw's original legal argument arose from cases where Black women could not bring discrimination suits because their experience was not covered by race discrimination law (which used Black men as the reference) nor by sex discrimination law (which used white women). Intersectionality specifically identifies that overlapping categories produce qualitatively distinct — not merely additive — forms of oppression. Option D describes a comparative measurement approach that might support intersectional research but is not itself an intersectional analysis.

questions.title: Philosophy of Free Will and Responsibility
questions.prompt: A hard determinist argues: 'Since every human action is the inevitable result of prior causes — genetics, upbringing, brain chemistry — no one is ever truly morally responsible for what they do.' Which response most effectively challenges this argument?

options.A: The argument is refuted because quantum indeterminacy at the subatomic level proves that some physical events are genuinely uncaused, making free will scientifically certain.
options.B: A compatibilist would challenge this by arguing that 'freedom' and 'moral responsibility' do not require the absence of causal determination — they only require that actions flow from the agent's own reasoning and desires without external coercion.
options.C: The argument is refuted because neuroscience has confirmed the existence of a non-physical mind (the soul) that operates independently of brain chemistry.
options.D: The argument cannot be challenged; determinism is accepted by all major branches of philosophy and science as the only coherent account of causation.

questions.explanation: Compatibilism (associated with philosophers like Hume, Frankfurt, and Dennett) holds that determinism and moral responsibility are not mutually exclusive; what matters is whether the action originates from the agent's own deliberative processes rather than external force. This directly challenges hard determinism without requiring indeterminism. Option A is tempting because quantum indeterminacy is real, but philosophers note that random quantum events do not produce meaningful free will — random ≠ free — making it an ineffective rebuttal.

questions.title: Adolescent Brain Development
questions.prompt: Neuroscientists have established that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is not fully myelinated until the mid-twenties. Which of the following adolescent behavioural patterns is MOST directly explained by this developmental fact?

options.A: Adolescents experience stronger emotions than adults because the limbic system develops before the PFC, creating a regulatory imbalance that biases decision-making toward immediate reward.
options.B: Adolescents are more creative than adults because incomplete myelination prevents the PFC from suppressing novel associations between unrelated ideas.
options.C: Adolescents have poorer long-term memory than adults because the PFC is responsible for encoding episodic memories in the hippocampus.
options.D: Adolescents sleep more than adults because the PFC regulates circadian rhythm and its incomplete development shifts the sleep-wake cycle later.

questions.explanation: The 'dual systems model' (Casey, Steinberg) proposes that the limbic/reward system (including the nucleus accumbens) matures earlier than the PFC, which provides inhibitory control and long-term planning. This developmental asynchrony produces heightened emotional reactivity and preference for immediate rewards over delayed ones, explaining risk-taking and peer-influenced decision-making in adolescence. Option D describes a real phenomenon (circadian phase delay in adolescence) but it is driven by melatonin timing changes and light-sensitivity shifts, not PFC myelination.

questions.title: Wellbeing Frameworks Compared
questions.prompt: The PERMA model (Seligman) and the WHO definition of health both address wellbeing, but they differ in scope. Compare these two frameworks: which statement most accurately identifies a key distinction between them?

options.A: PERMA focuses exclusively on positive emotions, while the WHO definition includes physical and social dimensions of health that PERMA ignores.
options.B: The WHO definition (1948) defines health as 'complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing' — a state-based model — whereas PERMA describes elements that contribute to flourishing, making it a process-oriented framework applicable to tracking growth over time.
options.C: PERMA is a clinical diagnostic framework used by psychiatrists, while the WHO definition is a philosophical aspiration with no practical application.
options.D: Both frameworks are functionally identical; PERMA was developed to operationalise the WHO definition for educational settings.

questions.explanation: The WHO definition establishes a holistic state of wellbeing as an endpoint ('complete... wellbeing'), which critics have noted sets an impossibly high bar. PERMA, by contrast, identifies five measurable and cultivatable elements — Positive Emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment — as contributors to flourishing, making it a dynamic, growth-oriented model more useful for intervention design. Option A is wrong because PERMA's 'R' (Relationships) and 'M' (Meaning) extend beyond positive emotion into social and purposive dimensions.

questions.title: Stereotype Threat and Performance
questions.prompt: Claude Steele's research on stereotype threat showed that Black college students performed worse on a difficult verbal test when told it measured intellectual ability, compared to a control group told it was a non-diagnostic puzzle task. What is the most accurate explanation for this performance gap?

options.A: The diagnostic framing activated anxiety about confirming a negative group stereotype, which consumed working memory resources and disrupted performance — not an actual difference in ability.
options.B: The participants in the diagnostic condition were less motivated because they believed the test was biased against them and chose not to try.
options.C: The test itself was harder in the diagnostic condition, introducing a confounding variable that explains the gap.
options.D: The diagnostic framing triggered the participants' fixed mindset, causing them to give up sooner than the control group.

questions.explanation: Steele and Aronson (1995) found that the mere awareness of a relevant negative stereotype created cognitive load — specifically, intrusive thoughts monitoring one's performance and the risk of confirming the stereotype — which impaired working memory and executive function on demanding tasks. The groups did not differ in actual ability or test difficulty. Option B is a common and appealing distractor, but Steele explicitly controlled for motivation and found that stereotype-threatened participants were actually over-motivated (trying harder) yet still performed worse.

questions.title: Moral Development Kohlberg
questions.prompt: Lawrence Kohlberg described three levels of moral development. A student justifies not cheating on a test by saying: 'Cheating is wrong because society depends on honest systems, and I want to uphold social order even when no one would catch me.' Which stage does this BEST represent?

options.A: Stage 1 (Obedience and Punishment): the student is avoiding punishment from authority.
options.B: Stage 3 (Good Interpersonal Relationships): the student wants to be seen as a good person by their peers.
options.C: Stage 4 (Maintaining Social Order): the student reasons from a commitment to upholding social systems and institutions regardless of personal benefit.
options.D: Stage 6 (Universal Ethical Principles): the student applies abstract universal principles of justice that transcend any specific legal or social system.

questions.explanation: Stage 4 in Kohlberg's framework is defined by law-and-order reasoning — moral decisions are made to preserve social institutions and systems, not for personal benefit or peer approval. The student's reference to 'society depends on honest systems' and their willingness to act rightly even unobserved are hallmarks of Stage 4 conventional morality. Option D is the most common student error: Stage 6 involves abstract universal principles (e.g., justice, human dignity) that may sometimes conflict with established social order, which this student's reasoning does not reach.

questions.title: Growth Mindset vs Fixed Mindset
questions.prompt: A student receives a poor grade on a mathematics test and tells herself: 'I'm just not a maths person — some people have it and some don't.' Evaluate this reasoning. Which response best identifies the psychological flaw in her conclusion?

options.A: Her reasoning is sound; neurological research confirms that mathematical ability is largely genetically determined.
options.B: She is displaying a fixed mindset, attributing ability to innate talent rather than recognising that neural pathways strengthen through deliberate practice.
options.C: She is correct that talent is fixed, but incorrect that the situation is hopeless, because motivation can compensate for low ability.
options.D: Her reasoning reflects a growth mindset because she is being self-aware about her current performance level.

questions.explanation: Dweck's research on mindset demonstrates that belief in fixed ability ('entity theory') reduces effort and resilience, whereas understanding that synaptic connections strengthen with practice ('incremental theory') correlates with higher achievement. Option A is a common misconception — twin studies show environment and practice account for substantial variance in mathematical skill beyond genetic baseline.

questions.title: Neuroscience of Adolescent Risk
questions.prompt: Neuroscientists note that the prefrontal cortex is not fully myelinated until approximately age 25. What is the most accurate implication of this finding for understanding adolescent decision-making?

options.A: Adolescents cannot experience empathy because empathy is processed entirely in the prefrontal cortex.
options.B: Incomplete myelination slows signal transmission in circuits governing impulse control, making risk assessment less efficient than in adults.
options.C: The limbic system is also underdeveloped in adolescents, so emotional reactions are weaker than in adults.
options.D: Myelination affects memory formation but has no measurable impact on risk-taking behaviour.

questions.explanation: Myelination speeds neural conduction; incomplete myelination of prefrontal circuits means the 'brakes' on the limbic system's reward-seeking signals are less effective, a finding supported by fMRI studies comparing adolescent and adult responses to risk. Option C is the key misconception — the limbic system matures earlier than the prefrontal cortex, which is precisely why the emotional-rational imbalance occurs.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning: Consequentialism
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Lying to protect a friend from embarrassment is acceptable because it prevents harm and increases overall happiness.' To what extent does this argument reflect a coherent consequentialist position, and what is its most significant vulnerability?

options.A: It is a fully coherent consequentialist position with no significant vulnerability, since outcomes are the only morally relevant factor.
options.B: It is coherent as consequentialism but vulnerable because it ignores Kant's categorical imperative, which is considered universally binding.
options.C: It is coherent as consequentialism but vulnerable because it requires accurate prediction of all consequences, which is practically impossible and may lead to rationalised self-interest.
options.D: It is incoherent because consequentialism only evaluates actions for society as a whole, not for individuals.

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism (a form of consequentialism) does judge actions by outcomes, so the argument is structurally consistent — but its weakness is epistemic: consequences cannot be fully known in advance, opening the door to motivated reasoning. Option B is a common error; citing Kant refutes the position from outside consequentialism rather than identifying an internal vulnerability of the consequentialist argument itself.

questions.title: Maslow's Hierarchy Applied
questions.prompt: A refugee student joining a new school has inconsistent access to food and safe housing. According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, why might a teacher's efforts to build the student's self-esteem have limited effect at this stage?
