questions.explanation: Metals expand when their particles gain thermal energy and vibrate more widely; because metal expands more than glass when heated, the lid's diameter increases slightly, reducing the friction and pressure holding it onto the jar. Option D is wrong because glass does not shrink when exposed to warm water — it would also expand slightly, but less than the metal.

questions.title: Ecosystems and Interdependence
questions.prompt: In a pond ecosystem, algae are eaten by water fleas, which are eaten by small fish, which are eaten by herons. If a disease suddenly kills most of the water fleas, predict what would most likely happen to the small fish population in the short term.

options.A: The small fish population would increase because herons would move away.
options.B: The small fish population would decrease because their main food source has become scarce.
options.C: The small fish population would stay the same because they can simply eat more algae instead.
options.D: The small fish population would increase because without water fleas, algae would grow more and feed the fish.

questions.explanation: Small fish depend on water fleas as their primary food source; if water fleas become scarce, fish have less to eat and their population would decline in the short term. Option D is wrong because small fish in this chain eat water fleas, not algae — they cannot simply switch food sources in the short term.

questions.title: Magnetic Fields
questions.prompt: A student sprinkles iron filings around a bar magnet and they form a pattern of curved lines. What do these lines represent, and where are they closest together?

options.A: They represent lines of electric current; they are closest together at the centre of the magnet.
options.B: They represent the magnetic field; they are closest together at the poles where the field is strongest.
options.C: They represent the magnetic field; they are closest together in the middle of the magnet where there is no pole.
options.D: They represent paths of heat energy; they are closest together at the north pole only.

questions.explanation: Iron filings align along magnetic field lines, and where field lines are densest (closest together) the magnetic force is greatest — this occurs at the poles (north and south ends) of the magnet. Option C is wrong because the middle of the magnet is where field lines are most spread out and the field is weakest.

questions.title: Cell Structure Basics
questions.prompt: Both plant cells and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and a nucleus. Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in typical animal cells?

options.A: Nucleus
options.B: Cell membrane
options.C: Cell wall
options.D: Cytoplasm

questions.explanation: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane, which gives the cell its fixed shape and extra support — animal cells do not have a cell wall. Options A, B, and D are all present in both plant and animal cells, making cell wall the only correct answer.

questions.title: Sound Transmission
questions.prompt: Astronauts on the Moon cannot hear each other speak without using radios, even when standing close together. Why can't sound travel between them through space?

options.A: The Moon is too cold for sound waves to form.
options.B: Sound waves need a medium (such as air, water, or a solid) to travel through; there is no atmosphere on the Moon.
options.C: Gravity on the Moon is too weak to carry sound waves from one person to another.
options.D: The helmets block all sound from leaving the astronaut's suit.

questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires particles to vibrate and pass energy along; in the vacuum of space there are no particles, so sound cannot travel at all. Option D is a common misconception — helmets do block some sound, but even without helmets there would be no air to carry vibrations between astronauts.

questions.title: Separating Mixtures
questions.prompt: A student has a mixture of salt dissolved in water and wants to recover the dry salt. Which method would most effectively separate the salt from the water?

options.A: Filtration — pouring the mixture through filter paper to catch the salt.
options.B: Evaporation — gently heating the mixture so the water turns to vapour and the salt remains.
options.C: Magnetism — passing a magnet through the liquid to attract the salt particles.
options.D: Sieving — using a fine sieve to separate the dissolved salt from the water.

questions.explanation: Because salt is dissolved in water, it passes straight through filter paper and a sieve; evaporation removes the water as vapour, leaving the solid salt behind as a dry residue. Option A is wrong because filtration only separates insoluble solids from liquids — dissolved salt particles are too small and pass through filter paper along with the water.

questions.title: Inherited vs Acquired Traits
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'If a bodybuilder develops very large muscles during their lifetime, their children will be born with naturally larger muscles too.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct — characteristics developed during a lifetime are passed on through DNA to offspring.
options.B: The claim is correct — muscles are controlled by genes, and exercise permanently changes those genes.
options.C: The claim is incorrect — muscle size gained through exercise is an acquired characteristic and is not passed on through genes to offspring.
options.D: The claim is partially correct — only characteristics developed before adulthood can be inherited by children.

questions.explanation: Only traits encoded in an organism's DNA can be inherited; muscles built through exercise are acquired characteristics caused by environment and behaviour, not changes to genetic code, so they are not passed to offspring. Option A is wrong because exercising does not alter the DNA in reproductive cells, which is what would be needed to pass the trait on.

questions.title: Forces and Balanced Systems
questions.prompt: A book rests on a table and does not move. Two forces act on it: gravity pulling it downward and the table pushing it upward. What can we say about these two forces?

options.A: They are unbalanced — gravity is stronger, which is why the book stays on the table.
options.B: They are balanced — they are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the book does not accelerate.
options.C: They are balanced — the table's force is slightly larger, which keeps the book pressed down.
options.D: They are unbalanced — the table's push is stronger, which is why the book doesn't fall through.

questions.explanation: Newton's first law states that an object at rest stays at rest when forces are balanced; the table exerts a normal reaction force equal and opposite to the book's weight, so the net force is zero and the book does not move. Options A and D are both wrong because if forces were unbalanced, the book would accelerate in the direction of the larger force.

questions.title: Soil Formation
questions.prompt: Compare physical weathering and chemical weathering of rocks. What is the key difference between these two processes?

options.A: Physical weathering always involves water; chemical weathering never involves water.
options.B: Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their mineral composition; chemical weathering changes the minerals themselves through chemical reactions.
options.C: Physical weathering is faster; chemical weathering takes millions of years and produces no soil.
options.D: Physical weathering only occurs in cold climates; chemical weathering only occurs in hot climates.

questions.explanation: Physical weathering (e.g., freeze-thaw, abrasion) breaks rock into fragments of the same material, while chemical weathering (e.g., acid rain dissolving limestone) changes the chemical composition of the minerals, forming new substances. Option A is wrong because water is involved in both types of weathering — for example, water is the agent in freeze-thaw (physical) and is also required for many chemical reactions that weather rock.

questions.title: Inherited Characteristics
questions.prompt: A student notices that tall plants grown from the seeds of a tall parent plant are sometimes short when grown in poor soil. What does this observation suggest about the relationship between genes and the environment?

options.A: Genes have no effect on height — only the environment determines how tall a plant grows.
options.B: The environment can change an organism's genes, making short plants pass on shortness to their offspring.
options.C: Both genes and environmental conditions can influence how characteristics like height are expressed in an organism.
options.D: Only plants that grow in good soil inherit genes from their parents; plants in poor soil have different genes.

questions.explanation: Genes provide the potential for a characteristic (like tallness), but environmental factors such as nutrient availability can affect how fully that potential is expressed — this is the interaction between genotype and phenotype. Option A is wrong because genes do influence height; in ideal conditions the tall genetic potential would be expressed.

questions.title: Renewable Energy Sources
questions.prompt: A student claims that solar panels and wind turbines are both 'renewable' energy sources because they produce electricity without burning fuel. What is the most accurate reason these sources are considered renewable?

options.A: They are renewable because the panels and turbines can be recycled at the end of their lives.
options.B: They are renewable because they use energy from sources — sunlight and wind — that are naturally and continuously replenished on a human timescale.
options.C: They are renewable because they produce more energy than they use, so they never run out.
options.D: They are renewable because they do not produce any waste products at all during their operation.

questions.explanation: A resource is renewable when it is naturally replenished much faster than it is used; sunlight and wind are driven by ongoing natural processes (the Sun's nuclear fusion and atmospheric circulation) so they will not be depleted by human use. Option A confuses the recyclability of the equipment with the renewability of the energy source itself — recyclability is a separate concept.

questions.title: Levers as Simple Machines
questions.prompt: A child uses a long metal bar as a lever to lift a heavy rock. She places the fulcrum very close to the rock. What effect does this position of the fulcrum have, and why?

options.A: It makes the rock harder to lift because the effort arm is shorter than the load arm.
options.B: It makes the rock easier to lift because the effort arm is longer than the load arm, increasing the mechanical advantage.
options.C: It has no effect — the position of the fulcrum only matters for seesaws, not for lifting levers.
options.D: It makes the rock easier to lift because the fulcrum absorbs some of the weight of the rock.

questions.explanation: When the fulcrum is close to the load (rock), the effort arm (the distance from the child's hands to the fulcrum) is much longer than the load arm, giving a high mechanical advantage — meaning a small effort force can lift a large load. Option A describes the opposite situation, where the fulcrum is far from the load, making lifting harder.

questions.title: Greenhouse Effect
questions.prompt: The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps Earth warm enough for life. Which of the following best describes how greenhouse gases cause warming?

options.A: Greenhouse gases trap sunlight before it reaches Earth's surface, heating the atmosphere directly.
options.B: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared (heat) radiation given off by Earth's surface and re-radiate some of it back, slowing the loss of heat to space.
options.C: Greenhouse gases reflect all radiation from the Sun back into space, preventing Earth from getting too cold.
options.D: Greenhouse gases increase the amount of solar energy reaching Earth's surface by acting as a magnifying lens.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases like CO₂ and water vapour are largely transparent to incoming shortwave solar radiation but absorb outgoing longwave infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward Earth — this is what slows heat loss and warms the planet. Option A is wrong because greenhouse gases mainly interact with outgoing infrared radiation from Earth, not with incoming sunlight.

questions.title: Lungs and Gas Exchange
questions.prompt: Inside the human lungs, oxygen moves from the air in tiny air sacs (alveoli) into the blood. Which feature of the alveoli is most important for making this gas exchange efficient?

options.A: Alveoli are large and balloon-like, providing a big space for air to be stored between breaths.
options.B: Alveoli are surrounded by a rich network of tiny blood vessels and have very thin, moist walls, maximising the surface area for diffusion.
options.C: Alveoli produce mucus that dissolves oxygen so it can be carried directly into the bloodstream.
options.D: Alveoli are made of muscle tissue that actively pumps oxygen into the blood vessels.

questions.explanation: Efficient gas exchange requires a large surface area, short diffusion distance, and moist surfaces — alveoli provide all three: millions of tiny sacs create enormous total surface area, their walls are just one cell thick, and they stay moist. Option A is wrong because alveoli being large individual structures would reduce surface area; it is their large number and small size that maximises the total surface area.

questions.title: Density and Floating
questions.prompt: A large steel ship floats on water even though steel is much denser than water. A small solid steel marble sinks immediately. What principle explains why the ship floats but the marble sinks?

options.A: The ship floats because it is much larger and heavier, so it is pushed up by a stronger gravitational force.
options.B: The ship floats because its hollow shape means its overall density (ship plus air inside) is less than water; the marble's overall density is greater than water.
options.C: The ship floats because steel becomes less dense when formed into a thin sheet, whereas the marble is made of very dense solid steel.
options.D: The ship floats because the large flat bottom spreads the weight over a greater area, reducing the force on any one part of the water.

questions.explanation: An object floats when its average density (total mass divided by total volume, including any enclosed air) is less than the fluid it is in; the ship's hull encloses a large volume of air, making its average density lower than water, while the solid marble has no air and its average density equals that of steel (about 8 times denser than water). Option C is wrong because the physical properties of steel do not change when it is shaped into a sheet — the steel itself remains just as dense.

questions.title: Plant Photosynthesis and Light
questions.prompt: A student grows two identical plants for four weeks. Plant A sits near a sunny window, and Plant B sits in a dim corner. Both receive the same amount of water and are in the same type of soil. Plant B grows taller but has thinner stems and paler leaves. What is the best explanation for Plant B's unusual height?

options.A: Plant B received more water than Plant A, causing it to stretch upward.
options.B: Plant B grew taller because it was stretching toward a stronger light source it could not reach.
options.C: Plant B grew taller because dim light triggers faster overall growth in plants.
options.D: Plant B used more nutrients from the soil to compensate for lower light levels.

questions.explanation: When plants receive insufficient light, they undergo etiolation — a process where cells elongate rapidly as the plant 'reaches' toward a brighter light source. This explains the taller but weaker, paler growth. Option C is wrong because dim light does not trigger genuinely faster growth; the elongation is a stress response that produces weaker tissue, not healthy faster growth.

questions.title: Food Web Disruption
questions.prompt: In a meadow ecosystem, hawks eat rabbits, rabbits eat grass, and grasshoppers also eat grass. Rabbits also eat grasshoppers. If a disease suddenly wiped out all the rabbits, which of the following would most likely happen over the next year?

options.A: Hawk populations would stay the same because they could switch to eating grasshoppers.
options.B: Grasshopper populations would decrease because more grass would grow and crowd them out.
options.C: Hawk populations would decline and grasshopper populations would increase.
options.D: Grass would disappear quickly because grasshoppers and hawks would both eat more of it.

questions.explanation: Without rabbits, hawks lose their main food source and their population falls due to starvation. With rabbits gone, grasshoppers face less predation and more available grass, so their numbers rise — a classic trophic cascade effect. Option A is wrong because hawks are not adapted to efficiently hunt grasshoppers, and simply switching prey is not guaranteed to sustain hawk populations.

questions.title: States of Matter and Particles
questions.prompt: A student heats a solid block of wax until it melts into a liquid, then heats it further until it becomes a gas. She claims that when the wax melted, the particles themselves got bigger. Evaluate her claim.

options.A: She is correct — particles expand when heated, just like a balloon expands with warm air.
options.B: She is partially correct — only the particles in the gas phase get bigger, not in the liquid phase.
options.C: She is incorrect — the particles stay the same size but move faster and spread further apart.
options.D: She is incorrect — the particles get smaller because some are lost as heat energy escapes.

questions.explanation: When a substance is heated, particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, overcoming the forces holding them together — this increases the spacing between particles, not the size of the particles themselves. The wax particles in liquid form are the same size as in solid form but are less rigidly arranged. Option A is a common misconception that confuses particle spacing with particle size.

questions.title: Adaptation and Natural Selection
questions.prompt: A population of beetles lives on brown tree bark. Most beetles are brown, but a few are bright green. Birds hunt these beetles by sight. Over many generations, what would you predict will happen to the population, and why?

options.A: Green beetles will learn to hide better over time, so both colours will survive equally.
options.B: Brown beetles will become more common because they are better camouflaged and survive longer to reproduce.
options.C: Brown beetles will increase because they actively choose to live on bark that matches their colour.
options.D: Green beetles will evolve brown colouring within their own lifetime to avoid predation.

questions.explanation: Natural selection acts because brown beetles are better camouflaged on brown bark, so they are eaten less often, survive longer, and pass their brown colouring to more offspring. Over generations, the proportion of brown beetles increases. Option D is wrong because individual organisms do not evolve within their lifetime — evolution occurs across generations through differential survival and reproduction.

questions.title: Heat Transfer Methods
questions.prompt: On a cold day, a student sits near a campfire and feels warm even though she is not touching the fire. She also notices the air directly above the flames shimmers and rises. Which two methods of heat transfer are described here?

options.A: Conduction from the fire to the student, and convection causing the rising air.
options.B: Radiation warming the student, and convection causing the rising shimmer of air.
options.C: Radiation warming the student, and conduction causing the air to rise above the fire.
options.D: Convection warming the student from a distance, and radiation causing the air to rise.

questions.explanation: The student feels warm without touching the fire because heat travels as infrared radiation through the air. The shimmering rising air above the flames is convection — hot air becomes less dense and rises, carrying heat energy upward. Option A is wrong because conduction requires direct physical contact between objects, which is not happening between the fire and the student.

questions.title: Water Cycle Processes
questions.prompt: On a warm morning, a student notices water droplets forming on the outside of a cold glass of juice. Her friend says the glass must be leaking. What is actually happening, and what process explains it?

options.A: Water is seeping through tiny holes in the glass — the friend is correct about leaking.
options.B: Water vapour in the warm air cools when it touches the cold glass and condenses into liquid droplets.
options.C: The cold glass is absorbing moisture directly from the juice inside, pushing it through the glass.
options.D: The warm air is evaporating the juice through the glass and depositing it on the outside.

questions.explanation: When warm, moist air meets the cold surface of the glass, it cools below its dew point — the temperature at which water vapour condenses into liquid. This is the same process that forms clouds and dew. Option A is a genuine misconception; the droplets appear on the outside, not the inside, which shows the water comes from the surrounding air, not from inside the glass.

questions.title: Forces and Falling Objects
questions.prompt: A student drops a large rock and a small pebble from the same height at the same time. She predicts the rock will hit the ground first because it is heavier. Assuming no significant air resistance, what will actually happen and why?

options.A: The rock hits first because gravity pulls harder on heavier objects, making them accelerate faster.
options.B: The pebble hits first because lighter objects experience less air resistance.
options.C: Both hit at the same time because gravity accelerates all objects equally regardless of mass.
options.D: Both hit at the same time because the heavier rock's greater air resistance cancels out the extra gravity.

questions.explanation: Galileo demonstrated that gravity accelerates all objects at the same rate (approximately 9.8 m/s² on Earth) regardless of mass, so both objects reach the ground simultaneously. The gravitational force is indeed greater on the heavier rock, but so is its inertia, and these effects cancel exactly. Option A is the classic misconception — more gravitational force does not mean greater acceleration when the mass is also greater.

questions.title: Rock Cycle and Erosion
questions.prompt: A geologist finds smooth, rounded pebbles in a riverbed far from any mountains. The same type of jagged rock exists in the mountains nearby. What process most likely transformed the jagged mountain rock into the smooth river pebbles?

options.A: The rocks melted underground and reformed as smooth shapes when they cooled in the river.
options.B: Water and other rocks gradually wore away the sharp edges as the rocks tumbled downstream over time.
options.C: Chemical reactions in the river water dissolved the outer layers of the rocks into a smooth coating.
options.D: The rocks compressed together underwater, fusing their edges into rounded shapes.

questions.explanation: This is physical weathering and erosion — as rocks are carried by river currents, they collide with each other and the riverbed, gradually abrading their sharp edges until they become smooth and rounded. This process can take thousands of years. Option C describes chemical weathering, which does occur but does not produce the rounded shapes seen here; that rounding is caused by physical abrasion.

questions.title: Electricity and Conductors
questions.prompt: A student tests several materials to see which ones allow electricity to flow. She finds copper wire works, but a plastic ruler and a rubber eraser do not. She then tests graphite (pencil lead) and is surprised it conducts electricity. What property do copper and graphite share that plastic and rubber lack?

options.A: Copper and graphite are both shiny, and shiny surfaces always conduct electricity.
options.B: Copper and graphite both contain electrons that are free to move and carry electrical charge.
options.C: Copper and graphite are both solid at room temperature, giving them stable conducting structures.
options.D: Copper and graphite are both found naturally in the Earth, while plastic and rubber are man-made.

questions.explanation: Electrical conductors contain electrons that are not tightly bound to individual atoms and can move freely through the material, carrying electric current. Graphite, despite being a non-metal, has a layered atomic structure with free electrons, making it a good conductor. Option A is incorrect because shininess is not related to conductivity — many shiny materials like certain plastics do not conduct electricity.

questions.title: Human Digestive System
questions.prompt: A student says that digestion begins in the stomach because that is where food gets broken down. Identify the error in her statement and explain where digestion actually begins.

options.A: She is correct — the stomach is the first organ to break down food using acid.
options.B: She is wrong — digestion begins in the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed.
options.C: She is wrong — digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth and saliva start breaking down food.
options.D: She is wrong — digestion begins in the oesophagus, which uses muscular contractions to crush food.

questions.explanation: Digestion begins in the mouth: teeth physically break food into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion) and saliva contains an enzyme called amylase that begins chemically breaking down starch. The stomach continues digestion but is not the starting point. Option B is wrong because by the time food reaches the small intestine, much digestion has already occurred in the mouth and stomach.

questions.title: Light Refraction
questions.prompt: A student places a straight pencil in a glass of water and notices the pencil appears bent at the water's surface. She concludes that the water physically bent the pencil. What is the actual cause of what she sees?

options.A: Light travels at different speeds in water and air, causing it to change direction at the surface — this is refraction.
options.B: The water exerts pressure on the pencil, compressing it slightly and causing the bend.
options.C: Light reflects off the water's surface and creates a double image of the pencil that looks bent.
options.D: Water magnifies objects beneath it, stretching the pencil's image to appear at an angle.

questions.explanation: Refraction occurs because light slows down when it passes from air into water (which is denser), causing the light rays to change direction at the boundary. This makes the submerged part of the pencil appear shifted from its actual position. Option C is wrong because while reflection does occur at the surface, it is refraction — not reflection — that causes the apparent bending of the pencil's image.

questions.title: Microorganisms and Disease
questions.prompt: Two students are discussing why covering a sneeze with a tissue helps stop illness from spreading. Student A says it traps the germs so they die. Student B says it stops droplets containing microorganisms from travelling through the air. Who is more scientifically accurate, and why?

options.A: Student A — tissues contain antibacterial chemicals that kill microorganisms on contact.
options.B: Student B — the tissue acts as a barrier, preventing infectious droplets from becoming airborne.
options.C: Both are equally correct — the tissue both kills germs and traps droplets simultaneously.
options.D: Neither is correct — sneezing only spreads illness through direct skin contact, not through the air.

questions.explanation: Respiratory illnesses spread when tiny droplets containing pathogens (bacteria or viruses) are expelled into the air and inhaled by others. A tissue physically blocks these droplets from travelling far. Student A's explanation is inaccurate because ordinary tissues do not contain antibacterial agents and trapping germs does not automatically kill them. Option D is wrong because many pathogens, including those causing influenza, are indeed airborne.

questions.title: Experimental Design Fairness
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether the colour of light affects how fast a plant grows. She places one plant under a red lamp and another under a blue lamp of the same brightness. She waters the red-lamp plant every day but waters the blue-lamp plant every three days. A classmate says this experiment is flawed. Which variable makes the test unfair?

options.A: The lamps are the same brightness, so the experiment cannot detect any difference.
options.B: Both plants should be the same species, which the student has not confirmed.
options.C: The watering frequency is different, so any growth difference could be caused by water, not light colour.
options.D: The experiment should use at least five plants under each colour, not just one.

questions.explanation: In a controlled experiment, only one variable — the independent variable — should change at a time. Here the student is changing both light colour and watering frequency, so any difference in growth could be due to water availability, not light colour. This means the results would be invalid as evidence about light colour. Option D identifies a real limitation (sample size) but is not the variable that makes the test unfair in the way described.

questions.title: Magnetic Fields and Compasses
questions.prompt: A hiker uses a compass to navigate. She notices that near a large iron ore deposit, her compass needle points toward the rocks rather than toward geographic north. What does this tell us about the iron ore deposit?

options.A: The iron ore deposit is producing electricity, which is interfering with the compass needle.
options.B: The iron ore deposit has magnetic properties strong enough to deflect the compass needle.
options.C: The iron ore deposit is reflecting Earth's magnetic field, causing the compass to reverse direction.
options.D: The compass is broken because iron ore has no effect on magnetic instruments.

questions.explanation: Iron is a ferromagnetic material, meaning it can become magnetised or already possesses magnetic properties. A large concentration of iron ore can create a local magnetic field strong enough to override Earth's magnetic field near the compass needle, pulling it away from north. Option A is incorrect because iron ore does not generate electricity passively; electricity and magnetism are related but the ore is not acting as a power source here.

questions.title: Carbon Cycle and Climate
questions.prompt: A scientist explains that burning forests releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere AND reduces the number of trees that absorb carbon dioxide. Why does deforestation have a double impact on the carbon cycle compared with simply releasing CO₂ from a factory?

options.A: Factories release a different type of carbon dioxide that does not affect the atmosphere as strongly.
options.B: Burning forests adds CO₂ to the atmosphere while simultaneously removing organisms that would have absorbed future CO₂.
options.C: Deforestation changes the soil temperature, which prevents any new plants from growing and absorbing CO₂.
options.D: Forests produce oxygen as well as absorb CO₂, so losing them only matters for the oxygen supply.

questions.explanation: Deforestation causes a double impact: combustion immediately releases stored carbon as CO₂, and the loss of trees removes future carbon sinks — organisms that would have absorbed atmospheric CO₂ through photosynthesis over decades. A factory releases CO₂ but does not reduce the ecosystem's capacity to absorb it. Option D is partially true but misses the key point about carbon absorption being the central climate issue.

questions.title: Sound Waves and Medium
questions.prompt: An astronaut outside the International Space Station bangs two metal pipes together. Her colleague inside the station cannot hear the sound through space, but does feel a faint vibration when holding a rope connected to the pipes. What does this tell us about how sound travels?

options.A: Sound travels only through air and cannot move through any solid material like a rope.
options.B: Sound requires a medium of particles to travel through — it moves through the solid rope but not through the vacuum of space.
options.C: Sound travels through space but is too quiet to hear because space absorbs all sound energy.
options.D: The colleague felt the vibration because light energy from the movement was converted to sound inside the station.

questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave that requires particles to compress and expand as it travels. Space is a near-perfect vacuum with almost no particles, so sound cannot propagate through it. The solid rope provides a medium of tightly packed particles that can carry the vibration efficiently. Option C is a common misconception — space does not 'absorb' sound; sound simply cannot exist without a medium to travel through.

questions.title: Inherited and Learned Traits
questions.prompt: A border collie puppy is raised in a city apartment and never herds sheep. Its sibling, raised on a farm, learns to herd sheep expertly. When the apartment dog is brought to a farm as an adult, it immediately begins herding behaviour without training. What does this most strongly suggest?

options.A: The apartment dog copied the herding behaviour by watching the farm dog at the moment they met.
options.B: Herding behaviour in border collies is entirely learned and the apartment dog must have practised secretly.
options.C: The herding instinct is an inherited trait passed down genetically, not solely dependent on environment or training.
options.D: All dogs have equal herding ability; border collies just look more like they are herding than other breeds.

questions.explanation: Border collies were selectively bred for herding instincts over many generations, encoding the behaviour genetically. The apartment dog displaying herding behaviour without training demonstrates that the instinct is inherited, not purely learned. Option A is implausible because the dogs were raised separately and the behaviour appeared immediately without observation time.

questions.title: Levers and Mechanical Advantage
questions.prompt: A student uses a long metal bar to lift a heavy boulder by placing the bar under the rock and resting it on a smaller rock close to the boulder. She pushes down on the far end. What would happen if she moved the small rock (the fulcrum) closer to her hand instead of closer to the boulder?

options.A: It would become easier to lift the boulder because more of the bar is under the rock.
options.B: It would become harder to lift the boulder because she reduces her mechanical advantage.
options.C: It would make no difference — the force needed depends only on the boulder's weight, not the fulcrum position.
options.D: The bar would snap because all the force would concentrate at the fulcrum point.

questions.explanation: In a lever, mechanical advantage increases when the effort arm (distance from fulcrum to where force is applied) is longer than the load arm (distance from fulcrum to the load). Moving the fulcrum closer to the effort reduces the effort arm relative to the load arm, decreasing mechanical advantage and making the boulder harder to lift. Option A is incorrect — it confuses which side of the fulcrum benefits from being longer.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Stability
questions.prompt: Two islands have the same total number of animals. Island A has 500 individuals all of the same species. Island B has 500 individuals spread across 20 different species. A new disease strikes both islands, affecting only one species. Which island's ecosystem is likely to recover better, and why?

options.A: Island A, because having one strong, well-adapted species makes the ecosystem more efficient.
options.B: Island B, because the other 19 species can continue ecosystem roles even if one is severely affected.
options.C: Island A, because a smaller number of species means fewer disease pathways.
options.D: Both islands would recover equally since the total number of animals is the same.

questions.explanation: Greater biodiversity provides ecosystem resilience — when one species is lost or reduced, others can fulfil similar ecological roles, maintaining functions like pollination, decomposition, or predation. Island A would completely collapse if its single species were devastated. Option D is wrong because total number of individuals matters less than the diversity of species filling different ecological roles.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation
questions.prompt: A student has a mixture of salt, sand, and iron filings. She wants to separate all three. She correctly identifies that a magnet will separate the iron filings first. What is the correct order of steps to separate all three components?

options.A: Use a magnet, then filter the remaining mixture, then evaporate the water to collect salt.
options.B: Filter the mixture first, then use a magnet on the filter residue, then boil the filtrate.
options.C: Dissolve everything in water, use a magnet, then filter, then evaporate.
options.D: Use a magnet, then dissolve the remaining mixture in water, filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to collect the salt.

questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: (1) use a magnet to remove iron filings, (2) add water to dissolve the salt while the sand remains undissolved, (3) filter to remove the sand, (4) evaporate the water to recover the salt crystals. Option A skips the dissolving step, so filtering alone cannot separate salt from sand because both remain as solids until the salt is dissolved.

questions.title: Solar System Scale
questions.prompt: A student builds a scale model of the Solar System using a basketball to represent the Sun. She is surprised to find that, at this scale, Earth would be represented by a small bead placed about 26 metres away. What does this model most powerfully demonstrate?

options.A: The Sun is the largest object in the Solar System and therefore the most important.
options.B: The vast distances between objects in the Solar System make space exploration extremely challenging.
options.C: Earth is relatively tiny compared with the Sun, and the distances in the Solar System are enormous compared with object sizes.
options.D: Planets close to the Sun are always small, while planets far away are always large.

questions.explanation: The model illustrates two related concepts: the enormous size difference between the Sun and Earth, and the vast empty space between them. At this scale, most of the Solar System is effectively empty space. Option D is incorrect — while inner rocky planets tend to be smaller, this is not a universal rule, and the model question is specifically about size and distance relationships, not a pattern about all planets.

questions.title: Comparing Vertebrate Characteristics
questions.prompt: A student is trying to classify a newly discovered animal. It has scales, lays eggs on land, and is cold-blooded. Another student says it must be a fish because it has scales. Which evidence most clearly shows it is NOT a fish?

options.A: It has scales — fish are the only vertebrates with scales, so this evidence is inconclusive.
options.B: It lays eggs on land — fish lay eggs in water, so laying eggs on land indicates it is a reptile.
options.C: It is cold-blooded — fish are warm-blooded, so this trait rules out it being a fish.
options.D: Its scale pattern is different — fish scales are always round, while reptile scales are always diamond-shaped.

questions.explanation: Most fish lay their eggs in water because fish eggs lack the protective membranes and shells needed to prevent drying out on land. Laying eggs on land with a protective shell or membrane is a key reptile characteristic. Option C contains a factual error — fish are cold-blooded (ectothermic) just like reptiles, so cold-bloodedness does not distinguish between the two groups.

questions.title: Greenhouse Effect Mechanism
questions.prompt: A student says the greenhouse effect is harmful and should be completely eliminated. Evaluate whether this is accurate, explaining the role the greenhouse effect normally plays on Earth.

options.A: She is correct — the greenhouse effect only causes harm and Earth would be better without any of it.
options.B: She is partially correct — the greenhouse effect is natural but all greenhouse gases are currently at harmful levels.
options.C: She is incorrect — the natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life; only the enhanced effect from extra gases is problematic.
options.D: She is incorrect — the greenhouse effect has no impact on temperature and only affects rainfall patterns.

questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect is essential: without it, Earth's average temperature would be approximately −18°C rather than the current +15°C, making liquid water and life as we know it impossible. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human emissions increasing concentrations of CO₂ and other gases. Option A dangerously misunderstands the natural process by treating all greenhouse warming as harmful.

questions.title: Density and Floating
questions.prompt: A solid steel ship floats, but a solid steel ball sinks. A student says this is impossible because both are made of the same material. What is the best explanation for why the ship floats?

options.A: The ship floats because steel becomes less dense when it is shaped into thin sheets.
options.B: The ship floats because its hull shape traps air, making the overall average density of the ship less than water.
options.C: The ship floats because moving water pushes upward on curved surfaces more than on flat ones.
options.D: The ship floats because large objects always displace enough water to float regardless of material.

questions.explanation: An object floats if its average density (total mass divided by total volume) is less than the density of water. A hollow ship hull contains a large volume of air, which dramatically reduces the ship's average density even though the steel itself is denser than water. Option A is incorrect — the density of steel does not change based on its shape; only the average density of the combined steel-and-air structure changes.

questions.title: Seed Dispersal Strategies
questions.prompt: Three plants have different seed structures: Plant X has seeds with hooks, Plant Y has seeds with light feathery fibres, and Plant Z has seeds inside sweet fleshy fruit. Which correctly matches each plant to its most likely dispersal method?

options.A: X: wind, Y: animals (external), Z: animals (eaten).
options.B: X: animals (external), Y: wind, Z: animals (eaten).
options.C: X: animals (eaten), Y: animals (external), Z: wind.
options.D: X: wind, Y: animals (eaten), Z: animals (external).

questions.explanation: Hooked seeds (Plant X) attach to fur or clothing and are carried by animals externally. Feathery fibres (Plant Y) catch air currents for wind dispersal. Sweet fleshy fruit (Plant Z) attracts animals that eat the fruit and deposit seeds elsewhere in their droppings. Option A incorrectly assigns wind dispersal to hooked seeds, which have no aerodynamic feature — hooks are specifically adapted for clinging to fur.

questions.title: Energy Transformation Chains
questions.prompt: A student rides a bicycle up a hill, then freewheels down the other side, brakes, and comes to a stop at the bottom. Arrange the main energy transformations in the correct order from start to finish.

options.A: Chemical energy → kinetic energy → gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy → heat energy.
options.B: Kinetic energy → chemical energy → gravitational potential energy → heat energy → kinetic energy.
options.C: Chemical energy → gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy → chemical energy → heat energy.
options.D: Gravitational potential energy → chemical energy → kinetic energy → heat energy → kinetic energy.

questions.explanation: The student's muscles convert chemical energy (from food) into kinetic energy as she pedals. This kinetic energy converts to gravitational potential energy as she climbs. Going downhill, potential energy converts back to kinetic energy. Braking converts kinetic energy to heat through friction, stopping the bicycle. Option C incorrectly inserts chemical energy in the middle of the sequence where potential energy converts to kinetic energy on the descent.

questions.title: Food Web Energy Flow
questions.prompt: In a grassland food chain, grass is eaten by grasshoppers, grasshoppers are eaten by frogs, and frogs are eaten by hawks. A scientist measures that the grass contains 10,000 units of energy. About how much energy would be available to the hawks, assuming only 10% of energy passes to the next level?

options.A: 1,000 units
options.B: 100 units
options.C: 10 units
options.D: 1,000 units passed directly from grass

questions.explanation: Energy is lost at each step in a food chain; with 10% transfer, 10,000 → 1,000 (grasshoppers) → 100 (frogs) → 10 units reach hawks. A common misconception is stopping at one transfer and choosing 1,000, but hawks are three levels away from the grass, so two more transfers are needed.

questions.title: States of Matter Change
questions.prompt: A student heats a block of ice in a pan. She notices the ice melts into liquid water, and eventually the water disappears as steam. What happens to the water molecules when liquid water becomes steam?

options.A: The molecules break apart into hydrogen and oxygen atoms
options.B: The molecules move faster and spread far apart from each other
options.C: The molecules disappear into the air permanently
options.D: The molecules slow down and lose their shape

questions.explanation: Evaporation is a physical change; water molecules gain enough energy to overcome attractions and move freely as gas, spreading far apart — they do not break apart chemically. Option A is a common misconception: molecules remain intact as H₂O during a change of state, which is a physical not chemical change.

questions.title: Natural Selection and Camouflage
questions.prompt: A population of moths lives on tree bark. Most moths are grey, but a few are white. Birds eat moths they can see easily. Over many generations, what would you expect to happen to the population if the trees are covered in grey lichen?

options.A: White moths would increase because they are healthier
options.B: Grey moths would increase because birds eat more white moths
options.C: Both colours would stay equally common because birds eat randomly
options.D: White moths would evolve grey colouring within their own lifetime

questions.explanation: Grey moths blend into grey lichen, so birds preferentially eat visible white moths, leaving grey moths to survive and reproduce more — this is natural selection. Option D reflects the misconception that individual animals consciously change to suit their environment, but evolution acts on populations across generations, not on single individuals.

questions.title: Electrical Conductors and Insulators
questions.prompt: A student tests several materials by placing them in a circuit between a battery and a bulb. The bulb lights up for copper wire and saltwater, but not for distilled water or rubber. What best explains why saltwater conducts electricity but distilled water does not?

options.A: Saltwater is denser, so electrons flow more easily through it
options.B: Salt dissolves to release charged particles called ions that carry the current
options.C: Distilled water is too cold to conduct electricity
options.D: Saltwater contains more hydrogen atoms that act as conductors

questions.explanation: When salt (sodium chloride) dissolves, it separates into positively and negatively charged ions that can move through the water and carry electric current — pure water has no such free charges. Option A is a misconception: density is not the reason a material conducts; what matters is the presence of free charged particles.

questions.title: Photosynthesis Inputs and Outputs
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Plants get all their food and energy from the soil through their roots.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of photosynthesis.

options.A: The claim is correct; roots absorb sugar and minerals that fuel plant growth
options.B: The claim is partly correct; roots provide water but sunlight provides all the energy
options.C: The claim is incorrect; plants make their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water
options.D: The claim is incorrect; plants get energy only from oxygen absorbed through their leaves

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide (from air) and water (from soil) into glucose — so plants manufacture their own food rather than absorbing it ready-made from soil. Option B is tempting but incomplete; roots supply water AND minerals, while leaves capture light energy, so it understates the root's role and misrepresents where energy comes from.

questions.title: Rock Cycle and Erosion
questions.prompt: A geologist finds a rock layer at the bottom of a river that contains rounded, smooth pebbles of many different rock types mixed together. What process most likely formed this layer?

options.A: Volcanic lava cooled and solidified in the riverbed
options.B: Rocks were transported by water, worn smooth by friction, then deposited as sediment
options.C: Pressure underground squeezed existing rocks into new rounded shapes
options.D: The rocks were formed from decayed plant material compressed over time

questions.explanation: Rounded, mixed pebbles are a classic sign of sedimentary processes: flowing water carries rock fragments, friction against each other wears away sharp edges, and they are eventually deposited together. Option C is a misconception conflating sedimentary and metamorphic processes — underground pressure changes rock type but does not sort or round river pebbles.

questions.title: Heat Transfer by Radiation
questions.prompt: On a sunny day, a student notices that a black car feels much hotter to touch than a white car parked in the same sunlight for the same time. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

options.A: Black surfaces absorb more radiant energy from the sun than white surfaces do
options.B: Black paint is thicker and traps heat inside the metal better than white paint
options.C: White cars reflect heat back into the air, which cools the surrounding air faster
options.D: Black cars have engines that produce more heat during the day

questions.explanation: Dark colours absorb a greater proportion of solar radiation and convert it to heat, while light colours reflect most radiation — this is why the black car's surface becomes hotter. Option B is a common misconception: paint thickness is negligible; it is the colour's absorption property that matters, not insulation.

questions.title: Human Digestive System
questions.prompt: Food passes through many organs during digestion. A student says the stomach is the most important organ because it is where all digestion happens. Identify the error in this claim.

options.A: The error is that digestion begins in the large intestine, not the stomach
options.B: The error is that digestion begins in the mouth, and most chemical digestion occurs in the small intestine
options.C: The error is that the stomach only digests liquids, not solid food
options.D: The error is that digestion is completed in the oesophagus before food reaches the stomach

questions.explanation: Digestion begins in the mouth with chewing and salivary enzymes breaking down starch; the small intestine, with help from the pancreas and liver, is where most chemical digestion and nutrient absorption occurs. Option A is wrong because the large intestine mainly absorbs water and compacts waste rather than digesting food.

questions.title: Acids, Bases, and Indicators
questions.prompt: A student tests four liquids with red cabbage indicator juice. Liquid 1 turns bright pink, Liquid 2 stays purple, Liquid 3 turns green, and Liquid 4 turns yellow-green. Which liquid is most likely a strong base?

options.A: Liquid 1, because bright pink shows a strong acid
options.B: Liquid 2, because purple is the neutral point
options.C: Liquid 3, because green indicates a mild base
options.D: Liquid 4, because yellow-green indicates a strong base

questions.explanation: Red cabbage indicator turns yellow-green in strongly alkaline (basic) solutions, green in mildly basic solutions, purple when neutral, and pink/red in acidic solutions. Option C is tempting because green does indicate a base, but yellow-green indicates a stronger base than green, making Liquid 4 the strongest base tested.

questions.title: Water Cycle Processes
questions.prompt: On a cold morning, the outside of a glass of iced water becomes covered in tiny water droplets, even though the glass has no holes. Where do these droplets come from, and what process forms them?

options.A: Water seeps through the microscopic pores in the glass from the inside
options.B: Water vapour in the surrounding air cools on the cold glass surface and condenses into liquid
options.C: The ice inside the glass melts and leaks through cracks in the glass
options.D: Oxygen and hydrogen in the air combine on the cold glass to form new water molecules

questions.explanation: The cold glass cools the air immediately around it below its dew point, causing invisible water vapour already present in the air to condense into visible liquid droplets on the glass surface — this is condensation. Option A is a common misconception; glass is not porous to water, and the droplets form on the outside, not from the inside.

questions.title: Gravity and Falling Objects
questions.prompt: A student drops a large iron ball and a small wooden ball from the same height at the same time in a room with no air. Which ball hits the ground first, and why?

options.A: The iron ball, because it is heavier and gravity pulls harder on heavier objects
options.B: The wooden ball, because it is lighter and falls more freely
options.C: Both balls hit at the same time, because gravity accelerates all objects equally regardless of mass
options.D: The iron ball, because it has more momentum pushing it downward

questions.explanation: In the absence of air resistance, gravity gives every object the same acceleration (9.8 m/s²) regardless of mass — this was famously demonstrated by Galileo and confirmed on the Moon by astronauts. Option A is perhaps the most widespread misconception in physics: heavier objects experience more gravitational force, but they also have more inertia, so these effects cancel out exactly.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Stability
questions.prompt: Ecologist Maria studies two islands. Island A has 50 species of plants and insects. Island B has only 5 species. A new plant disease arrives on both islands. Which island's ecosystem is more likely to survive with less damage, and why?

options.A: Island B, because fewer species means less competition for resources during the crisis
options.B: Island A, because greater biodiversity means more species can fill roles if one is lost
options.C: Island B, because the disease will spread more slowly with fewer organisms present
options.D: Both islands will be equally affected because disease does not care about species numbers

questions.explanation: High biodiversity gives an ecosystem resilience: if one species is wiped out, others can fulfil similar ecological roles, preventing collapse — this is called functional redundancy. Option A is a misconception; fewer species actually makes an ecosystem more fragile because there are no backup species to maintain vital functions like pollination or decomposition.

questions.title: Light Refraction and Lenses
questions.prompt: A student places a convex (magnifying) lens between a candle and a wall. She moves the lens back and forth until a sharp, clear image of the candle flame appears on the wall. The image is upside down. Why is the image inverted?

options.A: The glass in the lens flips the light rays because glass reverses direction
options.B: Light rays from the top and bottom of the flame cross over as they bend through the lens, swapping their positions
options.C: The wall reflects the image upside down because of its flat surface
options.D: The image is only upside down because the candle is held below the lens

questions.explanation: A convex lens refracts (bends) light rays so that rays from the top of an object converge to the bottom of the image and vice versa — the crossing of rays at the focal point causes the inversion. Option A is incorrect; glass does not inherently 'flip' or 'reverse' light; it is the geometry of converging rays crossing through the focal point that inverts the image.

questions.title: Inherited and Acquired Traits
questions.prompt: A farmer notices that his prize cow produces a lot of milk. He also notices that the cow has a scar on its leg from a fence injury. Which statement correctly distinguishes these two characteristics?

options.A: Both traits are inherited and will be passed to the cow's calves
options.B: High milk production is inherited; the scar is an acquired trait and will not be passed on
options.C: The scar is inherited because it was caused by the environment the cow lived in
options.D: Neither trait is inherited because both were influenced by the cow's environment

questions.explanation: Milk production is influenced by genes passed from parent to offspring (inherited trait), while a scar results from environmental experience and does not change the cow's DNA — so it cannot be inherited by calves. Option C reflects the historical misconception (Lamarckism) that environmentally acquired characteristics can be passed on genetically, which has been disproven.

questions.title: Levers and Mechanical Advantage
questions.prompt: Two children sit on opposite ends of a seesaw. Child A weighs 40 kg and sits 2 metres from the centre pivot. Child B weighs 20 kg. How far from the pivot must Child B sit to balance the seesaw?

options.A: 1 metre, because Child B is half the weight
options.B: 2 metres, because both children must sit the same distance away
options.C: 4 metres, because Child B must sit twice as far to compensate for half the weight
options.D: 3 metres, because you add the weight difference to the distance

questions.explanation: For a lever to balance, the turning force (torque) must be equal on both sides: 40 kg × 2 m = 80 units; Child B needs 20 kg × distance = 80, so distance = 4 m. Option B is wrong because simply matching distances only balances when weights are equal — the lighter child must sit further away to generate the same torque.

questions.title: Carbon Cycle and Greenhouse Effect
questions.prompt: A student explains: 'Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is bad for Earth because it prevents ALL heat from escaping into space, causing temperatures to rise.' Evaluate this explanation.

options.A: The explanation is correct; CO₂ traps all heat and this has always been harmful
options.B: The explanation is partly wrong; a natural level of CO₂ keeps Earth warm enough for life, but excess CO₂ traps more heat than needed
options.C: The explanation is wrong; CO₂ has no effect on temperature at all
options.D: The explanation is correct, but only CO₂ from volcanoes is harmful, not human-made CO₂

questions.explanation: A natural greenhouse effect, including CO₂, maintains Earth's average temperature around 15°C — without it, Earth would be about −18°C and mostly frozen; the problem is excess CO₂ from human activity enhancing this effect beyond the natural balance. Option A is wrong because the greenhouse effect is not inherently harmful; it is the amplification of it through excess emissions that causes climate change.

questions.title: Variables in Fair Testing
questions.prompt: Two students investigate which type of paper towel absorbs the most water. Student A uses one sheet of Brand X and two sheets of Brand Y, and dips them in water for different lengths of time. A classmate says the experiment is flawed. Which variable is NOT being controlled?

options.A: The type of paper towel being tested
options.B: The amount of water used in the bowl
options.C: The number of sheets used and the time each towel spends in the water
options.D: The colour of the paper towels

questions.explanation: In a fair test, all variables except the independent variable (brand of towel) must be kept the same — using different numbers of sheets and different dipping times means two variables are uncontrolled, making any result unreliable. Option A is actually the independent variable the students are intentionally changing, so it is correct that it differs between trials.

questions.title: Sound Waves and Medium
questions.prompt: An astronaut outside the International Space Station bangs two metal tools together. Her crewmate, standing 5 metres away outside the station, cannot hear the bang. Why not?

options.A: Sound waves travel too slowly in space to cover 5 metres
options.B: Space suits muffle all sound completely
options.C: Sound requires a medium such as air or water to travel, and space is a vacuum
options.D: The metal tools do not vibrate in zero gravity

questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles to vibrate and pass energy along — in the vacuum of space there are virtually no particles, so sound cannot propagate at all regardless of distance. Option A is a misconception; sound does not travel 'slowly' in space — it cannot travel through space at any speed because there is no medium.

questions.title: Adaptation and Habitat Change
questions.prompt: Polar bears have thick white fur, a thick layer of fat under their skin, and large padded paws. If global warming gradually melted Arctic sea ice over 100 years, which of these adaptations would become LEAST useful for surviving in a warmer, ice-free Arctic?

options.A: Large padded paws that spread weight across ice
options.B: Thick fat layer that provides energy reserves
options.C: Strong swimming ability for crossing open water
options.D: Ability to eat fish and seals

questions.explanation: Large paws are specifically adapted to distribute a polar bear's weight across thin or fragile ice — if sea ice disappears, this adaptation provides no advantage on open water or land. Options B and D remain useful regardless because fat stores provide energy during food scarcity, and hunting seals and fish would still be essential in an ice-free Arctic.

questions.title: Mixtures and Separation Techniques
questions.prompt: A student has a mixture of sand, salt, and iron filings. She wants to separate all three substances. Which sequence of steps would successfully separate them all?

options.A: Filter the mixture, then heat it, then use a magnet
options.B: Use a magnet to remove iron filings, then dissolve the rest in water, filter out sand, then evaporate the water to leave salt
options.C: Dissolve everything in water, then use a magnet, then filter
options.D: Evaporate the mixture first, then filter, then use a magnet

questions.explanation: Using a magnet first removes iron filings (which are magnetic); adding water dissolves the salt but not the sand, so filtering separates the sand; evaporating the water then yields pure salt — each step exploits a different physical property. Option A fails because filtering alone cannot separate dissolved salt from water, and heating the unseparated mixture would not cleanly isolate each substance.

questions.title: Human Impact on Soil
questions.prompt: Farmers in a valley have been growing the same single crop (a monoculture) on the same land for 20 years without adding compost or rotating crops. What is most likely to have happened to the soil over this time?

options.A: The soil has become richer because the crop roots add nutrients each year
options.B: The soil nutrients have been depleted because the same crop removes the same minerals year after year
options.C: The soil quality has improved because monocultures prevent weeds from taking nutrients
options.D: The soil has become denser and more fertile due to repeated rainfall compression

questions.explanation: Every crop removes specific minerals from the soil as it grows; without crop rotation or added compost to replenish them, the same nutrients are depleted year after year, reducing soil fertility. Option A is a misconception; roots do add some organic matter when they decay, but this is far outweighed by the nutrients removed by the harvested crop over 20 years.

questions.title: Pulse Rate and Exercise
questions.prompt: A student measures her resting pulse rate at 72 beats per minute. After running for 3 minutes, her pulse rises to 130 beats per minute. What is the most direct reason her heart beats faster during exercise?

options.A: The heart gets warm and expands during exercise, which forces it to beat faster
options.B: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose during exercise, so the heart pumps blood faster to deliver them
options.C: Breathing faster pushes the heart to speed up by pressing on it
options.D: The heart beats faster to produce more body heat and keep muscles warm

questions.explanation: Working muscles consume oxygen and glucose more rapidly and produce more carbon dioxide; the cardiovascular system responds by increasing heart rate to circulate blood more quickly, delivering supplies and removing waste. Option D is a misconception; heat is a by-product of muscle activity, not the goal — the heart rate increases to meet metabolic demands, not to generate warmth.

questions.title: Renewable Energy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A city council is deciding whether to build a large wind farm on a hillside outside town. A councillor says: 'Wind energy is perfectly clean and has no disadvantages.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; wind energy produces no pollution of any kind and has no negative effects
options.B: The claim is partly wrong; wind energy produces no air pollution during operation but can affect wildlife, habitats, and landscape, and only generates power when wind blows
options.C: The claim is wrong; wind turbines produce more carbon dioxide than coal power stations
options.D: The claim is correct, but only for turbines built near the coast where wind is strongest

questions.explanation: Wind turbines generate electricity without burning fuel or emitting greenhouse gases during operation, but they can kill birds and bats, create noise, alter habitats during construction, and produce no electricity during calm conditions — so they have real trade-offs. Option A is incorrect because 'perfectly clean with no disadvantages' ignores documented ecological and practical limitations of wind energy.

questions.title: Photosynthesis and Oxygen
questions.prompt: A student places an aquatic plant in bright sunlight and notices tiny bubbles rising from its leaves. She then moves the plant into a dark cupboard and the bubbles stop. What is the most precise explanation for why the bubbles stop in the dark?

options.A: The plant stops absorbing carbon dioxide because it no longer needs energy.
options.B: Without light, the plant cannot drive the chemical reactions that split water molecules and release oxygen gas.
options.C: Darkness causes the plant's stomata to seal completely, trapping all gases inside the leaf.
options.D: The plant switches to releasing carbon dioxide instead of oxygen, so no new bubbles form.

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires light energy to power the reactions that split water and produce oxygen as a by-product; without light those reactions halt entirely, so no oxygen bubbles are produced. Option D is a distractor because although plants do respire and release CO₂ at all times, that process does not stop the formation of observable bubbles—the key point is that oxygen production from photosynthesis has ceased, not that CO₂ replaces it in bubble form.

questions.title: Food Web Energy Loss
questions.prompt: In a grassland food chain — grass → grasshopper → frog → hawk — only about 10% of the energy at each level passes to the next. A student claims that removing all frogs would have no effect on the hawk population because hawks can eat other prey. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct; hawks are apex predators and always find alternative food sources easily.
options.B: The claim is partially correct; hawk numbers might drop temporarily but would recover because grasshoppers would become more abundant for them to eat directly.
options.C: The claim is incorrect; losing frogs removes a key energy link, and even if hawks switch prey, the grasshopper population would explode, over-consuming grass and destabilising the whole system.
options.D: The claim is incorrect; without frogs, hawks would immediately go extinct because they cannot digest any other prey.

questions.explanation: Removing frogs disrupts the energy flow and population balance: grasshoppers, no longer controlled, would over-eat grass, reducing plant cover and ultimately the energy base for all consumers including hawks. Option B is tempting but wrong because hawks are not well-adapted to catching large numbers of grasshoppers efficiently, and the ecological cascade affecting the grass layer is the deeper problem.

questions.title: States of Matter Particles
questions.prompt: A scientist heats a fixed amount of water in a sealed container until it completely turns to steam. Which statement correctly describes what happens to the particles during this change?

options.A: The water particles break apart into hydrogen and oxygen atoms, which then move freely.
options.B: The particles gain energy, move faster, and overcome the forces holding them close together, spreading to fill the container.
options.C: The particles shrink in size so they take up less space individually, allowing them to spread out.
options.D: The particles gain energy and arrange themselves into a new fixed pattern throughout the container.

questions.explanation: During evaporation and boiling, water molecules gain kinetic energy, move faster, and the intermolecular forces are overcome so they spread out to fill any available space — this is the defining particle model of a gas. Option A is wrong because changing state is a physical change, not a chemical one; the water molecules (H₂O) remain intact and do not decompose into hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.title: Thermal Expansion of Solids
questions.prompt: Engineers building a steel railway must leave small gaps between sections of track. A student argues that this is wasteful and the gaps should be welded shut to make the track stronger. Which reasoning best explains why the gaps are essential?

options.A: The gaps allow rainwater to drain away so the track does not rust as quickly.
options.B: Steel expands when heated; without gaps, sections would push against each other and buckle dangerously on hot days.
options.C: The gaps reduce vibration from passing trains, protecting the joints from metal fatigue.
options.D: Steel contracts when cold, so gaps prevent sections from pulling apart and snapping in winter.

questions.explanation: Metals expand when their temperature rises because the particles vibrate more vigorously and push further apart; without expansion gaps, the compressive force between sections can cause the track to bow upward — a dangerous buckling effect. Option D describes a real but secondary concern: contraction in winter creates tension, not compression, and the gaps are sized primarily to manage thermal expansion rather than contraction.

questions.title: Inherited vs Acquired Traits
questions.prompt: A champion weightlifter has very large muscles. Her daughter is born with average-sized muscles. The weightlifter claims her daughter will naturally develop large muscles too because she inherited them. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The error is assuming muscles are controlled by genes; muscle size is entirely determined by diet alone.
options.B: The error is confusing an acquired characteristic with an inherited one; large muscles built through training are not passed on through DNA.
options.C: The error is that daughters cannot inherit physical traits from their mothers, only from their fathers.
options.D: The error is assuming the daughter will train; if she trains equally hard she will definitely develop the same muscle size.

questions.explanation: Muscles enlarged through exercise are an acquired characteristic — a change in the body caused by the environment and effort, not a change to the DNA in reproductive cells, so they cannot be inherited. Option D is tempting because it sounds reasonable, but it misses the fundamental point: even with identical training, genetic variation means outcomes differ, and more importantly the claim itself about inheritance is still scientifically wrong regardless of training.

questions.title: Refraction of Light
questions.prompt: A straw placed in a glass of water appears to bend at the water's surface when viewed from the side, even though the straw is perfectly straight. What causes this optical effect?

options.A: Light reflects off the straw at a different angle underwater because water is denser and acts like a mirror.
options.B: Light travels at a different speed in water than in air, causing it to change direction as it crosses the boundary, shifting the apparent position of the submerged part.
options.C: Water magnifies objects because its molecules are larger than air molecules, stretching the image of the straw.
options.D: The water pressure pushes the light rays sideways, making the submerged straw look displaced.

questions.explanation: Refraction occurs because light slows down when it moves from air into water (a denser medium), causing the rays to bend at the boundary; this makes the underwater portion of the straw appear shifted from its actual position. Option A is wrong because, although some reflection does occur at the surface, the bending appearance is caused by refraction of transmitted light, not reflection.

questions.title: Water Cycle and Condensation
questions.prompt: On a cold morning, the outside of a glass of iced water becomes wet, even though no water was poured on it. A student says the cold is 'leaking' through the glass. What is actually happening, and why is the student's explanation incorrect?

options.A: Water vapour in the surrounding air is cooled by the glass below its dew point and condenses into liquid water on the outer surface; cold does not 'leak' because cold is an absence of heat, not a substance.
options.B: Water seeps through tiny pores in the glass from the cold liquid inside to the outside surface.
options.C: The glass attracts moisture from the air using static electricity generated by the temperature difference.
options.D: Cold air near the glass contains more water vapour than warm air, so the extra vapour settles on the glass surface.

questions.explanation: When the glass cools the air immediately surrounding it below the dew point, water vapour loses enough energy to change state and condense as liquid droplets on the outer surface — this is the same process that forms dew. Option B is wrong because standard glass is not porous to liquid water; the moisture comes from the atmosphere, not from inside the glass.

questions.title: Natural Selection Pressure
questions.prompt: A population of beetles lives on light-coloured sand. Most are pale, but a few are dark. A new predatory bird arrives that hunts by sight. Predict what will happen to the beetle population over many generations, and explain the mechanism.

options.A: Dark beetles will sense the danger and gradually change their colour to pale over their lifetime, passing this ability to their offspring.
options.B: Both colour types will survive equally well because the bird will adapt to hunting both colours at the same rate.
options.C: Pale beetles survive and reproduce at higher rates because they are camouflaged; over generations the proportion of pale beetles increases as dark ones are preferentially eaten.
options.D: The entire beetle population will go extinct within a few generations because no individual beetle can escape a predatory bird.

questions.explanation: Natural selection operates because pale beetles are better camouflaged on light sand, so they have a survival advantage, reproduce more, and pass their pale colouration genes to offspring; over many generations, pale colouration becomes more common in the population. Option A describes Lamarckian inheritance — the discredited idea that acquired changes during an organism's lifetime are passed to offspring — which is not how evolution works.

questions.title: Electrical Conductors and Insulators
questions.prompt: A student tests several materials by connecting them one at a time into a circuit with a battery and a bulb. Copper wire and graphite (pencil lead) both light the bulb, but rubber and glass do not. She concludes that only metals conduct electricity. What is wrong with her conclusion?

options.A: Nothing is wrong; rubber and glass are metals that have been chemically treated to stop conducting.
options.B: Her conclusion is too broad; graphite is a non-metal that also conducts electricity, which her own results already show.
options.C: Her conclusion is wrong because all non-metals conduct electricity just as well as metals if the battery is powerful enough.
options.D: Her conclusion is wrong because rubber can conduct electricity in very humid conditions, making it a metal-like material.

questions.explanation: Graphite is a form of carbon — a non-metal — yet it conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons that can move through its layered structure; her own data contradicts her conclusion. Option C is wrong because many non-metals (like rubber and glass) are excellent insulators regardless of voltage at normal levels, and increasing voltage does not convert an insulator into a conductor under everyday experimental conditions.

questions.title: Greenhouse Effect Mechanism
questions.prompt: A student says: 'The greenhouse effect is bad and should be completely eliminated.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of how Earth's atmosphere maintains temperatures suitable for life.

options.A: The claim is correct; the greenhouse effect only raises temperatures and has never had any beneficial role in Earth's history.
options.B: The claim is partially incorrect; a natural greenhouse effect is essential for keeping Earth warm enough for life, but the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by excess human-produced gases is the problem.
options.C: The claim is incorrect; the greenhouse effect is entirely caused by water vapour and is unaffected by human activities.
