options.A: The explanation is fully correct: the number of bonds made vs. broken determines whether a reaction is exothermic
options.B: The explanation is mostly correct but the key factor is the total energy of bonds made versus bonds broken, not the number of bonds — products must have stronger (lower energy) bonds than reactants
options.C: The explanation is incorrect: exothermic reactions release energy only because the products have fewer electrons than the reactants, reducing the system's electrical potential energy
options.D: The explanation is incorrect: breaking bonds always releases energy and making bonds always requires energy, so exothermic reactions actually break more bonds than they form

questions.explanation: Bond energy (enthalpy) determines exothermicity: energy is released when bonds form and absorbed when bonds break; a reaction is exothermic when the total energy released forming bonds in the products exceeds the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants — meaning the products contain stronger, lower-energy bonds. Option A is wrong because the number of bonds is irrelevant if those bonds are weak; for example, combustion of hydrogen forms only two O-H bonds but the energy of those bonds greatly exceeds the energy needed to break H-H and O=O bonds, making it strongly exothermic despite equal bond counts.

questions.title: Star Life Cycle Stages
questions.prompt: Astronomers classify the Sun as a main-sequence star. A student claims the Sun will eventually explode as a supernova, as stars do at the end of their lives. Evaluate this claim in the context of stellar evolution.

options.A: The claim is correct: all stars end their lives in a supernova explosion that disperses their material into space
options.B: The claim is incorrect: the Sun will expand into a red giant, then shed its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf — a supernova requires a star at least 8–10 times the Sun's mass
options.C: The claim is incorrect: the Sun will expand into a red giant and then collapse directly into a neutron star without a supernova because it lacks sufficient hydrogen
options.D: The claim is partially correct: the Sun will undergo a small-scale supernova called a nova when its outer layers are ejected, but it will not produce a neutron star or black hole

questions.explanation: Stellar evolution models show that low-to-medium mass stars (≤8 solar masses) like the Sun lack the core mass needed to generate the gravitational collapse and explosive shockwave of a Type II supernova; instead, the Sun will exhaust its hydrogen in ~5 billion years, expand as a red giant, and gently eject its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving behind a dense carbon-oxygen white dwarf. Option C is incorrect because a neutron star forms only from the supernova collapse of a massive star (>8–10 M☉); the Sun's remnant core is too small to overcome electron degeneracy pressure, so it stabilises as a white dwarf.

questions.title: Genetic Mutation vs Variation
questions.prompt: Two students debate the origin of genetic variation. Student A says mutations are always harmful and evolution would stop without them. Student B says mutations are the ultimate source of new alleles, but most are neutral, and natural selection acts on existing variation. Evaluate both positions.

options.A: Student A is correct: mutations cause diseases such as cancer, and without selection removing them, species would deteriorate
options.B: Both students are partially correct: mutations are the original source of alleles, but most are neutral or mildly deleterious; Student B is more accurate overall
options.C: Student B is entirely correct and Student A is entirely wrong: mutations are never harmful — natural selection ensures only beneficial mutations persist in a population
options.D: Student A is correct that evolution would stop without mutations, but incorrect that all mutations are harmful — evolution requires both beneficial and neutral mutations to operate

questions.explanation: Molecular evolutionary theory (the neutral theory proposed by Motoo Kimura, 1968) established that the majority of mutations are selectively neutral — they neither improve nor impair fitness — and drift randomly in populations; mutations are the ultimate source of new alleles without which no new variation could arise, but Student A is wrong to claim they are always harmful. Option C overstates Student B's position: some mutations are definitively harmful (e.g., those causing sickle cell disease in homozygous individuals), so the blanket claim that mutations are never harmful is scientifically inaccurate.

questions.title: Energy Transformation Efficiency
questions.prompt: A petrol car engine converts only about 25% of the fuel's chemical energy into kinetic energy; an electric motor converts about 85–90% into kinetic energy. A student concludes that electric vehicles are always more energy-efficient than petrol vehicles overall. Discuss whether this conclusion is fully justified.

options.A: The conclusion is fully justified: motor efficiency directly determines total vehicle efficiency, so electric vehicles are always more efficient
options.B: The conclusion is an oversimplification: total efficiency must include the efficiency of electricity generation and transmission, which varies by energy source — if the grid relies on coal, overall well-to-wheel efficiency may be similar to petrol
options.C: The conclusion is incorrect: electric motors are less efficient than stated because lithium batteries lose 50% of stored energy as heat during discharge
options.D: The conclusion is fully justified because even if electricity is generated by coal, the grid infrastructure converts heat to electricity far more efficiently than a car engine converts fuel

questions.explanation: A systems-level analysis (well-to-wheel efficiency) must account for all energy conversion steps: extracting fuel, generating and transmitting electricity, and the motor's efficiency; a coal-fired power plant operates at ~35–40% thermal efficiency, and after transmission losses (~5–8%), the electricity delivered to the EV may reflect an upstream efficiency that narrows the advantage over petrol vehicles — though EVs are still generally more efficient overall in most modern grid mixes. Option D is incorrect in its reasoning: a coal-fired power plant converting heat to electricity is not more efficient than a car engine at that step alone (~35% vs. ~25%), and the student's conclusion ignores the full system chain, making it an incomplete analysis.

questions.title: Acid Base pH Scale
questions.prompt: A student tests two acidic solutions: Solution X has a pH of 3 and Solution Y has a pH of 5. She states that Solution X is twice as acidic as Solution Y. Identify the error in her quantitative reasoning and provide a corrected statement.

options.A: The student is correct: a difference of 2 on the pH scale corresponds to twice the hydrogen ion concentration
options.B: The student is incorrect: the pH scale is logarithmic (base 10), so a difference of 2 pH units means Solution X has 100 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Solution Y
options.C: The student is incorrect: the pH scale is logarithmic, but a decrease of 2 units means Solution X has 20 times the hydrogen ion concentration of Solution Y
options.D: The student is incorrect: pH does not measure acidity directly; it measures alkalinity, so a lower pH value indicates a less acidic solution

questions.explanation: The pH scale is defined as pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], making it a logarithmic scale where each unit decrease in pH represents a tenfold increase in hydrogen ion concentration; therefore, pH 3 corresponds to [H⁺] = 10⁻³ mol/L and pH 5 to 10⁻⁵ mol/L — a factor of 100 difference, not 2. Option C is a common error: students sometimes multiply the pH difference (2) by 10 to get 20, confusing the logarithmic relationship (10² = 100) with a simple linear factor.

questions.title: Enzyme Activity and Temperature
questions.prompt: A student investigates the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at temperatures of 10°C, 20°C, 37°C, and 70°C. At 70°C the reaction rate drops to nearly zero. Which explanation best accounts for this observation?

options.A: The substrate molecules move too slowly at high temperatures to reach the active site
options.B: The enzyme's active site is permanently altered because high heat breaks bonds maintaining the tertiary structure
options.C: The enzyme is destroyed by oxidation when oxygen molecules collide more frequently at higher temperatures
options.D: High temperature causes the substrate to decompose before it can bind to the enzyme

questions.explanation: Above an enzyme's optimum temperature, the additional thermal energy breaks the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that maintain the tertiary structure, denaturing the enzyme and distorting the active site irreversibly. Option A is wrong because higher temperatures actually increase molecular kinetic energy and collision frequency — slow substrate movement is a low-temperature effect, not a high-temperature one.

questions.title: Natural Selection Evidence
questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is frequently cited as direct evidence for natural selection. Which statement most accurately explains why antibiotic use leads to resistant bacterial populations?

options.A: Bacteria sense the antibiotic and deliberately mutate their DNA to survive it
options.B: Antibiotics cause mutations that create resistance genes in all exposed bacteria
options.C: Resistant variants already present in the population survive and reproduce preferentially when antibiotic pressure is applied
options.D: Bacteria exchange resistance genes only after they detect a lethal chemical threat in the environment

questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on pre-existing genetic variation; resistant individuals already existed before antibiotic exposure and are selectively favoured to survive and reproduce, increasing resistance allele frequency in the population. Options A and B both imply directed or Lamarckian mutation in response to need, which contradicts the modern evolutionary synthesis — mutations are random and occur regardless of environmental pressure.

questions.title: Newton's Third Law
questions.prompt: A rocket in deep space fires its engine, expelling exhaust gases backward. A student claims the rocket accelerates because the exhaust gases push against the surrounding air. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; without air resistance the rocket would not accelerate
options.B: The claim is incorrect; the rocket accelerates because the engine pushes gases backward and by Newton's third law the gases exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket
options.C: The claim is partially correct; air resistance slows the rocket but the exhaust pressure against the air is still the primary driving force
options.D: The claim is incorrect; the rocket accelerates because the burning fuel increases the total mass of the system, providing greater inertia

questions.explanation: Rocket propulsion is an application of Newton's third law and conservation of momentum: the rocket exerts a backward force on expelled gases, and the gases exert an equal forward force on the rocket — no external medium is required, which is why rockets function in the vacuum of space. Option A is a common misconception arising from confusing jet propulsion with rocket propulsion; jets do rely on intake air but rockets carry their own oxidiser.

questions.title: DNA Replication Mechanism
questions.prompt: During DNA replication, a new strand is synthesised complementary to each template strand. Which base would be incorporated opposite a guanine (G) residue on the template?

options.A: Adenine, because purines always pair with purines to maintain strand width
options.B: Thymine, because G–T pairs are the most thermally stable in double-stranded DNA
options.C: Cytosine, because G and C form three hydrogen bonds according to Chargaff's complementary base-pairing rules
options.D: Uracil, because uracil replaces thymine whenever guanine is the template base

questions.explanation: Chargaff's rules state that guanine pairs exclusively with cytosine via three hydrogen bonds (and adenine with thymine via two), ensuring faithful complementary replication. Option D confuses DNA replication with RNA transcription — uracil is incorporated in RNA synthesis when the template base is adenine, not guanine, and it does not appear in newly synthesised DNA strands.

questions.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
questions.prompt: A sealed, thermally insulated container holds a gas. A paddle wheel inside is driven by an external motor, stirring the gas. What happens to the internal energy of the gas, and why?

options.A: Internal energy decreases because the rotating paddle compresses the gas, reducing molecular potential energy
options.B: Internal energy stays constant because the container is sealed and no heat can enter or leave
options.C: Internal energy increases because work is done on the gas by the paddle, and since the container is insulated no energy can leave as heat
options.D: Internal energy increases temporarily, then returns to its original value once the paddle stops, conserving total energy

questions.explanation: By the first law of thermodynamics, ΔU = Q + W; since the container is thermally insulated Q = 0, but the paddle does positive work on the gas (W > 0), so internal energy — and therefore temperature — rises permanently. Option B incorrectly equates a sealed container with a thermally insulated one; sealing prevents mass transfer but does not prevent work being done on the system.

questions.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Order
questions.prompt: Compare X-rays and radio waves in terms of their position in the electromagnetic spectrum. Which statement correctly describes a key difference between them?

options.A: X-rays travel faster than radio waves because higher frequency waves carry more energy per photon and therefore move more quickly
options.B: Radio waves have a longer wavelength and lower frequency than X-rays, though both travel at the same speed in a vacuum
options.C: X-rays have a longer wavelength than radio waves, which is why they can penetrate dense materials
options.D: Radio waves have a higher frequency than X-rays because they are produced by large antenna structures that oscillate more rapidly

questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum regardless of frequency; X-rays have wavelengths of roughly 0.01–10 nm whereas radio waves range from millimetres to kilometres, giving radio waves much lower frequencies. Option A is a classic misconception — wave speed in a vacuum is constant for all EM radiation; it is the photon energy (E = hf) that increases with frequency, not propagation speed.

questions.title: Mitosis vs Meiosis
questions.prompt: A student states: 'Meiosis and mitosis both produce genetically identical daughter cells.' Identify the error in this statement.

options.A: The statement is entirely correct; both processes use identical spindle mechanisms and therefore produce identical cells
options.B: Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells, but meiosis produces genetically varied haploid cells due to crossing over and independent assortment
options.C: Neither process produces genetically identical cells because random mutation occurs during every round of DNA replication
options.D: Meiosis produces identical cells, but mitosis introduces variation through homologous recombination at each division

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two diploid daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell (barring rare replication errors), whereas meiosis introduces genetic variation through crossing over in prophase I and random orientation of homologous pairs during metaphase I, yielding four haploid, genetically unique gametes. Option D reverses the processes — homologous recombination (crossing over) occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.

questions.title: Greenhouse Effect Mechanism
questions.prompt: Why does an increase in atmospheric CO₂ concentration lead to a rise in average global surface temperatures?

options.A: CO₂ absorbs incoming ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, preventing it from reaching the surface and heating the upper atmosphere instead
options.B: CO₂ molecules reflect incoming solar shortwave radiation back to Earth, effectively increasing the intensity of sunlight at the surface
options.C: CO₂ absorbs outgoing infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and re-emits it in all directions, reducing the net loss of energy to space
options.D: CO₂ reacts chemically with ozone, thinning the ozone layer and allowing more solar energy to penetrate to the surface

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases such as CO₂ are largely transparent to incoming shortwave solar radiation but absorb outgoing longwave (infrared) radiation emitted by Earth's surface; re-emission in all directions, including back toward Earth, reduces radiative cooling and raises equilibrium surface temperature. Option A is wrong because CO₂ does not significantly absorb UV radiation — that role belongs to stratospheric ozone — and the mechanism described would cool, not warm, the surface.

questions.title: Ohm's Law Application
questions.prompt: A resistor connected to a 12 V battery carries a current of 0.5 A. What is the resistance of the resistor?

options.A: 6 Ω

questions.explanation: Ohm's law states V = IR, so R = V/I = 12/0.5 = 24 Ω. Option A arises from the error of multiplying voltage by current (12 × 0.5 = 6) rather than dividing — a common procedural mistake when students confuse the formula rearrangements.

questions.title: Photosynthesis Light Reactions
questions.prompt: In the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, water molecules are split. What is the primary purpose of this process?

options.A: To release carbon dioxide that will be fixed in the Calvin cycle
options.B: To provide electrons that replace those lost from chlorophyll when it absorbs light energy, and to release oxygen as a by-product
options.C: To generate ATP directly by breaking high-energy hydrogen bonds in the water molecule
options.D: To supply hydrogen ions that combine with CO₂ to form glucose in the stroma

questions.explanation: Photolysis of water (2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂) replenishes electrons lost from the reaction centre of photosystem II when they are excited by light and passed to the electron transport chain; the oxygen released is a by-product. Option D conflates the role of hydrogen carriers (NADPH) with direct glucose synthesis — glucose is formed in the Calvin cycle using NADPH and ATP, not raw hydrogen ions combining with CO₂.

questions.title: Atomic Structure and Isotopes
questions.prompt: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are both isotopes of carbon. What do they have in common, and what makes them different?

options.A: They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons, giving them different chemical behaviours
options.B: They have the same number of protons and electrons but differ in neutron number, with Carbon-14 having two additional neutrons
options.C: They have the same mass number but different atomic numbers, placing them in different positions on the periodic table
options.D: They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of electrons, altering their ionic charge

questions.explanation: Isotopes of the same element have identical proton numbers (6 for carbon) and therefore the same electron configuration and chemical properties, but differ in neutron number; Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, giving them different mass numbers. Option A is incorrect because it reverses the definition — isotopes differ in neutron number, not proton number; different proton numbers would define entirely different elements.

questions.title: Predator-Prey Population Dynamics
questions.prompt: In a predator–prey system, a sudden large increase in the prey population is most likely to be followed by which sequence of events?

options.A: An immediate decline in prey numbers as the environment reaches carrying capacity, with no effect on predator numbers
options.B: A lagged increase in predator numbers due to greater food availability, followed by a decline in prey as predation pressure increases
options.C: A simultaneous increase in both predator and prey populations that continues indefinitely as resources expand
options.D: A rapid decline in predator numbers because increased prey density introduces new diseases that transfer to predators

questions.explanation: Classic Lotka–Volterra dynamics predict that prey population growth precedes a lagged increase in predator populations (due to improved predator survival and reproduction); rising predation eventually reduces prey numbers, subsequently causing predator numbers to fall — producing the characteristic oscillating cycles. Option A incorrectly attributes prey decline solely to carrying capacity and ignores the density-dependent predation feedback that is central to the model.

questions.title: Wave Refraction Principles
questions.prompt: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block at an angle. It bends toward the normal as it enters the glass. What does this tell us about the speed of light in glass compared with air?

options.A: Light travels faster in glass because denser materials give light more energy
options.B: Light travels at the same speed in both media but changes direction due to a change in wavelength
options.C: Light travels slower in glass; the reduction in speed causes the wavelength to decrease and the ray bends toward the normal
options.D: Light travels slower in glass because glass absorbs photons and re-emits them at a lower frequency, reducing speed

questions.explanation: When light enters an optically denser medium it slows down; by Snell's law (n = c/v), a higher refractive index means lower wave speed, shorter wavelength, and the ray bends toward the normal. Frequency remains constant across the boundary. Option D is a common misconception — frequency does not change upon refraction; only wavelength and speed change, not the photon frequency.

questions.title: Periodic Table Trends
questions.prompt: Moving from left to right across Period 3 of the periodic table, how does the atomic radius generally change, and what is the main reason for this trend?

options.A: Atomic radius increases because each successive element gains an extra electron shell, pushing outer electrons further from the nucleus
options.B: Atomic radius decreases because the increasing nuclear charge pulls the same outer electron shell closer to the nucleus
options.C: Atomic radius increases because additional protons repel each other, expanding the nucleus and pushing electrons outward
options.D: Atomic radius remains roughly constant because the extra proton and electron added at each step cancel each other's effects

questions.explanation: Across a period the principal quantum number (electron shell) stays the same, but the nuclear charge increases by one proton at each step; the greater electrostatic attraction pulls the outer electrons closer, decreasing atomic radius from Na to Cl. Option A describes the down-group trend (increasing shells), not the across-period trend, and is the most common confusion students make when comparing periodic trends.

questions.title: Tectonic Plate Boundaries
questions.prompt: At a subduction zone, an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate. Which combination of geological features is most likely to form at this boundary?

options.A: A mid-ocean ridge and frequent shallow-focus earthquakes only
options.B: A deep ocean trench, a volcanic arc on the continental plate, and deep-focus earthquakes along the subducting slab
options.C: A rift valley and basaltic flood plains as the plates diverge under compression
options.D: A mountain range formed purely by folding with no volcanic activity, because magma cannot form at convergent boundaries

questions.explanation: At an oceanic–continental subduction zone, the denser oceanic plate sinks into the mantle forming a deep trench; water released from the subducting slab lowers the melting point of mantle rock, generating magma that rises to create a volcanic arc on the overriding continent; deep-focus earthquakes occur along the subducting slab (Wadati–Benioff zone). Option A describes a divergent (constructive) boundary where new oceanic crust forms, not a convergent one.

questions.title: Mendelian Genetics Ratios
questions.prompt: Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed for a trait governed by simple dominance. What phenotypic ratio is expected in the offspring, and what is the underlying genotypic ratio?

options.A: Phenotypic ratio 1:2:1; genotypic ratio 3:1
options.B: Phenotypic ratio 3:1 (dominant : recessive); genotypic ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
options.C: Phenotypic ratio 1:1; genotypic ratio 1 AA : 1 aa
options.D: Phenotypic ratio 3:1; genotypic ratio 3 AA : 1 aa

questions.explanation: A Punnett square for Aa × Aa yields genotypes AA : Aa : aa in a 1:2:1 ratio; because A is dominant, both AA and Aa individuals display the dominant phenotype, giving a 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypic ratio. Option A reverses the two ratios — 1:2:1 is the genotypic ratio, not the phenotypic ratio, and 3:1 is the phenotypic ratio, not the genotypic one.

questions.title: Conservation of Momentum
questions.prompt: Two ice skaters, initially at rest, push off each other. Skater A has a mass of 50 kg and moves away at 3 m s⁻¹. Skater B has a mass of 75 kg. What is Skater B's speed immediately after the push?

options.A: 3 m s⁻¹, because both skaters experience the same force and therefore gain the same speed
options.B: 4.5 m s⁻¹, because the heavier skater receives more momentum proportional to the mass difference
options.C: 2 m s⁻¹, because total momentum is conserved and the heavier skater moves more slowly in proportion
options.D: 1.5 m s⁻¹, because kinetic energy is shared equally between both skaters

questions.explanation: Since the system starts at rest, total initial momentum = 0; by conservation of momentum, 50 × 3 = 75 × v, giving v = 2 m s⁻¹ for Skater B. Option A incorrectly applies Newton's third law to speeds rather than forces — equal and opposite forces act for the same time (equal impulses), but greater mass means smaller velocity change, not the same velocity.

questions.title: pH Scale and Acids
questions.prompt: A solution has a pH of 3. Another solution has a pH of 1. To what extent is the second solution more acidic than the first?

options.A: Twice as acidic, because the pH difference is 2
options.B: Ten times more acidic, because each pH unit represents a tenfold difference in H⁺ ion concentration
options.C: One hundred times more acidic, because a difference of 2 pH units corresponds to a 10² increase in H⁺ ion concentration
options.D: Twenty times more acidic, because pH is a linear scale and each unit adds a fixed increment of acidity

questions.explanation: pH = −log[H⁺], so a difference of 2 pH units means a 10² = 100-fold difference in hydrogen ion concentration; pH 1 has 100 times more H⁺ ions than pH 3. Option B would be correct for a difference of only 1 pH unit; students frequently stop at one order of magnitude when the actual difference spans two pH units.

questions.title: Nitrogen Cycle Processes
questions.prompt: Which process in the nitrogen cycle converts atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia (NH₃), making nitrogen available to living organisms?

options.A: Denitrification, carried out by anaerobic bacteria in waterlogged soils
options.B: Nitrification, in which nitrite bacteria oxidise ammonium ions to nitrates
options.C: Nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium that reduce N₂ to NH₃
options.D: Ammonification, in which decomposers break down organic nitrogen compounds into ammonia

questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation is the reduction of inert atmospheric N₂ to bioavailable ammonia (NH₃) by diazotrophic bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium in root nodules, Azotobacter in soil), using the enzyme nitrogenase; this is the primary entry point of nitrogen into biological systems. Option A describes denitrification, which is the reverse process — it returns fixed nitrogen back to N₂, removing it from the biological nitrogen cycle.

questions.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory
questions.prompt: What would happen if a fixed amount of ideal gas in a sealed, rigid container were heated from 300 K to 600 K? Assume volume remains constant.

options.A: The pressure would double, because at constant volume pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature
options.B: The pressure would remain constant while volume increases proportionally with temperature
options.C: The pressure would increase by a factor of four, because pressure depends on the square of the temperature
options.D: The pressure would double and the volume would halve, maintaining a constant product of pressure and volume

questions.explanation: Gay-Lussac's law states that for a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, P/T = constant; doubling the absolute temperature from 300 K to 600 K therefore doubles the pressure, because faster-moving molecules collide with container walls more frequently and with greater force. Option B describes Charles's law, which applies at constant pressure, not constant volume — in a rigid sealed container, volume cannot change.

questions.title: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
questions.prompt: The Hardy–Weinberg principle describes an idealised population in which allele frequencies do not change between generations. Which condition, if violated, would most directly cause allele frequencies to change?

options.A: The population reproduces sexually rather than asexually
options.B: Natural selection gives individuals with certain genotypes a reproductive advantage
options.C: All individuals in the population are diploid organisms
options.D: The population contains both male and female individuals in equal proportions

questions.explanation: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium requires no natural selection (all genotypes must have equal fitness); if selection favours certain alleles, the frequency of those alleles increases each generation, directly violating equilibrium. Options A, C, and D describe standard features of sexually reproducing diploid populations that are actually assumed or compatible with Hardy–Weinberg conditions, not violations of them.

questions.title: Specific Heat Capacity
questions.prompt: Equal masses of water (specific heat capacity 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and copper (specific heat capacity 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) receive the same amount of thermal energy. Which material undergoes the greater temperature rise, and approximately how many times greater is that rise?

options.A: Water rises more because it has a higher specific heat capacity, meaning it stores energy more efficiently
options.B: Copper rises more by a factor of approximately 11, because it has a much lower specific heat capacity so less energy is needed per degree
options.C: Both materials rise by the same temperature, because they receive identical amounts of thermal energy
options.D: Copper rises more by a factor of approximately 2, because metals always heat faster than liquids regardless of specific heat

questions.explanation: Using Q = mcΔT, for the same Q and m, ΔT ∝ 1/c; the ratio of temperature rises is c_water/c_copper = 4200/390 ≈ 10.8, so copper heats roughly 11 times more than water for the same energy input. Option A confuses cause with effect — a higher specific heat capacity means more energy is required per degree, so water actually rises less, not more.

questions.title: Nervous System Signal Transmission
questions.prompt: A student claims that nerve impulses travel along axons as an electrical current in the same way that current flows through a copper wire. Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; both involve electrons flowing continuously along a conductor at the speed of light
options.B: The claim is partially correct; both involve charge movement, but nerve impulses are propagated by sequential ion movements across the membrane rather than electron flow, and travel far more slowly
options.C: The claim is incorrect; nerve impulses are purely chemical signals carried by neurotransmitters along the entire length of the axon
options.D: The claim is partially correct; nerve impulses do involve electron flow but only in myelinated axons where the Schwann cells act as conductors

questions.explanation: An action potential is an electrochemical signal: voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels open sequentially along the axon membrane, producing a wave of depolarisation that propagates at 1–120 m s⁻¹ — far slower than the electron drift in a metal conductor. Option C is incorrect because neurotransmitters are released only at synapses to bridge the gap to the next neuron; signal transmission along the axon itself is electrical (ionic), not chemical.

questions.title: Carbon Cycle Flux
questions.prompt: Deforestation increases the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere. Which TWO processes that are disrupted by deforestation best explain this outcome?

options.A: Reduced photosynthesis (less CO₂ removed from air) and increased respiration or burning of felled trees (more CO₂ released)
options.B: Reduced transpiration (less water vapour produced) and increased nitrogen fixation by exposed soil bacteria
options.C: Increased photosynthesis by pioneer plants that colonise cleared land and increased CO₂ absorption by exposed soil
options.D: Reduced decomposition due to drier soil conditions and reduced respiration by soil organisms, causing net CO₂ accumulation

questions.explanation: Trees remove CO₂ via photosynthesis; when trees are cleared, this carbon sink is lost, and the carbon stored in biomass is released as CO₂ through burning or microbial decomposition of dead wood, simultaneously reducing uptake and increasing emission. Option B mentions transpiration, which affects the water cycle but not directly the carbon cycle flux that causes CO₂ accumulation.

questions.title: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life
questions.prompt: A radioactive sample initially contains 800 undecayed nuclei. Its half-life is 20 minutes. How many undecayed nuclei remain after 60 minutes?

options.A: 200 nuclei
options.B: 400 nuclei
options.C: 100 nuclei
options.D: 266 nuclei

questions.explanation: 60 minutes represents three half-lives (60 ÷ 20 = 3); after each half-life the number halves: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 undecayed nuclei remaining. Option A corresponds to only two half-lives (800 → 400 → 200), reflecting the common error of calculating elapsed time as two half-lives rather than three when dividing 60 by 20.

questions.title: Newton's Second Law
questions.prompt: A net force of 12 N acts on an object of mass 3 kg. What is the acceleration of the object, and which of Newton's laws directly predicts this?

options.A: 4 m/s², Newton's Second Law (F = ma)
options.B: 36 m/s², Newton's Second Law (F = ma)
options.C: 4 m/s², Newton's Third Law (action–reaction pairs)
options.D: 0.25 m/s², Newton's First Law (inertia)

questions.explanation: Newton's Second Law states F = ma, so a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m/s². Option B incorrectly multiplies force and mass rather than dividing, a common arithmetic error students make when rearranging the equation.

questions.title: DNA Base Pairing
questions.prompt: A segment of a DNA template strand reads 3′–ATCGTA–5′. What is the correct complementary coding strand sequence written in the conventional 5′ to 3′ direction?

options.A: 5′–TAGCAT–3′
options.B: 5′–ATCGTA–3′
options.C: 5′–UAGCAU–3′
options.D: 5′–TACGAT–3′

questions.explanation: Complementary base pairing (A–T, T–A, C–G, G–C) gives TAGCAT, and because the complementary strand runs antiparallel to the template, it is written 5′–TAGCAT–3′. Option C substitutes uracil for thymine, which only occurs in RNA transcription, not in the DNA double helix itself.

questions.title: Ideal Gas Law
questions.prompt: A sealed container holds a gas at pressure 100 kPa and temperature 300 K. The temperature is raised to 600 K while volume remains constant. What is the new pressure, assuming ideal gas behaviour?

options.A: 150 kPa
options.B: 200 kPa
options.C: 400 kPa
options.D: 50 kPa

questions.explanation: At constant volume, Gay-Lussac's Law gives P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂, so P₂ = 100 × (600/300) = 200 kPa. Option A (150 kPa) results from incorrectly using a 50% increase in Celsius rather than doubling the absolute Kelvin temperature.

questions.title: Natural Selection Mechanism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Giraffes grew longer necks because they needed to reach higher leaves.' Evaluate this statement in the context of Darwinian natural selection.

options.A: The statement is correct; organisms develop traits in direct response to environmental need.
options.B: The statement is incorrect; variation in neck length already existed, and individuals with longer necks had greater reproductive success over generations.
options.C: The statement is incorrect; neck length increased due to intentional selective breeding by early humans.
options.D: The statement is partially correct; need creates mutations that are then passed on to offspring.

questions.explanation: Darwinian natural selection acts on pre-existing heritable variation: giraffes with randomly longer necks survived better and reproduced more, gradually shifting population traits over generations. Option A describes Lamarckian inheritance — the discredited idea that acquired characteristics driven by need are inherited — a genuine misconception that confident students often confuse with evolution.

questions.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Order
questions.prompt: Which correctly ranks the following electromagnetic radiations in order of increasing frequency: infrared (IR), ultraviolet (UV), X-rays, and microwaves?

options.A: Microwaves → IR → UV → X-rays
options.B: IR → Microwaves → UV → X-rays
options.C: UV → IR → Microwaves → X-rays
options.D: Microwaves → UV → IR → X-rays

questions.explanation: The electromagnetic spectrum in increasing frequency order is: microwaves (~10⁹ Hz) → infrared (~10¹² Hz) → ultraviolet (~10¹⁶ Hz) → X-rays (~10¹⁸ Hz). Option B swaps microwaves and infrared, a common error because students associate 'infrared' with low energy heat and forget microwaves have even lower frequency.

questions.title: Enzyme Specificity
questions.prompt: Why does the enzyme amylase catalyse the breakdown of starch but NOT the breakdown of proteins such as collagen?

options.A: Amylase is too small to bind to the large collagen molecule.
options.B: The active site of amylase is complementary in shape only to the substrate starch, not to protein substrates.
options.C: Collagen has a higher activation energy than starch, so amylase cannot overcome it.
options.D: Amylase only functions in the mouth, where collagen is not present.

questions.explanation: Enzyme specificity arises from the precise three-dimensional shape of the active site, which is complementary to a specific substrate — the lock-and-key (or induced-fit) model. Collagen's molecular shape does not match amylase's active site, preventing binding. Option C incorrectly attributes specificity to activation energy differences rather than molecular shape complementarity.

questions.title: Wave Speed Equation
questions.prompt: A sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz and travels through air at 340 m/s. What is the wavelength of this wave?
questions.explanation: Using v = fλ, wavelength λ = v/f = 340/440 ≈ 0.77 m. Option B (1.29 m) results from inverting the formula and calculating f/v instead of v/f, a frequent algebraic error when rearranging the wave equation.

questions.title: Greenhouse Effect Mechanism
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's explanation: 'The greenhouse effect warms Earth because CO₂ and other gases block sunlight from reaching the surface, trapping heat inside the atmosphere.'

options.A: Greenhouse gases do not include CO₂; the main gas responsible is methane.
options.B: Greenhouse gases do not block incoming sunlight; they absorb and re-emit outgoing longwave infrared radiation from Earth's surface.
options.C: The atmosphere does not trap heat; instead, the ozone layer reflects solar radiation back to Earth.
options.D: The student is correct; CO₂ directly absorbs solar shortwave radiation before it reaches the surface.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases are largely transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation but absorb outgoing long-wave infrared radiation emitted by Earth's warmed surface, re-emitting it in all directions and raising surface temperatures. Option D incorrectly states that CO₂ blocks incoming solar radiation, confusing the mechanism with the behaviour of the ozone layer.

questions.title: Mendel's Law of Segregation
questions.prompt: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed. Using Mendelian genetics, what is the expected ratio of tall to short offspring in the F2 generation?

options.A: 1 tall : 1 short
options.B: 2 tall : 1 short
options.C: 3 tall : 1 short
options.D: 4 tall : 0 short

questions.explanation: A Tt × Tt Punnett square yields genotypes TT, Tt, Tt, tt in a 1:2:1 ratio; since T is dominant, phenotypically 3 plants are tall (TT or Tt) and 1 is short (tt), giving a 3:1 ratio. Option A (1:1) describes a test cross (Tt × tt), a common confusion students make when mixing up F2 and test-cross scenarios.

questions.title: Photosynthesis Reactants
questions.prompt: Which set of reactants and products correctly represents the overall equation for photosynthesis?

options.A: CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ (in the presence of light energy)
options.B: C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + ATP
options.C: CO₂ + O₂ → C₆H₁₂O₆ + H₂O (in the presence of light energy)
options.D: H₂O + O₂ → C₆H₁₂O₆ + CO₂ (in the presence of light energy)

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis converts 6CO₂ + 6H₂O into C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. Option B is the equation for aerobic cellular respiration, the reverse process, which is a common confusion because students see both equations but conflate which is anabolic and which is catabolic.

questions.title: Conservation of Momentum
questions.prompt: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg ball. They stick together after the collision. What is their combined velocity immediately after the collision?

options.A: 3 m/s
options.B: 6 m/s
options.C: 2 m/s
options.D: 4 m/s

questions.explanation: By conservation of momentum: p_before = 2 × 6 = 12 kg·m/s. After collision, total mass = 6 kg, so v = 12/6 = 2 m/s. Option A (3 m/s) results from dividing total momentum only by the moving ball's mass rather than the combined mass, a systematic error in applying the conservation equation.

questions.title: pH and Hydrogen Ions
questions.prompt: A solution has a pH of 3. A second solution has a pH of 5. How many times more concentrated in H⁺ ions is the first solution compared to the second?

options.A: 2 times more concentrated
options.B: 20 times more concentrated
options.C: 100 times more concentrated
options.D: 1000 times more concentrated

questions.explanation: pH = –log[H⁺], so a difference of 2 pH units corresponds to a factor of 10² = 100 in hydrogen ion concentration. Option A assumes the pH scale is linear rather than logarithmic, the most common error students make when comparing acidic solutions.

questions.title: Tectonic Plate Boundaries
questions.prompt: At a convergent boundary where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, which process most directly leads to the formation of a volcanic mountain range on the continent?

options.A: The less dense continental plate subducts beneath the oceanic plate, generating pressure ridges.
options.B: The denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate; as it descends, it partially melts and the magma rises to form volcanoes.
options.C: Both plates move apart, creating a rift valley that later fills with lava to form mountains.
options.D: Friction between the two plates compresses the crust equally, folding both plates upward symmetrically.

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, so it subducts; water released from the descending slab lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above, producing magma that rises through the continental crust to create volcanic arcs such as the Andes. Option A reverses the subduction direction, which would not occur because continental crust is less dense and resists sinking.

questions.title: Oxidation States in Redox
questions.prompt: In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, which species is oxidised and what is its change in oxidation state?

options.A: Cu²⁺ is oxidised; its oxidation state increases from 0 to +2.
options.B: Zn is oxidised; its oxidation state increases from 0 to +2.
options.C: SO₄²⁻ is oxidised; its oxidation state increases from –2 to 0.
options.D: Zn is oxidised; its oxidation state decreases from +2 to 0.

questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG); zinc metal (0) loses two electrons to become Zn²⁺ (+2), so its oxidation state increases from 0 to +2. Option A confuses oxidation with reduction — Cu²⁺ gains electrons and is reduced from +2 to 0, not oxidised.

questions.title: Carbon Cycle Pathways
questions.prompt: A student claims that burning fossil fuels and cellular respiration both release CO₂, so they have equivalent impacts on the global carbon cycle. To what extent is this claim valid?

options.A: Fully valid; both processes add exactly the same amount of CO₂ per year and are equally reversible.
options.B: Partially valid; both release CO₂, but fossil fuel combustion releases carbon stored for millions of years, adding net new carbon to the active cycle at a rate far exceeding natural uptake.
options.C: Invalid; cellular respiration does not release CO₂ — it only consumes oxygen.
options.D: Partially valid; the main difference is that respiration releases methane while combustion releases CO₂.

questions.explanation: While both processes chemically release CO₂, fossil fuel combustion transfers carbon sequestered in lithospheric deposits over millions of years into the atmosphere in decades, disrupting the balance between carbon sources and sinks. Respiration is part of a short-term cycle balanced by photosynthesis, whereas fossil fuel emissions represent a net addition to the active carbon pool. Option A ignores the critical distinction between the geological and biological carbon cycles.

questions.title: Electric Circuits: Ohm's Law
questions.prompt: A resistor connected to a 12 V battery draws a current of 0.4 A. What is the resistance of the resistor?
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law states V = IR, so R = V/I = 12/0.4 = 30 Ω. Option A (4.8 Ω) results from multiplying voltage and current (V × I = power) instead of dividing, a typical algebraic error when students confuse Ohm's Law with the power equation P = IV.

questions.title: Mitosis vs Meiosis
questions.prompt: Compare mitosis and meiosis. Which statement correctly distinguishes meiosis from mitosis?

options.A: Meiosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, while mitosis produces four haploid cells.
options.B: Meiosis involves two successive divisions and produces four genetically unique haploid cells for sexual reproduction.
options.C: Meiosis produces cells for growth and repair; mitosis produces gametes for reproduction.
options.D: Meiosis and mitosis are identical processes, but meiosis only occurs in plant cells.

questions.explanation: Meiosis consists of two sequential divisions (meiosis I and II), resulting in four haploid cells with unique genetic combinations due to crossing over and independent assortment — essential for producing gametes. Option A reverses the descriptions of meiosis and mitosis, a confusion very common among students who have memorised terms but not mechanisms.

questions.title: Atomic Structure: Isotopes
questions.prompt: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. What do these two atoms have in common, and how do they differ?

options.A: They have the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons.
options.B: They have the same number of protons (6) but different numbers of neutrons (6 and 8 respectively).
options.C: They have the same mass number but different numbers of electrons.
options.D: They have different numbers of protons but identical chemical properties.

questions.explanation: Isotopes of an element share the same atomic number (number of protons — 6 for carbon) but differ in neutron number; carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, giving mass numbers 12 and 14. Option A incorrectly states they differ in proton number, which would make them different elements entirely, not isotopes.

questions.title: Enthalpy Change Direction
questions.prompt: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, the solution becomes noticeably cold. What does this observation tell you about the enthalpy change (ΔH) of this process?

options.A: ΔH is negative; the reaction releases heat energy to the surroundings.
options.B: ΔH is positive; the reaction absorbs heat energy from the surroundings, making them cooler.
options.C: ΔH is zero; the temperature change is caused by increased molecular motion rather than energy change.
options.D: ΔH is negative; energy is absorbed by the solvent molecules as they expand.

questions.explanation: An endothermic process has a positive ΔH because the system absorbs thermal energy from the surroundings, lowering the surrounding temperature — as observed with cold packs. Option A describes an exothermic reaction (negative ΔH), which would produce a temperature increase, the opposite of what is observed.

questions.title: Ecological Succession
questions.prompt: A lava flow destroys all life on a hillside. Over the following decades, mosses establish first, then shrubs, then eventually a forest. What term describes this process, and what is it called when it begins on bare rock with no prior soil?

options.A: Secondary succession; climax community formation
options.B: Primary succession; pioneer colonisation
options.C: Primary succession; eutrophication
options.D: Secondary succession; biomass accumulation

questions.explanation: Primary succession occurs when communities establish on newly exposed, lifeless substrate such as bare rock or cooled lava, with no prior soil; pioneer species such as mosses and lichens colonise first. Option A incorrectly labels this secondary succession, which applies when disturbance destroys existing communities but soil and seed banks remain.

questions.title: Refraction and Snell's Law
questions.prompt: A ray of light passes from air (refractive index 1.0) into glass (refractive index 1.5). What happens to the ray's speed and direction as it enters the glass?

options.A: Speed increases; the ray bends away from the normal.
options.B: Speed decreases; the ray bends toward the normal.
options.C: Speed decreases; the ray bends away from the normal.
options.D: Speed stays constant; only wavelength changes.

questions.explanation: When light enters a denser medium (higher refractive index), its speed decreases (v = c/n), and by Snell's Law (n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂), with n₂ > n₁ the transmitted angle is smaller, meaning the ray bends toward the normal. Option C describes what happens when light moves from a denser to a less dense medium, reversing the direction of bending.

questions.title: Periodic Table Trends
questions.prompt: Moving from left to right across Period 3 of the periodic table (Na to Cl), which property shows a general increasing trend?

options.A: Atomic radius
options.B: First ionisation energy
options.C: Metallic character
options.D: Number of electron shells

questions.explanation: Across a period, nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, increasing effective nuclear charge and making it harder to remove an outer electron — so first ionisation energy generally increases from left to right. Option A is incorrect; atomic radius generally decreases across a period because greater nuclear charge pulls electron shells closer to the nucleus.

questions.title: Scientific Method: Variables
questions.prompt: A student investigates whether light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed. She counts oxygen bubbles produced per minute at different distances from a lamp. What is the independent variable in this experiment?

options.A: The number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute
options.B: The distance of the pondweed from the lamp
options.C: The temperature of the water surrounding the pondweed
options.D: The species of pondweed used in the investigation

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one deliberately manipulated by the experimenter — in this case, the distance from the lamp, which changes light intensity. Option A is the dependent variable (what is measured in response), a distinction students frequently blur when identifying variables in experimental design.

questions.title: Homeostasis: Blood Glucose
questions.prompt: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, blood glucose levels rise. Which hormone is released by the pancreas and what is its immediate effect on blood glucose?

options.A: Glucagon is released; it stimulates glycogen breakdown, raising blood glucose further.
options.B: Insulin is released; it promotes glucose uptake by cells and glycogen synthesis, lowering blood glucose.
options.C: Adrenaline is released; it diverts glucose to muscles, lowering blood glucose during digestion.
options.D: Insulin is released; it stimulates the liver to produce more glucose from amino acids.

questions.explanation: In response to elevated blood glucose, β-cells in the islets of Langerhans release insulin, which increases glucose uptake by cells (especially liver, muscle, and adipose tissue) and promotes glycogen synthesis in the liver, returning blood glucose to normal. Option A describes the action of glucagon, the antagonistic hormone released when blood glucose is low, a classic confusion in homeostasis questions.

questions.title: Half-Life Radioactive Decay
questions.prompt: A radioactive sample initially contains 800 undecayed atoms. The half-life of the isotope is 10 years. How many undecayed atoms remain after 30 years?

options.A: 200 atoms
options.B: 400 atoms
options.C: 100 atoms
options.D: 50 atoms

questions.explanation: 30 years equals three half-lives (30/10 = 3). After each half-life, the number of undecayed atoms halves: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100. Option A (200 atoms) reflects only two half-lives, an off-by-one error students make when miscounting the number of half-life periods elapsed.

questions.title: Entropy and Thermodynamics
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'When ice melts in a warm room, the process violates conservation of energy because the ice gains energy from nowhere.' Evaluate this claim, identifying the correct thermodynamic principle at work.

options.A: The claim is correct — energy is created during phase transitions, which is why temperature rises.
options.B: The claim is incorrect — the ice absorbs thermal energy from the warmer surrounding air, conserving total energy while increasing entropy.
options.C: The claim is incorrect — the ice spontaneously generates internal energy through molecular vibration without any external input.
options.D: The claim is partially correct — energy is conserved but the Second Law of Thermodynamics requires the room to gain energy overall.

questions.explanation: Energy flows from the warmer air to the cooler ice (First Law: energy is conserved), and the process is spontaneous because total entropy of the system increases — the ice's entropy gain exceeds the air's entropy loss. Option D is wrong because the room loses energy, not gains it; it is the universe's total entropy that increases, not the room's energy.

questions.title: Natural Selection and Fitness
questions.prompt: In a population of beetles, green individuals are better camouflaged on leaves than brown ones, and survive at a higher rate. After many generations, a student predicts the population will be entirely green. To what extent is this prediction accurate?

options.A: Fully accurate — natural selection will eliminate all brown alleles over time because they are disadvantageous.
options.B: Fully accurate — organisms deliberately choose to become green to improve survival chances.
options.C: Partially accurate — green frequency will increase, but genetic drift, mutation, and environmental changes mean fixation of green is not guaranteed.
options.D: Inaccurate — natural selection cannot change allele frequencies unless isolation between populations occurs first.

questions.explanation: Natural selection increases the frequency of advantageous alleles but rarely drives a population to absolute fixation; mutation continuously reintroduces variation, genetic drift can alter frequencies in small populations, and if the environment changes, selective pressure may reverse. Option A is wrong because it ignores these counteracting evolutionary forces that prevent guaranteed fixation.

questions.title: Electrochemical Cells
questions.prompt: In a standard Daniell cell (Zn | ZnSO₄ || CuSO₄ | Cu), a student proposes replacing the salt bridge with a wire to improve electron flow. Identify the error in this proposal.

options.A: The wire would slow electron flow because metals have higher resistance than ionic solutions.
options.B: The salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ion flow between half-cells; a wire cannot transport ions, so charge would build up and halt the reaction.
options.C: The wire would cause both half-cells to oxidise simultaneously, doubling current output.
options.D: Replacing the salt bridge with a wire is valid, but the cell voltage would drop because copper ions would migrate to the zinc half-cell.

questions.explanation: The salt bridge allows counter-ions to migrate and neutralise the charge build-up in each half-cell (e.g., SO₄²⁻ moving toward Zn²⁺ accumulation); without this ionic flow, an electric potential difference develops that opposes further electron flow, stopping the cell. Option D is wrong because a wire cannot transport ions at all — the issue is charge neutrality, not voltage drop from copper migration.

questions.title: Wave-Particle Duality
questions.prompt: The photoelectric effect cannot be explained by classical wave theory. Which observation specifically contradicts a wave-only model of light, and what does it imply?

options.A: Increasing light intensity below the threshold frequency eventually ejects electrons, implying energy accumulates over time in waves.
options.B: The kinetic energy of ejected electrons depends on light frequency, not intensity, implying energy is delivered in discrete quanta (photons).
options.C: Electrons are ejected with a time delay proportional to intensity, confirming that waves transfer energy gradually.
options.D: Higher intensity light ejects more electrons per second, which contradicts the wave model and implies particle behaviour.

questions.explanation: Classical wave theory predicts that increasing intensity (regardless of frequency) should eventually supply enough energy to eject electrons; the fact that no electrons are emitted below the threshold frequency — no matter how intense the light — proves energy is quantised into photons, each carrying energy E = hf. Option D describes a real observation but is consistent with the wave model (more wave energy = more electrons), so it does not by itself contradict classical theory.

questions.title: DNA Replication Fidelity
questions.prompt: DNA polymerase replicates DNA with very high fidelity. A student argues that any mutation introduced during replication will always be harmful to the organism. Critically assess this argument.

options.A: The argument is correct — all mutations disrupt protein structure and reduce organism fitness.
options.B: The argument is flawed — mutations in non-coding DNA or synonymous codons may have no phenotypic effect, and some mutations confer selective advantages.
options.C: The argument is flawed — DNA polymerase's proofreading mechanism eliminates all mutations before they can affect the organism.
options.D: The argument is correct — even silent mutations alter mRNA secondary structure, always affecting translation efficiency negatively.

questions.explanation: The majority of the human genome is non-coding, so many mutations have no effect on protein sequence or function; additionally, synonymous (silent) mutations do not change amino acid sequence. Some mutations, such as the sickle-cell allele in malaria-endemic regions, confer a net selective advantage in heterozygotes. Option C is wrong because proofreading reduces error rate to roughly 1 in 10⁹ base pairs but does not eliminate all mutations.

questions.title: Gravitational vs Electrostatic Force
questions.prompt: Compare gravitational and electrostatic forces. Which statement correctly identifies a fundamental difference between them?

options.A: Both forces follow an inverse-square law, but gravitational force can be repulsive while electrostatic force is always attractive.
options.B: Both forces follow an inverse-square law, but electrostatic force can be repulsive or attractive while gravitational force is always attractive.
options.C: Electrostatic force follows an inverse-square law, but gravitational force decreases linearly with distance.
options.D: Gravitational force depends on mass and charge, whereas electrostatic force depends on charge only.

questions.explanation: Both Coulomb's law (F = kq₁q₂/r²) and Newton's law of gravitation (F = Gm₁m₂/r²) are inverse-square laws; however, electric charges can be positive or negative, producing attraction or repulsion, while mass is always positive, making gravity exclusively attractive. Option A reverses the properties of the two forces — gravity is never repulsive under Newtonian mechanics.

questions.title: Climate Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: The melting of Arctic sea ice exposes darker ocean surface. A student describes this as a 'negative feedback' that helps stabilise global temperature. Evaluate this description.

options.A: The description is correct — exposed ocean absorbs more heat than ice, which cools the water and re-freezes it, stabilising temperature.
options.B: The description is incorrect — this is a positive feedback: lower albedo leads to more absorption of solar radiation, further warming and more ice melt.
options.C: The description is correct — ice-albedo feedback is negative because it reflects more solar energy back into space as ice reforms.
options.D: The description is incorrect — it is a neutral feedback because ocean heat capacity offsets the albedo reduction exactly.

questions.explanation: Ice has an albedo of approximately 0.8–0.9 (reflecting 80–90% of incoming solar radiation), whereas open ocean has an albedo of approximately 0.06; exposing more ocean therefore increases heat absorption, amplifying the original warming — this is a positive (amplifying) feedback loop. Option A incorrectly assumes the extra heat re-freezes the ocean, which would require cooling, not further warming.

questions.title: Molar Mass and Stoichiometry
questions.prompt: A student reacts 4 g of hydrogen gas (H₂) with excess oxygen to form water. They calculate that 4 moles of water are produced. Identify the error in their reasoning. (H = 1 g/mol, O = 16 g/mol)

options.A: There is no error — 4 g of H₂ is 4 moles, and each mole of H₂ produces one mole of H₂O.
options.B: The student correctly found 2 moles of H₂, but incorrectly applied a 1:1 ratio; the balanced equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O gives 2 moles of water.
options.C: The student used the wrong molar mass; H₂ has a molar mass of 2 g/mol, so 4 g is 2 moles of H₂, producing 2 moles of H₂O.
options.D: The student forgot to account for the molar mass of oxygen in water, so the product should be calculated using the molar mass of H₂O (18 g/mol).

questions.explanation: H₂ has a molar mass of 2 g/mol (two hydrogen atoms each of 1 g/mol), so 4 g ÷ 2 g/mol = 2 moles of H₂; the balanced equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O shows a 1:1 mole ratio of H₂ to H₂O, giving 2 moles of water, not 4. Option A is wrong because the student treated H₂ as having a molar mass of 1 g/mol, confusing atomic mass with molecular mass.

questions.title: Enzyme Inhibition Types
questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical compound reduces enzyme activity by binding to a site other than the active site, changing the enzyme's shape. Adding more substrate does not restore full enzyme activity. Which type of inhibition does this describe?

options.A: Competitive inhibition, because the inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site.
options.B: Non-competitive inhibition, because the inhibitor binds an allosteric site and cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.
options.C: Competitive inhibition, because the change in enzyme shape eventually allows the substrate to displace the inhibitor.
options.D: Uncompetitive inhibition, because the inhibitor only binds after the substrate has already attached to the active site.

questions.explanation: Non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitors bind at a site distinct from the active site, inducing a conformational change that reduces catalytic activity; because the inhibitor does not compete with the substrate, increasing substrate concentration cannot reverse the effect. Option A is wrong because competitive inhibitors bind the active site itself and their effect can be overcome by adding more substrate.

questions.title: Tectonic Plate Boundaries
questions.prompt: What would happen if two oceanic plates of similar density converged? Why does one plate subduct rather than both plates crumpling upward?

options.A: Both plates crumple upward because neither is denser than the other, forming a mid-ocean mountain range.
options.B: One plate subducts because slight differences in age and temperature make it marginally denser; the denser, cooler plate sinks into the mantle.
options.C: Neither plate subducts — instead, a transform fault forms and the plates slide past each other horizontally.
options.D: One plate always subducts because oceanic crust contains less silica than continental crust, making it inherently buoyant.

questions.explanation: Oceanic plate density increases with age as it cools and contracts; even between two oceanic plates, the older, cooler, and therefore denser plate will subduct, forming an oceanic trench and island arc (e.g., the Mariana Trench). Option A is wrong because crumpling (orogeny) typically occurs at continent-continent convergent boundaries where neither plate is dense enough to subduct.

questions.title: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
questions.prompt: A population geneticist applies the Hardy-Weinberg model to a small island population of birds experiencing strong directional selection. A student says the model will accurately predict allele frequencies next generation. To what extent is the student correct?

options.A: Fully correct — Hardy-Weinberg applies to all populations regardless of size or selection pressure.
options.B: Partially correct — Hardy-Weinberg is accurate when selection is present but the population is large enough to prevent drift.
options.C: Mostly incorrect — Hardy-Weinberg requires no selection, random mating, large population size, no mutation, and no migration; strong selection alone violates the model.
options.D: Fully incorrect — Hardy-Weinberg only applies to haploid organisms, not to diploid birds.

questions.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is maintained only when five conditions hold simultaneously: no natural selection, random mating, large population, no mutation, and no gene flow; directional selection directly violates the no-selection condition, so predicted frequencies will diverge from observed ones. Option B is wrong because even in a large population, selection alone is sufficient to break Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

questions.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
questions.prompt: In the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol), a student claims that raising the temperature always increases the yield of ammonia because particles move faster and collide more often. Identify the error.

options.A: There is no error — increased collision frequency always shifts equilibrium toward products.
options.B: The error is that increased temperature shifts equilibrium to the left (endothermic direction), reducing ammonia yield, even though the rate of reaction increases.
options.C: The error is that pressure, not temperature, is the key variable for ammonia yield; temperature has no effect on equilibrium position.
options.D: The error is that the reaction is endothermic, so raising temperature always favours the reverse reaction regardless of Le Chatelier's principle.

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle states that adding heat to an exothermic equilibrium (ΔH < 0) shifts the equilibrium toward the endothermic (reverse) reaction to absorb the extra energy, decreasing NH₃ yield; the student confuses rate of reaction (which does increase) with equilibrium yield (which decreases). Option A conflates collision frequency with equilibrium position — higher rates apply to both forward and reverse reactions, but the backward reaction is favoured more at higher temperatures for an exothermic process.

questions.title: Action Potential Propagation
questions.prompt: A neuroscience student reads that myelinated axons transmit signals faster than unmyelinated ones. Which mechanism best explains this speed advantage?

options.A: Myelin increases the diameter of the axon, allowing more ions to flow simultaneously and speeding up depolarisation at every point.
options.B: Myelin acts as an insulator so the action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), skipping most of the axon membrane.
options.C: Myelin provides a direct electrical pathway along its surface, replacing ion channel-based conduction entirely.
options.D: Myelin increases sodium ion concentration inside the axon, raising the resting potential and reducing the threshold for depolarisation.

questions.explanation: Myelin sheaths insulate the axon between nodes of Ranvier, forcing the action potential to 'jump' (saltatory conduction) from node to node rather than depolarising every point on the membrane; this saltatory conduction is roughly 50–100 times faster than continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibres. Option A describes the effect of larger axon diameter (a separate mechanism seen in squid giant axons), not the mechanism by which myelin itself speeds conduction.

questions.title: Conservation of Momentum
questions.prompt: Two ice skaters, A (mass 60 kg) and B (mass 80 kg), stand still on frictionless ice. Skater A pushes Skater B and they move apart. A student claims Skater A must experience no force because A did the pushing. Evaluate this claim using Newton's laws.

options.A: The claim is correct — the pusher exerts a force but does not receive one because action and reaction cannot occur simultaneously.
options.B: The claim is incorrect — by Newton's Third Law, Skater B exerts an equal and opposite force on Skater A, so A accelerates in the opposite direction.
options.C: The claim is partially correct — Skater A experiences a force, but it is smaller than the force A exerts because A has less mass.
options.D: The claim is incorrect — Skater A experiences a larger force than B because the total momentum must remain zero.

questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that forces always occur in equal and opposite pairs; when A pushes B, B simultaneously pushes A with the same magnitude of force but in the opposite direction, causing A to accelerate backward. Option C is wrong because Newton's Third Law pairs are always equal in magnitude — it is the resulting acceleration that differs (a = F/m), not the force.

questions.title: Carbon Cycle Disruption
questions.prompt: Synthesise your knowledge of the carbon cycle and climate science: why does burning fossil fuels increase atmospheric CO₂ more rapidly than natural carbon sources such as volcanic eruptions?

options.A: Fossil fuels release CO₂ that was previously sequestered over millions of years, adding carbon that was outside the active short-term cycle, at a rate far exceeding volcanic emissions.
options.B: Volcanoes release mostly water vapour, so they do not contribute CO₂ at all; fossil fuels are the only geological CO₂ source.
options.C: Burning fossil fuels produces a different isotope of carbon (¹⁴C) that accumulates more rapidly in the atmosphere than volcanic ¹²CO₂.
options.D: Fossil fuels release CO₂ faster because combustion is an exothermic reaction, generating heat that causes more ocean degassing simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Fossil fuels represent carbon stored by photosynthesis over hundreds of millions of years that has been removed from the active carbon cycle; human combustion releases approximately 35 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year, compared to roughly 0.3 billion tonnes from all volcanic activity — more than 100 times greater. Option B is wrong because volcanoes do emit CO₂ (alongside water vapour and SO₂), contributing measurably to atmospheric carbon.

questions.title: Oxidation States in Redox
questions.prompt: In the reaction MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O, a student claims that iron is reduced and manganese is oxidised. Identify the error and explain your reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct — iron gains electrons going from +2 to +3, which is reduction.
options.B: The student is incorrect — iron is oxidised (loses electrons: +2 to +3) and manganese is reduced (gains electrons: +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺).
options.C: The student is incorrect — both species are oxidised because the overall charge of the products is lower than the reactants.
options.D: The student is partially correct — manganese is oxidised but iron undergoes disproportionation rather than simple oxidation.

questions.explanation: Oxidation is defined as loss of electrons: Fe²⁺ loses one electron to become Fe³⁺ (oxidation state increases from +2 to +3), so iron is oxidised; Mn in MnO₄⁻ has oxidation state +7 (since each O is −2 and the ion is −1), and it is reduced to Mn²⁺ (gains 5 electrons). Option A confuses the direction: an increase in oxidation state signifies loss of electrons, which is oxidation, not reduction.

questions.title: Genetic Inheritance Patterns
questions.prompt: Two phenotypically normal parents have a child with cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive condition. What is the probability that their next child will be phenotypically normal but a carrier of one recessive allele?

options.A: 1/4, because one quarter of offspring from two carriers will be carriers.
options.B: 1/2, because half of all offspring from two carriers will be heterozygous carriers.
options.C: 2/3, because among phenotypically normal offspring from two carriers, two-thirds are carriers.
options.D: 3/4, because three-quarters of offspring will be phenotypically normal regardless of carrier status.

questions.explanation: A cross between two carriers (Aa × Aa) yields offspring ratios 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; the aa child has cystic fibrosis, so among the three-quarters who are phenotypically normal (AA and Aa), two out of three (2/3) are heterozygous carriers. Option B gives the overall probability of being Aa from the full cross (1/2), but the question asks for the conditional probability given the child is phenotypically normal.

questions.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Uses
questions.prompt: A student claims that X-rays and radio waves are fundamentally different types of radiation with different wave speeds in a vacuum. Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct — X-rays travel at the speed of light but radio waves travel slower because of their longer wavelength.
options.B: The claim is incorrect — both are regions of the electromagnetic spectrum and travel at the same speed (c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength, not fundamental type.
options.C: The claim is correct — X-rays are transverse waves and radio waves are longitudinal waves, making them fundamentally different.
options.D: The claim is partially correct — they share the same speed in vacuum but X-rays are particle-like photons while radio waves are purely waves, making them different in nature.

questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves, from radio waves to gamma rays, are transverse oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and travel at c ≈ 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum; they differ only in frequency (and consequently wavelength and photon energy). Option A is wrong because wave speed in a vacuum is independent of frequency — it is in a medium that different EM frequencies travel at different speeds (dispersion).

questions.title: Trophic Levels and Energy Transfer
questions.prompt: In a grassland food chain, only about 10% of energy transfers between each trophic level. A student uses this to argue that a human population can support ten times as many people by eating grain directly rather than beef. To what extent is this argument scientifically valid?

options.A: Fully valid — the 10% rule applies precisely, so eating grain supports exactly 10 times as many people as eating beef from grain-fed cattle.
options.B: Largely valid in principle — removing one trophic level does dramatically increase food energy available to humans, though the 10% figure is an approximation and nutritional factors also matter.
options.C: Invalid — the 10% rule only applies to wild ecosystems; agricultural systems recover nearly all energy, so there is no difference between eating grain and beef.
options.D: Invalid — humans cannot digest grain efficiently, so removing cattle from the food chain would reduce net energy available.

questions.explanation: The 10% rule (ecological efficiency) is an average approximation — actual values range from ~5% to ~20% depending on species and ecosystem; in principle, eliminating a trophic level does make far more energy available to humans, but factors such as human digestive capabilities, land use patterns, and protein quality mean the real-world ratio is not a precise factor of ten. Option A is wrong because treating the 10% figure as exact ignores the variability in ecological efficiency and oversimplifies a complex system.

questions.title: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life
questions.prompt: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 20 years. A 160 g sample is stored. How much of the original isotope remains after 80 years, and what reasoning leads to this answer?

options.A: 0 g — after four half-lives, all radioactive material has decayed completely.
options.B: 10 g — after 80 years (four half-lives: 160→80→40→20→10 g), one-sixteenth of the original remains.
options.C: 20 g — after 80 years, half of the original amount decays, leaving 80 g, and another halving leaves 20 g.
options.D: 40 g — 80 years is two half-lives for a 20-year half-life isotope, so one-quarter remains.
