options.C: Responsibility is shared across the chain — the mining company, the phone manufacturer, the government of Country B, and consumers all play a role, making it hard to pinpoint one party
options.D: The child using the phone has no connection to the mine and bears no responsibility whatsoever

questions.explanation: Global supply chains distribute both the benefits and the ethical responsibilities across multiple actors — mining companies set working conditions, manufacturers choose their suppliers, governments regulate or fail to regulate, and consumer demand drives production volume; this interconnection is why supply chain ethics is a complex international challenge. Option B ignores that international corporations and their customers are part of the system that creates demand for the minerals.

questions.title: Protected Areas and Local Communities
questions.prompt: A national park is created to protect endangered wildlife. However, the park boundaries include land that a local farming community has used for generations. The community is told they can no longer farm there. What is the MOST important tension this situation highlights?

options.A: The tension between protecting biodiversity for global benefit and respecting the land rights and livelihoods of local communities
options.B: The tension between two different endangered species competing for the same habitat
options.C: The tension between governments that want tourism income and farmers who prefer wilderness
options.D: There is no tension — conservation and community needs always align naturally

questions.explanation: Conservation biology and human rights scholars call this 'fortress conservation' — a model that protects nature by excluding local people, which can violate indigenous land rights and remove the communities best positioned to be long-term stewards; modern approaches increasingly seek to involve communities as partners. Option D is contradicted by numerous documented cases globally where conservation has displaced rural and indigenous communities.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: A lake is shared by five fishing villages, and no single village owns it. Each village knows that fishing more will hurt the lake long-term, but also fears the other villages will fish heavily anyway. What concept BEST describes this situation, and why does it make cooperation so difficult?

options.A: Circular economy — villages keep reusing the same fish stocks in a loop
options.B: Tragedy of the commons — individuals acting in self-interest deplete a shared resource even when everyone loses
options.C: Biodiversity loss — the fish species are becoming endangered because of climate change
options.D: Resource nationalisation — each village should claim legal ownership of one section of the lake

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons describes how a shared resource is overused because each individual benefits fully from taking more while the cost of depletion is shared by everyone, making cooperation feel risky. Option A is wrong because a circular economy refers to redesigning products and systems to eliminate waste, not to shared-resource decision-making between communities.

questions.title: SDG Goals and Connections
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) have nothing to do with each other — one is about weather and one is about food.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct; climate and food production are managed by entirely separate government departments
options.B: The error is that SDG 13 only applies to rich countries with high emissions, so it cannot affect food in poor countries
options.C: The error is that climate change causes droughts, floods, and extreme weather that directly reduce crop harvests, linking the two goals
options.D: The error is that SDG 2 is actually about water, not food, so the student has confused the two goals

questions.explanation: Climate change directly threatens food security because rising temperatures, shifting rainfall patterns, and extreme weather events reduce agricultural yields — for example, droughts in sub-Saharan Africa regularly cause crop failures. Option A is wrong because the SDGs were specifically designed to be interconnected, and governments worldwide are encouraged to address them together.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
questions.prompt: Bees pollinate roughly one-third of all food crops humans eat. A student claims that protecting bee populations is only important for nature lovers and has no economic value. What is the STRONGEST counter-argument to this claim?

options.A: Bees produce honey, which is a luxury product worth protecting for gourmet food markets
options.B: Without bee pollination, crop yields would fall dramatically, raising food prices and threatening food security for billions of people
options.C: Bees are a keystone species, meaning they directly control the weather patterns needed for farming
options.D: International law requires all countries to protect pollinators under the Convention on Biological Diversity

questions.explanation: Bees provide a free ecosystem service — pollination — that is estimated to be worth hundreds of billions of dollars annually to global agriculture; losing them would cause massive food shortages and economic damage. Option A is too narrow and misses the much larger connection to staple food crops like almonds, apples, and berries that depend on pollination.

questions.title: Circular Economy Choices
questions.prompt: A phone manufacturer offers two options: Model X is cheap but cannot be repaired and must be thrown away after two years. Model Y costs more upfront but has replaceable parts and can last ten years. From a circular economy perspective, which model is preferable and why?

options.A: Model X, because lower prices make technology accessible to more people, which is a social good
options.B: Model Y, because keeping materials in use longer reduces the need to mine new resources and creates less waste
options.C: Model X, because manufacturing fewer parts per unit means less energy is used overall
options.D: Model Y, because expensive products always have a smaller carbon footprint than cheap ones

questions.explanation: A circular economy aims to keep products and materials in use as long as possible; a phone lasting ten years means far fewer devices manufactured, less mining of rare metals like cobalt and lithium, and less electronic waste. Option A raises a real point about accessibility but does not address the circular economy principle, which is about resource stewardship rather than price.

questions.title: Environmental Stewardship Rights
questions.prompt: An indigenous community has protected a forest for generations using traditional practices. A national government grants a mining company rights to extract minerals from the same forest. Which tension does this scenario BEST illustrate?

options.A: The tension between short-term economic development and long-term environmental and cultural rights
options.B: The tension between national security and international trade agreements
options.C: The tension between urban and rural populations over land taxation
options.D: The tension between two competing mining companies over the same mineral deposit

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates a conflict where immediate economic gain from mining competes with the long-term rights of indigenous people to their land and the ecosystem services the forest provides — a recognised challenge in environmental justice. Option B is incorrect because national security and trade agreements are not the central issue; the community's rights and environmental protection are.

questions.title: Geopolitics of Climate Change
questions.prompt: Small island nations like Tuvalu and the Maldives produce almost no greenhouse gas emissions, yet they face the greatest threat from rising sea levels caused by climate change. What does this reveal about the relationship between who causes climate change and who suffers most?

options.A: It shows that climate change affects only coastal countries, so landlocked nations can ignore it
options.B: It reveals a deep unfairness — the countries least responsible for emissions often face the worst consequences
options.C: It shows that small countries produce more pollution per person than large industrial nations
options.D: It reveals that sea-level rise is caused by local factors like fishing and tourism rather than global emissions

questions.explanation: Small island developing states contribute less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions but are among the first nations that may become uninhabitable due to sea-level rise — a stark example of climate injustice. Option A is wrong because climate change affects landlocked countries too through droughts, heatwaves, and disrupted rainfall.

questions.title: Renewable Energy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A country replaces its oil-fired power stations with solar farms. A student says this is a perfect solution with no downsides. Which response BEST shows balanced, critical thinking about this change?

options.A: The student is right — solar energy produces zero pollution at every stage of its life cycle
options.B: The student is mostly right, but solar energy only works in countries near the equator where sunlight is strongest
options.C: Solar farms greatly reduce carbon emissions during operation, but manufacturing solar panels requires energy and rare minerals, and panels need land that could affect local ecosystems
options.D: Solar energy is worse than oil because it is unreliable and cannot power a whole country under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Solar power dramatically cuts operational carbon emissions, but producing solar panels requires mining materials like silicon and silver and uses significant energy, creating some environmental costs; additionally, large solar farms can alter local habitats. Option A is incorrect because the manufacturing phase of solar panels does produce emissions and environmental impacts, even if far less than burning fossil fuels.

questions.title: Resource Scarcity and Policy
questions.prompt: A government notices that its underground water supply (aquifer) is being used four times faster than rainwater can refill it. Which policy response BEST applies the principle of long-term environmental responsibility?

options.A: Drill deeper wells so that more water can be extracted before the aquifer runs out
options.B: Import water from neighbouring countries so the aquifer can be used for exports
options.C: Set legally enforceable limits on water extraction and invest in water recycling technology
options.D: Encourage farmers to plant more water-intensive crops to boost the economy before the water runs out

questions.explanation: Setting extraction limits and investing in recycling addresses the root problem by aligning usage with the natural recharge rate — a principle of sustainable resource management used in countries like Israel, which recycles over 85% of its wastewater. Option A only delays the crisis by increasing extraction rate, making the eventual collapse worse.

questions.title: Cause and Effect: Deforestation
questions.prompt: What would MOST likely happen to local rainfall patterns if a large tropical rainforest was completely cut down? Choose the answer that correctly links the cause to the effect through a specific natural process.

options.A: Rainfall would increase because there are fewer trees to block rain clouds from reaching the ground
options.B: Rainfall would decrease because trees release water vapour through transpiration, which forms clouds and rain
options.C: Rainfall would stay the same because rainfall is controlled entirely by ocean temperatures, not forests
options.D: Rainfall would increase because bare soil absorbs more heat, creating stronger updrafts that pull in rain clouds

questions.explanation: Tropical trees release enormous amounts of water vapour through transpiration — the Amazon rainforest alone creates 'flying rivers' of moisture that generate rainfall across South America; removing trees disrupts this cycle and causes regional drying. Option D contains a misconception — while bare soil does absorb more heat, this does not reliably increase rainfall and in practice deforested areas typically become drier.

questions.title: Peace and Environmental Conflict
questions.prompt: Two neighbouring countries share a large underground oil reserve. Scientists confirm the oil extends under both countries' borders. Country A begins drilling heavily. A student predicts this will lead to peaceful sharing. Which factor does the student's prediction MOST overlook?

options.A: Oil is a renewable resource, so both countries can drill indefinitely without conflict arising
options.B: Heavy extraction by one country reduces the pressure underground, causing oil to flow away from the other country's side, creating a resource dispute
options.C: International law automatically divides all underground resources equally between neighbouring countries
options.D: Oil is only valuable to countries that have their own cars and factories, so Country B would not care about the oil

questions.explanation: Underground oil and gas reservoirs are connected systems — aggressive drilling on one side draws resources away from the other side, a well-documented cause of real geopolitical disputes, such as those involving oil fields straddling the borders of Kuwait and Iraq. Option C is incorrect because international law on shared underground resources is complex and disputed, not automatic or equal.

questions.title: Evaluating Perspectives on Pollution
questions.prompt: A fishing community and a chemical factory owner look at water quality test results showing high levels of nitrogen in a local river. The factory owner says, 'Nitrogen is natural — plants need it, so there is no problem.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; since nitrogen is natural, high levels in rivers are always harmless to aquatic life
options.B: The claim is misleading; excess nitrogen from factories causes algal blooms that deplete oxygen in the water, killing fish
options.C: The claim is correct; the fishing community's concerns are based on cultural beliefs rather than science
options.D: The claim is partially right because nitrogen only harms rivers in cold climates, not warm ones

questions.explanation: Excess nitrogen triggers eutrophication — explosive algae growth that blocks sunlight and, when the algae die and decompose, depletes oxygen in the water, creating 'dead zones' where fish and other aquatic life cannot survive. Option A is a genuine misconception because many harmful substances occur naturally; what matters is concentration and context, not just whether something is 'natural.'

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities: Air
questions.prompt: City A burns large amounts of coal. Scientists measure increased acid rain falling in City B, 300 kilometres away, damaging its forests and lakes. City B's citizens say City A is violating their rights. Which principle BEST supports City B's argument?

options.A: The principle that air pollution is only the responsibility of the country that receives it
options.B: The polluter pays principle — those who cause environmental damage are responsible for its costs, even across borders
options.C: The principle of national sovereignty — City A has the absolute right to burn whatever fuels it chooses within its borders
options.D: The principle that environmental harm is only legally recognised when it occurs within the same country

questions.explanation: The polluter pays principle, embedded in international environmental agreements including the Rio Declaration of 1992, holds that entities causing pollution should bear the cost of managing or compensating for that damage, regardless of political borders. Option C is wrong because national sovereignty is limited by international environmental law when a country's actions cause measurable harm to other nations.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Monocultures
questions.prompt: A region replaces its mixed forest — containing hundreds of plant and animal species — with a single crop grown across thousands of hectares. A student says this is an improvement because it produces more food per hectare. What important risk does the student's reasoning ignore?

options.A: Monocultures always produce less food than mixed forests, so the student's basic claim about yield is wrong
options.B: A single crop with no genetic diversity is highly vulnerable to one disease or pest wiping out the entire harvest
options.C: Growing one crop improves soil quality over time by allowing it to specialise in one type of nutrient
options.D: International trade law forbids replacing forests with farmland, so the plan would be illegal

questions.explanation: Genetic uniformity in monocultures means one pathogen or pest can devastate an entire region's harvest — the 1840s Irish potato famine, which killed over one million people, was caused by a single fungus spreading through genetically identical potato crops. Option C is incorrect; monocultures typically deplete specific soil nutrients over time, requiring increasing amounts of artificial fertiliser.

questions.title: Carbon Footprint Comparisons
questions.prompt: Country A has 50 million people and releases 500 million tonnes of CO₂ per year. Country B has 500 million people and releases 600 million tonnes of CO₂ per year. A climate negotiator argues Country A should cut emissions more urgently. What is the MOST logical reason for this position?

options.A: Country A has a higher total emission count, so it is objectively the bigger polluter
options.B: Country A emits 10 tonnes per person per year while Country B emits only 1.2 tonnes per person — meaning each person in Country A creates far more climate impact
options.C: Country B has more people, so it should always reduce more regardless of per-person figures
options.D: Country A should cut first because smaller countries are always less economically important

questions.explanation: Per-capita emissions reveal how much each individual's lifestyle contributes to climate change; Country A at 10 tonnes per person versus Country B at 1.2 tonnes per person shows an eightfold difference in individual impact — a standard metric used in climate fairness discussions at the UN. Option A is misleading because total emissions alone ignore population size, which is why per-capita figures matter in equity arguments.

questions.title: Endangered Species Protection
questions.prompt: A conservation organisation argues that saving tigers from extinction is not just about the tigers themselves but benefits entire ecosystems. Which explanation BEST supports the idea that one species can affect an entire ecosystem?

options.A: Tigers are culturally important in many countries, so protecting them increases tourism revenues for local communities
options.B: As apex predators, tigers regulate deer and boar populations, which prevents overgrazing and allows forest vegetation to recover
options.C: Tigers compete with humans for land, so protecting them forces communities to use farmland more efficiently
options.D: Tigers only eat other endangered animals, so saving them automatically saves all other endangered species too

questions.explanation: Apex predators like tigers are keystone species — their presence controls herbivore populations, which prevents overgrazing and maintains plant diversity; when wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park, for example, similar trophic cascade effects restored river banks and increased biodiversity. Option A is true but only captures the economic argument for tourism, missing the ecological mechanism the question asks about.

questions.title: Fairness in Resource Use
questions.prompt: A student reflects: 'People in high-income countries use about ten times more energy per person than people in low-income countries. Since we all share the same atmosphere, is this fair?' Which response demonstrates the MOST thoughtful evaluation of this reflection?

options.A: It is fair because high-income countries earned their wealth through hard work and deserve to use more energy
options.B: It is unfair and should be solved by immediately cutting all energy use in high-income countries to zero
options.C: The disparity raises genuine equity concerns because higher energy use contributes more to shared atmospheric problems like climate change, affecting everyone — especially those who used least
options.D: It is neither fair nor unfair because energy use is a private choice and has no effect on others

questions.explanation: High energy consumption in wealthy nations historically accounts for the majority of accumulated greenhouse gases in the shared atmosphere, yet the worst climate impacts are felt in low-income countries — making this a core equity issue in international climate negotiations like the Paris Agreement. Option D is incorrect because atmospheric greenhouse gases accumulate globally, meaning individual and national energy choices directly affect people worldwide.

questions.title: Oceans as Global Commons
questions.prompt: The high seas — the parts of the ocean beyond any country's control — cover about 64% of the ocean surface. Because no country owns them, fishing fleets can operate there with very little regulation. What problem does this MOST clearly illustrate?

options.A: Circular economy failure, because fish caught at sea cannot be recycled after use
options.B: National sovereignty conflict, because countries are fighting over ownership of the high seas
options.C: Tragedy of the commons, because the absence of ownership means no one bears the full cost of overfishing shared fish stocks
options.D: Biodiversity economics, because fish in international waters are worth more than fish in national waters

questions.explanation: The high seas are a textbook example of the tragedy of the commons — without ownership or enforceable rules, fishing fleets have every incentive to catch as much as possible before others do, leading to stock collapses like the Grand Banks cod fishery in the 1990s. Option B is incorrect because the issue is not countries fighting to own the high seas but rather the lack of any ownership creating a governance gap.

questions.title: Soil Degradation and Agriculture
questions.prompt: Scientists warn that topsoil — the thin, fertile layer that grows most of the world's food — is being lost about 10 to 40 times faster than it forms naturally. A student claims this is only a problem for farmers, not for city dwellers. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct — city dwellers grow no food, so soil loss does not affect them
options.B: The student is wrong — soil degradation reduces global food supply, raising prices and threatening food security for urban and rural populations alike
options.C: The student is correct — advanced hydroponic farming in cities has already replaced the need for soil worldwide
options.D: The student is wrong — soil loss only affects countries that export food, not those that import it

questions.explanation: Topsoil loss reduces crop yields globally; the UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that at current rates of degradation, topsoil sufficient for crop production could be gone within 60 years, causing food shortages and price spikes that affect everyone who eats — including city populations. Option C overstates the current scale of hydroponics, which supplies only a tiny fraction of global food needs.

questions.title: International Climate Agreements
questions.prompt: The Paris Agreement asks every country to set its own targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions rather than imposing the same target on all countries. A student argues this approach is unfair. Which response BEST evaluates whether the student is right?

options.A: The student is right — only identical targets for all countries are truly fair in international agreements
options.B: The approach is actually unfair because it allows large countries to set very small targets with no penalty
options.C: The approach tries to balance fairness and effectiveness by allowing countries to set targets reflecting their different circumstances, though critics argue it lacks enforcement teeth
options.D: The student is wrong — the Paris Agreement gives all countries exactly equal reduction targets, so it is perfectly fair

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement uses nationally determined contributions (NDCs) because countries have vastly different economies, historical emission levels, and development needs; this flexibility helped achieve near-universal sign-up but is criticised because targets are self-set and there is no legal penalty for missing them. Option D is factually wrong — the Paris Agreement explicitly does not impose equal targets on all nations.

questions.title: Responsibility and Consumption
questions.prompt: A clothing brand makes T-shirts in a factory overseas that pollutes a local river. A child in another country buys the T-shirt. Who bears responsibility for the river pollution? Choose the answer that BEST reflects a nuanced view of shared responsibility.

options.A: Only the factory, because the child had no idea pollution was happening and lives far away
options.B: Only the government of the country where the factory is located, because it is their job to enforce pollution laws
options.C: Responsibility is shared among the factory, the brand that chose the factory, and consumers whose purchasing choices create demand — though not equally
options.D: No one is responsible because pollution is a natural by-product of manufacturing that no one can control

questions.explanation: Supply chain responsibility is a key idea in sustainability — the brand chose the factory knowing its practices, the factory carried out the pollution, and consumer demand drives the whole chain; this is why concepts like ethical consumption and corporate accountability have grown in importance. Option A is a genuine misconception because consumer demand is a real driver of production choices, even when consumers are unaware of specific harms.

questions.title: Wetlands and Ecosystem Value
questions.prompt: A city council plans to drain a wetland to build a shopping centre, arguing it will create jobs and tax revenue. Environmental scientists object. Which specific ecological function of wetlands MOST strengthens the scientists' case?

options.A: Wetlands are used for recreational activities like kayaking, which generates tourism income
options.B: Wetlands act as natural flood buffers and water filters, protecting downstream communities from flooding and providing clean water — services that would cost millions to replace artificially
options.C: Wetlands store large amounts of oil and gas underground that could be drilled for profit instead
options.D: Wetlands are habitats for migratory birds, which help spread seeds for forest regrowth globally

questions.explanation: Wetlands absorb excess rainwater during storms, reducing flood risk, and filter pollutants from water before it reaches rivers and reservoirs; the US Army Corps of Engineers estimated that restoring one acre of wetland provides flood protection worth up to $4,000 annually — making their destruction an economic loss, not just an ecological one. Option D is true but describes a less direct and less economically quantifiable benefit than flood control and water filtration.

questions.title: Stewardship Across Generations
questions.prompt: The concept of 'intergenerational equity' suggests that people alive today have a responsibility to future generations. A student says: 'Why should we sacrifice our comfort now for people who don't exist yet?' Which reasoning BEST challenges this view using an IB PYP concept?

options.A: Future generations will invent technology to fix any problem we create, so the student's concern is unnecessary
options.B: The concept of responsibility reminds us that our actions today have consequences for systems — like climate, soil, and biodiversity — that recover very slowly or not at all, meaning choices we make now permanently shape the options available to future people
options.C: The student's view is actually supported by international law, which states that only living people have legal rights
options.D: We should focus entirely on the present because predictions about the future are always unreliable

questions.explanation: The IB PYP concept of responsibility asks us to consider the long-term effects of our actions on shared systems; some environmental changes, like species extinction or aquifer depletion, are irreversible on human timescales, meaning today's choices permanently constrain what future generations can do — a foundation of the Brundtland Report's definition of sustainable development. Option A is a real misconception (sometimes called 'techno-optimism') that ignores the possibility that technology cannot solve all irreversible losses.

questions.title: Cause and Effect: Urban Heat
questions.prompt: Cities are often several degrees warmer than surrounding rural areas — a phenomenon scientists call the 'urban heat island' effect. What is the PRIMARY cause of this temperature difference?

options.A: Cities have more people, and human body heat from millions of residents warms the air significantly
options.B: Concrete, asphalt, and buildings absorb and retain far more heat from the sun than trees, grass, and soil do, and release it slowly at night
options.C: Cities are usually located in valleys where warm air naturally gets trapped by surrounding hills
options.D: Air conditioning units in cities pump cold air outside, which paradoxically heats the surrounding outdoor air while cooling interiors

questions.explanation: Dark surfaces like asphalt and concrete absorb up to 95% of incoming solar radiation and release it slowly as heat, whereas vegetation reflects more sunlight and cools air through transpiration — this is why cities with less green space are measurably hotter and why urban greening is a recognised climate adaptation strategy. Option D contains a partial truth — AC units do release waste heat outdoors — but this is a minor contributor compared to the massive heat-absorbing effect of built surfaces.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: A lake is shared by five villages. Each village is allowed to fish freely, and each knows that if they fish too much the lake will be emptied. Yet every village keeps increasing its catch. Which concept BEST explains why this happens even when everyone understands the risk?

options.A: The precautionary principle, because no one is certain the fish will run out
options.B: The tragedy of the commons, because individuals benefit from taking more while the cost of damage is shared by everyone
options.C: Resource nationalism, because each village wants to claim the lake as its own territory
options.D: The polluter-pays principle, because whoever fishes most should pay for restocking the lake

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons describes how individuals acting in self-interest deplete a shared resource, even when they know the collective harm — each village gains all the fish it catches but shares the loss with all others, making it rational to keep fishing more. The precautionary principle (A) is about halting actions under uncertainty, not explaining why overuse continues despite clear understanding of the risk.

questions.title: Circular Economy Limits
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If every country adopted a fully circular economy, resource scarcity would be completely eliminated because nothing would ever be wasted.' Identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Circular economies only work in wealthy countries, so poorer countries would still face scarcity
options.B: Recycling and reuse always consume some energy and materials, and some resources degrade each cycle, so losses cannot be reduced to zero
options.C: A circular economy focuses only on water, not on minerals or food, so other resources would still run out
options.D: Resource scarcity is caused by population growth alone, which a circular economy cannot control

questions.explanation: Even in a circular economy, the second law of thermodynamics means that every recycling process uses energy and causes some material degradation — for example, recycled paper fibres shorten with each cycle and eventually cannot be reused. Option A is incorrect because circular economy principles can be applied at various scales regardless of national income, and many low-income countries already use highly circular informal recycling systems.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
questions.prompt: Economists sometimes assign a monetary value to a forest's biodiversity. A logging company argues this is unfair because 'you cannot put a price on nature.' Which response BEST challenges the logging company's position using economic reasoning?

options.A: Forests are internationally protected by the Paris Agreement, so logging is already illegal
options.B: Assigning value to ecosystem services like pollination and flood control makes their economic contribution visible so it can be compared fairly against logging profits
options.C: Nature should never be given a monetary value because environmental protection is always more important than economics
options.D: The logging company is correct — pricing nature leads to it being sold to the highest bidder, which always causes more damage

questions.explanation: Ecosystem service valuation — used by economists and in reports like The Economics of Biodiversity (Dasgupta Review, 2021) — gives decision-makers a way to compare the full value of an intact forest (pollination, water filtration, carbon storage, tourism) against the one-time profit from logging, often showing forests are worth more standing. Option C is a moral argument, not an economic one, and does not actually challenge the logging company's economic reasoning.

questions.title: SDG Interconnections
questions.prompt: SDG 2 aims to end hunger and SDG 15 aims to protect life on land. A farmer clears a forest to grow more food for a hungry community. Which statement MOST accurately describes the relationship between these two SDGs in this scenario?

options.A: The SDGs never conflict because they were designed to support each other in every situation
options.B: SDG 2 is more important than SDG 15, so clearing the forest is always the correct decision
options.C: Progress on one SDG can sometimes undermine another, and solutions must consider both goals — for example by increasing yield on existing farmland instead
options.D: SDG 15 overrides SDG 2 in all cases because environmental protection is the foundation of all other goals

questions.explanation: The UN itself acknowledges that SDGs can create trade-offs — the Sustainable Development Goals Report notes that food production and land-use change are leading drivers of biodiversity loss, illustrating direct tension between SDG 2 and SDG 15. Option A is incorrect because SDG interactions include both synergies and trade-offs, and treating them as always complementary ignores documented conflicts.

questions.title: Climate Negotiations Fairness
questions.prompt: At an international climate summit, a delegate from a small island nation says: 'We produce almost no greenhouse gases, yet we face the worst consequences of climate change — rising seas threaten to erase our country.' Which ethical principle does this situation MOST clearly illustrate?

options.A: The precautionary principle, because the island nation is uncertain about future sea-level rise
options.B: Climate injustice, because those who contributed least to the problem suffer the greatest harm
options.C: The polluter-pays principle, because the island nation should charge large emitters for the damage
options.D: Common but differentiated responsibilities, because all nations agreed to the same emission reduction targets

questions.explanation: Climate injustice specifically describes the mismatch between who causes climate change and who bears its worst effects — small island developing states like Tuvalu contribute less than 0.1% of global emissions yet face complete territorial loss from sea-level rise. Option D is wrong because 'common but differentiated responsibilities' refers to recognising that countries have different historical responsibilities and capacities, not that they agreed to identical targets.

questions.title: Groundwater and Rights
questions.prompt: A large agricultural company drills deep wells to irrigate its crops, drawing from the same underground aquifer that local families use for drinking water. The families' wells begin to dry up. What does this scenario BEST demonstrate about rights to shared resources?

options.A: Whoever accesses a resource first automatically holds a permanent legal right to unlimited use
options.B: Private economic use of a shared resource can violate other users' rights when there is no regulation limiting extraction
options.C: Underground water is not a shared resource because it is located on private land
options.D: The families should move closer to the surface water instead of relying on groundwater

questions.explanation: Aquifers are transboundary shared resources — for example the Ogallala Aquifer in the USA is shared across eight states and is being depleted faster than it recharges, threatening both agriculture and community water supplies. Without regulation, one party's extraction can eliminate another's access, directly conflicting with the human right to water recognised by the UN in 2010. Option A is incorrect because prior appropriation law (where it exists) still includes limits and does not grant unlimited extraction rights.

questions.title: Carbon Footprint Responsibility
questions.prompt: Country A manufactures goods that are shipped to and consumed in Country B. When calculating greenhouse gas emissions, should these emissions be counted as Country A's responsibility, Country B's responsibility, or shared? Which approach do most international agreements currently use, and what is its main weakness?

options.A: Most agreements count emissions where goods are consumed (Country B); the weakness is that this unfairly ignores the manufacturing country's energy choices
options.B: Most agreements count emissions where goods are produced (Country A); the weakness is that this lets consuming countries appear cleaner than they truly are
options.C: Most agreements split emissions equally between both countries; the weakness is that it doubles the reporting burden
options.D: Most agreements count emissions by the shipping company; the weakness is that shipping companies operate across many countries

questions.explanation: The UNFCCC framework uses production-based accounting, meaning emissions are recorded in the country where goods are made — this is why China and other manufacturing nations show very high totals even though much of what they produce is consumed in wealthier countries. This system allows high-consuming nations to 'offshore' their real carbon footprint, a well-documented weakness called consumption-based versus production-based accounting. Option A describes the alternative consumption-based approach, which is advocated by researchers but not the current international standard.

questions.title: Overfishing and Regulation
questions.prompt: The European Union introduced fishing quotas in the North Sea that limit how many fish each country's boats can catch per year. Some fishing communities protested, saying the quotas destroyed their livelihoods. Evaluate: do short-term economic costs to fishing communities justify removing the quotas?

options.A: Yes, because local communities' immediate needs always take priority over environmental rules made by distant governments
options.B: No, because removing quotas would risk a fish population collapse, which would permanently destroy far more livelihoods than the quotas themselves
options.C: Yes, because fish populations recover naturally within a few years without any intervention, so quotas are unnecessary
options.D: No, because fishing communities should find entirely new industries rather than continuing to rely on a finite natural resource

questions.explanation: Historical evidence supports maintaining quotas: the Grand Banks cod fishery off Canada collapsed in 1992 after decades of overfishing, leading to a moratorium that has still not fully restored the stock, devastating communities far more than regulated fishing would have. Option C is incorrect because overexploited fish populations can take decades to recover — some North Sea species took 20+ years after reduced fishing pressure — and some may not recover at all if breeding populations fall below critical thresholds.

questions.title: Arctic Resource Geopolitics
questions.prompt: As Arctic sea ice melts, new shipping routes open up and previously inaccessible oil and mineral deposits become reachable. Several countries — including Russia, Canada, and the USA — have begun making competing territorial claims in the Arctic. What makes this situation a geopolitically complex example of 'sharing the planet'?

options.A: The Arctic is already fully governed by the United Nations, so these claims have no legal standing
options.B: The same climate change that creates new opportunities in the Arctic is worsened by exploiting those resources, while indigenous communities and global ecosystems bear the greatest harm
options.C: Because all Arctic resources lie in international waters, every country in the world has an equal legal right to extract them
options.D: The competing claims are only about shipping routes; oil and mineral rights in the Arctic are already settled by treaty

questions.explanation: This scenario embodies multiple layers of complexity: Arctic warming is driven by global fossil fuel use, yet countries now want to extract more fossil fuels from the newly accessible region, accelerating the very warming that enabled access — a reinforcing feedback loop. Additionally, indigenous peoples like the Inuit, who contribute minimally to emissions, face the destruction of their traditional ways of life, mirroring climate injustice. Option C is wrong because under UNCLOS, Arctic nations can claim extended continental shelf rights up to 350 nautical miles from their coasts, giving them exclusive resource rights in those zones.

questions.title: Invasive Species Economics
questions.prompt: The zebra mussel, originally from Eastern Europe, arrived in the Great Lakes of North America via ships' ballast water in the 1980s. It now costs the USA an estimated $1 billion per year in damage. Which chain of cause and effect BEST explains how one small organism creates such large economic costs?

options.A: Zebra mussels eat the fish that local industries harvest, so fishing revenues collapse directly
options.B: Zebra mussels filter so much plankton that native fish starve, and they clog water intake pipes for power plants and cities, requiring constant expensive cleaning
options.C: Zebra mussels produce toxins that poison drinking water, forcing cities to build new water treatment plants
options.D: Zebra mussels outcompete native mussels for territory, reducing biodiversity but not causing significant infrastructure damage

questions.explanation: Zebra mussels are filter feeders that remove phytoplankton at rates that collapse the base of the food web, starving native species like the lake whitefish; simultaneously, they attach in dense colonies to any hard surface, including water intake pipes for power stations, municipal water systems, and boat engines — US facilities spend hundreds of millions annually scraping and chemically treating these pipes. Option C is incorrect because zebra mussels do not produce toxins; they actually filter water and can concentrate existing pollutants but are not themselves the source.

questions.title: Environmental Policy Perspectives
questions.prompt: A government proposes a carbon tax that makes fossil fuels more expensive. An industrialist argues this will destroy jobs. An environmental scientist argues it will slow climate change. A social worker argues it will make energy unaffordable for poor families. Which statement BEST evaluates all three perspectives together?

options.A: The environmental scientist is right because climate change causes more harm than job losses or energy costs
options.B: A well-designed carbon tax can address all three concerns by using the revenue to support clean energy jobs and provide rebates to lower-income households
options.C: The industrialist is right because economic stability must be secured before environmental goals can be pursued
options.D: The social worker raises the only truly valid concern because poverty is always a more urgent problem than climate change

questions.explanation: Evidence from Canada's carbon pricing system, which includes direct rebates (the Climate Action Incentive Payment) to households, shows that most lower-income families receive more back in rebates than they pay in carbon costs, addressing the social worker's concern; revenue can also fund retraining programmes for fossil fuel workers. Option A presents a false hierarchy — the best policies seek to address economic, social, and environmental concerns simultaneously rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.

questions.title: Deforestation and Water Cycles
questions.prompt: Scientists studying the Amazon rainforest describe 'flying rivers' — vast streams of water vapour carried by wind from the forest inland, which then fall as rain on farms thousands of kilometres away. What does this reveal about the responsibility of people who live far from the Amazon?

options.A: People far from the Amazon have no responsibility because they do not live there and did not cause the deforestation
options.B: Because the Amazon's moisture cycle provides rainfall to distant agricultural regions, its destruction would harm food production far beyond Brazil, creating shared global responsibility for its protection
options.C: Only Brazil has the right to decide how to manage the Amazon, so other nations' concerns are not relevant
options.D: The flying rivers phenomenon shows that deforestation in one place increases rainfall in other places, so it is not necessarily harmful

questions.explanation: Research by Brazilian climate scientist Antonio Donato Nobre shows that the Amazon releases approximately 20 billion tonnes of water vapour daily — more than the Amazon River itself carries — providing rainfall that sustains agriculture in São Paulo state and as far as Argentina's Pampas grain belt. This hydrological service means Amazon deforestation would devastate farming across South America and potentially beyond, making its protection genuinely a shared global concern. Option D is wrong because deforestation disrupts the moisture cycle — transpiration from trees is what generates these 'rivers'; removing trees reduces rather than redistributes rainfall.

questions.title: Marine Protected Areas
questions.prompt: A government declares a large area of ocean a Marine Protected Area (MPA), banning all fishing within it. Local fishers protest. Five years later, fish catches outside the MPA have actually increased. Which concept BEST explains this unexpected result?

options.A: The fishers improved their technology during the five years, catching more fish with less effort
options.B: The MPA acted as a fish nursery — allowing populations to recover and 'spill over' into surrounding waters, increasing the overall number of fish available to catch
options.C: Fish migrated permanently into the MPA to avoid fishing, reducing competition in outer waters and letting remaining fish grow larger
options.D: The government secretly allowed limited fishing inside the MPA, which restocked the outer areas

questions.explanation: The 'spillover effect' is a well-documented phenomenon: a 2001 study of the Leigh Marine Reserve in New Zealand found that snapper densities inside the reserve were 14 times higher than outside, and adult fish regularly moved into adjacent fishing areas, significantly boosting nearby catches. This is a key scientific argument for MPAs — they function as reproductive refuges that ultimately benefit fishers. Option C is partially plausible but incorrect in mechanism: fish do not 'decide' to migrate permanently into protected zones; spillover is driven by population density pushing fish outward, not by fish avoiding fishing areas.

questions.title: Soil Degradation Causes
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Soil degradation is mainly caused by drought, so farmers can do nothing to prevent it — they just have to wait for better rains.' Identify the TWO most significant errors in this reasoning.

options.A: Error 1: Drought is not a real cause of soil degradation. Error 2: Farmers can make soil degradation worse but not better
options.B: Error 1: The main causes of soil degradation are human actions such as overgrazing, intensive tilling, and monoculture farming. Error 2: Farmers can prevent and reverse degradation through practices like crop rotation, cover cropping, and reduced tillage
options.C: Error 1: Soil degradation only happens in tropical regions. Error 2: Irrigation always prevents soil degradation regardless of how it is managed
options.D: Error 1: Drought is the only cause of soil degradation. Error 2: Better rainfall automatically restores degraded soil without any intervention

questions.explanation: According to the UN's Global Assessment of Soil Degradation, approximately 85% of soil degradation is caused by human activities — primarily overgrazing, unsustainable agricultural practices, and deforestation — not climate factors alone. Furthermore, regenerative practices such as cover cropping, no-till farming, and crop rotation are proven to rebuild soil organic matter and structure over time. Option D actually restates the student's flawed reasoning, making both listed 'errors' continuations of the original mistake rather than corrections.

questions.title: Fair Trade and Shared Benefit
questions.prompt: Coffee farmers in Ethiopia earn approximately $0.09 for every $3.50 cup of coffee sold in a European café. A student argues: 'This is simply how markets work — consumers get what they are willing to pay and farmers get what the market offers.' What is the STRONGEST counterargument to this position?

options.A: Coffee is not an essential product, so no one is obligated to ensure farmers are paid fairly
options.B: Global commodity markets are shaped by historical trade rules, subsidies to rich-country producers, and unequal bargaining power — meaning the outcome is not simply 'natural' but reflects structural unfairness that can be changed
options.C: The solution is for Ethiopian farmers to stop growing coffee and switch to more profitable crops
options.D: European consumers should stop buying coffee entirely to protest the unfair system

questions.explanation: Coffee markets are heavily influenced by historical colonial trade structures, WTO rules that have historically allowed wealthy nations to subsidise their agricultural exporters, and a trading system where farmers sell unprocessed beans at commodity prices set in New York and London — far removed from actual production costs. Fair Trade certification, which guarantees a minimum floor price to farmers, exists specifically to counter these structural disadvantages and has been shown to raise farmer incomes and community investment. Option A is not a counterargument at all — it actually supports the student's original position.

questions.title: Air Pollution and Borders
questions.prompt: Industrial pollution from factories in Country X is carried by wind patterns and falls as acid rain in Country Y, damaging forests and lakes there. Country X's government says: 'The pollution is in Country Y, not ours — it is their problem to solve.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Country X is correct because international law only governs pollution within a country's own borders
options.B: Country X's claim is legally and ethically flawed because the 'no harm' principle of international environmental law holds that states must not allow activities within their territory to cause significant damage to other states
options.C: Country Y should build a large barrier along its border to prevent the acid rain from entering its territory
options.D: Country X is partially correct because wind patterns are natural phenomena outside any government's control

questions.explanation: The 'no harm' principle, enshrined in Principle 21 of the 1972 Stockholm Declaration and reaffirmed in the 1992 Rio Declaration, establishes that states have a responsibility to ensure activities within their jurisdiction do not harm the environment of other states. The Trail Smelter Arbitration (1941), involving a Canadian smelter causing damage in the USA, was a landmark case establishing state responsibility for transboundary pollution. Option D confuses the mechanism (wind carries pollution) with responsibility — a country cannot avoid responsibility for the emissions it generates simply because nature transports them.

questions.title: Renewable Energy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A proposal to build a large solar farm in a desert region would require mining rare earth minerals, which causes significant environmental damage in the countries where those minerals are found. A student says: 'Solar energy is clean, so building more solar panels is always better for the environment.' What does this example reveal about the student's reasoning?

options.A: The student is correct — the long-term clean energy benefits of solar panels always outweigh the mining damage involved
options.B: The student is using incomplete reasoning by only considering emissions during operation and ignoring the full lifecycle environmental cost, including extraction of materials
options.C: The student is wrong because solar panels actually produce more greenhouse gases than coal when the full manufacturing process is counted
options.D: The student is correct that solar is always better, but wrong about which countries mine the minerals

questions.explanation: Lifecycle assessment (LCA) shows that while solar panels do generate far less CO₂ per kilowatt-hour than coal over their lifetime, the mining of minerals like lithium, cobalt, and rare earths causes significant local environmental and social harm — for example, cobalt mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been linked to deforestation and human rights abuses. A complete environmental evaluation must consider the full supply chain, not only operational emissions. Option C is factually incorrect — even accounting for manufacturing, solar panels produce roughly 20 times less CO₂ per kilowatt-hour than coal across their lifecycle.

questions.title: Food Miles and Local Food
questions.prompt: A student argues that buying locally grown food always has a lower carbon footprint than buying imported food. A researcher responds: 'Tomatoes grown in a heated greenhouse in Sweden can have a higher carbon footprint than tomatoes shipped from Spain.' Which concept does the researcher's response highlight?

options.A: Transport emissions are always the largest part of food's carbon footprint, confirming the student is right
options.B: The method of production (especially energy used for heating and growing) can matter more than distance travelled, so 'local' does not automatically mean lower carbon
options.C: Spanish farms always use renewable energy, making their produce carbon-neutral regardless of shipping distance
options.D: Food miles are the only relevant measure of a food's environmental impact, and the researcher is ignoring other important factors

questions.explanation: Research from the University of Manchester and confirmed by multiple lifecycle studies shows that for many vegetables, production-related energy use (such as greenhouse heating) accounts for a larger share of carbon emissions than transportation — Swedish greenhouse tomatoes can emit 2–3 kg CO₂ per kg versus 0.4 kg for Spanish open-field tomatoes shipped by truck. This means a simplistic 'buy local' rule can actually lead to higher-carbon choices. Option D is backward — it is the student (not the researcher) who is using food miles as the only measure, and the researcher is correctly pointing to additional factors.

questions.title: Indigenous Land Rights
questions.prompt: Many indigenous communities have managed forests sustainably for thousands of years without formal legal ownership. When governments open these same forests to commercial logging without consulting the communities, what rights and responsibilities are most directly violated?

options.A: The right to intellectual property, because indigenous communities own the scientific knowledge about the forest
options.B: The right to free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC), which under UNDRIP requires governments to consult and obtain agreement from indigenous peoples before projects affecting their lands begin
options.C: The right to economic development, because governments have a responsibility to create jobs through logging
options.D: The right to education, because indigenous communities should be taught about sustainable forestry methods before decisions are made

questions.explanation: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted in 2007, explicitly establishes Free, Prior, and Informed Consent as a right — meaning governments and companies must consult meaningfully with indigenous communities and obtain their agreement before undertaking projects on or near their traditional lands. Studies from the Amazon and Southeast Asia consistently show that forests managed under indigenous land rights have lower deforestation rates than those under government or commercial control. Option A, while related, is not the most directly violated right in this scenario — FPIC is the specific internationally recognised right most clearly at stake.

questions.title: Ocean Acidification Chain
questions.prompt: What would happen if atmospheric CO₂ concentrations doubled and remained elevated for 50 years? Arrange the following consequences in the correct cause-and-effect sequence: (1) shellfish and coral skeletons weaken; (2) more CO₂ dissolves into ocean water; (3) fish that rely on shellfish as food become scarcer; (4) ocean water becomes more acidic.
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: more CO₂ dissolves into seawater (2) → reacting with water to form carbonic acid, making the ocean more acidic (4) → the increased acidity reduces carbonate ions that shellfish and corals need to build their calcium carbonate shells and skeletons, weakening them (1) → as shellfish decline, fish species that depend on them as prey also become scarcer (3). Option B is wrong because acidification (4) cannot precede the increased CO₂ dissolution (2) that causes it — the chemistry must happen first.

questions.title: Water Pricing and Access
questions.prompt: Some economists argue that charging a higher price for water would reduce waste and fund better infrastructure. Critics argue this would make water unaffordable for the poor. Which approach BEST resolves this tension while respecting water as a human right?

options.A: Make all water completely free for everyone so that no one is excluded, regardless of the impact on conservation
options.B: Privatise all water utilities completely so that market competition drives down prices and improves quality
options.C: Use a rising block tariff — charge a low or zero price for a basic essential amount per household, then progressively higher prices for greater consumption — so basic needs are met while waste is discouraged
options.D: Allow each country to decide independently without international guidance, since water access is purely a national issue

questions.explanation: Rising block tariffs are used in countries including South Africa and parts of Chile, and align with the UN's recognition of water as a human right (Resolution 64/292, 2010) — the essential minimum (approximately 50 litres per person per day) is guaranteed cheaply or free, while higher consumption (associated with luxury uses like swimming pools and car washing) is priced more steeply to fund infrastructure and discourage waste. Option A ignores conservation incentives and fiscal sustainability — fully free water systems have often led to infrastructure neglect and illegal connections that paradoxically leave poorer communities without reliable supply.

questions.title: Ecological Footprint Comparison
questions.prompt: If everyone on Earth lived like an average person in the United Arab Emirates, we would need approximately 5.4 Earths to sustain that lifestyle. If everyone lived like an average person in India, we would need approximately 0.7 Earths. What does this comparison MOST reveal about the concept of 'sharing the planet' fairly?

options.A: People in India have achieved the ideal sustainable lifestyle and should be considered a global model without any further development
options.B: High-consumption lifestyles in wealthy nations use far more than their fair share of Earth's resources, making global equity and environmental sustainability inseparable challenges
options.C: Because India's footprint is below 1 Earth, it can increase consumption without any environmental concern
options.D: The comparison proves that population size is the most important factor in ecological footprint, since India has a much larger population

questions.explanation: Ecological footprint analysis, developed by Mathis Wackernagel and William Rees, shows that current global consumption already exceeds Earth's biocapacity by roughly 75% — primarily driven by high-consumption nations. The UAE's high footprint stems from energy-intensive lifestyles (heavy air conditioning, high car use, food imports) rather than population size, demonstrating that per-person consumption patterns are as critical as total numbers. Option D is directly contradicted by the data — India has over four times the UAE's population but a fraction of its footprint, showing that per-capita consumption, not raw population, drives the ecological footprint figure presented.

questions.title: Wetland Conservation Value
questions.prompt: A developer wants to drain a coastal wetland to build a hotel. A local government argues the wetland provides more long-term value than the hotel. Which combination of wetland functions BEST supports the government's argument in economic terms?

options.A: Wetlands are aesthetically pleasing and provide spiritual value to communities, which cannot be compared to economic value
options.B: Wetlands store large amounts of carbon, filter pollutants from water, buffer coastlines from storm surges, and provide nursery habitats for commercially important fish — each of these has a quantifiable economic value that often exceeds development profits
options.C: Wetlands are protected by international law in all countries, making the developer's project automatically illegal
options.D: The hotel would generate tourism revenue that could fund conservation of other wetlands nearby, making development the better environmental choice overall

questions.explanation: A 2014 study published in Global Environmental Change calculated that coastal wetlands provide storm protection services worth $23 billion annually in the USA alone, while wetlands are among the most carbon-rich ecosystems per unit area on Earth — peatlands store twice as much carbon as all the world's forests combined despite covering only 3% of land area. These quantifiable services (flood protection, water filtration, fishery support, carbon storage) typically far exceed one-time development value when calculated over decades. Option C is partly incorrect — the Ramsar Convention protects designated sites internationally, but not all wetlands are Ramsar sites, and legal protections vary widely by country.

questions.title: Responsibility for Space Debris
questions.prompt: There are now more than 27,000 pieces of trackable debris orbiting Earth, left by various nations' space missions. This debris threatens satellites that power GPS, weather forecasting, and internet communications worldwide. Which principle used in environmental governance on Earth MOST logically applies to this situation?

options.A: The principle of national sovereignty — each country's satellites are its own property and therefore its debris is also its own private matter
options.B: The tragedy of the commons — low Earth orbit is a shared resource being degraded by individual actors whose short-term benefit from launching satellites exceeds the cost they personally pay for leaving debris
options.C: The precautionary principle — because we are uncertain whether debris causes harm, no space launches should occur until debris is fully understood
options.D: The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities — wealthier spacefaring nations should clean up debris while poorer nations are exempt

questions.explanation: Low Earth orbit is a global commons — no single nation owns it — and every country and company that launches a satellite benefits individually from the mission while the cost of resulting debris (collision risk, orbital slot degradation) is shared by all users globally. NASA scientist Donald Kessler described the ultimate risk as a cascade where debris creates more debris, eventually making certain orbits unusable — precisely the collective action failure described by the tragedy of the commons. Option D is plausible but incorrect as the primary principle here: common but differentiated responsibilities addresses historical emission gaps, not the structural incentive problem that allows continued debris generation by all spacefaring actors regardless of wealth.

questions.title: Refugee Flows and Environment
questions.prompt: In recent decades, prolonged droughts in the Sahel region of Africa have contributed to large movements of people to cities and across borders. A student claims: 'These are economic migrants, not environmental refugees, so climate change is not responsible.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct because international law clearly distinguishes climate refugees from economic migrants and climate is never a primary cause of migration
options.B: The student oversimplifies: drought destroys crops and pastures, causing economic collapse and conflict over remaining resources, making the environment, economy, and conflict inseparably linked drivers of displacement
options.C: The student is wrong because all migration in the Sahel is caused by climate change alone, with no economic or political factors involved
options.D: The student is correct that climate is not responsible, because the Sahel has always experienced droughts and populations have always adapted without migrating

questions.explanation: The World Bank's Groundswell report (2021) projects that without climate action, up to 216 million people could become internal climate migrants by 2050, with the Sahel and sub-Saharan Africa among the most affected regions. In Lake Chad basin, the lake has shrunk by approximately 90% since the 1960s due to drought and overextraction, destroying fishing and farming livelihoods and fuelling conflict — making it impossible to separate environmental, economic, and security drivers. Option A is also partially correct that current international refugee law (1951 Refugee Convention) does not formally recognise climate refugees, but this is a legal gap, not evidence that climate is not responsible — and the student's claim goes further by denying climate's causal role entirely.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: A lake is shared by five villages. Each village is allowed to catch fish freely, and every village knows that if everyone catches too many fish, the lake will be empty within five years. Yet every village continues to catch as many fish as possible. Which concept BEST explains why individual villages act this way even when it harms everyone?

options.A: The precautionary principle, because villages are unsure whether the fish will really run out
options.B: The tragedy of the commons, because individuals benefit from overusing a shared resource while the cost is shared by all
options.C: The free-rider problem, because some villages secretly catch more fish than others without anyone knowing
options.D: Resource nationalism, because each village believes the lake belongs exclusively to its own community

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons describes situations where individuals acting in self-interest deplete a shared resource, because each person gains the full benefit of taking more while the damage is spread across everyone. The free-rider problem (C) is related but specifically refers to benefiting from a resource others pay to maintain, rather than explaining why overuse happens when everyone has equal access.

questions.title: Circular Economy Materials
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Recycling is always the best solution for waste because it turns old materials into new ones, so we should focus all our efforts on recycling rather than reducing how much we buy.' Evaluate this claim using the waste hierarchy principle.

options.A: The claim is correct because recycling recovers materials that would otherwise go to landfill, making it the most effective strategy
options.B: The claim is partly right because recycling is better than landfill, but the waste hierarchy places reducing consumption above recycling as a priority
options.C: The claim is wrong because recycling uses more energy than making products from raw materials, so it always increases environmental harm
options.D: The claim is correct because reducing purchases would hurt the economy, making recycling a better balance of environmental and economic goals

questions.explanation: The waste hierarchy ranks strategies as: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover — placing reduction above recycling because making fewer products in the first place uses the least energy and resources. Recycling still requires energy and processing, so it is not the top priority despite being better than landfill. Option C is wrong because recycling typically uses significantly less energy than producing from virgin raw materials for many materials like aluminium.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
questions.prompt: Bees pollinate approximately one-third of all the food crops humans eat. If a pesticide used on farms caused a 70% decline in wild bee populations, which chain of consequences would MOST likely follow?

options.A: Food prices would fall because farmers would need less labour to tend crops that no longer attract insects
options.B: Crop yields of many fruits and vegetables would decline, leading to food shortages and higher prices
options.C: Only honey production would be affected because other insects can pollinate all major food crops equally well
options.D: Farmers would immediately switch to wind-pollinated crops, preventing any significant impact on food supply

questions.explanation: Bees are the primary pollinators for around 75% of leading food crops worldwide, including fruits, nuts, and vegetables; a 70% decline would severely reduce yields of these crops, creating scarcity and price increases. Option C is wrong because while some insects pollinate some plants, bees are far more efficient and numerous than other pollinators for most major food crops, and wind pollination does not work for fruits and vegetables.

questions.title: Climate Geopolitics and Equity
questions.prompt: The Paris Agreement asks countries to set their own targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions rather than having a single global target enforced by one authority. What is the MOST significant weakness of this voluntary approach?

options.A: It makes it impossible for scientists to measure global emissions because each country uses different methods
options.B: Countries may set targets that are too weak or fail to meet them, since there is no binding penalty for non-compliance
options.C: It prevents developing countries from receiving any financial support for clean energy projects
options.D: It means the agreement only applies to the world's ten largest economies, leaving smaller countries without obligations

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement relies on Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which countries set themselves, and there is no international court or penalty system to punish countries that miss their targets, making enforcement a critical weakness. Option A is wrong because the UNFCCC has standardised reporting frameworks that allow consistent measurement of emissions across different countries.

questions.title: SDG Interconnections
questions.prompt: SDG 6 focuses on clean water and sanitation, while SDG 3 focuses on good health. A student argues these two goals are completely separate and should be funded independently. What evidence BEST challenges this view?

options.A: Both goals appear in the same United Nations document, which means they must be treated as one combined goal
options.B: Unsafe water causes around 485,000 diarrhoeal deaths per year globally, directly linking water access to health outcomes
options.C: Countries that achieve SDG 6 automatically receive UN funding to achieve SDG 3 as part of the same grant programme
options.D: Health workers require clean water to wash their hands, so SDG 3 depends on SDG 6 only in hospital settings

questions.explanation: Contaminated water is a leading cause of preventable disease globally; the WHO estimates unsafe water contributes to around 485,000 diarrhoeal deaths annually, showing a direct causal link between water quality (SDG 6) and health (SDG 3). Option D is too narrow — the relationship extends far beyond hospitals to entire communities, where drinking contaminated water causes widespread illness independent of healthcare settings.

questions.title: Resource Scarcity and Conflict
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen in a semi-arid region where two neighbouring countries share a river, if climate change caused that river's annual water flow to decrease by 40% over 20 years?

options.A: Both countries would independently develop desalination technology, eliminating the need to share the river
options.B: Tensions over water allocation would likely increase, potentially leading to diplomatic disputes or conflict
options.C: Farmers in both countries would spontaneously switch to crops that need no irrigation, solving the shortage
options.D: International organisations would immediately transfer water from a wetter region to replace the lost flow

questions.explanation: Historical evidence from regions like the Nile Basin and Tigris-Euphrates shows that declining shared water resources intensify competition and political tension between states, as each government faces pressure from its own population to secure sufficient supply. Option A is wrong because desalination is expensive, energy-intensive, and only feasible near coastlines, making it an impractical solution for landlocked semi-arid countries sharing an inland river.

questions.title: Environmental Rights and Law
questions.prompt: Some countries have added the 'right to a healthy environment' to their constitutions, while others have not. A student claims this legal difference makes no real practical difference because environmental protection depends on individual behaviour, not laws. Identify the strongest argument against this claim.

options.A: Constitutional rights give citizens the legal power to take their government to court if it fails to protect the environment, creating enforceable accountability
options.B: Countries without this right in their constitution have no environmental laws at all, so pollution is completely legal there
options.C: Individual behaviour can never reduce pollution, so only constitutional law can make any environmental difference
options.D: International law automatically gives all citizens a right to a healthy environment regardless of what national constitutions say

questions.explanation: When the right to a healthy environment is constitutionally protected, citizens and groups can bring legal cases against governments or companies that fail to uphold it, as seen in landmark cases in Colombia and the Netherlands where courts ordered stronger climate action. Option B is wrong because many countries without this specific constitutional right still have extensive environmental legislation; the constitutional provision adds an extra enforcement mechanism, not the only one.

questions.title: Carbon Footprint Comparison
questions.prompt: A family in a high-income country installs solar panels on their house and feels their environmental responsibility is fully met. A critic argues this is an example of 'individual action bias.' Which reasoning BEST supports the critic's position?

options.A: Solar panels do not actually reduce carbon emissions because manufacturing them releases more carbon than they save over their lifetime
options.B: Focusing only on home energy ignores the larger carbon footprint from aviation, consumption, and food, and can reduce pressure on governments to make systemic changes
options.C: Individual families in high-income countries have no measurable impact on global emissions, so personal actions are always pointless
options.D: Solar panels only work in sunny climates, so they are not a valid solution for most of the world's population

questions.explanation: Research shows that home energy is only one portion of a household's total carbon footprint, with aviation, diet, and consumer goods often contributing more; focusing on one visible action can create a false sense of completion and reduce motivation for wider advocacy or political pressure. Option A is factually incorrect — lifecycle analyses consistently show solar panels generate far more clean energy over their lifespan (typically 25–30 years) than the emissions produced during manufacturing.

questions.title: Soil Degradation and Food Security
questions.prompt: Scientists estimate that approximately 33% of the world's soil is moderately to highly degraded. Which combination of human activities is MOST responsible for this degradation?

options.A: Urban construction and road building, because covering soil with concrete prevents all natural recovery
options.B: Overgrazing, intensive agriculture with chemical inputs, and deforestation, which together remove protective cover and deplete nutrients
options.C: Acid rain caused by industrial air pollution, which is the single largest cause of soil damage worldwide
options.D: Natural erosion by wind and rain, which outpaces any human contribution to soil loss globally

questions.explanation: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization identifies overgrazing, unsustainable farming practices including excessive fertiliser use, and deforestation as the leading human-caused drivers of soil degradation globally, as they erode topsoil, reduce organic matter, and destroy soil microbiomes.
