Option D is wrong because while natural erosion occurs, human agricultural and land-use practices have accelerated erosion rates by 10 to 40 times beyond natural levels in many regions.

questions.title: Ocean Acidification Effects
questions.prompt: When oceans absorb excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, they become more acidic. Which organism is MOST directly harmed by ocean acidification, and why?

options.A: Large whales, because acidic water irritates their skin during long migrations
options.B: Shell-forming creatures like oysters and sea urchins, because acidic water dissolves the calcium carbonate they need to build shells
options.C: Saltwater fish like tuna, because their gills cannot filter acidic water as efficiently as neutral water
options.D: Seagrass beds, because acidic water prevents photosynthesis from occurring in underwater plants

questions.explanation: Ocean acidification reduces the concentration of carbonate ions in seawater, making it harder for marine organisms like oysters, mussels, sea urchins, and pteropods to build and maintain their calcium carbonate shells and skeletons — a process that is chemically disrupted as pH falls. Option C is plausible but wrong because fish gills are adapted to extract oxygen from water rather than filter acidity, and fish have other physiological buffers, making shell-forming invertebrates significantly more vulnerable.

questions.title: Fair Trade and Global Supply
questions.prompt: A chocolate bar sold in Europe for €2 contains cocoa grown by farmers in Ghana. Research shows the farmers receive less than 6% of the final sale price. Which principle from the concept of 'responsibility' in shared global trade BEST identifies the ethical problem here?

options.A: The polluter pays principle, because cocoa farming creates environmental damage that consumers must fund
options.B: Distributive justice, because the economic benefits of global trade are not shared fairly along the supply chain
options.C: The precautionary principle, because consumers cannot be sure the cocoa was grown without pesticides
options.D: Comparative advantage, because Ghana naturally produces cocoa more cheaply than Europe, making low prices inevitable

questions.explanation: Distributive justice concerns the fair distribution of benefits and burdens; when farmers who do the primary labour receive only 6% of the retail price while corporations and retailers take the majority, this represents an unjust distribution of the economic value created along the supply chain. Option D is wrong because comparative advantage is an economic theory explaining why countries specialise in certain goods, not an ethical justification for low producer payments — it describes what happens, not whether it is fair.

questions.title: Renewable Energy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A country plans to build large wind farms to generate clean electricity, but local communities protest because the turbines will be visible on hills they consider culturally important. Which framework BEST describes the type of conflict this situation represents?

options.A: A conflict between short-term economic costs and long-term economic benefits of energy investment
options.B: A conflict between global environmental responsibility and local community rights and cultural values
options.C: A conflict between government authority and private companies over who controls energy production
options.D: A conflict between different types of renewable energy, since wind power competes with solar power for funding

questions.explanation: This situation presents a genuine tension between the global benefit of reducing carbon emissions through wind energy and the local community's right to have their cultural landscape and values respected — a classic example of how environmental solutions can create conflicts between different scales of rights and responsibility. Option A is wrong because the community's objection is cultural and aesthetic, not primarily about economic costs, so framing it as a purely financial trade-off misrepresents the nature of the dispute.

questions.title: Biodiversity Economics
questions.prompt: An economist calculates that a wetland provides flood protection, water filtration, and fish nursery services worth $30,000 per hectare per year to nearby communities. A developer offers to buy and drain the wetland for $15,000 per hectare. Identify the error in the developer's economic reasoning.

options.A: The developer has not considered that wetlands are legally protected in all countries, making the purchase illegal regardless of price
options.B: The developer's offer ignores the ecosystem services the wetland provides, which are worth more than the purchase price and would be lost permanently
options.C: The developer has underestimated how much money can be made from selling the water drained from the wetland to nearby cities
options.D: The economist's figures are unreliable because ecosystem services cannot be measured in monetary terms under any accepted economic method

questions.explanation: The developer's reasoning is flawed because it only considers the land's market price (€15,000/hectare) while ignoring the ecosystem services — flood control, water purification, habitat — worth $30,000/hectare annually; these services would be permanently lost, costing communities far more than the sale generates. Option D is wrong because ecosystem service valuation is a well-established field in environmental economics, used by governments and organisations like the UN to guide policy decisions.

questions.title: Climate Migration and Rights
questions.prompt: Some Pacific Island nations may become uninhabitable due to rising sea levels within decades. Citizens who leave are sometimes called 'climate refugees,' yet international law does not currently recognise climate change as an official reason for refugee status. Why does this gap in law create a specific problem?

options.A: People displaced by climate change cannot access the legal protections given to refugees fleeing persecution, leaving them without guaranteed rights in other countries
options.B: Pacific Island nations cannot apply to join the United Nations if their territory is underwater, removing their voting rights
options.C: Other countries are required to pay compensation to climate migrants but only if they are officially recognised as refugees first
options.D: Climate migrants are automatically granted citizenship in the country that has produced the most historical greenhouse gas emissions

questions.explanation: The 1951 Refugee Convention protects people fleeing persecution but does not cover environmental displacement, meaning climate migrants have no guaranteed right to asylum, resettlement support, or protection from deportation under international law — a gap the UN Human Rights Committee highlighted in a landmark 2020 ruling. Option C is wrong because no international legal mechanism currently requires wealthy high-emitting countries to pay compensation to climate migrants; this is a proposed policy, not existing law.

questions.title: Overfishing and Quotas
questions.prompt: An international fishing agreement sets a maximum catch quota for Atlantic bluefin tuna. Country A follows the quota strictly. Country B secretly exceeds it by 30%. What is the MOST likely long-term consequence of Country B's behaviour, and why does it affect Country A too?

options.A: Country B will catch more fish in the short term, but tuna populations will decline for all fishing nations since fish migrate across national boundaries
options.B: Country A will be penalised by the international agreement for not catching its full quota, losing revenue unfairly
options.C: Tuna populations will recover quickly because Country A's restraint fully offsets Country B's excess catch
options.D: The agreement will automatically increase Country A's quota to match Country B's catch, ensuring equal treatment

questions.explanation: Atlantic bluefin tuna are highly migratory, crossing international waters, so overfishing by any one nation depletes the same shared stock that all nations depend on — Country A's compliance cannot protect the population if Country B undermines the total allowable catch. Option C is wrong because Country A's reduction only covers its own quota share; Country B exceeding by 30% adds additional pressure that Country A's restraint cannot cancel out.

questions.title: Green Economy vs Growth
questions.prompt: Some economists argue that economic growth and environmental protection are fundamentally incompatible — that you cannot have both at the same time. Other economists argue a 'green economy' can achieve both. Which piece of evidence MOST strongly supports the green economy view?

options.A: Some high-income countries have increased GDP while reducing total carbon emissions over the same period, a pattern called 'decoupling'
options.B: Renewable energy costs the same to produce as fossil fuels, so switching energy sources does not affect economic output at all
options.C: All countries that have signed the Paris Agreement have seen positive economic growth in every year since signing
options.D: Environmental regulations always create new jobs that exactly replace every job lost in polluting industries

questions.explanation: Countries including Denmark, the UK, and the USA have demonstrated 'absolute decoupling' — growing their economies as measured by GDP while simultaneously reducing total greenhouse gas emissions — providing empirical evidence that growth and reduced environmental impact can coexist. Option B is wrong because renewable energy is not always the same cost as fossil fuels in all contexts, and cost alone does not determine economic output; the relationship is far more complex than a simple price equivalence.

questions.title: Deforestation and Indigenous Rights
questions.prompt: A government grants a logging company permission to clear a forest that has been home to an indigenous community for hundreds of years. The community was not consulted before the decision was made. Which internationally recognised principle did the government MOST clearly violate?

options.A: The polluter pays principle, requiring industries to cover the cost of environmental damage they cause
options.B: Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), which requires governments to obtain indigenous communities' agreement before decisions affecting their land
options.C: The precautionary principle, which states that no development should proceed if any scientific uncertainty about harm exists
options.D: The common heritage of mankind principle, which means forests legally belong to all people on Earth equally

questions.explanation: Free, Prior and Informed Consent is enshrined in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) and requires that indigenous communities be genuinely consulted and give agreement before any project affecting their traditional lands proceeds — consultation after the decision is made violates this standard. Option C is wrong because the precautionary principle addresses responses to scientific uncertainty about environmental harm, not the rights of communities to participate in decisions about their land.

questions.title: Nitrogen Cycle Disruption
questions.prompt: Farmers apply large amounts of synthetic nitrogen fertiliser to grow more crops. Much of this nitrogen washes into rivers and eventually into coastal seas. What is the sequence of environmental consequences that MOST accurately describes what happens next?

options.A: Nitrogen makes seawater saltier, which kills freshwater fish that migrate into the sea to breed
options.B: Excess nitrogen causes algae to grow rapidly, the algae die and decompose, bacteria use up oxygen during decomposition, and fish suffocate in the low-oxygen water
options.C: Nitrogen reacts with ocean salt to form nitric acid, directly acidifying coastal waters and dissolving coral reefs
options.D: Nitrogen enriches the water, making it more productive so fish populations in coastal areas increase significantly

questions.explanation: This process is called eutrophication: excess nutrients trigger algal blooms, the algae die and are decomposed by bacteria that consume large amounts of dissolved oxygen, creating 'dead zones' where oxygen levels are too low for most marine life to survive — a documented problem in areas like the Gulf of Mexico. Option D is wrong because while algae initially grow, the resulting oxygen depletion during decomposition makes the water less hospitable for fish, not more productive.

questions.title: Urban Land Use and Equity
questions.prompt: In many cities, wealthier neighbourhoods have more trees, parks, and green spaces than poorer neighbourhoods. A student argues this is purely a matter of personal choice — wealthy residents simply prefer nature. Identify the strongest challenge to this explanation.

options.A: Wealthier people breathe more oxygen on average, so their bodies require access to more trees for health reasons
options.B: Green space distribution reflects historical planning decisions and property values, not individual preference, creating structural environmental inequality
options.C: Poorer communities actually prefer concrete because it is easier to clean and maintain than grass and trees
options.D: International urban planning law requires cities to provide equal green space per person, so any difference is simply a reporting error

questions.explanation: Urban ecology research consistently shows that green space is distributed unequally based on historical zoning, land values, and investment patterns rather than resident preferences — in many cities, low-income and minority neighbourhoods received less park investment over decades, a form of environmental injustice sometimes called 'green gentrification.' Option C is wrong and represents a harmful stereotype; survey evidence shows low-income urban residents value green spaces highly and often actively campaign for more.

questions.title: Energy Access and Development
questions.prompt: Approximately 775 million people globally still lack access to electricity. A student claims the solution is simple: give every community the same solar panels used in wealthy countries. What is the MOST important reason this suggestion oversimplifies the problem?

options.A: Solar panels do not work in tropical countries because the sun is too intense and damages the photovoltaic cells
options.B: Sustainable energy access requires infrastructure, maintenance skills, financing systems, and grid connections that cannot be solved by equipment alone
options.C: People in low-income countries prefer traditional energy sources like wood fires because they are more culturally familiar
options.D: Solar panels are currently too expensive to be manufactured in sufficient quantities to supply 775 million people within any realistic timeframe

questions.explanation: Energy poverty is a systemic challenge: even where panels are donated, projects fail without trained technicians for maintenance, financing for battery storage, distribution grids, and community engagement — evidence from failed aid projects in Sub-Saharan Africa demonstrates that hardware alone does not deliver sustained energy access. Option A is factually wrong: tropical and subtropical regions, including much of Africa and South Asia where energy poverty is concentrated, have excellent solar irradiance and are among the best locations for solar power generation.

questions.title: Migratory Species Protection
questions.prompt: Monarch butterflies migrate from Mexico to Canada and back, crossing three countries. Conservation efforts in Canada successfully increase butterfly numbers, but logging in Mexico destroys their overwintering forests. What does this situation BEST illustrate about protecting migratory species?

options.A: Conservation in one country alone is sufficient if the species breeds successfully there, because numbers will eventually recover globally
options.B: Effective protection of migratory species requires international cooperation because the species depends on habitats in multiple countries throughout its life cycle
options.C: Mexico's logging is justified because economic development must take priority over species that spend most of their time in other countries
options.D: Butterfly populations are too fragile to survive long-distance migration, so conservation should focus on breeding them in captivity instead

questions.explanation: Monarch butterflies depend on milkweed plants in Canada and the USA for breeding and on specific oyamel fir forests in Mexico for winter survival; protecting only one stage of the migration cannot sustain the population, illustrating why the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) requires coordinated multi-country action. Option A is wrong precisely because the Mexico overwintering sites are a critical bottleneck — without them, even large breeding populations cannot survive winter, as demonstrated by population collapses following forest loss in Mexican reserves.

questions.title: Electronic Waste Responsibility
questions.prompt: Millions of old smartphones and computers from wealthy countries are shipped to informal recycling sites in parts of West Africa and South-East Asia, where workers — often children — extract valuable metals without safety equipment. Which concept from environmental ethics MOST accurately describes what is happening here?

options.A: The precautionary principle, because wealthy countries are unsure whether e-waste recycling causes harm
options.B: Pollution haven effect, where countries with weaker environmental and labour regulations absorb harmful processes from wealthier nations
options.C: The circular economy, because metals recovered from old devices are used to make new electronics, completing the material loop
options.D: Comparative advantage, because lower-income countries are more efficient at recycling electronics due to lower labour costs

questions.explanation: The pollution haven effect describes how industries or waste streams relocate to countries with weaker regulations to avoid the costs of safe disposal — wealthy nations effectively exporting environmental and health harms to more vulnerable communities, a documented pattern in the global e-waste trade. Option C is wrong because a genuine circular economy requires safe, non-toxic material recovery with fair labour conditions; informal e-waste burning to extract metals is toxic and dangerous, the opposite of a sustainable circular model.

questions.title: Mangrove Loss and Coastal Risk
questions.prompt: Mangrove forests along tropical coastlines have been cleared at high rates to build shrimp farms. A student claims this is a good trade-off because shrimp farming creates jobs and food. Which multi-step consequence chain MOST effectively challenges this claim?

options.A: Mangrove loss reduces the carbon stored in coastal soils, which contributes to global warming, which eventually makes shrimp farming less profitable
options.B: Removing mangroves eliminates natural storm barriers and fish nurseries, increasing coastal flood damage and reducing wild fish catches that local communities depend on, often outweighing shrimp farm income
options.C: Shrimp farms pollute the water so heavily that they make nearby mangrove regrowth impossible, locking the coastline into permanent agricultural use
options.D: Mangroves provide the only source of wood fuel for coastal communities, so clearing them forces people to use more expensive fossil fuels for cooking

questions.explanation: Mangroves act as wave-breaks and storm surge barriers — studies show they reduce wave height by 50–70% — and serve as nurseries for up to 80% of tropical fish species, so their removal increases both flood damage costs and the collapse of wild fisheries that local communities often depend on more than shrimp farm wages. Option A describes a real consequence but is too indirect and long-term to challenge the immediate economic claim effectively, whereas the loss of storm protection and fisheries creates measurable short-term costs that directly undermine the trade-off argument.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: A lake is shared by five villages, each of which can fish as much as they want. Over time, the fish population collapses. Which concept BEST explains why individually rational decisions led to a collectively harmful outcome?

options.A: The free-rider problem
options.B: The tragedy of the commons
options.C: Market failure due to monopoly
options.D: The precautionary principle

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons, coined by Garrett Hardin in 1968, describes how individuals acting in self-interest deplete a shared resource, even when it is not in anyone's long-term interest — exactly what happens when unregulated fishing exhausts a shared lake. The free-rider problem is related but specifically describes benefiting from a resource without contributing to its maintenance, which is not the primary dynamic here.

questions.title: SDG Goals and Targets
questions.prompt: SDG 13 calls for urgent action on climate change. A student states: 'SDG 13 is only about reducing carbon emissions, so actions like adapting infrastructure to handle flooding are not part of it.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: SDG 13 focuses exclusively on developed nations, not all countries
options.B: SDG 13 includes both mitigation of emissions and adaptation to climate impacts
options.C: Flooding adaptation is covered under SDG 11, not SDG 13
options.D: Carbon emission reduction is not actually a target within SDG 13

questions.explanation: SDG 13 explicitly includes targets for both mitigation (reducing greenhouse gas emissions) and adaptation (strengthening resilience to climate-related hazards such as flooding), making the student's claim incorrect. While SDG 11 does address sustainable cities, climate adaptation measures are clearly listed under SDG 13's own targets and indicators.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: In a linear economy, materials follow a 'take-make-dispose' path. What is the KEY difference between a linear economy and a circular economy in terms of how waste is treated?

options.A: A circular economy eliminates all manufacturing waste by banning single-use products
options.B: A circular economy treats waste as a resource to be fed back into production cycles
options.C: A circular economy sends all waste to be buried in specially designed landfills
options.D: A circular economy focuses only on recycling plastic and ignores other materials

questions.explanation: The defining feature of a circular economy is that materials and products are kept in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and recycling — meaning waste from one process becomes the input for another. Option A is incorrect because the circular economy does not simply ban products but redesigns systems so materials loop back rather than being discarded.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
questions.prompt: Bees pollinate roughly one third of the food crops humans eat. If bee populations continue to decline due to pesticide use and habitat loss, which ecosystem service would be MOST directly threatened?

options.A: Climate regulation through carbon sequestration
options.B: Provisioning services related to crop food production
options.C: Cultural services such as nature-based tourism
options.D: Water purification and flood control

questions.explanation: Pollination by bees is a provisioning ecosystem service because it directly enables the production of food crops that humans and animals depend on for nutrition. Climate regulation through carbon sequestration is primarily performed by forests and oceans, not by bee pollination, making option A the most plausible but incorrect distractor.

questions.title: Resource Scarcity and Equity
questions.prompt: Analyse this statement: 'Scarcity of a resource always means there is not enough of it on Earth.' Why is this definition of scarcity incomplete?

options.A: Scarcity only applies to non-renewable resources like oil, not to renewable ones
options.B: Scarcity can result from unequal distribution even when total supply is sufficient
options.C: Scarcity is always caused by overpopulation rather than distribution problems
options.D: Resources become scarce only when governments fail to regulate their use

questions.explanation: Economic and geographical scarcity can exist even when Earth holds sufficient total quantities of a resource, because poor distribution systems, political barriers, or poverty prevent people from accessing it — this is called relative scarcity. Option A is incorrect because scarcity applies to any resource, renewable or not, and the distinction is not what makes the definition incomplete.

questions.title: Environmental Stewardship
questions.prompt: A government proposes a law requiring all new buildings to include rooftop solar panels. A citizen argues this infringes on private property rights. Which principle of environmental stewardship BEST justifies the government's position?

options.A: The polluter-pays principle
options.B: The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities
options.C: The idea that collective environmental well-being can justify shared obligations
options.D: The principle of state sovereignty over natural resources

questions.explanation: Environmental stewardship holds that individuals and societies have obligations to manage resources responsibly for the benefit of all, including future generations — this collective responsibility can justify regulations that place obligations on private actors. The polluter-pays principle (Option A) addresses who bears the cost of existing pollution, which is a different concept not directly relevant to the solar mandate.

questions.title: Carbon Footprint Basics
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Flying once from London to New York produces more CO₂ per passenger than driving a car for an entire year in Europe.' Evaluate whether this claim is accurate based on what you know about transport emissions.

options.A: The claim is false because long-haul flights are now carbon-neutral due to offset schemes
options.B: The claim is broadly accurate because a transatlantic flight produces roughly 1–3 tonnes of CO₂ per passenger, comparable to or exceeding average annual car use
options.C: The claim is false because cars always produce more emissions than planes due to daily use
options.D: The claim is accurate only for business-class passengers, not economy seats

questions.explanation: A return transatlantic flight produces approximately 1.5–3 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per economy passenger, which is similar to or greater than the roughly 1.5–2 tonnes produced by an average European car driven for a year — making the student's claim broadly accurate. Option C is incorrect because while cars are used daily, per-journey emissions of long-haul flights are extremely high due to the distance and fuel burned.

questions.title: Geopolitics of Climate Change
questions.prompt: Small island nations such as Tuvalu and the Maldives are among the countries MOST vulnerable to climate change, yet they contribute less than 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions. What does this situation reveal about the relationship between climate responsibility and climate vulnerability?

options.A: Countries with the lowest emissions are always the least developed economically
options.B: Those who contribute least to climate change often suffer its worst consequences, creating a fundamental injustice
options.C: Small island nations should increase their emissions to have more influence in climate negotiations
options.D: Vulnerability to climate change is primarily determined by a country's GDP, not its geography

questions.explanation: Small island developing states (SIDS) face existential threats from sea-level rise and extreme weather despite being responsible for a negligible share of historical emissions, illustrating the profound injustice at the heart of climate geopolitics. Option D is incorrect because geographic factors — low elevation, coastal exposure — are the primary drivers of vulnerability for these nations, not GDP alone.

questions.title: International Environmental Agreements
questions.prompt: The Paris Agreement asks countries to set their own emission-reduction targets, called Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). What is the MAIN criticism of this voluntary approach compared to a legally binding global emissions cap?

options.A: NDCs prevent developing countries from industrialising at all
options.B: Countries may set targets that are too weak or fail to meet them without facing legal penalties
options.C: The Paris Agreement does not cover the two largest emitting countries
options.D: Voluntary agreements are always more effective than binding ones because countries feel ownership

questions.explanation: Because NDCs are self-set and the Paris Agreement has no enforcement mechanism for missing targets, countries face only reputational rather than legal consequences for weak or unmet pledges — a major limitation for achieving the 1.5°C goal. Option D contradicts the core criticism and is the distractor students might choose if they confuse stakeholder ownership with effectiveness.

questions.title: Renewable vs Non-Renewable Energy
questions.prompt: Compare solar energy and coal as energy sources. Which comparison MOST accurately identifies a key difference relevant to long-term planetary sustainability?

options.A: Solar energy requires more land per unit of energy than coal in all circumstances
options.B: Coal releases stored carbon into the atmosphere when burned, while solar panels generate electricity without combustion emissions during operation
options.C: Solar panels produce more total lifetime energy than coal plants of the same initial cost
options.D: Coal is a renewable resource because new coal seams form naturally over time

questions.explanation: Burning coal releases carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that were stored underground for millions of years, contributing directly to climate change, whereas solar panels convert sunlight into electricity without combustion and produce no operational emissions. Option D is incorrect because coal takes hundreds of millions of years to form geologically, making it non-renewable on any human timescale.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: A mining company legally extracts copper from land it owns, but the process contaminates a river used by a downstream community for drinking water. Which framework BEST describes why the company's legal right to mine does not automatically justify the harm caused?

options.A: Rights always override responsibilities when they are protected by national law
options.B: Legal rights do not eliminate moral responsibilities to avoid harming others who depend on shared resources
options.C: The community should simply find another source of water rather than restrict the company
options.D: Only international courts have the authority to decide whether legal mining is harmful

questions.explanation: IB ethics frameworks and human rights principles hold that exercising a legal right does not excuse causing harm to others' access to essential shared resources like clean water — rights come paired with responsibilities. Option A is the main distractor because students may conflate legal permission with moral justification, but these are distinct concepts in both law and ethics.

questions.title: Biodiversity Economics
questions.prompt: An economist argues that assigning a monetary value to a mangrove forest — such as calculating its value as a storm barrier and fish nursery — will help protect it. What is the MAIN strength of this economic approach to conservation?

options.A: It proves that biodiversity is more important than human economic needs
options.B: It makes the economic case for conservation visible to decision-makers who use cost-benefit analysis
options.C: It ensures that local communities automatically receive payments for protecting the forest
options.D: It eliminates the need for environmental regulations by letting market forces protect ecosystems

questions.explanation: Valuing ecosystem services in monetary terms — a method used in tools like the UN's TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity) — allows conservationists to argue in the same economic language that governments and businesses use, making protection financially competitive with development. Option C describes payments for ecosystem services (PES), a specific mechanism that does not automatically follow from simply valuing a forest.

questions.title: Ocean Governance
questions.prompt: Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), a coastal country controls fishing rights within 200 nautical miles of its coast. What happens to fishing rights beyond this zone, in the open ocean?

options.A: The nearest country automatically gains control of fishing rights
options.B: Fishing in the open ocean is completely banned to protect marine biodiversity
options.C: The open ocean is treated as a global commons where any country may fish, often with limited regulation
options.D: The United Nations directly manages all fishing quotas in international waters

questions.explanation: Beyond the 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone, the high seas are considered a global commons — open to all nations for navigation and fishing — which creates governance challenges because no single authority enforces sustainable catch limits. Option D is incorrect because the UN does not directly manage fishing quotas in international waters; regional fisheries management organisations exist but have variable enforcement power.

questions.title: Peace and Environmental Conflict
questions.prompt: Research shows that prolonged drought in the Sahel region of Africa has contributed to conflicts between farming and herding communities. Which chain of causation BEST explains this link?

options.A: Drought → cultural differences intensify → communities stop trading → conflict
options.B: Drought → reduced arable land and water → competition over shrinking resources → conflict
options.C: Drought → governments increase taxes → poverty rises → political rebellion
options.D: Drought → population increases rapidly → cities become overcrowded → conflict

questions.explanation: Climate-linked resource stress — particularly shrinking pastureland and water sources — forces farmers and herders to compete for the same diminishing areas, which directly triggers territorial disputes and violence; this mechanism is documented in peer-reviewed research on climate-conflict linkages in the Sahel. Option A introduces cultural differences as the primary driver, which oversimplifies and misattributes the cause.

questions.title: Carbon Tax Policy
questions.prompt: A government introduces a carbon tax that makes fossil fuels more expensive for businesses. What is the intended economic mechanism by which this tax is supposed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions?

options.A: It directly bans the use of fossil fuels in all industries immediately
options.B: It raises the price of carbon-intensive activities, incentivising businesses to switch to cleaner alternatives
options.C: It funds research that automatically creates new renewable energy technologies
options.D: It transfers money from businesses to households to compensate for higher energy costs

questions.explanation: A carbon tax internalises the external cost of greenhouse gas emissions by making fossil fuel use more expensive, which gives businesses a financial incentive to invest in cleaner energy or more efficient processes — this is the core price-signal mechanism of carbon pricing. Option D describes a possible use of carbon tax revenue (dividend payments) but is not the mechanism by which the tax itself reduces emissions.

questions.title: Sustainable Development
questions.prompt: The Brundtland Report defined sustainable development as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' Which scenario BEST illustrates a violation of this principle?

options.A: A country builds wind farms to power its cities and exports surplus electricity
options.B: A country over-extracts groundwater for agriculture faster than aquifers can naturally recharge
options.C: A country plants trees to replace those harvested in sustainably managed forests
options.D: A country reduces industrial waste by investing in cleaner production technologies

questions.explanation: Extracting groundwater faster than it can recharge permanently depletes aquifers — a non-renewable stock on human timescales — directly compromising future generations' ability to access water for agriculture and drinking, violating the Brundtland definition. Option C actually exemplifies sustainable development through managed replenishment, making it the most likely distractor if students misread the question.

questions.title: Food Systems and Environment
questions.prompt: Examine this claim by a student: 'Buying locally grown food always has a lower carbon footprint than buying imported food.' Why is this statement an oversimplification?

options.A: Local food is always more expensive, which means it has a higher carbon footprint
options.B: The type of food and how it is grown can matter more than transport distance — for example, local greenhouse-grown tomatoes may emit more CO₂ than imported field-grown ones
options.C: Carbon footprint only measures water use, not transport emissions, so distance is irrelevant
options.D: Imported food always has a lower carbon footprint because ships are more efficient than trucks

questions.explanation: Research, including studies from Our World in Data, shows that transport accounts for a relatively small share of most foods' carbon footprint compared to production methods — energy-intensive local greenhouses can easily outweigh the shipping emissions of sun-grown imported produce. Option D is incorrect because although container ships are fuel-efficient per tonne, total food miles still contribute meaningfully to emissions, and the statement's 'always' is unjustified.

questions.title: Deforestation and Carbon
questions.prompt: When a tropical forest is cleared and burned, two separate environmental harms occur. What are these two harms related to carbon?

options.A: Carbon stored in the trees is released, and the land can no longer absorb future carbon dioxide
options.B: Carbon stored in the soil is released, and nearby rivers become too acidic to support fish
options.C: Carbon dioxide is released, and the ash from burning permanently increases soil fertility
options.D: Carbon monoxide is released, and satellite signals are disrupted by the smoke

questions.explanation: Burning forest vegetation releases the carbon stored in biomass as CO₂, while clearing the forest removes the ongoing carbon sink that would have absorbed future atmospheric CO₂ through photosynthesis — creating a double carbon penalty. Option B incorrectly attributes the primary carbon harm to soil rather than biomass, and the claim about river acidity conflates deforestation impacts with acid rain.

questions.title: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities
questions.prompt: The principle of 'Common But Differentiated Responsibilities' (CBDR) is central to international climate negotiations. Which statement MOST accurately describes what CBDR means in practice?

options.A: All countries share equal responsibility for reducing emissions regardless of their historical contributions
options.B: Developed countries should take greater action because of their larger historical emissions and greater capacity to act
options.C: Developing countries are exempt from all climate commitments until they reach high-income status
options.D: Responsibility for climate action is determined solely by current population size

questions.explanation: CBDR, established in the 1992 Rio Declaration and embedded in the UNFCCC, recognises that while all countries share the common challenge of climate change, wealthier nations that industrialised earlier bear a differentiated (greater) responsibility due to their larger cumulative historical emissions and greater financial and technological capacity. Option C misrepresents CBDR — developing countries still have obligations, just proportionally smaller ones.

questions.title: Biodiversity Loss Causes
questions.prompt: Scientists identify habitat destruction, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, and climate change as the five main drivers of global biodiversity loss. Which of these is currently considered the SINGLE largest driver worldwide?

options.A: Climate change
options.B: Pollution from plastics and chemicals
options.C: Habitat destruction, particularly land-use change for agriculture
options.D: Invasive species introduced through global trade

questions.explanation: According to the 2019 IPBES Global Assessment Report, land-use change — primarily conversion of natural habitats to agricultural land — is the leading driver of biodiversity loss, affecting 75% of the land surface and driving the extinction of more species than any other single factor. Climate change (Option A) is growing rapidly as a driver and will likely become dominant in coming decades, making it the top distractor.

questions.title: Water Governance Challenges
questions.prompt: An international river basin organisation (RBO) is created to manage a river shared by four countries. What is the PRIMARY advantage of this type of multilateral governance over each country acting independently?

options.A: It gives the most powerful country full control over water allocation decisions
options.B: It allows coordinated management of the whole river system, reducing conflicts and overuse
options.C: It transfers ownership of the river to the United Nations permanently
options.D: It eliminates the need for environmental monitoring by sharing costs equally

questions.explanation: River basin organisations like the Mekong River Commission allow all riparian states to coordinate water use, share data, and negotiate allocations across the entire hydrological system, which prevents upstream countries from unilaterally depleting resources that downstream countries depend on. Option A directly contradicts the purpose of multilateral governance, which distributes rather than concentrates decision-making power.

questions.title: Plastic Pollution Sources
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Reducing single-use plastic bags in wealthy countries is the most important action to tackle ocean plastic pollution.' Evaluate this claim using data about where ocean plastic pollution originates.

options.A: The claim is accurate because wealthy countries produce and export the most plastic waste globally
options.B: The claim is an oversimplification because most ocean plastic enters via rivers in rapidly industrialising countries with limited waste infrastructure
options.C: The claim is accurate because plastic bags are the single largest category of plastic found in oceans
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because ocean plastic pollution has no measurable impact on marine ecosystems

questions.explanation: Research published in journals such as Nature Communications shows that a large proportion of ocean plastic is carried by rivers, with the Yangtze, Ganges, and others in Asia and Africa among the top contributors — reflecting inadequate waste management infrastructure rather than simply high-income country consumption. Plastic bags, while visible, are not the largest category by mass in ocean plastic, making Option C incorrect.

questions.title: Precautionary Principle
questions.prompt: Scientists are uncertain whether a new agricultural chemical causes long-term harm to pollinators. Some argue the chemical should be banned immediately; others say wait for more evidence. Which environmental principle supports acting to restrict the chemical BEFORE certainty is established?

options.A: The polluter-pays principle
options.B: The precautionary principle
options.C: The principle of intergenerational equity
options.D: The principle of subsidiarity

questions.explanation: The precautionary principle, enshrined in the Rio Declaration (Principle 15), states that when there is scientific uncertainty about a potentially serious environmental harm, a lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason to postpone preventive measures. The polluter-pays principle (Option A) deals with who bears the cost of proven damage, not with action under uncertainty.

questions.title: Ecological Footprint
questions.prompt: The concept of 'ecological footprint' measures how much of the Earth's biological capacity a person or country uses. If humanity's total ecological footprint currently exceeds Earth's total biocapacity, what does this mean for the planet's resources?

options.A: Humans are using resources faster than ecosystems can regenerate them, causing a global ecological deficit
options.B: Earth's biocapacity is growing fast enough to keep up with human demand through technological progress
options.C: The surplus demand is being met by importing resources from other planets
options.D: A footprint larger than biocapacity only becomes a problem once it doubles in size

questions.explanation: According to the Global Footprint Network, humanity has been in ecological overshoot since the 1970s, meaning we consume renewable resources and generate waste faster than ecosystems can regenerate or absorb them — depleting natural capital stocks. Option B is the key distractor because students might assume technology automatically compensates for overuse, but biocapacity itself is not growing significantly.

questions.title: Green Economy Transition
questions.prompt: A country rich in coal exports is considering transitioning to a green economy based on renewable energy. A government official warns: 'This transition will destroy jobs in coal communities.' Which response BEST reflects a balanced evaluation of this concern?

options.A: The concern is fully valid and proves that green transitions are always economically harmful to workers
options.B: The concern is irrelevant because environmental protection must always come before economic considerations
options.C: The concern is partially valid, but 'just transition' policies such as retraining programmes can help workers adapt to new green industries
options.D: The concern is unfounded because renewable energy employs exactly the same number of people as coal in every country

questions.explanation: The International Labour Organization and UNFCCC both promote 'just transition' frameworks that acknowledge genuine short-term job losses in fossil fuel sectors while planning retraining, social protection, and investment in communities — recognising the concern without dismissing green transition as impossible. Option A overstates the harm by ignoring the capacity for policy interventions to manage the transition.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: A shared fishing lake is open to all villagers with no rules about how much fish each person can take. Over time, the fish population collapses. Which concept BEST explains why individuals acting in their own self-interest can destroy a shared resource?

options.A: The circular economy principle
options.B: The tragedy of the commons
options.C: The polluter-pays principle
options.D: The precautionary principle

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons, described by Garrett Hardin in 1968, explains how individuals overuse a shared resource because they each benefit fully from taking more while the cost of depletion is shared by everyone. The polluter-pays principle is a related but distinct idea that focuses on who should pay for environmental damage, not why overuse occurs in the first place.

questions.title: SDG Goals and Targets
questions.prompt: SDG 13 is called 'Climate Action.' A student says: 'SDG 13 is the only SDG that relates to the environment, so once we solve climate change all environmental problems will be solved.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct — climate change is the root cause of all environmental problems
options.B: The error is that SDG 13 does not exist; climate is covered under SDG 7
options.C: The error is that multiple SDGs address environmental issues, including SDG 14 (oceans), SDG 15 (land ecosystems), and SDG 6 (clean water)
options.D: The error is that climate change cannot be solved, making all other environmental SDGs irrelevant

questions.explanation: At least five SDGs directly address environmental sustainability: SDG 6 (clean water), SDG 13 (climate action), SDG 14 (life below water), SDG 15 (life on land), and SDG 7 (affordable clean energy). The top distractor (A) is wrong because many environmental problems — such as habitat loss, plastic pollution, and soil degradation — have causes and solutions distinct from climate change.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: In a linear economy, products follow a 'take-make-dispose' pattern. In a circular economy, this pattern changes. Which outcome is the MOST accurate description of what a circular economy tries to achieve?

options.A: Stopping all manufacturing to prevent resource depletion
options.B: Keeping materials in use as long as possible through reuse, repair, and recycling
options.C: Moving all production to countries with lower environmental standards
options.D: Relying entirely on renewable energy instead of non-renewable materials

questions.explanation: A circular economy aims to eliminate waste by keeping products, components, and materials at their highest utility for as long as possible — through strategies like reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling. Option D is a distractor because switching to renewable energy is part of sustainable development but is a separate concept from the circular management of material resources.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
questions.prompt: A government decides to drain a wetland to build a shopping centre. An ecologist argues that the wetland provides 'ecosystem services' worth more than the shopping centre. Which of the following is the BEST example of an ecosystem service that the wetland provides?

options.A: Providing land for commercial development
options.B: Supplying raw materials for manufacturing
options.C: Filtering water and reducing flood risk for nearby communities
options.D: Generating tax revenue for the local government

questions.explanation: Wetlands provide natural water filtration by trapping pollutants and absorbing excess water during storms, which directly reduces flood risk — a classic provisioning and regulating ecosystem service. Option B is wrong because wetlands do not typically supply significant raw materials for manufacturing; that function is more associated with forests or mines.

questions.title: Climate Justice and Equity
questions.prompt: Small island nations like Tuvalu and the Maldives contribute less than 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions yet face the greatest threat from rising sea levels. What does this situation BEST illustrate about the global climate crisis?

options.A: Countries with the smallest emissions are least affected by climate change
options.B: The impacts of climate change are distributed unevenly, creating a climate justice problem
options.C: Rising sea levels are caused mainly by local pollution rather than global emissions
options.D: International agreements have already resolved the issue of unequal climate impacts

questions.explanation: Climate justice refers to the ethical dimension of climate change — specifically, that those who contribute least to emissions (like small island states) often suffer the most severe consequences such as flooding and displacement. Option A directly contradicts this reality and is therefore the most tempting but clearly incorrect distractor.

questions.title: Renewable vs Non-Renewable Resources
questions.prompt: Examine the following student claim: 'Solar energy is renewable because the Sun produces energy continuously on a human timescale, whereas coal is non-renewable because it takes millions of years to form.' Is this reasoning correct, and why?

options.A: Incorrect — solar energy will eventually run out within 500 years
options.B: Incorrect — coal can be regrown in forests if managed carefully
options.C: Correct — the key distinction is whether the resource replenishes faster than humans use it
options.D: Correct — but only because solar panels themselves are made from renewable materials

questions.explanation: The defining characteristic of a renewable resource is that it replenishes naturally on a timescale relevant to human use, whereas non-renewables like coal form over millions of years and cannot be replaced once used. Option D is wrong because solar panels are made from materials like silicon and rare metals, which are not themselves renewable — yet solar energy is still classified as renewable.

questions.title: International Environmental Agreements
questions.prompt: The Paris Agreement (2015) asks countries to set their own targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions rather than imposing legally binding uniform cuts. What is the MAIN weakness of this approach?

options.A: It only applies to countries in Europe, excluding major emitters in Asia
options.B: It focuses on carbon dioxide but ignores methane and other greenhouse gases
options.C: Countries may set insufficiently ambitious targets and face no enforcement if they miss them
options.D: It requires developing nations to cut emissions before wealthy nations, which is unfair

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement relies on Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which are self-set targets with no binding enforcement mechanism — meaning countries can pledge modest reductions without legal consequences for failing to meet them. Option D is a plausible concern about climate equity but is factually incorrect as a description of the agreement, which explicitly includes principles of common but differentiated responsibilities.

questions.title: Geopolitics of Water Scarcity
questions.prompt: Ethiopia is building the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile River. Egypt argues this will reduce its water supply and threatens national security. Which term BEST describes the type of international conflict this represents?

options.A: A territorial sovereignty dispute over land borders
options.B: A transboundary resource conflict over shared water rights
options.C: A trade war caused by competing agricultural exports
options.D: A humanitarian crisis caused by voluntary water mismanagement

questions.explanation: The Nile Dam dispute is a classic example of a transboundary resource conflict, where a resource (the Nile River) crosses national borders and upstream use by one country directly affects downstream availability for another. Option A is wrong because the dispute is not about land borders but about the flow of a shared river that both countries depend on for survival.

questions.title: Polluter Pays Principle
questions.prompt: A chemical factory releases waste into a river, contaminating the drinking water of a downstream village. Authorities require the factory to pay for water purification and cleanup costs. Which environmental principle does this policy MOST directly apply?

options.A: The precautionary principle
options.B: The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities
options.C: The polluter-pays principle
options.D: The principle of intergenerational equity

questions.explanation: The polluter-pays principle holds that whoever causes environmental damage should bear the costs of managing it, including prevention and remediation — this is exactly what the factory is being required to do. The precautionary principle (A) applies before harm occurs, advising caution under scientific uncertainty, so it does not fit a situation where damage has already happened.

questions.title: Carbon Footprint Analysis
questions.prompt: A student calculates that flying from London to New York produces roughly 1.5 tonnes of CO₂ per passenger, whereas a year of daily car commuting produces about 2.4 tonnes. What should the student conclude from comparing these figures?

options.A: Flying is always more environmentally harmful than driving, regardless of distance
options.B: Both activities contribute significantly to personal carbon footprints, and reducing either has real impact
options.C: Car commuting causes more emissions overall so flying is not worth worrying about
options.D: CO₂ from aviation is less harmful than CO₂ from cars because it is released at high altitude

questions.explanation: The comparison shows that both activities are major sources of individual greenhouse gas emissions, and reducing either one meaningfully lowers a person's carbon footprint. Option C involves flawed logic — the fact that car commuting produces more total CO₂ over a year does not mean a single flight is negligible, especially since aviation also releases non-CO₂ warming agents at altitude.

questions.title: Biodiversity Economics
questions.prompt: Economists sometimes assign a monetary value to biodiversity, for example calculating that bees provide pollination services worth $235 billion annually to global agriculture. Why do economists use this approach?

options.A: To prove that nature has no real value unless humans can sell it
options.B: To make the economic cost of losing biodiversity visible to policymakers and businesses
options.C: To encourage countries to sell their biodiversity to the highest bidder
options.D: To replace international conservation laws with free-market pricing

questions.explanation: Valuing ecosystem services in monetary terms is a strategy to make the often-invisible economic costs of biodiversity loss tangible to decision-makers who might otherwise ignore them — bees pollinating crops is 'free' until they disappear. Option A misrepresents the goal; economists who value nature are typically trying to protect it by making its loss economically visible, not to claim it only matters if sold.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: A mining company has the legal right to extract minerals from land it owns, but the extraction poisons the groundwater used by neighbouring communities. Which statement BEST describes the ethical tension in this situation?

options.A: Legal rights always override community needs, so the company has no obligation to change
options.B: The company's legal right to mine conflicts with the community's right to clean water and a healthy environment
options.C: The community should move elsewhere to avoid the pollution, as the company arrived first
options.D: Only the national government has rights in this situation; neither the company nor the community has standing

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates the classic tension between individual or corporate legal rights and collective rights — the community's right to safe water is recognised in international frameworks including the UN's 2010 declaration on the human right to water. Option A is ethically flawed because legal permission does not automatically make an action morally acceptable or free from responsibility for harm caused.

questions.title: Intergenerational Equity
questions.prompt: The Brundtland Commission (1987) defined sustainable development as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' Which principle does this definition MOST directly express?

options.A: Intragenerational equity — fairness between people living today
options.B: The precautionary principle — avoiding uncertain environmental risks
options.C: Intergenerational equity — fairness between current and future generations
options.D: Common heritage of mankind — shared ownership of global resources

questions.explanation: Intergenerational equity is the ethical principle that present generations have a responsibility not to deplete or damage resources in ways that deny future generations equivalent opportunities — this is precisely what the Brundtland definition articulates. Intragenerational equity (A) is a related but different concept focusing on fairness among people alive today, particularly between rich and poor nations.

questions.title: Deforestation and Carbon Sinks
questions.prompt: Scientists describe forests as 'carbon sinks.' When large areas of forest are burned or cut down, what happens to the carbon stored in the trees?

options.A: The carbon is permanently locked in the soil and does not affect the atmosphere
options.B: The carbon is released into the atmosphere as CO₂, contributing to the greenhouse effect
options.C: The carbon is transferred to nearby living trees, increasing their growth rate
options.D: The carbon evaporates into space and is removed from the Earth's carbon cycle

questions.explanation: When trees are burned or decompose after being felled, the carbon they have stored through photosynthesis is oxidised and released as CO₂ into the atmosphere, where it acts as a greenhouse gas. Option A is partly misleading — some carbon does enter the soil, but burning releases the majority directly into the atmosphere, and soil carbon can also be lost through erosion after deforestation.

questions.title: Common but Differentiated Responsibilities
questions.prompt: The principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' (CBDR) is used in international climate negotiations. Which statement MOST accurately describes what this principle means?

options.A: All countries share responsibility for climate change and must therefore take identical actions
options.B: Only developed countries are responsible for climate change; developing nations have no obligations
options.C: All countries share responsibility for addressing climate change, but wealthier, historically higher-emitting nations have greater obligations
options.D: Responsibility for climate action should be distributed based on population size alone

questions.explanation: CBDR recognises that while climate change is a shared global problem requiring everyone's participation, historically industrialised nations bear greater responsibility because they have emitted far more greenhouse gases and have greater financial and technological capacity to act. Option A is incorrect because CBDR specifically rejects a one-size-fits-all approach, which is the whole point of the 'differentiated' aspect of the principle.

questions.title: Ocean Acidification
questions.prompt: When the ocean absorbs excess CO₂ from the atmosphere, a chemical reaction occurs that lowers the ocean's pH. Why does this process threaten marine organisms such as oysters, clams, and coral?

options.A: Lower pH raises ocean temperature, making it too warm for shell-forming organisms
options.B: Lower pH reduces the concentration of carbonate ions, which these organisms need to build their shells and skeletons
options.C: Lower pH increases the salinity of the ocean, dehydrating marine organisms
options.D: Lower pH reduces oxygen levels in the water, causing marine organisms to suffocate

questions.explanation: Ocean acidification reduces the availability of carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) in seawater, which are the building blocks that molluscs, corals, and other calcifying organisms use to form their calcium carbonate shells and skeletons — making it harder to grow or maintain them. Option A conflates ocean acidification with ocean warming; while both are caused by excess CO₂, they are separate processes with different mechanisms.

questions.title: Environmental Stewardship
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Environmental stewardship only applies to governments and large corporations. Individual people are too small to make any difference to global environmental problems.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — systemic change can only be achieved at the policy level
options.B: The claim is partially correct — individuals matter only in wealthy countries where consumption is highest
options.C: The claim is incorrect — individual actions collectively create large-scale change and individuals also influence corporate and political decisions
options.D: The claim is incorrect — governments have no role in environmental stewardship; it is entirely an individual responsibility

questions.explanation: Environmental stewardship applies at all scales; individual choices aggregate into significant demand signals that shape corporate behaviour, and citizens acting together can drive political change — for example, consumer pressure has led many companies to eliminate single-use plastics. Option D swings to the opposite extreme and is equally wrong — government policy, regulation, and international agreements are essential tools that individuals alone cannot replace.

questions.title: Soil Degradation and Food Security
questions.prompt: Topsoil, which supports most food production, takes approximately 1,000 years to form one centimetre through natural processes. Current agricultural practices are eroding topsoil at roughly 10 times the rate it forms. What does this imply for global food security?

options.A: Topsoil loss is a short-term problem that modern fertilisers have already solved permanently
options.B: Topsoil loss poses a serious long-term threat to agricultural productivity because it cannot be quickly replaced
options.C: Topsoil loss only affects developing countries because wealthy countries use hydroponics instead
options.D: Topsoil is classified as a renewable resource, so its depletion is not a concern for future generations

questions.explanation: Because topsoil forms over millennia, losing it faster than it regenerates is essentially irreversible on human timescales, threatening the foundation of agriculture worldwide — the UN estimates that if degradation continues at current rates, we have roughly 60 years of productive topsoil left. Option A is wrong because while fertilisers can supplement soil nutrients, they cannot replicate the complex biological structure and water-retention properties of healthy topsoil.

questions.title: Peace and Environmental Conflict
questions.prompt: Researchers have found a statistical link between prolonged droughts and increased rates of violent conflict in parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Which explanation BEST accounts for this link?

options.A: Droughts cause high temperatures which directly alter human brain chemistry, making people more aggressive
options.B: Droughts reduce agricultural output and water availability, increasing competition over scarce resources and weakening governments' ability to maintain stability
options.C: Droughts are caused by conflict, not the other way around; the causal direction is reversed
options.D: The link is coincidental — both droughts and conflicts are independently caused by population growth alone

questions.explanation: Resource scarcity caused by drought reduces livelihoods, increases food prices, drives displacement, and weakens state institutions — all of which are well-documented drivers of conflict, as seen in studies of the Sahel region. Option A is an overly simplistic and scientifically unsupported biological claim; while heat stress can affect behaviour, it is the socioeconomic consequences of drought that primarily explain the statistical link.

questions.title: Overfishing and Regulation
questions.prompt: The European Union uses a quota system to limit how many fish each member state's fishing fleets can catch each year. A fisherman argues the quotas are unfair because they reduce his income. An ecologist argues the quotas are essential. Which justification for the quotas is MOST scientifically sound?

options.A: Quotas are justified because they increase fish prices, benefiting fishermen who remain in the industry
options.B: Quotas are justified because fish populations need to stay above a minimum viable level to reproduce and sustain themselves
options.C: Quotas are justified because they prevent fish from migrating to non-EU waters
options.D: Quotas are justified because reducing fishing effort lowers carbon emissions from fishing vessels

questions.explanation: Fishing quotas are scientifically grounded in the concept of maximum sustainable yield — the idea that fish populations must maintain sufficient numbers to reproduce at a rate that replaces those caught; falling below this threshold can cause population collapse, as happened with Atlantic cod in the 1990s. Option A describes a potential economic side effect but is not the scientific justification for quota systems.

questions.title: Precautionary Principle
questions.prompt: A chemical company wants to release a new pesticide that tests suggest may harm bee populations, but the evidence is not yet conclusive. An environmental regulator decides to block its release until more studies are done. Which principle is the regulator applying?

options.A: The precautionary principle — act to prevent harm even under scientific uncertainty
options.B: The polluter-pays principle — make the company pay for potential damage in advance
options.C: The principle of common heritage — bees belong to all humanity and cannot be harmed
options.D: The principle of subsidiarity — local governments should make decisions, not national regulators

questions.explanation: The precautionary principle states that when an action raises threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not fully established scientifically — blocking the pesticide pending further study is a textbook application. Option B (polluter-pays) is wrong because it applies after harm occurs, requiring the responsible party to cover cleanup costs, not to prevent uncertain future harm.

questions.title: Urbanisation and Resource Demand
questions.prompt: By 2050, approximately 68% of the world's population is projected to live in cities. Compare the resource demands of urban versus rural populations. What does urbanisation MOST likely mean for global resource consumption?

options.A: Urbanisation will reduce resource consumption because cities use energy and transport more efficiently per person
options.B: Urbanisation will increase resource consumption because urban residents typically have higher incomes and consume more goods
options.C: Urbanisation will have no effect on global resource consumption because the total number of people stays the same
options.D: Urbanisation will eliminate food insecurity because cities are closer to food distribution networks

questions.explanation: Urban residents in developing regions typically experience income growth as they move to cities, which increases consumption of energy, manufactured goods, meat, and water — studies show that urbanisation correlates with rising per-capita resource use even when population totals are controlled. Option A is partially true at the infrastructure level (e.g. public transport), but this efficiency gain is generally outweighed by the consumption increases that accompany urban income growth.

questions.title: Ecological Footprint
questions.prompt: An ecological footprint measures how much land and water area a human population requires to produce what it consumes and absorb its waste. If Earth has approximately 1.6 global hectares of biocapacity per person but the average person currently uses 2.8 global hectares, what does this indicate?

options.A: Humanity is living within Earth's means and has surplus capacity for future growth
options.B: Humanity is consuming resources faster than Earth can regenerate them, creating an ecological deficit
options.C: The data shows that Earth's biocapacity is growing to match human consumption
options.D: The gap means that human technology will need to replace natural systems entirely within 50 years

questions.explanation: When consumption (2.8 gha) exceeds biocapacity (1.6 gha), humanity is running an ecological overshoot — drawing down natural capital faster than ecosystems can replenish it, which is unsustainable by definition. Earth Overshoot Day, the date when humanity has used nature's annual budget, now falls around late July each year. Option A directly contradicts the data provided in the question.

questions.title: Fast Fashion and Resource Use
questions.prompt: The fashion industry produces approximately 100 billion garments per year, and the average garment is worn only 7–10 times before being discarded. A student argues that buying second-hand clothing is a more responsible consumer choice. Which reasoning BEST justifies this claim?

options.A: Second-hand clothing is always cheaper, so it redistributes wealth from rich to poor consumers
options.B: Buying second-hand extends the useful life of existing garments, reducing demand for new production and its associated water use, chemical pollution, and carbon emissions
options.C: Second-hand clothing is made from better-quality materials than new fast fashion
options.D: Buying second-hand automatically makes a garment recyclable at the end of its life

questions.explanation: Producing a single cotton t-shirt requires approximately 2,700 litres of water and generates significant chemical waste and carbon emissions; buying second-hand keeps garments in use longer and reduces the demand that drives overproduction. Option A may sometimes be true but is an economic argument about cost rather than a justification based on environmental responsibility.

questions.title: Biodiversity Hotspots
questions.prompt: Conservation biologists use the term 'biodiversity hotspot' to prioritise areas for protection. Which TWO criteria must a region meet to qualify as a biodiversity hotspot?

options.A: It must be located in a tropical climate zone and contain at least one national park
options.B: It must contain a high number of endemic species AND have lost at least 70% of its original habitat
options.C: It must be home to endangered megafauna such as elephants or tigers AND be located near a human population centre
options.D: It must be formally recognised by the UN AND have received international conservation funding

questions.explanation: Conservation International's definition of a biodiversity hotspot requires that a region contain at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species AND have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation — this combination of irreplaceable biodiversity and severe threat justifies priority conservation status. Option A is wrong because hotspots exist in multiple climate zones, including Mediterranean climates, and do not require a national park.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: A shared fishing lake is open to all villagers with no rules. Each family reasons that if they don't catch as many fish as possible, others will. Analyse what will MOST likely happen to the fish population over time, and identify which concept this scenario illustrates.

options.A: Fish numbers will stabilise because families will voluntarily cooperate once they see the risk — illustrating collective action.
options.B: Fish numbers will collapse because individual self-interest depletes a shared resource — illustrating the tragedy of the commons.
options.C: Fish numbers will collapse because the lake's water quality decreases when more people use it — illustrating water pollution.
options.D: Fish numbers will stabilise because natural reproduction rates always match human harvesting — illustrating carrying capacity balance.

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons, coined by Garrett Hardin in 1968, describes how rational self-interest leads individuals to overuse shared resources until they are destroyed, which is exactly what this scenario demonstrates. Option A is wrong because without binding agreements or enforcement mechanisms, voluntary cooperation typically fails when personal gain is immediate and shared costs are deferred.

questions.title: Circular Economy Waste Hierarchy
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Recycling is the best solution to the global plastic waste crisis because it means plastic never becomes pollution.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of the circular economy waste hierarchy.

options.A: The claim is correct because modern recycling technology can process nearly all plastic types without energy loss.
options.B: The claim is partially correct; recycling helps but is less effective than reducing plastic production in the first place.
options.C: The claim is incorrect; recycling is harmful because it encourages people to buy more plastic.
options.D: The claim is correct because international recycling treaties ensure all plastic is processed responsibly.

questions.explanation: The circular economy waste hierarchy prioritises 'reduce' above 'recycle' because recycling still requires energy, produces emissions, and is only effective for certain plastic types — globally, only about 9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled. Option A is wrong because many plastic types (e.g., multi-layer packaging) cannot currently be recycled economically, meaning recycling alone cannot solve the crisis.

questions.title: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
questions.prompt: Examine the following: a government plans to drain a wetland to build a shopping centre. An environmental group argues this will cost more in the long run than any revenue the shopping centre generates. Which argument would the environmental group MOST likely use to justify this position?

options.A: Wetlands are aesthetically beautiful and their loss will reduce tourism permanently.
options.B: Wetlands provide ecosystem services such as flood control and water filtration whose economic value exceeds typical commercial development revenue.
options.C: International law forbids the draining of any wetland regardless of its size or location.
options.D: The shopping centre will create short-term jobs but wetland-based fishing provides more sustainable long-term employment.

questions.explanation: Economists who study ecosystem services have estimated that wetlands provide flood regulation, water purification, carbon storage, and habitat services worth tens of thousands of dollars per hectare annually — often far exceeding commercial land use value. Option D is a plausible distractor but misses the broader economic argument about ecosystem services, which goes beyond just fishing employment.

questions.title: SDG Goals and Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A developing country wants to achieve SDG 1 (No Poverty) by expanding its coal mining industry, which will create thousands of jobs. However, this conflicts with SDG 13 (Climate Action). What does this scenario BEST illustrate about the SDGs?

options.A: The SDGs are poorly designed because they create unavoidable contradictions that make them useless as policy tools.
options.B: SDG 1 is always more important than SDG 13 because human needs take priority over environmental concerns.
options.C: The SDGs can create genuine trade-offs, requiring governments to evaluate context-specific solutions that balance competing goals.
