questions.prompt: Mia argues: 'People should pay for every service they use, so there is no reason for a government to collect taxes at all.' Which example BEST shows a flaw in Mia's argument?

options.A: Street lighting — it is impossible to charge only the people who walk under a lamp, yet everyone benefits.
options.B: Cinemas — people pay per ticket so a government tax is clearly not needed to fund films.
options.C: Restaurants — private owners successfully sell food without government funding.
options.D: Hospitals — wealthy patients already pay privately so taxation is unnecessary for healthcare.

questions.explanation: Street lighting is a 'public good' — you cannot stop someone from benefiting from it, so no private business can charge each user individually; taxation is needed to fund it. Option D is wrong because it ignores people who cannot afford private healthcare, showing the argument fails for essential services needed by everyone.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Every student at a school has the right to a quiet learning environment. Some students also have the right to express themselves through music during break time. What does this situation BEST illustrate about rights in a community?

options.A: Rights are unlimited and schools should never restrict any form of self-expression.
options.B: Only the rights of the majority should be protected; minority preferences do not count.
options.C: Rights can conflict with each other, so communities create rules to balance them fairly.
options.D: Responsibilities always cancel out rights, so having one means giving up the other entirely.

questions.explanation: Rights frequently come into tension — the right to expression and the right to a quiet environment are both valid, so communities develop balanced rules such as designated music zones or specific times. Option A is wrong because unlimited rights would mean one person's freedom could completely override another person's equally valid right.

questions.title: Social Contracts
questions.prompt: When children join a classroom, they agree to follow certain rules even though nobody asked their opinion before the rules were made. A student says this proves rules in communities are always unfair. Which response MOST effectively challenges this claim?

options.A: Rules made before someone joins a group are always unfair and should be renegotiated every time someone new arrives.
options.B: Fairness depends only on whether rules were voted on, not on whether they protect everyone's ability to learn and belong.
options.C: Communities often establish rules that protect all members' ability to participate, and joining means accepting shared agreements that benefit everyone.
options.D: Children are too young to understand rules, so adult-made rules are automatically fair for everyone involved.

questions.explanation: The idea of a social contract holds that participating in a community means accepting its shared agreements, which exist to protect everyone's ability to function within it — this is different from unfairness. Option A is wrong because renegotiating every rule for every new member would make stable community life impossible.

questions.title: Goods and Services
questions.prompt: A student sorts items into two lists: List 1 has bread, shoes, and bicycles. List 2 has haircuts, teaching, and bus rides. What is the correct label for each list, and what is the KEY difference between them?

options.A: List 1 = wants; List 2 = needs. The difference is that needs are provided by governments and wants are bought privately.
options.B: List 1 = goods; List 2 = services. Goods are physical objects you can touch and keep, while services are actions performed for you.
options.C: List 1 = expensive items; List 2 = cheap items. The difference is based entirely on how much each costs in a market.
options.D: List 1 = services; List 2 = goods. Services require factories to produce, while goods are provided directly by people.

questions.explanation: Goods are tangible, physical products that can be owned and stored, while services are intangible actions or experiences performed by one person for another. Option D reverses the definitions — factories produce goods, not services, and services are performed directly by people.

questions.title: Democratic Voting
questions.prompt: In a class election, 15 students vote for Option A and 13 vote for Option B. A student says this proves Option A is definitely the right choice for the class. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: Voting is not a valid way to make decisions in classrooms because only governments should vote.
options.B: A majority vote shows what most people prefer, but it does not guarantee the choice is factually correct or best for all, especially minorities.
options.C: The result is invalid because a fair vote requires all options to receive exactly equal numbers of votes.
options.D: Option B must actually be correct because the minority is usually right in democratic systems.

questions.explanation: Majority rule reflects popular preference but does not prove correctness — the minority's valid interests still matter, which is why democracies also protect minority rights alongside majority decisions. Option D is wrong because democratic systems are not designed around the idea that minorities are usually right; they balance majority rule with minority protections.

questions.title: Global Institutions
questions.prompt: The United Nations has 193 member countries, but it cannot force a powerful country to follow its resolutions if that country refuses. What does this BEST tell us about how the UN is organised?

options.A: The UN is not a true world government because it relies on cooperation and agreement rather than binding legal force over all nations.
options.B: The UN fails at its job because a useful organisation should always be able to force members to comply.
options.C: The UN is more powerful than individual governments because it has more member countries than any single nation.
options.D: Countries that ignore UN resolutions automatically lose their membership and trade rights.

questions.explanation: The UN operates through diplomacy, consensus, and voluntary cooperation — it lacks the enforcement power of a national government, making it an international organisation rather than a world government. Option C confuses number of members with decision-making power; having many members does not mean the organisation can override national sovereignty.

questions.title: Market Supply and Demand
questions.prompt: Last summer, a drought destroyed most of the apple harvest. A student predicts apple prices will fall because farmers have fewer apples to sell. Evaluate this prediction.

options.A: The prediction is correct — when farmers produce less, they charge customers less to attract buyers.
options.B: The prediction is incorrect — when supply drops but demand stays the same, prices typically rise because fewer goods are competing for the same buyers.
options.C: The prediction is correct — governments always lower prices on food during shortages to help citizens.
options.D: The prediction is incorrect — drought has no connection to market prices because price is set only by production costs.

questions.explanation: When supply decreases and demand stays constant, sellers can charge more because buyers compete for fewer goods — this is a basic principle of supply and demand. Option A incorrectly assumes sellers lower prices when they have less to sell; in reality, scarcity usually gives sellers more pricing power.

questions.title: Community Roles
questions.prompt: In a town, the mayor makes new rules, the police enforce them, and judges decide if someone has broken them. A student asks: 'Why can't the mayor do all three jobs to make the system more efficient?' Which answer BEST explains why combining these roles would be problematic?

options.A: It would be too much work for one person, so decisions would take longer and the town would not function.
options.B: One person controlling all three functions could create rules that favour themselves and then enforce and judge those rules without any check on their power.
options.C: Towns legally require exactly three separate officials at all times, so combining roles breaks a universal law.
options.D: Police and judges always disagree with mayors, so giving one person all roles would create constant internal conflict.

questions.explanation: Separating powers prevents any single person from writing laws that benefit themselves and then enforcing and judging those laws unchallenged — this is the core reason for the separation of powers principle. Option A identifies a practical challenge but misses the crucial point about protecting citizens from abuse of power.

questions.title: Producers and Consumers
questions.prompt: A student says: 'In an economy, every person is either a producer OR a consumer, never both at the same time.' Which everyday example BEST disproves this claim?

options.A: A teacher who buys groceries on the way home from work, since teaching is a service she produces while groceries are goods she consumes.
options.B: A student who studies all day but buys nothing, showing that some people are neither producers nor consumers.
options.C: A factory that only makes products and never buys raw materials from any other business.
options.D: A government that collects taxes and spends them on services, acting only as a distributor rather than a producer or consumer.

questions.explanation: The teacher simultaneously produces a service (education) and consumes goods (groceries), demonstrating that most people in an economy play both roles at different moments of the same day. Option B is wrong because a student produces learning effort and often consumes goods and services like school supplies and meals.

questions.title: Fairness in Sharing
questions.prompt: Three children find a bag of 12 apples. Child A did most of the searching, Child B helped a little, and Child C did not help. They must decide how to split the apples. A student says equal shares are always the fairest method. Which principle BEST challenges this view?

options.A: Fairness can also mean distributing rewards according to contribution, so those who worked more might fairly receive more.
options.B: Equal sharing is always wrong; the person who worked most should always receive everything.
options.C: The only truly fair system is for an adult authority figure to decide the split without consulting the children.
options.D: Fairness is impossible to define, so the children should simply leave the apples unclaimed.

questions.explanation: There are different models of fairness: equity (rewards proportional to contribution) versus equality (identical shares) — both are recognised principles, meaning equal splitting is not automatically the fairest approach. Option B is wrong because it dismisses equality entirely and ignores that Child C may have other valid needs or circumstances.

questions.title: Laws and Their Purpose
questions.prompt: A country passes a law making it illegal to litter in public spaces. A student argues that this law takes away people's freedom unfairly. Which reasoning BEST explains why this law does NOT unfairly remove freedom?

options.A: Laws never restrict freedom because people can simply choose to disobey them if they disagree.
options.B: The law restricts one behaviour in order to protect the shared freedom of all community members to enjoy clean, safe public spaces.
options.C: Governments have unlimited power to make any law they wish, so questions of freedom are irrelevant.
options.D: The law is fair only if every single citizen voted in favour of it before it was passed.

questions.explanation: This law limits one individual behaviour to protect a collective right — clean public space — showing that some restrictions on individual freedom can expand the freedom and wellbeing of the wider community. Option D is wrong because democratic systems do not require unanimous agreement; laws made through representative processes are considered legitimate even without total consensus.

questions.title: Economic Inequality
questions.prompt: In City X, some families can easily afford healthy food, good schools, and doctors, while other families in the same city cannot. A student says this happens only because some families work harder than others. What important factor does this student's explanation ignore?

options.A: Some families choose to spend their money on unnecessary luxuries instead of essential needs.
options.B: Structural factors like the neighbourhood someone is born into, the quality of nearby schools, and inherited wealth affect opportunities independently of individual effort.
options.C: Wealthier families simply make better decisions in every area of their lives compared to poorer families.
options.D: City governments have no ability to influence whether families can afford food, schools, or healthcare.

questions.explanation: Research consistently shows that structural factors — birthplace, inherited resources, access to quality schools — shape economic outcomes significantly, independent of effort alone. Option A is wrong because it assumes inequality results from personal choices rather than acknowledging systemic differences in access and opportunity.

questions.title: Cooperation and Conflict
questions.prompt: Two neighbouring towns share a river. Town A wants to use the river for a factory that will create jobs but may pollute the water. Town B relies on the same river for clean drinking water. What kind of system would BEST help the towns resolve this disagreement fairly?

options.A: Town A should decide alone since the factory is in its territory and jobs benefit its own citizens.
options.B: A shared agreement or governing body with representatives from both towns, guided by clear rules, so all affected parties have a voice in the decision.
options.C: Town B should be allowed to block Town A's factory entirely since water safety is more important than jobs.
options.D: An outside country with no connection to the river should make the final decision to ensure complete neutrality.

questions.explanation: Shared resources that cross boundaries require cooperative governance structures where all affected parties are represented — this is the principle behind many international and regional agreements. Option A is wrong because decisions made unilaterally by one party about shared resources ignore the legitimate interests of others who are equally affected.

questions.title: Media and Information
questions.prompt: A student wants to find out whether a new school rule is fair. She reads one article by the school principal and one by a student leader. Both articles are about the same rule but reach opposite conclusions. What should the student do FIRST before deciding which view is correct?

options.A: Accept the principal's view because adults in authority always have more accurate information than students.
options.B: Accept the student leader's view because the student is more likely to be directly affected by the rule.
options.C: Consider what each author's role and possible interests are, and look for evidence and reasoning each provides to support their claims.
options.D: Ignore both articles entirely since neither can be trusted when the authors have a personal connection to the issue.

questions.explanation: Critical reading requires evaluating who is speaking, what their interests might be, and what evidence supports their position — not simply accepting or rejecting based on the author's role. Option D is wrong because discarding all sources with some connection to an issue would leave us unable to evaluate most real-world information.

questions.title: Budgeting and Planning
questions.prompt: A school council has 100 tokens to spend. Repairing the playground costs 60 tokens, buying new library books costs 50 tokens, and painting the hallways costs 40 tokens. A student says the council should do all three projects. What error is this student making?

options.A: The student is wrong to suggest spending on the library because books are less important than physical spaces.
options.B: The total cost of all three projects is 150 tokens, which exceeds the available budget of 100 tokens, so not all can be done.
options.C: The student is wrong because school councils are not allowed to spend money on painting projects.
options.D: The student is correct because combining projects always reduces the total cost through bulk purchasing savings.

questions.explanation: 60 + 50 + 40 = 150 tokens, which exceeds the 100 token budget — this is a straightforward budget constraint requiring the council to prioritise and make trade-offs. Option D is wrong because while bulk purchasing sometimes reduces costs, there is no basis in the question for assuming combined costs would fall within budget, and the principle of budget limits still applies.

questions.title: Government Structures
questions.prompt: Country A has a president elected directly by citizens every five years. Country B has a prime minister chosen by elected members of parliament. A student claims Country A is more democratic because citizens have a more direct say in choosing their leader. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is entirely correct — direct election of a leader is always a more democratic system than any parliamentary method.
options.B: The claim oversimplifies: in Country B, citizens still elect their representatives who then choose the leader, making it democratic in a different but equally legitimate way.
options.C: The claim is incorrect because presidential systems are never considered truly democratic by political scientists.
options.D: The claim is correct because parliamentary systems require citizens to vote twice, which reduces democratic participation.

questions.explanation: Both presidential and parliamentary systems are forms of representative democracy — in parliamentary systems, citizens elect representatives who reflect their will in choosing the executive, which is an indirect but legitimate democratic process. Option A is wrong because democracy is defined by representation and accountability, not solely by the directness of a single election.

questions.title: Civic Duties
questions.prompt: Lena says: 'Paying taxes, following laws, and voting are all things citizens do, but only voting is a civic duty because it is the only one that helps the whole community.' Which part of Lena's reasoning contains an error?

options.A: Lena is wrong that voting helps the community; individual votes almost never change election outcomes.
options.B: Lena is wrong that only voting is a civic duty — paying taxes funds shared services and following laws maintains order, both of which directly benefit the whole community.
options.C: Lena is correct that only voting qualifies as a civic duty because paying taxes and following laws are enforced by penalties, not chosen freely.
options.D: Lena is wrong that paying taxes helps the community; tax money is held by governments and rarely reaches the people who need it.

questions.explanation: Civic duties include actions that uphold community wellbeing — paying taxes funds schools, hospitals, and roads, while following laws ensures safety for all, making both genuine civic contributions. Option C is wrong because a duty can still be a duty even when it is enforced; coercion and obligation are different concepts from whether the action benefits the community.

questions.title: Organising Groups
questions.prompt: A group of 30 children wants to plant a community garden. Without any assigned roles, what problem is MOST likely to occur, even if all the children genuinely want the garden to succeed?

options.A: The children will immediately begin competing for leadership, making the garden impossible to start.
options.B: Tasks may be duplicated or left undone because no one is certain who is responsible for what, leading to confusion and inefficiency.
options.C: With 30 people all helping, the garden will definitely succeed because more helpers always means better results.
options.D: The children will lose interest within one day because people only work when they are paid or punished.

questions.explanation: Without clear roles, even motivated groups suffer from diffusion of responsibility — some tasks get done by many people while others are neglected because everyone assumes someone else will do them. Option C is wrong because adding more people without coordination can actually increase confusion rather than guarantee success.

questions.title: Local Versus National Government
questions.prompt: A national government passes a rule saying all schools must start at exactly 8:00 a.m. A local government argues that some communities, especially rural areas with long travel distances, need a later start time. What principle does the local government's argument BEST reflect?

options.A: Local governments should have no power at all, because national rules always serve everyone equally well.
options.B: Local governments are closer to the specific needs of their communities and may be better placed to make decisions that fit local conditions.
options.C: National governments should always overrule local governments because national rules are based on better information.
options.D: The local government is being selfish and trying to avoid following rules that most communities find perfectly acceptable.

questions.explanation: The principle of subsidiarity holds that decisions should be made at the lowest level of government capable of addressing them effectively — local governments often understand particular community needs, like geography and travel times, better than distant national governments. Option C is wrong because national governments lack the detailed local knowledge to make every decision optimally for all communities.

questions.title: Environmental Rules
questions.prompt: A fishing village has caught so many fish every year that the fish population is almost gone. Each family says it is not their fault because they only took a small amount. What problem does this situation illustrate about managing shared resources without rules?

options.A: Private ownership of the ocean would automatically solve the problem because owners always protect what belongs to them.
options.B: Each family individually acts reasonably, but without shared rules limiting total catch, the combined effect of many small decisions destroys a resource everyone depends on.
options.C: The fish population declined only because of natural weather changes, not because of the fishing families' behaviour.
options.D: The problem proves that fishing communities should stop fishing entirely and find a different food source.

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates the 'tragedy of the commons' — individually rational actions collectively destroy a shared resource, showing why communal rules and limits are necessary even when no single actor intends harm. Option A is wrong because private ownership of an ocean is impractical and would not automatically lead to sustainable management of migratory fish populations.

questions.title: Supply and Demand Basics
questions.prompt: A popular new video game is released and stores sell out within hours. The next week, the same game is being sold online for three times its original price. Which economic concept BEST explains why sellers can charge so much more than the original price?

options.A: Opportunity cost — buyers must give up other purchases to afford the game
options.B: Scarcity and high demand — limited supply with many buyers drives the price up
options.C: Taxation — the government adds extra charges when products sell too quickly
options.D: Comparative advantage — the seller is better at selling games than anything else

questions.explanation: When supply is limited and many people want the same product, sellers can charge higher prices because buyers compete for what is available — this is the basic principle of scarcity combined with high demand. Option A is wrong because opportunity cost describes what you give up by making a choice, not the mechanism that raises a seller's price.

questions.title: Role of Central Banks
questions.prompt: A country is experiencing inflation — prices for food, fuel, and goods are rising quickly, and people's money buys less each month. The central bank decides to raise interest rates. Why would raising interest rates help reduce inflation?

options.A: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so people and businesses spend less, reducing demand and slowing price rises
options.B: Higher interest rates force factories to produce more goods, increasing supply and automatically lowering prices
options.C: Higher interest rates allow the government to print more money to pay off its debts quickly
options.D: Higher interest rates punish shops that raise their prices, encouraging them to lower costs

questions.explanation: When borrowing costs rise, households and businesses take fewer loans and spend less; reduced spending means less money chasing the same goods, which slows price increases — this is a core tool central banks like the US Federal Reserve use to control inflation. Option B is a common misconception: interest rates affect demand and borrowing, not factories' production decisions directly.

questions.title: Purpose of Taxation
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'A country with no taxes at all would be the best place to live because everyone keeps all of their money.' Identify the most significant error in this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct — removing taxes always improves quality of life for everyone equally
options.B: The student ignores that taxes fund shared services like roads, hospitals, and schools that individuals cannot easily provide alone
options.C: The student forgets that taxes are required by international law, so no country is allowed to remove them
options.D: The student is wrong only because rich people would then have too much money compared to the poor

questions.explanation: Taxes are the primary way governments fund public goods and services — such as roads, emergency services, and public education — that benefit everyone and would be difficult for individuals to organise privately. Option C is incorrect because there is no international law forcing countries to collect taxes; taxation is a matter of domestic policy.

questions.title: How Laws Are Changed
questions.prompt: In many democracies, changing the constitution requires a much larger majority of votes than passing an ordinary law — sometimes two-thirds or three-quarters of all lawmakers must agree. Why is this higher barrier considered important rather than unfair?

options.A: It ensures that fundamental rights are only changed when there is very broad agreement, preventing a temporary majority from removing protections
options.B: It gives judges more power than elected politicians, which is fairer because judges are experts
options.C: It stops poor people from influencing the constitution because they vote less frequently
options.D: It makes democracy work faster by reducing the number of votes needed on small issues

questions.explanation: Constitutional protections are intended to be stable safeguards; requiring a supermajority means no single political party in a brief moment of power can easily strip away rights that protect minorities or future generations. Option B is incorrect because a supermajority requirement increases the bar for lawmakers, not judges — it does not transfer power to the judiciary.

questions.title: Social Contract in Schools
questions.prompt: A class creates a list of shared agreements: everyone listens when others speak, disagreements are solved by discussion, and no one is excluded from group work. Which concept from political philosophy does this classroom practice MOST closely reflect?

options.A: Comparative advantage — each student specialises in the task they do best
options.B: Separation of powers — different students hold different roles in the classroom
options.C: The social contract — members of a community agree to rules in exchange for a fair and orderly environment
options.D: Federalism — power is divided between the teacher and the students equally

questions.explanation: The social contract, developed by philosophers like Rousseau, describes the idea that people agree to follow common rules in exchange for protection and fairness — the classroom agreement mirrors this exactly. Option D is incorrect because federalism specifically describes the division of power between different levels of government, not a group's shared rules.

questions.title: Roles in Economic Systems
questions.prompt: In a command economy, the government decides what is produced, how much it costs, and who receives it. In a market economy, these decisions are made by buyers and sellers. What is a key risk of a pure command economy that a market economy is less likely to face?

options.A: A command economy may produce too many luxury goods because the government favours wealthy citizens
options.B: A command economy can struggle to match what people actually want because planners cannot easily gather and respond to millions of individual preferences
options.C: A command economy always collapses within ten years because it has no currency system
options.D: A command economy relies too heavily on international trade, leaving it vulnerable to foreign influence

questions.explanation: Central planners in a command economy face what economists call the 'knowledge problem' — it is extremely difficult to collect and process the preferences of millions of people, often resulting in shortages of wanted goods and surpluses of unwanted ones, as seen in the Soviet Union. Option A is incorrect; command economies typically set prices uniformly and often prioritised industrial goods over luxury items.

questions.title: United Nations Limitations
questions.prompt: The UN Security Council can authorise international action during conflicts, but any one of the five permanent members (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) can veto — block — that decision. A student says this makes the UN unfair and powerless. Which response BEST evaluates this claim?

options.A: The student is completely right — the veto power should be removed so all countries have equal votes on every issue
options.B: The student is partly right: the veto can block action, but it also encourages major powers to participate by ensuring they cannot be outvoted on issues vital to them
options.C: The student is wrong because all 193 UN member countries share the veto power equally, so it is perfectly democratic
options.D: The student is wrong because the veto has never actually been used, so it does not affect UN decisions

questions.explanation: The veto was deliberately designed so that major powers like the US and Russia would join the UN and remain members; without it, powerful nations might ignore or leave the organisation, making it even less effective. Option C is factually incorrect — only five permanent members hold veto power, not all 193 member states.

questions.title: Consequences of Rule-Breaking
questions.prompt: A small fishing community has agreed that no one should catch more than 50 fish per day from the shared lake, so the fish population can recover each year. One family secretly catches 200 fish daily because they believe their individual gain is worth it. What is MOST LIKELY to happen over time if others adopt the same reasoning?

options.A: The fish population will grow faster because more fishing removes competition between fish
options.B: The shared resource will be depleted until everyone suffers, even though each individual acted in their own short-term interest
options.C: The community will become wealthier overall because more fish are available to sell
options.D: Only the family that broke the rule will suffer consequences, while others remain unaffected

questions.explanation: This is a classic example of the 'tragedy of the commons' — when individuals overuse a shared resource for personal gain, the resource is destroyed and everyone loses in the long run, as happened with many real-world fisheries like the Grand Banks cod stocks. Option C is wrong because short-term surplus catches eventually lead to collapse of the fish population, causing economic loss for everyone.

questions.title: How Governments Represent Citizens
questions.prompt: In a representative democracy, citizens elect people to make decisions on their behalf. In a direct democracy, citizens vote on every law themselves. A student claims direct democracy is always better because people's voices are heard more directly. What is ONE significant problem with direct democracy that this student overlooks?

options.A: In a direct democracy, only wealthy citizens are allowed to vote on financial laws
options.B: Direct democracy becomes very difficult to manage when millions of people must vote on every single complex decision, and it can risk minority rights being overridden by majority opinion
options.C: Direct democracy is illegal under international law in countries with more than one million citizens
options.D: In a direct democracy, elected officials secretly still make all the final decisions, making it no different from representative democracy

questions.explanation: Ancient Athens used direct democracy but only had a small number of eligible citizens; modern nations of millions would struggle with constant referendums on complex technical laws, and majorities could vote away the rights of minorities without checks — this is why most democracies today use representative systems. Option A is incorrect because direct democracy does not inherently restrict voting by wealth.

questions.title: International Trade Benefits
questions.prompt: Country A can produce both cars and wheat more efficiently than Country B. A student argues that Country A should therefore make both products itself and not trade with Country B at all. Which concept challenges this reasoning most directly?

options.A: Opportunity cost and comparative advantage — Country A may gain more by specialising in its most efficient product and trading for the rest, even if it could make both
options.B: Inflation — producing two products at once always causes prices to rise uncontrollably
options.C: The social contract — trading partners must agree to share profits equally or the trade is unethical
options.D: Scarcity — Country A will always run out of resources if it tries to produce both products simultaneously

questions.explanation: Comparative advantage (developed by economist David Ricardo) shows that even if one country is better at producing everything, both countries benefit when each specialises in what it produces at the lowest relative cost and trades for the rest. Option D is a misconception — scarcity applies to all production decisions, but it does not specifically explain why specialisation and trade increase total output.

questions.title: Civic Responsibilities vs Rights
questions.prompt: A 10-year-old says: 'I have the right to free speech, so I can say anything I want anywhere, and no one can ever stop me.' Identify the most important flaw in this statement.

options.A: Children under 18 have no legal rights, so the claim is entirely false
options.B: Rights are not absolute — they exist alongside responsibilities and may be limited to protect other people's rights and public safety
options.C: Free speech only applies to written words, not to things said out loud
options.D: Rights can only be used in government buildings, not in schools or private spaces

questions.explanation: In democratic legal systems, even fundamental rights like free speech have recognised limits — for example, inciting violence or threatening individuals is not protected expression in most countries, because one person's rights end where they harm others. Option A is wrong because international frameworks like the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child explicitly recognise children as rights-holders.

questions.title: How NGOs Function
questions.prompt: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) like Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) provide medical care in conflict zones without being part of any government. Why is being independent from governments considered an important feature for such organisations?

options.A: Independence means the NGO can charge patients higher fees, which helps them raise more money
options.B: Independence allows them to operate in areas controlled by different sides of a conflict without being seen as favouring one government over another
options.C: Independence means they do not need any funding and can operate entirely for free
options.D: Independence from governments means they are not required to follow any laws in the countries where they work

questions.explanation: Neutrality and independence are core principles for humanitarian NGOs — by not being linked to any government, they can negotiate access to assist people on all sides of a conflict, as MSF does under principles established in the Geneva Conventions. Option D is incorrect; NGOs must still follow national and international laws, and their independence relates to political affiliation, not legal accountability.

questions.title: Purpose of a Free Press
questions.prompt: In Country Z, the government controls all newspapers, television channels, and websites. A student argues this is fine because the government can make sure only accurate information is shared. What is the MOST significant problem this student's reasoning misses?

options.A: Government-controlled media always uses more difficult language that ordinary citizens cannot understand
options.B: When governments control all media, they can hide their own mistakes and wrongdoing from citizens, removing a key check on their power
options.C: Government media is more expensive to run, so Country Z will quickly run out of money for other services
options.D: Citizens in Country Z will not know about international sports results because foreign news will be blocked

questions.explanation: A free press serves as a 'watchdog' — investigative journalism has historically exposed government corruption and abuse of power, such as the Watergate scandal in the US; without independent media, citizens lose a vital tool for holding leaders accountable. Option A is a generalisation with no basis in principle — government media could use any language register.

questions.title: Effects of Economic Inequality
questions.prompt: Two students are comparing two countries with similar average incomes. In Country J, most people earn close to the average. In Country K, a small number of people earn enormous amounts while most earn very little. A student says: 'The average income is the same, so people in both countries are equally well off.' What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.A: Nothing is wrong — average income is always the best and most complete way to measure how well off a population is
options.B: The student ignores income distribution — averages can be distorted by very high earners, meaning most people in Country K may actually be much poorer than the average suggests
options.C: The student is wrong because Country K must have a higher average due to its wealthy citizens, so the premise of the question is impossible
options.D: The student forgets that countries with the same average income always have the same tax rates

questions.explanation: A statistical mean (average) is pulled upward by extremely high values — if a few billionaires live in Country K, the average rises even if most citizens earn very little; economists use measures like the Gini coefficient and median income to better capture inequality. Option A is incorrect because average income alone cannot show how unevenly wealth is distributed across the population.

questions.title: Political Parties and Choice
questions.prompt: In a one-party state, citizens can vote, but there is only one party allowed to stand for election. A student claims this still counts as a democracy because elections are held. Which reasoning BEST challenges this claim?

options.A: Democracy requires elections, and elections are happening, so the student's claim is actually correct
options.B: Elections are only meaningful in a democracy if citizens have a genuine choice between different candidates or parties representing different ideas
options.C: A country is only a democracy if it has exactly two political parties, so one party is not enough
options.D: The student is wrong because democracy requires citizens to vote on every law, not just to choose leaders

questions.explanation: The defining feature of democratic elections is meaningful choice — if only one party is permitted, citizens cannot remove leaders they disapprove of or vote for alternative policies, which was the situation in countries like the Soviet Union despite regular elections. Option C is incorrect because many democracies, such as Germany and Sweden, have multiple parties, and two-party systems are not a requirement.

questions.title: Global Institutions and Cooperation
questions.prompt: After World War Two, countries created international institutions like the UN, World Bank, and IMF. What common cause-and-effect reasoning explains WHY these institutions were created at that specific moment in history?

options.A: Countries created these institutions to replace national governments, which were abolished after the war
options.B: The devastation of two world wars showed that nations acting alone could not prevent global conflict or economic collapse, creating urgent need for systems of cooperation
options.C: These institutions were created because newly independent colonies needed someone to manage their economies for them
options.D: International institutions were formed to help wealthy countries share their technology with less developed nations as a form of apology for colonialism

questions.explanation: The League of Nations had failed to prevent World War Two, partly due to limited membership and enforcement power; world leaders in 1945 deliberately designed the UN and Bretton Woods institutions to address international conflict and economic instability through structured cooperation. Option A is incorrect — national governments were preserved and indeed form the membership of these institutions.

questions.title: Local vs National Government
questions.prompt: A town council wants to introduce a recycling programme that suits local geography and community habits. The national government insists all towns must follow one identical recycling plan. What is a disadvantage of the national government's approach in this situation?

options.A: A national plan always costs less than a local plan, so the town will lose funding if it uses its own programme
options.B: A single national plan may not fit every community's specific needs, reducing effectiveness compared to locally designed solutions
options.C: Local governments are not legally allowed to organise recycling because it is an environmental issue handled only internationally
options.D: The town council is not elected, so its opinion about recycling should not be considered by the national government

questions.explanation: Local governments often have better knowledge of local conditions — for instance, a coastal town and a landlocked mountain village may need very different collection methods; this is one key argument for decentralisation and subsidiarity (the principle that decisions should be made at the lowest effective level). Option A is a generalisation that is not necessarily true — local programmes can sometimes be more cost-efficient due to community participation.

questions.title: Evaluating Propaganda
questions.prompt: A wartime government creates posters showing the enemy as monsters, and only reports stories of its own victories while hiding defeats. A student says this is acceptable because it helps keep citizens' morale high. Evaluate this claim using the concept of responsibility.

options.A: The student is correct because governments always have a responsibility to make citizens feel positive, even if this means hiding the truth
options.B: The student's claim overlooks the government's responsibility to provide citizens with accurate information so they can make informed decisions, and propaganda can fuel hatred and poor policy choices
options.C: The student is correct only if the posters were made by private companies rather than the government itself
options.D: The student is wrong because morale never affects the outcome of a war, making the posters pointless

questions.explanation: Governments have a responsibility of honesty to their citizens; propaganda that dehumanises enemies has historically contributed to atrocities such as genocide, and citizens who are misled cannot hold their government accountable for military or strategic failures. Option A is incorrect because responsibility in a democratic context includes transparency — morale-boosting cannot justify systematic deception.

questions.title: Interdependence in Communities
questions.prompt: In a modern city, farmers, truck drivers, supermarket workers, water engineers, and doctors all depend on each other to survive and function. What concept BEST describes this kind of relationship between people in an organised society?

options.A: Separation of powers — each person performs a different role so no one has too much control
options.B: Interdependence — individuals and groups rely on each other's specialised contributions for the community to function
options.C: Federalism — power and responsibilities are split between city and national levels equally
options.D: Scarcity — there are never enough workers in any one profession, forcing people to cooperate

questions.explanation: Interdependence is the key concept here — in complex societies, specialisation means no individual can meet all their own needs, so people depend on networks of others with different skills, which is a foundation of both economics and social organisation. Option A is incorrect because separation of powers specifically refers to the division of governmental authority among branches of government, not to general social roles.

questions.title: Budgets and Priorities
questions.prompt: A student government has a budget of $500. Members debate whether to spend it on a school party, new library books, or repairing the broken water fountain. They vote and decide on the library books. A classmate says the decision was unfair because not everyone wanted books. Which response BEST explains why the voting process was still fair?

options.A: It was fair because whoever spends the most time in the library should always make the decision
options.B: Fairness in collective decisions means every voice gets equal weight in the process; when a group disagrees, a transparent vote ensures the majority preference is respected while everyone had a chance to participate
options.C: It was fair only because $500 is a small amount — for larger amounts, all members must agree unanimously
options.D: It was unfair — any time someone disagrees with a group decision, that decision should be reversed

questions.explanation: Democratic fairness is procedural — it means the process (everyone votes, votes are counted equally) is just, even if not everyone prefers the outcome; this is a foundational principle of collective decision-making in democratic systems. Option D is incorrect because requiring unanimous agreement would give any single person a veto over all group decisions, making collective governance impossible.

questions.title: Changing Communities Over Time
questions.prompt: One hundred years ago, most people in a particular country lived in small farming villages with little contact with the outside world. Today, most live in large cities, buy food from global supply chains, and communicate instantly worldwide. Which TWO forces MOST directly caused this change?

options.A: Industrialisation and globalisation — factories drew people to cities, and improved transport and communications connected communities internationally
options.B: Colonialism and federalism — colonial powers moved people into cities, while federal systems encouraged international communication
options.C: The social contract and scarcity — people agreed to live in cities because governments told them to, and food became scarce in villages
options.D: Comparative advantage and the rule of law — countries specialised in different products, and legal systems forced people to relocate

questions.explanation: Industrialisation (beginning in the 18th–19th centuries) created factory jobs that pulled populations into urban centres, while globalisation — accelerated by container shipping, telecommunications, and trade agreements — connected these cities to global markets and cultures. Option B is partially historically relevant but federalism does not explain urbanisation or global communication as directly as industrialisation does.

questions.title: Rights of Minority Groups
questions.prompt: In a democracy, a vote is held and 80% of citizens support a law that would prevent a small religious minority from practising their religion in public. Should the law be passed simply because a large majority supports it? What principle challenges this?

options.A: Yes — in a true democracy, the majority always has the right to make any law it chooses, with no exceptions
options.B: No — constitutional rights and human rights frameworks exist specifically to protect minorities from 'tyranny of the majority,' where a large group uses its power to harm a smaller one
options.C: Yes — religious practices are personal choices, so restricting them publicly does not count as removing a right
options.D: No — but only if the religious group belongs to a larger international organisation that can intervene

questions.explanation: The concept of 'tyranny of the majority' — warned about by thinkers like John Stuart Mill — is exactly why constitutions and human rights instruments like the UN Declaration of Human Rights protect freedoms that cannot be removed by simple majority vote. Option A is a common misconception about democracy; democratic theory distinguishes between procedural majority rule and the protection of fundamental rights.

questions.title: How Rules Create Order
questions.prompt: Imagine a busy road junction with no traffic lights, no stop signs, and no road markings. Every driver tries to get through as quickly as possible. What would MOST LIKELY happen, and what does this illustrate about the function of rules in systems?

options.A: Traffic would flow smoothly because drivers would naturally take turns out of politeness, showing rules are unnecessary
options.B: Accidents and gridlock would increase, illustrating that agreed rules coordinate behaviour and allow complex systems to function more safely and efficiently
options.C: Only the fastest cars would get through, which is fair because they are contributing more to the economy
options.D: The government would immediately close the road, showing that rules only matter when officials are watching

questions.explanation: Research in urban planning shows that unregulated intersections cause significantly more accidents and congestion; traffic rules are a direct example of how shared agreements — even simple ones — coordinate large numbers of people to achieve outcomes better than unregulated self-interest alone. Option A is an idealistic assumption contradicted by real-world traffic studies and the game-theoretic concept of the prisoner's dilemma.

questions.title: International Aid and Development
questions.prompt: Country M receives large amounts of foreign aid for 20 years but remains poor. An economist argues that aid alone cannot create lasting development. Which explanation BEST supports the economist's view?

options.A: Aid fails because foreign money always loses its value when it crosses a border
options.B: Lasting development also requires strong institutions, rule of law, and local capacity — aid without these can create dependency rather than self-sustaining growth
options.C: Aid is always stolen by international organisations before it reaches the country, making it impossible for it to help
options.D: Poor countries can only develop if they completely copy the economic systems of wealthy countries

questions.explanation: Development economists like Dambisa Moyo have argued that aid without institutional reform can undermine local markets and create reliance on external funding; sustainable development requires governance improvements, education investment, and local enterprise, not just financial transfers. Option A is factually incorrect — money does not lose value simply by crossing national borders through aid transfers.

questions.title: Perspective and Policy Design
questions.prompt: A government is designing a new city park. A retired elderly person wants quiet benches and gardens. A parent of young children wants a large playground. A group of teenagers wants a skate park. A student says: 'The government should just pick the idea from the most important group.' What is wrong with this approach to policy design?

options.A: Nothing is wrong — governments should always prioritise the needs of whoever pays the most taxes
options.B: Deciding which group is 'most important' is itself a form of bias; good policy design considers multiple perspectives and tries to find solutions that serve diverse community needs
options.C: The approach is wrong because parks should always be designed by professional architects alone, without any public input
options.D: The approach is wrong only because teenagers are not yet citizens and should not be considered in government planning

questions.explanation: Inclusive policy design recognises that communities contain diverse groups with equally valid needs — urban planning research shows that parks serving multiple age groups (like Paley Park in New York) are used more frequently and create greater community benefit. Option A reflects a misconception that taxation determines whose needs matter most, which contradicts the principle of equal civic standing in a democracy.

questions.title: Supply and Demand Basics
questions.prompt: A new video game is released and becomes extremely popular. Stores quickly run out of stock, but the manufacturer hasn't yet increased production. Using what you know about markets, what would you expect to happen to the price of the game in the short term?

options.A: The price will likely rise because demand is high but supply is limited
options.B: The price will fall because sellers want to attract more customers quickly
options.C: The price will stay the same because the manufacturer controls all prices
options.D: The price will rise only after the manufacturer officially announces a shortage

questions.explanation: When demand is high and supply is low, sellers can charge more because buyers compete for limited goods — this is the core relationship between supply, demand, and price. Option C is a common misconception; in a free market, prices respond to shortages even without manufacturer control.

questions.title: Role of Central Banks
questions.prompt: A country's economy is growing very fast — so fast that prices for everyday goods like food and rent are rising quickly each month. The central bank decides to raise interest rates. Why would raising interest rates help slow down rising prices?

options.A: Higher interest rates make the government collect more taxes automatically
options.B: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, so people and businesses spend less
options.C: Higher interest rates force companies to lower their prices by law
options.D: Higher interest rates increase the amount of money printed, giving everyone more to spend

questions.explanation: When borrowing costs rise, consumers take fewer loans and businesses invest less, which reduces total spending and slows price increases — this is called contractionary monetary policy. Option D is the opposite of what happens; raising rates is meant to reduce money flow, not increase it.

questions.title: NGOs vs Governments
questions.prompt: An international non-governmental organisation (NGO) provides clean water to villages in a region where the local government has failed to do so. A student claims that since the NGO is doing the government's job, the government is no longer needed. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct — NGOs are more efficient and should replace governments entirely
options.B: The student is partly right because NGOs only help when funded by donations, which can run out
options.C: The student is wrong because governments have legal authority and accountability that NGOs lack
options.D: The student is wrong because NGOs are always controlled by governments anyway

questions.explanation: Governments hold legal responsibility to provide services as a right, can enforce laws, and are accountable through democratic processes — NGOs depend on funding and have no legal obligation to citizens. Option B contains a true fact but misses the deeper structural reason why governments remain essential.

questions.title: Public vs Private Goods
questions.prompt: A lighthouse warns all ships of nearby rocks, whether or not those ships have paid for the service. A private company refuses to build one because it cannot easily charge users. What economic concept does this illustrate, and why is it a problem for free markets?

options.A: Monopoly — one company controls the lighthouse and sets unfair prices
options.B: Public good — because no one can be excluded from its benefit, private companies won't profit from providing it
options.C: Opportunity cost — building the lighthouse means the company cannot build other things
options.D: Supply shortage — there are not enough lighthouses because the materials are rare

questions.explanation: A public good is non-excludable (you cannot stop anyone from benefiting) and non-rival (one ship using it doesn't reduce it for others), so private firms cannot recover costs — this is called the free-rider problem. Option C describes a real concept but does not explain why the market specifically fails to provide lighthouses.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principles
questions.prompt: In Country Z, even the president was prosecuted and fined after breaking an environmental law. A classmate says this is unusual because leaders normally make the laws, so the laws shouldn't apply to them. Which statement BEST explains why the classmate's view is mistaken?

options.A: Leaders should be exempt from laws they create because they understand them best
options.B: The rule of law means that all people, including leaders, are subject to the same laws
options.C: Environmental laws are international, so they automatically override leaders' immunity
options.D: Leaders can only be prosecuted by international courts, not their own country's courts

questions.explanation: The rule of law is the principle that no person is above the law, regardless of their position — this is fundamental to preventing abuse of power in democratic societies. Option C is wrong because environmental laws vary by country and are not automatically international.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: A remote village community agrees that everyone will contribute two hours of work per week to maintain shared paths and wells. A new family moves in and refuses, saying no one asked them to sign any agreement. What concept from social and political thought does this situation connect to?

options.A: Opportunity cost — the family is choosing not to work so they can do other things
options.B: The social contract — living in a community implies accepting shared responsibilities even without a written agreement
options.C: Federalism — the village cannot enforce rules without national government approval
options.D: Free trade — the family is exercising their right to not exchange labour

questions.explanation: Philosophers like Rousseau argued that the social contract means people implicitly agree to community norms and responsibilities by choosing to live in a community — no formal signature is needed. Option A misapplies opportunity cost, which is about choices between alternatives, not community obligation.

questions.title: Taxation and Public Services
questions.prompt: Country A has low taxes and relies on private companies to run schools and hospitals. Country B has higher taxes and funds public schools and hospitals for all citizens. A student argues that Country A's system is always fairer because people keep more of their own money. Identify the strongest flaw in this argument.

options.A: Country A's system is actually better for the environment
options.B: The argument ignores that people who cannot afford private services may be left without education or healthcare
options.C: The argument is correct — lower taxes always produce a fairer society
options.D: Country B's taxes are illegal under international trade law

questions.explanation: Fairness in a society must consider whether all citizens can access essential services — when only private options exist, those unable to pay may be excluded from healthcare or education entirely. Option C is factually incorrect; the relationship between tax levels and fairness is complex and debated by economists.

questions.title: Democracy and Representation
questions.prompt: In a representative democracy, citizens elect people to make decisions on their behalf. What is the KEY advantage of this system over direct democracy, where every citizen votes on every decision?

options.A: Representatives can be paid, which motivates better decision-making than volunteers
options.B: It allows decisions to be made efficiently by informed people in large, complex societies
options.C: It means the majority can never be wrong because they chose the representatives
options.D: Direct democracy is illegal under international law, making representation necessary

questions.explanation: In large modern societies, it is impractical for every citizen to study every complex policy — elected representatives can specialise and dedicate time to governance. Option C is a dangerous misconception; majorities can still make decisions that harm minority groups, which is why rights protections exist.

questions.title: Global Interdependence
questions.prompt: A disease outbreak in one country quickly affects the economies of countries thousands of kilometres away because supply chains are disrupted. What does this scenario BEST illustrate about how modern countries are organised?

options.A: Countries should avoid all trade to protect themselves from such risks
options.B: Global interdependence means events in one country can cause ripple effects worldwide
options.C: International organisations like the UN directly control all countries' economies
options.D: Only wealthy countries are affected by economic disruptions in other nations

questions.explanation: Modern economies are deeply connected through trade, supply chains, and finance — a disruption in one node (like a manufacturing hub) causes shortages and economic strain globally, as seen during the COVID-19 pandemic. Option A misunderstands the solution; isolation would reduce both risk and the significant benefits of trade.

questions.title: Civic Responsibility
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Voting is pointless because one vote never changes the outcome of an election.' What is the MOST effective response to challenge this reasoning?

options.A: Elections have been decided by a single vote, and widespread non-voting collectively changes outcomes
options.B: Voting is required by law in all democracies, so refusal results in punishment
options.C: One vote is statistically meaningless but voting is important for symbolic reasons only
options.D: The student is correct — individual votes have no measurable impact on large elections

questions.explanation: Several elections globally have been decided by very few votes, and when many people believe their vote doesn't matter and stay home, this collectively shifts outcomes — making individual participation systemically important. Option B is false; compulsory voting exists in some countries like Australia but not all democracies.

questions.title: Federal vs Unitary States
questions.prompt: In a unitary state, the central government makes all major decisions. In a federal state, power is shared between national and regional governments. Which situation would MOST LIKELY be managed more effectively by a federal system than a unitary one?

options.A: Signing a single international trade agreement on behalf of the whole country
options.B: Creating a national military defence force
options.C: Designing school curricula that reflect the unique languages and cultures of different regions
options.D: Issuing a common currency used by all citizens

questions.explanation: Federal systems allow regional governments to make decisions suited to local needs — education policy that reflects regional languages and cultures is a classic example where local knowledge leads to better outcomes. Options A, B, and D are areas where unified national action is more efficient, favouring a unitary approach.

questions.title: Checks and Balances
questions.prompt: A president vetoes a law passed by the legislature. The legislature then votes again and overrides the veto with a two-thirds majority, and the law passes. What does this sequence of events demonstrate about how well-organised governments function?

options.A: The president's power is absolute until the legislature gains enough support to resist
options.B: Checks and balances allow different branches to limit each other's power, preventing any one branch from dominating
options.C: This system slows government down unnecessarily and should be replaced with faster decision-making
options.D: The judiciary must approve all laws before they can override a presidential veto

questions.explanation: The veto and override process is a textbook example of checks and balances — the executive can block legislation, but the legislature can still prevail with sufficient support, ensuring no single branch is all-powerful. Option C reflects a misconception; the deliberate slow-down prevents hasty or harmful laws.

questions.title: Human Rights and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: The United Nations can recommend that member countries stop human rights violations within their borders, but cannot usually force them to comply. A student says this makes the UN useless. What is the BEST evaluation of this claim?

options.A: The student is correct — an organisation with no enforcement power has no value
options.B: The student is wrong because the UN can declare war on any country that disobeys
options.C: The student oversimplifies — the UN uses diplomacy, sanctions, and international pressure which can be effective without military force
options.D: The student is correct, but only for small countries; the UN controls large countries fully

questions.explanation: The UN's power lies in coordinating international pressure, applying economic sanctions, authorising peacekeeping missions, and shaping global norms — these tools have influenced behaviour even without direct enforcement. Option A wrongly equates usefulness only with coercive force.

questions.title: Market Failure and Pollution
questions.prompt: A factory produces cheap goods but releases harmful chemicals into a nearby river, damaging local fisheries. The factory pays nothing for this damage. What term describes the cost borne by others that the factory is not paying for, and what should a government do about it?

options.A: Comparative advantage — the factory should specialise in pollution and be left alone
options.B: Negative externality — the government should tax or regulate the factory to account for the damage it causes
options.C: Opportunity cost — the government gave up clean water when it chose to allow the factory
options.D: Inflation — too much production always causes environmental harm and price rises

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a third party bears costs from an economic activity they did not participate in — pollution is the classic case, and governments typically respond with taxes (like a carbon tax) or regulations. Option C misuses opportunity cost, which refers to trade-offs in choices, not harms passed to others.

questions.title: Rights vs Responsibilities
questions.prompt: What would MOST LIKELY happen if citizens in a democracy demanded all their rights but refused to accept any responsibilities — such as paying taxes, obeying laws, or participating in civic duties?

options.A: The democratic system would grow stronger because freedom without responsibility is the purest form of democracy
options.B: Nothing would change because rights and responsibilities are completely separate systems
options.C: The system would gradually break down because public services, law enforcement, and civic trust depend on shared obligations
options.D: International organisations would step in immediately to run the country instead

questions.explanation: Rights and responsibilities are interdependent — public services like schools and hospitals require tax funding, laws require compliance to function, and democracy requires participation; removing responsibilities collapses the foundation that makes rights possible. Option B incorrectly treats them as unrelated when they are deeply connected in organised societies.

questions.title: Immigration and Social Systems
questions.prompt: A country receives a large number of immigrants and some citizens worry this will reduce job opportunities for existing workers. An economist points out that immigrants also create new businesses and spend money. Which conclusion BEST reflects a balanced evaluation of immigration's economic effect?

options.A: Immigration always harms existing workers by increasing competition for every available job
options.B: Immigration has no economic effects at all — it is purely a social issue
options.C: Immigration has complex effects — it may increase competition in some sectors but also grows the economy by adding workers, consumers, and entrepreneurs
options.D: Immigration only benefits the economy if all immigrants are highly educated professionals

questions.explanation: Economic research, including studies by the IMF, consistently shows that immigration's effects are mixed and context-dependent — it can expand labour markets, increase consumer spending, and drive innovation while also creating short-term pressures in specific job categories. Option A reflects a common misconception that ignores the demand side of the economy that immigrants also stimulate.

questions.title: Propaganda and Media Literacy
questions.prompt: A government releases a poster showing its leader helping poor families, with the slogan 'Your government cares.' A critical thinker notices the poster shows no data and uses emotional images only. What skill is the thinker applying, and why does it matter in an organised society?

options.A: Mathematical reasoning — the thinker is calculating the cost of the poster
options.B: Media literacy — distinguishing emotional persuasion from evidence-based claims helps citizens make informed decisions
options.C: Legal analysis — the poster may be breaking advertising laws
options.D: Economic analysis — the thinker is assessing whether the government spent wisely on the poster

questions.explanation: Media literacy — the ability to analyse and evaluate messages in media — is essential in democracy because citizens who cannot distinguish propaganda from fact are more easily manipulated, weakening informed civic participation. Option D touches on a real skill but misidentifies the primary critical thinking act being performed.

questions.title: Globalisation and Local Culture
questions.prompt: As global companies spread into a small country, local shops close, traditional foods are replaced by international fast-food chains, and younger people adopt foreign fashions. A student says globalisation is entirely positive because it brings economic growth. Identify the most significant gap in this reasoning.

options.A: The student ignores that globalisation always causes inflation in small countries
options.B: The student ignores the potential loss of cultural identity and economic harm to local businesses
options.C: The student is correct — economic growth always outweighs cultural concerns
options.D: The student ignores that global companies are required to teach local languages

questions.explanation: While globalisation can bring economic benefits, it also risks homogenising cultures and displacing local businesses — a complete evaluation must weigh economic gains against cultural and social costs. Option C reflects an oversimplification; whether growth outweighs cultural loss is a values-based debate, not a settled fact.

questions.title: Authoritarian vs Democratic Leadership
questions.prompt: During a national emergency, an authoritarian leader can implement decisions in hours, while a democratic government may take weeks of debate. A student argues that authoritarian systems are therefore superior during crises. What is the MOST important counterargument?

options.A: Democratic systems are actually faster because voting can happen electronically
options.B: Speed is valuable, but authoritarian leaders can make unchecked decisions that cause serious harm with no way for citizens to correct them
options.C: Authoritarian leaders are always wrong during crises because they lack technical knowledge
options.D: Democratic systems never slow down during crises because emergency powers exist

questions.explanation: While speed is a genuine advantage of centralised authority, the absence of checks means poor or harmful decisions cannot be challenged or reversed — history shows authoritarian 'crisis responses' have sometimes caused greater harm than the original crisis. Option D is partially true (emergency powers exist in democracies) but overstates the case, as even emergency powers face scrutiny.

questions.title: Economic Inequality and Opportunity
questions.prompt: Two students grow up in the same city. Student A attends a well-funded school in a wealthy neighbourhood. Student B attends an underfunded school in a poorer area. Both work equally hard. A classmate says the outcome difference between them is entirely due to their personal choices. Evaluate this claim using what you know about how societies are organised.

options.A: The classmate is correct — personal effort is the only factor that determines success
options.B: The classmate is partly wrong — structural factors like unequal school funding shape opportunities before personal choices are even made
options.C: The classmate is correct because both students live in the same city and have equal access to the same resources
options.D: The classmate is wrong because Student B will always outperform Student A due to greater motivation

questions.explanation: Research in sociology and economics consistently shows that structural inequalities — such as unequal school funding linked to neighbourhood wealth — significantly shape life outcomes independently of individual effort. Option C confuses living in the same city with having equal access to resources, which the scenario explicitly contradicts.

questions.title: International Law and Enforcement
questions.prompt: A country signs an international treaty promising to reduce carbon emissions by 2030, but by 2028 it has increased emissions instead. Unlike domestic law, international law has no single global police force. What is the MOST realistic consequence the country might face?

options.A: The UN army will invade the country to enforce the treaty
options.B: Nothing at all — international treaties are simply suggestions with no consequences
options.C: The country may face diplomatic pressure, trade penalties, or damage to its international reputation
options.D: The country will automatically be expelled from all international organisations immediately

questions.explanation: International law relies primarily on diplomacy, reputation, and economic incentives rather than a single enforcement body — countries that breach treaties often face sanctions, reduced cooperation, and damaged trade relationships. Option A is incorrect; the UN does not have a standing army that enforces environmental treaties.

questions.title: Property Rights and Markets
questions.prompt: In Country X, entrepreneurs cannot legally own businesses outright — the state controls all production. In Country Y, private property rights are strongly protected by law. An economist argues Country Y will likely see more innovation over time. What reasoning BEST supports this argument?

options.A: Country Y's citizens are naturally more creative than Country X's citizens
options.B: When people can own and profit from their ideas and businesses, they have stronger incentives to take risks and innovate
options.C: Country X's state control always leads to war, which destroys innovation
options.D: Innovation only happens in countries that use a specific currency approved by the WTO

questions.explanation: Property rights create incentives — when individuals or companies can keep the rewards of their inventions and investments, they are more motivated to innovate, which is why patent law and private ownership are considered foundations of market-driven innovation. Option A falsely attributes outcomes to innate national characteristics rather than institutional structures.

questions.title: Refugee Rights and Global Responsibility
questions.prompt: Under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention, countries that have signed it are legally obliged to consider asylum claims from people fleeing persecution. A government official says: 'Our country's borders are our business alone — we owe nothing to people from other countries.' How does international law challenge this view?

options.A: The official is correct — national sovereignty means a country can ignore all international agreements
options.B: By signing the Refugee Convention, countries voluntarily accepted legal obligations that limit absolute sovereignty in exchange for global cooperation
options.C: The official is wrong because the UN can remove any government that refuses refugees
options.D: International law only applies to countries that are members of the WTO, not the UN

questions.explanation: When countries ratify international treaties, they voluntarily constrain their own sovereignty — the 1951 Refugee Convention, signed by over 140 countries, creates binding legal obligations to process asylum claims. Option A misunderstands sovereignty; it is not absolute once treaty obligations are voluntarily accepted.

questions.title: Entrepreneurship and Economic Change
questions.prompt: When a new ride-sharing app enters a city, many traditional taxi drivers lose income. Meanwhile, customers enjoy lower fares and more convenience. Economists call this process 'creative destruction.' What does this term mean, and what does it reveal about how market economies change over time?
