Government licensing creates a conflict of interest: the body being scrutinised controls the operating rights of those doing the scrutiny. Reporters Without Borders documents how press freedom restrictions through licensing and registration requirements have silenced opposition media in countries like Russia and Hungary. Option A is wrong in its absolutism: while broadcast spectrum licensing exists in democracies, content-based licensing by a political ministry is widely distinguished from technical regulatory licensing as incompatible with press freedom.

questions.title: International Trade Comparative Advantage
questions.prompt: Portugal can produce both wine and cloth more efficiently than England can produce either. An economist still argues Portugal should specialise in wine and trade with England for cloth. A student finds this counterintuitive: 'Why would Portugal buy cloth from a country that's worse at making it?' What principle resolves this apparent paradox, and what does it actually depend on?

options.A: Absolute advantage: Portugal should trade because England is geographically closer, reducing transport costs enough to make imports cheaper than domestic production.
options.B: Comparative advantage: even if Portugal is better at both, it benefits by specialising in wine if its relative efficiency advantage in wine is greater than in cloth, allowing both countries to consume more of both goods through specialisation and trade.
options.C: Competitive advantage: Portugal should specialise in wine because its brand reputation makes Portuguese wine worth more on international markets than any cloth it could produce.
options.D: Comparative advantage: Portugal must specialise in wine because international law requires countries to export only their single most efficiently produced good.

questions.explanation: David Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage (1817) demonstrates that trade is mutually beneficial when countries specialise in goods where their opportunity cost — not absolute productivity — is lower. If Portugal gives up less wine per unit of cloth than England does, England has a comparative advantage in cloth despite being worse in absolute terms; both countries end up consuming beyond their individual production possibility frontiers through trade. Option A confuses this with absolute advantage theory (Adam Smith's earlier concept), which only considers which country is simply more productive, missing Ricardo's more nuanced relative-cost insight.

questions.title: Organisational Decision-Making
questions.prompt: A large international humanitarian organisation must decide whether to centralise all decisions at its headquarters or allow regional offices to make independent decisions. A senior manager argues: 'Centralisation ensures consistency and prevents regional offices from acting against our values.' Evaluate the strongest counter-argument to this position.

options.A: Centralisation is always superior in humanitarian organisations because emergencies require immediate decisions and headquarters always has the best information.
options.B: Decentralisation allows regional offices with local knowledge to respond faster and more appropriately to on-the-ground realities, and over-centralisation can cause dangerous delays in crisis response when headquarters is geographically or culturally distant.
options.C: The counter-argument is that centralisation increases costs because it requires more senior staff at headquarters, while decentralisation reduces the administrative budget.
options.D: The counter-argument is that international law requires all NGOs to decentralise decision-making to the regional level to respect the sovereignty of host nations.

questions.explanation: Organisational theory distinguishes between the control benefits of centralisation and the responsiveness benefits of decentralisation; in humanitarian contexts, the SPHERE Handbook and after-action reviews of crises like the 2010 Haiti earthquake consistently show that slow centralised decision-making costs lives when conditions change rapidly on the ground. Regional offices that understand local languages, political dynamics, and access constraints are better positioned for timely, contextually appropriate responses. Option A is wrong because it assumes headquarters always has the best information — a factually incorrect premise in dynamic field environments where communication is often delayed or incomplete.

questions.title: Social Inequality and Meritocracy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'In a true meritocracy, everyone who works hard enough will succeed, so inequality in outcomes simply reflects differences in effort and talent — not unfair systems.' Examine which evidence most effectively challenges this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; sociological research consistently shows that effort accounts for more than 90% of lifetime income differences across all societies studied.
options.B: The claim is challenged by evidence that children's educational and economic outcomes are strongly correlated with the socioeconomic status of the family they are born into, suggesting that starting conditions — not only merit — determine success, and that equal opportunity is not guaranteed by meritocratic ideology alone.
options.C: The claim is challenged only in developing countries; in high-income OECD nations, meritocracy has been fully achieved and social mobility is no longer a concern.
options.D: The claim is challenged by the fact that effort and talent cannot be measured objectively, making all claims about meritocracy meaningless philosophical speculation rather than an empirical question.

questions.explanation: Research such as Raj Chetty's mobility studies (Opportunity Insights, Harvard) demonstrates that in the USA, a child born in the bottom income quintile has less than an 8% chance of reaching the top quintile — a finding replicated across many countries showing low intergenerational social mobility. This structural persistence of inequality across generations challenges the meritocratic assumption that effort and talent alone determine outcomes. Option C is factually wrong: the OECD itself has documented declining social mobility even in wealthy member states, with studies in the UK, USA, and Germany showing strong correlations between parental income and children's adult earnings.

questions.title: Democratic Backsliding
questions.prompt: A country has free elections, an independent judiciary, and freedom of the press. Over five years, the elected government passes laws that gradually reduce judicial independence, restrict press licences, and change electoral rules to disadvantage opposition parties — all through legal procedures. A student says: 'This can't be authoritarianism because everything was done legally.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct; actions taken through legal procedures are by definition democratic, and no legal process can produce authoritarian outcomes.
options.B: The student's reasoning is flawed because democratic backsliding often occurs through technically legal steps that systematically dismantle the institutional checks — judiciary, press, electoral fairness — that make democracy function, producing an 'elected autocracy' without an outright coup.
options.C: The student is correct for the first three years of changes but incorrect for the fifth year, because international law sets a five-year threshold after which legal changes to electoral rules become automatically authoritarian.
options.D: The student's reasoning is flawed only because press restriction is always unconstitutional under every democratic constitution, making at least one step in the process illegal regardless of how it was passed.

questions.explanation: Political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way coined the term 'competitive authoritarianism' to describe regimes that maintain formal democratic institutions but hollow out their independence; Hungary under Viktor Orbán after 2010 is a widely cited case where judicial packing, media licensing, and gerrymandering — all done through parliamentary majorities — systematically undermined liberal democratic norms while preserving the appearance of legality. The student's error is equating procedural legality with democratic legitimacy, ignoring the substantive requirements of democracy. Option A is wrong because it commits the same error the question identifies: legality of process does not guarantee democratic substance.

questions.title: UN Security Council Veto
questions.prompt: The UN Security Council has five permanent members (P5), each holding veto power over binding resolutions. A student argues this makes the Security Council the most democratically representative body in the UN system. Identify the error in the student's reasoning.

options.A: The veto system gives disproportionate power to five states regardless of population or current geopolitical weight, undermining equal representation.
options.B: The Security Council is undemocratic because it includes non-elected judges from the International Court of Justice.
options.C: Democratic representation requires that decisions be made by simple majority, which the Security Council actually uses for procedural votes.
options.D: The P5 were chosen by popular global referendum in 1945, making the system outdated but originally democratic.

questions.explanation: The P5 — USA, UK, France, Russia, and China — were designated in 1945 based on post-WWII power structures, and each can unilaterally block any substantive resolution, meaning 193 other UN member states have no equivalent influence. The top distractor (C) is wrong because while procedural votes do use simple majority, substantive decisions require P5 unanimity, and majority voting alone does not define democratic representativeness in an inter-state body.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principle
questions.prompt: Which statement BEST captures the core meaning of the 'rule of law' as used in political and legal theory?

options.A: Laws are valid only when approved by a two-thirds supermajority of elected representatives.
options.B: No individual or institution, including the government itself, is above the law, and laws are applied equally and consistently.
options.C: Legal systems must be based on written constitutions rather than unwritten conventions.
options.D: Citizens are obliged to follow every law regardless of whether it was created through a democratic process.

questions.explanation: The rule of law, articulated by theorists such as A.V. Dicey, means that law applies equally to all — rulers and ruled alike — and that government authority is constrained by law rather than arbitrary will. Option D is a common misconception: the rule of law is descriptive of legal equality, not a normative command for unconditional obedience, and it explicitly applies to governments themselves, not just citizens.

questions.title: Market Equilibrium Price
questions.prompt: In a free market, the price of a good settles where supply and demand intersect. If consumer incomes rise significantly and the good is a normal good, what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?

options.A: Price rises and equilibrium quantity rises, as higher demand shifts the demand curve rightward.
options.B: Price falls and equilibrium quantity rises, because producers compete more aggressively for wealthier consumers.
options.C: Price rises and equilibrium quantity falls, because higher incomes reduce the need to buy in bulk.
options.D: Both price and quantity remain unchanged because supply has not shifted.

questions.explanation: For a normal good, rising incomes increase consumer willingness to pay, shifting the demand curve right; with supply unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity both increase. Option D is wrong because equilibrium is determined by both curves — a rightward demand shift alone is sufficient to change price and quantity even without a supply shift.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: Thomas Hobbes described life without government as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' How does this view differ from Jean-Jacques Rousseau's conception of the natural state of humanity?

options.A: Hobbes believed humans are naturally cooperative; Rousseau believed they are naturally competitive.
options.B: Rousseau saw humans as naturally good and free, corrupted by society and inequality, whereas Hobbes saw the state of nature as dangerously conflictual.
options.C: Both agreed the state of nature was violent, but disagreed on whether a monarchy or democracy was the better solution.
options.D: Rousseau argued that governments must hold absolute power to prevent natural human aggression, unlike Hobbes who favoured limited government.

questions.explanation: Rousseau's concept of the 'noble savage' held that humans are naturally peaceful and equal, and that private property and social institutions introduced inequality and corruption — the direct opposite of Hobbes's war-of-all-against-all. Option C is wrong because Rousseau did not agree the state of nature was violent; his critique was precisely that civil society, not nature, created conflict and inequality.

questions.title: IMF Conditionality
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'The IMF gives grants to developing countries with no strings attached because its mission is to reduce global poverty.' Evaluate this claim. Which response BEST identifies the error?

options.A: The IMF does not work with developing countries at all; it exclusively assists high-income OECD nations facing currency crises.
options.B: The IMF primarily provides loans rather than grants, and attaches structural adjustment conditions such as fiscal austerity or market liberalisation.
options.C: The claim is mostly correct, but the IMF requires recipient countries to adopt a fixed exchange rate as the only condition.
options.D: The IMF provides grants, but only to countries that are members of the World Bank, making the claim partially correct.

questions.explanation: The IMF provides balance-of-payments loans, not grants, and typically requires 'conditionality' — policy reforms such as reducing government spending, privatising state enterprises, or liberalising trade — which critics argue can worsen poverty in the short term. Option C is wrong because IMF conditions vary widely and have often included moving away from fixed exchange rates, not toward them.

questions.title: GDP as Welfare Measure
questions.prompt: Why do many economists argue that GDP per capita is an insufficient measure of a population's wellbeing, even though it is widely used to compare living standards across countries?

options.A: GDP per capita overstates income because it includes government spending, which does not directly benefit citizens.
options.B: GDP per capita ignores income distribution, environmental quality, leisure time, and non-market activities like unpaid care work.
options.C: GDP per capita is calculated using purchasing power parity, which systematically favours smaller economies.
options.D: GDP per capita measures production output, which always rises faster than actual wages, creating a misleading picture.

questions.explanation: GDP per capita is an average that conceals inequality — a country where one person earns everything and others earn nothing would still show a high figure. It also excludes environmental degradation, health, education quality, and unpaid domestic labour, which all affect real wellbeing. Option A is wrong because including government spending is a deliberate feature (the G in the expenditure formula Y = C + I + G + NX), not a distortion, and it reflects real services provided to citizens.

questions.title: Civic Participation Forms
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the BEST example of direct democracy rather than representative democracy?

options.A: Citizens elect a parliament whose members then vote on whether to change the national constitution.
options.B: A president appoints judges to an independent supreme court to review legislation.
options.C: All eligible voters are asked to vote directly on a specific policy question in a national referendum.
options.D: A political party selects candidates through an internal primary election open to party members only.

questions.explanation: In direct democracy, citizens themselves make decisions on policy rather than delegating that authority to elected representatives; a national referendum is the clearest modern example. Option A is representative democracy — citizens elect intermediaries (parliament members) who then exercise decision-making power on their behalf, not the citizens themselves.

questions.title: Inflation and Purchasing Power
questions.prompt: A country experiences annual inflation of 8% while wages grow at 3% per year. What is the most accurate description of what happens to workers' real purchasing power?

options.A: Real purchasing power rises because workers are earning more money in nominal terms.
options.B: Real purchasing power is unchanged because both prices and wages are rising simultaneously.
options.C: Real purchasing power falls because prices rise faster than wages, reducing what workers can actually buy.
options.D: Real purchasing power falls only for workers who save money, not for those who spend all their income.

questions.explanation: Real purchasing power is measured by real wages (nominal wage growth minus inflation); at 3% wage growth and 8% inflation, real wages fall by approximately 5%, meaning workers can afford fewer goods and services despite earning more money. Option B is a common error — the fact that both prices and wages rise does not mean they cancel out; the relative rate of increase determines whether workers gain or lose.

questions.title: WTO Dispute Settlement
questions.prompt: Country A imposes a 40% tariff on Country B's steel exports, which Country B claims violates their bilateral trade agreement. Compare how this dispute would be handled under the WTO dispute settlement mechanism versus through direct diplomatic negotiation only.

options.A: The WTO mechanism is slower but legally binding, whereas direct negotiation is faster but relies on the goodwill of the stronger party.
options.B: Direct negotiation produces enforceable rulings, while WTO proceedings are only advisory and non-binding.
options.C: Both methods are equally effective because the WTO cannot impose any penalties beyond issuing a formal statement.
options.D: The WTO mechanism always favours larger economies because voting power is proportional to trade volume.

questions.explanation: The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body produces legally binding rulings and can authorise retaliatory tariffs if the losing party does not comply — giving smaller nations a formal avenue they would lack in pure power-based negotiation. Option B reverses the reality: WTO rulings are binding under international trade law, while direct diplomatic negotiations produce outcomes only as enforceable as the parties' political willingness to comply.

questions.title: Checks and Balances
questions.prompt: In the United States, the president can veto legislation passed by Congress, but Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers. Which political concept does this mechanism BEST illustrate?

options.A: Federalism, because power is shared between the national government and individual states.
options.B: Judicial review, because the courts can evaluate whether the president's veto is constitutional.
options.C: Checks and balances, because each branch has mechanisms to limit the power of the other branches.
options.D: Bicameralism, because two separate legislative chambers must both agree before a bill becomes law.

questions.explanation: The veto-override mechanism is a textbook example of checks and balances — the executive can restrain the legislature through the veto, and the legislature can restrain the executive through the override, preventing either branch from accumulating unchecked power. Option D describes bicameralism (the existence of two chambers), which is a structural feature of Congress but does not explain the veto-override dynamic between the executive and legislative branches.

questions.title: Comparative Advantage Trade
questions.prompt: Country X can produce 100 cars OR 200 tonnes of wheat per year. Country Y can produce 60 cars OR 180 tonnes of wheat per year. Which country has the comparative advantage in car production, and why?

options.A: Country X, because it has absolute advantage in both goods and therefore should specialise in cars.
options.B: Country X, because its opportunity cost of one car (2 tonnes of wheat) is lower than Country Y's (3 tonnes of wheat).
options.C: Country Y, because it produces cars at a lower absolute quantity, making each car relatively more valuable.
options.D: Country Y, because its opportunity cost of one car (3 tonnes of wheat) reflects greater sacrifice, indicating stronger productive commitment.

questions.explanation: Comparative advantage is determined by opportunity cost, not absolute output: Country X gives up 2 tonnes of wheat per car (200/100), while Country Y gives up 3 tonnes per car (180/60), so Country X has the lower opportunity cost and thus the comparative advantage in cars. Option A is wrong because absolute advantage (producing more overall) is irrelevant to comparative advantage — Ricardo's insight was precisely that trade benefits arise from relative cost differences, not raw productive capacity.

questions.title: Human Rights Universal Claim
questions.prompt: To what extent is the claim that human rights are 'universal' consistent with the fact that different cultures and legal systems recognise different sets of rights?

options.A: The claim is fully consistent because the UN Declaration of Human Rights was signed by every country, proving global agreement.
options.B: There is genuine tension: universality is a normative claim that rights apply to all humans by virtue of their humanity, but cultural relativists argue that rights are socially constructed and legitimately vary.
options.C: There is no tension because universal rights apply only to civil and political rights, while cultural variation is restricted to economic and social rights.
options.D: The claim is inconsistent because universality requires legal enforceability in every country, which does not currently exist.

questions.explanation: The universality of human rights is a philosophical and normative claim rooted in natural law traditions, but cultural relativism — held by many governments and scholars — argues that rights are embedded in specific cultural contexts, creating genuine philosophical tension. Option A is factually wrong: the UDHR (1948) was adopted without a unanimous vote, with eight abstentions including the Soviet Union and South Africa, and many states have since challenged specific rights on cultural or religious grounds.

questions.title: Public Goods Definition
questions.prompt: A student argues that national defence is just like any other good in a market economy and should be provided by private companies competing for customers. Which economic concept BEST explains why this argument is flawed?

options.A: National defence is a merit good, meaning individuals undervalue it but the government can correct this through subsidies.
options.B: National defence is a public good — non-excludable and non-rival — meaning markets will underprovide it due to the free-rider problem.
options.C: National defence creates negative externalities that private firms cannot price effectively, making government provision preferable.
options.D: Defence is a natural monopoly because its infrastructure costs are so high that only one provider can operate efficiently.

questions.explanation: A public good is defined by two properties: non-excludability (you cannot prevent anyone in the territory from benefiting) and non-rivalry (one person's protection does not reduce another's). These properties create a free-rider problem — individuals have no incentive to pay voluntarily — so private markets will under-supply it. Option A is wrong because a merit good is one where individuals undervalue it but it is excludable and rival (e.g., education, vaccines); the issue with defence is structural market failure due to non-excludability, not individual misvaluation.

questions.title: Electoral Systems Compared
questions.prompt: Country A uses First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) voting; Country B uses Proportional Representation (PR). A student says FPTP always produces fairer outcomes because the candidate with the most votes always wins. Identify the most significant error in this claim.

options.A: FPTP is unfair because it requires a runoff election whenever no candidate gets over 50%, wasting public resources.
options.B: FPTP can produce parliaments where a party wins a large majority of seats with a minority of the total popular vote, meaning many votes have no impact on the outcome.
options.C: FPTP is unfair because it allows multiple parties to compete, creating voter confusion and split outcomes.
options.D: FPTP is always biased toward smaller parties because single-member districts disadvantage large national parties.

questions.explanation: Under FPTP, a candidate only needs to beat all other candidates in a single constituency — not win a majority of all votes cast. This 'wasted vote' problem means parties can win commanding parliamentary majorities with 35–40% of the national vote, while parties with significant national support but diffuse geographic distribution win very few seats. Option D is wrong and is actually the reverse of reality: FPTP systematically advantages large parties with concentrated regional support and disadvantages smaller parties with broad but dispersed support.

questions.title: Globalisation and Labour
questions.prompt: What would MOST LIKELY happen to wages in a high-income country's manufacturing sector if that country removes trade barriers and allows imports of the same goods from a low-wage country?

options.A: Wages in manufacturing would rise as domestic producers compete harder to retain skilled workers.
options.B: Wages in manufacturing would fall or jobs would be lost as domestic producers face lower-cost competition they cannot match.
options.C: Wages across all sectors would rise because cheaper imports increase overall consumer purchasing power.
options.D: Manufacturing wages would remain stable because labour markets and goods markets operate independently of each other.

questions.explanation: When cheaper imports enter the market, domestic manufacturers face downward pressure on prices; to remain competitive, they typically cut costs by lowering wages, automating, or relocating production — leading to wage suppression or job losses in the affected sector. This effect is central to debates about deindustrialisation in countries like the UK and USA since the 1980s. Option C is partially true for consumers broadly (cheaper goods) but incorrectly applies that benefit to manufacturing workers specifically, who face job competition from lower-wage foreign labour.

questions.title: Monopoly Market Failure
questions.prompt: Why does a monopoly typically produce less output and charge a higher price than a perfectly competitive market for the same good?

options.A: A monopoly faces no demand curve and therefore sets price based purely on production cost plus a fixed profit margin.
options.B: Without competitive pressure, a monopoly maximises profit by restricting output to a level where it can charge a price above marginal cost.
options.C: A monopoly produces less because it lacks the economies of scale that multiple competing firms share across the industry.
options.D: Monopolies are legally required to limit output to prevent accusations of predatory pricing under competition law.

questions.explanation: A monopolist is the sole seller and thus faces the entire downward-sloping market demand curve; it maximises profit where MR = MC, which occurs at a lower quantity than the competitive equilibrium (where P = MC), allowing it to charge a higher price and capture economic profit. Option C is wrong because monopolies often have very large economies of scale — indeed, 'natural monopolies' arise precisely because average costs fall continuously with scale, making one large firm more efficient than many small ones.

questions.title: NGO Role in Global Governance
questions.prompt: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) like Amnesty International or Médecins Sans Frontières operate internationally but are not part of any government. What is the PRIMARY way NGOs influence global policy?

options.A: NGOs pass binding international laws through their consultative status at the United Nations General Assembly.
options.B: NGOs hold veto power over World Bank and IMF lending decisions that affect humanitarian conditions.
options.C: NGOs primarily influence policy through advocacy, public pressure, information campaigns, and providing expert testimony that shapes government and intergovernmental decisions.
options.D: NGOs replace government functions entirely in failed states, giving them de facto legislative authority in those regions.

questions.explanation: NGOs wield 'soft power' — they conduct research, mobilise public opinion, lobby governments, provide evidence to UN committees, and expose human rights violations, all of which create political pressure on states and international bodies without formal legal authority. Option A is wrong because NGO consultative status at the UN allows them to attend meetings and submit statements, not vote on or pass resolutions; legislative authority remains exclusively with member states.

questions.title: Taxation Types Compared
questions.prompt: A progressive tax system and a regressive tax system differ in how the tax burden is distributed across income levels. Which statement BEST describes a regressive tax?

options.A: A regressive tax takes a larger percentage of income from lower-income earners than from higher-income earners.
options.B: A regressive tax applies the same fixed amount in dollars to every taxpayer regardless of income.
options.C: A regressive tax is one where the government reduces the tax rate as the economy grows, to prevent overtaxing a prosperous population.
options.D: A regressive tax is one that decreases in absolute amount as income rises, so wealthier people pay less money overall.

questions.explanation: A regressive tax takes a higher share of income from low earners than from high earners — sales taxes and flat excise duties are classic examples, because a person earning $20,000 who pays $1,000 in sales tax loses 5% of income, while someone earning $200,000 paying the same $1,000 loses only 0.5%. Option B describes a poll tax (lump-sum tax), which is regressive in effect but is not the defining feature of a regressive tax system more broadly.

questions.title: Sovereignty and Globalisation
questions.prompt: A student claims that joining international organisations like the WTO or EU necessarily reduces a nation's sovereignty. To what extent is this claim accurate?

options.A: The claim is fully accurate: any treaty obligation means a nation has completely surrendered its sovereignty in that policy area.
options.B: The claim is partially accurate: nations voluntarily pool or constrain sovereignty in specific areas to gain cooperative benefits, but retain overall sovereignty as they can legally withdraw.
options.C: The claim is inaccurate: international organisations strengthen sovereignty by providing military and economic backing to member states.
options.D: The claim is inaccurate: sovereignty is only reduced when a country is invaded; treaty commitments are voluntary and therefore do not affect sovereignty.

questions.explanation: Pooled sovereignty is the accepted term in international relations — states cede decision-making authority in defined areas (e.g., EU single market regulations) in exchange for collective benefits, but retain the right to withdraw (as Brexit demonstrated). Option A overstates the loss: sovereignty is constrained in specific domains, not surrendered entirely, and the voluntary, revocable nature of treaty membership is what distinguishes it from conquest or subjugation.

questions.title: Authoritarian vs Democratic Systems
questions.prompt: Researchers find that a particular authoritarian country achieved faster economic growth over a 20-year period than most neighbouring democracies. A student concludes that authoritarianism is therefore superior for economic development. Which is the STRONGEST objection to this reasoning?

options.A: Economic growth was not high in that country because GDP statistics from authoritarian states are always falsified.
options.B: The conclusion commits a hasty generalisation: one case over 20 years cannot establish that authoritarianism causes better economic outcomes across all contexts, and other variables are ignored.
options.C: The comparison is invalid because neighbouring countries have different currencies, making growth comparisons meaningless.
options.D: Economic growth is irrelevant to evaluating political systems because quality of governance should only be measured by elections held.

questions.explanation: Drawing a universal causal conclusion from a single case study is a hasty generalisation — the correlation could reflect natural resource endowments, geographic advantages, a specific leader's policies, or global commodity prices rather than regime type. Cross-national studies (e.g., Acemoglu and Robinson's work) find no consistent causal link between authoritarianism and growth. Option A is too strong and factually problematic — some authoritarian states do grow rapidly (e.g., South Korea in the 1970s, China since 1980), and dismissing all such data as falsified is not a valid methodological objection.

questions.title: Fiscal vs Monetary Policy
questions.prompt: During a recession, a government increases its spending on public infrastructure while the central bank lowers interest rates. Which pair of terms CORRECTLY labels these two policy tools?

options.A: Both are examples of monetary policy, because they both aim to stimulate economic growth.
options.B: Increased government spending is fiscal policy; lowering interest rates is monetary policy.
options.C: Increased government spending is monetary policy; lowering interest rates is supply-side policy.
options.D: Increased government spending is fiscal policy; lowering interest rates is also fiscal policy because it affects the government's borrowing cost.

questions.explanation: Fiscal policy refers to government decisions on taxation and public expenditure, implemented by the finance ministry or treasury. Monetary policy refers to decisions about money supply and interest rates, typically made by an independent central bank (e.g., the Federal Reserve or Bank of England). Option D is wrong because although lower interest rates do reduce government borrowing costs, interest rate decisions are the domain of the central bank's monetary policy mandate, not fiscal policy.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: Unlike domestic law, international law lacks a single global police force to enforce it. What is the PRIMARY mechanism through which international law achieves compliance among sovereign states?

options.A: The UN Secretary-General can order military action against any state that violates international law without a Security Council vote.
options.B: Compliance depends on a combination of reciprocity, reputational costs, economic sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and in some cases UN Security Council-authorised enforcement.
options.C: The International Court of Justice has a standing army that can arrest heads of state who violate international law.
options.D: Compliance is guaranteed because all states sign binding treaties that automatically trigger financial penalties for any violation.

questions.explanation: International law operates in an anarchic system (no world government) and relies on self-interest mechanisms: states comply because reciprocity makes cooperation beneficial, reputation matters for future negotiations, and economic or diplomatic sanctions can impose real costs. The ICJ can adjudicate disputes but has no enforcement power of its own; enforcement requires voluntary compliance or Security Council action. Option C is false — the ICJ issues judgments and advisory opinions but has no police or military capacity.

questions.title: Unitary vs Federal States
questions.prompt: In a unitary state, the central government holds supreme authority and may grant or revoke powers to regional bodies. In a federal state, the constitution divides powers between central and regional governments. Which scenario BEST illustrates a feature unique to federalism?

options.A: The national parliament passes a law on immigration that overrides any conflicting local council policies.
options.B: A state government introduces its own income tax rate that the national government cannot legally abolish without amending the constitution.
options.C: Regional governors are appointed by the national president and can be removed if they disagree with central policy.
options.D: The national government devolves healthcare administration to regional councils but retains the right to reclaim it at any time.

questions.explanation: In a federal system, the division of powers is entrenched in the constitution, meaning neither level of government can unilaterally abolish the other's powers — this constitutional guarantee of regional authority is the defining feature of federalism (e.g., US states levying their own income taxes). Option D describes devolution, a feature of unitary states like the UK, where power is delegated from the centre but not constitutionally guaranteed and can be rescinded by parliamentary majority.

questions.title: Market Externalities
questions.prompt: A chemical factory legally dumps waste into a river, harming fishermen and local residents who use the water but receive no compensation. This situation is a classic example of which economic concept?

options.A: A positive externality, because the factory's production creates employment that benefits the surrounding community.
options.B: A negative externality, because the factory imposes costs on third parties who are not part of the market transaction between the factory and its customers.
options.C: A public goods problem, because clean water is non-excludable and non-rival and therefore the market cannot price it.
options.D: A moral hazard, because the factory takes excessive risk knowing the government will clean up pollution at public expense.

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when the production or consumption of a good imposes costs on parties external to the transaction without compensation — the factory's customers pay the market price but the fishermen and residents bear the pollution costs unpaid. This leads to overproduction relative to the socially optimal level. Option C is related but incorrect: while clean water has public good characteristics, the concept being illustrated here is the market's failure to internalise third-party costs (externalities), not the non-rivalry/non-excludability of water itself.

questions.title: Media and Democratic Accountability
questions.prompt: A free and independent press is often called the 'fourth estate' in democratic theory. What is the PRIMARY democratic function this label is meant to highlight?

options.A: The media has formal legislative power to propose bills, alongside the executive, judiciary, and legislature.
options.B: The media acts as an unofficial watchdog — investigating, reporting on, and scrutinising government and powerful institutions to keep them accountable to the public.
options.C: The media is the fourth branch of government because it is funded by the state and therefore subject to the same constitutional checks as the other three branches.
options.D: The press holds the fourth-highest formal authority in democratic systems, below the executive, legislative, and judicial branches.

questions.explanation: The 'fourth estate' is a metaphor, not a constitutional designation — it refers to the press's informal but vital democratic role in holding government to account through investigative journalism and public information, complementing the formal separation of powers. Option C is wrong because the independence of the press from state funding and control is precisely what makes it capable of fulfilling this watchdog role; state-funded media answerable to government would undermine rather than embody the fourth estate concept.

questions.title: UN Security Council Veto
questions.prompt: The UN Security Council has five permanent members, each holding veto power over binding resolutions. A student claims this arrangement ensures the most powerful nations always act in the global interest. Identify the core flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Veto power means permanent members can block resolutions that threaten their own national interests, not necessarily global welfare.
options.B: The veto is only symbolic because the General Assembly can override it with a two-thirds majority.
options.C: Permanent membership rotates every decade, so no single nation dominates long-term.
options.D: The Security Council only handles economic disputes, not political or military ones.

questions.explanation: Permanent members have used the veto to protect allies or national interests — for example, the US has vetoed resolutions critical of Israel, and Russia has vetoed resolutions on Syria — demonstrating that the veto serves national rather than global interests. Option B is wrong because the General Assembly cannot override Security Council veto decisions on peace and security matters; its resolutions are non-binding.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principle
questions.prompt: Which statement BEST captures the core meaning of 'the rule of law' as a principle of political organisation?

options.A: Laws must be written by professional legal experts to be considered valid.
options.B: The government itself is subject to the law and no individual or institution is above it.
options.C: Citizens must obey every law passed by their government without question.
options.D: Courts have the power to create new laws when existing ones are unclear.

questions.explanation: The rule of law means that legal authority applies equally to rulers and citizens — as established in foundational documents like Magna Carta (1215) — preventing arbitrary use of power. Option C confuses unconditional obedience with the rule of law; the concept actually protects citizens from unjust laws by holding governments accountable to constitutional limits.

questions.title: Market Price Signals
questions.prompt: In a free market economy, the price of a product rises sharply after a natural disaster destroys much of its supply. What role does this price increase play in the market system?

options.A: It signals producers to increase supply and encourages consumers to reduce demand, helping to restore equilibrium.
options.B: It shows the government should immediately impose price controls to protect consumers.
options.C: It permanently raises the cost of that good because production costs have risen.
options.D: It signals that the good is now inferior and consumers will switch to substitute goods only.

questions.explanation: Rising prices act as signals in a market economy: higher profits attract new producers and incentivise existing ones to increase output, while consumers are nudged to economise or find substitutes, moving the market back toward equilibrium. Option D is wrong because a price rise due to supply shock does not make a good 'inferior' in the economic sense — inferior goods are those whose demand falls as income rises, which is a separate concept.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: Thomas Hobbes and Jean-Jacques Rousseau both developed social contract theories, yet they reached very different conclusions about government. What is the key difference between their positions?

options.A: Hobbes believed humans are naturally cooperative, while Rousseau believed they are naturally competitive.
options.B: Hobbes argued that a powerful sovereign is needed to prevent chaos, while Rousseau argued that the general will of the people should guide government.
options.C: Hobbes supported democracy, while Rousseau supported absolute monarchy as the most natural system.
options.D: Both agreed on the need for strong central authority but disagreed only on how leaders should be elected.

questions.explanation: Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), argued that without a strong sovereign life would be 'nasty, brutish, and short,' justifying near-absolute authority. Rousseau, in The Social Contract (1762), argued that legitimate government must express the 'general will' of the people, making sovereignty rest with the community. Option A reverses their positions — Hobbes saw humans as naturally self-interested and conflicting, not cooperative.

questions.title: IMF Conditionality
questions.prompt: Critics of IMF loan programmes argue that the conditions attached — such as reducing government spending and privatising public services — can harm the poorest citizens of borrowing countries. Which reasoning BEST supports this critique?

options.A: IMF conditions prevent countries from ever borrowing money again in the future.
options.B: Cutting public spending typically reduces access to healthcare and education for low-income populations who depend most on state services.
options.C: Privatisation always leads to lower quality services regardless of the sector involved.
options.D: The IMF charges interest rates so high that repayment is mathematically impossible.

questions.explanation: Austerity conditions tied to IMF loans — such as those applied in Greece after 2010 or in Sub-Saharan African countries in the 1980s — have been documented to reduce access to public healthcare and education disproportionately affecting low-income groups. Option C overstates the case; privatisation outcomes vary significantly by sector, context, and regulatory environment, making a universal claim unsupportable.

questions.title: Electoral Systems Compared
questions.prompt: Country A uses a First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) electoral system. Country B uses Proportional Representation (PR). A student argues that FPTP is always fairer because it produces clear winners. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct because clear winners mean stronger, more decisive governments that serve citizens better.
options.B: The student's claim is flawed because FPTP can result in a party winning a majority of seats with a minority of total votes, misrepresenting voter preferences.
options.C: The student is correct because PR systems only work in countries with more than 50 political parties.
options.D: The student's claim is flawed because FPTP systems always produce coalition governments, which are less stable.

questions.explanation: In the 2015 UK general election, the Conservative Party won a majority of seats with only 36.9% of the popular vote, illustrating how FPTP can distort representation — a core fairness concern. Option D is wrong; it is PR systems, not FPTP, that typically produce coalition governments, since FPTP tends to favour two dominant parties.

questions.title: Comparative Advantage Basics
questions.prompt: Country X can produce 10 cars OR 20 tonnes of wheat per year. Country Y can produce 4 cars OR 16 tonnes of wheat per year. According to the principle of comparative advantage, which specialisation pattern maximises total output?

options.A: Country X should specialise in wheat; Country Y should specialise in cars.
options.B: Country X should specialise in cars; Country Y should specialise in wheat.
options.C: Both countries should produce equal amounts of both goods to avoid dependency.
options.D: Country X should specialise in both goods since it has an absolute advantage in each.

questions.explanation: Country X's opportunity cost of 1 car is 2 tonnes of wheat, while Country Y's opportunity cost of 1 car is 4 tonnes of wheat — so Country X has the comparative advantage in cars. Country Y has a lower opportunity cost in wheat (0.25 cars per tonne vs. 0.5 for Country X), so it should specialise there. Option A reverses the correct specialisation, confusing opportunity costs.

questions.title: Checks and Balances
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Checks and balances slow down government so much that they actually make democracy less effective.' Which response BEST challenges this view?

options.A: Speed of government action is the most important measure of democratic effectiveness.
options.B: Checks and balances are only relevant in presidential systems and do not apply to parliamentary democracies.
options.C: Deliberate slowness prevents hasty or unconstitutional decisions, protecting long-term rights over short-term efficiency.
options.D: Effectiveness in democracy is best measured by economic growth, which is unrelated to government structure.

questions.explanation: Checks and balances — such as judicial review, legislative override, and executive veto — exist specifically to prevent the abuse of power that rapid, unchecked decision-making can enable, as seen in historical examples of authoritarian consolidation. Option A is wrong because efficiency without accountability is the hallmark of authoritarian, not democratic, systems — making speed an inappropriate metric for democratic effectiveness.

questions.title: Public Goods Definition
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the BEST example of a public good as defined in economics, and why?

options.A: A toll motorway, because the government built it using public money.
options.B: National defence, because it is non-excludable and non-rivalrous — no citizen can be excluded and one person's protection does not reduce another's.
options.C: A public swimming pool, because anyone can use it regardless of income.
options.D: Electricity from the national grid, because it is provided by a state-owned company.

questions.explanation: A public good in economics must be both non-excludable (impossible to prevent people from using it) and non-rivalrous (one person's use does not diminish supply for others) — national defence fits both criteria precisely. A toll motorway is excludable (non-payers can be barred), so option A fails the definition; a public swimming pool is rivalrous when crowded, so option C also fails.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitary States
questions.prompt: What is the defining structural difference between a federal state and a unitary state?

options.A: Federal states always have elected presidents, while unitary states have prime ministers.
options.B: In a federal state, sovereign power is constitutionally divided between central and regional governments; in a unitary state, ultimate authority rests with the central government.
options.C: Unitary states have written constitutions, while federal states rely on unwritten traditions.
options.D: Federal states cannot be monarchies, while unitary states can take any form of government.

questions.explanation: In federal systems like the USA, Germany, or Australia, the constitution explicitly allocates powers to both national and sub-national levels, which cannot be removed by the centre alone. Unitary states like France or the UK concentrate sovereign authority at the centre, even if they devolve some administrative functions. Option A is factually incorrect — Germany is a federal republic with a chancellor, not a president as head of government.

questions.title: WTO Dispute Settlement
questions.prompt: The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) is described as 'the cornerstone of the rules-based trading system.' What makes it distinct from simply negotiating bilateral trade agreements between countries?

options.A: The DSB can impose military sanctions on countries that break trade rules.
options.B: It provides a neutral, binding arbitration process governed by agreed rules, reducing the advantage larger economies have in direct negotiations.
options.C: Bilateral negotiations are illegal under international law, so the DSB is the only permitted mechanism.
options.D: The DSB creates new trade laws, whereas bilateral agreements can only modify existing ones.

questions.explanation: The WTO's DSB operates under agreed rules and an appellate process, allowing small nations to successfully challenge major economies — for example, Antigua won a ruling against the USA over online gambling restrictions in 2004. Option A is wrong because the WTO has no military authority; its enforcement relies on authorising retaliatory tariffs, not sanctions.

questions.title: Civil Society Role
questions.prompt: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs), trade unions, and community associations are all examples of civil society. Why do political theorists consider a strong civil society important for democracy?

options.A: Civil society organisations replace elected governments when those governments become corrupt.
options.B: They provide channels for citizen participation, hold governments accountable, and protect individual rights outside formal political structures.
options.C: Civil society primarily serves economic functions by filling gaps in the market left by private companies.
options.D: Strong civil society guarantees that elections will always be free and fair.

questions.explanation: Civil society acts as an intermediary between citizens and the state, enabling advocacy, watchdog functions, and collective voice — as theorised by Alexis de Tocqueville, who observed that voluntary associations in America strengthened democratic culture. Option A is wrong; civil society organisations cannot replace elected governments — they operate alongside them, not as substitutes for legitimate political authority.

questions.title: Inflation and Central Banks
questions.prompt: A country's central bank raises interest rates in response to rising inflation. Which sequence of effects BEST explains the economic logic behind this decision?

options.A: Higher interest rates → government earns more tax revenue → public spending increases → inflation falls.
options.B: Higher interest rates → borrowing becomes more expensive → consumer and business spending falls → demand-pull inflation decreases.
options.C: Higher interest rates → currency depreciates → imports become cheaper → cost-push inflation decreases.
options.D: Higher interest rates → banks hold more reserves → money supply automatically doubles → prices stabilise.

questions.explanation: Raising interest rates increases the cost of borrowing, which discourages consumer credit spending and business investment, reducing aggregate demand — the primary driver of demand-pull inflation. This is the standard monetary policy transmission mechanism used by central banks such as the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. Option C is wrong because higher domestic interest rates typically cause currency appreciation (not depreciation), as foreign capital flows in seeking better returns.

questions.title: Human Rights Universality
questions.prompt: Some governments argue that human rights are culturally relative — meaning different societies may legitimately apply different standards. Which argument BEST supports the counter-position that human rights are universal?

options.A: Western nations have always had superior political systems, so their rights frameworks should apply globally.
options.B: If rights can be dismissed as culturally inappropriate, governments gain unlimited power to abuse citizens by claiming local custom.
options.C: Cultural relativism in rights is acceptable as long as it only applies to economic and social rights, not civil rights.
options.D: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was signed by every nation in 1948, making cultural objections legally invalid.

questions.explanation: The universalist position, articulated by philosophers like Martha Nussbaum through her capabilities approach, argues that permitting cultural exceptions creates a tool for authoritarian governments to justify oppression — the UDHR itself was designed to establish a floor of protections beyond which no cultural argument can reach. Option D is factually wrong; the UDHR was not signed as a binding treaty — it is a declaration, and not all states endorsed it without reservation.

questions.title: GDP as Welfare Measure
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A country with a higher GDP per capita is always better off than one with lower GDP per capita.' To what extent is this claim valid?

options.A: Fully valid — GDP per capita directly measures average citizen wellbeing by accounting for health, education, and income equally.
options.B: Largely invalid — GDP per capita ignores income inequality, environmental quality, and access to services, which significantly affect wellbeing.
options.C: Partially valid — GDP per capita is the only internationally comparable measure, so despite its flaws it should be used exclusively.
options.D: Fully valid — countries with higher GDP always score higher on all development indicators including health and education.

questions.explanation: GDP per capita measures average output per person but ignores distribution — a country could have high GDP driven by a wealthy elite while most citizens remain poor, as illustrated by the Gini coefficient gap visible in countries like Brazil or South Africa. The UN's Human Development Index (HDI) was specifically created to supplement GDP by incorporating health and education indicators. Option D is empirically false; the USA has very high GDP per capita but lower life expectancy than several countries with lower GDP.

questions.title: Separation of Church and State
questions.prompt: The principle of secularism in government holds that religious institutions should be separate from state authority. Which of the following BEST explains why many modern democracies adopt this principle?

options.A: Secular states forbid citizens from practising religion in private, ensuring uniform social values.
options.B: Separating religious and state authority protects both religious minorities and non-believers from laws based on one group's theological beliefs.
options.C: Secularism ensures that religious leaders can advise governments on moral matters without holding official positions.
options.D: Modern democracies adopted secularism primarily to increase economic productivity by reducing religious observance.

questions.explanation: Secularism, as articulated by John Stuart Mill and later enshrined in documents like the First Amendment to the US Constitution, prevents any single religious doctrine from being imposed through law on a diverse citizenry — protecting pluralism and individual conscience. Option A fundamentally misrepresents secularism; it protects freedom of private religious practice rather than restricting it.

questions.title: Negative vs Positive Rights
questions.prompt: Philosophers distinguish between 'negative rights' (freedoms from interference) and 'positive rights' (entitlements requiring active provision). Which pair BEST illustrates this distinction?

options.A: The right to vote (negative) and the right to free speech (positive).
options.B: The right to be free from torture (negative) and the right to free public education (positive).
options.C: The right to own property (negative) and the right to a fair trial (positive).
options.D: The right to free education (negative) and the right to free speech (positive).

questions.explanation: Freedom from torture is a negative right — it requires only that the state refrain from a harmful action. The right to free public education is a positive right — it requires the state to actively provide a service, allocate resources, and build institutions. Option A reverses the categories incorrectly; the right to vote actually requires active state infrastructure (polling stations, registration), making it closer to a positive right.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt: Garrett Hardin's 'Tragedy of the Commons' describes a situation where individuals, acting in their own rational self-interest, collectively deplete a shared resource. Which real-world scenario is the CLOSEST example of this concept?

options.A: A government nationalising a private company to prevent monopoly pricing.
options.B: Overfishing of international waters where no single country owns the ocean, leading to stock collapse.
options.C: A company raising its prices because a competitor has left the market.
options.D: Citizens refusing to pay taxes because they disagree with government spending priorities.

questions.explanation: International fisheries — especially in open ocean zones — are a textbook example of the Tragedy of the Commons: each fishing nation benefits from maximum catch while sharing the cost of depletion with all others, resulting in collective overexploitation as seen in the collapse of Grand Banks cod stocks by the 1990s. Option D describes a free-rider problem in public goods provision, which is related but distinct — the commons problem specifically involves a rivalrous shared resource being depleted, not a non-rivalrous public good.

questions.title: Judicial Independence
questions.prompt: Why is judicial independence — the principle that judges must be free from political pressure — considered essential to a functioning democracy?

options.A: It ensures judges can create new laws to fill gaps when the legislature is too slow to act.
options.B: Without it, courts could become tools of whoever holds political power, unable to protect citizens' rights against the state itself.
options.C: It prevents any citizen from challenging government decisions in court, maintaining social order.
options.D: Independent judges are more efficient because they do not need to consult elected officials before ruling.

questions.explanation: Judicial independence is necessary for courts to rule against the executive or legislature — as the US Supreme Court did in Marbury v. Madison (1803) establishing judicial review. If judges were politically appointed and removable at will, governments could stack courts to validate abuses of power. Option A misrepresents judicial independence; judges interpret and apply laws but do not have a general mandate to create legislation — that function belongs to the legislature.

questions.title: Globalisation and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Economic globalisation has made national sovereignty meaningless because multinational corporations are more powerful than most governments.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully valid — no government can regulate a multinational corporation operating across borders.
options.B: The claim is fully invalid — corporations have no influence on government policy in any country.
options.C: The claim overstates the case; governments retain significant regulatory powers and sovereignty, though globalisation does constrain some policy choices.
options.D: The claim is valid only for developing countries; all developed nations maintain complete sovereignty regardless of globalisation.

questions.explanation: While large MNCs such as Apple or ExxonMobil have revenues exceeding the GDP of many nations, states retain sovereign powers including taxation, regulation, and legal jurisdiction — the EU's €13 billion tax demand against Apple in Ireland (2016) demonstrates governments actively exercising authority over MNCs. Option A is an exaggeration; regulatory frameworks, international agreements, and national laws continue to constrain corporate behaviour significantly.

questions.title: Propaganda and Media Literacy
questions.prompt: A government-controlled broadcaster repeatedly describes political opponents as 'enemies of the nation' without providing evidence of wrongdoing. Which concept from media and political theory does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Agenda-setting theory, because the broadcaster chooses which topics to cover.
options.B: The use of propaganda through dehumanising language to delegitimise political opposition and manufacture consent for authoritarian control.
options.C: The marketplace of ideas, because citizens can still access alternative viewpoints online.
options.D: Yellow journalism, because the broadcaster is exaggerating stories to sell advertising space.

questions.explanation: Describing opponents as 'enemies of the nation' without evidence is a classic propaganda technique — dehumanisation — identified by scholars like Jacques Ellul and used historically in Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia to suppress political opposition and manufacture public consent. Option A describes agenda-setting theory, which concerns which topics receive media attention, not the use of emotional language to delegitimise opponents — a different mechanism.

questions.title: Collective Bargaining Rights
questions.prompt: Trade unions negotiate wages and working conditions on behalf of all workers in a sector, rather than each worker negotiating individually. What is the PRIMARY economic rationale for this collective approach?

options.A: It allows unions to fix prices for goods and services in the sector, maximising worker income.
options.B: Individual workers have much less bargaining power than employers; collective action corrects this power imbalance and can raise wages above the monopsony level.
options.C: Collective bargaining is required by WTO regulations in all member countries to prevent wage dumping.
options.D: It allows governments to intervene directly in private contracts to set wages efficiently.

questions.explanation: In labour markets where employers have significant market power (monopsony), individual workers face a take-it-or-leave-it wage offer; collective bargaining restores negotiating balance, and economic research — including work by economists like Alan Krueger — shows union presence is associated with reduced wage inequality. Option A is wrong; trade unions negotiate wages (a price of labour), not product prices — conflating these would make unions illegal price-fixing cartels under competition law.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: Unlike domestic law, international law lacks a single enforcing body with the power to compel sovereign states to comply with rulings. What does this reveal about the nature of the international system?

options.A: International law is entirely ineffective and should be replaced by bilateral agreements only.
options.B: The international system is anarchic in the structural sense — states remain the primary sovereign actors with no overarching authority above them.
options.C: The UN General Assembly can impose binding sanctions on any state that violates international law.
options.D: International law only applies to non-governmental organisations and multinational corporations, not to states.

questions.explanation: In international relations theory, 'anarchy' refers not to chaos but to the absence of a supreme authority above states — a foundational concept in realist and liberal IR theory as articulated by Kenneth Waltz. Compliance with international law depends on state consent, reputation, reciprocity, and collective pressure rather than centralised enforcement. Option C is wrong; the UN General Assembly passes non-binding resolutions — only the Security Council can impose binding Chapter VII sanctions.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Features
questions.prompt: Which combination of features BEST characterises a mixed economy, distinguishing it from both a pure market economy and a centrally planned economy?

options.A: All prices are set by the government, but private ownership of property is permitted.
options.B: Markets allocate most goods and services, but the government intervenes to provide public goods, correct market failures, and redistribute income.
options.C: The government owns all major industries but allows free international trade without tariffs.
options.D: Private firms compete freely with no government regulation, while the state manages only the military and foreign policy.

questions.explanation: A mixed economy, as seen in most modern democracies including France, Sweden, and Canada, combines private market mechanisms with government intervention in areas like healthcare, education, competition regulation, and welfare — addressing market failures that a pure market cannot correct. Option D describes a minimalist or laissez-faire economy, not a mixed one — in mixed economies, government regulation extends well beyond defence and diplomacy.

questions.title: Authoritarian vs Democratic Governance
questions.prompt: Both authoritarian and democratic governments claim to act in the interest of the people. What is the most fundamental structural feature that distinguishes a democratic government from an authoritarian one?

options.A: Democratic governments are always economically more successful than authoritarian ones.
options.B: Authoritarian governments are more stable because leaders do not face regular electoral challenges.
options.C: Democratic governments derive legitimacy from free, fair, and regular competitive elections with genuine transfer of power possible.
options.D: Democratic governments always have written constitutions, while authoritarian states always operate without any legal framework.

questions.explanation: The defining structural feature of democracy is accountable governance through free elections where incumbents can genuinely lose power — as codified by political scientists like Robert Dahl in his concept of 'polyarchy.' Authoritarian systems may hold elections but they are neither free nor genuinely competitive. Option D is wrong; several authoritarian states have written constitutions (e.g., China's 1982 constitution) — the presence of a constitution does not guarantee democratic governance.

questions.title: Comparative Advantage vs Absolute
questions.prompt: Country A can produce both cars and rice more efficiently than Country B. A student concludes that Country A should produce both goods and not trade with Country B. Evaluate this claim. Which response BEST identifies the flaw in the student's reasoning?

options.A: The student is correct — a country with absolute advantage in both goods gains nothing from trade.
options.B: The student ignores comparative advantage: Country B may still produce one good at a lower opportunity cost, making specialisation and trade mutually beneficial.
options.C: The student is wrong because trade is always beneficial regardless of production efficiency.
options.D: The student overlooks that Country A lacks the infrastructure to produce both goods simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Comparative advantage, developed by David Ricardo, shows that even if one country is absolutely more efficient, both countries gain if each specialises in the good with the lower opportunity cost — total output rises. Option A confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage, a very common misconception among students who conflate the two distinct concepts.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principles
questions.prompt: A government passes a law that applies only to political opponents of the ruling party, exempting its own members from the same penalties. To what extent does this scenario undermine the rule of law, and which principle is MOST directly violated?

options.A: It partially undermines rule of law because the law was still formally passed through parliament.
options.B: It does not undermine rule of law because a legitimate legislature approved the measure.
options.C: It fundamentally undermines rule of law by violating equality before the law — a core principle requiring laws to apply equally to all persons.
options.D: It undermines rule of law only if the courts later strike the law down as unconstitutional.

questions.explanation: The rule of law requires, as A.V. Dicey articulated, that no person is above the law and that laws apply equally to all — a selective law targeting opponents directly violates this equality principle. Options A and B both make the error of equating formal legislative process with legitimacy, ignoring that procedural passage does not satisfy substantive rule-of-law requirements.

questions.title: Market Failure and Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally discharges pollutants into a river, harming fishing communities downstream who have no legal agreement with the factory. A student claims the free market will solve this problem because the factory will eventually pay compensation voluntarily. Which response BEST challenges this claim?

options.A: The student is correct — reputational damage will force the factory to internalise the cost.
options.B: The student ignores negative externalities: the factory has no market incentive to compensate unless compelled, because the cost is borne by third parties outside the transaction.
options.C: The student is correct because property rights, once assigned to the fishing communities, automatically resolve pollution disputes.
options.D: The student is wrong because factories are legally prohibited from all river discharge under international law.

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a third party bears costs not reflected in the market price — the factory's profit motive gives it no incentive to compensate those outside the transaction. Option C misapplies the Coase Theorem, which requires well-defined property rights and low transaction costs — conditions rarely met in diffuse pollution cases.

questions.title: UN Security Council Structure
questions.prompt: The UN Security Council has five permanent members, each holding veto power over binding resolutions. A student argues this structure makes the UN more effective because powerful nations are more likely to enforce decisions they cannot be outvoted on. Which is the STRONGEST counter-argument to this view?

options.A: The veto undermines effectiveness because it allows any permanent member to block action even when a clear global consensus exists, as seen during Cold War deadlocks.
options.B: The counter-argument fails because without the veto, powerful nations would simply leave the UN.
options.C: The student is correct — the veto ensures all five major powers are always aligned before action is taken.
options.D: The veto is irrelevant because the General Assembly can override Security Council decisions by a two-thirds majority.

questions.explanation: During the Cold War, the USSR used its veto over 100 times, paralyzing Security Council action on numerous crises — demonstrating concretely how the veto blocks collective action even with broad support. Option D is factually incorrect: the General Assembly cannot override binding Security Council resolutions; it can only make non-binding recommendations.

questions.title: Social Contract and Rousseau
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that legitimate political authority rests on a 'general will' — the collective interest of all citizens — rather than on majority vote alone. How does this concept differ from simple majority-rule democracy?

options.A: They are identical — Rousseau defined the general will as whatever the majority votes for.
options.B: The general will represents the common good of the whole community, which may differ from the sum of individual preferences; majority decisions could still violate the general will if they serve only sectional interests.
options.C: Rousseau rejected democracy entirely and preferred rule by an enlightened monarch guided by reason.
options.D: The general will applies only to direct democracies and is irrelevant to representative systems.

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished between the 'will of all' (aggregated individual preferences) and the 'general will' (the common good), arguing that majority decisions could still betray the community if driven by private interest. Option A is a classic misreading — Rousseau explicitly warned that the will of all is not the same as the general will.

questions.title: IMF Conditionality Debate
questions.prompt: Critics argue that IMF structural adjustment programmes — which require recipient countries to cut public spending and privatise state industries — worsen inequality even while stabilising currencies. Synthesise the economic and social trade-offs this tension reveals.

options.A: There is no trade-off — fiscal austerity always produces both economic stability and improved social outcomes.
options.B: The trade-off is only short-term; social spending cuts have no lasting effect on inequality.
options.C: Austerity can restore macroeconomic stability and investor confidence, but reduced social spending disproportionately harms low-income populations, potentially deepening long-run inequality.
options.D: The IMF's primary goal is reducing inequality, so social spending cuts would never be required under its programmes.

questions.explanation: Evidence from IMF programmes in the 1980s–90s, including in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America, showed that fiscal austerity reduced deficits but also cut education and health budgets, widening inequality — a documented tension in development economics. Option A is empirically wrong and ignores distributional effects that economic literature consistently identifies.

questions.title: Civic Participation and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: In a country where 30% of eligible voters participate in elections, the winning party claims a strong democratic mandate. A student argues that low voter turnout does not affect the legitimacy of the result. To what extent is this argument convincing?

options.A: Fully convincing — electoral legitimacy depends solely on following correct procedures, not on turnout levels.
options.B: Partially convincing — procedural legitimacy is maintained, but low turnout raises questions about whether the government's decisions reflect the broader population's preferences.
options.C: Not convincing at all — any election below 50% turnout is constitutionally invalid in all democratic systems.
options.D: Fully convincing — non-voters implicitly consent to any outcome by choosing not to participate.

questions.explanation: Political theorists distinguish procedural legitimacy (following electoral rules) from substantive legitimacy (reflecting population preferences); at 30% turnout, a winning party may represent only 15–20% of eligible voters, weakening its claim to a broad mandate. Option D relies on the flawed 'tacit consent' argument — political philosophers like Hanna Pitkin have shown that non-participation does not constitute genuine consent.

questions.title: Globalisation and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: When a country joins the World Trade Organization, it agrees to have trade disputes resolved by WTO panels rather than its own courts. A student claims this arrangement proves globalisation inevitably destroys national sovereignty. Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — ceding any dispute mechanism is an absolute loss of sovereignty.
