options.B: The claim is overstated — nations voluntarily pool sovereignty through treaty to gain reciprocal market access, retaining the right to exit the agreement and to legislate domestically on non-trade matters.
options.C: The claim is correct because WTO membership is compulsory for all recognised states.
options.D: The claim is wrong because WTO panels have no enforcement power whatsoever.

questions.explanation: Sovereignty pooling — where states voluntarily delegate specific competencies to international bodies in exchange for mutual benefits — is distinct from sovereignty destruction; the WTO's 164 members joined by treaty and can withdraw. Option A conflates partial, voluntary delegation with total loss of sovereignty, ignoring the consensual and reciprocal nature of international agreements.

questions.title: Monetary Policy Tools
questions.prompt: A central bank raises its benchmark interest rate from 2% to 5%. What is the PRIMARY intended effect of this action, and which sector of the economy is MOST immediately affected?

options.A: To increase government tax revenue; the public sector is most immediately affected.
options.B: To reduce inflation by making borrowing more expensive, thereby cooling consumer spending and investment; credit-dependent sectors like housing are most immediately affected.
options.C: To strengthen exports by making domestic goods cheaper abroad; the manufacturing export sector is most immediately affected.
options.D: To increase the money supply so that businesses can expand production; the retail sector is most immediately affected.

questions.explanation: Raising interest rates is a contractionary monetary policy tool: higher borrowing costs reduce consumer loans and mortgage affordability, dampening demand and cooling inflation — the housing market typically reacts fastest, as seen after US Federal Reserve rate hikes in 2022–23. Option C reverses the mechanism — higher domestic interest rates typically strengthen the currency, making exports more expensive abroad, not cheaper.

questions.title: Federalism and Regional Autonomy
questions.prompt: In a federal system, a regional government passes an environmental law that is stricter than national standards. The national government argues this creates unfair competitive disadvantages for businesses. Which principle BEST explains why federal systems intentionally allow this kind of tension?

options.A: Federalism assumes regional governments always make better decisions than national governments.
options.B: Subsidiarity — the principle that decisions should be made at the lowest competent level of government — allows regions to respond to local priorities, acting as policy laboratories even if this creates variation.
options.C: Federal systems require all laws to be uniform, so regional variation would be unconstitutional in any true federation.
options.D: The tension exists only because federal systems are poorly designed and should eventually be replaced by unitary states.

questions.explanation: Subsidiarity, a core principle of federalism also enshrined in the EU's Treaty of Maastricht, holds that governance should occur at the most local effective level, enabling regional experimentation — US states have historically pioneered policies later adopted nationally. Option C is factually incorrect — federal systems by definition distribute powers between levels, explicitly allowing legislative variation within constitutional limits.

questions.title: Supply, Demand and Price Controls
questions.prompt: A government sets a maximum rent price (rent ceiling) below the market equilibrium price to make housing affordable. Identify the likely economic consequence that critics of this policy most commonly highlight.

options.A: Landlords will increase rents above the ceiling to compensate for lost profits.
options.B: Housing supply will decrease in the long run as landlords exit the market or reduce maintenance, potentially worsening housing shortages.
options.C: Demand for housing will fall because lower rents signal lower quality to consumers.
options.D: The government will earn higher tax revenues because more citizens can now afford housing.

questions.explanation: A rent ceiling below equilibrium creates excess demand (shortage) and discourages new construction and maintenance — a phenomenon documented in New York City and Stockholm, where rent controls contributed to housing shortages over decades. Option A is incorrect because a ceiling is a legal maximum landlords cannot legally exceed, though black markets may emerge — critics' primary concern is the supply reduction, not illegal price-setting.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge and Bias
questions.prompt: A government commissions its own economists to evaluate whether its economic policy has succeeded. A student reviewing this report argues that a government-commissioned study is just as reliable as an independent peer-reviewed study. Which ToK-informed response BEST challenges this claim?

options.A: The student is correct — professional economists follow objective methods regardless of who funds the research.
options.B: The student overlooks confirmation bias and motivated reasoning: researchers funded by institutions with an interest in a particular outcome may unconsciously — or deliberately — frame findings favourably, undermining epistemic objectivity.
options.C: The student is correct because government economists have superior access to data, making their studies more reliable.
options.D: The student is wrong only if the economists used qualitative rather than quantitative methods.

questions.explanation: In ToK terms, the knower's perspective — including institutional interests — shapes knowledge production; peer review by independent experts with no stake in the outcome is a key method for reducing confirmation bias in the human sciences. Option A commits the error of assuming methodological correctness automatically eliminates the influence of institutional context on research framing and variable selection.

questions.title: Electoral Systems Compared
questions.prompt: Country X uses First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) voting. In the most recent election, Party A won 55% of parliamentary seats with only 38% of the popular vote. Party B won 10% of seats with 22% of the vote. What systemic feature of FPTP BEST explains this outcome?

options.A: FPTP always produces proportional outcomes; the discrepancy must be due to voter fraud.
options.B: FPTP awards each seat to the candidate with the most votes in a geographic constituency, so parties whose support is geographically concentrated win more seats per vote than parties with diffuse support.
options.C: FPTP counts only first-preference votes and discards all others, making it identical to a single transferable vote system.
options.D: The outcome reflects the bonus seats automatically awarded to the winning party under FPTP rules.

questions.explanation: FPTP's winner-takes-all constituency structure means votes for losing candidates are 'wasted' — parties like the UK Liberal Democrats have repeatedly won ~20% of votes but far fewer seats because their support is geographically spread. Option D is incorrect — FPTP has no bonus-seat mechanism; the seat premium arises organically from geographic concentration, not a formal rule.

questions.title: Human Rights vs State Security
questions.prompt: A democratic government introduces legislation allowing security services to monitor citizens' private communications without individual court warrants, justified by counter-terrorism needs. A student argues that security always justifies suspending rights. Which response BEST evaluates this claim?

options.A: The student is correct — no rights can be maintained if physical security is compromised.
options.B: The claim is too absolute: rights frameworks distinguish between derogable rights (which may be limited proportionately during emergencies) and non-derogable rights (which cannot be suspended), meaning security needs must be balanced against proportionality and judicial oversight.
options.C: The student is wrong — security legislation is always unconstitutional in democratic systems.
options.D: The claim is correct because individual privacy rights are less important than collective security in all philosophical frameworks.

questions.explanation: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) Article 4 distinguishes derogable from non-derogable rights, and human rights law requires any limitation to be proportionate, necessary, and subject to oversight — bulk surveillance without warrants fails the proportionality test. Option A commits the 'security exceptionalism' fallacy, ignoring that unchecked surveillance powers have historically been used for political persecution, not only counter-terrorism.

questions.title: Fiscal Policy and Multiplier Effect
questions.prompt: During a recession, a government increases public spending on infrastructure by $10 billion. An economist claims the total increase in national income will be greater than $10 billion. What economic concept explains this prediction, and what condition MOST affects its magnitude?

options.A: The concept is the accelerator effect; its magnitude depends on exchange rate fluctuations.
options.B: The concept is the fiscal multiplier; its magnitude depends on the marginal propensity to consume — the higher the proportion of additional income spent domestically, the larger the multiplier.
options.C: The concept is comparative advantage; its magnitude depends on the country's trade balance.
options.D: The concept is quantitative easing; its magnitude is determined by the central bank's interest rate decisions.

questions.explanation: The Keynesian fiscal multiplier describes how initial government spending circulates through the economy — each recipient spends a fraction (marginal propensity to consume, MPC) of income received, generating further rounds of spending; a higher MPC produces a larger multiplier. Option A confuses the multiplier with the accelerator, which describes how changes in income drive investment rather than how spending injections ripple through income.

questions.title: NGOs and Global Governance
questions.prompt: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) like Amnesty International participate in UN conferences and influence international policy without being elected by any population. A student claims this undermines democratic accountability in global governance. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — only elected bodies should participate in international policy processes.
options.B: The claim has merit but is overstated: NGOs amplify voices of marginalised groups under-represented in official delegations, but they also lack electoral accountability, creating a legitimate tension in global governance.
options.C: The claim is incorrect because NGOs are formally elected by the communities they serve.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because NGOs have binding voting rights in UN resolutions.

questions.explanation: NGOs hold consultative status at the UN (under ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31), enabling advocacy without voting rights — they fill representation gaps for civil society but are accountable only to donors and members, not populations at large. Option C is factually wrong — NGOs are not democratically elected, which is precisely the source of the accountability tension the question raises.

questions.title: Authoritarian vs Democratic Resilience
questions.prompt: Some political analysts argue that authoritarian governments can respond to crises faster than democracies because they face fewer bureaucratic obstacles. Critically assess whether speed of response is a sufficient measure of governmental effectiveness.

options.A: Yes — speed is the most important measure; authoritarian systems are therefore more effective overall.
options.B: No — speed is one dimension of effectiveness, but democratic deliberation produces policies with broader legitimacy and error-correction through accountability mechanisms, which authoritarian systems suppress, often leading to larger long-run failures.
options.C: Yes — authoritarian governments always achieve better outcomes because citizens follow instructions without protest.
options.D: No — democracies always respond faster to crises because more decision-makers are involved.

questions.explanation: China's initial suppression of COVID-19 information in late 2019 illustrates how authoritarian speed can mask early-stage failures caused by information censorship — a classic accountability gap that democratic systems, despite slower deliberation, tend to correct through free press and opposition scrutiny. Option D is empirically wrong — democratic systems with coalition governments and legislative debate frequently respond more slowly in the immediate crisis phase.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Measurement
questions.prompt: Two countries both report an average (mean) GDP per capita of $20,000. Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.25 and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.55. What does this difference reveal that GDP per capita alone conceals?

options.A: Country B has a higher average income despite having the same GDP per capita figure.
options.B: Country B has far greater income inequality — a Gini of 0.55 indicates income is concentrated among few, while Country A's 0.25 reflects more even distribution — which GDP per capita disguises.
options.C: Country A is poorer because a lower Gini coefficient always indicates lower total output.
options.D: The Gini coefficient measures environmental sustainability, not income distribution.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (complete inequality) — South Africa's Gini of approximately 0.63 is among the world's highest, reflecting extreme wealth concentration despite moderate average income figures. Option C is a direct misconception — a low Gini measures distribution evenness, not total output; a poor country can have a low Gini if poverty is equally shared.

questions.title: Constitutional Amendments
questions.prompt: Most democratic constitutions require a supermajority (e.g., two-thirds of parliament) to amend foundational laws, rather than a simple majority. What is the PRIMARY justification for this higher threshold, and what risk does it carry?

options.A: The threshold ensures constitutional stability and protects minority rights from majority overreach, but risks entrenching outdated provisions that are difficult to reform even when reform enjoys broad public support.
options.B: The threshold is designed to give smaller political parties more legislative influence on routine policy decisions.
options.C: The threshold exists purely for historical reasons and has no contemporary democratic justification.
options.D: The threshold ensures only legal professionals can propose amendments, protecting constitutions from populist interference.

questions.explanation: Supermajority requirements, as in the US (two-thirds of Congress plus three-quarters of states for amendments), protect foundational rights from temporary majorities while ensuring changes reflect durable consensus — yet the US has not added a constitutional amendment since 1992, illustrating the entrenchment risk. Option D is factually wrong — constitutional amendments in most democracies can be proposed by elected legislators or through citizen referendum, not exclusively by legal professionals.

questions.title: Public Goods and Free Riders
questions.prompt: A coastal town is considering funding a lighthouse through voluntary contributions from shipping companies that benefit from it. An economist warns this plan will likely fail. Which concept BEST explains the economist's concern?

options.A: Shipping companies will over-contribute because they want to signal corporate responsibility.
options.B: The lighthouse is a public good — non-excludable and non-rival — so companies can benefit whether or not they contribute, creating a free-rider problem that makes voluntary funding inadequate.
options.C: The lighthouse is a private good, so companies will naturally fund it through profit motive alone.
options.D: The free-rider problem applies only to digital goods, not physical infrastructure like lighthouses.

questions.explanation: A lighthouse is the classic textbook example of a public good (Paul Samuelson used it): non-excludable because any passing ship benefits, and non-rival because one ship's use does not reduce availability to others — voluntary contribution schemes systematically under-provide such goods. Option C incorrectly classifies the lighthouse as a private good; excludability requires the ability to prevent non-payers from benefiting, which is physically impossible with a lighthouse beam.

questions.title: International Trade Agreements
questions.prompt: A bilateral free trade agreement between Country X and Country Y eliminates tariffs between them but keeps existing tariffs against all other nations. A student claims this agreement always benefits global free trade. Which concept BEST identifies a potential flaw in this reasoning?

options.A: Bilateral agreements always violate WTO rules, making them inherently harmful.
options.B: Trade diversion may occur: the agreement could redirect trade away from more efficient third-country producers toward less efficient partners simply because tariff preferences favour them, reducing overall global welfare.
options.C: The student is correct — any reduction in tariffs between two countries always increases global economic efficiency.
options.D: The agreement would be beneficial because bilateral agreements automatically trigger multilateral tariff reductions under WTO most-favoured-nation rules.

questions.explanation: Jacob Viner's classic 1950 analysis distinguished trade creation (efficiency gains) from trade diversion (efficiency losses when preferential access redirects imports from globally competitive to less competitive partners) — preferential agreements can produce net welfare losses if diversion outweighs creation. Option D misapplies the WTO's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) principle — bilateral FTAs are explicitly exempted from MFN under GATT Article XXIV and do not automatically multilateralise.

questions.title: Propaganda and Political Communication
questions.prompt: A government during wartime releases images of smiling, healthy soldiers while censoring reports of casualties. A media analyst describes this as 'manufacturing consent.' What does this concept, associated with Noam Chomsky and Edward Herman, claim about mass media?

options.A: Mass media accurately reflects public opinion and simply reports what citizens want to hear.
options.B: Corporate and state media systematically filter information to serve elite interests, shaping public consent for policies that might otherwise face opposition if people had access to full information.
options.C: Governments can only manufacture consent in authoritarian states; free press in democracies prevents this entirely.
options.D: The concept refers to the UN Security Council's procedure for reaching unanimous decisions.

questions.explanation: Chomsky and Herman's 'propaganda model' (Manufacturing Consent, 1988) identifies five filters — ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, and ideology — through which media systematically downplay information that challenges dominant power structures, applicable even in formally free democracies. Option C is precisely the misconception Chomsky targets — he argues the propaganda model applies most insidiously in liberal democracies where citizens believe the press is free.

questions.title: Property Rights and Development
questions.prompt: Economist Hernando de Soto argued that one reason many people in developing countries remain poor is not lack of assets but lack of formal legal title to those assets. What economic consequence does the absence of formal property rights most directly cause?

options.A: Without formal title, people cannot use property as collateral to access credit, preventing investment and entrepreneurship.
options.B: Informal property owners pay higher taxes, diverting resources from productive investment.
options.C: The absence of title causes governments to confiscate informally held property for redistribution.
options.D: People without formal title produce less because they lack the technical skills formal property owners possess.

questions.explanation: De Soto's 'Mystery of Capital' (2000) documented that billions of dollars in informal assets in developing nations are 'dead capital' — unable to serve as loan collateral because unregistered, thus cutting owners off from credit markets and preventing capital accumulation. Option D introduces a skills argument entirely absent from de Soto's framework, conflating the legal-institutional barrier with a human-capital deficit.

questions.title: Separation of Church and State
questions.prompt: In a secular democratic state, a political party wins a parliamentary majority and passes a law requiring all state schools to teach one religion's doctrine as scientific fact. A student argues this is democratic because the party won an electoral mandate. What is the MOST significant institutional objection to this argument?

options.A: Electoral mandates are never sufficient justification for any government action in a democracy.
options.B: A parliamentary majority cannot override constitutional protections — most democratic constitutions include secularism, freedom of conscience, or educational rights that no majority can legislate away.
options.C: The objection is purely religious, not institutional, and therefore irrelevant to political analysis.
options.D: The party's mandate is invalid because it did not win a supermajority in the election.

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracy distinguishes between procedural (majoritarian) legitimacy and substantive constraints — in France, secularism (laïcité) is a constitutional principle impervious to simple parliamentary majorities, illustrating how rights-protecting constitutions limit what majorities can enact. Option A is too absolute — electoral mandates are a valid and important source of governmental authority; the issue is that they operate within, not above, constitutional limits.

questions.title: Collective Action Problems
questions.prompt: Each of 50 fishing villages around a shared lake acts in its own short-term interest and overfishes, ultimately collapsing the fish stock that all villages depend on. This outcome occurs even though every village would prefer the stock to be preserved. What concept does this scenario BEST illustrate?

options.A: The invisible hand — market competition automatically produces the socially optimal outcome for shared resources.
options.B: The tragedy of the commons — individually rational resource extraction by multiple actors leads to collective ruin of a shared resource in the absence of coordinating rules.
options.C: Comparative advantage — each village specialises in the activity it does best, which happens to be fishing.
options.D: The prisoner's dilemma applies only to two actors; with 50 villages the outcome would be cooperative.

questions.explanation: Garrett Hardin's 1968 'Tragedy of the Commons' precisely describes how shared resources are over-exploited when individuals capture full benefits but share costs — Elinor Ostrom later showed that communities can overcome this through local governance institutions, winning the 2009 Nobel Prize. Option D is wrong — prisoner's dilemma logic extends to multi-player collective action problems; in fact, coordination becomes harder, not easier, as the number of actors increases.

questions.title: Political Spectrum Nuances
questions.prompt: A political party advocates for free markets and low taxes in economic policy, but also supports strong government control over social behaviour and opposes immigration. A student labels this party simply as 'right-wing.' What nuance does this label fail to capture?

options.A: The party cannot be right-wing because right-wing parties never support government intervention in any domain.
options.B: A single left-right axis cannot capture the combination of economic liberalism with social authoritarianism — two-dimensional models like the Political Compass separate economic and social axes, revealing that the party is economically right but socially authoritarian.
options.C: The party must be centrist because it combines elements from both sides of the political spectrum equally.
options.D: The student's label is accurate because all right-wing parties share identical positions on both economic and social issues.

questions.explanation: The Nolan Chart and Political Compass use two axes — economic (left/right) and social (authoritarian/libertarian) — recognising that a party can be pro-market while also advocating state control over social life, as characterised many national-conservative parties in Europe. Option A presents a false definition of 'right-wing' — classical conservatism has historically combined market economics with strong social conservatism and state enforcement of traditional norms.

questions.title: Separation of Powers Logic
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Montesquieu's separation of powers is outdated because modern democracies need fast, unified decision-making — having three branches just creates gridlock.' To what extent is this critique valid? Which response BEST evaluates the student's claim?

options.A: The critique is fully valid: coalition governments in parliamentary systems prove unified decision-making is always more efficient and equally safe.
options.B: The critique is partially valid — speed matters in crises — but it ignores that checks and balances prevent the concentration of power that historically leads to tyranny.
options.C: The critique is invalid because Montesquieu's model has never been altered in any democracy, proving it needs no reassessment.
options.D: The critique is valid because gridlock in legislatures has no democratic benefit and serves only to protect politicians from accountability.

questions.explanation: Separation of powers deliberately slows legislation to allow scrutiny, preventing abuses like those seen under unchecked executive authority — for example, the emergency powers misused by authoritarian regimes. Option A is wrong because parliamentary fusion of executive and legislature still relies on judicial independence and other checks; 'unified' does not automatically mean safe or more democratic.

questions.title: WTO Dispute Settlement Mechanics
questions.prompt: Country A imposes a 40% tariff on imported steel, claiming it is a national security measure. Country B challenges this at the WTO Dispute Settlement Body. Which statement BEST describes how the WTO can and cannot respond to this dispute?

options.A: The WTO can impose military sanctions on Country A if it refuses to comply with a ruling against it.
options.B: The WTO can rule the tariff illegal and authorise Country B to impose retaliatory tariffs, but it cannot physically force Country A to remove the tariff.
options.C: The WTO has no jurisdiction over tariffs framed as national security measures, so Country B's challenge will be immediately dismissed.
options.D: The WTO can directly lower Country A's tariff to 0% as an interim measure while the dispute is pending.

questions.explanation: The WTO Dispute Settlement Body can issue legally binding rulings and authorise retaliatory countermeasures, but it lacks an enforcement army — compliance ultimately depends on economic and diplomatic pressure. Option C is a common misconception: the WTO's national security exception (Article XXI of GATT) is not a blanket shield; panels have examined and ruled on such claims, as in Russia–Traffic in Transit (2019).

questions.title: Social Contract and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Rousseau distinguished between the 'will of all' (the sum of individual preferences) and the 'general will' (what is genuinely best for the community). Why does this distinction matter for evaluating whether a government's decision is truly legitimate?

options.A: It matters because Rousseau believed that majority vote always perfectly expresses the general will, making referendums the highest form of legitimacy.
options.B: It matters because a policy can win majority support yet still harm the long-term common good, meaning popular approval alone does not guarantee legitimacy.
options.C: It matters only in direct democracies; in representative systems the distinction has no practical relevance.
options.D: It matters because Rousseau argued that the general will is determined by an enlightened monarch, not by citizens themselves.

questions.explanation: Rousseau explicitly warned that citizens can vote for policies driven by private interest, making the 'will of all' diverge from the 'general will' — for example, majorities have historically voted to oppress minorities, which Rousseau would not consider legitimate. Option A is the most tempting misconception: Rousseau actually distrusted direct majoritarianism as a reliable indicator of the general will, arguing citizens must reason beyond self-interest.

questions.title: Market Failure and Public Goods
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Since national defence protects everyone in a country, private companies should provide it — they would be motivated by profit to do a better job than governments.' Identify the fundamental economic error in this reasoning.

options.A: The student is wrong because private companies are never allowed by law to operate in any security sector.
options.B: The student ignores that national defence is a public good — non-excludable and non-rivalrous — meaning free-rider problems make private provision economically unviable.
options.C: The student is wrong because profit motive always reduces quality in any service sector, including defence.
options.D: The student overlooks that defence is a natural monopoly, so only one government agency can legally provide it worldwide.

questions.explanation: National defence is a classic public good: you cannot exclude non-payers from being protected, and one person's protection does not reduce another's — this creates a free-rider problem that collapses private market provision. Option C is a misconception because profit motive improves quality in many sectors; the issue with defence is specifically its public-good characteristics, not profit itself.

questions.title: Federal vs Unitary Systems
questions.prompt: Switzerland operates as a federal state with 26 cantons that retain significant autonomy, including different official languages and education policies. What is the MOST compelling theoretical justification for this federal structure rather than a fully centralised unitary state?

options.A: Federalism is justified because it ensures that all regions adopt identical laws, creating perfect equality across the country.
options.B: Federalism is justified because it allows diverse regional populations to self-govern on local matters, reducing the risk that a distant central government imposes uniform policies unsuitable to local needs.
options.C: Federalism is justified solely on historical grounds — Switzerland adopted it in 1848 and tradition prevents any change.
options.D: Federalism is justified because it gives each canton a separate military, providing stronger collective defence than a unified army.

questions.explanation: Federalism's core theoretical justification is subsidiarity — decisions should be made at the lowest effective level — which suits Switzerland's four linguistic communities (German, French, Italian, Romansh) who have genuinely different cultural and policy needs. Option A is precisely wrong: federalism produces different regional laws, not identical ones; uniformity is a characteristic of unitary systems.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principles
questions.prompt: In 2018, a European court ruled that a government's anti-terrorism law violated citizens' right to privacy because it allowed surveillance without judicial oversight. Which principle of the rule of law does this ruling BEST illustrate?

options.A: The principle that governments may override any law during a national security emergency without judicial review.
options.B: The principle that even governments and their laws are subject to higher legal standards, and no law is automatically valid simply because a legislature passed it.
options.C: The principle that international courts have supreme authority over all domestic legislation in every country.
options.D: The principle that anti-terrorism laws are inherently unconstitutional in democratic states because security and rights are always incompatible.

questions.explanation: The rule of law includes the principle of legal hierarchy: ordinary legislation must conform to constitutional or higher human rights standards, and courts have the authority to strike down laws that violate those standards. Option C overstates the case — European courts (such as the ECHR) have jurisdiction only over signatory states under specific treaty obligations, not supreme authority over all domestic laws globally.

questions.title: Comparative Advantage Nuance
questions.prompt: Country X produces both wheat and textiles more efficiently than Country Y in absolute terms. A student concludes: 'Country X should produce both goods itself and not trade with Country Y.' Evaluate this reasoning using economic theory.

options.A: The student is correct: absolute advantage determines trade decisions, and Country X gains nothing by trading with a less efficient partner.
options.B: The student is correct only if Country Y has a comparative advantage in at least one good; otherwise, no trade should occur.
options.C: The student is wrong: even if Country X is more efficient at both, both countries can gain by specialising in the good where each has a lower opportunity cost — comparative, not absolute, advantage drives trade.
options.D: The student is wrong because the WTO legally requires all countries to trade with one another regardless of efficiency differences.

questions.explanation: David Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage shows that gains from trade arise from differences in opportunity costs, not absolute productivity levels — Country Y may still have a comparative advantage in one good even if it is less efficient overall. Option A is the classic student misconception: confusing absolute advantage with comparative advantage, which was Ricardo's key insight in overturning Adam Smith's simpler model.

questions.title: IMF Conditionality Ethics
questions.prompt: When the IMF provided a loan to a developing country in the 1990s, it required the government to cut public spending on healthcare and education. Critics argued this conditionality caused more harm than the debt crisis itself. Which analysis BEST synthesises the competing perspectives on IMF conditionality?

options.A: Conditionality is purely beneficial: it enforces fiscal discipline that invariably improves economic growth, and social spending cuts are always offset by private sector growth.
options.B: Conditionality reflects a genuine tension: stabilising government finances may require short-term austerity, but cuts to essential services can deepen poverty and undermine long-term human capital, creating a trade-off with no simple resolution.
options.C: Conditionality is entirely unjustified because the IMF has no legal authority to attach conditions to loans under any international agreement.
options.D: Conditionality only harms countries in the short term; all evidence shows that within one year economies fully recover and social outcomes improve.

questions.explanation: IMF structural adjustment programmes have been empirically linked to GDP stabilisation in some cases but also to reduced access to healthcare and increased inequality, as documented in studies of 1990s programmes in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America. Option A ignores substantial evidence that private sector growth does not automatically replace public services for the poorest populations, making it the most attractive but oversimplified distractor.

questions.title: Taxation and Redistribution
questions.prompt: A government introduces a progressive income tax where higher earners pay a larger percentage of their income. A critic argues: 'Progressive taxation punishes success and reduces the incentive to work hard.' Which response MOST effectively challenges this argument using economic reasoning?

options.A: The critic is entirely correct: all economic models confirm that any income tax above 0% reduces total economic output without exception.
options.B: Progressive taxation can maintain work incentives because marginal — not average — tax rates affect behaviour, and well-designed systems keep effective rates moderate while funding public goods that support economic activity.
options.C: Progressive taxation never reduces incentives because all economists agree people's motivation to work is completely unrelated to how much of their income they keep.
options.D: The critic is correct specifically about top earners, who empirically always reduce work hours when marginal tax rates exceed 30%.

questions.explanation: Economic debate centres on marginal tax rates and the Laffer Curve: at extreme rates disincentives appear, but moderate progressive systems fund infrastructure, education, and healthcare that increase overall productivity — making the blanket 'punishes success' claim too simplistic. Option D misrepresents the empirical evidence; studies such as those by Diamond and Saez (2011) suggest top earners' labour supply is relatively inelastic to tax rate changes within typical ranges.

questions.title: UN Security Council Veto Power
questions.prompt: The UN Security Council has five permanent members (P5), each holding veto power over resolutions. Critics argue this structure makes the UN unable to act in crises involving powerful states. What is the MOST accurate assessment of why the veto was originally included despite this limitation?

options.A: The veto was included to ensure the UN could override the domestic laws of any member state on human rights grounds.
options.B: The veto was included because the founders believed the UN would only function if the world's most powerful post-war states remained members, and those states would not join without a guarantee that resolutions could not be imposed against their vital interests.
options.C: The veto was included as a temporary measure designed to be eliminated once the UN had its own standing army.
options.D: The veto was included to give smaller nations a mechanism to block resolutions from larger powers.

questions.explanation: The 1945 San Francisco Conference designers pragmatically accepted the veto as the price of US, Soviet, and Chinese membership — without it, these powers would not have joined, rendering the UN irrelevant from the start. Option D reverses reality: the veto belongs exclusively to the P5 (USA, Russia, China, UK, France), giving large powers — not small ones — the blocking mechanism.

questions.title: Inflation and Central Bank Independence
questions.prompt: Many economists argue that central banks should be independent from elected governments. A student claims: 'This is undemocratic — monetary policy should be decided by elected politicians who are accountable to voters.' Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The student is entirely correct: all monetary decisions should be made by elected bodies because technical expertise is irrelevant to interest rate policy.
options.B: The student raises a legitimate democratic concern, but elected politicians have a structural incentive to inflate the money supply before elections, creating long-run inflation — central bank independence reduces this political business cycle problem.
options.C: The student is wrong because central banks are directly elected by citizens in most countries, making the accountability concern factually inaccurate.
options.D: The student is correct: historical evidence shows that independent central banks always produce worse inflation outcomes than politically controlled ones.

questions.explanation: The political business cycle theory (Nordhaus, 1975) demonstrates that politicians tend toward expansionary monetary policy pre-election, causing boom-bust cycles — independent central banks with clear mandates (e.g., the ECB's 2% inflation target) reduce this distortion. Option D contradicts evidence: countries with independent central banks, such as Germany under the Bundesbank, historically achieved lower inflation than those with politically directed monetary policy.

questions.title: Tragedy of the Commons Applied
questions.prompt: A coastal fishing community experiences rapidly declining fish stocks. Each fishing family rationally increases their own catch, reasoning that if they reduce fishing, others will simply take those fish instead. What does this scenario BEST illustrate, and what governance approach does economic theory suggest?

options.A: It illustrates perfect market competition, suggesting the solution is to remove all fishing regulations so prices rise and naturally reduce demand.
options.B: It illustrates the tragedy of the commons: individually rational decisions collectively destroy a shared resource, suggesting solutions such as regulated catch quotas, tradeable fishing licences, or community co-management agreements.
options.C: It illustrates comparative advantage: each family should specialise in the fish species they catch most efficiently to maximise total output.
options.D: It illustrates supply-side economics: the solution is to subsidise boats so families can fish more efficiently and increase total supply.

questions.explanation: Garrett Hardin's 'tragedy of the commons' (1968) describes exactly this dynamic — rational individual exploitation of a shared resource leads to collective ruin; Elinor Ostrom's Nobel Prize-winning research showed that community governance rules can sustainably manage common resources without full privatisation or state control. Option A is wrong because removing regulations intensifies the tragedy: rising prices incentivise more fishing, accelerating stock collapse rather than reducing it.

questions.title: Electoral Systems Compared
questions.prompt: Country A uses First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) voting; Country B uses Proportional Representation (PR). In Country A's last election, a party won 55% of seats with only 38% of the popular vote. Which statement BEST explains this outcome and its implications?

options.A: This outcome is impossible under FPTP; the system always ensures seat share exactly matches vote share.
options.B: FPTP's winner-takes-all constituency system rewards parties with geographically concentrated support, potentially giving strong majorities to parties without majority popular support — raising concerns about representational fairness.
options.C: This outcome proves Country A's election was fraudulent, because democratic systems cannot produce such a discrepancy.
options.D: This outcome is desirable because strong parliamentary majorities are always more democratic than coalition governments formed under PR systems.

questions.explanation: FPTP produces this result legitimately through the 'wasted votes' effect — a party winning many constituencies by small margins accumulates far more seats than its national vote share suggests; the UK's 2015 election is a notable example where the Conservative Party won a majority with 36.9% of votes. Option C is the most dangerous misconception: such disproportionate results are a structural, mathematically predictable feature of FPTP, not evidence of fraud.

questions.title: Globalisation and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: A government signs a trade agreement requiring it to treat foreign investors identically to domestic ones. A domestic court later rules against a foreign company on environmental grounds. The company sues the government in an international arbitration tribunal. What tension does this scenario most directly illustrate?

options.A: The tension between free trade and protectionism, resolvable by the WTO imposing a standard global environmental law.
options.B: The tension between national sovereignty — a state's right to regulate in the public interest — and international investment treaty obligations that can be used to challenge domestic policy decisions.
options.C: The tension between common law and civil law traditions, which requires harmonisation of all domestic legal systems.
options.D: The tension between democratic and authoritarian governance, since only authoritarian states face investor-state disputes.

questions.explanation: Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) mechanisms in trade agreements like NAFTA/USMCA allow foreign corporations to challenge domestic regulations, creating situations where legitimate environmental or public health laws can be contested — a direct conflict between treaty obligations and policy sovereignty. Option A misidentifies the issue: the WTO does not impose global environmental standards and is not the forum for investor-state arbitration.

questions.title: TOK: Knowledge and Political Systems
questions.prompt: A Theory of Knowledge student argues: 'In political science, the claim that democracy is the best system of government is an objective fact, proven by evidence.' What is the most significant epistemological problem with treating this as a purely factual claim?

options.A: There is no epistemological problem: political scientists have reached full consensus that democracy is objectively superior, so the student is correct.
options.B: The claim conflates empirical knowledge (measurable outcomes like life expectancy or GDP) with value judgements (what 'best' means), making it partly a normative claim that evidence alone cannot settle.
options.C: The problem is that political science uses no empirical methods, so all political claims are purely subjective with no role for evidence whatsoever.
options.D: The epistemological problem is that the student used inductive reasoning, which is only valid in natural sciences, not social sciences.

questions.explanation: The claim mixes the empirical (what outcomes democracies produce) with the normative (what outcomes we should value most), and what counts as 'best' depends on contested values such as freedom, stability, or equality that cannot be adjudicated by evidence alone — a classic is-ought distinction in TOK. Option C is wrong because political science does use empirical methods including statistical analysis and case studies; the issue is specifically the normative dimension of the claim, not a rejection of evidence.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democratic Health
questions.prompt: Research consistently shows that countries with strong civil society organisations — independent NGOs, free press, professional associations, community groups — tend to have more durable democracies. Which explanation BEST accounts for this relationship?

options.A: Civil society organisations replace elected governments, making formal democratic institutions unnecessary in countries where they are strong.
options.B: Civil society creates independent centres of power, information, and civic capacity that hold governments accountable between elections and resist authoritarian consolidation.
options.C: The relationship is coincidental: wealthy countries can afford both NGOs and democracy, but civil society itself has no causal effect on democratic durability.
options.D: Civil society strengthens democracy only in presidential systems; in parliamentary systems it has been shown to weaken governmental efficiency.

questions.explanation: Alexis de Tocqueville's observations in 'Democracy in America' and contemporary scholars like Robert Putnam demonstrate that civil society builds social capital and horizontal accountability — independent organisations that can monitor, criticise, and mobilise against government overreach. Option C confuses correlation with causation in the wrong direction: comparative studies, including of democratic backsliding in Hungary and Turkey, show that authoritarian governments specifically target civil society precisely because it is causally significant.

questions.title: Supply and Demand: Price Controls
questions.prompt: A government sets a maximum rent price (rent ceiling) below the market equilibrium rent in a major city to help low-income residents afford housing. What does economic theory predict will happen in the long term, and why might this contradict the government's intention?

options.A: The rent ceiling will increase housing supply because lower rents attract more tenants, signalling to developers to build more.
options.B: The rent ceiling will reduce housing supply over time because below-market rents discourage new construction and maintenance investment, creating shortages that harm the very residents it aimed to help.
options.C: The rent ceiling will have no effect because landlords will simply adjust quality to maintain profitability without reducing supply.
options.D: The rent ceiling will permanently fix the housing shortage because once government sets a price, markets always adjust to match that price with adequate supply.

questions.explanation: Price ceilings below equilibrium create persistent shortages: with reduced returns, landlords have less incentive to maintain properties or build new ones — Stockholm's rent control system, for example, has produced waiting lists of up to 20 years for rent-controlled apartments. Option A commits the error of treating demand-side signals as equivalent to supply-side incentives; increased demand at lower prices does not incentivise producers in a market economy — it is higher prices that do so.

questions.title: Bureaucracy and Organisational Theory
questions.prompt: Max Weber described an ideal-type bureaucracy as having fixed jurisdictional areas, hierarchical authority, written documentation, and appointment based on technical qualifications. A student claims: 'Weber's bureaucracy is simply an argument that all governments should be run like corporations.' Identify the error in the student's interpretation.

options.A: The student is wrong because Weber's model applies only to religious institutions, not governments or corporations.
options.B: The student misunderstands 'ideal-type' as a normative prescription: Weber used it as an analytical model to understand how modern organisations function, not to argue that bureaucracy is optimal or that governments should mimic private firms.
options.C: The student is correct: Weber explicitly stated that profit-driven management structures are superior to all other forms of public administration.
options.D: The student's error is assuming Weber supported democracy; in fact Weber was a committed advocate of monarchical systems as the only legitimate form of authority.

questions.explanation: Weber's 'ideal-type' (Idealtyp) is a methodological construct — an exaggerated, pure model used to compare real organisations against, not a normative blueprint; he was deeply ambivalent about bureaucracy, warning of an 'iron cage' of rationality. Option C inverts Weber's position entirely: he studied bureaucracy in both public and private contexts and explicitly contrasted bureaucratic with market logic rather than endorsing corporate management for governments.

questions.title: Human Rights vs State Sovereignty
questions.prompt: The UN Charter both affirms the principle of state sovereignty (Article 2.1) and protects human rights (Articles 55–56). When a government commits mass atrocities against its own citizens, these principles appear to conflict. How has the international community attempted to resolve this tension through the concept of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P)?

options.A: R2P resolves the tension by permanently abolishing state sovereignty for any country that has ever committed human rights violations.
options.B: R2P reframes sovereignty as conditional: states retain sovereignty as long as they protect their citizens, but if they commit atrocities, the international community acquires a responsibility to intervene — shifting sovereignty from an absolute right to a responsibility.
options.C: R2P resolves the tension by giving the UN Secretary-General personal authority to order military interventions without Security Council approval.
options.D: R2P resolves the tension by ruling that human rights law always supersedes state sovereignty in all circumstances, making the UN Charter's sovereignty clause legally void.

questions.explanation: Adopted at the 2005 World Summit, R2P established that sovereignty entails responsibilities, not just rights — and that the Security Council can authorise intervention in genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity. Option D overstates R2P's reach: it applies only to the four specific categories above and requires Security Council authorisation, meaning the P5 veto still constrains its application, as demonstrated by inaction in Syria.

questions.title: Gini Coefficient Interpretation
questions.prompt: Country X has a Gini coefficient of 0.28, and Country Y has a Gini coefficient of 0.52. A researcher concludes: 'Country X is a better place to live because it has less inequality.' Critically assess whether the Gini coefficient alone justifies this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is fully justified: the Gini coefficient comprehensively measures all aspects of quality of life, so a lower score definitively indicates a better country.
options.B: The conclusion is not fully justified: the Gini coefficient measures income distribution but not absolute living standards, so Country X could be more equal but at a lower overall income level — citizens in Country Y might be absolutely better off despite greater inequality.
options.C: The conclusion is correct because international organisations define 'better place to live' solely in terms of income equality, making the Gini coefficient the definitive measure.
options.D: The conclusion is flawed only because Gini coefficients cannot be compared across countries with different currencies.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient is dimensionless (0–1) and currency-independent, so cross-country comparison is valid, but it measures relative income distribution, not absolute wellbeing — a country with very equal distribution of low incomes can score better than one with unequal distribution of higher incomes. Option D is wrong about the currency limitation (Gini is a ratio and unaffected by currency units) but raises a superficially plausible technical objection that many students accept incorrectly.

questions.title: Political Ideology Spectrum
questions.prompt: A student places libertarianism on the 'far right' of a simple left-right political spectrum because libertarians oppose high taxes and government spending. What is the most significant limitation of this classification?

options.A: There is no limitation — the left-right spectrum fully and accurately captures all meaningful ideological differences between political positions.
options.B: The left-right spectrum conflates economic and social dimensions: libertarians favour minimal government in both economic AND personal/social matters, distinguishing them from social conservatives who also oppose high taxes but support government enforcement of traditional social norms.
options.C: The classification is wrong only because libertarians support higher taxes than conservatives do, making them centre-left on the economic axis.
options.D: The limitation is that the left-right spectrum applies only to European parliamentary systems and has no relevance to ideologies in the Americas.

questions.explanation: The Political Compass and similar multi-axis models separate economic (left-right) from social (authoritarian-libertarian) dimensions: libertarians are economically right but socially libertarian — opposing drug laws, surveillance, and military conscription — which a single axis cannot capture. Option C is factually wrong: libertarians typically advocate for lower taxes than most conservatives, placing them further right economically, not centre-left.

questions.title: NGO Accountability and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: An international NGO campaigns at the UN on behalf of communities affected by a dam project, claiming to represent local populations. A government delegate challenges the NGO: 'You were not elected by anyone — why should you have influence over international policy?' What is the MOST thoughtful response the NGO could give regarding its legitimacy?

options.A: NGOs have no legitimate role at the UN because all international policy decisions must be made exclusively by elected national governments.
options.B: The NGO can argue that electoral legitimacy is not the only form of legitimacy: it derives authority from technical expertise, direct relationships with affected communities, transparent funding, and a track record of accountability — forms of legitimacy that complement rather than replace democratic representation.
options.C: The NGO should respond that it is more legitimate than elected governments because NGOs are never corrupt, unlike politicians.
options.D: The NGO's legitimacy comes entirely from its UN accreditation, which is granted only to organisations that have been democratically elected by their member populations.

questions.explanation: Scholars of global governance distinguish between input legitimacy (participatory processes) and output legitimacy (effectiveness and accountability) — NGOs can claim both through community partnerships, published audits, and demonstrated impact, even without electoral mandate. Option C is the trap for students who sympathise with NGOs: the claim that NGOs are 'never corrupt' is empirically false and would undermine the NGO's credibility rather than bolster it.

questions.title: Constitutionalism and Amendment
questions.prompt: Some constitutions are 'rigid' — requiring supermajorities or special procedures to amend — while others are 'flexible' and can be changed by a simple parliamentary majority. A student argues: 'Flexible constitutions are more democratic because they allow the current majority to shape the law without being constrained by decisions made generations ago.' Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The student is entirely correct: rigid constitutions are fundamentally anti-democratic because any constraint on majority rule contradicts democratic theory.
options.B: The student raises a genuine concern about inter-generational democratic legitimacy, but rigid constitutions protect minority rights and fundamental freedoms from being dismantled by temporary majorities — a flexibility that allows majorities to entrench their own power or strip rights is a democratic risk, not just a democratic gain.
options.C: The student is wrong because flexible constitutions are only found in authoritarian states, where they are used to consolidate power.
options.D: The student is correct: all constitutional scholars agree that supermajority requirements have no justification in democratic theory.

questions.explanation: Constitutional theory recognises the 'counter-majoritarian dilemma' but also the danger of 'constitutional moments' being reversed — James Madison designed the US Constitution's amendment process specifically to prevent temporary majorities from eroding fundamental rights. Option C is factually wrong: the UK's uncodified and highly flexible constitutional arrangements are a prime example of flexibility in a long-established democracy, not an authoritarian system.

questions.title: Comparative Electoral Systems
questions.prompt: A political theorist argues that proportional representation (PR) always produces more democratic outcomes than first-past-the-post (FPTP) systems because it more accurately reflects the popular vote. Critically assess this claim. Which response BEST identifies the central weakness in this argument?

options.A: PR systems are less democratic because they exclude minority parties from coalition negotiations entirely.
options.B: PR can produce unstable coalition governments where smaller parties hold disproportionate veto power, undermining clear electoral mandates.
options.C: FPTP is more democratic because it always produces a majority government with over 50% of the popular vote.
options.D: PR is universally superior because every major democracy has now adopted it in preference to FPTP.

questions.explanation: PR systems often require coalition governments in which a minor party holding, say, 8% of seats can block legislation or collapse a government, giving it influence far beyond its electoral share — as seen repeatedly in Israeli Knesset politics. Option C is wrong because FPTP frequently produces majority governments on pluralities well below 50%, as occurred in the UK in 2005 when Labour won a majority with only 35% of the popular vote.

questions.title: WTO Dispute Settlement
questions.prompt: A confident student states: 'The WTO's Appellate Body ensures that all trade disputes between nations are resolved fairly and quickly, making it the most powerful supranational legal institution in existence.' Evaluate this claim by identifying its most significant factual error.

options.A: The Appellate Body has been effectively paralysed since 2019 because the United States blocked appointments of new judges, leaving it without a quorum.
options.B: The WTO has no dispute settlement mechanism; trade disagreements are handled entirely by bilateral negotiation between states.
options.C: The International Court of Justice, not the WTO, holds supreme authority over all international trade disputes.
options.D: The Appellate Body only handles disputes involving developing nations and has no jurisdiction over G7 members.

questions.explanation: From December 2019, the WTO Appellate Body lost its quorum when the US continued blocking new appointments, rendering it unable to hear appeals and severely compromising the dispute settlement system — a major institutional crisis. Option C is wrong because the ICJ handles state-to-state disputes under general international law and has no specific trade jurisdiction; WTO panels remain the designated forum for trade disputes.

questions.title: Social Contract Rousseau vs Locke
questions.prompt: Both Locke and Rousseau used the concept of a 'social contract', yet they reached different conclusions about legitimate government. Which statement MOST precisely captures a key philosophical difference between their positions?

options.A: Locke believed sovereignty resided permanently in a monarch by divine right, whereas Rousseau rejected any form of government authority.
options.B: Locke grounded legitimate government in the protection of pre-existing natural rights to life, liberty, and property; Rousseau grounded it in the 'general will', which may override individual preferences for the collective good.
options.C: Rousseau argued that individuals must surrender all rights unconditionally to the sovereign, while Locke believed no rights could ever be transferred to a government.
options.D: Both thinkers agreed that a government loses legitimacy only when it fails to protect private property rights above all other concerns.

questions.explanation: Locke's Second Treatise explicitly identifies life, liberty, and property as pre-political natural rights that government exists to protect, making its legitimacy conditional on that protection. Rousseau's 'general will' (volonté générale) in The Social Contract is a collective rational interest that can legitimately constrain individual desires, a fundamentally different basis for authority. Option C misrepresents Rousseau, who argued that individuals alienate rights to the community as a whole — of which they are part — not to an external sovereign, so they retain a form of self-governance.

questions.title: Market Failure and Externalities
questions.prompt: A steel factory produces goods efficiently at a price consumers are willing to pay, yet economists argue the free market 'fails' in this scenario. The factory emits pollution that causes respiratory illness in nearby communities. Which concept MOST precisely explains why this constitutes market failure, and what is the standard economic remedy?

options.A: This is a case of a public good problem; the remedy is full nationalisation of all steel production to internalise social costs.
options.B: This illustrates a negative externality where the social cost exceeds the private cost; the standard remedy is a Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost.
options.C: This represents a monopoly failure; the remedy is to break the factory into smaller competing firms so pollution is distributed more evenly.
options.D: This is demand-side market failure caused by consumers undervaluing clean air; the remedy is mandatory consumer education programmes.

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a third party bears costs not reflected in the market price; the factory's output is over-produced relative to the socially optimal level. A Pigouvian tax, named after economist Arthur Pigou, raises the private cost to match the social cost, restoring allocative efficiency — this is the canonical economic solution. Option A is wrong because pollution is a negative externality, not a public good problem (which involves non-excludability and non-rivalry), and full nationalisation is not the standard remedy in economic theory.

questions.title: UN Security Council Veto
questions.prompt: To what extent does the permanent members' veto power in the UN Security Council undermine the organisation's stated goal of maintaining international peace and security? Which evaluation BEST synthesises the competing arguments?

options.A: The veto completely undermines UN effectiveness because it has never allowed any peacekeeping resolution to pass since 1945.
options.B: The veto strengthens the UN because it prevents any single nation from dominating the Security Council's agenda.
options.C: The veto simultaneously enables great-power cooperation essential for implementation of resolutions while also allowing those powers to shield themselves and allies from accountability, creating a structural tension at the heart of the UN.
options.D: The veto is irrelevant to UN effectiveness because the General Assembly can override Security Council deadlock on any matter through a simple majority vote.

questions.explanation: Since 1945, the veto has been used over 300 times, including Russia and China blocking action on Syria and the US blocking resolutions on Israel-Palestine, demonstrating the accountability problem. However, the veto also incentivised the P5 to remain within the UN framework rather than exit it, which is why the organisation has survived — a genuine tension that cannot be resolved by claiming the veto is purely harmful or purely beneficial. Option D is wrong because the General Assembly can only make non-binding recommendations under the Uniting for Peace resolution; binding enforcement authority rests exclusively with the Security Council under the UN Charter.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principles
questions.prompt: A government passes a law retroactively criminalising an action that was legal when it was performed, and uses secret courts to try the accused without legal representation. Identify which principle of the rule of law is MOST directly violated, as defined by theorists such as A.V. Dicey.

options.A: The principle of parliamentary sovereignty, which holds that no parliament may bind its successors.
options.B: The principle of legal certainty and equality before the law, which requires that laws be prospective, public, and applied through open due process.
options.C: The principle of separation of powers, since the legislature is encroaching on judicial functions by defining guilt.
options.D: The principle of federalism, because only regional governments have the authority to prosecute crimes committed within their territories.

questions.explanation: Dicey's formulation of the rule of law explicitly requires that no person be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary courts, and that the law must be clear and prospective — retroactive criminalisation violates legal certainty. Secret courts without legal representation further violate the requirement of equality before the law in open proceedings, making B the most comprehensive and precise answer. Option C identifies a real but secondary concern; the more fundamental violation is against rule of law principles rather than separation of powers doctrine, since the scenario does not involve the legislature adjudicating guilt itself.

questions.title: IMF Conditionality Critique
questions.prompt: Critics of IMF structural adjustment programmes argue that conditionality requirements — such as cutting government spending, privatising state enterprises, and liberalising trade — often worsen inequality in recipient countries even when they stabilise macroeconomic indicators. Which reasoning MOST precisely supports this critical position?

options.A: IMF programmes always cause hyperinflation in recipient countries, which disproportionately harms the wealthy who hold savings.
options.B: Cuts to public spending on health and education reduce access for low-income populations precisely when economic contraction is already lowering household incomes, creating a pro-cyclical squeeze on the most vulnerable.
options.C: Privatisation of state enterprises always leads to monopoly formation, which the IMF is legally prohibited from monitoring under its articles of agreement.
options.D: Trade liberalisation under IMF programmes increases export revenue so rapidly that inequality automatically rises as a temporary but necessary side effect with no lasting harm.

questions.explanation: Pro-cyclical austerity during a crisis — as documented in Greece (2010–2015) and numerous sub-Saharan African cases in the 1980s–90s — cuts the social safety net when unemployment rises, disproportionately harming the poor who depend on public services; this is the core of the structural adjustment critique advanced by economists like Joseph Stiglitz. Option D is wrong because it misrepresents the critique as accepting inevitable but temporary harm, and empirical evidence (e.g., UNCTAD studies) shows inequality effects can be persistent, not merely transitional.

questions.title: Federalism and Subsidiarity
questions.prompt: The principle of subsidiarity holds that decisions should be made at the lowest level of government capable of effectively addressing the issue. A student claims subsidiarity is always superior to centralised decision-making because local governments understand local needs better. What is the MOST significant counter-argument to this claim?

options.A: Local governments have larger budgets than national governments in all federal systems, so they can always address issues more effectively.
options.B: Issues with cross-boundary externalities — such as river pollution, pandemic response, or climate change — cannot be solved effectively at the local level because the costs and benefits cross jurisdictional lines.
options.C: Subsidiarity is a principle exclusive to the European Union and has no application to other federal systems such as India or the United States.
options.D: Local governments always lack democratic legitimacy compared to national governments because voter turnout in local elections is higher.

questions.explanation: A classic example of subsidiarity's limits is transboundary river pollution: a city upstream may have no electoral incentive to reduce discharges because the costs fall on downstream communities in a different jurisdiction, requiring national or international coordination — a problem formally described as a 'spill-over' in public economics. Option D is factually inverted; local elections typically have lower, not higher, voter turnout than national elections, and the statement's conclusion about legitimacy is also contested.

questions.title: Fiscal Policy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: During a recession, a government increases public spending and cuts taxes simultaneously. A student argues this is always the optimal policy response because it stimulates aggregate demand. Which evaluation BEST identifies the conditions under which this Keynesian fiscal expansion could instead be harmful?

options.A: It is always harmful because government spending inevitably crowds out all private investment regardless of economic conditions.
options.B: It is harmful when the economy is already near full employment and low interest rates prevail, because additional demand primarily generates inflation rather than real output growth.
options.C: It is harmful specifically in economies with fixed exchange rates, because increased government spending always appreciates the currency, making exports cheaper.
options.D: Keynesian fiscal expansion is harmful only in command economies where the government already controls all factors of production.

questions.explanation: Keynesian stimulus is most effective when there is spare capacity (an output gap); when an economy approaches full employment, additional demand bids up prices rather than output, generating inflation — a limitation Keynes himself acknowledged and which underpins the Phillips curve relationship. Option A overstates the crowding-out effect; in a liquidity trap (near-zero interest rates with weak investment), government borrowing does not significantly displace private investment, which is precisely when Keynesian policy is most justified.

questions.title: Civic Participation and Deliberative Democracy
questions.prompt: Deliberative democracy theorists such as Jürgen Habermas argue that legitimate political decisions require open rational discourse among equal participants. A critic responds that this model is idealistic because real deliberation always reflects existing power imbalances. Which response MOST effectively synthesises both positions?

options.A: Habermas is entirely correct; studies of citizens' assemblies show that power imbalances disappear completely once formal deliberative rules are established.
options.B: The critic is entirely correct; because perfect equality is impossible, deliberative democracy has no value and should be replaced by technocratic expert rule.
options.C: Deliberative mechanisms can partially mitigate but not eliminate power imbalances; their value lies in improving decision quality and legitimacy relative to pure majority voting, even if the ideal of equal discourse is never fully achieved.
options.D: The disagreement is irresolvable because political philosophy has no empirical basis and neither claim can be evaluated against evidence.

questions.explanation: Empirical research on citizens' assemblies — such as Ireland's 2016–2017 assembly on abortion law — shows that structured deliberation does shift opinions and produce cross-partisan consensus, supporting the idea of practical improvement even without perfect equality, which aligns with Habermas's own acknowledgement that the 'ideal speech situation' is a regulatory ideal rather than a description of reality. Option A is wrong because research consistently finds that pre-existing social status, gender, and educational background still influence speaking time and perceived credibility in deliberative settings, even with procedural safeguards.

questions.title: Comparative Advantage Nuance
questions.prompt: Country A can produce both smartphones and rice more efficiently than Country B in absolute terms. A student concludes that Country A should produce both goods and not trade with Country B. Identify the precise economic error in this reasoning and state what trade theory actually predicts.

options.A: The student confuses comparative advantage with absolute advantage; trade theory predicts that even if Country A is more efficient at both, both countries gain if each specialises in the good for which its opportunity cost is lower.
options.B: The student is correct; absolute advantage is the only concept relevant to international trade decisions, and Country A has no reason to trade.
options.C: The student's error is assuming that efficiency differences exist; in reality, all countries have identical production possibilities in the long run due to technology transfer.
options.D: Trade theory predicts that Country B should pay Country A a tariff to compensate for the efficiency gap before any trade occurs.

questions.explanation: Ricardian comparative advantage (David Ricardo, 1817) shows that mutually beneficial trade is possible even when one country has an absolute advantage in all goods, as long as relative opportunity costs differ; Country A should export the good in which its comparative advantage is greatest and import the other. Option B is precisely the error the question targets: confusing absolute advantage (being more productive in all goods) with comparative advantage (having a lower opportunity cost in a specific good), a common misconception that Ricardo's model was designed to refute.

questions.title: Authoritarian Resilience
questions.prompt: Political scientists debate why some authoritarian regimes last for decades despite economic mismanagement and popular discontent. Which explanation MOST precisely reflects the academic consensus on the mechanisms of authoritarian durability?

options.A: Authoritarian regimes endure primarily because their populations are culturally predisposed to obedience and lack any desire for political change.
options.B: Authoritarian durability is explained by a combination of elite co-optation through selective patronage, repression of opposition coordination, and manipulation of information to prevent the formation of common knowledge among potential challengers.
options.C: All authoritarian regimes eventually collapse within 20 years because economic mismanagement inevitably triggers mass revolution.
options.D: Authoritarian regimes survive solely because of military loyalty, which is guaranteed by paying soldiers higher wages than the private sector.

questions.explanation: Scholars such as Milan Svolik (The Politics of Authoritarian Rule, 2012) identify elite co-optation and the management of the 'dictator's dilemma' — the need to balance satisfying ruling coalition members against popular demands — as central mechanisms; Sergei Guriev and Daniel Treisman add that modern 'spin dictators' rely more on information manipulation than brute repression. Option A is a culturalist argument widely criticised as essentialist and empirically unfounded; comparative evidence shows similar populations supporting both authoritarian and democratic regimes under different institutional conditions.

questions.title: TOK: Knowledge and Political Systems
questions.prompt: From a Theory of Knowledge perspective, a historian argues that describing a government as a 'dictatorship' or a 'democracy' is always a value-laden claim rather than a purely factual one. To what extent is this argument valid, and what implication does it have for political science as a knowledge system?
