options.A: The argument is entirely invalid because political science uses precise operational definitions — such as the Freedom House index — that make classifications purely objective and value-free.
options.B: The argument is entirely valid; because all political labels embed values, political science cannot produce any reliable knowledge and should be abandoned as a discipline.
options.C: The argument has significant validity because classifications depend on contested criteria (e.g., what counts as 'free' elections), but political science manages this through transparent operationalisation and inter-rater reliability, producing provisional rather than absolute knowledge.
options.D: The argument applies only to historical cases; contemporary governments can be classified as democratic or authoritarian with complete certainty using current data.

questions.explanation: In TOK, the distinction between value-laden and value-free claims is central to understanding the human sciences as a knowledge area; Polity IV, Freedom House, and V-Dem all make explicit methodological choices about what criteria constitute democracy, acknowledging that these are contestable — yet cross-dataset agreement on paradigm cases (e.g., Sweden as democratic, North Korea as authoritarian) shows the system produces useful if imperfect knowledge. Option A is wrong because even 'objective' indices like Freedom House have been criticised for ideological bias in borderline cases, demonstrating that operationalisation does not fully remove value-laden judgements.

questions.title: Central Bank Independence
questions.prompt: Many countries deliberately make their central banks independent from elected governments, preventing politicians from directing monetary policy. A student argues this arrangement is undemocratic and should be abolished. Which response MOST effectively evaluates this claim by acknowledging both its validity and its limits?

options.A: The student is fully correct; no institution in a democracy should operate without direct electoral accountability, and inflation control should be determined by popular vote.
options.B: Central bank independence is justified because elected politicians have short electoral cycles that incentivise inflationary monetary expansion before elections; independence addresses the 'time inconsistency problem', but accountability through transparent mandates and parliamentary oversight partially reconciles this with democratic values.
options.C: The student is wrong because central banks are always more competent than governments at economic management, making democratic oversight irrelevant in monetary affairs.
options.D: Central bank independence is undemocratic but this is acceptable because democracies routinely and without controversy remove all economic policy from political control.

questions.explanation: The time inconsistency problem, formalised by Kydland and Prescott (1977 Nobel Prize work), shows that governments facing elections have incentives to adopt short-term expansionary policies that generate long-run inflation, making credible commitment to price stability through an independent central bank welfare-improving — the empirical record of the Bundesbank and post-1997 Bank of England supports this. Option A ignores that direct democratic control of interest rates has a documented track record of political business cycles and inflation, which themselves harm democratic welfare, making the tradeoff more complex than the student's claim allows.

questions.title: NGO Legitimacy and Accountability
questions.prompt: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) often claim to represent the interests of marginalised communities in global governance forums. A critic argues that NGOs lack democratic legitimacy because their leaders are unelected and self-appointed. Evaluate this criticism. Which response MOST precisely identifies its strongest point AND its most significant limitation?

options.A: The criticism is entirely valid; because NGO leaders are unelected, all NGO participation in global governance is illegitimate and should be banned from international forums.
options.B: The strongest point is that NGOs lack formal accountability to the communities they claim to represent; the limitation is that elected governments themselves often fail to represent marginalised groups, meaning NGOs may provide a voice that formal democratic structures do not.
options.C: The criticism has no validity because NGOs are registered with the UN, which grants them full democratic legitimacy equivalent to member-state governments.
options.D: The criticism applies only to large international NGOs; local community organisations always have perfect democratic legitimacy regardless of how their leadership is selected.

questions.explanation: Political theorists such as Nadia Urbinati distinguish between electoral representation and other forms of advocacy representation; NGOs gain legitimacy through expertise, constituency relationships, and the 'politics of presence' where they amplify voices structurally excluded from formal politics — yet accountability deficits are real, as demonstrated by controversies over whether large NGOs like Oxfam reflect Northern donor priorities over Southern beneficiary needs. Option A is an absolutist claim that ignores the documented role NGOs have played in advancing human rights norms (e.g., the campaign for the Ottawa Mine Ban Treaty), which shows their influence can produce outcomes aligned with broad human interests.

questions.title: Gini Coefficient and Inequality
questions.prompt: Country X and Country Y both have a Gini coefficient of 0.40. A policy analyst concludes that inequality is therefore identical in both countries and that the same redistribution policy will have the same effect in each. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The Gini coefficient is only valid for countries with GDP above $10,000 per capita, so it cannot be compared across countries with different income levels.
options.B: The same Gini coefficient can result from very different distributions of income; two Lorenz curves can cross while yielding the same Gini, meaning the structure of inequality — who is poor, how the middle class fares — can differ substantially, affecting which policy interventions will be effective.
options.C: The Gini coefficient measures wealth, not income, so it cannot be used to design income redistribution policies under any circumstances.
options.D: A Gini of 0.40 represents perfect equality in both countries, so no redistribution is needed in either case.

questions.explanation: The 'Gini-crossing' problem is a well-known limitation: two different Lorenz curves can intersect and still produce the same Gini value, meaning one country might have severe rural poverty with a prosperous urban middle class while the other has moderate poverty spread evenly — the same aggregate statistic masking very different structural realities requiring different policy responses. Option D is factually wrong; a Gini of 0.00 represents perfect equality, while 0.40 indicates significant inequality (similar to the United States or China in recent decades).

questions.title: Judicial Review and Democracy
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Judicial review — courts striking down laws passed by elected legislatures — is inherently anti-democratic and should be abolished in all democratic systems.' What is the MOST sophisticated counter-argument to this position?

options.A: Judicial review is democratic because judges are elected by popular vote in all countries that practise it.
options.B: Judicial review is anti-democratic but this is irrelevant because courts have better judgement than elected parliaments on all issues.
options.C: Judicial review protects 'counter-majoritarian rights' — preventing temporary majorities from permanently disenfranchising minorities — and is thus consistent with a substantive rather than purely procedural conception of democracy, even though it does create a tension with electoral accountability.
options.D: Judicial review is only anti-democratic when courts consist of more than five judges; smaller courts maintain democratic legitimacy automatically.

questions.explanation: Alexander Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 78 that an independent judiciary is essential to prevent majorities from violating constitutional rights; scholars like Ronald Dworkin distinguish between 'democracy as majority rule' and 'democracy as equal concern and respect', with judicial review serving the latter conception — for example, the US Supreme Court's desegregation ruling in Brown v. Board (1954) protected minority rights that legislative majorities had refused to uphold. Option A is factually incorrect; in most countries with judicial review (UK, Germany, Canada, India), senior judges are appointed rather than popularly elected, specifically to insulate them from majoritarian pressures.

questions.title: Globalisation and State Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Critics of economic globalisation argue it erodes state sovereignty, while proponents claim it enhances national welfare. A researcher finds that countries deeply integrated into global supply chains have less policy autonomy over corporate taxation. Which evaluation MOST accurately characterises what this finding means for the globalisation debate?

options.A: The finding conclusively proves that globalisation is harmful and all countries should immediately adopt autarky (economic self-sufficiency) to restore full sovereignty.
options.B: The finding is consistent with the 'trilemma' argument: deep economic integration, national sovereignty, and democratic policy responsiveness cannot all be simultaneously maximised, requiring governments to make trade-offs among them.
options.C: The finding is irrelevant because corporate tax policy has never been an expression of state sovereignty in any theoretical framework.
options.D: The finding proves that globalisation only harms developing nations and has no effect on the policy autonomy of developed economies.

questions.explanation: Dani Rodrik's 'political trilemma of the world economy' (2011) formalises exactly this trade-off: nations can choose any two of deep integration, national sovereignty, and democratic governance but not all three — corporate tax competition, where countries lower rates to attract multinationals (as in the race to the bottom documented by OECD data), is a prime example of sovereignty constrained by integration. Option A is an extreme inference; the finding shows a specific constraint on one policy area, not that overall welfare is reduced by integration — these are empirically distinct claims requiring separate evidence.

questions.title: Public Goods and Free-Rider Problem
questions.prompt: A government considers whether to fund national defence through voluntary contributions rather than compulsory taxation, arguing that citizens who value security will pay willingly. An economist argues this policy will systematically fail. Which explanation MOST precisely identifies why, using the relevant economic concepts?

options.A: Citizens will overpay for national defence because they overestimate threats, leading to a military budget that is too large under voluntary contributions.
options.B: National defence is a pure public good — non-excludable and non-rival — so rational individuals will undercontribute, expecting others to pay while they benefit anyway; compulsory taxation solves this free-rider problem by forcing all beneficiaries to contribute.
options.C: Voluntary contributions fail because defence spending has a negative externality on neighbouring countries, which must be corrected by a Pigouvian subsidy rather than taxation.
options.D: The policy will fail only in countries with high income inequality; in equal societies, citizens voluntarily fund public goods at optimal levels.

questions.explanation: Pure public goods are defined by non-excludability (you cannot prevent non-payers from benefiting from national defence) and non-rivalry (one person's security does not reduce another's), making the dominant individual strategy to free-ride — contributing nothing while benefiting from others' payments, as formalised in Samuelson's 1954 paper on public expenditure. Option A describes an opposite problem (overconsumption) that applies to scenarios with subsidised private goods, not the structural under-provision problem created by non-excludability in pure public goods.

questions.title: Media and Political Agenda-Setting
questions.prompt: Agenda-setting theory (McCombs and Shaw, 1972) proposes that mass media does not tell people what to think, but is highly effective at telling people what to think about. A student argues that social media has made agenda-setting theory obsolete because anyone can now set the agenda. Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; empirical studies have confirmed that traditional media no longer influences public political priorities in any country with widespread internet access.
options.B: The student overstates the case; while social media enables distributed agenda-setting, algorithmic curation, platform concentration (Meta, Google), and the amplification of already-prominent voices mean power over agenda-setting remains significantly concentrated rather than democratised.
options.C: The student is wrong because agenda-setting only ever applied to television; it never applied to print media or online platforms at any point.
options.D: Agenda-setting theory is obsolete because citizens in the digital age have demonstrated they make political decisions based on fully rational evaluation of all available information, not media prominence.

questions.explanation: Research on platform algorithms shows that content amplification is not neutral — Meta's own internal documents (the 2021 'Facebook Papers') revealed that its algorithm systematically promoted outrage-inducing content, and studies show that a small number of 'super-spreader' accounts dominate viral political information, replicating concentration rather than eliminating it. Option A ignores substantial post-2010 research showing that legacy media gatekeepers still significantly shape which social media topics gain mainstream salience, a process Dafne Reymann-Weyde and others call 'intermedia agenda-setting'.

questions.title: Property Rights and Economic Development
questions.prompt: Economist Hernando de Soto argues in 'The Mystery of Capital' that the primary reason poor countries remain poor is not lack of resources or entrepreneurship but the absence of formal property rights systems. Which evaluation MOST effectively identifies both the strength and the limitation of this argument?

options.A: De Soto is entirely correct; all poverty is caused by informal property systems and no other institutional or structural factor contributes to underdevelopment.
options.B: De Soto's argument has no merit because economic development is determined solely by natural resource endowments, which property rights cannot alter.
options.C: De Soto correctly identifies that informal asset holders cannot use unregistered property as collateral to access credit markets, limiting capital formation; however, the argument underweights how formalisation can dispossess informal communities if titling processes are captured by elites, as documented in several land reform cases in Latin America.
options.D: De Soto's argument applies only to urban areas; rural agricultural property rights have no effect on economic development in any documented case.

questions.explanation: De Soto's central insight — that informally held assets (estimated at $9.3 trillion globally in 2000) cannot serve as capital because they lack legal recognition for collateralisation — is empirically grounded and has influenced World Bank policy. However, critics including Marxist geographers and development economists such as Ha-Joon Chang document that land formalisation in contexts such as post-1990s Peru and African land reforms has sometimes accelerated elite land grabs rather than benefiting the poor. Option A is wrong because it ignores well-documented contributions of colonial institutional legacies, geographic factors (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson 2001), credit market failures, and global trade structures to developmental outcomes.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: A state commits what the International Criminal Court (ICC) classifies as war crimes. The ICC issues an arrest warrant for the head of state. The accused remains in power and refuses to surrender. What does this situation MOST precisely reveal about the structural limitations of international law as a system of governance?

options.A: International law has no enforcement gap; the ICC can dispatch its own police force to any country to arrest indicted individuals without the cooperation of member states.
options.B: International law operates in an anarchic system where enforcement depends on state cooperation; the ICC has no independent enforcement capacity and relies on member states to execute warrants, creating a compliance gap when powerful or non-member states refuse.
options.C: The situation reveals that the ICC was designed only to prosecute individuals from non-permanent UN Security Council members, confirming that permanent members and their allies are automatically exempt.
options.D: This limitation exists only for heads of state; the ICC can independently arrest and try all lower-ranking officials without any state cooperation.

questions.explanation: The ICC's founding statute (Rome Statute, 2002) includes no independent enforcement mechanism; Article 86 requires state cooperation, and when the Security Council refers a case (as with Sudan's al-Bashir), P5 members can block enforcement through veto — al-Bashir travelled to multiple ICC member states after his 2009 warrant without being surrendered, illustrating the compliance gap. Option A is factually incorrect; the ICC has no police force, investigators, or powers of arrest independent of state cooperation, which is the defining structural limitation of most international legal institutions.

questions.title: Welfare State Models
questions.prompt: Sociologist Gøsta Esping-Andersen identified three 'worlds of welfare capitalism': liberal (minimal), conservative-corporatist (status-preserving), and social-democratic (universalist). A student claims Scandinavian countries are most prosperous simply because they are rich, and their welfare systems are a luxury caused by wealth rather than a contributor to it. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; wealth always precedes welfare states historically and no causal mechanism runs from welfare spending to economic productivity.
options.B: The claim contains a potential reverse causality error; empirical evidence suggests universal healthcare, early childhood education, and active labour market policies increase human capital accumulation and labour force participation, contributing to productivity growth rather than merely reflecting it.
options.C: The student is correct that welfare states are caused by wealth, but wrong that they are luxuries; welfare spending reduces GDP growth in all documented cases by increasing tax burdens.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because all Scandinavian countries adopted welfare states only after reaching per-capita GDP above $50,000 in today's prices, confirming that wealth came first in every case.

questions.explanation: The Nordic countries built expansive welfare states in the 1930s–1970s when they were considerably less wealthy than today; Sweden's welfare expansion in the 1950s preceded its peak economic growth in the 1960s, suggesting a causal contribution. Research by economists such as Torben Iversen shows that social investment policies — particularly childcare enabling female labour participation — are associated with higher long-run productivity, not just affordable by it. Option A ignores this evidence and the theoretical mechanisms (reduced poverty traps, better health outcomes, higher trust) through which welfare states can themselves generate economic returns.

questions.title: Monetary Union Trade-offs
questions.prompt: When a group of countries shares a single currency (as in the Eurozone), they give up an important macroeconomic adjustment tool. During the 2010 Greek debt crisis, critics argued Greece's situation was worsened by Eurozone membership. Which argument MOST precisely explains the economic mechanism behind this claim?

options.A: Greece's situation was worsened because the Eurozone prevented it from imposing tariffs on German goods, eliminating its competitive advantage in manufacturing.
options.B: By adopting the euro, Greece surrendered the ability to devalue its currency to restore export competitiveness during a crisis; the only available 'internal devaluation' required cutting wages and public spending, imposing severe social costs that a flexible exchange rate would have spread more gradually.
options.C: Greece's membership worsened the crisis because the European Central Bank is legally required to raise interest rates during any member state's recession, accelerating economic contraction.
options.D: The crisis was worsened by monetary union because the Eurozone treaty prohibits any member state from receiving loans from the IMF, leaving Greece without emergency financing options.

questions.explanation: Robert Mundell's Optimal Currency Area theory (1961) identifies exchange rate flexibility as a key adjustment mechanism; when Greece could no longer devalue the drachma (as it had done in previous crises), it was forced into 'internal devaluation' — a 25% reduction in wages and severe austerity — which contracted GDP by approximately 26% between 2008 and 2013, one of the deepest peacetime recessions in European history. Option C is factually wrong; the ECB's mandate is price stability for the Eurozone as a whole, not member-state-specific responses, and it actually cut rates and implemented quantitative easing during the crisis rather than raising them.

questions.title: Human Rights Universalism vs Relativism
questions.prompt: A government argues that internationally proclaimed human rights reflect Western cultural values and cannot legitimately be imposed on societies with different traditions. This position is known as cultural relativism in human rights. Critically assess this argument by identifying both its most valid point and its most significant weakness.

options.A: The relativist argument is entirely valid; universal human rights are a form of cultural imperialism with no empirical basis, and states should determine all rights standards domestically without external accountability.
options.B: The valid point is that the drafting of the UDHR (1948) was dominated by Western and Soviet bloc powers, underrepresenting many cultural traditions; the weakness is that this historical contingency does not logically prove that the rights themselves are only culturally valid — and the argument is frequently invoked by governments to shield specific elites from accountability rather than to protect genuine cultural practices.
options.C: The argument has no validity because the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was ratified unanimously by all nations in 1948, proving universal agreement on all rights standards.
options.D: Cultural relativism is valid only for civil and political rights; economic and social rights have always been universally agreed upon across all cultures and political systems.

questions.explanation: The UDHR drafting committee of 1946–1948 was indeed Western-dominated (led by Eleanor Roosevelt), and scholars like Makau Mutua have critiqued the document's liberal individualist assumptions as culturally specific; however, Amartya Sen argues in 'Human Rights and Asian Values' (1997) that invoking 'Asian values' has historically served authoritarian governments suppressing their own populations, exposing the relativist argument as frequently a rhetorical device for elite self-protection rather than a genuine defence of cultural traditions. Option C is wrong; the UDHR was adopted, not ratified, by 48 votes with 8 abstentions (including the USSR and Saudi Arabia) — it is a non-binding resolution, not a treaty, and consensus was not complete.

questions.title: Comparative Advantage vs Absolute
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Country A should always trade with Country B only if Country A is better at producing every good than Country B, because otherwise Country A gains nothing from trade.' Evaluate this claim. Which statement BEST identifies the flaw in the student's reasoning?

options.A: The student confuses comparative advantage with absolute advantage; trade is mutually beneficial when each country specialises in goods with the lowest opportunity cost, even if one country is more efficient at producing everything.
options.B: The student is correct that absolute advantage determines trade flows, but incorrect that all gains accrue to the more productive country.
options.C: The student ignores that trade is only beneficial when exchange rates are favourable, making currency policy the decisive factor.
options.D: The student fails to account for transportation costs, which can eliminate gains from trade entirely when one country dominates production.

questions.explanation: Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage shows that even if one country holds absolute advantage in all goods, both countries gain by specialising where their opportunity costs are lowest and trading. Distractor B is wrong because absolute advantage does not determine the terms of trade; comparative advantage does, and both parties can gain even when one is universally more productive.

questions.title: IMF Conditionality Debate
questions.prompt: Critics of IMF structural adjustment programmes argue that conditionality — requiring recipient countries to cut public spending, liberalise markets, and privatise state enterprises — often deepens inequality rather than restoring economic stability. To what extent is this critique valid when assessed against the IMF's stated objectives?

options.A: The critique is entirely invalid because IMF programmes have a perfect track record of restoring GDP growth within two years of implementation.
options.B: The critique has substantial merit: austerity conditions can reduce social spending, worsening poverty even as they stabilise exchange rates, creating tension with the IMF's own poverty-reduction goals articulated in its Articles of Agreement.
options.C: The critique is partially valid only for African nations; structural adjustment has uniformly succeeded in Latin America and Asia without adverse distributional effects.
options.D: The critique is misplaced because the IMF's primary mandate is military security, and economic conditions are secondary instruments toward that goal.

questions.explanation: The IMF's Articles of Agreement include promoting sustainable growth and reducing poverty, yet documented cases such as Argentina 2001 and Greece's post-2010 programme show that spending cuts reduced social services and raised unemployment, undermining these goals. Distractor C is wrong because structural adjustment in Latin America, notably in Mexico 1994 and Argentina, produced severe distributional crises, contradicting any claim of uniform success.

questions.title: Rule of Law Paradox
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following argument: 'A state fully satisfies the rule of law as long as its laws are consistently enforced by the police and judiciary, regardless of what those laws say.'

options.A: The argument is sound; consistency of enforcement is the only criterion legal positivists require for the rule of law to hold.
options.B: The error is conflating legality with justice; the rule of law also requires that laws themselves meet substantive standards — such as being prospective, publicly known, and not arbitrary — as articulated by theorists like Lon Fuller.
options.C: The error is that enforcement must be carried out by elected officials rather than an independent judiciary for the rule of law to apply.
options.D: The argument is flawed only in democratic states; in authoritarian states consistent enforcement does fully satisfy the rule of law by definition.

questions.explanation: Lon Fuller's 'inner morality of law' establishes that the rule of law requires laws to be general, public, prospective, clear, consistent, and capable of being followed — not merely enforced consistently. Apartheid South Africa enforced its laws consistently yet clearly violated the rule of law in its substantive content, demonstrating why option A is insufficient. Distractor A correctly notes legal positivist consistency but ignores that leading jurisprudential accounts require additional procedural and substantive criteria.

questions.title: Social Contract Rawls vs Hobbes
questions.prompt: Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment proposes that just principles of social organisation should be chosen without knowing one's place in society. How does this MOST fundamentally challenge Hobbes's conception of the social contract?

options.A: Rawls rejects any form of sovereign authority, whereas Hobbes requires an absolute sovereign, making their positions entirely incompatible on governance.
options.B: Rawls argues the social contract should produce fair distributive principles protecting the least advantaged, whereas Hobbes's contract is motivated purely by mutual security from violence and does not constrain the sovereign's distributive choices.
options.C: Rawls and Hobbes agree on outcomes but differ only in method: Rawls uses philosophy while Hobbes uses empirical political science.
options.D: Rawls challenges Hobbes by insisting that the state of nature is cooperative rather than competitive, eliminating the need for any social contract at all.

questions.explanation: Hobbes's Leviathan presents the contract as a rational response to the 'war of all against all,' granting the sovereign near-absolute power with no redistributive obligation; Rawls's difference principle, derived from the veil of ignorance, specifically requires institutions to maximise the welfare of the worst-off group. Distractor A overstates Rawls's position — he accepts legitimate authority and the state; he simply constrains what that authority may do by justice principles.

questions.title: WTO Dispute Settlement Mechanism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'The WTO's Appellate Body has the power to impose trade sanctions directly on member states that violate trade rules.' Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; the Appellate Body issues binding rulings and can levy financial penalties enforced by the WTO Secretariat.
options.B: The claim is incorrect; the Appellate Body issues recommendations adopted by the Dispute Settlement Body, and only if the losing party fails to comply can the winning party be authorised to impose proportionate countermeasures — sanctions are not imposed directly by the WTO.
options.C: The claim is partially correct; the Appellate Body can impose sanctions but only against developing nations that lack veto power in the General Council.
options.D: The claim is incorrect because the Appellate Body was permanently abolished in 2017 and replaced by bilateral arbitration panels, so no appellate authority currently exists.

questions.explanation: Under the WTO's Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU), rulings are adopted by the Dispute Settlement Body through reverse consensus; the aggrieved winning party may request authorisation to suspend concessions (countermeasures) proportional to the harm, but the WTO itself has no enforcement arm that directly imposes sanctions. Distractor D contains a partial truth — the Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019 due to the US blocking appointments, but it was not formally abolished, and MPIA arbitration has partly filled the gap.

questions.title: Market Failure and Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally produces steel but generates air pollution that raises healthcare costs for neighbouring residents who did not consent to this arrangement. Which economic concept BEST explains why the free market alone will produce too much steel in this scenario, and what is the standard policy remedy?

options.A: The factory creates a positive externality by providing employment; the remedy is a production subsidy to expand output further.
options.B: The factory creates a negative externality because its private marginal cost excludes social costs borne by others; the Pigouvian remedy is a tax equal to the marginal external cost, internalising the cost into the producer's decision.
options.C: The situation illustrates the free-rider problem; the remedy is to nationalise all steel production so the government absorbs health costs directly.
options.D: The factory's output reflects an information asymmetry between buyers and sellers; mandatory disclosure of pollution data would fully resolve the overproduction without any taxation.

questions.explanation: When a producer's private cost is below the full social cost — because health and environmental damage fall on third parties — the market equilibrium output exceeds the socially optimal level, the classic negative externality problem identified by Pigou. A corrective tax equal to the marginal external damage shifts the supply curve up to reflect true social cost. Distractor D is wrong because information asymmetry relates to buyers and sellers lacking equal knowledge about a product's qualities, which is a distinct market failure from externalities.

questions.title: UN Security Council Veto Power
questions.prompt: To what extent does the permanent members' veto in the UN Security Council undermine the organisation's stated principle of sovereign equality of all member states?

options.A: Not at all, because the UN Charter explicitly states that sovereign equality applies only to the General Assembly, not to the Security Council's enforcement functions.
options.B: Substantially, because P5 members can block binding resolutions even when a majority of the 193 member states oppose their position, giving five states structural power no other members possess — a direct contradiction of Article 2(1)'s equality principle.
options.C: Minimally, because the veto has never been used by any P5 member since 1990, making it a theoretical rather than practical concern.
options.D: Completely, because sovereign equality is not mentioned anywhere in the UN Charter and was invented by critics after the Cold War.

questions.explanation: Article 2(1) of the UN Charter declares the sovereign equality of all members, yet Chapter V grants each of the five permanent members (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) a unilateral veto over binding Security Council resolutions, allowing a single state to paralyse collective action regardless of majority opinion — a structural hierarchy directly at odds with formal equality. Distractor A is wrong because Article 2(1) is a general principle applying to the entire organisation, not exclusively to the General Assembly.

questions.title: Fiscal Policy and Multiplier Effect
questions.prompt: A government in recession increases public spending by $10 billion. An economist predicts that national income will ultimately rise by $25 billion. Which concept explains this amplified effect, and what assumption is MOST critical for the economist's prediction to hold?

options.A: The Laffer curve; the critical assumption is that tax rates are currently above the revenue-maximising point.
options.B: The Keynesian multiplier (k = 1/MPS); the critical assumption is that a significant proportion of additional income is spent domestically rather than saved or spent on imports, keeping the marginal propensity to consume high.
options.C: Monetarist crowding out; the critical assumption is that interest rates remain constant so private investment is not displaced by government borrowing.
options.D: The accelerator principle; the critical assumption is that consumer demand is growing at an accelerating rate independent of the government injection.

questions.explanation: The Keynesian multiplier equals 1/(1−MPC) or equivalently 1/MPS; a multiplier of 2.5 ($25bn from $10bn) implies MPS = 0.4 and MPC = 0.6. The critical condition is that recipients of government spending re-spend a large fraction domestically, triggering successive rounds of income generation. Distractor C conflates crowding out — which would reduce the multiplier — with the mechanism itself; monetarists argue crowding out negates the multiplier, which is the opposite of what the economist predicts.

questions.title: Electoral Systems Compared
questions.prompt: Country X uses First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) voting; Country Y uses Proportional Representation (PR). A student argues that FPTP is superior because it always produces strong single-party governments. Critically assess this claim, identifying both the strongest support for and the most significant challenge to it.

options.A: Supported: FPTP always produces majority governments. Challenged: PR produces more corruption because coalition bargaining enables backroom deals.
options.B: Supported: FPTP tends to produce majority governments with clear mandates. Challenged: it can deliver these majorities with a minority of the popular vote — in 2015 the UK Conservative Party won a majority of seats with 36.9% of votes — distorting representation.
options.C: Supported: FPTP eliminates wasted votes entirely. Challenged: single-party governments are unstable because they lack coalition support in the legislature.
options.D: Supported: FPTP produces strong governments because it is used by all developed democracies. Challenged: PR systems cannot form stable governments, as proved by the perpetual failure of German coalition governments.

questions.explanation: FPTP's concentration of representation in plurality winners can yield decisive single-party majorities, but this comes at the cost of representational accuracy: in the 2015 UK election, the Conservatives won 331 of 650 seats with only 36.9% of votes, while UKIP won 12.6% of votes but only 1 seat. Distractor D is wrong on both counts: many stable democracies use PR (Germany, Netherlands, Sweden), and German coalition governments have historically been among Europe's most stable.

questions.title: Globalisation and Tax Avoidance
questions.prompt: Multinational corporations often establish legal subsidiaries in low-tax jurisdictions, routing profits through them to minimise tax liabilities in countries where economic activity actually occurs. What systemic feature of the international order makes this practice possible, and which organisation has primarily coordinated responses to it?

options.A: The practice is possible because the WTO requires all member states to offer identical corporate tax rates; the IMF enforces compliance.
options.B: The practice is possible because national tax sovereignty means states set their own rates and bilateral tax treaties can be exploited through profit-shifting; the OECD has led the BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) project to coordinate responses.
options.C: The practice is possible only in non-democratic states; democratic governments have constitutional prohibitions on profit-shifting that corporations must respect.
options.D: The practice exploits the UN's mandatory tax harmonisation rules, which paradoxically created loopholes when implemented in 1995.

questions.explanation: Because each sovereign state sets its own corporate tax rate and the international system lacks a supranational tax authority, corporations can legally shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions through transfer pricing and subsidiary structures. The OECD's BEPS Action Plan (launched 2013) and the subsequent Inclusive Framework, including the 2021 global minimum corporate tax agreement (15%), represent the main coordinated institutional response. Distractor A is wrong because the WTO does not regulate corporate tax rates; its mandate covers trade in goods, services, and intellectual property.

questions.title: Checks and Balances Failure
questions.prompt: In a presidential democracy, the executive branch issues an emergency decree suspending judicial review of its actions for six months, citing national security. A student claims this is acceptable because the president was democratically elected and therefore represents the people's will. Evaluate this reasoning.

options.A: The reasoning is sound; democratic mandate gives the elected executive the authority to adjust the balance of powers as circumstances demand.
options.B: The reasoning conflates democratic legitimacy with constitutional legality; even a democratically elected executive is bound by constitutional constraints, and suspending judicial review removes the mechanism that prevents tyranny of the majority — a concern Madison articulated in Federalist No. 51.
options.C: The reasoning is correct in principle but flawed in practice because six months is too long; a two-week suspension would be constitutionally permissible.
options.D: The reasoning is invalid only if the opposition party disagrees; bipartisan support for the decree would make it constitutionally legitimate.

questions.explanation: Democratic election confers political legitimacy but does not override constitutional limits; the judiciary's role is precisely to check executive overreach, and its suspension removes the principal safeguard against majoritarian abuse. Madison's Federalist No. 51 explicitly argues that ambition must counteract ambition through structural design — not trust in electoral virtue. Distractor A is wrong because it conflates popular mandate with unlimited authority, a reasoning that historically enabled elected leaders like Hitler (1933 Enabling Act) to dismantle democracy legally.

questions.title: Oligopoly and Collusion
questions.prompt: In an oligopolistic market, four large firms control 80% of supply. A student argues that these firms will always compete fiercely because each wants to maximise its own profit. Which concept BEST explains why this reasoning may be flawed?

options.A: The prisoner's dilemma shows that individually rational strategies (competing) can produce outcomes worse for all firms than coordinated collusion, creating an incentive to collude even without formal agreement — a phenomenon studied as tacit collusion.
options.B: The student is correct; oligopolists always engage in price wars because the marginal cost pricing rule applies universally in concentrated markets.
options.C: The Coase theorem demonstrates that firms with well-defined property rights will always reach competitive equilibrium without government intervention.
options.D: The concept of diminishing marginal returns ensures that beyond a certain output level each firm reduces production voluntarily, mimicking competitive outcomes.

questions.explanation: Game theory — specifically the prisoner's dilemma applied to oligopoly — shows that even though competition is individually rational in the short run, firms recognise that mutual restraint (tacit collusion) can sustain above-competitive prices and profits. Industries like aviation and OPEC illustrate how firms coordinate without explicit contracts. Distractor C is wrong because the Coase theorem addresses bargaining over externalities between parties with defined property rights, not market competition between producers in concentrated industries.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democracy
questions.prompt: Synthesise the following: Alexis de Tocqueville argued that voluntary associations — civic groups, religious organisations, professional bodies — are essential to a healthy democracy. Why might a government that formally holds free elections nonetheless weaken democracy by restricting such associations?

options.A: Restricting associations weakens democracy only if they have formal legislative representation; informal civic groups have no constitutional role and their restriction is therefore politically neutral.
options.B: Voluntary associations build habits of cooperation, provide independent sources of political mobilisation, and act as intermediary institutions that check state power; restricting them eliminates the civil society infrastructure through which citizens organise dissent and hold governments accountable between elections.
options.C: Tocqueville's argument is valid only for the United States; European democracies do not depend on voluntary associations because their proportional electoral systems already aggregate diverse interests.
options.D: Restricting associations strengthens democracy by reducing factional conflict — the same concern Madison raised about factions in Federalist No. 10, which Tocqueville would have endorsed.

questions.explanation: Tocqueville, in 'Democracy in America' (1835), observed that Americans' habit of forming associations was their primary defence against the 'tyranny of the majority' and state encroachment; associations train citizens in self-governance and provide collective power independent of the state. Elections alone cannot ensure accountability if citizens cannot organise outside electoral cycles. Distractor D misuses Madison: Madison worried about factions distorting governance but proposed constitutional design as the remedy, not suppression; and Tocqueville explicitly valued associations as democracy's lifeblood — the opposite of suppressing them.

questions.title: Exchange Rate and Trade Balance
questions.prompt: Country A's central bank deliberately depreciates its currency by 20% against major trading partners. A student predicts that this will immediately improve Country A's trade balance by making exports cheaper. Identify the most significant limitation of this prediction.

options.A: The prediction ignores that currency depreciation always triggers retaliatory tariffs under WTO rules, eliminating any competitive advantage within 30 days.
options.B: The prediction ignores the J-curve effect: in the short run, import prices rise faster than export volumes adjust (due to existing contracts and demand inelasticity), often worsening the trade balance before it improves — improvement requires sufficient price elasticity of demand for exports and imports (Marshall-Lerner condition).
options.C: The prediction is entirely correct; a 20% depreciation mathematically guarantees a proportional improvement in the trade balance within the same fiscal quarter.
options.D: The prediction fails because exchange rate changes affect only capital account flows and have no theoretical relationship with the current account trade balance.

questions.explanation: The J-curve effect captures the empirically observed lag between depreciation and trade balance improvement: existing import contracts lock in higher prices immediately, while export volumes rise only after foreign buyers adjust their sourcing — typically 12–18 months. Furthermore, the Marshall-Lerner condition specifies that improvement occurs only if the sum of price elasticities of export and import demand exceeds one. Distractor D is wrong because the current account and exchange rates are theoretically and empirically linked through relative price effects on export and import competitiveness.

questions.title: Legitimacy and Authority
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three ideal types of legitimate authority: traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal. A revolutionary leader overthrows a centuries-old monarchy and rules on the basis of personal charisma alone, making laws by decree. According to Weber, what is the MOST significant long-term institutional risk of charismatic authority?

options.A: Charismatic authority is economically inefficient because charismatic leaders invariably pursue military expansion rather than economic development.
options.B: Charismatic authority is inherently unstable because it is vested in a single person; when that person dies or loses popular appeal, there is no institutionalised procedure for succession, creating a crisis of legitimacy — Weber called this the 'routinisation of charisma' problem.
options.C: Charismatic authority is risky because Weber showed it always devolves back into traditional authority within one generation, preventing modern state-building.
options.D: Charismatic authority violates international law under the UN Charter's self-determination clause, making the state illegitimate in the eyes of foreign governments.

questions.explanation: Weber argued in 'Economy and Society' that charismatic authority faces an acute succession problem: because legitimacy is personal, not institutional, the death or disgrace of the leader produces a vacuum unless authority is 'routinised' into either traditional or rational-legal forms (e.g., offices, bureaucracies, hereditary succession). Distractor C is wrong because Weber did not claim charisma always devolves to tradition; it can routinise into rational-legal bureaucratic authority, as occurred in revolutionary France transitioning from Napoleonic rule.

questions.title: Inflation Targeting Central Banks
questions.prompt: Many central banks, including the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, operate under an inflation-targeting mandate typically set at 2% per annum. A student claims: 'The ideal inflation target should be 0% because any rise in prices harms consumers.' Evaluate this claim using economic reasoning.

options.A: The claim is correct; 0% inflation is universally preferred by economists because stable prices maximise purchasing power and eliminate uncertainty.
options.B: The claim is flawed: very low or zero inflation raises the risk of deflation, which causes consumers to delay purchases (expecting further price falls), reduces corporate revenues and investment, increases the real burden of debt, and can trigger a deflationary spiral — the 2% target provides a buffer against these risks while keeping inflation manageable.
options.C: The claim is partially valid; 0% is ideal for consumers but harmful only to governments because inflation erodes the real value of public debt.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because central banks do not actually influence inflation; only governments can control price levels through fiscal policy.

questions.explanation: Economists favour a small positive inflation target (typically 2%) precisely because zero inflation creates a deflationary risk floor: if aggregate demand falls, prices drop, real wages become rigid downward, real debt burdens rise, and investment collapses — the experience of Japan's 'Lost Decade' and the 1930s Great Depression illustrate this trap. Distractor C is wrong because deflation harms not only governments but also private debtors, businesses, and workers through rising real debt costs and wage deflation pressures.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement Gap
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'International law is not really law because, unlike domestic law, there is no world police force to enforce it, meaning states can ignore it without consequence.' To what extent is this argument persuasive?

options.A: Fully persuasive; legal positivists like Austin define law as commands backed by a sovereign with coercive power, and since no world sovereign exists, international law is merely a set of moral norms.
options.B: Partially persuasive but overstated: while centralised enforcement is absent, states comply with international law through reputational costs, reciprocity, economic sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and internalisation in domestic legal systems — compliance rates for treaty obligations are empirically high despite the absence of a world police force.
options.C: Not persuasive at all; the UN Security Council acts as a fully effective world police force, enforcing all international law universally and without exception.
options.D: Persuasive only for customary international law; treaty law (such as the Geneva Conventions) is automatically self-enforcing through a mechanical compliance mechanism built into each treaty text.

questions.explanation: Scholars such as Louis Henkin famously observed that 'almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law almost all of the time' — compliance is maintained through iterated reputational incentives, domestic incorporation, and collective countermeasures rather than a central enforcer. Distractor A correctly identifies Austin's command theory but ignores Hart's critique that it fails to account for obligation-based legal systems, and overstates non-compliance; distractor C overstates Security Council capacity, which is frequently paralysed by P5 vetoes.

questions.title: Federalism Intergovernmental Conflict
questions.prompt: In a federal state, the national government passes a law requiring all schools to teach a standardised national curriculum. Several regional governments refuse, citing constitutional education jurisdiction. What does this conflict BEST illustrate about the design challenges of federal systems?

options.A: The conflict illustrates that federal systems are inherently unworkable and must eventually transition to unitary systems to function effectively.
options.B: The conflict illustrates the core tension in federalism between national uniformity — ensuring equal standards across territories — and sub-national autonomy — preserving regional capacity to govern according to local preferences — requiring constitutional courts to delineate jurisdictional boundaries.
options.C: The conflict illustrates only a fiscal issue: if the national government provided sufficient funding, regional governments would have no constitutional objection to the curriculum.
options.D: The conflict illustrates that constitutional jurisdiction clauses are irrelevant in practice because national governments always prevail over regional ones in federal systems.

questions.explanation: Federal constitutions deliberately divide sovereignty between levels of government, and conflicts over jurisdiction — as in US federalism disputes litigated under the Supremacy Clause, or Australian Section 109 constitutional conflicts — are intrinsic to the design, not a malfunction. Courts like the US Supreme Court or Germany's Federal Constitutional Court routinely arbitrate these boundaries. Distractor D is wrong: regional governments frequently prevail in federal courts; in the US, the 10th Amendment reserves unenumerated powers to states, and courts have struck down federal overreach in cases such as NFIB v. Sebelius (2012).

questions.title: Gini Coefficient and Inequality
questions.prompt: Two countries both report a GDP per capita of $30,000. Country P has a Gini coefficient of 0.28; Country Q has a Gini coefficient of 0.52. A student concludes: 'Since they have the same average income, citizens in both countries have similar living standards.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: There is no error; GDP per capita is the definitive measure of living standards and the Gini coefficient measures racial composition, not income distribution.
options.B: The student ignores that GDP per capita is a mean that obscures distributional differences: Country Q's Gini of 0.52 indicates highly unequal income distribution, meaning a small elite earns most of the income while the majority earns far less than $30,000 — median income and access to services will diverge significantly between the two countries.
options.C: The error is minor; the Gini coefficient affects only tax policy and has no bearing on the lived experience of typical citizens.
options.D: The student's error is that GDP per capita should be compared using Purchasing Power Parity before drawing any conclusions about living standards in different countries.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality); a score of 0.52 (similar to South Africa or Brazil) indicates that income is concentrated among a small proportion of the population, meaning the median income in Country Q will be substantially below $30,000, while a Gini of 0.28 (similar to Denmark) indicates more evenly distributed income closer to the mean. GDP per capita, as an arithmetic mean, is mathematically insensitive to this skew. Distractor D raises a legitimate methodological point about PPP but does not address the central flaw — distribution — making it a secondary issue, not the identified error.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge and News Bias
questions.prompt: A TOK student argues: 'All news sources are equally biased, so we should dismiss them all and rely only on our personal lived experience to understand political events.' From a TOK perspective, what is the primary epistemological problem with this argument?

options.A: The argument is epistemologically sound; lived experience is recognised by all major epistemologists as the most reliable source of political knowledge.
options.B: The argument commits a false equivalence by treating all bias as equal in magnitude and type, then compounds the error by privileging personal experience — which is inherently limited in scope, subject to confirmation bias, and incapable of accessing events beyond direct observation — over structured, corroborated, and methodologically transparent sources.
options.C: The only problem is that the student fails to specify which news sources are biased; once biased sources are identified and excluded, the remaining unbiased sources provide complete, objective knowledge.
options.D: The argument is flawed solely because emotional intelligence, not lived experience, is the proper alternative to news media for understanding political events.

questions.explanation: TOK distinguishes between ways of knowing; the student's 'all equal bias' claim is a false equivalence (peer-reviewed journalism with transparent methodology is not epistemically equivalent to anonymous social media), and individual sense perception is acknowledged in TOK as limited by perspective, scope, and availability. Corroboration, triangulation of sources, and methodological transparency are the epistemological tools for navigating bias — not wholesale dismissal. Distractor C is wrong because it presupposes a perfectly 'unbiased' source exists, a claim itself problematic in TOK's recognition that all knowledge is situated.

questions.title: Human Rights Universalism vs Relativism
questions.prompt: A government defends restricting women's right to vote by arguing that such rights are culturally specific Western constructs that do not apply universally. Critically assess this claim against the framework of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR).

options.A: The claim is valid; the UDHR itself contains a cultural exception clause that allows signatories to exempt practices they consider culturally essential.
options.B: The claim represents a cultural relativist position that directly contradicts the UDHR's foundational universalist premise — Article 1 declares all humans are born free and equal in dignity regardless of culture or geography, and Article 21 establishes political participation as a universal right; the relativist argument could logically justify any abuse by declaring it culturally normative.
options.C: The claim is partially valid; the UDHR universally protects civil rights but explicitly leaves political rights like voting to individual state determination.
options.D: The claim is invalid only if the country's constitution already guarantees women's suffrage; if no such constitutional provision exists, international human rights law does not apply.

questions.explanation: The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly with 48 votes in favour and none against (8 abstentions including Saudi Arabia and the Soviet bloc), asserting rights as inherent to all humans regardless of cultural context — this is its foundational universalist claim. The cultural relativist argument the government invokes is philosophically coherent but has been widely critiqued for potentially legitimising oppression by treating culture as immune from ethical evaluation. Distractor A is incorrect: the UDHR contains no cultural exception clause; the 1993 Vienna Declaration reaffirmed universality explicitly despite relativist objections.

questions.title: Principal-Agent Problem in Government
questions.prompt: In political science, the 'principal-agent problem' occurs when an agent (e.g., an elected official) acts in their own interests rather than those of the principal (e.g., voters) who authorised them. Which institutional mechanism MOST directly addresses this problem in representative democracies?

options.A: Compulsory voting laws, which increase turnout and thus align voter and politician incentives by ensuring all citizens are represented.
options.B: Regular elections combined with transparency mechanisms (freedom of information, public financial disclosure, independent audit institutions), which create accountability loops that threaten non-compliant agents with removal and expose self-interested behaviour.
options.C: Bicameral legislatures, which solve the principal-agent problem by requiring two chambers to approve any self-interested legislation proposed by elected officials.
options.D: Proportional representation electoral systems, which eliminate the principal-agent problem entirely by ensuring every vote translates proportionally into representation.

questions.explanation: The principal-agent problem in politics is primarily addressed through accountability mechanisms: elections enable principals to remove agents who diverge from their interests, while transparency institutions (such as freedom of information laws and independent anti-corruption bodies) reduce information asymmetry that allows agents to conceal self-interested behaviour. Distractor A is wrong because compulsory voting increases participation but does not solve the core information asymmetry that enables agents to act contrary to principal interests between elections.

questions.title: Refugee Law and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, states have a non-refoulement obligation — they cannot return a refugee to a territory where they face persecution. A state argues that this obligation violates its sovereign right to control its own borders. To what extent is this argument legally sustainable?

options.A: Fully sustainable; sovereign border control is an absolute right under the UN Charter's Article 2(7) non-interference principle, which supersedes all treaty obligations.
options.B: Not sustainable for signatory states: by ratifying the 1951 Convention, states voluntarily limit their sovereign discretion in this specific domain — sovereignty is not absolute but is exercised within treaty commitments states have freely undertaken; non-refoulement is also considered by many legal scholars to have attained the status of customary international law binding even non-signatories.
options.C: Sustainable only for non-signatory states; signatory states retain full sovereign discretion to return refugees if they pass a domestic parliamentary vote authorising it.
options.D: Fully sustainable, as the 1951 Convention was superseded by the 1967 New York Protocol, which returned all refugee decisions to state discretion.

questions.explanation: Sovereignty in the post-1945 international order is not absolute; states that ratify treaties accept binding obligations they have freely negotiated, limiting their discretion in the relevant domain — this is not a violation of sovereignty but an exercise of it. Non-refoulement under Article 33 of the 1951 Convention is widely considered jus cogens (peremptory norm), binding all states regardless of signature. Distractor D is factually incorrect: the 1967 Protocol expanded the Convention's geographic and temporal scope but did not return decisions to state discretion; non-refoulement obligations were maintained and extended.

questions.title: Public Goods and Free Rider Problem
questions.prompt: National defence is cited as a classic public good. A student argues: 'If national defence truly benefits everyone, then private companies would voluntarily provide it because they could profit by charging all beneficiaries.' Identify the specific economic flaw in this argument.

options.A: The argument is correct; private defence provision fails only because governments have made it illegal, not because of any inherent market failure.
options.B: The argument ignores that national defence is non-excludable — once protection is provided, no resident can be excluded from benefiting — which means rational individuals have no incentive to pay voluntarily when they receive protection regardless; the free rider problem causes private provision to under-supply or not supply the good at all.
options.C: The argument confuses national defence with a club good; the correct analysis is that defence should be funded through subscription fees charged only to those who want protection.
options.D: The argument is economically sound but politically infeasible because citizens distrust private military companies, not because of a structural market failure.

questions.explanation: Public goods are defined by two properties: non-rivalrous (one person's consumption does not reduce availability) and non-excludable (you cannot prevent non-payers from benefiting). Non-excludability creates the free rider problem: rational individuals wait for others to pay, resulting in market under-provision or complete absence of provision — this is why public goods must typically be financed through compulsory taxation. Distractor C misclassifies defence as a club good (excludable but non-rivalrous, like a private gym), ignoring that national defence is genuinely non-excludable — you cannot protect paying citizens from air attack while leaving non-payers exposed.

questions.title: Supranational vs Intergovernmental
questions.prompt: The European Union is often cited as the world's most advanced example of regional integration. A student claims: 'The EU is a supranational organisation because member states have transferred decision-making authority in some areas to EU institutions whose decisions can override national law.' Compare this with the claim that the EU remains fundamentally intergovernmental. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: The EU is purely intergovernmental; the European Commission merely coordinates national policies but all binding decisions require unanimous consent of all member states.
options.B: The EU is a hybrid: it has genuine supranational elements — the European Court of Justice's doctrine of supremacy and direct effect, qualified majority voting in the Council, and binding EU law under the doctrine established in Van Gend en Loos (1963) — but retains intergovernmental elements in areas like foreign policy and taxation where unanimity is required.
options.C: The EU is purely supranational and functions as a federal state in all policy domains, including full control of member states' military forces and taxation systems.
options.D: The student's supranational claim is correct only for the Eurozone; non-Eurozone EU members are subject exclusively to intergovernmental arrangements with no binding EU law.

questions.explanation: The EU's supranational character is most evident in its legal order: the ECJ's 1963 Van Gend en Loos ruling established direct effect, and Costa v. ENEL (1964) established supremacy of EU law over conflicting national law — binding without national parliamentary approval. However, the EU remains intergovernmental in Common Foreign and Security Policy and taxation, where Council unanimity preserves state vetoes. Distractor A is wrong because qualified majority voting in the Council frequently binds states that voted against a measure — a defining supranational feature.

questions.title: Fair Trade and Farmers
questions.prompt: A village in Ethiopia grows coffee that is sold in shops in Canada with a 'Fair Trade' label. The farmers earn a guaranteed minimum price for their coffee. Why does the Fair Trade label matter most to the farmers, not just the shoppers?

options.A: It tells shoppers the coffee tastes better than regular coffee
options.B: It protects farmers from earning too little when world coffee prices fall
options.C: It means the coffee was grown in a famous coffee region
options.D: It guarantees the coffee reaches shops faster than other brands

questions.explanation: Fair Trade certification sets a minimum price floor so that even when global market prices drop, farmers still receive enough income to cover their costs and support their families. Option A is wrong because the label is about payment fairness, not taste — a very common misconception shoppers hold.

questions.title: Migration Push and Pull
questions.prompt: A family moves from a drought-affected farming region to a large city in the same country. Which best describes the type of migration this is, and what is driving it?

options.A: International migration driven by a pull factor — better city schools
options.B: Internal migration driven by a push factor — environmental hardship at home
options.C: Refugee movement driven by a push factor — fear of government persecution
options.D: Internal migration driven by a pull factor — the family prefers city culture

questions.explanation: Moving within the same country is internal migration, and leaving because of drought — an environmental hardship — is a push factor forcing people away from their original home. Option D is tempting because it is also internal migration, but the driver is a pull factor, not the push factor that drought represents.

questions.title: Cultural Borrowing vs. Loss
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'When people in one country start celebrating another country's festival, it always means their own traditions are disappearing.' Evaluate this claim using what you know about cultural exchange.

options.A: The claim is correct because adding new traditions always replaces old ones
options.B: The claim is partly right — traditions only survive if kept completely unchanged
options.C: The claim is too simple — communities can adopt new celebrations while also keeping their own
options.D: The claim is correct because global companies deliberately erase local festivals

questions.explanation: Cultural exchange often adds layers rather than replacing existing traditions — many communities celebrate both borrowed and home-grown festivals simultaneously, as seen in countries like Malaysia where Chinese New Year, Diwali, and Eid are all celebrated widely. Options A and D both assume a zero-sum outcome that evidence from multicultural societies does not support.

questions.title: Water as a Shared Resource
questions.prompt: Many countries share underground water reserves called aquifers. If one country pumps out most of the shared water to grow crops for export, what global principle is most at risk?

options.A: The principle that natural resources belong only to the country where they are found underground
options.B: The principle that countries cooperating on trade must share equal profits
options.C: The principle that shared global resources should be used fairly so all who depend on them can benefit
options.D: The principle that agricultural nations have priority rights over water for food security

questions.explanation: Shared aquifers cross national borders, making them a common global resource; international frameworks like the UN Watercourses Convention stress equitable use so no single country depletes what others depend on. Option A is a real misconception — sovereignty over territory does not automatically grant unlimited rights to extract shared cross-border resources.

questions.title: Religion and Conflict
questions.prompt: Two groups fighting over land both claim their religion gives them the right to that territory. A student says, 'So religion causes all wars.' Which response best evaluates that conclusion?

options.A: The student is right — historical records show religion is always the main reason for conflict
options.B: The student overgeneralises — religion is sometimes used to justify conflicts that also have political and economic causes
options.C: The student is right — if people had no religion there would be no international conflicts
options.D: The student is partly right — only religions with sacred land teachings cause conflicts

questions.explanation: Historians and conflict researchers consistently find that most wars have overlapping causes — land, resources, power, and identity — with religion often used to motivate fighters rather than being the sole root cause. Option D is a plausible-sounding nuance but is still an overgeneralisation, since conflicts over sacred land appear in many different religious and non-religious contexts.

questions.title: Global Supply Chains
questions.prompt: A pair of trainers is designed in Germany, made from rubber grown in Thailand, stitched together in Vietnam, and sold in Brazil. What does this tell us about how modern goods are produced?

options.A: Most products today are still made entirely in one country from start to finish
options.B: Production is spread across many countries because each country specialises in different parts of the process
options.C: Countries only trade goods when they cannot make them at all on their own
options.D: Germany controls all the profits because it owns the design

questions.explanation: This is a global supply chain — different countries contribute what they do most efficiently, from design to raw materials to assembly, a pattern documented in nearly every major manufactured product today. Option A is a widespread misconception that students often hold before studying globalisation.

questions.title: Aid vs. Self-Sufficiency
questions.prompt: A region receives free food aid from another country for two years after a flood. A local leader says, 'We are grateful, but we need seeds and tools more than food packages.' What idea about development does the leader's comment reflect?

options.A: Short-term aid is unhelpful and should never be given after disasters
options.B: Receiving food aid makes communities permanently dependent on outside help
options.C: Sustainable development requires building local capacity, not only delivering immediate goods
options.D: Countries should only accept aid from countries that share the same culture

questions.explanation: The leader is expressing a key development principle: long-term well-being comes from strengthening local ability to produce and sustain livelihoods, which tools and seeds enable, rather than from continued delivery of finished goods. Option B is a genuine misconception — aid can create dependency, but that is a risk to manage, not a guaranteed permanent outcome.

questions.title: Citizenship and Belonging
questions.prompt: A child is born in Canada to parents who are citizens of Nigeria. When she grows up, which statement about her identity is most accurate from a global perspectives viewpoint?

options.A: She must choose only one national identity because holding two is legally impossible
options.B: She can hold multiple layers of cultural and national identity at the same time
options.C: She will automatically lose her Nigerian heritage because she was not born there
options.D: Her identity will be entirely Canadian because environment always overrides heritage

questions.explanation: Many countries including Canada allow dual citizenship, and individuals regularly hold layered identities that include birthplace, parental heritage, language, and community — scholars call this hybrid or hyphenated identity. Option D is a common misconception based on the idea that the country you grow up in completely replaces ancestral culture.

questions.title: Comparing Development Measures
questions.prompt: Country A has a very high average income, but most of that money is earned by a small number of very wealthy families. Country B has a lower average income, but wealth is shared more equally. Which measure would best reveal this difference that average income hides?

options.A: Total population size of each country
options.B: The Gini coefficient, which measures how equally income is distributed
options.C: Gross Domestic Product, which shows the total value of goods produced
options.D: The literacy rate, which shows how many people can read and write

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient is specifically designed to measure income inequality — a score of 0 means perfect equality and 1 means one person holds all income — making it the right tool to expose the hidden inequality that average income obscures. GDP (Option C) has the same averaging problem as average income and would not reveal internal distribution.

questions.title: Hinduism and Environmental Ethics
questions.prompt: In Hinduism, many rivers — including the Ganges — are considered sacred. Environmental activists have worked with Hindu religious leaders to protect these rivers from pollution. What does this collaboration suggest about the relationship between religion and environmental action?

options.A: Religious beliefs and environmental goals always oppose each other
options.B: Only scientific arguments can motivate communities to protect the environment
options.C: Religious values can provide powerful reasons for communities to protect natural spaces
options.D: Governments must separate religion from environmental policy completely

questions.explanation: The collaboration between Hindu leaders and activists around rivers like the Ganges shows that sacred status can motivate protective behaviour independently of scientific arguments — a principle recognised in global conservation frameworks that engage indigenous and religious communities. Option B is a misconception because it ignores the proven motivational power of cultural and spiritual values in driving community action.

questions.title: Digital Access Inequality
questions.prompt: During a global health emergency, schools in many countries switched to online learning. Students in rural areas of low-income countries were most affected. Which combination of factors best explains why?

options.A: Rural students prefer in-person learning and chose not to connect online
options.B: Limited internet infrastructure and fewer personal devices in low-income rural areas
options.C: Online platforms were designed only in languages those students do not speak
options.D: Low-income country governments banned online education during emergencies

questions.explanation: The digital divide — unequal access to internet and devices — is most acute in rural low-income regions; the International Telecommunication Union reports that billions of people still lack reliable broadband access. Option C is a partial truth in some contexts but is not the primary structural barrier compared to the infrastructure and device gap.

questions.title: Sanctions as Diplomacy
questions.prompt: Country A places economic sanctions on Country B, meaning it refuses to buy or sell goods with Country B. The goal is to pressure Country B's government to change a policy. What is a major risk of this approach?

options.A: Country B's government will immediately agree to all demands to protect its economy
