options.B: Ordinary citizens in Country B may suffer the most while its leaders remain protected
options.C: Country A will lose its military power by choosing economic tools instead
options.D: Sanctions always lead directly to armed conflict between the two countries

questions.explanation: A well-documented risk of economic sanctions is that governments can protect themselves and their supporters while the general population faces shortages of food, medicine, and energy — as seen repeatedly in case studies like those used by international relations scholars. Option A describes the intended best-case outcome, not a risk, making it a plausible but incorrect choice.

questions.title: Sustainable vs. Economic Growth
questions.prompt: A country discovers large oil reserves and plans to sell the oil to fund new schools and hospitals. An environmental group objects. Which statement best captures the tension between these two positions?

options.A: Economic development and environmental protection are always completely opposed and cannot both succeed
options.B: Environmental groups are always correct and economic growth should never be prioritised
options.C: Short-term human development gains may conflict with long-term environmental sustainability goals
options.D: Countries with oil are already wealthy, so they do not need new schools or hospitals

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates the classic sustainability dilemma: using a finite, polluting resource can fund immediate social needs but contributes to climate change and leaves future generations with depleted resources and environmental costs. Option A is a tempting but inaccurate claim — many countries and researchers have shown these goals can be balanced, just not easily.

questions.title: Gender and School Access
questions.prompt: In several countries, girls are more likely than boys to stop attending school by the age of twelve. A student says this is simply because families prefer boys. Which response shows more careful thinking about the causes?

options.A: The student is right — family preference is the only reason girls leave school early
options.B: Multiple factors overlap, including poverty, safety concerns on the journey to school, and cultural expectations around girls' roles
options.C: Girls leave school because they find the subjects harder than boys do
options.D: This only happens in countries where education is not valued at all by anyone

questions.explanation: UNESCO research identifies intersecting factors — household poverty requiring girls to work or care for siblings, distance and safety risks on school routes, and social norms about girls' roles — as interacting causes, not a single preference. Option A is the most common student misconception because it identifies a real factor but treats it as the only one.

questions.title: The Role of the United Nations
questions.prompt: The United Nations cannot force its member countries to follow its decisions. Yet countries still join and participate. Why would a country choose to remain part of an organisation whose rules it can ignore?

options.A: Because the UN secretly has a powerful army that enforces all its decisions
options.B: Membership offers diplomatic relationships, access to global programmes, and international legitimacy
options.C: Countries are legally required to join the UN once they declare independence
options.D: The UN pays countries large sums of money to remain as members

questions.explanation: UN membership provides access to forums for diplomacy, peacekeeping support, development funding programmes, and recognition on the world stage — benefits that make membership valuable even without binding enforcement. Option A is factually incorrect — the UN does have a small peacekeeping force, but it operates only where member states consent, and it does not enforce Security Council resolutions on powerful nations.

questions.title: Plastic Waste and Global Responsibility
questions.prompt: Rich countries ship plastic waste to poorer countries for recycling, but much of it ends up in rivers and oceans there. Which error in thinking does this practice expose?

options.A: Poorer countries are not capable of managing any kind of recycling
options.B: Assuming that moving a problem to another location solves it for everyone
options.C: Rich countries produce less waste than poorer countries overall
options.D: Recycling is never an effective strategy for managing plastic

questions.explanation: When waste is exported, it removes the visible problem from wealthy countries but often creates greater harm elsewhere — since 2018 bans by China and other countries have highlighted how this out-of-sight approach was never a real solution. Option A is a harmful generalisation that blames receiving countries rather than identifying the structural flaw in the export model.

questions.title: Buddhism and Interconnectedness
questions.prompt: A core Buddhist teaching is that all living things are interconnected and that actions affecting others will eventually return to affect yourself. How does this teaching relate to ideas in global sustainability?

options.A: It means Buddhists believe only their own community's environment matters
options.B: It supports the idea that environmental harm in one place eventually affects everyone everywhere
options.C: It teaches that natural disasters are punishments for bad individual behaviour
options.D: It suggests people should avoid all technology to protect the environment

questions.explanation: The Buddhist concept of interdependence (pratītyasamutpāda) parallels systems-thinking in sustainability — deforestation, ocean pollution, and climate change all demonstrate that harm to one part of a system ripples through to others across borders. Option C misrepresents the teaching by turning interconnectedness into a punishment framework, which is not part of this Buddhist concept.

questions.title: Comparing Rural and Urban Poverty
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this statement: 'Poverty only exists in rural areas of developing countries, not in cities or in wealthy nations.'

options.A: The error is that poverty is measured differently in rural and urban areas, so the comparison is unfair
options.B: The error is that poverty exists in urban areas of developing countries and in wealthy countries too
options.C: The error is that developing countries do not actually have rural areas
options.D: The error is that poverty in wealthy countries is always more severe than in developing ones

questions.explanation: Urban poverty is widespread in cities across all income levels of countries — for example, slums in Mumbai or Nairobi, and food insecurity in cities like London or Detroit — proving the statement geographically and economically incorrect. Option A sounds sophisticated but sidesteps the core factual error the question asks students to identify.

questions.title: Cultural Heritage and Tourism
questions.prompt: Thousands of tourists visit Machu Picchu in Peru each year, bringing money to the local economy but also damaging the ancient stonework. What would happen if the government allowed unlimited tourist numbers to continue?

options.A: The site would become more famous and the stonework would strengthen from use
options.B: The economic benefits would grow forever since more tourists always means more income
options.C: Physical damage could eventually destroy the site, ending the tourism that the local economy depends on
options.D: UNESCO would immediately take full ownership of the site away from Peru

questions.explanation: This is a sustainability paradox — the economic activity enabled by the site can destroy the very resource it depends on, a reason Peru now enforces daily visitor caps at Machu Picchu. Option B is the most tempting misconception because it follows straightforward economic logic without accounting for carrying capacity and irreversible heritage damage.

questions.title: Media and Global Events
questions.prompt: A natural disaster in a small, distant country receives very little news coverage compared to a similar disaster in a large, wealthy country. What does this difference in coverage most likely reveal?

options.A: Disasters in small countries are always less severe and cause less suffering
options.B: Media organisations make editorial choices influenced by audience interest and economic relationships
options.C: Journalists are not permitted to travel to small or distant countries
options.D: Small countries do not allow international media to report on their disasters

questions.explanation: Media research consistently shows that news coverage of disasters correlates with geographic and cultural proximity to the audience, and with the economic and political importance of the affected country — not only with the severity of the disaster. Option A is a dangerous misconception because it makes suffering invisible by attributing less coverage to less need.

questions.title: Indigenous Rights and Land
questions.prompt: An indigenous community has lived on a forest for hundreds of years but does not hold a government-issued land title. A mining company claims it has a legal right to dig there because the government granted it a licence. Which global principle is most in tension with the mining company's position?

options.A: The principle that only written documents can prove ownership of land
options.B: The principle of free prior and informed consent — that communities must agree before development affects their land
options.C: The principle that national governments have no authority over private companies
options.D: The principle that economic development always outweighs community land use

questions.explanation: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) establishes free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) as a standard — meaning development that affects indigenous lands requires the community's genuine agreement beforehand. Option A tempts students who focus on the document aspect of the dispute rather than the underlying rights principle.

questions.title: Islam and Zakat
questions.prompt: Zakat is one of the Five Pillars of Islam and requires Muslims who have wealth above a minimum level to give a portion — usually 2.5% — to those in need each year. How does Zakat function as a global development tool?

options.A: It functions by helping governments collect taxes more efficiently
options.B: It creates a regular, religion-motivated transfer of wealth from those who have more to those who have less
options.C: It encourages Muslims to invest in businesses to grow the economy
options.D: It requires wealthy nations to donate to poorer Muslim-majority countries specifically

questions.explanation: Zakat is estimated to generate between $200 billion and $1 trillion annually worldwide, functioning as a built-in redistribution mechanism rooted in religious obligation rather than government mandate. Option D is a common misconception — Zakat is directed toward individuals in need regardless of national location, and its categories are defined by need, not nationality.

questions.title: Climate Agreements and Fairness
questions.prompt: At a global climate meeting, representatives from low-income countries argue that they should not have to reduce their carbon emissions as much as high-income countries. What is the strongest reasoning behind this position?

options.A: Low-income countries do not have the science to measure their emissions accurately
options.B: High-income countries created most of the historical emissions that caused current climate problems and have more resources to make changes
options.C: Low-income countries have fewer people, so their emissions are naturally smaller
options.D: The climate only affects high-income countries, so they should bear the cost of fixing it

questions.explanation: The concept of 'common but differentiated responsibilities,' written into the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, recognises that wealthy industrialised nations emitted most of the greenhouse gases historically and have greater technological and financial capacity to act now. Option C is a misconception that confuses total emissions with per-person emissions and ignores rapidly growing populations in low-income countries.

questions.title: Stereotypes in Cross-Cultural Study
questions.prompt: A student researching Brazil writes: 'Brazilians love football and carnivals.' Another student writes: 'Football and carnival are culturally significant in Brazil, though individual Brazilians have varied interests.' Which statement is more appropriate for an IB inquiry, and why?

options.A: The first — it is simpler and easier for young readers to understand cultural facts
options.B: They are equally valid because both say the same thing in different ways
options.C: The second — it acknowledges cultural patterns without assuming every individual is the same
options.D: The first — using broad generalisations is always acceptable in social studies research

questions.explanation: IB inquiry standards require distinguishing between cultural patterns, which describe tendencies in a group, and universal truths about every individual — the second statement does this by using qualifying language. Option B is wrong because the two statements differ fundamentally: the first asserts a universal truth about all Brazilians, while the second correctly qualifies that claim.

questions.title: Remittances and Family Economics
questions.prompt: A worker moves from the Philippines to work in Qatar. Each month she sends part of her wages home to her family in the Philippines. These payments are called remittances. What effect do remittances have on a country like the Philippines at the national level?

options.A: They reduce the Philippines' total income because money is leaving Qatar
options.B: They have no economic effect because only government payments count toward national income
options.C: They bring foreign currency into the Philippines, supporting household spending and contributing significantly to the national economy
options.D: They weaken the Philippines by encouraging more people to leave the country permanently

questions.explanation: Remittances to the Philippines amount to roughly 9–10% of its GDP annually, making them one of the country's largest sources of foreign income and a lifeline for millions of families. Option D identifies a real tension — brain drain — but misrepresents remittances themselves as harmful when they are economically significant for the receiving country.

questions.title: Fair Trade Basics
questions.prompt: A village in Ethiopia grows coffee beans that are sold in supermarkets in Canada for ten times what the farmers were paid. A 'Fair Trade' label on a product is meant to change this situation. What does a Fair Trade label mainly promise?

options.A: The product was made without using any machines
options.B: Farmers received a price that covers their basic costs and is agreed to be fair
options.C: The product was grown in a rich country so workers are protected by strong laws
options.D: The packaging was made from recycled materials

questions.explanation: Fair Trade certification guarantees that producers receive a minimum price designed to cover the cost of sustainable production, plus a Fairtrade Premium for community investment. Option C is wrong because Fair Trade is specifically designed to help producers in lower-income countries, not those already protected by rich-country labour laws.

questions.title: Migration Push and Pull
questions.prompt: When people move from the countryside to cities within the same country, geographers call this 'internal migration.' Which combination correctly identifies one push factor and one pull factor that cause this movement?

options.A: Push: more hospitals in the city; Pull: fewer farms in the countryside
options.B: Push: lack of jobs in the countryside; Pull: better-paid work available in the city
options.C: Push: crowded city streets; Pull: quiet village life
options.D: Push: high city rents; Pull: cheaper land in rural areas

questions.explanation: A push factor is something that makes people want to leave a place, such as lack of jobs, while a pull factor attracts them to a new place, such as higher wages in cities. Option A reverses the logic — hospitals in the city are a pull factor, not a push factor, and fewer farms is a push factor, so the labels are swapped.

questions.title: Religions and Sacred Space
questions.prompt: The city of Jerusalem is considered sacred by three world religions. A student claims this must mean those three religions all worship in the same way and share the same holy texts. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The error is that Jerusalem is only sacred to one religion, not three
options.B: The error is that sharing a sacred place does not mean sharing the same practices or scriptures
options.C: The error is that sacred cities are always controlled by the religion that built them first
options.D: The error is that only ancient religions have sacred cities

questions.explanation: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam each consider Jerusalem sacred for different historical and theological reasons, yet they have distinct holy texts, practices, and beliefs. Sharing a location does not imply sharing a religion's traditions — the Wailing Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Dome of the Rock are all in Jerusalem but serve very different religious purposes. Option A is the top distractor but is factually wrong — Jerusalem is indeed sacred to all three Abrahamic faiths.

questions.title: Global Supply Chains
questions.prompt: A T-shirt sold in a shop in Germany was designed in France, made from cotton grown in India, sewn in Bangladesh, and shipped through a port in Singapore. What does this journey best illustrate about modern global trade?

options.A: Rich countries do all the important work while poorer countries only provide materials
options.B: Products today are created through global supply chains where different countries contribute different stages
options.C: Shipping goods across many countries always makes them cheaper for the customer
options.D: Each country involved earns an equal share of the final price of the T-shirt

questions.explanation: A global supply chain means that designing, sourcing raw materials, manufacturing, and distributing a product can each happen in a different country, allowing companies to use each region's strengths. Option D is a common misconception — in reality, the country doing the sewing (often Bangladesh) typically earns far less than the country doing the designing or selling.

questions.title: Climate Justice and Responsibility
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Countries that industrialised earliest, like the UK and USA, should pay more to help poorer countries adapt to climate change because they produced most of the greenhouse gases that exist in the atmosphere today.' What principle of global ethics supports this argument?

options.A: The principle that whichever country is richest today should pay the most, regardless of history
options.B: The principle of historical responsibility — those who caused more harm in the past owe more to fix it
options.C: The principle that all countries must contribute equally because climate affects everyone equally
options.D: The principle that only countries currently producing the most emissions should pay

questions.explanation: Historical responsibility holds that countries whose past industrial activity generated the most cumulative greenhouse gases bear a greater duty to fund climate solutions, even if they are no longer the top emitters today. Option D is a misconception because it ignores historical emissions — countries like China and India now emit heavily but industrialised far later than the UK or USA.

questions.title: Aid vs. Development
questions.prompt: After a major earthquake, Country A sends emergency food and tents. Five years later, Country B offers to build a school and train local teachers in the same region. Which type of support is more likely to help people in the long run, and why?

options.A: Country A's support, because immediate needs must always be met before anything else can work
options.B: Both are equally important because development cannot happen unless people are alive and fed
options.C: Country B's support, because building skills and local capacity creates lasting improvement beyond the emergency
options.D: Country A's support, because food and shelter have universal value while education depends on culture

questions.explanation: Development economists distinguish between humanitarian aid, which addresses immediate crises, and development aid, which builds lasting capacity through education, infrastructure, and training. Country B's investment in a school and teachers creates a local resource that keeps benefiting the community for generations. Option B is tempting because it sounds balanced, but it does not answer which is more effective in the long run.

questions.title: Cultural Diffusion Online
questions.prompt: A teenager in Nigeria learns Korean phrases and dances from K-pop videos online. A teenager in South Korea buys an Afrobeats song recorded in Lagos. What global process does this two-way exchange best represent?

options.A: Cultural imperialism, because one culture is replacing another
options.B: Cultural diffusion, where ideas and practices spread and mix across borders
options.C: Assimilation, where minority cultures adopt the habits of the majority
options.D: Nationalism, where people celebrate their own culture above all others

questions.explanation: Cultural diffusion refers to the spread of cultural elements — music, language, food, fashion — from one society to another, and digital technology has accelerated this process globally. The example shows a two-way exchange rather than one culture overpowering another, which rules out cultural imperialism. Option A is the top distractor but requires one culture to replace another, not a mutual exchange.

questions.title: Water Access and Rights
questions.prompt: In some countries, children walk more than two hours each day to collect clean water. A classmate says this is simply because those countries have less rainfall. What important factor does this explanation leave out?

options.A: It leaves out that children in those countries prefer walking to using taps
options.B: It leaves out inequality in access to water infrastructure, which means rainfall alone does not determine who gets clean water
options.C: It leaves out the fact that rainwater is always unsafe to drink anywhere in the world
options.D: It leaves out that wealthier countries receive more rainfall than poorer ones

questions.explanation: Many water-scarce communities are not in the driest regions — they lack pipes, pumps, purification systems, and the funding to build them, which is a development and governance issue, not simply a climate one. Countries like Bolivia or parts of South Asia face water access problems despite significant rainfall because infrastructure investment has not reached all communities. Option D is factually incorrect — some of the wettest countries in the world are low-income.

questions.title: Symbols and National Identity
questions.prompt: Many countries use a flag, an anthem, and a national language to help citizens feel connected to each other. What happens when a country has many different ethnic groups, each with their own language and traditions?

options.A: National symbols automatically unite all groups because everyone in a country shares the same values
options.B: Countries with multiple ethnic groups cannot develop a shared identity and always experience conflict
options.C: National symbols may not represent all groups equally, which can create tension alongside unity
options.D: Ethnic groups inside a country always choose to give up their own traditions to adopt national ones

questions.explanation: Countries like Canada, India, and South Africa are multicultural yet maintain national identities, though some groups feel their language or traditions are marginalised by majority symbols — for example, debates over official languages. Option B overstates the case by claiming conflict is inevitable, which ignores many peaceful multicultural nations.

questions.title: International Organisations
questions.prompt: The United Nations was created after World War Two. A student claims the UN can force any country in the world to obey its decisions, just like a national government can make laws for its citizens. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because the UN Security Council has the power to pass laws that automatically apply in every country
options.B: The claim is mostly correct but only applies to countries that joined the UN after 1990
options.C: The claim is incorrect because the UN relies on member countries to agree and cooperate — it cannot make binding domestic laws the way national governments do
options.D: The claim is incorrect because the UN only gives advice on environmental issues and has no political powers at all

questions.explanation: The UN is an intergovernmental organisation that depends on voluntary cooperation and consensus among sovereign member states; even UN Security Council resolutions require enforcement by member countries and can be blocked by a permanent member's veto. Option A is a common misconception — the UN has significant influence but cannot legislate inside sovereign nations the way a domestic parliament can.

questions.title: Religion and Shared Values
questions.prompt: Hinduism and Islam developed in very different parts of the world and have very different rituals. Yet both traditions teach that giving to those in need is an important duty. What can a student fairly conclude from this comparison?

options.A: Hinduism and Islam must have the same origin because they share this value
options.B: Religions that share some values must also share the same beliefs about God
options.C: Different religious traditions can arrive at similar ethical values through separate histories and teachings
options.D: Sharing a value about generosity means the two religions have more similarities than differences

questions.explanation: Dana (generosity) in Hinduism and Zakat (charitable giving) in Islam are both central duties, yet they emerge from completely distinct theological frameworks and scriptures — showing that comparable ethical values can develop independently. Option A is wrong because Hinduism and Islam have separate historical origins; a shared value does not imply a shared source.

questions.title: Debt and Development
questions.prompt: Country X borrowed money from international banks to build roads and hospitals. Now it spends more money every year repaying the loan interest than it spends on education. How does this situation connect to the idea of global inequality?

options.A: It shows that building roads and hospitals is always a bad investment for developing countries
options.B: It shows how debt repayments can trap lower-income countries in a cycle that limits spending on the services that help people develop
options.C: It shows that international banks are always trying to help poorer countries grow faster
options.D: It shows that Country X must have a corrupt government, because well-run countries never borrow money

questions.explanation: When debt repayment costs exceed spending on essential services like education, governments cannot invest in the human development that breaks cycles of poverty — this is sometimes called a 'debt trap.' Option C ignores the fact that loan conditions and interest rates have historically placed heavy burdens on lower-income borrowers, which is a well-documented development economics concern.

questions.title: Endangered Languages
questions.prompt: When the last speaker of a language dies, that language becomes extinct. A student argues this only matters to the families of those speakers. What would a global perspectives scholar most likely say in response?

options.A: The scholar would agree, because language is a private matter within families and communities
options.B: The scholar would note that each language encodes unique knowledge — about nature, medicine, and history — that is lost to all humanity when it disappears
options.C: The scholar would argue that having fewer languages makes international communication easier and is therefore a positive development
options.D: The scholar would say that language extinction only matters if the language had a written form that could be studied

questions.explanation: Linguists and anthropologists have documented that many indigenous languages contain ecological knowledge about local plants, animals, and environments that exists nowhere else — the extinction of a language can mean the permanent loss of this knowledge for everyone. Option C is a genuine misconception that prioritises efficiency over cultural and intellectual diversity.

questions.title: Gender and Education Access
questions.prompt: In several regions of the world, girls are less likely than boys to complete secondary school. A student suggests this is purely because girls are less interested in studying. What does research on global education inequality actually show?

options.A: Research shows girls score lower on tests globally, which explains why they leave school earlier
options.B: Research shows structural barriers — such as safety concerns, early marriage, and household responsibilities — often prevent girls from continuing school
options.C: Research shows that in all regions, boys and girls have equal access to education but make different personal choices
options.D: Research shows the gap is caused entirely by differences in national wealth and disappears in middle-income countries

questions.explanation: UNESCO data shows that structural factors — including distance to school, risk of violence on the way, expectations to care for siblings, and early marriage — are major reasons girls drop out, not lack of interest or ability. Option C is a misconception; access gaps are well-documented in regions across Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia even among countries with similar income levels.

questions.title: Comparing Government Systems
questions.prompt: Country A holds regular elections where all adults can vote for their leaders. Country B is led by one person whose family has ruled for generations and who does not hold elections. What is the key difference between these two systems of government?

options.A: Country A must be wealthier, because democracies always have higher incomes than monarchies
options.B: Country A uses democratic accountability, where leaders are chosen by citizens, while Country B uses hereditary or authoritarian rule without public elections
options.C: Country B must have better laws because a single leader can make decisions more quickly
options.D: Both systems are equally fair as long as the people are happy with the outcome

questions.explanation: The defining feature of a democracy is that citizens choose their government through free and fair elections, creating accountability — leaders can be voted out. Hereditary or authoritarian rule concentrates power without this public check. Option A is a misconception — several high-income Gulf states are not democracies, and some lower-income countries hold regular elections.

questions.title: Food Security and Globalisation
questions.prompt: A small island nation imports 80% of its food from other countries. When global shipping costs rise sharply, food prices on the island double. What does this situation reveal about a risk of deep economic globalisation?

options.A: It reveals that island nations should not be part of the global trading system at all
options.B: It reveals that importing food is always cheaper than growing it locally
options.C: It reveals that heavy dependence on global trade can make a country vulnerable when international conditions change
options.D: It reveals that shipping companies are responsible for ending world hunger

questions.explanation: Food security experts identify import dependence as a vulnerability — when supply chains are disrupted by rising fuel costs, pandemics, or conflicts, countries that produce little of their own food face sudden price shocks. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated this when shipping bottlenecks pushed up global food prices. Option B is a misconception; while imports can be cheaper in normal conditions, crises can reverse this rapidly.

questions.title: Refugees and Host Communities
questions.prompt: When a large number of refugees arrive in a new country, some local people worry about the impact on jobs and services. Others point out that refugees also contribute skills and labour to their new home. What does this tension best illustrate?

options.A: That refugees always cause economic harm to the countries that accept them
options.B: That migration has complex impacts and different groups within a host society may experience it differently
options.C: That host governments should always reduce the number of refugees they accept to protect citizens
options.D: That refugees and local workers always compete for exactly the same jobs

questions.explanation: Research from the World Bank and UNHCR shows that refugees can contribute to economic growth over time through labour, entrepreneurship, and taxes, though short-term pressures on housing and public services are real — the impacts are mixed and unevenly distributed. Option D is a misconception; refugees often fill different roles in the labour market, such as in sectors with shortages, rather than directly competing with local workers.

questions.title: Stewardship and Environment
questions.prompt: Many indigenous communities around the world have managed forests, rivers, and wildlife for thousands of years without destroying them. A development planner says this is simply luck because they had less technology. What does a global perspectives approach suggest instead?

options.A: That indigenous communities should now adopt modern farming and forestry techniques to improve results
options.B: That traditional ecological knowledge represents a systematic and proven form of environmental stewardship developed over generations
options.C: That lack of technology always leads to better environmental outcomes regardless of who is using the land
options.D: That luck is the main reason some ecosystems survive, and human decisions have little effect

questions.explanation: Studies published in journals including Science have found that indigenous-managed lands often have higher biodiversity and lower deforestation rates than state-managed or private lands, reflecting deep knowledge systems about seasonal patterns, species relationships, and sustainable harvesting. Option C oversimplifies by attributing outcomes to technology level alone rather than to cultural knowledge and values.

questions.title: Trade Sanctions Explained
questions.prompt: When one country refuses to buy or sell goods with another country as a way of pressuring it to change its behaviour, this is called a trade sanction. A student says sanctions always hurt only the government of the targeted country. Identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: The flaw is that sanctions always make the targeted government immediately change its behaviour
options.B: The flaw is that sanctions can harm ordinary citizens of the targeted country through shortages and rising prices, not just its leaders
options.C: The flaw is that governments are never affected by trade sanctions because they control their own money supply
options.D: The flaw is that only the country imposing the sanctions can be economically harmed, not the target

questions.explanation: Historical examples such as sanctions on Iran and North Korea show that while they create economic pressure on governments, ordinary citizens often experience food shortages, medicine scarcity, and unemployment — a well-documented unintended consequence. Option D is also partly wrong because imposing countries can face losses too, but B identifies the most significant flaw in the original claim.

questions.title: Measuring Poverty Fairly
questions.prompt: The international poverty line is set at a specific dollar amount per day. A student claims that if a person earns just above this amount, they are no longer poor. What important limitation does this view overlook?

options.A: It overlooks that the poverty line is set differently in every country, so comparisons are impossible
options.B: It overlooks that a fixed dollar threshold cannot capture differences in local costs, access to services, or social exclusion that still make life very difficult
options.C: It overlooks that people who earn more than the poverty line are always financially comfortable
options.D: It overlooks that poverty only refers to lack of food and has nothing to do with money

questions.explanation: The World Bank's poverty line (currently $2.15 per day in 2017 purchasing power parity) is a useful global comparison tool but misses multidimensional poverty — people just above the line may still lack clean water, healthcare, or schooling, and costs of living vary enormously between countries and cities. Option C is a direct misconception; earning just above the poverty threshold rarely means financial security.

questions.title: Borders and Belonging
questions.prompt: Some ethnic groups live across the borders of two or three different countries — for example, the Kurdish people live across parts of Turkey, Iraq, Iran, and Syria. What challenge does this create for understanding national identity?

options.A: It shows that political borders drawn by governments do not always match where cultural groups actually live or feel they belong
options.B: It proves that cultural groups divided by borders always want to form their own separate country
options.C: It shows that national identity is only meaningful when a country has defined borders recognised by all its neighbours
options.D: It shows that ethnic groups who cross borders are usually engaged in illegal migration

questions.explanation: Many modern national borders were drawn by colonial powers or through historical treaties without reference to where ethnic, linguistic, or cultural communities actually lived — the Kurdish example illustrates how political geography and cultural identity can be misaligned. Option B overstates the case; while some Kurds seek an independent Kurdistan, many others seek rights and recognition within existing states rather than full separation.

questions.title: Sustainable Development Tradeoffs
questions.prompt: A government wants to build a new coal power station to provide electricity to a rural community that currently has none. Environmentalists oppose the plan because coal produces greenhouse gases. What does this situation best illustrate about sustainable development decisions?

options.A: Environmental concerns are always more important than the needs of communities without electricity
options.B: Economic development always causes environmental damage and the two goals can never be balanced
options.C: Sustainable development often involves difficult tradeoffs between meeting people's current needs and protecting the environment for the future
options.D: The correct solution is always to choose the cheapest available energy source regardless of environmental impact

questions.explanation: The Brundtland Commission defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — a definition that acknowledges tension between development and environmental protection. Option A is wrong because it dismisses the real and urgent need for electricity access, which affects health, education, and economic opportunity for the rural community.

questions.title: Aid vs. Local Economy
questions.prompt: A charity sends free rice to a country experiencing hunger. Local rice farmers in that country then cannot sell their own rice because the free rice floods the market. What does this situation reveal about international aid?

options.A: Aid always helps the people who receive it most directly
options.B: Well-intentioned aid can sometimes harm the local economy it tries to help
options.C: Countries should refuse all international aid to protect their farmers
options.D: Free food aid is always better than sending money to a country

questions.explanation: When free goods flood a local market, local producers lose customers and income even though they were not in crisis — this unintended harm is a well-documented problem called 'aid dependency' or market distortion. Option A is wrong because the farmers, who are also local people, are made worse off by the very aid meant to help the country.

questions.title: Migration Push and Pull
questions.prompt: A student lists reasons people move to a new country: better hospitals, escaping flooding, family already living there, and higher wages. Which of these is BEST described as an environmental push factor rather than an economic pull factor?

options.A: Higher wages available in the new country
options.B: Family members already living in the new country
options.C: Escaping flooding in the home country
options.D: Better hospitals in the new country

questions.explanation: A push factor is something that drives people away from their home country, and when that reason is a natural event like flooding, it is classified as an environmental push factor. Higher wages and better hospitals are pull factors because they attract people toward the new country, and family ties are a social pull factor, not an environmental push.

questions.title: Religion and Sacred Spaces
questions.prompt: The city of Jerusalem is considered holy by three major world religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Why does this make Jerusalem a particularly complex place in international relations?

options.A: Religious cities are always richer than non-religious cities, causing economic jealousy
options.B: Multiple groups hold deeply sincere and overlapping claims to the same sacred sites, making political decisions affect religious identity
options.C: The United Nations does not recognise any religious sites as important, so there is no official protection
options.D: Only one religion at a time can legally own a holy site under international law

questions.explanation: Jerusalem contains sites like the Temple Mount, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Al-Aqsa Mosque, all in the same small area, meaning political decisions about who governs the city directly affect the religious lives of billions of people worldwide. Option D is incorrect because international law does not award exclusive religious ownership of shared sacred sites to a single group.

questions.title: Cultural Diffusion Effects
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'When a global music style becomes popular in a new country, the local traditional music always disappears forever.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from global cultural exchange.

options.A: The claim is correct because global styles have replaced every local music tradition studied so far
options.B: The claim is partly right because traditional music only survives if a government bans global music
options.C: The claim is too strong because many cultures blend global influences with local traditions to create new forms
options.D: The claim is correct because younger generations always prefer global music over traditional music

questions.explanation: Cultural diffusion often leads to hybrid or blended forms — for example, Afrobeats blends African rhythms with global pop — rather than complete replacement of local traditions. Option D is too absolute; many young people actively participate in reviving and celebrating traditional music, especially when it becomes a marker of cultural pride.

questions.title: Global Supply Chains
questions.prompt: A pair of trainers is designed in the United States, made with cotton from India, assembled in Vietnam, and sold in Germany. Which concept does this best illustrate?

options.A: Cultural assimilation across continents
options.B: A global supply chain connecting multiple countries in production
options.C: Bilateral trade, because only two countries are involved in making the product
options.D: Foreign direct investment, because money moves from the US to Germany

questions.explanation: A global supply chain is a network where different stages of making a product happen in different countries — the trainers example involves at least four countries each contributing a different step. Bilateral trade specifically means trade between just two countries, so option C is wrong because more than two countries are involved here.

questions.title: Fairtrade and Farmers
questions.prompt: A Fairtrade label on a product means the producer was paid a guaranteed minimum price. Which group benefits MOST directly from buying Fairtrade goods, and why?

options.A: Shipping companies, because Fairtrade products travel farther to reach shops
options.B: Supermarkets in wealthy countries, because Fairtrade products sell at higher prices
options.C: Farmers and workers in lower-income countries, because they receive a stable and fairer payment for their work
options.D: Governments of wealthy countries, because they collect more tax from Fairtrade product sales

questions.explanation: The Fairtrade system was specifically designed so that farmers and workers — often in low-income countries — receive a price floor that covers their costs and allows investment in their communities, regardless of how world commodity prices fluctuate. Supermarkets do charge more for Fairtrade products, but the extra revenue is meant to flow back to producers, not primarily to retailers.

questions.title: International Law Gaps
questions.prompt: Country A agrees to stop polluting a shared ocean, but Country B continues polluting because it never signed the international agreement. What does this situation reveal about how international agreements work?

options.A: International agreements are automatically enforceable against every country in the world
options.B: Country A made a mistake by signing the agreement because only the polluter benefits
options.C: International agreements only bind the countries that sign them, so non-signatories can act differently without breaking international law
options.D: The United Nations can send police to force Country B to stop polluting immediately

questions.explanation: International law is based on the consent of sovereign states — a country that does not sign a treaty is generally not legally bound by it, which is a major challenge for global environmental governance. The UN does not have its own police force that can compel sovereign states, making option D incorrect.

questions.title: Sustainable Development Tensions
questions.prompt: A developing country discovers large oil reserves. Its leaders want to sell the oil to fund schools and hospitals, but environmentalists argue this will worsen climate change. Which tension does this scenario best represent?

options.A: The tension between national development needs and global environmental sustainability
options.B: The tension between two countries both wanting to own the same oil field
options.C: The tension between religious values and scientific research
options.D: The tension between tourism and industrial farming within one country

questions.explanation: This is a classic sustainability dilemma: the country has a genuine human development need (schools and hospitals) but fulfilling it through fossil fuels contributes to a global problem that affects everyone, including the very people the revenue is meant to help. Option B does not apply because the scenario involves one country and its own discovered resource, not a competing claim from another nation.

questions.title: Refugee Rights Framework
questions.prompt: The 1951 Refugee Convention says countries must not return a refugee to a place where they face serious danger. What is the name of this legal principle?

options.A: Habeas corpus
options.B: Non-refoulement
options.C: Jus soli
options.D: Diplomatic immunity

questions.explanation: Non-refoulement is the core protection in international refugee law, prohibiting the return of a person to a territory where they would face persecution or serious harm — it is considered one of the most fundamental rules in international human rights law. Habeas corpus is a legal protection against unlawful detention, not a refugee protection rule, making it the most tempting but wrong distractor.

questions.title: Comparing Development Indicators
questions.prompt: Country P has a very high GDP per person but also has the highest rate of income inequality in its region. Country Q has a lower GDP per person but distributes income much more equally. Which statement about measuring development is most accurate?

options.A: Country P is clearly more developed because GDP per person is the only reliable measure of development
options.B: GDP per person alone does not tell us how fairly wealth is shared, so we need additional measures to compare development fairly
options.C: Country Q is clearly more developed because equal distribution of income always matters more than total wealth
options.D: Both countries are equally developed because each has one strength and one weakness

questions.explanation: GDP per capita shows average wealth but hides how that wealth is distributed — a country can have a very high average while most people remain poor if a small group is extremely wealthy. Option C overcorrects by claiming equality always matters more than total wealth, which ignores cases where a country may be equally poor and unable to fund essential services.

questions.title: Multicultural Identity
questions.prompt: Amara was born in Nigeria, moved to Canada at age five, and speaks Yoruba at home and English at school. She celebrates both Eid and Canadian Thanksgiving. Which concept best describes her relationship with culture?

options.A: Cultural assimilation, because she now lives fully within Canadian culture
options.B: Cultural isolation, because she maintains her home language separately from school
options.C: Bicultural or hybrid identity, because she actively participates in two cultural systems simultaneously
options.D: Cultural appropriation, because she celebrates a holiday from a culture she was not born into

questions.explanation: A bicultural or hybrid identity means a person authentically belongs to and practices two cultural systems at the same time — Amara's language use and celebration of both holidays is a clear example. Cultural assimilation would mean she had given up her Yoruba identity to fully adopt Canadian culture, which the scenario does not show.

questions.title: Global Commons Responsibility
questions.prompt: The open ocean beyond any country's border is called the 'global commons.' Which challenge does it face that is different from challenges faced by land owned by a single country?

options.A: It is impossible to travel across the open ocean, so countries ignore it
options.B: Because no single country owns it, it is harder to enforce rules about fishing or pollution
options.C: It belongs to the United Nations, which can easily stop any country from polluting it
options.D: Only wealthy countries are allowed to use the open ocean under current international agreements

questions.explanation: The 'tragedy of the commons' concept explains that when a resource belongs to everyone and no one in particular, individuals and countries may overuse or damage it because they are not directly responsible for its upkeep — enforcing fishing limits or pollution rules on the open ocean requires all countries to cooperate, which is very difficult. The UN does not own or fully control the high seas; rather, international conventions like UNCLOS set guidelines that are difficult to enforce against unwilling states.

questions.title: Hinduism and Global Ethics
questions.prompt: A core Hindu concept, ahimsa, means non-violence or doing no harm to any living being. How might a student studying global ethics use this concept when discussing environmental sustainability?

options.A: Ahimsa only applies to relationships between people and has no connection to the natural world
options.B: Ahimsa supports the idea that harming ecosystems and animals conflicts with a moral duty to avoid causing suffering
options.C: Ahimsa teaches that humans should avoid all contact with nature to prevent accidentally harming it
options.D: Ahimsa is a political concept used only by governments in South Asia and has no global relevance

questions.explanation: Ahimsa extends to all living beings in Hindu philosophy, which means destroying habitats, causing species extinction, or polluting water that harms animals and ecosystems can be seen as a violation of this principle — making it directly relevant to global environmental ethics. Option A is wrong because classical texts like the Mahabharata specifically extend ahimsa to animals and the natural world, not only to human relationships.

questions.title: Urbanisation and Inequality
questions.prompt: In many fast-growing cities in lower-income countries, some people live in very modern high-rise apartments while others live in informal settlements without clean water nearby. What does this pattern best illustrate?

options.A: Urban areas in lower-income countries are always poorer than rural areas in the same country
options.B: Rapid urbanisation can create extreme inequality within a single city, not just between countries
options.C: Modern buildings always replace informal settlements within a few years of being built nearby
options.D: Governments of lower-income countries always prioritise housing for the poorest residents first

questions.explanation: Intra-urban inequality — poverty and wealth existing side by side within the same city — is a documented feature of rapid urbanisation, seen in cities like Mumbai, Lagos, and São Paulo, where luxury towers can overlook large informal settlements. Option A is incorrect because many cities in lower-income countries actually have higher average incomes than rural areas in the same country, even while housing extreme inequality internally.

questions.title: Trade and Power Imbalance
questions.prompt: A large, wealthy country threatens to stop buying goods from a small, poorer country unless the small country changes a law the large country dislikes. What term describes using trade as a political tool in this way?

options.A: Economic sanctions used as diplomatic pressure
options.B: Fairtrade certification enforcement
options.C: Foreign direct investment incentive
options.D: Bilateral aid conditionality from a donor

questions.explanation: Economic sanctions — the threatened or actual restriction of trade — are a recognised tool of diplomatic pressure used by more powerful countries to influence the behaviour or policies of others, and this is exactly what the scenario describes. Fairtrade certification is a voluntary ethical labelling system with no power to threaten a country's laws, making it an appealing but clearly wrong option.

questions.title: Evaluating Stereotypes
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's argument: 'People in cold northern countries work harder than people in hot tropical countries. That is why northern countries are richer.'

options.A: The argument is flawed because it ignores historical factors like colonialism that shaped which countries became wealthy
options.B: The argument is correct because climate scientists agree that temperature directly determines economic output
options.C: The argument is flawed only because it does not mention the role of technology in economic growth
options.D: The argument is correct because countries closer to the equator have fewer natural resources

questions.explanation: Wealth differences between regions are heavily shaped by historical processes like colonialism, which extracted resources and disrupted economies in tropical regions for centuries — attributing wealth differences to climate and work ethic ignores this documented history. Option C is partially relevant but too narrow; the deeper error is the stereotyping of people by geography and ignoring the structural historical causes of inequality.

questions.title: Interconnected Environmental Risk
questions.prompt: Deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in South America affects rainfall patterns in countries thousands of kilometres away. What does this tell us about environmental problems?

options.A: Environmental damage is always contained within the country where it happens
options.B: Environmental systems are globally interconnected, so local damage can cause distant consequences
options.C: Only countries that share a land border with Brazil are affected by Amazon deforestation
options.D: Rainfall patterns are controlled by ocean temperature alone and are unaffected by forests

questions.explanation: The Amazon rainforest acts as a 'flying river,' releasing moisture that feeds rainfall across South America and beyond — scientific studies show that deforestation disrupts these patterns even in distant countries like Bolivia and Argentina. Option C is wrong because atmospheric circulation means impacts are not limited to neighbouring countries but can extend across continents.

questions.title: Citizenship and Belonging
questions.prompt: Some countries grant citizenship based on where a person is born (jus soli), while others grant it based on the citizenship of the parents (jus sanguinis). A child is born in Country X to parents who are citizens of Country Y. Under jus soli, which country's citizenship would the child receive at birth?

options.A: Country Y, because citizenship always follows the parents under all systems
options.B: Both Country X and Country Y automatically in every case
options.C: Country X, because jus soli grants citizenship based on the place of birth
options.D: Neither country, because a child must apply for citizenship after turning 18

questions.explanation: Jus soli is Latin for 'right of the soil,' meaning citizenship is granted to anyone born on a country's territory — so a child born in Country X would receive Country X's citizenship under this system, regardless of the parents' nationality. Option A describes jus sanguinis, not jus soli, so it confuses the two legal principles that the question asks students to distinguish.

questions.title: Media and Global Perspective
questions.prompt: A student in Europe reads only news from European outlets about a conflict in West Africa. Why might a global perspectives teacher caution the student about relying on only these sources?

options.A: European news outlets are always factually wrong about events in Africa
options.B: Reading multiple perspectives from different regions helps avoid unconscious bias and incomplete understanding
options.C: Students are not allowed to read international news until they are older
options.D: West African news sources write only in local languages and cannot be translated

questions.explanation: Media from one region may frame events through a particular cultural or political lens, emphasising certain causes, victims, or solutions while omitting others — this is called media bias, and it means that reading sources from multiple perspectives gives a more complete and fairer understanding. Option A is too absolute; European outlets can report accurately but may still prioritise angles or contexts that reflect their own readership's concerns.

questions.title: Multilateral Organisations
questions.prompt: The World Health Organization (WHO) coordinates global responses to disease outbreaks, but it cannot force any country to follow its advice. What does this limitation tell us about how international organisations work?

options.A: International organisations are completely useless because no country ever follows their guidance
options.B: International organisations rely mostly on persuasion, shared information, and voluntary cooperation rather than legal enforcement
options.C: The WHO should be replaced by a single world government that can force countries to act
options.D: Countries only follow WHO guidance if they are paid to do so

questions.explanation: The WHO's power rests on 'soft power' — producing scientific evidence, coordinating information sharing, and building consensus — because sovereign nations have not given it legal authority to compel them; during COVID-19, countries chose different levels of compliance with WHO recommendations. Option A overcorrects; many countries do voluntarily follow WHO guidance, and the organisation played a central role in eradicating smallpox, showing real impact through cooperation.

questions.title: Gender and Development
questions.prompt: Research shows that in countries where girls stay in school longer, overall economic development tends to improve. Which explanation best accounts for this connection?

options.A: Girls who study longer automatically earn more than boys in every country
options.B: Educated women tend to have healthier families, participate more in the workforce, and contribute to broader community wellbeing, creating a multiplier effect
options.C: Countries improve economically only because having girls in school means boys study harder to compete
options.D: Girls' education replaces the need for foreign aid, so countries spend less on imports

questions.explanation: Development economists describe girls' education as having a 'multiplier effect' — educated women tend to marry later, have healthier and fewer children, earn more income that stays in local communities, and invest more in their own children's health and education, all of which compound into broader social development. Option A is too absolute and ignores documented wage gaps that persist in most countries despite women's educational advances.

questions.title: Buddhism and Interconnection
questions.prompt: A Buddhist teaching called interdependence (pratītyasamutpāda) says that all things arise in relation to each other and nothing exists completely on its own. How might this idea connect to global sustainability thinking?

options.A: It supports the view that damaging one part of an ecosystem can affect many other parts and species
options.B: It teaches that humans should not make any decisions that affect nature
options.C: It only applies to relationships between Buddhist monks and has no broader meaning
options.D: It suggests that natural resources can always renew themselves without human help

questions.explanation: The Buddhist concept of interdependence mirrors the ecological understanding that ecosystems are webs of relationships — harming one species or habitat can cascade through the entire system, an idea central to sustainability science. Option B misapplies the teaching; interdependence does not prohibit human action but rather encourages mindful, compassionate action that acknowledges consequences for others.

questions.title: Climate Justice Claims
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Because wealthy countries produced most historical greenhouse gas emissions, they have a greater responsibility to fund climate solutions for poorer countries that did not cause the problem but suffer greatly from it.' What principle of global fairness does this argument use?

options.A: The precautionary principle, which says we should avoid any action until we are certain of the outcome
options.B: The polluter pays principle, applied across generations and countries to historic emissions
options.C: The principle of sovereign equality, which says all countries have the same rights and duties
options.D: The free rider principle, which says countries that benefit from a system should pay its costs

questions.explanation: The 'polluter pays' principle holds that those who caused environmental damage bear responsibility for remedying it — applying this historically means wealthy industrialised nations that emitted most greenhouse gases since the Industrial Revolution bear greater responsibility for funding adaptation in vulnerable countries. The precautionary principle (option A) is about avoiding uncertain future harms, not attributing responsibility for past actions.

questions.title: Cultural Heritage Preservation
questions.prompt: An international museum holds ancient sculptures that were taken from their country of origin during a period of colonial rule. The origin country now requests their return. Which competing value is at the centre of this debate?

options.A: The value of global free trade versus the value of national economic protectionism
options.B: The value of universal public access to culture in major museums versus the value of cultural sovereignty and repatriation of heritage
options.C: The value of scientific research versus the value of religious traditions
options.D: The value of national security versus the value of international tourism revenue

questions.explanation: Repatriation debates pit two genuine values against each other: museums argue that keeping objects in major institutions allows millions worldwide to access shared human heritage, while origin countries argue that objects taken under colonial coercion belong to their culture and should be returned to fulfil cultural sovereignty. Option A is unrelated to cultural heritage ownership and introduces a trade-economics frame that does not fit this debate.

questions.title: Food Security and Trade
questions.prompt: Country Z grows enough food to feed its population but exports most of its best crops to earn money from richer countries, leaving its own people to buy cheaper, less nutritious food. What does this reveal about the relationship between food trade and food security?

options.A: A country that produces enough food always guarantees food security for all its citizens
options.B: Producing food and being food secure are not the same thing if economic incentives drive exports over local needs
options.C: Food insecurity only exists in countries that do not grow any food of their own
options.D: Countries should never export food because it always causes hunger at home

questions.explanation: Food security requires that people have physical and economic access to sufficient, nutritious food — a country can produce plenty yet still have food insecurity if market forces direct the best food abroad and local people cannot afford adequate nutrition. Option A is the most tempting distractor but is incorrect because production quantity does not equal access — distribution, price, and economic power determine who actually eats well.

questions.title: Fair Trade vs Free Trade
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Free trade always benefits every country equally because goods flow freely across borders.' A classmate disagrees. Which response best challenges this claim using evidence from global economics?

options.A: Free trade helps all countries equally because competition lowers prices for everyone.
options.B: Wealthier countries often have advantages like better technology, so free trade can widen gaps between rich and poor nations.
options.C: Free trade only works between countries that share the same language and culture.
options.D: Poorer countries always refuse to join free trade agreements because they lose too much money.

questions.explanation: Wealthier countries often have stronger industries, better infrastructure, and advanced technology, which gives them a competitive advantage in free trade — meaning the benefits are not shared equally. Option A is wrong because lower prices alone do not account for how profits are distributed and which producers gain most from the arrangement.

questions.title: Migration Push and Pull
questions.prompt: A family moves from a drought-affected rural area to a busy city in the same country. Which term most accurately describes this type of movement, and why is it different from international migration?

options.A: Refugee movement, because drought is a natural disaster that forces people to flee.
options.B: International migration, because moving to a city is crossing into a new cultural zone.
options.C: Internal migration, because the family moves within the borders of one country.
options.D: Forced displacement, because drought removes all choice from the family's decision.

questions.explanation: Internal migration refers to movement within a single country's borders, such as from rural to urban areas — no international boundary is crossed. Option A is incorrect because refugee status is a legal category under international law that applies to people crossing international borders due to persecution, not to people moving within their own country.

questions.title: Cultural Identity and Globalisation
questions.prompt: A student notices that teenagers in many different countries listen to the same music, wear the same brands, and watch the same films. She concludes that cultural differences are disappearing entirely. What is the most accurate evaluation of her conclusion?

options.A: She is correct because shared media always replaces local traditions completely.
options.B: She is partly right — global culture spreads, but local traditions, languages, and customs often survive alongside it.
options.C: She is wrong because teenagers in different countries never share the same cultural products.
options.D: She is correct because cultural differences only existed before the internet was invented.

questions.explanation: Globalisation spreads shared cultural products widely, but local languages, festivals, foods, and customs continue to exist alongside global trends — this is sometimes called 'glocalisation.' Option A is wrong because evidence shows many local traditions remain strong even where global brands are popular, and the two forms of culture often blend rather than one erasing the other.

questions.title: International Aid Debate
questions.prompt: Country A sends large amounts of food aid to Country B after a flood. Some experts worry this could cause problems in Country B even though it helps immediately. Which concern do these experts most likely have?

options.A: People in Country B might eat too much and become unhealthy.
options.B: Free imported food may undercut local farmers, making it harder for them to sell their produce and recover long-term.
options.C: Country A will run out of food for its own people by sending too much.
options.D: Country B's government will become angry and refuse future aid from Country A.

questions.explanation: When large amounts of free food arrive, local farmers cannot compete on price, which can damage local agriculture and slow long-term food security recovery — a well-documented criticism of poorly targeted food aid. Option C is a plausible-sounding concern but is incorrect because aid is typically sourced carefully so it does not threaten the donor country's own food supply.

questions.title: World Religions: Sacred Spaces
questions.prompt: Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism each designate certain spaces or times as sacred. What does this similarity most strongly suggest when comparing world religions from a global perspectives viewpoint?

options.A: All three religions developed in the same geographic region and therefore share identical practices.
options.B: Separating the sacred from the everyday is a concept that appears across very different cultural and religious traditions.
options.C: Hinduism borrowed its idea of sacred spaces directly from Judaism.
options.D: A space can only be sacred if it is recognised as sacred by every religion in the world.

questions.explanation: The concept of distinguishing sacred time or space from ordinary life appears independently across many world religions, showing it is a cross-cultural human pattern rather than the result of shared origin. Option A is incorrect because while Islam and Judaism share some historical roots, Hinduism developed in South Asia through a very different history.

questions.title: Global Citizenship Rights
questions.prompt: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child states that every child has the right to education regardless of where they were born. Which situation most directly conflicts with this principle?

options.A: A country that teaches different subjects in primary school than a neighbouring country.
options.B: A country where children of undocumented migrants are denied enrolment in public schools.
options.C: A country that requires all children to wear uniforms to school.
options.D: A country where school starts at age six rather than age five.

questions.explanation: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child guarantees education to all children without discrimination, including those whose parents have irregular immigration status — denying enrolment directly violates this right. Option A is plausible but incorrect because different curricula do not deny children access to education; they simply vary the content taught.

questions.title: Sustainability and Consumption
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's reasoning: 'If every person on Earth recycled all their plastic, the problem of ocean plastic pollution would be completely solved.'

options.A: The error is claiming that plastic can ever be recycled, because plastic cannot be broken down.
options.B: The error is ignoring that plastic already in the ocean would remain, recycling systems are unequal globally, and production of new plastic would continue.
options.C: The error is assuming all people live near an ocean, when many people live far inland.
options.D: The error is suggesting recycling helps at all, since it uses more energy than making new plastic.

questions.explanation: Even universal recycling would not remove existing ocean plastic, and many low-income countries lack recycling infrastructure — plus ongoing plastic production would continue adding to the problem. Option D is a tempting distractor but is factually incorrect; recycling does reduce environmental impact in many contexts, even if it is not a complete solution.

questions.title: Comparing Development Measures
questions.prompt: Two countries both have a medium HDI score. Country P has much higher income per person, while Country Q has higher literacy rates and longer life expectancy. What does this comparison reveal about using HDI?

options.A: HDI is inaccurate because it gives the same score to countries that are completely different.
options.B: HDI combines income, education, and health equally, so different combinations of these can produce a similar overall score.
options.C: Country P is more developed because income is always the most important measure of development.
options.D: Country Q cannot have a higher literacy rate if it has a lower income, so the data must contain an error.

questions.explanation: HDI averages three dimensions — income, education (including literacy), and life expectancy — so a country can score higher on two dimensions and lower on one and still match another country's overall score. Option A misreads this as inaccuracy; the same composite score from different component strengths is a feature of the index, not a flaw in measurement.

questions.title: Multiculturalism in Schools
questions.prompt: A school celebrates cultural diversity by holding a 'World Food Day' once a year where students bring dishes from their heritage. A student argues this is not enough to build genuine multicultural understanding. Which reasoning best supports her argument?

options.A: Food events cost too much money and take time away from important lessons.
options.B: Sharing food is a disrespectful way to represent another culture.
options.C: Celebrating surface features like food once a year does not build understanding of values, histories, or perspectives different from one's own.
options.D: Students should only learn about cultures from their own country before studying international ones.

questions.explanation: Multicultural education researchers distinguish between surface-level cultural exchange (food, dress) and deeper engagement with histories, beliefs, and perspectives — a single annual event does not build the latter. Option A raises a practical concern but does not address the quality or depth of multicultural learning, making it a weaker counter-argument.

questions.title: Climate Justice and Responsibility
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Industrialised countries should contribute more to climate change funds than developing countries, even if both produce equal amounts of pollution today.' What is the strongest reasoning behind this position?

options.A: Industrialised countries have larger populations, so they have more people to contribute money.
options.B: Industrialised countries built wealth through decades of high emissions historically, creating a greater share of the total pollution causing current climate change.
options.C: Developing countries should not be asked to pay because they do not have governments capable of managing large funds.
options.D: It is fairer for industrialised countries to pay because they invented the technologies that caused pollution.

questions.explanation: The concept of 'historical responsibility' in climate justice holds that industrialised nations emitted the majority of greenhouse gases during their periods of rapid industrial growth, and those accumulated emissions are a primary cause of current climate change. Option D is plausible but too narrow — the argument is about cumulative emissions over time, not simply who invented a technology.

questions.title: Diplomacy and Conflict Resolution
questions.prompt: Two countries have a trade dispute. Country A imposes heavy taxes on goods from Country B. Country B threatens to do the same in return. What would most likely happen next if both countries follow through on these actions?

options.A: Prices for imported goods in both countries would fall as producers compete harder to sell.
options.B: Trade between the two countries would likely decrease and consumers in both countries could face higher prices.
options.C: Other countries would immediately stop all trade with both nations to show disapproval.
options.D: Country B would quickly surrender its position because small countries cannot sustain trade disputes.

questions.explanation: Mutual tariffs — sometimes called a 'trade war' — raise the cost of imported goods, which typically leads to reduced trade between the two nations and higher prices for consumers in both countries who relied on those imports. Option A is the opposite of what tariffs do; they make foreign goods more expensive, not cheaper.

questions.title: Indigenous Rights and Land
questions.prompt: A government gives a mining company permission to dig for minerals on land that an indigenous community has lived on for generations, without consulting the community. Which principle of international indigenous rights does this most directly violate?

options.A: The right of all citizens to vote in national elections.
options.B: The principle of free, prior, and informed consent, which requires governments to consult communities before decisions affecting their land.
options.C: The right of companies to operate freely in any country where they are registered.
