options.A: The error is that wealthy countries never send food aid; they only send money.
options.B: The error is assuming aid always has positive long-term effects; large food imports can undercut local farmers' prices, reducing their income and worsening long-term food security.
options.C: The error is using the word 'famine' — the correct term is 'food shortage.'
options.D: The error is that food aid can only be sent by international organisations like the United Nations, not by individual countries.

questions.explanation: When donor countries flood local markets with free or cheap food, local farmers cannot compete, which can destroy local agriculture and create dependency rather than recovery — a well-documented problem called 'aid dependency.' Option D is incorrect because individual nations do send bilateral food aid directly to affected countries.

questions.title: World Religions Comparison
questions.prompt: Ramadan in Islam, Yom Kippur in Judaism, and certain Buddhist retreats all involve periods of fasting or self-denial. What is the most academically careful conclusion to draw from this pattern?

options.A: All three religions originally developed in the same geographic region, so their practices are identical.
options.B: Fasting proves that all religions share the same core theology about the relationship between the body and the spirit.
options.C: Multiple distinct religious traditions have independently developed practices of fasting, suggesting it serves important spiritual or communal functions across cultures.
options.D: Fasting is only meaningful in religions that believe in one God, so Buddhism's inclusion of fasting disproves this idea.

questions.explanation: When unrelated cultures independently develop similar practices, it suggests those practices meet a deep human or spiritual need — scholars call this 'convergent cultural evolution.' Option A is incorrect because Buddhism originated in the Indian subcontinent while Judaism and Islam, though both Abrahamic, each developed distinct practices, and their similarities do not mean their practices are identical.

questions.title: Sustainability Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A developing country discovers large oil reserves beneath its national park. The government can earn billions by selling the oil, which would fund new schools and hospitals. Environmental groups argue the park must be protected. What does this scenario best demonstrate?

options.A: Developing countries do not have the right to use their own natural resources.
options.B: The tension between economic development goals and environmental sustainability, where choosing one can harm the other.
options.C: Environmental protection is always more important than economic growth, regardless of a country's wealth.
options.D: This is only a local issue and has no connection to global sustainability goals.

questions.explanation: This scenario is a classic example of the development-environment trade-off: burning the oil generates greenhouse gases affecting the global climate, while not drilling denies a poor country revenue it needs for human development, illustrating a real tension addressed by the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Option C presents one perspective as absolute fact, but development ethics requires weighing both environmental and human development needs rather than always prioritising one.

questions.title: Cultural Identity Change
questions.prompt: Over the past 50 years, fewer young people in South Korea have been learning traditional court music (jeongganbo notation), while K-pop has spread globally. Which PYP concept BEST frames what is happening to South Korean musical culture?

options.A: Form — because the physical instruments used in traditional and modern Korean music look different.
options.B: Responsibility — because Korean musicians are responsible for keeping all traditions alive.
options.C: Change — because globalisation and modernisation are transforming which aspects of culture are practised and valued.
options.D: Function — because music in all societies serves the single function of entertainment.

questions.explanation: The PYP concept of 'change' examines how things evolve over time and why; K-pop's global rise reflects how external market forces and technology alter what cultural practices thrive, while traditional forms risk being lost — a documented concern of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage programme. Option D is incorrect because music serves many functions beyond entertainment, including religious ritual, political expression, and community bonding.

questions.title: International Organisations Role
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'The United Nations can force any country to follow its resolutions because it is the world's highest authority.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; the UN Security Council can deploy armies to any country without permission.
options.B: The claim is partially correct; the UN can force economically weak countries but not permanent Security Council members.
options.C: The claim is incorrect; the UN relies on member states voluntarily complying, and permanent Security Council members can veto enforcement actions that threaten their interests.
options.D: The claim is incorrect; the UN has no power whatsoever and exists only to hold annual meetings.

questions.explanation: The UN's power depends heavily on member state cooperation; the five permanent members of the Security Council (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) each hold a veto, meaning they can block any resolution aimed at enforcing action against themselves or their allies. Option A overstates UN authority: the UN can only authorise peacekeeping forces with host country consent or a Security Council resolution not vetoed by a permanent member.

questions.title: Global Inequality Causes
questions.prompt: Country A was colonised for over 150 years; its resources were exported and profits sent abroad. Country B, never colonised, developed its own industries during the same period. Today Country A has much lower income levels. A student argues the gap is simply due to Country A having 'bad luck with geography.' What is the main weakness in this argument?

options.A: Geography has absolutely no effect on development, so the argument is irrelevant.
options.B: The argument ignores the documented economic impact of colonialism, which extracted wealth, disrupted local systems, and left lasting inequalities that geography alone cannot explain.
options.C: The argument is correct because tropical climates scientifically prevent economic growth.
options.D: The argument is weak because all colonised countries eventually become wealthier than non-colonised ones.

questions.explanation: Economic historians and development scholars, including Ha-Joon Chang and Walter Rodney, have documented how colonialism systematically transferred wealth from colonised nations to colonisers, undermined local governance, and created economic structures that persisted long after independence. Option C is a racist geographic determinism rejected by modern development economics; many tropical nations have achieved high development levels.

questions.title: Multiculturalism in Practice
questions.prompt: A school in Canada has students from 34 different countries. The school celebrates cultural heritage days but also teaches all students the same national curriculum in English. Which term BEST describes this approach to multiculturalism?

options.A: Assimilation, because students are being asked to abandon their cultures entirely and adopt Canadian culture.
options.B: Integration, because students participate in a shared national system while their cultural identities are also recognised and valued.
options.C: Segregation, because students from different countries are being separated into different heritage groups.
options.D: Isolationism, because the school is preventing outside cultural influences from entering the curriculum.

questions.explanation: Integration means that newcomers participate in shared institutions and public life while retaining elements of their own cultural identity — exactly what this school models through a common curriculum alongside heritage celebrations. Option A is incorrect because assimilation requires abandoning one's original culture, whereas the heritage days actively validate students' diverse backgrounds.

questions.title: Sustainable Development Goals
questions.prompt: SDG 10 aims to 'reduce inequalities within and among countries.' A government builds a motorway connecting a wealthy city to a port, claiming this achieves SDG 10 by boosting the national economy. A critic argues this does NOT reduce inequality. Who is more likely correct, and why?

options.A: The government is correct; any economic growth automatically reduces inequality.
options.B: The critic is more likely correct; infrastructure that primarily benefits wealthy areas may increase economic growth without closing the gap between rich and poor.
options.C: The critic is correct; motorways always harm the environment and therefore violate all SDGs simultaneously.
options.D: Neither is correct; SDG 10 only applies to inequalities between different countries, not within a single country.

questions.explanation: Research on infrastructure investment shows that when projects connect already-wealthy areas rather than underserved communities, GDP may grow but the benefits often flow to those already advantaged, actually widening the inequality gap — directly contradicting SDG 10's intent. Option A reflects 'trickle-down' thinking that is widely disputed by development economists, as growth does not automatically reach the poorest groups.

questions.title: Perspective on Borders
questions.prompt: What would happen if all countries removed their border controls completely and allowed anyone to move freely between nations? Consider both potential benefits AND likely challenges.

options.A: Only benefits would occur: all poverty would end immediately as people move to richer countries.
options.B: Only problems would occur: every country would immediately collapse due to uncontrolled population movement.
options.C: Some workers could access better opportunities and families could reunite more easily, but receiving countries might face rapid population growth that strains housing, services, and labour markets.
options.D: Nothing would change because most people do not want to move away from their home countries regardless of border rules.

questions.explanation: Open borders research, including studies by economist Michael Clemens, suggests significant global economic gains from labour mobility, yet even supporters acknowledge challenges such as rapid urban overcrowding, wage competition, and pressure on public services in destination areas. Option A is an oversimplification; while migration can lift incomes, the structural causes of poverty (governance, infrastructure, history) cannot be solved by movement alone.

questions.title: Environmental Justice
questions.prompt: A large multinational company operates a gold mine in a low-income country. The company pays taxes and creates local jobs, but the mining process pollutes the local river. Local people lose clean water access. Which framework from global ethics BEST applies here?

options.A: Cultural relativism — the mining company is simply following the business norms of its home country.
options.B: Environmental justice — the costs of economic activity (pollution, health risks) are being borne by a vulnerable local community while profits flow elsewhere.
options.C: Isolationism — the company should stop operating in foreign countries altogether.
options.D: Nationalism — the local government should nationalise the mine and run it itself.

questions.explanation: Environmental justice is the principle that no community — especially marginalised or low-income ones — should bear a disproportionate share of environmental harms caused by activities that primarily benefit others; this scenario is a textbook example. Option A is incorrect because cultural relativism concerns judging practices by their own cultural standards, not the distribution of economic harms and benefits.

questions.title: Comparing Development Measures
questions.prompt: Country P has a higher GDP per capita than Country Q, but Country Q has a higher HDI score. Which of the following BEST explains how this is possible?

options.A: It is impossible; a higher GDP always produces a higher HDI automatically.
options.B: Country Q may have lower average income but invests more effectively in healthcare and education, boosting life expectancy and literacy, which the HDI measures alongside income.
options.C: Country P must have a larger population, which always lowers the HDI score.
options.D: The HDI only measures environmental quality, so a cleaner country always scores higher regardless of income.

questions.explanation: The HDI (Human Development Index) combines income, life expectancy, and education into a single score; Cuba is a real-world example — it has a relatively low GDP per capita but achieves high HDI due to exceptional public healthcare and near-universal literacy. Option A is a key misconception: GDP measures total economic output per person but says nothing about whether that wealth is used to improve health or education outcomes.

questions.title: Religion and Conflict
questions.prompt: Two communities in the same country follow the same religion but have been in conflict for decades over land. A journalist reports this as a 'religious war.' What is the most significant problem with that label?

options.A: There is no problem; if both groups follow a religion, the conflict must be about religious beliefs.
options.B: The label oversimplifies by ignoring that shared-religion communities can have conflicts rooted in land rights, ethnicity, history, or political power, where religion is used to identify groups rather than cause the conflict.
options.C: The problem is that journalists are not allowed to report on religious conflicts.
options.D: The label is wrong because religious communities never fight over land — only secular communities do.

questions.explanation: Many scholars, including Karen Armstrong, argue that conflicts labelled 'religious wars' are typically driven by political, economic, or ethnic factors, with religion serving as a marker of group identity rather than the root cause. Option A is the most common misconception students hold: assuming shared religious labels mean the conflict must be about theology.

questions.title: Cause and Effect: Globalisation
questions.prompt: Since the 1990s, global clothing brands have moved production to countries with lower wages. As a result, clothing prices dropped for shoppers in wealthy countries. Which effect of this shift is most often OVERLOOKED in discussions that focus only on lower prices?

options.A: Shoppers in wealthy countries stopped buying clothes altogether.
options.B: Workers in producing countries often face low wages, long hours, and unsafe conditions, raising serious questions about labour rights in global supply chains.
options.C: Shipping clothing across oceans became impossible due to fuel shortages.
options.D: Wealthy country governments lost all tax revenue because factories moved abroad.

questions.explanation: The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh, which killed over 1,100 garment workers, highlighted how global fast fashion depends on labour conditions that would be illegal in the wealthy countries purchasing the clothes. Option D is a genuine misconception — while some corporate tax shifting does occur, wealthy governments still collect significant tax from retail sales, wages of local employees, and import duties.

questions.title: Interdependence and Risk
questions.prompt: During a global health crisis, many countries found they could not produce enough face masks because almost all mask manufacturing had moved to just a few countries. What lesson about globalisation does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Globalisation only creates benefits and this situation was caused by poor individual decisions, not the global system.
options.B: High economic interdependence can create efficiency in normal times but increases vulnerability when a single part of the supply network is disrupted.
options.C: Countries should never trade with each other because trade always causes crises.
options.D: The crisis proved that face masks are not important and countries were right not to produce them locally.

questions.explanation: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed how concentrating production of essential goods in a small number of countries — a logical outcome of comparative advantage in global trade — creates systemic fragility when those countries face their own emergencies and restrict exports. Option A denies a systemic cause: individual purchasing decisions were rational within a global system that created the concentration in the first place.

questions.title: Cultural Perspective and Bias
questions.prompt: A European textbook from 1920 describes certain African societies as 'primitive' because they did not use written language. Which concept from global perspectives best identifies the error in this description?

options.A: Ethnocentrism — judging another culture's practices using the standards and values of one's own culture as the benchmark.
options.B: Multiculturalism — celebrating the diversity of different cultural literacy traditions.
options.C: Relativism — accepting that all cultural practices are equally valid without judgement.
options.D: Nationalism — promoting European languages above all others for political reasons.

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism occurs when one culture uses its own practices as the universal standard of 'advancement,' leading to the false conclusion that societies organising knowledge differently (through oral traditions, art, or other means) are inferior — many African societies had highly sophisticated oral legal, historical, and scientific traditions. Option C (relativism) is the opposite error: it accepts all practices without evaluation, whereas the textbook made a negative judgement, which is the hallmark of ethnocentrism.

questions.title: Responsibility and Emissions
questions.prompt: Country X industrialised during the 1800s and built its wealth partly by burning coal for 200 years. Country Y is industrialising now and argues it should be allowed to use cheap coal to develop. Country X says both should cut emissions equally. Evaluate Country Y's argument.

options.A: Country Y's argument is completely invalid because climate change does not depend on historical emissions.
options.B: Country Y's argument has merit because historical cumulative emissions from already-wealthy nations are the largest cause of current climate change, raising questions of fairness in who should bear the cost of cutting emissions now.
options.C: Country Y's argument is valid only if Country X agrees to pay Country Y directly every year.
options.D: Country Y's argument is invalid because coal is now illegal worldwide under the Paris Agreement.

questions.explanation: The principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities,' embedded in the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, recognises that industrialised nations bear greater historical responsibility for cumulative greenhouse gas emissions and therefore should take on greater obligations and support developing nations financially. Option A is factually wrong — historical emissions are the dominant cause of current atmospheric CO₂ levels and cannot be separated from the fairness debate.

questions.title: Trade Agreements Impact
questions.prompt: When a free trade agreement removes import taxes between two countries, producers in the country with lower production costs often sell more goods. A student says this is always good for both countries. What is the MOST important nuance missing from this claim?

options.A: Free trade agreements never actually remove import taxes; they only reduce them temporarily.
options.B: While consumers may benefit from lower prices, local industries in the higher-cost country may lose business and workers may lose jobs, creating winners and losers within each country.
options.C: Free trade is only good if both countries are equally wealthy to begin with.
options.D: The student is entirely correct; economists unanimously agree free trade benefits everyone without exception.

questions.explanation: Free trade produces overall economic gains on average but distributes them unevenly: consumers gain from cheaper imports while workers in uncompetitive local industries can face unemployment — a real pattern seen when the USA signed NAFTA and some manufacturing towns lost factory jobs. Option D misrepresents economics; even mainstream economists acknowledge distributional effects and the need for transition support for displaced workers.

questions.title: Indigenous Rights Globally
questions.prompt: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) states that indigenous communities have the right to 'free, prior and informed consent' before governments approve development projects on their land. Why is the word 'prior' especially important in this phrase?

options.A: 'Prior' means the community must have lived on the land for at least 100 years before they can object.
options.B: 'Prior' ensures consent is sought BEFORE a project begins, not after damage is already done, giving communities real power to influence or stop harmful development.
options.C: 'Prior' refers to the fact that a government's rights always come before those of indigenous communities.
options.D: 'Prior' means communities must consult with other indigenous groups in different countries before they can give consent.

questions.explanation: Seeking consent after construction has begun or land has been cleared is meaningless; UNDRIP's insistence on 'prior' consultation means communities must be approached before any decision is made, giving them genuine agency rather than token consultation. Option C directly contradicts the intent of UNDRIP, which was designed to check government power over indigenous territories, not confirm it.

questions.title: Media and Global Events
questions.prompt: A student researching a conflict finds that news sources from Country A describe the fighting as a 'war of liberation,' while sources from Country B call it 'a terrorist uprising.' What does this difference MOST reveal about news media?

options.A: One source is telling the truth and the other is lying; the student just needs to find which is which.
options.B: News reporting reflects the perspective, values, and political context of its source, so the same events can be framed very differently; critical readers should compare multiple sources.
options.C: All media everywhere reports world events in exactly the same way, so the difference must be a translation error.
options.D: The student should only trust sources from neutral countries that are not involved in any conflicts.

questions.explanation: Media framing theory, studied in IB Global Perspectives, shows how word choices like 'freedom fighter' versus 'terrorist' reflect whose perspective the outlet privileges — neither source is simply lying, but each presents facts through a cultural and political lens that shapes meaning. Option A creates a false binary: most complex conflicts involve legitimate grievances on multiple sides, and reducing the question to 'true vs. false' misses the deeper issue of perspective.

questions.title: Water as a Global Resource
questions.prompt: Some experts argue that fresh water should be treated as a global commons — something belonging to everyone — while others say water rights should be managed by whichever country or company controls the land above an aquifer. Compare these two positions: which argument for treating water as a global commons is STRONGEST?

options.A: Water should be a global commons because it is heavy and difficult to transport, making private ownership impractical.
options.B: Water should be a global commons because underground aquifers and rivers cross national borders, meaning one country's or company's decisions about water use directly affect the survival and wellbeing of people elsewhere.
options.C: Water should be a global commons because all water eventually evaporates and returns to the atmosphere, so ownership is meaningless.
options.D: Water should be a global commons because companies always waste water more than governments do.

questions.explanation: The Guaraní Aquifer in South America, shared by Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay, illustrates how underground water systems ignore political borders; if one nation over-extracts, it depletes water others depend on, making unilateral national or corporate control a genuine justice issue. Option C is scientifically accurate about the water cycle but irrelevant to the governance argument about who decides how accessible fresh water is used on the ground.

questions.title: Cause of Global Poverty
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Countries remain poor simply because their governments are corrupt and their citizens do not work hard enough.' Which of the following responses BEST demonstrates a multi-causal understanding of global poverty?

options.A: The student is correct; corruption and work ethic are the only factors that explain why some countries are poorer than others.
options.B: The student is completely wrong; poverty is only caused by past colonialism and has nothing to do with local governance.
options.C: The student has identified some contributing factors, but poverty also results from historical exploitation, unequal trade rules, debt burdens, lack of infrastructure, and climate vulnerability — a complex web of causes, not a single explanation.
options.D: The student is correct about corruption but wrong about citizens; people in poor countries always work longer hours than people in wealthy countries.

questions.explanation: Development scholars like Amartya Sen emphasise that poverty is 'capability deprivation' caused by intersecting historical, structural, and political factors: for instance, many countries carry debt repayments that exceed their health budgets due to loans taken by previous governments under pressure, limiting current governments' choices regardless of their intentions. Option B is the opposite oversimplification — blaming everything on colonialism ignores the genuine role of current governance quality in how aid and resources are distributed within a country.

questions.title: Migration Push and Pull
questions.prompt: A family leaves their drought-stricken village in the Sahel region of Africa and moves to a nearby city, then later to Europe. Which statement best describes the CHAIN of forces driving their decisions at each stage?

options.A: Both moves are pulled by economic opportunity alone, since wage differences explain most migration patterns globally.
options.B: The first move is pushed by environmental stress; the second move combines push factors (urban poverty) and pull factors (better services abroad).
options.C: Both moves are pushed by political persecution, which is the leading cause of all international migration.
options.D: The first move is a pull toward city jobs; the second move is pushed entirely by cultural discrimination in the city.

questions.explanation: Migration scholars distinguish push factors (conditions forcing people to leave) from pull factors (conditions attracting people elsewhere). Environmental degradation in the Sahel pushes rural-to-urban movement, while urban poverty can then push onward migration, with perceived opportunities in Europe acting as a pull. Option A is wrong because it ignores environmental and social push factors, which the UN identifies as increasingly significant drivers distinct from pure wage differences.

questions.title: Fair Trade Mechanics
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Fair Trade certification always guarantees that farmers receive a higher income than they would on the regular market.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of how Fair Trade systems work.

options.A: The claim is fully correct because Fair Trade sets a minimum price floor that is always above world market prices.
options.B: The claim is partially correct because Fair Trade sets a minimum price floor, but when world market prices rise above that floor, conventional farmers can earn more.
options.C: The claim is fully incorrect because Fair Trade organisations do not involve themselves with pricing at all.
options.D: The claim is partially correct because Fair Trade doubles the price received by every certified farmer regardless of market conditions.

questions.explanation: Fair Trade guarantees a minimum floor price to protect farmers when world prices fall, but if global commodity prices rise above that floor, non-certified farmers selling on the open market can earn equal or more. This nuance makes the original claim too absolute. Option A is wrong because it ignores the scenario where market prices exceed the Fair Trade floor, which happens during commodity booms.

questions.title: UN Security Council Power
questions.prompt: Why does a small developing nation find it difficult to enforce an international ruling against a permanent member of the UN Security Council, even when the International Court of Justice has ruled in the small nation's favour?

options.A: Because the International Court of Justice can only hear cases involving trade disputes, not political conflicts.
options.B: Because enforcement of ICJ rulings depends on the UN Security Council, and each permanent member holds veto power over council decisions.
options.C: Because small nations are not permitted to bring cases to the International Court of Justice without sponsorship from a larger nation.
options.D: Because international law automatically overrides national law, making enforcement unnecessary if a ruling is issued.

questions.explanation: Under the UN Charter, the Security Council is the body responsible for enforcing International Court of Justice rulings, and each of its five permanent members (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) can veto any enforcement resolution. This means a P5 nation can simply block action against itself. Option D is wrong because international law does not automatically override domestic law; compliance depends on states choosing to act, and enforcement requires political mechanisms.

questions.title: Cultural Diffusion vs. Assimilation
questions.prompt: Compare cultural diffusion with cultural assimilation. A Korean family moves to Brazil and begins celebrating local festivals while also introducing kimchi to their neighbourhood restaurants. Which process is MOST accurately illustrated here?

options.A: Cultural assimilation only, because the family is adopting Brazilian customs.
options.B: Cultural diffusion only, because they are spreading Korean food culture to Brazilians.
options.C: Both cultural diffusion and cultural exchange, showing that influence flows in multiple directions simultaneously.
options.D: Cultural imperialism, because one culture is replacing another through economic pressure.

questions.explanation: The scenario shows two-way cultural flow: the family absorbs Brazilian festival traditions (receiving influence) while locals adopt kimchi (receiving Korean influence). This bidirectional process is best described as cultural exchange combined with diffusion, not one-way assimilation. Option A is wrong because it ignores the outward spread of Korean culture, which is a distinct and equally important process happening at the same time.

questions.title: Hinduism and Interconnection
questions.prompt: In Hinduism, the concept of 'ahimsa' (non-violence toward all living beings) has influenced environmental movements worldwide. What does this cross-cultural adoption of ahimsa BEST illustrate about the relationship between religion and global issues?

options.A: That Hinduism is the only world religion with teachings relevant to environmental protection.
options.B: That religious ideas can travel beyond their original communities and shape global conversations on shared problems.
options.C: That environmental activists must convert to Hinduism in order to use the concept of ahimsa correctly.
options.D: That global issues like climate change are primarily caused by religious differences between nations.

questions.explanation: Ahimsa originated in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions and was later adapted by figures like Mahatma Gandhi and global environmentalists who were not themselves Hindu, demonstrating that religious concepts can cross cultural boundaries to address universal concerns. Option A is incorrect because many other traditions, such as the Islamic concept of 'khalifa' (stewardship) and Christian creation care theology, also provide environmental frameworks.

questions.title: Gini Coefficient Meaning
questions.prompt: Country A and Country B both have a GDP per capita of $15,000. Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.25 and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.55. What does this tell us about the two countries that GDP per capita alone does NOT reveal?

options.A: Country B has a faster-growing economy than Country A, because higher Gini scores indicate economic dynamism.
options.B: Country A distributes its wealth more equally among citizens, while Country B has much greater inequality between rich and poor.
options.C: Country A is a smaller nation geographically, since lower Gini values are associated with compact territories.
options.D: Country B spends more on education, because nations with higher inequality always invest more in social services.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a scale of 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (total inequality). A score of 0.25 indicates relatively equal distribution, as seen in Nordic countries, while 0.55 indicates high inequality, closer to levels seen in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America. Option A is wrong because the Gini coefficient measures distribution, not growth rate; high inequality can actually slow long-term growth according to IMF research.

questions.title: Refugee Convention Obligations
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's statement: 'Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, any country can choose whether or not to accept refugees based purely on how many migrants it already has, with no legal obligations attached.'

options.A: The error is that the Convention only applies to refugees from Europe, not from other regions of the world.
options.B: The error is that signatory countries are legally bound by the principle of non-refoulement, meaning they cannot return refugees to places where they face serious harm.
options.C: The error is that the Convention gives refugees the right to choose which specific country they settle in permanently.
options.D: The error is that the Convention applies to economic migrants as well as refugees, so the distinction the student makes is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: The 1951 Refugee Convention's cornerstone is the principle of non-refoulement, which legally prohibits signatory states from returning a person to a territory where they face persecution or serious harm, regardless of how many people the country has already received. Option A is wrong because the 1967 Protocol removed the original geographic limitation to Europe, making the Convention universally applicable.

questions.title: Global Supply Chain Vulnerability
questions.prompt: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many hospitals in wealthy countries struggled to obtain personal protective equipment because most of it was manufactured in a single region. What does this BEST illustrate about globalised supply chains?

options.A: That globalised supply chains always reduce efficiency because goods must travel long distances.
options.B: That economic efficiency gained through geographic specialisation can create dangerous dependency and systemic risk.
options.C: That wealthy countries should always manufacture all their own goods domestically to avoid any foreign trade.
options.D: That the pandemic proved free trade agreements between nations cause more harm than benefit in all circumstances.

questions.explanation: Global supply chains concentrate production where it is cheapest, which improves efficiency in normal times but creates vulnerability when that concentrated source is disrupted. Around 70–80% of global PPE production was concentrated in China, making shortages severe when that supply was interrupted. Option C is wrong because complete self-sufficiency is economically impractical and ignores the many genuine benefits of trade specialisation in non-crisis periods.

questions.title: Buddhism and Impermanence
questions.prompt: A Buddhist teacher explains that attachment to possessions causes suffering. A student argues this teaching directly supports sustainability because it discourages overconsumption. Evaluate how well this connection holds up.

options.A: The connection is completely invalid because Buddhist teachings are only concerned with personal spiritual matters, never with economics or the environment.
options.B: The connection is reasonable but incomplete, because while reduced attachment could lower consumption, Buddhism also emphasises community action and interdependence, not only individual restraint.
options.C: The connection is perfect and fully supported, since Buddhist monks have historically led global campaigns against all forms of manufacturing.
options.D: The connection is invalid because Buddhism encourages followers to acquire wealth as proof of good karma in previous lives.

questions.explanation: Buddhist philosophy's concept of 'anicca' (impermanence) and the teaching that craving causes suffering do logically reduce the appeal of excessive consumption, supporting a sustainability link. However, Buddhism's concept of 'sangha' (community) and interdependence means that collective social action, not just individual non-attachment, is equally central to Buddhist ethical engagement. Option A is wrong because engaged Buddhism, championed by figures like Thich Nhat Hanh, explicitly connects spiritual practice to social and environmental responsibility.

questions.title: Water Scarcity and Equity
questions.prompt: In a country where water is scarce, a government must choose between giving priority access to water for farming communities who grow food for millions, or for a technology company that provides thousands of jobs but uses water for cooling its servers. Which framework from fairness and development is MOST relevant to evaluate this decision?

options.A: The framework of cultural relativism, because water use decisions depend entirely on local traditions and cannot be judged externally.
options.B: The framework of competing rights and resource equity, weighing food security as a basic human right against economic development needs.
options.C: The framework of comparative advantage, which states that whichever industry earns more foreign currency should always receive priority resources.
options.D: The framework of democratic deficit, which argues that only elected officials, not communities, should make resource allocation decisions.

questions.explanation: The UN recognises safe water and food security as fundamental human rights, placing them at the base of any equity analysis. Balancing these rights against economic development goals is a classic fairness and development dilemma, requiring consideration of who bears the greatest risk if deprived. Option C is wrong because comparative advantage is an economic trade theory about which goods nations should specialise in producing, not a framework for domestic resource equity decisions.

questions.title: Diaspora Cultural Identity
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to the cultural practices of an immigrant community if the host country introduced strict laws banning the use of languages other than the official national language in schools and public spaces?

options.A: The community's cultural practices would disappear completely within one generation because language is the only carrier of culture.
options.B: The community might preserve private cultural practices at home, but public expressions of their identity would be suppressed, accelerating assimilation over generations.
options.C: The community would likely thrive culturally because restrictions create pride and always strengthen minority identity movements.
options.D: The ban would have no effect because immigrant communities always maintain their culture regardless of legal pressures.

questions.explanation: Language policies that restrict minority languages in public typically push cultural expression into private spaces, which slows but does not immediately eliminate cultural transmission. Over generations, without institutional support, languages and associated practices do erode, as seen with Welsh before its revival or many indigenous languages globally. Option A overstates the speed of loss and ignores other cultural carriers like food, religion, and family rituals that persist even without language.

questions.title: Structural Adjustment Criticism
questions.prompt: In the 1980s and 1990s, the International Monetary Fund required many developing countries to cut government spending on health and education in exchange for loans. Critics argued this worsened long-term development. Which reasoning BEST supports the critics' position?

options.A: Because reducing government spending always causes immediate political revolutions, which destroy economic growth.
options.B: Because healthy, educated populations are more productive over time, so cutting health and education undermines the human capital needed for sustainable development.
options.C: Because the IMF had no legal authority to attach conditions to loans, making those agreements automatically invalid.
options.D: Because developing countries that refused IMF loans always grew faster, proving loans themselves cause poverty.

questions.explanation: Human capital theory, supported by economists like Amartya Sen, holds that investment in health and education raises long-term productivity and income. Cutting these services to balance budgets in the short term can reduce a country's ability to develop skilled workers and healthy citizens, slowing sustainable growth for decades. Option D is wrong because it makes an overgeneralised causal claim; some countries that refused IMF conditions did poorly, and the relationship between loan acceptance and growth is complex and contested.

questions.title: Islam Diversity and Sects
questions.prompt: A student researching Islam writes: 'The split between Sunni and Shia Muslims occurred after the death of the Prophet Muhammad and was originally a disagreement about political leadership, not about core beliefs like prayer or the Quran.' Evaluate this statement.

options.A: The statement is incorrect because Sunni and Shia Muslims use completely different versions of the Quran.
options.B: The statement is largely accurate; the original disagreement was about who should lead the Muslim community after Muhammad, though theological differences developed over time.
options.C: The statement is incorrect because the split happened centuries after Muhammad's death due to trade rivalries between Arab merchants.
options.D: The statement is accurate and there are currently no theological differences between Sunni and Shia Muslims.

questions.explanation: The Sunni-Shia split originated in 632 CE over succession: Sunnis accepted Abu Bakr as caliph, while Shia believed leadership should pass to Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law. Both groups share the Quran and core pillars of Islam, though distinct theological and legal traditions did develop over subsequent centuries. Option A is wrong because both Sunni and Shia Muslims use the same Arabic Quran; differences lie in hadith collections and jurisprudence, not scripture.

questions.title: Climate Justice Responsibility
questions.prompt: Historically, industrialised nations emitted most of the greenhouse gases currently in the atmosphere. Some developing nations argue they should receive financial support before being asked to limit their own emissions. Which principle MOST directly supports this argument?

options.A: The precautionary principle, which states that no country should act on climate until there is 100% scientific certainty about its causes.
options.B: The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, which recognises that all countries share responsibility for climate change but historical emitters bear a greater obligation.
options.C: The principle of sovereign equality, which gives every nation identical obligations regardless of historical emissions or current capacity.
options.D: The polluter pays principle applied only to individuals, not to nation states, making it irrelevant to international climate negotiations.

questions.explanation: The principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) is enshrined in the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and acknowledges that while all nations must act on climate, wealthier nations that caused most historical emissions have a greater duty to act first and support others financially. The Paris Agreement's climate finance provisions reflect this. Option C is wrong because sovereign equality in international law refers to equal legal standing, not equal obligations regardless of capacity or historical impact.

questions.title: Media Representation of Poverty
questions.prompt: A charity uses images of suffering children in advertisements to raise money for communities in sub-Saharan Africa. A student argues these images, although effective at fundraising, may cause long-term harm. Which argument BEST supports the student's concern?

options.A: Because photographs are always inaccurate representations of reality and should never be used in campaigns of any kind.
options.B: Because repeated images of helpless victims can create stereotypes that reduce entire regions to poverty and suffering, ignoring local agency, diversity, and strengths.
options.C: Because charities are legally prohibited from using images of children in any promotional material under international copyright law.
options.D: Because such images prove that wealthy donors are always motivated by guilt rather than genuine compassion, making fundraising unethical.

questions.explanation: Development scholars and organisations like Oxfam have critiqued 'poverty porn' because it reinforces one-dimensional narratives about Africa, erasing the continent's complexity, innovation, and people's own efforts to improve their lives. This can entrench harmful power dynamics and reduce affected communities to passive recipients of aid. Option A is wrong because it makes an absolute claim about all photographs, which is not supported; the issue is specifically about selective, decontextualised representation, not photography itself.

questions.title: Transboundary Pollution Ethics
questions.prompt: Country A's factories emit pollution that crosses into Country B, damaging crops and causing health problems. Country A argues it is acting within its own laws. Country B has no legal mechanisms to force Country A to stop. What does this scenario MOST reveal about current international environmental governance?

options.A: That international environmental law is fully effective and Country B simply chose not to use available legal tools.
options.B: That national sovereignty can conflict with global environmental responsibility, and enforcement gaps in international law allow harmful actions to go unaddressed.
options.C: That Country B should retaliate with its own pollution to create a balanced situation before negotiating.
options.D: That environmental problems only become international concerns when they affect wealthy nations, since poorer nations lack standing in international law.

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates the tension between the Westphalian principle of national sovereignty (each state governs its own territory) and the principle of 'no harm' in international environmental law, which holds that states should not allow their territory to be used in ways that harm other states. However, enforcement of the no-harm principle is weak without binding international mechanisms, as demonstrated by ongoing disputes over acid rain, river pollution, and transboundary air quality. Option A is wrong because international environmental enforcement is widely acknowledged as fragmented and lacks strong compulsory mechanisms.

questions.title: Indigenous Rights and Land
questions.prompt: A mining company wants to extract minerals from land that an indigenous community has used for centuries. The government has given the company legal permission, but the community was not consulted. Which internationally recognised principle does this process MOST likely violate?

options.A: The principle of eminent domain, which requires companies rather than governments to compensate communities for land use.
options.B: The principle of Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), which requires that indigenous communities are consulted and agree before projects affecting their lands begin.
options.C: The principle of comparative advantage, which states that natural resources must be developed by whoever can extract them most efficiently.
options.D: The principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows any country's courts to overrule a government's decision to grant mining licences.

questions.explanation: Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) is enshrined in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) and requires that indigenous communities give their free agreement, obtained before projects begin and based on full information, to any developments affecting their lands and resources. Bypassing this process, even with government approval, violates international standards. Option A is wrong because eminent domain is a domestic legal concept about government acquisition of private land for public use, not a mechanism requiring company-led community consultation.

questions.title: Ethnocentrism vs. Cultural Relativism
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Cultural relativism means we must accept every cultural practice without ever questioning it, because all cultures are equally valid.' Identify the problem with this position.

options.A: There is no problem; the student has correctly summarised what cultural relativism means in anthropology and international studies.
options.B: Cultural relativism is a methodological tool for understanding practices in their own context, but it does not require abandoning universal human rights standards when practices cause serious harm.
options.C: The problem is that cultural relativism only applies to Western cultures and cannot be used to analyse non-Western traditions.
options.D: The problem is that cultural relativism was disproven by scientists in the 20th century and is no longer used in academic study.

questions.explanation: Cultural relativism was developed in anthropology to help researchers avoid ethnocentric bias when studying other cultures, but most scholars, including the UN, distinguish between understanding a practice in its cultural context and endorsing practices that violate fundamental human rights such as freedom from torture or child labour. The student's version collapses into moral relativism, which is a different and more contested position. Option A is wrong because it accepts the student's conflation of methodological relativism with moral endorsement, which is not the standard academic definition.

questions.title: Urbanisation and Sustainability
questions.prompt: By 2050, the UN estimates that about 68% of the world's population will live in cities. A student claims this is purely negative for sustainability because cities consume enormous amounts of energy. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct because every study on cities shows they are more damaging to the environment than rural living in all measurable ways.
options.B: The claim is oversimplified because dense urban living can also reduce per-person energy use through shared infrastructure, public transport, and smaller homes compared to sprawling rural or suburban areas.
options.C: The claim is correct, but only applies to cities in developing countries; cities in wealthy nations are always carbon neutral.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because the UN's 68% estimate refers only to cities in Asia and does not apply globally.

questions.explanation: Research from the International Energy Agency shows that urban residents in dense cities often have lower per-capita carbon footprints than suburban or rural residents because they share walls, use public transit, and need less land per person. The sustainability impact depends heavily on how cities are designed and powered. Option A is wrong because it ignores the density advantages of city living and conflates total city energy use (high due to population size) with per-capita energy use (often lower than rural equivalents).

questions.title: Judaism Global Diaspora
questions.prompt: Jewish communities have maintained distinct cultural and religious practices across more than 70 countries for thousands of years, despite not having a single homeland for much of that period. What does this BEST demonstrate about the relationship between identity and place?

options.A: That religious and cultural identity requires a fixed geographic homeland to survive across generations.
options.B: That shared texts, rituals, calendar observances, and communal institutions can sustain a distinct cultural identity across diverse geographic locations over long periods.
options.C: That Jewish communities maintained their identity primarily through genetic isolation rather than shared cultural practices.
options.D: That diaspora communities always become identical to their host cultures within three generations, which proves culture is determined by geography.

questions.explanation: Jewish communities across Ethiopia, Yemen, India, Eastern Europe, and the Americas maintained recognisable shared practices, the Hebrew calendar, Torah study, and lifecycle rituals for millennia without a shared state. This demonstrates that a community of practice (shared texts, rituals, and institutions) can anchor identity more powerfully than territory. Option A is directly contradicted by the historical record of sustained Jewish identity during the diaspora period before 1948.

questions.title: Trade Sanctions Effectiveness
questions.prompt: When powerful countries impose economic sanctions on a nation to change its government's behaviour, research shows mixed results. Which explanation BEST accounts for why sanctions sometimes fail to achieve their political goals?

options.A: Because sanctions always harm the population of the sanctioning country more than the targeted country, so they are always abandoned quickly.
options.B: Because the economic hardship caused by sanctions often falls on ordinary citizens rather than the leaders making political decisions, and targeted governments may use sanctions to rally nationalist support.
options.C: Because international law prohibits any country from imposing economic sanctions under any circumstances without UN Security Council approval.
options.D: Because global markets always automatically compensate sanctioned countries by increasing prices for their exports, neutralising any economic pressure.

questions.explanation: Political science research, including work by Hufbauer et al. on sanctions effectiveness, shows that elites and government officials can often shield themselves from economic pain while ordinary people bear the costs of food and medicine shortages. Governments also frequently frame external sanctions as foreign aggression, increasing domestic solidarity. Option C is wrong because unilateral sanctions by individual countries or groups of countries are a common and legally practised foreign policy tool, distinct from UN-authorised multilateral measures.

questions.title: Gender Inequality Index
questions.prompt: Two countries have identical GDP per capita. Country X ranks much higher on the Gender Inequality Index than Country Y, meaning Country X has greater gender inequality. What can we most reasonably infer from this comparison?

options.A: Country X's women earn exactly half of what men earn, which is the definition of maximum gender inequality in economic measurement.
options.B: Economic wealth alone does not guarantee gender equality; Country X likely has greater gaps in areas such as parliamentary representation, maternal health, or labour force participation.
options.C: Country Y must have a lower crime rate than Country X, since gender equality and safety are always measured together in international indices.
options.D: Country X's government must be less democratic than Country Y's, because all authoritarian governments have higher gender inequality scores.

questions.explanation: The UNDP's Gender Inequality Index measures reproductive health, empowerment (parliamentary seats, educational attainment), and labour market participation. Countries with similar income levels can diverge sharply on these dimensions; for example, Gulf states have high GDP but relatively low female parliamentary representation, while some lower-income countries have achieved significant gender parity in politics. Option D is wrong because several democracies score poorly on gender equality and some non-democracies have passed progressive gender legislation.

questions.title: Multilateral vs. Bilateral Aid
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Bilateral aid, given directly from one government to another, is always more effective than multilateral aid channelled through international organisations, because bilateral donors know their own priorities best.' Evaluate the strength of this argument.

options.A: The argument is fully correct because international organisations have been proven to waste all the money they receive before it reaches recipients.
options.B: The argument is weak because bilateral aid is often tied to the donor country's political or commercial interests, while multilateral aid can apply shared expertise and reach more countries consistently.
options.C: The argument is fully correct because recipient countries always prefer bilateral arrangements and reject multilateral aid by a ratio of four to one.
options.D: The argument is partially correct; bilateral aid is more effective only when the donor country shares a language with the recipient country.

questions.explanation: Development economists note that bilateral aid is frequently 'tied', meaning recipients must spend it on goods or services from the donor country, which reduces its value by an estimated 15–30% according to the OECD. Multilateral agencies like UNICEF and WHO can apply technical expertise across many countries and are less likely to attach political conditions. Option A is wrong because it makes a sweeping, empirically unsupported absolute claim; multilateral organisations have documented, independently audited spending records and measurable outcomes.

questions.title: Cultural Heritage UNESCO Protection
questions.prompt: UNESCO's World Heritage List includes natural and cultural sites from many countries. A student argues that international protection of local heritage sites takes decision-making power away from the communities that live there. What is the STRONGEST counter-argument to this view?

options.A: UNESCO has military forces that can arrest local officials who disagree with heritage decisions, making the question irrelevant.
options.B: International status can attract funding, expertise, and tourism that local governments alone could not secure, potentially benefiting both the site and surrounding communities.
options.C: Communities near heritage sites have never expressed any concerns about UNESCO involvement, so the student's concern has no real-world basis.
options.D: International protection always overrides local law completely, which is justified because global culture is more important than local preferences.

questions.explanation: UNESCO World Heritage status brings access to international conservation funds, technical expertise, and tourist revenue that many national or local governments cannot independently generate. For example, sites like Angkor Wat in Cambodia have received substantial restoration funding tied to their international status. Option C is wrong because there are documented real-world tensions; for example, communities around Machu Picchu and Stonehenge have raised concerns about tourist management decisions made with limited local input.

questions.title: Remittances and Development
questions.prompt: In several low-income countries, remittances (money sent home by citizens working abroad) exceed the total amount of foreign aid the country receives. What does this suggest about the role of migration in development?

options.A: It suggests that foreign aid is completely useless and should be abolished immediately in all circumstances.
options.B: It suggests that individual migrant workers can be powerful economic actors in development, though brain drain and dependency risks must also be considered.
options.C: It proves that migration always increases inequality within sending countries because only wealthy families have relatives abroad.
options.D: It suggests that all developing countries should make it mandatory for citizens to work abroad for a minimum of five years.

questions.explanation: The World Bank reports that global remittances to low- and middle-income countries exceeded $650 billion in recent years, surpassing official development assistance. This demonstrates that migrant workers are significant development actors, funding education, healthcare, and housing for families. However, when skilled workers emigrate, 'brain drain' can deprive countries of doctors, teachers, and engineers, creating a trade-off that complicates the overall picture. Option C is wrong because remittances often reach households across income levels, and some research shows they reduce inequality by lifting the incomes of receiving families.

questions.title: Migration Push-Pull Factors
questions.prompt: A family leaves their home country because of drought destroying their crops, but they also know a nearby country has better hospitals and schools. Which statement most accurately describes their migration decision?

options.A: They are purely economic migrants because they want better services.
options.B: They are refugees because environmental disaster forced them to leave.
options.C: Their decision involves both push factors (drought) and pull factors (services), making it a complex migration.
options.D: They cannot migrate legally because environmental reasons are not recognised by any international body.

questions.explanation: Migration scholars use push-pull theory to explain that most real-world moves involve multiple motivations simultaneously; drought is a push factor while better healthcare is a pull factor, and these can coexist in one decision. Option B is wrong because refugee status under the 1951 Refugee Convention requires persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or social group — environmental disaster alone does not qualify under current international law.

questions.title: Global Supply Chain Fairness
questions.prompt: A garment is designed in France, made from cotton grown in Uzbekistan, sewn together in Bangladesh, and sold in Canada. Identify the error in this student's claim: 'Because Canada is the last country involved, it bears the most responsibility for the working conditions of the garment workers.'

options.A: The error is that France, as the designer, has no responsibility at all.
options.B: The error is assuming responsibility falls only on the last country; all actors in a supply chain share responsibility, especially the company that controls the brand.
options.C: The error is that Uzbekistan grows most cotton globally, not just for this garment.
options.D: The error is claiming Canada is involved; Canada only imports finished goods and cannot be held responsible.

questions.explanation: Supply chain responsibility in global ethics recognises that brands — often based in wealthy design countries — set price and quality standards that directly pressure factory conditions, meaning responsibility is distributed across the chain rather than sitting only at the point of sale. Option D is wrong because consumers and importing nations do bear some ethical and sometimes legal responsibility through trade regulations and consumer choices.

questions.title: World Religions Sacred Texts
questions.prompt: A student is comparing how different world religions guide daily life. She finds that Islam uses the Quran and Hadith together, while Judaism uses the Torah and the Talmud together. What does this pattern most suggest about how religions function?

options.A: Most religions require exactly two sacred texts to be considered complete.
options.B: Religious guidance often combines a primary scripture with additional interpretive tradition, showing that sacred texts alone may not answer every life question.
options.C: Islam and Judaism share the same core texts written at different times in history.
options.D: Only monotheistic religions use written texts to guide followers' daily behaviour.

questions.explanation: Both Islam and Judaism demonstrate that communities develop interpretive literature (Hadith records the Prophet's sayings; the Talmud records rabbinic legal debate) because scripture alone leaves many practical questions unanswered, pointing to a common function across traditions. Option A is wrong because there is no rule that religions must have exactly two texts — Hinduism, for example, has a vast range of sacred writings including the Vedas and Upanishads.

questions.title: Sustainable Development Tensions
questions.prompt: A developing country discovers large coal deposits. Mining the coal would create thousands of jobs and fund new schools, but would significantly increase national carbon emissions. Which tension does this scenario most precisely illustrate?

options.A: The tension between national sovereignty and international law.
options.B: The tension between short-term economic development and long-term global environmental sustainability.
options.C: The tension between rural and urban communities within one country.
options.D: The tension between democratic governments and authoritarian ones on energy policy.

questions.explanation: This is a classic sustainability dilemma where immediate human development needs (jobs, education funding) conflict with the long-term global goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions — a core tension addressed by the UN Sustainable Development Goals, which explicitly try to balance SDG 8 (decent work) with SDG 13 (climate action). Option A is wrong because the scenario does not involve any legal conflict between the country's laws and an international treaty.

questions.title: Cultural Diffusion vs. Imperialism
questions.prompt: Two students debate the global spread of English. Student A says it is a natural result of global trade and communication. Student B says it forces non-English cultures to lose their own languages. Which evaluation is most academically balanced?

options.A: Student A is completely correct because language spread is always voluntary.
options.B: Student B is completely correct because English has replaced every indigenous language it encountered.
options.C: Both students identify real effects; the spread of English creates economic opportunities but can marginalise speakers of minority languages, so the outcome depends on local policies.
options.D: Neither student is correct because French, not English, is the dominant global language today.

questions.explanation: Linguists and development scholars recognise that English functions as a global lingua franca that can open economic doors while simultaneously creating pressure on minority languages — UNESCO estimates that roughly one language dies every two weeks, often linked to dominant language pressure. Option B is factually wrong because many languages — Welsh, Māori, Swahili — continue to coexist actively alongside English.

questions.title: International Aid Dependency
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen if a low-income country became fully dependent on food aid from wealthier nations for more than a decade, according to development economists who study long-term fairness?

options.A: The country's farmers would steadily become more productive as they learn from aid workers.
options.B: Local food markets could be undermined because cheap or free imported food makes it hard for local farmers to sell their crops at a profit.
options.C: The country would quickly achieve food security because aid always increases agricultural investment.
options.D: Other countries would follow the same model to receive aid and improve their economies.

questions.explanation: Development economists, including Zambian economist Dambisa Moyo in her book 'Dead Aid,' argue that sustained food aid can collapse local agricultural markets because local farmers cannot compete with free goods, reducing investment in domestic food production. Option A is wrong because aid delivery does not typically transfer farming skills to local producers — it replaces local production rather than building it.

questions.title: UN Security Council Power
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council has five permanent members — the USA, UK, France, Russia, and China — each with veto power. A student claims this structure perfectly represents global fairness today. What is the strongest counter-argument?

options.A: The structure is unfair because the UN should have no permanent members at all.
options.B: The structure reflects the power balance of 1945, not today's world, leaving entire regions like Africa and Latin America without permanent representation.
options.C: The structure is unfair because permanent members should rotate every year among all nations.
options.D: The veto power is never actually used, so it does not affect global decision-making.

questions.explanation: The five permanent members were chosen after World War II based on the 1945 geopolitical order, but the world has changed dramatically — Africa contains 54 countries and over 1.4 billion people yet has no permanent seat, raising serious questions about equitable representation. Option D is factually incorrect: veto power has been used hundreds of times, including by Russia and the US in recent decades to block resolutions on conflicts.

questions.title: Gini Coefficient Meaning
questions.prompt: Country A and Country B have the same average income per person. However, Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.25 and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.55. What does this tell us about the two countries?

options.A: Country B's people are wealthier on average because a higher Gini score means higher income.
options.B: Country A has a more equal distribution of income, while Country B has much greater inequality between rich and poor.
options.C: Country A is poorer overall because a low Gini coefficient means a low GDP.
options.D: Both countries are equally unequal because they have the same average income.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a scale from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality), so Country A at 0.25 has income spread fairly evenly, while Country B at 0.55 has extreme gaps between its richest and poorest citizens — similar to real-world comparisons between Scandinavian countries and parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Option D is wrong because average income and income distribution are completely separate measures — two countries can have identical averages but vastly different equality.

questions.title: Hinduism Core Concepts
questions.prompt: A student studying Hinduism says: 'Karma is simply punishment for bad actions.' Which response shows the most precise understanding of the concept?

options.A: The student is correct — karma functions as a punishment system controlled by the gods.
options.B: Karma refers to the total consequences of all actions, good and bad, which shape future circumstances across lifetimes — it is a natural law of cause and effect, not a punishment assigned by a deity.
options.C: Karma only applies to actions performed during religious rituals, not everyday behaviour.
options.D: Karma is a concept unique to Buddhism and was later borrowed by Hinduism.

questions.explanation: In Hindu philosophy, karma (from Sanskrit meaning 'action') is understood as a universal law of cause and effect where every action — whether physical, verbal, or mental — produces consequences that influence one's present and future lives, without requiring a divine judge to assign outcomes. Option D is wrong because karma is a foundational concept in the Vedic tradition of Hinduism that predates Buddhism; Buddhism later adopted and adapted it.

questions.title: Fair Trade Certification
questions.prompt: When shoppers buy Fair Trade certified coffee, they pay a slightly higher price. A student claims this extra money goes directly to the coffee company's profits. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because Fair Trade is a marketing label with no actual financial standards.
options.B: The claim is incorrect because Fair Trade certification requires that farmers receive a guaranteed minimum price and an additional social premium used for community projects.
options.C: The claim is partly correct because half the premium goes to farmers and half goes to the certifying company.
options.D: The claim is correct because governments in consuming countries collect the extra money as an import tax.

questions.explanation: Fairtrade International sets legally binding standards requiring farmers to receive a minimum floor price (protecting them from market price crashes) plus a Fairtrade Premium — typically around $0.20 per pound of coffee — that farmer cooperatives democratically decide how to invest in schools, healthcare, or farming equipment. Option A is wrong because Fair Trade is an independently audited certification with specific financial and labour standards that companies must pass to use the label.

questions.title: Climate Justice Responsibility
questions.prompt: Historically, high-income industrialised countries emitted most of the greenhouse gases that caused current climate change. Today, some rapidly developing countries are increasing their emissions quickly. Which principle should most guide how emission reduction responsibilities are shared, according to climate justice frameworks?

options.A: All countries should reduce emissions by an identical percentage regardless of their history.
options.B: Countries should reduce emissions in proportion to their current population size only.
options.C: Responsibilities should reflect both historical emissions (who caused the problem) and current capacity to act (who can afford clean energy), as captured in the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities.'
options.D: Only countries that signed the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 bear any legal responsibility to reduce emissions.

questions.explanation: The principle of 'Common But Differentiated Responsibilities' (CBDR), established in the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and embedded in the Paris Agreement, recognises that while all nations share responsibility for climate action, wealthier nations that historically caused most emissions and have more technological resources must take on greater commitments. Option A is wrong because identical percentage cuts would ignore the fact that a 20% cut for a poor nation developing basic infrastructure causes far greater hardship than the same cut for a wealthy nation.

questions.title: Diaspora Cultural Identity
questions.prompt: A student whose grandparents emigrated from Nigeria to the UK celebrates Nigerian festivals, cooks Nigerian food at home, but speaks only English and has never visited Nigeria. Which concept from multiculturalism best describes her cultural identity?

options.A: Assimilation, because she speaks English and has adopted British culture completely.
options.B: A hybrid or hyphenated identity, where elements of Nigerian heritage and British upbringing combine into something new and complex.
options.C: Cultural appropriation, because she celebrates Nigerian traditions without living in Nigeria.
options.D: Monoculturalism, because she cannot speak a Nigerian language.

questions.explanation: Cultural theorists like Stuart Hall describe diaspora identity as hybrid — people simultaneously belong to multiple cultural worlds, inheriting traditions from their ancestral culture while living within and being shaped by their country of birth, creating a layered identity that is neither purely one nor the other. Option A is wrong because assimilation implies abandoning the heritage culture entirely, whereas this student actively maintains Nigerian cultural practices.

questions.title: Global Water Scarcity Causes
questions.prompt: Two regions both receive the same annual rainfall. Region X has widespread water scarcity while Region Y has no shortage. Which combination of factors most likely explains this difference?

options.A: Region X must have a larger population, which always causes water scarcity regardless of other factors.
options.B: Region X likely has higher water demand (from agriculture or industry), poorer water storage infrastructure, and greater pollution of available water sources compared to Region Y.
options.C: Region X has scarcity because its government has refused all international water aid.
options.D: Rainfall is the only factor that determines water scarcity, so the two regions must actually have different rainfall levels.

questions.explanation: Water scarcity experts distinguish between physical scarcity (not enough water) and economic scarcity (water exists but infrastructure to store, clean, and distribute it is lacking) — the same rainfall can produce very different outcomes depending on irrigation practices, industrial use, sanitation systems, and governance. Option D directly contradicts the premise of the question and ignores the well-established concept of economic water scarcity.

questions.title: Non-Governmental Organisations Role
questions.prompt: An NGO builds wells in a village in a drought-prone country. A government official argues that NGOs undermine state authority by taking over government responsibilities. A development worker argues NGOs fill gaps where governments cannot or will not act. Which evaluation best weighs both perspectives?

options.A: The development worker is completely right; governments should hand all development work to NGOs.
options.B: The government official is completely right; NGOs always cause more harm than good.
options.C: Both perspectives have merit: NGOs can provide vital services quickly and independently, but over-reliance on them can reduce pressure on governments to build lasting public systems.
