questions.explanation: The digital divide is fundamentally a structural inequality: in many low-income countries, fibre or mobile infrastructure does not exist in rural areas, data costs can consume a significant portion of daily wages, and unreliable electricity makes device use impractical — these are systemic barriers, not individual choices. Option D is a partial truth (language barriers do exist) but missing infrastructure and cost are far more fundamental obstacles than language alone.

questions.title: Role of International Organisations
questions.prompt: The World Trade Organization (WTO) aims to promote free trade globally. Critics argue it disproportionately benefits wealthy nations. Which argument most strongly supports the critics' view?

options.A: The WTO allows wealthy nations to subsidise their own farmers while pressuring developing nations to open their agricultural markets
options.B: The WTO prevents developing countries from trading with each other
options.C: The WTO was founded by wealthy nations and therefore only wealthy nations can be members
options.D: Free trade always reduces poverty in all countries equally, so critics are simply wrong

questions.explanation: Agricultural subsidies in wealthy nations (notably the EU's Common Agricultural Policy and US farm subsidies) allow their farmers to sell at artificially low prices, undercutting farmers in developing countries who are simultaneously pressured to lower trade barriers — a structural asymmetry that many economists and development advocates have documented as damaging. Option B is factually incorrect: the WTO explicitly facilitates trade among all member countries, including developing-nation-to-developing-nation trade.

questions.title: Nationalism vs. Global Citizenship
questions.prompt: A government decides to withdraw from several international climate agreements, arguing that national economic interests must come first. Evaluate the most significant global consequence of this reasoning if adopted widely by multiple nations.

options.A: International agreements would become stronger because remaining nations would be more committed
options.B: Global collective action problems like climate change cannot be solved when nations prioritise short-term national interests over shared long-term goals
options.C: Climate change would be resolved more quickly because individual nations can act faster than international bodies
options.D: Economic growth in withdrawing nations would automatically offset environmental damage globally

questions.explanation: Climate change is a classic 'collective action problem' — each nation has an individual incentive to free-ride on others' efforts, but if enough nations do so, the shared goal fails entirely; this is known as the 'tragedy of the commons' at a global scale. Option C is a misconception: historical evidence shows that unilateral national action has been insufficient to meet global emissions targets, which require coordinated international commitments.

questions.title: Hinduism and Global Misconceptions
questions.prompt: A student writes: 'Hinduism is a single, unified religion with one holy book, one god, and identical practices across all its followers.' Examine which specific feature of Hinduism most directly contradicts this claim.

options.A: Hinduism originated in India, not in multiple countries simultaneously
options.B: Hinduism encompasses a wide diversity of deities, philosophical schools, and sacred texts including the Vedas, Upanishads, and Bhagavad Gita, with no single unifying authority
options.C: Hinduism is the oldest religion in the world, which automatically makes it diverse
options.D: Hinduism allows conversion from other religions, which other unified religions do not

questions.explanation: Hinduism is often described by scholars as a 'family of religions' rather than a single system — it includes monotheistic, polytheistic, and non-theistic strands, multiple sacred texts, and varied practices across regions such as South India versus North India or the Indian subcontinent versus the Hindu diaspora. Option A is factually partially true but entirely irrelevant to the question of whether Hinduism is unified in belief and practice.

questions.title: Foreign Aid Dependency Debate
questions.prompt: Economist Dambisa Moyo argues that long-term aid to African governments has, in some cases, undermined economic development rather than supported it. Which mechanism best explains this argument?

options.A: Aid money is always stolen by foreign governments before reaching African nations
options.B: Consistent aid flows can reduce governments' incentive to develop domestic tax systems and can undermine local industries by flooding markets with free goods
options.C: African governments are constitutionally prevented from using aid money productively
options.D: Aid only damages development when it comes from former colonial powers

questions.explanation: Moyo's core argument in 'Dead Aid' (2009) is that predictable aid flows allow governments to bypass building tax-revenue relationships with citizens (weakening accountability), and that in-kind aid such as free food or clothing can destroy local markets by undercutting domestic producers. Option A is an oversimplification and a factual distortion — while corruption is a documented problem, Moyo's structural argument is distinct from blanket claims that all aid is stolen.

questions.title: Conflict Over Water Resources
questions.prompt: Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt all depend heavily on the Nile River. When Ethiopia began filling the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam in 2020, Egypt declared it a threat to national security. Which concept from international relations most accurately describes the underlying tension?

options.A: Cultural imperialism, because Ethiopia is imposing its development model on Egypt
options.B: Resource nationalism, where one country's sovereign development decisions directly threaten another's resource security
options.C: Brain drain, because engineers left Egypt to build the Ethiopian dam
options.D: Protectionism, because Egypt is trying to restrict Ethiopian economic activity

questions.explanation: The Nile dam dispute exemplifies resource nationalism and transboundary resource conflict: Ethiopia argues it has the sovereign right to develop its own rivers for energy and economic growth, while Egypt — which depends on the Nile for over 90% of its freshwater — sees upstream control as an existential threat. This is a documented real-world case studied in international relations and water security. Option A is incorrect because cultural imperialism involves cultural dominance, not infrastructure development affecting shared natural resources.

questions.title: Stereotyping vs. Generalisation
questions.prompt: A geography textbook states: 'People in collectivist cultures, such as many East Asian societies, tend to prioritise group harmony, though individual variation is significant.' A student rewrites this as: 'All East Asians always put their group before themselves.' Which academic skill best identifies what the student has done wrong?

options.A: The student has plagiarised the original source without citation
options.B: The student has replaced a qualified, evidence-based generalisation with an overgeneralisation that erases individual diversity and reinforces stereotyping
options.C: The student has correctly simplified a complex idea for a younger audience
options.D: The student has made a factual error because East Asian cultures are not collectivist at all

questions.explanation: The original textbook sentence uses hedging language ('tend to,' 'though individual variation is significant') that reflects academic rigour — acknowledging cultural tendencies while respecting individual differences. The student's rewrite uses absolute language ('all,' 'always') that transforms a nuanced cultural observation into a stereotype. This skill — recognising overgeneralisation — is central to MYP ATL critical thinking. Option C is wrong because simplification for accessibility is not the same as removing qualifiers that preserve accuracy.

questions.title: Debt and Development
questions.prompt: Several low-income countries have borrowed heavily from wealthier nations and international banks to fund infrastructure. When they struggle to repay, lenders sometimes require economic reforms — such as cutting public services — as conditions for new loans. What term describes these conditions, and what is a key criticism of them?

options.A: Structural adjustment programmes; critics argue they often worsen poverty by cutting healthcare and education spending on which poor populations depend
options.B: Fair Trade agreements; critics argue they force countries to export more than they import
options.C: Development grants; critics argue they create inflation in developing economies
options.D: Bilateral aid packages; critics argue they only benefit the lending country's exporters

questions.explanation: Structural adjustment programmes (SAPs), historically associated with the IMF and World Bank, required borrowing nations to reduce government spending, privatise state enterprises, and open markets as conditions of loans. Critics, including UNICEF's 1987 'Adjustment with a Human Face' report, documented that cuts to health and education disproportionately harmed the poorest populations. Option B confuses this concept with trade agreements, which are a separate mechanism and do not involve loan conditionality.

questions.title: Media Representation and Bias
questions.prompt: News coverage of natural disasters in wealthy countries typically lasts several weeks and includes detailed human stories, while coverage of equivalent disasters in low-income countries often lasts only a few days with limited personal narratives. What concept best describes the bias this reflects?

options.A: Confirmation bias, because audiences only seek news that confirms their existing beliefs
options.B: The proximity principle and ethnocentrism in media, where geographically or culturally 'closer' events receive more coverage, reflecting whose lives are implicitly valued more
options.C: Selection bias, because journalists choose to cover only stories where they have personal connections
options.D: Recency bias, because recent disasters always receive more coverage than older ones

questions.explanation: Media scholars describe two overlapping phenomena here: the 'news proximity principle' (audiences care more about geographically or culturally close events) and ethnocentrism (implicitly treating the lives of people from similar backgrounds as more newsworthy). This has been empirically documented in studies comparing international disaster coverage in Western media. Option A (confirmation bias) describes a different phenomenon — how individuals process information that aligns with pre-existing beliefs — and does not explain editorial decisions about coverage volume.

questions.title: Buddhism and Materialism
questions.prompt: Buddhist teachings emphasise the concept of 'non-attachment' — the idea that clinging to material possessions causes suffering. How might a Buddhist critique of modern consumer culture differ from an economist's critique of overconsumption?

options.A: They would not differ; both Buddhism and economics prioritise reducing material wealth
options.B: A Buddhist critique focuses on the spiritual and psychological harm of desire itself, while an economist's critique focuses on environmental or resource sustainability of consumption levels
options.C: Buddhism supports consumerism because trade historically spread Buddhist ideas along the Silk Road
options.D: An economist would agree with Buddhist non-attachment because all economic models oppose consumption

questions.explanation: The Buddhist concept of 'tanha' (craving or attachment) identifies desire itself as the root of suffering — the critique is fundamentally about inner psychological states and ethical living, not resource equations. An environmental economist, by contrast, would evaluate overconsumption through metrics such as planetary boundaries or carbon budgets, focusing on external consequences rather than internal spiritual states. Option C conflates historical trade routes carrying Buddhism with Buddhist endorsement of consumerism — a category error.

questions.title: Gender Inequality and Development
questions.prompt: The UN Gender Inequality Index (GII) shows that countries with greater gender equality tend to have higher overall HDI scores. A student claims this correlation proves that improving gender equality is the single cause of development. Identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct because the GII and HDI are produced by the same organisation
options.B: Correlation does not establish causation; both gender equality and development may be jointly influenced by other factors such as institutional quality, education investment, and political stability
options.C: The flaw is that gender equality is irrelevant to development outcomes
options.D: HDI is not a reliable measure, so any correlation with GII is meaningless

questions.explanation: While evidence strongly supports that gender equality and human development reinforce each other, claiming a single causal direction from a correlation commits the logical fallacy of 'cum hoc ergo propter hoc' (correlation implies causation). Development scholars like Amartya Sen argue the relationship is bidirectional and mediated by governance, education, and institutional factors. Option D is a common student misconception: HDI is a well-established, widely accepted composite measure despite its limitations.

questions.title: Sovereignty vs. Humanitarian Intervention
questions.prompt: When a government commits severe human rights abuses against its own citizens, some argue the international community has the right — or even duty — to intervene militarily without the government's permission. Which principle most directly opposes this view?

options.A: The Responsibility to Protect (R2P), which supports intervention in extreme cases
options.B: The principle of state sovereignty enshrined in the UN Charter, which protects nations from external interference in internal affairs
options.C: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which requires all nations to act the same way
options.D: The principle of multilateralism, which requires all nations to agree before any action can occur

questions.explanation: Article 2(1) of the UN Charter establishes the sovereign equality of states, and Article 2(7) prohibits intervention in matters 'essentially within the domestic jurisdiction' of any state — this is the foundational legal barrier to humanitarian intervention. The tension between sovereignty and the 'Responsibility to Protect' (R2P, adopted by the UN in 2005) is a defining debate in modern international relations. Option A is actually an argument in favour of intervention, not against it — students often confuse R2P's existence with its being universally accepted.

questions.title: Urbanisation and Inequality
questions.prompt: In many rapidly growing cities in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, millions of residents live in informal settlements (slums) without legal land ownership, clean water, or official addresses. What would happen if a city government demolished these settlements without providing alternative housing, claiming it needed the land for development?

options.A: Residents would easily find affordable housing because demolition creates economic growth that benefits everyone
options.B: Residents would likely form new informal settlements elsewhere, and the underlying causes of urban poverty would remain unaddressed while human rights to adequate housing would be violated
options.C: The action would immediately increase the city's HDI score because slums lower development indicators
options.D: Demolition without relocation primarily affects a city's GDP, not its residents' wellbeing

questions.explanation: Forced evictions without adequate resettlement have been extensively documented by UN-Habitat and human rights organisations as violating the right to adequate housing (recognised in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights). Studies in cities from Lagos to Mumbai show displaced residents typically rebuild informal settlements nearby, as the economic and social drivers of informal urbanisation remain unchanged. Option A reflects a common 'trickle-down' misconception that development benefits automatically reach the poorest urban residents.

questions.title: Indigenous Rights and Land
questions.prompt: A mining company receives government permission to extract minerals from land that an indigenous community has inhabited for generations, without consulting the community. The government argues the land legally belongs to the state. Analyse the strongest challenge to the government's position under international standards.

options.A: Mining is always environmentally harmful, so no government should permit it anywhere
options.B: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples requires 'free, prior and informed consent' from indigenous communities before projects affecting their lands proceed
options.C: The government's position is valid because national law always overrides international declarations
options.D: The community should accept compensation and relocate because economic development benefits the whole country

questions.explanation: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP, 2007) specifically enshrines the principle of Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), meaning indigenous communities must be genuinely consulted and give consent — not just be notified — before projects affecting their territories begin. Option C is a misconception: while international declarations are not always legally binding, they represent authoritative international standards that many domestic courts have begun to incorporate, and they challenge the claim that national law is the only relevant framework.

questions.title: Trade Protectionism Effects
questions.prompt: Country A imposes a high tariff (import tax) on foreign steel to protect its domestic steel industry and jobs. Analyse which group within Country A is most likely to be negatively affected by this policy.

options.A: Domestic steel workers, because the tariff reduces demand for their labour
options.B: Domestic manufacturers who use steel as an input, such as car or appliance makers, because they now pay higher prices for steel
options.C: Foreign governments, because tariffs directly reduce their national income
options.D: Domestic consumers of foreign-made goods, because tariffs reduce the variety of imported products available

questions.explanation: A steel tariff raises the cost of steel for all domestic industries that use it as a production input — this is called an 'upstream' or 'input cost' effect. Car manufacturers, construction companies, and appliance makers face higher costs, potentially reducing their competitiveness and leading to job losses in those sectors, even while steel jobs are protected. This is a well-documented trade-off studied in the 2018 US steel tariff analysis by the Federal Reserve. Option A is directly incorrect — domestic steel workers are specifically the group the tariff is designed to protect.

questions.title: Islam Diversity and Unity
questions.prompt: A student researching Islam notes that Sunni and Shia Muslims disagree on questions of religious leadership and some practices, yet both groups fast during Ramadan, pray five times daily, and accept the Quran as their holy text. What does this evidence best illustrate?

options.A: Sunni and Shia Muslims follow completely different religions that happen to share a name
options.B: Religious traditions can contain significant internal diversity in interpretation and practice while sharing core beliefs and texts that unite them as a single faith
options.C: The differences between Sunni and Shia Islam are purely political and have no religious dimension
options.D: All major world religions are internally identical in their practices, just as Islam is

questions.explanation: Sunni and Shia Muslims diverged historically over the question of succession after the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE — a theological and political split — yet both recognise the Five Pillars of Islam including the Shahada, Salat, Sawm, Zakat, and Hajj, and both revere the Quran. This exemplifies how religious traditions can have both unifying foundations and significant internal diversity, a nuanced point essential for cross-cultural understanding. Option C is incorrect: the Sunni-Shia split has both deeply religious dimensions (including different hadith collections and jurisprudential traditions) and political ones.

questions.title: Technology and Labour Markets
questions.prompt: Automation and artificial intelligence are replacing routine jobs in both wealthy and developing nations. A student claims this will affect all countries equally. Which factor most clearly shows why developing nations may face a greater challenge from automation?

options.A: Developing nations have more robots than wealthy nations, so they automate faster
options.B: Many developing nations' economies rely heavily on low-skill manufacturing and assembly jobs that are most vulnerable to automation, while having fewer resources to retrain workers or develop new industries
options.C: Workers in developing nations are less intelligent and therefore harder to retrain for technology jobs
options.D: Automation only affects agriculture, which wealthy nations have already moved away from

questions.explanation: A 2016 World Bank report estimated that up to 77% of jobs in developing countries are at high risk from automation, compared to approximately 47% in wealthy nations — largely because developing economies have higher concentrations of low-skill, routine-task manufacturing that is most easily automated. Additionally, weaker social safety nets and education systems in developing nations limit the ability to manage this transition. Option A is factually inverted: wealthy nations currently have significantly more industrial robots per worker than developing nations.

questions.title: Aid Versus Trade Debate
questions.prompt: A government in a low-income country receives a large grant of foreign aid to build schools, but a neighbouring country instead negotiates a long-term trade deal that removes tariffs on its agricultural exports. After ten years, which outcome is the trade-deal country most likely to have achieved that the aid-recipient country has not? Justify your reasoning.

options.A: A higher literacy rate, because trade funds more schools than aid does
options.B: Greater long-term economic self-sufficiency, because export revenue builds domestic industries rather than creating dependency
options.C: A stronger military, because trade agreements usually include defence clauses
options.D: Lower corruption, because international trade partners monitor government spending

questions.explanation: Trade deals generate ongoing export revenue that stimulates domestic production and reduces aid dependency — economists such as Dambisa Moyo in 'Dead Aid' argue this creates more durable growth than grants. Option A is wrong because aid specifically targets services like education, so the aid-recipient country, not the trade country, would more likely see faster literacy gains in the short term.

questions.title: Religious Diversity Within Islam
questions.prompt: A student preparing a presentation on Islam states: 'The Sunni–Shia divide is the only significant internal difference within Islam, so understanding it fully means you understand all Muslim communities.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The statement is correct; the Sunni–Shia divide does account for all major differences within Islam
options.B: The error is that Islam has no internal divisions — all Muslims follow identical practices globally
options.C: The error is that Islam also contains other significant traditions such as Sufism, regional cultural practices, and varied legal schools, meaning the Sunni–Shia split is only one dimension of diversity
options.D: The error is that the student should focus on differences between Islam and other religions rather than within Islam itself

questions.explanation: Islam includes Sufi mystical traditions, four major Sunni legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali), distinct regional practices in West Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, and communities like the Ibadi and Ahmadiyya, making the Sunni–Shia divide just one axis of diversity. Option A is wrong because reducing Islamic diversity to a single split is an oversimplification that ignores centuries of theological and cultural variation.

questions.title: Push and Pull Migration Factors
questions.prompt: A family leaves their home country after a factory that employed most of the town closes down, making work almost impossible to find. In the country they move to, they are attracted by high wages and family already living there. How should a geographer classify the primary factors driving this migration?

options.A: One push factor (unemployment) and two pull factors (wages and social networks)
options.B: Two push factors (unemployment and low wages) and one pull factor (family ties)
options.C: Entirely push factors, because the family had no real choice in where they went
options.D: Entirely pull factors, because economic decisions are always driven by opportunity rather than hardship

questions.explanation: Migration theory distinguishes push factors (conditions forcing people to leave, here: factory closure causing unemployment) from pull factors (attractions drawing them to a destination, here: high wages and family networks — two distinct pull factors). Option B is wrong because low wages in the home country is implied by the factory closure context but is not separately stated; the scenario identifies one push factor and two explicit pull factors.

questions.title: Evaluating Sustainable Development Goals
questions.prompt: Country A has achieved SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation for all citizens) but still ranks very low on the Human Development Index. A student argues this proves the SDGs and the HDI measure the same thing. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because clean water is one of the three dimensions the HDI uses to calculate scores
options.B: The claim is incorrect because the HDI measures health (life expectancy), education, and income, while the SDGs are a broader set of 17 goals covering many areas the HDI does not include, such as sanitation
options.C: The claim is correct because achieving any SDG automatically raises a country's HDI score
options.D: The claim is incorrect because the HDI measures military strength, while the SDGs focus on poverty

questions.explanation: The HDI specifically combines life expectancy, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per capita — sanitation is not one of its three components. The SDGs are a much wider framework of 17 goals; achieving one does not necessarily move any HDI indicator. Option A is a common misconception because students conflate 'health-related' goals with the health dimension of the HDI.

questions.title: Cultural Imperialism and Media
questions.prompt: Why might critics argue that the global dominance of English-language streaming platforms such as those producing American television series represents a form of cultural imperialism, even when no government forces anyone to watch them?

options.A: Because these platforms always broadcast government propaganda that promotes American political values directly
options.B: Because the economic dominance of a few large platforms crowds out local content industries, gradually shifting cultural norms, values, and aspirations toward those of the producing culture without overt force
options.C: Because watching foreign content is illegal in most countries, making the platforms inherently imperialist
options.D: Because all cultural exchange is by definition imperialist, regardless of economic power differences

questions.explanation: Cultural imperialism, as theorised by scholars like Herbert Schiller, does not require direct government coercion; when commercially dominant media from one culture displaces local industries — for example, Hollywood revenues enabling production budgets that local filmmakers cannot match — it can reshape aspirations and values indirectly. Option A is wrong because mainstream streaming content is generally commercial entertainment, not government propaganda, making that description factually inaccurate.

questions.title: International Law and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Country X is accused by a neighbouring country of violating an international human rights treaty it signed. Country X's government responds: 'We are a sovereign nation and our internal laws take precedence over any international agreement.' Analyse the tension this response illustrates.

options.A: The tension between free trade and protectionism in international economics
options.B: The tension between national sovereignty and the binding obligations states voluntarily accept when they ratify international treaties
options.C: The tension between democratic and authoritarian political systems
options.D: The tension between religious law and secular law within a single country

questions.explanation: When a state ratifies a treaty, it voluntarily limits aspects of its sovereignty by accepting legally binding international obligations; claiming domestic law overrides this contradicts the principle of pacta sunt servanda (agreements must be kept) under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969). Option C is a distractor because the scenario does not specify the type of political system of either country — the tension is about treaty law versus sovereignty, not regime type.

questions.title: Gender Inequality in Development
questions.prompt: A development organisation finds that when girls in a rural region stay in school for two additional years, community income, child health outcomes, and birth rates all improve significantly. Which development principle does this evidence most strongly support?

options.A: That economic growth always precedes improvements in social indicators such as health
options.B: That girls' education is a high-leverage investment because it generates cascading positive effects across multiple development dimensions simultaneously
options.C: That population reduction is the primary cause of economic growth in rural areas
options.D: That international aid organisations are more effective than governments at improving education

questions.explanation: Research by economists including Lawrence Summers and the World Bank has shown that each additional year of girls' schooling correlates with approximately 10–20% increases in future earnings and measurable improvements in child nutrition and reduced fertility rates, demonstrating education's multiplier effect across development dimensions. Option A is wrong because the scenario shows social indicators improving alongside income, not necessarily after it — the data supports education as a driver, not a result, of growth.

questions.title: Interpreting the Gini Coefficient
questions.prompt: Country P has a GDP per capita of $45,000 and a Gini coefficient of 0.52. Country Q has a GDP per capita of $18,000 and a Gini coefficient of 0.27. A student claims Country P is clearly a more developed and fairer society. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct because higher GDP per capita always means greater development and fairness
options.B: The claim is partially correct on development but incorrect on fairness, because Country P's high Gini coefficient indicates much greater income inequality than Country Q
options.C: The claim is entirely incorrect because GDP per capita is not a valid measure of economic development
options.D: The claim is correct on fairness but incorrect on development, because a higher Gini coefficient means more equal income distribution

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality); Country P's score of 0.52 indicates high inequality similar to South Africa, while Country Q's 0.27 reflects relatively equal distribution similar to Scandinavia. GDP per capita does indicate higher average income (a development indicator) but says nothing about how that income is distributed, so the fairness part of the student's claim is wrong. Option D contains a factual error about what a higher Gini score means.

questions.title: Refugee Rights Under International Law
questions.prompt: A group of people fleeing severe drought and famine in their home country arrives at the border of a neighbouring state and requests asylum. The neighbouring government argues these people do not qualify as refugees under international law. Examine whether this government's position is legally defensible.

options.A: The position is not defensible, because international law guarantees asylum to anyone fleeing difficult conditions regardless of cause
options.B: The position is legally defensible, because the 1951 Refugee Convention defines refugees as people fleeing persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or social group — not environmental or economic causes
options.C: The position is not defensible, because climate-related displacement is explicitly covered by the UN Charter
options.D: The position is defensible only if the neighbouring country has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention

questions.explanation: The 1951 UN Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol define refugee status based on a well-founded fear of persecution for specific protected characteristics; environmental displacement from drought or famine is not currently covered, leaving 'climate refugees' without formal legal protection under existing international refugee law. Option A is a common student misconception — international law does not grant asylum to all people in difficult circumstances, only to those meeting the specific legal definition.

questions.title: Multiculturalism vs. Assimilation
questions.prompt: Compare a country that adopts an official multiculturalism policy — encouraging immigrant communities to maintain their cultural practices — with one that expects immigrants to fully adopt the dominant national culture. What is the most significant trade-off each approach involves?

options.A: Multiculturalism risks cultural fragmentation and social cohesion challenges, while assimilation risks the loss of minority cultural heritage and can marginalise immigrant communities
options.B: Multiculturalism always leads to higher crime rates, while assimilation always produces economic growth
options.C: Assimilation protects human rights more effectively, while multiculturalism violates the UN Declaration of Human Rights
options.D: Both approaches have identical outcomes because culture always blends together naturally over one generation regardless of policy

questions.explanation: Political theorists such as Will Kymlicka note that multicultural policies preserve minority cultures but can create parallel communities with limited cross-cultural interaction, while assimilation policies promote a unified national identity at the cost of erasing immigrant cultural practices and can produce social exclusion. Option B presents unsupported causal claims — neither multiculturalism nor assimilation has a straightforward, universal link to crime or economic growth across all contexts.

questions.title: Global Supply Chain Responsibility
questions.prompt: A well-known sportswear brand headquartered in Europe contracts manufacturing to a factory in Southeast Asia where workers are paid below a living wage and work in unsafe conditions. The brand argues it is not legally responsible because it does not directly employ those workers. Evaluate this position from a global ethics perspective.

options.A: The brand's position is fully justified because legal liability ends at direct employment contracts
options.B: The brand's position may be legally arguable in some jurisdictions but is ethically weak, because corporations hold moral responsibility for conditions throughout their supply chains, especially when profit is derived from those conditions
options.C: The brand is fully responsible in both law and ethics because European law always applies to overseas factories used by European companies
options.D: The brand has no responsibility because workers in other countries choose their employment conditions freely

questions.explanation: The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011) established that companies have a responsibility to respect human rights throughout their value chains, even without direct legal employment relationships — this is distinct from formal legal liability, which varies by jurisdiction. Option A is a top misconception because students often conflate legal liability with ethical responsibility, which are separate standards.

questions.title: Comparing Sacred Spaces Across Religions
questions.prompt: A student notices that Judaism has the Western Wall, Islam has the Masjid al-Haram, and Hinduism has the Ganges River as important sacred sites. What conclusion is most analytically appropriate to draw from comparing these examples?

options.A: All three religions are essentially the same because they each have one central sacred site
options.B: The concept of sacred geography — places that hold special spiritual significance — appears across diverse religious traditions, though the specific beliefs, practices, and meanings attached differ substantially
options.C: Having a sacred site proves that a religion is more valid or older than religions without one
options.D: Sacred sites are only found in religions that originated in Asia or the Middle East

questions.explanation: Comparative religious studies show that sacred geography is a widespread cross-cultural phenomenon — from Jerusalem to the Ganges to Mecca — but the theological meanings are distinct: the Western Wall connects to the destroyed Temple, the Ganges is believed to purify karma, and the Masjid al-Haram surrounds the Kaaba, the direction of Muslim prayer. Option A commits the error of surface-level comparison, treating structural similarity as proof of sameness, which ignores profound doctrinal differences.

questions.title: Examining Climate Justice Arguments
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Wealthy industrialised countries should bear greater financial responsibility for helping developing nations adapt to climate change, because historically they produced most of the cumulative greenhouse gas emissions that caused the problem.' Which reasoning strategy is this student using?

options.A: Appeal to tradition — arguing that past practices should continue into the future
options.B: Polluter pays principle combined with historical responsibility — linking causal contribution to financial obligation
options.C: Utilitarian reasoning — arguing that maximising total global happiness justifies redistribution
options.D: Nationalist reasoning — arguing that wealthy countries should only act in their own economic self-interest

questions.explanation: The student's argument reflects the 'polluter pays' principle, a recognised concept in environmental law and the climate justice movement, combined with the notion of historical or 'common but differentiated' responsibilities enshrined in the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992). Option C is a misconception because the argument is based on causal responsibility and fairness, not on calculating aggregate happiness — a utilitarian framing would focus on outcomes, not on who caused the problem.

questions.title: Diaspora Identity and Belonging
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to a young person's sense of national and cultural identity if they grew up in a diaspora community — for example, as a third-generation Nigerian living in London — where their family maintained strong Nigerian cultural practices but all their schooling and friendships were in British institutions?

options.A: They would have no cultural identity because living between two cultures causes complete identity loss
options.B: They would likely develop a hybrid or hyphenated identity, drawing from both Nigerian heritage and British culture, potentially experiencing tension between the two but also gaining cross-cultural fluency
options.C: They would automatically identify fully as British because institutional culture always overrides family culture
options.D: Their identity would be identical to that of someone born and raised in Nigeria, because family practices preserve culture perfectly

questions.explanation: Research on diaspora communities, including Stuart Hall's work on cultural identity, shows that individuals in diaspora often develop hybrid identities that incorporate elements of both heritage and host cultures — sometimes called 'third culture' or 'hyphenated' identities — rather than choosing one exclusively. Option C is a misconception because studies consistently show family and community practices remain powerful identity influences even when individuals are educated entirely within the host country's system.

questions.title: Microfinance and Development Critique
questions.prompt: Microfinance programmes lend small amounts of money to poor entrepreneurs, especially women, in developing countries. Supporters call it transformative; critics argue it can trap borrowers in debt cycles. Which evaluation of microfinance is most analytically balanced?

options.A: Microfinance is entirely positive because giving money to poor people always improves their lives
options.B: Microfinance is ineffective because poor people cannot manage loans responsibly
options.C: Microfinance has demonstrated benefits in enabling small-scale enterprise and empowering women, but evidence also shows high interest rates and over-indebtedness can worsen poverty for some borrowers, meaning outcomes depend heavily on programme design and local context
options.D: Microfinance only works in Asia and is irrelevant to development in Africa or Latin America

questions.explanation: Large-scale studies including MIT economist Abhijit Banerjee's randomised control trials found that microfinance had modest positive effects for some borrowers but did not consistently lift people out of poverty, and that interest rates of 30–80% in some programmes created debt traps. Option A ignores the structural risks; Option B is a prejudiced generalisation unsupported by evidence — the issue is programme design, not borrower capacity.

questions.title: Nongovernmental Organisations and Accountability
questions.prompt: An international NGO raises millions of dollars in donations to provide food aid in a conflict zone. A journalist discovers that a large portion of the funds is spent on administrative costs and expatriate staff salaries in the NGO's home country rather than reaching affected people. Which concern about international development does this illustrate?

options.A: The problem of trade protectionism preventing aid from reaching its destination
options.B: The tension between aid effectiveness and organisational accountability, highlighting that donors and beneficiaries may have different interests and that aid architecture can prioritise the donor country's economy over recipient needs
options.C: Evidence that all NGOs are fraudulent and should be replaced by government programmes
options.D: The positive role of NGOs in creating employment in high-income countries through development work

questions.explanation: This scenario illustrates what development critics call 'phantom aid' — a concept examined in reports by ActionAid — where a significant percentage of official or charitable development funds cycle back to donor-country contractors, consultants, and staff rather than reaching beneficiaries, undermining aid effectiveness. Option C overgeneralises from one example to condemn all NGOs, which ignores the many organisations that do operate with high transparency and impact.

questions.title: Ethnocentrism in Historical Narratives
questions.prompt: A history textbook published in Country A describes the colonisation of a region in Africa as 'bringing civilisation and order to a primitive land.' A student from that same region reads this and finds it deeply offensive. Which concept best explains why the textbook's language is academically problematic?

options.A: Relativism — the idea that all cultural practices must be judged by the standards of the culture that performs them
options.B: Ethnocentrism — judging another culture using the values and standards of one's own culture as a superior benchmark, which distorts historical understanding
options.C: Nationalism — placing the interests of one's own nation above those of others in economic competition
options.D: Orientalism — the specific Western academic tradition of studying Eastern cultures

questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism, a concept developed in anthropology by William Graham Sumner, involves using one's own culture as the default measure of value and progress — the textbook's language assumes European definitions of 'civilisation' are universal and superior, erasing the complex political, social, and economic systems that existed in Africa before colonisation. Option D (Orientalism) is a related but specific concept coined by Edward Said referring to Western representations of the 'East' — it is not the broadest and most applicable term for this scenario.

questions.title: Water Scarcity and Global Equity
questions.prompt: In one country, households use an average of 300 litres of water per person per day, while in another country, households survive on fewer than 20 litres per person per day, which is below the WHO minimum of 50 litres. A student says this gap is entirely explained by different climates. What is the most significant error in this explanation?

options.A: Climate is completely irrelevant to water availability, so no part of the student's argument is valid
options.B: The explanation ignores the roles of economic inequality, infrastructure investment, governance quality, and historical patterns of development, which mean that water access reflects political and economic choices as well as geography
options.C: The explanation is correct — rainfall patterns fully determine household water consumption in all countries
options.D: The student's error is focusing on households rather than industry, which is the only relevant water user globally

questions.explanation: While climate affects water availability, countries with similar climates can have dramatically different access levels depending on infrastructure investment in piping and treatment, governance, and economic development — for example, Singapore and parts of sub-Saharan Africa have comparable rainfall but vastly different access to clean water. Option C is the key misconception to address: rainfall alone does not determine access because technology and investment can overcome geographic constraints, as Israel's desalination programme demonstrates.

questions.title: Secularism and Religious Freedom
questions.prompt: Country M has a strictly secular constitution that bans all religious symbols in public schools and government offices. Some religious minority communities argue this policy violates their religious freedom, while the government says it protects equality by treating all religions the same. Discuss which perspective presents the stronger argument.

options.A: The government is entirely correct because all secular states by definition respect human rights more than religious states
options.B: The minority communities are entirely correct because any restriction on religious expression is automatically a human rights violation
options.C: Both perspectives have merit: the government's position promotes formal equality but may produce substantive inequality by banning practices that are religious obligations for some groups but have no secular equivalent, suggesting context-sensitive accommodation may better balance rights
options.D: Neither perspective is valid because international law requires all countries to choose one official religion

questions.explanation: This scenario mirrors real debates in France (laïcité) where the European Court of Human Rights has ruled in multiple cases that blanket bans can disproportionately affect minority groups whose religious practice is more visibly expressed — distinguishing formal equality (same rules for all) from substantive equality (fair outcomes for all). Option A is wrong because secular constitutions can still produce unequal outcomes for minorities whose practices happen to be more visibly religious than the majority.

questions.title: Urbanisation and Inequality
questions.prompt: In many rapidly developing countries, rural populations are moving to cities in large numbers, yet surveys show urban slum residents often report lower subjective wellbeing than rural residents despite earning higher incomes. Which explanation is most consistent with a development studies framework?

options.A: Higher income always produces higher wellbeing, so the survey data must be incorrect
options.B: Urban slum conditions — overcrowding, pollution, weak social networks, insecure housing, and visible inequality — can offset income gains, showing that wellbeing is multidimensional and not reducible to income alone
options.C: Rural life is objectively better than urban life in all development contexts
options.D: People move to cities irrationally, since the data proves urban areas offer no economic benefit

questions.explanation: Amartya Sen's capabilities approach and the New Economics Foundation's research on wellbeing both demonstrate that income is only one dimension of human flourishing; loss of community networks, exposure to relative deprivation (seeing wealthy neighbours), and poor housing conditions in urban slums are documented factors that suppress subjective wellbeing even when income rises. Option A represents the common misconception that income and wellbeing are the same variable, which development economics has consistently challenged.

questions.title: Trade Blocs and National Sovereignty
questions.prompt: When a group of countries forms a trade bloc and agrees to follow shared regulations on product safety and labour standards, some citizens in member countries protest that their national parliament has lost meaningful power. Analyse whether this concern is well-founded.

options.A: The concern is completely unfounded because trade blocs have no legal authority over member states
options.B: The concern has genuine basis because member states do transfer some regulatory authority to bloc-level institutions, meaning domestic parliaments cannot set those specific rules independently, though they retain sovereignty in areas outside the bloc's scope
options.C: The concern is unfounded because joining a trade bloc increases a nation's total power by making it part of a larger unit
options.D: The concern is well-founded and proves that all international cooperation is harmful to democratic governance

questions.explanation: The European Union is the clearest example: member states cannot set independent tariff rates or diverge from single market product regulations, and the European Court of Justice can override national courts on matters within EU competence — this is a real, deliberate pooling of sovereignty. Option C conflates increased collective economic power with the separate question of national legislative autonomy, which are different things — a country can gain economic influence while simultaneously losing regulatory independence.

questions.title: Identifying Bias in Development Data
questions.prompt: A think-tank funded by a pharmaceutical company publishes a report arguing that patent protections on medicines in developing countries should be strengthened, citing evidence that this will increase investment in new drugs for tropical diseases. A student accepts the report without checking its funding source. Which ATL skill is the student failing to apply, and why does it matter in global perspectives?

options.A: Communication skills — the student is not presenting the information clearly enough to their teacher
options.B: Critical thinking and information literacy — failing to evaluate the source's potential conflict of interest means the student may mistake commercially motivated advocacy for objective evidence
options.C: Collaboration skills — the student should have worked in a group to find the report rather than reading it alone
options.D: Self-management skills — the student needs to improve their time management when conducting research

questions.explanation: In IB MYP ATL frameworks, information literacy includes evaluating the credibility, perspective, and potential bias of sources; a pharmaceutical company has a direct financial interest in stronger patent laws, which means its funded research may selectively present evidence — this matters in global perspectives because access to affordable medicines is a critical equity issue where biased data can influence harmful policy. Option A is wrong because the skill gap is not about how information is communicated but about how it is critically evaluated before being accepted.

questions.title: Migration Push-Pull Factors
questions.prompt: A family leaves their home country after the government collapses and armed conflict breaks out in their region. They cross into a neighbouring country and apply for official protection. A student claims they should be classified as economic migrants because they had jobs before leaving. Evaluate this claim using international refugee law.

options.A: The claim is correct because having prior employment disqualifies a person from refugee status under the 1951 Convention.
options.B: The claim is incorrect because the 1951 Refugee Convention protects people fleeing persecution or serious threats, regardless of their prior employment status.
options.C: The claim is correct because only people who have never worked can qualify for refugee status under UN definitions.
options.D: The claim is partially correct because refugee status applies only when a person crosses two or more international borders.

questions.explanation: The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as someone who cannot return home due to a well-founded fear of persecution or threats to life — employment history is entirely irrelevant to this definition. Option A is wrong because no clause in the Convention uses prior employment as a disqualifying criterion; conflating economic background with motive for flight is a common but inaccurate reasoning error.

questions.title: Trade Agreements and Inequality
questions.prompt: When a low-income country joins a free-trade agreement with high-income nations, some economists predict that domestic industries in the low-income country will suffer in the short term. Which reasoning best justifies why this short-term harm might still be considered acceptable from a development perspective?

options.A: Short-term harm is acceptable because high-income countries always compensate low-income partners directly through aid payments written into trade agreements.
options.B: Short-term harm is acceptable because free trade always produces equal benefits for all partner countries within the first decade.
options.C: Short-term harm may be offset by long-term gains such as access to larger markets, foreign investment, and technology transfer that can raise living standards over time.
options.D: Short-term harm is acceptable because the World Trade Organization legally requires low-income countries to enter such agreements regardless of domestic impact.

questions.explanation: Development economists who favour trade liberalisation argue that access to larger export markets, inflows of foreign direct investment, and the transfer of technology can generate sustained economic growth that eventually outweighs initial disruption to uncompetitive local industries. Option A is incorrect because direct compensation payments are not a standard feature of most free-trade agreements, making it a plausible but factually inaccurate claim.

questions.title: Global Commons and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: The high seas — ocean areas beyond any country's national jurisdiction — are sometimes called a 'global commons.' Countries have historically overfished these areas even when all parties agree it is unsustainable. Which concept from international relations most precisely names the dynamic causing this outcome?

options.A: Cultural imperialism, because wealthy fishing nations impose their practices on others.
options.B: The tragedy of the commons, because individual actors exploit a shared resource for personal gain, ultimately depleting it for everyone.
options.C: Comparative advantage, because each country focuses on the fishing activity it performs most efficiently.
options.D: Interdependence, because all countries rely on each other to set sustainable fishing limits.

questions.explanation: The 'tragedy of the commons,' articulated by ecologist Garrett Hardin in 1968, describes how rational self-interest by many individuals leads to collective overuse and destruction of a shared resource — precisely what occurs in unregulated international fisheries. Option D is plausible because interdependence is real in this context, but it names the relationship rather than the mechanism driving the destructive behaviour.

questions.title: Multiculturalism Policy Models
questions.prompt: France follows a policy sometimes called 'civic republicanism,' which discourages public displays of religious or ethnic identity and expects all citizens to share a single civic identity. Canada follows 'official multiculturalism,' which actively promotes cultural diversity within a shared civic framework. Compare these two approaches: which outcome does the French model prioritise above the others?

options.A: Preservation of minority cultural traditions within the public sphere.
options.B: State recognition of distinct ethnic communities as official groups with separate rights.
options.C: Equal treatment under a universal secular law that applies identically to all citizens regardless of background.
options.D: Government funding for multicultural festivals and community organisations representing different ethnicities.

questions.explanation: French civic republicanism is built on the principle that the state is blind to ethnicity and religion in the public sphere — the law applies identically to everyone, which its proponents argue prevents discrimination by treating all citizens as equal individuals rather than members of distinct groups. Options A and D describe outcomes the Canadian model pursues, making them plausible but opposite in orientation to France's approach.

questions.title: Climate Justice and Responsibility
questions.prompt: Evaluate the following student argument: 'Because China currently emits more total CO₂ than any other country, it bears the greatest responsibility for funding climate adaptation in vulnerable nations and should pay far more than the United States into the Green Climate Fund.'

options.A: The argument is fully sound because total current emissions are the only fair metric for assigning climate responsibility.
options.B: The argument oversimplifies responsibility because it ignores historical cumulative emissions, per-capita emissions, and the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities.'
options.C: The argument is correct because the Green Climate Fund's charter explicitly assigns contributions based solely on current total emissions.
options.D: The argument is flawed only because China's emissions figures are unreliable, not because the underlying reasoning is wrong.

questions.explanation: The UNFCCC's principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities' holds that countries which industrialised earlier and accumulated far more historical emissions — such as the United States and European nations — bear proportionally greater responsibility, even if a developing country's current total output is now higher. Option A is the top distractor because total current emissions seem like a straightforward metric, but it ignores the cumulative stock of greenhouse gases already in the atmosphere from decades of earlier industrialisation.

questions.title: Religion and Conflict Resolution
questions.prompt: In Northern Ireland, the 1998 Good Friday Agreement helped end decades of violent conflict between communities broadly identified as Protestant and Catholic. A student argues that this proves religion was the sole cause of the conflict. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The error is that the Good Friday Agreement was actually a religious treaty negotiated by church leaders, not a political document.
options.B: The error is that the conflict also involved competing national identities, colonial history, economic inequality, and political power — religion served as a marker of group identity rather than the sole driver.
options.C: The error is that both communities in Northern Ireland actually share identical religious beliefs, so religion could not have been a factor at all.
options.D: The error is that only conflicts involving three or more religious groups can be considered religiously motivated, so two-community conflicts are always purely political.

questions.explanation: The Northern Ireland conflict (the Troubles) was rooted in a complex mix of British colonial history, competing Unionist and Nationalist political identities, socioeconomic discrimination, and civil rights grievances — religious labels largely mapped onto these existing divisions rather than causing them independently. Option D is the strongest distractor because it sounds like a principled rule, but no such criterion exists in conflict studies or international relations.

questions.title: SDG Trade-offs in Practice
questions.prompt: A government in a low-income country wants to meet SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth) by attracting foreign manufacturing companies. Critics warn this conflicts with SDG 13 (climate action) because the factories will increase carbon emissions. What does this tension most clearly illustrate about the Sustainable Development Goals?

options.A: It illustrates that SDG 13 always takes legal precedence over SDG 8 under the UN Charter.
options.B: It illustrates that the SDGs can produce genuine trade-offs, requiring governments to weigh development priorities against environmental sustainability in context-specific ways.
options.C: It illustrates that economic growth goals were poorly designed and should be removed from the SDG framework.
options.D: It illustrates that low-income countries are exempt from SDG 13 obligations because they contributed least to global emissions.

questions.explanation: The 17 SDGs were designed as interconnected and mutually reinforcing goals, but in practice they can pull in different directions — especially for countries that must grow economically while managing environmental impact, a tension the UN itself acknowledges in SDG progress reports. Option D is a plausible distractor because the principle of differentiated responsibility is real, but no SDG framework grants formal exemptions from environmental goals based on income level.

questions.title: Cultural Diffusion vs. Imperialism
questions.prompt: Korean pop music (K-pop) has gained massive global audiences, influencing fashion, language learning, and consumer behaviour in countries from Brazil to Nigeria. A student labels this 'cultural imperialism by South Korea.' Analyse whether this label is accurate.

options.A: The label is accurate because any time one country's culture spreads globally, it constitutes imperialism by definition.
options.B: The label is accurate because South Korea's government forces foreign broadcasters to air K-pop content through international trade sanctions.
options.C: The label is inaccurate because cultural imperialism typically involves dominant powers using political or economic coercion to impose culture, whereas K-pop spread largely through voluntary audience demand and digital platforms.
options.D: The label is inaccurate because imperialism only applies to military conquest, making any cultural comparison to it inappropriate.

questions.explanation: Cultural imperialism, as theorised by scholars like Herbert Schiller, involves a power imbalance where dominant nations use economic or political leverage to displace local cultures — K-pop's rise was driven by consumer choice, social media, and the Korean Wave (Hallyu) strategy of soft power, not coercion. Option A is the top distractor because it conflates cultural spread with cultural imperialism, ignoring the critical element of coercion that distinguishes the two.

questions.title: Gini Coefficient and Inequality
questions.prompt: Country A and Country B have identical GDP per capita. Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.28 and Country B has a Gini coefficient of 0.52. What does this difference most precisely tell an analyst about the two countries?

options.A: Country B's citizens are, on average, twice as wealthy as Country A's citizens.
options.B: Income is distributed far more unequally in Country B than in Country A, meaning a larger share of national income is concentrated among fewer people in Country B.
options.C: Country B has a higher poverty rate than Country A because its GDP is spread across more people.
options.D: Country A must have stronger environmental protections because lower Gini scores correlate directly with sustainability policy.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient measures income inequality on a scale from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person holds all income); a score of 0.52 versus 0.28 means wealth is far more concentrated in Country B even though average incomes are the same. Option C is a strong distractor because high inequality can correlate with higher poverty rates, but GDP per capita is identical here, so the reasoning conflates distribution with overall wealth levels.

questions.title: Non-Governmental Organisations
questions.prompt: An NGO operating in a low-income country builds schools, trains teachers, and funds them for five years before withdrawing. A government official criticises this approach, arguing it undermines long-term development. Which reasoning best supports the official's concern?

options.A: NGOs are legally prohibited from operating in education sectors under international development law.
options.B: If the local government and community do not develop the capacity and funding structures to sustain the schools independently, the intervention creates dependency and collapses once the NGO leaves.
options.C: The schools will automatically be taken over by for-profit corporations once the NGO withdraws, harming local communities.
options.D: Five-year projects always fail because development research proves that only ten-year minimum commitments produce measurable outcomes.

questions.explanation: A core critique of short-term NGO projects is that they can foster dependency rather than building local institutional capacity — if the host government lacks the budget systems, trained administrators, and public funding mechanisms to continue the schools, the investment collapses, which is sometimes called the 'aid dependency trap.' Option C is a plausible-sounding distractor but introduces a specific claim (corporate takeover) that has no basis in the scenario or general development theory.

questions.title: Hinduism and Social Structure
questions.prompt: A student studying Hinduism writes: 'The caste system is an intrinsic part of Hindu religious teaching and is universally accepted by all Hindus today.' Evaluate this claim from a cross-cultural perspective.

options.A: The claim is accurate because the Vedas explicitly mandate caste as a universal eternal law observed identically across all Hindu communities.
options.B: The claim is oversimplified because while caste has historical roots in some Hindu texts, many Hindu reformers, scholars, and communities actively reject caste hierarchy, and India's constitution outlaws caste discrimination.
options.C: The claim is accurate because Hinduism, unlike other world religions, has no internal diversity of interpretation or practice.
options.D: The claim is partially accurate because caste is accepted in rural India but completely absent from all urban Hindu practice worldwide.

questions.explanation: Prominent Hindu reformers such as B.R. Ambedkar and Swami Vivekananda challenged caste hierarchy, and India's 1950 Constitution under Article 17 abolished untouchability — demonstrating that caste is contested, not universally accepted, within Hinduism. Option D is plausible because urbanisation does correlate with reduced caste observance in some contexts, but claiming it is 'completely absent' from all urban practice worldwide is factually inaccurate and overly sweeping.

questions.title: Globalisation and Labour Rights
questions.prompt: A multinational corporation relocates its manufacturing from a high-income country to a low-income country where labour laws are weaker and wages are lower. From the perspective of the low-income country's workers, which analysis is most nuanced and accurate?

options.A: The move is entirely beneficial because any paid employment is better than no employment in a low-income country.
options.B: The move is entirely harmful because multinationals never improve conditions for workers in low-income countries.
options.C: The impact is mixed: while the jobs may provide income and reduce unemployment, weak regulatory environments risk exploitation, poor safety conditions, and suppression of wages below a living wage.
options.D: The impact is irrelevant to fairness and development because workers freely choose whether to accept employment at offered wages.

questions.explanation: Development economists and labour rights organisations consistently find that foreign direct investment in manufacturing can reduce unemployment and provide income, but without strong labour protections it also enables wage suppression, unsafe conditions, and union busting — as documented in cases such as garment factories in Bangladesh before the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse. Option A is the top distractor because it contains a grain of truth (employment is valuable) but ignores the conditions and power imbalances under which that employment occurs.

questions.title: United Nations Security Council
questions.prompt: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States each hold a permanent seat on the UN Security Council with veto power. A student argues this structure perfectly reflects today's global balance of power and should remain unchanged. What is the strongest counter-argument to this position?

options.A: The counter-argument is that the UN Charter explicitly requires a review of permanent membership every ten years, which has never been conducted.
options.B: The counter-argument is that the P5 membership reflects post-World War II power dynamics, excluding major contemporary powers such as India, Brazil, and the African continent, which now represent billions of people with growing global influence.
options.C: The counter-argument is that veto power should be abolished entirely and replaced with a simple majority vote among all 193 member states.
options.D: The counter-argument is that only democracies should hold permanent seats, so Russia and China should be removed immediately under existing UN rules.

questions.explanation: The P5 was determined by the post-WWII geopolitical order of 1945; critics — including the UN's own reform proposals — argue that excluding Africa, South Asia, and Latin America from permanent representation makes the Council increasingly illegitimate relative to today's global population and economic weight. Option C is plausible as a reform proposal but goes far beyond a counter-argument to the student's claim, introducing a separate structural idea rather than directly challenging the premise about current relevance.

questions.title: Microfinance Effectiveness
questions.prompt: Microfinance institutions offer small loans to people in low-income communities, particularly women, who cannot access traditional bank credit. A researcher finds that in some programmes, borrowers fall into debt cycles rather than escaping poverty. What does this finding suggest about evaluating development interventions?

options.A: It suggests that microfinance is definitively harmful and should be immediately banned by international development organisations.
options.B: It suggests that development interventions must be evaluated in specific contexts, considering factors like interest rates, support services, and local markets rather than assuming universal success.
options.C: It suggests that women in low-income countries are inherently poor financial managers and require more supervision.
options.D: It suggests that poverty cannot be reduced through financial tools and that only political revolution produces lasting development.

questions.explanation: Research, including randomised controlled trials by economists like Esther Duflo, shows microfinance outcomes vary enormously depending on interest rates, whether complementary services (training, savings programmes) accompany loans, and local market conditions — supporting a context-specific, evidence-based approach to evaluating development tools. Option A is plausible because the finding is negative, but concluding total failure from mixed evidence commits the logical error of overgeneralisation.

questions.title: Diaspora Identity Formation
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to the cultural identity of a third-generation immigrant community — grandchildren of the original migrants — compared to the first generation, assuming no major policy changes and continued integration into the host society?

options.A: The third generation would adopt the host country's culture completely, with no retention of the ancestral culture, because full assimilation is biologically determined after three generations.
options.B: The third generation would likely develop a hybrid identity, possibly with selective or symbolic connections to ancestral culture — such as food, festivals, or family names — while primarily identifying with the host country.
options.C: The third generation would be more strongly connected to the ancestral homeland than the first generation because of increased nostalgia.
options.D: Cultural identity remains identical across all immigrant generations because identity is determined solely by ethnic heritage, not by social environment.

questions.explanation: Sociological research on 'segmented assimilation' and 'symbolic ethnicity' (Herbert Gans) shows that third-generation immigrants in integrated societies often maintain selective, low-cost cultural markers — such as heritage food or festivals — while primarily identifying with the host nation, producing a hybrid or hyphenated identity rather than complete erasure or full preservation. Option C is the top distractor because 'third-generation return' or Hansen's Law suggests some renewed interest in heritage, but this is a selective and debated phenomenon, not stronger overall ancestral connection than the first generation.

questions.title: Trade Protectionism Debate
questions.prompt: A government imposes high tariffs on imported steel to protect domestic steel jobs. Critics argue this harms the overall economy while supporters claim it protects workers. Which response most accurately presents both sides of this debate without misrepresenting either?

options.A: Supporters are correct and critics are wrong because protecting domestic industry always benefits a national economy in the long run.
options.B: Tariffs protect jobs in the steel sector and preserve strategic industrial capacity, but raise costs for industries that use steel as an input and may trigger retaliatory tariffs from trading partners, slowing overall growth.
options.C: Critics are correct and supporters are wrong because free trade is proven to benefit all workers in all sectors simultaneously.
options.D: Tariffs are always a short-term measure that automatically expire under WTO rules after two years, making the debate largely irrelevant.

questions.explanation: The US steel tariffs of 2018 illustrate this tension precisely: they preserved approximately 8,700 steel jobs but raised input costs for around 6.5 million workers in downstream manufacturing sectors and invited retaliatory tariffs from trading partners including the EU and China. Option A is the strongest distractor because it captures the pro-tariff argument but falsely presents it as universally correct, ignoring the well-documented costs to downstream industries.

questions.title: Buddhism's Spread and Adaptation
questions.prompt: Buddhism originated in South Asia but now has significant followings in East Asia, Southeast Asia, and increasingly in Western countries. In each region, local practices, rituals, and philosophies differ substantially. What does this pattern most accurately illustrate about world religions?

options.A: It illustrates that Buddhism is not a single unified religion but a collection of completely separate and unrelated belief systems that share only a name.
options.B: It illustrates that religions adapt to local cultural contexts as they spread, producing diverse expressions of shared core teachings while retaining common foundational elements such as the Four Noble Truths and the concept of nirvana.
options.C: It illustrates that Eastern religions are inherently more flexible than Western ones and therefore spread more successfully across cultures.
options.D: It illustrates that Buddhism has lost its original meaning through cultural contamination and that only South Asian Theravada Buddhism represents authentic practice.

questions.explanation: Scholars of comparative religion distinguish between the shared textual and doctrinal core of Buddhism (e.g., the Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, the concept of nirvana) and its culturally varied ritual expressions — a distinction that explains how Zen Buddhism in Japan, Tibetan Buddhism, and Theravada Buddhism in Sri Lanka are simultaneously different and related. Option A is a strong distractor because it acknowledges diversity but incorrectly severs the common foundations that link Buddhist traditions.

questions.title: Colonial Legacy and Development
questions.prompt: Some economists argue that colonial-era borders drawn by European powers in Africa, which often cut through ethnic and linguistic communities, are a significant cause of ongoing political instability and slower development in some African nations. A critic responds that this argument 'lets current African leaders off the hook for present-day governance failures.' Evaluate both positions.
