questions.prompt: In 2023, global remittance flows to low- and middle-income countries exceeded $650 billion — more than three times the total of official development assistance (ODA). A policymaker argues this makes foreign aid largely irrelevant. Critically assess this position.

options.A: The position is correct because remittances are always more efficiently allocated than ODA, which is often captured by corrupt governments.
options.B: The position is overstated because remittances flow predominantly to middle-income countries and to households with relatives abroad, whereas ODA can be targeted at the poorest populations and at public goods like health infrastructure that households cannot individually fund.
options.C: The position is correct because World Bank data confirms that countries receiving high remittances consistently outperform ODA-dependent countries on all HDI indicators.
options.D: The position is overstated because remittances decline during global recessions, whereas ODA is legally guaranteed to remain stable under UN treaties.

questions.explanation: While remittances do exceed ODA in aggregate, they are heavily concentrated in middle-income countries (e.g., India, Mexico, Philippines) and flow to households with diaspora connections, missing the poorest of the poor and unable to fund non-excludable public goods like disease surveillance or road networks. ODA, despite its inefficiencies, can be strategically directed toward these gaps. Option A is wrong because, while aid capture by elites is a real concern, the claim that remittances are 'always' more efficient is empirically unsupported — remittances are also partly spent on consumption goods rather than investment.

questions.title: Realism vs Liberalism in IR
questions.prompt: During a crisis in which State A threatens military action against State B unless B surrenders a disputed territory, State B appeals to a multilateral international organisation for protection. A realist IR scholar and a liberal institutionalist scholar would most likely disagree on which of the following?

options.A: Whether State A's behaviour constitutes a violation of sovereignty under the UN Charter.
options.B: Whether the multilateral organisation's intervention will be effective, since realists believe international institutions lack autonomous power and merely reflect the interests of powerful states, while liberals argue institutions can generate compliance beyond raw power calculations.
options.C: Whether State B has a legal right to self-defence, since realists reject international law entirely while liberals fully accept it.
options.D: Whether economic interdependence exists between States A and B, since realists deny that trade relationships exist between adversarial states.

questions.explanation: The central realist–liberal institutionalist disagreement concerns the independent causal power of international institutions. Realists like Mearsheimer contend institutions are epiphenomenal — they reflect underlying power distributions and cannot constrain great powers. Liberal institutionalists like Keohane argue institutions create credible commitment mechanisms, reduce transaction costs, and generate compliance beyond what power alone predicts. Option C is a common misconception: realists do not wholesale reject international law — they simply argue states comply only when it serves their interests, not because law has inherent binding force.

questions.title: Fair Trade Model Critique
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Fair Trade certification is the most effective mechanism for improving farmer welfare in developing countries because it guarantees a price floor above the market rate.' Critically assess this claim using evidence from development economics.

options.A: The claim is fully supported; economic studies consistently show Fair Trade farmers earn significantly higher incomes than non-certified counterparts.
options.B: The claim overstates the benefit because the price premium often does not reach individual farmers — much is retained by exporter cooperatives or used for certification costs — and only a fraction of Fair Trade-labelled produce is actually sold at the Fair Trade premium price.
options.C: The claim is wrong because Fair Trade certification sets a price ceiling, not a price floor, which depresses farmer incentives.
options.D: The claim is overstated because Fair Trade only operates in the coffee sector and cannot be applied to crops like cocoa or bananas.

questions.explanation: Rigorous studies, including a 2014 SOAS University of London report on Fairtrade in Ethiopia and Uganda, found that wages on Fairtrade farms were sometimes lower than on comparable non-certified farms, partly because cooperatives retained premiums for community projects and certification costs, and because only a minority of certified output is actually sold under Fairtrade terms. The price floor mechanism is real, but its transmission to individual farmers is frequently attenuated. Option A is the top distractor because students often accept the Fair Trade model uncritically, assuming the price premium directly and fully translates to higher farmer incomes.

questions.title: Nationalism and Globalisation Tension
questions.prompt: Several high-income democracies saw a significant rise in nationalist political movements during the 2010s, coinciding with decades of globalisation. Which explanation best synthesises the economic and cultural dimensions of this correlation?

options.A: Globalisation directly caused nationalism by making all citizens in wealthy countries economically worse off through trade competition.
options.B: Nationalist movements emerged purely as a cultural backlash against immigration, with no meaningful connection to economic grievances.
options.C: Rising nationalism reflects a convergence of distributional economic grievances — where trade and automation concentrated gains among the highly educated while displacing manufacturing workers — and identity-based anxieties about cultural change, both of which globalisation accelerated.
options.D: Nationalist movements rose because globalisation reduced national sovereignty to a point where democratic governance became impossible in most OECD countries.

questions.explanation: Research by economists such as David Autor (on the 'China shock') and political scientists like Ronald Inglehart and Pippa Norris identifies a 'dual backlash': communities facing deindustrialisation and wage stagnation proved more susceptible to nationalist appeals that also channelled cultural anxiety about demographic change. This is not a single-cause phenomenon. Option A overstates economic causation by claiming all citizens were made worse off — in aggregate, trade increases welfare, but its gains are unequally distributed, which is the crucial nuance.

questions.title: Islamic Finance Principles
questions.prompt: Islamic finance prohibits riba (usually translated as interest or usury). A Western banker argues that Islamic mortgage products are economically identical to conventional mortgages because the bank still profits proportionally. To what extent does this argument capture the significance of the distinction?

options.A: Fully — the banker is correct; the prohibition on riba is purely symbolic since profit in any form is economically equivalent to interest.
options.B: Partially — while the financial outcomes may be similar in some products, the Islamic finance framework shifts risk-sharing arrangements, prohibits investment in certain industries (e.g., alcohol, weapons), and is grounded in a distinct ethical philosophy of shared risk and social responsibility.
options.C: Not at all — Islamic mortgage products generate no profit for the bank whatsoever, making them fundamentally incompatible with commercial banking.
options.D: Partially — the distinction matters only in countries with Muslim majorities, where it has legal rather than ethical significance.

questions.explanation: Islamic finance products like murabaha (cost-plus financing) or musharakah (equity partnership) do generate returns for the bank, but the prohibition on riba has substantive implications: profits must be tied to real economic activity and shared risk, speculation (gharar) is restricted, and entire sectors are excluded from investment on ethical grounds. The Accounting and Auditing Organisation for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) provides standards that reflect these genuine structural differences. Option A is the top distractor because it represents a plausible but reductive economic critique that ignores the ethical architecture and risk-sharing principles that differentiate Islamic finance structurally.

questions.title: Neocolonialism in Resource Extraction
questions.prompt: Several African nations have signed agreements with foreign corporations granting long-term rights to extract mineral resources in exchange for infrastructure investment. Critics call this 'neocolonialism.' What is the most analytically precise definition of neocolonialism, and does it apply here?

options.A: Neocolonialism means direct military occupation of a sovereign state; since no troops are involved, the term does not apply here.
options.B: Neocolonialism, as defined by Kwame Nkrumah, refers to the exercise of economic and political control over formally independent states through trade, debt, and corporate arrangements — making these resource deals potentially neocolonial if they systematically transfer wealth while limiting the host country's policy sovereignty.
options.C: Neocolonialism applies only to relationships between European states and their former colonies; deals involving Chinese or American corporations cannot be described this way.
options.D: Neocolonialism refers to cultural domination through media and language, so economic resource agreements fall outside its scope by definition.

questions.explanation: Kwame Nkrumah coined and defined neocolonialism in his 1965 work 'Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism,' describing it as a situation where a state has nominal independence but its economic system and political policy are directed from outside. Resource agreements that lock in long-term profit repatriation, restrict export processing, and include investor-state dispute mechanisms that constrain government regulation fit squarely within this definition. Option A reflects a narrow, military-centric definition of colonialism that Nkrumah's framework was specifically designed to transcend.

questions.title: Amartya Sen Capabilities Approach
questions.prompt: Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum's 'capabilities approach' to human development challenges traditional welfare economics. Which of the following most accurately distinguishes it from utilitarian approaches to measuring development?

options.A: The capabilities approach measures total national happiness using subjective survey data, whereas utilitarianism focuses on objective economic outputs.
options.B: The capabilities approach focuses on what individuals are actually able to do and be — their substantive freedoms — rather than on aggregate welfare or income, recognising that people may adapt preferences to constrained circumstances.
options.C: The capabilities approach is distinguished by its exclusive focus on political freedoms, whereas utilitarianism addresses a broader range of human welfare dimensions.
options.D: The capabilities approach and utilitarianism are functionally equivalent because both ultimately seek to maximise human well-being, differing only in measurement units.

questions.explanation: Sen's capabilities approach holds that development should be evaluated by whether people have the substantive freedom to live lives they have reason to value — emphasising functionings (what people actually do) and capabilities (what they are free to do). A key insight is the 'adaptive preferences' problem: people in oppressive circumstances may report high satisfaction with low conditions, so subjective utility is a misleading measure. Option D is the top distractor because students who have engaged superficially with both frameworks may conclude they share the same end goal, missing the fundamental methodological and philosophical distinctions regarding whose preferences count and how freedom is conceptualised.

questions.title: Transnational Organised Crime
questions.prompt: The UN Office on Drugs and Crime estimates that transnational organised crime generates approximately $870 billion annually — nearly 1.5% of global GDP. A student argues this is a law enforcement problem that international development agencies should not address. Evaluate this view.

options.A: The view is correct because development agencies lack the legal mandate or technical expertise to address criminal networks.
options.B: The view is substantially flawed because organised crime undermines state institutions, distorts economies, fuels corruption, and entrenches poverty — making it directly relevant to development goals; a purely law-enforcement response ignores structural economic drivers like lack of licit livelihood alternatives.
options.C: The view is correct because the UNDP's mandate explicitly prohibits it from engaging with any issue that overlaps with criminal jurisdiction.
options.D: The view is partially correct because organised crime only affects development in transit countries but does not impact source or destination countries' development trajectories.

questions.explanation: Transnational organised crime is increasingly recognised as a development issue: illicit financial flows deprive states of tax revenue needed for public services, criminal networks corrupt public officials and undermine rule of law (a precondition for investment), and participation in drug economies often reflects the absence of legitimate economic alternatives. The UNDP and World Bank both have active programmes linking crime reduction to development. Option A is the top distractor: while development agencies do face jurisdictional boundaries, the claim that they should categorically not engage ignores the overwhelming evidence linking organised crime to developmental stagnation.

questions.title: Media Framing and Global Events
questions.prompt: Research in international communication has shown that Western news outlets devote significantly more coverage to natural disasters in high-income countries than to equally or more deadly disasters in low-income countries. Which concept from media studies and global perspectives most precisely describes this pattern and its consequences?

options.A: Agenda-setting theory — media organisations in wealthy countries intentionally suppress news of disasters in poor countries to protect economic interests.
options.B: The news value hierarchy and proximity bias — events are deemed more newsworthy when they involve populations culturally or geographically proximate to the audience, producing differential empathy and aid mobilisation that exacerbates global inequality.
options.C: Cultural imperialism — Western media corporations own all global news infrastructure, preventing any coverage of events in the Global South.
options.D: The CNN effect — real-time media coverage of disasters compels governments to intervene, but this mechanism only activates when coverage reaches a certain threshold of hours broadcast.

questions.explanation: Johan Galtung and Mari Ruge's foundational work on news values identified proximity (geographic and cultural) as a key factor in editorial selection. This creates a systematic bias: a disaster killing 10,000 in a distant low-income country may receive less coverage than one killing 100 in a proximate high-income country, influencing public sympathy, donor response, and political pressure on governments to act. Option A incorrectly implies intentional suppression for economic motives; the pattern is better explained by structural editorial norms and audience psychology rather than deliberate conspiracy, which makes B more analytically precise.

questions.title: Trade Terms of Trade Deterioration
questions.prompt: The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis, developed in the 1950s, predicted a long-run decline in the terms of trade for commodity-exporting developing countries relative to manufactured goods importers. To what extent has subsequent evidence supported or challenged this hypothesis?

options.A: The hypothesis has been fully confirmed: commodity prices have declined in every decade since the 1950s relative to manufactured goods without exception.
options.B: The evidence is mixed: while there is a long-run downward trend in real commodity prices for many goods, commodity booms (e.g., the 2000s 'super-cycle' driven by Chinese demand) produced significant reversals, suggesting the relationship is more volatile and contingent than Prebisch and Singer assumed.
options.C: The hypothesis has been entirely disproven because developing nations have consistently diversified into manufactured exports since the 1970s, eliminating commodity dependence.
options.D: The hypothesis remains unverifiable because no international institution has collected consistent commodity price data across the relevant time period.

questions.explanation: Empirical work by economists including Cashin and McDermott (2002) and the IMF has found that while there is a secular downward trend in real commodity prices over the very long run, this trend is punctuated by highly volatile booms and busts. The 2003–2011 commodity super-cycle, driven largely by Chinese industrialisation demand, significantly improved terms of trade for many commodity exporters in Africa and Latin America — temporarily. This contingency and volatility represents a genuine complication of the original Prebisch-Singer model. Option A is the top distractor as it overstates the hypothesis by removing the nuance of cyclical reversals that the evidence clearly shows.

questions.title: Indigenous Rights and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP, 2007) includes the principle of 'free, prior and informed consent' (FPIC) for decisions affecting indigenous territories. A state government argues that FPIC grants indigenous communities an absolute veto over national development projects. Evaluate this interpretation.

options.A: The interpretation is correct; UNDRIP's FPIC provision gives indigenous communities a legally binding absolute veto under international law.
options.B: The interpretation overstates FPIC's scope: the principle requires good-faith consultation and negotiation before decisions are made, but the Declaration itself is non-binding on states, and most legal interpretations treat FPIC as a procedural right to meaningful participation rather than an unconditional veto.
options.C: The interpretation is incorrect because FPIC applies only to decisions affecting land use, not to broader development or infrastructure projects.
options.D: The interpretation is correct because UNDRIP was incorporated directly into the domestic law of all UN member states upon adoption in 2007.

questions.explanation: UNDRIP is a General Assembly Declaration and is therefore non-binding under international law (unlike a convention or treaty). Moreover, even where FPIC is incorporated into domestic law (as in some Latin American countries via ILO Convention 169), courts have consistently interpreted it as a right to genuine consultation and negotiation rather than an absolute veto — as confirmed by rulings of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. Option A is the top distractor because the word 'consent' in FPIC leads well-read students to conclude it confers a veto, missing the crucial distinction between consultation obligations and binding consent requirements.

questions.title: Gender Inequality Index Components
questions.prompt: The UNDP's Gender Inequality Index (GII) measures gender-based disadvantage across three dimensions. A student lists these as: maternal mortality ratio, female educational attainment, and female labour force participation. Evaluate the accuracy of this list.

options.A: The list is correct; these are precisely the three dimensions used to calculate the GII.
options.B: The list is partially correct but incomplete in its health dimension: the GII uses both maternal mortality ratio AND adolescent birth rate together to capture reproductive health, so the student has omitted one of the two health indicators.
options.C: The list is incorrect because the GII does not measure labour force participation; it measures wage parity between men and women in the formal sector.
options.D: The list is incorrect because educational attainment is not a GII component; it uses female literacy rates instead.

questions.explanation: The UNDP's Gender Inequality Index comprises three dimensions: (1) Reproductive health — measured by BOTH maternal mortality ratio AND adolescent birth rate; (2) Empowerment — measured by share of parliamentary seats held by women AND population with at least some secondary education; (3) Labour market — female labour force participation rate. The student's list correctly identifies the health and labour dimensions but collapses the health dimension into one indicator, omitting the adolescent birth rate. Option D is a plausible distractor because the older Gender Development Index used literacy, but the GII specifically uses secondary education attainment.

questions.title: Cosmopolitanism vs Communitarianism
questions.prompt: A philosopher argues: 'Our primary moral obligations are to all human beings equally, regardless of national borders; special obligations to co-nationals are morally arbitrary.' A communitarian responds that deep obligations to particular communities are essential to human identity and moral life. Which framework does each position represent, and what is the most powerful communitarian counter-argument to the cosmopolitan view?

options.A: The philosopher represents liberalism and the respondent represents conservatism; the strongest counter-argument is that open borders would destabilise welfare states.
options.B: The philosopher represents cosmopolitanism and the respondent represents communitarianism; the strongest counter-argument is that moral obligations are constituted by actual relationships and shared practices — we are always 'situated selves' whose identities and moral motivations are inextricably embedded in particular communities, making impartial global obligations psychologically and motivationally unrealistic.
options.C: The philosopher represents utilitarianism and the respondent represents deontology; the key dispute is whether consequences or duties should govern international aid obligations.
options.D: The philosopher represents cosmopolitanism and the respondent represents nationalism; the strongest counter-argument is that international institutions are more corrupt than national governments and therefore cannot be trusted to distribute resources fairly.

questions.explanation: The debate is classic cosmopolitanism (associated with philosophers like Peter Singer and Thomas Pogge) versus communitarianism (Michael Walzer, Alasdair MacIntyre, Michael Sandel). The communitarian 'situated self' argument holds that the cosmopolitan 'view from nowhere' is a philosophical fiction — real moral agents are embedded in particular webs of relationship that are constitutive of identity, not merely chosen. This is philosophically more powerful than the empirical objections in Options A or D. Option A mislabels the frameworks; liberal cosmopolitanism and political conservatism are separate taxonomies, and the welfare state argument, while pragmatic, does not engage the cosmopolitan argument on its moral premises.

questions.title: Rules and Who Makes Them
questions.prompt: In Town A, all adults vote to choose leaders who then make the town's rules. In Town B, one family has always made every rule and no one else gets a vote. What is the most important difference between how power is shared in these two towns?

options.A: Town A has more people, so it can make better rules than Town B
options.B: Town A shares power among citizens, while Town B concentrates power in one group
options.C: Town B's rules are stricter, which always makes a place less safe
options.D: Town A's leaders are chosen by wealth, while Town B's leaders are chosen by skill

questions.explanation: In Town A, citizens collectively choose leaders through voting, which spreads political power broadly — this is the core idea of democracy. Town B describes an oligarchy or monarchy where power stays within one family regardless of citizens' wishes. Option A is wrong because the number of people does not determine how fairly power is shared.

questions.title: Fairness and Society's Rules
questions.prompt: A student says: 'A fair society is one where everybody gets exactly the same amount of everything — same food, same house, same clothes.' Which is the strongest reason why many political thinkers disagree with this idea?

options.A: Giving everyone the same things would mean no one could ever be creative
options.B: People have different needs, so giving everyone identical things may not treat them equally well
options.C: Societies can never produce enough goods to share them the same way with everyone
options.D: Only leaders deserve more than ordinary citizens because they work harder

questions.explanation: Political thinkers like Rawls argue that true fairness means meeting people's different needs, not giving identical amounts — a wheelchair user needs a ramp, not identical shoes. Simply distributing the same things ignores real differences in circumstances. Option C is a common misconception but is not the main philosophical objection; even wealthy societies with enough resources are still debated on this issue.

questions.title: Who Owns the Shops?
questions.prompt: In Country P, the government owns all the shops and factories and decides what prices things cost. In Country Q, private people own shops and prices change depending on how many buyers and sellers there are. What do we call the economic system used in Country Q?

options.A: A planned economy
options.B: A federal economy
options.C: A market economy
options.D: A mixed economy

questions.explanation: In a market economy, private individuals own businesses and prices are set by supply and demand — how many people want something compared to how much is available. Country P describes a planned (or command) economy where the government controls production and pricing. A mixed economy (Option D) combines both government and private ownership, which does not fully describe Country Q.

questions.title: Laws That Protect Everyone
questions.prompt: A constitution is a special set of rules that even the government must follow. Why is having a constitution important for protecting ordinary people's rights?

options.A: A constitution gives the government the right to make any law it wants without question
options.B: A constitution lists rights that leaders cannot take away, limiting what the government can do to people
options.C: A constitution ensures that the richest citizens always have the most political power
options.D: A constitution means judges, not elected leaders, make all decisions for a country

questions.explanation: A constitution places limits on government power by clearly stating rights — such as freedom of speech or the right to a fair trial — that leaders cannot remove. This protects citizens even if a powerful leader wants to ignore those rights. Option A is actually the opposite of a constitution's purpose; constitutions exist specifically to restrict unlimited government power.

questions.title: Sharing Power Between Levels
questions.prompt: In a federal system of government, some decisions are made by the national government and some are made by state or regional governments. What is the main advantage of sharing power this way?

options.A: It means every region must follow exactly the same rules, making the country more unified
options.B: It allows different regions to make rules that suit their own communities while staying part of one country
options.C: It removes the need for a national government because regions can do everything themselves
options.D: It gives citizens two sets of taxes but no extra rights or services in return

questions.explanation: Federalism lets regional governments handle issues that vary locally — like local languages or farming conditions — while a national government handles shared concerns like defence. This balance respects diversity within unity. Option A describes a unitary system, not a federal one, and is a common confusion students make.

questions.title: Why People Follow Leaders
questions.prompt: Some leaders are obeyed because people respect them and believe they deserve to lead. Other leaders are obeyed only because they have soldiers and police who punish anyone who disobeys. What is the key difference between these two situations?

options.A: The first leader uses authority based on legitimacy; the second relies on force alone
options.B: The first leader is always elected; the second leader always inherits their position
options.C: The first leader rules a democracy; the second leader always rules a federal system
options.D: The first leader has more money; the second leader has more supporters

questions.explanation: When people genuinely accept a leader's right to rule, that leader has legitimacy — a concept central to political science. A leader who relies only on force lacks legitimacy and must constantly use coercion to stay in power. Option B is a misconception; elected leaders can lose legitimacy, and inherited leaders can have it — what matters is whether people accept the right to rule, not how the position was obtained.

questions.title: Goods Everyone Can Use
questions.prompt: A lighthouse warns all ships of dangerous rocks. One shipping company pays for it, but every other ship also benefits without paying. Why does this create a problem for funding the lighthouse through a market alone?

options.A: Ships travel too fast for companies to charge them as they pass the lighthouse
options.B: Companies will not pay for something if others can use it for free without contributing
options.C: The government always builds lighthouses, so companies have no reason to try
options.D: Lighthouses are too expensive for any single company to afford on its own

questions.explanation: The lighthouse is a classic example of a public good: you cannot stop non-paying ships from benefiting (non-excludable), so private companies have no incentive to pay since others 'free-ride.' This is why markets underprovide such goods. Option D might sometimes be true but misses the core economic reason — even a cheap lighthouse would face the free-rider problem.

questions.title: Revolution: Causes and Change
questions.prompt: Before a revolution, people in a country are very unhappy with how things are run. A student claims: 'Revolutions happen only when people are extremely poor and have nothing to eat.' Which piece of evidence would most challenge this claim?

options.A: Many revolutions have happened in countries where the economy was growing but political rights were still denied
options.B: Revolutions always happen in countries with large populations and limited land
options.C: The poorest countries in the world have had the most revolutions throughout history
options.D: Revolutions need outside countries to support them before they can succeed

questions.explanation: Historians note that revolutions often occur when people gain enough wealth or education to demand rights, but political systems block their participation — this is called 'rising expectations.' The American Revolution (1776) involved relatively prosperous colonists who objected to political exclusion, not starvation. Option C is a misconception; many of the poorest nations have had authoritarian stability rather than revolution.

questions.title: Checks on Government Power
questions.prompt: In Country R, the president makes laws, judges whether people have broken those laws, and controls the army. A political thinker warns this is dangerous. What is the most important reason the thinker is concerned?

options.A: One person controlling all three functions means no separate group can stop them from abusing power
options.B: Having one leader makes decision-making too slow to respond to emergencies
options.C: Countries with one leader always become poorer because competition between leaders helps the economy
options.D: The president will not have enough time to do three jobs properly and will make mistakes

questions.explanation: The idea of separating government into different branches — legislature, judiciary, and executive — exists precisely so each branch can check the others. When one person controls all three, there is no independent body to prevent abuses of power; this principle is known as the 'separation of powers.' Option D is a common but shallow answer — the deeper concern is not efficiency but unchecked authority.

questions.title: Societies and Social Groups
questions.prompt: In some societies, people are grouped into social classes or castes and cannot easily move to a different group, even if they work very hard. What does this tell us about how that society is organised?

options.A: The society values individual achievement above family background
options.B: The society's structure is fixed and does not allow much social mobility
options.C: The society relies entirely on market competition to decide who gets which jobs
options.D: The society is democratic because groups are kept separate and equal

questions.explanation: When social position is determined by birth and cannot easily be changed, sociologists describe this as low social mobility and a rigid social structure — caste systems in some societies are a historical example. Option A is the opposite of what is described; fixed group membership denies individual achievement as a path upward. Option D confuses separation with democracy, which is a genuine misconception.

questions.title: Voting and Representation
questions.prompt: Imagine a country where only landowners are allowed to vote. A student says this is a democracy because people still vote. What is the most important flaw in this argument?

options.A: Voting is never a reliable way to find out what most people want
options.B: Democracy requires that all adult citizens have an equal say, not just a privileged group
options.C: Landowners are usually the most educated citizens and therefore represent everyone fairly
options.D: A country can only be a democracy if it has more than one political party to vote for

questions.explanation: A genuine democracy rests on universal suffrage — the idea that all adult citizens have an equal right to vote and participate in government, not just a wealthy subset. Restricting voting to landowners means the majority of citizens have no say in who governs them. Option C is a classic historical argument used to justify restricted voting but actually describes an oligarchy, not a democracy.

questions.title: Government and the Economy
questions.prompt: A country has private businesses but the government also provides free schools, free hospitals, and sets a minimum wage. Which type of economic system does this describe?

options.A: A planned economy, because the government is involved in the economy
options.B: A pure market economy, because private businesses still exist
options.C: A mixed economy, because both private enterprise and government services exist together
options.D: A federal economy, because different levels of government share economic responsibilities

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private ownership and market competition with government-provided services and regulations — most modern countries, including most of Europe, operate this way. Option A is a common misconception; a planned economy means the government controls all production and pricing, not just some services. Option D confuses a political structure (federalism) with an economic system.

questions.title: Power Without Permission
questions.prompt: A leader takes control of a country without being elected and uses soldiers to stay in power. Citizens who complain are arrested. Which term best describes this kind of political system?

options.A: Federal system
options.B: Representative democracy
options.C: Authoritarian system
options.D: Constitutional monarchy

questions.explanation: An authoritarian system is one where a leader or small group holds power without the consent of citizens, uses force to silence opposition, and does not allow free political participation. It is defined by control and suppression of dissent. A constitutional monarchy (Option D) still has legal limits on the ruler's power and often includes elected parliaments, which does not match this scenario.

questions.title: Agreements Between Countries
questions.prompt: Two neighbouring countries sign a treaty promising never to dump waste in the shared river between them. Three years later, one country begins dumping waste anyway. What does this situation reveal about the nature of agreements between countries?

options.A: Treaties are pointless because countries always break them eventually
options.B: International agreements depend on countries choosing to honour them, as there is no automatic enforcement
options.C: Only rich countries are able to follow international agreements because they have better resources
options.D: The agreement failed because it was not written down in a formal enough way

questions.explanation: Unlike laws within a country enforced by police and courts, international agreements rely heavily on countries voluntarily complying, diplomatic pressure, and international bodies like the UN — none of which can automatically force a sovereign nation. This is a central tension in international law. Option A overstates the case; many treaties are respected for long periods through mutual interest and reputation.

questions.title: What Makes a Rule Fair?
questions.prompt: Philosopher John Rawls suggested imagining that you do not know which family, country, or social group you will be born into before deciding what rules a society should have. What is the purpose of this thought experiment?

options.A: To prove that people who are born rich will always make fairer rules than those who are born poor
options.B: To help people design fair rules without being biased by their own personal advantages
options.C: To show that rules should always benefit the largest number of people, no matter who gets hurt
options.D: To argue that a society with no rules at all would actually be the most equal

questions.explanation: Rawls called this the 'veil of ignorance' — by imagining you could end up in any position in society, you are motivated to create rules that are fair for everyone, including those at the bottom. This removes personal bias from rule-making. Option C describes a different theory called utilitarianism, which Rawls actually argued against because it can justify harming minorities for the majority's benefit.

questions.title: Prices and Who Decides
questions.prompt: In a market economy, the price of umbrellas goes up whenever it rains a lot, but comes down when the sun shines for weeks. A student says: 'This is unfair — someone is controlling prices to make more money in bad weather.' What is the error in this reasoning?

options.A: Umbrella prices are actually set by the government, not by sellers
options.B: In a market economy, prices change automatically because more people want umbrellas in rain but supply stays the same
options.C: Only luxury goods change in price; everyday items like umbrellas always cost the same
options.D: Sellers are not allowed to raise prices in bad weather because of consumer protection laws

questions.explanation: In a market economy, prices respond to supply and demand automatically — when demand for umbrellas rises in rainy weather but supply does not immediately increase, prices go up without anyone specifically controlling them. This is the price mechanism at work. Option A is a misconception; in a market economy, the government does not typically set prices for everyday goods.

questions.title: Citizens and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: In a democracy, citizens have both rights (things the government must protect for them) and responsibilities (things citizens must do to keep democracy working). Which pairing below correctly matches a right with a responsibility?

options.A: Right to free speech / Responsibility to only say things the government approves
options.B: Right to vote / Responsibility to pay taxes that fund public services
options.C: Right to a fair trial / Responsibility to always agree with court decisions
options.D: Right to education / Responsibility to vote for the same party as your parents

questions.explanation: In civic life, the right to vote (participating in choosing leaders) pairs naturally with the responsibility to contribute to society through taxes, which fund shared services that make democratic life possible. Option A contradicts the very meaning of free speech — a right to speak freely cannot require government approval of content.

questions.title: Groups With Global Influence
questions.prompt: The International Red Cross helps people in wars and disasters in many different countries, even though it is not a government. A student asks: 'How can a non-government group have so much influence around the world?' What is the best explanation?

options.A: Non-government organisations gain influence by having their own armies and laws
options.B: The Red Cross has influence because governments have given it special permanent voting rights at the United Nations
options.C: Organisations can gain global influence through expertise, trusted reputation, and agreements with many governments
options.D: Only organisations based in wealthy countries can have worldwide influence

questions.explanation: International NGOs like the Red Cross build influence through specialised expertise, a strong reputation for neutrality, and formal agreements (such as the Geneva Conventions) that grant them access to conflict zones. Influence in global politics does not require an army or government status. Option B is incorrect; NGOs do not have voting rights at the UN, though some have observer status.

questions.title: Natural Rights and Society
questions.prompt: John Locke believed that before governments existed, people had natural rights to life, liberty, and property. He argued people created governments to protect these rights. What should happen, according to Locke, if a government destroys those rights instead of protecting them?

options.A: Citizens should always obey the government because it is more powerful than individuals
options.B: Citizens have the right to replace that government, because it has broken its agreement with the people
options.C: Citizens should leave the country, since natural rights only apply outside of government
options.D: The government should be allowed one warning before citizens take action

questions.explanation: Locke's social contract theory holds that government power comes from the consent of the governed, and if a government violates natural rights, citizens are justified in overthrowing it — an idea that directly influenced the American Declaration of Independence (1776). Option A contradicts Locke's entire argument; he specifically rejected the idea that might makes right.

questions.title: When Markets Do Not Help Everyone
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this statement: 'In a free market, competition always makes sure every community gets the goods and services it needs, so governments never need to provide anything.'

options.A: The error is that free markets never produce competition between businesses
options.B: The error is that markets may not provide goods where profit is low or absent, leaving some communities without essential services
options.C: The error is that governments always provide better services than businesses in every situation
options.D: The error is that competition always raises prices, so no one can afford market goods

questions.explanation: Markets work well when businesses can profit, but in remote communities or for goods like street lighting or basic healthcare for the very poor, profit may be too low to attract private providers — this is a market failure. Governments often step in precisely because markets leave gaps. Option C goes too far in the opposite direction; governments are not always better providers than businesses.

questions.title: Rousseau and the Common Good
questions.prompt: Jean-Jacques Rousseau believed that when people join together in a society, they should follow the 'general will' — what is best for the whole community, not just for one person. How is this idea different from simply doing whatever the majority wants?

options.A: The general will means the majority must always win every vote without exception
options.B: The general will focuses on what truly benefits everyone in society, which may differ from what most individuals want for themselves
options.C: The general will gives leaders the right to ignore all votes and decide alone what is best
options.D: The general will is the same concept as individual freedom and personal choice

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished the 'general will' (what genuinely serves the common good) from the 'will of all' (the sum of individual self-interests). A majority might vote to benefit themselves at the expense of a minority, which Rousseau would not consider the general will. Option A is a common misconception — Rousseau warned that the majority could be wrong if driven by self-interest rather than the community's true benefit.

questions.title: Comparing Economic Systems
questions.prompt: A student compares two countries: 'Country X's government decides how many cars to build each year. Country Y's car companies build as many as people are willing to buy.' Which challenge is Country X most likely to face that Country Y is less likely to face?

options.A: Country X may produce too many or too few cars because it cannot perfectly know what people want
options.B: Country X will always produce better cars because the government has higher standards
options.C: Country Y will run out of cars quickly because private companies do not produce enough
options.D: Country Y's car companies will always charge the same fixed price regardless of demand

questions.explanation: In a planned economy, central planners must estimate demand without using price signals, often leading to overproduction of unwanted goods or shortages of goods people actually want — a well-documented challenge of Soviet-style economies. Country Y's market system uses rising and falling prices to signal producers to make more or fewer cars. Option C is the opposite of typical market outcomes; competition usually incentivises more production.

questions.title: Political Ideas Spread and Change
questions.prompt: During the 1700s and 1800s, ideas about liberty, equality, and citizens' rights spread from books and pamphlets across many countries and inspired people to demand new political systems. What does this pattern show about how political change can begin?

options.A: Political change only begins when a country becomes wealthy enough to afford new systems
options.B: Ideas and shared beliefs can motivate people to challenge existing power structures and seek change
options.C: Political change always starts with military leaders deciding to reform the army first
options.D: Only countries that share the same language are influenced by the same political ideas

questions.explanation: The Enlightenment period showed that philosophical and political ideas — like those of Locke, Rousseau, and Voltaire — spread across national and language borders and inspired revolutions in America (1776) and France (1789). Ideas themselves can be a source of political power and change. Option A is a common misconception; many revolutionary movements have involved populations that were not primarily wealthy.

questions.title: Rules for the Whole World
questions.prompt: Some rules, like the law against torturing prisoners, are said to apply to every country in the world, even countries that never signed a treaty agreeing to them. What is the best explanation for why these rules are considered binding everywhere?

options.A: The United Nations has a global army that punishes every country that breaks these rules
options.B: These rules are part of customary international law, accepted as binding because all countries have long recognised them as fundamental
options.C: Wealthy countries created these rules and force poorer countries to follow them through trade penalties
options.D: Every country secretly agreed to these rules at a meeting that was never made public

questions.explanation: Customary international law develops when states consistently behave in a certain way over time because they believe it is legally required — the prohibition on torture is considered jus cogens, a fundamental norm no country can opt out of. Option A is incorrect; the UN does not have a standing army that automatically enforces international law on all nations.

questions.title: Communities and Belonging
questions.prompt: A new student joins a school and notices that different groups of children sit separately at lunch, share different traditions, and rarely mix. A teacher says this shows how social groups form naturally. What concept from social studies best describes how these separate groups maintain their own identity?

options.A: Economic class, because the groups probably have different amounts of money
options.B: Social mobility, because children are moving between groups every day
options.C: Cultural identity, because the groups share their own customs, practices, and sense of belonging
options.D: Federal structure, because different groups are like separate regions within the school

questions.explanation: Cultural identity refers to the shared values, practices, traditions, and sense of belonging that bind a social group together and distinguish it from others. The lunch table behaviour reflects how cultural groups maintain their distinctiveness within a larger community. Option B is incorrect because social mobility refers to movement between economic classes over time, not the everyday mixing of friendship groups.

questions.title: Rules and Who Makes Them
questions.prompt: In a democracy, citizens vote for leaders who make laws. In a country run by one ruler who never holds elections, laws are made by that ruler alone. What is the most important difference between these two systems?

options.A: Democracies always make better laws than single rulers do
options.B: In a democracy, the people have a say in choosing who makes the rules
options.C: Single rulers make decisions faster, so their systems are more efficient
options.D: Democracies only exist in rich countries with strong economies

questions.explanation: The core difference is accountability — in a democracy, citizens choose their leaders through elections, giving the people power over who governs them. Option A is wrong because democracies do not automatically produce better laws; the quality of laws depends on many factors beyond the system type.

questions.title: Sharing Power Fairly
questions.prompt: A student says: 'If everyone in a country votes, then the country must be treating all its citizens fairly.' Is this claim fully correct? Why or why not?

options.A: Yes, because voting means everyone has an equal voice in every decision
options.B: Yes, because elections are the only way fairness is measured in a society
options.C: No, because voting alone does not guarantee equal rights or opportunities in daily life
options.D: No, because fairness only happens when one strong leader makes all the decisions

questions.explanation: Voting is one important tool, but fairness also requires equal access to education, healthcare, and legal protection — things that elections alone cannot guarantee. Option A is wrong because even when people vote, some groups may still face discrimination or unequal treatment in laws and services.

questions.title: Who Owns What
questions.prompt: In Country A, the government owns all the factories and shops and decides what is made and sold. In Country B, private people and companies own businesses and set their own prices. Which pair of labels correctly matches these two economic systems?

options.A: Country A = market economy; Country B = planned economy
options.B: Country A = planned economy; Country B = market economy
options.C: Country A = mixed economy; Country B = planned economy
options.D: Country A = federal economy; Country B = market economy

questions.explanation: A planned economy is one where the government controls production and prices, as in Country A; a market economy lets private owners and competition determine what is made and sold, as in Country B. Option A reverses the labels, which is a common mix-up because students sometimes confuse who 'plans' things.

questions.title: Government Helping Markets
questions.prompt: A small town has only one hospital and it charges very high prices because there is no competition. The government steps in and sets a maximum price the hospital can charge. What kind of problem is the government trying to fix?

options.A: A revolution caused by unfair leadership
options.B: A federal disagreement between local and national governments
options.C: A market failure caused by a monopoly with too much power
options.D: A social structure problem caused by people not working hard enough

questions.explanation: When one provider has no competition, it can charge whatever it likes — this is called a monopoly, and it is a type of market failure where the market does not produce a fair outcome on its own. Option B is wrong because the problem is not about which level of government has authority; it is about the hospital's unchecked pricing power.

questions.title: Power and Authority
questions.prompt: A new school principal makes rules that the students feel are unfair. The students ask why they must follow someone they did not choose. What concept best explains why people are expected to follow the principal's rules even without voting for her?

options.A: Authority, because the principal holds a recognised role with the right to make rules
options.B: Democracy, because a principal is always chosen by a vote of the community
options.C: Revolution, because unfair rules always lead to people taking over
options.D: Federalism, because schools share power between teachers and students

questions.explanation: Authority refers to the recognised right to give orders and make rules within a role — principals have this because their position is formally established by the school system. Option B is wrong because principals are typically appointed by school boards, not elected by students, yet their authority is still considered legitimate.

questions.title: Rules That Protect Everyone
questions.prompt: A country writes a set of rules that even the president must follow, and no new law can go against these rules without a special process. What is this special set of rules called, and why is it important?

options.A: A budget, because it controls how the government spends money on everyone equally
options.B: A constitution, because it limits government power and protects citizens' basic rights
options.C: A treaty, because it makes agreements with other countries about shared rules
options.D: A census, because it counts the population to make sure laws apply to everyone

questions.explanation: A constitution is the highest law of a country — it sets out the rules that even the government must obey and protects citizens from the abuse of power. Option C is wrong because a treaty is an agreement between different countries, not an internal set of rules that limits a government's own power.

questions.title: Locke's Big Idea
questions.prompt: The philosopher John Locke believed that governments get their power from the people they govern. What did Locke say citizens should do if a government takes away their basic rights instead of protecting them?

options.A: Accept the situation because rulers always know what is best for everyone
options.B: Move to another country where the rules are different
options.C: Have the right to replace that government with a better one
options.D: Ask the United Nations to send its army to help them

questions.explanation: Locke argued that if a government breaks its duty to protect life, liberty, and property, citizens have the right — and even the responsibility — to remove and replace it. Option A directly contradicts Locke's view, which is that rulers do not have unlimited power and must earn the trust of the governed.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Jean-Jacques Rousseau believed that when people live together in a society, they must sometimes give up some personal wishes for the good of everyone. A student says: 'Rousseau thought people should always do exactly what they personally want.' Identify the error in this statement.

options.A: The error is that Rousseau thought only kings should decide what is good for everyone
options.B: The error is that Rousseau believed the common good of all people should sometimes come before personal wants
options.C: The error is that Rousseau lived before societies existed, so he had no opinion on this topic
options.D: The error is that Rousseau agreed with Locke on every point about how societies should work

questions.explanation: Rousseau's concept of the 'general will' holds that citizens must sometimes set aside personal desires to act in ways that benefit the whole community. Option A is wrong because Rousseau strongly opposed monarchy and believed power should come from the collective will of the people, not a king.

questions.title: Fairness Behind a Veil
questions.prompt: Philosopher John Rawls asked people to imagine designing society's rules without knowing whether they would be born rich or poor, healthy or sick. He called this the 'veil of ignorance.' Why did he use this thought experiment?

options.A: To show that rich people always make better rules than poor people do
options.B: To prove that no society can ever be truly fair under any circumstances
options.C: To help people design rules that are fair to everyone, since they could end up in any position
options.D: To argue that all people should earn exactly the same amount of money

questions.explanation: Rawls used the veil of ignorance to ensure fairness — if you do not know your place in society, you will choose rules that protect even the worst-off members, since you might be one of them. Option D is a misconception; Rawls did not argue for equal pay but rather for rules that benefit the least advantaged members of society.

questions.title: What Is a Social Contract
questions.prompt: When people form a government, philosophers say they make a kind of agreement called a 'social contract.' What does each side agree to in this contract?

options.A: Citizens agree to pay taxes, and the government agrees to spend all the money on roads
options.B: Citizens give up some freedoms, and the government agrees to protect their remaining rights
options.C: Citizens agree to obey every law forever, and the government agrees to never change any rules
options.D: Citizens agree to fight in wars, and the government agrees to give land in return

questions.explanation: The social contract idea, developed by philosophers like Locke and Rousseau, says citizens surrender some individual freedoms in exchange for the government's protection of their rights and safety. Option A is wrong because while taxes are part of civic life, they are not the defining exchange in the social contract — the core trade is freedom for protection of rights.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Balance
questions.prompt: Country Z has private businesses that compete with each other, but the government also runs public schools and provides free healthcare. What type of economic system does Country Z have, and why?

options.A: A planned economy, because the government controls healthcare and schools
options.B: A federal economy, because power is shared between the government and private businesses
options.C: A mixed economy, because it combines private businesses with government-provided services
options.D: A market economy, because private businesses are allowed to compete freely

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines elements of both market and planned systems — private businesses exist alongside government services like schools and hospitals. Option A is wrong because in a fully planned economy the government controls all production, not just certain services; Country Z still allows private competition.

questions.title: Why Revolutions Happen
questions.prompt: For many years, the farmers in a kingdom paid heavy taxes but had no voice in making laws. When a drought ruined their crops and the king still demanded full payment, the farmers rose up in rebellion. Which two conditions best explain why this revolution happened?

options.A: The farmers were uneducated and did not understand the importance of paying taxes
options.B: Long-term exclusion from power combined with a sudden crisis that made conditions unbearable
options.C: The king was foreign-born and therefore did not have the right to collect any taxes
options.D: The farmers were influenced by philosophers who told them to rebel against all rules

questions.explanation: Revolutions often occur when a group is systematically excluded from power over time and then a sudden crisis — like a famine — pushes them past the point of tolerance; this pattern matches what historians observe in events like the French Revolution. Option D is a distractor because while ideas can influence revolutions, it was the combination of structural inequality and immediate crisis, not philosophers alone, that drove this rebellion.

questions.title: Local and National Power
questions.prompt: In a federal system, some decisions are made by the national government and others are made by regional governments. A student claims: 'Federalism means the national government always has the final say on every single issue.' What is wrong with this claim?

options.A: Nothing is wrong — the national government in a federal system does control everything
options.B: The error is that in federalism, regional governments have their own areas of authority that the national government cannot override
options.C: The error is that federalism means there is no national government at all — only local ones
options.D: The error is that federal systems always give all power to citizens directly through referendums

questions.explanation: Federalism deliberately divides power between national and regional governments, and regional governments have recognised authority over certain policy areas — education and local taxation, for example — that the national government cannot simply overrule. Option C is wrong because federalism still includes a national government; it just shares power rather than concentrating it all centrally.

questions.title: Class and Opportunity
questions.prompt: Two children are born in the same city. One is born into a wealthy family with access to excellent schools, doctors, and networks. The other is born into a poor family with limited access to all three. A student says: 'Both children have equal opportunity because they live in the same country.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because laws treat all citizens the same regardless of wealth
options.B: The claim is correct because opportunity only depends on personal effort and attitude
options.C: The claim is incorrect because social structures like wealth and access to resources create unequal starting points
options.D: The claim is incorrect because children in the same city always attend the same schools

questions.explanation: Social structures — including wealth, family connections, and access to quality education — create very different starting points for children even within the same country, meaning formal legal equality does not equal real equality of opportunity. Option A is a common misconception; having the same legal rights does not remove the practical advantages that come from being born into a wealthy family.

questions.title: Authoritarian Control Methods
questions.prompt: A government bans all political parties except its own and controls all information on television and the internet. Which concept from political science best describes this type of rule, and what is its main goal?

options.A: Federalism — to share power more efficiently across the country
options.B: Authoritarianism — to prevent opposition and maintain the ruling group's total control
options.C: Democracy — to ensure the most popular ideas reach the largest number of citizens
options.D: Constitutionalism — to protect citizens from laws that violate their rights

questions.explanation: Authoritarianism involves concentrating power in a small group that suppresses opposition through censorship, banning rival parties, and controlling information — all aimed at staying in power. Option C is wrong because democracy requires free speech and political competition, which are the exact opposite of what this government is doing.

questions.title: What Governments Provide
questions.prompt: Street lighting makes a road safer for everyone, and it is impossible to stop one person from benefiting just because they did not pay for it. Why would a private company be unlikely to provide street lighting without government help?

options.A: Because private companies are not allowed to build anything on public roads
options.B: Because street lighting uses too much electricity for any company to afford
options.C: Because the company cannot stop non-payers from using the light, so it cannot earn enough profit
options.D: Because governments always do a better job of providing services than private companies do

questions.explanation: Street lighting is a public good — it is non-excludable (you cannot stop people from using it) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce it for others), which means companies cannot charge users and so cannot make a profit. Option D is wrong because the reason is not about which provider is better but about the economic impossibility of making a profit from something everyone can use for free.

questions.title: How Societies Change
questions.prompt: For centuries, women in many countries were not allowed to vote, own property, or go to university. Over time, laws changed and these rights were won through campaigning and protest. What does this tell us about the nature of social structures?

options.A: Social structures are permanent and cannot be changed by ordinary people
options.B: Social structures are created by people and can be changed through collective action over time
options.C: Social structures only change when a foreign country forces a government to reform
options.D: Social structures always improve automatically as countries become wealthier

questions.explanation: The history of women's rights shows that social structures — though often felt as fixed — are human-made systems that can be challenged and transformed through organised effort and persistent advocacy. Option A is a common but incorrect belief; it reflects how stable social structures feel, but history clearly shows they can and do change.

questions.title: International Agreements
questions.prompt: Two countries sign an agreement promising to protect the natural river that flows between them. Three years later, one country breaks the agreement by dumping waste in the river. What does this situation reveal about international law?

options.A: International law is completely useless because countries never follow any agreements
options.B: International law works perfectly because all countries always respect what they sign
options.C: International law can be difficult to enforce because there is no single world authority with the power to punish countries
options.D: International law only applies to wealthy countries that can afford to follow the rules

questions.explanation: International law lacks a single enforcing body like a world police force, so when a country breaks an agreement, consequences depend on diplomatic pressure, sanctions, or international courts — which are not always effective. Option A overstates the case; many international agreements are successfully followed, and international law shapes global behaviour even without perfect enforcement.

questions.title: Protecting Minority Rights
questions.prompt: In a democracy, decisions are made by majority vote. A student argues: 'Whatever the majority wants must always be right and fair because most people agree.' Identify the most important flaw in this argument.

options.A: The flaw is that the majority is usually wrong about most things it votes on
options.B: The flaw is that majorities can vote to take away the rights of smaller groups, which would be unfair even if popular
options.C: The flaw is that voting is never an accurate way to find out what most people think
options.D: The flaw is that fairness is only determined by expert leaders, not ordinary citizens

questions.explanation: Even in democracies, majority decisions can be unjust if they harm minority groups — which is why constitutional protections for minority rights exist to limit what majorities can do. Option A is wrong because it does not identify the real problem; the issue is not that majorities are usually wrong, but that popularity does not automatically equal fairness.

questions.title: Why Citizens Obey Laws
questions.prompt: People follow traffic lights even when no police officer is watching. A student wonders: 'If no one is checking, why do people still stop at red lights?' Which concept best explains this behaviour?

options.A: Authoritarianism, because the government forces everyone to obey all rules at all times
options.B: Legitimacy, because people accept that the rules are fair and benefit everyone including themselves
options.C: Federalism, because traffic rules are shared between local and national governments
options.D: Revolution, because people who do not obey laws are immediately replaced by new citizens

questions.explanation: Legitimacy refers to the widely shared belief that a rule or government is rightfully in place — when people believe a law is fair and useful, they follow it voluntarily without needing constant enforcement. Option A is wrong because authoritarianism relies on fear and force, not voluntary compliance; people stopping at red lights are not afraid of a ruler.

questions.title: Comparing Governance Systems
questions.prompt: Country A has one central government that makes all the laws. Country B has a national government plus state governments that make some of their own laws. What would happen in Country B if a state passed a law that the national government considered unconstitutional?

options.A: Nothing, because states in a federal system can never be challenged by the national government
options.B: The national government would likely have the power to override or strike down that law through courts
options.C: The state would automatically become an independent country with its own currency
options.D: All citizens of that state would lose their right to vote in national elections

questions.explanation: In federal systems like the United States, a supreme court or constitutional court can strike down state laws that conflict with the national constitution — this is a key check on state power. Option A is wrong because federal systems do not give states unlimited authority; the national constitution is still the supreme law.

questions.title: Propaganda and Information
questions.prompt: A government produces posters, songs, and films that always show its leaders as perfect heroes and never mention any problems in the country. What strategy is this government using, and what is its purpose?

options.A: Federalism — to share the government's successes with regional governments
options.B: Propaganda — to shape how people think by controlling the information they receive
options.C: Democracy — to keep citizens informed about the government's good work
options.D: International law — to show other countries that the government follows global standards

questions.explanation: Propaganda is the use of biased or one-sided information — through media, art, and symbols — to influence public opinion and maintain support for those in power. Option C is wrong because democracy requires honest and balanced information; presenting only a perfect image of leaders without any criticism is the opposite of a free press.

questions.title: Economic Decisions and Scarcity
questions.prompt: A town has enough money to build either a new hospital or a new sports stadium, but not both. The government must choose. What fundamental economic problem does this situation illustrate?

options.A: Market failure, because private companies refused to build either structure
options.B: Authoritarianism, because only the government is allowed to make building decisions
options.C: Scarcity, because limited resources mean not every need and want can be met at the same time
options.D: Federalism, because the town cannot spend money without permission from the national government

questions.explanation: Scarcity is the basic economic problem that resources — money, land, materials — are limited while human wants are unlimited, forcing societies and governments to make choices about priorities. Option A is wrong because this is not a market failure situation; the problem is not that markets are not working, but that there simply is not enough money to do everything at once.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: A student says: 'In a good society, I should have all my rights but no responsibilities to anyone else.' Using what you know about how societies work, explain what is wrong with this view.

options.A: Nothing is wrong — rights are more important than responsibilities in any society
options.B: The error is that rights and responsibilities are connected — a society only works when members both claim rights and accept duties toward others
options.C: The error is that only governments have rights, while citizens only have responsibilities
options.D: The error is that responsibilities are only required of adults, not of students or young people

questions.explanation: Rights and responsibilities are two sides of the same civic coin — for rights like safety, education, and fair treatment to exist for everyone, members of society must also accept duties such as paying taxes, following laws, and respecting others. Option A is wrong because a society where everyone demands rights but no one accepts responsibilities would quickly break down — this is a key idea in social contract theory.

questions.title: Comparing Economic Systems
questions.prompt: What would happen if a country switched from a planned economy to a market economy? Which change would most likely occur first?

options.A: The country would immediately become a democracy because free markets always lead to free elections
options.B: Private businesses and competition would begin to determine prices instead of the government
options.C: All citizens would instantly become wealthier because free markets always create equal wealth
options.D: The national government would gain more power because businesses need strong central control to survive

questions.explanation: The defining shift when moving from a planned to a market economy is that price-setting and production decisions move from government control to private competition — as happened in many Eastern European countries after 1989. Option A is a common misconception; while free markets and democracy can coexist, switching to a market economy does not automatically produce democratic elections.

questions.title: Democracy and Majority Rule
questions.prompt: In a democracy, the majority votes to remove the rights of a small minority group. A student says: 'This is fair because democracy means the majority decides everything.' What is the most important flaw in this thinking?

options.A: Democracies only allow adults to vote, so children are already excluded from decisions
options.B: Democracy includes protections for minority rights that limit what majorities can decide
options.C: The majority is usually wrong, so expert leaders should make decisions instead
options.D: Voting is only fair when every citizen agrees with the final result

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracies include bills of rights or charters precisely to protect minorities from majority overreach — majorities cannot legally vote away fundamental rights. Option A is true but irrelevant to the flaw in the argument, which is about the limits of majority power, not who is allowed to vote.

questions.title: Rousseau and General Will
questions.prompt: Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that citizens should follow the 'general will' even if it goes against what they personally want. Which statement best explains what Rousseau meant by the 'general will'?

options.A: The wishes of the most powerful group in society
options.B: Whatever the elected government decides to do
options.C: The shared interest of the whole community, not just individual desires
options.D: The combined total of every individual person's personal wishes

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished the 'general will' — what is genuinely good for the whole community — from the 'will of all,' which is simply the sum of private wishes. Option D describes the 'will of all,' which Rousseau explicitly said was different from and less important than the general will.

questions.title: Federalism and Power Sharing
questions.prompt: In a federal system, both national and regional governments have their own powers granted by the constitution. A student claims: 'In a federation, the national government can always overrule any regional law it dislikes.' Identify the error in this claim.

options.A: Regional governments actually have more power than national governments in all federations
options.B: The constitution in a federation protects certain regional powers from national interference
options.C: National governments in federations are not allowed to make any laws at all
options.D: Federations always require every citizen to vote before a law can be overruled

questions.explanation: A defining feature of federalism is that the constitution divides powers between levels of government, and neither level can simply eliminate the other's constitutionally guaranteed powers. Option A is wrong because federations vary — in some, national power is stronger, but the key point is constitutional protection of regional powers, not that regional governments are always stronger.

questions.title: Market Economy and Prices
