questions.prompt: In a free-market economy, the price of an item rises sharply after a flood destroys most of the supply. Which mechanism is responsible for this price change, and what signal does it send to producers?

options.A: Government regulation raises the price to protect consumers; producers are told to stop making the item
options.B: Supply and demand: lower supply with unchanged demand raises prices, signalling producers to make more
options.C: Supply and demand: higher supply with unchanged demand raises prices, signalling producers to make less
options.D: Central planning sets a higher price to share the item fairly among all citizens

questions.explanation: When a flood destroys supply, less of the good is available but buyers still want it, so competition among buyers pushes prices up; this higher price acts as a signal that more profit is possible, encouraging producers to increase output. Option C reverses the relationship — a flood reduces supply, it does not increase it.

questions.title: Authority and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A new leader takes power after winning a free and fair election. A second leader takes power after being appointed by a religious council that claims divine approval. What do these two leaders share, even though their authority comes from different sources?

options.A: Both use force as their primary method of keeping power
options.B: Both have legitimacy — people accept their right to rule, even if for different reasons
options.C: Both are accountable to the same international organisation
options.D: Both gained power through democratic processes recognised by citizens

questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the belief among the governed that a ruler has the right to hold power; it can come from elections, tradition, religion, or other sources — what matters is that people accept the authority. Option D is wrong because only the elected leader used a democratic process; the religious council's appointment is a different form of legitimacy, not a democratic one.

questions.title: Social Contract Origins
questions.prompt: Both Locke and Rousseau imagined a 'state of nature' before governments existed, but they described it very differently. Which statement correctly contrasts their views of the state of nature?

options.A: Locke saw it as peaceful and governed by natural law, while Rousseau saw early humans as selfish and dangerous
options.B: Locke saw it as a war of all against all, while Rousseau saw early humans as naturally free and good
options.C: Locke saw it as peaceful and governed by natural law, while Rousseau saw early humans as naturally free and good
options.D: Both saw the state of nature as violent and used this to justify strong government control

questions.explanation: Locke believed the state of nature was largely peaceful, governed by a natural moral law giving people rights to life, liberty, and property. Rousseau believed early humans were naturally good, innocent, and free — it was society and private property that corrupted them. Option B confuses Locke with Thomas Hobbes, who described the state of nature as 'war of all against all.'

questions.title: Planned Economy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A student evaluates a centrally planned economy and says: 'The biggest advantage is that the government can direct all resources toward national goals quickly.' What is the most significant trade-off this advantage creates?

options.A: The government earns too much profit and must give it all back to citizens
options.B: Individual choice and economic freedom are reduced because planners decide what is produced
options.C: Prices rise uncontrollably because there is no government oversight of markets
options.D: Foreign countries refuse to trade with planned economies, causing isolation

questions.explanation: Central planning allows rapid resource mobilisation for priority goals, but this requires planners to override individual preferences about what to buy, produce, or work on, significantly reducing personal economic freedom. Option D may sometimes occur for political reasons but is not a structural trade-off inherent to planned economies — the USSR traded internationally despite central planning.

questions.title: Rawls and Fair Inequality
questions.prompt: Rawls argued that people designing society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' would choose rules that help the least well-off members. Which economic arrangement would Rawls most likely reject as unjust?

options.A: A surgeon earns more than a cleaner, and some of the extra income funds healthcare for the poorest citizens
options.B: A society where everyone earns exactly the same wage regardless of their role or effort
options.C: Wealthy families pass enormous fortunes to children, leaving the poorest with no improvement in their situation
options.D: A government uses taxes from high earners to build schools in the poorest neighbourhoods

questions.explanation: Rawls's difference principle permits inequality only when it benefits the least advantaged group; inherited wealth that gives no benefit to the poorest fails this test. Option A would satisfy Rawls because the surgeon's higher pay funds benefits for the least well-off, which is exactly the condition his difference principle requires.

questions.title: Revolution and Social Change
questions.prompt: Historians note that many successful revolutions happen not when people are at their most oppressed, but when conditions have recently improved and then suddenly worsened again. Which concept best explains this pattern?

options.A: Relative deprivation — the gap between what people expect and what they actually have grows sharply
options.B: Absolute poverty — people revolt only when they have nothing left to lose
options.C: Elite fragmentation — the ruling class splits apart and loses control of the military
options.D: Social mobility — improving conditions allow more people to join the middle class and demand change

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation theory explains that revolution is triggered when rising expectations are suddenly frustrated — people feel more deprived compared to what they now expect, not just compared to an absolute level of suffering. Option B (absolute poverty) predicts revolution at the lowest point of suffering, which contradicts the pattern described where recent improvement precedes the crisis.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Government Role
questions.prompt: Country K has a mixed economy. The government provides public schools and hospitals, regulates food safety, and also allows private businesses to compete freely in most markets. A critic says this is contradictory. Which response best defends the logic of a mixed economy?

options.A: A mixed economy is contradictory and should choose either full government control or full private markets
options.B: Government provides goods and services where markets fail, while markets handle goods they supply efficiently
options.C: Government involvement always improves outcomes, so more intervention is always better in a mixed economy
options.D: Private businesses in a mixed economy are not truly free because the government sets all their prices

questions.explanation: Mixed economies are built on the idea that markets work well for many goods but fail in areas like public health and education where profit motives lead to underprovision or inequality, so government fills those gaps. Option C is wrong because mixed economies are defined by recognising that government intervention is not always better — the blend exists precisely because neither pure system is ideal in every situation.

questions.title: Power and Authoritarian Control
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government allows citizens to vote in elections, but only one party is ever permitted to stand as a candidate. A student argues: 'This country is democratic because it holds elections.' What is the strongest counterargument?

options.A: Elections are not necessary for democracy — a wise leader can make decisions without them
options.B: Democracy requires genuine competition among candidates so citizens have a real choice about who governs them
options.C: The country is democratic as long as all adult citizens are allowed to cast a vote
options.D: Elections are only legitimate when observed by international monitors from other countries

questions.explanation: Free and fair elections require meaningful competition; if only one party can stand, citizens have no real choice, making the election a performance of legitimacy rather than genuine democratic participation. Option C is incorrect because universal suffrage alone does not create democracy — North Korea, for example, holds elections in which nearly all citizens vote, yet it is not considered democratic.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Country P gives its parliament the power to make laws, its president the power to carry out laws, and its courts the power to decide whether laws follow the constitution. Why is this arrangement considered important for protecting citizens' freedom?

options.A: It makes government faster because three groups can each work on different problems at the same time
options.B: It prevents any single person or group from gaining enough power to abuse citizens' rights without being checked
options.C: It ensures that only trained experts make decisions, reducing mistakes in government
options.D: It allows citizens to appeal to whichever branch they prefer when they disagree with a decision

questions.explanation: The separation of powers, developed by thinkers like Montesquieu, is designed so that each branch limits the others — this system of 'checks and balances' prevents the concentration of power that historically has led to tyranny. Option A describes an efficiency argument, but the separation of powers actually slows government down by design, making abuse of power harder rather than making governance faster.

questions.title: Externalities and Market Failure
questions.prompt: A factory produces cheap steel but releases smoke that causes respiratory illness in nearby communities. The factory does not pay for the health costs it creates. Which economic concept describes the health costs borne by the community, and what does it suggest government should do?

options.A: A positive externality; government should subsidise the factory to produce even more steel
options.B: A negative externality; government should make the factory pay for or reduce the harm it causes others
options.C: A public good problem; government should take over the factory and run it as a public service
options.D: A monopoly problem; government should break up the factory so more companies compete

questions.explanation: Pollution that harms third parties who did not agree to bear the cost is a classic negative externality — the factory's true social cost is higher than its private cost, which is a market failure that governments address through taxes, regulations, or pollution limits. Option A confuses negative and positive externalities; a positive externality benefits third parties, while pollution harms them.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that governments are created to protect three natural rights. A student lists them as 'life, liberty, and happiness.' Identify the error and explain why it matters for Locke's overall theory.

options.A: The error is 'liberty' — Locke believed only life and property were natural rights, not freedom
options.B: The error is 'happiness' — Locke said 'property,' which matters because protecting ownership is a core purpose of government for him
options.C: There is no error — Locke and Jefferson used exactly the same list of three rights in their writings
options.D: The error is 'life' — Locke only protected liberty and property as natural rights, not the right to life

questions.explanation: Locke's three natural rights were life, liberty, and property; Thomas Jefferson changed 'property' to 'pursuit of happiness' in the US Declaration of Independence. This distinction matters because for Locke, government's primary duty was to protect private property, making property rights central to his justification for overthrowing unjust rulers.

questions.title: Comparing Governance Systems
questions.prompt: Country A elects a president directly by citizens and a parliament separately, so each has its own democratic mandate. Country B elects only parliament, and parliament then chooses the prime minister. What is a key difference in how power is structured between these two systems?

options.A: Country A is more authoritarian because one person has direct power, while Country B is always more democratic
options.B: Country A separates executive and legislative power, while Country B fuses them since the government depends on parliamentary confidence
options.C: Country B has weaker government because the prime minister was not directly elected by citizens
options.D: Country A and Country B are structurally identical because both systems ultimately trace power back to voters

questions.explanation: Country A describes a presidential system with separated powers, while Country B describes a parliamentary system where the executive is fused with the legislature through confidence requirements. Option D is misleading — while both trace power to voters, the structural difference between separated and fused powers has major consequences for how laws are passed and how governments fall.

questions.title: Social Structures and Class
questions.prompt: In medieval Europe, a person born into a peasant family was almost always a peasant their entire life, regardless of talent or effort. Which feature of that society most directly caused this pattern?

options.A: Peasants lacked the intelligence needed to rise to higher social positions
options.B: A rigid social hierarchy where birth determined status and social mobility was extremely limited
options.C: A free market economy that rewarded only those who could trade successfully
options.D: Democratic laws that restricted which jobs each social class was permitted to perform

questions.explanation: Medieval European feudalism was a rigid hierarchy based on birth — nobles, clergy, and peasants had fixed roles with almost no mechanism for moving between classes, a near-complete absence of social mobility. Option C is incorrect because medieval economies were not free markets; they were organised around feudal obligations, land ownership, and guilds, not open market competition.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council can authorise international action against countries that break international law, but any one of five permanent members can veto that decision. How does this structure affect the effectiveness of international law?

options.A: It makes international law stronger because five powerful countries must all approve any action, ensuring broad support
options.B: It weakens enforcement because a powerful rule-breaking country can block action against itself or its allies
options.C: It makes international law irrelevant because the Security Council has never successfully stopped any conflict
options.D: It has no effect because international courts can enforce law independently without Security Council approval

questions.explanation: The veto power means that if a permanent member (USA, Russia, China, UK, or France) breaks international law, or protects an ally who does, they can simply veto any Security Council resolution authorising a response, creating a significant enforcement gap. Option A misunderstands the veto — it does not require all five to approve; any single one can block action, which is a structural weakness, not a strength.

questions.title: Weber's Types of Authority
questions.prompt: A student learns about Max Weber's three types of authority: traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal. A beloved sports star becomes president of a country based entirely on their personal fame and the devotion of their fans. Which type of authority does this best represent?

options.A: Traditional authority, because the sports star follows long-established customs of leadership
options.B: Rational-legal authority, because the star won through a legally organised election process
options.C: Charismatic authority, because followers are devoted to the leader's exceptional personal qualities
options.D: Democratic authority, because citizens freely chose this leader through popular vote

questions.explanation: Weber defined charismatic authority as power based on followers' belief in a leader's extraordinary personal qualities — a sports celebrity president fits this category because support comes from personal devotion rather than tradition or legal rules. Option B is the strongest distractor: the election gives a legal process, but the source of authority is the personal charisma and fame, not the rules themselves.

questions.title: Free Trade and Protectionism
questions.prompt: Country M adds a large tax on all imported shoes to protect its own shoe factories from foreign competition. Domestic shoe prices rise. Evaluate: who benefits and who is harmed by this policy within Country M?

options.A: Domestic shoe workers benefit from protected jobs; domestic consumers are harmed by higher prices
options.B: Domestic consumers benefit from cheaper shoes; foreign shoe factories are harmed by lost sales
options.C: Domestic shoe workers are harmed because foreign competition increases; government loses tax revenue
options.D: Both domestic workers and consumers benefit, making protectionism always the best economic choice

questions.explanation: Import taxes (tariffs) protect domestic industries by making foreign goods more expensive, keeping domestic factories competitive and preserving jobs — but consumers pay more for shoes than they would in a free market. Option B reverses the consumer outcome: tariffs raise prices for domestic consumers, they do not lower them.

questions.title: Constitutional Rights and Limits
questions.prompt: A country's constitution guarantees freedom of speech. A new law bans citizens from publicly sharing instructions for making weapons. A citizen argues the law violates their constitutional right to free speech. Which reasoning best evaluates this dispute?

options.A: Constitutional rights are absolute and can never be limited under any circumstances by any government
options.B: The law is clearly unconstitutional because the constitution protects all speech without any exceptions
options.C: Most constitutional rights permit some limits when speech directly threatens public safety, so courts must weigh both claims
options.D: The citizen is wrong because freedom of speech only protects opinions, and instructions are not a form of opinion

questions.explanation: In constitutional democracies, courts regularly determine whether laws limiting rights are proportionate and justified — most legal traditions accept that safety-threatening speech can be restricted, but courts must balance the right against the harm. Option A is wrong because virtually all constitutional systems — including those with strong free speech protections like the US — recognise some limits on speech that presents clear and immediate danger.

questions.title: Propaganda and Political Power
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government teaches children from an early age that the ruling leader is wise and chosen by destiny, that all historical problems were caused by a named enemy group, and that questioning the government is unpatriotic. Which concept from political science best describes this strategy?

options.A: Socialisation through propaganda to shape citizens' beliefs and make the regime seem natural and legitimate
options.B: Democratic education to prepare citizens to make informed choices about their government
options.C: Federalism, distributing political education across different regions to suit local cultures
options.D: Market competition, where different political ideas compete for citizens' attention and belief

questions.explanation: Authoritarian governments use political socialisation through propaganda — especially targeting children in schools — to build loyalty, discredit opposition, and make the regime appear inevitable and just, reducing the likelihood of resistance. Option B is wrong because democratic education aims to develop critical thinking and informed citizenship, the opposite of the one-sided indoctrination described.

questions.title: Citizenship and Civic Duty
questions.prompt: Country Q makes voting in elections compulsory — citizens who do not vote must pay a fine. Critics say this violates freedom. Supporters say it strengthens democracy. Which argument best defends compulsory voting from a democratic theory perspective?

options.A: Compulsory voting ensures all citizens exercise a civic responsibility, producing governments that truly reflect the whole population's views
options.B: Compulsory voting is justified because citizens who do not vote clearly do not deserve to benefit from government services
options.C: Compulsory voting is wrong in all cases because it forces an action on citizens, which is always a form of oppression
options.D: Compulsory voting improves election quality because forced voters always research candidates more carefully than voluntary voters

questions.explanation: The democratic case for compulsory voting is that when only motivated minorities vote, election results reflect those groups' preferences rather than the whole society — compulsion corrects this by including all voices. Option D is factually unsupported and logically weak; compelled voters do not necessarily research more carefully, and this is not the standard democratic argument for the policy.

questions.title: Power of Non-State Actors
questions.prompt: A global environmental NGO campaigns to change the fishing rules of dozens of countries by providing research to governments, funding legal cases, and organising international public pressure. A student says: 'Real power in global politics belongs only to national governments.' What does this example reveal about that claim?

options.A: The claim is correct — the NGO only has influence because national governments have chosen to let it participate
options.B: The claim is too simple — non-state actors like NGOs can shape international policy through information, legal tools, and public opinion even without formal government power
options.C: The claim is wrong because NGOs have replaced national governments as the main decision-makers in global environmental policy
options.D: The claim is correct because the NGO's activities will ultimately fail without the backing of a powerful national military

questions.explanation: Non-state actors like NGOs exercise 'soft power' — influence through information, advocacy, and norm-setting — and have successfully changed international agreements without holding formal governmental authority. Option C overcorrects: NGOs have genuine influence but have not replaced states as primary actors; they work alongside and through state structures, not instead of them.

questions.title: Justice and Income Redistribution
questions.prompt: Country J collects high taxes from wealthy citizens and uses the money to provide free healthcare, housing support, and education for the poorest families. A wealthy citizen argues this is unfair because they earned their money through their own effort. Which philosophical response best challenges this argument?

options.A: Wealthy people did not really work hard — their success was entirely due to luck, so they owe everything to society
options.B: Individual success depends partly on social conditions — education, infrastructure, rule of law — that everyone contributes to and benefits from
options.C: Taxation is always wrong because governments have no right to take money that individuals earned legally
options.D: The wealthy citizen is correct because a truly just society would reward effort and never redistribute earnings

questions.explanation: Philosophers like Rawls and communitarian thinkers argue that individual success is built on shared social foundations — schools, laws, roads, security — and that redistributive taxation reflects the community's contribution to each person's success. Option A is an overstatement that weakens the argument; acknowledging that effort matters while still justifying redistribution through shared social foundations is a stronger philosophical position.

questions.title: Human Rights Universality Debate
questions.prompt: Some governments argue that human rights as defined by international declarations reflect Western values and should not be imposed on societies with different cultural traditions. A student evaluates this claim. Which response best identifies its strongest weakness?

options.A: The claim is wrong because Western countries wrote all international human rights documents entirely on their own
options.B: The claim can be used to justify serious harm to individuals within a society by making cultural tradition a shield against accountability
options.C: The claim is correct because every society should be free to define rights however its ruling government decides
options.D: The claim is right because human rights only apply in countries that have signed international treaties

questions.explanation: The key weakness in cultural relativist arguments about rights is that they can be exploited by governments to avoid accountability for abuses — the argument that 'our culture permits this' can shield torture, discrimination, or political oppression from international scrutiny. Option A is factually incorrect and weakens the counter-argument; the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights was drafted by a committee including representatives from China, Lebanon, Chile, and other non-Western nations.

questions.title: Democracy vs. Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A country holds elections every four years, but only one political party is allowed to put forward candidates. Citizens may vote, but they cannot vote for anyone outside that party. A student says this country is a democracy because it holds elections. What is the most important reason the student is wrong?

options.A: Democracy requires that elections happen more than once a year
options.B: Democracy requires that citizens can choose between competing candidates or parties
options.C: Democracy requires that every citizen must vote or face a penalty
options.D: Democracy requires that the winning leader must be approved by a foreign government

questions.explanation: A key feature of democracy is political competition — voters must have a genuine choice between different candidates or parties, otherwise the election does not reflect the people's will. Option A is wrong because the frequency of elections alone does not define democracy; what matters is whether real choice exists.

questions.title: Rule of Law Meaning
questions.prompt: In Country X, the president can order the arrest of any citizen without a trial, and judges are appointed by the president and can be dismissed if they give rulings the president dislikes. Which principle of good governance is most clearly being violated?

options.A: Federalism, because power is not shared between national and regional governments
options.B: Proportional representation, because the votes of citizens are not counted fairly
options.C: The rule of law, because no one — including the president — should be above the law
options.D: Socialism, because the government is controlling too many economic resources

questions.explanation: The rule of law means that every person, including leaders, must follow the same laws, and courts must be independent so they can apply the law fairly. Option A is wrong because federalism is about how power is divided between levels of government, not about whether leaders can escape legal consequences.

questions.title: Market Economy Prices
questions.prompt: In a free-market economy, when a new toy becomes extremely popular, shops quickly run out of stock. According to how market economies work, what would most likely happen next without any government involvement?

options.A: The price of the toy would fall because sellers want more children to afford it
options.B: The government would order factories to produce more toys at the original price
options.C: The price would rise, encouraging more producers to make the toy and eventually increasing supply
options.D: All toy shops would agree to split the remaining stock equally among all customers

questions.explanation: In a market economy, scarcity causes prices to rise, which acts as a signal to producers that they can earn more profit by making more of that good — this is called the price mechanism. Option A is wrong because sellers motivated by profit have no incentive to lower prices when demand exceeds supply; the opposite happens.

questions.title: Social Contract Ideas
questions.prompt: Rousseau believed that when people form a society, they agree to follow the 'general will' — what is best for the whole community, not just what each individual wants. A student argues: 'This means Rousseau thought individual freedom was more important than the community's decisions.' Identify the error in the student's claim.

options.A: The error is that Rousseau never wrote about freedom at all
options.B: The error is that Rousseau believed the general will of the community could rightfully override individual preferences when it serves the common good
options.C: The error is that Rousseau believed only kings and nobles should decide what the general will is
options.D: The error is that Rousseau thought society should never have any rules that limit personal behaviour

questions.explanation: Rousseau argued that by joining a community, individuals agree to be governed by the general will, which can require limiting personal desires for the benefit of all — this is the opposite of putting individual freedom first. Option C is wrong because Rousseau believed the general will comes from the people as a whole, not from rulers or elites.

questions.title: Power and Authority Types
questions.prompt: A village elder is respected and listened to by everyone in the community, not because she holds any official government position, but because people believe her wisdom and long experience make her judgements trustworthy. Which type of authority does she hold?

options.A: Legal-rational authority, because her authority is based on a written set of rules
options.B: Charismatic authority, because her authority comes from her special personal qualities and the trust of those who follow her
options.C: Coercive authority, because people feel they must obey or face punishment
options.D: Federal authority, because she has power over a specific region within a larger state

questions.explanation: Charismatic authority, described by sociologist Max Weber, is authority that comes from people believing in the exceptional personal qualities of a leader — not from law or tradition. Option A is wrong because legal-rational authority is based on formal rules and official positions, which this elder does not hold.

questions.title: Planned Economy Decisions
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, a government committee decides to produce ten million pairs of winter boots this year, the same number as last year. However, this year's winter is unusually mild and people buy far fewer boots than expected. What problem does this most clearly illustrate about planned economies?

options.A: Planned economies always produce too few goods because governments are not interested in people's needs
options.B: Planned economies struggle to respond quickly to changes in what people actually want or need because prices do not send signals to producers
options.C: Planned economies never allow citizens to buy winter clothing of any kind
options.D: Planned economies only fail when the weather is unpredictable, and work perfectly in stable conditions

questions.explanation: In a market economy, falling demand causes prices to drop, signalling producers to make less — but in a planned economy, central planners lack this automatic signal and may keep producing goods nobody wants, leading to waste. Option D is wrong because the deeper problem is that planners cannot gather and process all the information about changing needs quickly enough, regardless of whether the cause is weather or something else.

questions.title: Revolution Causes
questions.prompt: Historians note that many revolutions happen not when people are at their poorest, but when conditions have been improving for some time and then suddenly get worse again. A student claims: 'This shows that revolution is caused simply by poverty.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because the poorest people always lead revolutions
options.B: The claim is partly right because poverty is involved, but it misses that rising expectations followed by disappointment — not poverty alone — can trigger revolution
options.C: The claim is correct because once people have enough food and shelter, they never revolt
options.D: The claim is wrong because revolutions are only caused by foreign invasions, not by economic conditions

questions.explanation: The historian James Davies proposed the 'J-curve' theory: revolution is most likely when a period of improvement raises people's expectations, but then a sudden setback makes the gap between what people expect and what they have feel unbearable. Option A is wrong because the evidence described shows that the very poorest — who have never known improvement — are often less likely to revolt than those whose rising hopes have been frustrated.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Country P has a mixed economy. The government provides free public schools and hospitals, regulates pollution from factories, and also allows private businesses to compete freely in most other markets. Which statement best explains why Country P uses a mixed approach rather than a purely free-market system?

options.A: Because free markets always produce the wrong goods, so the government must control everything
options.B: Because some goods and services — like education and environmental protection — would be underprovided or harmful if left entirely to profit-seeking markets
options.C: Because the government earns more money when it runs schools and hospitals than when private companies do
options.D: Because international law requires every country to provide free schools and hospitals regardless of its economic system

questions.explanation: Mixed economies exist because free markets are efficient for many goods but fail in areas where profit motives lead to under-provision of public goods or negative side-effects like pollution — the government steps in specifically in these cases. Option C is wrong because governments typically spend more on public services than they earn from them; the goal is social benefit, not government profit.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that all people are born with natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and that governments exist only to protect these rights. Based on this idea, which action would Locke most strongly support?

options.A: A government that takes land from farmers without compensation to build military bases
options.B: A government that limits free speech to maintain order during peacetime
options.C: Citizens refusing to obey a government that seizes their property without any legal process
options.D: A government that requires all citizens to give up private property and share everything equally

questions.explanation: Locke believed that if a government violates natural rights — including property rights — without lawful process, citizens have the right to resist or replace it, because the government has broken the social contract. Option D contradicts Locke directly, as he considered the right to own private property one of the most fundamental natural rights that government must protect, not destroy.

questions.title: Constitutional Limits on Power
questions.prompt: A constitution divides government into three branches: one makes laws, one carries out laws, and one judges whether laws follow the constitution. Why is it important that each branch can limit the others' power, rather than one branch being the strongest?

options.A: Because having three branches makes government decisions three times faster
options.B: Because it prevents any single group from gaining too much control and abusing power, protecting citizens' rights
options.C: Because international organisations require all governments to have exactly three branches
options.D: Because it ensures that the branch making laws always has more power than the others

questions.explanation: The system of 'checks and balances' — where each branch can limit the others — is designed specifically to prevent tyranny, the idea being that concentrated power is dangerous to citizens' freedoms. Option D is the opposite of the principle: checks and balances are meant to ensure no branch dominates the others, not to guarantee legislative supremacy.

questions.title: Rawls and Fairness
questions.prompt: John Rawls asked people to imagine designing a society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' — not knowing whether they would be born rich or poor, healthy or ill, male or female. What was the main purpose of this thought experiment?

options.A: To prove that people naturally choose to keep all their personal wealth rather than share it
options.B: To show that people design fairer rules when they cannot predict which position in society they will occupy
options.C: To argue that the best society is one where everyone earns exactly the same income
options.D: To demonstrate that only philosophers are intelligent enough to design just laws

questions.explanation: Rawls argued that people behind the veil of ignorance would choose fair principles — like protecting the worst-off members of society — because they might end up in that position themselves; not knowing your place removes self-interest from decision-making. Option C is wrong because Rawls did not argue for strict equality of income; his 'difference principle' allows inequalities as long as they benefit the least advantaged members of society.

questions.title: Federalism and Local Power
questions.prompt: In a federal system, state governments have the power to make their own laws about education, while the national government cannot overrule them on this issue. A student says: 'This means the national government is weaker than the state governments in a federal system.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because state governments always have more total power than the national government in any federal system
options.B: The claim is misleading because federalism divides powers by area — the national government is supreme in its own areas, such as defence and foreign policy, while states are supreme in theirs
options.C: The claim is correct because in every federal country, states can ignore any national law they dislike
options.D: The claim is wrong because federal systems never allow state governments to have any independent lawmaking power

questions.explanation: Federalism is a system of divided sovereignty, where different levels of government each have defined areas of supreme power — the national government is not weaker overall, it is simply restricted to its own sphere. Option A is wrong because in most federal systems the national government has exclusive and supreme power over critical areas like national defence, currency, and foreign treaties.

questions.title: Propaganda and Information
questions.prompt: A government releases only positive news about its own performance and bans stories that show problems or failures. Citizens begin to believe the country is doing better than it actually is. Which concept best describes what the government is doing, and why is it a threat to democracy?

options.A: Taxation, because the government is taking something valuable from citizens without consent
options.B: Propaganda, because controlling information manipulates citizens' beliefs and prevents them from making informed choices about their leaders
options.C: Federalism, because the government is taking away powers that belong to regional authorities
options.D: Market failure, because the shortage of true information is like a shortage of goods in an economy

questions.explanation: Propaganda is the deliberate spread of biased or misleading information to shape public opinion, and it undermines democracy because democratic decisions rely on citizens having access to accurate, free information to hold leaders accountable. Option D is creative but wrong — while information asymmetry is a type of market failure, the political concept that precisely names state-controlled misleading communication is propaganda.

questions.title: Comparing Economic Systems
questions.prompt: Country A lets businesses and individuals decide what to produce and buy, with prices set by supply and demand. Country B's government makes all production and pricing decisions. Country C does both: the government runs some industries and lets private businesses run others. Match these correctly to market, planned, and mixed economies.

options.A: A = planned, B = market, C = mixed
options.B: A = mixed, B = planned, C = market
options.C: A = market, B = planned, C = mixed
options.D: A = market, B = mixed, C = planned

questions.explanation: A market economy is driven by private decisions and price signals (Country A), a planned economy has central government control over production and prices (Country B), and a mixed economy combines both private and government activity (Country C). Option D is wrong because Country B — where the government controls all production and prices — is the definition of a planned economy, not a mixed one.

questions.title: Civic Participation Importance
questions.prompt: In a democracy, voter turnout has fallen to 30% — meaning only 30 out of every 100 eligible citizens actually vote. A student argues: 'As long as elections still happen, low voter turnout does not matter.' Identify the strongest problem with this argument.

options.A: The argument is wrong because democracies are required by international law to achieve at least 80% voter turnout
options.B: The argument misses that when few people vote, elected governments may only represent a small portion of the population, weakening the legitimacy of their decisions
options.C: The argument is wrong because elections cannot legally take place if fewer than half of citizens vote
options.D: The argument misses that low turnout always leads immediately to a military takeover of government

questions.explanation: Democratic legitimacy — the idea that a government has the right to rule because it represents the people — depends on broad participation; a government elected by only 30% of eligible voters may not truly reflect the population's wishes. Option C is wrong because many democracies have no minimum turnout requirement for elections to be legally valid, though low turnout is widely seen as a sign of democratic weakness.

questions.title: Human Rights and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: A country's government is treating a group of its own citizens very cruelly. Other countries want to intervene to protect those people, but the government says: 'What happens inside our borders is our own business and no other country has the right to interfere.' Which tension in international relations does this situation best illustrate?

options.A: The tension between market economies and planned economies
options.B: The tension between national sovereignty — a government's right to control its own territory — and universal human rights that apply to all people everywhere
options.C: The tension between federalism and unitary government systems
options.D: The tension between proportional representation and first-past-the-post voting systems

questions.explanation: This is a classic conflict in international law and politics: state sovereignty means governments have authority within their borders, but the doctrine of universal human rights — established in agreements like the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights — argues some protections apply to all humans regardless of borders. Option A is wrong because the conflict described is about political authority and rights, not about how an economy is organised.

questions.title: Social Stratification Causes
questions.prompt: In Society X, wealthy families send their children to expensive private schools with excellent resources, while children from poor families attend underfunded schools. As adults, the privately educated children are more likely to get high-paying jobs. A student claims: 'This shows that social inequality is entirely caused by individual effort.' What is the most important flaw in this claim?

options.A: The flaw is that effort never matters at all in determining life outcomes
options.B: The flaw is that the claim ignores how structural advantages — like access to better schools based on family wealth — shape opportunities before individual effort even comes into play
options.C: The flaw is that only government policies, not schools, determine whether someone becomes wealthy
options.D: The flaw is that private schools always produce worse results than public schools

questions.explanation: Social stratification research shows that structural factors — inherited wealth, access to quality education, social networks — heavily influence life outcomes independently of individual effort; ignoring these starting-point differences gives an incomplete picture. Option A is wrong because it overcorrects in the opposite direction: individual effort does matter, but it operates within structural constraints that the original claim completely ignores.

questions.title: Legitimacy of Government
questions.prompt: Country A's leader was elected by a majority of voters and follows the constitution. Country B's leader inherited power from his father and rules according to ancient royal traditions. Both leaders claim their rule is legitimate. Which statement best explains how their legitimacy is different?

options.A: Country A's legitimacy comes from democratic consent and legal rules, while Country B's comes from traditional authority based on customs passed down through generations
options.B: Country A's legitimacy comes from military strength, while Country B's comes from popular elections
options.C: Both countries have identical sources of legitimacy because both leaders are obeyed by their citizens
options.D: Country A's legitimacy comes from traditional authority, while Country B's comes from legal-rational authority

questions.explanation: Max Weber identified distinct types of authority: legal-rational authority (based on rules and democratic consent, like Country A) and traditional authority (based on long-established customs and inherited positions, like Country B). Option D reverses the labels — it is Country A, not Country B, whose authority rests on legal-rational grounds.

questions.title: Global Trade and Interdependence
questions.prompt: Country A produces wheat cheaply and imports electronics. Country B produces electronics cheaply and imports wheat. Both countries benefit from trading with each other. A student argues: 'Each country should produce everything it needs itself so it never depends on others.' Identify the main economic problem with this argument.

options.A: The argument is flawed because trade always leads to war between trading partners
options.B: The argument misses the principle of comparative advantage — each country gains more by specialising in what it produces most efficiently and trading, rather than making everything itself at higher cost
options.C: The argument is flawed because international law requires every country to import at least some goods
options.D: The argument misses that countries can only produce goods if they are located near the equator

questions.explanation: The economic principle of comparative advantage shows that total production and living standards rise when countries specialise in goods they can make at lower relative cost and trade for the rest, rather than trying to be self-sufficient at a higher cost. Option C is wrong because there is no universal international law mandating imports; the argument is an economic one about efficiency, not a legal obligation.

questions.title: Political Ideology Spectrum
questions.prompt: Party X believes the government should own and run major industries, provide free healthcare and education for all, and tax the wealthy heavily to fund these services. Party Y believes private businesses should run most industries, taxes should be low, and individuals should pay for their own healthcare and education. Which labels most accurately describe these parties' positions on the political spectrum?

options.A: Party X = far-right, Party Y = far-left
options.B: Party X = left-wing, Party Y = right-wing
options.C: Party X = authoritarian, Party Y = democratic
options.D: Party X = federalist, Party Y = unitary

questions.explanation: Left-wing political positions generally favour government intervention in the economy, redistribution of wealth, and public provision of services — as Party X does — while right-wing positions generally favour free markets, lower taxes, and individual responsibility — as Party Y does. Option C is wrong because left/right describes economic and social policy preferences, not necessarily whether a government is democratic or authoritarian; parties across the spectrum can support either.

questions.title: Negative Externalities Explained
questions.prompt: A factory produces shoes and sells them profitably, but the chemicals it releases into a nearby river harm fish and make the water unsafe for a village downstream. The factory owner says: 'My business is successful, so there is no economic problem here.' What concept best explains why the factory owner is wrong?

options.A: The factory owner is wrong because profitable businesses always cause negative externalities
options.B: The factory owner ignores negative externalities — costs of production that fall on people outside the transaction who are harmed without receiving any compensation
options.C: The factory owner is wrong because the village should simply move away from the river
options.D: The factory owner ignores that under international trade law, downstream pollution always cancels a business's right to sell goods

questions.explanation: A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties — here, the village — who are not part of the transaction between the factory and its shoe buyers; the factory's private profit does not account for this wider social harm. Option A is wrong because not all profitable businesses create externalities; the problem arises specifically when the business shifts costs onto others who have no say in the transaction.

questions.title: Social Norms and Conformity
questions.prompt: In a society, people follow rules about queuing, saying 'please' and 'thank you', and dressing a certain way — even when no police officer is watching. These behaviours are not written in any law. What maintains these rules in society?

options.A: Legal sanctions, because breaking any social behaviour eventually leads to a criminal trial
options.B: Social norms enforced through informal social pressure — such as disapproval, embarrassment, or exclusion — rather than written law
options.C: Government propaganda, because the state programmes citizens to behave politely through television advertisements
options.D: Federalism, because regional governments create local customs that citizens must legally follow

questions.explanation: Social norms are unwritten rules maintained through informal mechanisms — peer pressure, social approval or disapproval, and the desire to belong — not through formal legal enforcement. Option A is wrong because the scenario specifically describes behaviour followed without any legal threat; social norms operate through social rather than legal consequences.

questions.title: Immigration and Identity
questions.prompt: A large number of people from one country move to live in another country, bringing their own language, food, religion, and customs. Some people in the new country welcome this as enrichment. Others worry it will threaten the existing culture. Which concept best describes what is happening when different cultures exist and interact within the same society?

options.A: Federalism, because people from different places must be governed by different sets of laws
options.B: Authoritarianism, because the arrival of new people reduces the freedom of existing citizens
options.C: Multiculturalism, which describes a society where multiple cultural groups live alongside each other, raising questions about integration, identity, and shared values
options.D: A planned economy, because the government must plan how many immigrants the country can support

questions.explanation: Multiculturalism is the term used in social and political science to describe the coexistence of multiple cultural, ethnic, or religious groups within one society, and the debates this raises about how much to integrate versus preserve distinct identities. Option A is wrong because federalism is about how political power is divided between levels of government, not about cultural diversity within a population.

questions.title: Voting Systems Evaluated
questions.prompt: In Country Z's first-past-the-post election, Party A wins 60% of parliamentary seats with only 40% of the total national vote, while Party B wins 10% of seats despite receiving 25% of the national vote. A student argues: 'This result is proof that the first-past-the-post system does not always translate votes into seats fairly.' Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The argument is wrong because first-past-the-post is defined as the fairest possible voting system by international law
options.B: The argument is well-supported: first-past-the-post awards seats by who wins each local district, not by total national vote share, so larger parties are often over-represented and smaller parties under-represented
options.C: The argument is wrong because seats must always equal the percentage of votes in every democratic system
options.D: The argument is well-supported, but only because Party A cheated in the election

questions.explanation: First-past-the-post systems frequently produce disproportionate results because a party can win many districts by small margins and lose others by large margins, accumulating more seats than its vote share warrants — a structural feature, not a sign of cheating. Option C is wrong because only proportional representation systems aim to match seat shares to vote shares; first-past-the-post is explicitly designed around district-level competition, not national totals.

questions.title: Power of International Institutions
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council can pass resolutions calling on countries to stop fighting or to impose sanctions, but its decisions can be blocked if any one of its five permanent members votes against them. A student says: 'This veto power means the Security Council can never be truly fair or effective.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is completely correct because the United Nations has never successfully resolved any international conflict
options.B: The claim identifies a real limitation — powerful states can block action that affects their interests — but overstates it by ignoring cases where the Council has achieved ceasefires, peacekeeping operations, and sanctions
options.C: The claim is wrong because the veto power actually makes decisions faster and more efficient
options.D: The claim is correct only when more than three permanent members use their veto at the same time

questions.explanation: The Security Council veto is a genuine structural problem — great powers can and do block action when their own allies are involved — but the Council has also authorised hundreds of peacekeeping missions and resolutions that have reduced conflicts, showing it is neither perfectly fair nor completely ineffective. Option A is factually wrong: the UN Security Council has successfully authorised peacekeeping missions in dozens of conflicts and played key roles in resolving disputes in countries like Namibia, East Timor, and Sierra Leone.

questions.title: Democracy Core Features
questions.prompt: Which feature is most essential for a political system to be called a democracy? Think carefully — all four options describe things that can exist in democracies, but only one is truly necessary.

options.A: A strong military to protect national borders
options.B: Regular free and fair elections where citizens choose leaders
options.C: A single powerful leader who makes quick decisions
options.D: High levels of economic wealth shared among citizens

questions.explanation: Democracy literally means 'rule by the people,' and regular free and fair elections are the core mechanism by which citizens exercise that rule — without them, governments cannot be held accountable. A strong military (A) exists in many non-democratic states, making it the top distractor, but military strength is not what defines a democracy.

questions.title: Market Economy Basics
questions.prompt: In a free-market economy, who mainly decides what goods and services are produced?

options.A: A national planning committee appointed by the government
options.B: International organisations such as the United Nations
options.C: Individual buyers and sellers responding to prices and profit
options.D: Trade unions negotiating with large corporations

questions.explanation: In a free market, the price mechanism guides decisions: producers make goods that earn profit, and consumers signal demand through purchasing choices — no central authority is needed. A national planning committee (A) describes a planned economy, the most common confusion students make when comparing economic systems.

questions.title: Federalism Defined
questions.prompt: A student says: 'In a federal system, the national government always has complete power over every decision made in the country.' Is this statement correct?

options.A: Yes, because the national government created the regional governments
options.B: Yes, because national law always overrides regional law in every area
options.C: No, because federalism deliberately divides powers between national and regional governments
options.D: No, because regional governments hold more power than the national government in federal systems

questions.explanation: Federalism is specifically designed to share power: the constitution usually lists which powers belong to the national government and which are reserved for states or regions, so neither level is completely dominant. Option D is wrong because regional governments do not automatically hold more power — the split depends on the constitution of each country.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: Historians often argue that revolutions happen when a large group of people feel that the existing system is deeply unfair AND believe that change is actually possible. Which term best describes the moment when people shift from accepting hardship to demanding change?

options.A: Colonisation
options.B: Rising expectations
options.C: Diplomatic negotiation
options.D: Economic globalisation

questions.explanation: Historians use the concept of 'rising expectations' to describe situations where people begin to expect better lives — often after small improvements — and then feel outrage when conditions worsen again, sparking revolution. Diplomatic negotiation (C) is a top distractor because it sounds like a reasonable response to injustice, but it describes a peaceful process, not the psychological trigger for revolution.

questions.title: Social Contract Idea
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that people form governments through a 'social contract.' What does Locke say should happen if a government seriously breaks this contract by violating citizens' natural rights?

options.A: Citizens must always obey the government because stability is more important than rights
options.B: Citizens have the right to overthrow and replace that government
options.C: Citizens should appeal to a higher international authority for help
options.D: Citizens must wait until the next scheduled election to change the government

questions.explanation: Locke explicitly wrote in his 'Second Treatise of Government' (1689) that if a government violates the natural rights of life, liberty, and property, citizens retain the right of revolution to replace it. Option D is a top distractor because waiting for elections seems reasonable, but Locke's theory gives citizens an active right to resist tyranny rather than a passive obligation to wait.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes what makes an economy a 'mixed economy' rather than a purely free market or purely planned system?

options.A: All businesses are owned by foreign investors
options.B: The government and private businesses both play significant roles in the economy
options.C: Citizens vote on every individual economic decision the government makes
options.D: Prices are set entirely by international trade agreements

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private enterprise (businesses making their own decisions) with government involvement (regulation, public services, and sometimes state-owned industries), sitting between the two extremes. Option C is a top distractor because democratic participation sounds related, but voting on individual economic decisions is not a defining feature of a mixed economy.

questions.title: Authority and Power
questions.prompt: A school principal has the official title and the school rules support her decisions. A popular student leader influences others through trust and admiration but holds no official position. Which statement correctly identifies the type of power each person holds?

options.A: Both hold formal authority because both influence others' behaviour
options.B: The principal holds formal authority; the student holds informal influence
options.C: The student holds formal authority because more people listen to her
options.D: Neither holds real power because power only comes from physical force

questions.explanation: Formal authority comes from an officially recognised position with rules that back it up — exactly the principal's role; informal influence relies on personal qualities like charisma or respect, which describes the student leader. Option A is a top distractor because influence and authority both affect behaviour, but confusing them misses the important distinction between official and unofficial power.

questions.title: Authoritarian Government
questions.prompt: What is the most important way an authoritarian government differs from a democratic one in terms of how it treats opposition?

options.A: Authoritarian governments always have stronger economies than democracies
options.B: Authoritarian governments typically suppress political opposition rather than allowing free competition for power
options.C: Authoritarian governments rely entirely on citizen consent to stay in power
options.D: Authoritarian governments allow free speech but control economic decisions instead

questions.explanation: The defining feature of authoritarianism is that the ruling group prevents meaningful political competition — through censorship, imprisonment of opponents, or banning rival parties — rather than risking losing power through fair elections. Option C is wrong and is a top distractor because authoritarianism fundamentally does not depend on broad citizen consent; it often relies on coercion.

questions.title: Rousseau General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau introduced the idea of the 'general will' — the shared interest of all people in a society. How does this idea differ from simply doing what the majority of individuals want?

options.A: The general will always agrees perfectly with what each individual privately wants
options.B: The general will refers to what is truly best for the whole community, which may differ from majority opinion
options.C: The general will is determined by a council of philosophers, not ordinary citizens
options.D: The general will only applies to economic decisions, not political ones

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished between the 'will of all' (the sum of individuals' selfish preferences) and the 'general will' (what genuinely benefits the whole community) — they can be different, which is why majorities can sometimes be wrong. Option A is the top distractor because students often assume Rousseau simply meant 'majority vote,' but he explicitly argued individual desires can conflict with the common good.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy
questions.prompt: Why does a constitutional democracy use a written constitution rather than allowing the elected parliament to make any law it chooses without limits?

options.A: To make government decision-making faster by reducing debate
options.B: To ensure wealthy citizens have more legal protection than others
options.C: To protect fundamental rights even when a majority might vote to remove them
options.D: To prevent regional governments from passing any laws independently

questions.explanation: A constitution places certain rights — such as freedom of speech or fair trial — beyond the reach of ordinary majority votes, preventing what theorists call the 'tyranny of the majority.' Option D is the top distractor because constitutions do interact with regional governments, but limiting regional lawmaking is not the main reason constitutions exist.

questions.title: Rawls Veil of Ignorance
questions.prompt: John Rawls asked people to imagine designing a society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' — not knowing what position they would hold in it. What is the main purpose of this thought experiment?

options.A: To show that the wealthiest citizens should design economic rules because they understand business
options.B: To help people choose fair principles for society without being biased by their own advantages
options.C: To prove that all societies should have identical laws regardless of their history
options.D: To demonstrate that people naturally choose the system with the greatest total wealth

questions.explanation: Rawls designed the veil of ignorance to strip away personal bias: if you do not know whether you will be rich or poor, healthy or ill, you are more likely to choose genuinely fair rules that protect everyone. Option D is a top distractor because some might think people would choose maximum total wealth, but Rawls argued they would instead choose to protect the worst-off position — the 'maximin' principle.

questions.title: Social Class Structures
questions.prompt: In a society with high social mobility, which of the following is most likely to be true?

options.A: People's social class is fixed at birth and does not change throughout their lives
options.B: Only people from wealthy families can access university education
options.C: Individuals can move into higher or lower social classes through effort, education, or opportunity
options.D: The government assigns each citizen a job based on their parents' occupation

questions.explanation: Social mobility describes the ability of individuals to move between social positions over time; high social mobility means birth circumstances are not destiny — education, skill, and effort can change one's class position. Option A is the top distractor because it describes a caste-like or low-mobility society, which is the direct opposite of high social mobility.

questions.title: Market Failure Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory produces cheap plastic toys but releases pollutants into a nearby river, harming local fish and making residents ill. The factory does not pay for this harm. In economics, what is the term for these costs that fall on people outside the business transaction?

options.A: Opportunity costs
options.B: Negative externalities
options.C: Scarcity premiums
options.D: Trade deficits

questions.explanation: A negative externality is a cost imposed on third parties (people not directly involved in buying or selling the product) — here, the river pollution harms residents who never bought the toys. Opportunity cost (A) is the top distractor because students often encounter it first in economics, but it refers to the next-best alternative given up when making a choice, not costs imposed on outsiders.

questions.title: International Law Purpose
questions.prompt: Which best explains the main purpose of international law, such as the Geneva Conventions or the United Nations Charter?

options.A: To allow the strongest nation to set rules that benefit its own economy
options.B: To create agreed standards for how countries should behave toward each other and protect human rights
options.C: To replace national governments with a single world government
options.D: To ensure all countries use the same economic system

questions.explanation: International law — including treaties, conventions, and charters — establishes shared norms and rules between sovereign states, covering areas like warfare, trade, human rights, and diplomacy, to promote cooperation and limit conflict. Option C is a top distractor because some students confuse international law with world government, but international law respects national sovereignty rather than replacing it.

questions.title: Power of the Press
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A free press has no real effect on how a democracy works — politicians make all decisions anyway.' Identify the most important reason this claim is incorrect.

options.A: The press is important mainly because it provides entertainment that keeps citizens happy
options.B: A free press holds government accountable by informing citizens, enabling them to make meaningful electoral choices
options.C: The press forces politicians to follow international law
options.D: A free press prevents other countries from interfering in elections

questions.explanation: A free press is considered a 'fourth estate' in democracy because investigative journalism exposes corruption and informs voters — without accurate information, citizens cannot meaningfully evaluate their leaders. Option C is a top distractor because international law sounds connected to accountability, but the press does not enforce international obligations; it primarily serves domestic democratic accountability.

questions.title: Planned Economy Features
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, the government decides what to produce, how much to produce, and at what price to sell goods. Which of the following is a genuine advantage often claimed for this system?

options.A: It always produces greater variety of consumer goods than a free market
options.B: It can rapidly direct resources toward national priorities such as defence or healthcare
options.C: It eliminates the need for any form of taxation
options.D: It automatically creates higher economic growth than market systems

questions.explanation: Historically, centrally planned economies like the Soviet Union were able to rapidly industrialise and mobilise resources toward specific goals (e.g., Sputnik space programme, wartime production) because central planners could redirect the whole economy. Option A is wrong and is a top distractor — planned economies are typically criticised for producing fewer consumer goods and less variety than market systems.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Most democratic governments divide power among a legislature (makes laws), an executive (carries out laws), and a judiciary (interprets laws). What is the main reason for keeping these three branches separate?

options.A: To make sure only educated citizens can participate in government
options.B: To ensure decisions are made as quickly as possible without delay
options.C: To prevent any single person or group from gaining unchecked control over all government power
options.D: To allow different political parties to each control one branch

questions.explanation: The doctrine of separation of powers, developed by Montesquieu and embedded in many constitutions, ensures that each branch can check the others — preventing tyranny by stopping power from concentrating in one place. Option D is a top distractor because in some coalition governments different parties do control different branches, but that is not the purpose of separation of powers — it is a system designed to check power, not share it between parties.

questions.title: Citizen Responsibilities
questions.prompt: In a democracy, citizens have both rights (things the government must allow or provide) and responsibilities (things citizens are expected to do). Which of the following is best described as a civic responsibility rather than a right?

options.A: The freedom to practise any religion
options.B: The right to a fair trial if accused of a crime
options.C: Participating in elections by voting and staying informed
options.D: Protection from unlawful search of one's home

questions.explanation: Voting and civic engagement are responsibilities — actions citizens are expected to perform to make democracy function — rather than entitlements the government must provide to individuals. Options A, B, and D are all classic rights (freedoms or protections), making option B the top distractor because a fair trial sounds active, but it is a protection citizens receive, not an obligation they perform.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Causes
questions.prompt: A researcher finds that in Country X, the wealthiest 10% of people own 70% of all land and property. Which structural factor most directly helps explain why this kind of wealth concentration tends to grow over time?

options.A: Wealthier people naturally work harder than poorer people
options.B: Wealth generates further income (through rent, investment, interest) making it easier to accumulate more
options.C: Poorer citizens choose not to participate in financial markets
options.D: International trade always benefits wealthy individuals more than governments can control

questions.explanation: Economists observe that existing wealth creates new income through returns on assets (rent from property, dividends from shares, interest on savings), creating a self-reinforcing cycle that widens inequality over time — a pattern Thomas Piketty analysed extensively. Option A is the top distractor because it reflects a common misconception that conflates effort with inherited advantage, ignoring structural causes of inequality.

questions.title: Comparative Governance
questions.prompt: Country A has a president directly elected by citizens who acts as both head of state and head of government. Country B has a prime minister who must keep the support of parliament to remain in power. Which system is Country A most likely using?

options.A: A parliamentary system
options.B: A federal system
options.C: A presidential system
options.D: A unitary authoritarian system

questions.explanation: In a presidential system (like the United States), the president is separately elected by the public and does not depend on parliamentary confidence to stay in office — combining the roles of head of state and head of government. Option A is the top distractor because Country B describes a parliamentary system, and students may confuse the two by focusing on Country B's description rather than Country A's.

questions.title: Human Rights Origins
questions.prompt: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states that rights belong to all human beings simply because they are human. Which philosophical tradition does this idea most closely reflect?

options.A: Rights are gifts granted by governments and can be taken away by law
options.B: Rights belong only to citizens of wealthy democratic nations
options.C: Rights are natural and universal — they exist independently of any government or law
options.D: Rights are earned through military service or civic contribution

questions.explanation: The UDHR is rooted in natural rights theory — the idea that rights are inherent to all humans regardless of nationality, gender, or status, predating and standing above any government's laws. Option A is the top distractor because it reflects legal positivism, the competing view that rights come from laws, which the UDHR specifically sought to challenge by anchoring rights in human dignity itself.

questions.title: Revolution and Change
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a reform and a revolution as methods of political change?

options.A: Reforms always improve society, while revolutions always make things worse
options.B: Reforms make gradual changes within the existing system; revolutions fundamentally overthrow and replace the system
options.C: Revolutions are always violent, while reforms always happen peacefully
options.D: Reforms only affect economic systems, while revolutions only change political systems

questions.explanation: By definition, reform works within existing institutions to improve them gradually, while revolution involves a rapid, fundamental break that replaces the old system with a new one — as seen in the French and American Revolutions. Option C is the top distractor because while many revolutions involve violence, some (like Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution) were largely peaceful, so violence is not the defining distinction.

questions.title: Government and Public Goods
questions.prompt: A lighthouse warns all passing ships of dangerous rocks and cannot prevent any ship from benefiting, whether or not that ship contributed to its construction costs. Why is a lighthouse considered a public good?

options.A: It is owned by the government rather than a private company
options.B: It is non-excludable (cannot stop anyone from benefiting) and non-rivalrous (one ship's use does not reduce it for others)
options.C: It is free to use and costs nothing to build or maintain
options.D: It benefits only the people who live near the coastline

questions.explanation: Economists define public goods by two technical properties: non-excludability (you cannot stop non-payers from benefiting) and non-rivalry (one person's use does not reduce availability for others) — the lighthouse fits both perfectly. Option A is the top distractor because government ownership does not make something a public good in the economic sense; some government-owned services are excludable.

questions.title: Global Governance Limits
questions.prompt: The United Nations can pass resolutions calling on countries to take action, but it cannot usually force a powerful member nation to comply. What does this reveal about the nature of power in the international system?

options.A: The international system is anarchic in the sense that no single authority sits above sovereign states
options.B: The United Nations was poorly designed and should be replaced immediately
