options.C: Powerful nations always follow international rules because they want to appear legitimate
options.D: International law is completely irrelevant to how countries actually behave

questions.explanation: International relations scholars describe the global system as 'anarchic' — not meaning chaotic, but meaning there is no supreme authority above sovereign states that can enforce compliance the way a national government enforces domestic law. Option C is the top distractor because while legitimacy does matter and influences state behaviour, the statement that powerful nations 'always' follow rules is clearly contradicted by historical examples.

questions.title: Connection: Trade and Power
questions.prompt: Country A exports most of its food to Country B. Country B then bans imports from Country A as a political punishment. What concept from political economy best describes the vulnerability this situation reveals for Country A?

options.A: Comparative advantage
options.B: Economic interdependence creating political vulnerability
options.C: Fiscal deficit
options.D: Protectionist tariff policy

questions.explanation: When two countries become economically connected through trade, both gain efficiency but also become vulnerable — Country A's heavy reliance on Country B as a buyer means that trade can be weaponised as a political tool, a concept central to discussions of economic interdependence and power. Comparative advantage (A) is the top distractor because it explains why countries trade, but does not describe the political vulnerability that results from dependence on a trading partner.

questions.title: Democracy vs. Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A country holds elections every four years, but only one political party is allowed to register candidates. Citizens can vote, but all candidates share the same ideology. A student claims this country is a democracy because it holds elections. What is the most accurate evaluation of this claim?

options.A: The claim is correct because elections are the only requirement for democracy.
options.B: The claim is wrong because democracy requires free competition between different political parties and genuine voter choice.
options.C: The claim is correct because citizens are still allowed to participate in voting.
options.D: The claim is wrong because democracies must hold elections every five years, not four.

questions.explanation: Democracy requires not just elections but meaningful competition — voters must be able to choose between genuinely different options representing different views. A single-party election removes real choice, making it authoritarian in practice. Option C is wrong because participation alone does not make a system democratic if the choices available are not free or competitive.

questions.title: Federalism and Local Power
questions.prompt: A flood destroys several towns in a federal country. The regional government wants to rebuild using a particular environmental design, but the national government insists on a standard cheaper design. In a federal system, how should this conflict most likely be resolved?

options.A: The national government always wins because it controls all funding in a federal system.
options.B: The regional government always wins because federalism means regions are fully independent from the national government.
options.C: Both levels of government negotiate, since federalism divides power between national and regional governments according to agreed rules.
options.D: An international court decides the outcome because federal disputes must be resolved globally.

questions.explanation: Federalism specifically divides governing power between national and regional levels, meaning neither automatically overrides the other — disputes are resolved through negotiation or constitutional courts. Option A is wrong because in a true federal system, regional governments retain genuine authority in certain policy areas and are not simply subordinate to central funding decisions.

questions.title: Market Economy Basics
questions.prompt: In a market economy, a sudden craze for a particular toy means shops sell out within days. Using your understanding of how markets work, predict what will most likely happen next.

options.A: The government will order factories to produce more toys to meet demand.
options.B: Producers will increase supply and may raise prices, attracted by the opportunity to make profit.
options.C: The price will be legally frozen so all children can afford the toy equally.
options.D: Shops will permanently close because they ran out of stock.

questions.explanation: In a market economy, the profit motive drives producers to respond to high demand by increasing supply, and prices often rise when demand exceeds supply — this is the price mechanism at work. Option A describes what would happen in a planned economy, not a market economy, where government directs production.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that when people join society, they give up some individual freedoms in exchange for the protection of the 'general will' — the shared good of the community. How does this idea challenge a purely individualist view of society?

options.A: It supports individualism by showing that personal rights are always more important than community decisions.
options.B: It challenges individualism by arguing that the community's shared interests can legitimately limit personal freedoms.
options.C: It agrees with individualism because Rousseau believed government should never restrict citizens.
options.D: It has no connection to individualism because Rousseau only wrote about economics.

questions.explanation: Rousseau's general will concept directly challenges pure individualism because it holds that what is best for the whole community can justifiably override individual preferences — citizens consent to this when joining society. Option A is the opposite of Rousseau's actual argument; he explicitly said personal freedom must sometimes be subordinated to collective welfare.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: What would most likely increase the risk of a political revolution in a country, based on patterns historians have observed across multiple revolutions?

options.A: A long period of economic growth shared equally across all social classes.
options.B: A growing gap between the expectations of ordinary people and what the government actually delivers, combined with weakened government authority.
options.C: A strong and popular military that supports civilian government decisions.
options.D: High rates of immigration that bring new cultural ideas into the country.

questions.explanation: Historians identify relative deprivation — the gap between what people expect and what they receive — combined with a loss of government legitimacy as core triggers of revolution, as seen in the French and Russian revolutions. Option A describes conditions that typically reduce revolutionary pressure rather than increase it.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: In Country P, the government runs public hospitals and schools, but most shops, farms, and factories are privately owned. A visitor concludes: 'This country has a planned economy.' Identify the error in the visitor's reasoning.

options.A: The error is that planned economies only exist in very large countries.
options.B: The error is that a planned economy means the government controls all production, whereas Country P has both government and private sectors — making it a mixed economy.
options.C: There is no error; a country with any government services must be a planned economy.
options.D: The error is that hospitals and schools are not part of any economy.

questions.explanation: A planned economy is defined by government control over nearly all production and resource allocation. Country P clearly has a large private sector alongside public services, which is the defining feature of a mixed economy. Option C reflects a common misconception — any government involvement in the economy does not automatically make it planned.

questions.title: Locke and Government Legitimacy
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that governments receive their authority from the consent of the governed. A king argues that his authority comes from God and therefore cannot be questioned by citizens. Which statement best explains why Locke would reject the king's argument?

options.A: Locke believed in God, so he would agree that divine authority is legitimate for rulers.
options.B: Locke would reject it because authority not based on popular consent can be withdrawn by citizens if their natural rights are violated.
options.C: Locke would reject it because he believed only elected parliaments, not kings, could ever rule.
options.D: Locke would agree with the king as long as the king protected the country from invasion.

questions.explanation: Locke's central argument in the Second Treatise of Government is that legitimate authority derives from a social contract with the people, not divine right — and citizens have the right to overthrow rulers who violate their natural rights to life, liberty, and property. Option A confuses Locke's personal religious beliefs with his political theory; he explicitly rejected divine right as a basis for political authority.

questions.title: Power vs. Authority
questions.prompt: A school bully forces younger students to give him their lunch money through threats. A school principal asks students to follow the same no-running rule every day and they comply. Compare these two situations: which concept best describes what the bully uses, and what does the principal have?

options.A: The bully uses authority; the principal uses power.
options.B: Both the bully and the principal use authority because both achieve compliance.
options.C: The bully uses power through coercion; the principal has authority because students accept her right to make rules.
options.D: The principal uses coercion and the bully has authority because the bully controls more people.

questions.explanation: Power refers to the ability to make others act, including through force or fear, while authority is power that is accepted as legitimate by those subject to it — the principal's rule-making is seen as rightful by students. Option A reverses these definitions, which is a very common student error when first encountering this distinction.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Limits
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'In a constitutional democracy, whatever the majority of citizens vote for must become law — majority rule is absolute.' What is the most important flaw in this claim?

options.A: The flaw is that majorities can never agree on any single issue.
options.B: The flaw is that constitutional democracies protect minority rights and fundamental freedoms that even majority votes cannot override.
options.C: The flaw is that in a constitutional democracy, only judges — not citizens — can make any laws.
options.D: There is no flaw; majority rule is indeed absolute in all democratic systems.

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracies deliberately limit majority rule through bills of rights and constitutional protections — for example, a majority cannot vote to eliminate free speech or imprison an ethnic minority, because the constitution protects these rights. Option D is a serious misconception; unconstrained majority rule is sometimes called 'tyranny of the majority,' which constitutions are designed to prevent.

questions.title: Rawls and Fairness
questions.prompt: Rawls asked people to imagine designing society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' — not knowing what family, income level, or talents they would be born with. Why is this thought experiment useful for thinking about justice?

options.A: It ensures wealthy people design the rules of society because they have the most experience.
options.B: It removes personal self-interest from decision-making so people are more likely to choose rules that are fair to everyone.
options.C: It proves that all inequalities are unjust and should be eliminated completely.
options.D: It is useful only in countries that already have democratic governments.

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance removes bias by making decision-makers uncertain of their own position — Rawls argued that rational people in this position would choose fair rules that protect even the worst-off members of society, since they could end up in that position. Option C misrepresents Rawls, who actually accepted some inequalities as just — specifically those that benefit the least advantaged group through his difference principle.

questions.title: Social Mobility and Structure
questions.prompt: Country X has free universities, strong public healthcare, and progressive taxation (higher earners pay a higher percentage). Country Y has expensive private universities, limited public healthcare, and flat taxation. Which country most likely has higher social mobility and why?

options.A: Country Y, because flat taxation means everyone pays equally and this is fairer.
options.B: Country X, because free education and healthcare reduce the advantages of being born wealthy, giving more people the chance to succeed.
options.C: Country Y, because private universities always produce better-educated graduates who can rise socially.
options.D: Both countries have equal social mobility because individual talent determines success in all societies.

questions.explanation: Social mobility research consistently shows that access to free education and healthcare removes structural barriers that keep lower-income families from advancing — countries like Denmark and Finland with these features regularly rank highest in social mobility indices. Option D ignores structural inequality; talent alone cannot overcome barriers created by unequal access to education and health resources.

questions.title: Market Failures Explained
questions.prompt: A factory releases chemical waste into a river, making the water undrinkable for downstream villages. The factory's products are cheaper because it does not pay for cleaning up this pollution. Which economic concept best describes this situation?

options.A: A positive externality, because cheaper products benefit consumers.
options.B: A monopoly, because the factory controls the entire river.
options.C: A negative externality, because the factory imposes costs on others that are not reflected in its prices.
options.D: Price discrimination, because different villages pay different prices for the same water.

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a producer's activity creates costs borne by third parties who had no say in the decision — the factory's pollution is a classic example used in economics textbooks. Option A is wrong because a positive externality benefits third parties; cheaper products help buyers, but those buyers are the factory's customers, not unrelated third parties being harmed.

questions.title: Comparative Governance
questions.prompt: In System A, the head of government is chosen by the parliament and can be removed by a parliamentary vote of no confidence. In System B, the head of government is elected directly by citizens in a separate election and cannot be removed by the legislature during their fixed term. Compare these: which system gives parliament greater control over the executive?

options.A: System B, because directly elected leaders have a stronger popular mandate.
options.B: System A, because parliament can remove the head of government, making the executive accountable to the legislature.
options.C: Both systems give parliament equal control because both have elected governments.
options.D: System B, because fixed terms make it easier for parliament to plan legislation.

questions.explanation: System A describes a parliamentary system (like the UK or Germany), where the prime minister depends on parliamentary support to remain in power — losing a confidence vote means losing office. System B describes a presidential system (like the USA), where the executive is separate from and cannot be routinely dismissed by the legislature. Option A confuses electoral mandate with parliamentary accountability — a strong mandate does not mean greater parliamentary control.

questions.title: International Law and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: The United Nations passed a resolution condemning Country Q for human rights abuses, but Country Q ignored it. A student argues that this proves international law is completely useless. Identify the strongest counterargument to this claim.

options.A: The student is correct because any law that is sometimes ignored has no value at all.
options.B: International law still shapes behaviour through reputation, diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions, and international courts — most countries comply most of the time.
options.C: International law is useless because the UN has no permanent army to enforce its decisions.
options.D: International law only applies to small countries, so powerful countries like Country Q are exceptions.

questions.explanation: International law scholars note that compliance with international law is actually very high across most routine areas — trade, aviation, postal systems, and treaties — and violations trigger diplomatic and economic consequences that matter to states. Option C is a genuine misconception that conflates enforcement mechanisms with effectiveness; domestic laws are also not always obeyed, but we do not therefore call them useless.

questions.title: Elections and Representation
questions.prompt: In a first-past-the-post election, Party A wins 55% of all seats in parliament but received only 38% of the total votes nationwide. A student says this outcome is unfair. Which concept best supports the student's concern?

options.A: The outcome is fair because the winning party followed all the rules of the electoral system.
options.B: The student's concern relates to representational fairness — the seats won do not proportionally reflect how citizens actually voted across the country.
options.C: The outcome proves that Party A cheated by manipulating votes in rural areas.
options.D: The student is wrong because in any democracy, 38% is always enough to win a majority.

questions.explanation: First-past-the-post systems regularly produce disproportionate outcomes where a party wins far more seats than its share of votes, which critics argue means millions of votes are effectively wasted — this is the central fairness critique of this electoral system. Option A is technically true but misses the point; legality and fairness are different things, and the student's concern is about fairness, not rule-breaking.

questions.title: Planned Economy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: Why does a centrally planned economy sometimes struggle to provide the exact goods and quantities that citizens actually want, even when the government is genuinely trying to meet people's needs?

options.A: Because planned economies are always run by corrupt leaders who steal the goods.
options.B: Because without price signals from buyers and sellers, planners lack accurate real-time information about what millions of people want and need.
options.C: Because citizens in planned economies are not allowed to express preferences about goods.
options.D: Because planned economies only produce military equipment and ignore civilian goods entirely.

questions.explanation: Economists describe this as the 'knowledge problem' — in a market, prices continuously communicate information about changing demand and supply across millions of transactions; central planners cannot replicate this information system, leading to chronic shortages of some goods and surpluses of others, as seen in the Soviet Union. Option A is a generalisation that confuses a structural economic problem with a moral or individual failing.

questions.title: Civic Responsibility
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Voting is optional in a democracy, so citizens who don't vote bear no responsibility for the government that gets elected.' Evaluate this claim using the concept of civic responsibility.

options.A: The claim is fully correct because rights are always separate from responsibilities.
options.B: The claim has a significant weakness: in a democracy, citizens collectively shape outcomes, so choosing not to participate still affects results and passes decision-making power to others.
options.C: The claim is correct because only politicians, not ordinary citizens, are responsible for government choices.
options.D: The claim is correct as long as the citizen pays taxes, because taxes are their main civic duty.

questions.explanation: Political theorists argue that in a democracy, the right to vote comes paired with the civic responsibility to participate — abstaining is itself a choice that shifts influence to those who do vote, affecting outcomes the non-voter must still live with. Option A misunderstands the relationship between rights and responsibilities in democratic theory; the two are generally considered inseparable.

questions.title: Media and Political Power
questions.prompt: Country T has a free press, but 90% of all media outlets are owned by individuals who all support the same political party. A student argues: 'This is fine because the media is technically free and not controlled by the government.' Identify the strongest challenge to this argument.

options.A: The student is right because freedom of the press only means government cannot control media.
options.B: The challenge is that concentrated private ownership can shape public opinion as effectively as government control, limiting the diversity of views citizens encounter.
options.C: The challenge is that 90% is not enough for ownership to influence politics — it requires 100%.
options.D: The student is right because citizens can always find alternative information on the internet.

questions.explanation: Media concentration in private hands can create the same distortion as state control — if most citizens receive news filtered through owners with aligned political interests, genuine democratic deliberation is undermined even without formal censorship. Option D is a common but flawed counterargument; internet access is unequal globally, and algorithmic filtering often reinforces rather than challenges dominant narratives.

questions.title: Social Class and Opportunity
questions.prompt: Research consistently shows that children born to wealthy parents in many countries are far more likely to attend elite universities than equally talented children from low-income families. Which concept best explains this pattern?

options.A: Meritocracy, because university admissions always reward the most talented students regardless of background.
options.B: Structural inequality, because social systems create advantages for wealthy families that talented students from poorer backgrounds cannot easily overcome.
options.C: Cultural determinism, because wealthy children are always naturally more intelligent than poor children.
options.D: Free market economics, because universities must charge high fees to remain financially viable.

questions.explanation: Sociologists use the concept of structural inequality to explain how wealth provides access to better schools, tutoring, social networks, and application support — advantages unrelated to individual talent that systematically favour wealthier applicants. Option A describes the ideal of meritocracy but ignores the structural barriers that prevent it from operating in reality for lower-income students.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: In Country M, the president has the power to make laws, enforce laws, AND judge whether laws have been broken — all without any other branch checking these decisions. What risk does this concentration of power create?

options.A: It makes the government more efficient, which is always beneficial for citizens.
options.B: It creates the risk of tyranny because no independent body can prevent the ruler from abusing power or acting unjustly.
options.C: It only creates problems if the president is personally dishonest, because good leaders use power fairly.
options.D: It means other countries will refuse to trade with Country M.

questions.explanation: The concept of separation of powers, developed by Montesquieu and built into many constitutions, exists precisely to prevent any one person or group from having unchecked authority — history shows that concentrated power frequently leads to abuses regardless of the ruler's initial intentions. Option C is wrong because the separation of powers was designed to be a structural safeguard, not one that depends on the individual character of leaders.

questions.title: Global Governance Challenges
questions.prompt: Climate change requires countries to reduce their carbon emissions, but each individual country benefits from other countries reducing emissions even if they do not reduce their own. What concept from political science best describes this challenge?

options.A: Nationalism, because countries always prioritise their own identity over environmental concerns.
options.B: The collective action problem, because individual actors have an incentive to benefit from others' sacrifices without contributing themselves.
options.C: Authoritarianism, because only authoritarian governments can force emissions reductions.
options.D: Market equilibrium, because countries will naturally find the right balance of emissions through trade.

questions.explanation: The collective action problem (sometimes called the free-rider problem) explains why globally beneficial actions, like reducing carbon emissions, are difficult to achieve: each country is tempted to let others bear the cost while benefiting from the result, leading to under-provision of the global good. Option A — nationalism — may contribute to the problem but does not specifically describe the structural incentive logic that makes global cooperation so difficult even for well-intentioned governments.

questions.title: Historical Change and Revolution
questions.prompt: A student studying the American Revolution (1776) notes that the colonists were not the poorest people in the world, yet they still revolted against British rule. Which explanation best accounts for this, using knowledge of why revolutions occur?

options.A: Revolutions only happen when people are starving, so this revolution must have been secretly caused by famine.
options.B: The colonists revolted because of political grievances — being taxed without representation in parliament — showing that revolutions can be driven by denied rights and loss of legitimacy, not just poverty.
options.C: Wealthy people never participate in revolutions, so the colonists must have been mostly poor.
options.D: The British army was too weak to stop the revolution, which is always the real cause of revolutionary success.

questions.explanation: The American Revolution illustrates that revolutions can be driven by political grievances — specifically the principle of 'no taxation without representation' — rather than purely economic desperation, showing that legitimacy and rights are powerful motivating forces. Option A reflects a misconception that absolute poverty is always the cause of revolution; the colonists were relatively prosperous by global standards but felt politically oppressed.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: Country H grants citizens the right to freedom of speech. However, the law also prohibits speech that directly incites violence against other citizens. A student argues this law violates freedom of speech entirely. What is the most accurate evaluation?

options.A: The student is correct because any restriction on speech eliminates the right entirely.
options.B: The student is incorrect because most rights have accepted limits that protect others from harm — restricting incitement to violence is widely considered a justifiable boundary, not an elimination of the right.
options.C: The student is correct because governments should never interfere with citizen speech under any circumstances.
options.D: The student is incorrect because freedom of speech only applies to written words, not spoken ones.

questions.explanation: Human rights frameworks, including the UN Declaration of Human Rights, recognise that rights can be limited when they directly threaten the rights of others — speech that incites violence endangers others' right to safety and is a standard, internationally recognised exception. Option A reflects a common misconception that any limitation equals elimination; in practice, almost all rights operate within boundaries that prevent harm to others.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Perspectives
questions.prompt: Two economists are debating inequality. Economist A says: 'Inequality motivates people to work harder and innovate.' Economist B says: 'Extreme inequality prevents equal opportunity and weakens social trust.' Which statement best evaluates these competing perspectives?

options.A: Economist A is completely right because more inequality always leads to more innovation.
options.B: Economist B is completely right because all inequality is harmful with no redeeming qualities.
options.C: Both perspectives capture partial truths — some inequality may incentivise effort, but extreme inequality can damage social mobility and cohesion, suggesting the level and type of inequality matters.
options.D: Neither perspective is valid because economists never agree on anything.

questions.explanation: Most economic research supports a nuanced view: moderate inequality can provide incentives, but extreme inequality — as shown in cross-national studies including those by the OECD — correlates with lower social mobility, poorer health outcomes, and reduced trust. Option A ignores substantial evidence that very high inequality reduces equality of opportunity, while Option B ignores research showing that some performance incentives do motivate productive behaviour.

questions.title: Identity and Political Participation
questions.prompt: Research shows that in many countries, younger citizens (ages 18–25) vote at much lower rates than older citizens. What is the most significant consequence of this pattern for democratic government?

options.A: It has no consequence because politicians represent all age groups equally regardless of who votes.
options.B: Politicians have an incentive to focus policies on older voters' interests since they are more likely to vote, potentially under-representing younger citizens' concerns.
options.C: It means younger citizens have no rights in the democratic system.
options.D: It proves that young people do not care about political issues.

questions.explanation: Political scientists document that elected officials tend to be responsive to their actual voters — lower youth turnout means pensions, healthcare for the elderly, and other older-voter priorities can receive more political attention than housing, climate policy, or education, which younger voters prioritise. Option A assumes perfect representative democracy that ignores empirical patterns; research consistently shows politicians respond disproportionately to groups that vote in higher numbers.

questions.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A country must be a democracy if its citizens are allowed to vote in elections.' Identify the most significant flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Democracies never hold elections because leaders are appointed by experts
options.B: Elections alone do not guarantee democracy if civil liberties, free press, and fair competition are absent
options.C: Only countries with a written constitution can be considered democratic
options.D: Voting is only meaningful when every citizen chooses to participate

questions.explanation: Democracy requires not just elections but also freedoms such as free speech, an independent press, and genuine competition between candidates — many authoritarian states hold elections that are not free or fair. Option C is wrong because several strong democracies, such as the United Kingdom, have no single written constitution.

questions.title: Market vs Planned Economy
questions.prompt: In a market economy, bread prices rise sharply after a poor wheat harvest. In a planned economy, the government keeps bread prices the same by law. What is the most likely consequence of the government's fixed price in the planned economy?

options.A: Bakers will produce more bread because they are following government orders
options.B: Consumers will buy less bread because they prefer the market system
options.C: Shortages may develop because suppliers have less incentive to produce at the artificially low price
options.D: The government will earn more tax revenue from bread sales

questions.explanation: When a government sets a price below what the market would naturally charge, suppliers earn less profit and may reduce production, while demand stays high — creating shortages. Option A is wrong because government orders alone do not automatically motivate efficient production; without profit incentive, output often falls.

questions.title: Social Contract Basics
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that true political authority comes from the 'general will' — the shared interest of all citizens. How does this idea challenge the authority of a king who inherited his throne?

options.A: It suggests kings are legitimate only if they are the strongest military leaders
options.B: It implies that authority is only legitimate when it reflects the collective agreement of the people, not birth or tradition
options.C: It proves that all monarchies are corrupt and must be abolished immediately
options.D: It argues that citizens should have no say in government because they lack wisdom

questions.explanation: Rousseau held that political power is legitimate only when it represents the general will of the community — not hereditary right or force. Option A is wrong because Rousseau based legitimacy on popular consent, not military strength.

questions.title: Federalism and Power
questions.prompt: In a federal system, both the national government and regional governments have their own areas of power guaranteed by the constitution. Why might a federal system be chosen by a large, diverse country rather than a unitary system?

options.A: A federal system is cheaper to run because there are fewer politicians
options.B: It allows different regions to make laws suited to their local needs while sharing national defence and trade
options.C: It guarantees that all regions will always vote the same way in national elections
options.D: It prevents any region from having a separate cultural identity

questions.explanation: Federal systems distribute power so that local governments can address regional differences in language, culture, or economic conditions, while the national government handles matters like defence — as seen in countries like India or the United States. Option A is incorrect; federal systems often require more layers of government and can be more expensive to administer.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen if a government consistently ignored the basic needs of its poorest citizens — such as food, shelter, and healthcare — while spending lavishly on the military and royal court?

options.A: Citizens would become more loyal because the strong military protects them
options.B: The economy would grow faster because military spending creates jobs
options.C: Social unrest and revolution become more likely as inequality and resentment grow
options.D: Other countries would invade, making the internal situation irrelevant

questions.explanation: Historians studying revolutions, including the French Revolution, consistently find that extreme inequality combined with government indifference to poverty fuels popular anger and collective action. Option A is a common misconception — military strength does not automatically create loyalty when basic needs are unmet.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'A government is only powerful if people fear it.' Compare this view with the concept of legitimate authority. Which statement best evaluates this claim?

options.A: The student is correct — fear is always the foundation of lasting political power
options.B: The student ignores that governments can also hold power through citizens' genuine consent and trust, which is often more stable
options.C: The student is wrong because governments only need economic strength, not fear or consent
options.D: Fear and legitimacy mean exactly the same thing in political science

questions.explanation: Political scientists distinguish between power based on coercion (fear) and legitimate authority based on consent — governments with high legitimacy, like stable democracies, often face less resistance and last longer. Option A is wrong because regimes based purely on fear tend to be unstable, as history shows with the eventual collapse of many authoritarian states.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: In Country M, the government runs public schools and hospitals but allows private businesses to sell food, clothing, and electronics freely. Which economic system does this describe, and why might a government choose this approach?

options.A: A planned economy, because the government controls at least one sector
options.B: A market economy, because private businesses are still allowed to operate
options.C: A mixed economy, combining government provision of essential services with private market activity
options.D: A traditional economy, because some services are shared among the community

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines government intervention in areas where markets might fail — such as education and healthcare — with free-market activity elsewhere, aiming to gain benefits of both systems. Option A is wrong because a planned economy means the government controls virtually all production and pricing, not just a few sectors.

questions.title: Locke and Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that all people are born with natural rights to life, liberty, and property. According to this view, what is the PRIMARY purpose of government?

options.A: To grant citizens their rights in exchange for obedience
options.B: To protect the natural rights that citizens already possess before government exists
options.C: To redistribute wealth equally among all members of society
options.D: To decide which citizens deserve more rights based on their contribution to society

questions.explanation: Locke believed natural rights exist before government — the state's job is to protect them, not create them. This idea directly influenced documents like the American Declaration of Independence. Option A is a common misconception; for Locke, rights are not gifts from government but pre-existing entitlements.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following statement: 'A constitutional democracy means the majority can always pass any law they want, because democracy means majority rule.'

options.A: The error is that majorities never actually agree on anything in real democracies
options.B: The error is that constitutional democracy limits majority power to protect the rights of minorities and individuals
options.C: The error is that constitutions only apply to economic laws, not political ones
options.D: The error is that democracies require unanimous agreement, not majority rule

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracy deliberately limits what a majority can do — constitutions typically protect minority rights and individual freedoms that cannot be voted away, as seen in the U.S. Bill of Rights. Option D is wrong because unanimity is not required in democracies; the point is that even majority decisions have constitutional boundaries.

questions.title: Market Failure: Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory produces shoes cheaply but releases pollution into a nearby river, harming fishing communities downstream. The factory owner pays nothing for this harm. Which economic concept does this situation illustrate, and what type of government action could address it?

options.A: A natural monopoly; the government should nationalise the factory
options.B: A negative externality; a pollution tax or regulation could make the factory pay for the harm it causes
options.C: A positive externality; the government should subsidise the factory to increase production
options.D: A public good problem; the government should provide shoes for free

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a third party bears costs they did not agree to — here, fishing communities suffer from pollution they did not cause. Governments address this with taxes (making polluters pay) or regulations (limiting pollution). Option C is wrong because positive externalities involve benefits spilling over to others, not costs.

questions.title: Social Inequality and Class
questions.prompt: Why does high social mobility in a society make it harder for rigid social class divisions to be maintained over time?

options.A: High social mobility means everyone eventually becomes wealthy, eliminating the need for class divisions
options.B: When people can move between classes through effort or education, the boundaries between classes become fluid and less fixed
options.C: Social mobility only applies to wealthy families moving to higher classes, not to poor families
options.D: High mobility causes governments to abolish all class-based laws automatically

questions.explanation: Social mobility means the position one is born into does not permanently determine one's place in society — people moving up and down between groups blurs rigid boundaries. Option A is wrong because mobility does not eliminate inequality or class differences; it simply makes them less fixed.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: Rawls asked us to imagine designing society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' — not knowing what position we would occupy in it. A student says this thought experiment is pointless because people will always design society to benefit themselves. Evaluate this objection.

options.A: The student is correct — Rawls himself admitted the veil of ignorance does not change human selfishness
options.B: The objection misunderstands the thought experiment: the veil of ignorance works precisely because people do not know their own position, so self-interest leads them to choose fairer rules
options.C: The student is correct because only philosophers, not ordinary people, can think fairly about justice
options.D: The objection is valid because Rawls only applied his theory to wealthy Western countries

questions.explanation: The whole point of the veil of ignorance is that uncertainty about one's own position makes rational self-interest produce fair principles — if you might end up poor, you design better safety nets. Option A is wrong; Rawls explicitly used self-interest as a feature, not a flaw, of his argument.

questions.title: Comparative Governance
questions.prompt: Country P has a president elected directly by citizens and a separately elected parliament. Country Q has a prime minister chosen by the parliament, not directly by citizens. Compare these two systems: which statement best identifies a key difference in accountability?

options.A: Country P's president is more powerful because direct election gives a stronger personal mandate from voters
options.B: Country Q's prime minister is always more democratic because parliament represents more people
options.C: In Country P, the president and parliament may have separate electoral mandates, creating potential conflict; in Country Q, the prime minister's survival depends on parliamentary confidence
options.D: Both systems are identical because all democratic leaders ultimately answer to voters

questions.explanation: Presidential systems (like Country P) can create deadlock when president and parliament disagree, since both have separate mandates; parliamentary systems (like Country Q) keep the executive dependent on the legislature, making them more directly accountable to it. Option D ignores the important structural differences in how accountability operates in each system.

questions.title: International Law Effectiveness
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council can authorise international action against countries that break international law, but five permanent members each hold a veto. How does this structure affect the effectiveness of international law?

options.A: It makes international law perfectly effective because five powerful countries always agree
options.B: It means international law cannot apply to any country at all, making it completely useless
options.C: It can weaken enforcement because a powerful country may veto action against itself or its allies, even when laws are broken
options.D: It strengthens international law by ensuring only the most serious violations are punished

questions.explanation: The veto power means that if a permanent member (like the US, Russia, or China) or one of its close allies violates international law, it or another permanent member can block UN action — creating unequal enforcement. Option B is too extreme; international law does function in many areas, especially when major powers agree.

questions.title: Propaganda and Media Control
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government controls all public media and only broadcasts positive stories about its leaders. A student claims: 'This is not a serious problem because people can tell when news is biased.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct — most people are naturally resistant to propaganda
options.B: The claim underestimates propaganda's power: when people have no alternative sources of information, repeated one-sided messages shape beliefs over time
options.C: The student is correct because authoritarian governments are always eventually exposed by foreign journalists
options.D: The claim is correct because biased media only affects uneducated citizens

questions.explanation: Research on propaganda shows that when people lack access to alternative information, repeated messages — even biased ones — can significantly shape their understanding of reality over time. Option A is a common misconception; access to independent information is what enables people to identify bias, and monopoly media removes that access.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Causes
questions.prompt: In Country R, the top 10% of earners own 70% of all wealth. A student argues this is entirely caused by some people being lazier than others. What is the most important flaw in this argument?

options.A: The argument is flawed because wealthy people always work harder than poor people
options.B: The argument ignores structural factors such as inherited wealth, unequal access to education, and systemic barriers that affect life outcomes regardless of individual effort
options.C: The argument is correct — inequality always reflects differences in personal effort and talent
options.D: The argument is flawed only because it does not account for differences in natural intelligence between people

questions.explanation: Economists and sociologists consistently show that factors like inherited wealth, quality of schooling, and discrimination significantly shape economic outcomes independently of individual effort — for example, children born into wealthy families have greater access to elite education. Option D is wrong because it simply replaces one reductive explanation with another.

questions.title: Revolution and Change
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen in a country where political reform is completely blocked — where peaceful protest, voting, and legal challenges all fail to change an unjust system?

options.A: Citizens would accept the situation permanently because they have no legal options
options.B: The probability of more radical or violent forms of resistance increases as peaceful channels are closed off
options.C: The economy would automatically collapse, forcing the government to change
options.D: Other countries would immediately intervene militarily to restore democracy

questions.explanation: Political scientists studying revolutions note that when all peaceful pathways for change are blocked, the perceived cost of radical action falls — historically, revolutions like those in France and Russia intensified after reform was repeatedly refused. Option A is contradicted by historical evidence showing that sustained injustice rarely produces permanent passive acceptance.

questions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
questions.prompt: A student says: 'In a democracy, I have the right to free speech, so I can say anything I want without any consequences.' Identify the most significant flaw in this view.

options.A: Free speech does not exist in any democracy — all speech is monitored by governments
options.B: Rights come with responsibilities; free speech in most democracies does not protect speech that harms others, incites violence, or constitutes defamation
options.C: The student is correct — democratic rights are always absolute and unlimited
options.D: Free speech only applies to politicians, not ordinary citizens

questions.explanation: Even in countries with strong free speech protections like the USA, legal limits exist — for example, the Supreme Court has ruled that falsely shouting 'fire' in a crowded theatre is not protected speech. Option C is wrong because no democratic country treats any right as completely unlimited.

questions.title: Globalisation and Governance
questions.prompt: As companies operate across many countries simultaneously, they can move their factories to whichever country has the lowest wages and weakest environmental rules. Which challenge does this create for individual national governments trying to protect workers and the environment?

options.A: Governments lose all power to make any laws once companies become multinational
options.B: Stricter national regulations may push companies to relocate, limiting a government's ability to enforce high standards without international cooperation
options.C: Multinational companies always prefer countries with stronger regulations because it signals stability
options.D: This is not a real problem because international trade agreements always protect workers automatically

questions.explanation: This 'race to the bottom' dynamic means individual governments face a dilemma: protect workers and the environment at the risk of losing jobs when companies move elsewhere, which is why international coordination on labour and environmental standards is increasingly seen as necessary. Option C is wrong because lower costs — not stronger regulation — typically attract companies seeking to maximise profit.

questions.title: Democratic Participation
questions.prompt: Voter turnout in Country S has fallen to 35% in national elections. A student argues this low participation strengthens democracy because only the most informed citizens are voting. Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The student is correct — smaller, more informed electorates always produce better government
options.B: Low turnout weakens democratic legitimacy because the elected government may not represent the views of the majority of citizens
options.C: Low turnout is only a problem if the non-voters are wealthy citizens
options.D: The student is correct because modern governments do not need mass participation to function effectively

questions.explanation: Democratic legitimacy depends partly on broad participation — when only 35% vote, a winning party might represent as little as 18–20% of all eligible voters, raising serious questions about whether the result truly reflects the public will. Option A is wrong because there is no reliable evidence that low turnout improves the quality of election results; it often means certain groups are systematically unrepresented.

questions.title: Perspective and Power
questions.prompt: The same government policy — increasing border controls — is described as 'protecting national security' by one newspaper and 'harming vulnerable refugees' by another. What does this difference most clearly illustrate about how we understand political events?

options.A: One newspaper is always correct and the other is always lying
options.B: Political events can look completely different depending on whose perspective and values shape the description, showing the importance of examining multiple viewpoints
options.C: This proves that governments should control media to prevent confusing citizens
options.D: Only experts in international law are qualified to judge government immigration policy

questions.explanation: The same policy genuinely affects different groups differently — security services and refugees have different experiences of the same law — so multiple perspectives reveal different aspects of political reality. Option A is wrong because it assumes only one account can be true, ignoring that both descriptions may reflect real but partial experiences of the same policy.

questions.title: Forms of Government
questions.prompt: Country J is governed by a small group of wealthy families who make all laws and control the military, with no elections or public participation. Which form of government best describes Country J, and how is it different from a democracy?

options.A: A theocracy, because religion controls law; democracies are ruled by elected officials
options.B: An oligarchy, because power is held by a small elite; in a democracy, authority comes from the broad participation of citizens
options.C: A federal system, because power is shared among families; democracies concentrate power centrally
options.D: A constitutional monarchy, because wealthy families can also hold royal titles; democracies have no monarchs

questions.explanation: An oligarchy is defined as rule by a small, privileged group — historically seen in ancient Sparta and in some modern states — contrasting with democracy where sovereignty rests with the broader citizenry. Option A is wrong because a theocracy specifically means rule by religious authority or clergy, which is not described in this scenario.

questions.title: Democracy vs. Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A country holds regular elections, but only one political party is legally allowed to stand for office, and all candidates must be approved by the ruling council. A student claims this system qualifies as a democracy because citizens still vote. What is the most precise flaw in the student's reasoning?

options.A: Voting alone does not make a system democratic if political competition and genuine choice are absent
options.B: The flaw is that democracies never require government approval for anything
options.C: The system is democratic as long as all adult citizens are permitted to cast a vote
options.D: The student is correct because the presence of elections is the only requirement for democracy

questions.explanation: Democracy requires not just the act of voting but genuine political competition — the ability for different parties and candidates to contest power freely. A system where only one party may participate removes meaningful choice, making elections ceremonial rather than democratic. Option C is the top distractor because it isolates one feature (universal suffrage) while ignoring the equally essential feature of competitive pluralism.

questions.title: Social Contract Philosophers
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that citizens give up their individual freedoms when they join society, receiving in return the protection of the 'general will.' Locke disagreed. Which statement best captures what Locke believed citizens retain even after forming a government?

options.A: Citizens surrender all natural rights permanently in exchange for security provided by the sovereign
options.B: Citizens retain their natural rights to life, liberty, and property, which government exists to protect rather than replace
options.C: Citizens keep only the right to vote but surrender economic and personal freedoms to the community
options.D: Citizens retain all freedoms without any obligation to obey laws they personally disagree with

questions.explanation: Locke specifically argued that natural rights — life, liberty, and property — pre-exist government and cannot be surrendered; government is created precisely to protect these rights, and any government that violates them loses its legitimacy. Option A describes Hobbes's view, not Locke's, making it the most tempting distractor for students who conflate the two thinkers.

questions.title: Federalism and Power
questions.prompt: In a federal system, a national government passes an education law. The regional government of State X argues the law violates its constitutional authority over education. Which feature of federalism makes this disagreement possible and meaningful?

options.A: In federalism, the national government always has unlimited power over regional governments
options.B: Federalism divides sovereign authority between levels of government, so each level has constitutionally protected areas of power
options.C: Regional governments in federal systems can only challenge national laws if they hold a referendum first
options.D: Federalism means regional governments are responsible for foreign policy while national governments handle domestic matters

questions.explanation: Federalism specifically distributes sovereign authority across levels of government through a constitution, meaning regional governments have legally protected powers that the national government cannot simply override. This constitutional division is what gives State X's objection real legal weight. Option A describes a unitary system, making it the most plausible distractor for students who confuse the two systems.

questions.title: Market Failures Explained
questions.prompt: A factory producing chemicals dumps waste into a river, harming fishing communities downstream. The factory pays nothing for this harm. An economist calls this a 'negative externality.' Why does this situation represent a market failure rather than simply unfair behaviour?

options.A: It is a market failure because the factory is acting illegally, which markets cannot tolerate
options.B: The market system produces too little of the chemical, making it a failure of supply
options.C: It is a market failure because the true social cost of production is not reflected in the factory's price, so too much of the harmful good is produced
options.D: It is unfair behaviour but not a market failure, since markets are only concerned with prices between buyers and sellers

questions.explanation: A negative externality is a market failure because the cost of environmental harm is borne by third parties — the fishing communities — rather than the factory, meaning the factory's price is artificially low and it overproduces relative to what is socially optimal. Option D is the top distractor because it correctly identifies that markets focus on buyer-seller transactions, but wrongly concludes this means the situation is not a market failure.

questions.title: Revolution and Causation
questions.prompt: Historians observe that revolutions rarely occur when people are at their absolute worst conditions. Instead, they often erupt after a period of improvement followed by a sudden setback. Which concept best explains why rising expectations, rather than deepest misery, can trigger revolution?

options.A: The J-curve theory, where improving conditions raise expectations that a sudden decline then violently frustrates
options.B: The idea that people only revolt when food shortages reach a level that causes mass starvation
options.C: The concept of social mobility, which guarantees revolution once citizens can move between classes freely
options.D: Relative deprivation only occurs when the wealthiest citizens lose income, triggering widespread unrest

questions.explanation: The J-curve theory, developed by sociologist James Davies, explains that revolutions are most likely when a period of improvement raises people's expectations, and a sudden reversal creates an intolerable gap between what people expect and what they have. Option B is plausible because famines have historically preceded revolutions, but it incorrectly limits the cause to absolute material conditions rather than the psychological gap between expectations and reality.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: Rawls imagined people choosing the rules of society from behind a 'veil of ignorance' — not knowing their own wealth, talents, or social position. What specific kind of reasoning does this thought experiment encourage, and why?

options.A: It encourages utilitarian reasoning, maximising the total happiness of the majority regardless of the least well-off
options.B: It encourages impartial reasoning by removing self-interest, so people choose principles fair to everyone including the worst-off
options.C: It encourages libertarian reasoning, where each person protects only their own pre-existing property rights
options.D: It encourages reasoning based on tradition, selecting rules that have historically worked in other societies

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance is designed to eliminate bias from self-interest: since you do not know whether you will be rich or poor, powerful or disadvantaged, you have a rational incentive to choose principles that protect the least well-off — leading Rawls to his difference principle. Option A is the strongest distractor because utilitarianism also aims at fairness, but it can justify harming minorities for the majority's benefit, which Rawls's approach specifically prevents.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A government has power if it can force people to obey, so power and legitimacy are the same thing.' Identify the most significant error in this claim.

options.A: The error is that governments only have power if they are elected through free and fair elections
options.B: The error is that power refers to the ability to enforce compliance, while legitimacy refers to whether authority is accepted as rightful — they are distinct concepts
options.C: The student is correct: any government that can enforce its rules automatically holds legitimate authority
options.D: The error is that legitimacy is only granted by foreign governments recognising a regime diplomatically

questions.explanation: Political theorists, including Max Weber, distinguish sharply between power (the capacity to compel behaviour through force or coercion) and legitimacy (the belief among citizens that authority is rightful and ought to be obeyed). A dictator may have power without legitimacy, and vice versa. Option C is the top distractor because it sounds logical — if compliance is achieved, authority seems legitimate — but it confuses the outcome of power with the moral acceptance that defines legitimacy.

questions.title: Economic Systems Comparison
questions.prompt: In Country A, prices are set by supply and demand and businesses decide what to produce. In Country B, a central authority decides production targets and sets prices. A student argues both systems face the same core economic problem. What is that shared problem?

options.A: Both systems must decide how to allocate scarce resources among unlimited human wants
options.B: Both systems rely on profit as the primary signal for what to produce
options.C: Both systems are equally vulnerable to inflation caused by excess money supply
options.D: Both systems eliminate inequality by distributing resources according to need

questions.explanation: The fundamental economic problem — scarcity — affects every economic system regardless of how it is organised: all societies must decide what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom, because resources are finite while wants are not. Option B is a strong distractor because profit does drive market economies, but centrally planned economies explicitly reject profit as a signal, so they do not share this feature.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Limits
questions.prompt: In a constitutional democracy, parliament passes a new law with 80% support from elected representatives. A court strikes it down, saying it violates citizens' fundamental rights. A student is angry: 'How can unelected judges overrule the democratic majority?' Which response best evaluates the student's concern?

options.A: The student is fully correct — in a democracy, the majority's elected representatives must always have the final say on all laws
options.B: The court is wrong because only a referendum of all citizens can override a parliamentary majority
options.C: Constitutional democracies deliberately protect minority rights from majority decisions, and courts enforce this to prevent 'tyranny of the majority'
options.D: Judges have democratic legitimacy equal to elected representatives because they are appointed by elected officials

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracies separate the will of the current majority from the foundational rights of all citizens; courts exist precisely to prevent a majority from using its power to violate the rights of minorities — a danger political theorists call 'tyranny of the majority.' Option D is the most tempting distractor because it offers a partial truth about judicial appointment, but it misrepresents the purpose of judicial independence, which is to apply constitutional principles rather than to represent political majorities.

questions.title: Social Structures and Mobility
questions.prompt: In feudal medieval Europe, a person born to a serf family was almost always legally required to remain a serf. Today, many societies use education and merit to determine social position. What does this shift primarily illustrate about how social structures change?

options.A: A move from an ascribed status system, where position is fixed at birth, toward an achieved status system, where position depends on individual effort and merit
options.B: A move from a democratic system to an authoritarian one, as governments gained more control over citizens' lives
options.C: A shift from a market economy to a planned economy, reducing inequality by redistributing inherited wealth
options.D: A change from horizontal social structures to vertical ones, meaning society became more hierarchical over time

questions.explanation: Sociologists distinguish between ascribed status (fixed at birth by factors like family, caste, or legal category) and achieved status (earned through education, skill, or effort); the move away from serfdom toward meritocratic systems is a classic example of this transition. Option D is a plausible distractor because vertical hierarchies do describe feudal society, but it describes a structural shape rather than the mechanism of change being asked about.

questions.title: International Law and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council passes a resolution demanding Country X stop a military action. Country X, which holds a permanent seat on the Security Council, had vetoed the resolution — but it passed anyway. Country X ignores the resolution entirely. What does this scenario most accurately reveal about international law?

options.A: International law is completely fictional because no country has ever followed a UN resolution
options.B: International law has real authority and can be enforced militarily against any country including permanent Security Council members
options.C: Enforcement of international law is constrained by state sovereignty and the political power of major states, especially permanent Security Council members
options.D: The UN Security Council has no legal authority whatsoever over member states' military actions

questions.explanation: International law operates in a system where states retain sovereignty, and the major powers that hold permanent veto seats on the Security Council have significant ability to block enforcement against themselves — making compliance partly a political rather than purely legal matter. Option B is the top distractor because the UN Charter does theoretically authorise collective military action, but in practice, the veto power of permanent members creates a political barrier that prevents enforcement against those very members.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Government Role
questions.prompt: Country M has a mixed economy. The government funds universal healthcare, regulates food safety standards, and also runs a state-owned railway. A student argues that only the healthcare funding is a legitimate government action because it corrects a market failure, while the railway is unnecessary government interference. Evaluate this position.

options.A: The student is correct: mixed economies only permit government intervention when a clear market failure can be identified
options.B: The student is wrong: governments in mixed economies also intervene for strategic, equity, or public interest reasons beyond correcting market failures
options.C: The student is correct about healthcare but wrong to include food safety regulation, which is always inappropriate government interference
options.D: The student is wrong because in a true mixed economy the government should own all industries equally

questions.explanation: Mixed economies blend market mechanisms with government intervention for multiple reasons: correcting market failures is one, but governments also act for equity (reducing inequality), strategic national interest (key infrastructure), and public welfare goals that markets might not serve. Option A is the strongest distractor because market failure correction is indeed a major justification for intervention, but it is not the only one — a student who has studied market failures without broader political economy would find it convincing.

questions.title: Cause and Effect: Revolutions
questions.prompt: Before the Russian Revolution of 1917, Russia had experienced military defeat in World War I, mass food shortages, and a Tsar who refused to share political power. Which best describes how these factors combined to cause revolution, using a multi-step causal chain?

options.A: Military defeat alone caused revolution because armies always overthrow governments after losing wars
options.B: War weakened the economy and military, food shortages created mass suffering, and the Tsar's refusal to reform removed peaceful alternatives — together making revolution the only outlet for grievances
options.C: Food shortages caused revolution directly, independently of political or military factors
options.D: The revolution was caused solely by foreign powers who wanted Russia to leave the war, not by internal conditions

questions.explanation: The Russian Revolution resulted from compounding causes: military failure destroyed the government's prestige and strained the economy, food shortages created desperate civilian suffering, and the Tsar's autocratic refusal to reform closed off peaceful political change — a combination that made violent revolution both likely and, in the eyes of many Russians, necessary. Option C is a tempting distractor because food shortages were a visible and immediate trigger, but reducing the revolution to a single cause ignores the political rigidity that prevented reform from addressing the crisis.

questions.title: Comparative Governance Systems
questions.prompt: In a presidential system, the head of government is elected separately from the legislature and has a fixed term. In a parliamentary system, the head of government depends on maintaining majority support in the legislature. What is the most significant consequence of this structural difference during a political crisis?

options.A: Parliamentary systems can replace an ineffective government more quickly by withdrawing confidence, while presidential systems lock in leadership for the fixed term
options.B: Presidential systems always produce more stable governments because the president answers directly to citizens
options.C: Parliamentary systems are more democratic because citizens vote directly for their prime minister
options.D: Presidential systems always lead to authoritarian rule because the president cannot be removed during a crisis

questions.explanation: In parliamentary systems, a vote of no confidence can remove a failing government quickly, allowing political adaptation during crises; presidential systems, by design, prevent removal except through impeachment (a lengthy process), which can mean rigidity during emergencies. Option B is the top distractor because it contains a partial truth — separation of powers can create stability — but 'always more stable' is inaccurate and ignores scenarios like political deadlock or poor crisis leadership.

questions.title: Propaganda and Information Control
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government funds schools that teach only officially approved history, controls all broadcasters, and arrests bloggers who post alternative views. Which concept from political science best explains the long-term goal of these combined strategies?

options.A: Hegemony — shaping citizens' beliefs so that the ruling group's dominance feels natural and inevitable rather than imposed
options.B: Pluralism — allowing many competing viewpoints to be debated in the public sphere simultaneously
options.C: Federalism — dividing information control between national and regional authorities to increase efficiency
options.D: Constitutionalism — using legal frameworks to guarantee citizens' rights to diverse information

questions.explanation: Antonio Gramsci's concept of cultural hegemony describes how a ruling group maintains power not just through force but by controlling ideas, values, and accepted 'common sense' — making its rule seem natural rather than contested. When schools, media, and public discourse all reinforce the same official narrative, citizens may internalise these views as their own. Option B is the strongest distractor because students might misread 'many sources' as producing pluralism, when in fact all sources in this scenario convey the same controlled message.

questions.title: Rousseau and the General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that citizens should obey the 'general will' — the common good of all — even when it conflicts with what an individual personally wants. A student argues this idea is compatible with modern liberal democracy. What is the strongest challenge to the student's argument?

options.A: Rousseau's general will can justify forcing individuals to obey the collective even against their own wishes, which conflicts with liberal democracy's protection of individual rights
options.B: Rousseau's idea is incompatible because he believed governments should never hold elections of any kind
options.C: Rousseau's general will is identical to majority voting, making it perfectly compatible with representative democracy
options.D: The challenge is that Rousseau only wrote about city-states, so his ideas cannot apply to any modern political system

questions.explanation: Rousseau's concept of the general will can, in extreme interpretations, justify overriding individual freedoms for the collective good — a tension that has historically been used to justify authoritarian measures; liberal democracy, by contrast, places individual rights as limits on what even popular majorities can do to a person. Option C is the most seductive distractor because Rousseau does connect the general will to community decision-making, but he explicitly distinguished it from mere majority preference, and it does not include liberal protections for dissenting individuals.

questions.title: Global Interdependence and Trade
questions.prompt: Country A produces grain very efficiently, while Country B produces electronics efficiently. Both countries currently produce some of each good. An economist argues both countries would benefit by specialising and trading. What economic principle supports this argument, and what risk does specialisation create?

options.A: Comparative advantage supports specialisation, but the risk is increased dependence on other countries — if trade is disrupted, a country may lack essential goods
options.B: Absolute advantage supports specialisation, and there is no meaningful risk because more efficient production always benefits everyone equally
options.C: Protectionism supports specialisation, and the main risk is that domestic producers become too powerful and monopolise the economy
options.D: Comparative advantage supports specialisation, and the main risk is that citizens will always prefer domestically produced goods and refuse to buy imports

questions.explanation: The principle of comparative advantage holds that countries benefit by producing what they are relatively most efficient at and trading for the rest — even if one country is better at everything, both gain from specialisation and exchange. However, specialisation creates vulnerability: if trade is blocked (by war, sanctions, or supply shocks), a country may lack critical goods it no longer produces. Option B is a distractor because it confuses comparative advantage with absolute advantage; comparative advantage is the correct principle, and the claim of 'no meaningful risk' ignores real-world supply chain vulnerabilities.

questions.title: Checks and Balances
questions.prompt: A president proposes a new law, the legislature passes it, but the supreme court rules it unconstitutional. The president argues: 'The court is blocking the democratic will — I was elected, and the court was not.' Evaluate whether the court's action is consistent with democratic principles.

options.A: The president is correct: in a democracy, elected officials must always have the final say because they have a popular mandate
options.B: The court's action is consistent with constitutional democracy because checks and balances exist to prevent any one branch from holding unchecked power, including elected branches
options.C: The court is acting undemocratically, but this is acceptable because courts are always wiser than elected officials
options.D: The court's action is unconstitutional because only the legislature, not the judiciary, can judge whether laws are valid

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracy is not simply rule by majority; it deliberately divides power so that no single branch — including popularly elected ones — can act without limit. Judicial review, the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the constitution, is a designed check against majoritarian overreach. Option A is the strongest distractor because the concept of democratic mandate is real and important, but it ignores the equally foundational principle that the constitution constrains all branches, including elected ones.

questions.title: Public Goods and Free Riders
questions.prompt: A lighthouse warns all ships of dangerous rocks, whether or not a ship's owner paid for its construction.
