A private company refuses to build one because it cannot stop non-paying ships from benefiting. What specific combination of characteristics makes the lighthouse a public good and explains the market's refusal to provide it?

options.A: The lighthouse is rival and excludable — only ships that pay can use it, which is why the private market won't fund it
options.B: The lighthouse is non-excludable and non-rival — you cannot stop non-payers from benefiting, and one ship using it doesn't reduce its benefit to others, so the private market cannot recover its costs
options.C: The lighthouse is a merit good — society values it more than individuals do, so private markets always underprice it
options.D: The lighthouse is non-excludable but rival — each additional ship that uses it reduces the warning signal, which is why private companies lose money providing it

questions.explanation: A public good is defined by being non-excludable (you cannot prevent people who haven't paid from benefiting) and non-rival (one person benefiting does not reduce availability for others); the lighthouse fits both criteria perfectly, creating a free-rider problem that means private firms cannot charge enough to cover costs. Option C is a strong distractor because merit goods are also underprovided by markets, but they are not the same as public goods — merit goods can be excludable (like education), which the lighthouse is not.

questions.title: Citizenship and Responsibility
questions.prompt: In ancient Athens, only free adult male citizens could vote in the assembly, yet Athens is often called the birthplace of democracy. A student argues this shows that citizenship has always been universal. What is the most precise error in the student's reasoning, and what does Athens' example actually demonstrate about democratic systems?

options.A: The student is correct: Athens proves democracy has always guaranteed equal rights to all people living in a society
options.B: The error is assuming historical democracies were universal — Athens excluded women, slaves, and non-citizens, showing that who counts as a 'citizen' with political rights has changed significantly over time
options.C: The error is calling Athens a democracy at all — it was actually an oligarchy because not every person participated
options.D: The student is correct that citizenship was universal in Athens, but wrong that Athens influenced later democracies

questions.explanation: Athenian democracy was real but deeply limited: women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners — who made up the majority of the population — were excluded from political participation. This shows that the concept of citizenship has been historically contested and expanded over time, not that it was ever universal. Option C is a tempting distractor because the exclusions were extensive, but political scientists still classify Athens as a form of democracy for its participating citizens — it was genuinely novel in giving those citizens direct participatory power.

questions.title: Non-State Actors' Global Influence
questions.prompt: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) operates in conflict zones regardless of which government controls the territory, sometimes criticising the actions of both governments and armed groups. Which concept best explains why this non-state actor can operate with this kind of independence?

options.A: It operates independently because it has military power that protects it from government interference
options.B: Its independence is based on its principle of neutrality and impartiality — refusing alignment with any political or military side gives it access and credibility across conflict lines
options.C: Non-state actors like this one are subject to full control by the United Nations, which grants them operating rights
options.D: It operates freely because international law gives all humanitarian organisations unlimited access to any territory in the world

questions.explanation: MSF's founding principles of neutrality (no taking sides in conflicts), impartiality (aid based on need, not identity), and independence (no government funding that would create political obligations) are what allow it to negotiate access across conflict lines; parties to conflicts are more likely to permit access if they trust the organisation will not take sides against them. Option D is a plausible distractor because humanitarian access is protected under international humanitarian law in principle, but in practice states and armed groups frequently violate these provisions — it is MSF's political neutrality that pragmatically enables access.

questions.title: Wealth Inequality and Taxation
questions.prompt: Country P uses a progressive tax system, where people with higher incomes pay a higher percentage of their earnings as tax. Country Q uses a flat tax, where everyone pays the same percentage. A student claims the flat tax is fairer because it treats everyone identically. Evaluate this claim using political philosophy.

options.A: The student is correct: treating everyone identically is the only definition of fairness in political philosophy
options.B: The claim confuses formal equality (same rules for everyone) with substantive equality (equal impact) — paying the same percentage is a much heavier real burden on low-income earners, which many philosophers argue is less fair
options.C: The student is correct because progressive taxation always reduces economic growth, making it both unfair and inefficient
options.D: The claim is correct from a Rawlsian perspective because Rawls believed all citizens should be treated with identical rules

questions.explanation: Political philosophers distinguish between formal equality (identical rules) and substantive equality (equal real-world impact): a flat tax percentage takes a much larger share of a poor person's spending power than a wealthy person's, meaning the burden is not equal in practice. Rawls, for example, would likely support progressive taxation as better protecting the least well-off. Option D is the strongest distractor because Rawls is associated with fairness, but his difference principle specifically justifies unequal treatment when it benefits the worst-off — contradicting the student's interpretation.

questions.title: State Formation and Authority
questions.prompt: Max Weber defined the state as the entity that holds a 'monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force' within a territory. A student argues that private security companies and licensed gun owners disprove this definition because they also use force legally. Identify the flaw in the student's argument.

options.A: The student is correct: Weber's definition is outdated because private actors now regularly use force without state involvement
options.B: The flaw is that private actors use force only because the state permits and regulates them — the state retains ultimate authority to grant, limit, or revoke that permission
options.C: The flaw is that Weber's definition applies only to dictatorships, not democracies where force is always distributed among citizens
options.D: The student is correct that private gun ownership disproves the monopoly, but private security companies actually support Weber's definition

questions.explanation: Weber's 'monopoly on legitimate force' does not mean only the state ever uses force; it means the state is the only entity that can authorise the use of force — private security and armed citizens act under state-granted licences and laws that the state can revoke. The student confuses 'delegated' use of force with an independent challenge to state authority. Option A is the strongest distractor because private military companies and armed groups do genuinely complicate state authority in fragile states, but in functioning states, their use of force is still state-regulated.

questions.title: Environmental Policy and Systems
questions.prompt: Scientists warn that fishing in international waters is collapsing because every fishing company takes as much as it can before competitors do, even though this will eventually destroy the fish population for everyone. This situation is called 'the tragedy of the commons.' Which response would best address this problem, and why?

options.A: Allow the free market to resolve it, since rising fish prices will eventually make fishing unprofitable, naturally stopping overfishing
options.B: Collective regulation — international agreements setting enforceable catch limits — because individual rational choices lead to collective ruin when a shared resource has no owner to protect it
options.C: Privatise the ocean by selling sections to fishing companies, since owners always protect their own property from overuse
options.D: Encourage voluntary restraint by individual companies, which is always sufficient to protect shared resources when the problem is clearly explained

questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons occurs precisely because individually rational behaviour (catch as much as possible) produces collectively irrational outcomes (resource collapse); the solution requires collective governance — binding international agreements with enforcement mechanisms — because voluntary restraint fails when competitors continue harvesting and individual companies bear all costs of restraint while sharing none of its benefits. Option A is a plausible distractor because market price signals do sometimes reduce demand, but fish populations can collapse before prices rise enough to deter overfishing, and the market signal comes too late.

questions.title: Historical Empires and Power
questions.prompt: The British Empire at its peak governed over 400 million people across multiple continents, using a combination of military force, economic control, and local administrators drawn from conquered populations. Which concept best explains how the Empire maintained control over far more people than Britain could physically station soldiers among?

options.A: The Empire maintained control purely through the threat of overwhelming military force deployed instantly anywhere in the empire
options.B: Indirect rule — using local elites and existing power structures to administer territories on Britain's behalf — reduced the number of British personnel needed while integrating local authority into the imperial system
options.C: The Empire succeeded primarily because colonised populations universally welcomed British governance as an improvement
options.D: Economic sanctions against any territory that resisted were the primary tool, as trade dependency made military force unnecessary

questions.explanation: The British Empire extensively used indirect rule — co-opting local kings, chiefs, and elites to enforce imperial authority — which dramatically reduced the personnel required for direct administration; in India, for instance, hundreds of millions were partly governed through local princes and a relatively small British civil service. Option A is the most tempting distractor because military force was certainly a foundation of imperial power, but the sheer geographic scale made direct military control alone logistically impossible — local collaboration was essential.

questions.title: Democracy vs. Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A country holds elections every four years, but only one political party is legally allowed to run candidates. Citizens may vote, but all candidates share the same ideology. A student claims this country is a democracy because it holds regular elections. What is the most precise reason this claim is incorrect?

options.A: Democracy requires elections to be held more frequently than every four years
options.B: Democracy requires genuine political competition and choice among candidates with different views
options.C: Democracy requires that every citizen, not just registered voters, must participate in elections
options.D: Democracy requires the leader to be chosen by a constitutional court rather than popular vote

questions.explanation: A core feature of democracy is meaningful electoral competition — voters must be able to choose between candidates representing different political options. A single-party election removes this choice, making it a tool of authoritarian control rather than genuine democratic representation. Option A is wrong because the frequency of elections is not the defining issue; four-year cycles are standard in many genuine democracies.

questions.title: Federalism and Power
questions.prompt: In a federal system, a national government passes an environmental law, but three regional governments refuse to enforce it, claiming it interferes with their local authority. Which principle of federalism best explains why this conflict can arise?

options.A: Federalism always grants regional governments supreme authority over national governments
options.B: Federalism divides sovereignty between levels of government, creating overlapping and sometimes competing jurisdictions
options.C: Federalism requires unanimous agreement among all regions before any national law can be passed
options.D: Federalism means the national government can only make laws about foreign policy and defence

questions.explanation: Federalism distributes sovereign power between national and regional governments, which creates jurisdictions that can overlap, especially in areas like environment, health, or education. This shared sovereignty is precisely what causes disputes when each level believes it has authority. Option A is incorrect because federalism does not automatically make regional governments supreme — the balance varies by constitution, and in most federal systems national law is supreme in defined areas.

questions.title: Market Failures Explained
questions.prompt: A factory produces cheap goods but releases pollution into a nearby river, harming fishing communities who were never consulted. The factory owner argues the market is working perfectly because supply meets demand and profit is being made. Evaluate this argument by identifying its central flaw.

options.A: The argument ignores that markets cannot function without government price controls
options.B: The argument fails to account for negative externalities — costs borne by third parties not involved in the transaction
options.C: The argument is flawed because profit-making is itself a sign of market failure
options.D: The argument overlooks the fact that pollution always reduces a firm's long-term profit, correcting itself automatically

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a transaction imposes costs on people outside the buyer-seller relationship — here, fishing communities suffer harm they did not agree to and are not compensated for. This is a classic market failure because the market price of the goods does not include the social cost of pollution. Option D is incorrect because pollution does not automatically reduce firm profits; firms often externalise costs indefinitely unless regulated.

questions.title: Locke's Social Contract
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that government authority comes from the consent of the governed and that people possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property. Which scenario would Locke most clearly use to justify citizens withdrawing their consent from a government?

options.A: A government raises taxes to fund public hospitals without holding a referendum on the specific amount
options.B: A government loses a close election and peacefully transfers power to the winning party
options.C: A government systematically seizes citizens' private property without compensation or legal process
options.D: A government signs an international trade treaty that some citizens believe harms local businesses

questions.explanation: Locke explicitly listed property as one of the three fundamental natural rights, and he argued that a government which violates these rights has broken the social contract, justifying resistance. Systematically seizing property without legal process is the most direct violation of Lockean principles. Option A is a distractor because Locke accepted that governments may levy taxes through legitimate legislative processes — taxation alone does not break the contract.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that true freedom comes from obeying the 'general will' — the collective good of society — rather than individual desires. A student claims this idea is identical to majority rule in a modern democracy. Identify the most important error in the student's claim.

options.A: The error is that Rousseau believed only educated citizens should vote, unlike majority rule which includes everyone
options.B: The error is that the general will refers to what is genuinely good for all of society, which may differ from what the majority actually votes for
options.C: The error is that Rousseau rejected all forms of government and believed people should live without any political authority
options.D: The error is that majority rule always produces the general will, so the two concepts are actually the same

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished the 'general will' — what is truly in society's collective interest — from the 'will of all,' which is simply the sum of individual preferences or majority votes. A majority could vote for something selfish or short-sighted that harms the common good, meaning majority rule and the general will can conflict. Option A is incorrect; Rousseau did not restrict voting to educated citizens — he was concerned with the quality of collective decision-making, not voter eligibility.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: Rawls proposed that fair principles of justice should be designed by people who do not know what position they will occupy in society — rich or poor, talented or not. What is the main purpose of this 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment?

options.A: To show that people who are ignorant make better political leaders than educated ones
options.B: To eliminate personal bias so that principles of justice are chosen impartially, protecting the most vulnerable
options.C: To argue that no one can ever know enough information to create a just society
options.D: To prove that equal distribution of all resources is the only morally acceptable outcome

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance is designed to remove self-interest from moral reasoning: if you do not know whether you will be born wealthy or poor, you are more likely to choose rules that protect everyone, especially the least advantaged. Rawls used this to derive his 'difference principle.' Option D is incorrect because Rawls did not demand equal distribution of everything — his difference principle allows inequalities if they benefit the worst-off members of society.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Country P has a mixed economy. The government provides universal healthcare, regulates banking, and owns the national railway, but most other industries are privately owned. Which statement best explains why mixed economies are more common globally than purely planned or purely free-market systems?

options.A: Mixed economies are more common because they are required by international law for all member states of the United Nations
options.B: Mixed economies attempt to balance the efficiency of markets with government intervention to correct failures and protect social welfare
options.C: Mixed economies guarantee equal wealth for all citizens while still allowing businesses to compete for customers
options.D: Mixed economies are more common because planned economies have never existed in any real country

questions.explanation: Mixed economies are widespread because neither pure markets nor pure planning works perfectly alone — markets generate growth but can fail to provide public goods or protect vulnerable people, while pure planning tends to cause inefficiency and lack of innovation. Most countries combine both approaches. Option C is incorrect: mixed economies do not guarantee equal wealth — they reduce inequality through welfare programs and regulation but do not eliminate income differences.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Limits
questions.prompt: In a constitutional democracy, a newly elected government with a large majority wants to pass a law removing freedom of speech protections from the constitution. The constitutional court blocks the law. A student argues the court is being undemocratic by overruling elected representatives. Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The student is correct because in a democracy, elected majorities should always have the final say on every law
options.B: The student is partially correct — courts should only block laws if they are requested to do so by citizens directly
options.C: The student is incorrect because constitutional democracy protects fundamental rights even from majority decisions, preventing 'tyranny of the majority'
options.D: The student is incorrect because the constitutional court was also elected by the people and therefore has equal democratic authority

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracy is built on the idea that certain fundamental rights cannot be removed even by a majority vote — this prevents a popular government from legally eliminating the rights of minorities or individuals. Judicial review exists precisely to enforce these limits. Option A reflects 'pure' majority rule but ignores the constitutional protection of rights, which is the defining feature that distinguishes constitutional democracy from unlimited majoritarian democracy.

questions.title: Cause of Revolutions
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen first when a government consistently ignores the economic needs of a large, poor population while visibly increasing the wealth of a small elite — even if the government maintains a strong military and controlled media?

options.A: The population will accept the situation because the military prevents any possibility of change
options.B: Grievances will build among the poor majority, increasing the likelihood of social unrest, protest, or revolutionary action
options.C: The economy will automatically correct itself as the elite invest their wealth back into society
options.D: International organisations will immediately intervene to redistribute wealth between the elite and the poor

questions.explanation: Historical patterns — including the French and Russian Revolutions — show that sustained economic inequality and political exclusion create deep social grievances that eventually drive unrest, even against militarily powerful regimes. The combination of deprivation and visible injustice is a well-established cause of revolutionary pressure. Option C is incorrect because the 'trickle-down' assumption is not reliable; historical evidence shows elite wealth does not automatically reach the poor without structural redistribution.

questions.title: Social Stratification Types
questions.prompt: In medieval feudal Europe, a serf could not legally leave the land they worked on, could not become a knight, and their children inherited the same status. Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes this as a 'closed' social stratification system?

options.A: People in the system lived in poverty, which always indicates a closed stratification system
options.B: Social position was fixed at birth and could not be changed through individual effort or achievement
options.C: The system was controlled by a military class, which always produces closed stratification
options.D: The system existed in Europe, where geography historically prevented social mobility

questions.explanation: A closed stratification system is defined by ascribed status — social position is inherited at birth and cannot be changed through personal achievement or effort. Feudal serfdom exemplifies this: birth determined one's legal, economic, and social standing permanently. Option A is incorrect because poverty alone does not define a closed system — open systems can also have poverty; the key distinguishing feature is whether mobility between strata is possible.

questions.title: Comparative Governance Systems
questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system, the head of government (Prime Minister) is chosen by the legislature and can be removed by a vote of no confidence. In a presidential system, the head of government is elected separately by citizens and serves a fixed term. Which statement best analyses a key consequence of this structural difference?

options.A: Presidential systems always produce stronger governments because the leader has a direct popular mandate
options.B: Parliamentary systems tend to produce faster policy responses to crises because the executive and legislature are fused, while presidential systems can experience gridlock when different parties control each branch
options.C: Parliamentary systems are less democratic because citizens do not directly vote for the head of government
options.D: Presidential systems guarantee more political stability because the fixed term prevents leadership changes during difficult periods

questions.explanation: Because the Prime Minister in a parliamentary system must maintain legislative support, the executive and legislature tend to work together more closely, allowing faster policy changes. Presidential systems can face 'divided government' — where the president's party differs from the congressional majority — creating legislative gridlock, as seen frequently in the United States. Option D is actually a disadvantage in disguise: a fixed term can prevent removal of a failing leader who a parliamentary no-confidence vote would remove quickly.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A government that uses force to stay in power has no legitimacy, while a government elected democratically always has full legitimacy.' Identify the most significant flaw in this argument.

options.A: The argument is flawed because legitimacy is entirely based on economic performance, not on how leaders come to power
options.B: The argument oversimplifies: democratic election can confer initial legitimacy, but governments can lose it through corruption or rights violations, and some non-elected authorities gain legitimacy through tradition or effectiveness
options.C: The argument is flawed only in its first part — force-based governments truly have no legitimacy, but elected governments always retain full legitimacy regardless of their actions
options.D: The argument is correct; political scientists universally agree that only democratic election produces legitimate authority

questions.explanation: Political legitimacy is multi-dimensional: Max Weber identified traditional, charismatic, and legal-rational sources of authority. An elected government can lose legitimacy through corruption, repression, or betrayal of voters, while a monarchy or traditional council may hold strong legitimacy through custom. Option C is wrong because even elected governments can become illegitimate — for example, Locke argued that a government violating natural rights loses its right to govern regardless of how it was elected.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council passed a resolution ordering Country X to stop its military actions, but Country X — a permanent member — vetoed enforcement measures. Which structural feature of the current international system does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: International law is completely ineffective because no country ever follows UN resolutions
options.B: The international system is anarchic in the sense that no overarching authority can compel the most powerful states to comply with international norms
options.C: The veto power proves that the UN was designed to benefit smaller nations over powerful ones
options.D: Security Council resolutions are only legally binding for countries that do not hold veto power

questions.explanation: International relations scholars describe the global system as 'anarchic' not because it is chaotic, but because there is no supreme authority above sovereign states that can force compliance — especially from powerful states with veto power. The five permanent Security Council members (US, UK, France, Russia, China) can each block enforcement actions against themselves. Option A overstates the case — many countries do follow international law most of the time for reasons of reputation, trade, and cooperation — but enforcement against great powers remains structurally weak.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Causes
questions.prompt: Country Q has a free-market economy. Over 30 years, the top 10% of earners have increased their share of total national income from 30% to 55%. Which combination of factors most plausibly explains this trend within a market system?

options.A: Government corruption and deliberate theft from the poor by political leaders
options.B: Returns to capital and skilled labour growing faster than wages for low-skilled workers, compounded by wealth generating further wealth over time
options.C: The poor deliberately choosing not to work hard enough to advance economically
options.D: Natural disasters repeatedly destroying assets owned only by lower-income groups

questions.explanation: In market economies, those who own capital (businesses, property, investments) tend to see their wealth grow faster than wages, especially for workers in low-skill sectors where automation competes. This compounding effect — wealth generating returns that are reinvested — is identified by economists including Thomas Piketty as a structural driver of inequality in capitalist systems. Option A may occur in some cases but is not a systemic explanation for a 30-year trend across a whole economy; structural economic forces are the primary driver.

questions.title: Propaganda and Political Control
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government funds all school textbooks, controls national television broadcasting, and requires patriotic ceremonies at all public events. Which concept from political science best describes the long-term political function of these policies?

options.A: Economic planning, because controlling information helps the government manage resource distribution
options.B: Political socialisation, in which the state systematically shapes citizens' values, beliefs, and loyalty from childhood to maintain regime support
options.C: Judicial review, because the government is using its authority to ensure laws are followed in educational settings
options.D: Federalism, because centralised control of education strengthens the national government over regional ones

questions.explanation: Political socialisation refers to the process by which individuals acquire political beliefs, values, and identities — authoritarian regimes deliberately control schools, media, and public rituals to shape citizens who accept and support the regime as natural and legitimate. This reduces the need for overt coercion. Option D has some surface logic but federalism describes how power is divided between government levels, not how governments shape citizen beliefs.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Country R has three branches of government: a legislature that makes laws, an executive that enforces them, and a judiciary that interprets them. The executive branch pressures judges to rule in its favour by threatening to cut the courts' budget. Which principle of democratic governance is most directly threatened?

options.A: Universal suffrage, because citizens lose the right to vote when courts are pressured
options.B: Judicial independence, which is essential for the rule of law and preventing the executive from placing itself above legal accountability
options.C: Proportional representation, because the court system should reflect the demographic composition of society
options.D: Federalism, because the executive is interfering with a regional government institution

questions.explanation: Judicial independence means courts must be free from political pressure so they can hold all branches of government accountable under the law. When an executive threatens the judiciary's budget to influence rulings, it undermines the rule of law and the separation of powers — a core pillar of constitutional democracy. Option A is incorrect because judicial independence and voting rights are separate principles; threatening courts does not directly remove citizens' right to vote.

questions.title: Nationalism and State Identity
questions.prompt: After a period of colonisation, Country S gains independence. Its new government promotes a single national language, rewrites school history to celebrate independence heroes, and creates national symbols like a flag and anthem. Which concept best explains why these actions are important for political stability in a newly independent state?

options.A: Nation-building: creating shared identity and loyalty to the new state among a potentially diverse population
options.B: Authoritarianism: imposing a single culture always indicates the suppression of minority political rights
options.C: Economic planning: controlling language and symbols is primarily a strategy for directing the economy
options.D: Federalism: recognising diverse groups within the country by giving each their own symbolic representation

questions.explanation: Nation-building is the deliberate process of constructing a shared national identity to unite citizens of a new or diverse state — it includes common symbols, narratives, and language policies. Newly independent post-colonial states often inherit diverse populations and borders drawn by colonial powers, making identity-building essential for cohesion and legitimate governance. Option B is a plausible distractor but is too broad — promoting national identity is not the same as authoritarianism, which involves suppressing political opposition and rights.

questions.title: Market vs. Planned Economy
questions.prompt: Country A uses a free market to set the price of bread. Country B's government sets the price of bread below market rate to ensure affordability. A student argues Country B's approach is always better because everyone can afford food. Evaluate the strongest challenge to this argument.

options.A: The strongest challenge is that governments should never interfere with any prices under any circumstances
options.B: The strongest challenge is that artificially low prices can reduce producers' incentive to make bread, potentially causing shortages that harm the people the policy intended to help
options.C: The strongest challenge is that bread is not important enough to justify government intervention in the economy
options.D: The strongest challenge is that the free market always produces lower prices than government price controls

questions.explanation: When governments set prices below the market rate (a price ceiling), producers receive less revenue, which can reduce their incentive to produce. This can lead to shortages — the opposite of what the policy intended. Historical examples include Soviet bread queues and Venezuelan food shortages. Option D is incorrect as a general claim — free markets do not always produce lower prices; they can produce monopoly pricing or exclude poor consumers entirely.

questions.title: Human Rights and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Country T's government argues that how it treats its own citizens is purely an internal matter and that other nations have no right to intervene, even if citizens are being severely oppressed. Which tension in international relations does this argument represent?

options.A: The tension between free trade and protectionism in global economic policy
options.B: The tension between state sovereignty — the right of nations to govern themselves without interference — and universal human rights norms
options.C: The tension between democratic and authoritarian states over which system produces better economic outcomes
options.D: The tension between national governments and multinational corporations over taxation rights

questions.explanation: The principle of state sovereignty (enshrined in the UN Charter) holds that each state governs its own territory without foreign interference. However, international human rights law — also part of the UN system — establishes standards that apply to all governments' treatment of people. These two principles can directly conflict when a state violates human rights and invokes sovereignty to block outside response. Option A describes a different international tension (trade policy) and is not relevant to the treatment of citizens.

questions.title: Cause and Effect in Policy
questions.prompt: A government cuts income taxes for all citizens, expecting higher consumer spending to grow the economy. Instead, wealthier citizens save most of their tax savings while poorer citizens spend their smaller savings quickly. Which concept best explains why the policy may have had unequal effects?

options.A: The marginal propensity to consume: lower-income households tend to spend a higher proportion of additional income than wealthy households
options.B: The law of supply and demand: cutting taxes always reduces consumer demand for goods
options.C: The principle of comparative advantage: wealthy citizens are better at making economic decisions than poor citizens
options.D: The concept of market failure: all tax cuts automatically create negative externalities for third parties

questions.explanation: The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) describes how much of an extra unit of income a person spends rather than saves. Lower-income households typically have a high MPC because they have unmet needs — they spend most of any additional money. Wealthier households, whose needs are already met, have a lower MPC and save more. This means tax cuts distributed equally across income groups tend to stimulate less spending than if directed at lower earners. Option C describes a normative opinion, not an economic concept, and has no basis in economic theory.

questions.title: Revolution and Social Change
questions.prompt: Historians note that revolutions often fail to achieve their stated goals: leaders who promised freedom sometimes create new dictatorships, and promised equality often benefits only a new elite. Which explanation best accounts for this recurring pattern?

options.A: Revolutions fail because the people who start them are always dishonest and never intended to fulfil their promises
options.B: Revolutionary leaders, once in power, face the same structural pressures as previous rulers — including threats to their authority — which often push them toward the same controlling behaviours they originally opposed
options.C: Revolutions fail because foreign countries always intervene militarily to restore the previous government
options.D: Revolutions are only successful when they are led by the military, not by civilian populations

questions.explanation: Political scientists and historians observe that revolutionary leaders often replicate authoritarian patterns not purely from personal dishonesty, but because governing is structurally difficult — threats of counter-revolution, economic crisis, and rival factions push leaders toward centralisation of power. The French Revolution's descent into the Reign of Terror and the Russian Revolution's shift to Stalinism illustrate this pattern. Option A assigns individual moral failure but ignores the structural and institutional pressures that shape behaviour in power.

questions.title: Citizenship and Rights
questions.prompt: Country U grants all adult citizens the right to vote but restricts free speech, requires government permission to hold public gatherings, and monitors citizens' private communications. A political philosopher would most likely describe Country U as what type of system?

options.A: A fully functioning liberal democracy, because universal suffrage is the only essential requirement
options.B: An electoral authoritarian regime, where elections exist but civil liberties required for genuine democracy are absent
options.C: A federal republic, because voting rights are shared between national and regional governments
options.D: A theocracy, because controlling speech and assembly indicates government based on religious law

questions.explanation: Electoral authoritarianism (sometimes called 'competitive authoritarianism') describes regimes that hold elections but repress the freedoms of speech, assembly, and press that make elections genuinely meaningful and competitive. Voting without these freedoms cannot produce real democratic accountability. Option A is incorrect: liberal democracy requires both electoral rights and civil liberties — suffrage alone is insufficient if citizens cannot freely organise, speak, or access information to make informed choices.

questions.title: Global Interdependence
questions.prompt: When a major earthquake struck Country V, neighbouring countries sent rescue teams and medical supplies, international NGOs provided food, and global media coverage attracted private donations from around the world. Which concept from international studies does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: Economic sanctions, because other countries used their resources as leverage to influence Country V's government
options.B: Complex interdependence, where states and non-state actors are connected through multiple channels — not only governments but also NGOs, media, and individuals
options.C: Realist power politics, where all assistance was given only because other countries calculated military advantage
options.D: Planned economy coordination, where international organisations directed all resource allocation globally

questions.explanation: Complex interdependence, developed by Keohane and Nye, describes a world in which states interact through many channels simultaneously — including NGOs, private actors, and media — not only through formal government-to-government relations. The earthquake response illustrates this perfectly: multiple non-state actors responded alongside governments. Option C incorrectly applies realist theory, which would predict states only act for strategic self-interest — but private citizens and NGOs who donated had no military calculation.

questions.title: Public Goods and Free Riders
questions.prompt: Country W builds a national flood defence system that protects all coastal towns. Some residents who never paid any taxes still receive protection from the flood barriers. A student argues the government should charge individual families for exactly how much flood protection they use. Identify the fundamental problem with this proposal.

options.A: The proposal would work perfectly in theory, but governments are too corrupt to collect the fees honestly
options.B: Flood protection is non-excludable — it is impossible to protect some houses in a coastal town while leaving neighbouring houses unprotected — making individual charging impractical
options.C: The proposal is unfair only because wealthier families would pay more than poor ones
options.D: Individual charging works for flood protection but fails for other public goods like street lighting

questions.explanation: Flood barriers are a public good partly because they are non-excludable — once a sea wall protects a coastline, it protects all nearby properties, and there is no practical way to withhold protection from those who do not pay. This makes individual pricing impossible to implement fairly or technically. Option D is incorrect because flood protection shares the same non-excludability problem as street lighting — both protect all nearby users regardless of payment.

questions.title: Perspective and Political Philosophy
questions.prompt: A libertarian argues that individuals should have maximum freedom from government interference, even if some become very wealthy and others very poor. A social democrat argues the government must reduce inequality through taxation and welfare. Both claim to value 'freedom.' How is it possible for both to use the same concept to reach opposite policy conclusions?

options.A: It is not possible; one side must be using the word 'freedom' dishonestly to mislead voters
options.B: They define freedom differently: libertarians emphasise negative freedom (freedom from interference), while social democrats emphasise positive freedom (freedom to actually achieve a good life, requiring resources and support)
options.C: Both mean the same thing by freedom, but they disagree only about which economic system produces faster growth
options.D: Freedom is a meaningless concept in political philosophy and politicians use it purely as an emotional slogan

questions.explanation: Political philosopher Isaiah Berlin distinguished 'negative liberty' (freedom from external constraint or interference) from 'positive liberty' (freedom to achieve one's potential, which requires having real opportunities and resources). Libertarians prioritise negative freedom — government should not restrict individuals. Social democrats prioritise positive freedom — without economic resources, formal rights mean little. Both concepts are genuinely about freedom, explaining the disagreement. Option A incorrectly treats this as dishonesty rather than a genuine philosophical distinction.

questions.title: Democracy Core Features
questions.prompt: Which feature most fundamentally distinguishes a liberal democracy from other forms of government that also hold elections?

options.A: Citizens vote for representatives in regular elections
options.B: Constitutional protections limit what even elected majorities can do
options.C: The government controls a large share of the national economy
options.D: A single national leader is chosen by popular vote

questions.explanation: Liberal democracy is defined not just by elections but by constitutional constraints — such as bills of rights and independent courts — that prevent majorities from violating individual freedoms. Option A is insufficient because authoritarian states like North Korea also hold elections, yet they are not considered democracies.

questions.title: Market Economy Basics
questions.prompt: In a free-market economy, prices rise sharply when a popular product becomes scarce. Which mechanism does this price rise perform in the market system?

options.A: It signals producers to increase supply and signals consumers to reduce demand
options.B: It allows the government to redistribute the product to those most in need
options.C: It guarantees that all consumers will eventually receive equal shares of the product
options.D: It encourages the government to set a price ceiling to protect consumers

questions.explanation: In market theory, rising prices serve as a signal: higher prices incentivise producers to supply more and simultaneously discourage consumers from buying as much, restoring equilibrium over time. Option B describes a planned economy response, not a market mechanism — markets allocate by price, not by need.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitarism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'In a federal system, regional governments have no real power because the national government can always overrule them.' Identify the error in this claim.

options.A: Regional governments in federal systems actually control the national military
options.B: Federalism constitutionally divides sovereignty, giving regional governments protected powers the centre cannot simply override
options.C: Federal systems require unanimous agreement among all regions before the national government can pass any law
options.D: In a federation, regional governments can veto any national election result

questions.explanation: Federalism is defined by a constitutional division of sovereign powers between levels of government; regional powers in areas like education or policing are legally protected, not subject to routine national override. The student's claim actually describes a unitary system, not a federal one. Options A and D describe powers that regional governments simply do not possess.

questions.title: Locke's Social Contract
questions.prompt: According to John Locke, governments derive their legitimate authority from the consent of the governed. Which of the following best states what this means in practice?

options.A: Citizens must obey any law passed by a majority, even if it violates their rights
options.B: A government that consistently violates natural rights loses its right to rule and may be replaced
options.C: Only property-owning citizens can give consent, so only they have political rights
options.D: Governments gain authority automatically once they win a military conflict

questions.explanation: Locke argued in his Second Treatise that government authority rests on protecting natural rights (life, liberty, property); a government that violates these rights breaks the social contract and citizens are justified in replacing it. Option A contradicts Locke's view — he explicitly held that majority rule cannot override fundamental natural rights.

questions.title: Planned Economy Features
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate description of how a centrally planned economy decides what goods are produced?

options.A: Firms independently compete to produce whichever goods yield the highest profit
options.B: International trade agreements determine which industries each country must develop
options.C: Central government authorities set production targets based on national plans rather than market prices
options.D: Consumer spending patterns automatically direct resources to the most popular products

questions.explanation: In a centrally planned economy, such as the Soviet Union under Stalin's Five-Year Plans, state planners rather than prices or consumer demand determine what is produced and in what quantities. Option A describes a free-market economy where profit signals guide production decisions.

questions.title: Power and Authority
questions.prompt: Max Weber distinguished between 'power' and 'authority.' Which statement most accurately captures the key difference between these two concepts?

options.A: Power refers to elected officials; authority refers to military commanders
options.B: Power is the ability to make others comply even against their will; authority is power that is recognised as legitimate
options.C: Power is always legal; authority can be used outside the law
options.D: Power belongs to democratic governments; authority belongs to authoritarian ones

questions.explanation: Weber defined power (Macht) as the capacity to impose one's will regardless of resistance, while authority (Herrschaft) is power that those subject to it accept as rightful and legitimate. Option D is incorrect because both democratic and authoritarian governments exercise both power and authority, though the sources of legitimacy differ.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau introduced the concept of the 'general will' as the basis for legitimate government. Which of the following best explains what Rousseau meant by this term?

options.A: The combined personal wishes of every individual citizen added together
options.B: The decision made by whichever political party wins the most votes in an election
options.C: The shared common good of the whole community, which may differ from what individuals personally want
options.D: The will of the monarch, who alone understands what is best for the nation

questions.explanation: Rousseau's 'general will' (volonté générale) refers to what is genuinely in the best interest of the whole community, which he distinguished from the 'will of all' — the mere sum of individual preferences. Option A describes the 'will of all,' which Rousseau explicitly contrasted with the general will as a different and inferior concept.

questions.title: Social Stratification Types
questions.prompt: In a caste system, a person born into the lowest caste is legally and socially prohibited from entering certain occupations or marrying outside their caste. Which type of social stratification does this describe?

options.A: Open stratification, because movement between castes occasionally happens
options.B: Meritocratic stratification, because skill still determines success within a caste
options.C: Closed stratification, because social position is fixed at birth with no legal path for movement
options.D: Class stratification, because economic wealth determines each person's social rank

questions.explanation: A caste system is the classic example of closed stratification: social position is ascribed at birth and movement between groups is legally or socially forbidden. Option D is incorrect because class stratification — unlike caste — is based on economic position and allows for social mobility through wealth or education.

questions.title: Authoritarianism Characteristics
questions.prompt: Which combination of features most accurately distinguishes an authoritarian regime from a democracy, even when both hold elections?

options.A: Authoritarian regimes have larger populations and more diverse economies
options.B: Authoritarian regimes restrict press freedom, limit opposition, and concentrate power without meaningful judicial independence
options.C: Authoritarian regimes always use violence against citizens, while democracies never do
options.D: Authoritarian regimes rely entirely on foreign aid and cannot sustain their economies independently

questions.explanation: Political scientists identify restricted civil liberties, controlled media, suppressed opposition parties, and weak judicial independence as hallmarks of authoritarianism — features that can coexist with staged elections. Option C is an oversimplification: democracies can use state force legally, and some authoritarian regimes maintain minimal stability without constant direct violence.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Country X has private businesses setting most prices, but the government runs public healthcare and regulates minimum wages. Which economic system does Country X most closely represent?

options.A: A centrally planned economy, because the government controls key services
options.B: A mixed economy, because both market mechanisms and government intervention operate simultaneously
options.C: A pure free-market economy, because private businesses still set most prices
options.D: A subsistence economy, because basic needs like healthcare are provided without payment

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private market activity with government provision of certain goods and regulatory oversight — exactly what Country X demonstrates with private pricing alongside public healthcare and wage laws. Option A is incorrect because a centrally planned economy would have government control over the majority of production and pricing, not just selected sectors.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: Political scientists often argue that revolutions are most likely when a gap exists between people's expectations and their actual conditions. What is the academic term for this gap?

options.A: Social mobility
options.B: Relative deprivation
options.C: Class consciousness
options.D: Structural functionalism

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation, developed by theorist Ted Gurr, refers to the perceived gap between what people feel they deserve and what they actually receive — a key driver of political grievance and revolution. Class consciousness (Option C) refers to Karl Marx's idea of workers recognising their shared economic interests, which is related but describes a different mechanism.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: John Rawls proposed the 'veil of ignorance' as a tool for thinking about fairness. What does reasoning behind the veil of ignorance require a person to do?

options.A: Prioritise the interests of the wealthiest citizens when designing laws
options.B: Design society's basic rules without knowing what position, wealth, or identity they will have within it
options.C: Ignore all inequalities and treat every citizen as if they have identical income
options.D: Consult only elected representatives when deciding what policies are just

questions.explanation: Rawls's veil of ignorance asks decision-makers to imagine they do not know their future social position, wealth, talents, or identity before agreeing on rules — ensuring impartiality. Option C misrepresents Rawls: he did not require ignoring inequalities but rather designing rules so that inequalities benefit the least advantaged (the difference principle).

questions.title: Market Failure: Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally produces steel but releases pollution that makes nearby residents sick. No compensation is paid to those residents. This is an example of which economic concept?

options.A: A positive externality, because the factory creates jobs for the community
options.B: A negative externality, because third parties bear costs not reflected in the factory's prices
options.C: A public good problem, because the air is shared by everyone in the region
options.D: A monopoly failure, because only one factory controls the steel market

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a third party — here, nearby residents — suffers costs from an economic activity without compensation, and these costs are not included in the producer's price. Option C conflates the concept with public goods theory; while air is shared, the specific issue here is cost imposition on third parties, which is the definition of an externality.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy
questions.prompt: Why do constitutional democracies typically establish an independent judiciary separate from the elected legislature and executive?

options.A: To give judges the power to create new tax policies without parliamentary approval
options.B: To ensure courts can strike down laws that violate constitutional rights, even if those laws are popular
options.C: To allow the judiciary to remove elected governments that perform poorly in opinion polls
options.D: To guarantee that all judges are elected by the public in regular competitive elections

questions.explanation: Judicial independence allows courts to act as a check on legislative and executive power by reviewing whether laws comply with the constitution — a function known as judicial review, famously established in the US by Marbury v. Madison (1803). Option C misrepresents the role: courts do not remove governments based on popularity but on legality.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: The principle of separation of powers divides government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches. What is the primary purpose of this division?

options.A: To increase government efficiency by specialising each branch in a different policy area
options.B: To prevent any single branch from accumulating unchecked power by having branches oversee each other
options.C: To ensure that economic policy is never influenced by political decisions
options.D: To allow regional governments to participate equally in national decision-making

questions.explanation: Montesquieu, who popularised the doctrine in 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748), argued that separating powers creates mutual oversight — a system of checks and balances — preventing tyranny. Option A reflects a misunderstanding: efficiency is not the goal; limiting arbitrary power is.

questions.title: International Law Sources
questions.prompt: International law does not have a single global legislature that passes binding laws on all countries. Which of the following is recognised as a primary source of international law?

options.A: Resolutions passed by any country's national parliament
options.B: Decisions made by multinational corporations about global trade standards
options.C: Treaties voluntarily signed by states, and customary practices states follow out of a sense of legal obligation
options.D: Rulings issued by the United Nations Security Council on all matters of global governance

questions.explanation: The Statute of the International Court of Justice (Article 38) identifies treaties and customary international law — practices followed by states from a sense of legal obligation (opinio juris) — as primary sources of international law. Option D is inaccurate: the UN Security Council's binding resolutions apply only to matters of international peace and security, not all areas of global governance.

questions.title: Political Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A new government came to power through a free and fair election but is making deeply unpopular economic decisions. A student argues the government has now lost its legitimacy. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because legitimacy in a democracy requires every policy to be popular
options.B: The claim is flawed because electoral legitimacy is based on the process of being elected, not on ongoing approval of each decision
options.C: The claim is correct because economic failure automatically removes the legal right to govern
options.D: The claim is flawed because governments can only lose legitimacy if a court formally rules against them

questions.explanation: Political legitimacy from democratic elections derives from the process — a free, fair vote — not from the continuous popularity of every subsequent decision. Governments routinely make unpopular choices between elections without losing their democratic mandate. Option A confuses popularity (measured by opinion polls) with legitimacy (based on recognised rightful authority).

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: Both Hobbes and Locke wrote about the 'state of nature' — life before government. Compare their views: which statement correctly identifies a key difference between them?

options.A: Hobbes believed the state of nature was peaceful; Locke believed it was violent and chaotic
options.B: Hobbes believed humans were naturally rational and cooperative; Locke believed they were naturally selfish
options.C: Hobbes described the state of nature as a war of all against all; Locke described it as governed by natural law and reason
options.D: Both philosophers agreed the state of nature was identical, but disagreed only on what type of government should replace it

questions.explanation: Hobbes famously described the state of nature in Leviathan (1651) as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a condition of constant war. Locke, by contrast, argued in his Second Treatise that natural law and reason gave people rights even before government. Option A reverses their actual positions entirely.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Measures
questions.prompt: The Gini coefficient is used to measure income inequality in a country. A country with a Gini coefficient of 0 would represent which situation?

options.A: Complete inequality, where one person holds all national income
options.B: Perfect equality, where every person has an identical share of national income
options.C: A situation where GDP per capita is exactly equal to the national average wage
options.D: Zero economic growth, meaning the country has not expanded its economy in one year

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality — everyone has the same income) to 1 (or 100) representing complete inequality where one person holds all income. Option A describes a Gini coefficient of 1, not 0 — students often reverse these two endpoints.

questions.title: Role of Civil Society
questions.prompt: Civil society organisations — such as charities, trade unions, and advocacy groups — operate between individuals and the state. Which function do they most commonly perform in a democracy?

options.A: They replace political parties as the main mechanism for choosing government leaders
options.B: They hold government accountable, represent citizen interests, and provide services the state does not deliver
options.C: They enforce laws on behalf of the government when police resources are insufficient
options.D: They negotiate international treaties on behalf of the nation's citizens

questions.explanation: Civil society organisations are recognised in democratic theory as a crucial 'third sector' that monitors government, advocates for specific groups, and fills gaps in public service provision — strengthening democratic accountability. Option A is incorrect: political parties, not civil society groups, are the primary mechanism for competitive elections in representative democracies.

questions.title: Nationalism and the State
questions.prompt: What does the principle of 'national self-determination' claim that a nation — a group sharing language, culture, and identity — has the right to do?

options.A: Impose its cultural practices on neighbouring countries through economic pressure
options.B: Govern itself independently, ideally through its own sovereign state
options.C: Automatically receive a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council
options.D: Exclude members of other national groups from living within its territory

questions.explanation: National self-determination — prominently promoted by US President Woodrow Wilson after World War I — holds that nations (cultural-linguistic communities) have the right to govern themselves, ideally through their own sovereign state. Option D describes ethnic exclusionism or xenophobia, which is a different and morally problematic concept unrelated to the formal principle.

questions.title: Propaganda and Authoritarian Control
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government funds artists, filmmakers, and teachers to promote a single approved version of national history. Which concept best describes this strategy of social control?

options.A: Judicial independence
options.B: Pluralism
options.C: Ideological hegemony through propaganda
options.D: Positive discrimination

questions.explanation: Using state-funded culture, education, and media to promote a single official ideology is a classic form of ideological hegemony and propaganda — used by regimes such as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union to shape how citizens think about society and history. Option B (pluralism) is the opposite: it describes societies where multiple competing viewpoints coexist freely.

questions.title: Comparative Governance: Parliaments
questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system, the head of government (Prime Minister) remains in office only as long as they retain majority support in the legislature. How does this differ from a presidential system?

options.A: In a presidential system, the president can also be removed at any time by a simple parliamentary majority
options.B: In a presidential system, the executive serves a fixed term and is independently elected, separate from the legislature
options.C: In a parliamentary system, the Prime Minister is always chosen by a national popular vote
options.D: Presidential systems always have stronger protections for civil liberties than parliamentary systems

questions.explanation: In presidential systems like the United States, the executive (President) is directly elected for a fixed term and cannot be removed by a simple legislative majority — creating a strict separation between executive and legislative branches. Option A describes a parliamentary vote of no confidence, which applies to parliamentary systems, not presidential ones.

questions.title: Human Rights Framework
questions.prompt: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) classifies rights into different categories. Which of the following is an example of an economic and social right, rather than a civil and political right?

options.A: The right to a fair trial before an independent court
options.B: The right to freedom from torture and cruel punishment
options.C: The right to an adequate standard of living, including food, housing, and healthcare
options.D: The right to vote and participate in free elections

questions.explanation: Economic and social rights (sometimes called 'second generation' rights) include the right to work, education, healthcare, and an adequate standard of living — enshrined in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966). Options A, B, and D are civil and political rights ('first generation'), which protect individuals from government abuse and guarantee participation in public life.

questions.title: Market Failure: Public Goods
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Street lighting is just like any other commercial product — if people value it, they will pay for it privately.' Identify the most significant flaw in this argument.

options.A: Street lighting is too expensive for any private company to produce at any price
options.B: Street lighting is non-excludable and non-rival, making it a public good that private markets systematically underprovide
options.C: Street lighting should be provided by international organisations rather than local governments
options.D: Street lighting is already profitable, so private companies would actually overprovide it without government involvement

questions.explanation: Street lighting is a classic public good: it is non-excludable (you cannot stop passersby from benefiting) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce availability for others). These properties create the free-rider problem, meaning private firms cannot efficiently charge users, so markets underprovide it. Option A is factually wrong — the issue is not cost impossibility but the inability to exclude non-payers.

questions.title: Democracy Core Features
questions.prompt: Which feature most directly distinguishes a liberal democracy from a system where leaders are elected but face no constitutional limits on their power?

options.A: Citizens vote in regular elections to choose their representatives
options.B: The rule of law constrains government power and protects individual rights
options.C: The government controls the economy to ensure equal distribution of resources
options.D: A single political party organises and runs all elections

questions.explanation: Liberal democracy requires not just elections but constitutional constraints — the rule of law — that prevent elected leaders from abusing power and that protect civil liberties. Option A describes a necessary but insufficient condition: even authoritarian regimes hold elections, so voting alone does not distinguish liberal democracy.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that governments derive their authority from the consent of the governed. Which of the following best states what Locke believed citizens were entitled to do if a government consistently violated their natural rights?

options.A: Accept the government's decisions because stability is more important than rights
options.B: Petition the monarch directly and await a royal pardon
options.C: Dissolve the government and establish a new one that protects their rights
options.D: Transfer authority to an international body such as the United Nations

questions.explanation: Locke's Second Treatise of Government explicitly states that when a government breaks the social contract by violating natural rights, citizens have the right to dissolve it and form a new government. Option A contradicts Locke's theory, which prioritises rights over mere stability.

questions.title: Market Economy Basics
questions.prompt: In a free-market economy, prices for goods and services are primarily determined by which mechanism?

options.A: Government ministers setting prices based on production costs
options.B: Trade unions negotiating with employers each year
options.C: The interaction of supply and demand between buyers and sellers
options.D: International agreements between trading nations

questions.explanation: The defining feature of a market economy is that prices emerge from the decentralised interaction of supply and demand — when demand rises or supply falls, prices increase, and vice versa. Option A describes how prices work in a centrally planned economy, not a free market.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitarianism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'In a federal system, the national government always has supreme authority over every area of policy.' Identify the most significant error in this claim.

options.A: Federal systems do not have a national government at all
options.B: Federalism divides powers between national and regional governments, so regional governments have constitutionally protected authority in certain areas
options.C: Federal systems give all power to regional governments, leaving the national government with only symbolic authority
options.D: In federal systems, the military controls final decision-making, not elected governments

questions.explanation: Federalism by definition divides sovereign authority between levels of government, with the constitution protecting regional powers in specified areas — the national government cannot override these without constitutional change. Option C is the opposite error: it over-corrects by eliminating national authority, which is equally inaccurate.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau introduced the concept of the 'general will' to explain legitimate political authority. Which statement most accurately describes what Rousseau meant by this term?

options.A: The personal wishes of the monarch as representative of the nation
options.B: The sum of every individual's private interests and desires
options.C: The collective interest of the whole community that aims at the common good
options.D: A majority vote on any single policy issue at a given moment

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished the general will — oriented toward the common good of the entire community — from the 'will of all,' which is merely the sum of individual self-interests. Option B describes the will of all, which Rousseau explicitly said was not the same as the general will.

questions.title: Authoritarian Control Methods
questions.prompt: Which of the following government actions is most characteristic of an authoritarian regime rather than a democratic one?

options.A: Holding regular elections with multiple competing political parties
options.B: Allowing independent courts to review the legality of government decisions
options.C: Banning opposition parties and prosecuting critics of the ruling government
options.D: Publishing a national budget that citizens can examine and debate

questions.explanation: Authoritarian regimes characteristically suppress political competition by banning opposition parties and silencing critics, often through legal prosecution or imprisonment, removing the checks that define democratic governance. Options A, B, and D all describe features of accountable, democratic governance.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Country M has private businesses that set their own prices, but the government also runs public hospitals and regulates pollution levels. Which economic system does Country M most closely represent?

options.A: A centrally planned economy
options.B: A mixed economy
options.C: A pure free-market economy
options.D: A barter economy

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private market activity with government intervention — including public services and regulation — which precisely describes Country M's combination of private pricing and state-run hospitals with environmental rules. A centrally planned economy would have the government controlling prices and production across the entire economy, not just specific sectors.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: Compare Locke's and Rousseau's views on the social contract. Which statement most accurately identifies a key difference between them?

options.A: Locke believed the state of nature was peaceful and cooperative, while Rousseau believed it was violent and dangerous
options.B: Locke emphasised protecting individual property rights, while Rousseau prioritised the collective general will above individual interests
options.C: Locke argued that governments should never be replaced, while Rousseau said citizens must always obey the sovereign
options.D: Rousseau believed only wealthy landowners should form the social contract, while Locke included all citizens equally

questions.explanation: Locke's social contract centres on protecting pre-existing natural rights — especially life, liberty, and property — as its primary purpose, whereas Rousseau subordinated individual interests to the general will of the community. Option A reverses their actual positions: Locke described the state of nature as largely peaceful, while Hobbes (not Rousseau) called it dangerous.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Why does a government that uses only force and fear to maintain control face greater long-term instability than one whose authority citizens regard as legitimate?

options.A: Force is always less expensive than building public consent, so governments that rely on it quickly run out of money
options.B: Citizens who accept a government's right to rule voluntarily comply, reducing the need for constant coercion and making the system more stable
options.C: International law prohibits governments from using force against their own citizens under any circumstances
options.D: Governments that rely on fear automatically lose all military support within five years

questions.explanation: Political scientists such as Max Weber distinguish power from legitimate authority: when citizens accept a government's right to rule, they comply voluntarily, which is far more sustainable than coercion that requires constant enforcement and breeds resistance. Option A contains a partial truth but is not the core political science explanation for why legitimacy matters.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: John Rawls proposed the 'veil of ignorance' as a tool for designing a just society. What did he mean by this concept?

options.A: Citizens should be kept unaware of government decisions to prevent protests
options.B: Judges must not see the faces of defendants to ensure impartial verdicts
options.C: People designing society's rules should imagine they do not know their own social position, wealth, or abilities
options.D: Voters should not be told which party a candidate belongs to before casting their ballot

questions.explanation: Rawls's veil of ignorance is a thought experiment in which individuals design social rules without knowing what position they will occupy in society — ensuring principles chosen are fair to all, including the worst-off. Option B confuses the metaphor with legal practice; judicial impartiality is a separate concept from Rawls's original position.

questions.title: Market Failure Concept
questions.prompt: A factory produces chemicals and releases waste into a nearby river, harming local fishing communities who have no part in the transaction. Economists call the cost imposed on those communities an example of which concept?

options.A: A positive externality
options.B: A negative externality
options.C: A merit good
options.D: A trade deficit
