questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a transaction imposes costs on third parties who did not agree to bear them — the factory's pollution harming fishers is a textbook example. A positive externality, option A, would involve benefits spilling over to third parties (such as a beekeeper whose bees also pollinate neighbouring farms).

questions.title: Revolution Causes
questions.prompt: Historians argue that revolutions rarely occur simply because people are poor — they are more likely when expectations rise faster than actual conditions improve. Which concept from social science best describes this gap?

options.A: Social mobility
options.B: Relative deprivation
options.C: Class consciousness
options.D: Political socialisation

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation refers to the sense of frustration created when people perceive a gap between what they expect and what they actually receive — this feeling, rather than absolute poverty, is a key driver of revolutionary action according to theorists like Ted Gurr. Class consciousness (option C) refers to workers recognising their shared class interests, which is a related but distinct Marxist concept.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy
questions.prompt: A constitution serves several functions in a democratic state. Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of a constitution?

options.A: To provide a detailed plan for the government's annual budget
options.B: To establish the fundamental rules governing the structure and limits of government power
options.C: To list every law that citizens must obey in daily life
options.D: To describe the country's history and cultural traditions

questions.explanation: A constitution's primary role is to set out the fundamental framework of government — how power is distributed, what rights citizens hold, and what limits apply to authorities — acting as the supreme law above ordinary legislation. Option A confuses constitutional function with budgetary legislation, which is a separate governmental process.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Why do many democratic systems divide government into separate legislative, executive, and judicial branches rather than concentrating all power in one body?

options.A: To make government decision-making faster and more efficient
options.B: To ensure each branch can check and limit the power of the others, preventing tyranny
options.C: To allow different political parties to each control one branch of government
options.D: To reduce the number of laws that a country needs to function

questions.explanation: The doctrine of separation of powers, developed by thinkers like Montesquieu, creates a system of checks and balances where each branch can restrain the others, preventing any single body from accumulating unchecked authority. Option A is actually a weakness of separation of powers, not a reason for it — shared power often slows decision-making.

questions.title: Social Stratification Types
questions.prompt: Examine the following: in caste systems, a person's social rank is fixed from birth and cannot be changed through personal achievement. Which sociological term best describes this type of social structure?

options.A: An open stratification system
options.B: A meritocracy
options.C: A closed stratification system
options.D: A pluralist society

questions.explanation: A closed stratification system assigns social position by birth with no possibility of movement between ranks — the caste system is the classic historical example of this structure. A meritocracy (option B) is the opposite: it rewards individual talent and effort rather than inherited status.

questions.title: International Law Basis
questions.prompt: International law differs from domestic law in an important structural way. Which statement most accurately describes this difference?

options.A: International law applies only to non-governmental organisations, not to states
options.B: International law is created by a single world government that all nations must obey
options.C: International law largely depends on the voluntary consent of states, with no single authority able to enforce it
options.D: Domestic law applies globally while international law applies only within one country

questions.explanation: Unlike domestic legal systems with police and courts that can compel compliance, international law primarily relies on state consent — through treaties and customary practice — and enforcement mechanisms remain weak and dependent on political will. Option B is incorrect because there is no world government; bodies like the UN Security Council have limited enforcement powers and members can veto actions against themselves.

questions.title: Planned Economy Features
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, which body makes the key decisions about what goods are produced, how they are produced, and who receives them?

options.A: Individual consumers expressing their preferences through purchasing choices
options.B: Private corporations competing with one another for profit
options.C: The central government or state planning authority
options.D: International trade organisations setting global quotas

questions.explanation: The defining characteristic of a centrally planned economy is that the state — through a planning authority — makes the fundamental economic decisions about production and distribution, replacing the price mechanism used in market economies. Option A describes how consumer sovereignty works in a market economy, not a planned one.

questions.title: Weber's Types of Authority
questions.prompt: A leader is obeyed because citizens believe in the sacred tradition that has always placed this family in power, passed from parent to child over centuries. According to Max Weber, which type of authority does this represent?

options.A: Rational-legal authority
options.B: Charismatic authority
options.C: Traditional authority
options.D: Bureaucratic authority

questions.explanation: Weber defined traditional authority as power accepted because of long-established customs and hereditary status — exactly the dynastic family scenario described. Charismatic authority (option B) rests on a leader's personal qualities and extraordinary appeal, not inherited tradition.

questions.title: Political Participation Forms
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Voting in elections is the only meaningful form of political participation in a democracy.' Evaluate this claim by identifying its most significant weakness.

options.A: The claim is correct because elections are the only mechanism citizens have to influence government
options.B: The claim ignores that citizens also shape policy through protests, petitions, joining parties, contacting representatives, and civil society organisations
options.C: The claim is flawed because voting has been abolished in most modern democracies
options.D: The claim understates the role of the military in shaping democratic decisions

questions.explanation: Democratic participation includes a wide range of activities — lobbying, protest, civil society engagement, party membership, public consultation — that influence policy between elections. Option A repeats the original error rather than identifying a flaw, while options C and D are factually incorrect.

questions.title: Comparative Governance
questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system, the head of government is drawn from and accountable to the legislature. In a presidential system, the head of government is separately elected and independent of the legislature. What is one significant consequence of this structural difference?

options.A: Presidential systems always produce stronger protection of civil liberties than parliamentary ones
options.B: In parliamentary systems, the government can lose power through a vote of no confidence in the legislature, creating direct legislative accountability
options.C: Parliamentary systems are only found in monarchies, while presidential systems exist only in republics
options.D: Presidential systems give courts more power than parliamentary systems do

questions.explanation: A vote of no confidence — where the legislature can remove the executive — is a defining feature of parliamentary systems that creates continuous accountability; this mechanism does not exist in presidential systems where the executive serves a fixed term. Option C is factually wrong: parliamentary republics such as Germany and India are common examples.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democracy
questions.prompt: Political scientists often argue that a strong civil society — including independent trade unions, religious organisations, and free press — is essential to a healthy democracy. Why?

options.A: Civil society organisations replace political parties and make elections unnecessary
options.B: Civil society provides space for citizens to organise, voice concerns, and hold government accountable between elections
options.C: Civil society ensures that only educated citizens can participate in political decisions
options.D: Civil society organisations control government spending and prevent corruption through direct financial oversight

questions.explanation: Civil society creates an independent sphere between the individual and the state where citizens can organise, advocate, and scrutinise power — performing a watchdog function that elections alone cannot provide. Option A is incorrect: civil society complements rather than replaces elections and political parties.

questions.title: Human Rights Universality
questions.prompt: Some governments argue that human rights are culturally relative — different societies have different values, so rights should vary by culture. Critics respond that rights are universal. Which argument best supports the universalist position?

options.A: Western nations invented the concept of rights and therefore their version is automatically correct
options.B: Because rights are created by governments, each government may define them differently for its own population
options.C: Certain rights — such as freedom from torture — protect human dignity that all people share regardless of culture, and were agreed upon by states from diverse regions in the 1948 Universal Declaration
options.D: Rights are universal because the United Nations can always enforce them against any government

questions.explanation: Universalists argue that some rights protect inherent human dignity shared by all people, and point to the 1948 UDHR — adopted by states from many cultural backgrounds — as evidence of cross-cultural agreement. Option D is incorrect because, as noted in international law, the UN cannot reliably enforce rights against powerful or non-compliant states.

questions.title: Government Revenue Sources
questions.prompt: Governments in market economies fund public services primarily through which mechanism?

options.A: Selling goods and services at market prices in competition with private businesses
options.B: Collecting taxes from individuals and businesses
options.C: Printing unlimited money to pay for any public expenditure needed
options.D: Borrowing from the World Bank, which never requires repayment

questions.explanation: Taxation — on income, goods, corporate profits, and other economic activities — is the primary revenue source for governments in market and mixed economies, enabling them to fund services without producing goods commercially. Option C is incorrect because printing money without limit causes inflation, undermining the economy.

questions.title: Globalisation and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to a nation's ability to set its own economic policies independently if it joined a deeply integrated economic union that required all members to follow shared trade rules and use a common currency?

options.A: Its economic sovereignty would increase because it gains access to larger markets
options.B: Its economic sovereignty would be reduced because key policy decisions are shared or transferred to the union level
options.C: Its political sovereignty would immediately disappear and the nation would cease to exist
options.D: There would be no change in its sovereignty, as economic unions are always purely voluntary and non-binding

questions.explanation: Joining a deep economic union — like the Eurozone — requires members to give up independent monetary policy (they cannot set their own interest rates or exchange rates) and align trade regulations, significantly constraining national economic decision-making. Option C overstates the effect: nations retain political sovereignty and legal existence even within economic unions.

questions.title: Propaganda and Ideology
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government funds school textbooks, produces all television news, and requires students to attend loyalty ceremonies. Which political concept best describes the government's systematic strategy in these actions?

options.A: Political socialisation through state-controlled propaganda
options.B: Federalism through regional education policy
options.C: Free-market competition among media providers
options.D: Judicial independence through civic education

questions.explanation: Political socialisation is the process by which people learn political values and beliefs; when the state monopolises this process through controlled media, education, and rituals, it constitutes state propaganda aimed at producing loyal, compliant citizens. Option C is the opposite of what is described — a government monopoly on information eliminates market competition among media.

questions.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A country that holds regular elections must be a democracy.' Evaluate this claim by identifying its most significant weakness.

options.A: The claim is correct because elections are the defining feature of democracy, and no other criteria are needed.
options.B: The claim is flawed because elections alone do not guarantee democracy if civil liberties, free press, and independent courts are absent.
options.C: The claim is flawed because democracies should never hold elections — decisions must be made by appointed experts.
options.D: The claim is correct as long as the winning party receives more than 50% of the vote.

questions.explanation: Elections are a necessary but not sufficient condition for democracy; authoritarian regimes such as Russia and Belarus regularly hold elections while suppressing opposition, limiting press freedom, and controlling the judiciary — so meaningful democracy requires these additional pillars. Option A is the top distractor because students often reduce democracy to the single feature of voting, missing the broader framework of civil liberties and institutional checks.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that individuals possess natural rights to 'life, liberty, and property' before any government exists. Which scenario would Locke most clearly identify as a violation of the social contract that justifies resistance?

options.A: A government raises income taxes to fund public hospitals without a referendum.
options.B: A government imprisons citizens without trial and confiscates their land to give to ruling-party members.
options.C: A government loses a war and is forced to cede territory to a neighbouring country.
options.D: A government passes an unpopular law through a legitimate parliamentary vote.

questions.explanation: Locke argued in his Second Treatise that when a government systematically violates property rights and denies liberty through arbitrary imprisonment, it destroys the very purpose of the social contract and citizens are justified in rebelling. Option A is a strong distractor because taxation can seem like a property violation, but Locke accepted taxation consented to by representatives — arbitrary confiscation without due process is the critical distinction.

questions.title: Market Failure and Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally produces cheap steel but releases pollution into a river, harming fishing communities downstream who receive no compensation. Which economic concept best describes this situation, and what does it suggest about the free market's ability to handle it?

options.A: This is a positive externality, showing that free markets efficiently distribute benefits to third parties.
options.B: This is a negative externality, showing that free markets can fail to account for costs imposed on parties outside the transaction.
options.C: This is a public goods problem, showing that the fishing community should have paid for cleaner production methods.
options.D: This is an income inequality problem, showing that fishing communities need higher wages rather than regulation.

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a production or consumption activity imposes costs on third parties not involved in the transaction — here, the factory's pollution harms fishers who bear costs without any market compensation, representing a classic market failure. Option A is a strong distractor because students sometimes confuse whether third parties are affected positively or negatively, and incorrectly label any spillover effect as positive.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau introduced the concept of the 'general will' — the collective interest of society as a whole. A student argues: 'Rousseau believed the general will is simply whatever the majority votes for.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: There is no error — Rousseau defined the general will as identical to the outcome of majority voting.
options.B: The error is that Rousseau distinguished the general will from the 'will of all'; the general will represents the common good, not merely the sum of private interests that a majority may vote for.
options.C: The error is that Rousseau believed the general will could only be expressed by a monarch, not by citizens voting.
options.D: The error is that Rousseau opposed all forms of collective decision-making and preferred individual contracts.

questions.explanation: Rousseau explicitly differentiated the 'will of all' (the aggregate of self-interested preferences) from the 'general will' (what is genuinely best for the whole community), arguing that a majority vote might simply reflect collective selfishness rather than the true common good. Option A is the top distractor because equating majority rule with the general will is the most intuitive but incorrect interpretation students adopt when first encountering Rousseau.

questions.title: Federalism and Power Distribution
questions.prompt: In Country X, regional governments can pass their own education and healthcare laws, collect their own taxes, and cannot be abolished by the national government. Which system of government does Country X most clearly illustrate, and what is its primary advantage?

options.A: Unitary system; it allows the central government to ensure equal standards across all regions.
options.B: Confederation; it means the national government has almost no real power over member states.
options.C: Federal system; it divides sovereign power between national and regional governments, allowing local policies to reflect local needs.
options.D: Theocracy; it ensures religious principles guide both regional and national legislation.

questions.explanation: Federalism constitutionally divides sovereignty between central and sub-national governments, with each having protected powers — as seen in countries like the USA, Germany, and India — allowing regions to tailor policies such as education to local contexts. Option B is a strong distractor because students often confuse federalism with confederation; in a confederation, the national government derives its authority from member states and is typically very weak, whereas in a federation the national government retains significant independent powers.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: Rawls argued that principles of justice should be chosen behind a 'veil of ignorance,' where decision-makers do not know their place in society. What would a person reasoning under this veil most rationally choose regarding income inequality?

options.A: Complete equality of income for everyone, since no one should earn more than another.
options.B: Unlimited inequality, because risk-takers deserve all the rewards they earn.
options.C: Inequality is acceptable only if it benefits the least advantaged members of society.
options.D: Whatever the current market produces, since market outcomes are always fair.

questions.explanation: Rawls's difference principle, developed in A Theory of Justice (1971), holds that inequalities are just only when they work to the greatest benefit of the worst-off group — since behind the veil of ignorance you might end up in the lowest position, you would rationally protect that position. Option A is the top distractor because many students assume that fairness from behind the veil of ignorance must mean absolute equality, but Rawls accepted incentive-driven inequality if it genuinely raises the floor for the poorest.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: In Country Z, rapid industrialisation has created a large urban working class living in poverty while a small elite controls nearly all wealth and political offices. Which combination of factors, drawn from theories of revolution, best explains why Country Z is at high risk of revolution?

options.A: Strong religious identity among the elite and weakening military discipline among soldiers.
options.B: Relative deprivation, where growing inequality creates the sense that the majority is unfairly excluded from power and prosperity.
options.C: Technological advancement that always produces political instability as a side effect.
options.D: The presence of a charismatic leader who personally inspires the population to revolt.

questions.explanation: The theory of relative deprivation, developed by sociologists including Ted Gurr, argues that revolutions arise not from absolute poverty but from the perceived gap between what people have and what they believe they deserve — the combination of economic inequality and political exclusion in Country Z fits this pattern closely, as seen historically in the Russian and French Revolutions. Option D is a strong distractor because students frequently overemphasise the role of individual leaders while underestimating structural economic and political conditions as the primary drivers of revolution.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Roles
questions.prompt: Country A has a mixed economy. The government provides universal healthcare and regulates bank lending, but most goods are produced and sold by private companies. A critic argues this system is contradictory because it mixes incompatible principles. Evaluate this criticism.

options.A: The criticism is valid because governments and markets always produce opposing outcomes and cannot function together.
options.B: The criticism is invalid because mixed economies deliberately combine market efficiency with government intervention to address failures the market cannot solve alone.
options.C: The criticism is valid because healthcare should always be left entirely to market forces to ensure quality.
options.D: The criticism is invalid because in a mixed economy the government must control all sectors equally, not just some.

questions.explanation: Mixed economies are intentionally designed to harness market competition for efficiency while using government intervention to provide public goods, correct externalities, and ensure social equity — most developed nations, including Germany and Canada, operate this way without contradiction. Option A is the top distractor because students often assume that combining market and government principles creates logical inconsistency, when in practice the two can be complementary and mutually reinforcing.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Compare the concepts of power and authority in political science. Which scenario best illustrates the difference between having power without authority and having authority without power?

options.A: A prime minister who wins elections has both power and authority; there is no meaningful distinction between the two.
options.B: A warlord who controls territory through armed force has power without authority; an exiled government recognised by other nations has authority without effective power.
options.C: A judge who sentences criminals has power without authority; a soldier who follows orders has authority without power.
options.D: A central bank governor who sets interest rates has power without authority; a popular celebrity who influences public opinion has authority without power.

questions.explanation: In political science, power is the capacity to compel obedience, while authority is legitimate, recognised power — the warlord example illustrates raw power without legitimacy, while an exiled government (such as France's government-in-exile during WWII) retains recognised authority despite lacking the ability to enforce decisions domestically. Option D is a plausible distractor because central bank governors and celebrities both exert influence, but their relationship to legitimacy and enforcement does not map cleanly onto the power/authority distinction in the way option B does.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy
questions.prompt: A newly elected government in Country P wins 65% of parliamentary seats and passes a law removing the independence of the supreme court, arguing that elected representatives should have supreme power. Analyse whether this action is consistent with constitutional democracy.

options.A: Yes, because constitutional democracy means the elected majority always has the final say on all government matters.
options.B: No, because constitutional democracy requires separation of powers and an independent judiciary to prevent any branch — including an elected majority — from becoming absolute.
options.C: Yes, because winning 65% of seats gives the government a mandate to restructure all state institutions.
options.D: No, because constitutional democracy forbids parliaments from passing any new laws without approval from courts.

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracy is explicitly designed to constrain even elected majorities through separation of powers, checks and balances, and judicial independence — removing court independence undermines the rule of law and has been cited as democratic backsliding in real cases such as Hungary and Poland. Option A is the top distractor because students commonly conflate democratic elections with unlimited majority rule, missing the constitutional limits that distinguish liberal democracy from majoritarian authoritarianism.

questions.title: Social Mobility and Class
questions.prompt: Two students debate whether their school system promotes equality. Student A says: 'Since anyone can apply to university, our society has equality of opportunity.' Student B responds: 'Students from wealthy families have private tutors, better schools, and more connections, so opportunity is not truly equal.' Which concept best supports Student B's argument?

options.A: Meritocracy — the idea that talent and effort alone determine outcomes regardless of background.
options.B: Structural inequality — the idea that social institutions and inherited advantages systematically favour certain groups over others.
options.C: Social contract — the idea that citizens agree to follow rules in exchange for government protection.
options.D: Positive discrimination — the idea that disadvantaged groups must receive preferences in all public institutions.

questions.explanation: Structural inequality refers to patterns embedded in social institutions — schools, housing, networks — that consistently advantage some groups before individual effort even enters the picture, which is precisely Student B's argument about inherited advantages distorting what appears to be open access. Option A is the top distractor because meritocracy is appealing to students as an explanation of equal opportunity, but it describes an ideal rather than the structural critique Student B is making.

questions.title: International Law Compliance
questions.prompt: Country M signs a United Nations treaty promising to reduce carbon emissions. Three years later it ignores the treaty and increases emissions. Which statement best analyses why states sometimes comply with international law even when there is no enforcement body to compel them?

options.A: States always comply with international law because signing a treaty is legally identical to following domestic law.
options.B: States comply when they calculate that the reputational damage, trade consequences, and loss of diplomatic partnerships from non-compliance outweigh the benefits of defection.
options.C: States comply only when a global army forces them to, so compliance never occurs voluntarily.
options.D: States comply because the UN Security Council monitors every country's behaviour and issues instant financial penalties.

questions.explanation: International relations scholars explain treaty compliance through rational self-interest: states value their reputation in repeated interactions, fear economic retaliation or exclusion from beneficial agreements, and depend on reciprocal cooperation — these incentives drive voluntary compliance even without a global police force. Option C is a strong distractor because students familiar with the lack of enforcement in international law sometimes incorrectly conclude that no voluntary compliance ever occurs, ignoring the substantial evidence that most treaty obligations are followed most of the time.

questions.title: Planned Economy Limitations
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, government planners must decide how much bread, shoes, and medicine to produce each year. What is the most significant economic problem this system faces compared to a market economy?

options.A: Planners cannot prevent workers from demanding higher wages than the state budget allows.
options.B: The information problem: planners lack the decentralised price signals that markets generate to efficiently coordinate millions of individual preferences and resource allocations.
options.C: Planned economies always produce too much of every good because governments want to demonstrate productivity.
options.D: Citizens in planned economies refuse to work because they receive goods for free and have no incentive.

questions.explanation: Economist Friedrich Hayek identified the 'knowledge problem' — no central authority can gather and process the vast, dispersed, constantly changing information that market prices automatically aggregate, leading to chronic misallocations like Soviet-era shortages of consumer goods and surpluses of military hardware. Option D is a genuine distractor because the incentive problem in planned economies is real, but it is secondary to the more fundamental information coordination failure that Hayek identified as the root cause of planning's inefficiency.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: A country's president has the power to write laws, enforce them, and also serve as the chief judge interpreting them. Which political concept is most clearly absent in this system, and what risk does this create?

options.A: Federalism is absent, creating a risk that regions will have unequal representation.
options.B: Separation of powers is absent, creating the risk that the president faces no checks on authority and can use the law to serve personal interests.
options.C: Universal suffrage is absent, creating the risk that citizens cannot vote the president out of office.
options.D: Proportional representation is absent, creating the risk that minority parties cannot gain seats in the legislature.

questions.explanation: Montesquieu's doctrine of separation of powers holds that legislative, executive, and judicial functions must be held by different institutions — concentrating all three in one person removes all checks and balances, enabling tyranny, as the president could write self-serving laws, enforce them selectively, and then rule in their own favour as judge. Option C is a strong distractor because students associate political accountability primarily with voting, but voting does not prevent abuse when unchecked power exists between elections.

questions.title: Comparative Political Systems
questions.prompt: Country A is a parliamentary democracy where the executive (prime minister) is chosen by and accountable to the legislature. Country B is a presidential democracy where citizens directly elect the executive separately from the legislature. Which statement best analyses a key difference in how accountability operates in these two systems?

options.A: In Country A, the prime minister can be removed by a parliamentary vote of no confidence, creating continuous legislative accountability; in Country B, the president serves a fixed term regardless of legislative support.
options.B: Country A is more democratic because parliamentary systems always produce better policy outcomes than presidential ones.
options.C: In Country B, the president is more powerful because citizens vote for the president, making the legislature irrelevant.
options.D: Both systems operate identically because all democracies ultimately answer to the same electorate.

questions.explanation: Parliamentary systems allow legislatures to remove executives through votes of no confidence (as happened in the UK multiple times in the 20th century), creating ongoing accountability; presidential systems insulate the executive from legislative removal during the fixed term, creating a different but not necessarily weaker form of accountability through direct popular election. Option B is a distractor that introduces a value judgement not supported by comparative political science — neither system is universally superior, and the question asks about accountability mechanisms, not outcomes.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Social contract theory proves that any government is legitimate as long as citizens have not actively rebelled against it. Silence means consent.' Identify the most significant weakness in this argument.

options.A: The argument is correct because tacit consent through non-rebellion is the standard most political philosophers accept.
options.B: The argument ignores that people may be unable to rebel due to fear, poverty, or repression, making silence an unreliable indicator of genuine consent.
options.C: The argument is flawed because social contract theory only applies to ancient societies, not modern nation-states.
options.D: The argument is flawed because social contract theory requires every citizen to sign a physical document to show consent.

questions.explanation: Philosophers including Hume challenged the idea of tacit consent by noting that most people lack realistic alternatives to living under their government — emigration is costly, rebellion is dangerous, and oppression prevents dissent — making silence a deeply unreliable proxy for genuine agreement. Option A is the top distractor because Locke did use tacit consent arguments, which makes it tempting for students to accept the claim, but even Locke required that citizens have meaningful freedom to leave the political community for consent to be genuine.

questions.title: Market Economy and Inequality
questions.prompt: In a free-market economy, two workers perform equally difficult jobs for the same number of hours. Worker 1 earns ten times more than Worker 2. A student says this must be the result of discrimination. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because equal effort always produces equal wages in a fair market.
options.B: The claim is overstated because wage differences in markets also reflect skill scarcity, negotiating power, industry profitability, and education — not only discrimination.
options.C: The claim is correct because free markets are inherently biased against lower-paid workers.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because governments in market economies always set wages to ensure equality.

questions.explanation: Labour economists explain wage gaps through multiple factors: supply and demand for specific skills, union membership, industry revenue, human capital investment, and bargaining power — discrimination is one potential cause but not the automatic explanation, requiring evidence of differential treatment rather than differential outcome alone. Option A is a strong distractor because students often assume that equal effort should produce equal pay, conflating inputs (effort) with market-valued outputs (skills, scarcity, productivity).

questions.title: Role of Civil Society
questions.prompt: A country has free elections and an independent judiciary, but the government consistently ignores citizens' concerns between election cycles. Which institution or mechanism is most likely to fill the accountability gap between elections?

options.A: A stronger military, which can step in to enforce citizen demands when politicians ignore them.
options.B: Civil society organisations such as trade unions, free press, NGOs, and protest movements that continuously apply pressure on government between elections.
options.C: More frequent elections held every six months to increase direct democratic pressure.
options.D: An international organisation that monitors all domestic political decisions in real time.

questions.explanation: Civil society — including independent media, organised interest groups, and social movements — functions as a continuous accountability mechanism between elections, as demonstrated by movements like Solidarity in Poland or the press exposés that contributed to Watergate in the USA. Option C is a genuine distractor because more frequent elections seem like a logical solution, but they are costly, create constant campaign mode governance, and do not address the gap in between electoral periods the way organised civil society does.

questions.title: Authoritarianism and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government delivers rapid economic growth, builds new hospitals, and reduces crime, but bans opposition parties and controls the media. A student argues: 'If citizens' living standards improve, the government is legitimate regardless of political rights.' Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The argument is valid because legitimacy is entirely based on economic performance — political rights are secondary.
options.B: The argument is partially valid but flawed because it confuses effectiveness with legitimacy; legitimacy also requires consent, transparency, and protection of fundamental rights.
options.C: The argument is entirely invalid because no government that bans parties can ever improve living standards.
options.D: The argument is valid because international law defines legitimacy purely in terms of a government's ability to maintain order.

questions.explanation: Political scientists distinguish between input legitimacy (consent and participation) and output legitimacy (effective delivery of public goods) — authoritarian developmental states like Singapore show that output legitimacy is real, but liberal democratic theory holds that legitimate government also requires meaningful consent and rights protection, not performance alone. Option A is the top distractor because the student's argument conflates effectiveness with full legitimacy, and many students find it intuitively persuasive when governments deliver visible improvements.

questions.title: Global Trade and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Country Q joins a regional trade agreement that requires it to lower tariffs and follow shared regulations set by a joint committee. Critics argue the country has 'given away its sovereignty.' Analyse whether this criticism is accurate.

options.A: The criticism is fully accurate because any shared regulation means the country no longer controls its own laws.
options.B: The criticism overstates the loss; the country voluntarily pooled certain sovereign powers to gain mutual economic benefits, and retains sovereignty in all areas outside the agreement.
options.C: The criticism is irrelevant because sovereignty only refers to military power, not economic rules.
options.D: The criticism is accurate because trade agreements are always imposed by more powerful countries against weaker ones.

questions.explanation: Political scientists describe this as 'pooled sovereignty' — when states voluntarily delegate certain decisions to shared bodies (as EU members do) they retain sovereignty overall and benefit from scale and reciprocity, meaning sovereignty is constrained rather than surrendered. Option A is a strong distractor because many students associate any external constraint with a total loss of sovereignty, missing the distinction between voluntary delegation of specific powers and coercive loss of independence.

questions.title: Types of Economic Systems
questions.prompt: Country X relies entirely on market forces for resource allocation, while Country Y's government makes all major production decisions. Country Z uses both private markets and government intervention. Identify the correct match of systems, and explain why Country Z cannot be classified as either X or Y.

options.A: X = planned, Y = market, Z = mixed; Z mixes private and public elements intentionally, so it fits neither pure category.
options.B: X = market, Y = planned, Z = mixed; Z combines private markets with government intervention, which is a distinct third category.
options.C: X = mixed, Y = market, Z = planned; Z is planned because any government involvement means central planning.
options.D: X = market, Y = mixed, Z = planned; Z is planned because governments always dominate when they intervene.

questions.explanation: A market economy uses price signals and private ownership; a planned economy uses central government decisions; a mixed economy intentionally uses both mechanisms — most real-world economies, including the UK and Australia, are mixed because governments intervene in healthcare, education, and regulation while leaving most production to private firms. Option C is a strong distractor because students who associate any government involvement with 'planning' misunderstand that planning implies comprehensive government control, not selective intervention.

questions.title: Political Ideology Spectrum
questions.prompt: A political party proposes: nationalising major industries, significantly increasing taxes on the wealthy, and expanding universal social services. A second party proposes: privatising state enterprises, cutting taxes, and reducing government regulation. Using political ideology, which labels best describe these parties?

options.A: The first party is right-wing and the second is left-wing, because expanding government is conservative.
options.B: The first party is left-wing and the second is right-wing, because left-wing ideologies favour government intervention and wealth redistribution while right-wing ideologies favour free markets and limited government.
options.C: Both parties are centrist because they both accept the existence of a government.
options.D: The first party is authoritarian and the second is democratic, because economic policy determines democratic status.

questions.explanation: On the conventional left-right political spectrum, left-wing positions support collective ownership, redistribution of wealth, and strong state involvement in the economy, while right-wing positions emphasise private ownership, free markets, and limited government — these are definitional characteristics used across comparative politics. Option A is the top distractor because students sometimes incorrectly invert the labels, associating 'conservative' with maintaining existing power structures without understanding how the economic left-right axis actually works.

questions.title: Human Rights and State Power
questions.prompt: During a national emergency, a government suspends freedom of assembly and imposes curfews. A human rights organisation argues this violates fundamental rights. The government argues emergencies justify temporary restrictions. Which principle from international human rights law best resolves this tension?

options.A: The principle of absolute rights — all human rights are absolute and can never be limited under any circumstances.
options.B: The proportionality principle — rights may be restricted during genuine emergencies only to the extent strictly necessary, for a limited time, and without discrimination.
options.C: State sovereignty — governments may suspend all human rights whenever they declare an emergency, without external scrutiny.
options.D: The principle of collective rights — individual rights must always be sacrificed when a majority of citizens support emergency measures.

questions.explanation: International human rights law, including the ICCPR Article 4, allows derogation from certain rights during public emergencies but imposes strict conditions: the restrictions must be proportionate, temporary, non-discriminatory, and cannot suspend non-derogable rights such as the prohibition on torture. Option A is a strong distractor because students learning about human rights often initially assume all rights are absolute, not yet distinguishing between derogable and non-derogable rights.

questions.title: Electoral Systems and Representation
questions.prompt: In Country T's election, Party A wins 40% of votes but receives 60% of parliamentary seats, while Party B wins 30% of votes but receives only 15% of seats. What does this outcome most likely indicate about Country T's electoral system?

options.A: Country T uses proportional representation, which always produces results that match vote shares exactly.
options.B: Country T uses a winner-takes-all system such as first-past-the-post, which tends to over-represent the leading party and under-represent parties whose votes are geographically spread.
options.C: Country T's election was fraudulent because seats and votes can never differ in a legitimate democracy.
options.D: Country T uses a two-round system, where the second round always amplifies the leading party's advantage proportionally.

questions.explanation: First-past-the-post (FPTP) systems consistently produce disproportionate outcomes because winning candidates need only a plurality in their individual district — concentrated geographic support gives Party A many seat wins while Party B's votes spread thinly across districts yield fewer seats, exactly as seen in UK general elections. Option A is the strongest distractor because students may assume that more votes should always produce more seats in any legitimate democratic system, not yet understanding how electoral system design shapes this relationship.

questions.title: Power of Non-State Actors
questions.prompt: A large multinational corporation operating in a developing country earns annual revenues larger than the country's entire government budget. The corporation employs 20% of the workforce and sets local environmental standards through its own policies. Which concept from international relations best describes this situation?

options.A: This illustrates imperialism — the corporation is acting as a colonial power and should be treated under colonial law.
options.B: This illustrates how non-state actors can exercise de facto governance power, challenging the assumption that states alone hold meaningful authority within their territories.
options.C: This illustrates comparative advantage — the corporation's size proves that specialisation always benefits developing countries.
options.D: This illustrates international law working correctly — corporations are legally recognised as equals to states under the UN Charter.

questions.explanation: When a corporation's economic footprint rivals or exceeds a state's resources, it can effectively set labour, environmental, and social standards within a territory — a phenomenon political scientists describe as 'private governance' or corporate quasi-sovereignty, raising questions about democratic accountability that traditional state-centred international relations theory does not fully address. Option A is a strong distractor because the comparison to imperialism has some historical merit in cases like the East India Company, but imperialism is a specific historical-political concept requiring territorial control by a foreign state, not simply corporate economic dominance.

questions.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A country holding regular elections must be a democracy, because elections prove the government has the consent of the governed.' Evaluate the most significant flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Elections are only meaningful if all citizens are required by law to vote, which most countries do not enforce.
options.B: Elections can exist without genuine competition, free press, or civil liberties, meaning they may legitimise authoritarian rule rather than reflect real consent.
options.C: Consent of the governed is a concept invented by Rousseau that only applies to direct democracies, not representative ones.
options.D: The flaw is that elections are too expensive to run fairly, so wealthier parties always win regardless of voter preference.

questions.explanation: Elections in authoritarian states — such as those held in Belarus or North Korea — often lack genuine opposition, press freedom, or independent courts, making them tools of legitimisation rather than real expressions of consent. Option C is wrong because Locke also wrote extensively about consent of the governed, and representative democracy is a widely accepted form of democratic consent.

questions.title: Locke and Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that a legitimate government must protect life, liberty, and property. Which scenario would Locke most clearly identify as a government acting beyond its legitimate authority?

options.A: A government taxes citizens to fund a national army that defends borders against foreign invasion.
options.B: A government passes laws punishing theft and enforcing contracts between private citizens.
options.C: A government seizes privately owned land without compensation to build a ruling party headquarters.
options.D: A government creates courts to settle disputes between citizens about property boundaries.

questions.explanation: Locke's Second Treatise explicitly states that government cannot take property from citizens without their consent, as property rights are natural and pre-political. Options A, B, and D all describe functions Locke considered core legitimate roles of government — protecting citizens, enforcing law, and resolving disputes.

questions.title: Market Failures and Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally produces steel but releases pollution into a river, harming fishing communities downstream who were never consulted. Which concept most precisely describes this situation, and what does it reveal about free-market pricing?

options.A: A positive externality — the market underproduces steel because the social benefits are not captured in the price.
options.B: A negative externality — the market overproduces steel because the social cost of pollution is not included in the price.
options.C: A public goods problem — steel is non-excludable, so the factory cannot prevent others from using the river.
options.D: A monopoly failure — the factory charges too high a price because it faces no competition in the steel market.

questions.explanation: Negative externalities occur when third parties bear costs not reflected in a product's market price; because pollution costs fall on fishing communities rather than the factory, steel is cheaper than its true social cost, causing overproduction. Option A is incorrect because the harm to downstream communities is a cost, not a benefit, making this a negative rather than positive externality.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that true political freedom means obeying the 'general will' rather than one's own private desires. A student claims this idea is simply another word for majority rule. Why is this interpretation inaccurate?

options.A: The general will refers to what the majority wants after an election, whereas majority rule describes parliamentary voting procedures.
options.B: Rousseau's general will represents the common good of the whole community, which may differ from what the majority of individuals actually want at any given moment.
options.C: Majority rule only applies in two-party systems, while the general will applies to all political systems regardless of the number of parties.
options.D: The general will is determined by a panel of philosophers, not by popular vote, so it cannot be compared to majority rule at all.

questions.explanation: Rousseau distinguished between the 'will of all' (the sum of private desires) and the 'general will' (what genuinely serves the community's common good), explicitly noting they could conflict — for example, a majority might vote for a policy that harms the collective. Option A incorrectly frames both concepts as procedural voting mechanisms, missing Rousseau's deeper normative distinction.

questions.title: Federalism and Power Distribution
questions.prompt: In a federal system, a national government passes an environmental law, but three state governments refuse to enforce it, arguing the issue falls under state jurisdiction. Which feature of federalism most directly creates this conflict?

options.A: Federalism requires all laws to be passed by both national and regional governments simultaneously, so national-only laws are automatically invalid.
options.B: The division of sovereignty between levels of government means jurisdictional boundaries are often contested, especially on issues not clearly assigned by the constitution.
options.C: Federal systems always give states the final word on environmental issues because natural resources are geographically local.
options.D: The conflict arises because federalism prohibits the national government from creating regulatory agencies without state approval.

questions.explanation: Federalism divides sovereignty, but constitutions rarely assign every policy area perfectly, creating 'concurrent powers' zones where both levels claim authority — environmental law is a classic example in countries like the USA and Australia. Option A is incorrect because federal systems do not universally require joint passage of all laws; many national laws are valid without regional co-passage.

questions.title: Rawls and the Veil of Ignorance
questions.prompt: Behind Rawls's 'veil of ignorance,' people do not know their place in society when designing its rules. A student argues: 'This means people behind the veil would always choose complete economic equality for everyone.' Identify the most precise error in this claim.

options.A: The error is that the veil of ignorance only applies to political rights, not to economic distribution, so Rawls never addresses income equality.
options.B: The error is that Rawls's difference principle permits inequalities that benefit the least advantaged members of society, so complete equality is not required.
options.C: The error is that people behind the veil would instead choose a meritocracy, rewarding the most talented individuals with higher incomes.
options.D: The error is that the veil of ignorance removes rational thinking, so no coherent principles of justice could be agreed upon.

questions.explanation: Rawls explicitly states in A Theory of Justice that the difference principle allows economic inequalities if — and only if — they improve the position of the worst-off group; this is not complete equality but regulated inequality. Option C is wrong because Rawls rejected pure meritocracy, arguing that natural talents are morally arbitrary and should not solely determine distribution.

questions.title: Planned Economy Trade-offs
questions.prompt: Country X operates a fully planned economy where the state allocates all resources. Economists observe persistent shortages of consumer goods alongside surpluses of military equipment. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.A: Planned economies cannot produce military goods efficiently because defence requires private sector innovation and competition.
options.B: Without price signals to convey consumer preferences, central planners allocate based on political priorities rather than actual demand, systematically mismatch supply.
options.C: Consumer goods shortages occur because citizens in planned economies deliberately consume less to support the state's goals.
options.D: Planned economies always prioritise exports over domestic consumption, so consumer goods are sent abroad while military goods remain at home.

questions.explanation: Friedrich Hayek's 'knowledge problem' explains this: prices in markets aggregate dispersed information about preferences, but central planners lack this signal and allocate according to political goals — historically seen in the Soviet Union, where heavy industry and military were over-resourced while consumer goods were chronically scarce. Option D is factually inaccurate; Soviet-style economies did not systematically export consumer goods — they simply underproduced them.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Limits
questions.prompt: A democratically elected parliament passes a law by a large majority that removes freedom of speech protections from a minority religious group. In a constitutional democracy, what is the most important mechanism that should prevent this outcome?

options.A: The ruling party voluntarily withdrawing the law after public protests demonstrate widespread disapproval.
options.B: An independent judiciary with the power of constitutional review, able to strike down laws that violate entrenched rights.
options.C: International organisations imposing trade sanctions on the country to pressure parliament into reversing the decision.
options.D: Requiring all laws to be approved by a supermajority of 90% of parliament before they can remove any rights.

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracies are distinguished by entrenched rights protected by judicial review — courts can invalidate majority decisions that violate the constitution, preventing 'tyranny of the majority'; this is the core role of bodies like the US Supreme Court or Germany's Federal Constitutional Court. Option A relies on political will rather than a structural mechanism and offers no guarantee — a determined majority could ignore protests.

questions.title: Social Stratification Mobility
questions.prompt: Research shows that in Country A, a child's future income is strongly predicted by their parents' income — more so than in Country B. Which conclusion is best supported by this evidence when comparing social structures?

options.A: Country A has a caste system, while Country B has a class system, because only caste systems use inheritance to determine status.
options.B: Country A has lower intergenerational social mobility than Country B, suggesting structural barriers limit individuals' ability to change economic position.
options.C: Country B must have a planned economy because equal opportunity requires government control of resource distribution.
options.D: Country A has higher social mobility because strong family ties ensure wealth is preserved and passed on efficiently.

questions.explanation: Intergenerational income elasticity is a standard measure of social mobility — a high correlation between parent and child income indicates low mobility due to structural factors like unequal access to education or inherited networks, as documented in studies comparing Scandinavian countries (high mobility) to the USA (lower mobility). Option A is incorrect because class systems can also transmit advantage intergenerationally; the distinction between caste and class is not solely about inheritance.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three types of authority: traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal. A new president is elected under a written constitution, but citizens only obey her because they admire her personally, not because they respect the electoral process. Which analysis of this situation is most accurate?

options.A: Her authority is purely rational-legal because she was elected through a constitutional process, regardless of citizens' personal motivations.
options.B: Her authority functions charismatically in practice, even though its formal basis is rational-legal — revealing a gap between institutional legitimacy and actual compliance.
options.C: Her authority is traditional because personal admiration reflects long-standing cultural norms about respected leaders.
options.D: Weber's framework cannot apply here because the president holds both elected and personal sources of authority simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Weber's types describe the basis on which citizens grant legitimacy; if compliance is driven by personal admiration rather than belief in the constitutional process, the operative authority is charismatic even if the formal source is rational-legal — this distinction is crucial for understanding fragile democracies where institutions are weak but leaders are popular. Option A conflates the formal source of authority with the actual basis of citizen compliance, which Weber's framework specifically distinguishes.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Country Z has a mixed economy. The government funds universal healthcare but allows private businesses to set prices for food and clothing. A critic argues: 'Providing free healthcare distorts the market and is therefore always economically harmful.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because any government provision of services creates dependency and reduces citizens' incentive to work and pay taxes.
options.B: The claim is partially correct: healthcare markets are perfectly competitive, so government provision is unnecessary and always less efficient than private supply.
options.C: The claim oversimplifies: healthcare has features of market failure — including information asymmetry and merit good characteristics — that can justify government provision on efficiency grounds, not just equity.
options.D: The claim is entirely wrong because mixed economies always outperform free markets in every sector, including consumer goods and services.

questions.explanation: Healthcare markets suffer from well-documented market failures: patients cannot easily evaluate the quality of treatment (information asymmetry), and healthy individuals may not purchase insurance until ill (adverse selection), justifying government intervention on efficiency grounds, not only social fairness. Option B is factually wrong — healthcare markets are notoriously imperfect and far from perfectly competitive due to licensing barriers, emergency demand, and information gaps.

questions.title: Revolutions and Social Change
questions.prompt: Scholars note that successful revolutions rarely occur at the absolute lowest point of oppression — instead, they often happen after a period of improvement followed by a sudden decline. Which theoretical concept best explains this pattern?

options.A: The iron law of oligarchy — every movement to overthrow elites eventually produces new elites, so revolution is most likely when citizens expect replacement rulers will be better.
options.B: Relative deprivation theory — people revolt not when suffering is greatest in absolute terms, but when a gap opens between their rising expectations and their actual conditions.
options.C: Social contract theory — citizens only rebel when the government completely fails to protect natural rights, which requires conditions to worsen to their worst possible point.
options.D: Structural functionalism — social systems seek equilibrium, so revolutions occur only when outside forces destabilise a previously stable society.

questions.explanation: James Davies's 'J-curve theory' of revolution, grounded in relative deprivation, argues that rising expectations created during improvement make a sudden reversal feel intolerable — this pattern is observed in the French Revolution and the 1979 Iranian Revolution. Option C is incorrect because Locke's social contract theory does not require conditions to reach their absolute worst; the threshold is the government's failure to protect rights, which can occur at various levels of oppression.

questions.title: Comparative Governance Systems
questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system, the head of government is chosen by the legislature and can be removed by a vote of no confidence. In a presidential system, the head of government is elected separately by citizens. Which outcome is more likely under a parliamentary system than a presidential one?

options.A: The executive branch is more likely to be completely independent of the legislature, reducing the chance of deadlock.
options.B: Policy gridlock is more likely because the legislature and executive are elected at different times with different mandates.
options.C: The executive is more likely to lose power quickly if it loses majority legislative support, increasing governmental accountability to parliament.
options.D: Citizens have more direct control over choosing the head of government because parliamentary elections always use proportional representation.

questions.explanation: The vote of no confidence is the defining mechanism of parliamentary accountability — prime ministers who lose majority support (e.g., the UK's Boris Johnson in 2022) must resign or face dissolution of parliament, making executive tenure directly dependent on legislative confidence. Option D is factually incorrect; parliamentary systems use a variety of electoral systems — the UK uses first-past-the-post for its parliamentary elections, not proportional representation.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) rules that Country A has violated international law by polluting a shared river. Country A ignores the ruling. A student argues this shows international law is effective only when powerful countries choose to comply. Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The argument is fully correct: international law has no enforcement mechanism whatsoever, making it completely meaningless as a system of rules.
options.B: The argument identifies a real limitation but overstates it: international law shapes behaviour through reputational costs, diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions, and treaty incentives even without a global police force.
options.C: The argument is wrong because the UN Security Council can always enforce ICJ rulings by sending peacekeeping troops to ensure compliance.
options.D: The argument is wrong because powerful countries consistently comply with international law, so the student's premise is based on a false assumption.

questions.explanation: International law lacks centralised enforcement but operates through mechanisms including reciprocity, reputational damage, diplomatic isolation, and economic pressure — states comply in the vast majority of cases because non-compliance has real costs, as demonstrated by decades of treaty adherence in areas like trade and diplomacy. Option C is incorrect because UN Security Council enforcement requires unanimous agreement among the five permanent members, and any one of them can veto action — making consistent enforcement far from guaranteed.

questions.title: Economic Systems and Incentives
questions.prompt: In Country P (market economy), doctors earn significantly more than teachers. In Country Q (planned economy), the government sets equal wages for both professions. A student argues Country Q's system is fairer because it treats all work as equally valuable. What is the most analytically complete response to this claim?

options.A: The student is correct: equal wages ensure social cohesion and remove harmful competition between professions.
options.B: The student's fairness claim has merit but ignores that equal wages may reduce incentives to undertake long, costly training — potentially causing shortages in skilled professions that require years of specialised education.
options.C: The student is wrong because market wages always accurately reflect social value, so doctors deserve higher pay by definition.
options.D: The student is correct that planned economies are fairer, but incorrect that equal wages are possible — central planners always end up paying workers differently based on political connections.

questions.explanation: Wage differentials in market economies serve as incentive signals: if medical training takes ten or more years and yields the same income as a shorter-training profession, fewer people will choose medicine — potentially causing critical shortages. This does not mean market wages are morally superior, but the student's argument ignores this efficiency trade-off. Option C incorrectly assumes market prices perfectly reflect social value, ignoring that wages reflect supply and demand rather than moral worth.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democracy
questions.prompt: Political scientists argue that a strong civil society — including independent trade unions, religious organisations, and advocacy groups — is essential for a healthy democracy. Why might this be the case, even when these groups disagree with the elected government?

options.A: Civil society groups replace political parties and make elections unnecessary by directly representing citizens' interests.
options.B: Independent organisations create alternative centres of power and information outside government control, holding leaders accountable between elections and protecting against the concentration of authority.
options.C: Civil society is only important in young democracies; once a country is well established, these organisations become obstacles to efficient governance.
options.D: The main democratic value of civil society is that it trains future politicians, ensuring that elected officials have prior experience in community organisations.

questions.explanation: Democratic theorists from Tocqueville onwards have argued that civil society creates 'countervailing power' — organisations independent of the state can monitor government, mobilise public opinion, and resist authoritarian consolidation; this is why authoritarian regimes typically restrict unions, religious organisations, and NGOs. Option A is incorrect because civil society organisations supplement rather than replace political parties and electoral processes; they lack formal governmental authority.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Country M's constitution grants the executive branch the power to appoint all judges, set all court budgets, and dismiss judges whose rulings it dislikes. A student claims this is acceptable because the executive was elected by the people. Identify the most significant constitutional problem with this arrangement.

options.A: The arrangement is problematic only if the executive appoints more than five judges, which exceeds the traditional limit in most constitutions.
options.B: Judicial independence is destroyed when the executive controls appointments, budgets, and dismissals — removing the courts' ability to act as a check on executive power, even if the executive was democratically elected.
options.C: The main problem is that elected executives lack the legal expertise to choose qualified judges, so judicial appointments should be made by legal professional associations.
options.D: The arrangement violates the social contract because Locke specified that only legislative bodies should control the judiciary.

questions.explanation: Separation of powers requires that branches check one another; if the executive fully controls the judiciary, courts cannot impartially review executive action — a pattern seen in Hungary under Orbán, where judicial reform enabled executive dominance. Option C focuses on competence rather than the constitutional principle of independence, missing the structural problem that courts must be able to rule against the government without fear of dismissal.

questions.title: Globalisation and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: When a country joins the World Trade Organization (WTO), it must change some domestic laws to comply with international trade rules, even if its own parliament voted for those laws. Which tension does this most clearly illustrate?

options.A: The tension between federalism and regional autonomy, since the WTO effectively acts as a federal government over member states.
options.B: The tension between national sovereignty and international governance, where states voluntarily constrain their own legislative freedom in exchange for the benefits of international cooperation.
options.C: The tension between democracy and authoritarianism, since international organisations always impose rules without any member state consent.
options.D: The tension between planned and market economies, since WTO rules require members to abandon all forms of government intervention in trade.

questions.explanation: WTO membership is voluntary but binding — states trade some legislative sovereignty (e.g., the ability to impose certain tariffs) for market access and dispute resolution mechanisms; this exemplifies the broader globalisation paradox where international cooperation requires limiting unilateral action. Option C is incorrect because WTO membership requires active state consent — countries choose to join and negotiate the terms of their obligations.

questions.title: Political Ideology Spectrum
questions.prompt: A political party supports reducing income taxes for all citizens, privatising state-owned enterprises, and cutting welfare programmes to encourage self-reliance. Which ideological position does this package of policies most closely represent, and what is its core philosophical justification?

options.A: Socialism — because reducing taxes increases disposable income for workers, which aligns with socialist goals of improving living standards.
options.B: Right-wing liberalism or economic conservatism — grounded in the belief that individual freedom and market competition produce better outcomes than state intervention.
options.C: Authoritarianism — because cutting welfare programmes concentrates economic power in the hands of the state.
options.D: Communism — because eliminating welfare dependency is a step toward achieving a classless, self-sufficient society.

questions.explanation: Tax cuts, privatisation, and welfare reduction are hallmarks of right-wing economic liberalism (or neoliberalism), philosophically rooted in thinkers like Friedrich Hayek and Milton Friedman who argued that free markets and individual responsibility produce superior outcomes to state provision. Option A is incorrect because socialism prioritises collective ownership, redistribution, and public welfare — directly contradicted by cutting welfare and privatising enterprises.

questions.title: Human Rights and Relativism
questions.prompt: Some governments argue that international human rights standards are Western cultural impositions that should not apply to countries with different traditions. A student claims this 'cultural relativism' argument fully justifies a government imprisoning political opponents. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct: if a culture accepts political imprisonment as normal, no external standard can legitimately challenge it.
options.B: The claim misuses cultural relativism: even if some cultural practices vary legitimately, jailing political opponents silences the very internal voices that could choose to change or preserve their own culture.
options.C: The claim is correct because the UN itself acknowledges that political rights are optional add-ons, not core human rights obligations.
options.D: The claim is partially correct: cultural relativism applies to economic rights but never to political rights, so the argument is invalid only in this specific case.

questions.explanation: A key counterargument to relativist justifications for political repression is that imprisoning dissidents eliminates the internal democratic process by which a society could legitimately debate and modify its own norms — the relativist defence thus undermines its own premise. Option C is factually wrong: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), ratified by most UN member states, treats political rights including freedom from arbitrary detention as binding obligations, not optional additions.

questions.title: Electoral Systems and Representation
questions.prompt: In the 2015 UK general election, UKIP received 12.6% of the national vote but won only 1 of 650 parliamentary seats. The SNP received 4.7% of the national vote but won 56 seats. Which feature of the UK's electoral system most directly explains this disparity?

options.A: The UK uses proportional representation, which rewards parties whose votes are geographically concentrated in specific constituencies.
options.B: The UK's first-past-the-post system rewards geographically concentrated support — the SNP's votes were concentrated in Scottish constituencies, while UKIP's support was spread thinly across the whole country.
options.C: UKIP was penalised by electoral law because it had fewer candidates standing for election than the SNP in the 2015 contest.
options.D: The disparity reflects the influence of campaign spending limits that disadvantaged UKIP relative to regionally focused parties.

questions.explanation: Under first-past-the-post, only the plurality winner in each constituency gains a seat, so parties with nationally spread but locally thin support (like UKIP) win few seats despite high total votes, while concentrated regional parties (like the SNP in Scotland) win many seats with fewer total national votes. Option A is factually wrong — the UK uses first-past-the-post, not proportional representation, for general elections.

questions.title: State and Non-State Power
questions.prompt: A large technology corporation collects detailed personal data on billions of users, can influence what political information people see, and operates across more than 100 countries. A student argues: 'Only governments hold real political power — private companies are purely economic actors.' Evaluate this claim in the context of contemporary political science.

options.A: The claim is correct: political power requires the ability to make binding laws, which only governments possess; corporations influence markets but not politics.
options.B: The claim is overstated: corporations that control information flows, shape public discourse, and lobby governments exercise a form of political power, even without formal legislative authority.
options.C: The claim is correct in democratic countries but wrong in authoritarian states, where corporations serve as arms of government.
