options.D: The claim is wrong because modern corporations have replaced governments as the primary source of law-making in globalised economies.

questions.explanation: Political scientists recognise that power includes agenda-setting, information control, and the capacity to shape political outcomes — capabilities large tech corporations demonstrably possess through algorithmic content curation and political advertising, as seen in debates about social media's role in elections. Option A adopts an overly narrow definition of political power focused exclusively on formal legislative authority, ignoring the influential concept of 'soft power' and agenda-setting power.

questions.title: Gender and Political Representation
questions.prompt: Research shows that countries using proportional representation electoral systems tend to elect significantly higher percentages of women to parliament than countries using first-past-the-post systems. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.A: Proportional representation countries have more progressive cultures, and cultural attitudes — not the electoral system itself — are the real cause of higher female representation.
options.B: Under proportional representation, parties compile ranked lists of candidates, creating pressure to include diverse candidates including women to appeal to a broad electorate; under first-past-the-post, parties field only one candidate per constituency and historically favour incumbents who are disproportionately male.
options.C: First-past-the-post systems legally prohibit women from running in more than half of all constituencies, reducing overall female representation.
options.D: Proportional representation gives political parties the power to appoint rather than elect members of parliament, making it easier to guarantee gender balance.

questions.explanation: Studies in comparative politics show that list-based proportional systems encourage 'zipper lists' alternating male and female candidates, and parties compete to appear broadly inclusive — structural incentives built into the electoral system itself, not just cultural attitudes. Option A commits the error of ignoring institutional factors; cross-national research shows electoral system type predicts female representation even after controlling for cultural variables.

questions.title: Taxation and Redistribution
questions.prompt: A progressive tax system charges higher earners a higher percentage of their income. A flat tax charges everyone the same percentage. A student argues: 'A flat tax is fairer because everyone pays the same rate — that is true equality.' Which philosophical response most effectively challenges this claim?

options.A: The student is correct: equal percentage rates satisfy the Rawlsian difference principle because no group is singled out for higher rates.
options.B: Formal equality of rates does not produce substantive equality of burden — a 20% tax on a low income may deprive someone of basic necessities, while the same rate on a high income barely affects living standards, making the flat tax regressive in real impact.
options.C: The student is wrong simply because progressive taxes generate more total revenue, which is always economically superior regardless of fairness arguments.
options.D: The flat tax is less fair because it violates Rousseau's general will, which explicitly requires tax rates to increase with income.

questions.explanation: The distinction between formal and substantive equality is central to political philosophy: equal percentage rates treat unequal circumstances identically, ignoring diminishing marginal utility — each additional dollar means less to a wealthy person than to a poor one, so equal rates create unequal sacrifices. Option A is incorrect: Rawls would not endorse a flat tax under the difference principle, because it does not maximise the position of the worst-off group and imposes proportionally heavier real burdens on low-income earners.

questions.title: Propaganda and Political Control
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government requires all schools to teach only government-approved history textbooks, bans foreign websites, and trains teachers to report students who express anti-government opinions. Which concept from political science best describes the long-term goal of this cluster of policies?

options.A: Gerrymandering — the government is redrawing political boundaries to ensure its preferred ideology wins in educational districts.
options.B: Ideological hegemony — the government is shaping the beliefs, values, and acceptable political imagination of citizens from childhood to make its rule seem natural and unchallenged.
options.C: Federalism — the government is centralising educational policy that would otherwise be managed by regional authorities.
options.D: Populism — the government is appealing directly to the people's desire for national pride by controlling the national narrative.

questions.explanation: Antonio Gramsci's concept of cultural hegemony describes how ruling groups maintain power not only through force but by shaping what citizens consider normal, natural, and common sense — controlling education and information from childhood is a systematic strategy for ideological reproduction. Option D is partially plausible but incorrect: populism describes a political style of appealing to 'the people' against elites, not the mechanism of indoctrination through information control.

questions.title: Decolonisation and Political Systems
questions.prompt: Many countries that gained independence after 1945 initially adopted democratic constitutions but later experienced military coups or one-party rule within a decade. Historians debate the causes. Which explanation is most analytically complete?

options.A: Democracy failed in post-colonial states because citizens in those countries were culturally unsuited to self-governance after centuries of colonial rule.
options.B: Democratic institutions were typically imposed rapidly without building supporting structures — independent courts, free press, civil society, and economic stability — while Cold War powers often backed coups that served their strategic interests.
options.C: Military coups occurred because post-colonial constitutions were always copies of Western models that were inherently incompatible with local legal traditions.
options.D: Democracy failed because newly independent governments lacked access to international trade, making economic failure inevitable and leading citizens to support authoritarian alternatives.

questions.explanation: Political scientists emphasise that democracy requires supporting institutions — judicial independence, civil society, free media — alongside the formal constitution; many post-colonial transitions lacked these, and Cold War interference (e.g., US support for the 1953 Iranian coup and 1973 Chilean coup) actively undermined democratic consolidation. Option A is a historically discredited and ethnocentric argument that ignores structural and geopolitical factors.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitary Power
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Federal systems always protect individual rights better than unitary systems because power is divided.' Evaluate this claim by identifying its most significant weakness.

options.A: The claim ignores that federal systems can allow regional governments to violate rights that a strong central government might protect uniformly.
options.B: The claim is correct because dividing power always prevents any single authority from becoming a tyranny.
options.C: The claim fails because unitary systems always have stronger bills of rights written into their constitutions.
options.D: The claim is wrong because federalism was only designed to manage economic policy, not protect rights.

questions.explanation: Federal systems can produce 'laboratories of repression' as well as innovation — historically, U.S. state governments used federalism to maintain segregation even when federal law moved toward equality, showing division of power does not automatically protect rights. Option B is the top distractor but is a logical fallacy: dividing power does not guarantee rights protection if both levels of government act oppressively or if one level actively suppresses minorities.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that citizens should obey the 'general will' even when it conflicts with their personal desires. A student argues this idea is fundamentally democratic because it reflects what the majority wants. What is the most precise error in this student's interpretation?

options.A: Rousseau believed the general will represents the common good of all citizens, which is not the same as majority opinion and can actually conflict with it.
options.B: Rousseau rejected democracy entirely and believed only a philosopher-king could identify the general will.
options.C: The error is that Rousseau said the general will only applies in direct democracies with fewer than 1,000 citizens.
options.D: Rousseau's general will is simply another term for a unanimous vote, making it identical to consensus democracy.

questions.explanation: Rousseau explicitly distinguished the 'general will' (volonté générale) — what is truly good for the whole community — from the 'will of all' (volonté de tous), which is merely the sum of individual preferences or majority opinion. A majority can be wrong about the common good, meaning the general will can diverge from majority rule. Option D is the top distractor because conflating general will with unanimity sounds sophisticated but misreads Rousseau, who said unanimous agreement is only a sign of the general will, not its definition.

questions.title: Market Failure and Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally produces steel and sells it profitably, but its smoke causes thousands of nearby residents to suffer respiratory illness, costing the public health system millions. Which concept most precisely describes this situation, and what does it reveal about the free market's limitation?

options.A: A negative externality, showing that free markets do not automatically include third-party costs in the price of goods.
options.B: A public good problem, showing that steel production requires government subsidy to remain viable.
options.C: A natural monopoly, showing that only one firm can efficiently produce steel in a region.
options.D: A merit good failure, showing that steel is underconsumed because buyers do not recognise its value.

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when the production or consumption of a good imposes costs on parties not involved in the transaction — here, the health costs borne by residents and the public system are not reflected in the steel price, a classic market failure identified by economists like Arthur Pigou. Option B is the top distractor because students sometimes confuse externalities with public goods problems, but a public good is defined by non-excludability and non-rivalry, neither of which applies to steel production.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Limits
questions.prompt: In a constitutional democracy, a newly elected government with 70% of parliamentary seats passes a law eliminating judicial review of its own legislation. Which principle of constitutional democracy is most directly undermined?

options.A: Popular sovereignty, because the majority no longer has the right to pass laws.
options.B: Separation of powers and the rule of law, because no branch should be able to exempt itself from legal accountability.
options.C: Universal suffrage, because removing judicial review prevents citizens from voting freely.
options.D: Federalism, because judicial review is the mechanism through which regional governments check the centre.

questions.explanation: Judicial review is a cornerstone of the separation of powers — it allows courts to check whether legislation conforms to the constitution, ensuring the rule of law applies even to elected majorities. When a legislature exempts itself from this check, it concentrates power in a single branch, which constitutional theorists like Montesquieu warned is the precondition for tyranny. Option A is the top distractor because students may confuse popular sovereignty with unlimited majority rule, but popular sovereignty in constitutionalism is bounded by the constitution itself.

questions.title: Authoritarian Legitimacy Strategies
questions.prompt: An authoritarian government dramatically increases spending on hospitals, schools, and roads, and its approval ratings rise sharply even though elections are not free or fair. Which concept best explains how this government is attempting to maintain power?

options.A: Performance legitimacy, where the regime justifies its authority through delivering economic and social outcomes rather than democratic consent.
options.B: Charismatic authority, where citizens obey solely because of the personal charm of the leader.
options.C: Traditional legitimacy, where citizens accept rule because it follows long-established customs and hereditary succession.
options.D: Legal-rational authority, where citizens obey because the government strictly follows a written constitution.

questions.explanation: Performance legitimacy is the concept — associated with scholars like Stein Ringen and used to analyse regimes like China's — where a government substitutes democratic legitimacy with demonstrated delivery of public goods, making citizens less likely to challenge the regime. Option B is the top distractor because charismatic authority (Weber's concept) focuses on a leader's personal qualities rather than policy outcomes, and the question emphasises spending programmes rather than a personality cult.

questions.title: Rawls and Inequality
questions.prompt: Two countries both have unequal income distributions. In Country P, the wealthiest 10% earn 40 times the poorest 10%, but the poorest group's absolute income has doubled in the last decade. In Country Q, the ratio is 15 to 1, but the poorest group's income has stagnated. Using Rawls' difference principle, which country has the more just arrangement, and why?

options.A: Country Q, because a smaller income gap always satisfies Rawls' principle of fairness.
options.B: Country P, because Rawls' difference principle permits inequality only if it improves the position of the least advantaged members of society.
options.C: Country Q, because Rawls believed equality of outcome is more important than equality of opportunity.
options.D: Country P, because Rawls argued that rapid economic growth always justifies inequality regardless of its effect on the poor.

questions.explanation: Rawls' difference principle, from 'A Theory of Justice' (1971), states that social and economic inequalities are just only if they benefit the least well-off group in society. Country P's larger gap is justified under this principle because the poorest have doubled their absolute income, meaning inequality is working to their advantage. Option A is the top distractor because students often misread Rawls as simply favouring smaller gaps, when he actually focuses on the absolute wellbeing of the worst-off, not the ratio of incomes.

questions.title: Revolution and Social Class
questions.prompt: Examine this claim: 'Revolutions occur primarily when a population is economically poor.' A student uses the fact that the leaders of the American Revolution (1775) were mostly wealthy landowners and lawyers to challenge this claim. Which theoretical framework best supports the student's counter-argument?

options.A: Relative deprivation theory, which argues that revolution is triggered not by absolute poverty but by the gap between what people expect and what they actually receive.
options.B: Dependency theory, which argues that revolutions only occur in countries exploited by wealthier foreign powers.
options.C: Modernisation theory, which predicts that as societies become wealthier, they inevitably become democratic and peaceful.
options.D: Structural functionalism, which argues that revolutions are caused by the failure of social institutions to adapt to population growth.

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation theory, associated with sociologist Ted Gurr, explains revolution through the frustration felt when people's rising expectations outpace reality — wealthy colonists in America were not poor in absolute terms, but felt deprived of the political rights and representation they believed they deserved as British subjects. Option B is the top distractor because dependency theory does describe external exploitation (which applies to American colonialism), but it focuses on economic extraction by foreign powers rather than on the psychology of revolutionary actors.

questions.title: Planned Economy Incentives
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, a factory manager is assigned a quota to produce 10,000 pairs of shoes per year. Historical records from the Soviet Union show managers frequently met quotas by producing very small shoe sizes that used less material. Which economic concept does this behaviour most precisely illustrate?

options.A: The principal-agent problem, where those implementing plans pursue their own interests rather than the planner's goals.
options.B: Comparative advantage, where managers specialise in the production they can do most efficiently.
options.C: Price elasticity, where demand for shoes falls when the government sets prices too high.
options.D: The free-rider problem, where factory workers benefit from state wages without contributing full effort.

questions.explanation: The principal-agent problem arises when an agent (the factory manager) has different incentives from the principal (the planning authority), leading to behaviour that meets the letter of the target but not its spirit — a well-documented dysfunction of Soviet central planning. Option D is the top distractor because the free-rider problem is also about misaligned incentives, but it specifically describes someone benefiting from a collective good without contributing, whereas the manager here is actively gaming the measurement system rather than simply shirking.

questions.title: Power vs Authority
questions.prompt: A school principal has the formal title and legal right to set school rules. A popular student leader has no official position but convinces most students to follow new social norms against bullying. Compare the type of influence each person holds and identify the most accurate description.

options.A: The principal holds authority while the student holds power; authority is legitimate and institutionally granted, whereas power can operate without formal legitimacy.
options.B: Both hold authority because both are able to change the behaviour of others effectively.
options.C: The principal holds power and the student holds authority because the student's influence is more widely accepted.
options.D: Neither holds true authority because only elected governments can possess legitimate authority.

questions.explanation: In political science, authority is power that is recognised as legitimate by those subject to it — the principal's authority derives from the institution's structure. Power, in contrast, is the ability to influence behaviour regardless of legitimacy, which describes the student's informal influence. Max Weber's typology distinguishes legal-rational authority (the principal) from influence without institutional backing (the student leader's social power). Option C is the top distractor because it confuses popularity with authority, but legitimacy in the formal sense requires institutional recognition, not just widespread acceptance.

questions.title: International Law Compliance
questions.prompt: Country A repeatedly violates international human rights law but faces no military intervention. A student argues this shows that international law is purely voluntary and therefore meaningless. Another student counters that even without enforcement, international law shapes state behaviour. Which argument is better supported by evidence?

options.A: The first student is correct because law without a centralised enforcer is not law in any meaningful sense.
options.B: The second student is better supported, because states often comply with international law to maintain reputation, access international institutions, and avoid economic sanctions even without military enforcement.
options.C: Both arguments are equally valid because international law is sometimes enforced and sometimes not, making it impossible to assess its overall effectiveness.
options.D: The first student is correct because the UN Security Council has never successfully enforced a human rights ruling against a powerful state.

questions.explanation: Scholars like Harold Koh have documented that states comply with international law far more often than violations make headlines, driven by reputational costs, treaty benefits, and domestic internalisation of norms — for example, most states honour thousands of trade and diplomatic treaty obligations annually without enforcement. Option D is the top distractor because while it is accurate that the Security Council rarely enforces rulings against powerful states, it conflates one mechanism of enforcement (military/political) with the full range of compliance incentives, ignoring economic and reputational pressures.

questions.title: Social Mobility and Meritocracy
questions.prompt: A government introduces free university education for all citizens, claiming this will create a true meritocracy. A sociologist responds that the policy alone cannot achieve meritocracy. Which argument best justifies the sociologist's position?

options.A: Free university education reduces social mobility by removing the motivation for students to work hard.
options.B: Meritocracy requires equal outcomes, not equal opportunities, so education reform is irrelevant to achieving it.
options.C: Structural inequalities such as differences in early childhood nutrition, school quality, and social capital mean that students arrive at university with vastly unequal preparedness, so access alone does not equalise opportunity.
options.D: The policy undermines meritocracy because university credentials become less valuable when everyone holds them.

questions.explanation: Sociologists like Pierre Bourdieu demonstrated that cultural capital — the knowledge, skills, and social networks passed down through families — means that children from privileged backgrounds benefit disproportionately from education systems even when access is equalised, because the inequalities begin long before university. Option D is the top distractor because credential inflation is a real economic concern, but it addresses the value of qualifications in the labour market rather than whether meritocracy itself is achieved.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that governments are formed to protect natural rights, but he also stated that some people could legitimately be excluded from the social contract. Which aspect of Locke's philosophy has been most criticised by later political thinkers as internally contradictory?

options.A: Locke's claim that property rights are natural contradicts his argument that governments should have unlimited power to redistribute wealth.
options.B: Locke's insistence that all humans possess natural rights by reason, while simultaneously justifying the exclusion of women, non-property owners, and colonised peoples from political participation, contradicts the universality he claimed.
options.C: Locke's social contract theory is contradictory because he argued both for revolution and for absolute obedience to the monarch.
options.D: Locke contradicted himself by arguing that the state of nature is peaceful while also claiming people need government to prevent constant war.

questions.explanation: Critics including feminist philosophers and postcolonial scholars have pointed out that Locke's Second Treatise simultaneously asserts universal natural rights grounded in reason and justifies the dispossession of Indigenous peoples and the exclusion of women from the polity, a contradiction that undermines the universalist foundation of his theory. Option D is the top distractor because it confuses Locke with Hobbes — Locke described the state of nature as relatively peaceful, and it was Hobbes who described it as a 'war of all against all.'

questions.title: Mixed Economy Government Roles
questions.prompt: Country R has a mixed economy. Its government provides universal healthcare, regulates pollution, and owns the national railway, but also allows private businesses to compete freely in most sectors. A libertarian critic argues the government should sell the railway and only regulate to correct market failures. Which response best challenges the libertarian position from a mixed economy perspective?

options.A: The critic is correct because public ownership always leads to inefficiency and higher costs for consumers.
options.B: Mixed economy theory justifies government ownership of natural monopolies like railways because privatising them may produce monopoly pricing that harms consumers and restricts access, a market failure that regulation alone may not solve.
options.C: The libertarian is wrong because mixed economies require governments to own all major industries to prevent inequality.
options.D: The critic's position is valid only in developed countries; in developing countries, governments must own all industries.

questions.explanation: Railways are a classic example of a natural monopoly — the infrastructure costs are so high that competition is impractical, meaning privatisation often results in a private monopoly that can extract high prices and underinvest in unprofitable routes. Mixed economy theory, as articulated by economists like John Maynard Keynes, recognises government ownership as legitimate where markets would otherwise fail to serve the public interest. Option A is the top distractor because while public ownership can be less efficient, this is an empirical generalisation, not a universal law, and ignores the specific market structure of natural monopolies.

questions.title: Democracy and Minority Rights
questions.prompt: A country holds a free and fair referendum in which 65% of voters support a law banning a religious minority from building new places of worship. A student argues: 'This is a legitimate democratic outcome because the majority decided.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct because in a democracy, majority decisions are always legitimate by definition.
options.B: The claim is partially correct in procedure but flawed in substance, because constitutional democracy distinguishes between legitimate majority rule and the 'tyranny of the majority,' where fundamental rights cannot be voted away.
options.C: The claim is wrong because referendums are never valid democratic instruments — only parliamentary votes count.
options.D: The claim is correct only if the religious minority had the opportunity to vote in the referendum.

questions.explanation: Liberal constitutional democracy, as theorised by thinkers from Madison to Dahl, explicitly protects certain fundamental rights from majority override — this is the purpose of bills of rights and constitutional entrenchment. The concept of 'tyranny of the majority,' warned about in Madison's Federalist No. 10, captures exactly this danger. Option D is the top distractor because allowing the minority to vote is a necessary condition for procedural fairness, but even if they voted, being outvoted on the removal of their own rights still constitutes a violation of liberal democratic principles.

questions.title: Globalisation and State Sovereignty
questions.prompt: As multinational corporations grow larger than many national economies and international trade agreements require countries to change their domestic laws, some political scientists argue that state sovereignty is being eroded. Others argue sovereignty remains intact. Which response best evaluates both positions?

options.A: Sovereignty is completely intact because states can always withdraw from trade agreements whenever they choose.
options.B: Sovereignty has been replaced by corporate power because multinational companies now make all significant economic decisions for national governments.
options.C: Both positions have merit: states formally retain sovereignty but face structural constraints from economic interdependence and international agreements that limit their practical policy choices.
options.D: Sovereignty is only eroded for developing countries; wealthy nations retain full control over their economic and political decisions.

questions.explanation: Political scientists like Stephen Krasner distinguish between formal (Westphalian) sovereignty — the legal right to self-governance — and operational sovereignty — the practical ability to make independent decisions. Globalisation has largely preserved the former while significantly constraining the latter, as seen when countries face investor-state dispute mechanisms or IMF conditionality. Option A is the top distractor because while withdrawal from agreements is technically possible (as with Brexit), the economic costs create powerful constraints that make the claim that sovereignty is 'completely intact' misleading.

questions.title: Comparative Electoral Systems
questions.prompt: In Country X's proportional representation system, a party wins 8% of the national vote and enters parliament. In Country Y's first-past-the-post system, the same party wins 8% of the national vote but wins zero seats in parliament. A student claims both systems are equally democratic. Identify the strongest challenge to this claim.

options.A: The claim is wrong because first-past-the-post systems always elect less qualified candidates than proportional systems.
options.B: The claim is challenged by the concept of 'wasted votes' — in Country Y, the 8% who voted for the party have no parliamentary representation, undermining the principle that all votes should carry equal weight.
options.C: The claim is correct because democracy is defined only by the freedom to vote, not by the translation of votes into seats.
options.D: The claim is wrong because proportional representation always produces more stable governments than first-past-the-post systems.

questions.explanation: Electoral systems scholars use the concept of 'wasted votes' to describe ballots cast for losing candidates in first-past-the-post systems that contribute nothing to representation — a party with 8% nationally but geographically dispersed support may win nothing, meaning those voters have no legislative voice. This challenges a core democratic principle of equal political weight for each citizen. Option C is the top distractor because it reflects a thin, procedural definition of democracy that ignores representational fairness — a definition that most democratic theorists consider inadequate.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democracy
questions.prompt: Political scientists often argue that a strong civil society — including independent trade unions, religious organisations, free press, and community groups — is essential for democracy to survive. Which reasoning best justifies this argument?

options.A: Civil society organisations replace the need for political parties, making elections unnecessary in mature democracies.
options.B: Civil society provides sources of power, information, and solidarity that citizens can use to resist government overreach, hold leaders accountable, and participate beyond election day.
options.C: Civil society is only important in authoritarian systems, where it substitutes for democratic elections that do not exist.
options.D: Strong civil society organisations reduce democracy by competing with elected governments for public loyalty and funding.

questions.explanation: Alexis de Tocqueville, studying American democracy in the 1830s, argued that voluntary associations were essential to preventing tyranny by creating intermediate institutions between the individual and the state — this analysis was later extended by scholars like Robert Putnam who showed that social capital built through civil society sustains democratic participation. Option C is the top distractor because while civil society is indeed crucial in authoritarian contexts, limiting its importance to non-democratic systems ignores the substantial evidence that it also sustains and deepens existing democracies.

questions.title: Social Contract and Consent
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Because I was born in my country and never signed any agreement, I am not actually bound by the social contract — the whole idea is fictional.' Which philosophical response best addresses this challenge?

options.A: The student is entirely correct; because no one literally signs a contract, governments have no legitimate authority over citizens.
options.B: Locke and later theorists use the concept of 'tacit consent' — by choosing to remain in a country and benefiting from its protections and services, citizens implicitly accept its authority, even without a literal signature.
options.C: The student is wrong because social contract theory is based on historical events when early humans literally gathered and agreed to form governments.
options.D: The social contract is binding because it was written into constitutions, which function as signed agreements between all citizens and the government.

questions.explanation: Locke introduced the concept of tacit consent in the Second Treatise, arguing that residing in a territory and enjoying its benefits — roads, security, legal system — constitutes implicit agreement to its governance. However, this concept has itself been criticised (notably by Hume) as insufficient to establish genuine moral obligation. Option C is the top distractor because students sometimes mistake social contract theory for a historical claim — but theorists from Hobbes to Rawls explicitly describe it as a hypothetical or analytical device, not a historical event.

questions.title: Income Inequality Measures
questions.prompt: Two economists debate Country Z's inequality. Economist A says the Gini coefficient has improved (fallen) over ten years, proving the country is becoming more equal. Economist B says the policy is failing the poor. Which scenario would allow both economists to be correct simultaneously?

options.A: The Gini coefficient measures absolute poverty, so a falling Gini always means the poor are better off in real terms.
options.B: The Gini coefficient could fall if middle-income groups gain relative to the very rich, even if the absolute income of the poorest group stagnates or falls.
options.C: Both economists cannot be correct because the Gini coefficient is a comprehensive measure of all aspects of poverty.
options.D: Economist B must be using incorrect data because the Gini coefficient is internationally standardised and cannot be disputed.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient measures relative income distribution across the whole population, not the absolute welfare of the poorest — it is possible for the Gini to fall (inequality narrows on average) while the poorest quintile sees no real income improvement if growth benefits the middle class at the expense of the top, leaving the bottom unchanged. This is a well-known limitation of single-metric inequality analysis. Option C is the top distractor because students may accept that the Gini is comprehensive, but it actually captures only income distribution, not absolute poverty, asset wealth, or access to services.

questions.title: Propaganda and Political Control
questions.prompt: A government mandates that all school textbooks describe the ruling party as the creator of the nation's prosperity and portray opposition leaders as traitors. Analyse which mechanism of political control this most precisely represents and why it is considered more durable than physical coercion.

options.A: Soft power projection, which is more durable because it influences other governments to support the regime internationally.
options.B: Ideological hegemony, where the ruling group shapes what people believe is natural, normal, and just, making resistance less likely because people may not recognise the system as oppressive.
options.C: Legal-rational authority, where citizens obey because the government has formalised its control through written laws and constitutions.
options.D: Charismatic domination, which is durable because the leader's personal appeal is passed on to future generations through the education system.

questions.explanation: Ideological hegemony, a concept developed by Antonio Gramsci, describes how ruling groups maintain power by shaping the dominant ideas, values, and beliefs in society so that their rule appears natural rather than imposed — when children are educated from birth to believe the current order is legitimate, they are less likely to organise resistance. This is considered more durable than coercion because it does not require constant force. Option A is the top distractor because soft power (Nye's concept) relates to international influence and attraction, not internal population control through education.

questions.title: Welfare State and Market Economy
questions.prompt: Country A is a market economy with an extensive welfare state providing universal healthcare, free education, and unemployment benefits funded by high taxes. Country B is a market economy with minimal government services and low taxes. A student claims Country A is not truly a market economy because of its high government spending. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct because a market economy by definition requires government spending to remain below 20% of GDP.
options.B: The claim is flawed because a market economy is defined by private ownership, price mechanisms, and competition — high government spending on services is compatible with these features, as demonstrated by Nordic countries.
options.C: The student is correct because government provision of services always crowds out private enterprise and eliminates market competition.
options.D: The claim is correct because welfare states require central planning of the entire economy, which contradicts market principles.

questions.explanation: The defining features of a market economy are private ownership of production, price signals allocating resources, and market competition — not the size of the public sector. Countries like Sweden, Denmark, and Norway have government expenditure exceeding 50% of GDP yet are consistently classified as market economies because most production occurs privately. Option D is the top distractor because students may conflate a large welfare state with central planning, but welfare states redistribute income and provide services without directing how private firms produce goods.

questions.title: Colonialism and Development
questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'The economic underdevelopment of many African and Asian nations today is primarily a result of colonial extraction and imposed borders, not cultural or geographic factors.' Which type of evidence would most directly support this historian's argument?

options.A: Evidence that former colonies with high geographic barriers such as landlocked territory consistently underperform economically, regardless of colonial history.
options.B: Evidence that regions within Africa with identical geographic and climatic conditions show significantly different levels of development based on the intensity and duration of colonial extraction they experienced.
options.C: Evidence that countries which adopted market economies after independence grew faster than those that adopted socialism, regardless of colonial history.
options.D: Evidence that former colonial powers have higher literacy rates than former colonies, demonstrating the cultural advantages of European civilisation.

questions.explanation: The historian's argument is a causal claim about colonialism specifically, so the strongest support would be evidence that controls for geographic and cultural variables and isolates colonial intensity as the differentiating factor — research like Daron Acemoglu's work on institutions and colonial legacy does exactly this, showing that extractive colonial institutions persistently damaged development regardless of geography. Option A is the top distractor because geographic determinism (associated with Jared Diamond) would actually undermine the historian's argument by attributing underdevelopment to geography rather than colonialism.

questions.title: Political Spectrum Limitations
questions.prompt: The traditional left-right political spectrum places socialist economic policies on the left and free-market policies on the right. A student argues this spectrum is insufficient to classify all political movements. Which example best justifies the student's argument?

options.A: Green political parties, which are simply an extension of the left wing and fit perfectly within the traditional spectrum.
options.B: Fascist movements, which combined far-right nationalism and authoritarianism with some state control of the economy, placing them in a position that the simple left-right axis cannot accurately represent.
options.C: Conservative parties, which have shifted from the right to the centre in most democracies, proving the spectrum needs only minor adjustment.
options.D: Anarchist movements, which are simply the extreme left of the spectrum and do not require any additional dimensions to classify.

questions.explanation: Fascism — as seen in Mussolini's Italy and Nazi Germany — combined extreme nationalism, authoritarian political control (neither left nor right on a civil liberties axis), and selective state economic intervention, which cannot be placed coherently on a one-dimensional left-right spectrum. This is why political scientists developed two-dimensional models like the Political Compass, adding an authoritarian-libertarian axis. Option D is the top distractor because anarchism does sit at the end of some left-leaning spectrums, but the student's argument requires an example that genuinely breaks the single axis — anarchism's rejection of all hierarchy also includes left-wing hierarchies, making it a poor fit for the simple left extreme.

questions.title: Separation of Powers Conflict
questions.prompt: The president of a democratic country issues an executive order banning immigration from three countries. Parliament passes a law reversing the ban. The supreme court rules the executive order constitutional. Which branch's action should take precedence, and which principle of constitutional government determines this?

options.A: The president's order, because executive power is supreme in matters of national security and immigration.
options.B: Parliament's law, because elected legislatures always override both executive orders and judicial rulings in constitutional democracies.
options.C: The supreme court's ruling supporting the executive order, because judicial review gives courts the final word on constitutionality, and a valid executive order cannot be overridden by ordinary legislation if the court deems it constitutional.
options.D: All three are equally valid and must be negotiated politically, because no branch has ultimate authority in a separation of powers system.

questions.explanation: In systems with strong judicial review — like the United States — the supreme court's determination of constitutionality is authoritative: if the court rules the executive order constitutional, parliament cannot simply override it with ordinary legislation, as that legislation itself could be struck down as unconstitutional. This is the principle of constitutional supremacy enforced through judicial review. Option B is the top distractor because parliamentary supremacy does apply in systems like the UK's Westminster model, but the question describes a system with a supreme court exercising constitutional judicial review, making parliamentary override legally contestable.

questions.title: Ethnic Conflict and State Formation
questions.prompt: After colonial powers drew borders in Africa that split ethnic groups across countries or merged rival groups into single states, post-independence conflicts frequently emerged. A student claims: 'These conflicts prove that ethnically homogeneous states are inherently more stable.' Evaluate the validity of this claim.

options.A: The claim is valid because all post-colonial conflicts demonstrate that diversity causes instability.
options.B: The claim oversimplifies the evidence: many diverse states are stable (Switzerland, India) while some homogeneous states have experienced significant internal conflict, suggesting institutional quality and political inclusion matter more than ethnic composition.
options.C: The claim is correct, and the solution is to redraw all national borders to match ethnic boundaries, which would eliminate future conflicts.
options.D: The claim is valid only in Africa and Asia, where ethnic identities are stronger than in Europe, where diversity produces stability.

questions.explanation: Comparative political research, including work by scholars like Arend Lijphart on consociational democracy, shows that diverse societies can achieve stability through inclusive political institutions, power-sharing arrangements, and federalism — Switzerland has four national languages and is among the world's most stable democracies. The root cause of post-colonial conflict was often poorly designed institutions that excluded groups from power, not diversity per se. Option C is the top distractor because redrawing borders sounds like a logical solution, but it ignores that borders cannot be cleanly drawn along ethnic lines (populations are intermixed), and the process of redrawing would itself likely cause massive conflict.

questions.title: Social Contract Foundations
questions.prompt: Thomas Hobbes described life in the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' Which conclusion does Hobbes draw from this premise to justify the existence of the state?

options.A: Citizens must retain the right to revolution when the sovereign acts unjustly
options.B: People rationally surrender rights to a sovereign in exchange for security and order
options.C: The general will of the population should guide all governmental decisions
options.D: Governments derive legitimacy only from the ongoing consent of the governed

questions.explanation: Hobbes argued in Leviathan (1651) that rational individuals escape the brutal state of nature by surrendering rights to an absolute sovereign (the Leviathan) in exchange for protection and civil order. Options A and D reflect Locke's more limited government theory, not Hobbes's absolutism; option C is Rousseau's concept of the general will.

questions.title: Market Failure Types
questions.prompt: A factory legally releases pollution into a river, harming downstream fishing communities who receive no compensation. In economic terms, which concept most precisely describes this situation?

options.A: A public good problem because the river is non-excludable
options.B: A moral hazard because the factory knows it will not be punished
options.C: A negative externality because a third party bears costs not reflected in market prices
options.D: A natural monopoly because only one factory controls the river access

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when production or consumption imposes costs on parties outside the transaction — here, fishing communities bear real economic harm not captured in the factory's pricing. Option A confuses externalities with public goods theory; option B describes moral hazard, which involves hidden risk-taking after an agreement, not third-party pollution harm.

questions.title: Democratic Electoral Systems
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A constitutional democracy is simply any country that holds regular elections.' Identify the most significant error in this claim.

options.A: Elections alone do not guarantee constitutional democracy; protection of civil liberties, rule of law, and separation of powers are also essential
options.B: Constitutional democracies do not require elections — appointed assemblies can represent citizens just as effectively
options.C: The claim is essentially correct because any state that holds elections qualifies as democratic by international law
options.D: The error is that elections must be proportional rather than first-past-the-post to count as truly democratic

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracy requires more than elections: it demands protection of fundamental rights, an independent judiciary, and institutional checks on power. Many authoritarian states hold elections while suppressing opposition — these are called 'electoral authoritarian' regimes. Option C is the top distractor because students conflate procedural elections with substantive democratic governance.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: John Rawls proposed the 'veil of ignorance' as a tool for designing fair social institutions. What is the core purpose of this thought experiment?

options.A: To show that individuals should follow the majority will even when it harms minorities
options.B: To ensure decision-makers do not know their place in society, producing impartial principles of justice
options.C: To demonstrate that markets naturally produce just outcomes when individuals act freely
options.D: To argue that governments should redistribute all wealth equally regardless of individual contribution

questions.explanation: Behind the veil of ignorance, individuals do not know their class, talents, or social position, so they choose principles of justice impartially — they would not risk favouring a system that might disadvantage them. Option D is a common misconception: Rawls's difference principle permits inequality if it benefits the worst-off, so he does not require total equality of wealth.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three 'ideal types' of legitimate authority. A monarch who rules because her family has governed for 400 years and citizens regard this as the natural order exemplifies which type?

options.A: Rational-legal authority, because the monarchy is embedded in the legal constitution
options.B: Charismatic authority, because citizens are personally devoted to the monarch's qualities
options.C: Traditional authority, because legitimacy rests on long-established customs and hereditary rules
options.D: Bureaucratic authority, because a professional civil service administers the monarch's decisions

questions.explanation: Weber's traditional authority is grounded in the sanctity of age-old rules and the personal status of the ruler — hereditary monarchy is his primary example. Option A is a common error: rational-legal authority refers to rule by codified law and elected or appointed officials whose power derives from legal procedures, not from dynastic tradition.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitarism
questions.prompt: Why do federal systems typically include a constitutional division of powers between national and regional governments, rather than leaving the division entirely to the national legislature?

options.A: To allow the national government to override regional decisions whenever it sees fit
options.B: To protect regional autonomy from being eliminated by a simple national parliamentary majority
options.C: To ensure all regions adopt identical laws and policies for administrative efficiency
options.D: To prevent regional governments from raising their own taxes independently

questions.explanation: A constitutional division of powers in federalism protects regional governments from being reduced or abolished at will by the national legislature — as seen in the US Tenth Amendment and Australia's federal constitution. Option A describes a unitary system, where the central government legally holds supreme authority over all sub-national units.

questions.title: Planned Economy Mechanics
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, what is the primary mechanism by which the government determines how resources are allocated across different industries?

options.A: The price mechanism, where rising prices signal producers to increase supply
options.B: Consumer sovereignty, where household spending decisions guide production priorities
options.C: Central planning targets set by the state, which direct firms on what and how much to produce
options.D: Competitive bidding among state-owned enterprises for government contracts

questions.explanation: In a centrally planned economy such as the Soviet Union under Stalin's Five-Year Plans, state planning agencies (e.g., Gosplan) set mandatory production quotas for industries and enterprises, replacing the price mechanism entirely. Options A and B describe market economy mechanisms, which central planners explicitly reject as inefficient or ideologically undesirable.

questions.title: Rousseau General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau distinguished between the 'will of all' and the 'general will.' Which statement best captures this distinction?

options.A: The will of all is the collective common good, while the general will is the sum of private interests
options.B: The general will represents the true common good of society, while the will of all is merely the aggregate of individual private interests
options.C: Both concepts are identical; Rousseau used them interchangeably in The Social Contract
options.D: The general will refers to majority rule, while the will of all refers to unanimous consent

questions.explanation: In The Social Contract, Rousseau explicitly separates these: the general will aims at the common good and cannot be divided or sold, while the will of all is simply the sum of what individuals privately desire, which may conflict with the common interest. Option A reverses the definitions — a mistake students commonly make when recalling the passage from memory.

questions.title: International Law Sources
questions.prompt: Under international law, which source is considered the most authoritative basis for legally binding obligations between sovereign states?

options.A: Resolutions passed by the United Nations General Assembly
options.B: Ratified international treaties and conventions signed by states
options.C: Rulings issued by international NGOs and human rights organisations
options.D: Statements of intent made by heads of state at diplomatic summits

questions.explanation: Under Article 38 of the ICJ Statute, ratified treaties are the primary source of binding international legal obligations — once a state ratifies a treaty it is legally bound by its terms under the principle pacta sunt servanda. Option A is frequently chosen in error: UNGA resolutions are not legally binding on member states, though they carry significant political weight.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Montesquieu argued in The Spirit of the Laws that political liberty depends on the separation of executive, legislative, and judicial powers. What is his core reasoning for this claim?

options.A: Separated powers increase government efficiency by allowing each branch to specialise in its function
options.B: When the same person or body holds multiple powers, there is no check to prevent tyrannical abuse of authority
options.C: Separation of powers ensures that elected officials are always more powerful than appointed judges
options.D: Multiple branches create competition that naturally leads to the best policy outcomes for citizens

questions.explanation: Montesquieu's central argument is that concentration of power corrupts — if the legislative and executive functions are held by the same body, that body can make oppressive laws and enforce them without restraint. Option A misrepresents his motive: Montesquieu was concerned with liberty, not administrative efficiency, which is a managerial argument foreign to his political philosophy.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: Relative deprivation theory, associated with Ted Gurr, explains revolutions by arguing that people rebel when there is a large gap between what they expect and what they actually have. Which historical case would BEST illustrate this theory?

options.A: A stable agrarian society with consistently low living standards and no recent economic change
options.B: A rapidly modernising society where rising middle-class expectations outpace actual political and economic access
options.C: A colonial state whose population has always lived under foreign rule and has never experienced self-governance
options.D: A wealthy democratic country experiencing mild inequality but robust civil society institutions

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation theory specifically predicts revolution when rising expectations are frustrated — a society modernising economically while political rights lag behind creates precisely this gap, as seen in pre-revolutionary Iran (1979). Option A describes absolute deprivation (consistently poor conditions), which Gurr distinguishes from relative deprivation; static misery does not necessarily produce rebellion.

questions.title: Market vs Mixed Economy
questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a mixed economy from a pure market economy?

options.A: In a mixed economy, all industries are nationalised and privately owned firms are banned
options.B: In a mixed economy, the government owns or regulates some industries and provides public services alongside private enterprise
options.C: A mixed economy uses central planning for consumer goods but allows market pricing for industrial goods only
options.D: In a mixed economy, prices are set by international trade agreements rather than domestic supply and demand

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private markets with state intervention — governments typically provide healthcare, education, or infrastructure and regulate key sectors while private enterprise operates freely in most areas, as seen in most Western European states. Option A describes a fully planned or command economy, where private ownership is abolished — the opposite extreme from a market economy.

questions.title: Social Stratification Concepts
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Meritocracy guarantees a fair society because talent and effort always determine success.' What is the most significant flaw in this argument from a sociological perspective?

options.A: Meritocracy is impossible because intelligence is entirely genetically fixed and cannot be changed by effort
options.B: It ignores how structural inequalities — such as unequal access to quality education — mean starting conditions are not equal for all individuals
options.C: Meritocracy actually produces more inequality than caste systems because it removes all social safety nets
options.D: The argument is essentially sound; sociologists broadly agree that modern societies are already fully meritocratic

questions.explanation: Sociologists like Michael Young (who coined the term 'meritocracy' critically in 1958) argue that meritocracy assumes a level playing field that does not exist — children from wealthier families access better schools, tutors, and networks, giving them structural advantages. Option A is factually wrong and represents a crude genetic determinism that modern sociologists reject.

questions.title: Authoritarianism Defined
questions.prompt: Which characteristic most fundamentally distinguishes authoritarian regimes from democratic ones, according to political scientists such as Juan Linz?

options.A: Authoritarian regimes are always led by military generals rather than civilian politicians
options.B: Authoritarian regimes limit political pluralism and restrict organised opposition to the ruling group
options.C: Authoritarian regimes always maintain a single official ideology that every citizen must publicly follow
options.D: Authoritarian regimes collapse more quickly than democracies because they lack popular support

questions.explanation: Juan Linz defined authoritarianism by its limited political pluralism — it suppresses organised opposition parties and civil society while not necessarily imposing a single total ideology (which distinguishes it from totalitarianism). Option C describes totalitarianism, not authoritarianism; many authoritarian regimes tolerate limited private beliefs as long as public political opposition is crushed.

questions.title: Locke Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that all individuals possess natural rights prior to the formation of any government. Which three rights did Locke specifically identify as natural and inalienable in his Second Treatise of Government?

options.A: Liberty, equality, and fraternity
options.B: Life, liberty, and property
options.C: Life, security, and the pursuit of happiness
options.D: Freedom, justice, and political representation

questions.explanation: Locke explicitly names life, liberty, and property as the three natural rights in the Second Treatise (1689); governments are formed to better protect these pre-political rights. Option C is frequently chosen because Jefferson adapted Locke when writing the Declaration of Independence — but Jefferson changed 'property' to 'pursuit of happiness,' and 'security' is Hobbes's focus, not Locke's triad.

questions.title: Information Asymmetry
questions.prompt: When a used-car seller knows far more about a vehicle's defects than the buyer, this situation can lead to 'adverse selection' in the market. Which economist's work first formally analysed this problem?

options.A: Milton Friedman, in his analysis of free-market price mechanisms
options.B: George Akerlof, in his 1970 paper 'The Market for Lemons'
options.C: John Maynard Keynes, in his critique of laissez-faire capitalism
options.D: Adam Smith, in his concept of the invisible hand in The Wealth of Nations

questions.explanation: George Akerlof's 1970 paper 'The Market for Lemons' demonstrated how information asymmetry causes market failure: sellers of bad cars (lemons) know more than buyers, driving good cars out of the market. Akerlof received the 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics for this work. Option A is a common distractor because Friedman is associated with market analysis, but he championed free markets rather than identifying their information failures.

questions.title: Comparative Political Systems
questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system, the executive (prime minister and cabinet) is accountable to and can be removed by the legislature. How does this differ from a presidential system?

options.A: In a presidential system, the president is elected by parliament and can be removed by a simple parliamentary vote
options.B: In a presidential system, the executive is separately elected and cannot normally be removed by the legislature through a vote of no confidence
options.C: Presidential systems always have weaker executives than parliamentary systems because the president lacks a party majority
options.D: In a presidential system, the judiciary appoints the executive and can dismiss it at any time

questions.explanation: The defining feature of presidentialism is the separate popular mandate of the executive — the president is directly elected and serves a fixed term independent of legislative confidence, as in the United States. Option A describes a parliamentary system; option C is factually false since the US president can be very powerful even without a congressional majority.

questions.title: Rule of Law Principle
questions.prompt: What does the principle of the 'rule of law' most precisely require of a government?

options.A: That the government must pass as many laws as possible to regulate every area of social life
options.B: That government officials and citizens alike are subject to publicly known, consistently applied laws rather than arbitrary personal rule
options.C: That laws must always reflect the preferences of the majority, even if they restrict minority rights
options.D: That courts must follow government instructions when ruling on cases involving state officials

questions.explanation: The rule of law, as articulated by A.V. Dicey and later the UN, requires that law is supreme over rulers and ruled alike, that laws are publicly known and applied equally, and that no one — including the government — is above the law. Option C confuses rule of law with majoritarian democracy; the rule of law specifically protects minorities from arbitrary majority power.

questions.title: Totalitarianism vs Authoritarianism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'All totalitarian states are authoritarian, but not all authoritarian states are totalitarian.' Evaluate whether this claim is accurate.

options.A: The claim is inaccurate; totalitarianism and authoritarianism are synonyms used interchangeably by political scientists
options.B: The claim is accurate; totalitarian states control all aspects of public and private life, while authoritarian states typically limit political opposition without mobilising all of society
options.C: The claim is inaccurate; authoritarian states are always more repressive than totalitarian ones because they use more direct violence
options.D: The claim is partially accurate but only applies to communist states; fascist states are neither totalitarian nor authoritarian

questions.explanation: Juan Linz's foundational work distinguishes totalitarianism (which seeks to transform all of society and private life through ideology and mass mobilisation — e.g., Nazi Germany, Stalinist USSR) from authoritarianism (which limits politics but tolerates private life). The student's logical subset claim is therefore correct. Option A is wrong because political scientists explicitly distinguish the two concepts.

questions.title: Public Choice Theory
questions.prompt: Public choice theory applies economic reasoning to political behaviour. Which of the following conclusions does public choice theory most typically draw about politicians and bureaucrats?

options.A: Politicians are primarily motivated by the desire to maximise social welfare above their personal interests
options.B: Self-interested actors in government pursue votes, budgets, and power, which can lead to policy outcomes that do not maximise public welfare
options.C: Democratic elections always force politicians to act in the public interest because voters can remove them from power
options.D: Bureaucrats are more efficient than private firms because they are shielded from market pressures and focus on service delivery

questions.explanation: Associated with James Buchanan (Nobel Prize 1986), public choice theory treats politicians as rational self-interested agents who maximise votes and bureaucrats who maximise budgets — leading to government failures such as over-spending, regulatory capture, and pork-barrel politics. Option C is the main distractor: public choice theorists argue that electoral incentives are imperfect and voters are often rationally ignorant.

questions.title: Social Contract and Consent
questions.prompt: What would happen if a government consistently broke the terms of the social contract, according to John Locke's political theory?

options.A: Citizens must continue to obey because any government is better than the chaos of the state of nature
options.B: The general will automatically transfers power to a new elected body chosen by the majority
options.C: Political power reverts to the people, who regain the right to replace or dissolve the government
options.D: The monarch gains absolute power because the original contract is void and no replacement is possible

questions.explanation: Locke argued in the Second Treatise that government is a conditional trust — if rulers violate natural rights or act against the public good, sovereignty reverts to the people, who may exercise the right to revolution and establish a new government. Option A describes Hobbes's view, not Locke's; Hobbes rejected the right of revolution even against an oppressive sovereign.

questions.title: Gender and Political Representation
questions.prompt: Compare the two main arguments used to justify gender quotas in parliamentary elections. Which statement most accurately captures the key debate?

options.A: Supporters argue quotas guarantee better policy outcomes; critics argue women are less effective legislators than men
options.B: Supporters argue quotas correct structural barriers to entry; critics argue they compromise merit-based selection and formal equality
options.C: Both supporters and critics agree quotas are needed but disagree on whether 30% or 50% is the correct threshold
options.D: Supporters argue quotas should apply only in authoritarian states; critics argue they are unnecessary in any democracy

questions.explanation: The core political philosophy debate is between substantive equality (correcting real structural disadvantage) and formal equality (treating all candidates identically regardless of outcome). Supporters cite evidence that structural bias excludes qualified women; critics invoke the principle that selection should be purely meritocratic. Option A introduces a factual claim about effectiveness that is not the basis of the mainstream philosophical debate.

questions.title: International Organisations
questions.prompt: The United Nations Security Council has five permanent members (P5) who each hold a veto. Why does this veto power create a structural limitation on the UN's ability to maintain international peace?

options.A: The veto means the Security Council cannot meet unless all five permanent members are physically present
options.B: Any P5 member can block enforcement action against itself or its allies, preventing collective security when major powers are involved
options.C: The veto transfers decision-making power to the General Assembly, which then becomes deadlocked
options.D: P5 members can only veto resolutions about their own territory, limiting broader Council effectiveness

questions.explanation: The P5 veto means that any major-power conflict or any situation where a P5 state sides with an aggressor is effectively immune from binding Security Council action — as seen during the Cold War and in more recent conflicts such as Russia's actions in Ukraine (2022). Option C is factually incorrect: the veto does not transfer power to the General Assembly, though the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution provides a limited workaround.

questions.title: Economic Inequality Measures
questions.prompt: The Gini coefficient is used to measure income inequality within a country. A Gini coefficient of 0 would indicate which economic condition?

options.A: One person receives all national income and everyone else receives nothing
options.B: The country has zero GDP and no income is generated at all
options.C: Every person in the country receives exactly the same share of national income — perfect equality
options.D: The top 10% of earners receive exactly ten times the income of the bottom 10%

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality — everyone has an identical income share) to 1 (maximum inequality — one person holds all income). It is derived from the Lorenz curve, measuring the area between the curve of actual distribution and the line of perfect equality. Option A describes a Gini coefficient of 1, the opposite extreme — a common mix-up for students who confuse the two endpoints.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democracy
questions.prompt: Political theorists such as Alexis de Tocqueville and Robert Putnam argue that a strong civil society (voluntary associations, civic groups, NGOs) is essential to healthy democracy. What is their core reasoning?

options.A: Civil society organisations replace political parties and eliminate the need for competitive elections
options.B: Civil society builds social trust, civic skills, and independent power centres that hold governments accountable and prevent tyranny
options.C: Civil society is only important in developing countries; established democracies do not depend on voluntary associations
options.D: Civil society weakens democracy by creating competing loyalties that undermine national unity and majority rule

questions.explanation: Tocqueville (Democracy in America, 1835) and Putnam (Bowling Alone, 2000) both argue that voluntary associations generate social capital — norms of trust and cooperation — and that they train citizens in democratic participation while providing institutional counterweights to state power. Option D is the top distractor: it represents an authoritarian critique of civil society, not the mainstream democratic theory position.

questions.title: Democracy Core Features
questions.prompt: Which feature most fundamentally distinguishes a liberal democracy from a system that holds elections but lacks other democratic guarantees?

options.A: Citizens vote in regular elections for representatives
options.B: The rule of law protects individual rights even from majority decisions
options.C: The government controls a military to enforce its authority
options.D: Economic policy is determined by elected officials

questions.explanation: Liberal democracy requires constitutional protections — the rule of law ensures that even a democratically elected majority cannot arbitrarily violate individual rights, distinguishing it from 'illiberal' or electoral-only regimes. Option A describes a necessary but insufficient condition; many authoritarian regimes hold elections without genuine liberal safeguards.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that legitimate political authority rests on the 'general will.' Which statement most accurately captures what Rousseau meant by this concept?

options.A: The sum of every individual's personal preferences at a given moment
options.B: The decision made by the most educated members of society
options.C: The collective interest of the community that individuals should subordinate personal desires to
options.D: The agreement reached between a monarch and the nobility

questions.explanation: Rousseau's 'general will' (volonté générale) refers to the shared common good of the whole community, distinct from the 'will of all' which is merely the aggregate of private interests. Option A is a common misconception — Rousseau explicitly contrasted the general will with the mere sum of individual wills.

questions.title: Market Failure: Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory legally releases pollution into a river, damaging fishing communities downstream who receive no compensation. Which economic concept does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: A positive externality, because the factory creates local employment
options.B: A negative externality, because third parties bear costs not reflected in the factory's prices
options.C: A public goods problem, because clean water is non-excludable
options.D: Regulatory capture, because the government allowed the pollution

questions.explanation: A negative externality occurs when a private transaction imposes costs on third parties outside the market exchange — here the fishing communities bear real economic harm not included in the factory's production costs. Option C is tempting but incorrect; clean water can be a public good issue in some contexts, but the specific mechanism here is the uncompensated external cost imposed on identifiable third parties.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Which three rights did Locke identify as inalienable natural rights that governments must protect?

options.A: Liberty, equality, and fraternity
options.B: Life, liberty, and property
options.C: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
options.D: Security, prosperity, and representation

questions.explanation: Locke's Second Treatise (1689) identifies life, liberty, and property as the fundamental natural rights that precede government and which the state is created to protect. Option C is a well-known distractor — Jefferson adapted Locke's phrasing in the Declaration of Independence, replacing 'property' with 'the pursuit of happiness.'

questions.title: Comparative Economic Systems
questions.prompt: In a command economy, which mechanism replaces the price system as the primary method for allocating resources?

options.A: Consumer demand signals transmitted through competitive markets
options.B: Central government planning and administrative directives
options.C: Negotiation between trade unions and employer associations
options.D: International trade agreements setting production quotas

questions.explanation: In a command (centrally planned) economy such as the Soviet Union under Stalin, a central planning authority issues directives determining what is produced, in what quantities, and at what prices, replacing the decentralised price signals of markets. Option A describes the market mechanism, which is precisely what a command economy replaces.

questions.title: Federalism vs Unitarism
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Federal systems always give more freedom to citizens than unitary systems.' Identify the most significant flaw in this generalisation.

options.A: Federal systems are actually more centralised than unitary systems
options.B: Regional governments in federal systems can restrict rights that national law would otherwise protect
options.C: Unitary systems always have stronger judiciaries than federal systems
options.D: Freedom depends only on economic development, not political structure

questions.explanation: Federalism divides power between national and subnational governments, but this can mean regional governments restrict minority rights in ways a unified national standard would prevent — for example, US states historically maintained racial segregation. Option A is factually incorrect; federalism by definition decentralises power rather than centralising it.

questions.title: Authoritarianism Defined
questions.prompt: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes an authoritarian regime from a totalitarian one?

options.A: Authoritarian regimes hold elections; totalitarian regimes do not
options.B: Authoritarian regimes seek to control only political life; totalitarian regimes attempt to dominate all aspects of society including culture and private life
options.C: Authoritarian regimes rely on charismatic leaders; totalitarian regimes rely on bureaucracies
options.D: Authoritarian regimes are always militaristic; totalitarian regimes are ideologically neutral

questions.explanation: Political scientists such as Hannah Arendt and Juan Linz draw the distinction by scope: authoritarian regimes suppress political opposition but tolerate private life, religion, and culture outside politics; totalitarian regimes seek comprehensive control over ideology, culture, education, and private belief. Option A is a common misconception — many authoritarian regimes do hold elections, but so have some totalitarian states.

questions.title: Social Contract Theory
