questions.prompt: Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau all proposed social contract theories. Which philosopher argued that life without government ('the state of nature') would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'?

options.A: John Locke
options.B: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
options.C: Thomas Hobbes
options.D: John Rawls

questions.explanation: This famous phrase appears in Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), where he argued that without a powerful sovereign, human life would be a war of all against all. Locke took a far more optimistic view of the state of nature, believing people could live relatively peacefully but needed government to adjudicate disputes — making him a popular but incorrect distractor here.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three types of legitimate authority. Which of the following correctly matches the type with its basis?

options.A: Traditional authority — based on the exceptional personal qualities of a leader
options.B: Charismatic authority — based on long-established customs and inherited positions
options.C: Legal-rational authority — based on formally established rules and offices
options.D: Charismatic authority — based on the legal right to hold an elected position

questions.explanation: Weber's legal-rational authority, the basis of modern bureaucracies and constitutional democracies, derives legitimacy from impersonal rules, laws, and formal procedures rather than tradition or personal qualities. Option A confuses charismatic authority (personal qualities) with traditional authority, a frequent error among students who partially remember Weber's typology.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy
questions.prompt: Why is an independent judiciary considered essential to constitutional democracy, even when its decisions are unpopular with the elected government?

options.A: Judges are more educated than politicians, so their decisions are more rational
options.B: It ensures that laws passed by elected majorities cannot violate constitutional rights of minorities
options.C: It removes economic policy decisions from political influence
options.D: It guarantees that all citizens have equal economic outcomes under the law

questions.explanation: An independent judiciary performs judicial review, striking down laws that violate constitutional protections even if those laws were democratically enacted — this is the key mechanism preventing 'tyranny of the majority.' Option A is elitist reasoning that does not reflect constitutional theory; judicial independence is valued for institutional checks, not personal intellect.

questions.title: Rawls and Justice
questions.prompt: John Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' is a thought experiment designed to achieve which goal in political philosophy?

options.A: To show that rational individuals will always prefer equal distribution of all resources
options.B: To design principles of justice by imagining choosers who do not know their place in society
options.C: To prove that free markets produce the most just outcomes over time
options.D: To demonstrate that utilitarianism is the most defensible ethical theory

questions.explanation: Rawls argues that if people chose the rules of society without knowing their gender, class, race, or talents (behind the 'veil of ignorance'), they would select fair principles because they could end up anywhere in the social hierarchy. Option A is a tempting misreading — Rawls's difference principle actually permits inequality, provided it benefits the least-advantaged group.

questions.title: Market vs Planned Economy
questions.prompt: Which of the following is identified by economists as a key advantage of market economies over centrally planned economies in allocating goods efficiently?

options.A: Prices automatically coordinate millions of decentralised decisions using dispersed information
options.B: Governments can ensure no citizen falls below the poverty line
options.C: Production targets are met reliably because firms are legally required to produce set quantities
options.D: Profit motive ensures equal distribution of goods across all social classes

questions.explanation: Friedrich Hayek's 'knowledge problem' argument holds that no central authority can possess the dispersed, local knowledge needed to allocate resources efficiently — only price signals in markets can aggregate this information. Option D is incorrect; the profit motive drives efficiency but does not produce equal distribution, which is a central criticism of market systems, not an advantage.

questions.title: Social Stratification
questions.prompt: A sociologist observes that in Country X, the top 1% of earners control 45% of national wealth, and this gap has widened every decade for fifty years. Which concept best describes this pattern?

options.A: Social mobility
options.B: Structural inequality
options.C: Cultural assimilation
options.D: Meritocracy

questions.explanation: Structural inequality refers to systematic, deeply embedded disparities in wealth, power, and opportunity that persist across generations due to how social, economic, and political institutions are organised. Option D (meritocracy) is the top distractor because some students confuse it with inequality; meritocracy is actually a normative ideal claiming rewards should reflect individual effort and talent, not a description of persistent gaps.

questions.title: Causes of Revolution
questions.prompt: Crane Brinton's comparative study of revolutions identified a common pattern. Which condition does Brinton cite as most typically present immediately before a revolution erupts?

options.A: The economy is in total collapse and mass starvation is occurring
options.B: The existing government is experiencing rising prosperity but fails to meet rising expectations
options.C: A foreign power has invaded and undermined national sovereignty
options.D: Religious institutions have lost all public credibility

questions.explanation: Brinton's Anatomy of Revolution (1938) and Alexis de Tocqueville's earlier observations both note that revolutions often occur not at the depths of misery but when conditions are improving yet expectations rise faster than reality — sometimes called the 'J-curve' or 'revolution of rising expectations.' Option A describes absolute deprivation, which Brinton found was not the typical trigger; extreme poverty can produce resignation rather than revolt.

questions.title: International Law Basics
questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains the primary source of binding obligations in international law between sovereign states?

options.A: Decisions made by the United Nations Security Council are automatically binding on all nations
options.B: Treaties voluntarily signed and ratified by states, creating consent-based legal obligations
options.C: Rulings by the International Court of Justice which all states must comply with
options.D: Universal moral principles that override national law in all circumstances

questions.explanation: The foundation of international law is state consent — states bind themselves by voluntarily ratifying treaties (e.g., the Geneva Conventions), a principle codified in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969). Option A is a common misconception; Security Council resolutions under Chapter VII can be binding, but they require a specific vote and can be vetoed, making them far from automatically universal.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Role
questions.prompt: Country Z has private firms producing most goods, but the government runs the healthcare and education systems and regulates pollution. Which type of economic system does this best represent?

options.A: Pure market economy
options.B: Command economy
options.C: Mixed economy
options.D: Traditional economy

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private markets for most goods with government provision of public services and regulatory intervention — exactly the pattern described, where private enterprise coexists with state-run healthcare, education, and environmental regulation. Option A is incorrect because a pure market economy has no government provision of services; most real-world economies are mixed.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Montesquieu argued that political liberty is best protected by separating governmental powers. Which problem does separation of powers most directly address?

options.A: Inefficiency caused by too many competing government agencies
options.B: The risk of tyranny when a single body makes, enforces, and judges the law
options.C: Voter apathy caused by complexity in government structures
options.D: Economic inequality arising from unregulated markets

questions.explanation: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that concentrating legislative, executive, and judicial powers in one body removes all checks on abuse — separation forces each branch to limit the others. Option A is a reasonable-sounding distractor; critics of separation of powers do cite gridlock and inefficiency, but this is a consequence of the system, not the problem it is designed to solve.

questions.title: Ethnic vs Civic Nationalism
questions.prompt: Country A defines national membership by descent and ethnicity. Country B defines it by shared civic values, laws, and citizenship regardless of ancestry. Which pair of concepts correctly labels these two approaches?

options.A: Federalism and unitarism
options.B: Ethnic nationalism and civic nationalism
options.C: Authoritarianism and liberalism
options.D: Populism and elitism

questions.explanation: Political scientists distinguish ethnic nationalism (membership defined by blood, ancestry, or culture) from civic nationalism (membership defined by shared laws and civic participation), associated with thinkers like Ernest Renan who emphasised 'daily plebiscite' over ethnic bonds. Option A is a structural rather than identity-based distinction and does not relate to definitions of nationhood.

questions.title: Public Goods Theory
questions.prompt: Which pair of characteristics do economists use to classify a good as a 'pure public good'?

options.A: Rival and excludable
options.B: Non-rival and non-excludable
options.C: Rival and non-excludable
options.D: Non-rival and excludable

questions.explanation: A pure public good is non-rival (one person's use does not reduce availability for others) and non-excludable (no one can be prevented from using it) — classic examples include national defence and street lighting. Option A describes a private good; Option C describes a common resource (e.g., fish in the ocean), and Option D describes a club good — students often confuse these four categories.

questions.title: Cold War Ideological Conflict
questions.prompt: During the Cold War, the United States and Soviet Union represented competing ideological systems. Which statement most accurately contrasts their core economic ideologies?

options.A: The US favoured state ownership of industries; the USSR favoured free-market competition
options.B: The US promoted market capitalism with private ownership; the USSR promoted state socialism with collective ownership of the means of production
options.C: Both systems were mixed economies but disagreed only on the role of religion
options.D: The US supported federalism; the USSR supported a unitary state — both used market systems

questions.explanation: The US promoted liberal market capitalism where private individuals own firms and prices are set by markets; the USSR operated a Marxist-Leninist planned economy where the state owned the means of production in the name of the working class. Option C is factually inaccurate — the ideological divide was fundamental, not a marginal disagreement about religion.

questions.title: Checks and Balances
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Checks and balances slow down government and are therefore a design flaw in democratic systems.' To what extent is this claim valid?

options.A: Fully valid — the main purpose of democratic systems is efficient policy delivery
options.B: Partially valid — slowing government is a deliberate feature to prevent unchecked power, not a flaw
options.C: Completely invalid — checks and balances always speed up legislation
options.D: Partially valid — checks and balances only apply to economic policy, not political decisions

questions.explanation: The Founders of the US Constitution, drawing on Montesquieu, intentionally designed friction into the system — slowing legislation protects against hasty or tyrannical action, making the delay a feature, not a bug, of constitutional design. Option A incorrectly prioritises efficiency over liberty as the primary democratic value, which misrepresents mainstream constitutional theory.

questions.title: Gender and Political Representation
questions.prompt: Research consistently shows women are underrepresented in national parliaments globally. Which structural factor do political scientists most frequently cite as a key cause?

options.A: Women are less interested in politics than men due to biological differences
options.B: Electoral systems, candidate selection processes, and unequal distribution of unpaid care work create systemic barriers
options.C: International law prohibits women from holding certain executive offices
options.D: Women's suffrage was only recently achieved in most countries, so representation will naturally equalise over time

questions.explanation: Political scientists point to structural factors including single-member district systems that disfavour outsider candidates, gatekeeping by party selection committees, and the 'double burden' of unpaid domestic labour that limits women's political availability — all documented in IPU and UN Women reports. Option A invokes biological determinism, which is not supported by political science evidence and represents a common but significant misconception.

questions.title: Democratic Backsliding
questions.prompt: Political scientists use the term 'democratic backsliding' to describe a trend seen in several countries since 2000. Which scenario best illustrates this concept?

options.A: A newly independent country holds its first free elections after decades of colonial rule
options.B: An elected government gradually undermines judicial independence, press freedom, and electoral integrity over several terms
options.C: A military coup immediately abolishes all democratic institutions in a single week
options.D: A country transitions from a monarchy to a parliamentary republic through constitutional reform

questions.explanation: Democratic backsliding, analysed by scholars such as Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way, refers to the gradual erosion of democratic norms and institutions by elected leaders — often through legal means — rather than sudden coups. Option C describes a sharp transition to authoritarianism, which is conceptually distinct from backsliding and is actually less common in the contemporary period.

questions.title: Globalisation and Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Critics of globalisation argue it erodes state sovereignty. Which of the following most accurately describes one mechanism through which economic globalisation can reduce a government's ability to act independently?

options.A: Multinational corporations can relocate investment if a government raises taxes or imposes regulation, constraining domestic policy choices
options.B: Globalisation forces all countries to adopt identical constitutions and legal systems
options.C: The United Nations passes laws that automatically override national legislation
options.D: International trade eliminates the need for domestic manufacturing, so governments lose tax revenue entirely

questions.explanation: Capital mobility means governments face a 'race to the bottom' pressure — if taxes or regulations become too burdensome, multinational firms can threaten or actually shift operations abroad, constraining policy autonomy without any formal legal compulsion. Option C is incorrect; the UN cannot pass laws that automatically supersede national law — international law is consent-based.

questions.title: Social Contract and Consent
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Because I never personally signed any agreement, I owe no obedience to my country's government.' Which philosophical response best challenges this argument using social contract theory?

options.A: Governments do not need consent because they are founded on tradition and divine right
options.B: Locke argued that residing in and benefiting from a state constitutes 'tacit consent,' implying ongoing voluntary acceptance of its authority
options.C: Rawls proved that formal contracts are unnecessary because justice is self-evident to rational people
options.D: Hobbes argued that once a sovereign is established, citizens permanently forfeit all rights and must obey unconditionally

questions.explanation: Locke introduced the concept of tacit consent in the Second Treatise — by choosing to remain in and benefit from a political community (roads, protection, courts), individuals implicitly accept its authority even without an explicit signed agreement. Option D misrepresents Hobbes, who did argue for near-absolute sovereign authority but crucially retained the right to self-preservation; this is a common but imprecise caricature of his position.

questions.title: Legitimacy vs Legality in Government
questions.prompt: A newly elected government passes a law through the correct constitutional procedures, but the law strips voting rights from all citizens who do not own property. A political philosopher argues the law is legal but not legitimate. Which concept best explains this distinction?

options.A: A law can be legal but lack legitimacy if it violates the foundational principles of justice or equal political standing that the system is meant to protect.
options.B: Legitimacy and legality are always identical — if a law passes through the correct procedures, it is automatically both legal and legitimate.
options.C: The law lacks legitimacy only because it was passed too quickly without enough public debate, not because of its content.
options.D: A law loses legitimacy only when citizens physically revolt against it; until then, legal passage is sufficient for full political authority.

questions.explanation: Legitimacy refers to whether authority is morally justified and widely accepted, not merely procedurally correct. Rawls and Locke both argue that laws undermining equal basic liberties — such as the right to vote — violate core principles of just governance, making them illegitimate regardless of procedural compliance. Option B is the top distractor but confuses procedural validity (legality) with substantive justification (legitimacy), a critical distinction in political philosophy.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau distinguished between the 'will of all' — the sum of individual private interests — and the 'general will' — what is genuinely best for the community as a whole. A student claims: 'Whatever the majority votes for in a democracy automatically equals the general will.' Identify the error in this claim.

options.A: The error is that majority decisions can reflect the aggregation of selfish private interests rather than genuine concern for the common good, so majority rule and the general will are not the same.
options.B: The error is that Rousseau believed only unanimous decisions, not majority votes, could reflect the general will.
options.C: The error is minor — Rousseau did accept that majority rule equals the general will in all but emergency situations.
options.D: The error is that Rousseau rejected democracy entirely, so no voting mechanism could produce the general will.

questions.explanation: Rousseau explicitly warned that the will of all (aggregate individual preferences) can diverge from the general will (the genuine common interest), especially when citizens vote out of self-interest rather than civic concern. A majority vote driven by factions or private gain does not automatically produce the general will. Option B is a plausible distractor but overstates Rousseau — he did not require unanimity for the general will; he required that citizens deliberate with the common good in mind.

questions.title: Market Failure: Negative Externalities
questions.prompt: A steel factory legally produces steel and sells it at a market price that covers all its private costs. However, the smoke it emits causes respiratory illness in nearby communities, costing the public health system millions annually. Why does this represent a market failure, and what is the economic term for this cost?

options.A: The factory charges too high a price, which is a case of monopoly pricing requiring antitrust regulation.
options.B: The health costs are a negative externality — a cost imposed on third parties not involved in the transaction — causing the market to overproduce steel relative to the socially optimal level.
options.C: The health costs represent a positive externality because the steel industry creates jobs that offset the medical expenses.
options.D: This is a problem of information asymmetry: the factory knows more about pollution than the government, causing inefficient regulation.

questions.explanation: A negative externality arises when a third party bears costs that are not reflected in the market price. Because the factory does not pay for the health damage it causes, its private marginal cost is below the social marginal cost, leading to overproduction — a classic market failure. Option C is a strong distractor because it confuses job creation (a separate economic benefit) with the definition of externality, incorrectly labelling a cost-imposing effect as positive.

questions.title: Authoritarian Consolidation of Power
questions.prompt: To what extent does control over the economy, rather than control over the military, determine whether an authoritarian regime remains stable over the long term? Consider historical examples in your reasoning.

options.A: Economic control is more decisive than military control because it creates a patronage network that incentivises loyalty among elites, as seen in resource-rich authoritarian states like Saudi Arabia.
options.B: Military control is always the sole determinant of authoritarian stability, as no economic wealth can compensate for a disloyal army.
options.C: Economic control is irrelevant to authoritarian stability — ideological propaganda is the only factor that truly sustains authoritarian regimes long-term.
options.D: Both military and economic control matter equally and always operate as independent variables with no interaction between them.

questions.explanation: Comparative politics research, including the 'selectorate theory' of Bueno de Mesquita, demonstrates that authoritarian stability often depends on distributing economic rents to a key group of supporters (winning coalition), making economic control central rather than incidental. Saudi Arabia's use of oil wealth to fund social services and elite patronage illustrates this. Option B is the top distractor because it contains a grain of truth — military loyalty matters — but it incorrectly treats it as the sole and always-dominant factor.

questions.title: Federalism and Minority Rights
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Federalism always protects minority groups because it divides power and prevents any one group from controlling everything.' Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — the division of power in federal systems mathematically prevents any majority from oppressing minorities at any level of government.
options.B: The claim is partially correct but overlooks that state or regional governments can themselves oppress local minorities, as occurred with Jim Crow segregation laws in US states.
options.C: The claim is entirely wrong because federalism always concentrates power in regional governments, which are more corrupt than central governments.
options.D: The claim is correct only in parliamentary federations; in presidential federations, federalism consistently fails to protect minorities.

questions.explanation: Federalism divides power vertically, but regional majorities can use that autonomy to oppress minorities within their jurisdiction. US history provides a clear example: between the 1870s and 1960s, Southern states used their federal autonomy to enforce racial segregation through Jim Crow laws, demonstrating that federalism can enable rather than prevent minority oppression at subnational levels. Option A is the strongest distractor because it correctly identifies the intent of federalism but ignores how the same mechanism can be turned against minorities.

questions.title: Veil of Ignorance Application
questions.prompt: Rawls proposed the 'veil of ignorance' as a tool for designing just institutions. If decision-makers behind the veil must choose between Society X, which guarantees equal outcomes for everyone, and Society Y, which allows inequality only where it maximally benefits the least advantaged group, which would Rawls endorse and why?

options.A: Rawls would endorse Society X because behind the veil of ignorance, rational agents would always choose perfect equality to avoid any risk of disadvantage.
options.B: Rawls would endorse Society Y because his difference principle holds that inequalities are just only when they benefit the least well-off members of society most.
options.C: Rawls would reject both societies because he argued that only a fully utilitarian system maximising total happiness is truly just.
options.D: Rawls would endorse Society Y only if the inequality also benefited the wealthiest members, since incentives are necessary for economic growth.

questions.explanation: Rawls's difference principle, the second part of his second principle of justice, explicitly permits inequalities provided they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. Society Y matches this criterion precisely. Option A is the top distractor and a very common misconception: students often assume the veil of ignorance leads to egalitarianism, but Rawls explicitly rejected strict equality in favour of maximin reasoning — choosing the arrangement that maximises the minimum position.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Safeguards
questions.prompt: Why do most constitutional democracies grant independent courts the power to strike down laws passed by an elected majority? Which principle of democratic theory best justifies this arrangement?

options.A: Constitutional review by courts protects against the 'tyranny of the majority' — the risk that elected majorities could enact laws that violate the fundamental rights of minorities or individuals.
options.B: Courts are given this power because elected legislatures are inherently corrupt and cannot be trusted to pass any just laws without judicial oversight.
options.C: This arrangement exists to ensure that trained legal experts, not uninformed voters, make all major policy decisions in a democracy.
options.D: Judicial review is justified because it allows courts to represent the interests of future generations who cannot vote in present elections.

questions.explanation: The doctrine of constitutional judicial review — most famously established in the US by Marbury v. Madison (1803) — rests on the principle that democracy requires not only majority rule but also the protection of rights that majorities cannot override. This addresses the tension between popular sovereignty and liberal rights. Option C is a strong distractor because it confuses the expertise of judges with the normative justification: judicial review is not about expert governance but about checking the majority's power to violate fundamental rights.

questions.title: Planned Economy: Price Signals
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, the state sets the price of bread below the market equilibrium price to ensure all citizens can afford it. Using economic reasoning, predict the most likely consequence of this policy.

options.A: The price ceiling will cause quantity demanded to exceed quantity supplied, leading to chronic shortages of bread.
options.B: The lower price will incentivise producers to make more bread, eliminating scarcity within months.
options.C: The policy will cause inflation in bread prices as consumers compete for limited supply.
options.D: Producers will raise quality standards to attract buyers since they cannot compete on price.

questions.explanation: When a price ceiling is set below equilibrium, it simultaneously increases quantity demanded (consumers want more at the lower price) and decreases quantity supplied (producers have less incentive to produce at lower profit margins), creating a persistent shortage. This was observed repeatedly in Soviet-era economies with price-controlled staples. Option B is the top distractor because students often conflate lower prices with greater consumer incentive, forgetting that it is the producer's incentive — not the consumer's — that drives supply.

questions.title: Social Contract: Hobbes vs Locke
questions.prompt: Thomas Hobbes argued that citizens should surrender nearly all freedoms to an absolute sovereign in exchange for security. John Locke disagreed fundamentally. Which statement most accurately identifies the core point of disagreement between their social contract theories?

options.A: Hobbes and Locke disagreed only on economics — Hobbes supported mercantilism while Locke supported free trade, which led to their different conclusions about government power.
options.B: The core disagreement is about the nature of the pre-political 'state of nature': Hobbes saw it as a war of all against all requiring absolute authority, while Locke saw it as generally peaceful with natural rights, meaning government authority should be limited and revocable.
options.C: Hobbes and Locke agreed on the state of nature but disagreed only on whether the social contract should be written or unwritten.
options.D: The core disagreement is that Locke believed in democracy while Hobbes believed in monarchy, but both shared identical views on the limits of government power.

questions.explanation: The fundamental divergence lies in their descriptions of the state of nature: Hobbes's 'Leviathan' (1651) describes it as 'nasty, brutish, and short,' necessitating an all-powerful sovereign to prevent chaos; Locke's 'Second Treatise' (1689) describes it as governed by natural law and natural rights, meaning sovereign authority is conditional and can be legitimately resisted if it violates those rights. Option D is a strong distractor because while the democracy/monarchy distinction contains a grain of truth, it misstates the argument — Hobbes did not focus on monarchy specifically, and both philosophers did not share identical views on government limits.

questions.title: Mixed Economy: Government Roles
questions.prompt: Country M has a mixed economy. Its government provides universal healthcare, regulates pollution, subsidises renewable energy, and also owns several commercial airlines that compete with private carriers. Which of these government activities goes furthest beyond the standard economic justification for state intervention?

options.A: Providing universal healthcare, because health services should be fully privatised in a mixed economy.
options.B: Regulating pollution, because externalities should be handled only by voluntary agreements between firms and communities.
options.C: Owning commercial airlines that compete with private firms, because this goes beyond correcting market failures into direct commercial competition where no clear market failure exists.
options.D: Subsidising renewable energy, because subsidies always distort markets and are never justified economically.

questions.explanation: Standard economic justifications for government intervention in mixed economies include correcting market failures such as externalities, public goods, and information asymmetries. Universal healthcare addresses equity and public good concerns; pollution regulation corrects a negative externality; renewable energy subsidies correct the positive externality of carbon reduction. Owning commercial airlines competing in normal markets has no standard market-failure justification and represents state enterprise beyond corrective intervention. Option D is a strong distractor because subsidies can be justified when positive externalities exist, which the renewable energy case illustrates.

questions.title: Power: Hard vs Soft Power
questions.prompt: Country A bases its international influence on its military presence and economic sanctions. Country B attracts allies through its cultural exports, educational exchanges, and reputation for democratic governance. Analyse how political scientist Joseph Nye would categorise these two approaches and evaluate which offers more durable influence.

options.A: Both countries use hard power; cultural influence is simply a form of economic investment and belongs to the same category as military force.
options.B: Country A uses hard power (coercion through military and economic tools) and Country B uses soft power (attraction through culture and values); soft power tends to be more durable because it generates willing alignment rather than compliance under threat.
options.C: Country B uses hard power because cultural exports generate revenue, and economic gain is always classified as hard power by Nye.
options.D: Country A uses soft power because sanctions are diplomatic tools, while Country B uses hard power because educational influence shapes foreign elites into agents of Country B's interests.

questions.explanation: Joseph Nye introduced the hard/soft power distinction in 'Bound to Lead' (1990): hard power involves coercion (military force, economic sanctions), while soft power involves attraction through culture, political values, and foreign policy legitimacy. Soft power is generally considered more durable because partners align voluntarily rather than under threat, and the influence persists even when coercive capacity is withdrawn. Option C is a classic misconception — students often categorise anything economic as hard power, but Nye specifically classifies economic attraction differently from economic coercion.

questions.title: Income Inequality: Gini Coefficient
questions.prompt: Country P has a Gini coefficient of 0.25 and Country Q has a Gini coefficient of 0.60. A student states: 'Country Q must have a lower average income than Country P.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because higher inequality always reduces GDP per capita through reduced consumer spending.
options.B: The claim is incorrect — the Gini coefficient measures income distribution, not average income level; a country can have high inequality alongside a high average income.
options.C: The claim is correct because the Gini coefficient directly measures the ratio of each country's GDP to its population size.
options.D: The claim is partially correct — a high Gini coefficient guarantees that the median income is below $10,000 per year.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality) and measures the distribution of income, not its absolute level. A country like the United States has a relatively high Gini (around 0.41) but also a very high average income — demonstrating that inequality and average wealth are independent variables. Option A is the top distractor because it contains an economic argument with some theoretical basis (inequality can reduce aggregate demand), but confuses a potential causal relationship with what the Gini coefficient itself measures.

questions.title: Revolution: Relative Deprivation Theory
questions.prompt: Sociologist Ted Gurr argued that revolutions occur not when people are at their most desperate, but when rising expectations outpace actual improvements — a concept called 'relative deprivation.' Which historical pattern best supports this theory?

options.A: The Russian Revolution of 1917 occurred after decades of unchanged poverty, confirming that absolute deprivation alone causes revolution.
options.B: Revolutions most commonly occur in the very poorest countries where citizens have no resources to organise collective action.
options.C: The period before the French Revolution of 1789 saw economic improvement under Louis XVI's reforms, raising expectations, yet political exclusion of the bourgeoisie remained — illustrating how the gap between rising expectations and limited political progress fuelled unrest.
options.D: Relative deprivation theory is best supported by post-World War II Europe, where stable democracies prevented revolution despite economic suffering.

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation theory predicts that revolution peaks when conditions have partially improved, raising expectations, but the improvement falls short of what people now believe they deserve. Pre-revolutionary France fits this precisely: the bourgeoisie had gained economic status and been influenced by Enlightenment ideas, raising political expectations, but the Ancien Régime's rigid hierarchy denied them corresponding political power. Option A is a strong distractor but actually contradicts relative deprivation theory by invoking absolute deprivation — the Russian Revolution involved other dynamics, and long-unchanged poverty is not what Gurr's model predicts.

questions.title: International Law: Sovereignty Tension
questions.prompt: The UN Responsibility to Protect (R2P) doctrine holds that the international community may intervene in a sovereign state if its government commits genocide or mass atrocities. A state's foreign minister argues: 'R2P fundamentally violates the Westphalian principle of sovereignty and should be rejected.' Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The argument is fully correct — sovereignty is absolute under international law and no doctrine can override it without unanimous global consent.
options.B: The argument correctly identifies a real tension between sovereignty and human rights norms, but overstates the case — R2P redefines sovereignty as conditional on protecting citizens, rather than being an outright violation of international law.
options.C: The argument is incorrect because the Westphalian system never included a principle of non-interference; sovereignty was always understood as conditional on good governance.
options.D: The argument is correct but irrelevant — R2P has never been applied and therefore poses no practical challenge to sovereignty.

questions.explanation: The Westphalian system (1648) established territorial sovereignty and non-interference as foundations of international order. R2P, adopted unanimously at the 2005 UN World Summit, explicitly reframes sovereignty not as a right but as a responsibility to protect citizens — creating a genuine normative tension. However, R2P does not simply violate sovereignty; it reconceptualises it. The foreign minister's argument identifies the tension but frames it too absolutely. Option A is the strongest distractor because sovereignty is a foundational international law principle, making the claim intuitively appealing, but absolute sovereignty is increasingly contested in modern international law.

questions.title: Comparative Governance: Checks and Balances
questions.prompt: In System A (presidential), the executive and legislature are elected separately and each can block the other's actions. In System B (parliamentary), the executive is drawn from and remains accountable to the legislature. Which statement best evaluates a key trade-off between these systems?

options.A: Presidential systems always produce more stable governments because the executive cannot be removed by a vote of no confidence.
options.B: Parliamentary systems always produce better policy outcomes because the executive is directly elected by citizens.
options.C: Presidential systems provide stronger protection against executive overreach through separation of powers, but may produce legislative gridlock when the executive and legislature are controlled by opposing parties.
options.D: Parliamentary systems are only suitable for small countries; presidential systems are necessary for large federal states regardless of political context.

questions.explanation: The separation of powers in presidential systems (as in the United States) creates structural checks on executive authority, but when different parties control the presidency and legislature, policy-making can become deadlocked — as seen repeatedly in US congressional-executive conflicts. Parliamentary systems avoid gridlock because the executive controls the legislature, but this reduces the separation of powers check. Option A is a strong distractor that contains a true element (presidents cannot be removed by no-confidence votes) but incorrectly equates this with overall stability — presidential systems have historically been more prone to democratic breakdown than parliamentary ones (Linz's 'perils of presidentialism').

questions.title: Globalisation and State Power
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Economic globalisation has fundamentally weakened the nation-state because multinational corporations can move capital across borders, making national economic policies ineffective.' To what extent is this claim accurate?

options.A: The claim is entirely accurate — nation-states are now irrelevant to economic governance and have been fully replaced by international institutions.
options.B: The claim identifies a real constraint on state power — capital mobility does limit unilateral tax and regulatory policy — but states retain significant tools including regulation, public spending, trade policy, and legal frameworks that multinationals must operate within.
options.C: The claim is entirely inaccurate — globalisation has strengthened nation-states by increasing their tax revenues from international trade, giving governments more resources than ever.
options.D: The claim is accurate only for developing countries; wealthy nations are completely immune to capital mobility pressures.

questions.explanation: Capital mobility does constrain state policy — the 'impossible trinity' in international economics shows that states cannot simultaneously maintain fixed exchange rates, free capital flows, and independent monetary policy — but states are far from irrelevant. They continue to set regulatory environments, provide public goods, negotiate trade agreements, and manage social safety nets. The hyperglobalisation thesis (states are powerless) is widely contested by political economists like Dani Rodrik. Option A is the top distractor because it logically extends the student's argument to its extreme, which many students find intuitively appealing but which overstates the erosion of state capacity.

questions.title: Democracy: Tyranny of Majority
questions.prompt: In a country where 80% of the population belongs to Group X and 20% belongs to Group Y, the parliament — elected by simple majority — passes a law banning Group Y's religious practices. Which concept from democratic theory most precisely identifies the problem with this outcome?

options.A: This represents electoral fraud, because a legitimate election cannot produce laws that affect minority groups.
options.B: This illustrates the 'tyranny of the majority' — where democratic procedures are used to systematically oppress a minority, violating the liberal component of liberal democracy that protects individual and group rights.
options.C: This represents an oligarchy, because only 80% of citizens effectively govern, which by definition is rule by the few.
options.D: This is an example of pluralism working correctly, as the majority interest has prevailed through democratic competition.

questions.explanation: The 'tyranny of the majority,' a concept discussed by both Tocqueville in 'Democracy in America' (1835) and Mill in 'On Liberty' (1859), describes how majoritarian democratic procedures can produce outcomes that oppress minorities and undermine the liberal rights that constitutional democracy is meant to protect. This scenario is precisely the kind of case that constitutional rights protections and judicial review are designed to prevent. Option D is a strong distractor because it correctly identifies that democratic competition has occurred but misapplies pluralism, which refers to competition among many groups — not the suppression of a minority's fundamental rights.

questions.title: Public Goods: Free Rider Problem
questions.prompt: A coastal town installs a lighthouse that warns all ships of dangerous rocks. No individual ship can be prevented from benefiting from the light. A private company refuses to build lighthouses without government funding, arguing it cannot make profit. Which economic concept explains the company's reasoning?

options.A: The free rider problem — because the lighthouse is non-excludable, ships benefit without paying, making it impossible for a private firm to recover costs through user fees alone.
options.B: Moral hazard — the existence of the lighthouse causes ship captains to take excessive navigational risks they would otherwise avoid.
options.C: Adverse selection — only reckless shipping companies operate near dangerous coasts, driving away cautious competitors.
options.D: Price discrimination — the company could charge different ships different prices, but government regulation prevents this profitable strategy.

questions.explanation: A lighthouse is a classic example of a public good: it is non-excludable (you cannot prevent ships from using the light) and non-rival (one ship's use does not diminish another's). Because non-excludability makes it impossible to charge users effectively, private firms face the free rider problem — rational actors benefit without paying — making private provision unprofitable and requiring public provision or subsidy. Option B is a plausible distractor because moral hazard does involve risk-taking in response to protection, which is superficially related, but it describes behavioural responses to insurance or safety nets, not the market provision problem of public goods.

questions.title: Power and Weber's Authority Types
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three ideal types of legitimate authority: traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal. A new revolutionary leader gains followers through personal magnetism and inspiring speeches, promising a complete transformation of society. Over time, as the revolution institutionalises, the leader creates written laws and bureaucracies. Which shift in authority type does Weber's framework predict?

options.A: The leader shifts from rational-legal to charismatic authority as the bureaucracy grows and replaces personal leadership.
options.B: The leader shifts from charismatic to traditional authority, as personal following always evolves into hereditary monarchy.
options.C: The leader shifts from charismatic authority to rational-legal authority, a process Weber called the 'routinisation of charisma,' where personal rule becomes institutionalised through laws and bureaucratic structures.
options.D: Weber's framework predicts no change — once a leader establishes charismatic authority, it remains fixed for the duration of their rule.

questions.explanation: Weber's concept of the 'routinisation of charisma' describes the process by which charismatic authority — based on extraordinary personal qualities — becomes institutionalised over time into rational-legal authority (based on codified rules and bureaucracy) or sometimes traditional authority. The scenario describes the rational-legal path: written laws and bureaucracies replace personal magnetism as the basis of rule. Option B is a strong distractor because Weber did acknowledge that routinisation can lead to traditional authority in some cases (hereditary succession), making students unsure which pathway applies here — but the specific clue of 'written laws and bureaucracies' points to rational-legal.

questions.title: Economic Systems: Opportunity Cost
questions.prompt: A government in a mixed economy chooses to spend an additional $10 billion on military defence rather than on public hospitals. A student says: 'This is a purely political decision with no economic dimension.' Identify the error in this claim using core economic reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct — government spending decisions are driven by political ideology and have no measurable economic consequences.
options.B: The error is ignoring opportunity cost — spending $10 billion on defence means forgoing the health outcomes and economic productivity that hospital investment would have generated; all resource allocation decisions carry an economic trade-off.
options.C: The error is assuming that $10 billion is a large sum; in modern economies, this amount is too small to carry significant economic consequences.
options.D: The error is that defence spending always generates higher GDP growth than hospital spending, making the decision economically optimal regardless of political motivations.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost — the value of the next-best alternative foregone — is a foundational economic concept that applies to all resource allocation decisions, including government spending. The $10 billion spent on defence cannot simultaneously be spent on hospitals; the foregone health improvements, workforce productivity gains, and lives saved represent the real economic cost of the choice. This makes the decision simultaneously political and economic. Option A is the top distractor because students sometimes treat government decisions as purely political, failing to apply the universal economic principle that scarcity means every choice involves a trade-off.

questions.title: Structural Inequality and Social Mobility
questions.prompt: Research shows that in Country W, children born to parents in the bottom income quintile have only a 7% chance of reaching the top income quintile as adults, compared to a 45% chance in Country V. A policymaker argues: 'This proves Country W's citizens simply lack ambition.' Critically assess this interpretation.

options.A: The interpretation is correct — differences in social mobility rates between countries are primarily explained by differences in individual motivation and work ethic.
options.B: The interpretation confuses correlation with causation — the data shows a statistical pattern of low mobility but cannot establish that ambition levels differ between countries.
options.C: The interpretation is flawed because it attributes a systemic, structural outcome to individual psychology, ignoring structural barriers such as unequal access to quality education, healthcare, and social networks that shape mobility regardless of individual effort.
options.D: The interpretation is partially correct — ambition matters, but the data also suggests Country W has a more efficient meritocracy because fewer low-income children advance.

questions.explanation: Social mobility research — including the work of economist Raj Chetty — demonstrates that low intergenerational mobility is strongly correlated with structural factors: inequality in school quality, residential segregation, access to healthcare, and inherited social capital. Attributing a society-wide statistical outcome to individual ambition is a form of individualist fallacy that ignores the sociological concept of social structure shaping life chances. Option B is a plausible distractor because correlation-causation reasoning is important, but it fails to identify the deeper flaw — the attribution of structural outcomes to individual psychology.

questions.title: International Organisations: UN Security Council
questions.prompt: The UN Security Council has five permanent members (P5) — the US, UK, France, Russia, and China — each holding veto power over binding resolutions. A student argues: 'The veto makes the Security Council the most effective decision-making body in international politics because any resolution that passes must have consensus among the most powerful states.' Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The argument is fully correct — a resolution that all five great powers support is always implemented effectively, making the veto a strength.
options.B: The argument identifies a real benefit of veto-backed consensus but critically overlooks that the veto also allows any single P5 member to block collective action even when four-fifths of the permanent members and the broader UN membership agree, enabling strategic paralysis during crises such as the Syrian civil war.
options.C: The argument is entirely wrong because the veto means no resolutions are ever passed, making the Security Council completely non-functional.
options.D: The argument is correct only when all five permanent members are liberal democracies, which has never historically been the case.

questions.explanation: The veto does provide a mechanism for great-power consensus, which can be a source of legitimacy when agreement is reached. However, the veto's most significant practical effect is enabling obstruction: during the Syrian civil war, Russia and China's vetoes blocked over a dozen resolutions on humanitarian intervention, preventing the Council from responding to mass atrocities. This demonstrates that the veto produces selective paralysis rather than consistent effectiveness. Option A is the top distractor because it correctly identifies the logic behind the veto system but ignores the empirical record of its use for obstruction.

questions.title: Political Ideology: Left vs Right Spectrum
questions.prompt: A political party advocates for high progressive taxation, nationalisation of key industries, strong labour union rights, and universal welfare programmes. Another party supports minimal taxation, privatisation of state enterprises, deregulation of labour markets, and means-tested welfare. Which framework best locates these parties on the political spectrum, and what is the core value that most clearly separates them?

options.A: Both parties are centrist; the left-right distinction is outdated and no longer applies to modern democratic politics.
options.B: The first party is broadly left-wing and the second broadly right-wing; the core separating value is the role of the state in redistributing wealth and managing the economy, with the left prioritising equality and collective welfare and the right prioritising individual freedom and market efficiency.
options.C: The first party is right-wing because nationalisation increases state control, and right-wing parties always support more government control than left-wing parties.
options.D: The first party is left-wing and the second is right-wing, with the core difference being their foreign policy positions on military intervention.

questions.explanation: The left-right political spectrum, originating in the French Estates-General seating arrangements of 1789, broadly maps onto attitudes toward equality versus hierarchy and state intervention versus market freedom. Left-wing positions historically favour redistribution, collective ownership, and social safety nets, while right-wing positions favour individual economic freedom, private enterprise, and limited government. The precise distinguishing value is the role of the state in economic redistribution. Option C is a strong misconception — students sometimes confuse 'state control' with right-wing ideology because of associations with authoritarian states, but economic state intervention is a left-wing rather than right-wing position in the democratic tradition.

questions.title: Decolonisation and State Formation
questions.prompt: Many African states gained independence in the 1960s with borders drawn by European colonial powers at the 1884-85 Berlin Conference, often splitting ethnic groups or merging traditional rivals. Evaluate how this historical process most directly contributed to governance challenges in post-colonial states.

options.A: Colonial borders had no lasting effect — post-colonial states quickly redrew boundaries to match ethnic and cultural realities within a decade of independence.
options.B: Arbitrary colonial borders created states where national identity was weak and ethnic or regional loyalties were stronger than loyalty to the central state, contributing to political instability, civil conflict, and challenges in building unified democratic institutions.
options.C: The main challenge created by colonial borders was economic — they disrupted trade routes rather than political identity, and political instability in Africa is primarily caused by post-independence economic mismanagement alone.
options.D: Colonial borders strengthened governance by creating clearly defined territories, and post-colonial instability resulted solely from Cold War interference by the US and USSR.

questions.explanation: The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 partitioned Africa with little regard for pre-existing ethnic, linguistic, or political boundaries. Research in comparative politics — including by scholars like Jeffrey Herbst in 'States and Power in Africa' — links this artificial state formation to weak national identity, ethnic competition for state resources, and recurrent civil conflicts such as those in Nigeria, DRC, and Sudan. Option C is a strong distractor because economic mismanagement and Cold War interference are genuine contributing factors to African political challenges, making it easy to mistake a partial cause for the complete answer — but it downplays the foundational governance problem created by arbitrary borders.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democratic Health
questions.prompt: Political scientist Robert Putnam argued that the strength of 'civil society' — voluntary associations, community groups, and social networks — is a better predictor of effective democratic governance than formal constitutional design. What would most directly challenge this hypothesis?

options.A: Evidence that countries with strong constitutions but weak civil society consistently maintain effective, accountable governments, suggesting formal institutions can substitute for social capital.
options.B: Evidence that countries with high voter turnout also tend to have strong civil society, confirming Putnam's view rather than challenging it.
options.C: Evidence that authoritarian regimes actively suppress civil society, which would support Putnam's hypothesis that civil society and good governance are related.
options.D: Evidence that civil society organisations in some countries are funded by foreign governments, raising questions about their independence but not directly challenging the hypothesis.

questions.explanation: Putnam's social capital thesis (developed in 'Making Democracy Work,' 1993) argues that dense networks of civic engagement generate trust and norms of reciprocity that make institutions function better. The strongest challenge to this hypothesis would be empirical evidence that robust formal institutions (well-designed constitutions, independent courts, strong rule-of-law frameworks) can produce effective democratic governance without high social capital — suggesting that institutional design may be a more direct causal factor. Option B actually confirms rather than challenges Putnam, which students may overlook; option D identifies a methodological concern but does not directly refute the causal claim.

questions.title: Populism and Democratic Erosion
questions.prompt: A populist leader wins a democratic election by campaigning as the voice of 'the real people' against a corrupt elite. Once in power, the leader attacks the judiciary, undermines press freedom, and uses electoral rules to entrench their party's advantage. Political scientists call this 'democratic backsliding.' Which feature of this scenario most clearly distinguishes democratic backsliding from an outright military coup?

options.A: Democratic backsliding, unlike a coup, occurs gradually through legal and electoral mechanisms, preserving the formal appearance of democratic institutions while hollowing out their actual function.
options.B: Democratic backsliding is identical to a coup in all politically relevant ways — both result in authoritarian rule and should be treated as the same phenomenon.
options.C: The key distinction is that democratic backsliding only occurs in young democracies, while coups occur in all regime types.
options.D: Democratic backsliding is less dangerous than a coup because elected leaders maintain popular legitimacy and therefore cannot become truly authoritarian.

questions.explanation: Political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way, along with scholars like Nancy Bermeo, distinguish democratic backsliding from sudden breakdowns precisely because it operates incrementally through ostensibly legal channels — court-packing, media regulation, gerrymandering — making it harder for citizens and international actors to identify a clear moment of democratic rupture. This gradualism is what makes backsliding particularly dangerous: the shell of democratic legitimacy remains even as its substance is removed, as seen in Hungary and Venezuela. Option D is the most dangerous distractor because it contains a half-truth — electoral legitimacy does persist initially — but it falsely concludes this prevents authoritarian consolidation.

questions.title: Democracy vs. Authoritarianism Spectrum
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A country holding regular elections must be a democracy, because free choice of leaders is the defining feature of democratic governance.' Evaluate the strength of this claim by identifying its most significant limitation.

options.A: The claim is largely correct, because elections are the single most important mechanism through which democratic accountability is maintained.
options.B: The claim is flawed because elections alone do not guarantee democracy if civil liberties, press freedom, and rule of law are absent.
options.C: The claim is flawed because democracy requires economic equality, and elections say nothing about wealth distribution.
options.D: The claim is correct as long as multiple political parties are permitted to appear on the ballot, which guarantees genuine competition.

questions.explanation: Elections are necessary but not sufficient for democracy; scholars like Robert Dahl define democracy ('polyarchy') as requiring not just elections but also freedoms of expression, alternative information sources, and associational autonomy. Option D is the top distractor — multi-party ballots can be manipulated through voter intimidation, gerrymandering, or media control, as seen in hybrid regimes like Russia, making the mere presence of parties insufficient.

questions.title: Locke's Natural Rights Theory
questions.prompt: According to John Locke, individuals in the state of nature already possess natural rights before any government exists. What is the primary purpose of forming a government, according to Locke's political philosophy?

options.A: To create rights for citizens that did not previously exist in the state of nature.
options.B: To redistribute property equally among all citizens so that no person dominates another.
options.C: To protect pre-existing natural rights — particularly life, liberty, and property — that individuals cannot reliably protect alone.
options.D: To merge individual wills into a single general will that overrides personal interests for the common good.

questions.explanation: Locke argued in the 'Second Treatise of Government' (1689) that government's sole legitimate purpose is to protect natural rights that individuals already hold, not to create or redistribute them. Option D describes Rousseau's concept of the 'general will,' not Locke — a common conflation that top students must carefully distinguish.

questions.title: Market Failure: Externalities
questions.prompt: A factory produces steel and releases pollutants into a nearby river, harming fishing communities downstream. The factory pays no compensation to those communities. Which concept best explains why the free market alone will not solve this problem, and what is the standard policy response?

options.A: Asymmetric information; the solution is mandatory disclosure laws requiring the factory to publish pollution data.
options.B: Negative externality; because the social cost exceeds the private cost, the market overproduces steel, and a corrective tax (Pigouvian tax) can restore efficiency.
options.C: Moral hazard; because the factory knows the government will clean up pollution, it takes excessive risks, requiring stricter liability laws.
options.D: Negative externality; because the private cost exceeds the social cost, the market underproduces steel, and a subsidy to the factory is the standard correction.

questions.explanation: Pollution is a textbook negative externality — a cost imposed on third parties not reflected in the factory's private costs, causing overproduction relative to the socially optimal level. A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost corrects this by internalising the externality. Option D reverses the cost relationship: when social cost exceeds private cost (not the other way), the market overproduces, so a subsidy would worsen, not fix, the problem.

questions.title: Rousseau's General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau argued that true freedom is achieved by obeying the 'general will' of society rather than one's own private desires. A student says: 'This makes Rousseau's theory fundamentally authoritarian, because it justifies forcing people to obey the collective.' To what extent is this student's critique valid?

options.A: The critique is entirely valid because Rousseau explicitly endorsed totalitarian government as the best way to enforce the general will.
options.B: The critique has merit because Rousseau did write that people could be 'forced to be free,' but he intended the general will to reflect genuine common interests, not ruler preferences — the tension is real but nuanced.
options.C: The critique is invalid because Rousseau's general will is identical to majority rule, which is inherently democratic and therefore cannot be authoritarian.
options.D: The critique is invalid because Rousseau argued private interests always align with the general will, so coercion would never be necessary.

questions.explanation: Rousseau did write in 'The Social Contract' (1762) that those who disobey the general will 'shall be forced to be free,' which critics like Benjamin Constant have used to argue his theory can justify authoritarianism. However, Rousseau distinguished the general will from the 'will of all' (mere majority preference), intending it to reflect genuine common good — making the tension real but not straightforwardly totalitarian. Option C conflates the general will with majority rule, which Rousseau explicitly rejected.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Structures
questions.prompt: In a constitutional democracy, why are certain rights — such as freedom of speech or protection from arbitrary arrest — placed beyond the reach of ordinary parliamentary majorities, even when those majorities represent the elected will of the people?

options.A: To give unelected judges more power than elected representatives, ensuring that experts rather than the public govern the country.
options.B: To protect minority rights and individual freedoms from the 'tyranny of the majority,' ensuring that democratic majorities cannot use their power to eliminate the very rights that make democracy legitimate.
options.C: To prevent any future changes to the system of government, ensuring permanent political stability regardless of changing social values.
options.D: To satisfy international organisations like the United Nations, which require all member states to entrench specific rights in their constitutions.

questions.explanation: Constitutional entrenchment of rights reflects the principle — central to theorists like Madison and Rawls — that democracy requires more than majority rule; it requires protection of the conditions (free speech, fair trial, minority rights) under which democratic competition itself can function. Without such protection, a majority could legitimately vote to oppress a minority, undermining democracy from within. Option A mischaracterises the purpose as elitist judicial supremacy rather than rights protection.

questions.title: Federalism and Power Distribution
questions.prompt: Compare the concepts of 'devolution' and 'federalism.' A student argues that both terms mean the same thing — that regional governments have powers that the central government cannot take away. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The error is that federalism applies only to large countries, while devolution applies only to small countries, regardless of constitutional arrangements.
options.B: The error is that in devolution, the central government grants powers to regional bodies but retains the constitutional authority to revoke them, whereas in federalism, regional powers are constitutionally guaranteed and cannot be removed by the central government alone.
options.C: The error is that devolution always leads to full independence for regions, whereas federalism permanently prevents regions from becoming independent.
options.D: There is no error — both devolution and federalism guarantee that regional governments have permanent, constitutionally protected powers independent of central government.

questions.explanation: In devolution (as in the UK's relationship with Scotland or Wales), Westminster retains parliamentary sovereignty and could theoretically repeal the devolution acts, meaning regional powers are delegated rather than constitutionally entrenched. In federal systems like the USA or Germany, regional powers are written into the constitution and cannot be unilaterally revoked by the central government. Option D repeats the student's error by treating the two concepts as equivalent.

questions.title: Economic Systems: Mixed Economy
questions.prompt: Why do most modern economies operate as mixed economies rather than as purely free-market or purely planned economies? Which explanation most accurately synthesises the theoretical and practical reasons?

options.A: Because international trade agreements require all countries to adopt a mixed model, preventing any nation from choosing a purely free-market or planned system.
options.B: Because free markets efficiently allocate most goods but produce market failures in areas like public goods, externalities, and natural monopolies, while fully planned systems have proven unable to process the vast information required to allocate resources efficiently across complex economies.
options.C: Because mixed economies always produce higher GDP growth than either pure system, making them objectively superior on every economic measure.
options.D: Because voters in democratic countries consistently prefer moderate policies, so governments are forced by electoral pressure to blend both systems regardless of economic theory.

questions.explanation: The mixed economy reflects both theoretical reasoning (market failures identified by welfare economics) and historical evidence (the collapse of Soviet central planning partly due to the 'knowledge problem' identified by Hayek — no central planner can process the decentralised information conveyed by price signals). Option C is incorrect because mixed economies do not universally outperform on every measure; the justification is based on correcting specific failures, not universal superiority.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three types of legitimate authority: traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal. A newly elected president governs according to a written constitution and established laws. Which type of authority does this represent, and why does the distinction matter?

options.A: Traditional authority, because the president follows established customs and norms that have governed the country for generations.
options.B: Charismatic authority, because elected presidents typically win office through personal appeal and the ability to inspire citizens.
options.C: Rational-legal authority, because the president's power derives from a codified legal framework rather than personal qualities or inherited tradition, making the office legitimate regardless of who holds it.
options.D: Rational-legal authority, but only if the president personally wrote or approved the constitution under which they govern.

questions.explanation: Weber's rational-legal authority is grounded in formally enacted rules and procedures — the authority belongs to the office, not the person, meaning any legitimately elected holder of that office commands obedience. This distinguishes modern bureaucratic states from traditional monarchies or charismatic movements. Option A is the key distractor — tradition involves long-established customs conferring legitimacy, not written legal frameworks, though the two can overlap.

questions.title: Rawls and Distributive Justice
questions.prompt: Rawls' 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment asks people to design a society without knowing their own position in it. A critic argues: 'Behind the veil of ignorance, a rational person would choose a completely equal society, because any inequality risks landing them at the bottom.' Critically assess this critique.

options.A: The critique is correct; Rawls concluded that perfect equality of wealth and income is the only arrangement rational agents would choose from behind the veil.
options.B: The critique is partially wrong because Rawls argued rational agents would accept inequalities that benefit the least-advantaged members of society, since such inequalities might produce greater overall resources even for those at the bottom.
options.C: The critique is correct because Rawls' first principle of justice demands equal distribution of all primary goods, including income and wealth, with no exceptions.
options.D: The critique is irrelevant because Rawls' theory applies only to political rights like voting, not to economic inequalities in wealth or income.

questions.explanation: Rawls' difference principle explicitly permits economic inequalities if — and only if — they work to the greatest benefit of the least-advantaged members of society. He used the 'maximin' strategy: maximise the minimum position. Complete equality is not his conclusion; it would be irrational if accepting some inequality makes even the worst-off better off. Option A directly contradicts this, reflecting a common misreading of Rawls as a strict egalitarian.

questions.title: Social Stratification and Class
questions.prompt: Karl Marx and Max Weber both analysed social inequality, but they differed significantly in their explanations. Which statement most accurately contrasts their approaches to understanding social class?

options.A: Marx saw class as determined solely by ownership of the means of production, while Weber argued class is multidimensional, also incorporating status (social prestige) and party (political power).
options.B: Marx focused on cultural factors like religion and education as drivers of inequality, while Weber focused exclusively on economic ownership as the sole determinant of class.
options.C: Both Marx and Weber agreed that economic ownership is the only significant factor in determining social class, but they disagreed on whether this would inevitably lead to revolution.
options.D: Weber rejected the concept of class entirely, arguing that only political party membership determines an individual's position in society.

questions.explanation: Marx's analysis in 'Capital' centres on binary class relations defined by ownership of the means of production (bourgeoisie vs. proletariat), treating economic position as the base that determines all social structures. Weber added 'status' (honour/prestige, not reducible to wealth) and 'party' (organised political power) as independent dimensions of stratification — a more pluralistic model. Option B reverses the theorists' actual positions, a misconception that confident but misinformed students often hold.

questions.title: Revolution: Causes and Conditions
questions.prompt: Political scientist Crane Brinton studied multiple revolutions (English, American, French, Russian) and found a recurring pattern. Which of the following best describes the conditions Brinton identified as most consistently preceding revolution?

options.A: Revolutions occur primarily in the world's poorest countries where citizens have never experienced prosperity, making desperation the single cause.
options.B: Revolutions typically occur during periods of improving conditions followed by a sudden downturn — when rising expectations are frustrated — rather than during the lowest point of misery.
options.C: Revolutions are caused exclusively by foreign military invasions that weaken central governments and create power vacuums exploited by radical factions.
options.D: Revolutions occur only when the ruling class is entirely unified and refuses all compromise, since internal divisions among elites prevent coordinated revolution.

questions.explanation: Brinton's 'Anatomy of Revolution' (1938) and related theories (like James Davies' 'J-curve') find that revolutions rarely occur at the absolute nadir of misery; instead, they follow a period of improvement that raises expectations, then a sharp reversal that frustrates those expectations — a phenomenon called 'relative deprivation.' The French Revolution occurred when France had experienced economic growth but fiscal crisis and food shortages hit simultaneously. Option A describes absolute deprivation, which research consistently shows is insufficient alone to generate revolution.

questions.title: International Law: Enforcement Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Unlike domestic law, international law has no single enforcement body equivalent to a national police force or courts with compulsory jurisdiction over all states. What mechanisms do exist to make international law function despite this gap?

options.A: International law functions purely on goodwill; because no enforcement exists, states comply only when it directly benefits them at that moment, making it entirely voluntary and unreliable.
options.B: The United Nations Security Council acts as a world government with binding authority over all states, ensuring all international laws are enforced equally regardless of a state's size or power.
options.C: Compliance is encouraged through reciprocity, reputational costs, economic sanctions, diplomatic pressure, international courts (for consenting states), and UN Security Council enforcement — though powerful states can still evade consequences.
options.D: International law is enforced identically to domestic law because states permanently surrender sovereignty when they sign the UN Charter, giving the UN binding jurisdiction over all national decisions.
