questions.explanation: International law relies on a decentralised enforcement system: states comply partly because they value reciprocal cooperation (if they break treaties, others will too), partly to protect their reputation in the international system, and partly because institutions like the ICJ, WTO dispute panels, and UN Security Council create structured consequences — though with significant limits, especially for permanent Security Council members who hold veto power. Option B is a serious misconception — the Security Council's enforcement power is limited by the veto system and only applies to peace and security matters, not all international law.

questions.title: Comparative Electoral Systems
questions.prompt: Country A uses a proportional representation system. After an election, five parties each win between 10% and 30% of seats, and no party has a majority. What is the most likely immediate consequence, and what does this reveal about the trade-off in proportional representation?

options.A: A second election must be immediately held because proportional representation rules require one party to hold a majority; the result is constitutionally invalid.
options.B: Parties must negotiate a coalition government, revealing that proportional representation increases parliamentary representation of diverse views but can reduce governmental decisiveness and stability.
options.C: The largest party automatically forms a majority government by absorbing the smallest parties, revealing that proportional representation ultimately produces the same outcome as first-past-the-post.
options.D: The result reveals that proportional representation always produces weaker democracies than first-past-the-post systems, because coalition governments are inherently less legitimate than single-party majorities.

questions.explanation: Coalition governments are the standard outcome of proportional representation when no single party wins a majority — as seen regularly in Germany, the Netherlands, and Israel. The trade-off is well-documented: PR systems better represent diverse voter preferences and reduce wasted votes, but coalition negotiations can be lengthy and governments may be less stable or decisive than single-party majority governments. Option D makes a normative judgement (coalitions are less legitimate) that is not supported by democratic theory — coalition governments can be highly legitimate.

questions.title: Public Goods vs. Merit Goods
questions.prompt: A student argues that education and national defence are both public goods and should therefore both be provided by the government for the same reasons. Identify the most significant error in this reasoning.

options.A: The error is that national defence should be privately provided, while education is the only true public good because it benefits individuals directly.
options.B: The error is that education is a merit good — excludable and rivalrous in consumption, but underprovided by markets because individuals undervalue its social benefits — whereas national defence is a pure public good that is non-excludable and non-rivalrous.
options.C: There is no error; both education and national defence are pure public goods because both benefit all citizens in society equally and neither can be provided efficiently by private markets.
options.D: The error is that national defence is a merit good while education is a pure public good, so the government justification for providing each is identical despite the different labels.

questions.explanation: National defence is a textbook pure public good: it is non-excludable (you cannot stop a citizen from benefiting from military protection) and non-rivalrous (one person's protection does not reduce another's). Education is excludable (students can be charged fees and excluded if they don't pay) and rivalrous (a seat in a classroom is used by one student), making it a merit good whose government provision is justified by positive externalities and information failures rather than by the public good definition. Option C conflates the two categories, a common student error.

questions.title: Authoritarianism: Propaganda and Control
questions.prompt: In authoritarian states, propaganda is used not only to promote positive images of the government but also — according to political theorist Hannah Arendt — to destroy citizens' capacity to distinguish truth from fiction altogether. Why would making citizens unable to evaluate truth be useful for an authoritarian regime?

options.A: Because citizens who cannot evaluate truth are more economically productive, which increases the regime's tax base and military capacity.
options.B: Because a population overwhelmed by contradictory information becomes politically passive and unable to coordinate effective resistance, making the regime more secure even without constant violent repression.
options.C: Because democratic opposition parties require access to true information to write their electoral platforms, so destroying truth primarily harms political competitors.
options.D: Because international organisations like the UN base sanctions decisions on documented human rights abuses, so obscuring truth protects the regime from foreign intervention.

questions.explanation: Arendt argued in 'The Origins of Totalitarianism' (1951) that total propaganda creates a population not of true believers, but of cynically disoriented citizens who give up trying to distinguish fact from fiction and become atomised and politically passive. This 'epistemic chaos' prevents collective action against the regime more effectively than simple censorship, because citizens cannot build shared reality needed for political coordination. Option D describes a real but secondary benefit — Arendt's argument focuses on domestic political control, not international relations.

questions.title: Cold War Ideological Conflict
questions.prompt: During the Cold War, the USA and USSR competed not just militarily but ideologically — each claiming their system represented the correct model for human development. What does this ideological dimension reveal about the nature of international power competition beyond simple military rivalry?

options.A: It reveals that military power is irrelevant in international relations, since both superpowers preferred ideas to weapons as their primary tools of influence.
options.B: It reveals that 'soft power' — the ability to attract other states through the appeal of one's values, culture, and political model — is a distinct and significant form of international power alongside military and economic coercion.
options.C: It reveals that ideological conflict always produces more stable international systems than military conflict, because ideas cannot cause physical destruction.
options.D: It reveals that the Cold War was fundamentally a religious conflict disguised as a political one, since both capitalism and communism functioned as substitute religions for their populations.

questions.explanation: Joseph Nye's concept of 'soft power' — the ability to achieve goals through attraction rather than coercion — is directly illustrated by Cold War ideological competition; both superpowers spent heavily on cultural diplomacy, broadcasting (Voice of America, Radio Free Europe), and foreign aid to demonstrate the superiority of their model. This shows power in international relations is multidimensional. Option A is incorrect — military power (the nuclear deterrent, arms race) remained central throughout the Cold War alongside ideological competition.

questions.title: Social Contract: Consent and Obligation
questions.prompt: A political philosophy student asks: 'If I was born in a country without ever signing a contract, why am I obligated to obey its laws?' Which of the following represents the most philosophically sophisticated response to this question?

options.A: You are not obligated to obey laws you never consented to; the social contract theory proves that all law is illegitimate unless citizens personally sign a founding document.
options.B: Locke argued that living in a country and benefiting from its protection constitutes 'tacit consent,' creating political obligation — though critics note this implies genuine freedom to leave, which many people lack.
options.C: You are obligated to obey the law because the state has superior force and will punish disobedience — obligation derives entirely from power, not from any form of consent.
options.D: Rawls' veil of ignorance proves that all rational people would consent to any set of laws produced by a democratically elected government, making political obligation universal and unconditional.

questions.explanation: Locke's doctrine of tacit consent (Second Treatise, §119) holds that residing in a territory and enjoying its benefits implies consent to its laws, even without an explicit agreement. However, philosophers like Hanna Pitkin have critiqued this: if people have no realistic alternative (no means to emigrate), tacit consent is not meaningful consent. This nuanced answer acknowledges both Locke's argument and its limits. Option C describes Hobbes' coercive view of political obligation, not the consent-based social contract tradition.

questions.title: Natural Monopoly and Regulation
questions.prompt: A natural monopoly exists when the most efficient number of producers in a market is one — typically because of very high fixed costs and low marginal costs. Why does a natural monopoly represent a market failure, and what is the government's standard regulatory response?

options.A: A natural monopoly is not a market failure; it is the efficient outcome of market competition and governments should never intervene in monopolistic industries.
options.B: It represents a market failure because a single unregulated producer will maximise profit by restricting output and raising price above marginal cost, causing allocative inefficiency and consumer harm; governments typically regulate prices or nationalise the industry.
options.C: It represents a market failure caused by negative externalities; governments should impose a Pigouvian tax equal to the external cost to restore efficiency.
options.D: It represents a market failure because multiple competing firms would produce more efficiently than one; the solution is to break up the monopoly into many small competing firms regardless of cost structures.

questions.explanation: In a natural monopoly (e.g., water supply networks, electricity grids), duplicating infrastructure for competition is wasteful, so one firm is efficient — but without regulation it will set price above marginal cost, extracting consumer surplus. Standard responses include price regulation (setting price equal to average cost to allow cost recovery) or public ownership. Option D would be counterproductive: forcing competition in a natural monopoly increases average costs because the high fixed costs are split among more firms, raising prices rather than lowering them.

questions.title: Globalisation and State Sovereignty
questions.prompt: Critics of economic globalisation argue that as countries become more deeply integrated through trade, investment, and international institutions, national governments lose meaningful sovereignty over economic policy. Evaluate the strength of this argument.

options.A: The argument is entirely correct; globalisation has completely eliminated national sovereignty because all economic decisions are now made by multinational corporations and international institutions like the IMF.
options.B: The argument has significant merit: membership in institutions like the WTO constrains trade policy, capital mobility limits tax and spending choices, and fear of capital flight restricts regulatory options — though states retain meaningful choices, particularly larger economies.
options.C: The argument is entirely incorrect; globalisation has no effect on national sovereignty because states can always simply withdraw from international agreements whenever they choose, at no cost.
options.D: The argument applies only to developing countries; wealthy countries with strong currencies like the USA or Germany face no constraints on economic policy from globalisation or international institutions.
options.E: The argument is invalid because globalisation increases total global wealth, and wealthier governments have more resources to pursue any economic policy they choose.

questions.explanation: The 'policy trilemma' (Mundell-Fleming) and empirical evidence from IMF conditionality both demonstrate genuine sovereignty constraints: countries that peg currencies, allow free capital movement, and seek foreign investment face real limits on independent monetary and fiscal policy. However, large economies (USA, China, EU) retain significantly more policy space than small open economies like Ireland or Singapore. Option A overstates the case — states clearly retain choices, as Brexit demonstrates — while Option C understates adjustment costs of withdrawal from international systems.

questions.title: Separation of Powers
questions.prompt: Montesquieu argued in 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748) that separating legislative, executive, and judicial powers among different institutions prevents tyranny. A student claims: 'Separation of powers is only effective if the three branches are completely independent and never interact.' Identify the error in this claim.

options.A: There is no error; complete independence of the three branches is exactly what Montesquieu intended and what modern democracies have successfully achieved.
options.B: The error is that effective separation of powers requires 'checks and balances' — mechanisms through which branches interact and constrain each other — not total independence, which would produce governmental deadlock and leave abuses within each branch unchecked.
options.C: The error is that Montesquieu only recommended separating the legislative and executive branches; he believed judges should be part of the executive branch to ensure consistent law enforcement.
options.D: The error is minor: the student is broadly correct, except that the judicial branch must always answer to the legislature to ensure judicial decisions reflect democratic values.

questions.explanation: The US Constitution — heavily influenced by Montesquieu — exemplifies that effective separation of powers works through overlap and mutual constraint: Congress passes laws but the President can veto them; the President nominates judges but the Senate must confirm them; courts can strike down laws passed by Congress. This 'checks and balances' system is the mechanism that prevents any single branch from accumulating tyrannical power. Option A reflects a common misconception that separation means isolation rather than structured interdependence.

questions.title: Nationalism and State Formation
questions.prompt: Benedict Anderson famously described nations as 'imagined communities.' What did he mean by this, and why is the concept important for understanding how states and national identities are formed?

options.A: Anderson meant that nations are fictional constructs with no real political power, and that ethnic or racial bonds are the only authentic basis for political community.
options.B: Anderson meant that national identity is socially constructed through shared symbols, print media, and collective narratives — people feel community with millions they will never meet — which reveals that nations are not natural givens but historical and cultural creations that can be built or dismantled.
options.C: Anderson meant that nations exist only in the imagination of political leaders who manipulate populations into false loyalty, proving all nationalism is inherently deceptive and harmful.
options.D: Anderson meant that nations are imagined because they rely on religious belief systems for their legitimacy, making secular states inherently less stable than religiously grounded political communities.

questions.explanation: Anderson's 'Imagined Communities' (1983) argues that the nation is imagined because no member can know all fellow members personally, yet each holds an image of their communion — sustained historically by print capitalism (shared newspapers, novels in vernacular languages). This constructivist insight is crucial for explaining why national identity varies across time and context and can be strengthened or weakened by political actors. Option A misreads 'imagined' as meaning 'fictional' or 'powerless' — Anderson argues imagined communities are entirely real in their political consequences.

questions.title: Civil Society and Democracy
questions.prompt: Political scientists like Robert Putnam argue that a strong 'civil society' — independent associations, clubs, religious organisations, and community groups — is essential for a healthy democracy. Why would organisations that are not part of the government strengthen democratic governance?

options.A: Because civil society organisations eventually become political parties, providing a direct pipeline of experienced leaders into government positions.
options.B: Because participation in voluntary associations builds social trust, civic skills, and norms of cooperation ('social capital') that citizens then bring into political life, making democratic institutions function more effectively.
options.C: Because civil society organisations are more efficient than governments at delivering public services, so strong civil society reduces the need for government intervention in most areas of social life.
options.D: Because international donors fund civil society organisations as an alternative to dysfunctional governments, so strong civil society compensates for weak democratic institutions rather than strengthening them.

questions.explanation: Putnam's 'Making Democracy Work' (1993) and 'Bowling Alone' (2000) demonstrate empirically that regions with denser networks of civil associations (even non-political ones like choral societies) exhibit higher levels of institutional performance and civic trust — 'bridging social capital' generalises from local associations to broader political cooperation. This is because citizens who practice cooperation in voluntary groups develop habits of trust and reciprocity that transfer to political engagement. Option C conflates civil society's civic function with economic efficiency, which was not Putnam's argument.

questions.title: Income Inequality: Measures and Effects
questions.prompt: The Gini coefficient measures income inequality within a country, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person holds all income). Country X has a Gini coefficient of 0.28, while Country Y has one of 0.52. A student claims: 'Country Y must have a lower standard of living than Country X, because higher inequality always means more poverty.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; economic research consistently shows that a Gini coefficient above 0.45 always produces absolute poverty rates above 30% regardless of overall GDP.
options.B: The claim is flawed because the Gini coefficient measures relative inequality, not absolute poverty levels — Country Y could have higher average income, meaning even the poorest citizens there are materially better off than the poorest in Country X.
options.C: The claim is correct because the Gini coefficient directly measures the percentage of the population living in poverty, so a score of 0.52 means 52% of Country Y's population is impoverished.
options.D: The claim is flawed but only because the Gini coefficient is an unreliable measure that should be replaced by GDP per capita, which accurately captures whether citizens are poor.

questions.explanation: The Gini coefficient measures the distribution of income relative to perfect equality, not absolute income levels. A country can have high inequality (high Gini) while still having high absolute living standards for most citizens — the USA has a Gini around 0.41 but higher average incomes than many more equal European countries. Standard of living depends on absolute income, access to services, and poverty thresholds, not solely on income distribution. Option C demonstrates a fundamental misreading of the Gini scale — it is not a percentage of people in poverty.

questions.title: Rousseau General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau's concept of the 'general will' is often contrasted with the 'will of all.' A student claims: 'For Rousseau, the general will is simply the majority vote of citizens on any given issue.' Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because Rousseau believed majority voting was the purest expression of collective reason.
options.B: The claim is flawed because the general will refers to what is genuinely good for the whole community, which may differ from what the majority actually votes for.
options.C: The claim is flawed because Rousseau argued that only unanimous consent, not majority rule, could express the general will.
options.D: The claim is partially correct because the general will equals majority will only when all citizens are equally educated.

questions.explanation: Rousseau explicitly distinguished the general will (volonté générale) from the will of all (volonté de tous): the former aims at the common good, the latter merely aggregates private interests, and a majority vote could reflect private interests rather than the common good. Option C is wrong because Rousseau did not require unanimity — he acknowledged majorities could vote, but warned that factional interests could corrupt votes so they no longer represent the general will.

questions.title: Federalism vs Devolution
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Federalism and devolution are essentially the same system because both involve regional governments holding some powers.' Identify the most significant error in this reasoning.

options.A: The error is that devolution always grants more powers to regions than federalism does, making the two systems opposites.
options.B: The error is that in federalism regional powers are constitutionally entrenched and cannot be removed by the central government alone, whereas in devolution the centre can legally reclaim delegated powers.
options.C: The error is that federalism only applies to republics, while devolution applies to constitutional monarchies.
options.D: The error is that both systems are identical in legal terms but differ only in name depending on the country.

questions.explanation: The defining distinction is constitutional entrenchment: in federal systems such as the USA or Germany, regional powers are guaranteed in the constitution and cannot be unilaterally removed by the central government, whereas devolution (as in the UK's relationship with Scotland) is a statutory grant that Westminster could theoretically repeal. Option A is incorrect because devolution does not necessarily grant more powers — in fact federal regions often have broader autonomous competences.

questions.title: Market Failure Externalities
questions.prompt: A steel factory releases pollution into a river, damaging fishing communities downstream. The factory pays no compensation and faces no government regulation. Which concept most precisely identifies the market failure here, and what is its direct consequence for resource allocation?

options.A: A public goods problem, leading to the underprovision of clean water by private firms.
options.B: A negative externality, causing the factory to overproduce steel relative to the socially optimal level because private costs are lower than social costs.
options.C: A monopoly failure, causing the factory to charge prices above the competitive equilibrium.
options.D: A negative externality, causing the factory to underproduce steel because the social cost exceeds the private benefit of production.

questions.explanation: When a producer does not bear the full social cost of its activity — here the damage to fishing communities — the private marginal cost is below the social marginal cost, so the firm produces more than is socially optimal. This is the standard negative externality mechanism. Option D is wrong because the factory underestimates its true costs and therefore overproduces, not underproduces — a common reversal error students make.

questions.title: Locke Property Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that legitimate government authority derives from the protection of natural rights, especially property. To what extent does this foundation create a tension with the goal of achieving distributive justice in modern liberal democracies?

options.A: There is no tension because Locke's theory requires governments to redistribute wealth whenever inequality grows too large.
options.B: The tension is significant because prioritising absolute property rights limits the government's legitimacy in taxing wealth for redistribution, which distributive justice may require.
options.C: The tension is minor because Locke's theory was designed specifically to address inequality through the labour theory of value.
options.D: The tension is resolved by Locke's proviso, which guarantees equal wealth outcomes for all citizens in a just society.

questions.explanation: Locke's labour theory of property treats legitimately acquired property as a natural right government must protect, which can be used — as Nozick later did in 'Anarchy, State, and Utopia' (1974) — to argue against redistributive taxation as a violation of rights, creating genuine tension with Rawlsian or utilitarian accounts of distributive justice. Option D misreads Locke's proviso: it states only that enough and as good must be left for others, not that equal outcomes are required.

questions.title: Authoritarian Legitimacy Strategies
questions.prompt: Compare the legitimation strategies of populist authoritarianism and traditional military dictatorship. Which statement most accurately synthesises a key difference in how each type of regime maintains popular support?

options.A: Populist authoritarianism relies on charismatic leaders who claim to represent 'the true people' against corrupt elites, whereas military dictatorships typically justify rule through appeals to national security and the restoration of order.
options.B: Military dictatorships rely on economic performance to maintain support, while populist authoritarianism relies solely on ideological indoctrination.
options.C: Both regimes use identical strategies but apply them to different social classes, with military dictatorships targeting urban workers and populist regimes targeting rural populations.
options.D: Populist authoritarianism is inherently more stable than military dictatorship because it holds regular elections, which provide genuine democratic accountability.

questions.explanation: Populist authoritarianism characteristically constructs a binary of 'the people' versus a corrupt elite — as theorised by Cas Mudde — and channels this into leader-cult legitimacy, while military regimes classically justify intervention as temporary guardianship restoring stability, as seen in Pinochet's Chile or the Greek junta. Option D is wrong because elections held under populist authoritarian regimes are typically manipulated or constrained and do not provide genuine accountability.

questions.title: Rawls Difference Principle Application
questions.prompt: A government proposes a tax cut for business owners, arguing it will grow the economy and eventually raise wages for the lowest-paid workers. Evaluate whether Rawls's difference principle would most likely justify or reject this policy.

options.A: Rawls would unconditionally reject the policy because his theory forbids any inequality between citizens.
options.B: Rawls would justify the policy only if there is robust evidence that it genuinely improves the absolute position of the least advantaged members of society.
options.C: Rawls would automatically justify the policy because any economic growth is compatible with the difference principle.
options.D: Rawls would reject the policy because the difference principle requires equal distribution of all economic benefits regardless of consequences.

questions.explanation: The difference principle permits inequalities only insofar as they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society — meaning the empirical claim that tax cuts raise wages for the poorest must be demonstrated, not simply asserted. Option C is wrong because Rawls does not endorse all growth-generating inequality, only inequality that maximally benefits the worst-off group; trickle-down assumptions are exactly the kind of claim the difference principle requires to be verified.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Judicial Review
questions.prompt: In constitutional democracies, unelected judges can strike down laws passed by elected parliaments through judicial review. A student claims this makes judicial review fundamentally anti-democratic. What is the most compelling counter-argument?

options.A: Judicial review is democratic because judges are indirectly elected by the public through their appointment by elected presidents.
options.B: Judicial review protects the constitutional rights of minorities against majority tyranny, which is itself a prerequisite for a functioning democracy rather than a contradiction of it.
options.C: Judicial review is not anti-democratic because courts have always agreed with parliamentary majorities in practice.
options.D: Judicial review is democratic because it gives the judicial branch equal power to the legislative branch, ensuring a perfectly balanced system.

questions.explanation: The standard counter-argument, developed by theorists such as Ronald Dworkin, is that democracy requires more than majority rule — it requires protection of fundamental rights, and judicial review prevents a tyranny of the majority from stripping minorities of constitutional protections, making it constitutive of rather than opposed to substantive democracy. Option A is incorrect as a general claim: in many systems such as the UK Supreme Court, judges are not appointed by elected presidents, and even where they are, this indirect link does not straightforwardly make their rulings democratic.

questions.title: Planned Economy Price Signals
questions.prompt: In a centrally planned economy, planners attempt to allocate resources without market prices. Which theoretical argument most precisely explains why this leads to chronic inefficiency in resource allocation, according to Friedrich Hayek?

options.A: Planners fail because they are always corrupt and prioritise their own interests over those of the population.
options.B: Planners cannot replicate the price signal system because prices in a market aggregate dispersed, localised knowledge that no single authority can collect or process efficiently.
options.C: Planners fail because citizens in planned economies always refuse to work productively without profit incentives.
options.D: Planners are inefficient because they rely on democratic voting to set prices, which introduces political bias into economic decisions.

questions.explanation: Hayek's 'knowledge problem,' articulated in 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945), holds that economic knowledge is inherently dispersed across millions of individuals and is often tacit or local — prices in a free market coordinate this knowledge automatically in a way that no central planner can replicate, leading to systematic misallocation. Option C, while a real concern in principal-agent theory, is a different argument (incentive problem) and does not capture Hayek's specific epistemological critique about the impossibility of gathering dispersed knowledge.

questions.title: Social Contract Legitimacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Because I never signed a social contract, I am not morally obligated to follow the laws of the state I was born into.' Evaluate this claim using political philosophy.

options.A: The claim is correct because all political philosophers agree that explicit written consent is necessary for legitimate state authority.
options.B: The claim has force but can be countered by Locke's concept of tacit consent — by residing in and benefiting from a state, individuals implicitly consent to its authority.
options.C: The claim is correct because Rousseau argued that citizens who do not vote in elections are exempt from legal obligations.
options.D: The claim is easily dismissed because political obligation derives from natural law, not consent, making the social contract irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Locke introduced tacit consent in the 'Second Treatise,' arguing that anyone who lives in a territory and uses its roads, protection, and institutions has implicitly consented to its governance — offering the most direct philosophical counter to the student's objection. Option D overstates the case: while natural law theories exist, dismissing the social contract tradition as 'irrelevant' ignores that consent-based theories remain the dominant framework in liberal political philosophy and are not simply superseded by natural law.

questions.title: Power Structures Class Analysis
questions.prompt: Marx argued that the state in capitalist society acts primarily as 'a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.' A contemporary pluralist theorist would most likely challenge this claim on which grounds?

options.A: Pluralists would argue that the bourgeoisie does not exist as a coherent class in modern economies.
options.B: Pluralists would argue that political power is distributed among many competing interest groups and that no single class consistently dominates state decisions.
options.C: Pluralists would argue that the state acts on behalf of the proletariat rather than the bourgeoisie in advanced democracies.
options.D: Pluralists would agree with Marx but argue that class domination is justified because the bourgeoisie creates economic growth for all.

questions.explanation: Pluralism, associated with Robert Dahl's study of New Haven in 'Who Governs?' (1961), holds that power is dispersed among competing groups — labour unions, business lobbies, civil society — such that no single class can consistently determine state policy, directly contradicting the Marxist base-superstructure model. Option A is wrong because pluralists do not typically deny the existence of business elites but rather argue that other groups counterbalance their influence through democratic competition.

questions.title: Democratic Backsliding Process
questions.prompt: Political scientists distinguish between democratic breakdown (sudden collapse by coup) and democratic backsliding (gradual erosion). Which pattern of events best exemplifies democratic backsliding rather than breakdown?

options.A: A military general seizes power overnight, dissolves parliament, and suspends the constitution by force.
options.B: An elected leader, using legal mechanisms, progressively weakens the constitutional court, restricts press freedom, and amends electoral rules to entrench the ruling party.
options.C: A foreign power invades a democracy and installs a puppet government aligned with its own interests.
options.D: A revolutionary movement overthrows an elected government after a series of mass street protests demanding systemic change.

questions.explanation: Democratic backsliding, as analysed by Levitsky and Ziblatt in 'How Democracies Die' (2018), occurs when elected leaders incrementally dismantle democratic institutions using legal means — court-packing, media restrictions, electoral manipulation — rather than through overt unconstitutional seizure of power, making it harder to identify and resist. Options A, C, and D all describe forms of sudden democratic breakdown or external imposition rather than the gradual internal erosion that defines backsliding.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Government Roles
questions.prompt: Evaluate this claim: 'A government operating a mixed economy should nationalise any industry that is strategically important, regardless of whether a market failure exists in that industry.'

options.A: The claim is correct because strategic importance is itself a sufficient economic justification for nationalisation in any mixed economy.
options.B: The claim conflates strategic importance with market failure; nationalisation may be justified for security reasons, but this is a political rather than purely economic rationale, and nationalisation carries its own efficiency costs.
options.C: The claim is wrong because mixed economies by definition prohibit any nationalisation of private industries.
options.D: The claim is correct because market failures are present in all strategically important industries by definition.

questions.explanation: Strategic importance — for example, defence manufacturing or energy infrastructure — is a political and security argument distinct from market failure (public goods, externalities, information asymmetry, monopoly), and conflating them ignores that nationalisation introduces government efficiency problems, potential political interference in management, and fiscal costs. Option D is false as a logical claim: strategic importance does not entail market failure — a defence sector could be competitive and efficient while still being deemed strategically sensitive.

questions.title: International Law Compliance
questions.prompt: Unlike domestic law, international law lacks a centralised enforcement authority. Which theoretical perspective best explains why states nonetheless comply with international law a significant proportion of the time?

options.A: Realists explain compliance by arguing that powerful states enforce international law on weaker states out of self-interest, creating a global rule of law.
options.B: Liberal institutionalists argue that repeated interaction within international institutions creates reputational incentives and reciprocity norms that make compliance rational even without a central enforcer.
options.C: Constructivists explain compliance by arguing that states are legally compelled by their constitutions to follow all international agreements they sign.
options.D: Compliance is best explained by the fact that international courts can imprison heads of state, providing a strong deterrent against violation.

questions.explanation: Liberal institutionalism, developed by theorists such as Robert Keohane in 'After Hegemony' (1984), holds that international institutions reduce transaction costs and create iterative games where states build reputations for compliance — defection risks future exclusion from cooperative arrangements, making compliance instrumentally rational without requiring a global police force. Option D is factually inaccurate as a general claim: only the International Criminal Court can issue arrest warrants for individuals, it has no enforcement mechanism of its own, and many major powers are not ICC members.

questions.title: Revolution Social Conditions
questions.prompt: Alexis de Tocqueville observed that revolutions are most likely to occur not when oppression is at its worst, but when conditions are improving. Which concept in political sociology best captures this counterintuitive pattern?

options.A: False consciousness — oppressed groups begin to see their own oppression only once education levels rise.
options.B: Relative deprivation — rising expectations that outpace actual improvements generate frustration and revolutionary grievance.
options.C: Class consciousness — the proletariat becomes unified precisely when living standards improve and leisure time increases.
options.D: Elite circulation — ruling classes are overthrown when a new elite with superior organisational capacity emerges during periods of economic growth.

questions.explanation: Relative deprivation theory, associated with James Davies's 'J-curve' model (1962) and Ted Gurr's 'Why Men Rebel' (1970), holds that the gap between rising expectations and reality — not absolute misery — is the key driver of revolutionary violence; Tocqueville's observation about the Ancien Régime reforming before 1789 is the classic historical illustration. Option D describes Pareto's elite circulation theory, which is a separate mechanism focused on elite replacement rather than the psychology of mass grievance.

questions.title: Separation of Powers Checks
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'A presidential system is always more democratic than a parliamentary system because in a presidential system, citizens directly elect both the executive and the legislature, creating two separate democratic mandates.' Identify the strongest flaw in this argument.

options.A: The argument is flawed because citizens in presidential systems do not vote directly for the legislature.
options.B: The argument is flawed because having two separately elected branches can produce constitutional deadlock, undermine accountability, and does not by itself ensure better democratic representation than parliamentary fusion of powers with strong legislative oversight.
options.C: The argument is correct; political scientists universally agree that presidential systems produce better democratic outcomes than parliamentary ones.
options.D: The argument is flawed because direct election of the executive gives presidents dictatorial powers that undermine democracy.

questions.explanation: Juan Linz's influential comparative work 'The Perils of Presidentialism' (1990) argued that dual democratic mandates in presidential systems create legitimacy conflicts during divided government, weaken accountability (a president cannot be removed by legislative vote except through cumbersome impeachment), and are statistically associated with higher rates of democratic breakdown in Latin America. Option D overstates the case — directly elected executives are not inherently dictatorial, which conflates potential abuse with structural design.

questions.title: Oligarchy Iron Law
questions.prompt: Robert Michels proposed the 'Iron Law of Oligarchy,' claiming that all organisations — even democratic ones — inevitably become controlled by a small elite over time. Which aspect of large democratic organisations most directly drives this tendency?

options.A: Large organisations are driven toward oligarchy primarily because wealthy members can purchase voting rights from poorer members.
options.B: Organisational complexity requires specialised leadership with communication and coordination advantages, allowing leaders to entrench themselves and marginalise rank-and-file participation.
options.C: Oligarchy emerges because democratic organisations always attract corrupt individuals who are more motivated to join than honest citizens.
options.D: Large democratic organisations become oligarchic because international law requires all major organisations to have a centralised governing board.

questions.explanation: Michels, writing in 'Political Parties' (1911) based on his study of the German Social Democratic Party, identified that as organisations grow, the division of labour creates a professional leadership class with superior information, resources, and communication networks, making it structurally difficult for ordinary members to challenge them — even when founding values are democratic. Option C describes a motivational selection argument (adverse selection) that is distinct from Michels's structural argument about the functional requirements of organisation.

questions.title: Welfare State Justifications
questions.prompt: Two students debate the welfare state. Student A says it is justified purely as insurance — rational citizens would choose it behind a 'veil of ignorance.' Student B says it is justified purely on utilitarian grounds — it maximises total societal happiness. Which statement best evaluates the key difference between these two justifications?

options.A: There is no meaningful difference because Rawlsian and utilitarian arguments always produce identical policy recommendations.
options.B: Student A's justification protects welfare rights even when they reduce total societal utility, whereas Student B's justification would cut welfare if doing so demonstrably produced greater overall happiness for the majority.
options.C: Student B's utilitarian justification is stronger because it is based on measurable outcomes, while Student A's Rawlsian argument is purely theoretical and cannot be applied to real policy.
options.D: Student A's argument requires unanimous public agreement on welfare levels, making it practically impossible to implement, unlike the utilitarian view.

questions.explanation: The critical divergence is that Rawlsian justice treats the welfare of the worst-off as lexically prior — a constraint not traded off against aggregate utility — while utilitarianism could in principle justify cutting welfare if the gains to the majority outweigh the losses to the few; this difference has concrete policy implications in means-testing and benefit caps. Option A is empirically false: Rawls himself explicitly developed his theory as a critique of utilitarian policy conclusions that could sacrifice individuals for the greater good.

questions.title: Ethnic Nationalism State Tension
questions.prompt: What would most likely happen to the stability of a multi-ethnic federal state if its constitution formally defined national citizenship primarily in terms of ethnicity rather than civic belonging?

options.A: Stability would increase because a clear definition of belonging reduces ambiguity and encourages social cohesion among all residents.
options.B: Stability would likely decrease because ethnic definitions of citizenship exclude minorities from full political membership, generating grievances that can fuel secessionist or conflict dynamics.
options.C: Stability would be unaffected because federal structures automatically accommodate ethnic diversity regardless of the citizenship definition used.
options.D: Stability would increase because ethnic federalism, as practised in Switzerland, shows that ethnic citizenship definitions promote peaceful coexistence.

questions.explanation: Ethnic definitions of citizenship create first- and second-class membership, as seen in the former Yugoslavia and post-Soviet republics, where ethnic constitutionalism marginalised minorities and contributed to violent fragmentation; civic nationalism — citizenship based on shared political values and legal equality — is more compatible with stable pluralism. Option D contains a factual error: Switzerland's stability is built on a civic, not ethnic, model of citizenship — its four linguistic communities are equally recognised as Swiss citizens regardless of ethnicity.

questions.title: Prisoner's Dilemma Collective Action
questions.prompt: Climate change negotiations often stall because each country calculates that the cost of reducing its own emissions is high while the benefits of other countries reducing theirs are shared globally. Which concept from game theory and political economy best explains this structural problem?

options.A: The tragedy of the commons — countries over-exploit a shared resource because property rights over the atmosphere are poorly defined.
options.B: The prisoner's dilemma — each country's dominant strategy is to free-ride on others' reductions, producing a collectively suboptimal equilibrium even when cooperation would benefit all.
options.C: Moral hazard — countries reduce emissions knowing that wealthier nations will pay to clean up any remaining pollution.
options.D: Adverse selection — countries that are most polluting are systematically more likely to enter climate negotiations, distorting the agreement.

questions.explanation: The multi-player prisoner's dilemma captures the climate negotiation structure precisely: each state's individually rational strategy (not reducing) dominates regardless of others' choices, leading to a Nash equilibrium in which all defect and the global public good of a stable climate is underprovided. Option A (tragedy of the commons, from Hardin 1968) is a related but distinct problem — it concerns overuse of a shared resource rather than the strategic interaction of rational actors with dominant strategies of non-cooperation.

questions.title: Propaganda Information Control
questions.prompt: In authoritarian regimes, scholars distinguish between 'preference falsification' (citizens publicly endorsing the regime while privately opposing it) and genuine 'preference change' (citizens internalising regime ideology). Why does this distinction matter for predicting regime stability?

options.A: It matters because regimes based on genuine preference change are less stable, since citizens who truly believe in the regime will eventually demand more political freedom.
options.B: It matters because regimes sustained by preference falsification can collapse rapidly and unpredictably once citizens learn others also privately oppose the regime, while regimes with genuine preference change face more stable, ideological support.
options.C: The distinction does not matter because authoritarian regimes maintain power through military force alone, making public opinion irrelevant to their survival.
options.D: It matters because preference falsification indicates higher economic development, which is the real predictor of regime stability.

questions.explanation: Timur Kuran's theory of 'preference falsification' in 'Private Truths, Public Lies' (1995) explains why communist regimes in Eastern Europe collapsed suddenly in 1989: once early defectors signalled that dissent was safe, cascading revelations of private opposition swept away systems that had appeared stable, because their apparent support was performative rather than genuine. Option C is wrong because both empirical research and case studies show that public opinion and legitimacy significantly affect authoritarian durability — purely coercion-based regimes are historically among the least stable.

questions.title: Comparative Electoral Systems
questions.prompt: A researcher finds that countries using proportional representation (PR) electoral systems tend to have higher voter turnout and more parties represented in parliament than first-past-the-post (FPTP) systems. A student concludes: 'Therefore, PR systems always produce more stable governments.' Evaluate this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is correct because more parties in parliament means more negotiation, which prevents hasty or extreme policy decisions.
options.B: The conclusion does not follow from the evidence: greater representativeness in PR systems often requires coalition governments, which can be inherently fragile and prone to collapse, as seen in Weimar Germany and interwar France.
options.C: The conclusion is correct because higher voter turnout statistically predicts government stability in all electoral systems studied.
options.D: The conclusion is partially correct because PR produces stability in foreign policy, though instability in domestic legislation.

questions.explanation: While PR systems do tend to produce broader representation and higher turnout, multi-party coalition governments are structurally more vulnerable to internal disagreement and collapse — Weimar Germany's proportional system is the textbook case of fragmentation contributing to democratic failure, and Israel's PR system produces governments that frequently fall within a single parliamentary term. Option C presents a false empirical claim: turnout correlates with democratic health indicators but is not a sufficient predictor of government stability.

questions.title: Asymmetric Information Markets
questions.prompt: George Akerlof's 'market for lemons' model describes how asymmetric information between buyers and sellers can cause markets to collapse. Which of the following scenarios is the most direct real-world application of this mechanism?

options.A: A government sets a maximum price for bread below the equilibrium price, causing shortages as supply falls and demand rises.
options.B: Private health insurance markets tend toward adverse selection because high-risk individuals know their own risk better than insurers, driving up premiums until low-risk individuals exit and the market unravels.
options.C: A monopoly firm charges prices above marginal cost, reducing consumer surplus and creating a deadweight loss.
options.D: Workers in a factory collude to limit production output, artificially raising their bargaining power in wage negotiations.

questions.explanation: Akerlof's 1970 model showed that when sellers know more about product quality than buyers, buyers discount all goods to the average quality price, driving high-quality sellers out — in health insurance, individuals know their health status better than insurers, causing adverse selection where only high-risk people buy insurance, pushing premiums up and potentially collapsing voluntary insurance markets, exactly the mechanism Akerlof described. Option A describes a price ceiling causing a shortage — a standard supply-demand distortion with no information asymmetry involved.

questions.title: Soft Power Global Influence
questions.prompt: Joseph Nye distinguished 'hard power' (military and economic coercion) from 'soft power' (attraction through culture, values, and diplomacy). A student claims: 'Soft power is always more effective than hard power because it creates willing compliance rather than forced obedience.' Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because empirical studies show soft power interventions consistently achieve foreign policy goals more reliably than military force.
options.B: The claim overgeneralises: soft power is slower-acting and ineffective in urgent security crises or against actors who reject the attracting state's values, whereas hard power may achieve immediate compliance despite its costs.
options.C: The claim is correct because soft power is free to deploy, making it superior in cost-effectiveness to any military operation.
options.D: The claim is partially correct but only for liberal democracies; authoritarian states cannot generate soft power under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Nye himself acknowledged that soft power operates slowly and requires receptive audiences — it is largely ineffective against actors ideologically opposed to the attracting state's model, as seen in US soft power failing to deter adversarial state or non-state actors who actively reject Western liberal values; hard power retains decisive advantages in immediate coercive contexts. Option C is factually wrong: soft power requires substantial investment in cultural diplomacy, broadcasting (e.g. BBC World Service, China's Confucius Institutes), and international aid — it is far from costless.

questions.title: Tocqueville Democracy Tyranny
questions.prompt: Alexis de Tocqueville warned of a 'tyranny of the majority' as a specific danger unique to democratic systems. Which mechanism did he identify as the primary driver of this risk?

options.A: Tocqueville argued that majority tyranny arises primarily through elected governments passing unconstitutional laws that courts are too weak to strike down.
options.B: Tocqueville was primarily concerned with social and moral conformism — the majority's power to suppress minority opinions through social pressure and reputational harm, rather than merely through formal legal coercion.
options.C: Tocqueville identified economic inequality as the primary mechanism, arguing that wealthy majorities use tax policy to oppress poorer minorities.
options.D: Tocqueville argued the tyranny of the majority was driven by voter fraud, which allowed dominant ethnic groups to permanently exclude minorities from elections.

questions.explanation: In 'Democracy in America' (1835), Tocqueville's most original concern was not legal but social tyranny: the pressure for conformity in an egalitarian society creates a climate in which independent thought is suppressed not by law but by the fear of social ostracism and reputational damage — a more subtle and pervasive form of control than state coercion. Option A describes a real concern about judicial weakness but was Madison's framing in the Federalist Papers rather than Tocqueville's distinctive contribution.

questions.title: Gender Social Stratification
questions.prompt: A sociologist studying gender inequality argues: 'The persistent gender pay gap in advanced economies is entirely explained by individual choices women make about career and family.' Identify the most significant methodological and theoretical flaw in this argument.

options.A: The argument is flawed because sociologists have proved that women are biologically programmed to prefer lower-paid professions.
options.B: The argument commits a methodological individualism error: it ignores structural factors such as occupational segregation, the undervaluation of feminised sectors, and the social construction of 'choices' that are shaped by unequal institutional norms.
options.C: The argument is flawed because individual choice cannot explain any social outcome — all inequality is structurally determined.
options.D: The argument is partially correct but applies only to developing countries; in advanced economies all gender pay differences have been eliminated by equal pay legislation.

questions.explanation: Controlled studies (e.g. Claudia Goldin's research, Nobel 2023) show that even after accounting for occupation, hours, and experience, an unexplained residual gap persists — and 'choices' themselves reflect structural constraints: socialisation, discriminatory hiring, lack of childcare infrastructure, and the fact that feminised occupations systematically pay less even when skill levels are comparable, showing that reducing all inequality to individual choice ignores social causation. Option C commits the opposite error — structural determinism that denies any explanatory role for individual agency — which is also rejected by mainstream sociology.

questions.title: Constitutional Entrenchment Rights
questions.prompt: Country A has no written constitution and parliament can pass any law by simple majority. Country B has a written constitution with an entrenched bill of rights that requires a supermajority to amend. A student claims Country B is necessarily more democratic. To what extent is this claim justified?

options.A: The claim is fully justified because written constitutions with bills of rights are universally recognised as superior democratic instruments.
options.B: The claim is only partially justified: Country B better protects minority rights and constrains majority overreach, but Country A's parliamentary sovereignty enables faster democratic responsiveness to changing public values without being bound by historical constitutional settlements.
options.C: The claim is not justified at all because written constitutions always lead to judicial activism that undermines democratic will.
options.D: The claim is fully justified because supermajority requirements ensure that only policies with overwhelming popular support become law, which is the highest form of democracy.

questions.explanation: The debate between constitutional entrenchment and parliamentary sovereignty reflects genuine trade-offs: entrenchment protects fundamental rights from temporary majorities (Country B's advantage) but can 'lock in' past constitutional settlements that majorities may legitimately wish to revise — the UK's uncodified constitution with parliamentary sovereignty has historically been responsive to evolving values such as expanded suffrage and human rights legislation. Option D incorrectly equates supermajority requirements with higher democratic quality, ignoring that requiring large majorities can itself entrench minority veto power over democratic majorities.

questions.title: Rousseau General Will
questions.prompt: Rousseau's concept of the 'general will' is often cited as a foundation of democratic theory. A student argues: 'The general will is simply the sum of what each individual citizen wants, so a majority vote always expresses it.' Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because Rousseau believed democratic majorities are the only legitimate source of political authority.
options.B: The claim is flawed because Rousseau distinguished the general will from the 'will of all,' arguing the general will reflects the common good, not aggregated private interests.
options.C: The claim is flawed because Rousseau rejected majority voting entirely, preferring decisions made by an enlightened philosopher-king.
options.D: The claim is correct because Rousseau's social contract requires unanimous consent, making majority votes a perfect expression of collective will.

questions.explanation: Rousseau explicitly separates the 'volonté générale' (general will) from the 'volonté de tous' (will of all) in The Social Contract — the general will aims at the common good and can be betrayed even by a majority if citizens vote from selfish motives. The top distractor (A) is wrong because Rousseau was deeply suspicious of factionalism and private interest distorting majority outcomes, which is why he opposed political parties.

questions.title: Locke Property Rights
questions.prompt: John Locke argued that legitimate government is founded on the protection of natural rights, including property. Which of the following most accurately identifies a critical tension in Locke's theory of property that later philosophers such as Rousseau and Marx exploited?

options.A: Locke failed to explain how a government could be formed without prior property ownership, making his theory circular.
options.B: Locke's labour theory of acquisition has no limit on accumulation once money is introduced, potentially justifying vast inequality while still claiming to protect natural rights.
options.C: Locke's theory only applied to land, leaving no basis for protecting intellectual or commercial property under natural law.
options.D: Locke contradicted himself by granting the legislature the right to tax property, which effectively denies property as an inalienable right.

questions.explanation: Locke's 'enough and as good' proviso initially limits acquisition, but he argues that the invention of money — which does not spoil — dissolves this limit, opening the door to unlimited accumulation. Critics like Rousseau used this to argue that Locke's liberalism naturalises inequality rather than protecting universal rights. Option D is plausible but incorrect because Locke explicitly permits taxation with the consent of the governed, which he does not see as contradicting inalienable rights.

questions.title: Rawls Veil of Ignorance
questions.prompt: A student applying Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' concludes: 'Rational agents behind the veil would always choose perfect equality of all goods, since no one knows their position.' To what extent is this conclusion supported by Rawls's own theory?

options.A: The conclusion is fully supported because Rawls's first principle of justice demands equal distribution of all primary goods without exception.
options.B: The conclusion is partially supported but overstated, as Rawls's difference principle permits inequalities that benefit the least-advantaged group.
options.C: The conclusion is unsupported because Rawls argued that agents behind the veil would use expected utility maximisation, not the maximin rule.
options.D: The conclusion is unsupported because Rawls believed natural talents justify unequal distributions without any constraint protecting the worst-off.

questions.explanation: Rawls's two principles of justice are not simply 'equal everything': the first principle guarantees equal basic liberties, but the second (the difference principle) explicitly allows socioeconomic inequalities provided they maximally benefit the least-advantaged members of society. The student's conclusion therefore overstates Rawls's position. Option C is wrong because Rawls specifically defended the maximin strategy — choosing to maximise the minimum — rather than expected utility, contra critics like Harsanyi.

questions.title: Market Failure Externalities
questions.prompt: A steel factory emits pollution that damages the health of nearby residents, but these residents are not compensated and the factory does not pay for the harm caused. Which economic concept explains this situation, and what does standard microeconomic theory predict will happen to output in such markets without intervention?

options.A: This is a positive externality; the market will under-produce steel relative to the socially optimal quantity.
options.B: This is a negative externality; the market will over-produce steel relative to the socially optimal quantity because private costs understate social costs.
options.C: This is a negative externality; the market will under-produce steel because producers internalise the cost of pollution in their pricing.
options.D: This is a public goods problem; the market will produce the efficient quantity of steel but distribute it inequitably.

questions.explanation: When a firm generates a negative externality it does not pay for, its private marginal cost is lower than the social marginal cost; this causes the supply curve to reflect only private costs, leading to output beyond the socially optimal level — a core result of Pigouvian economics. Option C is a common inversion error: producers who do not internalise pollution costs are precisely those who over-produce, not under-produce.

questions.title: Authoritarianism vs Totalitarianism
questions.prompt: Political scientists distinguish between authoritarian and totalitarian regimes. A student claims: 'Any government that restricts civil liberties and holds political prisoners is totalitarian.' Evaluate this claim using the standard political science distinction.

options.A: The claim is correct because any restriction on civil liberties meets the threshold for totalitarianism as defined by Hannah Arendt.
options.B: The claim is flawed because totalitarianism requires full ideological mobilisation and penetration of private life, whereas authoritarian regimes may repress opposition while tolerating a depoliticised private sphere.
options.C: The claim is flawed because totalitarian regimes never hold political prisoners — they eliminate opposition rather than imprison it.
options.D: The claim is correct because both authoritarian and totalitarian regimes are sub-types of the same political category and the distinction is merely semantic.

questions.explanation: The classic political science distinction, developed by scholars including Juan Linz and Hannah Arendt, holds that totalitarian regimes (e.g. Nazi Germany, Stalinist USSR) seek to reshape society through a single ideology, mass mobilisation, and control of private life, while authoritarian regimes (e.g. Franco's Spain) may tolerate a depoliticised private sphere as long as the regime's power is unchallenged. Option A misrepresents Arendt, who defined totalitarianism far more specifically than mere civil liberty restrictions.

questions.title: Constitutional Democracy Limits
questions.prompt: In a constitutional democracy, the legislature passes a law with 80% popular support that bans a religious minority from owning property. A student argues this is fully legitimate because it reflects the democratic will of the majority. Which principle of constitutional democracy most directly challenges this argument?

options.A: Separation of powers, because the judiciary should have proposed the law rather than the legislature.
options.B: Counter-majoritarian rights protection, because constitutional rights function precisely to shield minorities from majority preferences that violate fundamental freedoms.
options.C: Popular sovereignty, because 80% support is insufficient to constitute a true supermajority required for all legislation.
options.D: Federalism, because only regional governments have the authority to regulate property ownership under constitutional arrangements.

questions.explanation: Constitutional democracies embed counter-majoritarian mechanisms — such as bills of rights and judicial review — to protect minorities from what Madison called 'tyranny of the majority.' A supermajority in the legislature does not override constitutional rights; courts can strike down even unanimously popular laws that violate fundamental rights, as seen in landmark rulings like Brown v. Board of Education. Option A conflates the principle of separation of powers with rights protection, which is a different constitutional function.

questions.title: Comparative Economic Systems
questions.prompt: Country P operates a market economy; Country Q operates a centrally planned economy. Both countries face a sudden shortage of bread. Evaluate which system is more likely to resolve the shortage rapidly and through what mechanism.

options.A: Country Q resolves it faster because central planners can mandate increased production without waiting for price signals.
options.B: Country P resolves it faster because rising prices signal profit opportunities, attracting producers and increasing supply without requiring central coordination.
options.C: Both systems resolve shortages at identical speed because supply and demand pressures are independent of the political system.
options.D: Country Q resolves it faster because planned economies eliminate hoarding behaviour that delays resolution in market economies.

questions.explanation: In a market economy, a bread shortage raises prices, which simultaneously rations demand and signals producers to expand supply — Hayek's 'price signal' mechanism. This coordination is decentralised and rapid. Centrally planned economies historically suffered from information problems (Hayek's 'knowledge problem') meaning planners often failed to detect or respond to shortages quickly, as documented extensively in Soviet economic history. Option A is the key distractor: it assumes planners have both the information and logistics to act faster, which historical evidence contradicts.

questions.title: Power and Legitimacy
questions.prompt: Max Weber identified three ideal types of legitimate authority: traditional, charismatic, and rational-legal. A revolutionary leader who seizes power through popular uprising and governs through personal magnetism and emotional appeals later dies. Which Weberian prediction best describes what typically happens to such a regime?

options.A: The regime automatically reverts to traditional authority as followers seek a hereditary successor.
options.B: The regime faces a crisis of succession and must 'routinise' charismatic authority into either traditional or rational-legal forms to survive.
options.C: The regime collapses immediately because charismatic authority is entirely personal and cannot be transferred or institutionalised.
options.D: The regime transitions smoothly to rational-legal authority because Weber argued charismatic and rational-legal authority are complementary types.

questions.explanation: Weber explicitly theorised the 'routinisation of charisma': after a charismatic leader dies, followers must find ways to transfer or institutionalise the authority — either by designating a successor (moving toward traditional authority) or by creating bureaucratic structures (moving toward rational-legal authority). This does not happen automatically or without crisis. Option C overstates Weber's claim — he did not say charisma cannot be institutionalised, only that it faces an inherent succession problem.

questions.title: Federalism Revenue Sharing
questions.prompt: In a federal state, wealthier regions generate far more tax revenue than poorer regions. A student argues: 'True federalism requires that each region keep all taxes it collects, since fiscal transfers undermine regional autonomy.' To what extent does this argument reflect how federalism functions in practice?

options.A: The argument is fully accurate because fiscal transfers are a feature of unitary states, not federations.
options.B: The argument is overstated because most federal systems incorporate fiscal equalisation mechanisms to ensure baseline public services nationally, as seen in Germany and Australia.
options.C: The argument is accurate because the US federal system, the most prominent example of federalism, never transfers funds between states.
options.D: The argument is partially accurate because federalism only permits transfers for defence spending, leaving all other taxes entirely with regions.

questions.explanation: Most functioning federal systems — including Germany's Länderfinanzausgleich and Australia's GST distribution — include explicit fiscal equalisation transfers from wealthier to poorer regions, precisely to maintain national minimum standards without abolishing regional autonomy. Fiscal transfers and federalism are not contradictory. Option C is factually wrong: the US federal government operates extensive grant-in-aid programmes to states covering education, healthcare, and infrastructure.

questions.title: Social Contract Origins
questions.prompt: Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau each described a 'state of nature' before government. Which of the following most accurately synthesises a key difference between Hobbes's and Rousseau's depictions of human nature in the state of nature?

options.A: Hobbes saw humans as naturally cooperative but corrupted by government; Rousseau saw humans as naturally violent and in need of a strong sovereign.
options.B: Hobbes saw the state of nature as a war of all against all driven by rational self-interest; Rousseau saw natural humans as peaceful and self-sufficient, corrupted by society and private property.
options.C: Both Hobbes and Rousseau agreed the state of nature was violent, but disagreed on whether a monarch or a republic was the appropriate solution.
options.D: Hobbes argued for minimal government to preserve natural freedom; Rousseau argued for an absolute sovereign to prevent natural conflict.

questions.explanation: Hobbes's Leviathan describes the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — a condition of perpetual conflict arising from rational competition for scarce resources. Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality inverts this: natural humans are peaceful, compassionate 'noble savages' who are corrupted only by civilisation and the institution of private property. Option A precisely reverses both thinkers' positions, making it the most convincing wrong answer for a student who confuses them.

questions.title: Democratic Backsliding
questions.prompt: Political scientists use the term 'democratic backsliding' to describe a process distinct from sudden coups. Identify the statement that best characterises how contemporary democratic backsliding typically occurs, as documented in cases such as Hungary after 2010.

options.A: Democratic backsliding occurs when military leaders suspend elections, imprison the head of state, and dissolve parliament in a single swift action.
options.B: Democratic backsliding occurs incrementally through elected leaders who use legal mechanisms — packing courts, restricting media, and changing electoral rules — to entrench power while maintaining a democratic facade.
options.C: Democratic backsliding occurs when voter turnout falls below 50%, causing electoral outcomes to lack sufficient legitimacy for stable governance.
options.D: Democratic backsliding occurs primarily in new democracies and is impossible in states with more than 20 years of continuous democratic elections.

questions.explanation: Scholars like Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way document 'competitive authoritarianism' or backsliding through legal incrementalism: Hungary's Fidesz under Viktor Orbán systematically packed the constitutional court, changed electoral laws, and captured media through ostensibly legal acts rather than a coup. This gradualism makes it harder to identify and resist. Option A describes a classic coup, which is a distinct phenomenon that has become less common globally since the Cold War.

questions.title: International Law Enforcement
questions.prompt: The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for a sitting head of state. The state in question refused to arrest its own leader, and no other mechanism compelled compliance. Which theoretical framework in international relations best explains why this outcome was predictable?

options.A: Liberal institutionalism, because international institutions like the ICC have binding enforcement authority over all member states without exception.
options.B: Realism, because states prioritise sovereignty and national interest over international legal obligations when compliance conflicts with power considerations.
options.C: Constructivism, because state identities are fixed at founding and cannot be reshaped by international norms after a regime change.
options.D: Marxism, because international courts are created exclusively to serve the economic interests of capitalist states and are ignored by socialist governments.

questions.explanation: Realist IR theory predicts that states comply with international law only when it aligns with their interests or when a powerful actor enforces compliance — the ICC has no independent enforcement mechanism and relies entirely on state cooperation. The case of Sudan's Omar al-Bashir, for whom an ICC warrant was issued in 2009 but who travelled freely for years, exemplifies this. Option A misrepresents liberal institutionalism: even institutionalists acknowledge the ICC depends on voluntary state cooperation and lacks coercive power.

questions.title: Revolution Relative Deprivation
questions.prompt: Ted Gurr's theory of relative deprivation argues that revolutions arise not from absolute poverty but from the gap between what people expect and what they actually receive. A student critiques this theory: 'This cannot explain revolutions because the poorest people — who have the most to gain — rarely lead them.' Evaluate this critique.

options.A: The critique is fully valid because Gurr's theory has been empirically refuted in all case studies since 1970.
options.B: The critique actually strengthens Gurr's theory because relative deprivation is highest among rising groups whose expectations outpace gains, not among the absolutely poorest who have lower expectations.
options.C: The critique is valid because Gurr's theory requires that the poorest class leads revolutions, and historical evidence shows this never occurs.
options.D: The critique is invalid because it misidentifies Gurr's unit of analysis, which is states rather than individuals or social classes.

questions.explanation: Gurr's relative deprivation theory specifically predicts that the most revolutionary groups are those experiencing rising expectations frustrated by stagnant or declining outcomes — often the educated middle class, not the absolute poor. This is consistent with the bourgeois leadership of the French Revolution and the educated youth who led many 20th-century revolutions. The student's critique therefore misunderstands the theory by conflating absolute poverty with relative deprivation. Option C falsely claims Gurr requires the poorest to lead — his theory never specifies this.

questions.title: Mixed Economy Government Role
