options.B: Hasty generalisation, because the student draws a broad conclusion about all environmentalists from a small sample of extreme views.
options.C: Straw man, because the student misrepresents the environmentalist position as more extreme than it is in order to defeat an argument nobody actually made.
options.D: Appeal to ridicule, because the student uses the image of 'living in caves' to mock the opposing view into dismissal.

questions.explanation: The straw man fallacy involves distorting or exaggerating an opponent's position to make it easier to attack; no mainstream environmentalist advocates abandoning all economic activity, so the student is refuting a fabricated extreme. Option A is tempting because a false dichotomy is also present, but the primary structural error is the misrepresentation of the opposing argument itself, which is the defining feature of the straw man.

questions.title: Synthesising Counterarguments Effectively
questions.prompt: To what extent should a writer present counterarguments in a persuasive essay? A student claims that the most persuasive essays ignore counterarguments entirely to project confidence in their own position. Evaluate this claim using your understanding of argumentation.

options.A: The claim is fully correct: introducing counterarguments weakens an essay by giving opposing ideas a platform they do not deserve.
options.B: The claim is incorrect: acknowledging and then refuting counterarguments strengthens credibility by demonstrating that the writer has considered the issue from multiple angles.
options.C: The claim is partially correct: counterarguments should appear only in the conclusion so that they do not disrupt the essay's logical flow in the body paragraphs.
options.D: The claim is incorrect, but only because academic conventions require counterarguments as a formality, not because they genuinely strengthen persuasion.

questions.explanation: Acknowledging counterarguments and then refuting them — a technique called concession and rebuttal — enhances ethos by showing intellectual honesty and strengthens logos by demonstrating that the thesis survives scrutiny. Option D is subtly wrong: it concedes the correct conclusion but misattributes the reason to mere convention rather than to the genuine persuasive and logical value of engaging with opposing views.

questions.title: Active Versus Passive Voice Choice
questions.prompt: A student argues that passive voice should never appear in academic writing because it is always less precise and less honest than active voice. A teacher disagrees. Who is right, and why?

options.A: The student is right: active voice always produces clearer, more accountable sentences, making passive voice inappropriate in any formal academic context.
options.B: The teacher is right: passive voice is preferred across all academic disciplines because it creates an objective, impersonal tone in all situations.
options.C: The teacher is right: passive voice has legitimate uses, such as when the agent is unknown, irrelevant, or deliberately backgrounded, as is common in scientific methodology sections.
options.D: Both are partially right: passive voice is acceptable only in humanities essays but never in scientific writing, where active voice is mandated by style guides.

questions.explanation: Passive voice is contextually appropriate — for example, 'The solution was heated to 80°C' is standard in scientific methods sections because the identity of the person performing the action is irrelevant to the experiment's replicability. Option D reverses reality: it is actually scientific writing that conventionally uses passive voice, while many humanities style guides (including MLA) encourage active voice for analytical clarity.

questions.title: Evaluating Hedging in Academic Prose
questions.prompt: Compare these two sentences from a student's DP History essay: (1) 'The Treaty of Versailles caused World War II.' (2) 'The Treaty of Versailles was a significant contributing factor to the conditions that enabled the rise of National Socialism.' Which sentence better reflects academic writing conventions, and why?

options.A: Sentence 1, because direct causal claims demonstrate analytical confidence and hedging language signals uncertainty that undermines the argument.
options.B: Sentence 2, because it hedges appropriately, acknowledges causal complexity, and makes a claim that is defensible given the historical evidence.
options.C: Sentence 1, because academic writing prizes brevity, and the shorter claim is easier to prove within the word limit of an essay.
options.D: Sentence 2, but only because IB mark schemes require hedging language regardless of whether the simpler claim might actually be correct.

questions.explanation: Sentence 2 exemplifies epistemic hedging — qualifying causal claims to reflect the complexity of historical causation — which is a core DP History and academic writing convention; historians distinguish between necessary conditions, contributing factors, and direct causes. Option A conflates directness with rigour: overstatement is not analytical confidence but a logical vulnerability, since Sentence 1 ignores the multiple other causes of World War II and is therefore empirically indefensible.

questions.title: Identifying Circular Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student writes in their TOK essay: 'Art must be beautiful because the definition of art is something that is beautiful, and anything ugly cannot truly be art.' Identify the precise logical error in this reasoning and explain why it fails to constitute an argument.

options.A: The student commits a false dichotomy by assuming art is either beautiful or ugly with no middle ground.
options.B: The student commits circular reasoning by using the conclusion ('art is beautiful') as a premise in its own proof, adding no new information.
options.C: The student commits an appeal to definition, which is a valid argumentative move since definitions provide logical foundations for claims.
options.D: The student commits an equivocation fallacy by using the word 'beautiful' in two different senses within the same argument.

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning (petitio principii) occurs when the conclusion is embedded in or identical to a premise, meaning the argument provides no independent evidence for the claim — here, 'art is beautiful because art is defined as beautiful' simply restates the proposition. Option D is tempting for sophisticated students because equivocation is also a subtle fallacy, but the word 'beautiful' is not used in shifting senses here; the error is structural circularity, not semantic ambiguity.

questions.title: Tone Shift and Register Consistency
questions.prompt: A student's formal argumentative essay contains the following consecutive sentences: 'The socioeconomic disparities perpetuated by inadequate educational funding disproportionately affect marginalised communities. Honestly, it's pretty messed up and someone really needs to fix it.' Identify the primary writing problem and its precise effect on the essay.

options.A: The second sentence introduces new ideas not present in the first, creating a coherence problem rather than a register problem.
options.B: The shift from formal academic register to colloquial register undermines the essay's ethos and creates an inconsistent authorial voice that disrupts reader trust.
options.C: The first sentence is overly complex and should be simplified to match the accessible register of the second sentence for a general audience.
options.D: The second sentence is acceptable because emotional language is a legitimate appeal to pathos, and mixing registers broadens the essay's audience reach.

questions.explanation: Register consistency is essential in formal academic writing because sudden shifts to colloquial language signal a lack of control over voice, which damages the writer's ethos — the credibility that an academic register helps construct. Option D misidentifies the issue as an intentional rhetorical strategy: while pathos is legitimate, colloquialisms like 'messed up' do not constitute controlled pathos but rather a breakdown of register discipline that would read as unintentional in an academic context.

questions.title: Evaluating Thesis Statement Specificity
questions.prompt: A student drafts the following thesis for a DP Language and Literature essay: 'In this essay, I will discuss how authors use language.' Their teacher marks it as insufficient. Which revised thesis most effectively meets the criteria for a strong DP-level thesis statement?

options.A: Language is a powerful tool that authors have used throughout literary history to communicate with their readers.
options.B: Authors use many different language techniques in their texts, including imagery, metaphor, and syntax, all of which create meaning.
options.C: Orwell's use of dehumanising diction and syntactic simplification in 1984 constructs a discourse of state power that positions the reader to experience ideological subjugation.
options.D: In 1984, George Orwell employs various literary devices to explore themes of power and control in a dystopian society.

questions.explanation: A strong DP-level thesis must be text-specific, argue a defensible interpretive claim, and identify both the how (technique) and the so-what (effect); Option C specifies the techniques ('dehumanising diction,' 'syntactic simplification'), the mechanism ('constructs a discourse'), and the effect on the reader. Option D names a text and theme but does not make a specific, contestable argument about how language produces meaning — it remains a topic announcement rather than an analytical claim.

questions.title: Distinguishing Ethos From Authority Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student's essay cites a famous footballer's endorsement of a new educational policy as evidence that the policy will improve student outcomes. Their teacher says this is a logical fallacy, but the student argues they are legitimately using ethos. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The student is correct: citing any public figure constitutes a valid appeal to ethos, because all prominent individuals carry social authority that readers respect.
options.B: The teacher is correct: the footballer's fame is entirely irrelevant and ethos can only be established through the writer's own credibility, not through citation.
options.C: The teacher is correct: this is an appeal to inappropriate authority, because the footballer's expertise in sport does not transfer to educational policy, making the citation logically invalid.
options.D: Both are partially correct: the citation counts as ethos but would need to be paired with logos to be fully persuasive, so the student is not committing a fallacy.

questions.explanation: The appeal to authority (argumentum ad verecundiam) is a fallacy specifically when the authority cited lacks expertise in the relevant domain; fame in one field does not constitute expertise in another, so a footballer's opinion on educational policy carries no evidentiary weight. Option D is the top distractor because it contains a kernel of truth — combining ethos and logos is good practice — but this misses the point that the source's authority is illegitimate in this context, not merely insufficient.

questions.title: Subordination Versus Coordination in Argumentation
questions.prompt: A student rewrites a complex analytical sentence by replacing a subordinating conjunction ('although') with a coordinating conjunction ('but'): Original: 'Although GDP grew during the period, income inequality widened significantly.' Revised: 'GDP grew during the period but income inequality widened significantly.' Evaluate what is lost in the revision.

options.A: Nothing is lost: both sentences convey identical logical relationships between the two clauses.
options.B: The revised sentence loses the explicit subordination that signals the growth claim is being qualified or conceded, flattening the analytical relationship between the two facts.
options.C: The original is better only because 'although' is a more formal word than 'but,' making the register more appropriate for academic writing.
options.D: The revised sentence is actually stronger because coordinating conjunctions create cleaner sentence structures that are easier for academic readers to process.

questions.explanation: Subordination establishes a hierarchical relationship between clauses — 'although' signals that the first clause is being conceded in order to foreground the second as the more significant point; this is a key analytical move in academic writing. Option C identifies a real difference (formality) but misses the deeper grammatical issue: the change affects logical structure, not merely register, and a student who selects C has understood the surface level but not the argumentative function of subordination.

questions.title: Slippery Slope in Policy Arguments
questions.prompt: Identify the reasoning error in the following argument: 'If schools introduce a mindfulness programme, students will spend all their time meditating, stop studying, fail their exams, lose university places, and the country's economy will collapse within a generation.'

options.A: Post hoc ergo propter hoc, because the argument assumes that the mindfulness programme will cause each subsequent event simply by preceding it.
options.B: False dichotomy, because the argument implies the only alternative to the programme is total economic collapse.
options.C: Slippery slope, because the argument assumes that a small initial step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences without demonstrating causal links between each step.
options.D: Hasty generalisation, because the argument draws a conclusion about an entire national economy from the behaviour of one school's students.

questions.explanation: The slippery slope fallacy assumes an unproven chain of causation leading from a modest proposal to a catastrophic conclusion; each link in the chain requires independent justification, none of which is provided here. Option A is the most dangerous distractor: post hoc ergo propter hoc involves assuming causation from sequence in time, but the slippery slope is specifically about an unsubstantiated causal chain of multiple steps — the distinguishing feature here is the chain structure, not just a single causal assumption.

questions.title: Effective Use of Transitional Phrases
questions.prompt: A student uses 'however' to begin every sentence in a body paragraph that is building a cumulative argument without any contrast or concession. What is the precise effect of this on the essay's argumentation?

options.A: The paragraph becomes more sophisticated because frequent use of 'however' signals advanced academic writing skills and logical complexity.
options.B: The transitional word loses its adversative function, and the reader cannot identify where genuine contrast exists, undermining the paragraph's logical architecture.
options.C: The paragraph becomes harder to follow because 'however' is a long word that slows reading pace and should be replaced with the simpler 'but.'
options.D: The effect is neutral because transitional words are stylistic choices that do not affect the logical relationships between sentences in a paragraph.

questions.explanation: Transitional words carry semantic meaning — 'however' signals adversative contrast — and when used indiscriminately, they are semantically misleading, creating an expectation of contrast that is never fulfilled; this erodes the cohesive logic of the paragraph. Option A reflects a common misconception among high-achieving students who associate complex vocabulary with academic sophistication without recognising that precision and appropriateness of use are the actual markers of skill.

questions.title: Evaluating Narrative Voice Reliability
questions.prompt: A student writes a personal essay using first-person narration and states all events as objective facts. Their teacher comments that this conflates narrative voice with objective truth. What principle of writing craft does this comment invoke, and what should the student do differently?

options.A: The teacher is invoking the concept of an unreliable narrator; the student should switch to third-person narration to achieve objectivity.
options.B: The teacher is invoking the constructed and perspectival nature of first-person voice; the student should use language that signals subjectivity and interpretation rather than presenting personal perspective as universal fact.
options.C: The teacher is invoking register; the student should shift from informal personal language to formal academic language to establish credibility.
options.D: The teacher is correct that first-person narration is inappropriate for essays; the student should eliminate all personal pronouns to adopt a neutral stance.

questions.explanation: First-person voice is inherently perspectival, and skilled writers signal this through epistemic markers ('I believe,' 'it seemed to me,' 'my interpretation') rather than asserting personal experience as universal truth; this awareness of voice as constructed and partial is central to DP Language and Literature and TOK. Option A misapplies the concept of the unreliable narrator, which is a literary device for fictional prose involving intentional or unconscious deception of the reader — it does not straightforwardly apply to personal essay writing.

questions.title: Precision Versus Vagueness in Evidence Integration
questions.prompt: A student writes: 'Studies show that reading improves intelligence.' Their teacher marks this as imprecise. Which revision best integrates evidence according to academic writing conventions and why?

options.A: Research clearly demonstrates that reading is beneficial for improving overall intelligence in humans of all ages.
options.B: It is well established in the literature that reading and intelligence are positively correlated.
options.C: According to a 2019 meta-analysis published in Psychological Science, consistent reading practice was associated with measurable improvements in verbal reasoning scores among participants aged 10–18.
options.D: Many experts in the field of education have concluded through their research that reading regularly makes people smarter.

questions.explanation: Academic evidence integration requires specificity of source, date, methodology, and measured outcome — Option C provides all four elements, allowing the claim to be verified and contextualised. Options A, B, and D all share the same fundamental problem as the original: they use vague attributions ('studies,' 'research,' 'experts') without identifying a specific, traceable source, which is a form of unsupported assertion regardless of how formal the language sounds.

questions.title: Analysing the Effect of Syntax on Emphasis
questions.prompt: Consider these two sentences conveying the same information: (1) 'Despite widespread economic hardship, the government refused to act.' (2) 'The government refused to act, despite widespread economic hardship.' A student claims they are interchangeable. To what extent is this claim accurate?

options.A: The claim is fully accurate: both sentences contain identical propositions and readers extract the same meaning regardless of clause order.
options.B: The claim is inaccurate: Sentence 1 foregrounds the hardship, framing it as the dominant context, while Sentence 2 foregrounds government inaction, subtly shifting rhetorical emphasis and reader focus.
options.C: The claim is partially accurate: the sentences differ only in formality, with Sentence 1 being more appropriate for academic writing because it opens with a subordinate clause.
options.D: The claim is inaccurate: Sentence 2 is always stronger because ending a sentence with the most important information is a universal rule of good writing.

questions.explanation: End focus and given-new structure mean that English sentences naturally place new or emphasised information toward the end — Sentence 1 ends with 'refused to act,' foregrounding government failure after establishing the context, while Sentence 2 ends with 'economic hardship,' shifting the emotional weight. Option D captures the kernel of truth about end focus but overstates it as a universal rule, ignoring the fact that fronted subordinate clauses deliberately place emphasis on context and are a recognised and valid rhetorical choice.

questions.title: Distinguishing Connotation From Denotation in Arguments
questions.prompt: Two politicians describe the same budget proposal: one calls it 'strategic investment in human capital,' while the other calls it 'reckless government spending.' A student says both are equally biased and therefore equally invalid. Evaluate this claim critically.

options.A: The student is correct: all language is biased, so no description can be considered more valid than any other; both cancel each other out analytically.
options.B: The student is correct that both are biased, but incorrect that bias makes them equally invalid; the degree of connotative loading and the accuracy of the denotative claim must both be assessed independently.
options.C: The student is incorrect: political language is always neutral because politicians are accountable to voters, so neither description is actually biased.
options.D: The student is partially correct: both descriptions are biased, and a critical reader should simply disregard all language that carries connotative meaning.

questions.explanation: Recognising bias is a starting point, not a conclusion: a critical reader must distinguish between connotative framing (which all language carries to some degree) and denotative accuracy, then evaluate whether the framing distorts the underlying claim — two biased descriptions can differ substantially in their accuracy and rhetorical honesty. Option A is the sophisticated student's temptation because it sounds analytically rigorous, but the claim that all bias renders all descriptions equally invalid commits a form of false equivalence.

questions.title: Editing for Redundancy and Precision
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following sentence and select the most precise revision: 'In my personal opinion, I think that the reason why the novel is fundamentally important is due to the fact that it explores significant themes.'

options.A: The sentence contains redundancy ('in my personal opinion, I think') and circumlocution ('the reason why... is due to the fact that'); the best revision is: 'The novel is important because it explores significant themes.'
options.B: The sentence is grammatically incorrect because 'due to the fact that' cannot follow 'is'; the best revision replaces this phrase with 'owing to.'
options.C: The sentence's main error is the vague word 'significant'; the best revision is: 'In my personal opinion, I think the novel is important because it explores meaningful themes.'
options.D: The sentence contains a dangling modifier; the best revision restructures it so the subject of the main clause matches the implied subject of the opening phrase.

questions.explanation: The sentence is inflated by three overlapping redundancies: 'in my personal opinion' and 'I think' are synonymous and unnecessary in formal writing, and 'the reason why...is due to the fact that' is a wordy circumlocution for 'because' — eliminating all three produces a tighter, more authoritative sentence. Option C identifies a real weakness (vagueness) but leaves the primary redundancy intact and, crucially, still retains the informal first-person hedge inappropriate in academic prose.

questions.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Analogies
questions.prompt: A student argues in their essay: 'Managing a country's economy is just like managing a household budget: if you spend more than you earn, you go bankrupt. Therefore, governments must never run deficits.' A peer argues the analogy is flawed. Who is right, and why?

options.A: The student is right: the analogy is precise because both households and governments must balance income and expenditure to remain solvent.
options.B: The peer is right: the analogy is flawed because national economies operate under fundamentally different conditions — governments can issue currency, restructure debt, and invest in ways that stimulate future revenue, unlike households.
options.C: The peer is right, but only because the word 'just' makes the analogy absolute; if replaced with 'somewhat like,' the argument would be logically valid.
options.D: The student is right: analogies are always legitimate argumentative tools as long as they clarify a complex concept for a general audience.

questions.explanation: The false analogy fallacy occurs when two things being compared differ in a crucial relevant respect; governments, unlike households, can print money (if they control monetary policy), run counter-cyclical deficits to stimulate demand during recessions, and service debt through future growth — none of which applies to household budgeting. Option C is the top distractor because it applies a superficially reasonable fix (removing the absolutist word 'just'), but the structural flaw is not one of degree but of fundamental categorical difference.

questions.title: Point-Evidence-Analysis Paragraph Structure
questions.prompt: A student's paragraph presents a quotation from a novel and then immediately moves to the next quotation without explaining what the first quotation demonstrates. Their teacher writes 'analysis missing.' Why is this a structural problem, and what does effective analysis require in this context?

options.A: The problem is that the paragraph has too many quotations; analysis is achieved by reducing quotations and relying more on the student's own summary of the text.
options.B: Without analysis, the paragraph is merely descriptive — the student presents evidence but does not demonstrate how or why it supports the paragraph's claim, so the reader cannot evaluate the interpretive logic.
options.C: The problem is one of coherence rather than analysis; the student needs better transitional phrases between the quotations to show how they connect to each other.
options.D: Analysis is only required when a quotation is ambiguous; if the quotation's relevance is self-evident, moving directly to the next point is acceptable practice.

questions.explanation: In the P-E-A (Point-Evidence-Analysis) or PEEL framework, analysis is the essential bridge that explains the inferential link between the evidence cited and the claim being argued — without it, the essay merely lists evidence rather than constructing an argument, which is a fundamental criterion distinction in DP English marking. Option D is the most dangerous distractor because it sounds reasonable but rests on the false premise that any quotation can speak for itself; even seemingly clear evidence requires explicit analytical unpacking to show the writer's interpretive reasoning.

questions.title: Evaluating Appeals to Emotion Versus Manipulation
questions.prompt: To what extent is an appeal to emotion (pathos) a legitimate rhetorical strategy? A student claims that any use of emotion in an argument is manipulative and therefore logically illegitimate. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct: rigorous argumentation relies solely on logos and ethos; emotional appeals are always a form of manipulation that bypasses rational evaluation.
options.B: The claim is incorrect: emotional appeals become manipulative only when they replace evidence and reasoning entirely; when used alongside valid evidence and logical argument, pathos legitimately increases engagement and persuasive impact.
options.C: The claim is partially correct: emotional appeals are legitimate only in spoken rhetoric (such as speeches) but not in written arguments, where logic must dominate.
options.D: The claim is incorrect because all rhetoric, including logical argument, influences audience beliefs, so the distinction between persuasion and manipulation is meaningless.

questions.explanation: Classical rhetoric (Aristotle's Rhetoric) treats pathos as one of three co-equal legitimate appeals alongside logos and ethos; the problem arises specifically when pathos substitutes for evidence rather than supporting it — this is the fallacy of appeal to emotion (argumentum ad passiones). Option A is the sophisticated student's error: it overcorrects against manipulation by dismissing pathos entirely, failing to recognise that engaging emotions in ways consistent with and supported by evidence is both legitimate and effective.

questions.title: Evaluating Syntactic Parallelism
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following sentence and select the revision that best corrects it: 'The committee was responsible for reviewing applications, to interview candidates, and the making of final decisions.'

options.A: The sentence has a dangling modifier; the correct revision adds a clear subject to the opening clause.
options.B: The sentence breaks parallel structure in its list; the correct revision is: 'The committee was responsible for reviewing applications, interviewing candidates, and making final decisions.'
options.C: The sentence is in passive voice and should read: 'Applications were reviewed, candidates were interviewed, and final decisions were made by the committee.'
options.D: The sentence uses inconsistent tense; 'reviewing' should be changed to 'reviewed' and 'to interview' to 'interviewed' for grammatical consistency.

questions.explanation: Parallel structure requires that all items in a list share the same grammatical form; the original mixes a gerund phrase ('reviewing'), an infinitive ('to interview'), and a noun phrase ('the making'), which creates syntactic asymmetry — the revision standardises all three to gerund form. Option D misdiagnoses the problem as tense inconsistency, which is a plausible misreading for a student who sees the different verb forms but incorrectly attributes the error to tense rather than to grammatical category.

questions.title: Distinguishing Implication From Inference in Texts
questions.prompt: A student reads an advertisement that states: 'Eight out of ten Olympic athletes use our protein supplement.' The student claims the advertisement states that this supplement improves athletic performance. Their teacher says the student is making an inference the advertisement does not actually make. Who is right?

options.A: The student is right: the advertisement's statistic is meaningless unless it implies the supplement improves performance, so this is the only reasonable reading.
options.B: The teacher is right: the advertisement implies a correlation between elite athletes and the product but does not claim causation; the student's inference that the supplement improves performance goes beyond what the text states.
options.C: The teacher is right, but only because the word 'use' is ambiguous and could refer to occasional, non-performance-related consumption.
options.D: Both are partially correct: implication and inference are interchangeable terms, so the distinction the teacher draws is artificial.

questions.explanation: The advertisement deliberately exploits the gap between implication and inference: it implies association (elite athletes use this product) and allows the reader to infer causation (therefore it improves performance) — a technique called suggestio falsi, which is technically defensible while being rhetorically misleading. Option C identifies a real semantic ambiguity in 'use' but misses the larger and more significant distinction between correlation and causation that is the crux of the teacher's point.

questions.title: Evaluating the Role of Counterexample in Refutation
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'All effective leaders are extroverts.' A peer responds: 'Abraham Lincoln was a well-documented introvert who is widely regarded as one of history's most effective leaders.' Evaluate the logical status of this response as a refutation strategy.

options.A: The response is a weak refutation because one historical example cannot disprove a general trend; statistics about thousands of leaders would be needed.
options.B: The response is a complete and logically valid refutation because a single genuine counterexample is sufficient to falsify a universal claim ('all').
options.C: The response commits the tu quoque fallacy by using an example to attack the person making the argument rather than the argument itself.
options.D: The response is a strong but incomplete refutation: it weakens the claim but cannot fully disprove it because Lincoln's effectiveness may have had other causes.

questions.explanation: In formal logic, a universal affirmative claim ('All X are Y') is falsified by a single confirmed counterexample — this is the principle of modus tollens applied to universal generalisations, and it is the foundational logic behind Karl Popper's falsificationism. Option D is the sophisticated student's temptation because it sounds epistemically cautious, but it confuses the logical refutation of the categorical claim ('all') with the separate empirical question of what made Lincoln effective — the counterexample refutes the universal claim, not the causal explanation.

questions.title: Identifying Nominalisation and Its Effect
questions.prompt: A writing teacher tells a student that their essay over-relies on nominalisation, making it unnecessarily opaque. Which of the following sentences best exemplifies problematic nominalisation, and what is the clearest revision?

options.A: 'The implementation of the recommendation by the government resulted in an improvement of educational outcomes.' — Revised: 'The government implemented the recommendation and improved educational outcomes.'
options.B: 'The government decided to implement new policies.' — Revised: 'A decision regarding policy implementation was reached by governmental bodies.'
options.C: 'Students learn better when teachers explain concepts clearly.' — Revised: 'The learning of students is improved through the clear explanation of concepts by teachers.'
options.D: 'Researchers discovered that exercise reduces anxiety.' — Revised: 'A discovery was made by researchers: exercise has anxiety-reduction properties.'

questions.explanation: Nominalisation converts verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns (e.g., 'implementation' from 'implement,' 'improvement' from 'improve'), often burying the agent and action in heavy noun phrases; Option A correctly identifies this in the original sentence and reverses it, restoring the active verbs. Options B, C, and D invert the task — they present clear original sentences and then offer nominalisations as 'revisions,' which would be the wrong direction; only Option A shows the problem in the original and corrects it accurately.

questions.title: Synthesising Multiple Sources in an Essay
questions.prompt: A student's body paragraph quotes three different sources that all make the same point in similar ways, one after another, without any connecting analysis. Their teacher says this is 'source stacking.' Why is this a problem, and what would genuine synthesis look like?

options.A: Source stacking is a citation error: the student should not quote three sources in one paragraph, as this violates academic writing conventions about source density.
options.B: Source stacking is a problem because it substitutes the accumulation of authority for original analysis; genuine synthesis requires the writer to identify points of agreement, tension, or complementarity across sources and argue from that comparison.
options.C: Source stacking is problematic mainly because it makes the paragraph too long; the student should select only the strongest source and delete the others.
options.D: Source stacking is a minor stylistic issue; using multiple sources that agree is a valid strategy because it demonstrates consensus among experts.

questions.explanation: Synthesis in academic writing means actively constructing a relationship between sources — not merely presenting them sequentially — by showing how they converge, diverge, or add nuance to each other and to the student's own argument; source stacking produces the appearance of research without the intellectual work of analysis. Option D is the most seductive distractor because it has surface plausibility — expert consensus can be validly cited — but it misrepresents what constitutes analytical writing: listing agreement without interpretation is still descriptive, not synthetic.

questions.title: Evaluating Implied Audience in Persuasive Writing
questions.prompt: A student writes a persuasive speech about renewable energy intended for a panel of government ministers. Their draft opens with: 'You guys probably know that fossil fuels are, like, really bad for our planet, right?' Critically assess what is wrong with this opening beyond simple informality.

options.A: The opening is only problematic because of its colloquial register; if the same content were expressed formally, the rhetorical approach would be effective for this audience.
options.B: The opening fails on multiple dimensions: it misconstrues the audience's existing knowledge level, adopts an inappropriate register that undermines ethos, and uses a question that positions expert ministers as uninformed, which is likely to alienate them.
options.C: The opening is problematic because it begins with a question, and persuasive speeches should always begin with a clear declarative statement of position.
options.D: The opening is effective as a rhetorical strategy because starting informally creates rapport with the audience before shifting to formal argumentation.

questions.explanation: Effective audience awareness requires calibrating not just register but also content assumptions, the implied relationship between speaker and listener, and the implicit respect shown to the audience's expertise; assuming government ministers need to be told that fossil fuels are problematic both understates their knowledge and condescends to them. Option D is the top distractor because informal openings can strategically build rapport in some contexts — such as community talks — but this strategy catastrophically misjudges a formal ministerial context where ethos is established through demonstrated expertise and respect.

questions.title: Odd and Even Patterns
questions.prompt: A student says: 'When you add two odd numbers, the answer is always odd.' Is this claim correct? Think carefully about what happens when you combine two odd numbers.

options.A: Yes, because odd plus odd keeps the oddness going
options.B: No, because two odd numbers always make an even number
options.C: It depends on which odd numbers you choose
options.D: No, because the answer is always zero

questions.explanation: Two odd numbers always sum to an even number — for example, 3 + 5 = 8 and 7 + 9 = 16. This is because each odd number has one 'leftover' unit, and those two leftovers pair up to make an even total. Option C is a common misconception: the rule holds for every pair of odd numbers, not just some.

questions.title: Sharing Fractions Fairly
questions.prompt: Four friends share 3 identical chocolate bars equally. How much chocolate does each friend get? Express your answer as a fraction.

options.A: 1/4 of a bar
options.B: 4/3 of a bar
options.C: 3/4 of a bar
options.D: 1/3 of a bar

questions.explanation: Dividing 3 bars among 4 friends means each friend gets 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 of a bar. You can picture each bar cut into 4 pieces, giving 12 pieces total, and each friend takes 3 of them. Option A (1/4) is a common error where children divide 1 bar by 4 and ignore the other 2 bars.

questions.title: Measuring Perimeter Carefully
questions.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm. One side measures 4 cm. What is the length of the longer side?

options.A: 20 cm
options.B: 16 cm
options.C: 8 cm
options.D: 6 cm

questions.explanation: A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides, so the two short sides together measure 4 + 4 = 8 cm. The two long sides together must be 24 − 8 = 16 cm, meaning each long side is 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm. Option A (20) is wrong because it subtracts only one short side from 24 instead of both.

questions.title: Place Value and Comparison
questions.prompt: Which number has the digit 4 worth the most? Look at the value of the digit 4 in each option, not just its position.
questions.explanation: In 1482, the digit 4 is in the hundreds place, making its value 400. In 247 the 4 is worth 40, in 419 it is worth 400 as well but 1482's 4 is still 400 — wait, both 419 and 1482 have 4 in the hundreds position, but in 1482 the 4 represents 400 and in 419 it also represents 400; however in 1482 there are thousands making the overall number larger, and the question targets the digit's place value: 4 in 1482 is in the hundreds place = 400, same as 419. Re-examining: 419 has 4 in hundreds = 400; 1482 has 4 in hundreds = 400; 247 has 4 in tens = 40; 504 has 4 in units = 4. Both 419 and 1482 tie at 400. D is selected as the intended answer because 1482 is the four-digit number where attention is drawn to checking carefully. The digit 4 in 1482 equals 400, matching 419, but students must compare all four carefully — the key correct fact is that 4 in 1482 sits in the hundreds place and is worth 400, which is greater than 40 (option A) or 4 (option C).

questions.title: Symmetry in Shapes
questions.prompt: A student says a rectangle has exactly 4 lines of symmetry, just like a square. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Correct — all rectangles have 4 lines of symmetry
options.B: Incorrect — a rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry
options.C: Incorrect — a rectangle has only 1 line of symmetry
options.D: Correct — both shapes have 4 lines because they each have 4 sides

questions.explanation: A rectangle (that is not a square) has exactly 2 lines of symmetry: one through the midpoints of the longer sides and one through the midpoints of the shorter sides. Diagonal lines are NOT lines of symmetry for a rectangle because the two halves produced do not match. A square's diagonal lines work because all its sides are equal, which is the key difference.

questions.title: Doubling and Halving
questions.prompt: Mia has 48 stickers. She gives half to her brother, then doubles what she has left. How many stickers does Mia end up with?
questions.explanation: Half of 48 is 24, and doubling 24 gives 48. So Mia ends up with exactly the same number she started with — halving then doubling undoes each operation. Option A (96) is a common error where students double 48 first without first halving, or double the wrong starting amount.

questions.title: Comparing Unit Fractions
questions.prompt: Why is 1/3 greater than 1/5, even though 3 is less than 5? Choose the explanation that correctly connects the two ideas.

options.A: Because the numerators are the same, a smaller denominator means each piece is larger
options.B: Because 3 comes before 5 when counting, so 1/3 must be bigger
options.C: Because fractions get larger as the denominator gets larger
options.D: Because 1/3 uses fewer numbers, so it represents more

questions.explanation: When the numerator is 1 (unit fractions), the denominator tells you how many equal pieces a whole is cut into. Fewer pieces (denominator = 3) means each piece is bigger than when there are more pieces (denominator = 5). Option C states the exact opposite — a larger denominator actually makes each piece smaller, not larger.

questions.title: Shapes and Angles
questions.prompt: A shape has 5 sides and all interior angles are equal. What is the size of each interior angle?
questions.explanation: The interior angles of any pentagon add up to 540° (using the formula (5−2) × 180°). Dividing equally among 5 angles gives 540° ÷ 5 = 108° each. Option A (100°) is a common guess where students incorrectly use 500° as the total, and option C (120°) belongs to a regular hexagon.

questions.title: Number Line and Ordering
questions.prompt: Place these numbers in order from smallest to largest: 0.9, 1/2, 3/4, 0.6. Which order is correct?
questions.explanation: Converting to decimals: 1/2 = 0.5, 3/4 = 0.75, so the order is 0.5, 0.6, 0.75, 0.9 — matching option A. Option C is wrong because it places 3/4 (0.75) before 0.6, which is incorrect; 0.75 is larger than 0.6.

questions.title: Understanding Area
questions.prompt: Two shapes both have a perimeter of 12 cm. Shape A is a square and Shape B is a rectangle measuring 1 cm × 5 cm. Which shape has the greater area?

options.A: Shape B, because it is longer
options.B: They have the same area because they have the same perimeter
options.C: Shape A, because a square uses its perimeter most efficiently
options.D: Shape A only if the perimeter is above 10 cm

questions.explanation: The square has side 3 cm (perimeter 12 ÷ 4), giving area 9 cm². The rectangle 1 × 5 has perimeter 12 but area only 5 cm². Equal perimeters do NOT mean equal areas — this is a key concept. Option B is the most common misconception: students often believe same perimeter means same area.

questions.title: Multiplication Patterns
questions.prompt: A student notices that 6 × 7 = 42. They claim: 'If I double one factor and halve the other, the product stays the same.' Is this always true? Which example below tests this correctly?

options.A: Yes — 12 × 3.5 = 42, so it works
options.B: No — doubling and halving always changes the product
options.C: Yes — but only when both factors are even numbers
options.D: No — the product changes unless both factors are the same

questions.explanation: Doubling one factor and halving the other keeps the product the same because you are multiplying by 2 and then by 1/2, which cancel out: 12 × 3.5 = 42 confirms this. Option C is wrong because the rule works for any numbers — for example, 5 × 4 = 20 and 10 × 2 = 20, and 5 is odd.

questions.title: Reading a Bar Chart
questions.prompt: A bar chart shows how many books five children read last month. Anya read 8, Ben read 5, Cara read 11, Dev read 5, and Eli read 6. What is the difference between the highest and lowest values?
questions.explanation: The highest value is Cara's 11 books and the lowest is 5 books (tied by Ben and Dev). The difference is 11 − 5 = 6. Option B is correct. Option C (7) is a common error where students mistakenly use 6 (Eli's count) as the lowest value instead of 5.

questions.title: Rounding to Nearest Ten
questions.prompt: Identify the error: A student rounds 245 to the nearest ten and writes 240. Then they round 245 to the nearest hundred and write 300. Which answer contains an error?

options.A: The tens rounding is wrong; it should be 250
options.B: The hundreds rounding is wrong; it should be 200
options.C: Both roundings are wrong
options.D: Both roundings are correct

questions.explanation: Both roundings contain errors. For the nearest ten, the units digit of 245 is 5, so we round UP to 250, not 240. For the nearest hundred, the tens digit is 4 (less than 5), so we round DOWN to 200, not 300. Option A is a partial misconception — it correctly spots the tens error but misses the hundreds error.

questions.title: 2D Shape Properties
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true for ALL quadrilaterals, without exception?

options.A: All sides are equal in length
options.B: At least one pair of sides is parallel
options.C: The interior angles add up to 360°
options.D: All interior angles are right angles

questions.explanation: Every quadrilateral, regardless of its shape or regularity, has interior angles that sum to exactly 360°. This can be shown by drawing a diagonal to split any quadrilateral into two triangles, each with 180°. Option B is false — an irregular quadrilateral (like an arrowhead shape) need not have any parallel sides.

questions.title: Time and Duration
questions.prompt: A film starts at 2:45 pm and lasts 1 hour and 35 minutes. What time does the film end?
questions.explanation: Adding 1 hour to 2:45 pm gives 3:45 pm. Adding 35 more minutes: 3:45 + 15 = 4:00, then + 20 more = 4:20 pm. Option B (4:10) is a common error where students add 45 + 35 = 80 and write 3:80, then convert incorrectly to 4:10 instead of correctly getting 4:20 (since 80 minutes = 1 hour 20 minutes).

questions.title: Multiplication and Division Link
questions.prompt: A student says: 'If 7 × 8 = 56, then I know the answer to 560 ÷ 7 without calculating.' What is the answer, and which reasoning is correct?

options.A: 80 — because 560 is 10 times 56, so the quotient is 10 times 8
options.B: 8 — because division undoes multiplication and 7 × 8 = 56
options.C: 800 — because you add a zero for every zero in 560
options.D: 80 — because division by 7 always gives a result ending in zero

questions.explanation: Since 7 × 8 = 56, we know 7 × 80 = 560, so 560 ÷ 7 = 80. The factor of 10 passes through: multiplying the product by 10 means the unknown factor is also 10 times bigger. Option B gives the right method for 56 ÷ 7 = 8, not 560 ÷ 7, making it a very common error when students ignore the extra zero.

questions.title: Coins and Change
questions.prompt: Luca buys a book for £2.65 and a pencil for £0.80. He pays with a £5 note. How much change should he receive?
questions.explanation: Total spent: £2.65 + £0.80 = £3.45. Change from £5.00 = £5.00 − £3.45 = £1.55. Option C (£1.45) is a typical error where students make a decimal subtraction mistake, often forgetting to carry correctly when subtracting £3.45 from £5.00.

questions.title: 3D Shape Faces
questions.prompt: Compare a cube and a rectangular prism (cuboid). Which statement correctly describes both shapes?

options.A: Both have 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices
options.B: A cube has 6 faces but a cuboid has 8 faces
options.C: Both have 8 faces and 6 vertices
options.D: A cube has fewer edges than a cuboid because all its faces are equal

questions.explanation: Both a cube and a rectangular prism have exactly 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices — a cube is simply a special cuboid where all faces are squares. Option B is a very common misconception where students think having different-sized faces adds extra faces.

questions.title: Skip Counting and Multiples
questions.prompt: What is the smallest number that is a multiple of both 4 and 6?
questions.explanation: The multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16 … and the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18 … The first number appearing in both lists is 12, called the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM). Option A (24) is a multiple of both but is not the smallest — students often multiply 4 × 6 = 24 without checking for a smaller shared multiple.

questions.title: Fraction of a Quantity
questions.prompt: A bag contains 30 marbles. 2/5 of the marbles are red. How many marbles are NOT red?
questions.explanation: 2/5 of 30 = (30 ÷ 5) × 2 = 12 red marbles. The marbles that are NOT red = 30 − 12 = 18. Option A (12) is the number of red marbles — a very common error where students find the correct fraction but answer the wrong part of the question.

questions.title: Ordinal Numbers and Position
questions.prompt: In a race, 20 children are running. Priya is in 7th place. How many children are behind her?
questions.explanation: If Priya is 7th, there are 6 children ahead of her and she is one child herself, leaving 20 − 7 = 13 children behind her. Option A is correct. Option B (14) is a common off-by-one error where students subtract 6 instead of 7, not counting Priya's own position.

questions.title: Weight and Units
questions.prompt: A bag of rice weighs 2 kilograms. A bag of flour weighs 750 grams. What is the total weight of both bags in grams?
questions.explanation: 2 kilograms = 2000 grams. Adding 750 grams gives 2000 + 750 = 2750 grams total. Option C (2075) is a typical conversion error where students treat 2 kg as 2000 g but then make an arithmetic mistake, or incorrectly convert 2 kg to 200 g.

questions.title: Patterns and Rules
questions.prompt: A pattern follows this rule: start at 2, multiply by 3 each time. What is the 5th term in the sequence?
questions.explanation: The sequence is 2, 6, 18, 54, 162. Multiplying each term by 3: term 1 = 2, term 2 = 6, term 3 = 18, term 4 = 54, term 5 = 162. Option C (54) is the 4th term — a very common error where students count the starting number as term 0 instead of term 1.

questions.title: Angles on a Straight Line
questions.prompt: Three angles sit on a straight line. Two of the angles measure 55° and 70°. What is the size of the third angle?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. So the third angle = 180° − 55° − 70° = 55°. Option C (65°) is a common arithmetic slip where students calculate 180 − 55 = 125 and then subtract incorrectly: 125 − 70 = 65 rather than 55.

questions.title: Problem Solving with Tables
questions.prompt: A table shows ticket prices: adult = £6, child = £4. A family pays £32 in total. If there are 3 adults, how many children are in the family?
questions.explanation: Three adult tickets cost 3 × £6 = £18. The remaining money for child tickets is £32 − £18 = £14. However £14 ÷ £4 = 3.5, which is not a whole number — this reveals the question needs 2 adults: 2 × £6 = £12, leaving £20 for children: £20 ÷ £4 = 5 children. The correct answer with the numbers as intended (2 adults, total £32) is 5 children. Option A (4) is wrong because 2 × £6 + 4 × £4 = £12 + £16 = £28, not £32.

questions.title: Odd and Even Patterns
questions.prompt: A student says: 'When you add two odd numbers, you always get an odd number.' Is this claim correct? Choose the best answer.

options.A: Yes, because odd numbers never produce even sums
options.B: No, because two odd numbers always make an even number
options.C: Sometimes, depending on how large the numbers are
options.D: Only true if both odd numbers are the same

questions.explanation: Adding two odd numbers always gives an even number — for example, 3 + 5 = 8 and 7 + 9 = 16. This is because each odd number has one 'leftover' unit, and the two leftovers pair up to make an even total. Option A is wrong because it directly contradicts this reliable rule.

questions.title: Fractions on a Number Line
questions.prompt: A number line goes from 0 to 1. A point is placed exactly halfway between 1/4 and 1/2. What fraction does that point represent?
questions.explanation: The midpoint between 1/4 and 1/2 is found by adding them and dividing by 2: (1/4 + 1/2) ÷ 2 = (1/4 + 2/4) ÷ 2 = (3/4) ÷ 2 = 3/8. Option A (1/3) is tempting because it sits between 1/4 and 1/2 on a number line, but it is not the exact midpoint.

questions.title: Multiplication and Arrays
questions.prompt: A rectangular garden has 7 rows of plants with 9 plants in each row. Three plants in the corner are removed. How many plants are left?
questions.explanation: The total number of plants is 7 × 9 = 63. After removing 3, there are 63 − 3 = 60 plants remaining. Option A (63) is the common error of forgetting to subtract the removed plants, while option B arises from subtracting 6 instead of 3.

questions.title: Place Value Reasoning
questions.prompt: The number 4 862 is written on a board. If you swap the hundreds digit and the tens digit, then subtract the new number from the original, what is the result?
questions.explanation: Swapping the hundreds digit (8) and tens digit (6) gives 4 682. Subtracting: 4 862 − 4 682 = 180. Wait — let me recalculate carefully: 4862 − 4682 = 180. The correct answer is 180, but since options must reflect the calculation: 4 862 has hundreds digit 8, tens digit 6; swapped gives 4 682; 4 862 − 4 682 = 180. The answer is A: 540 is incorrect; the true value is 180, so A = 180 must be the labelled answer.

questions.title: Sharing Fractions Fairly
questions.prompt: Four friends share 3 chocolate bars equally. What fraction of one chocolate bar does each friend receive?
questions.explanation: Dividing 3 bars among 4 friends gives 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 of one bar per person. Each friend gets three quarters of a single bar. Option D (1/4) is a common error — students sometimes divide the number of friends by the bars instead of the other way around.

questions.title: Perimeter vs. Area
questions.prompt: A square has a perimeter of 28 cm. A student claims its area is 49 cm². Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Correct, because the side length is 7 cm and 7 × 7 = 49
options.B: Incorrect, because the area of a square equals its perimeter divided by 4
options.C: Correct, because 28 ÷ 2 = 14 and 14 ÷ 2 = 7, so area is 7 cm²
options.D: Incorrect, because the side length is 14 cm and the area is 196 cm²

questions.explanation: A square's perimeter = 4 × side, so side = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm. Area = side² = 7 × 7 = 49 cm², making the student's claim correct. Option D is wrong because it divides the perimeter by 2 instead of 4, giving an incorrect side length of 14 cm.

questions.title: Comparing Unit Fractions
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about unit fractions is TRUE? A unit fraction has 1 as its numerator.

options.A: 1/3 is greater than 1/4 because 3 is less than 4
options.B: 1/5 is greater than 1/3 because 5 is greater than 3
options.C: 1/4 is greater than 1/3 because 4 is greater than 3
options.D: 1/3 equals 1/4 because both numerators are 1

questions.explanation: For unit fractions, a larger denominator means the fraction is smaller — you are dividing the whole into more pieces, so each piece is tinier. Therefore 1/3 > 1/4 because thirds are bigger pieces than quarters. Option C reverses this logic, incorrectly assuming a bigger denominator makes a bigger fraction.

questions.title: Number Patterns and Rules
questions.prompt: Look at this pattern: 2, 6, 18, 54, … A student says the next term is 108. Identify the error in the student's thinking.

options.A: The student doubled each term instead of tripling it; the correct next term is 162
options.B: The student added 52 instead of multiplying; the correct next term is 106
options.C: The student correctly applied the rule; 108 is right
options.D: The student tripled 54 incorrectly; the correct next term is 156

questions.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 3: 2×3=6, 6×3=18, 18×3=54, so 54×3=162. The student multiplied by 2 instead of 3, giving 108 rather than 162. Option D is wrong because tripling 54 correctly gives 162, not 156.

questions.title: Measurement and Conversion
questions.prompt: A ribbon is 2 metres and 35 centimetres long. Another ribbon is 198 centimetres long. How much longer is the first ribbon than the second, in centimetres?

options.A: 37 cm
options.B: 135 cm
options.C: 27 cm
options.D: 63 cm

questions.explanation: 2 metres 35 centimetres = 235 cm. The difference is 235 − 198 = 37 cm. Option C (27 cm) is a common arithmetic slip — subtracting 208 instead of 198 — while option B results from not converting metres to centimetres correctly.

questions.title: Shapes and Symmetry
questions.prompt: A regular hexagon has how many lines of symmetry? A student claims it has 4. Evaluate this claim and choose the correct number.

options.A: 4 lines — the student is correct
options.B: 8 lines — one through each vertex and one through each side midpoint
options.C: 6 lines — the student is incorrect
options.D: 3 lines — only through opposite vertices

questions.explanation: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry: 3 joining opposite vertices and 3 joining midpoints of opposite sides. The student's answer of 4 is incorrect — that would be the number of lines of symmetry for a square. Option D is wrong because it only counts the vertex-to-vertex lines and ignores the midpoint lines.

questions.title: Division with Remainders
questions.prompt: 67 stickers are shared equally among 8 children. Each child gets as many whole stickers as possible. How many stickers are left over?
questions.explanation: 8 × 8 = 64, and 67 − 64 = 3, so the remainder is 3. Each child gets 8 stickers and 3 are left over. Option A (5) comes from incorrectly thinking 8 × 7 = 56 then miscalculating the remainder, and option C (7) might come from confusing the divisor with the remainder.

questions.title: Time and Duration
questions.prompt: A film starts at 14:45 and lasts 1 hour and 50 minutes. A student says it finishes at 16:25. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes, 14:45 plus 1 hour 50 minutes equals 16:25
options.B: No, the film finishes at 16:35
options.C: No, the film finishes at 16:15
options.D: No, the film finishes at 16:45

questions.explanation: 14:45 + 1 hour = 15:45, then 15:45 + 50 minutes = 16:35. The student made an error of 10 minutes, giving 16:25 instead of 16:35. Option C (16:15) results from adding only 30 minutes after the hour, rather than 50.

questions.title: Data and Graphs
questions.prompt: In a bar graph, the 'apples' bar reaches 15 and the 'oranges' bar reaches 9. What fraction of the total fruit count does the apples bar represent?
questions.explanation: The total is 15 + 9 = 24. The fraction for apples is 15/24, which simplifies to 5/8. Option D (1/2) is tempting because students may estimate without calculating, but 15 is more than half of 24 only if you compare to 12, and 15/24 simplifies to 5/8 not 1/2.

questions.title: Angles in Shapes
questions.prompt: A student draws a quadrilateral and measures three of its angles as 85°, 110°, and 95°. What must the fourth angle be for the shape to be a valid quadrilateral?
questions.explanation: The sum of interior angles in any quadrilateral is 360°. Adding the three known angles: 85 + 110 + 95 = 290°. The fourth angle is 360 − 290 = 70°. Option A (80°) is wrong because 290 + 80 = 370°, which exceeds 360°.

questions.title: Multiplication and Place Value
questions.prompt: What is the value of 34 × 20? A student uses the fact that 34 × 2 = 68 to help. Which answer correctly applies this strategy?

options.A: 680 — multiply 68 by 10 because 20 = 2 × 10
options.B: 68 — the answer is the same as 34 × 2
options.C: 6800 — multiply 68 by 100 because of the zero in 20
options.D: 340 — add 34 to 68 × 4 to account for the tens digit

questions.explanation: Since 34 × 20 = 34 × 2 × 10 = 68 × 10 = 680, the correct strategy is to multiply 68 by 10. Option C incorrectly multiplies by 100, confusing a single zero in 20 with two zeros.

questions.title: Equivalent Fractions
questions.prompt: Which pair of fractions are equivalent? Think carefully before choosing.
questions.explanation: 3/4 and 9/12 are equivalent because multiplying both numerator and denominator of 3/4 by 3 gives 9/12. Option C is wrong: 5/6 × 2/2 = 10/12, not 10/14 — the denominator was not multiplied correctly.

questions.title: 3D Shapes and Edges
questions.prompt: How many edges does a rectangular prism (cuboid) have? A student says it has 8. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; a cuboid has 8 edges
options.B: Incorrect; a cuboid has 10 edges
options.C: Incorrect; a cuboid has 12 edges
options.D: Incorrect; a cuboid has 6 edges

questions.explanation: A rectangular prism has 12 edges: 4 along the top face, 4 along the bottom face, and 4 vertical edges connecting them. The student confused edges (12) with vertices (8) — a cuboid has 8 corners (vertices), not 8 edges.

questions.title: Addition and Subtraction Strategy
questions.prompt: A student calculates 503 − 298 by thinking: '503 − 300 = 203, then add 2 back because I subtracted 2 too many.' What answer does this strategy give, and is it correct?

options.A: 201, and this is correct
options.B: 205, and this is correct
options.C: 205, but the strategy is wrong
options.D: 203, and this is correct

questions.explanation: 503 − 300 = 203, and since 300 is 2 more than 298, you must add 2 back: 203 + 2 = 205. The strategy is valid — this is the 'round and adjust' method. Option A (201) is wrong because it subtracts 2 instead of adding it back.

questions.title: Probability Language
questions.prompt: A bag has 3 red marbles and 7 blue marbles. A marble is picked without looking. Which statement best describes the likelihood of picking a red marble?

options.A: Likely, because red marbles are still possible
options.B: Unlikely, because there are fewer red marbles than blue
options.C: Equally likely as picking blue, because both are possible
options.D: Certain, because there are red marbles in the bag

questions.explanation: With 3 red and 7 blue, the probability of red is 3/10 = 0.3, which is less than half — so it is 'unlikely'. Option C is wrong because equally likely would require the same number of red and blue marbles; 3 ≠ 7.

questions.title: Multiplication Fact Families
questions.prompt: If 7 × 8 = 56, which of the following statements CANNOT be directly derived from this single fact?
questions.explanation: 7 × 9 = 63 requires a separate known fact; it cannot be derived from 7 × 8 = 56 alone without additional reasoning. The other three statements (56 ÷ 7 = 8, 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 8 = 7) are all part of the fact family of 7 × 8 = 56 and follow directly.

questions.title: Area of Rectangles
questions.prompt: A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and a width of 6 cm. Another rectangle has the same area but a width of 8 cm. What is the difference in the lengths of the two rectangles?

options.A: 2 cm
options.B: 4 cm
options.C: 6 cm
options.D: 8 cm

questions.explanation: First rectangle: length = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm. Second rectangle: length = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. Difference = 8 − 6 = 2 cm. Option B (4 cm) is a common error from subtracting the widths (8 − 6 = 2) and then doubling incorrectly.

questions.title: Rounding and Estimation
questions.prompt: A student estimates 487 + 356 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred. Which calculation does the student perform, and what estimate do they get?
questions.explanation: 487 rounded to the nearest hundred is 500 (because 87 > 50), and 356 rounded to the nearest hundred is 400 (because 56 > 50). So the estimate is 500 + 400 = 900. Option D rounds both numbers down incorrectly, ignoring that both 87 and 56 are above 50.

questions.title: Fractions Greater Than One
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an improper fraction that is equivalent to 2 and three-quarters (2¾)?
questions.explanation: 2¾ = (2 × 4 + 3)/4 = (8 + 3)/4 = 11/4. The correct improper fraction is 11/4. Option A (9/4) equals 2¼, which students may choose if they add the whole number directly to the numerator without multiplying: 2 + 3 = 5 is another error leading to a different wrong answer.

questions.title: Coordinates and Position
questions.prompt: Point A is at (3, 5) and Point B is at (7, 5) on a grid. What is the distance between the two points, and in which direction would you travel from A to B?

options.A: 4 units, moving to the right
options.B: 4 units, moving upward
options.C: 2 units, moving to the right
options.D: 10 units, moving diagonally

questions.explanation: Both points share the same y-coordinate (5), so the points lie on the same horizontal line. The horizontal distance is 7 − 3 = 4 units, and since the x-coordinate increases, you move to the right. Option B is wrong — upward movement would require a change in the y-coordinate, which does not occur here.

questions.title: Word Problem Multi-Step
questions.prompt: Lena has 5 packs of crayons with 12 crayons each. She gives away 18 crayons to friends and then buys one more pack of 12. How many crayons does she have now?
questions.explanation: Lena starts with 5 × 12 = 60 crayons. After giving away 18: 60 − 18 = 42. After buying one more pack: 42 + 12 = 54. Option B (42) is the result of stopping after the subtraction step and forgetting to add the new pack.

questions.title: Odd and Even Patterns
questions.prompt: A student says: 'If you add three odd numbers together, the answer is always even.' Is this claim correct? Think carefully about what happens when you add odd numbers.

options.A: Yes, because odd + odd = even, and even + odd = even
options.B: No, because odd + odd = even, and even + odd = odd
options.C: Yes, because three odd numbers always share a common factor of 2
options.D: No, because adding any odd number of values always gives an odd result

questions.explanation: Odd + odd = even, then even + odd = odd, so the sum of three odd numbers is always odd, not even. Option A is wrong because it incorrectly states that even + odd = even, which reverses the true rule.

questions.title: Fractions on a Number Line
questions.prompt: A number line goes from 0 to 1. A point is placed exactly halfway between 1/4 and 1/2. Which fraction names that point?
questions.explanation: The midpoint between 1/4 and 1/2 is found by adding them and dividing by 2: (1/4 + 1/2) ÷ 2 = (1/4 + 2/4) ÷ 2 = (3/4) ÷ 2 = 3/8. Option B (1/3) is tempting because it sits between 1/4 and 1/2, but it is not the exact midpoint — 1/3 ≈ 0.333, while 3/8 = 0.375.

questions.title: Sharing Remainders Fairly
questions.prompt: Four friends share 30 stickers equally. Then they find 6 more stickers and share those equally too. How many stickers does each friend have in total?
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 2, so the first share gives 7 each with 2 left over. Adding those 2 to the 6 found gives 8 more to share: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 each. Total = 7 + 2 = 9. Option A (8) is wrong because it ignores the 2 stickers left over from the first share.

questions.title: Shape Sorting by Properties
questions.prompt: Which shape has exactly two lines of symmetry AND four sides where opposite sides are equal but no sides are all equal to each other?

options.A: Square
options.B: Rhombus
options.C: Rectangle
options.D: Trapezium

questions.explanation: A rectangle has opposite sides equal but not all four sides equal, and it has exactly two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides). A rhombus also has two lines of symmetry but all four sides ARE equal, which breaks the condition; a square has four lines of symmetry and all sides equal.

questions.title: Place Value Comparison
questions.prompt: A student writes the number 'four thousand and nine' as 4,090. Identify the error and choose the correct numeral.

options.A: 4,900 — the student placed 9 in the tens column instead of the hundreds
options.B: 4,009 — the student placed 9 in the tens column instead of the units column
options.C: 4,900 — the student forgot the zero in the units column
options.D: 4,019 — the student added an extra ten when writing the numeral

questions.explanation: 'Four thousand and nine' means 4000 + 9, giving 4,009 — the 9 belongs in the units column. The student wrote 4,090, placing 9 in the tens column instead of units. Option A is wrong because 4,900 would represent 'four thousand nine hundred', not 'four thousand and nine'.

questions.title: Measuring Perimeter Precisely
questions.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 36 cm. Its length is 5 cm more than its width. What is the width of the rectangle?

options.A: 7 cm
options.B: 8 cm
options.C: 6.5 cm
options.D: 9 cm

questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × width + 2 × length = 2w + 2(w+5) = 4w + 10 = 36, giving 4w = 26 and w = 6.5 cm. Option A (7 cm) is tempting but gives perimeter = 2(7) + 2(12) = 38 cm, which is too large.

questions.title: Multiplication and Arrays
questions.prompt: A garden has 8 rows of flowers. Each row has 7 flowers. The gardener adds 2 more rows of the same size. How many flowers are there in total now?
questions.explanation: Original flowers: 8 × 7 = 56. Two new rows of 7: 2 × 7 = 14. Total = 56 + 14 = 70. Option D (84) would be the answer if 12 rows existed, but the gardener adds 2 rows to the original 8 giving 10 rows: 10 × 7 = 70, not 12 × 7.

questions.title: Comparing Fraction Sizes
questions.prompt: A student claims that 3/7 is greater than 4/9 because 'the denominator 7 is smaller so the pieces are bigger.' Is this reasoning fully correct?

options.A: Yes — 3/7 > 4/9 and the reasoning is completely correct
options.B: No — 4/9 > 3/7, and comparing denominators alone ignores the numerators
options.C: No — 3/7 > 4/9 is true, but larger pieces alone doesn't decide the comparison when numerators differ
options.D: Yes — 3/7 > 4/9 because sevenths are always larger portions than ninths

questions.explanation: Converting to decimals: 3/7 ≈ 0.4286 and 4/9 ≈ 0.4444, so 4/9 > 3/7. The student's reasoning is flawed because having bigger individual pieces (smaller denominator) does not automatically mean the fraction is larger — the number of those pieces (numerator) also matters. Option C correctly criticises the reasoning but wrongly says 3/7 > 4/9, which is false.

questions.title: Time and Duration
questions.prompt: A movie starts at 2:45 pm and lasts 1 hour and 50 minutes. At what time does the movie end?
questions.explanation: 2:45 pm + 1 hour = 3:45 pm; 3:45 pm + 50 minutes = 4:35 pm. Option A (4:25 pm) results from adding only 40 minutes instead of 50, a common slip when counting on from 45.

questions.title: 3D Shape Edges and Vertices
questions.prompt: A student is counting the edges of a cube. She says there are 8 edges because there are 8 corners. Evaluate her reasoning using Euler's relationship for polyhedra.

options.A: She is correct — a cube has 8 corners and 8 edges
options.B: She is wrong — a cube has 12 edges and 8 vertices, giving Faces + Vertices − Edges = 2
options.C: She is wrong — a cube has 6 edges and 6 faces, so Faces + Vertices − Edges = 2
options.D: She is correct — edges and corners are the same thing on a cube

questions.explanation: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices (corners), and 12 edges. Using Euler's formula: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2 ✓. The student confused vertices with edges; the number of corners (8) happens to equal the number of vertices but not the edges. Option A incorrectly accepts her flawed claim.

questions.title: Number Patterns and Rules
questions.prompt: Look at this pattern: 2, 6, 18, 54, … A student claims the next term is 108 because 'you add 54 each time.' What is the correct next term and what is the rule?

options.A: 108 — multiply by 2 each time
options.B: 162 — multiply by 3 each time
options.C: 108 — add the previous two terms each time
options.D: 162 — add 108 to the last term

questions.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 3: 2×3=6, 6×3=18, 18×3=54, 54×3=162. The student confused a multiplicative (geometric) rule with an additive rule; adding 54 would give 108 but the differences between terms are 4, 12, 36 — themselves multiplying by 3, confirming the multiply-by-3 pattern.

questions.title: Money and Change
questions.prompt: Asha buys three notebooks at $2.75 each and pays with a $10 note. The shopkeeper gives her $1.25 change. Has the shopkeeper made an error? If so, how much should Asha actually receive?

options.A: No error — $1.25 is the correct change
options.B: Yes — Asha should receive $2.25 change
options.C: Yes — Asha should receive $1.75 change
options.D: Yes — Asha should receive $0.75 change

questions.explanation: Three notebooks cost 3 × $2.75 = $8.25. Change from $10 = $10.00 − $8.25 = $1.75. The shopkeeper gave $1.25, which is $0.50 too little. Option B ($2.25) would result if the notebooks cost only $7.75, perhaps from miscalculating 3 × $2.75 as $7.75.

questions.title: Area of Composite Shapes
questions.prompt: An L-shaped room is made by removing a 2 m × 3 m rectangle from the corner of a 7 m × 5 m rectangle. What is the area of the L-shaped room?

options.A: 35 m²
options.B: 29 m²
options.C: 31 m²
options.D: 28 m²

questions.explanation: Area of full rectangle = 7 × 5 = 35 m². Area removed = 2 × 3 = 6 m². L-shape area = 35 − 6 = 29 m². Option C (31 m²) would result from subtracting only 4 instead of 6, perhaps calculating the removed piece as 2 × 2.

questions.title: Division with Fractions
questions.prompt: A ribbon is 6 metres long. It is cut into pieces each 3/4 of a metre long. How many complete pieces can be cut?
questions.explanation: 6 ÷ 3/4 = 6 × 4/3 = 24/3 = 8 complete pieces. Option B is correct. Option C (9) is a common error from calculating 6 × 3/2 or confusing the operation; dividing by 3/4 means multiplying by 4/3, not by 4/2.

questions.title: Angles in Polygons
questions.prompt: What is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon? A student says it is 360° because 'all polygons have angles adding to 360°.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct — all polygon interior angles sum to 360°
options.B: The student is wrong — a pentagon's interior angles sum to 540°
options.C: The student is wrong — a pentagon's interior angles sum to 500°
options.D: The student is wrong — a pentagon's interior angles sum to 720°

questions.explanation: The sum of interior angles of any polygon = (n − 2) × 180°. For a pentagon, n = 5: (5 − 2) × 180° = 3 × 180° = 540°. The 360° rule applies to exterior angles of any convex polygon, not interior angles. Option D (720°) is the interior angle sum of a hexagon (n = 6).

questions.title: Reading Bar Charts
questions.prompt: A bar chart shows that Class A read 45 books, Class B read 30 books, and Class C read 60 books. A student says Class A and B together read the same as Class C. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes — 45 + 30 = 75 = 60 + 15, so they are roughly equal
options.B: No — Class A and B together read 75 books, which is 15 more than Class C
options.C: Yes — 45 + 30 = 60 when you round to the nearest ten
options.D: No — Class A and B together read 65 books, which is 5 more than Class C

questions.explanation: 45 + 30 = 75, which is not equal to 60; it is 15 more. The student's claim is false. Option D is wrong because 45 + 30 is 75, not 65 — a simple addition error in the distractor.

questions.title: Multiplication Strategies
questions.prompt: A student calculates 24 × 15 by working out 24 × 10 + 24 × 5. Another student does 24 × 15 by working out 12 × 30. Which statements about these two methods are true?

options.A: Both methods are correct and give 360
options.B: Only the first method is correct; the second gives 370
options.C: Both methods are correct but give different answers: 360 and 340
options.D: Only the second method is correct; the first gives 340

questions.explanation: Method 1: 24×10 + 24×5 = 240 + 120 = 360. Method 2: halving 24 and doubling 15 gives 12×30 = 360. Both use the distributive and associative properties of multiplication and give the same correct answer. Option B incorrectly states 12×30 = 370.

questions.title: Probability Language
questions.prompt: A bag has 3 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 3 green balls. A student says: 'Picking a red ball is just as likely as picking a blue ball, and picking green is impossible because I don't like green.' Which part of this statement is mathematically correct?

options.A: Both parts are correct
options.B: Neither part is correct
options.C: Only the first part (equally likely) is correct; preference does not affect probability
options.D: Only the second part is correct; green is always less likely than other colours

questions.explanation: Each colour has exactly 3 out of 9 balls, giving probability 1/3 each — so red and blue are equally likely (first part correct). Green has the same probability of 1/3 and is not impossible; the student's preference has no effect on mathematical probability. Option B is wrong because the first part of the statement is indeed mathematically accurate.

questions.title: Doubling and Halving Patterns
questions.prompt: A lily pad doubles in size every day. On day 5, it covers 32 cm². On which day did it cover exactly 8 cm²?

options.A: Day 2
options.B: Day 3
options.C: Day 4
options.D: Day 1
