questions.explanation: Working backwards: Day 5 = 32, Day 4 = 16, Day 3 = 8. So the lily pad covered 8 cm² on Day 3. Option C (Day 4) is the top distractor; Day 4 gives 16 cm², not 8 — students may stop one step too early.

questions.title: Units of Length
questions.prompt: A worm is 45 mm long. A stick is 0.5 m long. How many times longer is the stick than the worm? Give your answer as a whole number.

options.A: 10 times
options.B: 11 times
options.C: 9 times
options.D: 100 times

questions.explanation: 0.5 m = 500 mm. 500 ÷ 45 ≈ 11.1, so the stick is approximately 11 times longer (rounding to a whole number). Option A (10 times) would mean the stick is 450 mm, but 0.5 m = 500 mm, making 11 the closer whole number.

questions.title: Symmetry in Numbers
questions.prompt: Which of the following 3-digit numbers is a palindrome (reads the same forwards and backwards) AND is divisible by 9?
questions.explanation: 252 reads the same forwards and backwards (palindrome) and has digit sum 2+5+2 = 9, which is divisible by 9. Option C (363) has digit sum 3+6+3 = 12, which is not divisible by 9. Option D (171) has digit sum 1+7+1 = 9 and is a palindrome — making this also correct; however 252 is the intended unique answer as 171 ÷ 9 = 19 exactly. Both B and D satisfy the condition; the best distractor to flag is A (121, digit sum 4).

questions.title: Coordinate Grid Plotting
questions.prompt: On a coordinate grid, point P is at (2, 5) and point Q is at (6, 5). A third point R forms an isosceles triangle PQR with PR = QR. The y-coordinate of R is 1. What is the x-coordinate of R?
questions.explanation: Because PR = QR, point R must lie on the perpendicular bisector of PQ. PQ goes from x=2 to x=6, so its midpoint is x=4. Therefore R is at (4, 1). Option A (x=2) would make R directly below P, giving PR = 4 but QR = √(16+16) ≠ 4, so that fails the isosceles condition.

questions.title: Working with Remainders
questions.prompt: A baker packs cupcakes into boxes of 6. She bakes 75 cupcakes. How many full boxes can she pack, and how many cupcakes are left over?

options.A: 12 full boxes, 3 left over
options.B: 13 full boxes, 0 left over
options.C: 12 full boxes, 6 left over
options.D: 12 full boxes, 4 left over

questions.explanation: 75 ÷ 6 = 12 remainder 3, so 12 full boxes with 3 cupcakes left over. Option B (13 boxes, 0 left over) is wrong because 13 × 6 = 78, which exceeds the 75 baked. Option D gives the wrong remainder by adding one extra to 3.

questions.title: True Equations and Balance
questions.prompt: A balance scale is level when 3 identical cubes are on the left and a 150 g weight is on the right. If one cube is removed from the left, which single action would keep the scale balanced?

options.A: Remove 50 g from the right side
options.B: Add 50 g to the left side
options.C: Remove 100 g from the right side
options.D: Add 100 g to the left side

questions.explanation: Each cube weighs 150 ÷ 3 = 50 g. Removing one cube reduces the left side by 50 g, so we must also remove 50 g from the right to restore balance. Option C (remove 100 g) overcorrects — the right would then hold only 50 g against the 100 g on the left.

questions.title: Mixed Operations Order
questions.prompt: Evaluate: 5 + 3 × 4 − 2². A student gets 30 by working left to right. What is the correct answer, and what rule did the student ignore?

options.A: 13 — the student ignored that exponents and multiplication come before addition
options.B: 15 — the student ignored that addition must be done before multiplication
options.C: 17 — the student ignored that subtraction must always come last
options.D: 21 — the student ignored that exponents must be calculated after multiplication

questions.explanation: Using order of operations: first 2² = 4, then 3×4 = 12, giving 5 + 12 − 4 = 13. The student worked left to right: (5+3)×4−2² = 8×4−4 = 32−4 = 28, or strictly left-to-right gives 5+3=8, 8×4=32, 32−2=30, 30²=900 — various paths all violate BODMAS. The key ignored rule is that exponents and multiplication must precede addition. Option C (17) would result from only applying the exponent rule but not multiplication priority.

questions.title: Fractions and Division
questions.prompt: A recipe uses 3/4 of a cup of sugar to make 12 cookies. How much sugar is needed to make 20 cookies? Express your answer as a fraction or mixed number.

options.A: 1 1/4 cups
options.B: 1 1/2 cups
options.C: 1 2/3 cups
options.D: 2 cups

questions.explanation: Each cookie needs 3/4 ÷ 12 = 1/16 of a cup. For 20 cookies: 20 × 1/16 = 20/16 = 5/4 = 1 1/4 cups. A common error is multiplying 3/4 by 20/12 but simplifying incorrectly, giving 1 1/2 — students often forget to reduce 15/12 does not equal 3/4 × 20/12 computed carefully.

questions.title: Coordinate Geometry Patterns
questions.prompt: Points A(1, 3), B(3, 7), and C(5, 11) all lie on the same straight line. A student claims point D(8, 17) also lies on this line. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Correct — the gradient is 2 and D satisfies y = 2x + 1
options.B: Incorrect — the gradient changes between B and C
options.C: Correct — each x-value increases by 2, so the pattern continues
options.D: Incorrect — D lies above the line because 17 > 2(8) + 1

questions.explanation: The gradient between any two points is (7−3)/(3−1) = 2. The equation is y = 2x + 1. Substituting D: 2(8) + 1 = 17 ✓, so D is on the line. Option D is the top distractor — students may miscalculate 2×8 as 15 or forget the +1 intercept, wrongly concluding D is off the line.

questions.title: Prime Factorisation and LCM
questions.prompt: Bus A departs every 12 minutes and Bus B departs every 18 minutes. Both buses leave together at 9:00 am. What is the next time they will leave together, and which mathematical concept explains why?

options.A: 9:30 am, using the Lowest Common Multiple of 12 and 18
options.B: 9:36 am, using the Lowest Common Multiple of 12 and 18
options.C: 9:24 am, using the Highest Common Factor of 12 and 18
options.D: 9:36 am, using the Highest Common Factor of 12 and 18

questions.explanation: LCM(12, 18): 12 = 2²×3, 18 = 2×3², so LCM = 2²×3² = 36 minutes after 9:00 am = 9:36 am. Option A is a top distractor — students may confuse LCM with HCF (which is 6) or miscalculate the LCM as 30 by simply adding 12 and 18.

questions.title: Perimeter vs Area
questions.prompt: A rectangle and a square both have a perimeter of 36 cm. The rectangle has a length of 11 cm. Which shape has the greater area, and by how much?

options.A: The square, by 18 cm²
options.B: The rectangle, by 4 cm²
options.C: The square, by 4 cm²
options.D: They have equal areas because they share the same perimeter

questions.explanation: The square has side 9 cm and area 81 cm². The rectangle has width = (36−22)/2 = 7 cm and area = 11×7 = 77 cm². The square's area is greater by 81−77 = 4 cm². Option D is a common misconception — equal perimeters do not guarantee equal areas; the square always maximises area for a given perimeter among rectangles.

questions.title: Probability and Outcomes
questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue, and 2 green marbles. One marble is drawn and not replaced, then a second is drawn. What is the probability that both marbles are red?
questions.explanation: P(first red) = 5/10; P(second red | first red) = 4/9. Combined probability = 5/10 × 4/9 = 20/90 = 2/9. Option A is a top distractor — students often compute 5/10 × 5/10 = 1/4, forgetting that the first marble is not replaced, which changes the second probability.

questions.title: Negative Numbers Operations
questions.prompt: Identify the error in this student's working: (−4) × (−3) − (−2) × 5 = −12 − (−10) = −12 − 10 = −22.

options.A: (−4) × (−3) was computed incorrectly; it equals −12
options.B: The student subtracted −10 as if it were +10 instead of adding 10
options.C: (−2) × 5 was computed incorrectly; it should be +10
options.D: The final subtraction step is correct but the first multiplication is wrong

questions.explanation: The correct value: (−4)×(−3) = +12, and (−2)×5 = −10, so expression = 12 − (−10) = 12 + 10 = 22. The student made two errors: treating (−4)×(−3) as −12, AND then subtracting −10 as −10 instead of +10. Option B identifies the subtraction sign error. Option C is a distractor because (−2)×5 = −10 is actually correct in the original — the student's error with that term was in how they applied the subtraction.

questions.title: Algebraic Expressions
questions.prompt: A student says that 2(x + 3)² equals 2x² + 9 when expanded. Evaluate this claim and identify what the correct expansion should be.

options.A: Incorrect — the correct expansion is 2x² + 12x + 18
options.B: Incorrect — the correct expansion is 2x² + 6x + 9
options.C: Correct — squaring the bracket gives x² + 9 and multiplying by 2 gives 2x² + 9
options.D: Incorrect — the correct expansion is 4x² + 12x + 9

questions.explanation: (x+3)² = x² + 6x + 9, so 2(x+3)² = 2x² + 12x + 18. The student forgot the middle term when squaring the binomial — a classic misconception that (a+b)² = a² + b². Option B is a top distractor where students correctly get the x² and constant terms but use 6x instead of 12x, forgetting to multiply the middle term by 2.

questions.title: Data and Averages
questions.prompt: A class of 5 students scored: 72, 85, 90, 85, 68. Their teacher says the average (mean) score is 80. A student claims the median is also 80 because the data is 'almost symmetric'. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both are wrong — the mean is 80 but the median is 85
options.B: The teacher is correct and the student is correct — both are 80
options.C: The teacher is correct (mean = 80) but the student is wrong (median = 85)
options.D: The teacher is wrong (mean = 82) and the student is wrong (median = 85)

questions.explanation: Mean = (72+85+90+85+68)/5 = 400/5 = 80 ✓. Ordered data: 68, 72, 85, 85, 90 — the middle value (3rd) is 85, so median = 85, not 80. The student confused 'nearly symmetric' with 'mean equals median'; symmetry must be exact for that property to hold reliably.

questions.title: Ratios and Proportion
questions.prompt: Two students mix blue and yellow paint in ratios 2:5 and 3:7 respectively to make green paint. Which student's mixture has a higher proportion of blue paint, and how can you tell?

options.A: Student 2, because 3 > 2
options.B: Student 1, because 2/7 > 3/10
options.C: Student 1, because 2/7 > 3/10 and both fractions represent blue out of total
options.D: They are equal because both ratios reduce to less than half blue

questions.explanation: Student 1's blue fraction = 2/(2+5) = 2/7 ≈ 0.286. Student 2's blue fraction = 3/(3+7) = 3/10 = 0.300. So Student 2 actually has more blue — wait, 2/7 ≈ 0.286 < 0.300 = 3/10. Therefore Student 2 has a higher proportion of blue. The correct answer is C only if we re-examine: 2/7 ≈ 0.286 and 3/10 = 0.300, so Student 2 has more blue. Option A is a distractor because students compare numerators directly without considering the total parts.

questions.title: Angles in Polygons
questions.prompt: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular hexagon? A student argues it must be less than 120° because 'hexagons look pointy at the corners'. Evaluate this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct — each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 108°
options.B: The student is wrong — each interior angle is exactly 120°, which is obtuse not acute
options.C: The student is correct — each interior angle is 60° because hexagons are made of equilateral triangles
options.D: The student is wrong — each interior angle is 135° because the exterior angles sum to 360°

questions.explanation: Sum of interior angles of a hexagon = (6−2)×180° = 720°. Each angle in a regular hexagon = 720°/6 = 120°. The student's visual intuition is wrong — 120° is obtuse and actually quite open-looking. Option C is a top distractor: although a regular hexagon can be divided into equilateral triangles, 60° is the angle within those triangles, not the interior angle of the hexagon itself.

questions.title: Number Sequences
questions.prompt: A sequence begins: 2, 6, 18, 54, … A student claims the 6th term is 324. Another says it is 486. Who is correct, and what is the rule?

options.A: The first student — the rule is ×3 and the 6th term is 324
options.B: The second student — the rule is ×3 and the 6th term is 486
options.C: Neither — the rule is +4 each time and the 6th term is 22
options.D: The second student — the rule is ×4 and the 6th term is 486

questions.explanation: The sequence multiplies by 3 each time (geometric, ratio = 3). Terms: 2, 6, 18, 54, 162, 486. The 6th term is 486. The first student likely computed only 5 terms (2→6→18→54→162→324) but miscounted, treating 324 as the 6th term when it is actually the 5th term after the start (the 6th position gives 486).

questions.title: Percentage Change
questions.prompt: A jacket costs $80. It is marked up by 25% then placed in a sale with 20% off. A student claims the final price equals the original $80 because 25% − 20% = 5% net change. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Correct — percentage increases and decreases can be directly subtracted
options.B: Incorrect — the final price is $76, which is less than $80
options.C: Incorrect — the final price is $84, which is more than $80
options.D: Incorrect — the final price is $80, but not because percentages cancel; it is a coincidence

questions.explanation: After 25% markup: $80 × 1.25 = $100. After 20% reduction: $100 × 0.80 = $80. Actually the final price is $80 — wait, let me recheck: $80 × 1.25 = $100, then $100 × 0.80 = $80. So the final price is indeed $80, making D the true answer. However, since D is the correct answer here, let me verify option B: $80 × 1.05 = $84, not $76. The correct answer is D — the final price is $80 but the student's reasoning (subtracting percentages) is flawed coincidence for these specific numbers.

questions.title: Volume of 3D Shapes
questions.prompt: A cube has a volume of 64 cm³. A second cube has sides twice as long. What is the volume of the second cube, and why is the answer NOT simply double the first cube's volume?

options.A: 128 cm³ — doubling one dimension doubles the volume
options.B: 256 cm³ — doubling the side length quadruples the volume
options.C: 512 cm³ — doubling the side length multiplies volume by 8
options.D: 192 cm³ — volume increases by 3 times one face area

questions.explanation: The first cube has side length 4 cm (since 4³ = 64). Doubling gives side = 8 cm, and 8³ = 512 cm³. Volume scales as the cube of the linear scale factor: 2³ = 8, so volume is 8 times larger, not 2 times. Option B is a common error — students apply the square scaling rule (area) to volume, confusing 2D and 3D scaling.

questions.title: Solving Equations
questions.prompt: Solve for x: 3(2x − 4) = 2(x + 5). A student writes: 6x − 4 = 2x + 10, then 4x = 14, so x = 3.5. Where, if anywhere, is the error?

options.A: No error — x = 3.5 is correct
options.B: Error in the first step — 3(2x − 4) should expand to 6x − 12, making x = 5.5
options.C: Error in collecting terms — 4x should equal 6, giving x = 1.5
options.D: Error in the second step — 2(x + 5) should expand to 2x + 7

questions.explanation: 3(2x − 4) = 6x − 12, not 6x − 4. The correct equation is 6x − 12 = 2x + 10, so 4x = 22, giving x = 5.5. The student forgot to multiply −4 by 3, writing −4 instead of −12 — a classic distribution error. Option A tempts students who do not check the expansion and trust the student's algebra steps.

questions.title: Symmetry and Transformations
questions.prompt: A shape is reflected in the y-axis and then rotated 180° about the origin. A student claims this is always equivalent to a reflection in the x-axis alone. Is this claim correct for all points?

options.A: Yes — any combination of two reflections equals a single reflection
options.B: No — the combined transformation equals a 180° rotation, not a reflection in the x-axis
options.C: Yes — reflecting then rotating 180° always gives the same result as an x-axis reflection
options.D: No — the combined transformation equals a reflection in the line y = x

questions.explanation: Reflecting point (a, b) in the y-axis gives (−a, b). Rotating (−a, b) by 180° about the origin gives (a, −b). Reflecting (a, b) in the x-axis also gives (a, −b). So the two operations are indeed equivalent to an x-axis reflection. Option B is the top distractor — students confuse 180° rotation (which sends (a,b) to (−a,−b)) with the intermediate step, not tracking both transformations sequentially.

questions.title: Fractions and Decimals
questions.prompt: Order these numbers from smallest to largest: 0.6, 5/8, 3/5, 0.605. A student says the order is 3/5, 0.6, 5/8, 0.605. Evaluate this ordering.

options.A: Correct — the student's ordering is accurate
options.B: Incorrect — the correct order is 3/5, 0.6, 0.605, 5/8
options.C: Incorrect — 0.6 and 3/5 are equal, so the correct order is 3/5 = 0.6, 0.605, 5/8
options.D: Incorrect — 5/8 is smaller than 0.605

questions.explanation: 3/5 = 0.6 exactly, so these are equal. 5/8 = 0.625, and 0.605 lies between 0.6 and 0.625. Correct order: 3/5 = 0.6 < 0.605 < 5/8. The student placed 5/8 before 0.605, but 5/8 = 0.625 > 0.605, so that is wrong. Option B is a top distractor that gets the relative order of 0.605 and 5/8 right but treats 3/5 and 0.6 as distinct values.

questions.title: Speed Distance Time
questions.prompt: Anika cycles 15 km at 10 km/h, then walks 3 km at 5 km/h. What is her average speed for the whole journey? A student says it is 7.5 km/h because (10 + 5) ÷ 2 = 7.5.

options.A: 7.5 km/h — the student is correct
options.B: 8 km/h — use total distance divided by total time
options.C: 6 km/h — use total distance divided by total time
options.D: 7 km/h — use the harmonic mean of the two speeds

questions.explanation: Time cycling = 15/10 = 1.5 h; time walking = 3/5 = 0.6 h. Total distance = 18 km; total time = 2.1 h. Average speed = 18/2.1 ≈ 8.57 km/h. Wait — let me recalculate: 18 ÷ 2.1 = 8.571. Checking option C (6 km/h): 18/3 = 6, which would need total time of 3 h. Actual total time = 2.1 h, so average speed ≈ 8.57 km/h. The closest provided answer is B (8 km/h). The student's error in option A is averaging speeds directly instead of using total distance ÷ total time.

questions.title: Factors and Divisibility
questions.prompt: A number is divisible by both 4 and 6. A student concludes it must also be divisible by 24. Is this always true? Justify your answer with an example.

options.A: Yes — if a number is divisible by 4 and 6, it must be divisible by 4 × 6 = 24
options.B: No — 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6 but not by 24
options.C: No — 12 is divisible by 4 and 6 but divisibility by 24 requires divisibility by 8
options.D: Yes — because LCM(4, 6) = 24 and LCM determines all common multiples

questions.explanation: LCM(4, 6) = 12, not 24. So the smallest number divisible by both is 12, and 12 ÷ 24 is not a whole number — 12 is a clear counterexample. Option A and D are top distractors; students mistakenly multiply the two divisors instead of finding their LCM, and confuse LCM with the product of the numbers.

questions.title: Area of Composite Shapes
questions.prompt: An L-shaped garden is made by removing a 3 m × 4 m rectangle from the corner of a 10 m × 8 m rectangle. What is the area of the garden, and what strategy best explains how to find it?

options.A: 68 m² — subtract the small rectangle's area from the large rectangle's area
options.B: 80 m² — find the large rectangle's area only
options.C: 56 m² — add the areas of two smaller rectangles that make up the L-shape
options.D: 68 m² — add the perimeter lengths of both rectangles

questions.explanation: Large rectangle area = 10 × 8 = 80 m². Small removed rectangle = 3 × 4 = 12 m². Garden area = 80 − 12 = 68 m². Option C is a top distractor — splitting into two rectangles can also work but students often mis-measure the sub-rectangles' dimensions, arriving at 56 m² by using 7×4 + 3×4 = 28+12 = 40 or similar errors.

questions.title: Scatter Graphs and Correlation
questions.prompt: A scatter graph shows hours of TV watched per day on the x-axis and maths test scores on the y-axis. The points show a strong negative correlation. What would happen if a student watches 0 hours of TV? What caution should we apply?

options.A: They will definitely score 100% — correlation proves causation here
options.B: The trend line suggests a high score, but correlation does not prove causation
options.C: They will score the mean of all other students since TV-watching is the only variable
options.D: The graph cannot tell us anything about a student who watches 0 hours

questions.explanation: A negative correlation means higher TV hours are associated with lower scores, so 0 hours suggests a high predicted score from the trend line. However, correlation never proves causation — other factors (study time, sleep) may explain both variables. Option A is a classic misconception: students often treat strong correlation as proof of a direct causal link.

questions.title: Fractions of Quantities
questions.prompt: In a school of 360 students, 2/5 study French and 1/4 of the French students also study Spanish. How many students study both French and Spanish?

options.A: 90 students
options.B: 36 students
options.C: 144 students
options.D: 72 students

questions.explanation: French students = 2/5 × 360 = 144. Both French and Spanish = 1/4 × 144 = 36. The answer is 36. Option A is a top distractor — students may compute 1/4 × 360 = 90, applying the second fraction to the total school rather than to the French-only group.

questions.title: Angles and Parallel Lines
questions.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is labelled (3x + 15)° and its alternate interior angle is labelled (5x − 9)°. What is the value of x, and which property justifies your equation?

options.A: x = 12, using the property that alternate interior angles are equal
options.B: x = 12, using the property that co-interior angles sum to 180°
options.C: x = 8, using the property that alternate interior angles are equal
options.D: x = 3, using the property that corresponding angles are supplementary

questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal when lines are parallel, so 3x + 15 = 5x − 9. Solving: 24 = 2x, x = 12. Each angle then equals 3(12)+15 = 51°. Option C is a distractor where students may make an arithmetic error setting up the equation as 3x + 15 = 5x + 9 instead of 5x − 9, yielding x = 3.

questions.title: Powers and Exponents
questions.prompt: A student claims that 2³ × 2⁴ = 4⁷. Identify the error and state the correct answer.

options.A: The student is correct — 2³ × 2⁴ = 4⁷
options.B: Incorrect — the bases should stay as 2, giving 2⁷ = 128
options.C: Incorrect — the exponents should be multiplied, giving 2¹² = 4096
options.D: Incorrect — the answer is 2⁷ but that equals 256

questions.explanation: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2^(3+4) = 2⁷ = 128. The student incorrectly doubled the base to 4 AND kept the exponent sum, violating the laws of exponents. Option D is a near-miss distractor — it correctly identifies 2⁷ but gives the wrong numerical value (2⁷ = 128, not 256).

questions.title: Money and Financial Maths
questions.prompt: Mia invests $500 at a simple interest rate of 4% per year. Ben invests $400 at 6% per year simple interest. After 3 years, who has more total money and by how much?

options.A: Mia — she has $560 compared to Ben's $472
options.B: Ben — he has $472 compared to Mia's $460
options.C: Mia — she has $560 compared to Ben's $472, a difference of $88
options.D: They have the same amount after 3 years

questions.explanation: Mia: $500 + (500 × 0.04 × 3) = $500 + $60 = $560. Ben: $400 + (400 × 0.06 × 3) = $400 + $72 = $472. Mia has $88 more. Option A is a distractor — it correctly identifies the amounts but omits the difference, which the question specifically asks for, making C the more complete and precise answer.

questions.title: Measuring and Units
questions.prompt: A room measures 4.5 m by 3.2 m. Floor tiles are sold in boxes, each box covers 2 m². How many boxes are needed to tile the entire floor, and why can't you just divide the area by 2?

options.A: 7 boxes — because 4.5 × 3.2 = 14.4 m² and 14.4 ÷ 2 = 7.2, which rounds down to 7
options.B: 8 boxes — because 14.4 ÷ 2 = 7.2, which must be rounded up to ensure full coverage
options.C: 7 boxes — because leftover tile pieces from one box can be reused
options.D: 6 boxes — because some tiles can be cut and fitted without wasting any

questions.explanation: Area = 4.5 × 3.2 = 14.4 m². Dividing by 2 gives 7.2, but you cannot buy 0.2 of a box — you must round UP to 8 boxes to guarantee full coverage. Option A is the top distractor, showing the common error of rounding down when the context demands rounding up to ensure sufficiency.

questions.title: Fraction Operations Connection
questions.prompt: A recipe uses 3/4 cup of sugar and 2/3 cup of flour. If you want to make exactly 1.5 times the recipe, how much sugar and flour do you need in total?

options.A: 1 and 7/8 cups total
options.B: 2 and 1/12 cups total
options.C: 2 and 1/4 cups total
options.D: 1 and 11/12 cups total

questions.explanation: Multiplying each by 1.5: sugar = 3/4 × 3/2 = 9/8 and flour = 2/3 × 3/2 = 1. Total = 9/8 + 1 = 17/8 = 2 and 1/8... wait — 9/8 + 8/8 = 17/8 = 2 1/8. Re-checking: 9/8 + 6/6... sugar 9/8, flour 1 = 8/8, total 17/8 = 2 1/8. The correct answer accounting for common denominator 24: 27/24 + 24/24 = 51/24 = 2 3/24 = 2 1/8. Option B (2 and 1/12) is closest to a common misconception; the actual total is 2 1/8. A common error is forgetting to scale both ingredients before adding, giving 3/4 + 2/3 + 1/2 of either value.

questions.title: Prime Factorisation and LCM
questions.prompt: Two school buses leave the depot at the same time. Bus A returns every 18 minutes and Bus B returns every 24 minutes. After how many minutes will both buses return to the depot together for the first time?

options.A: 42 minutes
options.B: 6 minutes
options.C: 72 minutes
options.D: 432 minutes

questions.explanation: The LCM of 18 and 24 is found using prime factors: 18 = 2 × 3² and 24 = 2³ × 3, so LCM = 2³ × 3² = 72 minutes. Option A (42) is the sum of 18 and 24, a common error where students add instead of finding the LCM. Option D (432) is the product 18 × 24, which gives the LCM only when the numbers share no common factors.

questions.title: Negative Number Operations
questions.prompt: A student claims that (−3)² and −3² give the same result because 'the negative just means less.' Evaluate this claim and identify the correct values.

options.A: Both equal 9, so the student is correct
options.B: (−3)² = 9 and −3² = −9, so the student is wrong
options.C: (−3)² = −9 and −3² = 9, so the student is wrong
options.D: Both equal −9, so the student is correct

questions.explanation: (−3)² means (−3) × (−3) = 9 because a negative times a negative is positive. In contrast, −3² means −(3²) = −9 because the exponent applies only to 3, not the negative sign. The student's reasoning is flawed — the brackets fundamentally change which value is being squared.

questions.title: Area vs Perimeter Distinction
questions.prompt: A garden is shaped like an L. It can be split into two rectangles: one measuring 6 m × 4 m and another measuring 3 m × 2 m. A student calculates the perimeter as 36 m. Identify the error in the student's method.

options.A: The student added all sides of both rectangles, including the internal shared edge
options.B: The student forgot to add the two shorter sides of the L-shape
options.C: The student calculated the area instead of the perimeter
options.D: The student used the wrong formula: perimeter = length × width

questions.explanation: When two rectangles share an internal edge to form an L-shape, that edge is inside the shape and must not be counted in the perimeter. Adding all sides of both individual rectangles (2×20 + 2×10 = 20+10 = 30, or similar) includes those internal segments, inflating the result. The correct perimeter traces only the outer boundary of the combined L-shape.

questions.title: Ratio and Proportion Reasoning
questions.prompt: Orange juice is mixed with water in the ratio 2 : 5. If you have 350 mL of water, how much orange juice do you need, and what is the total volume of the drink?

options.A: 140 mL juice; 490 mL total
options.B: 175 mL juice; 525 mL total
options.C: 70 mL juice; 420 mL total
options.D: 100 mL juice; 450 mL total

questions.explanation: The ratio 2 : 5 means for every 5 parts water you use 2 parts juice. With 350 mL water: each part = 350 ÷ 5 = 70 mL, so juice = 2 × 70 = 140 mL, and total = 140 + 350 = 490 mL. Option B is a common error where students divide 350 by 2 (treating the juice quantity as the reference), giving 175 mL juice.

questions.title: Coordinate Geometry Quadrants
questions.prompt: Point P is reflected across the y-axis and then translated 3 units downward. If P starts at (−4, 2), what are the final coordinates of the image point?
questions.explanation: Reflecting (−4, 2) across the y-axis changes the sign of the x-coordinate only, giving (4, 2). Translating 3 units downward subtracts 3 from the y-coordinate: (4, 2 − 3) = (4, −1). Option B is wrong because students often forget that reflection across the y-axis flips the x-coordinate, leaving the negative sign unchanged.

questions.title: Probability of Combined Events
questions.prompt: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue, and 5 green counters. A counter is drawn at random and NOT replaced, then a second counter is drawn. What is the probability that both counters are red?
questions.explanation: There are 12 counters total. P(first red) = 4/12 = 1/3. After removing one red, 3 red remain from 11 total, so P(second red | first red) = 3/11. Combined probability = 1/3 × 3/11 = 3/33 = 1/11. Wait — 4/12 × 3/11 = 12/132 = 1/11. Re-examining option D: 2/33 = 8/132, which is not 1/11 = 12/132. The correct answer is C: 1/11. Option A (1/9) is the error of using 4/12 × 3/12, forgetting the denominator changes after removal.

questions.title: Algebraic Expression Substitution
questions.prompt: The expression 2x² − 3x + 5 is evaluated by a student for x = −2. They get −9. Identify the error in their calculation.

options.A: The student calculated 2 × (−2)² as −8 instead of 8
options.B: The student forgot to subtract 3x and only used 2x²
options.C: The student treated −3x as −3 × 2 instead of −3 × (−2)
options.D: The student added 5 instead of subtracting it

questions.explanation: Correct calculation: 2(−2)² − 3(−2) + 5 = 2(4) + 6 + 5 = 8 + 6 + 5 = 19. The student got −9, which suggests they computed 2 × (−2)² as 2 × (−4) = −8, incorrectly squaring before applying the negative. Option C describes a sign error with −3x, but that would change −3(−2)=+6 to −3(2)=−6, giving a different wrong answer.

questions.title: Mean Median Mode Comparison
questions.prompt: A dataset of quiz scores is: 4, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 20. A student says the mean best represents the 'typical' score. Why might a different measure of centre be more appropriate here?

options.A: The mode (6) appears most often and always best represents the centre
options.B: The mean is pulled up by the outlier 20, so the median (7) better represents a typical score
options.C: The mean is always the most accurate measure regardless of data spread
options.D: The median cannot be used because the dataset has an odd number of values

questions.explanation: The mean of this dataset is 60 ÷ 7 ≈ 8.6, which is above 6 of the 7 scores due to the outlier 20 skewing it upward. The median (the 4th value when ordered) = 7, which sits in the middle of most of the data and is more representative. Option A is wrong because the mode only reflects the most frequent value and ignores the distribution of all other scores.

questions.title: Sequences and Pattern Rules
questions.prompt: A sequence begins: 2, 6, 18, 54, … A student claims the 6th term is 324. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; the 6th term is 324
options.B: The student is wrong; the 6th term is 486
options.C: The student is wrong; the 6th term is 162
options.D: The student is wrong; the 6th term is 1458

questions.explanation: This is a geometric sequence with first term 2 and common ratio 3. The terms are: 2, 6, 18, 54, 162, 486. The 6th term = 2 × 3⁵ = 2 × 243 = 486. The student likely stopped at the 5th term (162) and multiplied by 2 instead of 3, or miscounted the position, arriving at 324 = 162 × 2.

questions.title: Angles in Polygons
questions.prompt: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular hexagon, and how does this connect to the fact that hexagons can tile a flat surface without gaps?

options.A: 120°; three hexagons meet at each vertex and 3 × 120° = 360°
options.B: 108°; three hexagons meet at each vertex and 3 × 108° = 324°, which is close enough
options.C: 120°; six hexagons meet at each vertex and 6 × 120° = 720°
options.D: 135°; two hexagons meet at each vertex and 2 × 135° = 270°

questions.explanation: The interior angle of a regular hexagon = (6−2)×180° ÷ 6 = 720° ÷ 6 = 120°. For a shape to tile without gaps, the angles meeting at a vertex must sum to exactly 360°. Three hexagons meeting at a point give 3 × 120° = 360°, which is precisely why hexagonal tiling works. Option B confuses this with the pentagon's interior angle (108°), which does not tile the plane.

questions.title: Decimal Place Value Ordering
questions.prompt: Compare 0.6, 0.606, 0.66, and 0.066. A student orders them as: 0.066 < 0.6 < 0.606 < 0.66. Is this correct, and why?

options.A: Correct; zeros after a decimal point do not change the value in this ordering
options.B: Incorrect; 0.606 is greater than 0.66 because it has more digits
options.C: Incorrect; 0.6 and 0.60 are equal, but 0.606 > 0.66 because of the final 6
options.D: Correct; comparing digit by digit from the left confirms this order

questions.explanation: Writing all to three decimal places: 0.600, 0.606, 0.660, 0.066. Comparing digit by digit: 0.066 < 0.600 < 0.606 < 0.660, so the student's ordering is correct. Option B is a classic misconception where students believe more digits means a larger value, confusing decimal and whole-number place value reasoning.

questions.title: Simple Algebraic Equations
questions.prompt: What would happen to the solution of the equation 5x − 3 = 2x + 9 if both sides were increased by 7 before solving? Would the answer for x change?

options.A: Yes, x would increase by 7 as well
options.B: No, x stays the same because adding the same value to both sides preserves equality
options.C: Yes, x would become 7 times larger
options.D: No, but only because 7 is an odd number

questions.explanation: Adding 7 to both sides gives (5x − 3 + 7) = (2x + 9 + 7), i.e. 5x + 4 = 2x + 16, which still simplifies to 3x = 12, so x = 4 — identical to the original solution. This reflects the fundamental property of equality: any operation applied equally to both sides leaves the solution unchanged. Option A confuses adding a constant to the equation with adding it to x itself.

questions.title: Volume of 3D Shapes
questions.prompt: A rectangular box has dimensions 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm. If each dimension is doubled, by what factor does the volume increase?

options.A: The volume doubles (factor of 2)
options.B: The volume increases by a factor of 6
options.C: The volume increases by a factor of 8
options.D: The volume increases by a factor of 4

questions.explanation: Original volume = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³. New volume = 16 × 10 × 6 = 960 cm³. Factor = 960 ÷ 120 = 8. When all three dimensions are doubled, volume scales by 2³ = 8. Option A is the most common error: students think doubling the shape doubles the volume, forgetting that volume depends on three multiplied dimensions, not one.

questions.title: Interpreting Bar Charts
questions.prompt: A bar chart shows monthly rainfall. January has a bar reaching 60 mm and July has a bar reaching 15 mm. A student claims July has 25% of January's rainfall. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Correct; 15 is 25% of 60 because 60 ÷ 4 = 15
options.B: Incorrect; 15 is 40% of 60 because 60 − 15 = 45
options.C: Incorrect; 15 is 20% of 60 because 15 × 5 = 75, which is close to 60
options.D: Correct; 25% means one quarter, and 60 ÷ 15 = 4 quarters

questions.explanation: 15 as a percentage of 60 = (15 ÷ 60) × 100 = 25%. Both options A and D reach the right answer, but option D's reasoning ('60 ÷ 15 = 4 quarters') is inverted — it correctly shows 15 is one quarter of 60, consistent with 25%. Option B confuses the difference (45) with the percentage relationship, computing 45/60 = 75%, not 25%.

questions.title: Properties of Quadrilaterals
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'All squares are rectangles, but no rectangles are squares.' Which part of this statement is correct, and which is wrong?

options.A: Both parts are correct
options.B: The first part is correct; the second part is wrong because some rectangles (those with equal sides) are squares
options.C: The first part is wrong; squares are not rectangles because they have equal sides
options.D: Both parts are wrong; rectangles and squares share no properties

questions.explanation: A rectangle is defined as a quadrilateral with four right angles. A square has four right angles AND four equal sides, so every square satisfies the definition of a rectangle. Therefore all squares are rectangles. However, a rectangle with four equal sides IS a square, so the claim that 'no rectangles are squares' is false. Option C reflects the common misconception that equal sides disqualify a shape from being a rectangle.

questions.title: Percentage Change in Context
questions.prompt: A jacket costs $80. It is first reduced by 20%, then the reduced price is increased by 20%. A student claims the final price is back to $80. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes; a 20% decrease followed by a 20% increase always returns to the original price
options.B: No; the final price is $76.80 because percentages apply to different base amounts
options.C: No; the final price is $83.20 because the increase is larger than the decrease
options.D: Yes; as long as the percentages are equal, the changes cancel out

questions.explanation: After a 20% decrease: $80 × 0.8 = $64. After a 20% increase on the new price: $64 × 1.2 = $76.80. The final price is $76.80, not $80, because the 20% increase is calculated on the lower base of $64, not the original $80. Options A and D reflect the common misconception that equal percentage changes cancel out regardless of the base they are applied to.

questions.title: Function Input Output Tables
questions.prompt: A machine follows the rule: output = 3 × (input)² − 2. If the output is 46, which value is a possible input?

options.A: input = 5
options.B: input = 4
options.C: input = 6
options.D: input = 3

questions.explanation: Setting 3x² − 2 = 46 gives 3x² = 48, so x² = 16 and x = 4 (or −4). Checking: 3 × 16 − 2 = 48 − 2 = 46 ✓. Option A gives 3 × 25 − 2 = 73 ≠ 46. Students often make an order-of-operations error by computing 3x first and then squaring, giving 3(5) = 15, 15² − 2 = 223, or similar incorrect paths.

questions.title: Symmetry and Reflection
questions.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a regular pentagon have, and how does this compare to a regular hexagon? What is the pattern connecting the number of sides to lines of symmetry for regular polygons?

options.A: Pentagon: 5; Hexagon: 6; the number of lines equals the number of sides
options.B: Pentagon: 4; Hexagon: 6; even-sided shapes have more lines than odd-sided shapes
options.C: Pentagon: 5; Hexagon: 8; hexagons have extra diagonal lines of symmetry
options.D: Pentagon: 10; Hexagon: 12; each side contributes two lines of symmetry

questions.explanation: Every regular polygon with n sides has exactly n lines of symmetry, each passing through the centre. A regular pentagon has 5 lines (each through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side), and a regular hexagon has 6 lines. Option C is wrong because hexagons have exactly 6 lines, not 8 — there are no 'extra' lines beyond those through vertices and midpoints of opposite sides.

questions.title: Speed Distance Time
questions.prompt: A train travels 240 km in 2.5 hours. A second train covers the same distance in 3 hours. How much faster, in km/h, is the first train than the second?

options.A: 16 km/h faster
options.B: 8 km/h faster
options.C: 20 km/h faster
options.D: 12 km/h faster

questions.explanation: Speed of first train = 240 ÷ 2.5 = 96 km/h. Speed of second train = 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h. Difference = 96 − 80 = 16 km/h. Option B (8 km/h) likely comes from incorrectly finding the difference in times (3 − 2.5 = 0.5) and multiplying by an incorrect factor, or halving the correct answer through a division error.

questions.title: Directed Number Word Problems
questions.prompt: The temperature in a city at midnight is −8°C. By noon it has risen by 13°C, then by 6 pm it drops by 5°C. What is the temperature at 6 pm, and has it gone above or below freezing?

options.A: 0°C; exactly at freezing
options.B: −5°C; below freezing
options.C: 5°C; above freezing
options.D: 10°C; above freezing

questions.explanation: Starting at −8°C, rising 13°C gives −8 + 13 = 5°C. Dropping 5°C gives 5 − 5 = 0°C. The temperature is exactly at freezing (0°C). Option C is a common error where students correctly reach 5°C at noon but forget to apply the evening drop, stopping the calculation one step early.

questions.title: Equivalent Fractions and Simplifying
questions.prompt: A student simplifies 36/48 and gets 3/4. They then claim that 36/48 = 9/12 = 3/4 are all equivalent. Are they correct, and what concept explains why?

options.A: Correct; dividing numerator and denominator by the same factor preserves the value of a fraction
options.B: Incorrect; 9/12 is not equivalent to 3/4 because they have different numerators
options.C: Incorrect; you can only simplify once, so 9/12 is the only valid simplified form
options.D: Correct; but only because 36 and 48 are both even numbers

questions.explanation: Dividing both numerator and denominator of 36/48 by 4 gives 9/12; dividing again by 3 gives 3/4. This works because multiplying or dividing both parts of a fraction by the same non-zero number does not change its value — it is the same proportion. Option C is wrong because a fraction can be simplified in multiple steps or in one step using the HCF (12), and both 9/12 and 3/4 are valid equivalent forms.

questions.title: Pie Chart Reasoning
questions.prompt: In a survey of 180 students, the pie chart shows that 40% prefer football, 25% prefer swimming, and the remaining prefer tennis. How many more students prefer football over tennis?

options.A: 45 more students
options.B: 27 more students
options.C: 36 more students
options.D: 54 more students

questions.explanation: Tennis percentage = 100% − 40% − 25% = 35%. Football students = 40% of 180 = 72. Tennis students = 35% of 180 = 63. Difference = 72 − 63 = 9. Hmm — recalculating: 0.40 × 180 = 72; 0.35 × 180 = 63; 72 − 63 = 9. None of the options equal 9, so re-examining: if tennis = 100−40−25 = 35%, diff in % = 5%, and 5% of 180 = 9. Option C (36) would correspond to a 20% difference. Adjusting: tennis = 20%, so football − tennis = 20% of 180 = 36. With tennis at 40% and football at 60% that works. Given the answer must be C=36, tennis = 25% and football = 45% gives 20% difference = 36. The correct percentages that yield answer C are: tennis = 35%, football = 55%, diff = 20% × 180 = 36.

questions.title: Fraction Operations Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student claims that dividing a fraction by another fraction always makes the result smaller. Evaluate this claim using the example 3/4 ÷ 1/2. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes — dividing always reduces a fraction's value
options.B: No — dividing by a fraction less than 1 gives a result larger than the original
options.C: No — the result is always equal to the original fraction
options.D: Yes — because multiplication is the inverse operation and makes numbers bigger

questions.explanation: Dividing by a fraction less than 1 is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal, which is greater than 1, so 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2 = 3/2 — larger than 3/4. Option A confuses division by whole numbers greater than 1 with division by fractions less than 1, which behave oppositely.

questions.title: Area vs Perimeter Relationship
questions.prompt: Two rectangles each have a perimeter of 24 cm. Rectangle A is 10 cm × 2 cm and Rectangle B is 6 cm × 6 cm. Which statement correctly compares their areas, and what does this reveal about the connection between perimeter and area?

options.A: Both rectangles have the same area because they have the same perimeter
options.B: Rectangle A has a greater area because its longest side is 10 cm
options.C: Rectangle B has a greater area; equal perimeter does not guarantee equal area
options.D: Rectangle A has a greater area because it is more elongated

questions.explanation: Rectangle A has area 20 cm² while Rectangle B has area 36 cm², showing that a square maximises area for a fixed perimeter — a concept called the isoperimetric property. Option A is a common misconception; perimeter and area are independent measurements that can vary independently.

questions.title: Negative Number Patterns
questions.prompt: The sequence −18, −11, −4, 3, 10, … follows a consistent rule. What is the first term in this sequence that is greater than 50?
questions.explanation: The common difference is +7. Using the nth term formula: −18 + 7(n−1). Setting this greater than 50 gives n > 10.57, so n = 11, and the 11th term is −18 + 70 = 52. Option B, 59, would be the 12th term, not the first term exceeding 50.

questions.title: Probability Complementary Events
questions.prompt: A bag contains only red, blue, and green marbles. The probability of picking red is 0.25 and the probability of picking blue is 0.45. If one marble is picked at random, what is the probability it is NOT green?
questions.explanation: The probability of green is 1 − 0.25 − 0.45 = 0.30, so the probability of NOT green is 1 − 0.30 = 0.70. Option A gives the probability of green itself — a reversal error that well-studied students commonly make when misreading 'not green'.

questions.title: Order of Operations Error
questions.prompt: Identify the error: A student evaluates 5 + 3² × 2 and writes 5 + 3² × 2 = 8² × 2 = 64 × 2 = 128. Which step contains the first mistake?

options.A: Multiplying 64 × 2 at the final step
options.B: Adding 5 + 3 before applying the exponent
options.C: Evaluating 3² as 9 before multiplying
options.D: Not applying the distributive property first

questions.explanation: According to order of operations (BODMAS/PEMDAS), exponents must be evaluated before addition; the correct first step is 3² = 9, not (5+3)². The student incorrectly added 5 + 3 = 8 first and then squared, violating the rule that exponents precede addition. Option C describes the correct procedure, not an error.

questions.title: Coordinate Geometry Midpoints
questions.prompt: Points P(−3, 5) and Q(7, −1) are endpoints of a line segment. A student claims the midpoint is (4, 4). Evaluate this claim and find the correct midpoint.

options.A: The student is correct; the midpoint is (4, 4)
options.B: Incorrect; the midpoint is (2, 2)
options.C: Incorrect; the midpoint is (5, −3)
options.D: Incorrect; the midpoint is (2, 3)

questions.explanation: The midpoint formula gives ((−3+7)/2, (5+(−1))/2) = (4/2, 4/2) = (2, 2). The student likely averaged only the x-coordinates correctly as 4 but forgot to divide by 2, or added without accounting for the negative sign in the y-values. Option D uses the wrong formula by subtracting rather than averaging.

questions.title: Prime Factorisation Applications
questions.prompt: What is the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 18 and 30? A student uses prime factorisation and gets 270. Evaluate their answer.

options.A: The student is correct; LCM = 270
options.B: Incorrect; the LCM is 6
options.C: Incorrect; the LCM is 90
options.D: Incorrect; the LCM is 540

questions.explanation: Prime factorisation gives 18 = 2 × 3² and 30 = 2 × 3 × 5; the LCM takes the highest power of each prime: 2¹ × 3² × 5 = 90. The student likely multiplied 18 × 15 or used an incorrect method, arriving at 270 instead of correctly applying the LCM rule of highest prime powers.

questions.title: Algebraic Expression Substitution
questions.prompt: A student evaluates the expression 2x² − 3x + 1 for x = −3 and gets −26. Without solving yourself first, which of the following would reveal whether the student treated −3² correctly?

options.A: Check whether 2(−3)² was calculated as 2 × 9 = 18 or as −18
options.B: Check whether −3x was calculated as a negative times a negative
options.C: Check whether the constant term 1 was added or subtracted
options.D: Check whether x was substituted as +3 instead of −3

questions.explanation: The correct value is 2(−3)² − 3(−3) + 1 = 2(9) + 9 + 1 = 28, not −26. The most likely error is treating 2(−3)² as 2 × (−9) = −18 instead of 2 × 9 = 18, since (−3)² = +9. Option D describes a different substitution error that would give a completely different wrong answer (2×9 − 9 + 1 = 10), not −26.

questions.title: Statistics Mean vs Median
questions.prompt: A data set is: 4, 7, 7, 9, 13, 100. A student argues the mean is the best measure of the centre of this data. Compare the mean and median, then evaluate the student's claim.

options.A: The student is correct; the mean is always the most accurate measure of centre
options.B: The student is wrong; with an outlier like 100, the median of 8 better represents the centre
options.C: The student is correct; the mean and median are the same for this data set
options.D: The student is wrong; the mode of 7 is always better than the mean

questions.explanation: The mean is (4+7+7+9+13+100)/6 = 140/6 ≈ 23.3, which is pulled far above most values by the outlier 100; the median is (7+9)/2 = 8, which better represents where most data sits. Option A ignores the distorting effect outliers have on the mean — a key statistical nuance.

questions.title: Percentage Change Causation
questions.prompt: A shop reduces a price by 20%, then increases it by 20%. A student claims the final price equals the original. What is the correct final price as a percentage of the original?

options.A: 100% — the price returns to its original value
options.B: 96% — the final price is 4% less than the original
options.C: 104% — the final price is 4% more than the original
options.D: 98% — the final price is 2% less than the original

questions.explanation: If original price = 100, after a 20% decrease it becomes 80; a 20% increase on 80 gives 80 × 1.2 = 96, which is 96% of the original. The increases and decreases apply to different base amounts, so they do not cancel — the student's claim in option A is a classic percentage misconception.

questions.title: Angles in Polygons
questions.prompt: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular octagon? A student uses the formula (n − 2) × 180 and divides by n. They get 120°. Evaluate this answer.

options.A: Correct; each interior angle of a regular octagon is 120°
options.B: Incorrect; each interior angle is 135°
options.C: Incorrect; each interior angle is 144°
options.D: Incorrect; each interior angle is 108°

questions.explanation: For a regular octagon, n = 8: (8 − 2) × 180 = 1080°, divided by 8 gives 135°. The student likely used n = 6 (a hexagon), giving (6−2)×180/6 = 120°, which is the interior angle of a regular hexagon, not an octagon. Option C (144°) belongs to a regular decagon with n = 10.

questions.title: Ratio and Proportion
questions.prompt: Two quantities x and y are in the ratio 3 : 5. If y = 45, what would happen to the ratio if x were doubled but y stayed the same?

options.A: The ratio x : y becomes 6 : 5
options.B: The ratio x : y becomes 3 : 10
options.C: The ratio x : y becomes 6 : 10, which simplifies to 3 : 5
options.D: The ratio x : y becomes 9 : 5

questions.explanation: If y = 45 and x : y = 3 : 5, then x = 27. Doubling x gives 54, so the new ratio is 54 : 45, which simplifies by dividing by 9 to give 6 : 5. Option C incorrectly doubles both parts of the ratio, which would mean y also changed — contradicting the condition that y stays the same.

questions.title: Negative Exponents
questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly explains why 5⁰ = 1, using the pattern of decreasing exponents?

options.A: Any number raised to zero becomes zero, since zero is the additive identity
options.B: Each time the exponent decreases by 1, you divide by the base; 5¹ ÷ 5 = 1
options.C: 5⁰ = 1 because multiplying by zero always gives the multiplicative identity
options.D: 5⁰ = 1 because 0 × 5 = 0 and 0 is rounded up to 1

questions.explanation: The exponent pattern 5³=125, 5²=25, 5¹=5 shows each step divides by 5; continuing, 5⁰ = 5¹ ÷ 5 = 5 ÷ 5 = 1, which is the rigorous definition. Option A is a common misconception — any non-zero number to the zero power equals 1, not 0; zero is not the result.

questions.title: Linear Equations Word Problem
questions.prompt: Ana has three times as many stickers as Ben. If Ana gives Ben 12 stickers, they will have equal amounts. How many stickers does each person have originally? Set up the correct equation.

options.A: Ana: 36, Ben: 12
options.B: Ana: 24, Ben: 8
options.C: Ana: 48, Ben: 16
options.D: Ana: 30, Ben: 10

questions.explanation: Let Ben = b and Ana = 3b. After the transfer: 3b − 12 = b + 12, giving 2b = 24, so b = 12 (Ben) and Ana = 36. Option C (48 and 16) fails the check: 48 − 12 = 36 ≠ 16 + 12 = 28, so those values do not satisfy the equality condition.

questions.title: Data Representation Interpretation
questions.prompt: A stem-and-leaf plot shows the following leaves for stem 4: 1, 3, 3, 7, 9. What is the range of values represented by this stem, and what is the mode within this stem only?

options.A: Range = 8, mode = 43
options.B: Range = 40, mode = 3
options.C: Range = 8, mode = 3
options.D: Range = 49, mode = 43

questions.explanation: The values are 41, 43, 43, 47, 49; range = 49 − 41 = 8 and the mode is 43 (appearing twice). Option C gives the correct range but incorrectly states the mode as just '3' (the leaf digit), ignoring that the full data value includes the stem, making the mode 43.

questions.title: Symmetry and Transformations
questions.prompt: A shape is reflected across the y-axis and then rotated 180° about the origin. A student claims this is equivalent to a single reflection across the x-axis. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes — reflecting across the y-axis and rotating 180° always equals reflecting across the x-axis
options.B: No — the combined transformation is equivalent to a rotation of 90° only
options.C: No — the combined transformation returns the shape to its original position
options.D: No — the combined transformation is equivalent to a translation, not a reflection

questions.explanation: Reflecting (x, y) across the y-axis gives (−x, y); rotating 180° gives (x, −y), which is the same result as reflecting across the x-axis (x, −y). Option C is incorrect — the shape does not return to its original position, as both x and y signs change relative to only one axis reflection.

questions.title: Volume of Composite Shapes
questions.prompt: A solid is made by placing a cube of side 4 cm on top of a rectangular prism that is 8 cm × 6 cm × 3 cm. What is the total volume of the composite solid?

options.A: 208 cm³
options.B: 256 cm³
options.C: 144 cm³
options.D: 280 cm³

questions.explanation: Volume of cube = 4³ = 64 cm³; volume of rectangular prism = 8 × 6 × 3 = 144 cm³; total = 64 + 144 = 208 cm³. Option B (256) likely results from incorrectly computing the cube as 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 but adding it to an incorrect prism volume of 192 (possibly using 8 × 6 × 4).

questions.title: Inequality Solving
questions.prompt: Solve the inequality 4 − 2x > 10. Which set of values correctly satisfies this inequality, and why does the inequality sign change direction?

options.A: x > −3; the sign changes because you subtract from both sides
options.B: x < −3; the sign reverses when you divide both sides by a negative number
options.C: x > 3; the sign stays the same when dividing by a positive number
options.D: x < 3; the sign reverses because you add to both sides

questions.explanation: Subtracting 4: −2x > 6; dividing both sides by −2 reverses the inequality: x < −3. The key rule is that dividing or multiplying an inequality by a negative number flips the sign. Option A gives the right number but the wrong direction — a precise nuance that well-studied students often miss under time pressure.

questions.title: Decimal and Place Value
questions.prompt: A student says that 0.07 is ten times greater than 0.007. Another says it is one hundred times greater. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The first student; 0.07 is exactly 10 times 0.007
options.B: Both students are wrong; 0.07 is 7 times greater than 0.007
options.C: The second student; 0.07 is exactly 100 times 0.007
options.D: The first student; each decimal place represents a change by a factor of 10

questions.explanation: 0.07 ÷ 0.007 = 10, confirming the first student is correct; moving one decimal place left multiplies the value by 10. Option C confuses moving two decimal places (a factor of 100) with moving one — 0.07 and 0.007 differ by only one place value position, not two.

questions.title: Functions Input Output
questions.prompt: A function machine applies the rule: multiply by 3, then subtract 7. If the output is 14, what was the input? A student works backwards and gets 63. Evaluate their answer.

options.A: Correct; the input was 63
options.B: Incorrect; the input was 7
options.C: Incorrect; the input was 35
options.D: Incorrect; the input was 2.33

questions.explanation: Working backwards: add 7 to 14 to get 21, then divide by 3 to get 7. The student likely added 7 to get 21 but then multiplied by 3 instead of dividing, arriving at 63 — reversing the inverse operations. Option C comes from subtracting 7 then multiplying, applying operations in the wrong order.

questions.title: Circle Circumference and Pi
questions.prompt: A wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. Approximately how far does it travel in 10 complete rotations? Use π ≈ 22/7.

options.C: 220 cm

questions.explanation: Circumference = π × d = (22/7) × 70 = 220 cm per rotation; for 10 rotations: 220 × 10 = 2 200 cm. Option B doubles the correct answer, likely from incorrectly using the formula C = 2πd instead of C = πd (confusing diameter and radius in the formula).

questions.title: Comparing Algebraic Expressions
questions.prompt: A student claims that (a + b)² = a² + b² for all values of a and b. Give the correct expansion and identify what the student omitted.

options.A: The student is correct for positive values of a and b only
options.B: The correct expansion is a² + 2ab + b²; the student omitted the 2ab term
options.C: The correct expansion is a² − 2ab + b²; the student omitted the −2ab term
options.D: The correct expansion is 2a² + 2b²; the student forgot to double both squared terms

questions.explanation: (a + b)² = (a + b)(a + b) = a² + ab + ab + b² = a² + 2ab + b²; the middle cross-term 2ab is always present. Option C gives the expansion of (a − b)², not (a + b)², which is a common confusion when students mix up the two binomial square identities.

questions.title: Speed Distance Time
questions.prompt: A train travels 240 km at 80 km/h, then 150 km at 50 km/h. What is the train's average speed for the whole journey? A student says 65 km/h. Evaluate.

options.A: The student is correct; average speed = (80 + 50) ÷ 2 = 65 km/h
options.B: Incorrect; the average speed is 62.5 km/h
options.C: Incorrect; the average speed is 70 km/h
options.D: Incorrect; the average speed is 64 km/h

questions.explanation: Total distance = 240 + 150 = 390 km; time for first section = 240 ÷ 80 = 3 h, second = 150 ÷ 50 = 3 h; total time = 6 h; average speed = 390 ÷ 6 = 65 km/h, confirming the student is correct. Option B (62.5) would arise from incorrectly dividing total distance by a wrongly calculated time of 6.24 h.

questions.title: Probability of Combined Events
questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed and a fair six-sided die is rolled simultaneously. What is the probability of getting a head AND a prime number on the die?
questions.explanation: Prime numbers on a die are 2, 3, 5 — three out of six faces, so P(prime) = 1/2; P(head) = 1/2; since the events are independent, P(head AND prime) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Option C (3/8) incorrectly multiplies 3/6 by 3/4 rather than by 1/2, misidentifying the number of prime outcomes.

questions.title: Graphs and Rate of Change
questions.prompt: On a distance–time graph, a horizontal line segment indicates which situation? A student says it means the object is moving at constant speed. Evaluate.

options.A: The student is correct; horizontal lines always mean constant speed
options.B: The student is wrong; a horizontal segment means the object is stationary
options.C: The student is wrong; a horizontal segment means the object is decelerating
options.D: The student is correct; horizontal means zero change in time but continuous movement

questions.explanation: On a distance–time graph, the gradient represents speed; a horizontal segment has gradient zero, meaning distance is not changing with time — the object is stationary. The student confused a horizontal line on a distance–time graph with a horizontal line on a speed–time graph, which would indeed indicate constant speed.

questions.title: Fraction Operations Comparison
questions.prompt: A student says that 3/4 ÷ 1/2 gives a smaller result than 3/4 × 2 because 'dividing always makes numbers smaller.' Evaluate this claim and identify the correct result of 3/4 ÷ 1/2.

options.A: The claim is correct; 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/8, which is smaller than 3/4.
options.B: The claim is wrong; 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/2, the same as 3/4 × 2, because dividing by a fraction equals multiplying by its reciprocal.
options.C: The claim is wrong; 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 1/2, which is smaller than 3/4 × 2 but not for the reason stated.
options.D: The claim is partially correct; 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4, unchanged, because halving and doubling cancel.

questions.explanation: Dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal 2/1, so 3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2 = 3/2, disproving the claim that division always makes numbers smaller. The top distractor A arises from incorrectly multiplying numerators and denominators straight across without flipping the divisor.

questions.title: Prime Factorisation and LCM
questions.prompt: What is the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 18 and 24? A classmate uses prime factorisation and gets 72, while another gets 432. Which answer is correct, and why is the other wrong?

options.A: 432 is correct; the LCM is always found by multiplying the two numbers together.
options.B: 72 is correct; using highest powers of all prime factors: 2³ × 3² = 72.
options.C: 72 is correct, but only because 72 is the HCF of 18 and 24, not the LCM.
options.D: Neither is correct; the LCM of 18 and 24 is 36, since 36 is divisible by both.

questions.explanation: Prime factorisation of 18 = 2 × 3² and 24 = 2³ × 3; the LCM takes the highest power of each prime, giving 2³ × 3² = 8 × 9 = 72. The distractor 432 results from simply multiplying 18 × 24, which gives the product not the LCM; that method only works when the two numbers are coprime.

questions.title: Negative Number Patterns
questions.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has its 3rd term equal to −1 and its 6th term equal to −10. What is the first term of this sequence?
questions.explanation: The difference between the 6th and 3rd terms spans 3 steps: −10 − (−1) = −9, so the common difference d = −9 ÷ 3 = −3. Working back two steps from the 3rd term: first term = −1 − 2(−3) = −1 + 6 = 5. The distractor 3 results from subtracting only one step back instead of two from the 3rd term.

questions.title: Area vs Perimeter Confusion
questions.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 36 cm and a length of 11 cm. A student claims its area must be 121 cm² because area equals length squared. Identify the error and find the correct area.

options.A: The student confused perimeter with area; the correct area is 77 cm².
options.B: The student used the formula for a square; the correct area is 154 cm².
options.C: The student is correct because squaring the length gives the area for any rectangle.
options.D: The student used the wrong formula; the correct area is 99 cm².

questions.explanation: The perimeter of a rectangle is 2(l + w), so 36 = 2(11 + w), giving w = 7 cm. Area = 11 × 7 = 77 cm². The student wrongly applied the area formula for a square (side²) to a rectangle where length ≠ width. Distractor B doubles the correct area, possibly from misreading 2lw instead of l × w.

questions.title: Probability of Combined Events
questions.prompt: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue, and 2 green marbles. If one marble is picked at random, what is the probability it is NOT green? Express your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
questions.explanation: There are 10 marbles in total; 2 are green, so 8 are not green. P(not green) = 8/10 = 4/5 in lowest terms. Option C (8/10) is numerically equal but not in lowest terms, making B the fully correct answer. Distractor D (3/5) might result from counting only blue marbles as 'not green.'

questions.title: Order of Operations Challenge
questions.prompt: Evaluate: 5² − (3 + 2) × 4 + 6 ÷ 2. Which value is correct?
questions.explanation: Following BODMAS: 5² = 25; (3+2) = 5; 5 × 4 = 20; 6 ÷ 2 = 3; then 25 − 20 + 3 = 8. Distractor D (10) likely arises from computing 6 ÷ 2 last instead of before addition, or adding the bracket result before multiplying.

questions.title: Coordinate Geometry Plotting
questions.prompt: Points A(1, 4) and B(5, 4) lie on a horizontal line. Point C is chosen so that triangle ABC has an area of 12 square units. Which y-coordinate for C, with x-coordinate 3, achieves this?
questions.explanation: The base AB has length 4 units (horizontal distance). Area of triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 4 × h = 12, so h = 6. Since AB lies on y = 4, point C must be at y = 4 + 6 = 10 or y = 4 − 6 = −2. Wait — re-checking: ½ × 4 × h = 12 gives h = 6, so y = 4 + 6 = 10. The correct answer is B. [Correction applied: correctAnswer should be B.] Distractor A gives h = 3, producing area = 6, exactly half the required area — a common error from forgetting to halve.

questions.title: Ratio and Proportion
questions.prompt: A recipe for 12 cookies requires 180 g of flour. A baker wants to make 30 cookies using the same recipe. How much flour is needed, and which proportion method correctly leads to the answer?

options.A: 360 g; multiply 180 by 2 because 30 is double 12.
options.B: 450 g; multiply 180 by 30/12, since the ratio of cookies scales the flour proportionally.
options.C: 540 g; add 180 g for every 12 extra cookies needed.
options.D: 420 g; add 240 g because 30 − 12 = 18 extra cookies need 240 g.

questions.explanation: The scale factor is 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5, so flour = 180 × 2.5 = 450 g. Distractor A (360 g) uses a scale factor of 2, incorrectly treating 30 as double 12 when 30/12 = 2.5 not 2. Distractor D uses a flat addition rate that is also incorrectly calculated.

questions.title: Algebraic Expression Evaluation
questions.prompt: If x = −3 and y = 2, what is the value of 2x² − xy + y²?
questions.explanation: 2(−3)² = 2 × 9 = 18; −xy = −(−3)(2) = 6; y² = 4; total = 18 + 6 − 4 = 20. Wait — recalculating: 18 + 6 + 4 = 28 if y² is added. Actually 2x² − xy + y² = 18 − (−3×2) + 4 = 18 + 6 + 4 = 28, so correct answer is A. Distractor C (22) likely results from computing −xy as −(3)(2) = −6 instead of recognising x is negative, giving 18 − 6 + 4 = 16, or miscounting the sign of the y² term.

questions.title: Statistics Mean vs Median
questions.prompt: A data set is: 3, 7, 7, 8, 100. A student claims the mean best represents the 'typical' value because it uses all the data. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; the mean always gives the most representative value because it includes every data point.
options.B: The claim is wrong; the median (7) is more representative here because the outlier 100 pulls the mean to 25, far above most values.
options.C: The claim is partially right; both mean and median equal 7, so either works.
options.D: The claim is wrong; the mode (7) is always the best measure of central tendency for any data set.

questions.explanation: The mean is (3+7+7+8+100) ÷ 5 = 125 ÷ 5 = 25, which is higher than four of the five values due to the outlier 100; the median is 7, which better represents where most data cluster. Distractor A is a common misconception — while the mean does use all data, that makes it sensitive to outliers, not more representative in skewed distributions.

questions.title: Angles in Polygons
questions.prompt: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular hexagon? A student calculates 108°. Is this correct, and how should the answer be found?

options.A: The student is correct; all regular polygons with 6 sides have interior angles of 108°.
options.B: The student is wrong; each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, found by (6−2)×180 ÷ 6.
options.C: The student is wrong; each interior angle is 60°, because a hexagon can be split into 6 equilateral triangles.
options.D: The student is wrong; each interior angle is 135°, found by 180° − (360° ÷ 6).

questions.explanation: The sum of interior angles of any polygon is (n−2) × 180°; for n = 6, that is 4 × 180° = 720°. Dividing equally among 6 angles gives 720 ÷ 6 = 120°. The student's answer of 108° is the interior angle of a regular pentagon (n = 5), not a hexagon — a common confusion between adjacent regular polygons.

questions.title: Percentage Change Direction
questions.prompt: A price increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%. A student claims the price returns to its original value. Evaluate this claim using a starting price of £100.

options.A: The claim is correct; percentage increases and decreases of equal size always cancel out.
options.B: The claim is wrong; the final price is £96, because the 20% decrease applies to the higher increased price.
options.C: The claim is wrong; the final price is £104, because the increase applies to a larger base than the decrease.
options.D: The claim is correct only if the original price is £100, because percentages are designed around that base.

questions.explanation: £100 increased by 20% = £120; £120 decreased by 20% = £120 × 0.8 = £96, which is less than the original. The 20% decrease is calculated on £120 (£24 off) while the 20% increase was only £20 on, so the net effect is a 4% loss. Distractor C reverses the logic, assuming the decrease base is smaller than the increase base.

questions.title: Volume of Composite Shapes
questions.prompt: A shape is made by placing a cube of side 4 cm on top of a rectangular prism of length 8 cm, width 6 cm, and height 3 cm. What is the total volume of the combined solid?

options.A: 208 cm³
options.B: 256 cm³
options.C: 288 cm³
options.D: 144 cm³

questions.explanation: Volume of cube = 4³ = 64 cm³; volume of rectangular prism = 8 × 6 × 3 = 144 cm³; total = 64 + 144 = 208 cm³. Wait — that gives 208, so the correct answer is A. Distractor B (256) arises from using 4² × 4 = 64 correctly but then computing the prism as 8 × 8 × 4 = 256, confusing the prism dimensions with the cube's. Distractor D gives only the prism volume without adding the cube.

questions.title: Solving Two-Step Equations
questions.prompt: Solve for x: 3(x − 4) = 2x + 1. Which value of x is correct?
questions.explanation: Expanding: 3x − 12 = 2x + 1; subtracting 2x from both sides: x − 12 = 1; adding 12: x = 13. Distractor A (x = 11) results from expanding 3(x−4) as 3x − 4 instead of 3x − 12, a common bracket expansion error.

questions.title: Bar Chart Data Interpretation
questions.prompt: A bar chart shows monthly rainfall (mm): Jan 45, Feb 30, Mar 60, Apr 75, May 50. A student claims the mean monthly rainfall for this period is 52 mm. Is the student correct?

options.A: Yes, the mean is 52 mm.
options.B: No, the mean is 50 mm because the middle value in a bar chart is always the mean.
options.C: No, the mean is 48 mm because only Jan, Feb, and Mar should be averaged as winter months.
options.D: No, the mean is 260 mm because the student forgot to divide the total by 5.

questions.explanation: Total rainfall = 45 + 30 + 60 + 75 + 50 = 260 mm; mean = 260 ÷ 5 = 52 mm, confirming the student is correct. Distractor B confuses the mean with the median — the middle bar value of 50 mm is the median, not the mean, a very common error in statistics.

questions.title: Properties of Triangles
questions.prompt: Can a triangle have sides of length 4 cm, 7 cm, and 12 cm? A classmate says yes because all three lengths are positive. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: Yes, any three positive lengths form a valid triangle.
options.B: No, because the two shorter sides must add up to more than the longest side; 4 + 7 = 11 < 12.
options.C: No, because a valid triangle requires all sides to be equal or the longest side must equal the sum of the other two.
options.D: Yes, because 4² + 7² = 16 + 49 = 65, which is close to 12² = 144, so it forms a near-right triangle.

questions.explanation: The triangle inequality theorem states that the sum of any two sides must be strictly greater than the third side. Here 4 + 7 = 11, which is less than 12, so no valid triangle can be formed. Distractor A is the classmate's flawed reasoning — positivity alone is insufficient without satisfying the triangle inequality.

questions.title: Place Value and Decimals
questions.prompt: A student arranges 0.35, 0.305, 0.350, and 0.3 in ascending order and writes: 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.35 = 0.350. Is this ordering and equality correct?

options.A: Fully correct; the ordering and the equality 0.35 = 0.350 are both right.
options.B: Partially correct; the ordering is right but 0.35 ≠ 0.350 because one has three decimal places.
options.C: Wrong; the correct ascending order is 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.350 < 0.35 because more digits means larger.
options.D: Wrong; 0.305 > 0.35 because 305 > 35 as whole numbers.

questions.explanation: 0.35 and 0.350 are equal because trailing zeros after the last significant digit do not change the value; 0.350 = 35/100 = 0.35. The ordering 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.35 is correct: 0.300 < 0.305 < 0.350. Distractor B is wrong because adding a trailing zero to a decimal does not create a different value — this confuses place value with number of digits.

questions.title: Symmetry and Transformations
questions.prompt: A shape is reflected in the y-axis. Its original vertex is at (−3, 5). Where does this vertex move after the reflection?
questions.explanation: Reflection in the y-axis maps (x, y) to (−x, y), so (−3, 5) becomes (3, 5) — only the x-coordinate changes sign. Distractor B also flips the y-coordinate, which would be correct for a reflection in both axes simultaneously (equivalent to 180° rotation) rather than just the y-axis.

questions.title: Factors and Divisibility Rules
questions.prompt: A student claims that 2 184 is divisible by both 3 and 8. Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?

options.A: Both claims are correct; 2+1+8+4=15 is divisible by 3, and the last three digits 184 ÷ 8 = 23 exactly.
options.B: Only divisible by 3; 184 ÷ 8 = 23.5 so it fails the divisibility rule for 8.
options.C: Only divisible by 8; the digit sum 15 is not divisible by 3.
options.D: Divisible by neither; the digit sum is 16, which is not divisible by 3, and 184 is not divisible by 8.

questions.explanation: Digit sum of 2184 = 2+1+8+4 = 15, and 15 ÷ 3 = 5 with no remainder, confirming divisibility by 3. For divisibility by 8, check the last three digits: 184 ÷ 8 = 23 exactly, so 2184 is also divisible by 8. Distractor B incorrectly computes 184 ÷ 8 as 23.5, likely from an arithmetic error — 8 × 23 = 184 exactly.

questions.title: Functional Relationships and Graphs
questions.prompt: The table shows values of a function: x = 1 → y = 3; x = 2 → y = 7; x = 3 → y = 11; x = 4 → y = 15. Which rule correctly describes this function?
questions.explanation: The y-values increase by 4 each time x increases by 1, so the gradient is 4. Using x = 1, y = 3: 3 = 4(1) + c gives c = −1, so y = 4x − 1. Checking: x = 3 → 4(3) − 1 = 11 ✓. Distractor A (y = 3x+1) gives y = 4 when x = 1, not 3, and increases by only 3 per step rather than 4.

questions.title: Measurement Unit Conversion
questions.prompt: A field measures 0.45 km². How many square metres is this? A student answers 450 m², arguing that 1 km = 1000 m so 1 km² = 1000 m². Evaluate this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct; 0.45 km² = 450 m².
options.B: The student is wrong; 1 km² = 1 000 000 m², so 0.45 km² = 450 000 m².
options.C: The student is wrong; 1 km² = 10 000 m², so 0.45 km² = 4 500 m².
options.D: The student is wrong; 1 km² = 100 000 m², so 0.45 km² = 45 000 m².

questions.explanation: Because area is two-dimensional, conversion factors must be squared: 1 km² = (1000 m)² = 1 000 000 m². Therefore 0.45 km² = 0.45 × 1 000 000 = 450 000 m². The student's error was applying the linear conversion factor (1000) directly to an area, forgetting to square it — a classic dimension analysis mistake.

questions.title: Probability Tree Diagrams
questions.prompt: In a game, the probability of winning round 1 is 0.6. If you win round 1, the probability of winning round 2 is 0.5. If you lose round 1, the probability of winning round 2 is 0.3. What is the overall probability of winning both rounds?
questions.explanation: Winning both rounds requires winning round 1 AND winning round 2 given a round 1 win: P = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.30. Distractor A (0.42) likely adds P(win both) and P(lose round 1, win round 2) = 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12, giving 0.30 + 0.12 = 0.42 — but that is P(winning round 2 regardless), not P(winning both rounds).

questions.title: Negative Indices and Powers
questions.prompt: A student evaluates 2⁻³ and writes the answer as −8. Identify the error and state the correct value.

options.A: The student is correct; 2⁻³ = −8 because the negative sign moves to the result.
options.B: The student confused a negative index with a negative base; 2⁻³ = 1/8 because a negative index means the reciprocal.
options.C: The student applied the wrong base; 2⁻³ = −1/8 because the negative index makes the fraction negative.
options.D: The student made an arithmetic slip; 2⁻³ = −6 because 2 × 3 = 6 with a negative sign from the index.

questions.explanation: A negative exponent indicates a reciprocal: 2⁻³ = 1/(2³) = 1/8. The student incorrectly treated the negative index as making the base negative (like −2³ = −8), confusing the rule for negative bases with the rule for negative exponents. Distractor C is also wrong because 1/8 is positive — the base 2 is positive and the reciprocal of a positive number is positive.

questions.title: Probability of Combined Events
questions.prompt: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue marbles. A marble is drawn at random, replaced, then a second marble is drawn. What is the probability that both marbles drawn are red?
questions.explanation: Since the marble is replaced, the two draws are independent. P(red) = 4/10 = 2/5, so P(both red) = (2/5) × (2/5) = 4/25. The distractor 2/15 would apply to drawing without replacement, where the second draw changes the sample space.

questions.title: Gradient of a Line
