questions.prompt: You walk into the kitchen and find an empty biscuit tin, crumbs on the table, and your little brother's shoes by the door. Using abductive reasoning, what is the most justified conclusion?

options.A: Your little brother definitely ate all the biscuits.
options.B: Your little brother most likely ate the biscuits, as this is the simplest explanation fitting all the clues.
options.C: Someone broke into the house and ate the biscuits.
options.D: The tin was empty before anyone came home.

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the most plausible explanation that accounts for all the available evidence — shoes, crumbs, and an empty tin all point to the brother being present and eating. Crucially, abductive reasoning gives us the best guess, not certainty, so saying he 'definitely' ate them (option A) overclaims what the evidence supports.

questions.title: Argument Strength Comparison
questions.prompt: Two students argue about whether screen time harms sleep. Carlos says: 'I always sleep fine after watching TV.' Dana says: 'Dozens of studies involving thousands of children show blue light delays sleep.' Whose argument is stronger, and why?

options.A: Carlos, because personal experience is the most reliable form of evidence.
options.B: Dana, because evidence from many studies across large groups is more reliable than one person's experience.
options.C: Both are equally strong because each person is speaking from their own knowledge.
options.D: Carlos, because he is talking about his own body, which he knows better than any study.

questions.explanation: Scientific studies using large samples reduce the influence of individual differences and chance, making them far more reliable than a single anecdote. Carlos may genuinely sleep well, but his experience cannot rule out effects in other people — this is why researchers study thousands of participants. Personal experience is valuable but extremely limited in what it can prove about a general rule.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Logic
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If the light is on, someone is home. Premise 2: Nobody is home. What can be logically concluded?

options.A: Someone must have just left the house.
options.B: The light is not on.
options.C: The light might or might not be on — we cannot tell.
options.D: Someone is home but hiding.

questions.explanation: This is the logical pattern called modus tollens: if 'P implies Q' is true and Q is false, then P must also be false. Since 'light on → someone home' and nobody is home (not-Q), the light cannot be on (not-P). Option C is tempting but wrong — the logical structure does allow a definite conclusion here.

questions.title: Circular Reasoning Error
questions.prompt: A student says: 'This book must be interesting because interesting books are the kind I enjoy, and I enjoy this book.' Identify the logical error in this statement.

options.A: Hasty generalisation — she has only read one book.
options.B: Ad hominem — she is making the argument about herself rather than the book.
options.C: Circular reasoning — she is using the conclusion to prove the premise that proves the conclusion.
options.D: Straw man — she is misrepresenting what makes a book interesting.

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning (also called begging the question) happens when the conclusion is secretly hidden inside the premise — here, 'interesting books are ones I enjoy' and 'I enjoy this book' together just mean 'this book is interesting,' which is exactly what she is trying to prove. Option A describes a different error about drawing broad conclusions from too few examples.

questions.title: Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge thinking, a young student says: 'I know the stove is hot because I touched it once and got burned.' Which 'way of knowing' is the student mainly using?

options.A: Language, because they described the event in words.
options.B: Sense perception, because they used direct physical experience to gain knowledge.
options.C: Reason, because they used logic to decide the stove is hot.
options.D: Memory, because they are recalling a past event.

questions.explanation: In IB Theory of Knowledge, sense perception means gaining knowledge through the senses — touch, sight, smell, taste, or hearing. The student touched the stove and felt heat, making sense perception the primary source. Memory (option D) is involved in recalling the event, but the original knowledge came through touch, not through the act of remembering.

questions.title: Identifying Hidden Assumptions
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'We should not change the school lunch menu because the current menu has been the same for ten years.' What hidden assumption is the student making?

options.A: Students always prefer familiar food to new food.
options.B: If something has existed for a long time, it must be good or correct.
options.C: Changing menus is always more expensive than keeping them the same.
options.D: The school does not have enough money to buy new ingredients.

questions.explanation: The argument appeals to tradition — assuming that something is right or good simply because it has been around for a long time, which is a logical fallacy. Ten years of use does not logically prove the current menu is the best option; it could have been poor for all ten years. Option A is a plausible assumption but is not the one driving the logical structure of this particular argument.

questions.title: Sorting Fact from Opinion
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is a fact rather than an opinion?

options.A: Autumn is the most beautiful season of the year.
options.B: Dogs make better pets than cats.
options.C: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
options.D: Reading is more important than playing sport.

questions.explanation: A fact is a statement that can be tested and verified objectively — water's boiling point at sea level is 100°C and can be measured by anyone anywhere. The other options express preferences or value judgements that different people can reasonably disagree about, making them opinions rather than facts.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Evaluation
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If our school allows one free dress day, soon we will have no uniform at all, and then nobody will respect the school.' Evaluate this reasoning.

options.A: The reasoning is strong because small changes always lead to larger ones.
options.B: The reasoning uses a slippery slope fallacy by assuming each step will automatically lead to the next without evidence.
options.C: The reasoning is a false dilemma because it only considers two options.
options.D: The reasoning is an ad hominem because it attacks the idea of school pride.

questions.explanation: A slippery slope argument claims that one small step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences, but it provides no evidence that each step in the chain will actually occur — many schools have occasional free dress days without abandoning uniforms entirely. Option C (false dilemma) describes a different error where only two options are offered, which is not the structure of this argument.

questions.title: Sampling in Research
questions.prompt: A student surveys five of her close friends to find out whether all 400 students in her school prefer art or music. She concludes that art is more popular school-wide. What is the main flaw in her research?

options.A: She should have asked teachers instead of students.
options.B: Her sample is too small and not representative, so her conclusion cannot apply to the whole school.
options.C: She gave students only two choices, which is never acceptable in research.
options.D: Art and music are too similar to compare in a survey.

questions.explanation: A reliable survey needs a sample that is large enough and representative of the whole group — five close friends are likely to share similar tastes and cannot speak for 400 diverse students. This is called a sampling bias, and it makes the conclusion unreliable. Option A is incorrect because student opinions on student preferences are exactly the right source; teachers are not the relevant population.

questions.title: Logical Negation
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some cats are black.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: Some cats are not black.
options.B: All cats are black.
options.C: No cats are black.
options.D: Most cats are not black.

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'some X are Y' is 'no X are Y' — to make 'some cats are black' false, there must be zero black cats, not just fewer. Option A is tempting because it sounds like an opposite, but 'some cats are not black' can be true at the same time as 'some cats are black,' so it is not a true negation.

questions.title: Appeal to Popularity
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Everyone in my class thinks this movie is the best ever made, so it must be.' Identify the logical error.

options.A: Circular reasoning, because the student is using the class's opinion to prove the class's opinion.
options.B: Appeal to popularity, because the number of people who believe something does not make it true.
options.C: Hasty generalisation, because one class cannot represent all moviegoers.
options.D: Straw man, because the student is exaggerating the class's actual opinion.

questions.explanation: An appeal to popularity (also called 'ad populum') is the error of thinking that if many people believe something, it must be correct — history shows that majorities have held false beliefs many times. Option C (hasty generalisation) is close but describes drawing a broad conclusion from too few examples, whereas the error here is specifically about treating popularity as proof of quality.

questions.title: Evaluating Evidence Quality
questions.prompt: A student is researching whether exercise improves mood. Which source of evidence would give the strongest support for a conclusion?

options.A: A diary entry from one person who felt happier after jogging.
options.B: An advertisement from a gym claiming exercise makes people happier.
options.C: A study that tracked the moods of 500 children over six months, comparing those who exercised regularly with those who did not.
options.D: A social media post by a sports celebrity saying exercise changed their life.

questions.explanation: A controlled study with a large sample, a comparison group, and a long time period provides far stronger evidence because it reduces the effect of chance, personal bias, and individual differences. The advertisement (option B) comes from a source with a financial interest in the outcome, which makes it less trustworthy even if it cites some evidence.

questions.title: Anchoring Bias in Decisions
questions.prompt: A shop marks a toy as 'Was £40, now £25!' A child immediately thinks £25 is a great deal. Which cognitive bias is influencing the child's thinking?

options.A: Confirmation bias, because the child only notices information that supports buying the toy.
options.B: Sunk-cost bias, because the child feels committed to buying something they have already looked at.
options.C: Anchoring bias, because the original price of £40 is being used as a reference point that makes £25 seem cheap.
options.D: Availability bias, because the child can easily imagine owning the toy.

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias occurs when the first number we see (the 'anchor') shapes how we judge a later number — the child does not know whether £25 is a fair price without the £40 anchor, but the anchor makes it feel like a bargain. Confirmation bias (option A) involves selectively noticing supporting information, which is a different process from being influenced by an initial number.

questions.title: Spotting Hidden Assumptions
questions.prompt: A student says: 'My older sister studied hard and got into a great school, so if I study hard, I will too.' Which hidden assumption makes this argument weak?

options.A: That studying hard is the only reason her sister succeeded, ignoring other factors
options.B: That her sister actually studied hard at all
options.C: That great schools are better than average schools
options.D: That the student is as intelligent as her sister

questions.explanation: The argument assumes studying hard alone caused the sister's success, ignoring factors like tutoring, luck, or connections — this is the hidden assumption that undermines the reasoning. Option D is tempting because intelligence seems relevant, but the core flaw is treating one cause as the only cause, not comparing ability levels.

questions.title: Valid Syllogism Testing
questions.prompt: Premise 1: All mammals are warm-blooded. Premise 2: Whales are mammals. A student concludes: 'Therefore, whales are warm-blooded.' Is this argument valid, and is it sound?

options.A: Valid but not sound, because whales live in water so the conclusion is false
options.B: Both valid and sound, because the conclusion follows from true premises
options.C: Neither valid nor sound, because mammals cannot always be trusted as a category
options.D: Sound but not valid, because the conclusion is true even though the logic is flawed

questions.explanation: A valid argument means the conclusion follows logically from the premises; a sound argument is valid AND has true premises. Both premises here are scientifically true, and whales really are warm-blooded, so the argument is both valid and sound. Option A is wrong because living in water does not affect warm-bloodedness — whales genuinely are warm-blooded mammals.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Overlap
questions.prompt: In a group of 20 children, 12 like painting and 10 like dancing. If the Venn diagram shows exactly 4 children in the overlapping section, how many children like neither painting nor dancing?
questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: children who like at least one activity = 12 + 10 − 4 = 18. So 20 − 18 = 2 children like neither. Option A is a common error made by students who subtract the overlap from the total without first combining both sets correctly.

questions.title: Inductive Pattern Limits
questions.prompt: Every morning for a year, the sun has risen at roughly the same time. A student concludes: 'The sun will definitely rise tomorrow at the same time.' What is the strongest criticism of this reasoning?

options.A: One year is too short a sample to notice any pattern at all
options.B: Inductive conclusions are never certain because past patterns cannot guarantee future events
options.C: The student should have used deductive reasoning instead to be sure
options.D: Sunrise times actually vary too much to form a reliable pattern

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning builds probable conclusions from observed patterns, but it can never provide logical certainty — this is called the 'problem of induction,' noted by philosopher David Hume. Option C is wrong because even deductive reasoning about sunrise would still require premises about physical laws, which themselves rest on inductive observations.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias Explained
questions.prompt: Priya believes that eating breakfast makes you smarter. She notices every time a classmate does well on a test, asks if they ate breakfast, and records 'yes' answers carefully — but ignores classmates who skipped breakfast and also did well. Which error in thinking is Priya making?

options.A: Overgeneralisation from a single case
options.B: Confirmation bias — only collecting evidence that supports her existing belief
options.C: The post hoc fallacy — assuming breakfast caused the good score
options.D: Circular reasoning — using her belief to design her research

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias occurs when a person seeks out or pays attention only to evidence that confirms what they already believe, while ignoring contradictory evidence. Priya is systematically ignoring breakfast-skippers who succeed. Option C (post hoc) is plausible but describes a different error — assuming causation from sequence — which is not the main flaw Priya is showing here.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Is being at least 7 years old a necessary condition, a sufficient condition, or neither for being in Year 2 at most IB PYP schools?

options.A: Both necessary and sufficient, because Year 2 students are always exactly 7
options.B: Sufficient but not necessary, because turning 7 automatically places you in Year 2
options.C: Neither necessary nor sufficient, because age alone does not determine year group placement
options.D: Necessary but not sufficient, because you must be old enough but age alone does not guarantee Year 2 placement

questions.explanation: A necessary condition must be present for the outcome, but does not alone cause it. Being old enough is required for Year 2, but placement also depends on enrolment, assessment, and other factors, so age alone is not sufficient. Option C is tempting but incorrect — age is genuinely required (necessary), just not enough on its own.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogies
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Practising maths is just like exercising muscles — the more you do it, the stronger you get.' Evaluate this analogy. What is its most significant weakness?

options.A: Muscles can be injured by over-exercise, but maths practice cannot harm the brain in the same way
options.B: Maths is a subject, not a skill, so the comparison does not apply at all
options.C: The analogy is fully accurate and has no significant weakness
options.D: Muscles grow automatically with rest, while maths understanding requires conscious reflection, not just repetition

questions.explanation: The analogy breaks down because muscles strengthen through physical stress and recovery even without thinking, whereas maths understanding requires active sense-making — rote repetition without understanding produces little deep learning. Option A is plausible and partially true, but it addresses a side detail rather than the core difference between physical and cognitive development.

questions.title: Deductive Modus Tollens
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If the classroom light is on, the teacher is inside. Premise 2: The teacher is not inside. What must be true, using only these two premises?

options.A: The classroom light is off
options.B: The classroom light might be on or off — we cannot be sure
options.C: The teacher left the light on by accident
options.D: Another adult is in the classroom instead

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. If the light being on guarantees the teacher is inside, and the teacher is not inside, then the light cannot be on. Option B is a common mistake — students think uncertainty exists, but the logical form removes it entirely given the stated premises.

questions.title: False Dichotomy Identification
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Either you are good at art or you are good at science — you cannot be good at both.' Which logical error does this statement contain?

options.A: Circular reasoning, because the student is using one claim to prove the same claim
options.B: A false dichotomy, because it presents only two options when more are possible
options.C: Hasty generalisation, because the student has not surveyed enough people
options.D: Ad hominem, because the student is attacking people's abilities rather than evidence

questions.explanation: A false dichotomy (or false dilemma) forces a choice between two options as if no other possibilities exist. Many people are talented in both art and science — Leonardo da Vinci is a famous historical example. Option C is tempting because the claim does feel like a generalisation, but the specific logical structure here is the either/or constraint, which defines a false dichotomy.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Fairness
questions.prompt: Two students test whether salt makes water boil faster. Student A uses a large pot with 2 litres of water and adds salt. Student B uses a small cup with 200 ml of water and no salt. They compare boiling times. Why is this experiment unfair?

options.A: Salt always makes water boil faster, so the result is already known
options.B: Multiple variables are changed at once — both the amount of water and the presence of salt differ
options.C: The experiment should use a thermometer rather than timing the boil
options.D: Student B's cup is too small to produce reliable bubbles for observation

questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one variable at a time — here, both the volume of water and the salt are different, so any difference in boiling time cannot be attributed to salt alone. This violates the principle of controlling variables. Option D sounds practical and reasonable, which makes it a good distractor, but it misses the fundamental flaw in experimental design.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Choice
questions.prompt: You find your friend's umbrella inside the school entrance, still dripping with water, on a day the forecast predicted sunshine. Using abductive reasoning, which conclusion is most justified?

options.A: Your friend deliberately spilled water on the umbrella as a prank
options.B: It rained unexpectedly and your friend used the umbrella to stay dry
options.C: Your friend borrowed someone else's wet umbrella by mistake
options.D: The umbrella was stored wet from a previous rainy day and brought in today

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the simplest and most likely explanation for the available evidence. A dripping umbrella at the entrance on a day it rained unexpectedly most simply explains all the clues together. Option D is plausible but requires an additional assumption (that the umbrella was stored wet), making it a less economical explanation than unexpected rain.

questions.title: Counterexample Disproving Rules
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'All prime numbers are odd.' Which single counterexample is enough to disprove this claim?

options.A: The number 9, which is odd but not prime
options.B: The number 2, which is prime but even
options.C: The number 1, which is neither prime nor composite
options.D: The number 15, which is odd and not prime

questions.explanation: The number 2 is the only even prime number, making it a perfect counterexample that disproves the claim that all primes are odd. Options A and D describe numbers that are odd and not prime, which actually do not challenge the claim — they show the reverse relationship, not a counterexample to what was stated.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Trap
questions.prompt: A student sees the pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and says the rule is 'add the next odd number each time.' Another student says the rule is 'square the position number.' Are these two rules the same or different?

options.A: Different, because squaring always gives bigger numbers faster than adding odd numbers
options.B: The same for this sequence, because both rules produce identical outputs for every term
options.C: Different, because one rule works forwards and the other works backwards
options.D: The same only for the first three terms, then they start to diverge

questions.explanation: Both rules describe perfect square numbers and produce exactly the same sequence indefinitely: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36… This is because each perfect square equals the previous square plus the next odd number (e.g., 9 = 4 + 5; 16 = 9 + 7). Option D is wrong — the rules never diverge; they are mathematically equivalent for all whole-number positions.

questions.title: Evaluating Source Credibility
questions.prompt: A student researching whether screen time harms sleep finds two sources: a five-year study published in a science journal, and a blog post by a well-known YouTuber who agrees with the same conclusion. Which source should be weighted more heavily, and why?

options.A: The blog post, because it is written in simpler language and easier to understand
options.B: Both equally, because they reach the same conclusion so they support each other
options.C: The journal study, because it used systematic evidence gathered over time and reviewed by experts
options.D: The blog post, because the YouTuber has personal experience with screens every day

questions.explanation: Peer-reviewed journal studies carry more evidential weight because they use controlled methods, large samples, and expert review to reduce error and bias. Option B is a tempting error — agreement between sources does not make a weak source stronger; the blog post's reliability does not increase just because its conclusion matches the study.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: Juno says: 'We should eat less meat to help the environment.' Kai responds: 'Juno wants everyone to become vegetarian and never eat any animal products ever again — that is impossible!' Which logical error has Kai made?

options.A: Ad hominem — attacking Juno personally rather than the argument
options.B: False dichotomy — suggesting only two extreme choices exist
options.C: Straw man — misrepresenting Juno's position to make it easier to attack
options.D: Circular reasoning — Kai is using Juno's own words against her

questions.explanation: The straw man fallacy occurs when someone distorts or exaggerates an opponent's argument to make it easier to knock down. Juno said 'less meat,' but Kai responded to a fabricated extreme version. Option B is plausible because Kai does imply an extreme, but the defining feature here is the misrepresentation of Juno's original claim, which is the straw man.

questions.title: Counterfactual Cause and Effect
questions.prompt: Imagine that paper had never been invented. Which chain of counterfactual effects would most logically follow?

options.A: Writing would not exist, because writing was invented alongside paper
options.B: Books, written laws, and widespread literacy would have developed much more slowly or differently
options.C: Mathematics would not exist, because numbers need to be written down to be understood
options.D: Schools would not exist at all, because teaching requires paper-based materials

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning traces the most plausible consequences of a changed historical condition. Writing pre-dates paper (clay tablets and papyrus were used first), so Option A is factually wrong. Without paper, the mass production of books and written laws would have been far harder, slowing literacy — but alternatives like clay, bark, or stone might still exist, so schools and mathematics would not simply vanish.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: A student discovers that cities with more hospitals have more people who die in them. She concludes that hospitals cause death. Evaluate this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is correct — being in a hospital does increase the chance of catching other illnesses
options.B: The conclusion is flawed — larger cities have more hospitals AND more people, so more deaths happen there regardless
options.C: The conclusion is flawed — death rates at hospitals are actually tracked and corrected by governments
options.D: The conclusion is correct — the data clearly shows that where hospitals go up, death numbers rise

questions.explanation: This is a classic correlation-does-not-imply-causation error. Bigger cities have both more hospitals and larger populations, so more deaths occur simply due to population size — hospitals are not causing the deaths. Option A introduces a real phenomenon (hospital-acquired infections) but does not address the core logical error in the student's reasoning, which is confusing correlation with causation.

questions.title: Argument Strength Comparison
questions.prompt: Two students debate screen-free Sundays at school. Cara says: 'I feel less stressed when I don't look at a screen.' Dayo says: 'A study of 500 students across ten schools found lower stress levels on screen-free days.' Whose argument provides stronger evidence?

options.A: Cara's, because personal experience is more honest and direct than numbers
options.B: Both are equally strong, because feelings and data each tell a different kind of truth
options.C: Dayo's, because the study covers many students and schools, reducing the chance that one person's experience is the whole picture
options.D: Cara's, because she has actually lived the experience, while the study may contain errors

questions.explanation: Dayo's study has a large, diverse sample across many schools, which controls for individual differences and makes the finding more generalisable — a core principle of research methodology. Cara's personal experience is anecdotal: it may be true for her but cannot be assumed to apply to everyone. Option B sounds balanced but is incorrect, because in formal reasoning, systematic evidence outweighs personal testimony.

questions.title: Logical Negation Practice
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some cats have orange fur.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: All cats have orange fur
options.B: Some cats do not have orange fur
options.C: No cats have orange fur
options.D: Most cats do not have orange fur

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'Some X are Y' (at least one) is 'No X are Y' (zero). If it is false that even one cat has orange fur, then no cats have orange fur. Option B is a very common error — 'some cats do not have orange fur' does not contradict the original statement; both could be true at the same time.

questions.title: Sunk Cost Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student has spent three weeks building a model that is not going well. She says: 'I have to keep going — I've already put so much time into it!' Which error in thinking does this show?

options.A: Anchoring bias — she is stuck on the original plan and cannot adjust
options.B: Sunk cost fallacy — letting past effort influence a decision that should be based on future outcomes
options.C: Overconfidence bias — she believes she can fix the model despite evidence against it
options.D: Availability heuristic — she is overestimating how much time she spent because it feels recent

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when someone continues a failing course of action because of resources already invested, rather than evaluating future costs and benefits freshly. Time already spent cannot be recovered, so it should not drive future decisions. Option A (anchoring) is plausible — she is stuck on her original plan — but anchoring specifically refers to over-relying on the first piece of information received, not to past effort.

questions.title: Ways of Knowing Comparison
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge terms, a student uses reason to work out that 2 + 2 = 4, and then uses perception to see that two apples plus two apples make four apples. Which statement best describes the relationship between these two ways of knowing?

options.A: They are the same way of knowing described with different words
options.B: Reason is weaker than perception because mathematics is abstract and cannot be touched
options.C: They are complementary — reason works with abstract rules while perception provides concrete evidence from the world
options.D: Perception is unreliable, so it cannot support or confirm conclusions made by reason

questions.explanation: IB Theory of Knowledge treats reason and perception as distinct and complementary ways of knowing: reason operates on abstract logical principles, while perception provides sensory evidence from the real world. Together they can reinforce each other. Option D overstates perception's unreliability — while perception can be deceived, it remains a valid and important source of knowledge that science depends upon.

questions.title: Appeal to Authority Error
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'My football coach says vaccines cause illness, so vaccines must be dangerous.' Evaluate this argument. What is the main logical problem?

options.A: The student should not trust any adult's opinion on any topic
options.B: The coach may be an expert in football but has no special expertise in medicine, so their claim lacks authority in this area
options.C: The student is committing ad hominem by using the coach's identity as proof
options.D: The argument would be valid if the coach were also a nurse or doctor

questions.explanation: An appeal to authority is only valid when the authority cited has genuine expertise in the relevant field. A football coach has no medical training, so their opinion on vaccines carries no more evidential weight than any non-expert's. Option D is a tempting partial truth — expertise does matter — but accepting a claim solely based on any authority figure, without evidence, remains a logical problem even when the authority is more relevant.

questions.title: If–Then Converse Error
questions.prompt: The rule is: 'If an animal is a dog, then it is a mammal.' A student concludes: 'This animal is a mammal, therefore it must be a dog.' What error has the student made?

options.A: Denying the antecedent — the student is incorrectly using the negative form of the rule
options.B: Affirming the consequent — the student treats a result as if it proves its cause
options.C: False dichotomy — the student assumes there are only two kinds of mammals
options.D: Circular reasoning — the student uses 'mammal' to prove 'dog' and 'dog' to prove 'mammal'

questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent is a formal logical fallacy: just because being a dog guarantees being a mammal does not mean every mammal is a dog — cats, whales, and horses are all mammals too. Option A (denying the antecedent) is a similarly structured formal fallacy but involves negating the 'if' part, not incorrectly reversing the 'then' conclusion as this student did.

questions.title: Sampling Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student surveys 50 children at her school to find out whether children worldwide prefer reading or playing video games. She finds 70% prefer reading. Why might this result not represent children worldwide?

options.A: 50 students is too small a sample to count as data at all
options.B: The sample is taken from one school in one location, which may not reflect the diversity of children worldwide
options.C: Children's answers about preferences cannot be trusted because they change their minds often
options.D: The question is biased because it only gives two choices

questions.explanation: Sampling bias occurs when the group studied does not represent the wider population. One school's students share a location, culture, language, and likely socioeconomic background — none of which reflects the variety of children globally. Option D raises a fair point about question design, but it is not the main reason the result fails to represent worldwide preferences — the sampling problem is more fundamental.

questions.title: Logical Equivalence Testing
questions.prompt: Statement: 'If you do not practise, you will not improve.' Which of the following statements is logically equivalent — meaning it expresses exactly the same relationship?

options.A: If you improve, then you must have practised
options.B: If you practise, you will improve
options.C: You can improve without practising
options.D: Practising always guarantees improvement

questions.explanation: The original statement 'If not P, then not Q' is logically equivalent to its contrapositive: 'If Q, then P' — meaning 'If you improve, you must have practised.' These two statements always have the same truth value. Option B is the converse of the original, which is a common confusion — the converse of a true conditional is not necessarily true.

questions.title: Syllogism Validity Check
questions.prompt: Read these two premises carefully: 'All mammals breathe air. Dolphins breathe air.' A student concludes: 'Therefore, dolphins are mammals.' Is this conclusion logically valid?

options.A: Yes, because both premises are true and dolphins really are mammals.
options.B: No, because the conclusion is false — dolphins are fish.
options.C: No, because breathing air does not only apply to mammals, so the logic has a gap.
options.D: Yes, because if the conclusion happens to be true, the argument must be valid.

questions.explanation: A syllogism is only valid if the conclusion must follow from the premises — here, 'breathes air' is shared by non-mammals too (e.g., birds, reptiles), so the logic does not force the conclusion even though dolphins are indeed mammals. Option A confuses a true conclusion with a valid argument — an argument can reach a true conclusion by faulty reasoning, which does not make the reasoning valid.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Overlap
questions.prompt: In a group of 24 children, 15 like painting, 13 like coding, and 4 like neither. How many children like both painting and coding?
questions.explanation: Children who like at least one activity = 24 − 4 = 20. Using the inclusion-exclusion rule: both = 15 + 13 − 20 = 8. Option A (6) is a common error made by subtracting 4 from the overlap calculation instead of from the total, mixing up where the 'neither' group belongs in the formula.

questions.title: Inductive vs. Deductive
questions.prompt: A student notices that every time she waters her plant in the morning, it looks healthier by evening. She concludes: 'Morning watering always makes plants healthier.' Which type of reasoning is she using, and what is its biggest risk?

options.A: Deductive reasoning; the risk is that one of her premises could be false.
options.B: Inductive reasoning; the risk is that future observations might not match past ones.
options.C: Abductive reasoning; the risk is that a simpler explanation might exist.
options.D: Inductive reasoning; the risk is that she used too many observations to be reliable.

questions.explanation: Moving from specific observations to a general rule is inductive reasoning, and its key weakness is that even many confirming cases cannot guarantee the rule will always hold — one counter-example can disprove it. Option D is wrong because using more observations actually strengthens inductive arguments rather than weakening them.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias Spotting
questions.prompt: Priya believes that eating breakfast makes students smarter. She surveys her classmates and only writes down the scores of children who ate breakfast that morning. Which cognitive bias is Priya showing?

options.A: Anchoring bias, because she fixed her belief before gathering data.
options.B: Confirmation bias, because she only collects evidence that could support her belief.
options.C: Availability bias, because she uses the most recent scores she can remember.
options.D: Sunk-cost bias, because she has already spent time on the survey.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, record, or favour information that supports a pre-existing belief — Priya ignores the non-breakfast group entirely, which is a textbook example. Anchoring bias (Option A) refers to over-relying on the first piece of information encountered, not to selectively collecting data.

questions.title: Necessary vs. Sufficient
questions.prompt: A student says: 'Being over 18 is sufficient to vote in most countries, but it is not the only condition — you usually need to be a registered citizen too.' Which statement about these conditions is most logically precise?

options.A: Being over 18 is both necessary and sufficient on its own to guarantee the right to vote.
options.B: Being over 18 is necessary but not sufficient, because citizenship is also required.
options.C: Being over 18 is sufficient but not necessary, because some countries allow younger voters.
options.D: Being over 18 is neither necessary nor sufficient because laws change between countries.

questions.explanation: A condition is necessary if you must have it, and sufficient if having it alone guarantees the outcome. Since citizenship is also required, being over 18 alone does not guarantee the right to vote — making it necessary (you need it) but not sufficient (it is not enough on its own). Option C misuses 'sufficient': the existence of exceptions in other countries does not change whether the condition alone guarantees voting rights within a given system.

questions.title: False Analogy Evaluation
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training a dog is exactly like teaching a younger sibling — if you reward good behaviour consistently, both will learn.' Evaluate the strength of this analogy. What is its most important weakness?

options.A: The analogy is strong because reward systems work identically in all learning situations.
options.B: The analogy is weak because dogs and children live in different places.
options.C: The analogy is weak because children use language and abstract reasoning in ways dogs cannot, so the learning processes differ importantly.
options.D: The analogy is strong because both dogs and children can be stubborn.

questions.explanation: Analogies break down when the compared things differ in a way that matters for the claim — children's capacity for language, self-reflection, and complex motivation means their learning process differs fundamentally from a dog's conditioned responses, undermining the 'exactly like' claim. Option A is wrong because reward systems, while present in both cases, operate through very different cognitive mechanisms.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Reasoning
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a shape is a square, then it has four equal sides. Premise 2: This shape does NOT have four equal sides. What must be true?

options.A: This shape is not a square.
options.B: This shape might still be a square with unequal sides.
options.C: This shape could be a rectangle because rectangles have four sides.
options.D: We cannot conclude anything without knowing what shape it is.

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: 'If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.' Since having four equal sides is a necessary property of a square, and this shape lacks it, the shape cannot be a square. Option D is incorrect because the logical form of modus tollens gives a definite conclusion regardless of knowing the shape's name — we do not need extra information.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Sam says recycling programmes save money for cities. Jake replies: 'Why should we listen to Sam? He forgot his homework twice this week.' Which logical error has Jake made?

options.A: Straw man, because Jake is distorting Sam's argument.
options.B: Ad hominem, because Jake attacks Sam's character instead of the argument.
options.C: False dichotomy, because Jake is presenting only two choices.
options.D: Appeal to authority, because Jake is dismissing Sam's expertise.

questions.explanation: Ad hominem means attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself — Jake's comment about homework is irrelevant to whether recycling saves cities money. Straw man (Option A) would require Jake to misrepresent Sam's claim, which he does not do here; he simply ignores it.

questions.title: Pattern Rule Testing
questions.prompt: A student sees the pattern: 3, 6, 12, 24 and says the rule is 'double each time.' Another student says the rule is 'add the previous term.' Are both students correct, and why?

options.A: Both are correct because doubling a number and adding the same number to itself give the same result.
options.B: Only the first student is correct because 'add the previous term' would give 3, 6, 9, 12.
options.C: Only the second student is correct because addition is simpler than multiplication.
options.D: Neither is correct because the pattern could also be explained by cubing each position number.

questions.explanation: Doubling a number (×2) and adding the number to itself (n + n) are mathematically identical operations, so both descriptions produce the same sequence and are equivalent rules. Option B misunderstands 'add the previous term' — the second student means add each term to itself, not add consecutive different terms, so it does produce 3, 6, 12, 24.

questions.title: Hypothesis Falsifiability
questions.prompt: A student's hypothesis is: 'Invisible fairies help plants grow, but they hide whenever anyone looks.' A teacher says this hypothesis is not scientific. What is the best reason why?

options.A: Because fairies have never been observed, so the hypothesis must be false.
options.B: Because the hypothesis cannot be tested or proven wrong by any possible observation.
options.C: Because plants are known to grow due to sunlight and water, leaving no room for other causes.
options.D: Because a good hypothesis must be simple, and this one uses too many ideas.

questions.explanation: A scientific hypothesis must be falsifiable — there must be some observation that could prove it wrong. Since the fairies are defined as hiding when observed, no experiment could ever disprove the claim, making it non-scientific. Option C is wrong because discovering one cause of plant growth does not logically rule out the existence of other contributing factors.

questions.title: Counterfactual Cause and Effect
questions.prompt: A student says: 'If our school had never started a reading programme, fewer students would enjoy books today.' Which type of thinking does this statement use, and what does it assume?

options.A: Deductive thinking; it assumes the premises are logically guaranteed.
options.B: Counterfactual thinking; it assumes the programme was the main cause of students enjoying reading.
options.C: Inductive thinking; it assumes past reading habits predict future ones.
options.D: Abductive thinking; it assumes the simplest explanation is always the best.

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning imagines an alternative past ('if X had not happened') to understand causation — here, the student pictures a world without the programme to claim it caused the love of reading. The key assumption is that no other factor (home libraries, family habits, teachers) would have produced the same outcome, which may not be true.

questions.title: Evaluating Competing Evidence
questions.prompt: Two students research whether screen time affects sleep. Mia finds a study of 500 children showing less sleep with more screens. Leo finds one study of 20 children showing no effect. Who has the stronger evidence, and what is the key reason?

options.A: Leo, because his study found no effect, which is harder to achieve.
options.B: Mia, because her study used a much larger sample, making the findings more reliable.
options.C: Leo, because a recent small study is more up to date than a large old one.
options.D: Both are equally strong because each study was conducted by researchers.

questions.explanation: Sample size is a key factor in research reliability — a study of 500 children is far less likely to be distorted by individual differences than a study of 20, making Mia's evidence stronger. Option D is wrong because being conducted by researchers does not make studies equal; methodology and sample size matter greatly.

questions.title: Appeal to Popularity Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Everyone in my class uses this brand of calculator, so it must be the best one for maths.' Identify the logical problem with this argument.

options.A: The student is using a straw man because she ignores other calculators.
options.B: The student is using an appeal to popularity, because how many people use something does not prove it is the best.
options.C: The student is using circular reasoning because 'best' and 'most used' mean the same thing.
options.D: The student is using an appeal to authority because classmates are treated as experts.

questions.explanation: Appeal to popularity (also called argumentum ad populum) is the error of thinking that widespread use proves quality or truth — popularity reflects habit, price, or availability, not necessarily excellence. Option D would require the classmates to be cited as expert authorities, which is not what the argument does; it cites their sheer number.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In a TOK discussion, a student says: 'Sense perception is the most reliable way of knowing because we can always trust what we see.' Which response provides the strongest challenge to this claim?

options.A: Sense perception is reliable, so the student is correct and no challenge is needed.
options.B: Optical illusions and optical tricks show that what we see can be systematically wrong, so perception can mislead us.
options.C: Reasoning is a better way of knowing, so sense perception should be replaced entirely.
options.D: We should trust memory more than perception because memory combines many past experiences.

questions.explanation: Optical illusions — such as lines appearing different lengths when they are equal — demonstrate that the visual system can produce consistent errors, showing that sense perception is not automatically reliable. Option C sets up a false choice; challenging perception does not require replacing it entirely, and reasoning also has its own limitations.

questions.title: Circular Reasoning Detection
questions.prompt: A student writes: 'We know this rule is fair because fair rules are always like this one.' Identify the logical error in her reasoning.

options.A: False dichotomy, because she only considers two types of rules.
options.B: Circular reasoning, because the conclusion is used as part of the evidence for itself.
options.C: Hasty generalisation, because she assumes all rules of this type are fair.
options.D: Appeal to tradition, because she implies that existing rules must be followed.

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning (begging the question) occurs when the conclusion is smuggled into the premises — 'the rule is fair because fair rules are like this' simply restates 'fair' without providing independent evidence for it. A hasty generalisation (Option C) would involve jumping from a few cases to a broad rule, which is not the structure of this argument.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Best Explanation
questions.prompt: You come home and find the back door open, muddy paw prints on the floor, and your dog looking guilty in the corner. Using abductive reasoning, what is the most justified conclusion?

options.A: A stranger entered through the back door and walked through mud.
options.B: The dog went outside through the open door, walked in mud, and came back in.
options.C: The door was left open by the wind and the paw prints were there from yesterday.
options.D: Another pet from a neighbour's house entered and left the prints.

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the explanation that best fits all available evidence with the fewest assumptions — the dog being present and 'looking guilty,' combined with paw prints and an open door, makes the dog's own muddy trip outside the simplest and most coherent account. Option A requires assuming an additional agent (a stranger) with no supporting evidence.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Evaluation
questions.prompt: A teacher argues: 'If we allow students to redo one test, soon they will want to redo every test, then every assignment, and eventually no grade will mean anything.' Evaluate whether this is a sound argument.

options.A: It is sound, because each step in the chain is likely and the conclusion follows.
options.B: It is unsound, because the chain of consequences is exaggerated and each step is not shown to be inevitable.
options.C: It is sound, because teachers have experience and their predictions are usually correct.
options.D: It is unsound, because redoing tests is always a good idea and the teacher is simply wrong.

questions.explanation: A slippery slope argument is only valid if each step in the chain is shown to follow necessarily — here, allowing one retest does not logically or inevitably lead to all grades becoming meaningless, so the argument exaggerates without proof of each link. Option A is wrong because asserting that each step is 'likely' is not the same as demonstrating it, and likeliness alone does not make a chain argument sound.

questions.title: Controlled Variable Identification
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether adding fertiliser makes tomato plants grow taller. She uses two plants: one gets fertiliser and one does not. She keeps them in the same room, same pot size, and same amount of water. Which variable is the one she is deliberately changing?

options.A: The height of the plants, because that is what she measures.
options.B: The room temperature, because both plants share the same room.
options.C: The amount of fertiliser, because one plant receives it and the other does not.
options.D: The amount of water, because water affects plant growth too.

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes — in this case, whether fertiliser is given, making it the variable being tested. Plant height (Option A) is the dependent variable — what is being measured as a result — not what is being changed.

questions.title: Logical Negation Precision
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some students always finish their homework on time.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: All students always finish their homework on time.
options.B: No students ever finish their homework on time.
options.C: No students always finish their homework on time.
options.D: Some students never finish their homework on time.

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'Some X are Y' is 'No X are Y' — to disprove that at least one student always finishes on time, you must show that zero students do so. Option B ('No students ever finish') is too strong — it negates both 'some' and 'always' simultaneously, going further than a precise logical negation requires.

questions.title: Correlation vs. Causation
questions.prompt: A student notices that on days when more ice cream is sold in her town, more people go to the hospital. She concludes: 'Ice cream causes illness.' What is the most likely error in her reasoning?

options.A: She has used too small a sample to notice any pattern at all.
options.B: She is confusing correlation with causation — a third factor like hot weather may cause both.
options.C: She is using circular reasoning because her conclusion repeats her observation.
options.D: She is committing the appeal to authority fallacy by relying on hospital data.

questions.explanation: When two things rise together, a third variable (confounding variable) may explain both — hot weather increases ice cream sales and also causes heat-related illness and accidents, explaining the correlation without any causal link between ice cream and hospitalisation. Circular reasoning (Option C) would require the conclusion to be built into the premises, which is not the case here.

questions.title: Argument Structure Mapping
questions.prompt: Claim: 'We should plant more trees in our city.' Evidence given: 'Trees reduce air pollution, provide shade, and improve mental wellbeing.' A student adds: 'Also, my neighbour likes trees.' Which piece of evidence is weakest, and why?

options.A: Trees reduce air pollution, because not all cities have pollution problems.
options.B: Trees provide shade, because shade is only useful in summer.
options.C: Trees improve mental wellbeing, because this is hard to measure scientifically.
options.D: The neighbour likes trees, because one person's preference gives no reason for a city-wide policy.

questions.explanation: An argument for a city-wide policy must be supported by evidence relevant to many people or the city as a whole — one neighbour's preference affects only that individual and gives no reason for others to support the policy. Option C is weaker than it might seem because mental wellbeing research on nature is well-established, even if complex to measure.

questions.title: Deductive Argument Soundness
questions.prompt: Premise 1: All living things need energy. Premise 2: Rocks do not need energy. A student concludes: 'Therefore, rocks are not living things.' Is this argument valid AND sound?

options.A: Valid but not sound, because Premise 1 is false — some living things do not need energy.
options.B: Valid and sound, because the logic works and both premises are true.
options.C: Not valid and not sound, because the conclusion does not follow from the premises.
options.D: Sound but not valid, because the conclusion is true even if the logic has a gap.

questions.explanation: An argument is valid if the conclusion must follow from the premises, and sound if it is valid AND the premises are true — here both conditions are met. Premise 1 (living things need energy) and Premise 2 (rocks do not need energy) are accepted scientific facts, and the conclusion follows correctly by modus tollens. Option A incorrectly claims Premise 1 is false; all known living organisms require energy for metabolic processes.

questions.title: Availability Bias Recognition
questions.prompt: After watching several news stories about plane crashes, Tomás decides never to fly and tells his family planes are extremely dangerous. What cognitive bias is most influencing Tomás, and what information is he ignoring?

options.A: Anchoring bias; he is ignoring the first safety report he ever read.
options.B: Availability bias; he is ignoring statistics showing flying is statistically safer than many other forms of travel.
options.C: Confirmation bias; he is only watching news programmes that show crashes.
options.D: Sunk-cost bias; he is ignoring the money he has already spent on flights.

questions.explanation: Availability bias causes people to judge how common or dangerous something is based on how easily dramatic examples come to mind — plane crashes are heavily reported and therefore feel frequent, even though flying has a very low accident rate per journey compared with car travel. Confirmation bias (Option C) would require Tomás to be actively seeking out only crash stories, but the question says he is responding to stories he has seen, not filtering for them.

questions.title: Identifying Hidden Assumptions
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Children who read more score higher on tests, so schools should assign more reading homework.' What hidden assumption does this argument make that could be challenged?

options.A: That tests are the only way to measure learning.
options.B: That assigning reading as homework will cause children to read more, rather than just causing stress.
options.C: That all children currently read the same amount.
options.D: That schools are responsible for improving test scores.

questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation (reading more → higher scores) to a policy (assign reading homework), but assumes the policy will actually produce more reading — children may ignore or rush assigned reading differently from self-chosen reading, breaking the assumed link. Option A is a valid concern but is not the assumption hidden in this specific argument, which focuses on reading and scores rather than whether tests are a good measure.

questions.title: Epistemology: Belief vs. Knowledge
questions.prompt: In TOK, there is a difference between believing something and knowing it. A student says: 'I believe the sun will rise tomorrow, and since I'm very confident, I know it.' What key ingredient of knowledge is the student overlooking?

options.A: Confidence, because knowledge requires feeling less certain than belief does.
options.B: Justification, because knowledge traditionally requires a good reason or evidence — not just strong confidence.
options.C: Memory, because the student has not experienced enough sunrises to count as knowing.
options.D: Agreement, because something counts as knowledge only when a whole community accepts it.

questions.explanation: The classical definition of knowledge (from philosophy/TOK) is 'justified true belief' — confidence alone is not enough; you must have good reasons or evidence supporting the belief. The student confuses the strength of a feeling with the quality of justification. Option D describes social constructivism, which is one view of knowledge but not the standard condition the student is missing in this argument.

questions.title: Deductive Reasoning Basics
questions.prompt: Premise 1: All mammals are warm-blooded. Premise 2: A whale is a mammal. What must be true according to deductive reasoning?

options.A: Whales are probably warm-blooded, but exceptions may exist
options.B: Whales are warm-blooded
options.C: All warm-blooded animals are mammals
options.D: Whales are mammals because they are warm-blooded

questions.explanation: In a valid deductive syllogism, if both premises are true, the conclusion must be true with certainty — whales are definitely warm-blooded. Option A is wrong because deductive conclusions are certain, not probabilistic, when premises are accepted as true.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: A student notices that towns with more libraries also tend to have lower crime rates. She concludes that libraries cause crime to fall. What is the most significant problem with her conclusion?

options.A: Her sample size might be too small to draw any pattern at all
options.B: Correlation between two variables does not prove that one causes the other
options.C: Libraries are not relevant to crime in any way
options.D: She should have used a survey rather than observational data

questions.explanation: Correlation shows that two things change together but cannot by itself establish that one causes the other — a third factor, such as overall wealth of a town, could explain both. Option A is plausible but is not the most significant logical flaw identified here; the core error is confusing correlation with causation.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Logic
questions.prompt: In a group of 20 students, 12 like art, 10 like music, and 5 like both. How many students like neither art nor music?
questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: students who like art or music = 12 + 10 − 5 = 17, so students who like neither = 20 − 17 = 3. Option D is wrong because it incorrectly subtracts only the overlap from 20 without adding both sets first.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Basics
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether drinking water before a test improves scores. She gives water to her friends and checks their scores, but does not compare them to a group that did not drink water. What essential element is missing from her experiment?

options.A: A large enough sample of different test subjects
options.B: A control group that did not receive the treatment
options.C: A written hypothesis stating her prediction
options.D: Permission from the school to run the experiment

questions.explanation: Without a control group — participants who do not drink water — there is nothing to compare the results against, making it impossible to determine whether water made any difference. A written hypothesis (Option C) is good practice but is not what makes a comparison possible.

questions.title: Identifying Assumptions
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'My older brother studied medicine, so I should study medicine too — it clearly runs in the family.' What hidden assumption is this argument making?

options.A: Medicine is the most prestigious career available
options.B: Career choices are determined mainly by family background, not individual interest
options.C: Her brother chose medicine for financial reasons
options.D: Studying medicine is too difficult for most people

questions.explanation: The argument assumes that because one family member chose a career, the same career is automatically right for another — treating family pattern as a determining factor rather than personal choice or ability. Option A is an opinion not embedded in the argument's logic.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: Every morning for a year, the school bell rings at exactly 8:30 a.m. A student concludes it will ring at 8:30 a.m. forever. Which statement best identifies the weakness of this inductive conclusion?

options.A: One year is not enough observations to see any pattern at all
options.B: Past observations cannot guarantee future outcomes with certainty
options.C: The student should have used deductive reasoning instead
options.D: The bell schedule is set by the government, not the school

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning builds probable conclusions from repeated observations, but no number of past cases can guarantee the future will be identical — the bell schedule could change. Option C is wrong because deductive reasoning also requires reliable premises and cannot replace observation-based prediction here.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Priya argues that the school should switch to renewable energy. Tomás responds: 'Why should anyone listen to Priya? She failed her science test last week.' Which logical error has Tomás made?

options.A: False dilemma — presenting only two choices
options.B: Ad hominem — attacking the person rather than the argument
options.C: Circular reasoning — using the conclusion as evidence
options.D: Hasty generalisation — drawing a conclusion from too few cases

questions.explanation: An ad hominem fallacy attacks the character or personal qualities of the person making an argument instead of addressing the argument's actual content — Priya's test score is irrelevant to whether renewable energy is a good idea. A false dilemma (Option A) would involve presenting only two options where more exist.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Is having electricity a necessary condition, a sufficient condition, or both for a lamp to produce light? Choose the most precise answer.

options.A: Both necessary and sufficient — electricity is all a lamp ever needs
options.B: Sufficient only — electricity guarantees the lamp will light up
options.C: Necessary but not sufficient — electricity is required but a working bulb and connection are also needed
options.D: Neither — a lamp can produce light through chemical reactions alone

questions.explanation: Electricity is necessary because without it the lamp cannot work, but it is not sufficient on its own — the bulb must also be functional and correctly connected. Option A is wrong because electricity alone does not guarantee light if the bulb is broken.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias
questions.prompt: A student believes that eating breakfast makes you smarter. When doing research, she only reads articles that agree with her view and ignores studies that show no effect. Which cognitive bias is she demonstrating?

options.A: Anchoring bias — relying too heavily on the first piece of information
options.B: Availability heuristic — judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
options.C: Confirmation bias — seeking only evidence that supports an existing belief
options.D: Sunk cost fallacy — continuing because of past investment

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias occurs when a person actively searches for, favours, or remembers information that confirms their pre-existing belief while dismissing contradicting evidence. The anchoring bias (Option A) refers specifically to over-relying on the first piece of data encountered, which is not what is described here.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition in Sequences
questions.prompt: A student examines the sequence: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. She claims the rule is 'add 3 each time.' Evaluate her claim and identify the correct rule.

options.A: She is correct; the rule is to add 3 each time
options.B: She is wrong; the rule is to multiply each term by 2
options.C: She is wrong; the rule is to add the previous two terms together
options.D: She is partially correct; the rule alternates between adding and multiplying

questions.explanation: Each term is double the previous one: 3×2=6, 6×2=12, 12×2=24, 24×2=48 — this is a geometric sequence with a common ratio of 2. Adding 3 each time (Option A) would give 3, 6, 9, 12 — which does not match the sequence after the second term.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian writes: 'If the printing press had never been invented, the spread of scientific ideas during the Renaissance would have been much slower.' What type of reasoning is the historian using?

options.A: Inductive reasoning — building a general rule from many historical examples
options.B: Counterfactual reasoning — imagining an alternative past to understand causation
options.C: Deductive reasoning — applying a known law to reach a certain conclusion
options.D: Abductive reasoning — finding the simplest explanation for observed evidence

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning explores what would have happened if a key condition had been different, helping us understand the causal role of that condition — here, the printing press's role in spreading ideas. Abductive reasoning (Option D) is about inferring the best explanation for existing evidence, not imagining alternative histories.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogies
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training for a marathon is just like studying for an exam — both require consistent daily practice.' What is the most significant weakness of this analogy?

options.A: Marathon training is physically dangerous, making the comparison unfair
options.B: The analogy ignores important differences, such as physical vs. cognitive effort and how progress is measured
options.C: Not everyone can run a marathon, so the analogy excludes some students
options.D: Studying does not require daily practice — weekly revision is equally effective

questions.explanation: Analogies are weakened when the two things being compared differ in ways relevant to the conclusion — marathon training builds physical endurance measured in race times, while exam study builds knowledge measured differently. Option A is a distractor that focuses on safety rather than the logical structure of the analogy.

questions.title: Modus Ponens Logic
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a shape has four equal sides and four right angles, then it is a square. Premise 2: Shape X has four equal sides and four right angles. What must be true?

options.A: Shape X is probably a square, but could be a rectangle
options.B: Shape X is a rhombus
options.C: Shape X is a square
options.D: All squares have four equal sides and four right angles

questions.explanation: This is modus ponens: if 'P then Q' and P is true, then Q must be true — Shape X meets both conditions exactly, so it is definitively a square. Option A is wrong because the premises fully satisfy the definition given, leaving no room for uncertainty.

questions.title: Hasty Generalisation
questions.prompt: After surveying five students in her class, Sofia concludes: 'All students at this school prefer science to humanities.' Which logical error has Sofia made?

options.A: False dilemma — she has assumed students can only prefer one subject
options.B: Ad hominem — she has dismissed students who disagree
options.C: Hasty generalisation — she has drawn a broad conclusion from too small a sample
options.D: Circular reasoning — she used her conclusion to justify her survey method

questions.explanation: A hasty generalisation occurs when a conclusion about a large group is drawn from an unrepresentatively small or non-random sample — five students cannot represent the whole school. Option A (false dilemma) would apply if Sofia had presented only two rigid choices, which is not the main error here.

questions.title: Ways of Knowing: Perception
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, two students look at the same optical illusion and disagree about what they see. A student argues this proves that perception is a completely unreliable way of knowing. Which response best challenges this claim?

options.A: Optical illusions are designed to deceive, so they are not fair tests of perception
options.B: Perception can be unreliable in some cases yet still be a valuable source of knowledge in many everyday situations
options.C: Students should rely on technology rather than human perception for all observations
options.D: Perception is the most reliable way of knowing because it is direct and immediate

questions.explanation: In TOK, saying a way of knowing is sometimes unreliable does not mean it is completely unreliable — perception provides enormous amounts of valid knowledge in daily life and science. Option D overcorrects by claiming perception is the most reliable, which is also an extreme and unsupported position.

questions.title: Variable Control in Experiments
questions.prompt: Two students test whether salt water or plain water makes pasta cook faster. Student A uses the same pot, same stove, and same amount of water for both trials. Student B uses different pots on different days. Whose method is more reliable, and why?

options.A: Student B, because testing on different days removes the risk of carry-over effects
options.B: Student A, because keeping all other variables constant means differences in cooking time are more likely due to the salt
options.C: Student B, because using different pots gives a more varied and realistic result
options.D: Both methods are equally reliable because they both test the same question

questions.explanation: Fair testing requires controlling all variables except the one being tested (the independent variable); Student A's method ensures that any difference in cooking time can be attributed to the salt. Student B's different pots and days introduce multiple confounding variables, making conclusions unreliable.

questions.title: Logical Negation
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some students in the class enjoy reading.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: All students in the class enjoy reading
options.B: Most students in the class do not enjoy reading
options.C: No students in the class enjoy reading
options.D: Some students in the class do not enjoy reading

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'Some X are Y' is 'No X are Y' — denying that even one instance exists. Option D ('Some students do not enjoy reading') could be true at the same time as the original statement, so it is not a true logical negation.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student comes home to find the front door unlocked, muddy footprints leading to the kitchen, and a note on the table saying 'Took your lunch — sorry!' Using abductive reasoning, what is the most justified conclusion?

options.A: A burglar entered the house but only stole the lunch
options.B: A known person — likely a family member or friend — entered and took the lunch
options.C: The student's lunch was taken by an animal that can write notes
options.D: The student forgot to lock the door and the note was already there from the day before

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the simplest and most plausible explanation fitting all available evidence — a note written in human language suggests a person who knows the student, making a known acquaintance the best explanation. Option A is possible but less justified because a burglar would typically take more than just food.

questions.title: Evaluating Evidence Quality
questions.prompt: A student researching climate change finds two sources: (1) a peer-reviewed journal article written by 30 climate scientists, and (2) a blog post by an anonymous writer. Which source should she trust more, and what is the most important reason?

options.A: The blog post, because it is written in simpler language she can understand
options.B: The journal article, because it has been checked by other experts and the authors are accountable
options.C: The journal article, because scientific sources are always more up-to-date than blogs
options.D: Both equally, because all sources have potential bias regardless of their origin

questions.explanation: Peer review means that independent experts have evaluated the methodology and conclusions before publication, and named authors are professionally accountable for their claims — both increase reliability. Option C is wrong because scientific journals are not always more current than online sources; peer review, not timing, is the key advantage.

questions.title: False Cause Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student notices that every time she wears her lucky pencil case, she does well on tests. She concludes the pencil case causes good performance. Identify the most precise name for this logical error.

options.A: Hasty generalisation — drawing a wide conclusion from limited evidence
options.B: False cause (post hoc) fallacy — assuming that because one event follows another, the first caused the second
options.C: Anchoring bias — relying too heavily on her first test result
options.D: Ad hominem — dismissing evidence that contradicts her belief

questions.explanation: The post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this') fallacy occurs when a person assumes that because B followed A, A must have caused B — the pencil case did not cause the results, though the two occurred together. Hasty generalisation (Option A) refers to sample size problems, not mistaking sequence for causation.

questions.title: Perspective and Bias in Sources
questions.prompt: A student reads two newspaper articles about a new sports stadium: one from a paper owned by the stadium's construction company, and one from an independent local paper. Why is it important to consider who owns a source when evaluating information?

options.A: Owners always instruct journalists to write false information
options.B: Ownership can create financial or political interests that influence how information is selected and presented
options.C: Independent papers are always more accurate than company-owned papers
options.D: The owner's name tells you how recently the article was written

questions.explanation: A source's owner may have financial or ideological interests that shape which facts are included, emphasised, or omitted — this is known as perspective or bias in TOK and media literacy. Option A overstates the case; ownership creates potential bias, not automatic falsehood.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If our school allows students to use phones during lunch, soon everyone will be on their phones in every lesson, and no one will ever learn anything again.' Evaluate whether this is a sound argument.

options.A: It is sound because phone use in schools is a proven cause of falling grades
options.B: It is unsound because it assumes a chain of increasingly extreme consequences without evidence for each step
options.C: It is sound because each step in the chain follows logically from the one before
options.D: It is unsound because it contains an ad hominem attack on phone users

questions.explanation: This is a slippery slope fallacy — it jumps from a modest policy change (lunch-time phone use) to extreme consequences (complete academic failure) without providing evidence that each step in the chain must follow. Option C is wrong because the steps are not logically guaranteed; each would require separate justification.

questions.title: Argument Structure: Premises and Conclusions
questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the role of a premise in a logical argument?
