options.A: A premise is the final statement that the argument is trying to prove
options.B: A premise is a statement offered as evidence or a reason to support the conclusion
options.C: A premise is an example used to make an argument more interesting
options.D: A premise is a question that the argument is designed to answer

questions.explanation: In formal logic, premises are the foundational statements whose truth is used to support and lead to the conclusion — they supply the reasoning. Option A describes the conclusion, not the premise, which is a common confusion.

questions.title: Evaluating a Scientific Claim
questions.prompt: A company claims: 'Nine out of ten dentists recommend our toothpaste.' A student wants to evaluate this claim critically. Which question is MOST important for her to ask?

options.A: What country are the dentists from?
options.B: How many dentists were surveyed, how were they selected, and were they paid by the company?
options.C: What flavour is the toothpaste?
options.D: Did the dentists also recommend a rival toothpaste at the same time?

questions.explanation: Evaluating statistical claims requires knowing the sample size, sampling method, and any conflicts of interest — a survey of only ten dentists chosen by the company is far less reliable than an independent survey of thousands. Option D is worth asking but is less fundamental than the issues of sample quality and independence.

questions.title: Thinking About Thinking: Metacognition
questions.prompt: After receiving a low mark on an essay, a student spends time identifying exactly which parts of her reasoning were weak before starting the next draft. Which ATL thinking skill is she most clearly demonstrating?

options.A: Creative thinking — generating new ideas for the essay
options.B: Reflection and metacognition — thinking critically about her own thought processes
options.C: Information literacy — finding better sources for evidence
options.D: Transfer — applying skills from one subject to another

questions.explanation: Metacognition means thinking about one's own thinking — analysing where reasoning went wrong is a core reflective and metacognitive skill in the IB ATL framework. Creative thinking (Option A) involves generating ideas, which is not the primary focus of reviewing and diagnosing reasoning errors.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Basics
questions.prompt: Premise 1: All mammals are warm-blooded. Premise 2: A dolphin is a mammal. What must be true according to deductive reasoning?

options.A: Dolphins are the only warm-blooded sea animals
options.B: A dolphin is warm-blooded
options.C: All warm-blooded animals are mammals
options.D: Dolphins evolved from land mammals

questions.explanation: Deductive reasoning moves from general rules to specific conclusions: if all mammals are warm-blooded and a dolphin is a mammal, the dolphin must be warm-blooded — this follows with certainty. Option A is wrong because the premises say nothing about other sea animals being warm-blooded or not.

questions.title: Correlation vs. Causation
questions.prompt: A student notices that towns with more hospitals have more deaths per year. She concludes that hospitals cause deaths. What is the main flaw in her reasoning?

options.A: She has not drawn a Venn diagram to show the relationship
options.B: Her sample of towns is too small to draw any conclusion
options.C: She is confusing correlation with causation — larger towns have both more hospitals and more people who may die
options.D: She should have used inductive rather than deductive reasoning

questions.explanation: Correlation means two things change together; causation means one thing directly produces another. Larger populations naturally have more hospitals AND more deaths, so a third factor (population size) explains both — hospitals do not cause the deaths. Option B is tempting but misses the point: even with many towns, the logical error of assuming causation from correlation would remain.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Steps
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether cold water boils faster than warm water. Before starting her experiment, what must she clearly identify?

options.A: The colour of the pots used in the experiment
options.B: A testable hypothesis, independent variable, and controlled variables
options.C: The conclusion she expects to publish after the experiment
options.D: Whether other students agree with her prediction

questions.explanation: A valid experiment requires a testable hypothesis (a specific, falsifiable prediction), an independent variable (starting water temperature), and controlled variables (same pot, volume, heat source) so the test is fair. Option C describes stating a conclusion before testing, which is the opposite of the scientific method — conclusions come after evidence is collected.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias
questions.prompt: Maya believes that students who sit at the front of class always get better grades. She only pays attention to front-row students who do well and ignores those who do poorly. Which cognitive bias is Maya showing?

options.A: Anchoring bias
options.B: Availability bias
options.C: Confirmation bias
options.D: Sunk cost bias

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, notice, and remember only information that supports an existing belief while ignoring contradictory evidence — exactly what Maya is doing. Anchoring bias refers to over-relying on the first piece of information encountered, which is not what this scenario describes.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: Every morning for a year, the school bell rings at 8:30 am. A student concludes it will ring at 8:30 am tomorrow. Why is this inductive conclusion not guaranteed to be true?

options.A: Inductive reasoning only works with numbers, not events
options.B: Past observations can support but never guarantee future outcomes
options.C: The student should have used a Venn diagram to check the pattern
options.D: One year of data is always too small a sample

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning draws probable conclusions from repeated observations, but probability is not certainty — the bell could be broken, school cancelled, or the schedule changed. Option D is tempting but wrong: the issue is not sample size alone; even millions of observations cannot logically guarantee the next instance in inductive reasoning.

questions.title: Necessary vs. Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Is having electricity a necessary condition, a sufficient condition, or neither for a lamp to produce light? Choose the most precise answer.

options.A: It is sufficient but not necessary, because battery lamps also exist
options.B: It is both necessary and sufficient for a lamp to produce light
options.C: It is necessary but not sufficient, because the bulb must also be working
options.D: It is neither necessary nor sufficient on its own

questions.explanation: Electricity is necessary for most standard lamps — without it they cannot light up — but it is not sufficient on its own because the bulb, switch, and wiring must also function correctly. Option A incorrectly treats battery power as electricity-free; batteries are a form of electrical energy, so electricity remains necessary even in battery-powered lamps.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Priya argues that the school should have a longer lunch break. Her classmate responds, 'We shouldn't listen to Priya — she's always late to class.' Identify the logical error in this response.

options.A: False dilemma — only two options are presented
options.B: Ad hominem — attacking the person rather than the argument
options.C: Circular reasoning — the conclusion repeats the premise
options.D: Slippery slope — assuming extreme future consequences

questions.explanation: Ad hominem is a fallacy where someone attacks the character or personal behaviour of the speaker instead of addressing their argument — Priya's punctuality has no logical bearing on whether a longer lunch break is a good idea. A false dilemma (Option A) would require two extreme choices being falsely presented as the only options, which is not what happens here.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning
questions.prompt: You walk into the kitchen and see muddy footprints, an open window, and the dog looking guilty. Using abductive reasoning, what is the most justified conclusion?

options.A: A stranger broke in through the window and left the footprints
options.B: The dog came in through the window and made the muddy footprints
options.C: Someone left the window open accidentally and the rain blew mud inside
options.D: The footprints were already there before the window was opened

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the simplest and most likely explanation that fits all the available evidence — the dog, the open window, and the muddy footprints all connect most simply as the dog entering through the window. Option A is possible but introduces a new, less probable actor (a stranger) when the dog already accounts for all the evidence.

questions.title: Modus Ponens Logic
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a shape has three sides, it is a triangle. Premise 2: This shape has three sides. What must follow according to the rule of modus ponens?

options.A: This shape might be a triangle if all its angles are equal
options.B: All triangles have three sides
options.C: This shape is a triangle
options.D: The shape is a triangle only if it has equal sides

questions.explanation: Modus ponens is the valid argument form: 'If P then Q; P is true; therefore Q is true.' Since the shape has three sides (P), and three sides means triangle (Q), we can conclude with certainty it is a triangle. Option D wrongly adds the condition of equal sides, which is not in either premise.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogies
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training for a sport is just like studying for an exam — both require repetition and discipline, so the same practice schedule should work for both.' What is the most significant weakness in this analogy?

options.A: Sport training never requires discipline, so the comparison is completely false
options.B: The analogy ignores key differences: sport training is physical while exam study is cognitive, requiring different recovery and methods
options.C: The student has not defined what 'repetition' means in each context
options.D: Analogies can never be used to support arguments about learning

questions.explanation: A good analogy must share the relevant features; while both involve practice and discipline, physical training fatigues muscles and requires rest in different ways than cognitive study, so the same schedule would not necessarily transfer. Option C is a minor weakness about definition clarity, not the most significant flaw in the overall reasoning.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Rules
questions.prompt: A student sees the sequence: 3, 6, 12, 24, __. She claims the rule is 'add 3 more each time.' A second student says the rule is 'multiply by 2 each time.' Which student is correct, and why?

options.A: The first student, because adding 3 produces consistent differences
options.B: Both students are correct since the terms match either rule equally well
options.C: The second student, because multiplying by 2 produces each term from the previous one
options.D: Neither student, because the sequence follows a Fibonacci pattern

questions.explanation: Multiplying by 2 correctly generates every term: 3×2=6, 6×2=12, 12×2=24, so the next is 48. The first student's 'add 3 more each time' rule would give 3, 6, 9, 12 — not this sequence — because the differences between terms are 3, 6, 12, not constant. Option B is wrong because only one rule correctly produces all the given terms.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student asks: 'If penicillin had never been discovered, what would most likely have happened to the death rate from bacterial infections in the 20th century?' Which answer best uses counterfactual reasoning?

options.A: Death rates would have remained exactly the same because other medicines exist
options.B: Death rates from bacterial infections would likely have remained much higher, since penicillin was the first widely available antibiotic treatment
options.C: Bacteria would have evolved to be harmless without the pressure of antibiotics
options.D: Scientists would have invented something identical within a few years anyway

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning asks what would have changed if a key event had not occurred. Penicillin, discovered in 1928, was the first effective antibiotic and dramatically reduced deaths from previously fatal infections like pneumonia and sepsis; without it, those death rates would have stayed high. Option D assumes a near-inevitable replacement, but counterfactual reasoning requires us to change only the named condition, not assume identical substitutes.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: Eva proposes that the school library should open 30 minutes earlier. Her classmate responds: 'Eva wants students to spend all day in the library instead of having lessons — that's a terrible idea.' Which fallacy has the classmate committed?

options.A: Ad hominem — attacking Eva personally
options.B: Straw man — misrepresenting Eva's argument to make it easier to attack
options.C: False dilemma — presenting only two extreme choices
options.D: Circular reasoning — using the conclusion as a premise

questions.explanation: A straw man fallacy occurs when someone exaggerates or distorts another person's argument into an extreme version and then attacks that distorted version. Eva only suggested 30 extra minutes; her classmate invented the extreme claim about 'all day.' Ad hominem (Option A) attacks the person, not their argument, which is not what the classmate did here.

questions.title: Ways of Knowing — Perception
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, a student argues that perception through our senses is the most reliable way of knowing because 'seeing is believing.' Which response best challenges this claim?

options.A: Perception is always reliable because our senses have evolved to detect truth
options.B: Optical illusions and optical phenomena demonstrate that our senses can be systematically deceived
options.C: Reasoning and logic are also ways of knowing, so perception is not the only one
options.D: Most scientists rely only on perception, so it must be the most reliable method

questions.explanation: Optical illusions — such as the Müller-Lyer illusion where two equal lines appear different lengths — show that perception can be systematically and predictably wrong, undermining the claim that seeing is always believing. Option C is true but does not challenge the reliability claim directly; it only points out that other ways of knowing exist.

questions.title: Valid vs. Sound Arguments
questions.prompt: Consider this argument: 'All fish can fly. Salmon are fish. Therefore, salmon can fly.' Is this argument valid, sound, or neither?

options.A: It is sound because the logical structure is correct
options.B: It is neither valid nor sound because the conclusion is false
options.C: It is valid but not sound — the logic is correctly structured but a premise is false
options.D: It is sound but not valid because one premise is true

questions.explanation: Validity means the conclusion follows logically from the premises — if both premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true, and this structure achieves that. Soundness additionally requires all premises to be actually true; since 'all fish can fly' is false, the argument is valid but not sound. Option B incorrectly states the argument is not valid; validity is about structure, not truth of premises.

questions.title: Availability Bias
questions.prompt: After watching several news reports about plane crashes, Tomás decides that flying is more dangerous than driving, even though statistics show the opposite. Which cognitive bias best explains Tomás's thinking?

options.A: Confirmation bias — he only watches news that supports his fear of flying
options.B: Sunk cost bias — he has already paid for flights he now regrets
options.C: Availability bias — he overestimates the risk because vivid media reports are easy to recall
options.D: Anchoring bias — the first crash report he saw set a fixed impression

questions.explanation: Availability bias causes people to judge the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind; dramatic plane crash stories are memorable and frequently reported, making the risk feel greater than the statistical reality. Confirmation bias (Option A) would require Tomás to be seeking out crash stories to confirm a pre-existing belief, but the scenario describes passive viewing changing his opinion.

questions.title: Logical Negation
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some students in this class enjoy mathematics.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: All students in this class enjoy mathematics
options.B: Most students in this class do not enjoy mathematics
options.C: No students in this class enjoy mathematics
options.D: Some students in this class do not enjoy mathematics

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'some X are Y' is 'no X are Y' — to make the original statement false, it must be the case that zero students enjoy mathematics. Option D ('some do not enjoy it') is compatible with the original statement being true, so it is not a true negation.

questions.title: Control Variables in Experiments
questions.prompt: Two students test whether fertiliser helps tomatoes grow. Student A uses fertiliser, ten hours of light, and daily watering. Student B uses no fertiliser, six hours of light, and weekly watering. What is the main problem with this experiment?

options.A: Tomatoes are not a suitable plant for this type of experiment
options.B: Multiple variables differ between the two groups, so no reliable conclusion about fertiliser can be drawn
options.C: The experiment needs at least five plants per group to be valid
options.D: The hypothesis was not stated before the experiment began

questions.explanation: A fair test requires only one variable to change at a time (the independent variable); here, light and watering also differ, so any difference in growth could be caused by light or water, not necessarily fertiliser. Option C refers to sample size, which is a separate issue and not the 'main' problem identified in this scenario.

questions.title: Perspective and Bias in Sources
questions.prompt: A student researches whether video games affect children's behaviour. She finds one study funded by a gaming company showing no negative effects, and five independent studies showing mixed results. How should she weigh the evidence?

options.A: She should trust the gaming company study most, as it is the most recent
options.B: She should ignore all studies and form her own opinion through experience
options.C: She should treat all six studies equally, as each represents one data point
options.D: She should note the potential conflict of interest in the funded study and give greater weight to independent research

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest — where the funder benefits from a particular result — does not automatically make research false, but it is a recognised reason to scrutinise it more carefully; independent research with no financial stake is generally considered more credible. Option C incorrectly treats all studies as equal regardless of funding source or potential bias.

questions.title: If-Then Conditional Statements
questions.prompt: A rule states: 'If a student scores above 80%, they receive a merit certificate.' A student did NOT receive a merit certificate. What can be logically concluded?

options.A: The student scored exactly 80%
options.B: The student did not score above 80%
options.C: The student was absent during the assessment
options.D: The teacher forgot to issue the certificate

questions.explanation: This is modus tollens: 'If P then Q; Q is false; therefore P is false.' If scoring above 80% guaranteed a certificate (Q), then not receiving one (not Q) means the student did not score above 80% (not P). Option D introduces an external explanation not supported by the logical premises given.

questions.title: Generalisation Errors
questions.prompt: After interviewing five students from one school, a researcher concludes: 'Children worldwide prefer online learning to classroom learning.' Identify the most significant error in this conclusion.

options.A: The researcher should have used a survey instead of interviews
options.B: The sample is too small and unrepresentative to support a worldwide claim
options.C: The conclusion uses the word 'prefer,' which is an opinion, not a fact
options.D: The researcher forgot to define what 'online learning' means

questions.explanation: Generalising from a small, non-representative sample to a worldwide population is a hasty generalisation fallacy — five students from one school cannot represent the diversity of children globally. Option C is partially valid but misses the main logical error; 'prefer' can be measured systematically, but the sampling problem is the central flaw.

questions.title: Argument Structure Identification
questions.prompt: A student writes: 'We should plant more trees in our city because trees reduce air pollution, and clean air improves public health.' Which part of this passage is the conclusion?

options.A: Trees reduce air pollution
options.B: Clean air improves public health
options.C: We should plant more trees in our city
options.D: Air pollution is caused by human activity

questions.explanation: In an argument, the conclusion is the main claim that the premises are designed to support — 'We should plant more trees in our city' is what the student is arguing for, while the other statements are the reasons (premises) that support it. Option A is a premise (a reason given to support the conclusion), not the conclusion itself.

questions.title: Falsifiability in Science
questions.prompt: A student proposes the hypothesis: 'Invisible dragons cause thunder, but they cannot be detected by any instrument.' Why is this hypothesis problematic from a scientific point of view?

options.A: The hypothesis uses imaginative language, which is not allowed in science
options.B: It is not falsifiable — no possible observation could prove it wrong
options.C: The hypothesis needs to be tested in at least three different countries first
options.D: Science only studies things that are visible to the naked eye

questions.explanation: Karl Popper's principle of falsifiability states that a scientific hypothesis must be testable and potentially disprovable; if the hypothesis claims the cause cannot be detected by any instrument, no experiment could ever refute it, making it unscientific. Option A is wrong because creative language is not the problem — the untestable nature is the issue.

questions.title: Deductive Argument Evaluation
questions.prompt: Evaluate this argument: 'No reptiles are warm-blooded. All snakes are reptiles. Therefore, no snakes are warm-blooded.' Is this argument valid AND sound?

options.A: Valid but not sound, because some snakes are actually warm-blooded
options.B: Sound but not valid, because the premises are true
options.C: Neither valid nor sound, because the conclusion contradicts common knowledge
options.D: Both valid and sound — the logic is correct and both premises are true

questions.explanation: The argument is valid because the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises. It is also sound because both premises are factually true: reptiles are indeed cold-blooded (ectothermic), and snakes are indeed reptiles. Option A is wrong because snakes are not warm-blooded — the premise is accurate, making the argument sound.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this argument: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Whales are mammals. Therefore, whales are warm-blooded.' A classmate says the conclusion is only probably true, not definitely true. Is the classmate correct?

options.A: Yes, because science can always be proven wrong by new discoveries
options.B: No, because if both premises are true the conclusion must be true — this is a valid deductive argument
options.C: Yes, because whales live in the ocean, which creates an exception to the rule
options.D: No, but only because whales are large animals, making the rule more reliable

questions.explanation: In a valid deductive syllogism, if all premises are true the conclusion is guaranteed — not just probable. The classmate is confusing deductive certainty with the uncertainty found in inductive reasoning. Option A is wrong because questioning scientific facts is separate from evaluating the logical structure of the argument; even if the premises were hypothetically accepted as true, the logic forces the conclusion.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Overlap Error
questions.prompt: In a survey of 40 children, 22 like painting, 17 like coding, and 9 like both. A student draws a Venn diagram and says 30 children like at least one activity. Is the student right?

options.A: No, the correct answer is 39 because you add all three numbers together
options.B: Yes, 30 is correct because 22 plus 17 minus 9 equals 30
options.C: No, the correct answer is 48 because you must count the overlap twice
options.D: No, the correct answer is 31 because you subtract the total from 40

questions.explanation: The inclusion-exclusion principle states that to find those who like at least one activity, you add the two groups and subtract the overlap: 22 + 17 − 9 = 30. This avoids double-counting the 9 children who like both. Option A is wrong because simply adding 22, 17, and 9 gives 48, which double-counts the overlap group and exceeds the total survey size.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student wants to find out whether video games make children less focused. She only interviews children who have been told off for playing games too long and ignores children who play games and do well in school. What reasoning error is she making?

options.A: Ad hominem bias, because she is judging people instead of evidence
options.B: Confirmation bias, because she is only collecting evidence that supports her existing belief
options.C: False dilemma, because she is treating focus as either present or absent
options.D: Slippery slope, because she assumes gaming always leads to worse focus

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias occurs when a person seeks out or notices only evidence that confirms what they already believe, ignoring contradictory evidence. By selecting only children who have been told off for gaming, the student is pre-filtering her sample to support her hypothesis. Option D describes a different error — slippery slope — which would involve claiming one step automatically causes an extreme end result, which is not what the student is doing here.

questions.title: Necessary vs. Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Priya says: 'Being over 12 years old is enough to join the school's debate club.' If this is true, which of the following statements is also definitely true?

options.A: Every member of the debate club must be over 12 years old
options.B: Any student over 12 years old can join the debate club
options.C: Students under 12 years old are never good at debating
options.D: Being over 12 years old is the only way to join the debate club

questions.explanation: If being over 12 is a sufficient condition, it guarantees the outcome — any student over 12 can join. A sufficient condition does not mean it is the only route in, so other ages might also qualify. Option A is wrong because it describes a necessary condition (you must be over 12), but Priya only said being over 12 is enough — she did not say it is required.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: Every Monday for six weeks, the school canteen has served pizza. A student concludes: 'Pizza will definitely be served next Monday.' What is the most accurate evaluation of this reasoning?

options.A: The reasoning is valid because six observations make the conclusion certain
options.B: The reasoning is strong but not certain, because a pattern in the past does not guarantee the future
options.C: The reasoning is invalid because you need at least ten observations to draw any conclusion
options.D: The reasoning is strong and certain because canteens always follow a fixed schedule

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion, which makes it probable but never logically guaranteed — the canteen could change its menu at any time. Six consistent observations increase confidence but cannot produce certainty. Option A is wrong because no number of past observations can make an inductive conclusion logically certain; that is the fundamental limitation of induction.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Flaw
questions.prompt: A student tests whether fertiliser helps plants grow. She gives fertiliser to five plants but waters them more often than the five plants without fertiliser. She finds the fertilised plants grew taller and concludes fertiliser works. Identify the main problem with her experiment.

options.A: She used too few plants to draw any conclusion at all
options.B: She changed two variables at once, so she cannot know which caused the growth
options.C: She should have used a different type of plant to make the results more general
options.D: She measured height instead of leaf count, which is a less reliable measure

questions.explanation: A fair experiment changes only one variable at a time (the independent variable) while keeping all others constant. By also watering the fertilised plants more, she introduced a second variable, meaning the extra growth could be due to more water, not the fertiliser. Option A is a genuine concern but is not the main flaw — even with more plants, changing two variables simultaneously would still make the conclusion unreliable.

questions.title: Appeal to Authority Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'We should eat less sugar because a famous footballer said so in an interview.' A second student disagrees with this as evidence. Which of the following best explains why the second student is right to be cautious?

options.A: Footballers are never correct about nutrition, so the claim can be dismissed
options.B: Being famous and skilled in one area does not make someone a reliable expert in a different area
options.C: The argument would only be valid if more than one footballer agreed with the claim
options.D: Personal opinions are always weaker than scientific studies, so this evidence counts for nothing

questions.explanation: An appeal to authority is only logically strong when the authority cited has relevant expertise in the subject being discussed. A footballer may be expert in sport but has no special knowledge of nutrition science unless separately qualified. Option D is too extreme — personal testimony can sometimes be relevant evidence, but in this case the issue is specifically the mismatch between the person's fame and their expertise in the topic.

questions.title: Counterfactual Cause and Effect
questions.prompt: What would most likely have happened if Alexander Fleming had cleaned his laboratory dishes properly and not noticed the mould killing bacteria in 1928? Use counterfactual reasoning to choose the best answer.

options.A: Penicillin would never have been discovered, because only Fleming could have found it
options.B: The discovery of penicillin might have been delayed, but other scientists could eventually have made a similar observation
options.C: Medicine would be exactly the same today because other antibiotics already existed in 1928
options.D: Fleming would have discovered something even more important instead

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning asks what would follow if a past event had been different, tracing probable consequences. While Fleming's accidental observation was historically important, other researchers were studying bacteria and moulds, making an independent discovery plausible over time. Option A is too absolute — it assumes Fleming was uniquely positioned, ignoring that scientific discovery often happens independently across multiple researchers, as seen with Darwin and Wallace on evolution.

questions.title: Modus Ponens Application
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a shape has exactly three sides, it is a triangle. Premise 2: This shape has exactly three sides. What must be true?

options.A: This shape might be a triangle, but we need to measure its angles to be sure
options.B: This shape is a triangle
options.C: All triangles have exactly three sides, so the shape could be any polygon
options.D: This shape is probably a triangle, but quadrilaterals can also have three visible sides

questions.explanation: This is a straightforward application of modus ponens: if P then Q; P is true; therefore Q is certain. Given both premises are accepted as true, the conclusion follows necessarily without needing further measurement. Option A is wrong because it adds an extra condition not required by the logical structure — once the premises are accepted, no additional information is needed to reach the conclusion.

questions.title: Spotting the False Analogy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training your brain with puzzles is just like training muscles at the gym — the more you practice, the stronger you get, so doing one puzzle a day will definitely raise your IQ score.' What is the most significant weakness in this analogy?

options.A: Puzzles are not physical activities, so the comparison cannot work at all
options.B: Brain training may improve specific skills but research does not confirm it reliably raises overall IQ, unlike the predictable gains from physical exercise
options.C: The analogy is perfect because neuroscientists have proven the brain and muscles follow identical rules
options.D: The analogy fails only because one puzzle a day is too few — the argument would be correct with more puzzles

questions.explanation: An analogy is weak when the two things being compared differ in a key way. Muscle growth from exercise follows well-documented, consistent biological rules, but the transfer of puzzle-solving gains to general intelligence (IQ) is not reliably supported by research — a crucial disanalogy. Option D is wrong because it accepts the flawed logic and only disputes the quantity, missing that the core claim about IQ improvement lacks scientific support regardless of how many puzzles are done.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Best Explanation
questions.prompt: You come home and find your dog is muddy, the back gate is open, and there are paw prints leading to the garden. Which conclusion best demonstrates abductive reasoning?

options.A: The dog definitely escaped into the garden because that is the only logical possibility
options.B: The dog most likely escaped into the muddy garden, because this explanation accounts for all three clues together
options.C: Someone must have broken into the garden and brought mud inside the house
options.D: It is impossible to know what happened without more information

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning means choosing the simplest explanation that best fits all available evidence — sometimes called 'inference to the best explanation.' The dog escaping through the open gate into the garden explains the mud, the open gate, and the paw prints as a single coherent story. Option A is wrong because abductive conclusions are the most probable, not certain — new evidence could always reveal a different explanation.

questions.title: Evaluating Circular Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student says: 'I know my memory is always accurate because I clearly remember never making a memory mistake.' Identify the logical error in this statement.

options.A: Slippery slope — the student is assuming one good memory leads to always having good memory
options.B: Circular reasoning — the student is using the very thing being proved as evidence for itself
options.C: False dilemma — the student is treating memory as either perfect or completely unreliable
options.D: Ad hominem — the student is attacking the credibility of people who say memories can be wrong

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning (also called begging the question) occurs when the conclusion is hidden inside the premise — the student is using their memory to prove their memory is reliable, which provides no independent evidence. This is also known as a self-referential fallacy. Option A describes a slippery slope, which involves a chain of increasingly extreme consequences — that structure is not present in this argument.

questions.title: Correlation vs. Causation
questions.prompt: A study finds that children who own more books at home score higher on reading tests. A newspaper headline reads: 'Buying more books makes children smarter readers.' What is the main problem with this headline's reasoning?

options.A: The study is too small to be meaningful, so the headline should not have been written
options.B: The headline confuses correlation with causation — a third factor, like a reading-focused home environment, could explain both
options.C: The headline is correct because having more books gives children more practice material
options.D: The study measures the wrong thing — it should test writing scores instead of reading scores

questions.explanation: Correlation means two things are associated, but it does not prove one causes the other. Both owning more books and scoring well on reading tests could both be caused by a third factor — such as parents who value education, read to their children, and have higher incomes. Option C is wrong because it assumes the causal direction stated in the headline, which is precisely the unjustified leap the question asks students to identify.

questions.title: Perspective and Bias in Sources
questions.prompt: Two reports about a new shopping centre are published. One is written by the company building it; the other by a local environmental group. A student says both reports are equally unreliable because they are both biased. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct — any source with a viewpoint is completely unreliable and should be ignored
options.B: The student is partially right: both sources may be biased, but understanding each perspective still provides useful information when read critically
options.C: The student is wrong — the environmental group's report is always more trustworthy because it protects nature
options.D: The student is wrong — the building company's report is more reliable because it is based on technical data

questions.explanation: Almost all sources carry some perspective or interest, but that does not make them worthless — it means they must be read critically and cross-checked. A skilled reasoner identifies potential bias and weighs claims accordingly rather than simply discarding sources. Option A represents an extreme view that would make research impossible, since even peer-reviewed science is produced by researchers with interests and funding sources.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: Yusuf argues: 'Schools should teach students how to cook simple meals.' His classmate replies: 'Yusuf wants to turn school into a cooking competition and stop teaching maths!' Which logical error has the classmate made?

options.A: Appeal to emotion — the classmate is trying to make students feel worried about losing maths
options.B: Straw man — the classmate has exaggerated and distorted Yusuf's argument to make it easier to attack
options.C: False dilemma — the classmate is saying schools must choose between cooking and maths
options.D: Hasty generalisation — the classmate has drawn a broad conclusion from one comment

questions.explanation: A straw man fallacy involves misrepresenting someone's argument in an exaggerated or distorted form, then attacking that distortion rather than the actual claim. Yusuf said nothing about removing maths or holding competitions — the classmate invented a more extreme version of the argument. Option C describes a false dilemma, which presents only two choices; while there is a hint of that here, the core error is the distortion of Yusuf's original, much more modest claim.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition and Exceptions
questions.prompt: A student studying number patterns notices: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and says the rule is 'add the next odd number each time.' Another student says the rule is 'square the position number.' Are these rules different, or do they always give the same sequence?

options.A: They are different rules that happen to match for the first five terms but will diverge later
options.B: They are the same rule expressed differently — both always produce the same sequence of square numbers
options.C: The squaring rule is correct and the odd-number rule is an approximation that eventually fails
options.D: They are different because one uses addition and the other uses multiplication

questions.explanation: Both rules are equivalent descriptions of the square numbers: the nth square number equals n², and it is also true that n² equals the sum of the first n odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7…). This equivalence holds for every positive integer, not just the first five terms. Option A is wrong because these rules are mathematically proven to be identical — they will never diverge at any term in the sequence.

questions.title: Evaluating Anecdotal Evidence
questions.prompt: A classmate says: 'My grandmother smoked all her life and lived to 95, so smoking cannot be that harmful.' A second student challenges this. Which response best explains why the second student is right?

options.A: The classmate is wrong because personal stories should never be used in arguments
options.B: One exceptional case does not disprove a statistical risk — most smokers do face significantly higher health risks according to large studies
options.C: The classmate's grandmother must have had unusually good genes, which proves genetics matters more than behaviour
options.D: The classmate is right because lived experience is always more reliable than scientific statistics

questions.explanation: A single anecdote cannot overturn statistical evidence from large populations. The grandmother's longevity is a real but rare outcome — the fact that some smokers live long lives does not change the well-documented finding that smoking dramatically increases the risk of cancer, heart disease, and early death at a population level. Option D is wrong because personal experience, while valuable, is subject to selection bias and cannot reliably detect small or medium-sized risks across millions of people.

questions.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
questions.prompt: Amara has spent three months learning to play a piece of piano music she dislikes. She wants to quit but says: 'I have to keep going — I've already put in so much time.' Which cognitive error is influencing Amara's reasoning?

options.A: Anchoring bias — she is too focused on her original decision to change course
options.B: Sunk cost fallacy — she is letting past investment influence a decision that should be based on future benefit
options.C: Optimism bias — she believes future practice will eventually make her enjoy the piece
options.D: Availability heuristic — she remembers the hard work more easily than the reasons she chose the piece

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when someone continues an action because of past investment (time, money, effort) rather than evaluating whether continuing is worthwhile going forward. The three months already spent cannot be recovered, so the decision to continue should depend only on future enjoyment or benefit. Option A (anchoring) refers to over-relying on the first piece of information received when making decisions — a different mechanism from being swayed by past effort.

questions.title: Connecting Cause and Effect Chains
questions.prompt: A town closes its only public library. Which multi-step chain of effects is most logically supported?

options.A: Fewer people read → children's literacy scores may fall → job opportunities for residents could decrease over time
options.B: Fewer books exist → printing companies close → the town's economy collapses immediately
options.C: People use the internet instead → literacy improves because screens are more engaging than books
options.D: Local schools gain more funding from the saved money → academic standards rise and replace library benefits

questions.explanation: A logical cause-and-effect chain must have each step plausibly caused by the previous one. Closing the library reduces access to free books and reading spaces, which research links to lower literacy outcomes, which in turn can affect long-term employment and economic opportunity. Option B is wrong because closing a public library does not reduce the total number of books in existence or cause printing companies to close — the causal link is broken at the first step.

questions.title: Ways of Knowing: Perception
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, two students look at the same optical illusion and disagree about what they see. One says: 'This proves that perception is completely unreliable as a way of knowing.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct — if two people disagree on what they see, perception can never be trusted
options.B: The claim is too strong — optical illusions show that perception has limits and can be influenced by context, but perception also provides reliable information in most everyday situations
options.C: The claim is correct because science has replaced perception and we no longer need our senses to gain knowledge
options.D: The claim is wrong — optical illusions are simply mistakes made by careless observers, not a real limit of perception

questions.explanation: Optical illusions demonstrate that perception can be influenced by context, expectation, and brain processing — showing it has genuine limitations. However, concluding that perception is completely unreliable goes too far: our senses successfully navigate the world in countless everyday situations and form the basis of all empirical science. Option A commits the hasty generalisation error — moving from one type of case (illusions) to an absolute conclusion about all cases.

questions.title: Argument Structure: Hidden Premise
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'We should eat local food because it is better for the environment.' Which hidden premise must be true for this argument to work?

options.A: Local food tastes better than imported food
options.B: Doing what is better for the environment is something we should do
options.C: All imported food causes environmental damage
options.D: Local farmers always use more sustainable methods than large corporations

questions.explanation: The argument moves from a factual claim ('local food is better for the environment') to a recommendation ('we should eat it'). For this leap to work, there must be a hidden value premise connecting environmental benefit to moral obligation — that we ought to do what is better for the environment. Without this assumption, the environmental fact alone does not generate the 'should.' Option C is wrong because the argument does not require all imported food to be harmful — it only claims local food is comparatively better.

questions.title: Falsifiability in Science
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'There is an invisible dragon in my room that cannot be detected by any instrument, cannot be touched, and leaves no trace.' A classmate says this claim cannot be part of a scientific investigation. Why is the classmate right?

options.A: Science only investigates living things, so invisible objects are outside its scope
options.B: The claim is not falsifiable — no possible observation could prove it wrong, which means it cannot be tested scientifically
options.C: The claim is false because dragons do not exist according to biology textbooks
options.D: Science requires claims to be made by qualified scientists, and the student has not been trained

questions.explanation: For a claim to be scientific, philosopher Karl Popper argued it must be falsifiable — there must be some possible observation or test that could show it is wrong. By defining the dragon as undetectable by any means, the student has made a claim where no evidence could ever count against it, making it untestable and therefore non-scientific. Option C is wrong because simply appealing to existing textbooks is not the core reason — the issue is the logical structure of the claim itself, not what is currently known.

questions.title: Hasty Generalisation Detection
questions.prompt: After visiting Paris for two days, a tourist says: 'All Parisians are rude — every person I asked for directions ignored me.' Identify the reasoning error and explain why it matters.

options.A: This is a slippery slope because the tourist assumes rudeness will get worse over time
options.B: This is a hasty generalisation because the tourist is drawing a conclusion about millions of people from a small, possibly unrepresentative sample
options.C: This is confirmation bias because the tourist only visited Paris to find evidence of rudeness
options.D: This is circular reasoning because the tourist is using rudeness to define what counts as a Parisian

questions.explanation: A hasty generalisation occurs when someone draws a broad conclusion from too small or unrepresentative a sample. Two days of asking for directions involves perhaps a dozen people out of a city of over two million — the sample is far too small and context-specific to support a claim about all Parisians. Option C is wrong because confirmation bias requires the person to have a pre-existing belief they are seeking to confirm — the tourist's claim appears to be formed from the experience itself, not used to confirm an earlier assumption.

questions.title: Using a Venn Diagram for Syllogisms
questions.prompt: Premise 1: All scientists read research papers. Premise 2: Dr Patel reads research papers. A student concludes: 'Therefore, Dr Patel is a scientist.' Is this conclusion valid?

options.A: Yes, because the two premises together confirm Dr Patel belongs to the scientist category
options.B: No, because reading research papers could be true of many non-scientists — the premises do not rule this out
options.C: Yes, because Premise 1 tells us scientists read papers, and Dr Patel does the same thing
options.D: No, because we would need a third premise confirming Dr Patel works in a laboratory

questions.explanation: This is a classic logical error called 'affirming the consequent.' Premise 1 says if someone is a scientist, they read research papers — but it does not say that only scientists read research papers. A journalist, teacher, or curious reader could also read research papers without being a scientist. Option A is wrong because it mistakes correlation of behaviour with membership in a category — the Venn diagram would show research-paper-readers as a large circle that includes but extends beyond scientists.

questions.title: Evaluating Sample Size and Bias
questions.prompt: A school magazine surveys 10 students in the library about their favourite hobby and reports: 'Reading is the most popular hobby among all 600 students at our school.' A student challenges this finding. Which challenge is strongest?

options.A: The survey should have been done online so more students could see it
options.B: The sample is too small and was collected in a location that almost certainly over-represents students who enjoy reading, making it biased
options.C: Hobby preferences change over time, so any survey result will quickly become outdated
options.D: The magazine should have asked students to rank hobbies rather than choose one favourite

questions.explanation: Two separate problems combine here: the sample of 10 is too small to represent 600 students reliably, and crucially, surveying only students already in the library introduces sampling bias — those in the library are far more likely than average students to enjoy reading. Option A addresses format but does not fix the bias problem — an online survey could still be answered by a skewed group and would not resolve the core methodological flaw.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider these two premises: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Dolphins are mammals.' A student concludes: 'Therefore, dolphins are warm-blooded.' Is this argument valid, and why?

options.A: Valid, because the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises
options.B: Invalid, because we need more evidence that dolphins are truly mammals
options.C: Valid, but only because dolphins happen to be warm-blooded in real life
options.D: Invalid, because a syllogism needs at least three premises to work

questions.explanation: A deductive argument is valid when the conclusion must be true if both premises are true — the logical form here is a classic valid syllogism (All A are B; C is A; therefore C is B). Option C confuses logical validity with factual truth: validity is about the argument's structure, not whether the conclusion matches reality independently.

questions.title: Correlation vs. Causation
questions.prompt: A student notices that towns with more ice cream shops also have higher rates of drowning. She concludes that eating ice cream causes drowning. What is the most accurate evaluation of her reasoning?

options.A: Her reasoning is sound because the data shows a clear pattern
options.B: Her reasoning is flawed because correlation does not prove causation — a third factor likely explains both
options.C: Her reasoning is flawed only because her sample size is too small
options.D: Her reasoning is correct, but she needs a lab experiment to confirm it

questions.explanation: Both ice cream sales and drowning rates rise in summer, meaning hot weather is a confounding variable that explains both — this is a classic example of a spurious correlation. Option A mistakes a pattern in data for a causal relationship, which is a fundamental error in scientific reasoning.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a class of 28 students, 15 like science, 12 like art, and 5 like both. How many students like neither science nor art?
questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: students who like science OR art = 15 + 12 − 5 = 22. Students who like neither = 28 − 22 = 6. Option D (11) is a common error made by students who forget to subtract the overlap and calculate 28 − 15 − 12 = 1, or who add incorrectly.

questions.title: Identifying Hidden Assumptions
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'We should ban video games in schools because screen time is harmful to children.' What hidden assumption must be true for this argument to work?

options.A: That video games are more entertaining than other school activities
options.B: That the screen time from video games contributes meaningfully to harmful levels of overall screen exposure
options.C: That all teachers currently allow video games in class
options.D: That banning video games would make students study harder

questions.explanation: The argument only holds if school video game time actually adds to a harmful level of screen exposure — without this assumption, limiting games at school might make no meaningful difference to health outcomes. Option D introduces a separate claim about study habits that is not required for the original argument to function.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Strength
questions.prompt: A student tests five different metals and finds that each one conducts electricity. She concludes: 'All metals conduct electricity.' Which statement best evaluates the strength of this inductive argument?

options.A: It is a strong argument because inductive conclusions based on any evidence are always reliable
options.B: It is a weak argument because five examples are too few and the conclusion cannot be proven with absolute certainty by examples alone
options.C: It is a strong argument because the conclusion happens to be scientifically accurate
options.D: It is a weak argument because she should have used deductive reasoning instead

questions.explanation: Inductive arguments move from specific observations to general conclusions, so they can never guarantee certainty — a single counterexample could disprove the rule, and five cases is a limited sample. Option C confuses the logical strength of the argument with whether the conclusion is factually true; a lucky guess does not make an argument logically strong.

questions.title: Necessary vs. Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Is being over 18 years old a necessary condition, a sufficient condition, or neither for voting in most national elections? Choose the most precise answer.

options.A: It is sufficient — anyone over 18 is automatically guaranteed the right to vote
options.B: It is necessary — you cannot vote without it, but it alone does not guarantee voting rights
options.C: It is both necessary and sufficient — age is the only factor that matters
options.D: It is neither — age has no logical connection to voting eligibility

questions.explanation: Being over 18 is a necessary condition because you must be that age to vote, but it is not sufficient because other requirements — such as citizenship and registration — are also usually required. Option A is wrong because meeting one condition alone (age) does not guarantee voting rights when additional requirements exist.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student believes that listening to music helps concentration. When designing her experiment, she decides only to interview classmates who already listen to music while studying. What cognitive error is she making?

options.A: Anchoring bias — she is over-relying on the first piece of information she encountered
options.B: Confirmation bias — she is only gathering evidence that is likely to support her existing belief
options.C: Sunk cost fallacy — she has already invested too much time in her original idea
options.D: Availability heuristic — she is choosing participants based on how easily she can remember them

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias occurs when a person selectively collects or interprets evidence to support a pre-existing belief, ignoring contradictory data — by only asking students who already use music, she excludes those who might report it harms concentration. Option D describes availability heuristic, which is about ease of recall, not deliberate selection to match a hypothesis.

questions.title: Counterexample Disproving Rules
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'If a number is even, then it is not prime.' What is the best way to evaluate this claim logically?

options.A: Test many even numbers and if most are not prime, accept the claim as true
options.B: Accept it, because even numbers are always divisible by 2 so they cannot be prime
options.C: Reject it using the counterexample of 2, which is both even and prime
options.D: Reject it, because the definition of even numbers already includes prime numbers

questions.explanation: A single counterexample is enough to disprove a universal claim — the number 2 is even (divisible by 2) and also prime (its only factors are 1 and itself), directly falsifying the student's statement. Option A is flawed because a universal claim ('all even numbers') cannot be established as true merely by testing many cases; one exception destroys it.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Reasoning
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a shape is a square, then it has four equal sides. Premise 2: This shape does NOT have four equal sides. What must be logically true?

options.A: The shape must be a circle
options.B: The shape is not a square
options.C: The shape might still be a square with slightly unequal sides
options.D: No conclusion can be drawn without seeing the shape

questions.explanation: This is the valid logical form called modus tollens: if P implies Q, and Q is false, then P must also be false — so if 'square implies four equal sides' and the shape lacks four equal sides, it cannot be a square. Option C contradicts the definition given in Premise 1, which stated categorically that squares have four equal sides.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: Sofia argues: 'We should have healthier options in the school canteen.' Rory responds: 'Sofia wants to ban all fun food and make everyone miserable.' Which logical error has Rory made, and why does it weaken his response?

options.A: Ad hominem — he is attacking Sofia's character rather than her argument
options.B: False dichotomy — he is suggesting there are only two extreme options
options.C: Straw man — he is misrepresenting Sofia's position to make it easier to attack
options.D: Circular reasoning — he is using his conclusion as evidence for itself

questions.explanation: A straw man fallacy occurs when someone distorts or exaggerates an opponent's argument to make it easier to knock down — Sofia only said 'healthier options,' not a total ban, but Rory responded to the extreme version he invented. Option A (ad hominem) involves attacking the person's character, which Rory did not do; he attacked a fabricated version of her idea.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Design
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether fertiliser makes tomato plants grow taller. She uses three identical pots with the same soil and sunlight. She adds fertiliser to two pots and nothing to the third. What is the role of the third pot?

options.A: It is the dependent variable — it measures the effect of fertiliser
options.B: It is the control — it provides a baseline to compare against the fertilised plants
options.C: It is a repeated trial — it confirms the results of the second fertilised pot
options.D: It is the independent variable — it is what the student deliberately changes

questions.explanation: A control group receives no treatment and establishes a baseline growth rate, so any difference in height between the fertilised and unfertilised plants can be attributed to the fertiliser. Option D confuses the control with the independent variable — the independent variable is the fertiliser itself (what is deliberately changed), not the pot that receives nothing.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Limits
questions.prompt: A student sees the sequence: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and confidently states the rule is 'add the next odd number each time.' Her classmate says the rule is 'square the position number.' Are these two rules different, and what does this reveal about pattern reasoning?

options.A: The rules are different and will eventually produce different sequences, showing that only one can be correct
options.B: The rules are the same — they always produce identical results — showing that one pattern can have multiple valid descriptions
options.C: The rules are different, which proves that pattern recognition is always unreliable
options.D: The rules are the same, but only because the sequence is short; longer sequences would diverge

questions.explanation: Both rules are mathematically equivalent descriptions of the perfect squares (1²=1, 2²=4, 3²=9…) and will produce identical results for every term — this illustrates that a single pattern can be correctly described in more than one way. Option A incorrectly claims they must eventually diverge, which is false because both descriptions are different expressions of the same underlying mathematical relationship.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogical Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training for a marathon is just like revising for exams — both require regular practice and a plan.' What is the strongest criticism of this analogy?

options.A: Analogies can never be used in logical arguments, so the comparison is automatically invalid
options.B: The analogy ignores key differences — physical stamina can be built through repetition alone, but exam revision also requires understanding new concepts
options.C: The analogy is completely useless because marathons and exams have nothing in common
options.D: The analogy proves that exam revision is always harder than marathon training

questions.explanation: Analogies are weakened when the two things being compared differ in a relevant and significant way — physical training responds predictably to repetition, but academic understanding sometimes requires conceptual insight that mere repetition cannot provide. Option A is wrong because analogies are a legitimate and widely used form of reasoning; the issue is not that analogies are invalid but that this one has important limits.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Everyday
questions.prompt: You walk into the kitchen and see muddy paw prints on the floor, an overturned bin, and a half-eaten sandwich on the ground. Using abductive reasoning, what is the most justified single conclusion?

options.A: A burglar broke in and was interrupted while eating
options.B: A pet dog most likely entered the kitchen and knocked over the bin
options.C: A younger sibling made the mess and tried to hide it
options.D: An earthquake caused the bin to fall and scatter food

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the simplest explanation that accounts for all the available evidence — muddy paw prints, an overturned bin, and eaten food together most straightforwardly point to a dog. Option A is less justified because a burglar scenario does not explain paw prints and requires additional unsupported assumptions.

questions.title: False Cause Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student notices that every time she wears her lucky bracelet, her football team wins. She concludes the bracelet causes the wins. Identify the logical error and explain the strongest reason it is a mistake.

options.A: Hasty generalisation — she has drawn a conclusion from an unrepresentative sample of matches
options.B: False cause — she has assumed that because two events happen together, one must cause the other
options.C: Appeal to authority — she is relying on the bracelet's reputation rather than evidence
options.D: Slippery slope — she is assuming one small event will lead to a chain of consequences

questions.explanation: The false cause fallacy (post hoc ergo propter hoc) is the error of assuming that because B follows A, A must have caused B — her bracelet cannot physically influence her team's performance, so the association is coincidental. Option A (hasty generalisation) involves drawing broad conclusions from too few examples, which is a different error from wrongly assuming one thing causes another.

questions.title: Evaluating Source Credibility
questions.prompt: A student is researching whether sugar is harmful. She finds two sources: (1) a peer-reviewed nutrition journal article, and (2) a blog post by someone who sells a sugar-free diet plan. Which source should she trust more, and why?

options.A: The blog post, because personal experience is always more reliable than academic studies
options.B: The journal article, because peer review means other experts have checked the methodology and conclusions
options.C: Both equally, because all published sources must meet the same accuracy standards
options.D: The blog post, because it is written in simpler language and is easier to understand

questions.explanation: Peer-reviewed journal articles go through expert scrutiny before publication, which significantly reduces errors and bias — the blog author also has a financial conflict of interest that may distort their claims. Option A reverses the logic of evidence quality; personal or commercial experience is more prone to bias than systematically reviewed scientific research.

questions.title: Counterfactual Thinking Chains
questions.prompt: Imagine that the printing press had never been invented in the 1400s. Which chain of counterfactual effects is most logically justified?

options.A: Scientific knowledge would have spread just as quickly because people would have found another way to share ideas
options.B: Books would have remained rare and expensive, slowing the spread of literacy and scientific ideas across Europe
options.C: Only mathematics would have been affected, since other subjects did not depend on written text
options.D: The internet would have been invented earlier to compensate for the lack of printed material

questions.explanation: Before the printing press, books were hand-copied and extremely costly, limiting literacy and the exchange of ideas — the press directly enabled rapid sharing of scientific, religious, and political texts, so its absence would logically have slowed these developments. Option A is unjustified counterfactual optimism; it assumes an equivalent alternative would emerge without providing a logical mechanism.

questions.title: Distinguishing Fact from Opinion
questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion or value judgement?

options.A: Mathematics is the most important subject in school
options.B: Students should be allowed to choose their own homework topics
options.C: The human brain uses approximately 20% of the body's total energy
options.D: Art is more creative than science

questions.explanation: A verifiable fact is a claim that can be tested and confirmed or disproved using evidence — the brain's energy use is a measurable physiological fact, estimated at around 20% of total caloric energy. Options A and D involve value comparisons ('most important,' 'more creative') that depend on personal criteria and cannot be objectively measured.

questions.title: Spotting Equivocation Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'The law says I have the right to a fair trial. School tests are trials. Therefore, school tests must be fair by law.' What is the logical error in this argument?

options.A: Circular reasoning — the conclusion is used to support one of the premises
options.B: Equivocation — the word 'trial' is used with two different meanings in the same argument
options.C: Ad hominem — the argument attacks the legal system rather than addressing the real issue
options.D: Overgeneralisation — the student is applying a rule designed for one situation to too many cases

questions.explanation: Equivocation is the fallacy of using the same word with different meanings within one argument — 'trial' in law means a legal proceeding, while a 'trial' at school is simply a test or exam; the argument only seems to work by exploiting this ambiguity. Option D (overgeneralisation) involves applying a rule too broadly but does not capture the specific problem of deliberately or accidentally shifting the meaning of a key word.

questions.title: Perspectives and Bias in Knowledge
questions.prompt: Two historians write about the same battle. Historian A, from the winning country, describes it as a glorious victory. Historian B, from the losing country, describes the same event as a devastating attack. What does this example best illustrate about knowledge?

options.A: One of the historians must be lying and their account should be discarded
options.B: Historical facts are always wrong and cannot be trusted
options.C: The perspective and context of the knower can shape how the same event is interpreted and described
options.D: Only accounts from neutral countries provide accurate historical knowledge

questions.explanation: This illustrates a core IB Theory of Knowledge idea: the same facts can be framed very differently depending on the cultural, national, or personal perspective of the person recording them — both historians may be describing real events while emphasising different aspects. Option A incorrectly assumes bias equals dishonesty; a historian can genuinely believe their interpretation while still being shaped by their perspective.

questions.title: Evaluating Sample Representativeness
questions.prompt: A student wants to find out whether people in her city prefer cats or dogs. She surveys 50 students at her own school and reports her findings as representing the whole city. What is the main problem with her methodology?

options.A: 50 people is always too small a number for any valid survey
options.B: Her sample is not representative because it excludes different age groups, backgrounds, and areas of the city
options.C: She should have asked about more than two animals to make the survey scientific
options.D: Surveys are not a reliable method of research and she should use experiments instead

questions.explanation: A representative sample must reflect the diversity of the population being studied — surveying only students from one school excludes adults, elderly people, and residents from other areas who may have very different preferences. Option A is incorrect because sample size alone does not determine validity; a carefully selected sample of 50 diverse people can be more informative than 500 people from the same narrow group.

questions.title: Logical Negation Precision
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some students in this class enjoy reading.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: All students in this class enjoy reading
options.B: Most students in this class do not enjoy reading
options.C: No students in this class enjoy reading
options.D: Some students in this class do not enjoy reading

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'Some A are B' (there exists at least one) is 'No A are B' (there does not exist even one) — if it is false that even one student enjoys reading, then no student does. Option D is a common misconception; 'Some do not' can be true at the same time as 'Some do,' so it does not actually contradict the original statement.

questions.title: Appeal to Popularity Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Millions of people believe that the earth is the centre of the universe, so it must be true.' Which logical fallacy does this argument commit, and what is the strongest reason it fails?

options.A: Slippery slope — the argument wrongly predicts a chain of negative consequences from this belief
options.B: Appeal to popularity — the number of people who believe something has no bearing on whether it is true
options.C: False dichotomy — the argument ignores other possible positions about the structure of the universe
options.D: Hasty generalisation — the argument draws a conclusion based on a sample of people that is too small

questions.explanation: Appeal to popularity (ad populum) is the fallacy of claiming something is true simply because many people believe it — historically, the majority once believed the Earth was the centre of the solar system, yet Copernicus and Galileo showed this was false through evidence. Option D does not apply here because the argument is about all of humanity ('millions'), not a small sample.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this argument: 'All mammals breathe air. Whales breathe air. Therefore, whales are mammals.' A student says this syllogism is valid because the conclusion is true. Is the student correct, and why?

options.A: Yes — the argument is valid because whales really are mammals and the premises support this
options.B: No — the argument is invalid because 'breathes air' is not a property unique to mammals, so the conclusion does not follow logically from the premises
options.C: No — the argument is invalid because whales live in water, which contradicts the first premise
options.D: Yes — the argument is valid because both premises are true statements about the natural world

questions.explanation: A syllogism is logically valid only if the conclusion must follow from the premises — not merely if the conclusion happens to be true. Here, the middle term 'breathes air' applies to things beyond mammals (e.g., birds, reptiles), so the structure commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent. Option A confuses a true conclusion with a valid argument; having a true conclusion does not make the logical structure sound.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 40 students, 22 like science, 17 like art, and 9 like both. A student draws a Venn diagram and claims that 14 students like neither subject. Evaluate this claim carefully.

options.A: The claim is correct — adding 22 and 17 and subtracting 9 gives 30, so 10 like neither
options.B: The claim is incorrect — the correct number is 10 students who like neither subject
options.C: The claim is correct — 22 plus 17 minus 9 equals 30, and 40 minus 30 equals 10, which rounds to 14
options.D: The claim is incorrect — the correct number is 14, found by subtracting both totals from 40 without accounting for overlap

questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: students who like at least one subject = 22 + 17 − 9 = 30. Students who like neither = 40 − 30 = 10, not 14. Option A accidentally states the correct answer of 10 but labels the original claim as correct, which is contradictory; the claim of 14 is wrong.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: A student notices that every prime number she has checked above 2 is odd, so she concludes: 'All prime numbers are odd.' Which statement best evaluates her reasoning process?

options.A: Her reasoning is strong inductive reasoning and her conclusion is fully justified because no even prime above 2 has ever been found
options.B: Her reasoning is deductive and valid because odd numbers and prime numbers are defined to overlap above 2
options.C: Her reasoning is inductive and her conclusion is technically false — 2 is a prime number and it is even, so the generalisation fails
options.D: Her reasoning is inductive but the conclusion is acceptable because 2 is usually treated as a special case and excluded from general prime number rules

questions.explanation: The number 2 is the only even prime number, which is a well-established mathematical fact. Because 2 is both prime and even, the student's generalisation 'all prime numbers are odd' is false — a single counterexample is enough to disprove a universal claim. Option D is tempting but incorrect: 2 is not excluded from the definition of prime; it is the canonical example of an even prime.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: Priya wants to prove that listening to music helps concentration. She designs a study but only asks students who already believe music helps them. Which specific problem does this introduce, and what is it called?

options.A: Placebo effect — participants may perform better simply because they expect music to help, regardless of whether it actually does
options.B: Selection bias — choosing participants who already favour music skews the sample so results cannot apply to all students
options.C: Confirmation bias — Priya is unconsciously looking only for evidence that supports her existing belief about music
options.D: Overgeneralisation — drawing a broad conclusion from a group that is too small to be statistically meaningful
