questions.explanation: The specific flaw in Priya's design is selection bias: by recruiting only students who already believe music helps, the sample is not representative of the wider population, so any findings cannot be generalised. Confirmation bias (Option C) refers to selectively interpreting or seeking evidence — it describes a reasoning error in the analyst's mind, but the structural flaw in the study design itself is the biased sampling method.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Practising every day is sufficient to become a great musician.' Which of the following most precisely identifies the error in this claim?

options.A: Daily practice is neither necessary nor sufficient — some great musicians practise irregularly and still succeed
options.B: Daily practice may be necessary but is not sufficient — other factors like quality of instruction and innate ability also matter
options.C: Daily practice is sufficient but not necessary — there are many paths to greatness that do not require daily effort
options.D: The claim is correct — sufficient conditions by definition guarantee the outcome when present, and practice guarantees improvement

questions.explanation: A sufficient condition alone guarantees the outcome, but daily practice does not guarantee greatness because factors such as quality of teaching, feedback, and natural aptitude are also required. Practice is plausibly necessary (hard to become great without it) but not sufficient on its own. Option A is tempting but overstates the case — most evidence suggests consistent practice is at least necessary even if not sufficient.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Reasoning
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a shape is a square, then it has four equal sides. Premise 2: This shape does not have four equal sides. What is the only logically valid conclusion?

options.A: This shape might or might not be a square — we need more information about its angles
options.B: This shape is not a square
options.C: This shape is a rectangle, since rectangles are the closest shape to a square
options.D: This shape is not a square and therefore has no equal sides at all

questions.explanation: This argument uses modus tollens: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Since the shape lacks four equal sides, it cannot be a square by definition. Option D adds an unwarranted extra claim — knowing the shape is not a square tells us nothing about whether it has any equal sides; for example, a rhombus has four equal sides but is not a square.

questions.title: Hasty Generalisation Fallacy
questions.prompt: After interviewing five students from one school, a journalist writes: 'Young people today have no interest in environmental issues.' A classmate says this conclusion is unfair. Which objection is logically strongest?

options.A: The journalist has not spoken to adults, so the comparison group is missing
options.B: Five students from one school cannot represent all young people — the sample is too small and unrepresentative
options.C: The journalist should have used a survey instead of interviews to get more reliable data
options.D: The word 'today' makes the claim unprovable because it changes over time

questions.explanation: The core logical error is hasty generalisation: drawing a broad conclusion about all young people from a tiny, non-random sample of five students at a single school. The sample is both too small and likely unrepresentative because school culture, location, and demographics vary widely. Option C identifies a methodological improvement but does not name the logical flaw that makes the existing conclusion unjustified.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning Chains
questions.prompt: Consider: 'If penicillin had never been discovered, which sequence of consequences is most logically supported by cause-and-effect reasoning?' Evaluate the options below.

options.A: Surgeries would be riskier → more deaths from post-operative infection → average life expectancy would likely be lower today
options.B: Fewer medicines would exist → hospitals would close → modern science would not have developed at all
options.C: People would avoid hospitals → governments would invest less in education → literacy rates would fall
options.D: Bacterial infections would be untreatable → all infectious diseases would spread uncontrolled → human population would have collapsed by 1950

questions.explanation: Penicillin, discovered in 1928, was the first effective antibiotic and dramatically reduced deaths from bacterial infections including those following surgery. Without it, surgical procedures would carry far higher mortality risk from post-operative bacterial infection, logically lowering life expectancy. Option D overstates the effect — other antiseptic methods existed before penicillin and some infections are viral, not bacterial, so a total population collapse is not logically supported.

questions.title: False Cause Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student notices that countries with more hospitals have higher death rates, and concludes: 'Hospitals must be causing people to die.' Identify the precise logical error in this reasoning.

options.A: Circular reasoning — the student is using the conclusion to support the premise about hospitals
options.B: False cause (post hoc) — the student assumes that because two things are correlated, one must cause the other, ignoring that sick people go to hospitals
options.C: Straw man — the student is misrepresenting what hospitals are designed to do
options.D: Slippery slope — the student is assuming one observation will lead to an extreme and unrelated consequence

questions.explanation: This is a false cause fallacy: the student mistakes correlation for causation. Wealthier, older, or sicker populations both build more hospitals and have people who die — the hospital is not causing death but rather treating people who are already ill. The Latin phrase for this error is 'cum hoc ergo propter hoc' (with this, therefore because of this). Option A (circular reasoning) would require the student to use the conclusion as evidence for itself, which is not what is happening here.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Design
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether cold water or warm water makes sugar dissolve faster. She stirs the cold water twice as vigorously as the warm water and measures which dissolves sugar more quickly. What is the fundamental problem with her experiment?

options.A: She should have used salt instead of sugar to get clearer results
options.B: She has not controlled the stirring variable — two variables are changing at once, so she cannot know which caused any difference in dissolving speed
options.C: She should have used more trials to ensure her results are repeatable before drawing any conclusion
options.D: The experiment is invalid because temperature and stirring are unrelated variables that cannot be compared in the same test

questions.explanation: A fair test requires that only one variable changes (the independent variable — here, water temperature) while all others remain constant (controlled variables). By stirring the cold water more vigorously, she has introduced a confounding variable: stirring speed. Any difference in dissolving rate could be due to stirring rather than temperature. Option C (more trials) addresses reliability, not the fundamental validity flaw caused by two changing variables.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogical Arguments
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'The human brain is just like a computer — it stores memories like files and processes information like a processor. Therefore, if we upgrade the brain like we upgrade a computer, it will work better.' What is the most significant weakness of this argument?

options.A: The analogy is weak because computers cannot feel emotions, making them completely unlike brains in every way
options.B: The analogy breaks down because brains store memories through dynamic neural connections that change with use, not as fixed digital files, so 'upgrading' does not translate meaningfully
options.C: The argument is invalid because analogies can never be used as evidence in logical reasoning
options.D: The analogy fails because computers were invented by humans, which means the comparison is biased from the start

questions.explanation: The brain–computer analogy is useful up to a point but fails when applied to 'upgrading' because brain memory is stored through synaptic plasticity — connections between neurons that strengthen with use — not as discrete, retrievable files. The biological mechanism is so different from digital storage that the conclusion about upgrading does not follow from the analogy. Option A overstates the failure by claiming computers and brains are unlike in every way, which ignores genuine similarities in information processing.

questions.title: Epistemology and Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In a Theory of Knowledge discussion, a student claims: 'Sense perception is the most reliable way of knowing because we can directly observe the world.' Which example most effectively challenges this claim?

options.A: Different people find different foods delicious, showing that taste perception is subjective and unreliable
options.B: A straight stick appears bent when placed in water, demonstrating that sense perception can systematically mislead us even under normal conditions
options.C: We cannot see ultraviolet light, which proves that sense perception only gives us a partial view of reality
options.D: Dreams feel real while we are having them, which shows that the brain can generate convincing false perceptions

questions.explanation: The bent-stick optical illusion is a classic example of how sense perception can be systematically and predictably wrong — the stick is straight but appears bent due to the refraction of light in water. This directly challenges the claim that direct observation is reliable because it shows the sensory system producing a false reading under ordinary, repeatable conditions. Option C is valid but addresses the limitations of the range of perception rather than its reliability within that range.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Yusuf argues that the school canteen should serve more vegetables. His opponent responds: 'Why should we listen to Yusuf? He failed his last health project.' Which logical fallacy does the opponent commit, and why does it matter?

options.A: Straw man — the opponent distorts Yusuf's argument to make it easier to attack
options.B: Ad hominem — the opponent attacks Yusuf's personal record rather than addressing the argument about vegetables, which may still be logically sound
options.C: Appeal to authority — the opponent implies that only people with perfect academic records can make valid arguments
options.D: False dichotomy — the opponent implies you either trust Yusuf completely or reject everything he says

questions.explanation: Ad hominem (Latin for 'to the person') is the fallacy of attacking the speaker rather than their argument. Yusuf's past academic performance is irrelevant to whether the claim 'the canteen should serve more vegetables' is well-reasoned or supported by evidence. Option A (straw man) would require the opponent to misrepresent the argument itself, not to attack the person making it.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition and Rules
questions.prompt: A student sees the sequence: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. She says the rule is 'multiply by 2 each time.' Her partner says the rule could also be 'add the previous number to itself.' A third student claims these are actually two different rules. Who is correct?

options.A: The third student is correct — multiplying by 2 and adding a number to itself are mathematically different operations that will eventually produce different sequences
options.B: The first student is correct — 'multiply by 2' is the standard mathematical way to describe this pattern and all other descriptions are informal
options.C: The third student is wrong — both descriptions always produce identical results because multiplying any number by 2 is the same operation as adding that number to itself
options.D: The partner is correct — 'add the previous number to itself' is more precise because it describes what is physically happening to each term

questions.explanation: Multiplying any number n by 2 (n × 2) is mathematically identical to adding n to itself (n + n), because 2n = n + n is a fundamental arithmetic identity. The two rules generate exactly the same sequence for every term, so they are not different rules — they are two descriptions of the same operation. This illustrates that a sequence can be described in multiple equivalent ways, and having multiple descriptions does not mean the underlying rule differs.

questions.title: Evaluating Source Reliability
questions.prompt: A student researching climate change finds two sources: Source A is a peer-reviewed paper by 47 climate scientists published in a scientific journal; Source B is a blog post by a popular science communicator with 2 million followers. Which source should she prioritise, and why?

options.A: Source B — a large audience suggests the content has been widely tested and accepted by the public, which is a strong indicator of reliability
options.B: Source A — peer review means other expert scientists have checked the methodology and findings before publication, adding a layer of verification
options.C: Both are equally reliable — popularity and peer review are both valid ways of testing whether an idea is correct
options.D: Source A — academic papers are always correct because scientists are trained to be objective and cannot be biased

questions.explanation: Peer review is a formal quality-control process in which independent experts evaluate a study's methodology, data, and conclusions before it is published. This makes Source A more reliable for scientific claims about climate change. Option D is tempting but wrong — peer-reviewed papers can still contain errors or be retracted, and scientists can have biases; the peer review process reduces but does not eliminate error.

questions.title: Anchoring Bias in Decisions
questions.prompt: A shopkeeper first shows customers a jacket priced at £200, then offers them a 'bargain' jacket for £90. Research shows customers feel the £90 jacket is a great deal. Which cognitive bias best explains this effect, and why does the order of presentation matter?

options.A: Availability bias — customers remember the £200 price more easily because it was shown first, making it more mentally available
options.B: Anchoring bias — the first price (£200) sets a mental reference point that makes the second price seem cheaper by comparison, regardless of its actual value
options.C: Sunk cost fallacy — customers feel they have already invested attention in the expensive jacket, so they feel compelled to buy something
options.D: Framing effect — the shopkeeper uses positive language about the second jacket, which changes how customers perceive its value

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias occurs when an initial piece of information (the anchor) disproportionately influences subsequent judgments. Psychologists Kahneman and Tversky demonstrated that people estimate values by adjusting from the first number they encounter rather than evaluating objectively. The £200 anchor makes £90 feel cheap even if £90 is still overpriced for that item. Option D (framing effect) would apply if the description of the jacket changed, not the numerical anchor.

questions.title: Evaluating Competing Hypotheses
questions.prompt: Two students investigate why plants grow taller near windows. Sana says: 'Plants grow toward light because they need energy from sunlight.' Riku says: 'Plants grow toward windows because windows are warmer.' Both explanations fit the observation. How should they proceed to determine which is better supported?

options.A: They should accept Sana's hypothesis because photosynthesis is a well-known scientific process and is therefore more likely to be correct
options.B: They should design an experiment that separates light from warmth — for example, using a grow lamp away from the window — to test each variable independently
options.C: They should research what other scientists have concluded and accept the most popular scientific view without conducting their own experiment
options.D: They should present both hypotheses as equally valid since both explain the same observation and no experiment can distinguish between them

questions.explanation: When two hypotheses both fit an observation, the correct scientific response is to design an experiment that can distinguish between them by isolating the variables. Placing a grow lamp away from the warm window separates light from heat, allowing each to be tested independently (controlled experimentation). Option A commits the appeal-to-authority fallacy — prior scientific knowledge is useful context but does not replace testing the specific competing claims.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning in Context
questions.prompt: A student opens her locker and finds that her textbook, which she left at school, is now wet and smells of river water. Using abductive reasoning, which explanation is most justified given only this evidence?

options.A: The school's water pipe must have burst near her locker and flooded it during the night
options.B: Someone who had been near a river accessed her locker and handled the textbook, or it was transported near river water
options.C: The textbook absorbed moisture from the air because school lockers are often humid environments
options.D: A classmate spilled a drink on the textbook, and the smell is from chemicals in the drink

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning means choosing the simplest, most plausible explanation that accounts for all the evidence. The combination of wetness and the specific smell of river water — not just generic moisture — makes the most parsimonious explanation one involving contact with river water, either directly or via someone who had been near a river. Option A (burst pipe) would explain wetness but not the distinctive river-water smell, making it a less complete explanation.

questions.title: Appeal to Popularity Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Astrology must be a valid science because millions of people around the world read and believe their horoscopes every day.' Identify the logical fallacy and explain why the evidence does not support the conclusion.

options.A: False dichotomy — the student implies that something is either a valid science or completely useless, with no middle ground
options.B: Appeal to popularity (ad populum) — the number of people who believe something has no bearing on whether it is scientifically valid
options.C: Anecdotal evidence — the student is relying on individual personal stories rather than controlled scientific data
options.D: Circular reasoning — the student uses the conclusion that astrology works to prove that people believe in it, and uses belief to prove it works

questions.explanation: The appeal to popularity (ad populum) fallacy assumes that widespread belief makes something true or valid. Historically, the majority once believed the Earth was flat — popularity did not make that correct. Scientific validity requires testable predictions, reproducible evidence, and peer review — not a count of believers. Option C (anecdotal evidence) would apply if the student cited personal experiences, but the argument is specifically about the number of believers, not personal stories.

questions.title: Deductive vs Inductive Conclusions
questions.prompt: Compare these two arguments: Argument 1 — 'All metals conduct electricity; copper is a metal; therefore copper conducts electricity.' Argument 2 — 'Copper, iron, and aluminium all conduct electricity; therefore all metals conduct electricity.' Which statement about these arguments is most accurate?

options.A: Both arguments are deductive because they both reach a conclusion about metals and electricity
options.B: Argument 1 is deductive and its conclusion is certain if its premises are true; Argument 2 is inductive and its conclusion could be disproved by finding one non-conducting metal
options.C: Argument 1 is inductive because it uses general knowledge about metals; Argument 2 is deductive because it lists specific examples
options.D: Both arguments are equally strong because they both produce true conclusions about electricity and metals

questions.explanation: Argument 1 is a deductive syllogism: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true with certainty — this is the defining feature of deductive reasoning. Argument 2 moves from specific observations to a general rule, which is inductive reasoning. Inductive conclusions are never guaranteed — for example, mercury is a metal that does not conduct electricity in the same straightforward way as solid metals, showing that the generalisation can fail. Option C reverses the definitions of inductive and deductive reasoning.

questions.title: Perspective and Argument Strength
questions.prompt: A student evaluates this claim: 'School uniforms reduce bullying.' She finds one study showing a 15% reduction in bullying and another showing no significant change. Which conclusion is most logically justified from this mixed evidence?

options.A: School uniforms definitely reduce bullying — one positive study is sufficient evidence to support the claim
options.B: School uniforms do not reduce bullying — if they worked, all studies would show the same result
options.C: The evidence is mixed and inconclusive — multiple studies with different results suggest the effect may depend on context, and more research is needed
options.D: The study showing no change should be rejected because it contradicts established policy in many schools

questions.explanation: When studies on the same question produce contradictory results, the most logically responsible conclusion is that the evidence is mixed and context-dependent rather than definitively supporting or rejecting the claim. This reflects the IB ATL skill of evaluating the quality and consistency of evidence before drawing conclusions. Option B commits the error of setting an unrealistically high standard — real-world phenomena rarely produce perfectly consistent results across all studies.

questions.title: Spotting Equivocation in Arguments
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Laws can be broken. The laws of mathematics are laws. Therefore, the laws of mathematics can be broken.' Identify the precise logical error in this argument.

options.A: Hasty generalisation — the student is making a broad claim about all laws based on only one type of law
options.B: Equivocation — the word 'law' is used in two different senses: legal rules (which can be violated) and mathematical principles (which describe necessary truths)
options.C: False cause — the student wrongly assumes that the existence of mathematical laws causes legal laws to be breakable
options.D: Circular reasoning — the student uses the premise about laws being broken to reach the same conclusion without adding new information

questions.explanation: Equivocation is the fallacy of using the same word in two different meanings within one argument. 'Law' in 'laws can be broken' refers to legal or social rules that people can choose to disobey. 'Laws of mathematics' refers to logical necessities that cannot be otherwise — you cannot 'break' the law that 2 + 2 = 4. The argument looks valid on the surface but fails because 'law' shifts meaning between the premises. Option A (hasty generalisation) would require the student to generalise from too few examples of the same type, which is not what is happening here.

questions.title: Cause Effect and Responsibility
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Social media companies are solely responsible for the rise in teenage anxiety because teenagers spend more time on social media and anxiety has increased at the same time.' Evaluate the strength of this causal claim.

options.A: The claim is strong because the simultaneous rise of both social media use and anxiety is powerful evidence of a direct causal link
options.B: The claim is weak because correlation does not establish causation, and other factors — such as academic pressure or economic stress — may also explain the rise in anxiety
options.C: The claim is strong because social media companies design their platforms to maximise engagement, which proves intention to cause harm
options.D: The claim is weak because teenage anxiety existed long before social media, which proves social media cannot be a cause

questions.explanation: The argument relies on correlation (both trends rising together) to conclude sole causation, which is a logical error. Multiple factors such as exam pressure, economic instability, and reduced sleep may independently contribute to rising anxiety. Furthermore, claiming sole responsibility requires ruling out all other causes, which has not been done. Option D is tempting but commits the opposite error — the fact that anxiety existed before social media does not rule out social media as a contributing (though not sole) cause.

questions.title: Validity vs Soundness of Arguments
questions.prompt: Consider: 'All fish can breathe underwater. Dolphins can breathe underwater. Therefore, dolphins are fish.' A student says this argument is valid because the conclusion follows from the premises. Is the student right?

options.A: Yes — the argument is valid and sound because the logical structure is correct and dolphins genuinely live in the sea like fish
options.B: Yes — the argument is valid in structure, but it is not sound because the first premise ('all fish can breathe underwater') is too narrow and excludes dolphins, which are mammals
options.C: No — the argument is invalid in logical structure because the conclusion does not follow from the premises even if we accept them as true; and it is also unsound because the first premise is false
options.D: No — the argument is neither valid nor sound: it is invalid because the conclusion is known to be false, and soundness requires a true conclusion

questions.explanation: This syllogism commits the same error as the whale example: the middle term 'can breathe underwater' does not uniquely identify fish — dolphins also breathe underwater yet are mammals. The argument structure is invalid (the conclusion does not follow logically) AND unsound (the premise that only fish breathe underwater is false). Option B incorrectly claims the argument is structurally valid; validity requires that IF the premises were true, the conclusion would follow — but even granting the premises, the structure has an undistributed middle term.

questions.title: Dunning-Kruger and Metacognition
questions.prompt: Research shows that people with low skill in a subject often overestimate their ability, while experts sometimes underestimate themselves. This is known as the Dunning-Kruger effect. Which scenario below most accurately illustrates this effect?

options.A: A student who has studied chess for ten years says she is 'probably decent' at it, while a student who has played three times says he could easily beat a grandmaster
options.B: A student who scored 95% on a test feels proud, while a student who scored 40% feels embarrassed
options.C: An expert scientist says she is certain her new theory is correct, while a student doubts the same theory because it seems complex
options.D: A beginner runner overestimates how far he has run because he is too tired to judge distance accurately

questions.explanation: The Dunning-Kruger effect, described by psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger in 1999, specifically predicts that novices overestimate competence because they lack the skill to recognise what they do not know, while experts underestimate because they are acutely aware of complexity. Option A captures both halves of this effect: the beginner (three games) confidently claims he could beat a grandmaster, while the experienced player (ten years) modestly says she is 'probably decent.' Option B describes appropriate emotional responses to test results and does not illustrate the effect.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this syllogism: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Whales are mammals. Therefore, whales are warm-blooded.' Evaluate whether this argument is valid, invalid, sound, or unsound.

options.A: Valid and sound, because the conclusion follows necessarily from true premises
options.B: Valid but unsound, because the conclusion does not follow from the premises
options.C: Invalid but sound, because the premises are true even though the logic is flawed
options.D: Invalid and unsound, because mammals are not always warm-blooded

questions.explanation: A deductive argument is valid when the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises, and sound when it is both valid and has true premises. Both premises here are scientifically true and the conclusion follows logically, making the syllogism valid and sound. Option B is wrong because 'valid but unsound' requires true form but at least one false premise, which is not the case here.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: A survey of 40 students found that 22 study French, 17 study Spanish, and 5 study both. A student claims that 6 students study neither language. Justify whether this claim is correct by applying set logic.

options.A: Incorrect — the number who study neither is 4
options.B: Correct — the number who study neither is exactly 6
options.C: Incorrect — the number who study neither is 8
options.D: Incorrect — the number who study neither is 1

questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: students studying at least one language = 22 + 17 − 5 = 34. Subtracting from 40 gives 40 − 34 = 6, confirming the claim is correct. Option A (4) is a common error made by subtracting 5 twice or miscounting the union.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias Identification
questions.prompt: A student researching climate change only reads articles that support her existing belief that humans cause it, ignoring studies she disagrees with. Which cognitive bias does this best illustrate?

options.A: Anchoring bias
options.B: Confirmation bias
options.C: Availability heuristic
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, favour, and recall information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence. The student's selective reading perfectly matches this definition. Anchoring bias involves over-relying on the first piece of information encountered, which is not what is described here.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Studying hard is a sufficient condition for passing the exam.' Which statement best evaluates this claim using the correct logical definition of sufficiency?

options.A: The claim is correct because studying hard guarantees passing in all possible cases
options.B: The claim is correct because passing requires studying hard as a minimum
options.C: The claim is questionable because sufficiency means studying hard alone must guarantee passing, which is not always true
options.D: The claim is correct because sufficiency and necessity mean the same thing in this context

questions.explanation: A sufficient condition means that if the condition is met, the outcome must follow with certainty — studying hard alone guaranteeing a pass. In reality, other factors like exam difficulty or illness can prevent passing even after hard study, making this claim logically questionable. Option A is wrong because it restates the claim without evaluating whether real-world exceptions exist.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: A student notices that every time she eats breakfast, she performs well on morning quizzes. She concludes: 'Eating breakfast causes better quiz performance.' Identify the primary logical weakness in this inductive conclusion.

options.A: The sample is too large to draw a reliable conclusion
options.B: Correlation does not establish causation — a third factor may explain both
options.C: Inductive reasoning can never produce any useful conclusions
options.D: The conclusion is deductively invalid because one counterexample disproves it

questions.explanation: The classic flaw in inferring causation from correlation is that an unobserved third variable — such as getting enough sleep — could cause both breakfast-eating and better performance. This is known as a confounding variable. Option D is incorrect because the argument is inductive, not deductive, so the standard of a single counterexample refuting it does not directly apply here.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Application
questions.prompt: Examine this argument: 'If a shape is a square, then it has four equal sides. This shape does not have four equal sides. Therefore, this shape is not a square.' Which valid argument form does this demonstrate?

options.A: Modus ponens
options.B: Affirming the consequent
options.C: Modus tollens
options.D: Denying the antecedent

questions.explanation: Modus tollens follows the form: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Here, P = square, Q = four equal sides; the argument denies Q and concludes not-P, which is the exact modus tollens structure. Modus ponens would instead affirm P to conclude Q, which is the opposite direction of reasoning used here.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Sofia argues that schools should reduce homework in lower years. Her opponent replies: 'Sofia wants students to do nothing at home and learn nothing at all.' Which logical error has Sofia's opponent committed?

options.A: Ad hominem fallacy
options.B: False dilemma fallacy
options.C: Slippery slope fallacy
options.D: Straw man fallacy

questions.explanation: A straw man fallacy occurs when someone misrepresents an opponent's argument in an exaggerated or distorted way to make it easier to attack. Sofia said 'reduce homework,' not 'eliminate all learning,' so her opponent has created a distorted version of her position. An ad hominem attacks the person rather than their argument, which is different from what is described here.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Design
questions.prompt: A researcher wants to test whether caffeine improves concentration in teenagers. She gives caffeine to one group and nothing to a second group, then compares their concentration scores. What critical element is missing from her experimental design?

options.A: A larger sample size of at least 1000 participants
options.B: A placebo condition so participants do not know which group they are in
options.C: A second researcher to repeat the experiment independently
options.D: A longer time period of at least one year for data collection

questions.explanation: Without a placebo, participants who know they received caffeine may perform better simply because they expect to — this is called the placebo effect or demand characteristics. A proper control group receives an identical-looking drink without caffeine to isolate the true effect of the substance. A larger sample is helpful but does not address the fundamental bias introduced by participants knowing their condition.

questions.title: False Dilemma Recognition
questions.prompt: A school announcement states: 'Either students attend every single after-school activity, or they simply do not care about their education.' Analyse what is logically problematic about this statement.

options.A: It commits an ad hominem fallacy by attacking students personally
options.B: It presents only two options when many other possibilities exist, creating a false dilemma
options.C: It uses circular reasoning by defining education through activity attendance
options.D: It is a hasty generalisation based on insufficient evidence about students

questions.explanation: A false dilemma (also called a false dichotomy) artificially reduces a complex situation to exactly two options, ignoring the full spectrum of possibilities — for example, attending some activities, having legitimate conflicts, or caring about education in other ways. Ad hominem would involve a personal attack on an individual's character, which is distinct from the all-or-nothing framing used here.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In a TOK discussion, a student argues: 'Scientific knowledge is the only reliable way of knowing because it can be tested.' Which response most effectively challenges this claim using TOK terminology?

options.A: The claim is correct because all other ways of knowing are entirely subjective and unreliable
options.B: Mathematical knowledge is reliable and logical yet does not depend on empirical testing in the same way
options.C: Science cannot test anything because all experiments contain some degree of human error
options.D: Emotion is more reliable than science because it is felt directly without any interpretation

questions.explanation: Mathematics produces certain, reliable knowledge through deductive proof rather than empirical experiment — for example, we know the Pythagorean theorem is true without running physical tests. This demonstrates that testability is not the only path to reliable knowledge, directly challenging the claim. Option D overclaims the reliability of emotion and does not use TOK reasoning about the nature of different knowledge frameworks.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Rule Testing
questions.prompt: A student sees the sequence 3, 6, 12, 24 and claims the rule is 'multiply by 2 each time.' Another student says the rule could instead be 'add the previous term.' Evaluate which student is correct about the relationship between these two proposed rules.

options.A: The first student is correct and the second is wrong because multiplication is always the primary rule
options.B: Both rules are different and produce different sequences from the fifth term onwards
options.C: Both rules produce identical results for this sequence because doubling equals adding the previous term
options.D: Neither rule is valid because sequences must be defined by subtraction or addition only

questions.explanation: For any term n, multiplying by 2 gives 2n, and adding the previous term (n) to itself also gives n + n = 2n — these are mathematically equivalent operations. Both rules generate 3, 6, 12, 24, 48… identically, so neither can be distinguished from this data alone, illustrating the problem of underdetermination in pattern recognition. Option B is incorrect because both rules continue to produce the same sequence indefinitely, not just for the first four terms.

questions.title: Circular Reasoning Detection
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'The school rules are fair because the principal says so, and we know the principal is fair because she created the school rules.' Identify the logical error in this argument.

options.A: Slippery slope — the argument implies one step leads inevitably to another
options.B: Circular reasoning — the conclusion is used as a premise to support itself
options.C: Appeal to authority — the argument relies solely on the principal's position
options.D: Hasty generalisation — too few examples are used to reach a broad conclusion

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning (also called begging the question) occurs when the conclusion is embedded in or identical to the premises — here, the rules' fairness proves the principal's fairness, which in turn proves the rules' fairness, creating a closed logical loop with no independent evidence. An appeal to authority would cite the principal's expertise without the self-referential loop, making it a distinct type of error.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'If the printing press had never been invented, the Protestant Reformation would not have spread as rapidly.' What type of reasoning is this, and what is its core logical feature?

options.A: Deductive reasoning — it draws a certain conclusion from established historical facts
options.B: Counterfactual reasoning — it explores what would have happened under a different set of conditions
options.C: Inductive reasoning — it generalises from many specific historical examples
options.D: Abductive reasoning — it selects the simplest explanation for an observed historical outcome

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning involves constructing hypothetical scenarios that contradict known facts ('counter to fact') to explore causal relationships — here, imagining a world without the printing press to assess its causal role in the Reformation. This is a standard tool in historical analysis and TOK discussions about causation. Abductive reasoning selects the best explanation for an existing observation rather than hypothesising an alternative past.

questions.title: Argument Strength Evaluation
questions.prompt: Two students debate screen time limits. Carlos says: 'A meta-analysis of 40 studies found that screen time over three hours daily reduces sleep quality in adolescents.' Diana says: 'My cousin uses screens for five hours a day and sleeps perfectly well.' Compare the strength of these two arguments.

options.A: Diana's argument is stronger because personal experience is more vivid and reliable than statistics
options.B: Both arguments are equally strong because each provides one piece of valid evidence
options.C: Carlos's argument is stronger because a meta-analysis across many studies provides broader, more reliable evidence
options.D: Neither argument is strong because neither comes from a qualified sleep researcher

questions.explanation: A meta-analysis synthesises data from multiple studies, dramatically increasing sample size and reducing the influence of individual variation — it is considered one of the highest levels of evidence in research methodology. Diana's example commits the anecdotal fallacy: a single case cannot override a pattern found across many studies, since her cousin may be an outlier. Option B is incorrect because evidence quality and scope differ significantly between the two arguments.

questions.title: Affirming the Consequent Error
questions.prompt: Examine this reasoning: 'If it is snowing, the playground will be white. The playground is white. Therefore, it must be snowing.' Identify the logical error and explain why the conclusion is not guaranteed.

options.A: The error is denying the antecedent — the argument incorrectly negates the first premise
options.B: The error is affirming the consequent — other causes could also make the playground white
options.C: The error is modus tollens — the argument incorrectly denies the conclusion
options.D: There is no error — the argument is a valid form of deductive reasoning

questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent takes the invalid form: if P then Q; Q is true; therefore P is true. This is a fallacy because Q (white playground) can have multiple causes — paint, frost, chalk, or snow — so observing Q does not confirm P specifically. Denying the antecedent is a different formal fallacy that would instead say 'it is not snowing, therefore the playground is not white.'

questions.title: Epistemology Justified Belief
questions.prompt: In TOK, knowledge is often defined as 'justified true belief.' A student correctly guesses that it is raining outside without any evidence. She says: 'I knew it would rain.' Evaluate whether she genuinely had knowledge according to this definition.

options.A: Yes — because her belief turned out to be true, it qualifies as knowledge
options.B: Yes — because she held the belief confidently, which counts as justification
options.C: No — although her belief was true, it lacked justification, so it does not meet the full definition
options.D: No — because weather cannot be known in advance by any means

questions.explanation: The classical 'justified true belief' (JTB) definition of knowledge, associated with Plato's Theaetetus, requires all three conditions: the belief is held, it is true, and there is adequate justification for holding it. A lucky guess satisfies the first two but lacks the third, so it does not constitute knowledge under JTB. Option A is incorrect because truth alone is insufficient — a stopped clock is 'right' twice a day but gives no knowledge.

questions.title: Hasty Generalisation Fallacy
questions.prompt: After interviewing five students at her school, a researcher concludes: 'Teenagers worldwide prefer online learning to classroom learning.' Identify the logical problem with this conclusion.

options.A: Circular reasoning — the conclusion repeats what the sample already stated
options.B: False dilemma — the researcher ignores a third option between online and classroom learning
options.C: Hasty generalisation — the conclusion extends far beyond what the small, non-representative sample can support
options.D: Appeal to authority — the researcher relies on her own expertise rather than data

questions.explanation: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from an insufficient or unrepresentative sample. Five students from one school cannot represent 'teenagers worldwide' given enormous differences in culture, technology access, and educational context globally. A false dilemma would involve reducing choices artificially to two, which is not the structural error in this argument.

questions.title: Analogical Reasoning Evaluation
questions.prompt: A debater argues: 'Running a country is just like running a business — so we should elect a successful CEO as president.' Evaluate the strength of this analogy, identifying its most significant weakness.

options.A: The analogy is strong because both involve managing large numbers of people and resources
options.B: The analogy is weak because countries prioritise citizen welfare over profit, unlike businesses
options.C: The analogy is strong because CEOs and presidents both make decisions under uncertainty
options.D: The analogy is weak because businesses are always larger than countries in population

questions.explanation: An analogy is evaluated by comparing relevant similarities and differences between the two things compared. The critical disanalogy is that businesses are designed to maximise profit for shareholders, while governments are accountable to all citizens and must balance competing values like equity, rights, and welfare — goals that can directly conflict with profit motives. Option D is factually incorrect and irrelevant as a logical critique of the analogy.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Best Explanation
questions.prompt: You find your locker door open, your books scattered on the floor, and your pencil case missing. Using abductive reasoning, which conclusion is most justified?

options.A: Someone opened the locker by accident and the pencil case fell without anyone noticing
options.B: An earthquake caused the books to fall and the pencil case to slide away
options.C: Someone deliberately opened the locker and took the pencil case, explaining all three observations together
options.D: The locker was never properly closed and the pencil case was lost days earlier

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning — sometimes called 'inference to the best explanation' — selects the hypothesis that most simply and completely accounts for all available evidence. Option C explains all three observations (open door, scattered books, missing pencil case) as the result of one intentional act, giving it greater explanatory power than alternatives. Options A and B require multiple independent coincidences, making them less parsimonious explanations.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Assessment
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If we allow phones in school for one lesson, soon students will be on them all day, learn nothing, and schools will collapse.' Evaluate whether this is a strong or weak argument and why.

options.A: Strong — because each step in the chain is well-evidenced and logically inevitable
options.B: Strong — because the conclusion is extreme enough to justify the initial caution
options.C: Weak — because it is a slippery slope fallacy that assumes each step follows without providing evidence
options.D: Weak — because schools have never used phones in lessons before, so no comparison exists

questions.explanation: A slippery slope fallacy asserts that one small step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences, without providing evidence that each intermediate step is actually likely. The argument leaps from 'phones in one lesson' to 'schools will collapse' without justifying why controlled use would spiral out of control. Option A is incorrect because no evidence is actually given in the argument to support the inevitability of each step.

questions.title: Research Bias and Sampling
questions.prompt: A study on student happiness surveys only pupils who voluntarily attend an after-school wellbeing club. A student argues this sample accurately represents the whole school. Examine the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: The flaw is that the sample is too large and introduces too many variables
options.B: The flaw is selection bias — students who join a wellbeing club likely differ systematically from those who do not
options.C: The flaw is that happiness cannot be measured in any scientifically valid way
options.D: The flaw is that after-school clubs are held at inconvenient times, reducing data quality

questions.explanation: Selection bias occurs when the sample is not randomly chosen and systematically differs from the wider population in a way that affects the variable being measured. Students who voluntarily attend a wellbeing club are likely already more engaged with their wellbeing, skewing happiness scores upward. Option C overstates the problem — psychological research has developed validated tools for measuring happiness, so the issue is the sampling method, not the measurability.

questions.title: Logical Negation of Statements
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'Some students always complete their homework.' What is the correct logical negation of this statement?

options.A: All students always complete their homework
options.B: Some students never complete their homework
options.C: No student always completes their homework
options.D: Most students do not always complete their homework

questions.explanation: The logical negation of an existential statement 'Some X are Y' is the universal negative 'No X are Y' — it must deny that even a single instance of the original claim is true. 'No student always completes their homework' is the precise negation because it contradicts the existence of any student who always completes homework. Option B ('some students never') does not contradict the original — both could be true simultaneously.

questions.title: Availability Heuristic Bias
questions.prompt: After watching a documentary about plane crashes, a student decides flying is far more dangerous than driving and refuses to travel by plane. Which cognitive bias best explains this decision?

options.A: Sunk cost fallacy
options.B: Availability heuristic
options.C: Bandwagon effect
options.D: Overconfidence bias

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut where people judge the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind — vivid, emotionally charged media coverage makes plane crashes feel far more common than they statistically are. In reality, driving is significantly more dangerous per mile travelled than flying. The sunk cost fallacy involves continuing with something because of prior investment, which is unrelated to this scenario.

questions.title: Validity vs Truth in Arguments
questions.prompt: Consider: 'All fish can fly. Salmon are fish. Therefore, salmon can fly.' Analyse whether this argument is valid, and whether it is sound.

options.A: Valid and sound — the conclusion follows from the premises and all premises are true
options.B: Invalid and unsound — the conclusion does not follow and the first premise is false
options.C: Valid but unsound — the conclusion follows logically from the premises, but the first premise is false
options.D: Invalid but sound — the premises are true even though the conclusion does not follow

questions.explanation: Validity concerns logical structure only: if the premises were true, would the conclusion follow? Here, 'all fish fly + salmon are fish → salmon fly' is a structurally perfect syllogism, so it is valid. However, it is unsound because the first premise ('all fish can fly') is factually false. This question demonstrates the important distinction that a valid argument can have false premises and a false conclusion.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a debate about nutrition policy, a doctor argues that sugar taxes reduce obesity. An opponent responds: 'We shouldn't listen to her — she was once seen eating a cake.' Identify the logical error in the opponent's response.

options.A: False dilemma — the opponent reduces the debate to only two positions
options.B: Straw man — the opponent misrepresents the doctor's argument
options.C: Ad hominem — the opponent attacks the doctor's character rather than her argument
options.D: Appeal to ignorance — the opponent claims the argument is wrong because it has not been proven

questions.explanation: An ad hominem fallacy attacks the person making the argument rather than addressing the argument itself — here, the opponent criticises the doctor's personal behaviour instead of evaluating the evidence about sugar taxes. Whether the doctor eats cake has no logical bearing on the validity of the research supporting sugar taxation. A straw man would involve distorting the argument's content, which is not what happens here.

questions.title: Falsifiability in Science
questions.prompt: A student proposes the hypothesis: 'There is an invisible force that controls luck, but it cannot be detected by any instrument or experiment.' A scientist responds that this is not a scientific hypothesis. Justify the scientist's position using the concept of falsifiability.

options.A: The scientist is wrong — any idea about the world counts as a scientific hypothesis
options.B: The scientist is correct — a hypothesis must be testable and potentially provable false to be scientific
options.C: The scientist is correct — a hypothesis must be proven true by at least three experiments before it is scientific
options.D: The scientist is wrong — invisible phenomena have been studied scientifically before, so this qualifies

questions.explanation: Karl Popper proposed that a statement is scientific only if it is falsifiable — meaning it is possible, in principle, to design an observation or experiment that could prove it wrong. A hypothesis that is 'undetectable by any instrument' is constructed to be immune to falsification, placing it outside the domain of science. Option C confuses falsifiability with verification — scientific hypotheses must be testable, not necessarily already confirmed.

questions.title: Deductive Reasoning Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this argument: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Whales are mammals. Therefore, whales are warm-blooded.' A student claims this argument is valid but might not be sound. What does it mean for an argument to be VALID, as distinct from being SOUND?

options.A: Valid means the conclusion is true; sound means the premises are also true
options.B: Valid means the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises; sound means the argument is both valid AND has true premises
options.C: Valid means all premises are true; sound means the conclusion is widely accepted
options.D: Valid means the argument uses formal logic symbols; sound means it is written in standard form

questions.explanation: An argument is valid when its conclusion must follow from its premises — if the premises were true, the conclusion could not be false. Soundness adds the additional requirement that the premises are actually true; option A confuses the two terms by reversing their definitions.

questions.title: Identifying Confirmation Bias
questions.prompt: A student researching climate change only reads articles that agree with her existing belief and dismisses sources that challenge it without reading them. Which cognitive bias does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Anchoring bias
options.B: Dunning-Kruger effect
options.C: Confirmation bias
options.D: Availability heuristic

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and favour information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence. Anchoring bias, by contrast, refers to over-reliance on the first piece of information encountered when making decisions.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 40 students, 22 study Spanish, 17 study French, and 5 study both. A student claims that 6 students study neither language. Evaluate this claim by calculating the correct number.

options.A: The claim is correct; 6 students study neither
options.B: The claim is wrong; 4 students study neither
options.C: The claim is wrong; 8 students study neither
options.D: The claim is wrong; 1 student studies neither

questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: students studying at least one language = 22 + 17 − 5 = 34, so students studying neither = 40 − 34 = 6. Wait — that gives 6, making the claim correct. Re-checking: 22 + 17 = 39, minus 5 who do both = 34; 40 − 34 = 6. The claim is actually correct at 6 students. Option D is incorrect; the calculation confirms the claim in option A is right.

questions.title: Inductive vs Deductive Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student notices that every time she studies with background music, she scores above 80% on the next test. She concludes: 'Background music always helps me score above 80%.' Which type of reasoning is this, and what is its PRIMARY limitation?

options.A: Deductive reasoning; the conclusion may contradict the premises
options.B: Inductive reasoning; the conclusion goes beyond what the evidence strictly proves
options.C: Abductive reasoning; the best explanation may not be the only one
options.D: Deductive reasoning; the sample size is too small to generalise

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion, but that conclusion is never guaranteed — a future test could break the pattern. Option A is wrong because deductive reasoning's weakness is not contradiction between premises; it produces certainty when premises are true.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Syllogism
questions.prompt: Examine this argument: Premise 1: If the school canteen serves pizza, students are happy. Premise 2: Students are not happy. What conclusion follows by modus tollens?

options.A: The school canteen does not serve pizza
options.B: Students are unhappy because of the canteen
options.C: The school canteen serves pizza but students are still unhappy
options.D: If students are happy, the canteen must serve pizza

questions.explanation: Modus tollens follows the form: If P then Q; not-Q; therefore not-P. Since students are not happy (not-Q), we conclude the canteen does not serve pizza (not-P). Option D describes the logical fallacy of affirming the consequent, which is not valid.

questions.title: False Dichotomy Fallacy
questions.prompt: A politician states: 'Either we increase defence spending or our country will be invaded.' A student says this contains a logical error. Which fallacy is MOST clearly present, and why?

options.A: Ad hominem, because the politician attacks opponents personally
options.B: Slippery slope, because invasion is an extreme outcome
options.C: False dichotomy, because there are other options besides increasing defence spending
options.D: Straw man, because the politician misrepresents the opposing view

questions.explanation: A false dichotomy presents only two options as if they are the only possibilities, when others exist — for example, diplomacy or alliances could also prevent invasion. Option B (slippery slope) would require a chain of events leading to the extreme outcome, which is not what is explicitly stated here.

questions.title: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: In logic, having oxygen present is described as a necessary condition for fire, but not a sufficient condition. Which statement BEST explains what 'necessary but not sufficient' means in this context?

options.A: Oxygen guarantees fire will occur, but fire can also occur without oxygen
options.B: Without oxygen there can be no fire, but oxygen alone does not guarantee fire will occur
options.C: Oxygen is the most important factor in causing fire, but other factors matter equally
options.D: Oxygen and fire always occur together and neither can exist without the other

questions.explanation: A necessary condition must be present for the outcome to occur, but its presence alone does not cause the outcome — fire also requires fuel and heat (the fire triangle). Option A incorrectly states that oxygen guarantees fire, which would make it a sufficient condition.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Design
questions.prompt: A student hypothesises that caffeine improves reaction time. She tests 20 students who drink coffee and records their reaction times, but does not include a group that drinks no caffeine. What is the MAIN methodological problem with her study?

options.A: The sample of 20 students is too large for a valid experiment
options.B: She has not included a control group, so she cannot compare results against a baseline
options.C: Reaction time cannot be measured accurately, making the experiment unreliable
options.D: She should have used a double-blind method before choosing caffeine as a variable

questions.explanation: Without a control group (participants who receive no caffeine), there is no baseline to compare against, so it is impossible to know whether caffeine caused any difference in reaction time. Option D, while relevant to some studies, addresses blinding, which is a separate concern from the absence of a control group.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a school debate, one student argues: 'We shouldn't listen to Paulo's argument about reducing screen time — he spends hours on his phone every day.' Which logical fallacy does this response commit?

options.A: Straw man fallacy
options.B: Ad hominem fallacy
options.C: Circular reasoning
options.D: Appeal to authority

questions.explanation: An ad hominem fallacy attacks the person making the argument rather than addressing the argument itself; Paulo's phone use is irrelevant to whether his argument about screen time is logically sound. A straw man fallacy, by contrast, involves distorting the opponent's argument, which does not happen here.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: A study finds that countries with more television sets per household also have higher life expectancy. A journalist concludes: 'Watching television makes people live longer.' Evaluate this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is justified because the correlation is measured across many countries
options.B: The conclusion is flawed because a correlation between two variables does not establish that one causes the other
options.C: The conclusion is flawed because television sets are not related to health in any known way
options.D: The conclusion is justified if the study was conducted by a reputable research institution

questions.explanation: Correlation shows that two variables move together but does not prove causation; a confounding variable — wealth — likely explains both higher TV ownership and better healthcare access. Option A is incorrect because a large number of countries increases correlation reliability but still cannot establish causation.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Best Explanation
questions.prompt: You open your front door in the morning and find the path is wet, but the sky is now clear and sunny. Using abductive reasoning, which conclusion is MOST justified?

options.A: A neighbour deliberately poured water on the path last night
options.B: It rained during the night and stopped before morning
options.C: The path is wet because the material absorbs atmospheric moisture
options.D: A burst pipe somewhere on the street caused water to flow onto the path

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the simplest and most probable explanation given the available evidence; overnight rain that stopped before sunrise best explains both the wet path and the current clear sky. Option A is possible but requires assuming deliberate action with no supporting evidence, making it a less parsimonious explanation.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In TOK, 'sense perception' is listed as one of the ways of knowing. A student argues that sense perception is the MOST reliable way of knowing because it gives us direct access to reality. Which example BEST challenges this claim?

options.A: Mathematical proofs are sometimes wrong, showing that all knowledge is fallible
options.B: Optical illusions demonstrate that our senses can systematically mislead us about physical reality
options.C: Language shapes what we can think, making sense perception less important than communication
options.D: Historical records show that many things believed through sense perception were later revised

questions.explanation: Optical illusions — such as the Müller-Lyer illusion where two equal lines appear different lengths — show that sensory perception can be systematically and predictably wrong, directly undermining the claim that it gives reliable direct access to reality. Option D refers to historical revision but is a weaker direct challenge because it does not isolate sense perception as the specific source of error.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If we allow mobile phones in class for research, students will be texting all day, teachers will give up, and education will collapse.' Identify and evaluate the reasoning used.

options.A: This is a valid inductive argument because each step is probable
options.B: This is a slippery slope fallacy because it assumes a chain of extreme consequences without justifying each link
options.C: This is a false dichotomy because it ignores the option of banning phones entirely
options.D: This is an appeal to emotion because it makes the audience fear for education

questions.explanation: A slippery slope fallacy assumes that one action will inevitably lead to a series of increasingly extreme consequences without providing evidence for each causal link in the chain. Option D has some merit but misidentifies the primary structural error, which is the unjustified causal chain rather than emotional manipulation.

questions.title: Logical Negation of Statements
questions.prompt: A student is asked to write the logical negation of the statement: 'Some students in this class have never been late.' Which option is the correct negation?

options.A: No students in this class have ever been late
options.B: All students in this class have been late at least once
options.C: Most students in this class have been late at least once
options.D: Some students in this class have been late at least once

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'Some X have never done Y' is 'All X have done Y at least once,' because negating an existential claim that some exist with a property requires asserting that none exist without it — i.e., all possess the opposite property. Option D is actually consistent with the original statement being true, so it cannot be its negation.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: Mia argues that school lunches should include more vegetarian options. Jake responds: 'Mia wants to force everyone to become vegetarian and ban all meat from the school.' Which error in reasoning has Jake committed?

options.A: Ad hominem, because Jake is criticising Mia personally
options.B: False dichotomy, because Jake implies there are only two options
options.C: Straw man, because Jake distorts Mia's argument into a more extreme version to attack it
options.D: Circular reasoning, because Jake's conclusion assumes his premise is already true

questions.explanation: A straw man fallacy occurs when someone misrepresents an opponent's argument — often making it more extreme — to make it easier to attack; Mia said nothing about banning meat. Option A is incorrect because Jake attacks the argument's content, not Mia's personal character.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogical Arguments
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training for a marathon is just like revising for exams — both require consistent daily effort over months.' Evaluate the strength of this analogy and identify its MOST significant weakness.

options.A: The analogy is strong with no significant weakness because both activities require discipline
options.B: The analogy is weak because marathon training is physical while exam revision is mental, so strategies may not transfer reliably
options.C: The analogy is weak because exams take one day while marathons are longer events
options.D: The analogy is strong because both have a fixed end-point goal to achieve

questions.explanation: Analogies are weakened when the two things being compared differ in ways relevant to the conclusion; physical endurance training and cognitive study involve different types of fatigue, recovery, and learning mechanisms, so study strategies may not mirror training strategies. Option C identifies a real difference but it is less relevant to whether the strategies transfer than the physical-versus-mental distinction.

questions.title: Occam's Razor Principle
questions.prompt: Two doctors propose explanations for a patient's symptoms: Doctor A suggests a rare tropical disease requiring six specific conditions; Doctor B suggests a common viral infection. Neither explanation has been confirmed by tests yet. Which principle of reasoning supports preferring Doctor B's explanation at this stage?

options.A: The principle of falsifiability, because Doctor B's claim can be tested more easily
options.B: Occam's Razor, which states that among competing explanations, the one requiring fewer assumptions should be preferred
options.C: The principle of charity, which requires us to always accept the most generous interpretation
options.D: Confirmation bias, because we naturally prefer the more familiar explanation

questions.explanation: Occam's Razor (the law of parsimony) holds that explanations should not multiply entities beyond necessity — the simpler explanation with fewer required conditions is preferable in the absence of distinguishing evidence. Option A (falsifiability) is a related concept from Popper but addresses testability rather than simplicity.

questions.title: Epistemology Justified True Belief
questions.prompt: In TOK, the classical definition of knowledge is 'justified true belief.' A student guesses correctly on a multiple-choice test with no reasoning. She got a true belief. Does she KNOW the answer according to this definition?

options.A: Yes, because she believed it and it turned out to be true
options.B: Yes, because the test result proves she had correct knowledge
options.C: No, because although her belief is true, it lacks justification — she had no reasoned basis for the answer
options.D: No, because multiple-choice tests do not test genuine understanding

questions.explanation: According to the classical JTB definition, knowledge requires a belief that is both true and justified through reasoning or evidence; a lucky guess satisfies only the first two conditions. Option A incorrectly conflates having a true belief with having knowledge, ignoring the justification requirement.

questions.title: Counterfactual Conditional Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian writes: 'If the printing press had not been invented in the 15th century, the Protestant Reformation would not have spread as quickly.' What type of reasoning is this, and what is its MAIN challenge?

options.A: Deductive reasoning; the challenge is ensuring the premises are logically consistent
options.B: Counterfactual reasoning; the challenge is that we cannot observe or test what did not actually happen
options.C: Inductive reasoning; the challenge is that one historical example is not enough to generalise
options.D: Abductive reasoning; the challenge is identifying which explanation is the simplest

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning speculates about alternative outcomes if a past event had been different; its fundamental challenge is that the alternative scenario is unobservable and untestable, so conclusions remain speculative. Option C is incorrect because inductive reasoning moves from multiple observations to a general rule, which is not what this historical argument does.

questions.title: Availability Heuristic Bias
questions.prompt: After watching several news reports about plane crashes, a student decides that flying is more dangerous than driving, even though statistics show driving has a higher fatality rate per kilometre. Which cognitive bias BEST explains this judgment?

options.A: Confirmation bias, because the student selectively watches news about crashes
options.B: Anchoring bias, because the first news report sets the reference point for all future judgments
options.C: Availability heuristic, because the student judges probability based on how easily examples come to mind
options.D: The Dunning-Kruger effect, because the student overestimates their own knowledge of transport safety

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic leads people to estimate the likelihood of events based on how easily related examples are recalled; vivid news coverage of plane crashes makes them feel more frequent than statistics justify. Option A is less precise because the student is not shown to be actively seeking out only crash reports — the bias operates on ease of mental retrieval.

questions.title: Appeal to Authority Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'We should eat less red meat because a famous footballer posted about it online.' A classmate challenges this reasoning. Which response BEST identifies the logical problem?

options.A: The argument commits an ad hominem fallacy by using someone's identity to make a point
options.B: The argument commits a false dichotomy by implying we must either eat red meat or follow the footballer
options.C: The argument commits an appeal to authority fallacy by citing someone famous but not expert in nutrition
options.D: The argument commits the bandwagon fallacy by assuming popularity proves correctness

questions.explanation: An appeal to authority is a fallacy when the cited authority lacks relevant expertise; a footballer is not qualified in nutrition or public health, so their opinion does not constitute valid evidence. Option D (bandwagon) would require the argument to reference how many people hold the belief, which is not present here.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Limits
questions.prompt: A student sees the number sequence: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and confidently states the rule is 'square numbers.' Her teacher points out the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 42 fits a different rule. What does this demonstrate about pattern recognition?

options.A: Pattern recognition is useless unless you have an infinite number of data points
options.B: A finite sequence can be consistent with multiple different rules, so confirming a pattern does not prove it is the only rule
options.C: The student should have used deductive reasoning instead of looking at examples
options.D: Sequences with more than five terms are always ambiguous and cannot be analysed logically

questions.explanation: Any finite sequence of numbers is technically consistent with infinitely many different rules; observing that a pattern fits your hypothesis does not eliminate all alternative hypotheses, which is why pattern recognition must be combined with rigorous testing. Option A overstates the conclusion — pattern recognition is useful, just not conclusive on its own.

questions.title: Falsifiability in Science
questions.prompt: Philosopher Karl Popper argued that a claim is scientific only if it is FALSIFIABLE. Which of the following statements is NOT falsifiable, and therefore not scientific according to Popper?

options.A: Objects fall at 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface in a vacuum
options.B: All events happen for a cosmic reason that cannot be measured by science
options.C: Plants exposed to more light grow taller on average
options.D: Vaccines reduce the incidence of measles in vaccinated populations

questions.explanation: Popper held that a statement is falsifiable if an observation could, in principle, prove it wrong; the claim about unmeasurable cosmic reasons is constructed to be immune to any possible evidence, making it unfalsifiable and therefore non-scientific. Options A, C, and D all describe claims that could be tested and potentially contradicted by experimental results.

questions.title: Circular Reasoning Identification
questions.prompt: Identify the logical error in this argument: 'This news website is trustworthy because it only publishes reliable information, and we know the information is reliable because the website is trustworthy.'

options.A: False dichotomy — it implies news is either fully trustworthy or completely unreliable
options.B: Circular reasoning — the conclusion is used as a premise to support itself
options.C: Slippery slope — it assumes trustworthiness automatically leads to reliability
options.D: Appeal to authority — it relies on the reputation of the website rather than evidence

questions.explanation: Circular reasoning (also called begging the question) occurs when the conclusion of an argument is smuggled into its premises; here, 'trustworthy' and 'reliable information' are used to define each other with no independent evidence offered. Option D has surface plausibility but no external authority is cited — the fallacy is purely the self-referential loop.

questions.title: Evaluating Argument Strength
questions.prompt: Two students present arguments about whether zoos should be abolished. Kai says: 'Zoos cause animal suffering, and several peer-reviewed studies show captive animals display stress behaviours at higher rates than wild counterparts.' Priya says: 'My neighbour who works at a zoo says the animals are happy.' Whose argument is stronger, and why?

options.A: Priya's, because a direct eyewitness account is more reliable than published studies
options.B: Kai's, because peer-reviewed studies provide systematic, replicable evidence across multiple animals
options.C: Both are equally strong because they both cite named sources of information
options.D: Priya's, because her neighbour has direct professional experience with zoo animals

questions.explanation: Peer-reviewed studies involve systematic methodology, large samples, and expert scrutiny, making them stronger evidence than a single anecdotal account from one observer. Option A is incorrect because a single eyewitness has limited scope and potential bias, whereas peer-reviewed research controls for such limitations.
