questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this syllogism: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Dolphins are mammals. Therefore, dolphins are warm-blooded.' A classmate says the conclusion is only probably true, not certainly true. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The classmate is correct because biological rules always have exceptions
options.B: The classmate is wrong; the conclusion follows with certainty if both premises are true
options.C: The classmate is correct because inductive reasoning can never guarantee conclusions
options.D: The classmate is wrong because dolphins have been individually tested and confirmed

questions.explanation: A valid deductive argument guarantees the conclusion if its premises are true; this syllogism follows the standard form 'All A are B; C is A; therefore C is B,' making the conclusion logically certain. The top distractor (A) confuses logical validity with empirical uncertainty — the question of whether exceptions exist is about premise truth, not whether the conclusion follows from the premises.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 40 students, 22 like science, 17 like art, and 9 like both. A student draws a Venn diagram and claims that 30 students like at least one of these subjects. Is this correct? Justify your answer.

options.A: Yes, because 22 + 17 − 9 = 30, so the claim is correct
options.B: No, because you must add all three numbers: 22 + 17 + 9 = 48
options.C: Yes, because overlapping sets always reduce the total by the overlap amount, giving 39
options.D: No, because only students who like both subjects should be counted, giving 9

questions.explanation: The inclusion-exclusion principle states that |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|, which gives 22 + 17 − 9 = 30; the claim is correct. Option B is a common misconception where students add the overlap rather than subtract it, double-counting the 9 students who like both subjects.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student researching the benefits of social media only reads articles that support a positive view and dismisses critical studies as 'biased.' Which cognitive bias is most precisely demonstrated here, and why does it undermine her conclusion?

options.A: Anchoring bias, because she fixed her view on the first information she found
options.B: Confirmation bias, because she selectively gathers evidence that supports her existing belief
options.C: Availability heuristic, because she relies on information that is easiest to recall
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect, because she overestimates her ability to evaluate sources

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias specifically describes the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs, which is exactly what the student is doing by excluding critical studies. Anchoring bias (A) refers to over-relying on the first piece of information encountered, which is a distinct phenomenon not described in this scenario.

questions.title: Necessary vs. Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Practising every day is sufficient to become a professional musician.' Compare this with the claim that daily practice is merely necessary. Which statement is more defensible, and why?

options.A: Sufficient is more defensible, because consistent effort always produces professional results
options.B: Neither claim is defensible, because music ability is entirely innate
options.C: Necessary is more defensible, because daily practice alone does not guarantee professional success
options.D: Both claims are equally defensible, because necessary and sufficient mean the same thing

questions.explanation: A necessary condition must be present but is not enough on its own; daily practice is required but additional factors such as quality of instruction, talent, and opportunity also determine professional success, making 'necessary' the more defensible claim. Option A confuses sufficiency with necessity — just because practice is required does not mean it alone guarantees the outcome.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Application
questions.prompt: Identify the error: A student is given — Premise 1: If Maria studied, she passed. Premise 2: Maria did not study. The student concludes: 'Therefore, Maria did not pass.' Evaluate whether this conclusion is logically valid.

options.A: Valid, because denying the antecedent always produces a valid conclusion
options.B: Invalid, because the premises do not rule out Maria passing without studying
options.C: Valid, because if studying causes passing, not studying must cause failing
options.D: Invalid, because the premises are contradictory and cannot both be true

questions.explanation: The student commits the fallacy of 'denying the antecedent': the premise only says studying leads to passing, not that studying is the only way to pass — Maria could have passed through prior knowledge or other means. Option C is a common misconception that treats a conditional statement as a biconditional ('if and only if'), which is not logically warranted.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Design
questions.prompt: A student wants to test whether caffeine improves concentration. She gives coffee to ten friends and asks them to rate their own concentration. What is the most significant methodological flaw in this design?

options.A: The sample size of ten is too small and the results lack a control group and objective measurement
options.B: Caffeine has already been scientifically proven to improve concentration, so the test is unnecessary
options.C: The experiment cannot be ethical because it involves giving substances to participants
options.D: Self-rating is reliable because participants know their own mental states better than any instrument

questions.explanation: The design has multiple compounding flaws: no control group means there is no baseline for comparison, self-reported concentration is subjective and susceptible to placebo effects, and a sample of ten friends is too small and not randomly selected. Option C is a distractor — caffeine in coffee is generally considered safe for research, and ethics, while relevant, is not the most significant methodological flaw here.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: A student notices that every prime number she has checked greater than 2 is odd, so she concludes: 'All prime numbers greater than 2 are odd.' Analyse whether this inductive conclusion is justified and identify its logical vulnerability.

options.A: Unjustified, because inductive reasoning is always unreliable and should never be used in mathematics
options.B: Justified and safe, because mathematical patterns proven by observation are as strong as formal proofs
options.C: Justified as a working hypothesis, but it remains vulnerable to a single counterexample disproving it
options.D: Unjustified, because she has not checked every prime number, so the claim has no value

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning from observed cases can produce strong working hypotheses, and in this case the claim is actually mathematically provable — but the inductive reasoning itself is always vulnerable to falsification by a counterexample, which is the defining weakness of induction. Option B is wrong because observational patterns in mathematics do not constitute proof; formal deductive proof is required, as famously demonstrated by cases like Euler's conjecture.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Priya argues that the school should switch to renewable energy. James responds: 'Why should we listen to Priya? She failed her geography test last week.' Examine the logical error James is making.

options.A: James is using a false dilemma by implying Priya either knows geography or knows nothing
options.B: James is making an ad hominem attack by targeting Priya's character instead of her argument
options.C: James is using the appeal to authority fallacy by suggesting only experts can speak on energy
options.D: James is making a hasty generalisation by judging Priya's knowledge from one test result

questions.explanation: Ad hominem is the fallacy of attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself; James dismisses Priya's claim about renewable energy by referencing her test result, which is entirely irrelevant to the merits of the energy proposal. Option D is a genuine misconception — while one could argue James generalises, the primary and most precise error is that he attacks Priya personally rather than engaging with her argument.

questions.title: Counterfactual Causal Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'If penicillin had not been discovered in 1928, millions more people would have died from bacterial infections by 1950.' What type of reasoning is this, and what is its main epistemological challenge?

options.A: Deductive reasoning; its challenge is that premises about the past cannot be verified
options.B: Counterfactual reasoning; its challenge is that we cannot observe what actually would have happened in an alternate timeline
options.C: Abductive reasoning; its challenge is that the best explanation may not be the correct one
options.D: Analogical reasoning; its challenge is that historical events are never truly comparable

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning involves imagining an alternative past and inferring its consequences; its core epistemological problem is that there is no observable evidence for events that did not happen, making the conclusions inherently speculative. Option A is wrong because deductive reasoning moves from accepted premises to certain conclusions — it does not involve imagining alternate histories, which is the defining feature of counterfactual thinking.

questions.title: False Cause Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student notices that ice cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer and concludes: 'Eating ice cream increases the risk of drowning.' Identify the precise logical error and the concept that explains the real relationship.

options.A: Hasty generalisation; the student should have surveyed more people before drawing conclusions
options.B: False cause (post hoc); the student assumes correlation implies causation, ignoring the confounding variable of hot weather
options.C: Circular reasoning; the conclusion restates the correlation without adding new information
options.D: False dilemma; the student implies ice cream or safety are the only two variables that matter

questions.explanation: The false cause fallacy (often called post hoc or 'correlation does not imply causation') occurs when a causal link is assumed from mere correlation; here, hot weather is a confounding variable that independently increases both ice cream consumption and swimming activity. Option A is a misconception — the problem is not sample size but the logical error of inferring causation from correlation.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge — Perception
questions.prompt: In TOK, two students look at the same ambiguous image: one sees a duck, the other sees a rabbit. A student argues: 'This proves perception cannot be a reliable way of knowing.' Evaluate whether this conclusion is too strong.

options.A: The conclusion is justified because any single failure of perception invalidates it as a way of knowing
options.B: The conclusion is too strong; ambiguous images show perception's limits but do not eliminate its general reliability
options.C: The conclusion is justified because modern science has replaced perception with instruments entirely
options.D: The conclusion is too strong, but only because the rabbit interpretation is objectively correct

questions.explanation: One ambiguous case demonstrates that perception can be fallible and context-dependent, but this does not mean perception is unreliable in all situations — it establishes a nuanced limit rather than a wholesale dismissal. TOK epistemology recognises that ways of knowing each have strengths and limitations; a single counterexample cannot invalidate a way of knowing entirely. Option A represents the hasty generalisation error of moving from one case to a universal claim.

questions.title: Analogical Argument Strength
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training for a marathon is just like studying for exams — both require consistent daily effort, a long-term plan, and mental resilience.' Evaluate the strength of this analogy by identifying its most significant weakness.

options.A: The analogy is strong with no significant weakness because both activities are fundamentally identical
options.B: The analogy breaks down because marathon training is physical while studying is cognitive, creating different recovery needs and skill types
options.C: The analogy is weak because it uses the word 'just like,' which always signals a flawed comparison
options.D: The analogy breaks down because exams are shorter than marathons, making them incomparable in duration

questions.explanation: A strong analogy requires that the two things being compared share relevant structural features; while the surface similarities are real, the physical-cognitive distinction means that overtraining a body and cognitive overload have entirely different physiological and neurological recovery processes, limiting how far the comparison can guide decisions. Option D identifies a real difference but focuses on a superficial feature (duration) rather than the more fundamental distinction in the type of demand placed on a person.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Evaluation
questions.prompt: A school board argues: 'If we allow students to use calculators in maths tests, they will stop learning arithmetic, then lose all problem-solving ability, and eventually be unable to function in society.' Evaluate whether this is sound reasoning.

options.A: Sound reasoning, because each step in the chain logically and inevitably follows from the previous one
options.B: Unsound; it is a slippery slope fallacy because the chain of consequences is asserted without evidence that each step is likely
options.C: Sound reasoning, because technology always reduces human cognitive ability over time
options.D: Unsound; it is an ad hominem attack on students who prefer using calculators

questions.explanation: The slippery slope fallacy occurs when a chain of consequences is presented as inevitable without justifying why each step must lead to the next; there is no demonstrated mechanism linking calculator use to total loss of societal functioning. Option A is a misconception — logical inevitability must be demonstrated with evidence or valid inference, not merely asserted through a dramatic chain of events.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Best Explanation
questions.prompt: A student walks into school and notices her friend's desk is empty, his bag is missing, and his lunch box is gone. Using abductive reasoning, which conclusion is most justified?

options.A: Her friend has permanently left the school, because all his belongings are gone
options.B: Her friend is absent today, as this best explains all three observations with the fewest assumptions
options.C: Her friend was late and has not yet arrived, so his belongings were placed somewhere else
options.D: Her friend's belongings were stolen, because no other explanation accounts for their absence

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning selects the hypothesis that best explains all available evidence with the fewest unwarranted assumptions — absence from school accounts for the empty desk, missing bag, and missing lunch in a single, simple explanation. Option A is a common over-inference; it leaps to a dramatic conclusion (permanent departure) without any evidence beyond what absence would equally explain.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: Sofia argues: 'We should have shorter school days to reduce student stress.' Her opponent replies: 'Sofia wants students to learn nothing and waste their entire day.' Examine the logical error in the opponent's response.

options.A: False dilemma, because the opponent implies the only two options are long school days or no learning
options.B: Straw man fallacy, because the opponent misrepresents Sofia's position in an extreme form to attack it more easily
options.C: Appeal to emotion, because the opponent is trying to make Sofia's idea sound absurd to provoke a reaction
options.D: Circular reasoning, because the opponent assumes that fewer hours means less learning without proof

questions.explanation: The straw man fallacy involves distorting or exaggerating an opponent's argument into a weaker or more extreme version, then attacking that version; the opponent has replaced Sofia's moderate claim (shorter days) with an extreme caricature (no learning at all). Option A is a genuine misconception — while there is an implicit false contrast, the defining feature of this exchange is the misrepresentation of Sofia's actual position, which is the straw man.

questions.title: Occam's Razor Principle
questions.prompt: Two students try to explain why their school's test scores improved. One says: 'A new teacher, better resources, and a full moon all worked together.' The other says: 'The new teacher alone explains the improvement.' Which reasoning principle supports the second student, and why?

options.A: The principle of charity, because we should assume the most generous interpretation of available evidence
options.B: Occam's Razor, because when multiple explanations fit the data, the simplest one requiring fewest assumptions should be preferred
options.C: Falsifiability, because the second student's explanation can be more easily tested and disproven
options.D: The burden of proof, because the first student must prove each cause individually before making claims

questions.explanation: Occam's Razor (the principle of parsimony) states that among competing hypotheses that equally explain observed evidence, the one making the fewest assumptions should be preferred — the second student correctly avoids introducing the unverified lunar variable. Option C is a common confusion: falsifiability (Popper's criterion) is about whether a theory can in principle be disproven, not about choosing between simpler and more complex explanations.

questions.title: Bias in Data Sampling
questions.prompt: A student surveys 50 classmates about their favourite school subject to represent the views of all students in her country. Analyse the most significant problem with generalising from this sample.

options.A: The sample is too small; she needs at least 1,000 responses for any conclusion to be valid
options.B: The sample is biased because classmates share the same school environment and are not representative of all students nationally
options.C: The survey method is flawed because students may lie about their favourite subjects
options.D: The generalisation is invalid because different countries have different school subjects, making comparison impossible

questions.explanation: The core problem is sampling bias — classmates from the same school share teachers, curriculum, and culture, making them a non-representative subset of all students nationally; valid generalisation requires a random, representative sample across diverse contexts. Option A represents a common misconception that sample validity is purely about size; a biased sample of any size, including 10,000, would still produce unreliable generalisations.

questions.title: Appeal to Authority Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'My favourite footballer says this energy drink improves athletic performance, so it must be true.' Compare this to a sports scientist citing a peer-reviewed study on the same drink. Why is one argument stronger?

options.A: The footballer's argument is stronger because personal experience is more reliable than theoretical studies
options.B: Both arguments are equally strong because both cite an authority in their respective fields
options.C: The scientist's argument is stronger because peer-reviewed evidence represents relevant expertise and methodological scrutiny
options.D: Neither argument is valid because no study or testimony can prove a product's effectiveness

questions.explanation: Appealing to a celebrity who lacks relevant expertise in a domain is a logical fallacy; the sports scientist's peer-reviewed study carries legitimate epistemic weight because it represents domain-relevant expertise and has undergone methodological review by other experts. Option B is a key misconception — not all authorities are equal; the fallacy of appeal to authority specifically concerns citing someone outside their area of genuine expertise.

questions.title: Contrapositive Logic
questions.prompt: A rule states: 'If a student completes all assignments, they pass the course.' Which of the following is the logically equivalent contrapositive of this statement?

options.A: If a student does not complete all assignments, they do not pass the course
options.B: If a student passes the course, they completed all assignments
options.C: If a student does not pass the course, they did not complete all assignments
options.D: If a student completes some assignments, they may pass the course

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'If P then Q' is 'If not Q then not P,' which is logically equivalent to the original; for this statement, that becomes 'If a student does not pass the course, they did not complete all assignments.' Option A is the common confusion of the contrapositive with the 'inverse' (negating both parts without switching them), which is not logically equivalent to the original.

questions.title: Evaluating Statistical Claims
questions.prompt: A headline reads: 'New study: 80% of people who eat breakfast get better grades.' A student concludes breakfast causes better grades. What additional information is most critical before accepting this causal claim?

options.A: The total number of people in the study and whether the sample was large enough
options.B: Whether the study controlled for confounding variables like socioeconomic status and sleep quality
options.C: Whether the researchers liked breakfast themselves, as this could indicate personal bias
options.D: The type of breakfast eaten, because healthy and unhealthy breakfasts may have different effects

questions.explanation: To establish causation rather than mere correlation, a study must control for confounding variables — factors like socioeconomic status affect both the likelihood of eating breakfast and academic performance, making the relationship potentially spurious without controls. Option A addresses statistical power (sample size), which is relevant but secondary; the more fundamental issue is whether the study design can distinguish correlation from causation at all.

questions.title: Equivocation Fallacy
questions.prompt: Identify the error: 'A sharp mind is valuable. This knife has a sharp blade. Therefore, this knife has something valuable in common with a great thinker.' What logical error makes this argument flawed?

options.A: False analogy, because knives and minds cannot be meaningfully compared
options.B: Equivocation, because the word 'sharp' is used with two different meanings across the argument
options.C: Circular reasoning, because the argument assumes sharpness is valuable without proving it
options.D: Hasty generalisation, because not all minds are sharp and not all knives are sharp

questions.explanation: Equivocation occurs when a key word shifts meaning between premises — 'sharp' means intellectually acute when applied to a mind but physically keen-edged when applied to a blade, making the syllogism deceptively invalid. Option A is a misconception; the flaw is not that the two things are incomparable in general, but that a single word is being used in two distinct senses to create a misleading connection.

questions.title: Falsifiability and Science
questions.prompt: A student proposes: 'There is an invisible dragon in my room that cannot be detected by any instrument, leaves no footprints, and makes no sound.' A classmate argues this claim is unscientific. Evaluate the classmate's objection using the concept of falsifiability.

options.A: The classmate is wrong; the claim is scientific because it is about something that could exist in nature
options.B: The classmate is correct; because no possible observation could disprove the claim, it is not falsifiable and falls outside science
options.C: The classmate is wrong; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, so the dragon could still be real
options.D: The classmate is correct, but only because dragons are mythological and therefore automatically unscientific

questions.explanation: Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion holds that a claim is scientific only if there is some conceivable observation or experiment that could prove it false; by making the dragon undetectable by any means, the student has deliberately removed every possible disconfirmation, which is what makes it non-scientific. Option C, while philosophically interesting, misunderstands the issue — the problem is not whether the dragon exists but whether the claim is structured in a way that could in principle be tested.

questions.title: Bandwagon Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Everyone in my school uses this revision app, so it must be the best way to study.' Examine the logical weakness of this argument and compare it with evidence-based reasoning.

options.A: The argument is strong because widespread use indicates a product has been tested by many people
options.B: The argument commits the bandwagon fallacy; popularity does not establish effectiveness, which requires empirical evidence
options.C: The argument commits a hasty generalisation because the student has not surveyed every student in the school
options.D: The argument is weak only because 'everyone' is an exaggeration, but the underlying logic is sound

questions.explanation: The bandwagon fallacy (argumentum ad populum) assumes that something is good or correct because many people believe or do it; popularity is a social fact, not evidence of effectiveness, which would require controlled comparison of learning outcomes. Option D is a subtle misconception — even if the claim were literally true that every student used the app, consensus among users would still not constitute evidence of effectiveness.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Limits
questions.prompt: A student examines the sequence: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and confidently states: 'The rule is perfect squares.' Another student points out the rule could equally be 'differences increase by 2 each time.' Analyse what this situation reveals about pattern-based reasoning.

options.A: The first student is correct because perfect squares is the most common mathematical sequence
options.B: The second student is wrong because an equivalent rule expressed differently does not constitute a different rule
options.C: Both rules describe the same sequence so far, illustrating that data alone cannot uniquely determine the underlying rule
options.D: Pattern recognition is always unreliable and should be replaced entirely by algebraic proof

questions.explanation: Both rules — perfect squares and 'differences increase by 2' — generate exactly the same sequence up to the observed terms; this illustrates that any finite set of data is compatible with multiple hypotheses, known in philosophy of science as the problem of underdetermination. Option B is incorrect because even though the two descriptions are mathematically equivalent here, they represent genuinely different generative rules that would diverge for sequences modified slightly differently.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning and Logic
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If it is wrong to harm one person for the benefit of five, then it is always wrong to sacrifice one person's interests for the majority.' Evaluate whether this principle applies consistently across all ethical situations.

options.A: Yes, the principle is consistent because ethical rules must apply universally without exception to have any meaning
options.B: No, because the principle ignores the scale of harm — taxing individuals to fund hospitals sacrifices some personal wealth for majority benefit without being clearly unethical
options.C: Yes, because utilitarian ethics, the dominant ethical framework, agrees that individual rights should always override majority interests
options.D: No, because the principle only applies to physical harm, not to economic or social trade-offs

questions.explanation: The student's principle overgeneralises from a specific context (physical harm to one person) to all situations; everyday social arrangements like taxation involve individuals contributing resources for collective benefit and are widely considered ethically acceptable, showing the principle does not apply universally. Option C is a significant misconception — utilitarianism actually holds the opposite view, prioritising the greatest good for the greatest number, even at individual cost.

questions.title: Loaded Question Fallacy
questions.prompt: A survey asks students: 'How often do you waste time on social media instead of studying?' Identify the logical problem embedded in this question and explain how it affects the validity of responses.

options.A: The question is too vague because 'social media' could mean many different platforms
options.B: The question contains a loaded presupposition — 'waste time' assumes social media use is unproductive, biasing responses before they are given
options.C: The question commits a false dilemma by implying students only study or use social media
options.D: The question is an example of leading evidence because it presents social media as the cause of poor study habits

questions.explanation: A loaded question embeds a presupposition that the respondent has not agreed to — by using 'waste time,' the question assumes social media is unproductive before any answer is given, making it impossible to respond without implicitly accepting this characterisation. Option C is a misconception; while the question implies a contrast, it does not present only two exclusive options — it specifically uses the loaded framing as its primary flaw.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this syllogism: Premise 1: All mammals are warm-blooded. Premise 2: Whales are mammals. Conclusion: Whales are warm-blooded. A student says the argument is strong because the conclusion sounds true. Evaluate whether the argument is valid, sound, or both, and explain why the student's reasoning is insufficient.

options.A: It is valid and sound, but the student's reasoning is wrong because truth of conclusion alone does not establish logical validity
options.B: It is valid but not sound, because the premises have not been scientifically verified in this context
options.C: It is sound but not valid, because the conclusion follows from the premises but the premises are unproven
options.D: It is neither valid nor sound because syllogisms only work with abstract categories, not real animals

questions.explanation: A deductive argument is valid if the conclusion must follow from the premises, and sound if it is valid AND its premises are true. Here both premises are factually true and the structure is formally valid, making it sound. The student's error is thinking that a true conclusion alone proves the argument is good — a conclusion can be true even in an invalid argument, so truth of conclusion is not sufficient evidence of validity.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student investigating whether social media causes anxiety only reads articles that support her hypothesis and ignores three peer-reviewed studies showing no clear link. Which cognitive bias does this best illustrate, and why does it undermine her conclusion?

options.A: Availability heuristic, because she is using the most memorable information rather than all available data
options.B: Confirmation bias, because she is selectively gathering only evidence that supports her pre-existing belief
options.C: Anchoring bias, because her initial hypothesis acts as an anchor that skews all subsequent judgements
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect, because she overestimates her ability to evaluate complex psychological research

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias specifically describes the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence — exactly what this student is doing by disregarding peer-reviewed studies. The availability heuristic (Option A) refers to judging likelihood based on how easily examples come to mind, not selective reading of sources, so it does not accurately describe this scenario.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a group of 40 students, 22 study French, 18 study Spanish, and 5 study both. A student claims that exactly 5 students study neither language. Analyse this claim using set logic and identify whether it is correct.

options.A: Correct, because 22 + 18 − 5 = 35, and 40 − 35 = 5 study neither
options.B: Incorrect, because 22 + 18 − 5 = 35, and 40 − 35 = 5, so 0 study neither
options.C: Incorrect, because you must add both groups first giving 40, meaning everyone studies at least one language
options.D: Correct, because subtracting the overlap from both sets gives 15 + 13 = 28, and 40 − 28 = 12 study neither

questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: |French ∪ Spanish| = 22 + 18 − 5 = 35. Subtracting from the total gives 40 − 35 = 5 students who study neither, confirming the claim is correct. Option C incorrectly adds the two groups without subtracting the overlap, yielding 40, which would wrongly imply every student studies at least one language.

questions.title: Inductive vs Deductive Reasoning
questions.prompt: Compare inductive and deductive reasoning. A doctor examines 200 patients and notices that those who sleep fewer than six hours consistently score lower on memory tests. She concludes: 'Sleep deprivation reduces memory performance.' Which type of reasoning is this, and what is its primary limitation?

options.A: Deductive reasoning; it is limited because the sample of 200 may not represent all humans
options.B: Inductive reasoning; it is limited because the conclusion could still be false even if all observations are true
options.C: Inductive reasoning; it is limited because the premises are not stated explicitly in formal logical form
options.D: Deductive reasoning; it is limited because the conclusion goes beyond what can be proven from the premises

questions.explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion, which is precisely what the doctor does — observing a pattern across 200 cases and generalising. Its defining limitation is that no finite number of confirming observations guarantees the truth of the general conclusion; a single counter-example could disprove it. Option A correctly identifies the reasoning as inductive but misidentifies its primary logical limitation as sample size, when the deeper issue is the logical gap between observations and universal conclusions.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Flaws
questions.prompt: A student hypothesises that drinking water before a test improves scores. She gives water to the ten highest-achieving students in her class and compares their scores to the rest. Identify the most significant flaw in her experiment design.

options.A: She did not measure how much water each student drank, so the variable is not precisely controlled
options.B: Her sample is too small to draw any conclusions regardless of the results
options.C: She selected participants based on prior achievement, creating a biased sample that confounds her variable
options.D: She failed to get parental consent before conducting her experiment on classmates

questions.explanation: By choosing the ten highest-achieving students to receive water, she introduces a confounding variable: their superior performance may be due to prior ability rather than hydration. This selection bias makes it impossible to isolate the effect of water on scores. Option A is a real concern but is secondary — the more fundamental problem is that the two groups are not comparable to begin with, so even precise measurement of water quantity would not rescue the design.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Application
questions.prompt: A logician presents the following argument: Premise 1: If the alarm is working, it will sound when triggered. Premise 2: The alarm did not sound when triggered. What is the logically valid conclusion, and which argument form does this represent?

options.A: The alarm was not triggered; this is modus ponens
options.B: The alarm is not working; this is modus tollens
options.C: The alarm may or may not be working; this is a fallacy of denying the antecedent
options.D: The alarm is not working; this is affirming the consequent

questions.explanation: Modus tollens has the form: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Here, P = alarm is working, Q = alarm sounds when triggered. Since Q is false (alarm did not sound), we validly conclude P is false (alarm is not working). Option D incorrectly labels this as affirming the consequent, which would be the invalid form: If P then Q; Q is true; therefore P — the opposite logical structure.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a debate about school canteen food, a student says: 'We should ignore Priya's argument for healthier options — she failed her last science test, so she clearly doesn't understand nutrition.' Evaluate this reasoning and identify the logical error.

options.A: It is a false dilemma, because it implies the only options are accepting or rejecting Priya's argument based on her test score
options.B: It is an ad hominem fallacy, because it attacks the person rather than engaging with the content of her argument
options.C: It is an appeal to authority, because it uses academic performance as a measure of credibility
options.D: It is a hasty generalisation, because one test result cannot represent Priya's overall knowledge

questions.explanation: An ad hominem fallacy occurs when someone attacks the character or personal qualities of the person making the argument instead of addressing the argument itself. The student's test performance is irrelevant to whether her claims about nutrition are correct or not. Option D describes a hasty generalisation, which is about drawing broad conclusions from limited data — it partially applies but does not capture the core logical error, which is the redirection from argument to person.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Practising every day is sufficient to become an expert musician.' Examine this claim carefully. Is daily practice sufficient, necessary, both, or neither for achieving musical expertise?

options.A: It is both necessary and sufficient, because expertise is defined by the accumulation of practice hours alone
options.B: It is necessary but not sufficient, because practice alone does not guarantee expertise without factors like quality of instruction and talent
options.C: It is sufficient but not necessary, because some musicians achieve expertise through intensive short bursts rather than daily practice
options.D: It is neither necessary nor sufficient, because expertise is entirely determined by innate musical ability

questions.explanation: A necessary condition is one that must be present for the outcome to occur — regular, sustained practice is generally considered necessary for expertise. However, it is not sufficient on its own because research such as Ericsson's deliberate practice studies shows that quality of feedback, instruction, and other factors also play crucial roles. Option C is tempting but incorrectly implies daily practice is not required at all, when in fact consistent engagement is widely recognised as a prerequisite for high-level skill.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: A data analyst finds a strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and drowning rates across summer months. A newspaper headline reads: 'Ice cream causes drowning!' Evaluate the headline's reasoning and identify what logical step is missing.

options.A: The headline is correct because a strong correlation in multiple months provides sufficient evidence of causation
options.B: The headline ignores that both variables are likely caused by a third variable — hot weather — making the correlation spurious
options.C: The headline is wrong because correlations between unrelated items are always the result of data collection errors
options.D: The headline should instead claim that drowning causes ice cream sales to increase, which is the more logical direction

questions.explanation: This is a classic example of a spurious correlation driven by a confounding variable: hot weather increases both swimming activity (raising drowning risk) and ice cream consumption simultaneously. Correlation, even when strong, does not establish a causal mechanism without ruling out alternative explanations. Option A is a common misconception — the number of data points increases statistical reliability but still cannot by itself establish causation, which requires controlled experimental evidence.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'If penicillin had never been discovered, the average human lifespan in the 20th century would have been significantly shorter.' Evaluate this counterfactual claim. Which response best assesses its strength?

options.A: The claim is weak because counterfactual statements can never be verified and are therefore meaningless in historical analysis
options.B: The claim is strong and certain because penicillin is scientifically proven to kill bacteria
options.C: The claim is reasonably strong but must acknowledge that alternative antibiotics or treatments might have been developed instead
options.D: The claim is weak because lifespan is determined primarily by diet and genetics, not medical treatments

questions.explanation: A well-constructed counterfactual identifies a plausible chain of consequences while acknowledging alternative pathways. The historian's claim is grounded in real evidence — penicillin dramatically reduced death from bacterial infections — but a rigorous counterfactual must consider that other researchers were close to similar discoveries, meaning alternative antibiotics could have emerged. Option A is wrong because historians widely use counterfactuals as legitimate analytical tools; the inability to verify them directly does not make them meaningless, as they help identify causal significance.

questions.title: Epistemology and Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, a student argues: 'Sense perception is the most reliable way of knowing because we can all see and touch the same physical world.' Which response provides the strongest challenge to this claim?

options.A: Sense perception is actually the least reliable way of knowing because mathematics does not rely on it at all
options.B: Optical illusions and perceptual differences show that sensory data can be systematically misleading, undermining the claim of universality
options.C: The claim is correct because scientific instruments are extensions of our senses and science is our most reliable knowledge system
options.D: The student should have said reason rather than sense perception, since logical deduction produces certain knowledge

questions.explanation: Sense perception is demonstrably fallible: optical illusions like the Müller-Lyer illusion cause virtually all observers to misjudge lengths, and perceptual differences due to culture, expectation, and neurological variation mean we do not all experience the same physical world identically. This directly undermines the claim that shared access to the physical world makes perception reliable. Option C conflates the reliability of scientific methodology with the reliability of raw sensory experience — science is trustworthy precisely because it adds controls and replication to correct for perceptual errors.

questions.title: False Cause Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student notices that countries with more televisions per household tend to have higher life expectancy. She concludes: 'Owning televisions makes people live longer and governments should distribute them to poorer nations.' Identify the primary error in her reasoning.

options.A: She commits the false cause fallacy by inferring that television ownership directly causes longer life when both are likely products of higher national wealth
options.B: She commits a hasty generalisation because she should have examined more countries before drawing a conclusion
options.C: She commits an appeal to ignorance because no evidence has proven that televisions do not improve health
options.D: She commits a slippery slope fallacy because her policy recommendation goes far beyond what the data suggests

questions.explanation: The false cause fallacy (post hoc or non causa pro causa) involves treating a correlation as proof of direct causation. Here, wealth is a confounding variable: wealthier countries can afford both more televisions and better healthcare, explaining the correlation without any causal link between the two. Option B is partially valid — more data is always useful — but the fundamental error is not sample size; it is the unwarranted leap from correlation to causation, which would persist even with a larger dataset.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Limits
questions.prompt: A student examines the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and confidently states: 'The rule is perfect squares, so the pattern will always continue as n².' A second student argues that infinitely many different rules could produce the same first five terms. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The first student is correct because n² is the simplest and therefore the only mathematically valid rule for this sequence
options.B: The second student is correct because any finite set of data points is consistent with infinitely many underlying rules
options.C: Both students are partially correct — n² is the best rule, but only for sequences with fewer than ten terms
options.D: The second student is correct, but this problem only arises when the sequence contains repeated values

questions.explanation: This reflects a fundamental insight in the philosophy of science known as the underdetermination of theory by data: any finite set of observations is logically compatible with infinitely many theories or rules. For five data points, a polynomial of degree five or higher can be constructed to fit them while diverging dramatically at the sixth term. Option A confuses simplicity (Occam's razor) with logical necessity — n² may be the most elegant rule, but parsimony is a practical preference, not a logical proof that it is the only correct rule.

questions.title: Argument Structure Mapping
questions.prompt: Examine this argument: 'Schools should teach coding because coding develops logical thinking, and logical thinking is essential for success in any career.' Which statement best evaluates the logical structure of this argument?

options.A: The argument is valid and sound because both premises are widely accepted and the conclusion follows logically
options.B: The argument is valid in structure but requires examination of whether coding uniquely develops logical thinking better than other subjects
options.C: The argument is invalid because the conclusion is stated before the evidence, which violates logical form
options.D: The argument is a circular argument because it uses success to define logical thinking and logical thinking to define success

questions.explanation: The argument has a valid deductive structure: if coding develops logical thinking and logical thinking is career-essential, then schools should teach coding. However, a key hidden assumption is that coding is a unique or superior way to develop logical thinking — mathematics, chess, and philosophy might achieve the same outcome equally well, weakening the specific conclusion about coding. Option A is overly accepting; it fails to question whether the premises are actually true and whether the argument for coding in particular (as opposed to other subjects) is justified.

questions.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
questions.prompt: After spending three months and significant effort on a science fair project she now realises is deeply flawed, Maria decides to continue anyway, saying: 'I've put too much work into this to quit now.' Evaluate whether Maria's reasoning is logically sound.

options.A: Maria's reasoning is sound because abandoning a project wastes the skills and knowledge already gained
options.B: Maria commits the sunk cost fallacy — past effort that cannot be recovered should not influence future decisions
options.C: Maria's reasoning is sound because perseverance is an important academic skill that should be encouraged
options.D: Maria commits a false dilemma fallacy because she assumes the only options are continuing or quitting entirely

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when past irrecoverable investments (time, money, effort) are used to justify continuing a poor course of action, rather than evaluating the future costs and benefits objectively. Rationally, only future outcomes should guide the decision — if the project is deeply flawed, continuing wastes additional resources for little gain. Option C describes a genuine virtue (perseverance) but conflates it with rational decision-making; perseverance is valuable when applied to viable goals, not when it means continuing with a recognised failure out of psychological discomfort.

questions.title: Logical Negation of Conditionals
questions.prompt: A rule states: 'If a student submits work late, they will receive a penalty.' A student argues: 'I submitted on time, so I definitely won't receive a penalty.' Identify whether the student's conclusion is logically valid.

options.A: Valid, because submitting on time is the logical opposite of submitting late, so the rule guarantees no penalty
options.B: Invalid, because the student commits the fallacy of denying the antecedent — the rule says nothing about consequences of on-time submission
options.C: Valid, because a conditional rule logically implies its contrapositive, which covers on-time submissions
options.D: Invalid, because conditional rules in school contexts are never logically binding and always have exceptions

questions.explanation: The fallacy of denying the antecedent occurs when someone argues: If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q. This is formally invalid. The rule 'if late, then penalty' says nothing about what happens when work is submitted on time — there could be other reasons for a penalty such as plagiarism or incomplete work. Option A is the classic misconception: students often assume that reversing the condition reverses the consequence, but this confuses the conditional with its (invalid) inverse.

questions.title: Evaluating Source Credibility
questions.prompt: A student cites a website that claims a popular vitamin supplement cures colds. The website has no author listed, no references, and sells the supplement directly. Another source is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of 40 studies showing no significant effect. Which principle of argument evaluation best justifies preferring the second source?

options.A: The second source is better because it was published more recently, and newer evidence always supersedes older evidence
options.B: The second source is better because peer review, transparency, and absence of financial conflict of interest make it more epistemically reliable
options.C: The second source is better because it has a larger sample — 40 studies are always more reliable than a single website
options.D: The first source could be equally valid because personal testimonials on commercial websites reflect real human experience

questions.explanation: Epistemic reliability in research depends on peer review (independent expert scrutiny), transparency (named authors, disclosed methods), and absence of conflicts of interest that might bias results. The commercial website fails all three criteria and has a direct financial incentive to promote the product. Option C identifies a relevant factor but is imprecise — the key advantage is not merely quantity but the methodology of meta-analysis and absence of bias, since 40 poorly designed studies would still be less reliable than one rigorous experiment.

questions.title: Applying Occam's Razor
questions.prompt: Two students observe that their school's test results improved after a new timetable was introduced. Student A argues: 'The new timetable caused the improvement.' Student B argues: 'The improvement was caused by the new timetable, combined with a cosmic alignment of planets that boosted student intelligence.' Apply Occam's razor to evaluate these explanations.

options.A: Student B's explanation is better because it considers more variables and is therefore more thorough
options.B: Student A's explanation is preferable because Occam's razor favours the explanation that introduces the fewest unnecessary assumptions
options.C: Neither explanation is valid because neither student conducted a controlled experiment to test their hypothesis
options.D: Student A's explanation is preferable because it was proposed first, giving it priority over later theories

questions.explanation: Occam's razor (the principle of parsimony) states that among competing hypotheses, the one with the fewest unnecessary assumptions should be preferred. Student B's explanation adds an untestable and unsupported claim about planetary alignment, introducing complexity with no evidential basis. Student A's simpler explanation should be provisionally preferred until evidence demands additional complexity. Option C raises a valid methodological concern about causation, but it does not address the question of which explanation is preferable given current information — Occam's razor applies even before controlled experiments are conducted.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Strength
questions.prompt: A student finds her bike lock open and her bicycle missing, and notices fresh tyre tracks leading away from the rack. Using abductive reasoning, she concludes her bike was stolen. Which statement best evaluates the strength of this abductive inference?

options.A: The inference is strong because abductive reasoning always produces the correct explanation when physical evidence is present
options.B: The inference is weak because abductive reasoning can only be applied to scientific experiments, not everyday situations
options.C: The inference is the best available explanation given the evidence, but remains provisional since alternative explanations cannot yet be ruled out
options.D: The inference is strong and certain because theft is the only explanation consistent with an open lock and missing bike

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning (inference to the best explanation) selects the hypothesis that best explains the available evidence, but it is inherently provisional — alternative explanations might exist, such as a family member borrowing the bike or the student misremembering where she parked. The conclusion is the most reasonable inference, not a certain one. Option D overstates certainty: abductive conclusions are always open to revision when new evidence emerges, which is a defining feature of this type of reasoning.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning and Logic
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Lying is always wrong because if everyone lied, society would collapse.' A second student responds: 'But what if lying to a bully prevents serious harm to someone?' Evaluate which type of ethical reasoning each student is using.

options.A: Both students use consequentialist reasoning, because both refer to outcomes — collapse of society and prevention of harm
options.B: The first student uses deontological reasoning based on universal rules; the second uses consequentialist reasoning based on outcomes
options.C: The first student uses virtue ethics by asking what a good person would do; the second uses deontological reasoning
options.D: Both students use deontological reasoning because both are discussing what people should or should not do

questions.explanation: The first student's reasoning echoes Kant's categorical imperative — a rule is moral if it can be universalised without contradiction, placing duty above consequences. This is deontological reasoning. The second student focuses on the real-world outcome (preventing harm), which is the defining feature of consequentialism, particularly utilitarianism. Option A misidentifies the first student's reasoning: the universalisability test is a criterion for the validity of the rule itself, not an analysis of actual consequences, making it deontological in character.

questions.title: Statistical Reasoning Traps
questions.prompt: A school reports: 'Our students' average test score increased by 15 points this year!' However, 80% of students scored between 50 and 55, while a small group of exceptional students scored above 95. Which statistical concept explains why the average may be misleading here?

options.A: Sampling error, because the school did not test a representative sample of students
options.B: The mean is skewed by outliers, making the median a more representative measure of typical student performance
options.C: Regression to the mean, because high scores in one year tend to decrease in the following year
options.D: Placebo effect, because students may have performed better simply because they expected improvement

questions.explanation: When a distribution is skewed by a small number of extreme high scores (outliers), the mean is pulled upward and no longer represents the typical student. In this case, the median — the midpoint of scores when ranked — would remain in the 50–55 range and give a more accurate picture of most students' performance. Option C describes regression to the mean, which is a real statistical phenomenon but refers to the tendency of extreme measurements to move toward the average over time, not the problem of outliers distorting a reported average.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogical Arguments
questions.prompt: A politician argues: 'Running a country is just like running a business — so we should hire a successful CEO as our leader.' Evaluate the strength of this analogy and identify its most significant weakness.

options.A: The analogy is strong because both governments and businesses manage large budgets and teams of people
options.B: The analogy is weak because it ignores fundamental differences: governments must balance competing social values and cannot simply maximise profit
options.C: The analogy is weak because CEOs are not elected, meaning they lack public speaking skills needed for political leadership
options.D: The analogy is strong if the CEO has international business experience, which is equivalent to foreign policy expertise

questions.explanation: An analogy is only as strong as the relevant similarities between the two things being compared. While governments and businesses share some features (managing resources, decision-making), the differences are fundamental: governments must weigh justice, equality, welfare, and democratic accountability rather than profit, and their 'failure' cannot be resolved through bankruptcy. Option A acknowledges superficial similarities but ignores the disanalogies that matter most for the conclusion being drawn — that a CEO skill-set transfers directly to political leadership.

questions.title: Distinguishing Evidence Types
questions.prompt: A student wants to justify the claim that 'teenagers sleep less than the recommended eight hours.' Rank the following pieces of evidence from most to least convincing: (i) a peer-reviewed sleep study of 2,000 adolescents; (ii) a survey of her twelve classmates; (iii) a quote from a celebrity who says she only needs five hours. Which ranking is correct?

options.A: i, ii, iii — because sample size and peer review make (i) most reliable, (ii) provides some local data, and (iii) is anecdotal
options.B: ii, i, iii — because the classmate survey is most relevant to this specific student's local context
options.C: iii, i, ii — because celebrity endorsements reach the widest audience and therefore reflect broader public experience
options.D: i, iii, ii — because expert celebrities often have access to research that informs their personal choices

questions.explanation: Evidence quality depends on sample size, representativeness, and methodological rigour. A peer-reviewed study of 2,000 adolescents meets all three criteria, making it the strongest support for a general claim. The classmate survey has a tiny, unrepresentative sample but at least consists of actual data. A celebrity quote is anecdotal and has no methodological basis — the celebrity's personal sleep needs may be atypical and provide no information about teenagers generally. Option B incorrectly prioritises local relevance over scientific reliability when making a general empirical claim.

questions.title: Evaluating Syllogism Validity
questions.prompt: Consider this argument: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. All dogs are mammals. Therefore, all dogs are warm-blooded.' A student claims this syllogism is valid AND sound. Evaluate: under what condition could a syllogism be valid but NOT sound?

options.A: When the conclusion follows from the premises, but at least one premise is false
options.B: When the conclusion is false, even though both premises are true
options.C: When the argument contains more than two premises
options.D: When the conclusion introduces a new concept not present in the premises

questions.explanation: Validity means the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises; soundness additionally requires all premises to be true. A valid argument can have a false premise — e.g., 'All fish are mammals; salmon are fish; therefore salmon are mammals' is valid in form but unsound because the first premise is false. Option B is wrong because if both premises are true and the argument is valid, the conclusion must also be true — a true-premise valid argument cannot produce a false conclusion.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student researching the effects of social media on mental health only reads articles that support her hypothesis that social media is harmful, dismissing contrary studies as 'poorly designed.' Which cognitive bias is most precisely at work, and why does it undermine her research methodology?

options.A: Availability heuristic, because she only recalls vivid examples of harm
options.B: Confirmation bias, because she selectively gathers evidence that supports her pre-existing belief
options.C: Anchoring bias, because her first reading sets the benchmark for all later judgements
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect, because she overestimates her ability to assess study quality

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias specifically describes the tendency to seek, interpret, and remember information in a way that confirms one's existing beliefs — exactly what the student is doing by filtering out contradictory studies. This undermines research methodology because it violates the principle of falsifiability and prevents objective evaluation. The availability heuristic (Option A) concerns how easily examples come to mind, not selective reading; it does not capture the systematic dismissal of contrary evidence.

questions.title: Necessary vs. Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Analyse this claim: 'Practising for 10,000 hours is sufficient to become an expert in any field.' A classmate counters: 'But 10,000 hours of poor practice won't make you an expert.' Which logical concept does the classmate's counter-example best illustrate?

options.A: That 10,000 hours is a necessary but not sufficient condition for expertise
options.B: That 10,000 hours is neither necessary nor sufficient for expertise
options.C: That quality of practice is a necessary condition, showing 10,000 hours alone is not sufficient
options.D: That 10,000 hours is a sufficient condition only when combined with talent

questions.explanation: The classmate's counter-example shows that mere quantity of hours does not guarantee expertise if quality is absent — demonstrating that 10,000 hours is not, by itself, sufficient. The counter-example specifically highlights that deliberate, high-quality practice is a necessary additional condition. Option A is wrong because the classmate's point is specifically about sufficiency, not about whether 10,000 hours is necessary; some experts reach mastery in far fewer hours in certain domains.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: A student notes that the sun has risen every single day in recorded human history and concludes it will definitely rise tomorrow. Evaluate: which philosopher's argument most directly challenges the reliability of this type of reasoning, and what is the core problem identified?

options.A: Descartes, who argued that sensory experience is always potentially deceptive
options.B: Hume, who argued that past regularities give no logical guarantee of future events
options.C: Popper, who argued that scientific claims must be falsifiable to be meaningful
options.D: Aristotle, who argued that inductive reasoning only applies to particular cases

questions.explanation: David Hume formulated the 'problem of induction,' arguing that no matter how many times an event has occurred, logic alone cannot justify certainty about future occurrences — the connection between past and future is a habit of mind, not a logical necessity. This directly challenges the student's leap from repeated observations to certainty. Popper (Option C) responded to Hume by proposing falsifiability, but his contribution is specifically about scientific methodology, not the core philosophical problem of inductive justification.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 50 students, 30 like science, 25 like art, and 10 like neither. A student draws a Venn diagram and claims the overlap — students who like both — must be exactly 15. Justify or refute this claim using set logic.

options.A: The claim is wrong; the overlap must be 5 because 30 + 25 = 55 and the survey has 50 students
options.B: The claim is correct; 15 students must like both because the two groups together account for exactly 65 students
options.C: The claim is correct; 15 is the overlap because (30 + 25) − (50 − 10) = 15
options.D: The claim is wrong; without additional data about preferences, the overlap cannot be determined

questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: |Science ∪ Art| = 50 − 10 = 40 students like at least one subject. Therefore |Science ∩ Art| = |Science| + |Art| − |Science ∪ Art| = 30 + 25 − 40 = 15. The student's claim of 15 is correct, and Option C expresses this calculation accurately. Option A is wrong because it subtracts from the total of 50 without first removing the 10 who like neither, misapplying the formula.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Application
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by both 2 and 3. Premise 2: The number 49 is not divisible by 2. What can be logically concluded using modus tollens, and which of the following precisely captures that conclusion?

options.A: 49 is not divisible by 3
options.B: 49 is not divisible by 6
options.C: 49 is divisible by neither 2 nor 6
options.D: No conclusion can be drawn because the premises only refer to numbers divisible by 6

questions.explanation: Modus tollens states: if P → Q and ¬Q, then ¬P. Here, P = 'divisible by 6' and Q = 'divisible by 2 AND 3.' Since 49 is not divisible by 2, Q is false, so we can conclude P is false: 49 is not divisible by 6. Option A ('not divisible by 3') cannot be concluded — 49 = 7×7, so it actually is not divisible by 3 either, but this cannot be derived from these premises alone; the logic does not reach that conclusion.

questions.title: False Dichotomy Identification
questions.prompt: A school council member argues: 'Either we increase the school day by one hour to improve results, or we accept that our students will fall behind globally.' Identify the precise logical flaw in this argument and explain why it weakens the council member's position.

options.A: Ad hominem, because the argument attacks students' work ethic rather than the evidence
options.B: False dichotomy, because it presents only two options when multiple alternatives exist
options.C: Hasty generalisation, because global comparisons involve too many variables
options.D: Circular reasoning, because improved results are used to justify the longer school day

questions.explanation: A false dichotomy (also called a false dilemma) artificially restricts a debate to two options, ignoring others — such as improving teaching quality, curriculum reform, or better use of existing time. This weakens the argument because the council member has not justified why only these two outcomes are possible. Option C (hasty generalisation) concerns drawing broad conclusions from limited samples, which is not the primary error here; the flaw is in the structure of the choice presented, not the sample size.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Design
questions.prompt: A student hypothesises that caffeine improves short-term memory. She tests 20 students who volunteered after seeing a poster in the cafeteria, gives them all caffeine, then measures their memory scores. Compare this method to a controlled experiment and identify the most critical design flaw.

options.A: The sample is too small to produce statistically significant results
options.B: There is no control group, so there is no baseline to compare memory improvement against
options.C: The students self-selected, introducing sampling bias that may skew who participates
options.D: Memory was only measured once, so changes over time cannot be tracked

questions.explanation: The most critical flaw is the absence of a control group — without students who received no caffeine under identical conditions, there is no way to determine whether any observed memory scores are due to caffeine or other factors such as test familiarity or natural variation. This is the fundamental requirement for a controlled experiment. Self-selection bias (Option C) is also a real problem, but it is secondary: even with a perfectly random sample, without a control group the comparison needed to test the hypothesis is impossible.

questions.title: Analogical Reasoning Strength
questions.prompt: A politician argues: 'Running a country is just like running a business — you need to cut costs and maximise profit.' Examine the strength of this analogy. What is the most significant structural weakness that undermines it?

options.A: Countries are larger than businesses, so management techniques cannot scale effectively
options.B: Governments have obligations to equity and public welfare that conflict with profit maximisation as a goal
options.C: Politicians rarely have business experience, making the comparison misleading in practice
options.D: Both entities deal with budgets, so the analogy may actually be stronger than it appears

questions.explanation: The core weakness is a difference in purpose: businesses aim to maximise profit for shareholders, while governments must balance competing obligations — healthcare, education, justice, and the welfare of all citizens, including those who are not profitable to serve. When the goals differ fundamentally, key conclusions drawn from the analogy (e.g., cut unprofitable services) break down. Option A is wrong because scale is not the primary structural failure; the analogy fails because of mismatched objectives, not size.

questions.title: Counterfactual Causal Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'If penicillin had not been discovered in 1928, millions more would have died from bacterial infections during World War II.' A student challenges this by saying, 'Someone else would have discovered it soon anyway.' Evaluate which reasoning strategy the student is using and assess its validity.

options.A: The student uses inductive reasoning, generalising from past patterns of scientific discovery
options.B: The student uses a counterfactual claim to challenge the historian's counterfactual, which is logically legitimate but empirically uncertain
options.C: The student commits a post hoc fallacy by assuming discovery follows a fixed timeline
options.D: The student uses deductive reasoning, proving the historian's conclusion is necessarily false

questions.explanation: The student is constructing an alternative counterfactual — imagining a scenario where discovery still occurs — to challenge the historian's hypothetical. This is a legitimate logical strategy; one can challenge a counterfactual with another. However, it remains empirically uncertain because there is no guarantee another scientist would have made the same discovery in time for WWII — Florey and Chain's work developing penicillin for clinical use was itself a complex, historically contingent process. Option C is wrong because post hoc fallacy concerns incorrectly inferring causation from sequence, which is not what the student is doing.

questions.title: Identifying Ad Hominem
questions.prompt: During a class debate on climate policy, Riya presents data from three peer-reviewed studies. Her opponent responds: 'Riya only cares about this because her parents are environmental activists — she's biased.' Identify the precise logical error in the opponent's response and justify your answer.

options.A: Straw man, because the opponent misrepresents Riya's argument as purely personal
options.B: Ad hominem, because the opponent attacks Riya's character rather than the evidence she presented
options.C: Appeal to authority, because Riya's use of peer-reviewed studies is itself a form of bias
options.D: Genetic fallacy, because the opponent dismisses the argument based solely on its origins

questions.explanation: The genetic fallacy occurs when an argument is dismissed or accepted based on its source or origin rather than its content — the opponent rejects Riya's data because of where her motivation comes from, not because the studies are flawed. While this overlaps superficially with ad hominem, the genetic fallacy is the more precise term when the attack specifically concerns the origin of a belief or argument rather than a personal insult. Option B (ad hominem) is the closest distractor and partially correct, but the genetic fallacy more precisely names the error of dismissing evidence based solely on its origins.

questions.title: TOK Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, a student argues: 'Mathematics is the only area of knowledge where we can achieve absolute certainty, because its truths are derived purely through reason.' Which counterargument most effectively challenges this claim using a specific example from mathematics itself?

options.A: Mathematical models of the real world often produce inaccurate predictions, showing that applied maths is uncertain
options.B: Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that in any sufficiently complex formal system, there are true statements that cannot be proven within that system
options.C: Mathematicians frequently disagree about definitions, proving that even pure mathematics involves subjective judgement
options.D: Historical changes in the acceptance of zero and negative numbers show that mathematical knowledge evolves over time

questions.explanation: Kurt Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) proved that within any consistent formal mathematical system powerful enough to describe arithmetic, there exist true statements that cannot be proved within the system itself. This fundamentally challenges the claim that mathematics offers absolute certainty purely through reason — some truths are beyond formal proof. Option D (evolution of mathematical concepts) is a plausible historical challenge but addresses changing conventions rather than a logical limit on certainty within mathematics.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Limits
questions.prompt: A student observes the sequence: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and concludes the rule is 'square numbers.' She predicts the next term is 36. A second student argues the rule could be a polynomial fitting all five points that gives a different sixth term. Which statement best evaluates this dispute?

options.A: The first student is correct because square numbers are the simplest explanation and simplicity guarantees correctness
options.B: Both rules are equally valid; additional terms are needed to test which rule is more predictive
options.C: The first student's rule is preferable under parsimony, but the second student is logically correct that infinitely many rules fit any finite sequence
options.D: The second student is wrong because polynomials cannot produce sequences that include only perfect squares

questions.explanation: By Lagrange interpolation, infinitely many polynomial functions pass through any finite set of points, meaning any finite sequence has infinitely many valid generating rules. The first student's rule is preferable by Occam's Razor (parsimony — prefer the simpler explanation) but this is a methodological preference, not a logical proof of uniqueness. Option A is wrong because simplicity is a heuristic, not a logical guarantee — parsimony guides us but does not prove a rule correct.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Evaluation
questions.prompt: A school administrator argues: 'If we allow students to use calculators in Year 7, they will never learn basic arithmetic, and by Year 10 they won't be able to do any mathematics at all.' Evaluate whether this constitutes a slippery slope fallacy and under what conditions it might be a legitimate concern.

options.A: It is a slippery slope fallacy because each step in the chain is asserted without evidence that one stage leads inevitably to the next
options.B: It is not a fallacy because research consistently confirms that calculator use eliminates arithmetic skill development
options.C: It is a hasty generalisation because the administrator is assuming all students will respond identically to calculator use
options.D: It is a legitimate causal chain because technological dependence in schools is a well-documented phenomenon

questions.explanation: A slippery slope fallacy occurs when a chain of consequences is asserted without sufficient evidence that each step necessarily leads to the next. The administrator's argument skips from 'calculator use' to 'complete mathematical inability' without justifying the intermediate steps. It would be a legitimate concern — not a fallacy — only if empirical evidence demonstrated each causal link in the chain. Option C (hasty generalisation) is partially relevant but does not identify the primary structural flaw, which is the unsubstantiated causal chain.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Precision
