questions.prompt: A doctor observes a patient with fever, swollen lymph nodes, and fatigue. She concludes: 'The most likely explanation is a bacterial infection.' A student says this is deductive reasoning. Examine whether the student is correct and justify your answer.

options.A: The student is correct — the doctor is using deductive reasoning by applying a general medical rule to a specific case
options.B: The student is incorrect — the doctor is using inductive reasoning by generalising from one patient's symptoms
options.C: The student is incorrect — the doctor is using abductive reasoning by inferring the best explanation for observed symptoms
options.D: The student is partially correct — medical diagnosis uses a hybrid of deductive and inductive reasoning simultaneously

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning — introduced by philosopher C.S. Peirce — involves inferring the most plausible explanation for a set of observations, rather than deriving a certain conclusion. The doctor is not deducing (which requires the conclusion to follow necessarily) nor purely inducing (which generates generalisations); she is identifying the best hypothesis that accounts for all symptoms. Option D is plausible but imprecise; the specific name for reasoning from evidence to the best explanation is abduction, and that is what the doctor is primarily doing.

questions.title: Evaluating Correlation Claims
questions.prompt: A study finds a strong positive correlation (r = 0.89) between the number of fire stations in a city and the number of building fires recorded. A journalist concludes: 'Fire stations cause fires.' Evaluate this conclusion and identify what the data most likely actually shows.

options.A: The conclusion is valid because a correlation of 0.89 is strong enough to establish causation
options.B: The conclusion is flawed; a confounding variable — city population size — likely explains both the number of stations and fires
options.C: The conclusion is flawed; fire stations reduce fires, so the correlation must be incorrectly calculated
options.D: The conclusion is valid because the data is observational and therefore more reliable than experimental data

questions.explanation: This is a classic example of a confounding variable: larger cities have both more fire stations and more buildings, therefore more fires — population size drives both variables simultaneously. The correlation is real but the causal inference is false. Even a correlation of r = 0.89 cannot establish causation; correlation and causation are logically distinct. Option A is wrong because statistical strength of correlation never, by itself, establishes a causal direction — this is a foundational principle of research methodology.

questions.title: Argument by Analogy Limits
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'The human brain is like a computer — it processes input, stores memory, and produces output. Therefore, we should be able to upgrade human intelligence the way we upgrade computer hardware.' What is the most precise logical weakness in this argument?

options.A: The analogy is too simple because computers are made of silicon while brains are biological
options.B: The argument uses the analogy to justify a practical conclusion in a domain where the analogy's differences are decisive — brains lack modular, replaceable hardware components
options.C: The argument commits a false dichotomy by implying intelligence can only be improved through hardware, not software
options.D: The student is committing an appeal to technology fallacy by assuming newer is always better

questions.explanation: Analogies justify conclusions only when the similarities are relevant and the differences are not decisive. Here, the crucial difference is that brains are not modular: neurons are interconnected through billions of synaptic connections that develop over time, cannot be 'swapped out,' and are biologically unique to each individual — unlike replaceable RAM or CPU chips. Simply sharing functional descriptions (input/processing/output) does not mean the physical mechanisms can be treated the same way. Option A is too superficial; the material difference alone is not the logical weakness — the decisive issue is whether the analogy's disanalogies undermine the conclusion.

questions.title: Epistemic Humility and Bias
questions.prompt: The Dunning-Kruger effect describes a cognitive bias where individuals with limited knowledge in a domain overestimate their competence. Which scenario most precisely illustrates the Dunning-Kruger effect rather than simple overconfidence?

options.A: An expert surgeon believes she performs operations better than most colleagues, though peer review shows average results
options.B: A student who has read one article on economics confidently tells his class he fully understands macroeconomic policy
options.C: A chess grandmaster underestimates a novice opponent and loses due to overconfidence
options.D: A student refuses to answer any question she is not completely certain about, fearing mistakes

questions.explanation: The Dunning-Kruger effect specifically involves low-competence individuals who lack the metacognitive ability to recognise their own incompetence — they don't know enough to know what they don't know. The student with one article's worth of knowledge who believes he fully understands complex macroeconomics exemplifies this. Option A describes an expert with mildly inflated self-assessment — this is closer to the inverse Dunning-Kruger pattern (experts sometimes underestimate their ability relative to others) and is not the classic low-competence case.

questions.title: Deductive Argument Structure
questions.prompt: Examine this argument: 'No reptiles are warm-blooded. Some dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Therefore, some dinosaurs were not reptiles.' Determine whether the conclusion follows validly from the premises and whether the argument is sound given current scientific understanding.

options.A: The argument is both valid and sound because all three statements are accepted as true by modern science
options.B: The argument is valid — the conclusion follows from the premises — but unsound because Premise 1 is disputed by evidence that some reptiles may regulate temperature
options.C: The argument is invalid because the conclusion introduces the concept of warm-bloodedness, which is not in both premises
options.D: The argument is valid in form, but unsound because modern palaeontology classifies birds (warm-blooded dinosaur descendants) as a subset of reptiles, making Premise 1 false

questions.explanation: The argument's form is valid: if no reptiles are warm-blooded and some dinosaurs are warm-blooded, then those warm-blooded dinosaurs cannot be reptiles — the conclusion follows. However, it is unsound because Premise 1 is false under modern cladistic taxonomy: birds are warm-blooded, birds are living dinosaurs, and birds are classified within Reptilia — making warm-blooded reptiles demonstrably real. Option B is partially correct about Premise 1 being disputed, but Option D is more precise and scientifically grounded, identifying the specific mechanism (bird-dinosaur-reptile classification) that falsifies Premise 1.

questions.title: Occam's Razor Application
questions.prompt: Two students explain why their school's internet went down. Student A says: 'A cable was probably cut near the building.' Student B says: 'The internet provider had a regional outage, which caused the school's router to overheat, which triggered an automatic shutdown.' The internet provider later confirms a regional outage. Which reasoning principle should have guided the initial evaluation, and does the confirmed outage settle the dispute?

options.A: Occam's Razor initially favours A's simpler explanation, but evidence from the provider confirms B's explanation — showing parsimony is a guide, not a proof
options.B: Occam's Razor confirms A is correct because the confirmed outage still does not match the complexity of B's chain of events
options.C: The principle of falsifiability should guide the evaluation; since neither explanation was testable, no reasoning applies
options.D: Occam's Razor favours B because a regional outage is a single cause that explains the event more completely than a local cable cut

questions.explanation: Occam's Razor (parsimony) states we should prefer the hypothesis with fewer unnecessary assumptions — initially favouring the simpler local cable explanation. However, new evidence (provider confirmation) updates the justified belief, demonstrating that parsimony is a defeasible heuristic rather than a logical law. Even if B's chain of events is more complex, it becomes the better-supported explanation when confirmed. Option D misapplies Occam's Razor — a regional outage is simpler in terms of causes than a local physical cut combined with hardware failure, so parsimony still initially favoured A.

questions.title: Appeal to Nature Fallacy
questions.prompt: A classmate argues: 'We should never use synthetic medicines — anything artificial is harmful to the body. Natural remedies are always safer because they come from nature.' Identify the fallacy and provide the most effective single counter-example to dismantle this reasoning.

options.A: The classmate commits a false dichotomy; the counter-example is that most medicines are partially derived from natural sources anyway
options.B: The classmate commits an appeal to nature fallacy; the counter-example is that botulinum toxin is entirely natural yet is one of the most lethal substances known
options.C: The classmate commits hasty generalisation; the counter-example is that some synthetic medicines like aspirin have been proven safe over decades
options.D: The classmate commits circular reasoning; the counter-example is that 'natural' and 'safe' are not equivalent terms and the argument assumes what it needs to prove

questions.explanation: The appeal to nature fallacy assumes that what is natural is good or safe and what is artificial is harmful — a non-sequitur because the origin of a substance does not determine its safety. Botulinum toxin (produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum) is entirely natural yet is the most acutely toxic protein known to science, with a lethal dose in micrograms. This single counter-example demolishes the claim that 'natural always equals safer.' Option D raises a valid point about circular reasoning but does not provide the precise fallacy name nor a concrete counter-example that would be most persuasive.

questions.title: Falsifiability and Science
questions.prompt: Karl Popper argued that a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable. A student claims: 'The theory that invisible dragons cause earthquakes is just as scientific as plate tectonics, because neither has been fully proven.' Evaluate this student's reasoning and identify the specific flaw.

options.A: The student is correct that proof and falsifiability are the same standard, so both theories should be judged equally
options.B: The student confuses proof with falsifiability — plate tectonics makes testable, falsifiable predictions while the invisible dragon theory, by definition, cannot be tested or refuted
options.C: The student is wrong because plate tectonics has been fully proven through GPS measurements, making it categorically superior
options.D: The student's error is in claiming that dragons are invisible — a falsifiable version of the theory would be scientific

questions.explanation: Popper's criterion is falsifiability, not proof — a scientific theory must make predictions that could in principle be shown to be false by experiment. Plate tectonics predicts measurable continental drift, seismic patterns at specific boundary types, and ocean floor age gradients — all of which have been confirmed and could have been falsified. The invisible dragon theory, because the dragons are stipulated to be invisible and undetectable, cannot generate any testable prediction; it is unfalsifiable and therefore non-scientific. Option C is wrong because Popper explicitly argued that science never 'fully proves' theories — it only corroborates them by surviving falsification attempts.

questions.title: Logical Biconditional Analysis
questions.prompt: A teacher states: 'You will pass the exam if and only if you score 60% or above.' A student scores 58% and fails. Another student claims: 'The teacher's rule also means that anyone who scores 60% or above is guaranteed to pass.' Evaluate whether the second student's claim follows logically from the teacher's statement.

options.A: The second student is wrong — 'if and only if' only tells us what causes failure, not what guarantees passing
options.B: The second student is correct — 'if and only if' is a biconditional that makes scoring 60%+ both necessary and sufficient for passing
options.C: The second student is partially correct — scoring 60%+ is necessary for passing but the teacher may impose additional conditions
options.D: The second student is wrong — 'if and only if' is equivalent to 'if... then' and does not confirm the reverse direction

questions.explanation: A biconditional (if and only if, written P ↔ Q) means both 'if P then Q' AND 'if Q then P.' Here: P = scores ≥60%, Q = passes. The statement establishes scoring ≥60% as both necessary and sufficient for passing. Therefore, the second student's claim is logically correct: anyone scoring 60%+ is guaranteed to pass, and anyone scoring below 60% is guaranteed to fail. Option C incorrectly suggests the biconditional only establishes necessity — this confuses a biconditional with a simple conditional ('if...then'), which only goes one direction.

questions.title: Anchoring Bias in Judgement
questions.prompt: During a charity auction, the auctioneer opens bidding for a painting by announcing: 'Shall we start at $10,000?' The painting sells for $8,500. At a second auction, the same painting is opened at $1,000 and sells for $3,200. Which cognitive phenomenon best explains the price difference, and how does it challenge the assumption of rational decision-making?

options.A: Availability heuristic, because the high opening price makes expensive artworks more memorable and desirable
options.B: Anchoring bias, because the initial price sets a psychological reference point that disproportionately influences subsequent bids
options.C: Sunk cost fallacy, because bidders who heard the high opening price feel committed to higher bids
options.D: Framing effect, because the same painting is presented as more valuable in the first auction than the second

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias (identified by Tversky and Kahneman) occurs when people rely too heavily on the first piece of information received — the anchor — when making judgements. The opening price serves as a cognitive anchor; bidders adjust from it insufficiently, producing final prices that mirror the starting point. This challenges rational decision-making models because the painting's intrinsic value has not changed — only the arbitrary starting number has, yet it dramatically affects outcomes. Option D (framing effect) concerns how presentation of options influences choice, but the specific mechanism here — the numerical anchor — is more precisely captured by anchoring bias.

questions.title: Evaluating Competing Evidence
questions.prompt: Two studies examine whether class size affects student achievement. Study 1 (n=1,200, randomised controlled trial) finds smaller classes improve outcomes significantly. Study 2 (n=80, teacher survey) finds no relationship. A student concludes: 'The evidence is mixed, so no conclusion is possible.' Evaluate this conclusion and identify what a stronger analytical response would be.

options.A: The student is correct — two studies with opposing findings produce genuine equipoise and no conclusion should be drawn
options.B: The student's conclusion is too weak; Study 1 should be weighted more heavily due to its larger sample, randomised design, and reduced risk of bias compared to Study 2
options.C: The student is wrong; Study 2 should be trusted more because teacher surveys capture qualitative nuance that quantitative studies miss
options.D: The student's conclusion is acceptable; in social science research, mixed findings always indicate that more data is needed before any position is defensible

questions.explanation: Not all evidence is equal — a strong analytical response weighs studies by methodological quality. A randomised controlled trial (RCT) with 1,200 participants minimises confounding variables through random assignment and provides high statistical power; this is the gold standard in experimental research. A teacher survey of 80 participants is subject to response bias, self-selection, and lacks experimental control. Concluding 'mixed evidence, no conclusion possible' falsely treats both studies as equally valid. Option A is wrong because equipoise requires comparable quality of evidence on both sides — which is not the case here.

questions.title: Modus Ponens Application
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a number is divisible by 4, then it is divisible by 2. Premise 2: 36 is divisible by 4. Using modus ponens, what is the valid conclusion?

options.A: 36 is divisible by 2
options.B: 36 is divisible by 4 because it is divisible by 2
options.C: All numbers divisible by 2 are divisible by 4
options.D: 36 is not divisible by any number other than 2 and 4

questions.explanation: Modus ponens states: if P then Q; P is true; therefore Q is true. Since the premise guarantees divisibility by 4 implies divisibility by 2, and 36 satisfies the antecedent, the conclusion is simply that 36 is divisible by 2. Option B reverses the direction of the conditional, which is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias Identification
questions.prompt: A student researching whether social media causes anxiety only reads studies that support that conclusion and discards studies that show no link. Which cognitive bias is most precisely demonstrated here?

options.A: Availability heuristic
options.B: Confirmation bias
options.C: Anchoring bias
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, favour, and recall information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs — exactly what the student does by selectively reading supportive studies. The availability heuristic is incorrect here because it refers to overweighting information that is easy to recall, not the deliberate filtering of evidence by direction.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: Set A contains all multiples of 3 up to 30. Set B contains all multiples of 5 up to 30. How many elements are in A ∪ B but NOT in A ∩ B?
questions.explanation: Set A = {3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27,30} (10 elements), Set B = {5,10,15,20,25,30} (6 elements), A ∩ B = {15,30} (2 elements). |A ∪ B| = 10 + 6 − 2 = 14, and removing the 2 intersection elements gives 12 elements in the union but outside the intersection. Option B (14) is a common error because students calculate the union correctly but forget to subtract the overlap from the final count.

questions.title: Inductive vs Deductive Reasoning
questions.prompt: A student notices that the sum of any two odd numbers she has tested is always even and concludes 'The sum of any two odd numbers is always even.' Which type of reasoning is this, and what would make the conclusion logically certain?

options.A: Deductive reasoning; a formal algebraic proof using (2m+1)+(2n+1) = 2(m+n+1)
options.B: Inductive reasoning; a formal algebraic proof using (2m+1)+(2n+1) = 2(m+n+1)
options.C: Inductive reasoning; testing every pair of odd numbers up to 1000
options.D: Abductive reasoning; finding the simplest explanation for the observed pattern

questions.explanation: The student generalises from specific examples, which is inductive reasoning; inductive conclusions are probable but not logically certain. Logical certainty requires deductive proof: writing odd numbers as (2m+1) and (2n+1) and showing their sum equals 2(m+n+1), which is definitionally even. Option C is wrong because no finite number of tests can prove a universal claim — a counterexample could always exist beyond those tested.

questions.title: Fallacy of Affirming Consequent
questions.prompt: A student reasons: 'If it snows, school is cancelled. School was cancelled today. Therefore it must have snowed.' Identify the logical error in this argument.

options.A: Straw man fallacy
options.B: Affirming the consequent
options.C: Denying the antecedent
options.D: False dichotomy

questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent is the invalid form: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P.' The conditional only guarantees that snow causes cancellation, not that cancellation proves snow — a fire alarm or teacher strike could equally cause cancellation. Denying the antecedent (option C) would look like: 'It did not snow, therefore school was not cancelled,' which is a different invalid form.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly identifies oxygen as a necessary but not sufficient condition for fire?

options.A: Oxygen alone guarantees fire will occur, but fire can sometimes exist without oxygen
options.B: Fire cannot occur without oxygen, but oxygen alone does not guarantee fire will occur
options.C: Oxygen guarantees fire and fire guarantees oxygen equally
options.D: Oxygen is irrelevant to fire if fuel and ignition are present

questions.explanation: A necessary condition is one without which the outcome cannot occur: fire cannot exist without oxygen (in standard combustion). However, oxygen alone does not guarantee fire — fuel and an ignition source are also required — so it is not sufficient. Option A confuses the definitions by reversing which direction of the conditional holds.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: A scientist presents peer-reviewed evidence that a new vaccine is safe. A critic responds: 'She received funding from a pharmaceutical company, so her conclusions cannot be trusted.' Evaluate whether the critic's response is logically sound.

options.A: The critic is correct because financial conflicts of interest always invalidate scientific findings
options.B: The critic commits an ad hominem fallacy by attacking the scientist rather than the evidence
options.C: The critic uses a legitimate appeal to authority to undermine a weaker claim
options.D: The critic correctly applies the precautionary principle to reject uncertain data

questions.explanation: Actually, option B is correct — the critic dismisses evidence by attacking the source rather than engaging with the data or methodology, which is the ad hominem (circumstantial) fallacy. Funding creates a conflict of interest worth noting but does not by itself make findings false; the peer-reviewed evidence must be evaluated on its merits. Option C is wrong because an appeal to authority supports a claim rather than attacks a person, and no authority is cited here.

questions.title: TOK: Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, which of the following best describes why 'reason' is considered a more reliable way of knowing than 'intuition' for establishing mathematical truth?

options.A: Reason always produces results that match empirical observation, while intuition does not
options.B: Reason follows explicit, checkable logical steps from axioms, making conclusions verifiable by others
options.C: Intuition is subjective and therefore has no role in any knowledge-producing discipline
options.D: Reason is faster and more efficient than intuition for complex problems

questions.explanation: Mathematical proof via reason is intersubjectively verifiable: any trained mathematician can follow and check each deductive step from agreed axioms, making the conclusion certain within that axiomatic system. Intuition, while useful for generating conjectures, cannot on its own provide the logical warrant required. Option A is incorrect because mathematics is not empirical — mathematical truths are established through logical proof, not observation.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Logic
questions.prompt: A student hypothesises that caffeine improves reaction time. She designs an experiment with a control group and a caffeine group. Which outcome would most directly falsify her hypothesis?

options.A: The caffeine group shows no statistically significant difference in reaction time compared to the control group
options.B: The control group shows high variability in reaction times
options.C: Some participants in the caffeine group drink coffee regularly in daily life
options.D: The sample size is smaller than ideal for the study

questions.explanation: Falsification requires a result that contradicts the prediction: if caffeine truly improves reaction time, the caffeine group should outperform the control. A null result — no statistically significant difference — directly contradicts the hypothesis. Options C and D identify confounding variables and limitations respectively, which weaken the study's validity but do not themselves constitute evidence against the hypothesis.

questions.title: Contrapositive Reasoning
questions.prompt: The statement is: 'If a quadrilateral is a square, then it has four equal sides.' Which of the following is the logically equivalent contrapositive?

options.A: If a quadrilateral does not have four equal sides, then it is not a square
options.B: If a quadrilateral is not a square, then it does not have four equal sides
options.C: If a quadrilateral has four equal sides, then it is a square
options.D: A quadrilateral with four equal sides must also have four equal angles

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'If P then Q' is 'If not Q then not P,' and is logically equivalent to the original. Negating the consequent ('does not have four equal sides') and the antecedent ('is not a square') in the correct order gives option A. Option B is the inverse ('If not P then not Q'), which is not logically equivalent to the original statement and is a common student error.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Evaluation
questions.prompt: A school board argues: 'If we allow students to use calculators in one exam, soon they will use them in all exams, and eventually students will be unable to perform any mental arithmetic at all.' To what extent is this a valid argument?

options.A: It is fully valid because each step in the chain follows necessarily from the previous
options.B: It commits the slippery slope fallacy because the causal chain between steps is assumed, not demonstrated
options.C: It is a sound inductive argument because trends in education consistently support the predicted outcome
options.D: It is a valid deductive argument but uses a false premise about mental arithmetic

questions.explanation: The slippery slope fallacy assumes that one action will inevitably trigger a cascade of increasingly extreme consequences without providing evidence for each causal link. Each step in the argument — from one exam to all exams to total arithmetic inability — needs independent justification. Option A is incorrect because the steps do not follow necessarily; controlled policies could allow calculators in some contexts without the predicted outcome.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: Data shows a strong positive correlation between the number of swimming pools in a city and the city's ice cream sales. A student concludes that buying more swimming pools causes ice cream sales to rise. Identify the most precise flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: The student has made a sampling error by using city-level data
options.B: The student conflates correlation with causation, ignoring a confounding variable — hot weather
options.C: The student's conclusion is invalid because correlation coefficients cannot exceed 1
options.D: The student has committed confirmation bias by selecting favourable data

questions.explanation: Both swimming pool construction and ice cream sales are driven by a third variable — hot weather — making this a classic case of a confounding variable creating a spurious correlation. Inferring that one causes the other ignores this common cause. Option D is incorrect because the prompt describes a data conclusion, not selective reading; the student is not filtering evidence to support a prior belief.

questions.title: Deductive Validity and Soundness
questions.prompt: Consider the argument: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Dolphins are mammals. Therefore, dolphins are warm-blooded.' Which statement best describes this argument?

options.A: Valid but not sound, because the conclusion about dolphins is false
options.B: Sound and valid, because the argument form is correct and both premises are true
options.C: Invalid, because dolphins live in the ocean and the premise about mammals is too broad
options.D: Valid but not sound, because 'warm-blooded' is an ambiguous term in the argument

questions.explanation: A sound argument is one that is both deductively valid (the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises) and has true premises. Both premises here are biologically true — all mammals are indeed warm-blooded, and dolphins are classified as mammals — so the argument is sound. Option A is incorrect because dolphins actually are warm-blooded; the conclusion is true, not false.

questions.title: Falsifiability in Science
questions.prompt: Karl Popper argued that a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable. Which of the following claims best illustrates an unfalsifiable statement?

options.A: All copper conducts electricity
options.B: There exists an invisible force that helps athletes when they believe in themselves, but disappears when measured
options.C: Increasing CO₂ concentration raises average global temperature
options.D: Objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum regardless of mass

questions.explanation: A claim is unfalsifiable if no possible observation could count as evidence against it. The claim about an invisible force that vanishes under measurement cannot be tested by definition — any negative measurement is explained away by the claim itself. Options A, C, and D are all falsifiable: each makes a specific prediction that could in principle be contradicted by experimental results.

questions.title: Logical Negation of Statements
questions.prompt: What is the correct logical negation of the statement: 'Some students in the class passed the exam'?

options.A: Some students in the class did not pass the exam
options.B: No students in the class passed the exam
options.C: All students in the class failed the exam
options.D: Most students in the class did not pass the exam

questions.explanation: The logical negation of 'Some X are Y' (∃x: Px) is 'No X are Y' (¬∃x: Px), equivalently 'All X are not Y.' The statement 'Some students passed' is false if and only if zero students passed — i.e., no students passed. Option A ('Some did not pass') is actually compatible with the original statement being true, so it is not its negation.

questions.title: Occam's Razor Principle
questions.prompt: Two theories explain the same astronomical data equally well. Theory X requires the existence of five new unobserved entities; Theory Y requires only one. According to Occam's Razor, which theory should be preferred initially, and why?

options.A: Theory X, because more entities provide more explanatory power and thus greater predictive accuracy
options.B: Theory Y, because the simpler theory makes fewer unverified assumptions and is easier to falsify
options.C: Theory X, because complex phenomena require complex explanations by definition
options.D: Neither — Occam's Razor states that all theories must be tested empirically before any preference is justified

questions.explanation: Occam's Razor (the principle of parsimony) states that among competing hypotheses explaining the same evidence equally well, the one requiring fewer assumptions should be preferred. Theory Y's single unobserved entity involves fewer unverified claims, making it simpler. Option A is incorrect because additional entities that are unobserved do not inherently increase explanatory or predictive power — they introduce more untested assumptions.

questions.title: Argument Structure Identification
questions.prompt: A student writes: 'We should reduce screen time for teenagers. High screen time is linked to sleep disruption, and poor sleep impairs academic performance. Therefore, reducing screen time should improve academic outcomes.' Identify the role of 'High screen time is linked to sleep disruption' in this argument.

options.A: It is the main conclusion of the argument
options.B: It is an intermediate premise that supports the overall conclusion
options.C: It is a counterargument that the student is attempting to rebut
options.D: It is a definitional claim that establishes the meaning of screen time

questions.explanation: In argument mapping, intermediate premises (also called sub-conclusions or supporting premises) provide evidence that feeds into further reasoning leading to the main conclusion. Here, the link between screen time and sleep disruption supports the chain leading to the main conclusion that reducing screen time improves academic outcomes. Option A is incorrect — the main conclusion is the first sentence: 'We should reduce screen time for teenagers.'

questions.title: Hasty Generalisation Fallacy
questions.prompt: After surveying 12 students from one school, a researcher concludes: 'Teenagers globally prefer online learning to classroom learning.' Which fallacy does this conclusion commit?

options.A: False dichotomy
options.B: Appeal to ignorance
options.C: Hasty generalisation
options.D: Post hoc ergo propter hoc

questions.explanation: Hasty generalisation occurs when a conclusion about a large population is drawn from a sample that is too small or unrepresentative to support it. Twelve students from a single school cannot represent global teenage preferences. Option D (post hoc ergo propter hoc) refers to incorrectly inferring causation from temporal sequence, which is a different type of fallacy not applicable here.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning
questions.prompt: Historians debate whether World War I would still have occurred without the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Which statement best captures the correct use of counterfactual reasoning in this context?

options.A: Since the assassination did occur, it is pointless to speculate about what would have happened otherwise
options.B: Counterfactual reasoning examines what outcomes would likely follow if a specific historical condition were changed, helping identify which causes were necessary
options.C: Counterfactual reasoning proves that the assassination was the single sufficient cause of the war
options.D: Counterfactual reasoning in history is identical to controlled experiments in science because both isolate variables

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning asks 'what if a specific condition were different?' and is used in historical analysis to assess which causes were necessary versus merely contributory. If the war likely would have occurred anyway due to underlying tensions, the assassination may have been a trigger rather than a necessary cause. Option D is incorrect because historians cannot control variables or repeat history — counterfactuals in history remain speculative, unlike controlled scientific experiments.

questions.title: Anchoring Bias in Judgement
questions.prompt: A student is told that a used car 'normally sells for $20,000' before being offered it for $15,000. She feels it is a good deal even though independent research shows the car's fair market value is $12,000. Which cognitive bias is at work?

options.A: Availability heuristic
options.B: Dunning-Kruger effect
options.C: Anchoring bias
options.D: Framing effect

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias occurs when an initial piece of information (the 'anchor') disproportionately influences subsequent judgements. The $20,000 figure acts as an anchor, making $15,000 feel like a saving even though the true value is $12,000. The framing effect (option D) is related but specifically refers to how the presentation of choices as gains or losses alters decisions — here the bias is specifically about the numerical anchor distorting value judgement.

questions.title: Deductive Proof by Contradiction
questions.prompt: A student wants to prove that √2 is irrational. She begins by assuming √2 is rational and derives a contradiction. What is the name of this proof technique?

options.A: Proof by induction
options.B: Proof by exhaustion
options.C: Proof by contrapositive
options.D: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum)

questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) assumes the negation of what you want to prove and shows this leads to a logical contradiction, thereby confirming the original claim. The classic proof of √2's irrationality assumes √2 = p/q in lowest terms and derives that both p and q must be even — contradicting the lowest-terms assumption. Proof by induction (option A) is used to prove statements about all natural numbers through a base case and inductive step.

questions.title: Epistemic Humility in TOK
questions.prompt: A Theory of Knowledge student argues: 'If a claim cannot be proven with absolute certainty, we have no reason to believe it at all.' Evaluate this position.

options.A: The position is correct because knowledge requires certainty by definition
options.B: The position is too strong; most knowledge is probabilistic, and strong evidence justifies belief even without absolute certainty
options.C: The position is correct for scientific knowledge but not for mathematical knowledge
options.D: The position is too weak because it allows belief in any unproven claim

questions.explanation: Virtually all empirical knowledge is probabilistic rather than absolutely certain — even well-established scientific theories like evolution or germ theory are justified by overwhelming evidence, not logical certainty. Demanding absolute certainty as a condition for any belief leads to radical scepticism, making knowledge of the external world impossible. Option A conflates justified belief with certainty; TOK explicitly distinguishes between knowledge and absolute certainty.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition Limits
questions.prompt: A student observes the sequence: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and concludes the rule is 'multiply by 2.' Another student points out a polynomial that also fits all five terms. What does this illustrate about pattern recognition from finite data?

options.A: A finite sequence always has exactly two possible generating rules
options.B: Without additional data or constraints, infinitely many rules can fit any finite sequence, so the simplest rule is not necessarily the correct one
options.C: Polynomial rules are always superior to geometric rules when both fit the same data
options.D: Pattern recognition is reliable only when the sequence has at least ten terms

questions.explanation: By Lagrange interpolation, a polynomial of degree n can be constructed to pass through any n+1 data points, meaning infinitely many functions can fit a finite sequence. The 'multiply by 2' rule is parsimonious but is not uniquely determined by the data. Option A is incorrect because it severely understates the number of possible rules — there is no finite upper bound on the rules that can generate a given finite sequence.

questions.title: Analogical Reasoning Strength
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Training for a marathon is just like studying for exams — both require consistent daily effort, a long-term plan, and recovery periods.' Critically assess the strength of this analogy.

options.A: The analogy is strong and without significant weakness because physical and cognitive tasks are governed by the same neurological principles
options.B: The analogy is moderately useful for motivational purposes but breaks down because physical overtraining causes injury in a way that cognitive overwork does not mirror precisely
options.C: The analogy is entirely invalid because physical and cognitive activities involve completely different processes
options.D: The analogy is weak because marathons are always harder than exams, making the comparison misleading

questions.explanation: Analogies are useful when the compared domains share relevant structural features but must be evaluated on how far the similarities hold. The shared features (consistency, planning, recovery) make the analogy pedagogically useful. However, physical overtraining leads to stress fractures and muscle tears — specific physiological consequences with no precise cognitive parallel — limiting the analogy's precision. Option C is too dismissive; structural similarities in process do exist and make the analogy partially valid.

questions.title: Sampling Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A researcher surveys 500 people about their dietary habits by posting a questionnaire on a fitness forum. She concludes that 78% of the general population exercises at least four times per week. What is the primary methodological problem?

options.A: The sample size of 500 is too small to draw any conclusions
options.B: The sample is self-selected from a fitness forum and therefore systematically unrepresentative of the general population
options.C: The survey question about diet is irrelevant to a conclusion about exercise frequency
options.D: The researcher has committed confirmation bias by using an online survey format

questions.explanation: Sampling bias occurs when the method of selecting participants systematically excludes or overrepresents certain groups. Fitness forum users are disproportionately interested in exercise, making them unrepresentative of the broader population — a form of self-selection bias. Option A is incorrect because 500 is actually a reasonable sample size for population research when randomly selected; the problem is the non-random, biased selection method, not the number.

questions.title: Valid vs Sound Arguments
questions.prompt: A student presents the following argument: 'All mammals are cold-blooded. Whales are mammals. Therefore, whales are cold-blooded.' Which of the following best describes this argument?

options.A: Valid and sound, because the conclusion follows from true premises
options.B: Invalid and unsound, because the conclusion does not follow from the premises
options.C: Valid but unsound, because the logical form is correct but the first premise is false
options.D: Invalid but sound, because the premises are true even though the form is flawed

questions.explanation: An argument is valid if the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises, regardless of whether the premises are true. Here the form 'All A are B; C is A; therefore C is B' is valid, but the first premise ('All mammals are cold-blooded') is factually false, making the argument unsound. Option A is wrong because soundness requires both validity AND true premises; the first premise here is false.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Reasoning
questions.prompt: Consider the argument: Premise 1 — If a number is divisible by 4, it is divisible by 2. Premise 2 — 17 is not divisible by 2. What can be validly concluded using modus tollens?

options.A: 17 is divisible by 4
options.B: 17 is not divisible by 4
options.C: All numbers not divisible by 2 are odd
options.D: No conclusion can be drawn because 17 is prime

questions.explanation: Modus tollens has the form: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Here P = 'divisible by 4' and Q = 'divisible by 2'. Since 17 is not divisible by 2 (not Q), we conclude 17 is not divisible by 4 (not P). Option A commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent, which is a common error among students who confuse the direction of the conditional.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias Identification
questions.prompt: A student researching climate change only reads articles that support her existing belief that human activity is the primary cause, dismissing contradictory sources as 'biased.' Which cognitive bias most precisely describes her approach?

options.A: Availability heuristic
options.B: Confirmation bias
options.C: Anchoring bias
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs, which is exactly what the student is doing by only accepting supporting evidence. The availability heuristic, option A, refers to judging probability based on how easily examples come to mind — a different mechanism not demonstrated here.

questions.title: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: In formal logic, being a square is described in relation to being a rectangle. Which statement most precisely captures the logical relationship between these two concepts?

options.A: Being a square is both necessary and sufficient for being a rectangle
options.B: Being a rectangle is necessary but not sufficient for being a square
options.C: Being a rectangle is sufficient but not necessary for being a square
options.D: Being a square and being a rectangle are logically independent properties

questions.explanation: Every square must be a rectangle (having four right angles), so being a rectangle is a necessary condition for being a square. However, being a rectangle is not sufficient — a rectangle does not have to have equal sides, so it need not be a square. Option A is wrong because being a square is sufficient for being a rectangle but is not necessary, since many non-square rectangles exist.

questions.title: Ad Hominem Fallacy
questions.prompt: During a class debate, Priya argues that the school cafeteria should serve more vegetarian options. Her opponent responds: 'Why should we listen to Priya? She failed her biology test last week.' Identify the logical fallacy in the opponent's response.

options.A: False dilemma
options.B: Appeal to authority
options.C: Ad hominem
options.D: Post hoc ergo propter hoc

questions.explanation: Ad hominem (Latin: 'against the person') is the fallacy of attacking the character or personal circumstances of the arguer rather than engaging with the argument itself. Priya's biology grade is irrelevant to the merits of the cafeteria argument. Option B, appeal to authority, would involve incorrectly citing an expert — the opposite of what is happening here.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 40 students, 22 study French, 18 study Spanish, and 7 study both. How many students study neither French nor Spanish?
questions.explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle: |F ∪ S| = 22 + 18 − 7 = 33. Students studying neither = 40 − 33 = 7. Option C is correct. Option D (11) is a common error made by students who forget to subtract the overlap and simply compute 40 − 22 − 18 + 7 incorrectly, or who add rather than subtract the intersection.

questions.title: Inductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: A student tests 200 batteries from a production line and finds all of them last more than 10 hours. She concludes: 'All batteries from this factory last more than 10 hours.' Which statement best evaluates the strength of this inductive conclusion?

options.A: The conclusion is logically certain because the sample size is large enough
options.B: The conclusion is strong but not logically guaranteed, since unexamined batteries could still fail
options.C: The conclusion is weak because inductive reasoning is always invalid
options.D: The conclusion is strong only if the student used deductive reasoning to verify it

questions.explanation: Inductive conclusions are probabilistically supported but never logically certain — even a large sample cannot guarantee a universal claim, as a single counterexample could falsify it. This is known as the 'problem of induction,' associated with philosopher David Hume. Option A is wrong because no sample size, however large, makes an inductive universal conclusion logically certain.

questions.title: Hypothesis Falsifiability
questions.prompt: Karl Popper argued that a hypothesis must be falsifiable to be considered scientific. Which of the following hypotheses is NOT falsifiable in Popper's sense?

options.A: All copper conducts electricity
options.B: Exercise reduces resting heart rate over six weeks
options.C: An invisible force guides all human decisions but leaves no measurable trace
options.D: Increasing CO₂ concentration raises global average temperature

questions.explanation: Popper's criterion of falsifiability requires that a hypothesis must be capable of being shown false by some conceivable observation or experiment. A hypothesis about an invisible, undetectable force by definition cannot be tested or refuted, making it unfalsifiable. Options A, B, and D can all be tested experimentally and potentially disproved, satisfying Popper's criterion.

questions.title: Deductive Syllogism Form
questions.prompt: Identify which of the following represents a valid categorical syllogism in standard form.

options.A: All athletes are disciplined. Some students are disciplined. Therefore, some students are athletes.
options.B: All prime numbers greater than 2 are odd. 7 is a prime number greater than 2. Therefore, 7 is odd.
options.C: Most scientists accept evolution. Evolution must therefore be correct.
options.D: If it snows, school is cancelled. School was cancelled. Therefore, it snowed.

questions.explanation: Option B is a valid syllogism of the form: All A are B; X is A; therefore X is B. The premises are also true, making it both valid and sound. Option A commits the fallacy of the undistributed middle — 'disciplined' appears in both premises but is not universally distributed, so the conclusion does not follow. Option D commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: A study finds that countries with higher chocolate consumption per capita have more Nobel Prize winners per capita. A journalist concludes that eating chocolate boosts intelligence and creativity. Evaluate this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is well supported because the correlation is cross-national and therefore reliable
options.B: The conclusion is flawed because correlation does not establish causation; a confounding variable such as national wealth may explain both
options.C: The conclusion is flawed only because the sample size of Nobel winners is too small
options.D: The conclusion is valid because Nobel Prizes are an objective measure of intelligence

questions.explanation: Correlation indicates that two variables move together but does not prove that one causes the other. Wealthier countries can afford both more chocolate and more investment in research and education, making national wealth a classic confounding variable. Option A is wrong because cross-national scope does not overcome the fundamental problem that correlation alone cannot establish causation.

questions.title: Theory of Knowledge: Perception
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, a student claims: 'Sense perception is the most reliable way of knowing because it gives us direct access to reality.' Which response most effectively challenges this claim?

options.A: Sense perception is reliable in science but not in the arts, so it cannot be universally most reliable
options.B: Optical illusions and perceptual limitations show that perception can systematically misrepresent reality, undermining the claim of direct access
options.C: Reason is more reliable than perception because mathematics is certain, so perception is the least reliable way of knowing
options.D: Perception is reliable only when combined with memory, so memory is actually the primary way of knowing

questions.explanation: Well-documented phenomena such as optical illusions (e.g., the Müller-Lyer illusion), colour constancy, and perceptual adaptation demonstrate that the senses do not give unmediated access to reality — they construct and sometimes distort it. This directly challenges the premise of 'direct access.' Option A is too narrow in scope and does not address the core claim about directness of perceptual access.

questions.title: Straw Man Fallacy
questions.prompt: A politician argues for a moderate increase in the minimum wage. Her opponent responds: 'My opponent wants to destroy small businesses by forcing them to pay wages they cannot possibly afford.' Identify the logical error in the opponent's response.

options.A: False dilemma, because only two economic options are presented
options.B: Appeal to emotion, because the opponent is trying to frighten listeners
options.C: Straw man fallacy, because the opponent misrepresents the original position to make it easier to attack
options.D: Hasty generalisation, because not all small businesses would be affected equally

questions.explanation: A straw man fallacy occurs when an arguer distorts or exaggerates an opponent's position and then attacks that distorted version instead of the actual claim. The politician advocated a moderate increase, but her opponent reframed this as wanting to 'destroy small businesses' — a far more extreme position. Option B is partially relevant but does not name the primary structural fallacy, which is the misrepresentation of the original argument.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning
questions.prompt: A doctor notes that a patient has a high fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes. She concludes the most likely diagnosis is a bacterial throat infection. Which type of reasoning best describes her thinking?

options.A: Deductive reasoning, because she is applying a general rule to a specific case
options.B: Inductive reasoning, because she is generalising from a pattern of symptoms
options.C: Abductive reasoning, because she is inferring the best explanation for the observed evidence
options.D: Analogical reasoning, because she is comparing this patient to previous cases

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning, sometimes called 'inference to the best explanation,' involves forming the most plausible hypothesis that accounts for the available evidence — exactly what the doctor is doing by identifying bacterial infection as the best explanation for the symptom cluster. Option A is wrong because deductive reasoning guarantees the conclusion from the premises; the doctor's conclusion here remains probabilistic, not certain.

questions.title: Counterfactual Conditional Logic
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If Isaac Newton had never been born, the laws of gravity would never have been discovered.' Critically assess the logical strength of this counterfactual claim.

options.A: The claim is strong because Newton's Principia Mathematica was uniquely transformative and irreplaceable
options.B: The claim is weak because it conflates the discovery of a law with the existence of the underlying physical phenomenon
options.C: The claim is strong because no other scientist of the era had sufficient mathematical ability to develop calculus
options.D: The claim is weak only because Gottfried Leibniz also developed calculus, making Newton replaceable in mathematics

questions.explanation: Gravity as a physical reality exists independently of any human observer or theorist; what Newton discovered was not gravity itself but a mathematical description of it. The counterfactual confuses the discovery (a human act) with the phenomenon (a feature of the universe). Option D raises a valid historical point about Leibniz, but the deeper logical error in the original claim is the conflation of phenomenon and discovery, making B the more precise answer.

questions.title: Slippery Slope Assessment
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'If we allow students to use calculators in maths class, they will never learn arithmetic, and soon no one will be able to do any maths at all.' To what extent is this a logically sound argument?

options.A: It is sound because each step in the chain of consequences is inevitable given the first
options.B: It is a slippery slope fallacy because it assumes a chain of increasingly severe consequences without providing evidence that each step will occur
options.C: It is sound because empirical research confirms that calculator use always reduces arithmetic ability
options.D: It is a hasty generalisation because the student is applying one classroom's experience to all students

questions.explanation: The slippery slope fallacy occurs when an argument asserts that one event will inevitably trigger a chain of increasingly negative consequences without demonstrating that each step necessarily follows from the previous one. The student provides no evidence that calculator use leads to total mathematical incapacity. Option A is wrong because inevitability must be demonstrated, not assumed — the chain of consequences here is asserted rather than argued.

questions.title: Research Methodology: Control Groups
questions.prompt: A researcher tests a new study drug by giving it to 50 students before an exam, and their average score is 78%. She concludes the drug improves performance. What is the most significant methodological flaw in her study?

options.A: The sample size of 50 is too small to draw any conclusions
options.B: She did not use a control group, so there is no baseline to compare the score of 78% against
options.C: The study lacks internal validity because exam scores are an unreliable measure of performance
options.D: She should have used a double-blind procedure to control for researcher bias

questions.explanation: Without a control group — a comparable group of students who did not take the drug — the researcher cannot determine whether 78% is higher, lower, or the same as typical performance. The score of 78% is meaningless in isolation. Option D identifies a real concern about double-blind design, but the most fundamental flaw is the complete absence of any comparison group, which prevents any causal conclusion.

questions.title: Logical Biconditional
questions.prompt: In formal logic, the biconditional statement 'P if and only if Q' is true under which condition?

options.A: When P is true and Q is false, or when P is false and Q is true
options.B: When P is true regardless of the truth value of Q
options.C: When P and Q have the same truth value — both true or both false
options.D: When at least one of P or Q is true

questions.explanation: A biconditional (P ↔ Q) is true exactly when both components share the same truth value: true-true or false-false. It is false when one is true and the other is false. Option A describes the exclusive-or (XOR) operator, which students frequently confuse with the biconditional because both involve comparing truth values of two propositions.

questions.title: Anchoring Bias in Estimation
questions.prompt: Participants in an experiment were first asked whether Gandhi died before or after age 9, then asked to estimate his actual age at death. A second group was first asked whether he died before or after age 140. The second group gave significantly higher estimates. Which cognitive bias best explains this result?

options.A: Confirmation bias
options.B: Anchoring bias
options.C: Hindsight bias
options.D: Representativeness heuristic

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias occurs when an initial piece of information (the anchor) disproportionately influences subsequent judgements. The absurd reference point of age 140 pulled estimates upward relative to the anchor of age 9, even though both anchors are obviously wrong. This was famously demonstrated by Tversky and Kahneman. Option C, hindsight bias, involves believing after the fact that one 'knew it all along,' which is not what this experiment tests.

questions.title: Mathematical Proof by Contradiction
questions.prompt: A student attempts to prove that √2 is irrational. She begins by assuming √2 is rational, writes √2 = p/q in lowest terms, and derives a contradiction. What is the name of this proof technique?

options.A: Proof by induction
options.B: Proof by exhaustion
options.C: Proof by contrapositive
options.D: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum)

questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) assumes the negation of what you wish to prove and then shows this assumption leads to a logical impossibility, thereby establishing the original claim. The classic proof that √2 is irrational, attributed to ancient Greek mathematicians, uses exactly this structure. Option C, proof by contrapositive, proves 'if not Q then not P' instead of 'if P then Q' — a related but distinct technique that does not involve assuming the negation of the conclusion.

questions.title: Appeal to Nature Fallacy
questions.prompt: A health blogger writes: 'This herbal remedy is completely natural, therefore it is safe and beneficial. You should choose it over any synthetic medicine.' Evaluate the logical quality of this argument.

options.A: The argument is strong because natural substances have fewer side effects than synthetic ones by definition
options.B: The argument commits the appeal to nature fallacy — being natural does not entail being safe or beneficial
options.C: The argument is weak only because herbal remedies are not regulated, not because of any logical error
options.D: The argument commits a hasty generalisation by applying one remedy's properties to all natural substances

questions.explanation: The appeal to nature fallacy treats 'natural' as inherently good or safe, ignoring counterexamples like arsenic, cyanide, and deadly nightshade, which are entirely natural yet highly toxic. The natural/synthetic distinction does not determine safety or efficacy. Option A is false by counterexample — many synthetic medicines are safer than natural alternatives — and it essentially accepts the fallacious premise rather than identifying it as an error.

questions.title: TOK: Shared Knowledge
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, which of the following best distinguishes 'shared knowledge' from 'personal knowledge'?

options.A: Shared knowledge is always more reliable than personal knowledge because it has been tested by more people
options.B: Shared knowledge belongs to groups or disciplines and is built collaboratively, while personal knowledge is individual and shaped by direct experience
options.C: Shared knowledge is produced only by scientists, while personal knowledge is produced by everyone else
options.D: Personal knowledge is subjective and therefore excluded from academic disciplines, which rely solely on shared knowledge

questions.explanation: In the IB TOK framework, shared knowledge refers to knowledge that is accumulated, tested, and held collectively by communities — such as scientific consensus, historical narratives, or mathematical proofs — whereas personal knowledge is grounded in individual experience, intuition, and perspective. Option A is too absolute; shared knowledge can reflect collective biases and is not automatically more reliable than well-grounded personal expertise.

questions.title: Equivocation Fallacy
questions.prompt: Identify the logical error in the following argument: 'The end of something is its goal. Death is the end of life. Therefore, death is the goal of life.'

options.A: Appeal to authority, because the argument assumes a widely held view without evidence
options.B: Equivocation, because the word 'end' shifts meaning from 'purpose' to 'termination' between premises
options.C: Circular reasoning, because the conclusion restates the first premise
options.D: False dilemma, because it presents only two possible roles for death

questions.explanation: Equivocation occurs when a key word is used with two different meanings within the same argument, producing a misleading appearance of valid reasoning. Here 'end' means 'goal/purpose' in premise one but 'final point/termination' in premise two — a shift that makes the argument appear logically tight while being fundamentally invalid. Option C is wrong because the conclusion does not simply restate a premise; it introduces a new (false) claim about purpose.

questions.title: Experimental Variables
questions.prompt: In a controlled experiment testing whether caffeine improves reaction time, a researcher measures the reaction times of participants before and after consuming caffeine. What is the dependent variable in this experiment?

options.A: The amount of caffeine consumed
options.B: The reaction time of participants
options.C: The participants' age and body weight
options.D: The time of day the experiment is conducted

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured to assess the effect of the manipulation. In this experiment, reaction time is what changes (or is expected to change) as a result of caffeine intake, making it the dependent variable. Option A is the independent variable — the factor deliberately manipulated by the researcher. Options C and D are control variables — factors held constant to ensure a fair test.

questions.title: Deductive Proof in Mathematics
questions.prompt: A student wants to prove that the sum of any two even integers is always even. She writes: 'Let the two even integers be 2m and 2n where m, n ∈ ℤ. Their sum is 2m + 2n = 2(m+n), which is even.' What type of proof is this?

options.A: Proof by induction, because she is building from a base case upwards
options.B: Proof by exhaustion, because she is checking all possible pairs of even numbers
options.C: Direct deductive proof, because she derives the conclusion necessarily from a general algebraic definition
options.D: Empirical proof, because she uses specific integer values m and n to support the claim

questions.explanation: A direct proof establishes a conclusion by constructing a logical chain from accepted definitions and axioms without assuming the negation or using induction. By defining even integers algebraically as 2m and 2n and manipulating them to produce 2(m+n), the student proves the result for all even integers simultaneously. Option B is wrong because proof by exhaustion requires checking every single case individually, which is impossible for an infinite set like all even integers.

questions.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student has spent four months writing a novel she no longer enjoys and finds poorly structured. She decides to keep writing because 'I've already put in so much time that stopping now would be a waste.' Identify the reasoning error.

options.A: Availability heuristic, because she is overweighting her recent emotional experience
options.B: Sunk cost fallacy, because she is letting irrecoverable past investment determine a future decision
options.C: Optimism bias, because she believes the novel will improve if she persists
options.D: Representativeness heuristic, because she assumes future effort will resemble past effort

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy involves continuing a course of action because of previously invested resources (time, money, effort) that cannot be recovered, rather than evaluating the future costs and benefits rationally. The time already spent is gone regardless of what the student does next; rational decision-making should focus on future outcomes only. Option A is incorrect because the availability heuristic concerns how easily information comes to mind, not the role of prior investment in decision-making.

questions.title: Validity vs Soundness
questions.prompt: A student presents the following argument: 'All mammals breathe air. Dolphins are mammals. Therefore, dolphins breathe air.' She then presents: 'All fish live on land. Salmon are fish. Therefore, salmon live on land.' Evaluate which argument is valid, which is sound, and what the distinction reveals.

options.A: Both arguments are valid; only the first is sound, because soundness requires true premises
options.B: Both arguments are sound; validity is a weaker condition than soundness
options.C: Only the first argument is valid, because the second has a false conclusion
options.D: Neither argument is valid, because validity depends on whether the premises are true

questions.explanation: An argument is valid if the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises, regardless of whether those premises are true; both syllogisms have that property. Soundness additionally requires all premises to be true — the salmon argument fails this test because salmon do not live on land. Option C is a common misconception: validity is determined by logical form alone, not by the truth of the conclusion.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A psychologist studying whether social media causes anxiety only interviews teenagers who already attend therapy for anxiety disorders. She concludes: 'My data strongly supports the link between social media and anxiety.' Identify the most significant flaw in her methodology.

options.A: She has used too small a sample to detect statistical significance
options.B: Her sample is not representative, creating selection bias that pre-selects for anxious individuals
options.C: She failed to use a double-blind procedure, so participants knew the study's aim
options.D: She relied on self-report data, which is inherently unreliable

questions.explanation: By recruiting exclusively from therapy populations, the psychologist ensures her sample already has elevated anxiety, making it impossible to establish whether social media use — rather than pre-existing vulnerability — is causal; this is textbook selection bias. Option A is a genuine concern but secondary: even a large sample drawn from this skewed group would produce the same flaw.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Application
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by both 2 and 3. Premise 2: The number 35 is not divisible by 2. What conclusion can be drawn using modus tollens, and is that conclusion correct?

options.A: 35 is not divisible by 6 — correct conclusion reached by valid deduction
options.B: 35 is not divisible by 3 — correct, because failing one condition implies failing the other
options.C: 35 might or might not be divisible by 6, because modus tollens does not apply here
options.D: 35 is not divisible by 6 — but this conclusion is reached by inductive reasoning, not modus tollens

questions.explanation: Modus tollens states: if P implies Q, and Q is false, then P is false. Here P = 'divisible by 6', Q = 'divisible by 2'. Since 35 is not divisible by 2, Q is false, so P must be false — 35 is not divisible by 6. Option B is a misconception: failing to be divisible by 2 does not, by this argument alone, allow us to conclude anything about divisibility by 3 (35 is actually divisible by neither, but that requires separate reasoning).

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 50 students, 30 study Biology, 25 study Chemistry, and 10 study both. A student claims that 5 students study neither subject. Critically assess this claim using set theory.

options.A: The claim is correct: |B ∪ C| = 30 + 25 − 10 = 45, so 5 study neither
options.B: The claim is incorrect: |B ∪ C| = 30 + 25 + 10 = 65, which exceeds 50, so the data is contradictory
options.C: The claim is incorrect: |B ∪ C| = 30 + 25 − 10 = 45, but neither = 50 − 45 = 5, which is wrong because overlap students must be subtracted twice
options.D: The claim is correct, but only if Biology and Chemistry are mutually exclusive sets

questions.explanation: The inclusion-exclusion principle gives |B ∪ C| = 30 + 25 − 10 = 45; since the total is 50, the number studying neither is 50 − 45 = 5, so the claim is correct. Option B is a common misconception where students add the overlap rather than subtract it, incorrectly treating the 10 'both' students as an additional group rather than those already counted in both sets.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Studying hard is sufficient for passing the exam, and it is also necessary.' Her friend disagrees: 'Some students pass without studying hard — so it cannot be necessary.' Evaluate who is logically correct.

options.A: The friend is correct: if students can pass without studying hard, then studying hard is not a necessary condition for passing
options.B: The student is correct: studying hard guarantees passing, which makes it both necessary and sufficient
options.C: Both are partially right: studying hard is necessary but not sufficient, since other factors also matter
options.D: Neither is correct: necessity and sufficiency cannot apply to real-world situations like exam performance

questions.explanation: A necessary condition is one without which the outcome cannot occur. If even one student passes without studying hard, that single counterexample proves studying hard is not necessary for passing. The original student conflates 'studying hard leads to passing' (sufficiency claim) with necessity, which is a separate logical relationship requiring that passing is impossible without it.

questions.title: Evaluating Inductive Strength
questions.prompt: A historian notes that every empire she has studied — Roman, Ottoman, British, Mongol — eventually declined. She concludes: 'All empires must inevitably decline.' To what extent is this a strong inductive argument?

options.A: It is a moderately strong inductive argument — the pattern is consistent but cannot be logically guaranteed to extend to all future cases
options.B: It is a deductively valid argument because the sample of empires is sufficiently large to prove the rule
options.C: It is a weak argument because the historian has only studied Western empires, introducing sample bias
options.D: It is a strong argument because inductive conclusions that have no known exceptions are treated as laws in historical methodology

questions.explanation: Inductive arguments can be strong without being conclusive — the consistent historical pattern provides genuine evidential support, but induction by nature cannot guarantee universal truths; one counter-example would falsify the claim. Option B is a critical misconception: no accumulation of empirical cases converts an inductive argument into a deductively valid one — these are categorically different forms of reasoning.

questions.title: Argument Ad Hominem
questions.prompt: During a TOK presentation, Priya argues that climate change is human-caused and cites three peer-reviewed studies. Her classmate responds: 'You failed your geography test last week, so why should we trust your analysis of climate science?' Identify and evaluate the logical error.

options.A: This is an ad hominem attack — it targets Priya's credibility rather than engaging with the evidence she presented
options.B: This is a straw man fallacy — the classmate misrepresents Priya's argument to make it easier to attack
options.C: This is an appeal to authority — the classmate implies only experts should make such arguments
options.D: This is a false dichotomy — the classmate implies either Priya is credible in all areas or none

questions.explanation: Ad hominem (Latin: 'to the person') is the fallacy of attacking the person making an argument rather than the argument itself; Priya's geography test result is irrelevant to the validity of the peer-reviewed studies she cited. Option B (straw man) is a plausible distractor but incorrect — the classmate does not misrepresent her argument, they simply dismiss her as a person.

questions.title: Hypothesis Falsifiability
questions.prompt: A student proposes the hypothesis: 'There exists an invisible, undetectable force that makes some people luckier than others, but it cannot be measured by any instrument.' Evaluate this hypothesis from a scientific methodology perspective.

options.A: The hypothesis is unfalsifiable — because no possible observation could prove it false, it fails Popper's criterion for scientific hypotheses
options.B: The hypothesis is falsifiable — we could test it by comparing outcomes for people who believe in the force versus those who do not
options.C: The hypothesis is valid as a scientific claim because it makes a specific prediction about luck distribution
options.D: The hypothesis is weak but acceptable — science often begins with untestable ideas that later become measurable

questions.explanation: Karl Popper argued that a hypothesis is scientific only if it is in principle falsifiable — i.e., there must be some observation that could prove it wrong. By definition, a force that is 'undetectable by any instrument' cannot be falsified, placing it outside the domain of empirical science. Option B is a tempting misconception — comparing belief groups tests psychological effects of belief, not the existence of the force itself.

questions.title: Deductive Proof by Contradiction
questions.prompt: A student attempts to prove that √2 is irrational. She begins: 'Assume √2 is rational, so √2 = p/q where p and q share no common factors.' She shows this leads to both p and q being even — a contradiction. What proof method is she using, and why does the contradiction validate her conclusion?

options.A: Proof by contradiction — the assumption that √2 is rational leads to a logical impossibility, so the assumption must be false
options.B: Proof by induction — she tests the base case and assumes the result holds for all fractions
options.C: Abductive reasoning — she infers the best explanation for why p and q cannot both be even
options.D: Proof by exhaustion — she checks all possible values of p and q to show none satisfy the equation

questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) assumes the negation of the desired conclusion and demonstrates that this leads to a logical impossibility; since the assumption 'p and q have no common factors' contradicts the derived result 'both are even', √2 cannot be rational. Option B is wrong because mathematical induction requires a base case and inductive step over natural numbers — it does not apply to proving irrationality.

questions.title: False Cause Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student notices that ice cream sales and drowning rates both rise in summer and concludes: 'Eating ice cream increases your risk of drowning.' Identify the reasoning error and explain what concept best accounts for the observed correlation.

options.A: This is the false cause (post hoc) fallacy — both variables are driven by a confounding variable: hot weather increases both swimming and ice cream consumption
options.B: This is an anecdotal evidence fallacy — the student relies on personal observation rather than controlled data
options.C: This is a hasty generalisation — the student draws a universal rule from a single summer's worth of data
options.D: This is a circular argument — the student uses the correlation to prove causation and causation to explain the correlation

questions.explanation: The correlation between ice cream sales and drowning is a classic example of a confounding variable — hot weather causes both increases simultaneously, with no causal link between the two. This is the false cause (or 'cum hoc ergo propter hoc') fallacy. Option C is a tempting distractor, but hasty generalisation concerns the sample size, not the misattribution of a shared cause.

questions.title: Counterfactual Reasoning History
