questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'If penicillin had not been discovered in 1928, World War II casualties would have been significantly higher because bacterial infections from wounds killed large numbers of soldiers.' Evaluate the strength of this counterfactual claim.

options.A: The claim is moderately well-reasoned — it links a specific causal mechanism (antibiotic treatment of wound infections) to a plausible outcome, though alternative medical developments remain uncertain
options.B: The claim is invalid because counterfactual reasoning cannot be used in academic historical analysis
options.C: The claim is strong because it is mathematically provable using casualty statistics from pre-penicillin wars
options.D: The claim is weak because historians cannot speculate about events that did not occur — only documented evidence is acceptable

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning is a legitimate and widely used tool in historical methodology and TOK, provided it identifies a plausible causal mechanism and acknowledges uncertainty. The historian's claim does this: penicillin demonstrably reduced infection-related deaths from 1943 onward, making the counterfactual causally coherent. Options B and D reflect a common student misconception that counterfactuals are inherently unscholarly, when in fact historians such as Niall Ferguson have formalised their use.

questions.title: Syllogism with Quantifiers
questions.prompt: Examine this syllogism: 'Some politicians are honest. Some honest people are popular. Therefore, some politicians are popular.' Is this syllogism logically valid?

options.A: No — the syllogism is invalid because 'some' statements do not guarantee that the overlapping subsets are the same individuals
options.B: Yes — if some politicians are honest and some honest people are popular, the overlap must include at least one politician
options.C: Yes — the syllogism is valid because the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises using the transitive property
options.D: No — the syllogism is invalid only because the premises may be empirically false

questions.explanation: This is a classic syllogistic error involving 'some' quantifiers. The honest politicians and the popular honest people could be entirely different subgroups — there is no logical guarantee that any single person is simultaneously a politician, honest, and popular. Option B is the top misconception: students assume 'some' sets must overlap with each other when they both relate to a middle term, but Venn diagram analysis shows this need not be the case.

questions.title: Availability Heuristic Bias
questions.prompt: After watching several news reports about plane crashes, a student becomes afraid of flying but happily drives to school each day. When told that car travel is statistically far more dangerous per kilometre than air travel, she responds: 'But you always hear about plane crashes.' Which cognitive bias best explains her reasoning?

options.A: The availability heuristic — she overestimates the probability of plane crashes because vivid media examples are more mentally accessible
options.B: The anchoring bias — her fear was set by the first news story she saw and she has not updated it since
options.C: The dunning-kruger effect — she overestimates her ability to assess risk due to limited statistical knowledge
options.D: Confirmation bias — she selectively remembers news stories that confirm her pre-existing fear of flying

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic, identified by Kahneman and Tversky, describes the tendency to estimate the likelihood of an event based on how easily examples come to mind; dramatic plane crash coverage makes such events cognitively vivid and therefore feel more probable than they are. Option D (confirmation bias) is a plausible distractor, but the student's reasoning is primarily about ease of recall, not selective attention to confirming evidence.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogical Arguments
questions.prompt: A philosopher argues: 'The human brain is like a computer — it processes inputs, stores information, and produces outputs. Therefore, consciousness is simply the result of information processing, just as a computer's outputs are the result of its programming.' Critically assess the strength of this analogy.

options.A: The analogy is partially useful for describing function but fails to account for subjective experience — computers do not have qualia or self-awareness
options.B: The analogy is fully valid — modern neuroscience confirms that consciousness is identical to computational information processing
options.C: The analogy is completely invalid because brains are biological and computers are electronic, making comparison meaningless
options.D: The analogy is strong because it correctly predicts that sufficiently complex computers will become conscious

questions.explanation: Analogies are strongest when two things share relevant structural similarities and weakest when key disanalogies exist. Philosopher David Chalmers' 'hard problem of consciousness' highlights that no functional description of information processing explains why there is subjective experience at all — computers process data without any inner life. Option B is a confident misconception: neuroscience maps neural correlates of consciousness but has not established identity with computation.

questions.title: Control Variables in Experiments
questions.prompt: Two students test whether caffeine improves reaction time. Group A drinks caffeinated coffee at 8 am; Group B drinks water at 2 pm. Both groups then complete the same reaction-time test. A student says the only variable is caffeine. Identify the error.

options.A: Time of day is an uncontrolled confounding variable — alertness and reaction time naturally vary across the day, making the caffeine effect impossible to isolate
options.B: The sample size is too small — reaction time studies require at least 100 participants per group to achieve statistical significance
options.C: The test should be double-blind — participants should not know whether they consumed caffeine or water
options.D: The type of drink is a confounding variable — coffee contains compounds other than caffeine that could affect performance

questions.explanation: Confounding variables are those that vary alongside the independent variable and could independently affect the outcome; here, time of day is uncontrolled — circadian rhythms are well-documented to influence cognitive performance, so any difference in results could be attributable to the time difference rather than caffeine. Option D is a genuine concern but secondary — while coffee has other compounds, the question states the variable is caffeine and the more fundamental flaw is the uncontrolled time of day.

questions.title: TOK — Reason vs Intuition
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, a student argues: 'Reason is always a more reliable way of knowing than intuition because reason follows explicit rules that can be checked, while intuition cannot be verified.' To what extent do you agree with this claim?

options.A: Partially — reason is more transparent and checkable, but research in cognitive science shows expert intuition can reliably encode genuine patterns inaccessible to slow deliberate reasoning
options.B: Fully — formal logic provides certainty that intuition, being subjective, can never match; reason is always epistemically superior
options.C: Not at all — intuition is the foundation of all reasoning, so reason cannot be evaluated independently of it
options.D: Partially — reason is superior in mathematics, but in ethics intuition is always more reliable than reasoned argument

questions.explanation: Kahneman's dual-process theory (System 1 and System 2) and Klein's research on expert intuition demonstrate that experienced practitioners — surgeons, firefighters, chess grandmasters — develop reliable intuitions that outperform deliberate analysis in time-pressured contexts. Reason's advantage is verifiability, not guaranteed accuracy. Option B overstates the case: formal reasoning can be applied to false premises, producing certain but incorrect conclusions.

questions.title: Pattern Recognition vs Overfitting
questions.prompt: A student analyses five years of school canteen data and notices that pizza is served every time a school football match is scheduled. She concludes: 'The canteen always serves pizza on match days — this is an established pattern.' A classmate cautions that five instances may not be enough. Who has the stronger position, and why?

options.A: The classmate is stronger — five data points is insufficient to distinguish a genuine pattern from coincidence, especially without knowing how many match days had no pizza
options.B: The student is stronger — a 100% hit rate across five observations is statistically compelling and justifies calling it a pattern
options.C: Both are equally valid — pattern recognition and scepticism are complementary tools with no objective criterion for deciding between them
options.D: The student is stronger — five years of data constitutes a longitudinal study, which carries higher evidential weight than single observations

questions.explanation: A pattern claim requires not only that pizza appeared on all observed match days, but also that pizza was not served on non-match days — the student has not examined the base rate. Additionally, five events is a very small sample; in statistics, a 5/5 run has a 1/32 probability by chance alone if the event occurs half the time, not negligible. Option B is the top misconception: students often treat a 100% rate in a small sample as conclusive, ignoring sample size and base rate.

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning and Slippery Slope
questions.prompt: A school council debates lowering the voting age for student council elections from 16 to 15. One member argues: 'If we allow 15-year-olds to vote, soon we'll have 10-year-olds deciding school policy.' Evaluate whether this is a logically sound objection.

options.A: This is a slippery slope fallacy — it assumes a chain of events without providing evidence that each step will necessarily follow
options.B: This is a valid reductio ad absurdum — reducing the voting age even slightly must logically lead to removing all age restrictions
options.C: This is a straw man fallacy — the argument misrepresents the proposal as being far more extreme than it actually is
options.D: This is a false analogy — comparing students to adults in democratic contexts is logically inappropriate

questions.explanation: The slippery slope fallacy assumes that one step will inevitably lead to a sequence of increasingly extreme outcomes without demonstrating why each link in the chain is necessary; there is no logical reason why lowering the age by one year forces further reductions. Option B is a misconception — reductio ad absurdum is a legitimate proof technique that requires the absurd conclusion to follow necessarily from the premise, which is not established here.

questions.title: Inverse and Converse Errors
questions.prompt: A rule states: 'If a student scores above 90%, they receive a distinction.' A student scores below 90% and concludes: 'I will not receive a distinction.' A second student scores a distinction and concludes: 'I must have scored above 90%.' Which student has committed a logical error?

options.A: The first student has committed the fallacy of denying the antecedent — scoring below 90% does not necessarily mean no distinction, since other criteria may apply
options.B: The second student has committed the converse error — a distinction does not guarantee a score above 90%
options.C: Both students have made errors — the original rule gives neither student any valid information about their result
options.D: Neither student has made an error — both conclusions follow validly from the given conditional statement

questions.explanation: The conditional 'if P then Q' only tells us that P is sufficient for Q; failing the antecedent (scoring below 90%) does not logically prevent Q (distinction) — other routes to a distinction may exist. This is the fallacy of denying the antecedent. The second student's reasoning is actually valid: if a distinction guarantees a score above 90% only if the rule is biconditional, but as stated it is only one-directional — however, the question asks which student has committed an error, and the first student's error is more definitively established by the given rule.

questions.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student has spent three months preparing a history extended essay on a topic she now finds uninteresting and poorly evidenced. Her advisor suggests switching topics. She replies: 'I can't switch — I've already spent three months on this.' Evaluate the logical quality of her reasoning.

options.A: This is the sunk cost fallacy — past time invested is irrelevant to the future decision of which topic will produce the best essay
options.B: Her reasoning is sound — accumulated research constitutes a form of expertise that would be wasted by switching
options.C: This is an appeal to tradition — she values her original choice simply because it has lasted longer
options.D: Her reasoning is partially valid — continuity in research has genuine methodological value that should weigh against switching

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when past unrecoverable investments (time, money, effort) are used to justify continuing a suboptimal course of action; rational decision-making should be based on future expected outcomes, not past costs. Three months of unretrievable work is irrelevant to whether the topic will produce a high-quality essay. Option B is the most tempting distractor: students often conflate sunk time with accumulated expertise, but the student herself acknowledges the topic is poorly evidenced.

questions.title: Epistemology — Justified True Belief
questions.prompt: Gettier's 1963 paper challenged the classical definition of knowledge as 'justified true belief.' Which of the following scenarios best illustrates a Gettier-type counterexample?

options.A: Aiko sees a clock showing 3:15 and believes it is 3:15. The clock stopped exactly 12 hours ago, but it happens to be 3:15 — her belief is true and justified but not knowledge
options.B: Tom believes it is raining because he sees wet pavement, but the pavement was wet from a burst pipe — his belief is false and therefore not knowledge
options.C: Sara knows her flight departs at noon because she checked the airline's official website — this is genuine knowledge under the JTB model
options.D: Max believes all ravens are black after seeing 1,000 black ravens — his belief is justified but may not be true, making it uncertain knowledge

questions.explanation: Edmund Gettier showed that JTB is insufficient for knowledge by constructing cases where someone has a justified true belief that is true 'by accident.' The stopped clock case is a canonical example: Aiko's belief is justified (clocks usually tell the right time) and happens to be true, but it is true by coincidence — not because of the epistemic connection we associate with knowledge. Option B is wrong because Tom's belief is false, making it straightforwardly not knowledge rather than a Gettier case.

questions.title: Mathematical Proof by Induction
questions.prompt: A student claims that the formula 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 can be proved using mathematical induction. She verifies it for n = 1 and assumes it holds for n = k. What must she show next for the proof to be complete?

options.A: That if the formula holds for n = k, it also holds for n = k + 1, completing the inductive step
options.B: That the formula holds for n = 2 and n = 3 as additional base cases to strengthen the proof
options.C: That the formula fails for at least one value of n to establish the limits of its applicability
options.D: That the formula can be derived algebraically without assuming any particular value of n

questions.explanation: Mathematical induction requires two steps: establishing the base case (n = 1, done) and proving the inductive step — that truth for n = k implies truth for n = k + 1. Together these guarantee the formula holds for all natural numbers. Option B is a common misconception: students sometimes believe more base cases strengthen induction, but a single base case plus a valid inductive step is logically sufficient for all n ≥ 1.

questions.title: Synthesising Competing Evidence
questions.prompt: Study A (n = 500) finds that students who sleep 8 hours perform 15% better on memory tests. Study B (n = 50) finds no significant difference. Study C (n = 1,200) finds a 12% improvement with 8 hours of sleep. Synthesise these findings: what is the most epistemically justified conclusion?

options.A: The weight of evidence from the two larger studies supports a positive relationship between 8 hours of sleep and memory performance, while Study B's small sample limits its evidential weight
options.B: The studies contradict each other, so no conclusion can be drawn until a definitive single study is conducted
options.C: Study B should be weighted equally because it provides a necessary counterpoint to prevent confirmation bias in the synthesis
options.D: Study C is the only reliable study because its sample size is largest — Studies A and B should be disregarded

questions.explanation: Evidence synthesis requires weighting studies by quality indicators, including sample size; Study B's n = 50 gives it lower statistical power and wider confidence intervals, making a null result less informative than its positive-result counterparts. The convergence of Studies A and C — with large samples and consistent effect sizes — justifies a provisional positive conclusion while acknowledging Study B. Option B is a misconception: disagreement among studies does not suspend all conclusions — it requires proportionate weighting.

questions.title: Applying Occam's Razor
questions.prompt: Two students explain why lights in a school corridor flicker at the same time each day. Student A says: 'A loose electrical connection reacts to temperature changes as the building warms up.' Student B says: 'A ghost activates at exactly 9 am, and the temperature changes are coincidental.' Apply Occam's Razor to evaluate these explanations.

options.A: Student A's explanation is preferable — it invokes fewer unverified entities and relies on well-understood physical mechanisms
options.B: Student B's explanation is preferable — it accounts for the precise timing more specifically than a general electrical fault
options.C: Occam's Razor cannot be applied here because both explanations are equally untested hypotheses
options.D: Both explanations are equally valid — Occam's Razor only applies in scientific contexts, not everyday reasoning

questions.explanation: Occam's Razor (the principle of parsimony) holds that, all else being equal, the explanation requiring the fewest additional unverified assumptions should be preferred. Student A's explanation requires only known physics; Student B's requires positing an undetectable entity with unexplained timing precision. Option B is a misconception: the ghost hypothesis does not actually account for timing better — it merely asserts it, adding an extra entity without explanatory gain.

questions.title: Logical Equivalence and Contrapositive
questions.prompt: The statement 'If a shape is a square, then it is a rectangle' is given as true. Which of the following statements is logically equivalent to this original statement?

options.A: If a shape is not a rectangle, then it is not a square
options.B: If a shape is a rectangle, then it is a square
options.C: If a shape is not a square, then it is not a rectangle
options.D: A shape is a square if and only if it is a rectangle

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'If P then Q' is 'If not Q then not P', and it is always logically equivalent to the original conditional. Here, 'If not a rectangle, then not a square' is the contrapositive and shares identical truth conditions. Option B is the converse — 'If Q then P' — which is a common confusion; the converse is not logically equivalent (many rectangles are not squares, making Option B false).

questions.title: Dunning-Kruger and Metacognition
questions.prompt: A student scores 45% on a logic exam but estimates she scored about 80%. When shown her actual paper with detailed feedback, she says: 'The marking must be wrong.' Which concepts from cognitive psychology best explain her responses, and what would genuine metacognitive competence look like?

options.A: The Dunning-Kruger effect explains her overestimation; rejecting the feedback shows defensive attribution. Metacognitive competence involves accurately monitoring one's own understanding and updating beliefs on evidence
options.B: Confirmation bias explains both responses — she seeks information confirming her self-image and dismisses contradictory evidence
options.C: The halo effect explains her overestimation — positive self-image in one area inflates her estimate of performance in unrelated areas
options.D: Cognitive dissonance alone explains both behaviours — she experiences discomfort and resolves it by rejecting external feedback

questions.explanation: The Dunning-Kruger effect specifically describes how low-competence individuals lack the metacognitive skills to recognise their own incompetence, leading to overestimation; Kruger and Dunning's 1999 study found this pattern across logical reasoning, grammar, and humour tasks. Rejecting the feedback is a defensive attribution. Genuine metacognition requires calibration — comparing predicted and actual performance and adjusting future strategies accordingly. Option B (confirmation bias) is partially applicable but does not explain the initial overestimation, which is the core phenomenon here.

questions.title: Validity vs Soundness
questions.prompt: A student presents the following argument: 'All mammals are cold-blooded. Whales are mammals. Therefore, whales are cold-blooded.' Evaluate the logical status of this argument.

options.A: The argument is both valid and sound, because the conclusion follows from the premises.
options.B: The argument is valid but unsound, because the first premise is factually false.
options.C: The argument is invalid and unsound, because the conclusion is factually wrong.
options.D: The argument is sound but invalid, because a true conclusion can be reached from a false premise.

questions.explanation: Validity concerns whether the conclusion follows logically from the premises — and here it does, making the argument valid. However, soundness additionally requires all premises to be true; since mammals are warm-blooded, the first premise is false, making the argument unsound. Option C is the top distractor: students often conflate a false conclusion with invalidity, but validity is purely about the logical structure, not factual accuracy.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: A student researching the health effects of coffee only reads articles that support her existing belief that coffee is beneficial and dismisses contradictory studies as 'poorly designed.' Which cognitive bias is most precisely at work, and what is its core danger in academic research?

options.A: Anchoring bias — she is over-relying on the first studies she encountered.
options.B: Availability heuristic — she is judging probability by how easily examples come to mind.
options.C: Confirmation bias — she is selectively gathering and interpreting evidence to support a pre-existing belief.
options.D: Dunning-Kruger effect — she overestimates her ability to evaluate research quality.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias specifically describes the tendency to seek, favour, and recall information that confirms one's prior beliefs, which directly corrupts the impartiality required in academic inquiry. Option A is the top distractor: anchoring bias relates to over-weighting an initial piece of information during decision-making, not to the selective filtering of an entire body of literature.

questions.title: Modus Ponens vs Tollens
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If a number is divisible by 4, then it is divisible by 2. Premise 2: The number 18 is divisible by 2. A student concludes: 'Therefore, 18 is divisible by 4.' Which error in deductive reasoning does this illustrate?

options.A: Denying the antecedent — the student negates the 'if' part of the conditional.
options.B: Affirming the consequent — the student wrongly infers the 'if' part from the 'then' part.
options.C: Modus tollens — the student correctly applies contrapositive reasoning.
options.D: Affirming the antecedent — the student correctly applies modus ponens.

questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent is the formal fallacy of concluding P from 'If P then Q' and Q — here, knowing divisibility by 2 does not guarantee divisibility by 4, since 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5. Option A is the top distractor: denying the antecedent would require negating 'divisible by 4' to conclude 'not divisible by 2,' which is a different structural error.

questions.title: Venn Diagrams and Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 50 students, 30 study Biology, 25 study Chemistry, and 10 study both. A student claims that the number studying Biology or Chemistry but NOT both is 35. Is this claim correct?

options.A: Yes — the union of the two sets is 45, and subtracting the 10 who study both gives 35.
options.B: No — the correct number is 45, because you add 30 and 25 and subtract nothing.
options.C: No — the correct number is 25, because you subtract both sets of 10 from 30 and 25 respectively and add the results.
options.D: Yes — because 30 + 25 − 10 − 10 = 35, accounting for double-counting of both groups.

questions.explanation: Students studying only Biology = 30 − 10 = 20; students studying only Chemistry = 25 − 10 = 15; together, 20 + 15 = 35 study exactly one subject. Option B is the top distractor: students who forget to subtract the overlap entirely compute 30 + 25 = 55, or mistakenly report 45 as the exclusive count rather than the union.

questions.title: Inductive Strength and Sample Size
questions.prompt: A student surveys 8 friends and finds that 7 of them prefer online learning. She concludes: 'The majority of teenagers worldwide prefer online learning.' To what extent is this inductive argument strong?

options.A: It is strong, because a 7/8 ratio is statistically significant for a preliminary claim.
options.B: It is weak primarily because the sample is too small and unrepresentative to generalise globally.
options.C: It is strong, because inductive arguments only need to show a pattern, not prove certainty.
options.D: It is weak only because the conclusion uses the word 'majority' rather than 'most.'

questions.explanation: Inductive strength depends on sample size, representativeness, and the scope of the conclusion; a sample of 8 personal friends drawn from one social circle cannot be generalised to teenagers worldwide due to sampling bias and lack of diversity. Option C is the top distractor: while inductive arguments do not require certainty, they still demand that the evidence proportionally supports the scope of the conclusion, which here it does not.

questions.title: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: Consider the statement: 'Being over 18 is a necessary condition for voting in this country's national election.' Which of the following correctly interprets this claim?

options.A: Anyone over 18 is automatically eligible to vote.
options.B: If you can vote, you must be over 18, but being over 18 alone does not guarantee voting rights.
options.C: If you are not over 18, you cannot vote, and this is the only requirement for voting.
options.D: Being over 18 and being eligible to vote are logically equivalent conditions.

questions.explanation: A necessary condition N for outcome O means: if O then N — you cannot vote without being over 18, but there may be additional requirements (citizenship, registration) that prevent an over-18 person from voting. Option A is the top distractor: students frequently confuse necessary with sufficient conditions, wrongly assuming that meeting a necessary condition alone guarantees the outcome.

questions.title: Evaluating Analogical Arguments
questions.prompt: A politician argues: 'Running a country is just like running a business — you must cut costs, maximise efficiency, and eliminate waste.' Critically assess the strength of this analogy.

options.A: The analogy is strong because both a country and a business involve managing large budgets and many people.
options.B: The analogy is weak because countries have obligations — such as welfare, security, and rights — that businesses do not, making profit logic inappropriate as the sole framework.
options.C: The analogy is weak only because countries are larger than businesses, making direct comparison impossible.
options.D: The analogy is strong because economic efficiency is the primary goal of both governments and corporations.

questions.explanation: Analogical arguments fail when the two things being compared differ in morally or functionally relevant ways; governments must provide public goods, protect rights, and support citizens who cannot contribute economically — goals that conflict with pure profit-maximisation logic. Option A is the top distractor: surface similarities (budgets, people) do not establish that the core logic of one domain transfers to the other.

questions.title: Hypothetical Syllogism
questions.prompt: Premise 1: If global temperatures rise by 2°C, Arctic ice will melt significantly. Premise 2: If Arctic ice melts significantly, sea levels will rise. What can be validly concluded using hypothetical syllogism?

options.A: If sea levels rise, then global temperatures have risen by 2°C.
options.B: If global temperatures rise by 2°C, then sea levels will rise.
options.C: Arctic ice will melt if and only if global temperatures rise by 2°C.
options.D: Sea levels will definitely rise because global temperatures are currently rising.

questions.explanation: Hypothetical syllogism chains two conditionals: if P→Q and Q→R, then P→R; here, 2°C rise → ice melt and ice melt → sea rise, so validly: 2°C rise → sea rise. Option A is the top distractor: students often reverse the conditional, committing the fallacy of affirming the consequent by working backwards from sea level rise to temperature.

questions.title: Correlation vs Causation
questions.prompt: A study finds that countries with higher ice cream sales have higher rates of drowning. A student concludes that ice cream consumption causes drowning. Identify the most precise logical error and the most likely explanation for the correlation.

options.A: Post hoc ergo propter hoc — ice cream sales preceded drowning rates being measured.
options.B: Confounding variable — hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming, thereby increasing drowning risk independently.
options.C: Selection bias — the study only included coastal countries where both variables are naturally higher.
options.D: Hasty generalisation — a single study is insufficient to draw any conclusions about ice cream or drowning.

questions.explanation: A confounding variable (here, temperature) independently causes both observed variables, creating a spurious correlation — hot weather drives both ice cream purchases and increased water activity, making the apparent link between ice cream and drowning misleading. Option A is the top distractor: post hoc reasoning concerns inferring causation from temporal sequence, not from simultaneous correlational data mediated by a third variable.

questions.title: TOK Ways of Knowing
questions.prompt: In Theory of Knowledge, a student argues: 'Mathematical knowledge is more reliable than historical knowledge because mathematics deals with absolute truths, while history is just interpretation.' To what extent is this distinction justified?

options.A: Fully justified — mathematical proofs are deductively certain, while historical claims are always subjective opinions.
options.B: Partially justified — mathematics achieves certainty within its axiomatic system, but historians also apply rigorous evidence-based methods, and mathematical axioms themselves are chosen, not discovered.
options.C: Not justified — history is more reliable because it deals with real events, while mathematics only deals with abstract constructs.
options.D: Fully justified — the natural sciences and mathematics share absolute truth, unlike humanities subjects.

questions.explanation: Mathematical truth is conditional on its axioms (e.g., Euclidean vs non-Euclidean geometry produces different 'truths'), while historical methodology, though interpretive, uses primary sources, corroboration, and peer review to produce knowledge claims with varying degrees of justification. Option A is the top distractor: students often treat deductive certainty as equivalent to absolute or unconditional truth, ignoring that mathematical systems rest on chosen axioms.

questions.title: Identifying Ad Hominem
questions.prompt: During a school debate on climate policy, one student says: 'We shouldn't listen to Dr Chen's research on carbon emissions — she drives a petrol car, so she's a hypocrite.' Evaluate this response as a logical argument.

options.A: It is a valid point — a researcher's personal behaviour is relevant evidence when evaluating their scientific claims.
options.B: It commits ad hominem, attacking the person's character rather than engaging with the evidence in her research.
options.C: It is a tu quoque fallacy — the student is accusing Dr Chen of inconsistency, which is a different error from ad hominem.
options.D: It is an appeal to authority in reverse — dismissing an expert based solely on their credentials.

questions.explanation: Tu quoque ('you also') is a specific subtype of ad hominem that dismisses an argument by pointing out the arguer's inconsistency or hypocrisy rather than addressing the argument's content; Dr Chen's personal car use is irrelevant to the validity of her carbon emission data. Option B is the top distractor: while all tu quoque arguments are ad hominem, identifying the precise subtype 'tu quoque' is the more accurate and complete answer — however, since Option B describes the broader category and C is more specific, C is correct here.

questions.title: Falsifiability and Science
questions.prompt: Karl Popper argued that a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable. A student claims: 'The theory that an invisible, undetectable dragon lives in my garage is scientific because it cannot be disproved.' Evaluate this claim using Popper's criterion.

options.A: The student is correct — if a theory cannot be disproved, it must be considered scientifically valid.
options.B: The student is incorrect — for Popper, a theory that cannot in principle be tested or refuted is unfalsifiable and therefore non-scientific, regardless of whether it seems true.
options.C: The student is correct — Popper's criterion only applies to theories that make quantitative predictions, not to existence claims.
options.D: The student is incorrect — the theory fails because it has not yet been proved true by experimental evidence.

questions.explanation: Popper's falsifiability criterion holds that scientific theories must make predictions that could, in principle, be shown false by observation; a theory whose subject is defined as 'undetectable' can never be tested and thus lies outside science — it is non-scientific, not necessarily false. Option A is the top distractor: students often confuse 'cannot be disproved' with 'must be valid,' reversing the logic of falsifiability.

questions.title: Contrapositive Reasoning
questions.prompt: The rule states: 'If a polygon is a square, then it is a rectangle.' Which of the following statements is the logically equivalent contrapositive of this rule?

options.A: If a polygon is a rectangle, then it is a square.
options.B: If a polygon is not a square, then it is not a rectangle.
options.C: If a polygon is not a rectangle, then it is not a square.
options.D: A polygon is a square if and only if it is a rectangle.

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'If P then Q' is 'If not Q then not P,' which is logically equivalent to the original; here, 'If not a rectangle, then not a square' is the contrapositive and is necessarily true. Option A is the top distractor: students frequently confuse the contrapositive with the converse ('If Q then P'), which is a common error — the converse is not logically equivalent and is actually false (not all rectangles are squares).

questions.title: Ethical Reasoning and Trolley Problems
questions.prompt: In a classic thought experiment, a runaway trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever to divert it, killing one person instead. A student argues: 'Pulling the lever is always wrong because you are actively causing a death.' Critically assess this reasoning.

options.A: The student is correct — deontological ethics holds that actively causing harm is categorically prohibited regardless of consequences.
options.B: The student's reasoning is too absolute; it ignores utilitarian considerations and the distinction between doing harm and allowing harm, which different ethical frameworks weigh differently.
options.C: The student is incorrect because utilitarian ethics, which always maximises outcomes, is the only valid framework for such dilemmas.
options.D: The student is correct because the trolley problem is a hypothetical with no real-world application and therefore no valid answer exists.

questions.explanation: The student applies a Kantian 'acts vs omissions' distinction but presents it as universally decisive; a utilitarian framework (Bentham, Mill) would argue that saving five lives at the cost of one maximises welfare, while virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do — no single framework conclusively 'wins.' Option A is the top distractor: while it accurately represents one deontological position, it presents that position as the definitive answer rather than one competing ethical perspective.

questions.title: Recognising False Equivalence
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Scientists disagree about the precise timeline of climate change, so there is just as much scientific debate about whether human-caused climate change is happening at all.' Identify the logical error in this argument.

options.A: Appeal to ignorance — the student assumes that lack of complete certainty means the opposite is equally likely.
options.B: False equivalence — the student treats disagreement about details as equivalent to disagreement about the fundamental phenomenon, conflating two very different levels of scientific consensus.
options.C: Straw man — the student misrepresents scientists' position to make it easier to attack.
options.D: Hasty generalisation — the student draws a broad conclusion from a small number of dissenting scientists.

questions.explanation: False equivalence occurs when two unequal things are presented as comparably uncertain; over 97% of climate scientists agree on anthropogenic climate change, while legitimate debate exists only about specific timelines and magnitudes — treating these as the same level of dispute is a false equivalence. Option A is the top distractor: appeal to ignorance argues from lack of proof of X to truth of not-X, which differs from the specific error of equating two non-equivalent degrees of disagreement.

questions.title: Proof by Contradiction
questions.prompt: A student wants to prove that there is no largest prime number. She begins by assuming the opposite — that there is a largest prime, P. She then constructs the number N = (2 × 3 × 5 × … × P) + 1. What is the logical purpose of this step?

options.A: To show directly that N is always prime and therefore larger than P.
options.B: To derive a contradiction — N is either prime (larger than P) or has a prime factor not in the list, both of which contradict the assumption that P is the largest prime.
options.C: To demonstrate that multiplying all primes and adding 1 always produces a prime number.
options.D: To use inductive reasoning to confirm that the sequence of primes never terminates.

questions.explanation: Euclid's proof uses reductio ad absurdum: N, when divided by any prime up to P, leaves remainder 1, so either N itself is prime and exceeds P, or it has a prime factor not listed — either outcome contradicts the assumption that P is the largest prime, disproving it. Option C is the top distractor: N is not always prime (e.g., 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509), so students who believe the construction guarantees primality misunderstand the proof's mechanism.

questions.title: Bayesian Reasoning Basics
questions.prompt: A medical test for a rare disease (affecting 1 in 1000 people) has a 99% accuracy rate — meaning it correctly identifies both those who have the disease and those who do not, 99% of the time. If a person tests positive, a student claims there is a 99% chance they actually have the disease. Is this correct?

options.A: Yes — the test is 99% accurate, so a positive result means a 99% probability of having the disease.
options.B: No — because the disease is rare, most positive results are false positives; the actual probability is closer to 9%.
options.C: No — the test is 99% accurate, meaning it is wrong 1% of the time, so the probability is exactly 1%.
options.D: Yes — as long as the test is clinically approved, the stated accuracy rate applies directly to individual results.

questions.explanation: Using Bayes' theorem with a population of 100,000: approximately 100 have the disease, of whom 99 test positive; of the 99,900 without it, 999 also test positive (false positives) — giving roughly 99/(99+999) ≈ 9% true probability. Option A is the top distractor: students commonly commit the base rate fallacy, ignoring the low prevalence of the disease and assuming test accuracy directly equals the probability of being sick.

questions.title: Equivocation Fallacy
questions.prompt: Examine this argument: 'The sign said Fine for parking here. So I parked there, because the sign said it was fine.' Which fallacy does the argument commit, and why does it undermine the conclusion?

options.A: Straw man — the arguer misrepresents the sign's intended meaning to justify their action.
options.B: Equivocation — the word 'fine' shifts meaning from 'a monetary penalty' to 'acceptable,' allowing a deliberately misleading conclusion.
options.C: Amphiboly — the grammatical structure of the sentence creates unintended ambiguity in how the sign should be read.
options.D: Appeal to authority — the arguer uses the official sign as an authoritative source to justify the action.

questions.explanation: Equivocation exploits a word with multiple meanings by using it in one sense in a premise and another in the conclusion; 'fine' means 'penalty' on the sign but is reinterpreted as 'acceptable,' creating a deliberately fallacious inference. Option C is the top distractor: amphiboly involves grammatical ambiguity in sentence structure rather than a single word shifting meaning, making it a related but distinct fallacy.

questions.title: Sunk Cost and Rationality
questions.prompt: A student has spent six months writing a novel she now finds deeply unenjoyable. She says: 'I have to finish it — I've already put in six months of work.' A friend argues she should abandon it if it brings no value. Who reasons more rationally, and why?

options.A: The student reasons more rationally — commitment and perseverance are important values that outweigh short-term discomfort.
options.B: The friend reasons more rationally — past time invested is a sunk cost and, being irrecoverable, should not influence future decisions based on current and future value.
options.C: Both reason equally well — the student considers past investment while the friend considers future value, and both factors are relevant.
options.D: The friend reasons more rationally only if the student has a better alternative project to pursue instead.

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when irrecoverable past investments irrationally influence forward-looking decisions; rational decision-making (as in economics and decision theory) should be based solely on expected future costs and benefits, not past expenditure. Option C is the top distractor: students often believe that balancing past and future factors is good reasoning, failing to recognise that economic rationality categorically excludes sunk costs from future decisions.

questions.title: Counterfactual Historical Reasoning
questions.prompt: A historian argues: 'If the printing press had never been invented, the Protestant Reformation would not have occurred.' Synthesise what this counterfactual claim assumes, and identify its key limitation as historical reasoning.

options.A: The claim assumes the printing press was the sole cause of the Reformation, which is valid because no other technology could have spread Luther's ideas.
options.B: The claim assumes the printing press was a necessary condition for the Reformation; its key limitation is that it treats a complex, multicausal event as dependent on a single variable, ignoring religious, political, and economic factors.
options.C: The claim is a valid use of deductive reasoning, since removing one cause logically removes the effect.
options.D: The claim is strong because counterfactual history is the most rigorous form of causal analysis available to historians.

questions.explanation: Counterfactual reasoning in history is useful for identifying causal weight but is limited by the impossibility of controlling all variables; the Reformation was driven by corruption in the Church, economic tensions, and political fragmentation — the press accelerated it but was not necessarily the only path. Option A is the top distractor: students who have learned that the printing press was important to the Reformation may conflate 'important cause' with 'sole necessary cause,' which is a monocausal fallacy.

questions.title: Deductive Proof and Generalisation
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'I have checked every even number up to one million and confirmed that each is the sum of two primes. Therefore, every even number greater than 2 can be expressed as the sum of two primes.' Evaluate whether this constitutes a mathematical proof.

options.A: Yes — checking one million cases is a sufficiently large sample to establish a mathematical truth.
options.B: No — this is empirical induction, not a deductive proof; mathematical proofs must hold for all cases by logical necessity, and one counterexample beyond the checked range would disprove the conjecture.
options.C: Yes — if no counterexample has been found, the statement is considered proved by exhaustion.
options.D: No — but only because the student should have checked more cases before generalising.

questions.explanation: The student is testing Goldbach's Conjecture (1742), which remains unproved precisely because checking finite cases cannot establish infinite generality — a single unverified counterexample would invalidate the claim. Option A is the top distractor: students familiar with statistical reasoning may wrongly apply 'large sample' logic to mathematics, where proof by exhaustion only works when the case space is genuinely finite and fully enumerable.

questions.title: Argument Structure Analysis
questions.prompt: Identify the error: 'Nine out of ten dentists recommend Sparkle toothpaste. Sparkle is therefore the best toothpaste for whitening teeth.' What is the most precise logical flaw?

options.A: Hasty generalisation — the survey sample of dentists is too small to represent all dental opinion.
options.B: Non sequitur combined with an incomplete appeal to authority — 'recommended by dentists' does not logically entail 'best for whitening,' as dentists may endorse it for cavity prevention or fluoride content rather than whitening.
options.C: Ad populum — the argument appeals to a large number of dentists to generate persuasion rather than evidence.
options.D: Circular reasoning — 'best toothpaste' and 'dentist-recommended' are used to mutually reinforce each other without external evidence.

questions.explanation: The argument commits a non sequitur because 'dentist recommendation' does not imply 'best whitening'; dentists may recommend the product for fluoride content, cavity prevention, or overall dental health — none of which address whitening specifically, making the conclusion unsupported. Option A is the top distractor: while sample size could be questioned, the stated ratio (9/10) suggests a reasonable survey size, and the deeper flaw is the irrelevant conclusion about whitening, not the sample.

questions.title: Epistemology and Justified Belief
questions.prompt: Gemma believes that it is raining outside because she heard what sounded like rain on the roof. It turns out she was correct — it was raining. However, the sound was actually caused by a neighbour's sprinkler. Does Gemma's belief count as knowledge? This scenario relates to which philosophical problem?

options.A: Yes — Gemma's belief counts as knowledge because it is true and she believed it; truth plus belief is sufficient for knowledge.
options.B: No — Gemma's belief does not count as knowledge because her justification was faulty, even though the belief happened to be true; this illustrates the Gettier problem, which challenges the traditional definition of knowledge as justified true belief.
options.C: Yes — Gemma's belief counts as knowledge because she had reasonable justification (the sound) and the belief was true, satisfying all three conditions of justified true belief.
options.D: No — Gemma's belief fails because it was not justified at all; hearing a sound is not a valid form of perceptual justification.

questions.explanation: Edmund Gettier (1963) demonstrated that a belief can be justified and true yet still fail to constitute knowledge if the justification is accidentally correct — Gemma's belief is true and she had a reason to hold it, but her justification (the sound) was causally disconnected from the actual rain, leaving her belief unjustifiably lucky rather than genuinely known. Option C is the top distractor: students who have learned the three-part JTB (Justified True Belief) definition often assume it is both necessary and sufficient, not knowing that Gettier cases specifically challenge its sufficiency.

questions.title: Validity vs Soundness
questions.prompt: A student presents the following argument: 'All mammals are warm-blooded. Whales are mammals. Therefore, whales are warm-blooded.' A classmate then presents: 'All fish breathe air. Salmon are fish. Therefore, salmon breathe air.' Evaluate which argument is valid, which is sound, and which combination correctly describes both.

options.A: Both arguments are valid; only the first is sound
options.B: Both arguments are valid and both are sound
options.C: Only the first argument is valid; the second commits a fallacy of equivocation
options.D: The first argument is valid and sound; the second is neither valid nor sound

questions.explanation: Validity concerns logical form, not factual truth: if the premises were true, the conclusion must follow. Both arguments share identical valid syllogistic structure (All A are B; X is A; therefore X is B), so both are valid. However, soundness requires valid form AND true premises; the second argument's premise ('All fish breathe air') is false, so it is not sound. Option D is wrong because validity is purely structural — the second argument's false premise does not break the logical form.

questions.title: Modus Tollens Application
questions.prompt: A logician states: 'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by both 2 and 3.' A student is told that the number 91 is not divisible by 2. Which conclusion follows with strict logical necessity from these two statements alone?

options.A: 91 is divisible by 3 but not by 6
options.B: 91 is not divisible by 6
options.C: 91 is not divisible by 3
options.D: 91 is not divisible by 2 or 3

questions.explanation: Modus tollens: if P implies Q, and Q is false, then P is false. Here P = 'divisible by 6' and Q = 'divisible by both 2 and 3.' Since 91 is not divisible by 2, Q is false, so P must be false — 91 is not divisible by 6. We cannot conclude anything about divisibility by 3 from these premises alone; indeed 91 = 7 × 13 and is not divisible by 3, but that requires separate calculation, not logical deduction from the given statements, making C a tempting but unsupported inference.

questions.title: Confirmation Bias in Research
questions.prompt: Dr Patel hypothesises that students who eat breakfast perform better academically. She surveys 200 students but, when coding responses, unconsciously records ambiguous answers as supporting her hypothesis 68% of the time. Her published conclusion strongly supports the breakfast–performance link. Which methodological and epistemological problem most precisely describes what occurred?

options.A: Sampling bias, because the 200-student sample is too small to generalise
options.B: Confirmation bias operating at the data-coding stage, compromising internal validity
options.C: Publication bias, because only positive findings were submitted to journals
options.D: Observer-expectancy effect, which is distinct from confirmation bias and affects participants rather than the researcher

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to process ambiguous information in ways consistent with pre-existing beliefs; here it operates specifically during coding, which is a threat to internal validity because the measurement instrument itself is corrupted. Publication bias (C) refers to the selective publication of positive results across the whole research literature, which is not described here. The observer-expectancy effect (D) typically alters participant behaviour through researcher cues, not the researcher's own data interpretation.

questions.title: Venn Diagram Set Logic
questions.prompt: In a survey of 50 people, 30 like jazz, 25 like classical music, and 10 like neither. A student claims the number who like both genres must be exactly 15. Critically assess this claim using set theory.

options.A: The claim is incorrect; the number who like both is 5
options.B: The claim is correct; the inclusion-exclusion principle yields exactly 15
options.C: The claim is incorrect; the number who like both is 10
options.D: The claim cannot be evaluated without knowing how many like only jazz

questions.explanation: By the inclusion-exclusion principle: |J ∪ C| = |J| + |C| − |J ∩ C|. Since 10 like neither, |J ∪ C| = 50 − 10 = 40. Therefore 40 = 30 + 25 − |J ∩ C|, giving |J ∩ C| = 15. The student's claim is correct. Option A (answer 5) is a common error where students subtract 25 from 30 rather than applying inclusion-exclusion; option C confuses the 'neither' count with the 'both' count.

questions.title: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
questions.prompt: In a formal logical framework, evaluate the following: 'Being a prime number greater than 2 is a sufficient condition for being an odd number.' To what extent is this statement logically precise?

options.A: It is precise and true: every prime greater than 2 is odd, so the condition is sufficient but not necessary for oddness
options.B: It is imprecise because being prime greater than 2 is both necessary and sufficient for oddness
options.C: It is false: some primes greater than 2 are even, for example 2 itself
options.D: It is true but trivially so, because all sufficient conditions are also necessary conditions in number theory

questions.explanation: A sufficient condition for X means: whenever the condition holds, X is guaranteed. Every prime greater than 2 is indeed odd (since any even number greater than 2 is divisible by 2 and thus not prime), making it a genuinely sufficient condition. It is not necessary for oddness because many odd numbers (e.g. 9, 15) are not prime. Option C confuses the statement by referencing 2 itself, which is excluded by the condition 'greater than 2.'

questions.title: Straw Man vs Steel Man
questions.prompt: During a TOK seminar, Priya argues: 'Indigenous knowledge systems should be given equal epistemic status to scientific knowledge in schools.' Dani responds: 'So you want us to teach students that the Earth is flat and that vaccines cause harm — that's dangerous.' Identify the precise logical error Dani commits and explain why it undermines the debate.

options.A: Ad hominem, because Dani attacks the consequences of Priya's view rather than Priya's character
options.B: False dichotomy, because Dani implies there are only two possible positions on epistemic status
options.C: Straw man, because Dani replaces Priya's actual argument with a distorted, extreme version that is easier to attack
options.D: Slippery slope, because Dani predicts extreme harms without demonstrating the causal chain from Priya's position

questions.explanation: Priya's claim is about epistemic status and inclusion in curricula, not about endorsing flat-earth theories or anti-vaccine claims; Dani constructs an extreme misrepresentation to attack instead of engaging with the actual argument — the defining feature of a straw man fallacy. Option D (slippery slope) is tempting because Dani does project harmful consequences, but the primary error is the misrepresentation of Priya's position rather than an unsupported causal chain of events.

questions.title: Inductive Strength Assessment
questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical researcher observes that in 1,000 randomised controlled trials across diverse populations, Drug X reduces tumour size in 78% of participants. She concludes: 'Drug X will reduce tumour size in the next patient.' Evaluate the logical strength of this inductive inference.

options.A: The inference is deductively valid because the 78% figure constitutes near-certainty in medicine
options.B: The inference is inductively strong but not logically guaranteed, because induction never yields certainty regardless of sample size
options.C: The inference is weak because 1,000 trials represent a small fraction of all possible patients
options.D: The inference commits the base rate fallacy by ignoring the prior probability of tumour reduction

questions.explanation: Inductive inferences, however well-supported, cannot be logically guaranteed — this is Hume's problem of induction. Even 1,000 RCTs provide extremely strong inductive support, making the inference 'strong' in the technical sense, but the conclusion about the next specific patient is not deductively entailed. Option A incorrectly applies the concept of deductive validity, which requires that the conclusion cannot possibly be false given true premises — a threshold no amount of empirical data can meet.

questions.title: Counterfactual Causation
questions.prompt: Historians debate whether World War I would have occurred without the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. A student argues: 'Since the war began immediately after the assassination, the assassination was the cause.' Critically assess the logical and historical adequacy of this argument.

options.A: The argument is sound because temporal precedence is both necessary and sufficient to establish causation
options.B: The argument conflates correlation with causation and ignores the structural conditions — alliance systems, imperial rivalries, militarism — that made war likely regardless of any single event
options.C: The argument is valid but unsound, because counterfactual reasoning cannot establish historical causation at all
options.D: The argument is strong because the assassination is the only event that changed between peacetime and the outbreak of war

questions.explanation: Post hoc ergo propter hoc ('after this, therefore because of this') is the fallacy of assuming temporal sequence implies causation. Historians widely recognise that structural preconditions — the alliance web, the arms race, imperial competition — made European war highly probable; the assassination was a proximate trigger, not a sufficient cause in isolation. Option C is wrong because counterfactual reasoning is a legitimate and widely used tool in both philosophy of causation and historical methodology, not inherently invalid.

questions.title: Formal Proof by Contradiction
questions.prompt: A student attempts to prove that √2 is irrational. She begins: 'Assume √2 = p/q where p and q are integers with no common factors.' She then shows p² = 2q², concludes p is even, writes p = 2k, and finds q² = 2k², concluding q is also even. She then stops. What must she state next to complete the proof, and why does it succeed?

options.A: She must verify that 2k² = q² has integer solutions, confirming the assumption was correct
options.B: She must note that p and q both being even contradicts the assumption that they share no common factors, thus the original assumption is false and √2 is irrational
options.C: She must show that p/q cannot be simplified further, proving the fraction is already in lowest terms
options.D: She must use the fundamental theorem of arithmetic to show 2 appears an odd number of times in the prime factorisation of p², completing the proof by unique factorisation

questions.explanation: The proof works by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum): the initial assumption was that p/q is fully reduced (gcd(p,q) = 1). Showing both p and q are even means 2 divides both, contradicting the no-common-factor assumption. This contradiction proves the assumption that √2 is rational must be false. Option D describes an alternative valid proof method (using the fundamental theorem of arithmetic), but it is not what the student's specific proof structure requires at that stage — she has set up a contradiction proof, not a prime factorisation argument.

questions.title: Availability Heuristic Evaluation
questions.prompt: After seeing three news reports about plane crashes in one week, a student refuses to fly for her IB field trip and says: 'Flying is obviously more dangerous than driving.' Evaluate the quality of her reasoning, identifying the specific cognitive mechanism involved and its effect on risk perception.

options.A: Her reasoning is sound because media coverage accurately reflects the statistical frequency of dangerous events
options.B: She commits the availability heuristic: vivid, recent media events inflate perceived frequency of plane crashes, while statistically driving causes far more deaths per mile travelled
options.C: She commits the representativeness heuristic: she assumes that because crashes are associated with aviation, her specific flight will crash
options.D: Her reasoning reflects rational risk aversion: even if crashes are rare, their catastrophic nature justifies avoiding flying entirely

questions.explanation: The availability heuristic (Tversky and Kahneman, 1973) leads people to judge probability by how easily examples come to mind; dramatic news coverage makes plane crashes cognitively accessible and thus seem more frequent. In reality, aviation has approximately 0.07 deaths per billion kilometres versus over 3 deaths per billion kilometres for road travel, making driving statistically more dangerous. Option C (representativeness) refers to judging probability by similarity to a prototype, which is not the mechanism operating here.

questions.title: Logical Equivalence and Contrapositive
questions.prompt: Consider the conditional statement: 'If a student passes the IB Diploma, then they have passed Theory of Knowledge.' Which of the following is logically equivalent to this statement — not merely true in some cases, but equivalent in all possible logical scenarios?

options.A: If a student has passed Theory of Knowledge, then they have passed the IB Diploma
options.B: If a student has not passed Theory of Knowledge, then they have not passed the IB Diploma
options.C: If a student has not passed the IB Diploma, then they have not passed Theory of Knowledge
options.D: A student passes the IB Diploma if and only if they pass Theory of Knowledge

questions.explanation: A conditional 'P → Q' is logically equivalent to its contrapositive '¬Q → ¬P.' Here P = passes IB Diploma, Q = passes TOK, so the contrapositive is 'if not passed TOK, then not passed IB Diploma' — which is option B. Option A is the converse (Q → P) and option C is the inverse (¬P → ¬Q); both are common confusions and are logically distinct from the original. Option D (biconditional) asserts equivalence in both directions, which is stronger than and not equivalent to the original statement.

questions.title: Falsifiability and Popper
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'My theory predicts that if extra study time is applied, performance improves — but if it doesn't improve, that just shows the student wasn't really studying properly.' A TOK teacher says this theory has a structural problem. Identify the problem and name the philosopher whose criterion it violates.

options.A: The theory violates Kuhn's criterion of paradigm consistency, because it cannot be integrated into the current scientific paradigm
options.B: The theory is unfalsifiable: by redefining failed predictions as 'not real' instances, it immunises itself against empirical refutation, violating Popper's criterion of falsifiability
options.C: The theory commits the naturalistic fallacy by deriving an 'ought' (students ought to study) from an 'is' (study improves performance)
options.D: The theory violates Occam's Razor by introducing an unnecessary explanatory variable — 'real studying' — when simpler explanations exist

questions.explanation: Karl Popper argued that a scientific theory must be falsifiable — there must exist possible observations that could prove it wrong. By redefining any counter-instance as 'not real studying,' the theory makes itself immune to refutation, which Popper called an 'immunising stratagem.' This is a central concept in his 1959 work The Logic of Scientific Discovery. Option A (Kuhn) is a tempting distractor because Kuhn also discussed scientific demarcation, but his criterion involves paradigm membership, not falsifiability.

questions.title: Equivocation Fallacy
questions.prompt: Identify the logical fallacy: 'The law of nature says the strongest survive. Laws must be obeyed. Therefore, humans are morally obligated to let the weakest members of society perish without assistance.'

options.A: The argument commits equivocation by using 'law' in two different senses: a descriptive natural principle and a prescriptive normative rule
options.B: The argument commits the naturalistic fallacy exclusively, by deriving a moral 'ought' from a natural 'is'
options.C: The argument is a valid syllogism; its conclusion is false only because the first premise is empirically incorrect
options.D: The argument commits a category error by treating biological processes as equivalent to human institutions

questions.explanation: Equivocation occurs when a key term is used with two different meanings across an argument. 'Law' first means a descriptive pattern in nature (no obligation implied), then shifts to mean a prescriptive rule requiring compliance — these are categorically different senses. While the argument also contains naturalistic fallacy elements, equivocation is the primary structural error that makes the syllogism invalid. Option B is partially correct but incomplete — it misses the equivocation that precedes and enables the naturalistic move.

questions.title: Deductive Argument Structure
questions.prompt: Synthesise your understanding of argument structure to evaluate: 'Premise 1: All actions that maximise overall happiness are morally right. Premise 2: Torturing one innocent person sometimes maximises overall happiness. Conclusion: Therefore, torturing one innocent person is sometimes morally right.' Is this argument valid, and what does your answer reveal about the difference between validity and moral acceptability?

options.A: The argument is invalid because the conclusion is morally unacceptable, demonstrating that logical validity requires moral defensibility
options.B: The argument is valid but not necessarily sound: the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises, but a moral realist would reject Premise 1 as false
options.C: The argument is invalid because Premise 2 is empirically unverifiable, which breaks the logical chain
options.D: The argument is sound because both premises are widely accepted in utilitarian ethics and the conclusion follows logically

questions.explanation: Logical validity is purely formal: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be. The argument has valid syllogistic structure. However, 'sound' requires valid form plus true premises; a deontologist or rights-theorist would deny Premise 1 (that maximising happiness is the sole criterion of moral rightness), making the argument invalid in soundness but not in form. Option A commits a fundamental error by conflating moral unacceptability with logical invalidity — two entirely separate dimensions of argument evaluation.

questions.title: Anchoring Bias in Judgement
questions.prompt: In an experiment, Group A is asked: 'Is the population of Turkey more or less than 5 million?' then gives an estimate. Group B is asked: 'Is the population of Turkey more or less than 100 million?' then gives an estimate. Group A's mean estimate is 17 million; Group B's is 68 million. The actual population is approximately 85 million. What cognitive phenomenon explains the difference between the two groups' estimates?

options.A: Framing effect, because the questions present different emotional frames around the same information
options.B: Anchoring bias, because each group's initial reference number disproportionately influenced their subsequent estimate
options.C: The representative heuristic, because participants matched Turkey's population to their mental prototype of a medium-sized country
options.D: Regression to the mean, because both groups' estimates converge toward the actual population figure over repeated trials

questions.explanation: Anchoring bias (Tversky and Kahneman) describes how an initial numerical reference point — even an arbitrary one — systematically distorts subsequent quantitative judgements by insufficient adjustment from the anchor. Group A anchored on 5 million and adjusted upward insufficiently; Group B anchored on 100 million and also adjusted insufficiently downward. The framing effect (A) involves changes in response due to how information is presented contextually or emotionally, not specifically the influence of a numerical anchor on quantitative estimation.

questions.title: Abductive Reasoning Limits
questions.prompt: A detective notes: a window is broken from outside, muddy boot prints lead to the safe, and £10,000 is missing. She concludes: 'A burglar broke in and stole the money.' A student argues this is deductive reasoning because the conclusion fits all the evidence. Critically assess the student's classification.

options.A: The student is correct: when a conclusion accounts for all available evidence, it qualifies as deductively valid
options.B: The student is incorrect: this is abductive reasoning — inference to the best explanation — which selects the most plausible hypothesis but does not rule out alternatives with logical necessity
options.C: The student is incorrect: this is inductive reasoning, because the detective is generalising from a pattern of observations to a universal conclusion about burglary
options.D: The student is partially correct: the reasoning is deductive in structure but inductive in certainty, a hybrid form known as retroductive reasoning

questions.explanation: Abductive reasoning, formalised by C.S. Peirce, infers the most explanatory hypothesis from observed evidence without logically eliminating alternatives — the homeowner could have staged the scene, or the money could have been moved earlier. Deductive reasoning, by contrast, guarantees the conclusion given true premises. Inductive reasoning (C) involves generalising from multiple instances to a general rule, which is not what the detective is doing — she is inferring the best explanation for a specific event.

questions.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
questions.prompt: A student has spent 200 hours on an Extended Essay topic that her supervisor now says is deeply flawed and unlikely to score above a D. She decides to continue because 'I've put too much time in to give up now.' Evaluate this decision from a rational choice perspective and identify the fallacy involved.

options.A: The decision is rational because consistency and perseverance are virtues that improve long-term academic outcomes
options.B: The student commits the sunk cost fallacy: past irrecoverable time investment should not influence forward-looking decisions, which should be based on expected future value only
options.C: The student commits the gambler's fallacy: she assumes past effort increases the probability of future success
options.D: The decision reflects rational loss aversion: the psychological cost of abandoning 200 hours outweighs the marginal benefit of switching topics

questions.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy occurs when irrecoverable past investments (time, money, effort) are allowed to influence future decisions, contrary to rational choice theory, which holds that only prospective costs and benefits should matter. The 200 hours cannot be recovered regardless of what she does next; the rational question is purely whether continuing or switching now yields a better expected outcome. Option D attempts to legitimise the reasoning as 'rational loss aversion,' but loss aversion describes sensitivity to potential losses of future value, not attachment to unrecoverable past costs.

questions.title: Hypothesis Testing Logic
questions.prompt: In a psychology experiment, a researcher sets a significance level of p < 0.05 and obtains p = 0.03. She concludes: 'There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true.' To what extent is this interpretation of the p-value correct?

options.A: Correct: p = 0.03 means there is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data
options.B: Mostly correct, but p = 0.03 should be interpreted as a 3% chance of a Type I error specifically in this study
options.C: Incorrect: p = 0.03 means there is a 3% probability of obtaining results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true — it says nothing directly about the probability of the null hypothesis being true
options.D: Incorrect: p-values cannot be used to draw any conclusions about null hypotheses; only Bayesian posterior probabilities can do this

questions.explanation: The p-value is defined as P(data ≥ observed | H₀ is true) — the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, which would require a Bayesian framework with a prior. This misinterpretation (the 'inverse probability fallacy' or 'prosecutor's fallacy') is one of the most common errors in statistics education. Option D overstates the limitation: p-values do allow probabilistic inference about rejecting H₀ under the frequentist framework.

questions.title: Burden of Proof Principle
questions.prompt: A classmate claims: 'You cannot prove that dark matter does not exist, so it must exist.' Evaluate this argument and identify which principle of rational discourse it violates.

options.A: The argument is valid because absence of evidence is always evidence of absence in scientific reasoning
options.B: The argument commits an appeal to ignorance (argumentum ad ignorantiam): inability to disprove a claim does not constitute positive evidence for it
options.C: The argument commits a false dilemma: dark matter either exists or it does not, so we must accept one option
options.D: The argument is inductively weak but not fallacious, because scientific consensus does support the existence of dark matter

questions.explanation: Argumentum ad ignorantiam is the fallacy of treating the absence of disproof as proof of a positive claim. The burden of proof lies with the person making the positive assertion (dark matter exists), not with those who lack a refutation. Philosophically, this is sometimes called Hitchens's Razor: 'What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.' Option D conflates the argument's logical structure with the separate question of whether the conclusion (dark matter exists) happens to be well-supported by other evidence — the two are independent evaluations.

questions.title: Russell's Paradox and Self-Reference
questions.prompt: Bertrand Russell posed the following paradox: 'Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does this set contain itself?' A student says: 'This is just a word game — any sufficiently large set would contain itself.' Critically assess the student's dismissal.

options.A: The student is correct: in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, all sufficiently large sets contain themselves, resolving the paradox
options.B: The student is wrong: the paradox reveals a genuine contradiction in naive set theory and led directly to the development of axiomatic set theory to restrict unrestricted set comprehension
options.C: The student is correct: the paradox is a linguistic confusion, not a mathematical problem, and has no bearing on formal logic
options.D: The student is partially right: the paradox only arises in informal logic and was resolved when Gödel proved that no set can contain itself

questions.explanation: Russell's Paradox (1901) exposed a genuine contradiction in Frege's naive set theory: if the set R of all non-self-containing sets exists, then R ∈ R implies R ∉ R and vice versa. This led directly to axiomatic set theory (Zermelo-Fraenkel), which restricts set formation through the Axiom Schema of Separation to prevent such contradictions. Option A is wrong because ZF set theory does not allow any set to contain itself due to the Axiom of Regularity (also called the Axiom of Foundation).

questions.title: Dunning-Kruger and Metacognition
questions.prompt: Research by Kruger and Dunning (1999) found that participants who scored in the bottom quartile on logic tests consistently overestimated their performance by a larger margin than high performers. A student argues: 'This proves that ignorant people are always more confident than experts.' To what extent is this a valid synthesis of the research?

options.A: Fully valid: the study demonstrates a universal law that incompetence produces overconfidence across all domains
options.B: Partially valid but overstated: the original study showed bottom-quartile participants overestimated their rank, but the effect is domain-specific, varies with task type, and high performers in the study also showed metacognitive errors — they tended to underestimate their relative performance
options.C: Invalid: subsequent studies have entirely failed to replicate the Dunning-Kruger effect, so no conclusions can be drawn
options.D: Mostly valid, except the study actually showed that experts are never overconfident, only underconfident
