The thermostat itself does not convert energy into heat, so calling it a process stage is incorrect.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright
questions.prompt: A student creates an original drawing and shares it on a class website. Does copyright protection apply automatically, or does the student need to register it with a government office first?

options.A: Copyright applies only after the student registers the drawing with a government copyright office
options.B: Copyright applies automatically the moment an original creative work is created
options.C: Copyright applies only if the drawing is printed and not shared digitally
options.D: Copyright applies only to adults, not to work made by children

questions.explanation: Under international copyright law (including the Berne Convention), copyright protection is automatic from the moment an original work is created — no registration is needed. Children's creative works receive the same copyright protection as those made by adults.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment: End of Life
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment (LCA) of a plastic toy shows that most of its environmental impact happens during manufacturing, not disposal. A classmate concludes: 'Then we don't need to worry about what happens to it after children stop playing with it.' Evaluate this conclusion.

options.A: The conclusion is correct — if manufacturing causes the most harm, end-of-life disposal is unimportant
options.B: The conclusion is incorrect — end-of-life disposal still contributes to total environmental impact and affects ecosystems even if it is a smaller share
options.C: The conclusion is correct — plastic toys are always recycled, so disposal has zero impact
options.D: The conclusion is incorrect — disposal always causes more environmental harm than manufacturing

questions.explanation: An LCA measures impact at every stage, and even a smaller end-of-life contribution — such as plastic entering landfill or waterways — is still a real environmental harm that designers should minimise. Option D is also wrong because it overclaims: disposal is not always the largest impact stage, as the LCA in this case clearly shows manufacturing is greater.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Automation and Jobs
questions.prompt: A factory installs robots that can pack boxes three times faster than human workers. The factory now needs fewer packers. Which ethical question should designers and engineers consider BEFORE introducing such automation?

options.A: Should the robots be painted the same colour as the factory walls?
options.B: How will the workers who lose their jobs be supported, and is this a fair outcome for them?
options.C: Will the robots be able to pack boxes of every colour equally well?
options.D: Is packing boxes a task that requires a university degree?

questions.explanation: Technology ethics requires designers and engineers to consider the human consequences of their solutions — including whether people who lose work due to automation can retrain, are compensated, or face hardship. The colour of robots and box colour compatibility are engineering details, not ethical questions about fairness to people.

questions.title: Iterative Design: Test and Refine
questions.prompt: What would happen if a design team skipped the testing stage and went straight from their first prototype to mass production?

options.A: The product would automatically be better because it was made faster
options.B: Unsolved problems discovered only by real users could be produced in large quantities, making them costly to fix
options.C: Testing is optional in professional design, so nothing bad would necessarily happen
options.D: The product would be safer because fewer people handled it during development

questions.explanation: Skipping testing means undetected flaws — such as a part that breaks under normal use — get reproduced across thousands of units, making repairs or recalls extremely expensive and potentially dangerous. Testing is considered a required stage in iterative design precisely because it catches problems before they are multiplied at scale.

questions.title: UX Research: Observation vs. Interview
questions.prompt: A designer wants to understand how six-year-olds actually use a new puzzle app. She could interview children about their experience, or she could watch them play the app silently. Which method would more accurately reveal problems the children cannot easily put into words?

options.A: Interviewing, because children can explain exactly what they find confusing
options.B: Silent observation, because it captures actual behaviour including moments of confusion children may not notice or be able to describe
options.C: Interviewing, because it produces data that is easier to count and compare
options.D: Silent observation, because children always perform better when no one speaks to them

questions.explanation: Observation captures real-time behaviour — such as a child pausing, backtracking, or accidentally pressing the wrong button — that users often cannot recall or articulate in an interview. Interviews rely on self-reporting, which young children find especially difficult for sub-conscious actions; Option A overstates their ability to verbalise subtle usability problems.

questions.title: Material Properties: Flexibility vs. Rigidity
questions.prompt: A designer needs a material for the frame of children's glasses. The frame must bend slightly without breaking if a child sits on them, but must spring back to its original shape. Which combination of properties is most important?

options.A: High hardness and high density, so the frame resists all bending
options.B: Flexibility and elasticity, so the frame bends and then returns to its original shape
options.C: High thermal conductivity, so the frame feels comfortable in cold weather
options.D: Brittleness and low mass, so the frame is as light as possible

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the property that allows a material to return to its original shape after being deformed — combined with flexibility, this is exactly what a glasses frame needs when accidentally bent. A hard, rigid material (Option A) would not bend and might instead snap, making it unsuitable for this purpose.

questions.title: Design Brief: Constraints vs. Criteria
questions.prompt: A design brief says: 'The lunchbox must keep food cold for at least four hours, must cost under ten dollars to make, and must fit inside a standard school bag.' Which part of this brief describes a CONSTRAINT rather than a success criterion?

options.A: Keeping food cold for at least four hours, because this is what success looks like
options.B: Costing under ten dollars to make, because this is a fixed limit the design cannot exceed
options.C: Fitting inside a standard school bag, because this is what success looks like
options.D: All three requirements are success criteria because they describe desired outcomes

questions.explanation: A constraint is a fixed boundary that cannot be crossed — a budget cap of ten dollars is a hard limit imposed from outside the design itself. A success criterion describes measurable performance the design should achieve, such as keeping food cold for four hours. Both keeping food cold and fitting in a bag are performance targets, making them criteria rather than constraints.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: Compare a linear economy and a circular economy. In a linear economy, a company makes a product, a customer uses it, and it is thrown away. What is the KEY difference in a circular economy?

options.A: Products are made faster so they can be replaced more often
options.B: Materials and products are kept in use as long as possible through repair, reuse, or recycling instead of disposal
options.C: Products are always manufactured closer to where customers live
options.D: Companies charge higher prices so customers value products more and use them longer

questions.explanation: A circular economy is defined by keeping resources in use at their highest value for as long as possible — through reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and recycling — so that waste is designed out of the system. Making products faster (Option A) actually accelerates the linear take-make-dispose pattern, which is the opposite of circular.

questions.title: Ideation: Convergent Thinking
questions.prompt: After a brainstorming session, a team has 40 different ideas. They now need to choose the two or three best ideas to develop further. Which type of thinking are they using in this selection step?

options.A: Divergent thinking, because they are reviewing many possibilities
options.B: Empathic thinking, because they must consider the user while choosing
options.C: Convergent thinking, because they are narrowing many ideas down to the most promising few
options.D: Lateral thinking, because they are looking at ideas from unusual angles

questions.explanation: Convergent thinking is the process of evaluating and narrowing multiple options down to the best solution — it follows divergent thinking (generating many ideas) in the design process. Divergent thinking is what happened during brainstorming; the selection step is explicitly convergent, not divergent.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trademark
questions.prompt: A student designs a logo and name for a lemonade stand. Her friend starts using the exact same name and logo on his competing stand. Which type of intellectual property protection would have been MOST useful to prevent this?

options.A: A patent, because it protects new products from being copied
options.B: A trademark, because it protects brand names and logos from being used by others
options.C: A trade secret, because keeping the logo private would have stopped copying
options.D: Creative Commons licensing, because it tells others how they may use the design

questions.explanation: A trademark specifically protects brand identifiers — names, logos, and symbols — that distinguish one business's goods or services from another's. A patent protects inventions and processes, not brand identity, so it would not apply to a logo and name used commercially.

questions.title: Sustainability: Embodied Energy
questions.prompt: Two bags are being compared. Bag A is made of cotton and Bag B is made of recycled polyester. A student says cotton is always more sustainable because it is natural. Why is this claim too simple?

options.A: The claim is too simple because cotton bags are always less sustainable than any synthetic material
options.B: The claim is too simple because growing cotton requires large amounts of water and pesticides, giving it a significant environmental footprint
options.C: The claim is too simple because natural materials cannot be used to make bags
options.D: The claim is too simple because only bags made in one country can be called sustainable

questions.explanation: Cotton is natural but not automatically low-impact — conventional cotton farming is one of the most water-intensive and pesticide-heavy agricultural processes, sometimes giving it a higher environmental cost than recycled synthetics across its full lifecycle. 'Natural' and 'sustainable' are not synonyms, which is why a full lifecycle assessment is needed rather than simple category labels.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystems
questions.prompt: A school designs a system that collects rainwater, filters it, and delivers it to garden taps. Which correctly identifies two separate SUBSYSTEMS within this larger system?

options.A: The rain and the garden are the two subsystems
options.B: The collection subsystem (gutters and tank) and the filtration subsystem (filter and pipes) are two distinct parts
options.C: The water and the electricity are the two subsystems
options.D: The students and the teachers who manage the system are the two subsystems

questions.explanation: In systems engineering, a subsystem is a self-contained part of a larger system that performs a specific function — here, collection and filtration are two distinct functional groups, each with their own components. The rain itself is an input to the system, not a subsystem within it.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: First Mover
questions.prompt: Being first to market with a new product can give a company a big advantage, but it also carries risks. Which risk is MOST specific to being a first mover in a new market?

options.A: Having to spend money on advertising, which all companies must do
options.B: Educating customers about a product type that does not yet exist, while later competitors can simply offer an improved version once the market is established
options.C: Being unable to patent the product because it is too new
options.D: Finding it impossible to hire staff because no one has heard of the company yet

questions.explanation: First movers bear the cost of building consumer awareness and acceptance of an entirely new product category, then risk losing market share to 'fast follower' competitors who learn from the pioneer's mistakes and offer refined versions. Advertising costs and hiring challenges affect all companies, not specifically first movers.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Data Privacy
questions.prompt: A children's game app collects players' ages, locations, and game scores and shares this information with advertising companies. A designer argues this is acceptable because the app is free to download. Identify the ethical problem with this reasoning.

options.A: There is no ethical problem — free services always require data sharing
options.B: Children cannot legally give meaningful consent to data collection, and their location data creates safety risks regardless of the app's price
options.C: The ethical problem is only that game scores should be kept private
options.D: The problem is that the app should charge a fee instead of using advertising

questions.explanation: Children cannot give fully informed consent to data collection and sharing, and location data in particular creates real child safety risks; these harms exist independently of whether the app is free. The argument that a free price justifies any data practice is an ethical fallacy — the value of the service does not override children's rights to privacy and safety.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Visibility and Contrast
questions.prompt: A student designs an emergency exit sign for a school corridor. She uses light grey text on a white background because she thinks it looks clean and modern. Why is this likely to fail as an ergonomic design?

options.A: Emergency signs must always be circular, not rectangular
options.B: Low colour contrast between text and background makes the sign very hard to read quickly, especially in smoke or dim lighting
options.C: Modern-looking designs are not permitted in school buildings
options.D: Grey text fades faster than other colours, so the sign will need replacing sooner

questions.explanation: Ergonomic signage for safety must prioritise legibility under difficult conditions — high contrast (such as the internationally standard green/white or red/white) allows people to read signs rapidly even in low visibility. Low contrast between similar tones drastically reduces reading speed and distance, which is dangerous in an emergency.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Levels
questions.prompt: A team is at the very beginning of a project and wants to quickly test three very different ideas for a new school locker design. Which type of prototype is MOST appropriate at this early stage?

options.A: A high-fidelity prototype made from the final materials, finished to look like the real product
options.B: A low-fidelity prototype such as a cardboard model or sketch, made quickly to explore ideas without large investment
options.C: A digital simulation run on a computer to test structural strength
options.D: A written report listing all the advantages of each locker design

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes — rough physical models or sketches — are ideal for early-stage exploration because they are fast and cheap to make and easy to change, allowing many different ideas to be tested without committing time and money. High-fidelity prototypes are valuable later, once the concept is more developed and needs detailed evaluation.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Process
questions.prompt: A design team wants to create a new backpack for young children. Before they start sketching ideas, they spend a whole day watching children pack and carry their bags at school. Why is this observation step done BEFORE ideation rather than after?

options.A: To decide which materials will be cheapest to buy
options.B: To discover real problems users face before inventing solutions
options.C: To check whether a prototype already solves the problem
options.D: To write the design brief that lists the budget

questions.explanation: The empathise stage comes first so designers discover genuine user needs before they invent anything; this stops them solving the wrong problem. Checking a prototype (C) belongs to the test stage, which happens much later in the process.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Choice
questions.prompt: A student is designing a new pencil grip for children with small hands. She has limited time. Should she build a detailed, painted model or a rough cardboard mock-up first, and why?

options.A: The detailed model, because users give more honest feedback on finished-looking products
options.B: The rough mock-up, because it lets her test the basic shape quickly and cheaply before investing more effort
options.C: The detailed model, because the IB design cycle requires a fully finished prototype at every stage
options.D: The rough mock-up, because materials do not matter at all in the testing stage

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes are built early to test core ideas quickly and cheaply, so changes are easy to make without wasting resources. Option A is wrong because while a polished look can affect feedback, the main reason for a rough prototype is speed and cost, not the appearance preference of users.

questions.title: Material Thermal Properties
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable lunch box that must keep food warm for three hours. She compares two materials: aluminium foil lining and foam padding. Which material property makes foam the better choice for keeping heat inside?

options.A: Foam is waterproof, so it stops steam escaping
options.B: Foam is a thermal insulator, so it slows the movement of heat through the walls
options.C: Foam is lightweight, so it reduces the overall temperature loss
options.D: Foam is rigid, so it prevents heat from escaping through cracks

questions.explanation: Foam traps air in tiny pockets, making it a poor conductor of heat — this is the property called thermal insulation, which slows heat transfer. Aluminium, by contrast, is a good thermal conductor and would let heat escape quickly, which is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: After interviewing users, a team writes this problem statement: 'We need to make a better product.' A classmate says this statement is not useful. What is the MAIN reason the classmate is correct?

options.A: It does not mention a specific budget or timeline for the project
options.B: It does not name a specific user, a specific problem, or a measurable goal
options.C: It was written before any prototypes were tested, so it cannot be accurate
options.D: It is too short to count as a proper design brief in the IB process

questions.explanation: A good problem statement from the define stage must identify who the user is, what specific challenge they face, and what success would look like — without these, designers cannot judge whether their solution is good. Mentioning budget (A) is part of specifications, not the core purpose of a problem statement.

questions.title: Sustainability and Material Choice
questions.prompt: A company is choosing between two materials for a children's toy: recycled plastic and freshly cut wood from a certified sustainable forest. Which statement best explains why BOTH options can be considered more sustainable than using non-recycled, non-certified materials?

options.A: Both materials are biodegradable, so they break down safely after disposal
options.B: Both reduce demand for extracting new raw materials from the environment
options.C: Both are cheaper to produce, which makes the toy more affordable
options.D: Both materials can be melted and reformed into new products easily

questions.explanation: Recycled plastic reuses existing plastic instead of making new plastic from oil, and certified sustainable wood comes from forests that are replanted, so neither requires large amounts of new raw material to be taken from nature. Recycled plastic is not biodegradable (A), so that reason does not apply to both.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Fit
questions.prompt: A class is evaluating two designs for a child's scissors. Design A has handles that open and close smoothly with a spring but are the same size for all users. Design B has handles that can be squeezed to different widths but require more force to cut. Which design better applies the principle of ergonomics, and why?

options.A: Design A, because the spring reduces the effort needed and effort reduction is the core of ergonomics
options.B: Design B, because adjustable handles fit a wider range of hand sizes, reducing strain for more users
options.C: Design A, because a uniform size is easier to manufacture and ergonomics includes production efficiency
options.D: Design B, because requiring more force builds hand strength, which is an ergonomic health benefit

questions.explanation: Ergonomics means designing products that fit the physical characteristics of their users; adjustable handles accommodate different hand sizes, directly reducing discomfort or strain across a wider group. Design A's spring helps with force but ignores the variation in hand sizes among children, which is the more fundamental ergonomic issue here.

questions.title: Iterative Testing and Feedback
questions.prompt: A team tests their prototype water bottle with five classmates. Three say the lid is hard to open; two say it is fine. A teammate says, 'Most people struggle, so we should redesign the lid.' Another says, 'Two people were okay with it, so the lid is good enough.' Whose reasoning is stronger, and why?

options.A: The second teammate, because if some users can manage the lid, the problem is with user skill, not the design
options.B: The first teammate, because a majority finding it hard signals a real design problem worth fixing
options.C: Neither, because five users is too small a sample to draw any conclusion at all
options.D: The second teammate, because design changes are costly and should only happen after much larger tests

questions.explanation: When 60% of test users identify the same difficulty, that pattern is strong evidence of a design flaw that should be iterated on; the design process treats repeated user difficulty as a signal to improve. Option C overstates the limitation — even small tests provide actionable feedback in early-stage prototyping, especially when a clear majority agrees.

questions.title: Innovation vs. Invention
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Creating something that has never existed before and creating something that improves an existing product are both called inventions.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct, because any new or improved product counts as an invention in design
options.B: The claim is partly correct: a completely new creation is an invention, but improving an existing product is called an innovation
options.C: The claim is incorrect: improving an existing product is an invention, and creating something brand new is an innovation
options.D: The claim is correct, because patents are granted for both types, which means they share the same name

questions.explanation: An invention is a brand-new creation that did not exist before, while an innovation is an improvement or new application of something that already exists; these are distinct terms in design and economics. Patents can be granted for both inventions and some innovations, so the patent argument in option D does not prove they are the same thing.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Stages
questions.prompt: A student says the lifecycle of a plastic ruler ends when a child stops using it and throws it away. A classmate disagrees. Which stage is the student MISSING from a complete lifecycle assessment?

options.A: The design and testing stage, where the ruler shape was decided
options.B: The marketing stage, where the ruler was advertised to customers
options.C: The end-of-life stage, which includes what happens to the material after disposal
options.D: The distribution stage, where the ruler was transported to shops

questions.explanation: A lifecycle assessment must include the end-of-life stage — what happens to the product after disposal, such as landfill, recycling, or decomposition — because this stage can have significant environmental impact. The student's error is treating disposal as the final point, when the material continues to exist and affect the environment after that.

questions.title: Systems Input and Feedback
questions.prompt: In a simple system, a thermostat detects that a room is too cold and turns on a heater until the room reaches the right temperature, then turns it off. What role does the thermostat's temperature reading play in this system?

options.A: It is the output, because temperature is what the system produces
options.B: It is the process, because measuring is the main action the system performs
options.C: It is the feedback, because it sends information back to control what the system does next
options.D: It is the input, because temperature data enters the system from outside

questions.explanation: The thermostat's reading is feedback — information about the output (room temperature) that is sent back into the system to adjust the process (turning the heater on or off); this feedback loop is what keeps the room at the right temperature. Calling it simply an input (D) misses the key point that it is information generated by the system's own output being fed back to control the system.

questions.title: UX Research Method Selection
questions.prompt: A designer wants to know how many children out of 200 find a new game app confusing to navigate. Which UX research method is MOST appropriate for this goal?

options.A: A one-on-one interview with five children, asking them to describe their experience
options.B: A survey with a clear question sent to all 200 children to collect countable responses
options.C: An observation session where the designer watches three children play the game
options.D: A focus group where eight children discuss what they like about the app

questions.explanation: When the goal is to measure how many people share a particular experience, a survey collects quantitative data from a large group, which is exactly what is needed here. Interviews and observation (A, C) give rich qualitative detail about why something is confusing, but they cannot reliably count how many out of 200 are affected.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Types
questions.prompt: A student invents a new shape for a building block toy. She also writes a short story about characters who play with the blocks. Which types of intellectual property protection apply to EACH creation?

options.A: Patent for the toy shape; trademark for the story
options.B: Trademark for the toy shape; copyright for the story
options.C: Patent for the toy shape; copyright for the story
options.D: Copyright for the toy shape; patent for the story

questions.explanation: Patents protect new inventions and functional designs, so a new toy shape would be covered by a patent; copyright automatically protects original written works like a story from the moment they are created. A trademark (A, B) protects brand names and logos, not inventions or written works.

questions.title: Fair Testing in Design
questions.prompt: Two students each build a bridge from paper to hold the most weight. Student A uses a single folded sheet; Student B uses three sheets glued together. They test both bridges and Student B's holds more weight. A third student says the test proves that gluing is better than folding. Identify the error in this conclusion.

options.A: The test is unfair because the bridges were not painted the same colour
options.B: The test is unfair because two variables changed at once — the number of sheets and the joining method — so neither alone is proved better
options.C: The test is unfair because paper bridges should not be used to test real weight-bearing structures
options.D: The test is unfair because Student B spent more time building, giving her an advantage unrelated to the design

questions.explanation: A fair test changes only one variable at a time; here both the number of sheets and the joining method are different, so any result could be caused by either factor or both together, making the conclusion invalid. Time spent building (D) could be a secondary concern, but it is not the fundamental flaw in the experimental design.

questions.title: Technology Ethics and Privacy
questions.prompt: A new smartwatch for children can track their exact location at all times and share it with the maker's servers. A parent says this is perfectly safe because the company promises to keep the data private. What is the strongest reason to be cautious about this promise?

options.A: The watch will use too much battery if it is always sending location data
options.B: Stored data can be hacked, shared, or misused even if the company intends to keep it safe
options.C: Children's watches should not include technology more advanced than telling time
options.D: The parent should trust the company's promise because companies are legally required to keep data safe in all countries

questions.explanation: Even well-intentioned companies have suffered data breaches, and permanently stored location data about children is particularly sensitive; a promise does not eliminate the technical and security risks of holding that data. Option D is wrong because data protection laws vary significantly between countries and do not guarantee breaches will never happen.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: A shoe company designs its trainers so that when they wear out, the rubber sole can be melted and made into new soles, and the fabric upper can become insulation material. Which economic model does this best represent, and what is its key idea?

options.A: A linear economy, where materials move from production to use to recycling in a straight line
options.B: A circular economy, where materials are kept in use for as long as possible by cycling back into new products
options.C: A sharing economy, where products are shared between users to reduce total waste
options.D: A green economy, where companies reduce their carbon footprint during manufacturing

questions.explanation: A circular economy is specifically designed so that materials are recovered and reused at the end of a product's life, forming a loop rather than ending in a landfill; the shoe company's plan to remelt the sole and reuse the fabric is a textbook example of this. A linear economy (A) actually ends in disposal — the word 'recycling' in option A makes it sound circular but the model itself is defined by a one-way flow.

questions.title: Ideation Technique Comparison
questions.prompt: A team uses mind-mapping during ideation. Another team uses a SCAMPER checklist (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse). A student claims mind-mapping is always better because it shows connections between ideas. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct, because showing idea connections always produces more creative results than a checklist
options.B: The claim is incorrect, because SCAMPER is always better since it gives structured prompts that guarantee new ideas
options.C: The claim is partly wrong, because different ideation tools suit different problems and teams, and both have genuine strengths
options.D: The claim is correct, because mind-mapping is the only IB-approved ideation method for design projects

questions.explanation: Mind-mapping excels at exploring free associations and connections between ideas, while SCAMPER provides structured prompts that help teams think beyond obvious solutions; neither is universally superior, and good designers choose the tool that fits the problem. The IB design curriculum encourages using a variety of ideation methods rather than favouring one exclusively.

questions.title: Design Specifications and Constraints
questions.prompt: A student writes these two design requirements for a new school chair: (1) 'The chair must be comfortable.' (2) 'The seat height must be between 38 cm and 42 cm.' Which requirement is more useful to a designer, and why?

options.A: Requirement 1, because comfort is the actual goal and measurable sizes are just guesses
options.B: Requirement 2, because it gives a specific, measurable range that can be tested and checked objectively
options.C: Both are equally useful, because design needs both a goal and a measurement
options.D: Requirement 1, because it tells the designer what the user feels, which is more important than any number

questions.explanation: A useful design specification must be measurable so the designer and tester can objectively check whether the solution meets it; 'between 38 and 42 cm' can be confirmed with a ruler, while 'comfortable' is subjective and untestable without further definition. While the underlying goal is comfort (A), a vague requirement cannot guide design decisions or fair testing.

questions.title: Material Durability vs. Sustainability
questions.prompt: A designer must choose between two materials for reusable shopping bags: woven polypropylene plastic (lasts 10 years, hard to recycle) and organic cotton (lasts 3 years, fully biodegradable). A classmate says organic cotton is definitely the greener choice. Is this claim fully correct?

options.A: Yes, because biodegradable materials are always better for the environment than plastics
options.B: No, because polypropylene is recyclable, which makes it greener than any natural material
options.C: Not necessarily, because organic cotton requires significantly more water and land to grow, and its shorter lifespan means more bags are needed over time
options.D: Yes, because anything that comes from a natural source has a lower environmental impact than a synthetic material

questions.explanation: Studies have shown that producing organic cotton uses large amounts of water and agricultural land, and if a cotton bag needs to be replaced three times as often, its total environmental cost over a decade could exceed that of the longer-lasting plastic bag. Biodegradability (A, D) is one factor in sustainability, not the only one — production impacts must also be counted.

questions.title: User-Centred Design Inclusivity
questions.prompt: A student designs a museum audio guide app. She tests it with 20 visitors and finds it works well. Later, a visitor who is deaf reports the app is useless for them. What design principle did the student most likely fail to apply?

options.A: Sustainability, because the app should have used less energy
options.B: Inclusive design, because the app was not tested with users who have a range of different needs and abilities
options.C: Iterative design, because she should have tested more than one prototype before releasing the app
options.D: Systems thinking, because she did not consider how the app connects to other museum technology

questions.explanation: Inclusive design requires that products are developed by considering a wide range of users, including those with disabilities; only testing with hearing visitors meant the deaf visitor's needs were never discovered or addressed. Iterative design (C) relates to repeating the prototype–test cycle, which is a different principle from ensuring diverse user groups are included.

questions.title: Innovation Economics and Incentive
questions.prompt: A company invests a large amount of money to develop a new type of long-lasting battery. They apply for a patent. What is the MAIN economic reason companies seek patents on innovations?

options.A: Patents allow companies to receive government grants to fund future research
options.B: Patents give companies exclusive rights to make and sell the invention for a set period, so they can earn back what they spent
options.C: Patents prevent universities from studying the technology and publishing findings about it
options.D: Patents guarantee that the product will be certified as safe before it reaches customers

questions.explanation: A patent grants the inventor exclusive rights to produce and sell the innovation for a limited time (usually 20 years), allowing the company to recoup its investment before competitors can copy the product — this exclusivity is the core economic incentive for costly innovation. Government grants (A) are a separate form of funding and are not provided automatically by a patent.

questions.title: Prototyping Material Selection
questions.prompt: A team is building a quick prototype of a new helmet shape. They choose to use paper and tape instead of hard foam. A classmate says this is a mistake because paper cannot show how well the helmet protects. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The classmate is correct, because a prototype must always use the same materials as the final product to be valid
options.B: The team is correct if they are testing only the shape and fit; paper is fine for that stage
options.C: The classmate is correct, because helmet safety cannot be evaluated at all without professional testing equipment
options.D: The team is correct, because any material that holds its shape is acceptable for all types of prototype testing

questions.explanation: Early prototypes are often built from cheap, easy-to-work materials to test specific aspects like shape, size, and user fit — not final performance; only later-stage prototypes need realistic materials to test protective qualities. Option A is wrong because using final materials at every stage would make prototyping extremely expensive and slow, defeating its purpose.

questions.title: Systems Engineering Subsystems
questions.prompt: A student says a bicycle is 'just one system.' A teacher says a bicycle is made of multiple subsystems working together. Which answer best supports the teacher's view?

options.A: A bicycle has one purpose — moving the rider — so it counts as a single system by definition
options.B: The braking system, gear system, and steering system each have separate inputs and outputs but work together to make the bicycle function
options.C: A bicycle is too simple to be called a system at all, since systems must include electronic components
options.D: The teacher is wrong because a subsystem must be able to work independently, and bicycle parts cannot work alone

questions.explanation: In systems engineering, complex products like bicycles are analysed as collections of subsystems — each with its own inputs, processes, and outputs — that interact to create overall function; identifying subsystems helps engineers design, test, and repair each part independently. Option D misunderstands the definition: subsystems do not need to be fully independent to qualify — they just need to perform a distinct function within the larger system.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Automation
questions.prompt: A factory replaces ten workers with a robot that can do their jobs faster and without breaks. The company says this is good because products become cheaper for everyone. Identify the strongest ethical concern with this situation.

options.A: Robots use electricity, which increases the factory's carbon footprint
options.B: The ten workers have lost their income, which may cause real hardship for them and their families
options.C: The robot may make errors that a human worker would not, reducing product quality
options.D: Cheaper products may reduce the perceived value of the item among customers

questions.explanation: The central ethical concern in automation is the human impact — workers who lose their jobs face loss of income and livelihood, raising serious questions about fairness and responsibility even if the overall economy benefits. While energy use (A) and quality (C) are real concerns, they are practical rather than the strongest ethical argument about human welfare in this scenario.

questions.title: Design Thinking Empathy Tools
questions.prompt: A designer creates an 'empathy map' for a user. What information does an empathy map mainly help the designer collect?

options.A: The specific dimensions and measurements needed to build the prototype
options.B: What the user thinks, feels, says, and does in relation to a problem or experience
options.C: The cost of materials and time required to complete the design project
options.D: A ranked list of every feature the final product must include

questions.explanation: An empathy map is a tool used in the empathise stage of design thinking to capture what a user thinks, feels, says, hears, and does — building a deep understanding of their experience before any solution is designed. Measurements and specifications (A, D) belong to the define and planning stages, not to empathy mapping.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Trade-Offs
questions.prompt: An LCA shows that an electric car produces more environmental harm during manufacturing than a petrol car, but less harm during its years of use. A student concludes that petrol cars are therefore greener. What error is the student making?

options.A: The student is ignoring the fact that electric cars are more expensive, which is the real environmental issue
options.B: The student is only looking at one stage of the lifecycle rather than comparing the total impact across all stages
options.C: The student is correct, because manufacturing harm is the most important stage in any lifecycle assessment
options.D: The student is ignoring the fact that LCAs are only valid for comparing products in the same price range

questions.explanation: A lifecycle assessment requires comparing total environmental impact across all stages — manufacturing, use, and end-of-life; if an electric car's lower emissions during years of use outweigh its higher manufacturing impact, its overall LCA score may still be better than a petrol car's. The student's error is cherry-picking one stage instead of evaluating the full picture.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: A team is designing a school bag for students who use wheelchairs. They read reviews online and decide they have enough information. A classmate suggests they should also spend time watching wheelchair users navigate hallways with their current bags. Why is the classmate's suggestion a better empathy strategy?

options.A: Reading reviews is always unreliable, so observation must replace it entirely.
options.B: Watching users in context reveals problems they may not think to mention in a review.
options.C: Observation is faster than reading, saving the team time in the design process.
options.D: Reviews only come from adults, so they cannot apply to a student product.

questions.explanation: Direct observation in context — called contextual inquiry — uncovers hidden pain points that users experience but never think to report, because those problems feel normal to them. Option A is wrong because online reviews do provide useful data; the issue is that observation adds a different, richer layer of insight rather than replacing reviews.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A student writes this design brief: 'I will make a better water bottle.' Her teacher says the brief is too vague. Which rewritten brief is MOST useful for guiding the design process?

options.A: I will design a leak-proof 600 ml water bottle that 8–12-year-olds can open with one hand, for use during sports.
options.B: I will make a water bottle that looks nice and is easy to use for everyone.
options.C: I will create the best water bottle possible by researching many designs.
options.D: I will improve a standard water bottle so that it is more convenient and modern.

questions.explanation: A strong design brief includes specific, measurable criteria — such as capacity (600 ml), a target user group (8–12-year-olds), a functional requirement (one-hand opening), and a context (sports) — so success can be clearly tested. Options B, C, and D all use vague language like 'nice,' 'best possible,' and 'more convenient,' which cannot be objectively measured during testing.

questions.title: Material Properties and Function
questions.prompt: An engineer is designing a helmet for young cyclists. She needs the outer shell to resist scratches and the inner lining to compress and absorb energy during a crash. Which pair of material properties best matches these two needs?

options.A: Outer shell: high hardness; inner lining: high elasticity.
options.B: Outer shell: high hardness; inner lining: low density only.
options.C: Outer shell: high flexibility; inner lining: high hardness.
options.D: Outer shell: high conductivity; inner lining: high elasticity.

questions.explanation: Hardness describes a material's resistance to surface scratching or denting, making it ideal for the protective outer shell. Elasticity (the ability to deform and absorb energy) is what allows inner foam liners to crush on impact and protect the skull. Option B is wrong because low density alone does not explain energy absorption — a material needs compressibility or elasticity for that function.

questions.title: Prototyping Purposes
questions.prompt: A student builds a prototype of her new pencil grip using cardboard and tape, even though the final product will be made from silicone rubber. Her classmate says this is a waste of time because the materials are completely different. What is the BEST reason the cardboard prototype is still valuable?

options.A: Cardboard is cheaper than silicone, so the prototype saves money that can be spent on marketing.
options.B: The prototype tests the shape and fit on real users quickly before committing to expensive materials.
options.C: The prototype proves that cardboard is a better material than silicone for pencil grips.
options.D: Cardboard prototypes always look more professional than silicone ones at the early stage.

questions.explanation: Early-stage prototypes — sometimes called 'lo-fi' or low-fidelity models — are used to explore and test form, size, and ergonomic fit rapidly and cheaply before investing in final materials or manufacturing. The classmate's distractor (Option A about marketing) confuses cost-saving with the prototype's design purpose; saving money is a benefit, but the primary reason is rapid learning about shape and usability.

questions.title: Sustainability and Material Choice
questions.prompt: A company makes children's toys and wants to reduce its environmental impact. It is choosing between two plastics: Plastic A is made from oil and lasts 20 years, while Plastic B is made from plants and breaks down in a landfill within 2 years. Which statement BEST evaluates these options?

options.A: Plastic B is always better because anything made from plants is automatically sustainable.
options.B: Plastic A is always better because longer-lasting products reduce waste over time.
options.C: The best choice depends on factors like how each plastic is produced and whether it can be recycled or composted properly.
options.D: Neither plastic matters because the environmental impact of toys is too small to be significant.

questions.explanation: Sustainability requires evaluating the full lifecycle — including raw material sourcing, manufacturing energy, and end-of-life disposal. A bio-based plastic (Plastic B) can still have a high environmental impact if it requires land cleared for farming or if it releases methane in a landfill rather than being industrially composted. Option A is a common misconception — 'plant-based' does not automatically mean low environmental impact.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Groups
questions.prompt: A designer creates a kitchen knife with a handle shaped perfectly for an average adult right hand. A classmate says this is excellent ergonomic design. Identify the most important flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Kitchen knives should never have shaped handles because straight handles are safer.
options.B: Designing for only the 'average' user excludes people with smaller hands, larger hands, or who are left-handed.
options.C: Ergonomic design only applies to chairs and keyboards, not to kitchen tools.
options.D: The handle shape does not matter as long as the blade is sharp enough.

questions.explanation: Good ergonomic design considers the full range of users, including those at the extremes of hand size and both left- and right-handed users — a principle sometimes called designing for the 5th–95th percentile. Designing for an 'average' user can make the product uncomfortable or even unsafe for a large portion of the real population. Option C is wrong because ergonomics applies to any product a human interacts with physically.

questions.title: Innovation Economics and Cost
questions.prompt: A startup invents a new type of reusable lunch box that keeps food warm for 8 hours. The production cost is $40 per box, but similar insulated boxes already sell for $15. What economic challenge does this startup face, and what is the MOST realistic strategy to address it?

options.A: The startup should give the boxes away for free to build popularity, then raise the price later.
options.B: The startup faces a price competitiveness problem and could try to reduce costs by producing larger quantities.
options.C: The startup should immediately patent the design so competitors cannot make anything similar.
options.D: The startup should ignore the price difference because customers always prefer newer products.

questions.explanation: Economies of scale mean that manufacturing costs per unit typically fall as production volume increases, allowing the startup to close the price gap over time. A patent (Option C) protects intellectual property but does not directly address the production cost problem; it would prevent copying but not make the box cheaper to produce.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Automation
questions.prompt: A supermarket replaces its human cashiers with self-checkout machines. A student argues this is purely a positive innovation because it saves shoppers time. What is the MOST important ethical concern this student has overlooked?

options.A: Self-checkout machines use electricity, which has an environmental cost.
options.B: Automation eliminates jobs, which can harm workers and their families who depended on that income.
options.C: Some shoppers may prefer talking to a human cashier, so customer satisfaction could drop slightly.
options.D: Self-checkout machines require more floor space, which increases the store's costs.

questions.explanation: When automation replaces workers at scale, it can cause significant social harm — unemployment, loss of income, and difficulty retraining for new roles — particularly for people with fewer formal qualifications. This is a core ethical concern in technology deployment. Option C (customer preference) describes a user experience issue, not an ethical harm to a group of people who lose their livelihoods.

questions.title: Ideation and Concept Selection
questions.prompt: After generating 30 ideas during brainstorming, a design team needs to choose which idea to develop into a prototype. They decide to pick the idea that sounded the most exciting in the room. Why is this method problematic?

options.A: Excitement in the room usually means the idea is too simple to be worth developing.
options.B: Choosing by excitement ignores whether the idea actually meets the design brief's criteria for the user.
options.C: Teams should always choose randomly to avoid any bias in the selection process.
options.D: The most exciting idea is always the one that was suggested first, which introduces recency bias.

questions.explanation: Selecting ideas based on enthusiasm rather than criteria — such as feasibility, user need, and alignment with the design brief — can lead to developing a concept that fails to solve the original problem. Design teams use structured tools like decision matrices to evaluate ideas against specific criteria objectively. Option C is wrong because random selection is also an unstructured method that ignores the design brief.

questions.title: Systems Engineering Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: A smart thermostat measures the temperature in a room. When it is too cold, it turns the heater on; when warm enough, it turns it off. This is an example of which systems engineering concept?

options.A: An open-loop system, because the heater operates without human input.
options.B: A closed-loop system with negative feedback, because the output (temperature) is measured and used to adjust the input.
options.C: A closed-loop system with positive feedback, because the heater increases the temperature over time.
options.D: A linear system, because the temperature changes in a straight line from cold to warm.

questions.explanation: A closed-loop system uses its own output as feedback to control future inputs — here, the measured room temperature tells the thermostat whether to activate the heater. Negative feedback means the system works to reduce the difference between the current state and the target state (the set temperature), keeping the output stable. Option C is wrong because positive feedback would mean the output amplifies itself — like a system that makes the room hotter and hotter without stopping.

questions.title: UX Research Survey Design
questions.prompt: A student surveys users about her new app with this question: 'Don't you agree that our app is easy to use?' A classmate says this is a poorly designed survey question. What is the main problem?

options.A: The question is too short; good survey questions should be at least two sentences long.
options.B: The question is leading because it suggests the 'correct' answer is agreement, biasing the results.
options.C: The question should only be asked in a face-to-face interview, not in a written survey.
options.D: The question uses the word 'our,' which makes it informal and unprofessional.

questions.explanation: A leading question steers respondents toward a particular answer — in this case, agreeing — which means the data collected will not accurately reflect users' true opinions. This is a fundamental flaw in UX research design that produces unreliable results. Option D is a distraction; informal wording is a minor stylistic issue and does not explain why the question produces biased data.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Types
questions.prompt: A student creates a logo for her school club — a unique drawing of a running fox. She also invents a new way to fold paper that makes origami 50% faster. Which combination of intellectual property protections is MOST appropriate?

options.A: A trademark for the logo and a copyright for the folding method.
options.B: A patent for the logo and a trademark for the folding method.
options.C: A copyright for the logo and a patent for the folding method.
options.D: A patent for the logo and a copyright for the folding method.

questions.explanation: Copyright automatically protects original creative works — like drawings and artwork — as soon as they are created. A patent protects new inventions and processes, such as a novel paper-folding technique. Option A is wrong because a trademark protects brand identifiers (names, logos used in trade) rather than pure artistic works, and copyright — not trademark — is the standard protection for original artwork.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment compares a cotton tote bag and a plastic shopping bag. The study finds that a cotton bag must be used more than 130 times before its total environmental impact is lower than a single-use plastic bag. What does this tell us about sustainability decisions?

options.A: Plastic bags are always more sustainable than cotton bags because they require less use.
options.B: Cotton bags are always better because they are natural and biodegradable.
options.C: A product's sustainability cannot be judged by its material alone — how often it is actually used matters too.
options.D: Lifecycle assessments only measure carbon emissions, so this comparison is incomplete.

questions.explanation: This real finding from lifecycle research illustrates that the environmental benefit of a reusable item only emerges after many uses, because producing cotton requires large amounts of water, land, and energy. Simply choosing a 'natural' material without considering the full lifecycle can be misleading. Option B is a common misconception — natural or biodegradable does not automatically mean low environmental impact across all lifecycle stages.

questions.title: Design Thinking Iteration
questions.prompt: After three rounds of testing and improving, a team's prototype still does not solve the user's problem. A student says they should start completely over with a new idea. Another says they should keep iterating on the current design. What principle of design thinking should guide their decision?

options.A: They should always keep the original idea because changing direction wastes all previous work.
options.B: They should return to the empathise and define stages to check if they correctly understood the user's real problem.
options.C: They should ask their teacher to choose the correct solution for them to save time.
options.D: After three iterations, design thinking rules require the team to submit what they have.

questions.explanation: Design thinking is non-linear — if repeated testing shows a solution is not working, designers are encouraged to loop back to earlier stages, especially to re-examine whether the problem was correctly defined in the first place. A poorly defined problem leads to well-executed solutions for the wrong need. Option A is wrong because sunk cost (previous effort) is not a good reason to continue in a failing direction.

questions.title: Fair Testing in Design
questions.prompt: Two teams each design a solar-powered phone charger. Team A tests theirs on a sunny day in July, and Team B tests theirs on a cloudy day in November. Team A claims their charger is better because it charged the phone faster. Identify the flaw in this conclusion.

options.A: Solar chargers cannot be tested outdoors because sunlight is too variable for any accurate measurement.
options.B: The test is unfair because the variable of sunlight intensity was not controlled, so the results cannot be compared.
options.C: Team A's charger must be better because summer sunlight proves it works in real-world conditions.
options.D: The test is unfair because phone models were not mentioned, making the charging speed irrelevant.

questions.explanation: A fair comparative test requires all variables to be the same except the one being tested — in this case, the charger design. Testing in different light conditions changes a key external variable (solar irradiance), making any performance difference impossible to attribute to the charger design alone. Option D raises a valid but secondary concern; the primary and most significant flaw is the uncontrolled environmental variable.

questions.title: User-Centred Design Perspectives
questions.prompt: A designer creates a beautifully detailed map app with 20 different features. User testing shows that most people only ever use 3 of those features and find the rest confusing. What does this reveal about the designer's approach?

options.A: Users should be better trained so they can take advantage of all 20 features.
options.B: The designer prioritised technical capability over the actual needs and mental models of real users.
options.C: Having more features always creates a better product, so the users are wrong to find it confusing.
options.D: The app only needs a better colour scheme to reduce the feeling of confusion.

questions.explanation: User-centred design requires identifying what users actually need and prioritising those functions, rather than maximising technical features. This is sometimes called the principle of 'less is more' in UX — unnecessary features add cognitive load and reduce usability. Option A places the blame on users, which contradicts the core principle that good design should fit the user, not require users to adapt to the design.

questions.title: Innovation and Cause-Effect Chains
questions.prompt: The invention of the smartphone led to the decline of many separate devices: cameras, alarm clocks, maps, and music players. What concept in innovation economics BEST describes this effect?

options.A: Economies of scale, because smartphones are produced in very large quantities.
options.B: Disruption, because the smartphone replaced existing markets and products by offering their functions in one device.
options.C: Iteration, because the smartphone went through many small improvements to replace these devices.
options.D: Intellectual property, because smartphone makers patented all the features of other devices.

questions.explanation: Disruptive innovation describes a new product or technology that fundamentally changes or eliminates existing markets by offering a simpler, more integrated, or more accessible alternative. The smartphone is a classic example studied in innovation economics. Option C is wrong because iteration describes the process of improving a single product over time, not the market-level effect of one product making others obsolete.

questions.title: Sustainability and Responsibility
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'It is the consumer's responsibility to recycle, so product designers do not need to think about what happens to a product after it is sold.' Do you agree? Choose the response that BEST evaluates this claim.

options.A: Agree — once a product is sold, the designer has no further legal or ethical responsibility for it.
options.B: Disagree — designers share responsibility because they choose materials and structures that determine whether recycling is even possible.
options.C: Agree — consumers are the ones who throw products away, so all end-of-life responsibility is theirs.
options.D: Disagree — the government is solely responsible for recycling infrastructure, not designers or consumers.

questions.explanation: Designers make decisions — such as gluing parts together, mixing material types, or using non-recyclable composites — that can make recycling impossible regardless of consumer intent. This is why concepts like Design for Disassembly exist, requiring designers to consider the end-of-life stage as part of their work. Option A is wrong because extended producer responsibility laws in many countries specifically hold manufacturers accountable for their products' end-of-life impact.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Safety
questions.prompt: A student designs a school chair and sets the seat height at 52 cm because that matches the average height in her class. After testing, several shorter students say their feet dangle, causing discomfort after 30 minutes. What ergonomic principle did the designer fail to apply?

options.A: The designer should have made the chair lighter so shorter students could adjust it themselves.
options.B: The designer should have designed for the range of users, not just the average, or included an adjustable height mechanism.
options.C: The designer should have surveyed students about colour preferences before fixing the seat height.
options.D: The chair only needs a footrest added at the testing stage, which resolves all ergonomic concerns.

questions.explanation: Ergonomic design for a diverse group should accommodate users from roughly the 5th to 95th percentile of the relevant measurement — in this case, leg length — rather than designing only for the mean. An adjustable seat height is the standard solution for shared furniture used by people of different sizes. Option D identifies a partial fix (footrest) but misses the deeper principle that a good design anticipates this range from the start, rather than patching it during testing.

questions.title: Intellectual Property and Open Source
questions.prompt: Some software developers choose to release their code as 'open source,' meaning anyone can read, use, and improve it for free. A student says this is bad for innovation because companies won't invest in creating new software if they can't protect it with patents. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct — without patents, no software innovation has ever occurred.
options.B: The claim is partially wrong — open source has driven major innovations like the Linux operating system, showing that collaboration can also fuel development.
options.C: The claim is fully correct because open source means no company can ever earn money from software.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because software cannot legally be patented in any country.

questions.explanation: Open-source software, including the Linux kernel (which powers Android and most internet servers), demonstrates that collaborative sharing can produce highly innovative and widely-used technology. Companies also build profitable services and products on top of open-source foundations. Option C is wrong because companies routinely make money through services, support, and complementary products built around open-source software.

questions.title: Material Properties — Conductivity
questions.prompt: A student wants to design a reusable coffee cup that keeps drinks hot for 2 hours. She is comparing two designs: Design X has a single aluminium wall, and Design Y has two stainless steel walls with a vacuum between them. Which design will perform better and why?

options.A: Design X, because aluminium conducts heat well, which spreads warmth evenly throughout the drink.
options.B: Design Y, because the vacuum between the walls eliminates conduction and convection, greatly slowing heat loss.
options.C: Design X, because a single wall is lighter, meaning less material absorbs heat from the drink.
options.D: Design Y, because stainless steel is magnetic, which traps heat inside the cup.

questions.explanation: A vacuum is an absence of matter, so heat cannot travel through it by conduction or convection — the two main ways heat escapes from a hot drink. This is the principle behind vacuum-insulated (double-walled) flasks. Option A is actually the opposite of what is needed; high thermal conductivity in aluminium means heat transfers rapidly from the drink to the outside air, making it a poor insulator.

questions.title: Design for Inclusion
questions.prompt: A designer is creating a public information sign for a city park. She includes only written text in English. What principle of inclusive design has she failed to consider, and what is the MOST significant consequence?

options.A: She has ignored colour theory, which will make the sign harder to photograph.
options.B: She has excluded people who cannot read English — such as tourists, young children, or people with certain reading difficulties — reducing the sign's usefulness.
options.C: She has failed to consider font size for people standing far away, which is the most significant accessibility barrier.
options.D: She has used too much text, which always reduces the impact of a public sign.

questions.explanation: Inclusive design means creating products and communications that work for the broadest possible range of people, including those with different languages, literacy levels, and abilities. Using internationally recognised icons alongside text significantly expands who can access the information. Option C raises a valid accessibility concern (legibility at distance), but language exclusion affects a far larger group of people and is therefore the more significant flaw in this context.

questions.title: Systems Thinking — Unintended Consequences
questions.prompt: A city installs hundreds of bright LED streetlights to improve safety. Months later, scientists report a sharp drop in the local bat population. What systems thinking concept BEST explains what happened?

options.A: The city caused a positive feedback loop because bright lights attract more insects, which attracts more bats.
options.B: The city experienced an unintended consequence because the design change in one part of the system (lighting) affected another part (wildlife) that was not considered.
options.C: The bat population declined because LEDs produce ultraviolet light that is toxic to bats.
options.D: This is an example of a closed-loop system failure because the streetlights did not monitor bat numbers.

questions.explanation: Systems thinking recognises that changing one element of a complex system often causes ripple effects in other parts of the system — these are called unintended consequences. Bright streetlights disrupt bats' nocturnal hunting and navigation, reducing insect prey availability near the lights. Option A describes the opposite of what happened — if bats were attracted to insects near lights, populations would rise, not fall.

questions.title: Evaluating Design Criteria
questions.prompt: A team's design brief states that their new reusable water bottle must weigh less than 200 g and cost under $10 to manufacture. Their finished prototype weighs 185 g and costs $9.50 to make, but it leaks when tilted. How should the team evaluate their prototype?

options.A: The prototype is fully successful because it meets both the weight and cost criteria exactly.
options.B: The prototype is partially successful — it meets weight and cost targets but fails a core function (being leak-proof), which must be fixed.
options.C: The prototype has failed completely and should be discarded because it leaks.
options.D: The leaking is not important because most users will keep their bottles upright at all times.

questions.explanation: Evaluation against a design brief requires checking all success criteria, including implicit functional requirements. A water bottle that leaks fails a fundamental function — containing liquid safely — even if it meets explicit numeric targets. Option A ignores the leaking flaw entirely, which is a critical error because a core function failure means the product does not fulfil its basic purpose.

questions.title: Technology Ethics and Privacy
questions.prompt: A new smartwatch for children can track the child's location and send it to parents in real time. A student says this is an ethically perfect design because safety is always the most important value. What tension does this student's reasoning overlook?

options.A: Smartwatches use too much battery, which is a more pressing ethical concern than location tracking.
options.B: Constant location tracking can conflict with a child's right to privacy and the development of personal independence.
options.C: The design is ethically flawed because parents should not be involved in their child's safety.
options.D: The watch's safety feature is only ethical if it also tracks heart rate and sleep data.

questions.explanation: Tech ethics rarely involves a single value — safety must be weighed against privacy and autonomy, which are also recognised rights. Continuous surveillance, even by parents, can undermine a child's developing sense of independence and normalise the idea that constant monitoring is acceptable. Option A (battery life) is a design concern but not an ethical one in the same sense as rights and values.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: A design team wants to create a better school lunchbox for students. They have time for only one research activity before defining the problem. Which method would give them the DEEPEST understanding of how students actually use their lunchboxes every day?

options.A: Sending an online survey to 200 students asking what they like about their current lunchbox
options.B: Watching students unpack and eat their lunches in the cafeteria without telling them they are being observed
options.C: Reading reviews of popular lunchboxes on a shopping website
options.D: Asking the school principal what complaints parents have made about lunchboxes

questions.explanation: Observing users in their real environment (a technique called naturalistic observation) reveals genuine behaviours, workarounds, and frustrations that people often forget or do not mention in surveys. A survey only captures what students consciously remember and can put into words, so it misses unspoken habits like struggling with zips or having no space for a drink bottle.

questions.title: Material Properties Selection
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable coffee cup meant to keep drinks hot for at least two hours. She shortlists two materials: stainless steel with a vacuum layer, and thick ceramic. Which property makes stainless steel with a vacuum layer the better choice for this specific function?

options.A: Stainless steel is heavier, so it holds heat better than ceramic
options.B: The vacuum layer removes air, which dramatically reduces heat loss by conduction and convection
options.C: Stainless steel has a higher melting point, so it can store heat at higher temperatures
options.D: Ceramic is porous, which means it cannot hold liquids without leaking

questions.explanation: Heat travels through materials by conduction and through air by convection; a vacuum eliminates both pathways because there is no matter to carry the heat, making vacuum-insulated steel far more effective than thick ceramic. The distractor about weight is a common misconception — mass alone does not determine insulation; the structure and air gaps matter far more.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: After interviewing elderly users, a student writes this design brief statement: 'I will design something that helps old people.' A classmate says this is not a good problem statement. What is the MAIN reason the classmate is correct?

options.A: The statement does not mention what materials will be used
options.B: The statement is too vague — it does not specify the user need, context, or measurable goal
options.C: The statement should be written from the user's point of view, not the designer's
options.D: The statement focuses on elderly people, which is too narrow an audience for a successful product

questions.explanation: A strong problem statement must clearly describe who the user is, what specific need they have, and what success looks like so the designer can evaluate solutions — 'helps old people' gives none of these. Option C (point of view) is a real design concept but it is a refinement technique, not the main flaw; the fundamental issue is the lack of specificity.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Choices
questions.prompt: A team is designing a new app to help students track their homework. They are in the early ideation stage and want to test whether their navigation layout makes sense to users. Which type of prototype is MOST appropriate at this stage?

options.A: A fully coded app with a working database and final colour scheme
options.B: A paper sketch showing the screen layouts and how buttons connect to other screens
options.C: A written description of every feature the app will eventually have
options.D: A video advertisement showing what the app will look like when finished

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity paper prototypes are ideal in early stages because they are quick and cheap to make and change, letting the team test navigation logic before investing time in coding. A fully coded app would waste significant effort if the layout turns out to be confusing and needs redesigning.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Fit
questions.prompt: A student claims that an ergonomic keyboard is better than a standard keyboard simply because it looks more modern and costs more. Evaluate this claim. Why is the student's reasoning flawed?

options.A: Ergonomic design is always about aesthetics, so appearance is a valid measure of ergonomic quality
options.B: Ergonomic quality is measured by how well the design reduces strain and fits the user's body, not by price or appearance
options.C: Cost is actually the best indicator of ergonomic quality because expensive products are tested more thoroughly
options.D: Ergonomics only applies to furniture and chairs, so keyboards cannot be ergonomic at all

questions.explanation: Ergonomics is specifically the science of fitting a design to the physical and cognitive needs of the user to reduce discomfort or injury — a keyboard is ergonomic if it reduces wrist strain, regardless of how it looks or what it costs. The idea that higher price guarantees better ergonomic testing is a plausible but incorrect generalisation, as many affordable products are well-tested.

questions.title: Sustainability and Material Choice
questions.prompt: A company is designing a children's toy and must choose between two plastics: one made from fossil fuels that is fully recyclable, and one made from plants (bioplastic) that is NOT recyclable in most local facilities. Which factor should MOST influence the sustainability decision?

options.A: The bioplastic is automatically more sustainable because it comes from plants, not oil
options.B: The fossil-fuel plastic is more sustainable because it is recyclable and can re-enter the production cycle
options.C: Both materials have trade-offs, and the best choice depends on whether local recycling infrastructure actually exists for the recyclable plastic
options.D: Sustainability only concerns energy used in manufacturing, so neither material's origin or end-of-life matters

questions.explanation: A lifecycle assessment must consider end-of-life disposal: a recyclable plastic is only sustainable if people actually have access to facilities that recycle it; if not, it goes to landfill like any other plastic. The assumption that bioplastic is automatically greener (Option A) is a very common misconception — if it cannot be composted or recycled locally, it may have a worse real-world impact.

questions.title: Innovation Economics Basics
questions.prompt: A student says, 'If a new product is cheaper to make, it will always sell better than an older, more expensive product.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: The statement is correct — lower manufacturing cost always leads to a lower selling price and higher sales
options.B: The statement ignores factors like brand loyalty, quality perception, and whether the product solves a real user need better than competitors
options.C: The statement should say 'faster to make' rather than 'cheaper to make' for it to be accurate
options.D: Manufacturing cost is irrelevant to product success because marketing is the only factor that matters
