questions.explanation: A product's commercial success depends on many factors beyond cost: users may prefer a trusted brand, perceive a cheaper product as lower quality, or simply not need what the product offers — all factors the student's claim ignores. Option D is also wrong because marketing is important but not the only factor; cost, quality, and need all play roles.

questions.title: Systems Thinking and Feedback
questions.prompt: A smart thermostat measures the temperature in a room and switches the heater on when it gets too cold, then switches it off when the target temperature is reached. What type of system feature does this describe?

options.A: An open-loop system, because the thermostat always runs on a fixed schedule
options.B: A feedback loop, because the system's output (room temperature) is used to control its own input (heater on/off)
options.C: A linear process, because energy travels in one direction from heater to room
options.D: A prototype stage, because the thermostat is still being tested before final use

questions.explanation: A feedback loop is when a system monitors its own output and uses that information to adjust its inputs — the thermostat measures the result of the heater's work and feeds that data back to decide whether to keep heating. An open-loop system (Option A) would run on a fixed timer with no awareness of actual temperature, which is the opposite of what a smart thermostat does.

questions.title: UX Research: Comparing Methods
questions.prompt: A design team wants to know WHY users keep abandoning their checkout process in an online shop. They already have data showing that 60% of users leave before paying. Which research method would best help them understand the reason?

options.A: Collecting more website data to see exactly which page users leave on
options.B: Running a think-aloud usability test where real users narrate their thoughts as they attempt to buy something
options.C: Redesigning the checkout page with a new colour scheme and testing if the abandonment rate drops
options.D: Sending a follow-up email survey asking users if they enjoyed shopping on the website

questions.explanation: A think-aloud test reveals users' real-time reasoning and frustrations as they navigate, explaining the 'why' behind a behaviour — something analytics data alone cannot do. More website data (Option A) would show where users leave but still not explain their reason for leaving.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Bias
questions.prompt: An AI tool is trained to select job applicants. Researchers discover it recommends men far more often than equally qualified women. What is the MOST likely cause of this problem, and what does it reveal about design responsibility?

options.A: The AI is working correctly because it is simply reflecting the most common applicant type
options.B: The training data likely contained historical hiring decisions that favoured men, so the AI learned and repeated that bias
options.C: The problem is caused by women applying for fewer jobs, which is outside the designer's control
options.D: AI tools cannot be biased because they use mathematics rather than personal opinions

questions.explanation: AI systems learn patterns from training data, so if historical data reflects past discrimination, the AI reproduces it — this is called algorithmic bias, and designers are responsible for checking their training data for such patterns. The idea that AI cannot be biased (Option D) is a very common misconception; bias enters AI through the data and design choices humans make.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trademarks
questions.prompt: A student designs a logo for her handmade jewellery business and starts selling online. A year later, a larger company begins using a nearly identical logo. What type of intellectual property protection would have BEST prevented this, and why?

options.A: A patent, because patents protect original visual creations like logos
options.B: A trademark, because trademarks protect brand identifiers like logos and prevent others from using confusingly similar marks
options.C: A copyright, because copyright automatically protects all creative work including logos from any commercial use by others
options.D: A trade secret, because keeping the logo design confidential would stop others from copying it

questions.explanation: A registered trademark specifically protects brand identifiers such as logos, names, and slogans used in commerce, and gives the owner the legal right to stop others from using confusingly similar marks in the same industry. Copyright (Option C) does protect the artistic expression in a logo automatically, but it does not prevent someone from creating a similar-looking logo independently — only a trademark blocks confusingly similar commercial use.

questions.title: Cause and Effect in Design Iterations
questions.prompt: A team tests their prototype water bottle and finds two problems: the lid leaks, and users say it is too heavy. They decide to fix only the leaking lid before the next test. What is the BEST reason for addressing one problem at a time?

options.A: Fixing both problems at once would confuse users in the next test, making it impossible to know which change caused any improvement
options.B: Designers should always fix cosmetic problems before structural ones to make a better first impression
options.C: The weight problem is not a real design problem because users can choose to carry less water
options.D: Fixing one issue at a time saves money, which is the only reason iterative design exists

questions.explanation: Changing one variable at a time is a principle of fair testing: if both problems were fixed simultaneously and user feedback improved, the team could not determine which change caused the improvement, making it impossible to learn from the test. Cost savings (Option D) are a benefit but not the primary reason — the core purpose is to isolate cause and effect.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: A shoe company collects old trainers from customers, grinds them into rubber granules, and uses those granules to make the soles of new trainers. Which circular economy principle does this BEST demonstrate?

options.A: Reduce — the company is using less rubber overall by making thinner soles
options.B: Upcycling — the old trainers are turned into a product of higher value than the original
options.C: Recycling — materials from used products are reprocessed and returned into production as raw material
options.D: Planned obsolescence — products are designed to wear out quickly so customers return them sooner

questions.explanation: Recycling in a circular economy means collecting used products, breaking them back into raw materials, and reintroducing those materials into manufacturing — exactly what grinding trainers into rubber granules achieves. Upcycling (Option B) is a plausible distractor but specifically means transforming waste into something of greater value or quality, not simply reprocessing it into the same type of material.

questions.title: Form Versus Function Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A designer creates a beautifully curved chair that wins an art award but causes back pain for anyone who sits in it for more than ten minutes. Using design thinking concepts, what does this chair FAIL to achieve?

options.A: It fails to achieve good form, because its curved shape is not visually appealing enough
options.B: It fails to achieve its function, because a chair's primary purpose is to support the user comfortably
options.C: It fails because it has not been tested with enough users from different countries
options.D: It fails because winning an art award is not a valid measure of design success in any context

questions.explanation: In design, function refers to how well a product fulfils its intended purpose; a chair's core function is to support a person comfortably, and causing pain after ten minutes means it fundamentally fails at this. Form (aesthetic appearance) is important but secondary when it conflicts with function — the chair has excellent form but poor function.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Stages
questions.prompt: A company claims its new electric scooter is '100% green' because it produces zero emissions while riding. A student argues this claim is misleading. Which lifecycle stage is the company IGNORING?

options.A: The distribution stage, because delivering scooters by truck produces emissions
options.B: The use stage, because electric scooters do produce some emissions from their motors
options.C: The manufacturing and end-of-life stages, where mining battery materials and disposing of batteries can cause significant environmental harm
options.D: The retail stage, because selling scooters in physical shops uses electricity

questions.explanation: A lifecycle assessment covers raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life — lithium batteries require environmentally damaging mining and are difficult to recycle safely, meaning the scooter's true environmental impact is much greater than zero even if it emits nothing while riding. Option A (distribution) is a real impact but a minor one compared to battery production and disposal.

questions.title: Perspective in User Research
questions.prompt: A team designs a navigation app and tests it only with university students who are very comfortable with smartphones. They conclude the app is easy to use. Why might this conclusion be UNRELIABLE?

options.A: University students always give dishonest feedback to seem more helpful
options.B: The test group does not represent all potential users; older adults or people less familiar with technology may find the app much harder
options.C: Navigation apps should only be tested by professional drivers, making any other test group invalid
options.D: The conclusion is reliable because smartphone-comfortable users represent the majority of the population

questions.explanation: Testing with a narrow group that shares the same characteristics (technology confidence, age range, education level) creates a biased sample that does not represent the full range of intended users — a phenomenon called sampling bias. Option D is a common error; even if tech-confident users are common, designing only for them excludes and disadvantages other legitimate users.

questions.title: Innovation vs Invention Distinction
questions.prompt: Gutenberg did not invent paper or ink, but he combined a screw press, movable type, and oil-based ink to create the printing press, which transformed how books were made and spread across Europe. Is this best described as invention or innovation, and why?

options.A: Invention, because Gutenberg created a completely new machine that had never existed before
options.B: Neither — it is imitation because he used existing technologies that others had already developed
options.C: Innovation, because he combined existing ideas in a new way that created significant value and changed society
options.D: Innovation only applies to digital technology, so this historical example cannot be classified that way

questions.explanation: Innovation means applying existing knowledge in a new combination or context to create significant value — Gutenberg did not invent the individual components but his novel system transformed book production and spread of ideas, which is the hallmark of innovation. Option A is tempting because the printing press was genuinely new, but since it was built from pre-existing technologies rather than entirely new principles, 'innovation' is the more precise term.

questions.title: Responsible Design and Inclusivity
questions.prompt: A student designs a voice-controlled smart speaker and only tests it with native English speakers in a quiet room. Identify TWO potential problems this testing approach could cause when the product is used in the real world.

options.A: The speaker may fail to recognise accents and may struggle with background noise, excluding many real users
options.B: The speaker may be too expensive for most people and may break easily in humid climates
options.C: The speaker may be too large for small rooms and may use too much electricity in developing countries
options.D: The speaker may not connect to the internet reliably and may be incompatible with older phones

questions.explanation: Testing only native English speakers in a quiet room means the voice recognition system was never exposed to accents, dialects, or ambient noise — in reality, people speak with varied accents and use devices in noisy kitchens or outdoors, causing the system to misunderstand them. This is a documented real-world problem with voice assistants and reflects a failure of inclusive, responsible design.

questions.title: Planned Obsolescence Ethics
questions.prompt: A phone manufacturer designs its battery so that it cannot be replaced by the user and degrades significantly after two years, encouraging customers to buy a new phone. A student says this is good for the economy but bad for the environment. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct — more phone sales always boost the economy, and discarded phones always harm the environment
options.B: The claim is partially correct — while more sales generate revenue, the environmental cost of e-waste and repeated manufacturing may outweigh the economic benefit
options.C: The claim is fully wrong — planned obsolescence is illegal in most countries so it cannot exist
options.D: The claim is fully wrong — short product lifespans reduce manufacturing because fewer parts are needed overall

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence does drive short-term sales revenue, but the environmental costs include toxic e-waste, repeated energy-intensive manufacturing, and resource depletion — a lifecycle assessment shows these harms can outweigh the economic gains, making the student's nuanced view partially correct. Option A overstates both sides; economic and environmental relationships are more complex than 'always' good or bad.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystems
questions.prompt: A designer breaks a bicycle into these parts to understand it better: frame, braking system, gear system, and wheel system. What is the correct systems engineering term for each of these separate parts, and why is thinking this way useful?

options.A: They are called modules; breaking a system into modules makes it impossible to see how the parts affect each other
options.B: They are called subsystems; identifying subsystems helps designers understand, test, and improve each part independently while seeing how they connect
options.C: They are called prototypes; each part must be built and tested separately before the bicycle can be assembled
options.D: They are called inputs; every part of a system is an input because they all contribute energy to the final output

questions.explanation: In systems engineering, a subsystem is a self-contained part of a larger system that performs a specific function — identifying subsystems lets engineers isolate problems and improve components without having to redesign the whole system. Option A confuses 'modules' with subsystems and incorrectly states that decomposing a system prevents understanding connections — the opposite is true.

questions.title: Ideation: Convergent Thinking
questions.prompt: After a brainstorming session, a design team has 40 different ideas for a new school locker system. They now need to narrow down to the three best ideas to prototype. Which type of thinking are they using in this next step?

options.A: Divergent thinking, because they are still exploring many possible directions
options.B: Empathic thinking, because selecting ideas requires imagining how users would feel about them
options.C: Convergent thinking, because they are evaluating and narrowing multiple ideas down to the most promising ones
options.D: Lateral thinking, because choosing between options requires creative connections across unrelated fields

questions.explanation: Convergent thinking is the process of evaluating, filtering, and selecting the best options from a wide set — it follows divergent thinking (generating many ideas) and is essential in design to move from exploration to focused development. Divergent thinking (Option A) is the opposite phase: it is about generating ideas, not selecting them.

questions.title: Sustainability: Design for Disassembly
questions.prompt: A laptop is designed so that all its screws are standard sizes, the battery snaps out without tools, and all plastic parts are clearly labelled with their material type. What sustainability strategy does this BEST represent?

options.A: Design for obsolescence — making the product easy to replace when newer models come out
options.B: Design for disassembly — making it easy to take a product apart so components can be repaired, reused, or correctly recycled
options.C: Modular design — allowing users to customise the laptop by swapping in different processor types
options.D: Minimal design — using fewer parts overall to reduce the environmental impact of manufacturing

questions.explanation: Design for disassembly (DfD) is a sustainability strategy where products are engineered to be easily taken apart at end-of-life, enabling efficient repair, component reuse, and accurate material sorting for recycling. Modular design (Option C) is related and a genuine concept but focuses on interchangeable functional units, not specifically on end-of-life disassembly for sustainability.

questions.title: Copyright and Open Source
questions.prompt: A student finds a piece of computer code online marked 'MIT Licence.' She uses it in her school project app without asking the original author. A classmate says she is breaking copyright law. Who is correct?

options.A: The classmate is correct — all code is automatically copyrighted and can never be reused without written permission
options.B: The student is correct — the MIT Licence is a type of open-source licence that explicitly allows others to use, modify, and distribute the code, usually just requiring credit
options.C: The classmate is correct — school projects are not allowed to use any code found on the internet, regardless of its licence
options.D: The student is correct — copyright does not apply to computer code because code is a functional tool, not a creative work

questions.explanation: The MIT Licence is a well-known open-source software licence that grants anyone permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute the code, typically with just a credit requirement — the student's use is therefore legal and permitted. Option D is wrong: code is protected by copyright as a creative work, which is precisely why the open-source licence is needed to grant usage rights.

questions.title: Change: Unintended Design Consequences
questions.prompt: A city installs a new app that shows real-time bus locations, expecting it to reduce passenger wait times. Instead, traffic near bus stops increases as more people drive to catch buses rather than walking. What design concept does this scenario BEST illustrate?

options.A: A design failure — the app does not work correctly because it shows wrong bus locations
options.B: An unintended consequence — a solution that works as designed but produces unexpected negative effects in a connected system
options.C: A prototype stage — the city released the app too early before finishing the testing phase
options.D: A circular economy problem — the app should have been designed to reduce car use from the start

questions.explanation: An unintended consequence occurs when a solution works exactly as intended but triggers unexpected effects in the broader system it is part of — the app functioned correctly but changed user behaviour in an unforeseen way. This is why systems thinking requires designers to map how a change in one part of a system affects all connected parts.

questions.title: Reflection in Iterative Design
questions.prompt: After completing and presenting their final design project, a student writes: 'If I could do this again, I would interview more users before building the prototype, because our first version solved a problem our users did not actually have.' Which IB design concept does this reflection MOST strongly demonstrate?

options.A: Responsibility — the student recognises their duty to make a product that does not harm users
options.B: Reflection — the student critically evaluates their own process to identify what should change in future projects
options.C: Empathy — the student feels sorry for the users who were given a product they did not need
options.D: Causation — the student explains what caused the prototype to be built incorrectly

questions.explanation: Reflection in design means critically looking back at decisions, identifying what worked and what did not, and using that understanding to improve future practice — the student is doing exactly this by pinpointing the root cause of their project's weakness. Causation (Option D) is a genuine IB concept and relevant here, but the primary act being demonstrated is reflective evaluation of process, not simply explaining cause and effect.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Assumption in Design
questions.prompt: A student designing a school lunchbox surveys only her best friends to understand user needs. A classmate says this approach has a serious flaw. Which explanation BEST identifies the problem with her research method?

options.A: Surveys always produce less reliable data than interviews, so any survey is flawed.
options.B: Her sample is too small and not representative, so her findings may not reflect the needs of all lunchbox users.
options.C: She should have skipped empathy research and moved straight to ideation to save time.
options.D: Friends always give honest answers, so their feedback will be biased toward positive responses only.

questions.explanation: A non-representative sample means the designer only understands the needs of one narrow group, missing important perspectives from users with different diets, allergies, or physical abilities. Option D is tempting but reverses the logic — friends may give overly positive feedback, yet the core flaw is still the unrepresentative sample, not dishonesty alone.

questions.title: Material Properties: Conductivity
questions.prompt: A student building a simple electric circuit for a model lighthouse chooses wooden dowels to connect the battery to the bulb. The bulb does not light up. What is the MOST precise material-science reason for this failure?

options.A: Wood is too brittle and will snap before electrons can travel through it.
options.B: Wood is an electrical insulator because its electrons are tightly bound and cannot move freely to carry charge.
options.C: Wood is a poor conductor because it is a natural material, and only synthetic materials conduct electricity.
options.D: Wood has too high a density, which prevents electrical current from flowing.

questions.explanation: Electrical conduction depends on the availability of free electrons; in wood, electrons are tightly bound in covalent bonds, so no current flows. Option C is wrong because the natural versus synthetic distinction is irrelevant — graphite is a natural material that conducts electricity well.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A team is in the early ideation stage of designing a new school bag. They debate whether to spend two weeks building a fully finished, detailed prototype or a quick rough model made from cardboard. Evaluate: what is the STRONGEST reason to choose the rough model at this stage?

options.A: A rough model is always cheaper, and cost is the most important factor in every design decision.
options.B: A rough model allows the team to test and discard multiple ideas quickly before investing time in a concept that may not work.
options.C: A finished prototype would confuse users during testing because it looks too realistic.
options.D: The IB design cycle requires cardboard models at every stage, regardless of the project.

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes enable rapid iteration — teams can explore many directions cheaply and pivot when an idea fails, which is the core purpose of early prototyping. Option A is wrong because cost alone does not justify prototype choice; the primary reason is the ability to test ideas quickly without commitment.

questions.title: Sustainability: Material Selection
questions.prompt: A company is choosing between two materials for a reusable water bottle: stainless steel and single-use plastic. A student claims stainless steel is always more sustainable because it lasts longer. Which response BEST evaluates this claim?

options.A: The student is completely correct; durability is the only factor that determines sustainability.
options.B: The student is partially correct; stainless steel lasts longer, but its production requires more energy and mining of raw materials, so the full lifecycle must be considered.
options.C: The student is wrong; plastic is always more sustainable because it is lighter and cheaper to manufacture.
options.D: The student is correct because steel is a natural element found in the earth, making it automatically eco-friendly.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle assessment shows that stainless steel production is energy-intensive and involves mining iron ore, so its environmental advantage depends on how many times it replaces single-use plastic — typically breaking even after many reuses. Option A is wrong because durability is just one stage of the lifecycle; extraction and manufacturing impacts also matter.

questions.title: UX Research: Observation Methods
questions.prompt: A design team wants to understand how young children interact with a new educational tablet app. They have two options: (1) ask children to fill in a written questionnaire, or (2) watch children use the app without interrupting and take notes. Which method is MORE suitable, and what is the key reason?

options.A: The questionnaire, because written answers are always more detailed and accurate than observations.
options.B: The questionnaire, because children enjoy filling in forms and will provide richer data.
options.C: Direct observation, because young children may struggle to articulate their frustrations in writing, while observation captures real behaviour as it happens.
options.D: Direct observation, because it is faster to complete than a questionnaire and saves the research team time.

questions.explanation: Observational research captures actual user behaviour, including hesitation, errors, and confusion that users themselves may not be able to describe — especially young children with limited writing skills. Option D is wrong because speed is not the primary reason; the depth and authenticity of behavioural data is what makes observation more appropriate here.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Anthropometrics
questions.prompt: A manufacturer is designing a children's classroom chair for students aged 9–11. A student suggests using the average height of all children in that age group to set the seat height. Identify the flaw in this approach.

options.A: Using the average means the chair will fit the majority perfectly and disadvantage no one.
options.B: Designing for the average excludes children at the extremes of the height range, meaning the tallest and shortest students will be uncomfortable.
options.C: Anthropometric data from one country cannot be used in classrooms, so the data itself is invalid.
options.D: Seat height is unrelated to user height; only arm length determines ergonomic comfort in chairs.

questions.explanation: Designing for the average, known as 'designing for the average user', actually fits very few individuals perfectly; ergonomic best practice designs for a range (e.g., 5th to 95th percentile) to accommodate most users. Option A is incorrect because statistical averages do not represent the majority — many individuals sit outside that single average value.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: A smart thermostat senses room temperature and automatically turns the heater off when the room reaches 20 °C, then turns it back on when the temperature drops below 18 °C. What type of system behaviour does this describe, and why?

options.A: An open-loop system, because the thermostat sends information out of the room to a central server.
options.B: A positive feedback loop, because the system amplifies temperature changes to make the room hotter.
options.C: A closed-loop system with negative feedback, because the output (temperature) is fed back to control the input (heater on/off) and keep the system stable.
options.D: A linear system, because the heater follows a straight sequence of on and off steps without any feedback.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback in a closed-loop system means the output measurement is used to reduce the difference between the current state and the desired state, maintaining stability — exactly what the thermostat does. Option B is wrong because positive feedback would amplify the change (making a hot room hotter), which is the opposite of what a thermostat does.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: First-Mover Risk
questions.prompt: Company A launches the world's first foldable paper tablet and spends heavily on marketing. A year later, Company B releases a similar but improved product at a lower price. A student claims Company A had an advantage because it was first. Which response BEST evaluates this claim?

options.A: The student is fully correct; being first always guarantees long-term market success.
options.B: The student is partially correct; first-mover advantages include brand recognition and loyal early customers, but Company A also bore the high cost of educating the market and risk of technical failure.
options.C: The student is wrong; being second is always better because the second company can copy the first with no legal consequences.
options.D: The student is wrong; innovation economics shows that only the cheapest product survives regardless of who launched first.

questions.explanation: First-mover advantages are real — early brand recognition and switching costs for customers — but first movers also absorb research costs and market education costs that later entrants avoid, a phenomenon called the 'pioneer's curse'. Option C is wrong because intellectual property law (patents, trade secrets) means copying is not always legal.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A school uses an AI program to recommend which students should receive extra reading support. A teacher notices that the program almost never recommends students from one cultural group, even when those students are struggling. What is the MOST likely cause of this problem?

options.A: The AI has developed personal opinions about students after working for too long.
options.B: The training data used to build the AI was likely unrepresentative, causing the algorithm to reflect existing biases in that data.
options.C: All AI systems must be manually programmed to exclude certain groups, so someone deliberately set this up.
options.D: The AI is correct because cultural background is a reliable predictor of reading ability.

questions.explanation: Algorithmic bias most commonly arises when training datasets are skewed — if historical support decisions underrepresented a cultural group, the AI learns to replicate that pattern. Option C is wrong because bias can emerge unintentionally from data patterns without any deliberate exclusion being programmed.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secret
questions.prompt: A bakery invents a unique recipe for a flavoured bread. The owner decides NOT to apply for a patent but instead keeps the recipe completely secret. What is the MAIN advantage of this strategy over filing a patent?

options.A: Trade secrets provide stronger legal protection than patents in every country and in every court.
options.B: A trade secret can theoretically protect the recipe indefinitely, whereas a patent expires after a set period (typically 20 years), after which anyone can use the invention.
options.C: Keeping a secret is always cheaper than a patent, so the bakery automatically saves money.
options.D: A patent only protects inventions in science, so a recipe cannot be patented under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Patents expire — in most countries after 20 years — at which point the invention enters the public domain; a trade secret like Coca-Cola's formula has been kept protected for over a century. Option C is tempting but incorrect as the primary advantage; while secrecy can reduce legal fees, the core strategic benefit is unlimited duration of protection.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A student's design brief says: 'Build something to help people.' A mentor says this brief needs to be improved. Which version of a revised brief BEST follows good design-brief writing principles?

options.A: 'Design a mobile app for elderly residents aged 70–85 in our neighbourhood that helps them track daily medication schedules, measured by whether users can set a reminder in under two minutes.'
options.B: 'Build a really good product that elderly people will enjoy using every day of their lives.'
options.C: 'Create the most innovative solution possible for any problem facing society today.'
options.D: 'Improve technology for older people by making it simpler and more colourful.'

questions.explanation: A strong design brief specifies a target user, a defined problem, a context, and measurable success criteria — all present in Option A. Option D is plausible because it names older people and mentions simplicity, but it lacks a specific measurable criterion and a concrete context.

questions.title: Material Properties: Malleability
questions.prompt: A jeweller needs a metal that can be hammered into thin sheets without cracking. Which property is she looking for, and which metal is the BEST example of a material with this property?

options.A: Hardness; diamond is the best example because it resists scratching.
options.B: Malleability; gold is an excellent example because it can be beaten into sheets less than 0.1 mm thick without breaking.
options.C: Tensile strength; steel is the best example because it can be stretched without breaking.
options.D: Malleability; glass is a good example because it can be shaped when heated.

questions.explanation: Malleability is the specific property of a material that allows it to be deformed under compressive stress (hammering) without fracturing; gold is famously malleable and can be beaten into gold leaf thinner than 0.1 micrometres. Option D incorrectly classifies glass as malleable — glass is brittle at room temperature and is shaped through viscous flow when molten, not malleability.

questions.title: Cause and Effect: Product Failure
questions.prompt: A company releases a new folding bicycle without testing the hinge mechanism with real users over many weeks. Six months after launch, hinges begin to break under normal cycling conditions. Trace the MOST complete cause-and-effect chain that explains this outcome.

options.A: The company used cheap materials → the hinge broke immediately → users complained.
options.B: The design skipped extended real-world testing → stress from repeated folding over time was not measured → a fatigue weakness in the hinge was undetected → the hinge failed after months of use.
options.C: Users folded the bike incorrectly → the hinge broke → the company was not responsible.
options.D: The company released the bike too quickly → customers bought it → they used it too much → the hinge wore out normally.

questions.explanation: Metal fatigue — the weakening of a material under repeated cyclic stress — can take many months of real use to manifest and is precisely what extended durability testing is designed to detect. Option A implies an immediate failure from cheap materials, but the six-month delay points to fatigue, not instant material cheapness.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: A student claims that recycling is the most important strategy in a circular economy. A classmate disagrees, saying that reducing consumption ranks higher. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The first student is correct; recycling recovers the most material value and is therefore ranked first in circular economy models.
options.B: The classmate is correct; in the waste hierarchy, reducing consumption is ranked above recycling because it prevents resource use and energy expenditure from occurring in the first place.
options.C: Both students are wrong; in a circular economy, reusing products ranks above both recycling and reducing.
options.D: The first student is correct; recycling is ranked above reducing because modern recycling technology recovers nearly 100% of a material's energy.

questions.explanation: The widely used waste hierarchy (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) places reduction first because avoiding consumption entirely saves the energy, water, and raw materials that recycling still requires. Option C is plausible because reuse does rank above recycling, but the classmate's specific claim — that reducing ranks above recycling — is correct.

questions.title: Ideation: SCAMPER Technique
questions.prompt: A design team is using the SCAMPER technique to improve a standard wooden ruler. One student suggests: 'What if we put a magnifying strip along one edge so users can see tiny measurements more easily?' Which SCAMPER action does this BEST represent?

options.A: Substitute — replacing the wood with a different material to change the ruler's feel.
options.B: Eliminate — removing the millimetre markings to make the ruler simpler.
options.C: Put to other uses — using the ruler as a bookmark in a textbook.
options.D: Add (Adapt/Modify) — adding a new feature (the magnifying strip) to improve the ruler's existing function.

questions.explanation: The SCAMPER letter 'A' stands for Adapt or Add; adding a magnifying strip is an adaptation that enhances the ruler's core measuring function without replacing or removing anything. Option C is plausible because SCAMPER includes 'P' for Put to other uses, but that action involves using the object differently, not modifying it.

questions.title: Sustainability: Planned Obsolescence
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer designs its phone so that the battery cannot be replaced by the user, and software updates slow down older models after two years. What design strategy does this describe, and what is its MAIN sustainability problem?

options.A: Universal design; the problem is that not all users can access the phone's features equally.
options.B: Planned obsolescence; the strategy deliberately shortens the product's useful life, increasing electronic waste and encouraging unnecessary new purchases.
options.C: Modular design; the problem is that users cannot swap components to customise their phone.
options.D: Open-source design; the problem is that competitors can copy the phone's software freely.

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence is a deliberate design strategy to make products outdated or unusable sooner than their physical lifespan requires, driving consumers to buy replacements and generating large volumes of e-waste. Option C is wrong because modular design is actually the opposite — it allows parts to be swapped and updated independently, extending product life.

questions.title: User Testing: Validity of Results
questions.prompt: A team tests their new app by asking users to complete tasks while the lead designer watches and gives hints when users get stuck. A supervisor says the test results are not valid. What is the MOST accurate reason?

options.A: The test is invalid because usability tests must always be conducted online, not in person.
options.B: The hints from the designer interfere with the test — they mask real usability problems, making the app appear easier to use than it actually is.
options.C: The test is invalid because only professional UX researchers are legally allowed to conduct usability tests.
options.D: The results are not valid because users always perform worse when they know they are being watched.

questions.explanation: When a designer provides hints during a usability test, the results no longer reflect authentic user behaviour with the product — failures that real users would encounter are hidden, a violation of test validity. Option D describes the 'observer effect', which is a real concern but is not the primary reason the supervisor identifies the test as invalid here.

questions.title: Innovation vs. Invention Distinction
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following student statement: 'Alexander Graham Bell's telephone was an innovation because it changed how society communicated, even though nothing like it had existed before.'

options.A: The error is that the telephone did not change society — its impact was minimal.
options.B: The error is in the word 'innovation'; because the telephone was a completely new device with no prior version, it is correctly classified as an invention, not an innovation.
options.C: The error is that Bell did not create the telephone — it was invented by a team of engineers.
options.D: The error is that innovation only applies to software products, not physical devices.

questions.explanation: An invention is the creation of something entirely new; an innovation improves or applies an existing idea in a new way. Since nothing like the telephone existed before Bell's patent in 1876, it qualifies as an invention. Option C introduces a historical debate about co-inventors but does not address the conceptual error in the student's use of 'innovation'.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment: Hidden Impacts
questions.prompt: A student argues that electric cars are completely zero-emission because they produce no exhaust fumes while driving. Evaluate this claim using lifecycle assessment thinking.

options.A: The student is correct; because no exhaust is produced during driving, the car has no environmental impact.
options.B: The student is partially correct; electric cars produce no exhaust during use, but manufacturing the battery requires mining lithium and cobalt and releases significant CO₂, so total lifecycle emissions are not zero.
options.C: The student is wrong; electric cars produce more exhaust than petrol cars because charging electricity always comes from coal power plants.
options.D: The student is correct; lifecycle assessment only measures emissions during the use phase of a product.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle assessment considers all stages — raw material extraction, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life — and lithium-ion battery production is energy-intensive and involves environmentally damaging mining, so electric cars are not truly zero-emission across their full lifecycle. Option D is factually wrong; LCA specifically accounts for all lifecycle stages, not only the use phase.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Defining vs. Assuming
questions.prompt: A student skips the 'define' stage of the design cycle and moves straight from empathy research to ideation. What is the MOST likely consequence of this shortcut?

options.A: The student will generate too many ideas during ideation, making it impossible to choose one.
options.B: Without a clearly defined problem statement, the student's ideas during ideation may address the wrong problem or solve symptoms rather than root causes.
options.C: The student will have to redo the empathy stage because skipping definition always resets the process.
options.D: Ideas generated without a define stage are automatically creative because they are not constrained by rules.

questions.explanation: The 'define' stage transforms raw empathy data into a precise problem statement (often called a 'Point of View' or 'How Might We' question), giving ideation a clear target; without it, solutions may be creative but address the wrong need. Option A is wrong because the number of ideas is not reduced by having a clear problem statement — in fact, a focused prompt often generates more targeted and useful ideas.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Data Privacy in Products
questions.prompt: A company designs a smart toy that records children's conversations to improve its voice recognition. The toy's privacy policy is written in complex legal language that parents are unlikely to read. Which ethical principle does this MOST clearly violate?

options.A: The principle of sustainability, because recording uses device battery power unnecessarily.
options.B: The principle of informed consent, because users (parents and children) cannot meaningfully agree to data collection they do not understand.
options.C: The principle of universal design, because the toy's features are inaccessible to children with hearing difficulties.
options.D: The principle of ergonomics, because the toy's microphone placement may not be comfortable for small children.

questions.explanation: Informed consent requires that users understand what data is collected, how it is used, and who has access to it before agreeing — deliberately obscuring this in complex legal language prevents genuine informed consent. Option C is plausible in a broader access context but does not address the specific ethical issue of hidden data collection described in the question.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Sensory Design
questions.prompt: A designer creates a warning alarm for a factory. She makes it a high-pitched beep at 18,000 Hz. A safety inspector rejects the design. What is the MOST likely ergonomic reason for the rejection?

options.A: High-pitched sounds travel more slowly through air and would not reach workers across a large factory floor in time.
options.B: Many adult workers, especially older ones, lose the ability to hear very high frequencies above about 16,000 Hz, so a large portion of the workforce might not hear the alarm.
options.C: Sounds above 10,000 Hz are illegal in workplace environments under international safety law.
options.D: High-pitched sounds always cause more hearing damage than low-pitched sounds of the same volume.

questions.explanation: High-frequency hearing loss (presbycusis) is a well-documented effect of aging — many adults over 40 cannot hear frequencies above 15,000–16,000 Hz, making a 18,000 Hz alarm functionally silent for a significant portion of the workforce. Option D is wrong because the risk of hearing damage depends on sound intensity (decibels), not frequency alone.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright Duration
questions.prompt: A student finds a beautiful illustration made by an artist who died in 1953. She wants to use it freely in her design project without asking permission. In most countries, is this likely to be legal, and why?

options.A: No, because copyright lasts forever once an artist creates a work.
options.B: Yes, because in most countries copyright expires 70 years after the author's death, and a work from an artist who died in 1953 would enter the public domain after 2023.
options.C: Yes, because any work created before the year 2000 is automatically in the public domain.
options.D: No, because the artist's family automatically inherits copyright indefinitely and can prevent any use.

questions.explanation: In most countries that follow the Berne Convention, copyright lasts for 70 years after the creator's death, meaning the work of an artist who died in 1953 would enter the public domain in 2024, making free use legal in those jurisdictions. Option D is wrong because copyright is not inherited indefinitely — it expires after the statutory period regardless of who holds it.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystems
questions.prompt: A student is mapping the systems inside a modern aircraft. She lists the engine as the only system. Her teacher says this is an oversimplification. Which response BEST explains why?

options.A: An aircraft has only two systems: the engine and the wings, so the student is almost correct.
options.B: A modern aircraft is a complex system made of many interacting subsystems — propulsion, navigation, hydraulics, electrical, and cabin life support — each of which must function and communicate with the others for the aircraft to operate safely.
options.C: The teacher is wrong; in systems engineering, the engine is defined as the entire system because it powers all other parts.
options.D: An aircraft is too complex to be described using systems engineering, so the student should use a different method.

questions.explanation: Systems engineering defines a complex system as a set of interacting subsystems that together produce a function no single subsystem could achieve alone; an aircraft's safety depends on the integration of propulsion, avionics, hydraulics, and life support. Option A is wrong because it still oversimplifies — a real aircraft has many more subsystems than just engines and wings.

questions.title: Reflection in the Design Process
questions.prompt: After completing a design project, a student writes: 'My product looked great and I enjoyed making it.' Her teacher gives low marks for the reflection section. What is MOST likely missing from her reflection?

options.A: She should have written more words, because a longer reflection always earns higher marks.
options.B: She has not evaluated her product against the original design brief criteria, identified what worked and what failed, or explained what she would change if repeating the project.
options.C: She should have included photographs, because reflections without images are always incomplete.
options.D: She described her feelings, which is not allowed in IB reflections — only technical facts should be included.

questions.explanation: Effective design reflection requires evaluating the product against specific success criteria from the design brief, analysing failures and successes with evidence, and proposing concrete improvements — mere aesthetic approval and enjoyment show no critical thinking. Option A is wrong because word count alone does not determine reflection quality; depth of analysis does.

questions.title: Inclusive Design Principles
questions.prompt: A student claims that designing a product specifically for wheelchair users will make it less useful for everyone else. Evaluate this claim using the principle of inclusive design.

options.A: The student is correct; designing for one group always compromises the design for all other groups.
options.B: The student is partially correct; specialised design features can sometimes reduce portability for non-wheelchair users.
options.C: The student is wrong; inclusive design often produces solutions that benefit a wider population — for example, kerb cuts designed for wheelchairs also help pushchairs, cyclists, and delivery trolleys.
options.D: The student is correct because inclusive design is only required by law and has no practical benefit for mainstream users.

questions.explanation: The 'kerb cut effect' is a well-documented inclusive design phenomenon: features created to remove barriers for people with disabilities frequently improve usability for a much wider group. Option B is a partial concession that sounds reasonable but misses the broader principle that inclusive features commonly become universal benefits.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Assumption in Design
questions.prompt: A student designing a lunchbox for elderly users skips the empathise stage and moves straight to ideation, saying, 'I already know what old people need.' Which consequence is MOST likely to result from this decision?

options.A: The prototype will take longer to build because no research was done
options.B: The final product may not solve the real problems users actually face
options.C: The team will generate too many ideas and become confused
options.D: The design brief will be missing a success criterion

questions.explanation: The empathise stage exists to uncover real user needs that designers cannot guess accurately; skipping it means solutions are based on assumptions, producing a product that may miss genuine problems entirely. Option A is wrong because prototype speed depends on the ideation and prototyping stages, not on whether empathy research was conducted.

questions.title: Material Properties: Conductivity
questions.prompt: A student needs to choose a material for the blade of a pair of scissors. She lists four properties: hardness, electrical conductivity, flexibility, and transparency. Which TWO properties are most important for this specific use, and why is one common answer incorrect?

options.A: Hardness and flexibility, because blades must bend when cutting
options.B: Hardness and electrical conductivity, because metals conduct electricity and are hard
options.C: Hardness and low flexibility, because blades must stay rigid to cut cleanly
options.D: Transparency and hardness, because users need to see through the blade

questions.explanation: Scissor blades need hardness to maintain a sharp edge and low flexibility (rigidity) so they do not deform under cutting force, which would make them ineffective. Option A incorrectly includes flexibility as a benefit; a flexible blade would bend rather than cut, making the scissors useless.

questions.title: Defining a Design Problem
questions.prompt: Two students are writing a design brief. Student A writes: 'We will make a better school bag.' Student B writes: 'We will design a school bag that weighs less than 400 g when empty and evenly distributes load across both shoulders for users aged 10–12.' Which statement is correct about these two briefs?

options.A: Student A's brief is better because it leaves room for creative solutions
options.B: Student B's brief is better because it includes measurable criteria that define success
options.C: Both briefs are equally useful because they describe the same product
options.D: Student B's brief is worse because specific numbers limit the designer's choices too much

questions.explanation: A strong design brief contains measurable success criteria so the designer and evaluators can objectively judge whether the solution works; Student B's brief provides weight and ergonomic distribution targets that allow testing. Student A's brief cannot be tested because 'better' has no agreed meaning or metric.

questions.title: Sustainability: Trade-off Thinking
questions.prompt: A company switches from single-use plastic straws to bamboo straws. A student claims this is always better for the environment. Which piece of evidence would MOST strongly challenge the student's claim?

options.A: Bamboo straws cost more money to produce than plastic straws
options.B: Bamboo straws must be used at least 50 times to offset the energy used in shipping them from farms overseas
options.C: Some customers prefer the texture of plastic straws
options.D: Bamboo grows faster than most trees used to make paper straws

questions.explanation: Lifecycle assessment thinking shows that the environmental benefit of a product depends on its full lifecycle, including production and shipping energy; if bamboo straws are rarely reused, the carbon cost of transporting them can exceed the benefit of avoiding plastic. Option A is a financial concern, not an environmental one, so it does not challenge an environmental claim.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Levels
questions.prompt: A design team is at the very beginning of testing an idea for a new chair. They build a rough model from cardboard and tape in 30 minutes. A classmate says they should have used real wood to get accurate results. Who is correct, and what design principle explains the answer?

options.A: The classmate is correct; accurate materials always produce more reliable feedback
options.B: The team is correct; low-fidelity prototypes allow quick, cheap testing of basic form and function early in the process
options.C: The team is correct; cardboard is stronger than wood for a first prototype
options.D: The classmate is correct; users cannot give useful feedback about a cardboard model

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes are deliberately rough so teams can test fundamental design ideas (shape, size, form) cheaply before committing to expensive materials; this is a core principle of iterative design thinking. The classmate's claim is wrong because using expensive final materials at the earliest stage wastes resources if the basic concept needs to change.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Diversity
questions.prompt: A company designs a computer keyboard using measurements from a study of adult men aged 20–40. Children and elderly users later report discomfort. What ergonomic principle did the company most likely violate?

options.A: They should have used softer key materials to reduce finger strain
options.B: They failed to design for a representative range of users, ignoring anthropometric diversity
options.C: They chose the wrong colour scheme for the keys, reducing visibility
options.D: They did not test the product in different lighting conditions

questions.explanation: Ergonomics relies on anthropometric data (measurements of human bodies), and designing only for one narrow demographic ignores the variation in hand size, reach, and strength across different ages and groups; this is called designing for the average and excluding outliers. Option A relates to material comfort but does not explain why different user groups experience structural mismatch.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: First-Mover Advantage
questions.prompt: Company X launches a new type of foldable water bottle and gains many customers quickly. Company Y releases a very similar bottle six months later at a lower price. A student claims Company X will always stay ahead because it was first. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; first-mover advantage always guarantees long-term market leadership
options.B: The claim is partly correct; being first builds brand recognition, but a later competitor offering lower price or better quality can overtake the leader
options.C: The claim is incorrect; the first company to market always loses because early products have more flaws
options.D: The claim is correct; customers never switch products once they have chosen a brand

questions.explanation: First-mover advantage gives early brand recognition and customer loyalty, but history shows that later entrants (fast followers) can gain market share by offering lower prices or improved features; for example, many early internet companies were overtaken by later rivals. Option A is wrong because first-mover advantage is real but not permanent or guaranteed.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart home heating system, a thermostat measures room temperature and switches the heater off when the target temperature is reached. This is an example of which type of system behaviour?

options.A: An open-loop system, because the heater runs on a fixed timer
options.B: A closed-loop system with negative feedback, because the output (temperature) is used to control the input (heater on/off)
options.C: A closed-loop system with positive feedback, because more heat causes even more heating
options.D: An open-loop system, because the thermostat is a separate device from the heater

questions.explanation: A closed-loop system uses feedback from its output to adjust its input; negative feedback reduces the difference between the actual and desired state, which is exactly what a thermostat does — it feeds back temperature data to stop the heater when the goal is reached. Option C describes positive feedback, which would cause runaway heating and is the opposite of what a thermostat does.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A school uses an AI program to recommend which students need extra reading support. The program was trained mostly on data from students in wealthy urban schools. What is the most likely ethical problem with using this program in a rural school?

options.A: The program will be too slow to run on rural school computers
options.B: The program may give biased recommendations because it was not trained on data representing rural students' needs and backgrounds
options.C: Rural students will find the program's interface too complicated to use
options.D: The program will recommend too many students for support, wasting school resources

questions.explanation: AI systems reflect the biases in their training data; a model trained on urban wealthy-school data may not recognise the literacy patterns, resources, or challenges of rural students, leading to inaccurate and potentially unfair recommendations. Option A is a technical concern about hardware, not an ethical concern about fairness or bias.

questions.title: UX Research: Survey vs. Observation
questions.prompt: A designer wants to know how children actually use a new tablet app in class. She chooses between a survey and silent observation. A classmate says surveys are always more accurate because children can describe their own behaviour. Is the classmate correct?

options.A: Yes; surveys capture both how users feel and what they do, making them more complete
options.B: No; people often cannot accurately recall or describe their own behaviour, so observation of real use is frequently more reliable
options.C: Yes; silent observation makes children nervous and changes how they behave
options.D: No; surveys should never be used in UX research because the sample size is always too small

questions.explanation: Research in UX and psychology consistently shows that users have poor recall of their own behaviour and often describe what they think they should do rather than what they actually do — a phenomenon known as self-report bias; direct observation captures genuine, in-context behaviour. Option C raises a valid concern (the observer effect), but this does not make surveys more accurate for capturing actual behaviour.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secret
questions.prompt: A food company keeps its recipe for a popular sauce completely secret and does not register it anywhere. A competitor hires a former employee who knows the recipe and uses it. Which type of intellectual property protection BEST describes what the food company was relying on, and why did it fail here?

options.A: Copyright; it failed because recipes cannot be copyrighted
options.B: Trade secret; it failed because once the secret is disclosed by a person, legal protection depends on confidentiality agreements, which may not have been in place
options.C: Patent; it failed because the company did not file the patent in time
options.D: Trademark; it failed because the sauce was not given a registered brand name

questions.explanation: A trade secret protects information that gives a business advantage as long as it remains confidential; famous examples include the Coca-Cola formula. If employees share the secret without a confidentiality (non-disclosure) agreement, the company loses protection because the information is no longer secret. Option C is wrong because a patent requires public disclosure of the invention, which would defeat the purpose of keeping it secret.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment: Hotspot Identification
questions.prompt: An LCA of a cotton T-shirt finds that 70% of its total water consumption occurs during the growing of the cotton, 5% during manufacturing, and 25% during consumer washing over its lifetime. Which stage should a designer target FIRST to reduce the shirt's overall water footprint?

options.A: Manufacturing, because factories can install water recycling systems most easily
options.B: Consumer washing, because educating users is cheaper than changing materials
options.C: Cotton growing, because it accounts for the largest share of water use and offers the greatest reduction potential
options.D: End-of-life disposal, because landfill leachate contaminates water supplies

questions.explanation: LCA hotspot analysis directs designers to the life-cycle stage with the largest impact; since cotton cultivation accounts for 70% of water use, switching to less water-intensive fibres (such as recycled polyester or organic cotton with drip irrigation) would deliver the biggest reduction. Option B targets only 25% of the problem and relies on changing consumer behaviour, which is harder to guarantee than a material design change.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Define Stage
questions.prompt: After interviewing users, a design team writes this problem statement: 'We need to design an app.' A mentor says this is too vague. Which version of the problem statement best follows the 'point of view' format used in design thinking?

options.A: A busy 10-year-old student needs a way to organise homework reminders because she often forgets tasks given verbally by teachers
options.B: We need a homework app with a calendar, notifications, and a colour-coded system
options.C: Students should use technology more often to help with school work
options.D: We will build a mobile app that solves the problem of forgotten homework for all students

questions.explanation: A point-of-view statement in design thinking follows the structure: [user] needs [need] because [insight]; Option A identifies a specific user, her real need, and the underlying reason, without jumping to a solution. Option B is a solution statement, not a problem statement, and skips the empathy insight entirely.

questions.title: Materials: Biodegradability Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A student argues that all products should be made from biodegradable materials because they always break down harmlessly. Identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: Biodegradable materials are always more expensive, making them impractical
options.B: Some biodegradable materials release methane or other gases when they decompose in landfills, and they may degrade before the product's useful life is over
options.C: Biodegradable materials cannot be recycled, so they must go to landfill
options.D: Biodegradable materials are weaker than plastics and cannot be used for structural products

questions.explanation: Biodegradable materials can create environmental problems when they decompose anaerobically in landfills, producing methane — a potent greenhouse gas; additionally, a material that degrades too quickly may fail before the product is meant to be replaced. Option A is sometimes true but is a cost argument, not a flaw in the environmental reasoning the student presented.

questions.title: Ideation: Convergent vs. Divergent Thinking
questions.prompt: A team has finished brainstorming and has 40 ideas for a new water bottle design. Their teacher says it is time to switch from divergent to convergent thinking. What should the team do NEXT?

options.A: Generate even more ideas to make sure no option has been missed
options.B: Evaluate and narrow down ideas using criteria linked to the design brief
options.C: Begin building a high-fidelity prototype of every idea
options.D: Return to the empathise stage and conduct more user interviews

questions.explanation: Convergent thinking means moving from many possibilities to a focused selection by applying design criteria and constraints; this is the natural follow-up to divergent brainstorming and leads towards a chosen concept to prototype. Option A continues divergent thinking, which is counterproductive once sufficient ideas exist and time is needed to select and develop one.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Cognitive Load
questions.prompt: An app for 10-year-olds displays 15 different options on its home screen at once. Users report feeling confused and making many mistakes. Which ergonomic concept best explains this problem?

options.A: Poor colour contrast, making it hard to distinguish the options visually
options.B: Excessive cognitive load, because the number of choices exceeds the user's working memory capacity
options.C: Inadequate font size, causing physical eye strain that leads to errors
options.D: Lack of haptic feedback, leaving users unsure if they have pressed a button

questions.explanation: Cognitive ergonomics recognises that human working memory can hold approximately 7 (plus or minus 2) chunks of information at once (Miller's Law); presenting 15 simultaneous options overwhelms this capacity, causing confusion and errors. Option A relates to visual ergonomics and could cause problems, but it does not explain the confusion from having too many choices.

questions.title: Innovation: Incremental vs. Radical
questions.prompt: Company A releases a new smartphone that is thinner and has a longer battery life than last year's model. Company B releases the world's first phone that projects a holographic screen into the air. Which statement correctly classifies these innovations?

options.A: Both are radical innovations because both involve new technology
options.B: Company A's is incremental; Company B's is radical, because Company B introduces an entirely new way of displaying information that did not exist before
options.C: Company A's is radical; Company B's is incremental, because holographic technology already exists in research labs
options.D: Both are incremental innovations because both are still smartphones

questions.explanation: Incremental innovation improves existing products in small steps (thinner, longer battery), while radical innovation introduces a fundamentally new concept that changes how a product works or is used; a holographic display phone creates a new product category. Option D is wrong because the category of device does not determine whether the innovation is radical — the nature of the change does.

questions.title: Sustainability: Planned Obsolescence
questions.prompt: A student reads that some electronics companies deliberately design products to stop working after a few years so customers buy new ones. This practice is called planned obsolescence. What is the PRIMARY sustainability argument AGAINST this practice?

options.A: It forces customers to spend more money, which is unfair
options.B: It increases the volume of electronic waste containing toxic materials, accelerating resource depletion and pollution
options.C: It reduces competition between companies because weaker products drive customers away
options.D: It prevents designers from developing creative new features for future models

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence dramatically shortens product lifespans, generating large quantities of e-waste that contains hazardous substances like lead and mercury; this depletes finite raw materials and creates toxic pollution in ecosystems. Option A is a valid ethical concern but relates to economics and fairness rather than to environmental sustainability.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystem Interaction
questions.prompt: A student designs an electric scooter and finds that when she makes the motor more powerful to go faster, the battery runs out twice as quickly. What does this illustrate about systems engineering?

options.A: Each subsystem can be improved independently without affecting the others
options.B: Optimising one subsystem can negatively impact the performance of another, requiring the designer to balance trade-offs across the whole system
options.C: The motor and battery are not part of the same system and should be designed separately
options.D: A more powerful motor always requires a smaller battery, so the total weight stays the same

questions.explanation: Systems engineering recognises that subsystems are interdependent; changing one component's performance creates ripple effects across others, requiring engineers to optimise the whole system rather than individual parts in isolation. Option A is the misconception the question is testing — it describes a non-systems way of thinking that ignores interdependence.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Automation and Employment
questions.prompt: A factory introduces robots that can pack products 10 times faster than human workers. The company claims this is good for everyone because products become cheaper. A student challenges this claim. Which argument BEST supports the student's challenge?

options.A: Robots sometimes break down, so production is not always faster
options.B: Workers who lose their jobs may not have the skills to find new employment quickly, causing hardship for individuals and communities
options.C: Cheaper products reduce company profits, harming shareholders
options.D: Robots cannot check product quality as carefully as human workers

questions.explanation: The ethical concern with automation is that displaced workers, especially those in low-skill roles, face structural unemployment because the new jobs created by technology often require different and higher-level skills; communities dependent on factory work can suffer significant economic harm. Option A is a reliability concern, not an ethical argument about the impact on people.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright Duration
questions.prompt: A student wants to use a song in her design presentation. She finds out the songwriter died in 1960. She assumes the song is now free to use because so much time has passed. Is she correct, and what does she need to check?

options.A: She is correct; all works become public domain 50 years after the creator's death in every country
options.B: She may be incorrect; copyright duration varies by country and is typically 70 years after the creator's death, meaning the song may still be protected
options.C: She is correct; songs can never be copyrighted, only the written lyrics can be
options.D: She may be incorrect; she needs to check whether the song was published online, because only printed works are protected by copyright

questions.explanation: In most countries following the Berne Convention, copyright lasts for 70 years after the author's death; since 1960 + 70 = 2030, the song would still be protected in many jurisdictions as of now. Option A is wrong because the duration is not uniformly 50 years — many countries including EU members use 70 years post-mortem.

questions.title: User Testing: Evaluating Results
questions.prompt: After testing a new pencil grip with five users, a student reports: 'Four out of five users said it was comfortable, so our design is a success.' Identify the strongest weakness in this conclusion.

options.A: The student should have tested at least ten materials before choosing one
options.B: A sample of five users is too small to draw reliable conclusions, and the test ignored whether comfort was maintained after extended use
options.C: The student forgot to include a control group using a standard pencil grip
options.D: User opinions are never valid evidence in design; only measurement data should be used

questions.explanation: Five participants is a very small sample that may not represent the range of users the product is designed for; additionally, comfort after only one brief use session does not predict long-term ergonomic performance, which is a key criterion for a grip. Option C raises a valid research design point but is less central to the specific flaws in the student's conclusion than sample size and test duration.

questions.title: Circular Economy: Design for Disassembly
questions.prompt: A designer creates a laptop where all parts are glued together permanently, making it impossible to replace a broken screen or a dead battery. From a circular economy perspective, what is the PRIMARY design failure here?

options.A: The laptop will be too heavy because of all the glue used in assembly
options.B: The design prevents repair and part recovery, shortening the product's useful life and making material recycling nearly impossible
options.C: Gluing parts together makes the laptop look unattractive to consumers
options.D: The laptop cannot receive software updates because the hardware cannot be upgraded

questions.explanation: In a circular economy, products should be designed for disassembly so components can be repaired, reused, or recovered at end of life, keeping materials in circulation and reducing waste; permanent bonding makes all of this impossible and forces the whole device into the waste stream when one component fails. Option D is about software, not the physical design failure central to circular economy principles.

questions.title: Design Responsibility: Inclusive Design
questions.prompt: A team designs a public water fountain at a height that works perfectly for an average adult but cannot be reached by a child in a wheelchair. A classmate says, 'We designed it for most people, so it is fine.' Which principle of responsible design does this attitude most directly violate?

options.A: Sustainability, because the fountain uses too much water
options.B: Inclusive design, because a well-designed public product should be usable by people across a wide range of abilities and body types without requiring special adaptation
options.C: Aesthetics, because the fountain should look appealing to all users regardless of their height
options.D: Iterative design, because the team did not test enough prototypes

questions.explanation: Inclusive (or universal) design is the principle that products, especially public ones, should be accessible and usable by the widest possible range of people without exclusion; designing only for the statistical average actively excludes users with disabilities, different ages, or body sizes. Option D (iterative design) relates to process methodology and does not address the ethical responsibility to include all users.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: During the empathise stage of the design thinking process, a student wants to understand why elderly users struggle with a new TV remote. Which data-collection approach would BEST reveal the root causes of their difficulty?

options.A: Distributing a written survey with yes/no questions about the remote's features
options.B: Observing elderly users interacting with the remote in their own homes
options.C: Asking a group of teenagers to predict what elderly users would find difficult
options.D: Counting how many buttons the remote has compared to older models

questions.explanation: Observation in the user's natural environment is a core empathy tool in design thinking because it reveals behaviours and frustrations users cannot always articulate themselves. A written survey with yes/no questions (option A) captures opinions but misses the non-verbal cues and real-time struggles that direct observation uncovers.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A team has finished their empathy research and now must write a problem statement. Which of the following is the MOST effective problem statement for the define stage of design thinking?

options.A: We need to build a better water bottle for students.
options.B: Students aged 10–14 who walk to school need a way to stay hydrated throughout the day because they frequently forget to refill heavy bottles.
options.C: Water bottles are inconvenient and students do not drink enough water.
options.D: The design team will create a lightweight, insulated water bottle with a reminder alarm.
