questions.explanation: An effective problem statement from the define stage names the specific user, their need, and the insight behind the problem — not the solution. Option D describes a solution rather than a problem, which belongs in the ideate stage, not the define stage.

questions.title: Material Properties: Conductivity
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable coffee cup that keeps drinks hot for at least two hours. She must choose between a stainless-steel shell and a ceramic shell. Which property makes stainless steel with an air gap BETTER than solid ceramic for this purpose?

options.A: Stainless steel has higher density, so it stores more heat energy
options.B: Stainless steel is opaque, preventing heat loss through radiation
options.C: A double-walled stainless-steel construction creates a vacuum gap that greatly reduces conductive heat transfer
options.D: Stainless steel has a higher melting point, so it absorbs heat more slowly

questions.explanation: Double-walled vacuum flasks work because removing air between the walls eliminates conduction and convection, the two main heat-transfer pathways — a principle used in stainless-steel travel cups. Higher density (option A) is a physical property unrelated to insulation; it does not determine how quickly heat escapes.

questions.title: Sustainability: Material Choice
questions.prompt: Examine the following claim: 'Bamboo is always a more sustainable material than plastic because it is natural.' Is this claim fully accurate? Evaluate.

options.A: Yes, because natural materials are biodegradable and plastics never decompose
options.B: Yes, because bamboo grows faster than any other plant used for materials
options.C: No, because sustainability depends on the full lifecycle, including processing, transport, and end-of-life disposal
options.D: No, because plastic is stronger than bamboo and therefore lasts longer, reducing waste

questions.explanation: Lifecycle assessment (LCA) considers all stages from raw material extraction to disposal, not just whether a material is natural. Bamboo processed with heavy chemicals or shipped long distances may have a higher overall environmental impact than locally recycled plastic in some contexts. Option A oversimplifies by ignoring processing and transport emissions.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Levels
questions.prompt: A design team is in the early ideation phase and wants to quickly test whether their layout concept for a new app screen makes sense to users. Which type of prototype is MOST appropriate at this stage?

options.A: A fully coded, interactive app with final colours and fonts
options.B: A low-fidelity paper sketch showing the rough layout of the screen
options.C: A written description of all the app's planned features
options.D: A high-resolution digital mockup with animations and real data

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes such as paper sketches are used early in the design process because they are fast and cheap to produce, allowing teams to test core layout ideas before investing time in detailed development. A fully coded app (option A) is a high-fidelity prototype better suited to later-stage testing when design decisions are nearly finalised.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Fit
questions.prompt: A student is designing a school backpack for children aged 8–12. She discovers that the shoulder straps on most commercial bags are set at a fixed width, causing discomfort for narrower-shouldered users. Which ergonomic design principle does adjustable strap width BEST apply?

options.A: Designing for the average user so the product fits most people reasonably well
options.B: Designing for adjustability so the product accommodates a range of body sizes
options.C: Designing for the extreme user so the product works for the largest and smallest users only
options.D: Designing for aesthetics so the product looks proportional on different body types

questions.explanation: Designing for adjustability is a key ergonomic principle that allows a single product to be adapted to different users' anthropometric measurements — in this case, varying shoulder widths. Designing for the average (option A) typically excludes users at both ends of the measurement range, meaning many children would still experience discomfort.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: Pricing
questions.prompt: A startup releases a new smartwatch that costs far more to produce than existing models but sells it at a very low price initially to build a large customer base quickly. What economic strategy is this company using?

options.A: Price skimming, charging the highest price the market will bear at launch
options.B: Cost-plus pricing, adding a fixed percentage profit to production costs
options.C: Penetration pricing, setting a low price to rapidly gain market share
options.D: Premium pricing, signalling high quality through a high price point

questions.explanation: Penetration pricing involves deliberately setting a low initial price to attract customers away from competitors and quickly establish a user base, with the intention of raising prices later once the brand is established. Price skimming (option A) is the opposite strategy — charging the highest price first, then lowering it over time, which is common with new technology launches.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Data Privacy
questions.prompt: A company builds a free educational game for children and collects detailed data on every mistake a player makes, storing it indefinitely and sharing it with advertising partners. Identify the PRIMARY ethical concern with this practice.

options.A: The game may not be entertaining enough to hold children's attention
options.B: Children cannot give informed consent to data collection, raising serious privacy and exploitation concerns
options.C: Sharing data with partners will make the game run more slowly
options.D: Collecting mistake data may discourage children from trying difficult challenges

questions.explanation: Children are considered a vulnerable group in data ethics frameworks; they cannot meaningfully give informed consent, and indefinite data collection shared with advertisers potentially exposes them to manipulation and privacy violations. Option D describes a pedagogical concern about game design, not an ethical concern about data handling.

questions.title: UX Research: Surveys vs Interviews
questions.prompt: A designer wants to find out how 500 students feel about the school canteen's online ordering system. She considers using either an online survey or one-to-one interviews. Compare the two methods: which advantage does the online survey have over interviews for this specific goal?

options.A: The survey provides deeper insight into the reasons behind user frustration
options.B: The survey allows all 500 students to be reached efficiently, producing quantitative data at scale
options.C: The survey eliminates all forms of response bias from participants
options.D: The survey reveals non-verbal cues that indicate user confusion

questions.explanation: Surveys are efficient for gathering quantitative data from large samples quickly, making them ideal when a designer needs to understand patterns across a broad group such as 500 students. Deeper insight into reasons and non-verbal cues (options A and D) are advantages of interviews, not surveys.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In systems engineering, a thermostat in a home heating system detects room temperature and switches the heater off when the target temperature is reached. What type of system mechanism does this demonstrate?

options.A: An open-loop system that processes inputs without monitoring outputs
options.B: A negative feedback loop that uses output information to stabilise the system
options.C: A positive feedback loop that amplifies the heating effect over time
options.D: A subsystem that operates independently of the main heating system

questions.explanation: A thermostat is the classic example of a negative feedback loop: the output (room temperature) is measured and fed back to the controller, which reduces the system's action (turns off the heater) to maintain a stable state. A positive feedback loop (option C) would cause the system to amplify its output — the heater would keep heating even above the target temperature.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright
questions.prompt: A student creates an original logo for her school project and saves it to her computer. She does not register it anywhere. Does copyright protection apply to her logo? Justify your answer.

options.A: No, because copyright only protects works that have been officially registered with a government office
options.B: No, because logos must be trademarked, not copyrighted, to receive any protection
options.C: Yes, copyright protection applies automatically to original creative works as soon as they are created and fixed in a tangible form
options.D: Yes, but only after the student publishes the logo publicly online or in print

questions.explanation: Under most international copyright frameworks (including those aligned with the Berne Convention), copyright is automatic and arises the moment an original work is created in a fixed form — no registration is required. Option A is incorrect because registration is not a condition for copyright to exist, though it can help in legal disputes.

questions.title: Design Criteria and Constraints
questions.prompt: In an MYP Design project, a student lists 'the product must cost less than $10 to manufacture' and 'the product should look attractive to teenagers.' Which statement BEST describes the difference between these two requirements?

options.A: The first is a design criterion and the second is also a criterion; they are the same type of requirement
options.B: The first is a constraint because it sets a non-negotiable limit, while the second is a criterion because it is a measurable success indicator
options.C: The first is a design criterion and the second is a constraint because aesthetics are more flexible than cost
options.D: Both are constraints because they both limit what the designer can do

questions.explanation: In MYP Design, constraints are non-negotiable limits (such as a fixed budget) that the design must not exceed, while criteria are measurable conditions the design should meet to be considered successful. The cost cap is a hard limit (constraint), whereas 'looks attractive' is a success indicator that can be tested and refined (criterion).

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment: End of Life
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment of a smartphone reveals that the end-of-life stage produces the LEAST greenhouse gas emissions compared to manufacture and use. Why does manufacture typically produce the MOST emissions in a smartphone's lifecycle?

options.A: Because smartphones must be shipped globally, and transport produces more emissions than any other stage
options.B: Because mining rare earth metals and assembling complex components requires enormous amounts of energy and resources
options.C: Because users charge their phones daily, generating large cumulative emissions over the product's life
options.D: Because recycling facilities use more electricity than factories that produce new components

questions.explanation: Smartphone manufacturing involves energy-intensive mining of rare earth elements (such as cobalt and lithium) and highly complex, multi-stage assembly processes, making it the most emission-heavy phase of the lifecycle. Daily charging (option C) does contribute to use-phase emissions, but the energy cost of manufacturing consistently exceeds use-phase emissions for most smartphones.

questions.title: Iterative Design: Concept Testing
questions.prompt: A student builds a cardboard model of a new chair design and shows it to five classmates. Three say the seat seems too narrow. What should the student do NEXT according to iterative design principles?

options.A: Discard the entire design concept and restart the empathy stage from the beginning
options.B: Ignore the feedback because cardboard models are not accurate representations of the final product
options.C: Record the feedback, modify the seat width in the design, and create a revised prototype to test again
options.D: Conduct more empathy interviews before making any changes to the prototype

questions.explanation: Iterative design requires designers to record user feedback, make targeted improvements, and then test again — the cycle of prototype, test, refine is repeated until the design meets its criteria. Discarding the whole concept (option A) is rarely appropriate when feedback highlights a specific, addressable issue like seat width.

questions.title: Material Property: Tensile Strength
questions.prompt: An engineer is selecting a material for a suspension bridge cable that must support enormous weight without snapping. Which material property is MOST critical for this application?

options.A: High thermal conductivity, so the cable can release heat generated by friction
options.B: High tensile strength, so the cable resists being pulled apart under heavy load
options.C: High malleability, so the cable can be bent into shape without breaking
options.D: High hardness, so the cable resists surface scratching from environmental exposure

questions.explanation: Tensile strength is the maximum stress a material can withstand when being stretched or pulled before it breaks, making it the most critical property for suspension cables under tension. Malleability (option C) describes a material's ability to be shaped by compression — a different property that is more relevant to sheet metal forming.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Ideation Techniques
questions.prompt: A design team is stuck and cannot move past two or three similar ideas. A facilitator suggests using SCAMPER as an ideation technique. What does SCAMPER encourage designers to do?

options.A: Rank existing ideas by cost and eliminate the most expensive ones
options.B: Apply systematic prompts such as Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, and Reverse to develop new ideas
options.C: Survey users with structured questions to generate ideas based on their preferences
options.D: Sketch, Create, Analyse, Model, Plan, Evaluate, and Report on a single chosen idea

questions.explanation: SCAMPER is a creative ideation technique where each letter stands for a prompt that pushes designers to think about their concept differently — for example, 'Substitute' asks what materials or components could be swapped. Option D invents a plausible-sounding acronym but does not reflect SCAMPER's actual meaning.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trademark
questions.prompt: A food company uses a distinctive swoosh symbol on all its packaging for five years. A rival company begins using a nearly identical symbol on similar food products. Which form of intellectual property protection would BEST prevent this kind of copying?

options.A: A patent, which protects the technical process used to manufacture the food
options.B: A trademark, which protects distinctive brand symbols, names, and logos from being used by competitors
options.C: A copyright, which automatically protects creative works from being reproduced
options.D: A trade secret, which keeps the symbol's design confidential within the company

questions.explanation: A trademark specifically protects brand identifiers — such as logos, symbols, and names — that distinguish one company's goods from another's, and it can be renewed indefinitely as long as the mark is in use. Copyright (option C) protects original creative expression but does not prevent competitors from using a confusingly similar logo in a commercial context the way trademark law does.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystems
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A bicycle is a single, unified system with no separate subsystems.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because all parts of a bicycle work together toward one purpose
options.B: The claim is incorrect; a bicycle contains distinct subsystems such as braking, steering, and drivetrain, each with its own components and function
options.C: The claim is correct because subsystems only exist in electronic or digital systems
options.D: The claim is incorrect because a bicycle has too few parts to be considered a system at all

questions.explanation: In systems engineering, complex systems are composed of subsystems — groups of interacting components that perform a specific function within the larger system. A bicycle's braking subsystem (brake levers, cables, callipers) operates somewhat independently from its drivetrain subsystem (pedals, chain, gears). Option A confuses the idea of a shared purpose with the absence of subsystems.

questions.title: Sustainability: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
questions.prompt: The waste hierarchy ranks strategies for managing materials from most to least preferable. Place these options in the CORRECT order from most to least sustainable: (1) recycling the material, (2) refusing to use the material at all, (3) reusing the material multiple times.

options.A: Recycle → Reuse → Refuse
options.B: Reuse → Refuse → Recycle
options.C: Refuse → Reuse → Recycle
options.D: Recycle → Refuse → Reuse

questions.explanation: The waste hierarchy prioritises prevention (refusing) first because it avoids resource use entirely, followed by reuse (extending the product's life), and then recycling (which still requires energy and processing). Option A places recycling first, which is incorrect because recycling consumes energy and resources even though it is better than landfill.

questions.title: UX Research: Usability Testing
questions.prompt: During a usability test of a new library website, a researcher asks participants to 'think aloud' while completing tasks. What is the PRIMARY purpose of the think-aloud protocol?

options.A: To measure how quickly users complete each task on the website
options.B: To reveal users' moment-to-moment thoughts, confusion, and decision-making as they interact with the interface
options.C: To compare the performance of different users and rank them by ability
options.D: To allow researchers to correct users' mistakes before they give up on a task

questions.explanation: The think-aloud protocol is a qualitative usability research technique that makes users' cognitive processes visible — they verbalise what they are looking at, thinking, and feeling, giving designers insight into confusion points that would be invisible from task completion times alone. Option A describes a quantitative measure (task time) that does not require a think-aloud approach.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: Market Disruption
questions.prompt: Digital music streaming services disrupted the CD market by offering all-you-can-listen access for a monthly fee. Which economic term BEST describes what streaming did to the price of listening to individual songs?

options.A: Deflation of the marginal cost of accessing each song toward near zero
options.B: Inflation of the average price consumers pay for music overall
options.C: Price skimming that allowed streaming companies to charge more for new releases
options.D: Market saturation that caused all music prices to stabilise at a fixed rate

questions.explanation: Streaming platforms drove the marginal cost of accessing any individual song toward near zero for subscribers, because the additional cost of listening to one more song on a subscription service is essentially nothing — a classic feature of digital goods economics. Option B is incorrect because most consumers now pay less for music access than they did when buying individual CDs.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A student discovers that a hiring algorithm used by a company recommends male candidates at a much higher rate than equally qualified female candidates. What is the MOST likely explanation for this bias?

options.A: The algorithm was deliberately programmed to favour male candidates by the engineers
options.B: The training data reflected historical hiring patterns that already favoured male candidates, and the algorithm learned and replicated that bias
options.C: Female candidates submitted applications with weaker qualifications on average
options.D: The algorithm was not given enough data and therefore made random errors

questions.explanation: Algorithmic bias most commonly arises when machine learning models are trained on historical data that reflects existing social inequalities — the algorithm learns to reproduce those patterns, even when there is no deliberate intention to discriminate. Option A (deliberate programming) is possible but far less common than bias embedded in training data.

questions.title: Material Property: Elasticity
questions.prompt: A designer is choosing material for the soles of running shoes. She wants a material that returns to its original shape after each footstrike, providing energy return. Which property is she looking for?

options.A: Plasticity, so the material permanently deforms to match the runner's foot shape
options.B: Brittleness, so the material resists cracking under repeated impact
options.C: Elasticity, so the material stores and releases energy by returning to its original shape after deformation
options.D: Porosity, so the material absorbs moisture and reduces shoe weight

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the property that allows a material to deform under stress and then return to its original shape when the stress is removed — exactly what is needed for energy-returning shoe soles. Plasticity (option A) is the opposite: a plastic material permanently deforms rather than recovering its shape.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Testing Stage
questions.prompt: A team has tested their prototype alarm clock with ten users. Seven users said the alarm sound was 'too quiet in a noisy bedroom.' The team decides to present the current prototype to their teacher without making changes. Identify the error in their approach.

options.A: Testing with ten users is not a large enough sample to draw any conclusions
options.B: The team should have tested with professional designers rather than general users
options.C: The team failed to use testing feedback to iterate on the design before proceeding, violating iterative design principles
options.D: Alarm volume cannot be changed at the prototype stage and must wait until manufacturing

questions.explanation: In iterative design, testing is only valuable if the findings are used to improve the prototype before the next stage; presenting an unchanged prototype despite clear, repeated user feedback contradicts the core principle of using testing to drive refinement. Option A is a reasonable concern but is not the central error — the team had actionable feedback from seven out of ten users and chose to ignore it.

questions.title: Sustainability: Design for Disassembly
questions.prompt: A mobile phone manufacturer designs its new model so that the battery, screen, and main circuit board can each be removed with a standard screwdriver in under five minutes. What sustainability principle does this design apply?

options.A: Design for aesthetics, making the product visually appealing throughout its life
options.B: Design for disassembly, enabling components to be separated easily for repair, reuse, or recycling
options.C: Design for durability, ensuring the phone survives physical damage over many years
options.D: Design for modularity, allowing users to upgrade individual components without changing the exterior

questions.explanation: Design for disassembly (DfD) is a sustainability strategy that ensures products can be taken apart at end of life so materials are recovered efficiently for recycling or parts are reused — reducing landfill waste. Design for modularity (option D) is closely related but specifically focuses on swappable upgradeable parts rather than end-of-life disassembly for material recovery.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: During the empathise stage of design thinking, a student interviews five classmates about their school bag problems. Which type of information is MOST valuable at this stage?

options.A: Numerical data showing how many students own each bag brand
options.B: Descriptions of how students feel when their bag is too heavy or hard to open
options.C: A list of materials used in competing bag designs
options.D: Technical specifications of bag zippers from the manufacturer

questions.explanation: The empathise stage focuses on understanding users' lived experiences, emotions, and frustrations — qualitative insight that reveals unmet needs. Numerical brand data (option A) belongs more to market research and does not capture the emotional or experiential dimension that empathy requires.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A team has gathered research about users and now needs to write a problem statement. Which of the following is the BEST example of a well-defined problem statement?

options.A: We need to build an app because technology is popular.
options.B: Busy secondary school students need a way to track homework deadlines because they frequently forget assignments and feel stressed.
options.C: Students do not have enough time to study, so we will create more time in the school day.
options.D: Our product will use a calendar interface with colour-coded subjects.

questions.explanation: A well-defined problem statement identifies who the user is, what they need, and why — without prescribing a solution. Option D describes a specific solution rather than a problem, which skips the define stage and risks designing for the wrong need.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Choices
questions.prompt: A student claims that building a low-fidelity prototype out of cardboard is a waste of time because it does not look like the final product. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct, because users cannot give useful feedback on rough models.
options.B: The claim is correct, because prototypes must accurately represent materials to be meaningful.
options.C: The claim is incorrect, because low-fidelity prototypes are quick and cheap ways to test core ideas before committing resources.
options.D: The claim is incorrect, because cardboard is always stronger than the final material will be.

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes allow designers to test fundamental concepts and gather early feedback at minimal cost — a core principle of iterative design. Option A is wrong because users can and do provide useful feedback on rough models, especially regarding layout, size, and basic function.

questions.title: Material Conductivity Properties
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable coffee cup intended to keep drinks hot for longer. Which material property is MOST important for the outer layer that the user holds?

options.A: High thermal conductivity, so heat moves away from the liquid quickly
options.B: Low thermal conductivity, so the outside stays cool enough to hold comfortably
options.C: High electrical conductivity, so the cup can be charged wirelessly
options.D: High density, so the cup feels premium and does not tip over easily

questions.explanation: Low thermal conductivity means heat transfers slowly from the hot liquid through the outer wall, keeping the surface comfortable to hold — this is why materials like silicone sleeves are used on takeaway cups. High thermal conductivity (option A) would make the outer surface dangerously hot, directly contradicting the ergonomic goal.

questions.title: Sustainability and Material Choice
questions.prompt: Examine the following claim: 'Biodegradable plastics are always more sustainable than conventional plastics.' Which response BEST evaluates this statement?

options.A: The claim is fully correct, because biodegradable materials decompose and therefore have no environmental impact.
options.B: The claim is fully correct, because biodegradable plastics use less energy to manufacture.
options.C: The claim is an oversimplification, because biodegradable plastics often require specific industrial conditions to break down and may still harm ecosystems if improperly disposed of.
options.D: The claim is fully incorrect, because biodegradable plastics are always more expensive and therefore worse for society.

questions.explanation: Many biodegradable plastics require industrial composting facilities with controlled temperature and humidity; in a landfill or ocean, they behave similarly to conventional plastic. Option A is wrong because decomposition is not automatic and can still produce methane or micro-fragments depending on disposal conditions.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Fit
questions.prompt: A company is redesigning a computer mouse for professional graphic designers who use it for eight hours a day. Which ergonomic consideration should have the HIGHEST priority?

options.A: Making the mouse available in a bright colour palette to improve desk aesthetics
options.B: Ensuring the shape supports the natural curve of the hand to reduce repetitive strain injury
options.C: Adding extra buttons so the mouse can perform more functions simultaneously
options.D: Reducing the mouse's weight to the absolute minimum regardless of grip stability

questions.explanation: Ergonomics prioritises the physical fit between product and user to prevent injury and fatigue; for prolonged use, supporting the hand's natural posture is critical to avoiding repetitive strain. Adding extra buttons (option C) addresses functionality but not the physical health risk that is the central ergonomic concern.

questions.title: Innovation vs Invention
questions.prompt: A student argues that Thomas Edison's commercialisation of the light bulb was more important than the original invention of incandescent light. Which concept from innovation economics BEST supports this argument?

options.A: Intellectual property law, which protects the first inventor above all others
options.B: Diffusion of innovation, which recognises that widespread adoption creates greater societal value than the original idea alone
options.C: Lifecycle assessment, which shows that older technologies always have lower environmental impact
options.D: Systems engineering, which focuses on how individual components are assembled into a working product

questions.explanation: Diffusion of innovation theory, developed by Everett Rogers, argues that an invention only creates value when it spreads broadly through society — Edison's system of power distribution made electric light practically useful for millions. Intellectual property (option A) actually protects inventors, which would support the original inventor's claim, not the commercialiser's.

questions.title: UX Surveys vs Interviews
questions.prompt: A UX researcher wants to gather opinions from 500 users about a new app in a short time. Compare surveys and in-depth interviews: which method is MORE appropriate here, and why?

options.A: In-depth interviews, because they allow the researcher to ask follow-up questions to all 500 users efficiently
options.B: Surveys, because they can be distributed quickly and collect structured data from a large number of users at once
options.C: Surveys, because they always produce richer qualitative insights than interviews
options.D: In-depth interviews, because surveys cannot include rating scales or multiple-choice questions

questions.explanation: Surveys are scalable — a single digital survey can reach hundreds of respondents simultaneously, producing quantitative data suitable for large-sample analysis. Option A is incorrect because conducting in-depth interviews with 500 people would take an impractically long time and is not the purpose of that method.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Stages
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following student statement: 'A lifecycle assessment only measures the pollution created when a product is being manufactured in a factory.'

options.A: The statement is correct; LCA focuses exclusively on manufacturing emissions.
options.B: The error is that LCA also includes raw material extraction but not end-of-life disposal.
options.C: The error is that LCA covers all stages — raw material extraction, manufacturing, distribution, use, and end-of-life — not just manufacturing.
options.D: The error is that LCA measures financial cost rather than environmental pollution.

questions.explanation: A lifecycle assessment follows a 'cradle-to-grave' approach, evaluating environmental impacts across every stage from resource extraction through to disposal or recycling. Option B is a partial correction that still omits distribution and use-phase impacts, making it an incomplete answer.

questions.title: Systems Engineering Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a central heating system, a thermostat measures room temperature and switches the boiler on or off. What type of systems control mechanism does this BEST represent?

options.A: Open-loop control, where the output is monitored and used to adjust the input
options.B: Closed-loop control, where output information is fed back to regulate the system
options.C: Open-loop control, where the system runs at a fixed rate regardless of conditions
options.D: Manual control, where a human must physically adjust the boiler every time

questions.explanation: A closed-loop (feedback) control system uses information about the output — room temperature — to adjust the input (boiler on/off), maintaining a set point automatically. Option A uses the term 'open-loop' incorrectly; open-loop systems do not use output data to modify the input.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Types
questions.prompt: A fashion designer creates a distinctive logo for her clothing brand. Which form of intellectual property protection is MOST appropriate for protecting that logo?

options.A: Patent, which protects new inventions and technical processes
options.B: Trademark, which protects brand identifiers such as logos and names
options.C: Copyright, which automatically protects original creative written or artistic works
options.D: Trade secret, which keeps manufacturing processes confidential within a company

questions.explanation: A trademark specifically protects brand identifiers — including logos, symbols, and names — used in commerce to distinguish one business's goods from another's. Copyright (option C) could technically apply to an artistic logo, but trademark is the standard and more robust protection for commercial brand identity.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A student designs a facial recognition system trained only on images of adults. She then tests it on children and finds it performs poorly. Which ethical principle does this design process MOST clearly violate?

options.A: Privacy, because facial recognition stores biometric data without consent
options.B: Inclusivity, because the system was not designed or tested to work fairly for all intended user groups
options.C: Sustainability, because training AI models uses large amounts of energy
options.D: Intellectual property, because using photographs of people without permission infringes copyright

questions.explanation: Inclusivity in design requires that products work fairly and effectively for all members of the intended user group; training only on adult images creates algorithmic bias that disadvantages children. Privacy (option A) is a genuine concern with facial recognition but is not the primary violation demonstrated by the testing failure described.

questions.title: Design Brief Success Criteria
questions.prompt: A student writes a design brief for a new school locker. She states: 'The locker should look good and be useful.' Why is this criterion insufficient for evaluating design success?

options.A: It is insufficient because a design brief should not mention appearance at all.
options.B: It is insufficient because it uses subjective, unmeasurable language that cannot be tested objectively.
options.C: It is insufficient because lockers do not require a design brief.
options.D: It is insufficient because the brief should only focus on manufacturing cost, not user needs.

questions.explanation: Effective design criteria must be measurable and testable — for example, 'the locker must fit a standard 30 cm ruler and an A4 folder' rather than 'be useful.' Terms like 'look good' are subjective and cannot be objectively evaluated during testing. Option A is incorrect because aesthetic criteria are entirely valid in design briefs when expressed precisely.

questions.title: Iterative Design Process
questions.prompt: What does the term 'iterative' mean in the context of the design process, and why does it matter?

options.A: It means the design is completed in one attempt, saving time and resources.
options.B: It means the design is shared publicly so many people can suggest improvements simultaneously.
options.C: It means the design goes through repeated cycles of testing and refinement, each improving on the last.
options.D: It means the designer waits until all research is finished before beginning any creative work.

questions.explanation: Iteration in design means repeatedly cycling through stages — prototype, test, analyse, refine — so each version incorporates lessons from the previous one, steadily improving the solution. Option A describes a linear, non-iterative approach, which is less effective because it does not incorporate user feedback.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: A shoe company collects worn-out trainers from customers, grinds the rubber soles into pellets, and uses those pellets to make new sports surfaces. Which circular economy strategy does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Reduce — using less material during the original manufacturing process
options.B: Reuse — selling the trainers second-hand to another customer
options.C: Recycle — recovering material from used products and processing it into new raw material
options.D: Repair — fixing the soles so customers can continue wearing the same pair

questions.explanation: Recycling involves processing used materials back into raw or secondary materials for new production — grinding soles into rubber pellets is exactly this. Reuse (option B) would mean using the shoes again in the same form, not breaking them down and reprocessing them.

questions.title: User Testing Sample Selection
questions.prompt: A design team has created a walking aid for elderly users. They test it only with members of their own school's design class. Analyse why this sample is problematic.

options.A: The sample is too large, making the data too complex to analyse.
options.B: The sample does not represent the target users, so feedback will not reflect the needs of elderly people.
options.C: The sample is problematic because students are not allowed to conduct testing during school hours.
options.D: The sample is problematic because all testing must be done by qualified engineers, not students.

questions.explanation: Valid testing requires representative users — people whose characteristics match those of the intended audience. Teenagers testing a walking aid would not replicate the mobility limitations, grip strength, or visual needs of elderly users, making the data misleading. Option A is incorrect because the sample described is likely quite small, not large.

questions.title: Open Source vs Proprietary
questions.prompt: A software company releases its code so that anyone can read, modify, and share it freely. Compare this approach to keeping the code private. What is a key ADVANTAGE of releasing code openly?

options.A: The company earns higher licensing fees because more people use the software.
options.B: A global community of developers can identify bugs and contribute improvements, accelerating innovation.
options.C: The company can prevent competitors from ever copying any feature of the software.
options.D: The code automatically becomes patented, giving the company legal protection worldwide.

questions.explanation: Open-source development harnesses collective intelligence — thousands of independent developers can spot errors, suggest features, and adapt the software far faster than a closed team. Option A is incorrect because open-source software is typically free; the business model relies on support services, not licensing fees.

questions.title: Tensile vs Compressive Strength
questions.prompt: An engineer is selecting a material for a bridge cable that must withstand being pulled from both ends by heavy loads. Which material property is MOST critical?

options.A: High compressive strength, so the cable does not crack under squeezing forces
options.B: High tensile strength, so the cable resists breaking when stretched by pulling forces
options.C: High thermal conductivity, so heat does not build up inside the cable
options.D: High porosity, so the cable remains lightweight and allows water to pass through

questions.explanation: Tensile strength is resistance to being pulled apart — exactly the force acting on a suspension bridge cable under load. Compressive strength (option A) is critical for materials that are squeezed, such as columns or foundations, not cables, which experience tension.

questions.title: Ideation Techniques
questions.prompt: A design team is stuck after generating the same ten ideas repeatedly. Which ideation technique would BEST help them break out of conventional thinking?

options.A: Revisiting their design brief and reading it aloud to each other again
options.B: SCAMPER — a structured method that prompts new ideas by asking how a product could be Substituted, Combined, Adapted, Modified, Put to other uses, Eliminated, or Reversed
options.C: Conducting another round of user interviews to confirm that their existing ideas are correct
options.D: Building a high-fidelity prototype of their best current idea to see if it works

questions.explanation: SCAMPER is a creative ideation tool designed to stimulate novel thinking by systematically challenging every aspect of an existing concept, helping teams move beyond familiar ideas. Revisiting the brief (option A) helps clarify constraints but does not actively generate new concepts.

questions.title: Design for Disassembly
questions.prompt: A furniture manufacturer designs its tables so that each part can be unscrewed and separated without damage. Why does this design choice support sustainability goals?

options.A: It makes the table cheaper to produce in the factory.
options.B: It ensures that materials can be easily separated for recycling or component reuse at end of life.
options.C: It prevents customers from modifying the product in ways that might void the warranty.
options.D: It makes the table stronger, because screws provide more structural support than glue.

questions.explanation: Design for disassembly is a sustainability strategy that makes it straightforward to separate materials (e.g., metal, wood, plastic) at end of life so each can be recycled or reused rather than sent to landfill as a mixed-material product. Option A may be true in some cases but is not the sustainability rationale being described.

questions.title: Data Privacy in UX Design
questions.prompt: A student designs a fitness-tracking app that collects users' heart rate, sleep hours, and location. Her teacher asks her to justify what data is truly necessary. Which ethical principle is the teacher applying?

options.A: Planned obsolescence — building products that stop working after a set period
options.B: Data minimisation — collecting only the personal data that is strictly needed for the product to function
options.C: Open licensing — making all user data publicly available to improve community research
options.D: Interoperability — ensuring the app works across all operating systems equally

questions.explanation: Data minimisation is an ethical and legal principle (embedded in regulations like the GDPR) requiring that only the minimum necessary personal data be collected. Collecting location data for a heart rate app, for example, may be unnecessary and increases privacy risk. Planned obsolescence (option A) is unrelated to data collection.

questions.title: Aesthetic vs Functional Design
questions.prompt: A classmate argues: 'A product only needs to work correctly — how it looks is irrelevant.' Evaluate this claim using design principles.

options.A: The claim is correct; function is the only criterion a designer should consider.
options.B: The claim is correct; aesthetics can be added by a graphic designer after the product is complete.
options.C: The claim is an oversimplification, because aesthetics influence user trust, emotional response, and willingness to use a product.
options.D: The claim is correct for industrial products, but aesthetics matter only for consumer fashion items.

questions.explanation: Research in design psychology, including Don Norman's work on emotional design, shows that a product's appearance significantly affects users' perception of quality, trust, and enjoyment — all of which influence adoption and satisfaction. Option A ignores the established field of emotional design and the commercial reality that aesthetics drive purchasing decisions.

questions.title: Planned Obsolescence Ethics
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer releases a software update that slows down older phone models, encouraging users to buy newer ones. Which term BEST describes this practice, and why is it ethically controversial?

options.A: Planned obsolescence — intentionally limiting a product's useful life to drive sales, which raises concerns about consumer deception and increased electronic waste
options.B: Lifecycle assessment — measuring how long a product lasts in order to plan recycling programmes
options.C: Innovation diffusion — accelerating the adoption of new technology by making older products incompatible
options.D: Open-source development — sharing software updates freely to benefit as many users as possible

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence describes deliberately shortening a product's effective lifespan to stimulate replacement purchases; it is ethically controversial because it misleads consumers and contributes to e-waste. Innovation diffusion (option C) describes how new technologies spread naturally through society, not how manufacturers artificially degrade existing products.

questions.title: Usability Testing Methods
questions.prompt: A design team asks users to complete a task on their new website while speaking their thoughts aloud. What is the name of this UX research technique, and what is its main benefit?

options.A: A/B testing — comparing two versions of a page to see which performs better statistically
options.B: A think-aloud protocol — revealing users' real-time reasoning and confusion as they interact with the product
options.C: A focus group — gathering opinions from multiple users simultaneously in a discussion format
options.D: An eye-tracking study — recording exactly where on the screen users look using specialised cameras

questions.explanation: The think-aloud protocol captures users' moment-by-moment thought processes, making hidden decision-making and points of confusion visible to researchers — information that surveys and analytics alone cannot provide. A/B testing (option A) compares design variants quantitatively but does not explain why users behave as they do.

questions.title: Trade-offs in Sustainable Materials
questions.prompt: A company wants to replace the polystyrene packaging for its electronic products with a mushroom-based biodegradable alternative. What is the most significant TRADE-OFF the company must consider?

options.A: The mushroom material will conduct electricity and could damage the products inside.
options.B: The mushroom material may have higher production costs or lower protective performance than polystyrene, requiring evaluation of both environmental and functional criteria.
options.C: The mushroom material will require a new patent, which takes ten years to be approved.
options.D: The mushroom material is heavier than polystyrene and will therefore double shipping emissions, making it less sustainable overall.

questions.explanation: Sustainable material substitutions often involve trade-offs between environmental benefit and practical factors such as cost, strength, or manufacturing scalability — designers must weigh all these dimensions, not just environmental credentials. Option A is incorrect because mushroom composite packaging is not electrically conductive.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Assumption in Design
questions.prompt: A student designing a school planner skips the empathise stage and goes straight to sketching ideas, claiming he already knows what students need. Evaluate this decision and identify the most likely consequence.

options.A: The planner will be well-designed because the student shares the same context as the users.
options.B: The planner may not meet real user needs because assumptions replace evidence-based insights.
options.C: Skipping empathy saves time without affecting quality, since ideation is the most important stage.
options.D: The planner will fail only if the student does not also skip the define stage.

questions.explanation: The empathise stage exists specifically to uncover real, often unexpected user needs through observation and interviews; assumptions frequently miss these insights. Option A is a common misconception — sharing a context does not eliminate bias or guarantee representative understanding of diverse users.

questions.title: Define Stage Problem Statements
questions.prompt: Two students are writing a problem statement for the define stage. Student A writes: 'We need to build a better lunchbox.' Student B writes: 'Active 12-year-olds need a lunchbox that keeps food at the correct temperature for six hours without leaking.' Which statement better satisfies the define stage, and why?

options.A: Student A, because a shorter statement leaves more creative freedom during ideation.
options.B: Student B, because specifying the user, need, and measurable criteria gives clear design direction.
options.C: Student A, because problem statements should not include technical requirements.
options.D: Both are equally valid because any clear sentence can serve as a problem statement.

questions.explanation: An effective problem statement in the define stage names the user, the need, and success criteria so designers can evaluate solutions objectively — Student B's statement does all three. Student A's statement is too vague to guide ideation or evaluation, which is a frequent student error.

questions.title: Material Properties and Conductivity
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable coffee cup that must keep drinks hot for at least two hours and be safe to hold. She is choosing between stainless steel with a silicone sleeve and thick ceramic with no sleeve. Analyse which choice better meets both criteria and why.

options.A: Thick ceramic, because ceramic is a better thermal insulator than stainless steel.
options.B: Stainless steel with a silicone sleeve, because the steel retains heat while the silicone insulates the hand.
options.C: Thick ceramic, because its higher density means it conducts heat away from the liquid faster.
options.D: Stainless steel with a silicone sleeve, because stainless steel is transparent to infrared radiation.

questions.explanation: Stainless steel combined with a silicone sleeve leverages each material's properties: the steel's low porosity and high durability retain heat in the liquid, while silicone's very low thermal conductivity (~0.2 W/m·K) prevents burns. Option A is plausible but ceramic alone transfers heat to the outer surface quickly, making the cup uncomfortable to hold.

questions.title: Prototyping Fidelity Choices
questions.prompt: A team is designing a new app interface. They must decide whether to build a low-fidelity paper prototype or a high-fidelity digital prototype for their first round of user testing. Which choice is most justified at this early stage, and why?

options.A: High-fidelity, because users cannot give useful feedback on a paper prototype.
options.B: High-fidelity, because the app must look finished to attract investment.
options.C: Low-fidelity, because it is faster and cheaper to test and change core layout ideas before coding.
options.D: Low-fidelity, because digital prototypes always introduce bias in user responses.

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes allow teams to test fundamental navigation and layout assumptions rapidly and at minimal cost before investing development time — this aligns with iterative design principles. Option A is a misconception; research shows users can provide highly actionable feedback on paper prototypes precisely because they focus on structure rather than aesthetics.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Inclusive Design
questions.prompt: A designer is creating a public information kiosk for a city centre. She must decide the height of the touchscreen. Which approach best reflects ergonomic and inclusive design principles?

options.A: Set the screen at the average adult eye level so the majority of users are comfortable.
options.B: Set the screen at the height preferred by the design team after testing among themselves.
options.C: Set the screen at a height that accommodates both wheelchair users and standing adults, using anthropometric data from diverse populations.
options.D: Set the screen as high as possible to prevent vandalism, since security outweighs comfort.

questions.explanation: Inclusive ergonomic design uses anthropometric data from diverse user groups — including people with disabilities — to ensure access for all, not just the statistical average. Option A is the most attractive distractor but designing for the average excludes users at both extremes of the population, a known failure mode called 'average user fallacy'.

questions.title: Sustainability and Material Selection
questions.prompt: A shoe company wants to reduce its environmental impact. It is considering three sole materials: (1) virgin synthetic rubber, (2) recycled rubber from old tyres, and (3) natural latex from sustainably managed plantations. Evaluate which option is MOST sustainable overall, considering both production and end-of-life factors.

options.A: Virgin synthetic rubber, because it has consistent quality and fewer defects.
options.B: Recycled rubber from old tyres, because it diverts waste and uses less new raw material.
options.C: Natural latex, because it is biodegradable and comes from a renewable biological source that can be managed sustainably.
options.D: All three are equally sustainable because soles eventually wear out regardless of material.

questions.explanation: Sustainably sourced natural latex scores well across lifecycle stages: it is renewable, can be biodegradable, and its production supports forest ecosystems when certified. Option B is a strong distractor because recycled rubber does reduce waste, but it still degrades into microplastics and is not biodegradable, meaning end-of-life impact remains significant.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart home heating system, a thermostat measures room temperature and turns the heater on or off to maintain a target temperature. What type of system mechanism does this represent, and why is it important in systems engineering?

options.A: An open-loop system, because the heater operates on a fixed schedule regardless of temperature.
options.B: A negative feedback loop, because the system uses output information to counteract deviation from the target state.
options.C: A positive feedback loop, because the heater reinforces heating until it is manually stopped.
options.D: A redundant system, because two sensors are always needed for the system to function safely.

questions.explanation: A negative feedback loop uses the output (current temperature) as input to reduce the difference between actual and desired states, which is exactly how thermostats maintain stability. Option C is a common misconception — positive feedback loops amplify change rather than correct it, which would cause uncontrolled heating.

questions.title: UX Research: Comparing Methods
questions.prompt: A design team wants to understand why users abandon their checkout page. They are deciding between sending a survey to 500 users or conducting 8 in-depth interviews. Compare these methods and identify which is more appropriate for this specific goal.

options.A: The survey, because a larger sample size always produces more reliable insights about user behaviour.
options.B: The interviews, because open-ended conversations reveal the reasoning and emotions behind user behaviour that surveys cannot capture.
options.C: The survey, because interviews are too time-consuming to be used in professional UX research.
options.D: Both methods are equally appropriate because the goal is simply to collect any user data.

questions.explanation: Understanding why users abandon a process requires qualitative depth — interviews allow follow-up questions that uncover emotional and cognitive barriers, whereas surveys only reveal what happens, not why. Option A is a seductive distractor because larger samples do improve quantitative reliability, but they cannot explain causal reasoning behind behaviour.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: First-Mover Advantage
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'The first company to release a new product always has a permanent advantage over competitors.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of innovation economics.

options.A: The claim is correct because first movers build brand loyalty that cannot be overcome.
options.B: The claim is partially correct; first movers gain early market share but can be overtaken by fast followers who improve on the original design.
options.C: The claim is incorrect because being first always causes financial losses before the market is ready.
options.D: The claim is correct because intellectual property law permanently protects the first product released.

questions.explanation: First-mover advantage is real but temporary — companies like Google (following earlier search engines) and Facebook (following MySpace) demonstrate that fast followers with superior execution can displace pioneers. Option A overstates brand loyalty as a permanent moat, which is contradicted by many market examples.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: An AI system used to screen job applications was trained mostly on data from male applicants who were hired in the past. A student claims this system is fair because it uses objective data. Identify the ethical flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: The system is unfair only if the company deliberately programmed it to discriminate.
options.B: Historical data can encode existing biases, so a system trained on it will replicate and scale those biases even without deliberate intent.
options.C: The system is fair because algorithms cannot be biased — only humans can be biased.
options.D: The system would only be unfair if fewer than 50% of the training data came from male applicants.

questions.explanation: Algorithmic bias occurs when training data reflects historical inequalities — Amazon's real recruiting AI, scrapped in 2018, systematically downgraded female applicants because it learned from historically male-dominated hiring records. Option A is the most common misconception: intent is not required for discriminatory outcomes to occur.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secrets
questions.prompt: A soft drinks company keeps its flavour formula secret internally rather than applying for a patent. What is the key trade-off the company is making with this decision?

options.A: The company avoids paying taxes on the formula but risks it being copied legally.
options.B: The company gains potentially unlimited protection if the secret is kept, but loses all protection if the secret leaks, unlike a patent which gives legal recourse.
options.C: The company gains 70 years of legal protection automatically, the same as a copyright.
options.D: The company avoids the need to innovate further because trade secrets never expire by law.

questions.explanation: Trade secrets like Coca-Cola's formula offer indefinite protection as long as secrecy is maintained, but provide no legal remedy if independently discovered or leaked — a fundamental difference from patents, which grant 20-year exclusivity in exchange for public disclosure. Option C confuses trade secret law with copyright duration, a common student error.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment: Hidden Impacts
questions.prompt: A manufacturer replaces plastic bags with cotton tote bags, claiming this is always more environmentally friendly. Examine whether this claim is fully accurate from a lifecycle assessment perspective.

options.A: The claim is fully accurate because cotton is a natural material and plastics are synthetic.
options.B: The claim is inaccurate because cotton bags are heavier and therefore more expensive to ship.
options.C: The claim oversimplifies the issue; a cotton tote must be reused many times to offset the water and energy used in cotton farming and production.
options.D: The claim is accurate only if the cotton bag is made in the same country as the plastic bag.

questions.explanation: A Danish Environmental Protection Agency study found a conventional cotton tote must be used at least 7,100 times to match a plastic bag's overall environmental footprint, mainly because cotton farming is water- and pesticide-intensive. Option A is a misconception — 'natural' does not automatically mean lower environmental impact across the full lifecycle.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Testing Validity
questions.prompt: A team tests their ergonomic chair prototype by asking only design students in their class to evaluate comfort. Identify the most significant limitation of this testing approach.

options.A: The sample is too knowledgeable about design, so they will give overly positive feedback.
options.B: The sample is not representative of the intended users, so the results may not transfer to the real target group.
options.C: The test is invalid because comfort can only be measured using digital sensors, not human feedback.
options.D: The test is invalid because prototypes should never be tested by the same age group as the designers.

questions.explanation: Valid user testing requires participants who match the target user profile — testing a chair meant for office workers with teenage design students introduces sampling bias that may produce misleading comfort data. Option A has some plausibility but design expertise would more likely produce harsher aesthetic critique, not uniformly positive comfort feedback.

questions.title: Biomimicry in Innovation
questions.prompt: Engineers designing a high-speed train noticed it created a loud sonic boom when exiting tunnels. By studying the beak shape of a kingfisher bird, they redesigned the train's nose. What design approach does this represent, and why is it effective?

options.A: Reverse engineering, because the engineers took apart an existing product to understand it.
options.B: Biomimicry, because nature has already optimised solutions to physical challenges like air-pressure transition over millions of years.
options.C: Incremental innovation, because the engineers only changed one small part of the train.
options.D: User-centred design, because birds are the primary users of air-pressure environments.

questions.explanation: Biomimicry is the practice of using nature's proven designs to solve human engineering problems — the Shinkansen 500 Series redesign reduced noise by 30% and improved energy efficiency by mimicking the kingfisher's beak, which minimises pressure wave disruption when diving. Option C is plausible but misidentifies the method; changing one component is incremental, but the source of inspiration defines this as biomimicry.

questions.title: Cradle-to-Cradle Design Principle
questions.prompt: Compare the 'cradle-to-grave' and 'cradle-to-cradle' product design philosophies. Which statement most accurately describes the key distinction between them?

options.A: Cradle-to-grave designs are always cheaper to produce; cradle-to-cradle designs are always more expensive.
options.B: Cradle-to-grave treats disposal as the end point, while cradle-to-cradle designs materials to cycle back into production or nature indefinitely.
options.C: Cradle-to-cradle simply means a product is recyclable; cradle-to-grave means it is not.
options.D: Cradle-to-grave applies only to food products; cradle-to-cradle applies only to electronics.

questions.explanation: The cradle-to-cradle framework, developed by architect William McDonough and chemist Michael Braungart, designs products so materials either re-enter biological cycles (biodegradable) or technical cycles (recovered and remanufactured) — waste becomes food for the next cycle. Option C is a misconception; recyclability alone does not constitute cradle-to-cradle design, which requires intentional material flow planning from the outset.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright vs. Patent
questions.prompt: A student writes and illustrates an original graphic novel and also invents a new method for binding the pages so they never fall out. Which statement correctly identifies the appropriate IP protection for each creation?

options.A: Both the graphic novel and the binding method are protected by copyright automatically upon creation.
options.B: The graphic novel is protected by copyright automatically; the binding method requires a patent application to gain protection.
options.C: The binding method is protected by copyright; the graphic novel requires a patent because it is a novel product.
options.D: Both require trademark registration to prevent unauthorised copying.

questions.explanation: Copyright protects original creative expression (art, writing, music) automatically from the moment of creation, while a patent must be applied for and granted to protect a novel functional invention or process. Option A is the most common student error — conflating copyright with patent protection because both prevent copying.

questions.title: Ideation: SCAMPER Technique
questions.prompt: A student uses the SCAMPER technique during ideation, applying the 'Adapt' step to a standard bicycle. Which of the following responses best demonstrates the 'Adapt' step?

options.A: Remove the handlebars entirely to reduce manufacturing cost.
options.B: Combine the bicycle with a solar panel to charge a phone while riding.
options.C: Borrow the shock-absorption system used in mountain bike suspension and apply it to a city commuter bike to reduce road vibration.
options.D: Make the bicycle much larger so it can carry more passengers.

questions.explanation: In SCAMPER, 'Adapt' means borrowing or modifying something from another context to solve a problem — applying mountain bike suspension technology to commuter bikes directly demonstrates this step. Option B represents 'Combine', another SCAMPER step, which is the most likely student confusion since combining and adapting both involve bringing elements together.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystem Interaction
questions.prompt: In a complex system, a change to one subsystem can have unintended effects on others. A school installs an automatic door to improve accessibility but notices the heating bill increases significantly. What systems engineering concept does this illustrate?

options.A: Redundancy, because two door systems are now operating simultaneously.
options.B: System interdependence, because changing the door subsystem created an unintended impact on the heating subsystem.
options.C: Positive feedback, because the door opening causes the heating to increase, which causes the door to open more.
options.D: A design defect, because any well-engineered system prevents all unintended consequences.

questions.explanation: System interdependence describes how subsystems within a larger system affect each other — the automatic door (accessibility subsystem) held open longer than a manual door, allowing heat to escape and burdening the heating subsystem. Option D is an attractive distractor but is factually wrong; even well-engineered systems can have emergent, unintended interactions.

questions.title: Material Properties: Strength vs. Flexibility
questions.prompt: An engineer is selecting a material for a sports mouthguard. She needs a material that absorbs impact without cracking and can be moulded to fit individual teeth. Identify the combination of properties that best fits these requirements.

options.A: High hardness and high brittleness, so the mouthguard maintains its shape under pressure.
options.B: High elasticity and high toughness, so it deforms under impact and returns to shape without fracturing.
options.C: High density and low malleability, so it is heavy enough to resist movement.
options.D: High thermal conductivity and low viscosity, so it spreads heat evenly and flows into gaps.

questions.explanation: Toughness (energy absorbed before fracture) and elasticity (ability to recover shape) are the key properties for impact protection — thermoplastic elastomers used in mouthguards possess both. Option A is tempting because hardness sounds protective, but brittleness causes catastrophic cracking under sudden impact, which is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Data Privacy in Design
questions.prompt: A team designs a children's fitness tracker that collects daily step count, heart rate, and sleep data. A classmate suggests sharing this data with partner companies to generate app revenue. Evaluate the primary ethical concern with this proposal.

options.A: It is unethical only if the partner companies are located in another country.
options.B: Sharing sensitive health data of minors without informed parental consent violates privacy rights and may breach regulations like COPPA and GDPR.
options.C: It is acceptable because the data is anonymised and therefore no longer personal.
options.D: It is unethical only if the revenue model was not disclosed in the original marketing materials.

questions.explanation: Children's health data is classified as sensitive personal data under frameworks like GDPR and COPPA; sharing it commercially without explicit, informed consent from parents is both an ethical violation and illegal in many jurisdictions. Option C is a common misconception — health and biometric data can often be re-identified even when supposedly anonymised, and regulations still apply.

questions.title: User-Centred Design: Personas
questions.prompt: A design team creates a detailed user persona named 'Marco, age 13, uses a wheelchair, attends a state school, and struggles with small touchscreen buttons.' What is the primary purpose of creating this persona during the design process?

options.A: To replace the need for interviews by inventing a fictional user who summarises all possible needs.
options.B: To give the design team a concrete, empathy-building reference point representing a specific user segment's needs and constraints.
options.C: To satisfy a legal requirement that design teams must document imagined users before testing.
options.D: To ensure the final product is designed exclusively for users who match Marco's exact profile.

questions.explanation: Personas synthesise real research data into a vivid character that keeps design decisions anchored to specific user needs — they build empathy and guide trade-off decisions throughout the process. Option A is a frequent misconception; personas should be based on actual user research data, not invented assumptions, and they complement rather than replace interviews.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: Disruptive vs. Sustaining
questions.prompt: A student argues that all new technology is disruptive innovation. Examine this claim using your knowledge of innovation economics. Which response most accurately evaluates it?

options.A: The student is correct because any technology that is new automatically disrupts the market.
options.B: The student is incorrect; disruptive innovation specifically targets overlooked markets or lower-end users and eventually displaces established products, unlike sustaining innovations that improve existing products for existing customers.
options.C: The student is correct because all innovation eventually replaces old technology, making it disruptive by definition.
options.D: The student is incorrect because disruptive innovation only applies to digital technology, not physical products.

questions.explanation: Clayton Christensen defined disruptive innovation as a process where a simpler, more affordable product initially targets overlooked segments before improving and displacing incumbents — this is distinct from sustaining innovations that improve existing products for existing customers. Option C conflates long-term replacement (which all innovation may eventually cause) with the specific mechanism of disruption.

questions.title: Sustainability: Planned Obsolescence
questions.prompt: Some electronics manufacturers design products to become outdated or stop working within a few years, encouraging consumers to buy replacements. Discuss the main sustainability criticism of this practice.

options.A: It is unsustainable only if consumers choose not to recycle the old products.
options.B: It deliberately shortens product lifespans, increasing raw material extraction, energy use, and e-waste generation beyond what would occur if products were designed for longevity.
options.C: It is unsustainable because it reduces company profits, leaving less money for environmental research.
options.D: It is only a sustainability problem when applied to food products, not electronics.

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence artificially accelerates the product lifecycle, driving unnecessary resource extraction and contributing to the 50+ million tonnes of e-waste generated globally each year — a direct contradiction of circular economy principles. Option A is a common deflection; even with recycling infrastructure, planned obsolescence creates net excess material throughput that recycling cannot fully offset.

questions.title: Design Criteria: Constraints vs. Specifications
questions.prompt: A student confuses design constraints with design specifications when writing her design brief. Which statement correctly distinguishes between these two concepts?

options.A: Constraints are optional guidelines; specifications are mandatory rules that must be followed.
options.B: Constraints are the limits within which the design must operate (e.g., budget, materials, size); specifications describe the measurable performance the solution must achieve.
options.C: Specifications describe the appearance of the product; constraints describe how it must be manufactured.
options.D: Constraints and specifications mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably in a design brief.

questions.explanation: In design briefs, constraints are external boundaries that cannot be changed (e.g., must cost under £10, must use recyclable materials), while specifications are measurable success criteria the solution must meet (e.g., must hold 1 litre, must withstand a 1-metre drop). Option D is a very common student error — conflating these distinct concepts leads to briefs that cannot be used for objective evaluation.

questions.title: Accessibility and Universal Design
questions.prompt: The 'curb cut effect' describes how design features created for people with disabilities (like pavement ramps) end up benefiting the wider population (like parents with pushchairs). What does this effect suggest about the relationship between accessibility and universal design?

options.A: Accessibility features should only be added if they also benefit non-disabled users, to justify the cost.
options.B: Designing for the most constrained users often produces solutions that improve usability for all users, meaning accessibility and broad usability are complementary goals.
options.C: Universal design means creating one identical product for every person, eliminating the need for specialised accessibility features.
options.D: The curb cut effect shows that non-disabled users should be the primary focus of all design decisions.

questions.explanation: The curb cut effect demonstrates that solving for extreme use cases (severe mobility limitations) produces better general solutions — this is a core principle of universal design, which seeks to make products inherently usable by the widest possible range of people. Option C is a misconception; universal design does not mean identical products, but rather intentional design that does not require separate adaptation for different users.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: A design team is creating a new school locker system. They survey 200 students online to gather data. A mentor suggests they also spend a morning watching students actually use their lockers. Why would the observation method add value that the survey alone cannot provide?

options.A: Observations always produce more accurate numerical data than surveys do
options.B: Watching users reveals unspoken behaviours and pain points that users may not think to report
options.C: Survey data is legally unreliable and cannot be used in a design brief
options.D: Observations guarantee a larger sample size than online surveys

questions.explanation: Observation during the empathise stage captures tacit knowledge — behaviours users perform habitually and therefore do not consciously notice or mention in a survey, such as struggling with a stiff latch. Option A is wrong because observations typically generate qualitative, not more accurate numerical, data; surveys are better for large-scale quantitative trends.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A student writes the following problem statement: 'We need to design a better app.' A classmate argues this is not a useful define-stage output. Evaluate the classmate's claim and identify what is missing from the statement.

options.A: The classmate is wrong; a short problem statement is always preferable to avoid over-constraining the design
options.B: The classmate is correct; the statement lacks a specific user, a clear need, and measurable success criteria
options.C: The classmate is correct; the statement should name the specific technology to be used before proceeding
options.D: The classmate is wrong; the define stage only requires a list of materials, not a problem statement

questions.explanation: A strong define-stage problem statement must identify who the user is, what problem they face, and what success looks like — often called a 'point of view' statement in design thinking. Without these elements the team has no clear direction for ideation. Option C is wrong because the define stage should not prescribe solutions or technologies; that prematurely closes off creative exploration.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Choice
