questions.prompt: A team designing a new café seating arrangement has limited time and budget. They must choose between building a high-fidelity physical model with real materials and creating a low-fidelity paper floor-plan mock-up. At this early stage of prototyping, which choice is more appropriate, and why?

options.A: The high-fidelity model, because stakeholders will only trust feedback given on realistic prototypes
options.B: The low-fidelity mock-up, because it allows rapid iteration and testing of layout ideas at low cost
options.C: The high-fidelity model, because early prototypes should always match the final product exactly
options.D: The low-fidelity mock-up, because paper prototypes are the only format accepted in professional design practice

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes are deliberately rough and cheap, enabling teams to explore multiple layout concepts quickly and discard poor ideas before investing significant resources. This is a core principle of iterative design. Option A is a common misconception — early-stage feedback on general concepts and spatial flow is often more honest with simple models because users focus on the idea rather than surface-level finish.

questions.title: Material Properties and Function
questions.prompt: An engineer is selecting a material for a children's outdoor climbing frame. She needs the material to resist corrosion when wet, support heavy loads without bending permanently, and be safe if a child falls against it. Which combination of properties is MOST important to prioritise?

options.A: High thermal conductivity, high density, and low cost
options.B: Corrosion resistance, high tensile strength, and sufficient toughness
options.C: High transparency, low weight, and high electrical conductivity
options.D: High hardness, low ductility, and high thermal resistance

questions.explanation: Corrosion resistance prevents structural weakening in wet outdoor conditions; high tensile strength allows the frame to bear loads without permanent deformation; and toughness (the ability to absorb energy before fracturing) reduces injury risk during impact. Option D is tempting but wrong — high hardness combined with low ductility means the material is brittle, which is dangerous in a children's play context as it may shatter rather than deform.

questions.title: Ergonomics and User Fit
questions.prompt: A designer is developing a backpack for students aged 10–14. She collects anthropometric data showing that students in this group vary significantly in shoulder width and torso height. Which design decision BEST applies this data ergonomically?

options.A: Designing the bag to fit the average shoulder width and torso height only
options.B: Including adjustable straps that can be customised to different body sizes
options.C: Making the bag as light as possible regardless of strap position
options.D: Producing three fixed sizes based on age groups rather than body measurements

questions.explanation: Adjustable straps directly respond to anthropometric variability by allowing each user to position the load optimally for their specific torso length and shoulder width, reducing strain on the spine. Designing for the average (Option A) is a classic ergonomic mistake — it can fit no one perfectly and excludes users at both ends of the distribution, a concept highlighted in MYP Design ergonomics units.

questions.title: Sustainability Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A clothing company is deciding between two manufacturing changes: (1) switching to organic cotton, which uses no pesticides but requires more water; (2) switching to recycled polyester, which uses less water but is derived from plastic and sheds microplastics when washed. Evaluate which choice has the clearer sustainability advantage.

options.A: Organic cotton is clearly superior because it is a natural fibre with no trade-offs
options.B: Recycled polyester is clearly superior because recycling is always better than growing new materials
options.C: Neither choice is clearly superior; each has distinct environmental costs that depend on local water scarcity and ocean pollution impact
options.D: The decision is irrelevant because textiles have a negligible environmental footprint compared to other industries

questions.explanation: Lifecycle assessment thinking shows that both options involve genuine environmental costs: organic cotton's high water demand is critical in water-scarce regions, while recycled polyester contributes to microplastic pollution in waterways. A context-dependent trade-off analysis is required rather than a blanket conclusion. Option B reflects the misconception that 'recycled' automatically means more sustainable across all impact categories.

questions.title: UX Research Method Selection
questions.prompt: A team is designing a new library app for teenagers. They want to understand not just what features users want, but also how users currently feel about finding books. Which UX research method would BEST capture both behavioural patterns and emotional responses?

options.A: An anonymous multiple-choice survey sent to 500 students
options.B: A contextual interview combined with observation of users searching for books
options.C: An A/B test comparing two versions of the app's colour scheme
options.D: A focus group where a designer presents their preferred solution for feedback

questions.explanation: Contextual interviews combine open questioning — which surfaces emotional responses and motivations — with real-time observation of actual behaviour, giving both qualitative depth and behavioural data. A/B testing (Option C) is a late-stage quantitative method that tests specific design variables, not early-stage emotional or behavioural understanding, making it inappropriate at this research phase.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Types
questions.prompt: A student invents a new board game with unique rules, original artwork, and a distinctive logo. She wants legal protection for three different aspects of her creation. Which combination of intellectual property protections would cover all three elements?

options.A: Three separate patents — one for each element of the game
options.B: A patent for the rules, copyright for the artwork, and a trademark for the logo
options.C: A single copyright registration covering all creative elements simultaneously
options.D: A trade secret agreement prevents anyone from ever copying any part of the game

questions.explanation: Patents protect novel functional inventions (such as a unique game mechanism or ruleset), copyright automatically protects original creative works like artwork, and trademarks protect brand identifiers like logos. These are three legally distinct forms of intellectual property, each covering different aspects. Option C is wrong because copyright does not protect functional inventions like game rules — that is the domain of patents.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: A smart thermostat measures room temperature and adjusts heating to maintain a set temperature. When the room gets too warm, it turns the heater off; when it cools below the target, it turns the heater on. What type of system mechanism is this, and why is it essential for stable operation?

options.A: A positive feedback loop, because the system reinforces each temperature change to reach extremes faster
options.B: A negative feedback loop, because the system counteracts deviations to maintain a stable target state
options.C: An open-loop system, because the thermostat does not use any external information to make decisions
options.D: A redundant system, because having two states (on/off) is unnecessary for simple heating

questions.explanation: A negative feedback loop reduces the difference between actual and desired output — here, the thermostat detects deviation from the set temperature and acts to correct it, maintaining stability. This is the fundamental control mechanism in most automated systems. Option A is a frequent misconception; positive feedback amplifies change (e.g., a microphone squealing near a speaker) rather than stabilising a system.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: First-Mover
questions.prompt: A student claims that being the first company to release a new product always gives the greatest long-term business advantage. Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of innovation economics.

options.A: The claim is fully correct; first movers always capture the entire market before competitors can enter
options.B: The claim is partially correct; first movers gain early brand recognition but may face high development costs and early adopter risks that later entrants avoid
options.C: The claim is fully incorrect; being first is always a disadvantage because the market is untested
options.D: The claim is irrelevant; product release timing has no measurable effect on business success

questions.explanation: First-mover advantage is real — early entrants can establish brand loyalty and set industry standards — but it is not absolute. First movers bear higher R&D costs, educate the market at their own expense, and risk investing in technologies that may not succeed, allowing fast followers to learn from their mistakes and enter with improved products. The history of search engines (Google overtaking early movers) illustrates this. Option A ignores the well-documented fast-follower phenomenon in innovation economics.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A hiring company uses an AI algorithm trained on ten years of its own employees' data to shortlist job applicants. The algorithm consistently ranks male applicants higher than equally qualified female applicants. Identify the MOST likely root cause of this bias.

options.A: The algorithm was programmed by a female developer who introduced deliberate errors
options.B: The training data reflects historical gender imbalances in hiring, so the algorithm learned and replicated those patterns
options.C: AI algorithms are mathematically perfect and cannot produce biased outcomes
options.D: The bias is caused by the applicants providing inaccurate information in their applications

questions.explanation: Machine learning algorithms identify patterns in training data, so if historical hiring data under-represented women due to past discrimination, the algorithm treats maleness as a predictor of success and replicates the bias systematically. Amazon publicly retired a similar recruitment tool in 2018 for exactly this reason. Option C is a dangerous misconception — algorithms are not inherently neutral; they reflect the biases embedded in their training data and design choices.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Stages
questions.prompt: A designer performs a lifecycle assessment of a disposable plastic pen. She focuses only on the manufacturing and end-of-life disposal stages. A peer says her LCA is incomplete. Justify whether the peer is correct.

options.A: The peer is wrong; manufacturing and disposal are the two most important stages and together form a complete LCA
options.B: The peer is correct; a full LCA must also include raw material extraction, distribution, and the use phase
options.C: The peer is correct; a full LCA only requires adding the distribution stage to be complete
options.D: The peer is wrong; LCA applies only to electronic products and is not relevant to a plastic pen

questions.explanation: A complete LCA — as defined in ISO 14040 — covers all stages: raw material extraction (cradle), processing, manufacturing, distribution, the use phase, and end of life (grave). Omitting raw material extraction ignores the environmental cost of petroleum-based plastic sourcing, and omitting the use phase ignores ink consumption and refill possibilities. Option C is wrong because adding only distribution still leaves out raw material extraction and the use phase.

questions.title: Design Specifications vs. Brief
questions.prompt: Compare a design brief and a design specification. A student argues they are interchangeable documents because both relate to the same project. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; the brief and specification contain identical information presented in different formats
options.B: The student is incorrect; the brief describes the problem and context broadly, while the specification lists precise, measurable criteria the design must meet
options.C: The student is incorrect; the brief is written after testing, while the specification is written before any research
options.D: The student is correct; in professional design practice only one document is ever produced per project

questions.explanation: A design brief outlines the client's problem, goals, target user, and constraints in qualitative terms, while a design specification translates those goals into precise, testable criteria (e.g., 'the product must weigh less than 300g'). They serve different functions at different stages of the design process. Option A is wrong because the two documents differ in purpose, detail level, and the stage at which they are created.

questions.title: Planned Obsolescence Ethics
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer designs its batteries so they cannot be replaced by users and become noticeably slower after two years, encouraging customers to buy a new model. Examine the ethical and sustainability concerns raised by this practice.

options.A: There are no concerns; companies must increase sales to remain profitable and this is a standard business practice
options.B: The main concern is purely aesthetic; customers simply prefer the look of new phones
options.C: It raises concerns about consumer deception, increased electronic waste, and resource consumption from manufacturing replacement devices
options.D: The only concern is legal; planned obsolescence is illegal in all countries and will result in prosecution

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence deliberately shortens product lifespan, which generates e-waste containing hazardous materials (lead, mercury), consumes new raw materials unnecessarily, and may deceive consumers who are not aware the slowdown is engineered. Apple was fined by French and Italian regulators over this practice in 2018. Option D is wrong because planned obsolescence is not universally illegal — regulations vary significantly by country, and legality is only one dimension of the broader ethical concern.

questions.title: Inclusive Design Principles
questions.prompt: A student designs a public water fountain at two heights: one for adults and one for wheelchair users. A classmate says this is inclusive design. Another classmate says it is only accessible design, not truly inclusive. Who is more accurate, and why?

options.A: The first classmate is correct; any design that accommodates more than one user type is fully inclusive
options.B: The second classmate is more accurate; true inclusive design creates one solution usable by all people without segregation, whereas two separate heights still divide users into categories
options.C: Both classmates are wrong; water fountains cannot be redesigned using design thinking principles
options.D: The second classmate is correct; inclusive design requires that wheelchair users and adults use exactly the same fountain at the same height

questions.explanation: Inclusive (or universal) design aims to create a single product or environment that works for the widest possible range of users without requiring separate or specialised versions. Two separate heights is an accessible design solution but implicitly categorises users, which is distinct from inclusive design's goal of seamless integration. Option D is wrong because it conflates the principle of a single solution with a physically impossible requirement — a single height cannot optimally serve both standing adults and seated wheelchair users simultaneously.

questions.title: Ideation: Divergent vs. Convergent
questions.prompt: During a design project, a team generates 40 different ideas in 20 minutes using mind-mapping. Their teacher then asks them to identify the three most promising ideas using a decision matrix. Which design thinking phases do these two activities respectively represent?

options.A: Both activities are part of the empathise phase, gathering different types of user data
options.B: Mind-mapping is divergent thinking in the ideate phase; the decision matrix is convergent thinking used to select ideas
options.C: Mind-mapping is the define phase; the decision matrix is the prototype phase
options.D: Both activities are convergent thinking, because all creative tasks aim to produce a single correct answer

questions.explanation: Divergent thinking generates many possibilities without judgement — this is the ideation phase's core purpose. Convergent thinking then evaluates and narrows options using structured tools like a decision matrix, which scores ideas against criteria. These are two complementary cognitive modes in design thinking, not separate phases. Option D is a misconception — the ideation phase is specifically defined by divergent (non-convergent) thinking; convergence comes afterwards.

questions.title: Open Source vs. Proprietary
questions.prompt: A software company releases its new code as open source, meaning anyone can view, use, and modify it. A rival company keeps its code proprietary. Analyse ONE likely advantage the open-source company gains that the proprietary company does not.

options.A: The open-source company earns more direct revenue from software licence fees
options.B: The open-source company benefits from a global community of developers who can identify bugs and contribute improvements at no direct cost
options.C: The open-source company retains exclusive control over all modifications made to its code
options.D: The open-source company faces less competition because rivals cannot study the code

questions.explanation: Open-source projects like Linux demonstrate that distributed, voluntary contributor communities can accelerate development and quality assurance beyond what a single company could afford internally, as thousands of developers worldwide review and improve the code. Option A is the opposite of reality — open-source software typically cannot charge per-licence fees for the code itself, and companies usually monetise through services, support, or complementary products instead.

questions.title: Biomimicry in Design
questions.prompt: Engineers designing a new high-speed train studied the beak of the kingfisher bird, which dives from air into water with minimal splash, to solve a noise problem when the train exited tunnels at speed. What design approach does this example best illustrate?

options.A: Planned obsolescence, because natural forms change over time just as products do
options.B: Biomimicry, because engineers derived a functional design solution by emulating a biological structure evolved for a similar physical challenge
options.C: Systems engineering, because the bird and train are both complex systems with inputs and outputs
options.D: User-centred design, because engineers interviewed kingfisher birds to understand their needs

questions.explanation: Biomimicry is the practice of learning from and emulating nature's strategies to solve human design challenges. The Shinkansen bullet train's nose was redesigned based on the kingfisher's beak, reducing the sonic boom when exiting tunnels by 30% and improving energy efficiency. Option C is a plausible distractor but wrong — while both involve systems, the defining feature of this example is the deliberate biological inspiration, which is the hallmark of biomimicry specifically.

questions.title: Cradle-to-Cradle Design
questions.prompt: A furniture company designs its chairs so that every component can be fully composted or safely recycled into new chairs at the end of their life, with zero waste sent to landfill. Which design philosophy does this BEST represent, and how does it differ from a traditional linear economy approach?

options.A: Planned obsolescence; the chairs are designed to be replaced frequently, stimulating demand
options.B: Cradle-to-cradle design; materials cycle continuously as nutrients, unlike the linear take-make-dispose model
options.C: Lean manufacturing; the company eliminates waste during production but not after the product's life
options.D: Cradle-to-gate assessment; the company measures impact only up to the factory gate

questions.explanation: Cradle-to-cradle (C2C) design, developed by McDonough and Braungart, treats all materials as biological or technical 'nutrients' that flow in closed loops with no waste — a fundamental departure from the linear 'take, make, dispose' economy. Option C is wrong because lean manufacturing focuses on reducing waste during production processes, not on designing for end-of-life material recovery or closed material loops.

questions.title: Human-Centred vs. Technology-Centred
questions.prompt: A company develops a highly advanced voice-assistant device but does not test it with elderly users. When released, elderly customers report they cannot hear its responses clearly and find the voice commands confusing. What error in the design process led to this outcome?

options.A: The company used too many prototypes, confusing the development team
options.B: The company failed to include representative users — particularly elderly users — in testing, prioritising technical capability over user needs
options.C: The company should have chosen a simpler technology that did not involve voice recognition
options.D: The company's lifecycle assessment was incomplete, causing the design flaws

questions.explanation: Human-centred design requires testing with representative users from the actual target population throughout development. Excluding elderly users meant the team had no data on auditory or cognitive accessibility needs, resulting in a product that fails this group. This illustrates the risk of technology-centred design, where engineering excellence is prioritised over user fit. Option D is a misconception — lifecycle assessment evaluates environmental impact, not usability or accessibility issues.

questions.title: Composite Materials
questions.prompt: A student claims that carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) is the best material for every structural application because it is both lighter and stronger than steel. Identify the flaw in this reasoning.

options.A: There is no flaw; CFRP is universally superior to steel in every measurable property
options.B: The claim ignores cost, repairability, and recyclability — CFRP is significantly more expensive, difficult to repair after impact damage, and harder to recycle than steel
options.C: The claim is flawed because CFRP is actually heavier than steel per unit volume
options.D: The claim is flawed only because CFRP is not available in sufficient quantities for large-scale use

questions.explanation: While CFRP does offer a superior strength-to-weight ratio, material selection always involves trade-offs across multiple criteria. CFRP costs roughly 10–20 times more than structural steel, delamination damage from impact is difficult to detect and repair, and recycling carbon fibre composites remains technically challenging and costly. Material selection must match context, not always optimise a single metric. Option C is factually wrong — CFRP's low density (approximately 1.6 g/cm³ vs. steel's 7.8 g/cm³) is one of its genuine advantages.

questions.title: Privacy by Design
questions.prompt: A developer builds a fitness app that collects users' heart rate data, location, and sleep patterns. A design ethics expert recommends applying 'privacy by design.' Which approach BEST reflects this principle?

options.A: Adding a privacy policy page that users must scroll through before signing up
options.B: Collecting all available data by default and giving users an option to delete it later on request
options.C: Building the system to collect only the minimum data necessary, storing it encrypted, and giving users clear control over their data from the start
options.D: Hiring a legal team to review data practices after the app has been released to the public

questions.explanation: Privacy by design, formalised by Ann Cavoukian and embedded in regulations like GDPR, means privacy protections are embedded into the architecture of a system from the outset, not added later. This includes data minimisation, encryption, and user control by default. Option B describes the opposite — 'privacy by exception' — where data collection is maximal by default and users must actively opt out, which contradicts the principle's core requirement.

questions.title: Disruptive vs. Sustaining Innovation
questions.prompt: A new company begins selling digital music downloads for $0.99 per song, attracting customers who previously could not afford or access full CD albums. Established record companies initially dismiss it as a niche market. Over five years, CD sales collapse. Which type of innovation does this scenario describe, and what is its key characteristic?

options.A: Sustaining innovation; it improved an existing product for existing customers who already bought CDs
options.B: Disruptive innovation; it initially targeted overlooked or new customers with a simpler, more accessible product before eventually displacing the dominant market
options.C: Incremental innovation; digital downloads are only a minor modification of the existing music delivery system
options.D: Process innovation; the main change was in the manufacturing process rather than the product itself

questions.explanation: Clayton Christensen's theory of disruptive innovation describes a product that starts by serving non-consumers or low-end customers with a simpler, cheaper alternative, then improves until it displaces incumbents — exactly what digital downloads did to the CD market. Option A is wrong because sustaining innovation improves products for existing customers of established companies (e.g., a higher-quality CD player), rather than creating a new access model that undermines the entire format.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Assumption in Design
questions.prompt: A student designing a backpack for elderly users skips the empathise stage and moves straight to ideation, arguing that 'everyone knows what old people need.' Evaluate this decision using design thinking principles.

options.A: It is acceptable because ideation produces more creative solutions when designers are not constrained by user data.
options.B: It is flawed because assumptions replace observed user needs, leading to a design that may not solve the real problem.
options.C: It is acceptable because elderly users form a well-documented demographic with known, stable needs.
options.D: It is flawed only if the student has never interacted with an elderly person before starting the project.

questions.explanation: The empathise stage exists specifically to replace assumptions with direct observation and interview data; skipping it means the design brief is built on unverified beliefs rather than real user pain points, a foundational error in design thinking. Option C is the top distractor because demographic data does exist for elderly users, but generalised statistics cannot replace contextual empathy research that reveals the specific, nuanced needs of a target group.

questions.title: Material Selection Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable water bottle intended for outdoor use. She narrows her choice to polypropylene and stainless steel. Compare these two materials in terms of durability, weight, and sustainability to justify the better choice for this context.

options.A: Polypropylene, because it is lighter, cheaper to produce, and fully biodegradable at end of life.
options.B: Stainless steel, because it is more durable, does not leach chemicals, and is infinitely recyclable without quality loss.
options.C: Polypropylene, because it has a higher tensile strength than stainless steel and therefore withstands outdoor impacts better.
options.D: Stainless steel, because it is lighter than polypropylene and therefore more suitable for carrying during outdoor activity.

questions.explanation: Stainless steel is highly durable, does not leach BPA or other chemicals into liquids, and can be recycled repeatedly without degradation in material quality, making it the strongest choice across all three criteria for a reusable outdoor bottle. Option A is the top distractor because polypropylene is indeed lighter and cheaper, but it is not biodegradable — it is a petroleum-based polymer that persists in the environment, which contradicts the sustainability criterion.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Types
questions.prompt: A graphic designer creates a distinctive logo for her company and also writes the software code that animates it on the company's website. Which combination of intellectual property protections best covers both the logo and the code?

options.A: A patent for the logo and a trademark for the software code.
options.B: A trademark for the logo and copyright for the software code.
options.C: Copyright for both the logo and the software code, since both are original creative works.
options.D: A patent for the software code and copyright for the logo.

questions.explanation: A trademark protects brand identifiers such as logos to distinguish a company's goods in the marketplace, while copyright automatically protects original creative works including software code from the moment of creation. Option C is the top distractor because copyright does apply to creative works, and a logo can receive copyright protection, but a distinctive logo used as a brand identifier is most strategically and legally protected as a trademark, which can be renewed indefinitely unlike copyright.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Anthropometric Data
questions.prompt: A product designer is using anthropometric data to design a school desk. She uses measurements from the 50th percentile of her target age group as her single design standard. Identify the error in this approach.

options.A: The 50th percentile represents the average, so designing for it excludes users at the extremes of the range, such as very tall or very short students.
options.B: Anthropometric data should never be used for furniture design because people's posture varies too much to be measured accurately.
options.C: The 50th percentile is too high a target; designers should always use the 5th percentile to ensure smaller users are accommodated.
options.D: The error is using age-group data rather than weight-group data, since desk height depends on body weight, not age.

questions.explanation: Ergonomic best practice requires designing for a range, typically the 5th to 95th percentile, so that the product accommodates the full diversity of users; a single 50th-percentile standard means roughly half of all users are outside the optimal fit zone. Option C is the top distractor because while designing for smaller users matters, using only the 5th percentile would exclude the majority of users — the correct approach is to design for a range or provide adjustability, not to replace one extreme with another.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Hotspots
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment (LCA) of a cotton T-shirt reveals that the manufacturing stage produces 15% of total carbon emissions, while the use stage (repeated washing at 60°C) produces 60%. Which design intervention would most effectively reduce the T-shirt's overall environmental impact?

options.A: Switching to a more energy-efficient factory to reduce manufacturing emissions.
options.B: Redesigning the T-shirt with a label instructing users to wash at 30°C, targeting the highest-impact stage.
options.C: Using organic cotton to eliminate pesticide use during the raw material extraction stage.
options.D: Improving the end-of-life recycling programme so that more T-shirts are recovered rather than landfilled.

questions.explanation: LCA data shows the use stage accounts for 60% of emissions, so the greatest leverage for reduction is influencing user behaviour during washing; designing for lower-temperature washing directly addresses the dominant hotspot in the product's lifecycle. Option A is the top distractor because manufacturing is a visible, controllable stage, but at only 15% of emissions, improving it yields far less impact reduction than addressing the 60% use-stage hotspot identified by the LCA.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Decisions
questions.prompt: A design team is testing whether users can navigate a new mobile app intuitively. They have limited time and budget. Which prototype type is most appropriate at this stage, and why?

options.A: A high-fidelity coded prototype, because users need to experience the real interaction speed to give valid navigation feedback.
options.B: A low-fidelity paper prototype, because it can be quickly created, allows rapid iteration, and is sufficient to test navigation logic.
options.C: A fully functional beta version, because any prototype with missing features will confuse participants and skew results.
options.D: A physical 3D model, because users respond more honestly to tangible objects than to screens during usability testing.

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity paper prototypes are a well-established UX method for testing information architecture and navigation flow cheaply and quickly, allowing the team to identify usability problems before investing in coding; research shows users readily engage with paper interfaces when task scenarios are clearly framed. Option A is the top distractor because interaction speed is a real usability factor, but it is irrelevant at this stage — the research question is about navigation logic, not performance, making high-fidelity development unnecessary and wasteful.

questions.title: Systems Thinking and Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart home heating system, a thermostat measures room temperature and turns the boiler off when the target temperature is reached. What type of feedback loop is this, and why is it important for system stability?

options.A: A positive feedback loop, because the system amplifies the heating signal to reach the target temperature faster.
options.B: A negative feedback loop, because the system uses output information to reduce the gap between actual and desired states, creating stability.
options.C: An open-loop system, because the boiler operates on a fixed timer regardless of the measured temperature.
options.D: A positive feedback loop, because the boiler and thermostat reinforce each other's operation until the room is warm.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback loops use the system's output to counteract deviation from a set point — here, when temperature rises above the target, the thermostat sends a signal that reduces heating, stabilising the system around the desired value; this is the defining mechanism of controlled, self-regulating systems. Option A is the top distractor because 'amplifying' sounds like it could describe faster heating, but positive feedback loops amplify deviation away from the target rather than correcting it, which would cause the system to overheat uncontrollably.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'If a hiring algorithm was trained only on data from past successful employees who were mostly men, it will automatically produce fair results because it is just following mathematical patterns.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct; algorithms are inherently objective because they do not have personal biases or emotions.
options.B: The claim is incorrect; the algorithm will likely replicate and amplify the historical gender bias present in its training data.
options.C: The claim is correct, provided the mathematical model used is statistically significant and peer-reviewed.
options.D: The claim is incorrect only if the programmers intentionally coded discriminatory rules into the algorithm.

questions.explanation: Machine learning algorithms learn patterns from training data; if that data reflects historical bias — such as predominantly male success profiles — the algorithm codifies and can amplify that bias, producing discriminatory outputs even without intentional programming, a phenomenon documented in real hiring tools including Amazon's 2018 recruiting tool which was scrapped for this reason. Option A is the top distractor because the idea that mathematics is neutral is intuitive but incorrect — objectivity depends on the quality and representativeness of the data, not merely on the use of mathematics.

questions.title: Innovation Economics and First-Mover Advantage
questions.prompt: Company A releases the world's first smartwatch but makes little profit, while Company B releases a similar smartwatch two years later and dominates the market. Which economic concept best explains why the second mover outperformed the first?

options.A: Economies of scale, because Company B produced more units and therefore had lower average costs.
options.B: First-mover disadvantage, where Company B learned from Company A's mistakes, avoided R&D costs, and entered a market with proven demand.
options.C: Comparative advantage, because Company B specialised in manufacturing while Company A specialised in research.
options.D: Monopoly pricing, because Company A set prices too high, allowing Company B to undercut them and capture the market.

questions.explanation: First-mover disadvantage occurs when an early entrant bears the high costs of market education, technology development, and early adopter limitations, allowing later entrants to free-ride on proven demand, learn from the pioneer's failures, and use more mature technology — a pattern observed with companies like Apple entering markets pioneered by earlier, less successful products. Option A is a plausible distractor because economies of scale do benefit later, larger producers, but this concept explains cost reduction rather than the strategic advantage of learning from a pioneer's market-building efforts.

questions.title: Define Stage and Problem Framing
questions.prompt: After empathising with users, a design team writes this problem statement: 'We need to build a better website.' A classmate argues this is an inadequate define-stage output. Justify whether the classmate is correct.

options.A: The classmate is incorrect; a broad problem statement gives the design team maximum creative freedom during ideation.
options.B: The classmate is correct; the statement is solution-oriented and lacks a specific user, identified need, and insight from empathy research.
options.C: The classmate is correct, but only because the statement does not include a measurable success criterion.
options.D: The classmate is incorrect; the define stage is meant to summarise what the team will build, so focusing on the website is appropriate.

questions.explanation: A strong 'How Might We' or point-of-view problem statement must identify a specific user, their unmet need, and an insight drawn from empathy data; 'build a better website' is solution-focused rather than problem-focused and contains none of these elements, violating the core purpose of the define stage. Option C is the top distractor because success criteria are important, but the deeper flaw is that the statement is solution-oriented and user-free — without knowing who has the problem or what need exists, adding a metric would still not fix the fundamental framing error.

questions.title: UX Research Method Selection
questions.prompt: A design team wants to understand how teenagers actually use a study planning app in their natural environment over two weeks, rather than how they say they use it. Which research method is most appropriate?

options.A: A large-scale online survey distributed to 500 students, to collect statistically significant self-reported usage data.
options.B: Diary studies or experience sampling, where participants log their real interactions with the app in context over the two-week period.
options.C: A controlled lab usability test in which participants complete set tasks on the app while a researcher observes.
options.D: A focus group with eight participants who discuss their ideal study planning features after a demo of the app.

questions.explanation: Diary studies and experience sampling methods capture authentic, in-context behaviour over time, bridging the gap between what users say and what they actually do — a known validity problem called the 'say-do gap'; this method is specifically designed for longitudinal, naturalistic observation. Option C is the top distractor because usability testing does observe real behaviour, but it occurs in an artificial lab environment with pre-set tasks, which does not reflect how teenagers spontaneously use the app in their own study routines over two weeks.

questions.title: Sustainability and Cradle-to-Cradle
questions.prompt: Examine the difference between a 'cradle-to-grave' and a 'cradle-to-cradle' design philosophy. Which statement most accurately describes what makes cradle-to-cradle design fundamentally different?

options.A: Cradle-to-cradle design focuses on reducing waste during manufacturing, while cradle-to-grave includes the disposal stage.
options.B: Cradle-to-cradle design eliminates the concept of waste by ensuring all materials continuously cycle back as nutrients into biological or technical systems.
options.C: Cradle-to-cradle design is identical to recycling, but applied at an industrial scale rather than at the household level.
options.D: Cradle-to-cradle design requires that products last longer than cradle-to-grave products to justify their higher production cost.

questions.explanation: Cradle-to-cradle, developed by architect William McDonough and chemist Michael Braungart, reframes waste as a design flaw by ensuring materials flow endlessly in either biological cycles (composting) or technical cycles (industrial reuse), fundamentally eliminating the endpoint of 'grave.' Option C is the top distractor because recycling is part of cradle-to-cradle thinking, but conventional recycling often degrades material quality (downcycling), whereas cradle-to-cradle design specifies materials remain at full value indefinitely — a qualitatively different goal.

questions.title: Tensile Strength vs. Hardness
questions.prompt: A student designing a climbing carabiner states: 'I should choose the hardest material available, because hardness means it won't break under the load of a climber.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: There is no error; hardness and resistance to breaking under tensile load are the same material property.
options.B: Hardness measures resistance to surface scratching and indentation, not resistance to breaking under tension; tensile strength is the relevant property.
options.C: The error is that the student should prioritise density over hardness, since lighter materials always have higher load-bearing capacity.
options.D: The error is that carabiners require ductility rather than hardness, but ductility and tensile strength are the same thing.

questions.explanation: Hardness is defined as a material's resistance to surface deformation (scratching or indentation), measured on scales such as the Vickers or Mohs scales, whereas tensile strength measures how much pulling force a material can withstand before fracturing — these are distinct properties, and a very hard material can be brittle and fail catastrophically under tensile load. Option D is the top distractor because ductility (the ability to deform plastically before breaking) is indeed important for carabiners to avoid sudden fracture, but ductility and tensile strength are separate properties and conflating them is a different error from the one in the question.

questions.title: Open Source vs. Proprietary Design
questions.prompt: A student argues: 'Open-source design always leads to better innovation than proprietary design because more people can contribute improvements.' Evaluate whether this claim is always true.

options.A: The claim is always true; distributed collaboration consistently outperforms single-company development in every industry.
options.B: The claim is sometimes true; open-source models excel in software but rarely produce innovation in hardware due to manufacturing cost barriers.
options.C: The claim is not always true; proprietary models can fund sustained R&D and quality control that fragmented open-source contributions may lack.
options.D: The claim is false; proprietary design always outperforms open-source because financial incentives drive higher quality output.

questions.explanation: While open-source projects like Linux demonstrate powerful collaborative innovation, proprietary models allow companies to invest large, coordinated R&D budgets, enforce consistent quality standards, and develop long-term technology roadmaps — advantages that fragmented volunteer-driven development may struggle to match for complex, resource-intensive innovations. Option B is a plausible distractor because manufacturing cost barriers for hardware are real, but the open-source hardware movement (e.g., Arduino, RepRap 3D printers) has produced genuine innovations, so the claim that open-source 'rarely produces hardware innovation' is an overstatement that makes B incorrect.

questions.title: Iterative Design vs. Linear Design
questions.prompt: A project manager insists her team follow a strict linear design sequence: research → design → build → launch, with no going back to earlier stages. Compare this approach with iterative design, and identify the most significant risk of the linear model.

options.A: The linear model risks producing a product that is over-engineered, because teams spend too long on each stage.
options.B: The linear model risks launching a product that fails to meet user needs, because problems discovered late cannot be corrected without restarting from the beginning.
options.C: The linear model is only risky for digital products; for physical products, a single design-to-build sequence is industry standard.
options.D: The linear model risks creating too many prototypes, whereas iterative design limits prototype production to reduce costs.

questions.explanation: In a linear (waterfall) model, user feedback is only received at the end, meaning that fundamental design flaws discovered at launch require expensive, time-consuming rework from early stages — a risk that iterative design mitigates by building in feedback loops at every stage so problems are caught and corrected early. Option A is a plausible distractor because over-engineering is a real project risk, but it is not caused by linearity — in fact, a linear model often under-tests assumptions rather than spending too long on each stage.

questions.title: Biomimicry in Innovation
questions.prompt: Engineers studying the microscopic structure of shark skin discovered it reduces drag by disrupting water flow. They replicated this structure on Olympic swimsuits. This is an example of which design approach, and what is its primary advantage?

options.A: Ergonomic design, because the swimsuit is shaped to fit the human body more comfortably during athletic performance.
options.B: Biomimicry, because it draws on solutions refined by millions of years of natural selection to solve a human engineering problem.
options.C: Reverse engineering, because the designers disassembled an existing product to understand and replicate its function.
options.D: Biomimicry, because using biological materials rather than synthetic ones reduces the environmental impact of production.

questions.explanation: Biomimicry is the practice of emulating structures, processes, or systems found in nature to solve human design challenges; shark skin's dermal denticle structure has been refined over approximately 450 million years of evolution, providing a highly optimised drag-reduction solution that engineers adapted into Speedo's Fastskin swimsuit technology. Option D is the top distractor because it correctly names biomimicry, but its justification is wrong — biomimicry involves replicating natural structures or principles, not necessarily using biological materials, and the swimsuits were made from synthetic fibres.

questions.title: Data Privacy in Product Design
questions.prompt: A fitness tracker company proposes sharing anonymised user heart-rate and location data with insurance companies to help them set premiums. A student argues this is acceptable because the data is anonymised. Evaluate this ethical position.

options.A: The position is sound; anonymisation completely eliminates privacy risk, so sharing the data with third parties raises no ethical concerns.
options.B: The position is weak; anonymised datasets can often be re-identified when combined with other data, and users may not have consented to this specific use.
options.C: The position is sound, provided the company notifies users after sharing occurs, in accordance with standard data transparency practice.
options.D: The position is weak only if the insurance company is located in a different country, where different data protection laws apply.

questions.explanation: Research, including a landmark 2019 MIT study, has demonstrated that anonymised location data can be re-identified with high accuracy when cross-referenced with other datasets; additionally, using health and movement data to influence insurance premiums may discriminate against people with chronic conditions, raising serious ethical concerns beyond anonymisation alone. Option A is the top distractor because anonymisation does reduce risk and is a genuine privacy safeguard, making it plausible — but it does not 'completely eliminate' risk, and the consent issue remains regardless of anonymisation quality.

questions.title: Morphological Analysis in Ideation
questions.prompt: During ideation, a student uses a morphological chart by listing key functions of a product along one axis and possible solutions for each function along the other. What is the primary advantage of this method over simple brainstorming?

options.A: It generates ideas faster because participants can work in silence without being influenced by others' suggestions.
options.B: It systematically explores combinations of solutions across all key functions, reducing the chance of overlooking viable design solutions.
options.C: It eliminates weak ideas early by requiring each function's solution to pass a feasibility test before being recorded in the chart.
options.D: It is more creative than brainstorming because it encourages designers to copy solutions from nature rather than inventing new ones.

questions.explanation: A morphological chart structures ideation by decomposing a design problem into its essential functions and then systematically generating and combining solutions for each function, creating a combinatorial solution space that is far more comprehensive than unstructured brainstorming, which tends to cluster around familiar ideas. Option A is the top distractor because silent individual idea generation (brainwriting) is a real technique that reduces social influence bias, but morphological charts are not specifically a silent method — their defining advantage is systematic combination, not silencing social pressure.

questions.title: Planned Obsolescence Ethics
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer releases a software update that slows down older phone models. The company claims this is done to protect battery life. Analyse this practice from an ethical standpoint, considering both the company's claim and an alternative interpretation.

options.A: The practice is entirely ethical because companies are legally obligated to extend the functional life of their products through software updates.
options.B: The practice raises ethical concerns because it may constitute planned obsolescence — artificially shortening product life to drive new purchases — even if the battery justification is partially valid.
options.C: The practice is unethical only if the company does not inform users, but transparent communication makes it fully acceptable regardless of intent.
options.D: The practice is ethical because consumer electronics are designed with fixed lifespans, and slowing older devices is a necessary technical consequence.

questions.explanation: Apple was fined hundreds of millions of euros by regulators in France and Italy for precisely this practice, which courts found constituted planned obsolescence; while battery management is a genuine engineering concern, throttling performance without disclosure or user consent undermines autonomy and drives unnecessary consumption, creating both ethical and environmental harms. Option C is the top distractor because transparency is indeed an important ethical principle, but transparency alone does not make the underlying practice ethical if the intent is to manipulate users into purchasing new devices — disclosure and acceptability are separate questions.

questions.title: Universal Design Principles
questions.prompt: A student designing a public park water fountain applies the principle of 'equitable use' from universal design. Which design decision best demonstrates this principle?

options.A: Installing two separate fountains — one at standard height and a lower one specifically labelled for wheelchair users.
options.B: Designing a single fountain at an accessible height with a hands-free sensor, usable comfortably by standing adults, children, and wheelchair users.
options.C: Adding a non-slip surface around the fountain's base to prevent accidents, improving safety for all users.
options.D: Placing the fountain near a park bench so that elderly users can sit and rest immediately after drinking.

questions.explanation: The principle of equitable use, as defined by the Center for Universal Design, requires that a design be usable by people with diverse abilities in the same or equivalent way without segregation or stigmatisation; a single fountain accessible to all achieves this, whereas separate facilities (Option A) explicitly violates equitable use by stigmatising wheelchair users with a labelled 'special' fountain. Option A is the top distractor because it does accommodate wheelchair users and may even comply with some accessibility codes, but it achieves access through segregation rather than equity — a critical distinction in universal design theory.

questions.title: Cost-Benefit Analysis in Innovation
questions.prompt: A company spends $2 million developing a new biodegradable packaging material. It saves $500,000 per year in waste disposal fees and generates $300,000 per year in additional sales from eco-conscious customers. Approximately how many years will it take to break even, and what economic concept does this calculation represent?

options.A: 4 years; this represents the concept of economies of scale.
options.B: 2.5 years; this represents the concept of sunk cost.
options.C: 2.5 years; this represents the concept of return on investment (payback period).
options.D: 4 years; this represents the concept of opportunity cost.

questions.explanation: The annual benefit is $500,000 + $300,000 = $800,000; dividing the $2,000,000 investment by $800,000 per year gives a payback period of 2.5 years, which is a specific form of return on investment (ROI) analysis used to determine when an innovation becomes profitable. Option D is the top distractor because 4 years would result from incorrectly using only the waste disposal savings ($500,000/year) and ignoring the additional sales revenue — a calculation error that produces the wrong answer and attributes it to an unrelated economic concept.

questions.title: Disruptive vs. Sustaining Innovation
questions.prompt: Clayton Christensen distinguished between 'sustaining' and 'disruptive' innovation. A budget airline offers basic flights with no meals or reserved seats, initially targeting travellers who previously took buses or drove, not existing airline customers. Which category does this represent, and why?

options.A: Sustaining innovation, because the airline is still operating in the existing aviation industry and competing for similar routes.
options.B: Disruptive innovation, because it initially targets non-consumers at the low end of the market with a simpler, cheaper product that later moves upmarket.
options.C: Disruptive innovation, because it forces existing airlines to immediately lower their prices, destroying the established market.
options.D: Sustaining innovation, because budget airlines improve the overall flying experience by making air travel affordable to more people.

questions.explanation: Christensen's definition of disruptive innovation specifically describes a product that starts by serving non-consumers or the low end of a market — those ignored by incumbents — with a simpler, cheaper offering, then improves over time to challenge established players; budget airlines like Ryanair followed exactly this pattern, initially targeting bus and car travellers before eventually competing for business travellers. Option A is the top distractor because operating in the same industry does superficially resemble the incumbent market, but Christensen's theory explicitly distinguishes disruptive from sustaining innovation by initial target market and performance trajectory, not by industry.

questions.title: Failure Mode Analysis
questions.prompt: An engineering team uses Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) to assess a new electric scooter design. For one component, they rate severity as 9/10, occurrence as 2/10, and detectability as 8/10. What is the Risk Priority Number (RPN), and what does it suggest about this failure mode?

options.A: RPN = 144; the failure is high priority because the severity is catastrophic, even though it is unlikely to occur.
options.B: RPN = 19; the failure is low priority because the average score across the three dimensions is low.
options.C: RPN = 144; the failure is low priority because the overall score is below the maximum of 1000.
options.D: RPN = 72; the failure is moderate priority and requires monitoring but not immediate redesign.

questions.explanation: RPN is calculated by multiplying severity × occurrence × detectability: 9 × 2 × 8 = 144; this score signals a high-priority failure mode because a severity of 9 indicates a potentially catastrophic outcome (such as brake failure causing injury), and even a low probability of occurrence warrants serious attention when consequences are this severe. Option C is the top distractor because it correctly calculates the RPN as 144 but misinterprets its significance — an RPN of 144 out of a maximum of 1000 is not inherently 'low priority'; the severity sub-score of 9 alone triggers mandatory review in most FMEA protocols regardless of the total RPN.

questions.title: Design for Manufacture and Assembly
questions.prompt: A product designer applies Design for Manufacture and Assembly (DFMA) principles to a new lamp. Which design change best reflects DFMA principles?

options.A: Adding more decorative components to increase perceived value and justify a higher retail price.
options.B: Reducing the number of separate parts by combining the switch housing and base into a single moulded component.
options.C: Using a wider variety of materials to ensure each part has the optimal property profile for its function.
options.D: Increasing the number of assembly steps so that each worker specialises in one task, improving quality control.

questions.explanation: DFMA is a methodology that aims to reduce production costs and errors by minimising part count, simplifying assembly steps, and standardising components; combining the switch housing and base into one moulded part directly reduces the number of parts, assembly operations, and potential failure points. Option C is the top distractor because using optimal materials for each function sounds like good engineering, but DFMA specifically discourages material variety because it complicates supply chains, tooling, and recycling — standardising materials is a core DFMA recommendation.

questions.title: Trade-offs in Sustainable Materials
questions.prompt: A company switches from petroleum-based plastic bags to bags made from corn-based bioplastic (PLA), claiming this is a more sustainable choice. Evaluate this claim by identifying a significant limitation of PLA that undermines the sustainability argument.

options.A: PLA is less durable than conventional plastic, so the bags must be replaced more often, increasing overall material consumption.
options.B: PLA requires industrial composting conditions to break down and will persist in landfill or oceans similarly to conventional plastic if not properly processed.
options.C: PLA is derived from corn, which is a food crop, raising concerns about diverting agricultural land and water from food production.
options.D: PLA cannot be recycled in conventional plastic streams and produces toxic gases if incinerated at low temperatures.

questions.explanation: PLA is compostable only under industrial conditions of approximately 60°C for several weeks; in home compost, landfill, or marine environments, it degrades extremely slowly, behaving similarly to conventional plastic and potentially contributing to microplastic pollution — a fact that directly undermines the claim that switching to PLA automatically improves sustainability. Option C is the top distractor because land use and food competition are genuine sustainability concerns in bioplastic production (the 'food vs. fuel' debate), but the most immediate and direct limitation that undermines the specific sustainability claim about end-of-life is the composting infrastructure requirement, which is the most commonly misunderstood aspect of PLA.

questions.title: Inclusive Design vs. Universal Design
questions.prompt: A classmate states: 'Inclusive design and universal design are the same thing — both aim to make products work for everyone.' Evaluate this claim by identifying the most important distinction between the two approaches.

options.A: The claim is correct; inclusive design and universal design are interchangeable terms used in different countries for the same set of principles.
options.B: The claim is partially incorrect; universal design seeks one solution usable by all, while inclusive design may involve multiple solutions tailored to different groups, including those historically excluded from design processes.
options.C: The claim is incorrect; universal design applies only to physical products, while inclusive design applies only to digital interfaces and software.
options.D: The claim is partially incorrect; inclusive design focuses on aesthetics and cultural representation, while universal design focuses on physical accessibility only.

questions.explanation: Universal design, codified by Ron Mace, aims to create a single design solution that works for the widest possible range of users without adaptation; inclusive design, as articulated by Microsoft's Inclusive Design toolkit, takes a broader approach by actively involving excluded groups in the design process and may deliberately create multiple pathways or solutions for different user needs rather than seeking one universal solution. Option A is the top distractor because the terms are frequently used interchangeably in casual conversation and even in some educational materials, making this a genuine source of confusion — but they represent philosophically distinct approaches particularly regarding process (who is involved) and output (one solution vs. multiple).

questions.title: Empathy vs. Assumption in Design
questions.prompt: A design team skips the empathise stage and moves straight to ideation, arguing they already understand their users because they are the same age. Evaluate this decision using design thinking principles.

options.A: It is acceptable because peers share the same lived experience, making formal empathy research redundant.
options.B: It is flawed because empathy research uncovers specific user needs that personal assumptions often miss or distort.
options.C: It is efficient because ideation produces prototypes faster, and testing will correct any misunderstandings later.
options.D: It is acceptable as long as the team conducts a survey after the prototype is built to confirm their assumptions.

questions.explanation: The empathise stage exists precisely because designers—even those similar to users—hold unconscious biases that skew their assumptions; structured methods like interviews or observation reveal latent needs invisible to insiders. Option C is tempting but wrong: errors embedded at ideation compound throughout the process, making late-stage testing far more costly and less likely to produce a fundamentally user-centred solution.

questions.title: Material Properties Under Stress
questions.prompt: A student is designing a reusable sports water bottle. She narrows her choice to two materials: high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and borosilicate glass. Compare these materials and justify which is more appropriate, considering durability, weight, and chemical safety.

options.A: Borosilicate glass, because it is chemically inert, thermally stable, and lighter than HDPE.
options.B: HDPE, because it is chemically inert, impact-resistant, and significantly lighter than glass.
options.C: Borosilicate glass, because its high tensile strength makes it less likely to crack under repeated impact than HDPE.
options.D: HDPE, because it is the only food-safe plastic approved for repeated use, unlike all other polymers.

questions.explanation: HDPE is classified food-safe, resists most chemicals, has a density of about 0.95 g/cm³ (far lighter than borosilicate glass at ~2.23 g/cm³), and absorbs impact without shattering—critical for a sports context. Option A is wrong because borosilicate glass is heavier, not lighter, than HDPE, and despite its thermal resistance it remains brittle under impact.

questions.title: Defining the Design Problem
questions.prompt: A student writes the following design specification criterion: 'The product should be good and easy to use.' A teacher marks this as inadequate. Identify the primary reason this criterion fails and explain what a measurable alternative would look like.

options.A: It fails because it does not mention the target user group; adding a demographic description would make it sufficient.
options.B: It fails because it uses subjective language with no measurable standard, so success cannot be objectively tested.
options.C: It fails because design criteria must always include cost constraints to be considered complete.
options.D: It fails because criteria should describe the manufacturing process rather than the final product's performance.

questions.explanation: A valid design criterion must be testable: words like 'good' and 'easy' are entirely subjective and cannot be measured. A measurable alternative would specify, for example, '90% of test users complete the primary task in under 30 seconds without assistance.' Option A identifies a real gap but is not the primary failure; subjective language is the core problem that prevents any objective evaluation of success.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Anthropometrics
questions.prompt: A designer is creating a school desk for students aged 12–14. She uses the average sitting height of her class to set the desk height. Analyse why using only the average measurement may result in a poorly ergonomic design.

options.A: Because averages are always statistically inaccurate and should be replaced with the median value instead.
options.B: Because designing for the average excludes the tallest and shortest users, who may experience discomfort or injury.
options.C: Because ergonomic furniture must be designed for the 95th percentile user to ensure comfort for the entire population.
options.D: Because sitting height is irrelevant to desk design; only arm reach and hand span measurements should be used.

questions.explanation: Anthropometric design for the average fits only a narrow band of the population; students significantly taller or shorter will adopt awkward postures leading to musculoskeletal strain. Option C states a common rule but overgeneralises: designers typically use the 5th–95th percentile range or adjustable designs rather than optimising exclusively for the 95th percentile, making B the more precisely correct and broadly applicable answer.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Decision
questions.prompt: A team is at the early ideation stage and must choose between a paper prototype and a fully coded digital prototype to test their app concept with users. Which choice is most justified at this stage, and why?

options.A: The fully coded prototype, because users cannot give reliable feedback on a product that does not function as the final version will.
options.B: The paper prototype, because low-fidelity models are faster to build and cheaper to change, enabling more iterative cycles.
options.C: The fully coded prototype, because digital interfaces require real interaction to reveal usability problems accurately.
options.D: The paper prototype, because IB Design regulations require low-fidelity prototypes before digital work can begin.

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototyping at early ideation stages is a core design thinking principle: paper prototypes can be created in minutes, iterated rapidly, and allow teams to test fundamental concepts before investing significant time in coding. Option A sounds logical but is contradicted by established UX research showing that paper prototypes reliably surface major navigation and layout issues that are identical to those found in coded versions at a fraction of the cost.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Trade-offs
questions.prompt: An LCA comparing cotton tote bags and single-use plastic bags finds that a cotton tote must be reused at least 131 times to have a lower climate impact than a single-use plastic bag. A student claims cotton bags are always the more sustainable choice. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because cotton is biodegradable, which always makes it environmentally superior to plastic regardless of use frequency.
options.B: The claim is partially correct: cotton bags are superior in end-of-life impact but inferior in water consumption during production.
options.C: The claim is incorrect because the high resource cost of cotton production means a tote bag only becomes more sustainable after sufficient reuse, which many consumers do not achieve.
options.D: The claim is incorrect because LCA results are unreliable; only carbon footprint data should be used to compare product sustainability.

questions.explanation: Studies including a UK Environment Agency LCA found cotton bags require over 100 uses to offset their production impact, which includes high water use, pesticide application, and energy-intensive manufacturing; consumers who use them only a few times can have a higher environmental impact than single-use plastic users. Option A is wrong because biodegradability addresses only one end-of-life impact category and does not offset the large upstream resource burden of cotton cultivation.

questions.title: Innovation Economics and Diffusion
questions.prompt: According to Everett Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations model, which group adopts a new technology only after seeing credible evidence of its success from peers, and why does targeting this group matter for a product's commercial survival?

options.A: Innovators, because they drive initial sales that fund further research and development.
options.B: Early majority, because they represent a large market segment whose adoption tips the product into mainstream success.
options.C: Early adopters, because they write influential reviews that convince innovators to fund the product.
options.D: Laggards, because converting the most resistant users signals total market saturation and maximum profit.

questions.explanation: Rogers identified the early majority as roughly 34% of the market; their adoption follows the 'chasm' identified by Geoffrey Moore and represents the tipping point at which a product shifts from niche to mainstream—critical for financial viability. Option C conflates early adopters (who adopt before seeing peer evidence) with the early majority, and misrepresents the direction of influence in the diffusion model.

questions.title: UX Research Method Selection
questions.prompt: A company wants to understand why users abandon their checkout process partway through. They have two weeks and access to 200 existing users. Which combination of research methods would most effectively diagnose the problem?

options.A: A large-scale online survey followed by a focus group to discuss the most common survey responses.
options.B: Heuristic evaluation by the design team followed by a competitive analysis of rival checkout flows.
options.C: Analytics funnel analysis to identify where drop-offs occur, combined with moderated usability testing to observe why.
options.D: Card sorting to reorganise the product categories, followed by A/B testing two new homepage designs.

questions.explanation: Analytics data pinpoints the exact step where users abandon the funnel (quantitative 'where'), while moderated usability testing reveals the cognitive and interaction barriers causing abandonment (qualitative 'why')—together providing actionable diagnosis. Option A generates opinion data but does not reveal actual behaviour; surveys suffer from self-reporting bias and cannot capture real-time decision-making during checkout.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A student claims that an AI hiring tool is fair because it was trained on ten years of a company's successful employee data. A classmate disagrees. Who is correct, and what specific ethical concept explains the flaw?

options.A: The first student is correct; historical data from within the company is the most relevant and unbiased training source available.
options.B: The classmate is correct; the tool likely encodes historical bias, as past hiring patterns may have systematically excluded certain groups.
options.C: The classmate is correct; AI tools cannot be used ethically for hiring decisions under any circumstances due to privacy laws.
options.D: Both are partially correct; the tool is fair for candidates similar to past hires but unfair only if the company operates in a regulated industry.

questions.explanation: Training on historical data embeds historical discrimination: if past hiring favoured certain demographics, the model learns to replicate that pattern—a documented case occurred with Amazon's recruiting tool, which downgraded CVs mentioning women's colleges. Option A is wrong because the relevance of data does not guarantee its fairness; data can be highly relevant to past decisions while encoding systemic bias against under-represented groups.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart thermostat system, the room temperature reading is continuously compared to the target temperature, and the heater is switched on or off accordingly. What type of system mechanism is this, and why is it essential for stable operation?

options.A: A positive feedback loop, because the heater output reinforces the system's initial action and drives it toward the target.
options.B: An open-loop control system, because the thermostat does not need sensor input once the target temperature is set.
options.C: A negative feedback loop, because the system's output (room temperature) is fed back to reduce the gap between actual and target values.
options.D: A closed-loop amplifier, because electrical signals are continuously amplified to maintain a steady temperature output.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback loops are self-correcting: when the output (temperature) rises above the target, the feedback signal reduces the heater's activity, stabilising the system around the set point—a fundamental principle of control engineering. Option A describes a positive feedback loop, which amplifies deviation rather than correcting it and would cause the temperature to overshoot indefinitely, the opposite of stable thermostat behaviour.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secrets
questions.prompt: A company keeps its manufacturing process confidential rather than applying for a patent. Analyse the key trade-off this decision involves compared to patent protection.

options.A: A trade secret provides indefinite protection as long as secrecy is maintained, but offers no legal recourse if a competitor independently discovers the same process.
options.B: A trade secret is registered with a government agency, giving the company exclusive rights without requiring public disclosure.
options.C: A patent provides broader protection than a trade secret because it prevents independent discovery, whereas trade secrets only prevent direct copying.
options.D: A trade secret is always inferior to a patent because patents protect all forms of intellectual property simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Unlike a patent, a trade secret has no fixed expiry and does not require public disclosure, but it provides no protection against a competitor who independently reverse-engineers or discovers the same process—Coca-Cola's formula is a classic example of a company accepting this risk. Option C is wrong because patents do not prevent independent discovery either; they prevent use of the patented invention regardless of how it was developed, which is actually a stronger protection than trade secrets in that specific regard.

questions.title: Sustainability: Cradle-to-Cradle Design
questions.prompt: A designer claims her product follows a 'cradle-to-grave' model. A classmate argues that 'cradle-to-cradle' is always preferable. Examine the classmate's argument and identify a scenario where cradle-to-grave might be justified.

options.A: The classmate is entirely correct; cradle-to-cradle is preferable in all contexts because it eliminates waste by definition.
options.B: The classmate is mostly correct, but cradle-to-grave may be justified for single-use medical devices where contamination risks make reprocessing unsafe or impractical.
options.C: Cradle-to-grave is always preferable for electronic products because recycling electronics releases toxic materials that outweigh recovery benefits.
options.D: The classmate is incorrect; cradle-to-cradle only applies to biological materials and cannot be implemented for synthetic products.

questions.explanation: Cradle-to-cradle design (materials cycling back as nutrients) is generally superior, but single-use sterile medical devices such as syringes or surgical tools carry infection risks if reprocessed; safe disposal (cradle-to-grave) is justified to protect patient safety. Option A overgeneralises: cradle-to-cradle may require complex disassembly infrastructure, use of rare materials, or energy-intensive recycling that can outweigh its benefits in specific contexts.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Define Stage
