questions.prompt: After conducting user interviews, a team creates a 'Point of View' (POV) statement: 'We want to build an app.' A mentor says this is not a proper POV statement. Identify the error and explain what a correct POV statement should include.

options.A: The error is that it proposes a solution rather than defining a user, their need, and an insight derived from research.
options.B: The error is that it does not specify a budget or timeline, which are required components of a POV statement.
options.C: The error is that it focuses on digital technology; POV statements must remain technology-agnostic and describe only physical interactions.
options.D: The error is that it is too short; a proper POV statement must be at least three paragraphs and include competitive analysis.

questions.explanation: A properly structured POV statement follows the format: '[User] needs [need] because [insight]'—it names the specific user, articulates their unmet need derived from research, and provides the surprising insight that reframes the problem. Proposing a solution ('build an app') bypasses this structure and short-circuits creative problem-solving by constraining ideation before the problem is well defined. Option B invents requirements; budget and timeline belong in a design brief, not a POV statement.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystem Failure
questions.prompt: An autonomous drone delivery system fails to deliver packages when outdoor temperatures exceed 35°C. The engineers discover the battery management subsystem shuts down to prevent overheating. Examine why this is described as an 'emergent' system behaviour.

options.A: Because the battery subsystem was programmed to fail under these conditions as a deliberate design feature for all delivery scenarios.
options.B: Because the failure arises from the interaction between the thermal environment and the battery subsystem in a way not fully anticipated at the whole-system level.
options.C: Because emergent behaviour refers specifically to software bugs that only appear during real-world operation, not during testing.
options.D: Because the drone's navigation subsystem independently decided to cancel deliveries based on weather forecast data it was programmed to receive.

questions.explanation: Emergence in systems engineering describes properties or behaviours that arise from subsystem interactions rather than being a designed feature of any single component; the battery protection feature (designed for safety) interacting with high ambient temperatures produces a system-level delivery failure that was not the intended outcome. Option A incorrectly describes the shutdown as a deliberately designed whole-system feature, when it is actually a subsystem-level safety response whose system-wide consequence was not fully foreseen.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright vs. Patent
questions.prompt: A student writes original code for a mobile game and also invents a new physical controller device for it. Compare the intellectual property protections that would automatically apply to each creation without any registration.

options.A: Both the code and the controller are automatically protected by copyright the moment they are created and fixed in a tangible form.
options.B: The code is automatically protected by copyright upon creation, but the physical controller requires a patent application to receive any protection.
options.C: The controller is automatically protected by a design patent, while the code must be registered as a trademark to prevent copying.
options.D: Neither creation receives automatic protection; both require government registration before any intellectual property rights exist.

questions.explanation: Copyright arises automatically at the moment an original work is fixed in tangible form (including software code) in most jurisdictions under the Berne Convention; no registration is required. Patent protection for a physical invention, however, must be actively applied for—it is not automatic—and requires disclosure, novelty, and non-obviousness criteria to be met. Option A incorrectly extends automatic copyright to the physical device, which is a novel functional invention requiring patent registration.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Cognitive Load
questions.prompt: A student argues that adding more features and menu options to a productivity app always improves its usability because users have more choices. Evaluate this argument using the concept of cognitive ergonomics.

options.A: The argument is correct because more features increase perceived value and experienced users will learn to navigate complex interfaces over time.
options.B: The argument is incorrect because increasing the number of choices raises cognitive load, slowing decision-making and increasing error rates.
options.C: The argument is partially correct: additional features improve usability for expert users but reduce it only for novices.
options.D: The argument is correct because usability is determined solely by visual design, not by the number of available features.

questions.explanation: Hick's Law states that decision time increases logarithmically with the number of choices, and cognitive ergonomics research consistently shows that interface complexity raises working memory demand, increasing errors and user frustration for all experience levels. Option C is a plausible nuance but overstates expert immunity: even expert users experience degraded performance when cognitive load exceeds working memory capacity, and feature proliferation reduces discoverability for everyone.

questions.title: Sustainable Materials: Bioplastics
questions.prompt: A company replaces conventional plastic packaging with PLA (polylactic acid) bioplastic, marketing it as fully compostable. Analyse the most significant limitation of this claim for a consumer who disposes of it in a home compost bin.

options.A: PLA is not actually derived from plant material, so the 'compostable' label is entirely false advertising.
options.B: PLA requires industrial composting conditions (around 58°C sustained heat) to break down; it will not compost effectively in a typical home bin.
options.C: PLA releases methane when composted, making it more harmful than conventional plastic in any composting scenario.
options.D: PLA composting is only limited by the fact that home bins lack sufficient moisture, which can be solved by adding water regularly.

questions.explanation: PLA (made from fermented plant starch, typically corn) is certified industrially compostable under EN 13432, requiring sustained temperatures around 58°C and specific microbial conditions found only in commercial facilities; in a home compost bin it typically persists for years like conventional plastic. Option D is wrong because the primary limiting factor is temperature and the specific thermophilic microbial community required, not moisture, which home bins generally possess adequately.

questions.title: Design Ethics: Planned Obsolescence
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer designs its latest model so the battery cannot be replaced by the user, and software updates intentionally slow down older models. Examine the ethical issues this raises from the perspective of both the consumer and the environment.

options.A: There are no significant ethical issues because consumers voluntarily purchase the product and manufacturers must innovate to remain competitive.
options.B: The primary ethical issue is aesthetic: the sealed design reduces the product's visual appeal, lowering consumer satisfaction.
options.C: It raises issues of consumer autonomy, deceptive practice, and increased electronic waste as devices are discarded prematurely due to artificially reduced performance.
options.D: The sole ethical concern is environmental; consumer interests are protected because manufacturers are legally required to provide free replacements.

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence through non-replaceable batteries and performance-throttling software (as documented in Apple's 'batterygate' controversy) reduces product lifespan artificially, forcing premature replacement and generating e-waste containing toxic materials like lithium and cobalt; it also undermines consumer autonomy by concealing the practice. Option A dismisses ethical responsibility by citing voluntary purchase, ignoring that consumers cannot give fully informed consent when the performance-throttling mechanism is undisclosed.

questions.title: Innovation: Disruptive vs. Sustaining
questions.prompt: Clayton Christensen distinguished between 'sustaining' and 'disruptive' innovations. A new electric car that is faster, more luxurious, and more expensive than existing models is released. Classify this innovation and justify your answer.

options.A: Disruptive, because electric technology fundamentally changes the automotive industry's energy source.
options.B: Sustaining, because it targets existing high-end customers with superior performance metrics, improving on what established players already offer.
options.C: Disruptive, because it creates an entirely new market segment that did not previously exist in the automotive industry.
options.D: Sustaining only if it is produced by an existing manufacturer; if produced by a new entrant, the same product would be classified as disruptive.

questions.explanation: Christensen's model defines sustaining innovation as improvements to existing products that serve established customers better—a faster, more expensive luxury electric car targets current high-end buyers with incremental performance gains, matching the definition exactly. Option A confuses the technology type with the market dynamic; electric propulsion itself is not inherently disruptive unless it first targets overlooked, low-end, or non-consuming markets—which an expensive luxury vehicle does not do.

questions.title: UX: Accessibility and Inclusive Design
questions.prompt: A developer designs an app where all interactive elements are distinguished only by colour (e.g., red means stop, green means go). Identify the design principle being violated and the specific user group most immediately excluded.

options.A: The principle of minimalist design is violated; elderly users who prefer simpler interfaces are the most affected group.
options.B: The principle of redundant coding is violated; users with colour vision deficiency (colour blindness) cannot reliably distinguish the interface states.
options.C: The principle of affordance is violated; users who are blind cannot interpret the colour signals, making screen readers essential.
options.D: The principle of consistency is violated; users who switch between apps with different colour conventions are confused by non-standard choices.

questions.explanation: Redundant coding requires that critical information is conveyed through at least two perceptual channels (e.g., colour plus shape or colour plus label); relying solely on colour excludes the approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women with colour vision deficiency, who cannot reliably distinguish red from green. Option C is plausible but less precise: blind users rely on screen readers which do not interpret colour at all, making colour irrelevant rather than ambiguous for them; the most immediately and specifically harmed group by a red/green distinction is those with red-green colour blindness.

questions.title: Iterative Testing: Validity of Results
questions.prompt: A student tests her ergonomic chair prototype with five members of her family in their home living room. A classmate argues the test results are not valid for the intended school environment. Examine this argument and identify the TWO most significant threats to validity.

options.A: Sample bias (family members share genetics and habits) and environmental mismatch (home setting differs from classroom tasks and furniture context).
options.B: Observer effect (family members perform better to please the designer) and insufficient prototype fidelity (the prototype is too rough to yield meaningful data).
options.C: Lack of a control group (no existing chair is tested simultaneously) and absence of quantitative measurement tools.
options.D: Time of day effects (testing at home occurs outside school hours) and seasonal variation (temperature differs between home and school).

questions.explanation: Sample bias is a critical threat because family members are not representative of the diverse range of student body sizes, postures, and school task behaviours; environmental mismatch means feedback about sitting comfort during home leisure activities will not accurately predict performance during sustained desk work in a classroom. Option B raises real concerns but observer effect (social desirability bias) is a secondary issue compared to representativeness, and there is no information suggesting the prototype's fidelity is inadequate.

questions.title: Data Privacy in Product Design
questions.prompt: A fitness tracker collects users' heart rate, sleep patterns, and GPS location continuously. The company's terms of service state that this data may be shared with 'third-party partners.' Evaluate the primary ethical design failure in this scenario.

options.A: The primary failure is technical: the device should use stronger encryption to prevent data interception by hackers.
options.B: The primary failure is commercial: sharing data with partners reduces the company's competitive advantage by revealing proprietary user insights.
options.C: The primary failure is one of informed consent: vague language about 'third-party partners' does not allow users to meaningfully understand or control how sensitive biometric data is used.
options.D: The primary failure is ergonomic: continuous data collection drains battery life, reducing the product's usability and therefore its ethical standing.

questions.explanation: Informed consent requires that users are given clear, specific, and understandable information about data usage; 'third-party partners' is deliberately vague and fails the principle of transparency required by frameworks like the GDPR, which mandates explicit purpose specification for sensitive biometric data. Option A identifies a real technical risk but is not the primary ethical design failure in the scenario described, which centres on how data is disclosed and shared rather than how it is secured in transit.

questions.title: Material Selection: Strength-to-Weight Ratio
questions.prompt: An aerospace engineer needs to select a material for a structural component that must be as light as possible while maintaining high tensile strength. Which material property ratio should she prioritise, and which material is most likely to be selected?

options.A: Stiffness-to-cost ratio; structural steel is selected because it offers the best balance of rigidity and low procurement cost.
options.B: Specific strength (tensile strength divided by density); carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) is selected for its exceptionally high specific strength.
options.C: Hardness-to-weight ratio; titanium alloy is selected because hardness is the most critical property in all structural aerospace applications.
options.D: Thermal conductivity-to-mass ratio; aluminium is selected because managing heat dissipation is the primary structural concern in aerospace.

questions.explanation: Specific strength (strength per unit density) is the key metric for weight-critical structural applications; CFRP has a specific tensile strength roughly five times that of structural steel, which is why it is used extensively in modern aircraft fuselages and wings. Option C is wrong because hardness measures resistance to surface deformation and scratch, not structural load-bearing capacity; titanium alloys have excellent specific strength but CFRP surpasses them in this metric for many aerospace applications.

questions.title: Empathy in Design Thinking
questions.prompt: During the 'empathise' stage of design thinking, a student interviews potential users about their daily routines. What is the PRIMARY goal of this stage?

options.A: To generate as many design solutions as possible before constraints are set
options.B: To deeply understand the needs, emotions, and contexts of the people you are designing for
options.C: To evaluate competing products already on the market
options.D: To define measurable success criteria for the final design

questions.explanation: The empathise stage is specifically about building a human-centred understanding of users — their feelings, motivations, and lived experiences — before any problem is defined or solutions considered. Option D describes the 'define' stage, and option A describes ideation, both of which come later in the design thinking process.

questions.title: Material Thermal Properties
questions.prompt: A designer is selecting a material for an outdoor bench that must remain comfortable to sit on even in hot summer sun. Which thermal property is MOST relevant to this decision?

options.A: High thermal conductivity, so heat dissipates quickly away from the surface
options.B: Low thermal conductivity, so the material does not absorb and transfer heat to the user
options.C: High specific heat capacity, so the material stores heat rather than releasing it
options.D: Low specific heat capacity, so the material heats and cools rapidly with ambient temperature

questions.explanation: A material with low thermal conductivity — such as wood or certain plastics — transfers heat slowly to the user's skin, keeping the surface feeling cooler. High thermal conductivity (option A) would actually make metal benches uncomfortably hot, as metals rapidly conduct heat from the sun directly to the sitter.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Types
questions.prompt: A fashion company creates a distinctive swoosh logo that it uses on all its products. Which form of intellectual property protection is MOST appropriate for protecting this logo?

options.A: Patent
options.B: Copyright
options.C: Trademark
options.D: Trade secret

questions.explanation: A trademark protects brand identifiers such as logos, names, and symbols that distinguish one company's goods from another's; it can be renewed indefinitely. Copyright protects original creative works like music and literature automatically upon creation, and would not be the primary protection for a commercial logo used as a brand identifier.

questions.title: Sustainability and Lifecycle
questions.prompt: In a lifecycle assessment (LCA), the 'cradle-to-gate' scope differs from 'cradle-to-grave'. Which statement BEST describes the cradle-to-gate scope?

options.A: It covers all stages from raw material extraction through to final disposal by the consumer
options.B: It covers only the use phase and end-of-life disposal of the product
options.C: It covers raw material extraction and manufacturing up to the point the product leaves the factory
options.D: It covers distribution and retail stages only, excluding manufacturing

questions.explanation: Cradle-to-gate analysis measures environmental impact from resource extraction through manufacturing, ending when the finished product leaves the production facility — before distribution or use. Option A describes cradle-to-grave, which is the full lifecycle including disposal.

questions.title: UX Research Validity
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'A survey with 500 responses always gives more useful UX data than a usability test with 5 participants.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because larger sample sizes always produce more statistically reliable results
options.B: The claim is incorrect because surveys measure stated preferences, while usability tests reveal actual behaviour and hidden usability problems
options.C: The claim is correct because usability tests are too time-consuming to provide actionable data
options.D: The claim is incorrect because surveys cannot be analysed quantitatively and are therefore always inferior

questions.explanation: Nielsen's research shows that testing with just 5 users uncovers approximately 85% of major usability problems, and observational usability tests capture real behaviour rather than self-reported opinions. Surveys gather breadth of preference data but miss the 'why' behind user struggles that direct observation reveals.

questions.title: Systems Engineering Feedback
questions.prompt: In systems engineering, what distinguishes a closed-loop system from an open-loop system?

options.A: A closed-loop system has no inputs; an open-loop system requires constant human input
options.B: A closed-loop system uses feedback from the output to automatically adjust the process; an open-loop system does not
options.C: A closed-loop system operates without any energy source; an open-loop system requires external power
options.D: A closed-loop system can only be digital; an open-loop system can be mechanical or digital

questions.explanation: The defining feature of a closed-loop (feedback) system is that output information is fed back to the controller to correct or adjust the process automatically — for example, a thermostat measuring room temperature to regulate a heater. An open-loop system, like a simple toaster timer, applies a fixed process regardless of the actual output state.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Choices
questions.prompt: A design team is in the early ideation stage and wants to test whether their concept layout makes intuitive sense to users. Which type of prototype is MOST appropriate at this point?

options.A: A high-fidelity digital prototype with full colour, fonts, and working interactions
options.B: A low-fidelity paper prototype or wireframe sketching key layout and flow
options.C: A functional engineering prototype built from the final chosen materials
options.D: A scale model manufactured using CNC machining for dimensional accuracy

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes such as paper sketches and wireframes are deliberately quick and cheap to produce, allowing rapid iteration on layout and conceptual flow before investing resources in detailed design. High-fidelity prototypes (option A) are more appropriate for later-stage testing of visual and interactive details, not early concept validation.

questions.title: Innovation Economics Basics
questions.prompt: In innovation economics, 'first-mover advantage' refers to the competitive benefit gained by the first company to enter a new market. Which scenario BEST illustrates a risk that can undermine first-mover advantage?

options.A: The first company sets the industry standard, forcing all competitors to adopt its format
options.B: Later entrants learn from the pioneer's mistakes and enter with a more refined, cheaper product
options.C: The first company builds strong brand loyalty that is difficult for competitors to erode
options.D: The first company secures exclusive long-term contracts with key suppliers

questions.explanation: A classic risk to first movers is the 'fast-follower' effect: competitors observe what works, avoid early costly mistakes, and launch improved or lower-priced alternatives — as seen when later smartphone manufacturers improved on early touchscreen designs. Options A, C, and D all describe advantages of being first, not risks.

questions.title: Ergonomics Anthropometric Data
questions.prompt: A designer uses the 5th-to-95th percentile anthropometric range when sizing a new office chair. Why is designing for this range, rather than the average (50th percentile) alone, considered better ergonomic practice?

options.A: It ensures the chair is comfortable for the largest possible range of body sizes in the target population
options.B: It reduces manufacturing cost by standardising a single size for most users
options.C: It complies with international patent law requirements for adjustable furniture
options.D: It guarantees the chair will be aesthetically acceptable to all cultural groups

questions.explanation: Designing only for the 50th-percentile 'average' user means the product fits no one particularly well and excludes those at the extremes of the distribution. The 5th-to-95th percentile range captures 90% of the target population's body dimensions, maximising comfort and usability across diverse users.

questions.title: Tech Ethics and Bias
questions.prompt: An AI hiring tool is trained exclusively on a company's historical recruitment data from the past 20 years. A student argues this approach could produce biased outcomes. What is the MOST likely source of that bias?

options.A: The algorithm will run too slowly on large datasets, causing random errors
options.B: Historical hiring decisions may reflect past discrimination, which the AI will learn and replicate
options.C: The company's data is stored digitally and is therefore vulnerable to hacking
options.D: Training on company-specific data violates international copyright law

questions.explanation: If historical hiring data reflects systemic biases — for example, favouring certain demographics — the AI learns those patterns as desirable predictors of success, perpetuating discrimination at scale. Amazon famously scrapped such a tool in 2018 after discovering it systematically downranked CVs mentioning women's colleges. Data security (option C) is a separate concern unrelated to algorithmic bias.

questions.title: Define Stage Problem Statement
questions.prompt: In the design thinking process, the 'define' stage produces a Point of View (POV) statement. Which of the following is a correctly structured POV statement?

options.A: 'We will build an app that sends daily reminders to elderly users to take their medication.'
options.B: 'Elderly users need a way to remember their medication schedule because cognitive load increases with age and multiple prescriptions.'
options.C: 'The problem is that 40% of elderly patients miss doses, so we should survey them about their habits.'
options.D: 'Our goal is to increase medication adherence by 25% within six months using a digital solution.'

questions.explanation: A POV statement follows the structure: [User] needs [need] because [insight] — it centres on the user's need and the underlying reason, without prescribing a solution. Option A jumps directly to a solution (an app), and option D states a business metric goal rather than articulating a user-centred need.

questions.title: Material Sustainability Properties
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following student statement: 'Biodegradable plastics are always more sustainable than conventional plastics because they break down naturally and leave no waste.'

options.A: The error is that conventional plastics also biodegrade, just at a slower rate, making them equally sustainable
options.B: The error is that many biodegradable plastics only break down under specific industrial composting conditions and may persist in landfill
options.C: The error is that biodegradable plastics are always more expensive, which makes them unsustainable from an economic perspective
options.D: The error is that biodegradation always releases toxic chemicals, making biodegradable plastics more harmful

questions.explanation: Many plastics labelled 'biodegradable' or 'compostable' require elevated temperatures and specific microbial conditions found only in industrial composting facilities; in a standard landfill they degrade at rates comparable to conventional plastic. This means the environmental benefit depends entirely on the disposal infrastructure available.

questions.title: UX Persona Development
questions.prompt: A UX designer creates a 'persona' as part of their research process. What is the PRIMARY purpose of a persona in design?

options.A: To provide a legally binding description of the target customer for marketing contracts
options.B: To create a fictional but research-based representation of a typical user, keeping design decisions focused on real user needs
options.C: To replace the need for actual user interviews by imagining what users might want
options.D: To document the technical specifications the engineering team must meet during development

questions.explanation: Personas synthesise real research data — interviews, observations, surveys — into a representative fictional character that helps designers empathise with and make decisions for their target users throughout the project. They are grounded in actual data, not invented to replace research, which distinguishes a valid persona from mere assumption.

questions.title: Circular Economy Principles
questions.prompt: A furniture company redesigns its chairs so that all components can be disassembled and each material returned to a separate recycling stream. This strategy is BEST described as which circular economy principle?

options.A: Planned obsolescence, to stimulate regular repurchasing cycles
options.B: Design for disassembly, to maintain material value through multiple use cycles
options.C: Vertical integration, to control all stages of the supply chain
options.D: Lean manufacturing, to minimise waste during the production process

questions.explanation: Design for disassembly (DfD) is a core circular economy strategy in which products are engineered so components can be easily separated at end of life, allowing materials to re-enter production streams at high quality. Planned obsolescence (option A) is the opposite philosophy — deliberately shortening product life to drive new sales.

questions.title: Compression vs Tension Strength
questions.prompt: An architect selects concrete for the columns of a building and steel cables for the suspended bridge deck. What material property principle justifies these different choices?

options.A: Concrete has high compressive strength but low tensile strength; steel has high tensile strength suitable for cables under tension
options.B: Concrete has high tensile strength but low compressive strength; steel is used in columns because it is cheaper
options.C: Both materials have equal tensile and compressive strength, but concrete is chosen for aesthetics
options.D: Steel has higher compressive strength than concrete, making it ideal for load-bearing columns

questions.explanation: Concrete can withstand large compressive forces (around 20–50 MPa) but has very low tensile strength (roughly 2–5 MPa), making it ideal for columns in compression. Steel has extremely high tensile strength (up to 500 MPa for structural grades), making it the correct choice for cables and reinforcement elements that must resist pulling forces.

questions.title: Innovation Diffusion Curve
questions.prompt: Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovations theory describes how new technologies spread through a population. Which group adopts a new technology LAST, according to this model?

options.A: Early adopters
options.B: Late majority
options.C: Laggards
options.D: Early majority

questions.explanation: Rogers' model places adoption groups in order: innovators → early adopters → early majority → late majority → laggards. Laggards are the last to adopt, often doing so only when a technology becomes unavoidable or when older alternatives are discontinued. The late majority (option B) adopts before laggards, driven by social pressure and necessity.

questions.title: Ethical Design Data Privacy
questions.prompt: A smart speaker company stores all voice recordings from users' homes indefinitely on its servers to improve speech recognition. What ethical design principle does this practice MOST clearly violate?

options.A: The principle of universal design, which requires products to be accessible to all users
options.B: The principle of data minimisation, which holds that only the minimum necessary data should be collected and retained
options.C: The principle of open-source development, which requires companies to share their source code
options.D: The principle of iterative design, which requires products to be regularly updated based on feedback

questions.explanation: Data minimisation is a core principle of privacy frameworks including GDPR, requiring organisations to collect only what is strictly necessary and retain it no longer than needed. Storing all voice recordings indefinitely goes far beyond what is required for the stated purpose, violating this principle. Universal design (option A) concerns accessibility for people with varying abilities, not data handling.

questions.title: Iterative Design Process
questions.prompt: What would happen if a design team skipped the testing phase entirely and moved straight from prototype to full production?

options.A: The product would automatically meet user needs because the prototype stage already incorporates user research
options.B: Undetected usability flaws and design errors could be replicated at scale, making corrections extremely costly
options.C: The product would reach market faster with no disadvantage, because testing only identifies minor cosmetic issues
options.D: Regulatory bodies would approve the product more quickly because fewer stages are documented

questions.explanation: Testing exists to identify errors, mismatches with user needs, and safety issues before mass production commits resources. A flaw undetected at prototype stage becomes embedded in thousands or millions of units, making recalls or redesigns exponentially more expensive — a risk exemplified by high-profile product recalls in the automotive and electronics industries.

questions.title: Design for Sustainability Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A student claims: 'Using recycled aluminium is always better for the environment than using virgin aluminium.' To what extent is this claim accurate?

options.A: The claim is entirely accurate because recycling always uses less energy than primary production for any metal
options.B: The claim is largely accurate: recycling aluminium uses approximately 95% less energy than smelting bauxite, though collection and sorting logistics still carry some environmental cost
options.C: The claim is inaccurate because recycled aluminium is structurally weaker and must be replaced more often, increasing overall environmental impact
options.D: The claim is inaccurate because the energy used in recycling aluminium exceeds that of primary smelting

questions.explanation: Recycling aluminium requires only about 5% of the energy needed for primary production from bauxite ore via the Bayer and Hall-Héroult processes, making it one of the most energy-efficient recycling processes for any metal. However, transport, sorting, and contamination handling in the recycling supply chain do carry residual environmental costs, so 'always better in every dimension' overstates the case.

questions.title: Systems Thinking Emergence
questions.prompt: In systems thinking, 'emergence' refers to properties that arise from the interaction of system components. Which of the following is the BEST example of an emergent property?

options.A: A bicycle wheel's mass, which equals the sum of the masses of its individual spokes and rim
options.B: The ability of a flock of birds to navigate and avoid obstacles collectively, despite no single bird directing the flock
options.C: The voltage across a battery, which remains constant regardless of the circuit it is connected to
options.D: The hardness of a steel bolt, which is a property measurable in any single component in isolation

questions.explanation: Flocking behaviour — collective navigation without central control — emerges only from the interactions between individual birds following simple local rules; it cannot be observed by studying a single bird in isolation. This is the defining characteristic of emergence: properties that exist at the system level but not in any individual component.

questions.title: Intellectual Property Open Source
questions.prompt: A software developer releases their code under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. What does this licence specifically require of anyone who uses or modifies the code?

options.A: Users must pay a royalty fee to the original developer for every copy distributed
options.B: Users must credit the original creator when sharing or building upon the work
options.C: Users must release any modified version under an identical open-source licence
options.D: Users are prohibited from using the work for any commercial purpose

questions.explanation: The Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) licence requires only that the original creator is credited — it permits use, modification, and even commercial use without payment, provided attribution is given. Requiring derivative works to use the same licence is the 'ShareAlike' condition (CC BY-SA), which is a separate and more restrictive licence variant.

questions.title: Planned Obsolescence Ethics
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer releases a software update that measurably slows down older phone models, encouraging users to buy new ones. Critically assess the primary ethical concern with this practice.

options.A: It violates patent law because the manufacturer is modifying its own previously sold product
options.B: It manipulates consumers into unnecessary purchases, generating electronic waste and undermining user autonomy
options.C: It is primarily a technical problem because slower software reduces battery efficiency
options.D: It is ethically acceptable because manufacturers have a legal obligation to encourage upgrades for security reasons

questions.explanation: Deliberately degrading performance to drive sales is a form of planned obsolescence that removes consumer choice, generates significant electronic waste — e-waste is the world's fastest-growing waste stream — and breaches the ethical principle of user autonomy. Apple was fined €25 million by French authorities in 2020 for exactly this practice without informed user consent.

questions.title: Ideation SCAMPER Technique
questions.prompt: A product design team uses the SCAMPER ideation technique. The 'R' in SCAMPER stands for 'Reverse or Rearrange.' How would a team CORRECTLY apply this prompt to redesign a conventional backpack?

options.A: Replace the canvas fabric with a waterproof polymer composite
options.B: Ask: what if the storage compartments opened from the bottom rather than the top, or the straps were on the front?
options.C: Combine the backpack with a sleeping bag to create a multifunctional camping product
options.D: Eliminate all internal dividers to create a single open-storage volume

questions.explanation: The 'Reverse or Rearrange' prompt asks designers to invert assumptions about how or where elements are positioned — for example, flipping the opening direction or swapping front and back to prompt novel configurations. Option A describes 'Substitute' (replacing a material), and option C describes 'Combine', both of which are different SCAMPER letters.

questions.title: Material Hardness vs Toughness
questions.prompt: Compare hardness and toughness as material properties. A student states: 'A harder material is always tougher.' Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.A: There is no error; hardness and toughness always increase together in engineering materials
options.B: Hardness measures resistance to surface scratching or indentation, while toughness measures energy absorbed before fracture; highly hard materials are often brittle and therefore low in toughness
options.C: The error is that toughness refers to a material's density, not its resistance to fracture
options.D: The error is that hardness can only be measured at temperatures above 200 °C, making room-temperature comparisons invalid

questions.explanation: Glass and ceramics are extremely hard (high scratch resistance) but fracture with little energy absorption, making them brittle and low in toughness. Tough materials like rubber or mild steel can absorb significant impact energy before breaking. This inverse relationship is a fundamental concept in materials science — increasing hardness through heat treatment often reduces toughness.

questions.title: Human-Centred Design Principles
questions.prompt: Don Norman's concept of 'affordance' in design refers to which of the following?

options.A: The financial cost a user must pay to access a product or service
options.B: A design quality that clearly communicates to a user how an object is meant to be used or interacted with
options.C: The minimum level of accessibility a product must achieve to meet disability legislation
options.D: The range of cultural contexts in which a product can be used without modification

questions.explanation: Norman defined affordance as the perceived and actual properties of an object that suggest how it should be used — a door handle's shape affords pulling, a flat plate affords pushing. It is a perceptual cue embedded in the design itself, not a legal standard or cost factor. Confusing affordance with accessibility requirements (option C) is a common misconception.

questions.title: Design Thinking: Empathy Stage
questions.prompt: During the empathise stage of design thinking, a student interviews potential users about their daily routines. Which type of question will yield the most useful data for defining the design problem?

options.A: Closed questions with yes/no answers to gather measurable data quickly
options.B: Open-ended questions that invite users to describe experiences and feelings
options.C: Leading questions that confirm the designer's existing assumptions
options.D: Hypothetical questions asking users to predict their future behaviour

questions.explanation: Open-ended questions allow users to express needs, frustrations, and contexts in their own words, producing rich qualitative insight that defines the real problem. Closed yes/no questions generate limited data and miss the nuance needed to empathise deeply; hypothetical questions are unreliable because people often misjudge their own future behaviour.

questions.title: Material Properties: Tensile Strength
questions.prompt: A student claims that a material with high tensile strength is automatically the best choice for a climbing rope. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully correct because tensile strength is the only property that prevents a rope from snapping under load
options.B: The claim is partially correct; tensile strength matters, but elongation and flexibility are also critical for absorbing sudden loads safely
options.C: The claim is incorrect because climbing ropes rely entirely on compressive strength rather than tensile strength
options.D: The claim is partially correct; tensile strength matters, but thermal conductivity is equally important for rope safety

questions.explanation: Climbing ropes must have high tensile strength to resist breaking, but they also require controlled elongation (dynamic stretch) to absorb the energy of a fall without injuring the climber — a property known as impact absorption. Compressive strength is irrelevant to ropes, which experience tension not compression; thermal conductivity has negligible relevance in standard climbing conditions.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trademark vs Patent
questions.prompt: A beverage company has a distinctive bottle shape that customers associate with their brand. Which form of intellectual property protection is most appropriate for this shape?

options.A: Patent, because the shape represents a novel functional invention
options.B: Copyright, because the shape is an original artistic creation
options.C: Trade secret, because the shape can be kept confidential from competitors
options.D: Trademark, because the shape serves as a brand identifier distinguishing it in the marketplace

questions.explanation: A distinctive product shape that identifies a brand's origin can be registered as a three-dimensional trademark (trade dress), as seen with the Coca-Cola contour bottle. A patent protects novel functional inventions with limited duration, not brand identifiers; copyright protects artistic expression but does not cover product shapes used as brand signals.

questions.title: Sustainability: Cradle-to-Cradle Concept
questions.prompt: The cradle-to-cradle (C2C) design philosophy differs from traditional cradle-to-grave thinking. What is the defining principle of C2C design?

options.A: Products are made as cheaply as possible so consumers can afford to replace them frequently
options.B: All materials in a product are designed to be safely cycled back into either biological or technical systems indefinitely
options.C: Products are designed to last as long as possible before being sent to landfill
options.D: Manufacturing waste is minimised by using only recycled inputs at the start of production

questions.explanation: C2C, developed by McDonough and Braungart, holds that every material should re-enter either a biological cycle (safely composting) or a technical cycle (returned to manufacturers for reuse) — eliminating the concept of waste entirely. Extended product lifespan is a related but different strategy (longevity design), and using recycled inputs addresses only the beginning of a product's life rather than its end-of-life destination.

questions.title: UX Research: Think-Aloud Protocol
questions.prompt: A UX researcher asks participants to speak their thoughts out loud while navigating a new website. What is the primary purpose of this think-aloud protocol?

options.A: To measure how quickly users complete tasks and generate quantitative performance benchmarks
options.B: To reveal users' real-time cognitive processes, confusion points, and mental models
options.C: To allow researchers to correct users' mistakes before they become frustrated
options.D: To validate that the website meets the technical specifications in the design brief

questions.explanation: The think-aloud protocol, developed by Ericsson and Simon, externalises users' inner reasoning so researchers can identify where mental models diverge from the interface design — information unavailable from task-completion times alone. Intervening to correct users (option C) would contaminate the data; technical specification checks are done through functional testing, not observational UX research.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a home thermostat system, the thermostat measures room temperature and switches the heater off when the target temperature is reached. Which systems engineering concept does this illustrate?

options.A: A positive feedback loop that amplifies the heating effect over time
options.B: An open-loop control system that ignores actual room temperature
options.C: A negative feedback loop that maintains the system near a set point
options.D: A feedforward control system that predicts temperature before it changes

questions.explanation: A thermostat uses negative feedback: the output (room temperature) is measured and compared to the desired set point, and the difference (error) is used to reduce the gap by switching the heater off — a self-correcting mechanism. A positive feedback loop would amplify the deviation rather than reduce it; an open-loop system would not use temperature measurement to adjust its behaviour.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: First-Mover Advantage
questions.prompt: To what extent does being the first company to introduce a new product to market guarantee long-term commercial success?

options.A: Completely, because customers always remain loyal to the brand they encountered first
options.B: Not at all, because early entry always gives competitors time to study and improve upon the product
options.C: To a limited extent, because first-mover advantages such as brand recognition can be eroded by fast-follower competitors with superior resources
options.D: Completely, because patents automatically prevent any competitor from entering the same market

questions.explanation: First-mover advantages — including brand loyalty, network effects, and resource pre-emption — are real but not permanent; fast followers like Google (not the first search engine) or Facebook (not the first social network) can displace pioneers by learning from their mistakes. Customer loyalty is not guaranteed, and patents are time-limited and market-specific, so they do not permanently block all competition.

questions.title: Prototyping: Fidelity Levels
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following statement: 'A high-fidelity prototype should always be built first because it most accurately represents the final product and therefore gives the most useful feedback.'

options.A: There is no error; high-fidelity prototypes consistently produce the most actionable user feedback at every stage
options.B: The error is that high-fidelity prototypes are too expensive to build and should be avoided entirely
options.C: The error is that early low-fidelity prototypes allow rapid, cheap testing of core concepts before investing resources in detailed builds
options.D: The error is that only digital products use high-fidelity prototypes; physical products always use low-fidelity models

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes (e.g., paper sketches, cardboard models) let designers test fundamental assumptions quickly and cheaply, reducing the risk of expensive mistakes in high-fidelity builds; this is a core principle of iterative design. High-fidelity prototypes are valuable later in the process but are costly to revise if major concept flaws are discovered; saying all prototypes should be high-fidelity ignores the strategic value of early rough testing.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A facial recognition system used by a school for attendance performs significantly less accurately for students with darker skin tones. What is the most likely cause of this disparity?

options.A: The camera hardware physically cannot detect darker skin tones due to sensor limitations
options.B: The algorithm was trained on a dataset underrepresenting darker skin tones, embedding bias into its outputs
options.C: Students with darker skin tones are statistically more likely to be absent, skewing the data
options.D: Darker skin tones reflect less infrared light, making any camera-based system inherently inaccurate

questions.explanation: Research — including the MIT Gender Shades study — has demonstrated that facial recognition systems trained on non-diverse datasets consistently show higher error rates for underrepresented demographic groups, a classic case of algorithmic bias. While lighting can affect image quality, the primary documented cause is dataset imbalance, not a physical impossibility of detection; option C introduces a false and harmful statistical claim.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment: Hotspot Analysis
questions.prompt: An LCA of a cotton T-shirt reveals that 70% of its total water consumption occurs during raw material cultivation. In LCA terminology, what is this stage called?

options.A: An end-of-life burden, because it represents the disposal impact of the product
options.B: A hotspot, because it is the lifecycle stage with the greatest environmental impact
options.C: A functional unit, because it defines the baseline measurement for comparison
options.D: A system boundary, because it marks the limit of the assessment's scope

questions.explanation: In LCA methodology, a 'hotspot' refers to the lifecycle stage or process responsible for a disproportionately large share of a specific environmental impact — here, water use during cotton cultivation. A functional unit is the reference unit used for comparison (e.g., 'one T-shirt worn 50 times'), not a stage with high impact; system boundary defines what is included or excluded from the study.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Anthropometric Data
questions.prompt: A chair designer uses the 5th-percentile female and 95th-percentile male anthropometric measurements when setting the adjustable height range of a new office chair. Why are these specific percentiles chosen rather than the average?

options.A: Because the average excludes extreme users and designing for the range from 5th to 95th percentile accommodates 90% of the target population
options.B: Because designing for the average automatically includes all users at both extremes of the population
options.C: Because the 5th and 95th percentiles represent the smallest and tallest individuals ever recorded
options.D: Because regulatory standards legally require chair heights to be set at exactly these percentiles

questions.explanation: Designing for the 5th-to-95th-percentile range ensures the product accommodates 90% of the target population — a standard ergonomic design strategy that avoids excluding the smallest and largest users while keeping the design practical. Designing for the average (50th percentile) would fit only one data point and exclude most users at the extremes; the percentiles do not represent absolute biological limits.

questions.title: Define Stage: Problem Statement
questions.prompt: After empathising with users, a design team writes: 'We need to build a faster website.' A design teacher says this is not a proper problem statement. What is missing?

options.A: A specific technology stack specifying which programming language will be used
options.B: A user-centred framing that identifies who has the problem and what human need is unmet
options.C: A budget figure indicating how much the solution will cost to implement
options.D: A timeline showing the project's Gantt chart milestones

questions.explanation: A well-formed problem statement in design thinking is user-centred: it names a specific user group, describes their unmet need, and avoids prescribing solutions — for example, 'Elderly users need a way to access health information online because slow-loading pages cause them to give up.' The statement 'build a faster website' jumps directly to a solution. Budget and timelines belong in the design brief, not the problem statement.

questions.title: Sustainability: Embodied Energy
questions.prompt: Which of the following best defines 'embodied energy' in the context of sustainable design?

options.A: The electrical energy a product consumes during its operational lifespan
options.B: The total energy required to extract, process, manufacture, and transport a product before it is used
options.C: The energy released when a product is incinerated at the end of its life
options.D: The solar energy captured by renewable materials used in a product's construction

questions.explanation: Embodied energy encompasses all energy inputs upstream of a product's use phase — resource extraction, material processing, manufacturing, and transport — and is a key metric in LCA for understanding a product's total environmental footprint. Operational energy (option A) is a separate category; incineration energy recovery is an end-of-life consideration, not embodied energy.

questions.title: Innovation: Disruptive vs Sustaining
questions.prompt: A student claims that a new smartphone with a 20% better camera is a disruptive innovation because it changes how people take photos. Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct because any improvement that changes user behaviour qualifies as disruptive innovation
options.B: The claim is incorrect; a 20% camera improvement is a sustaining innovation that improves an existing product for existing customers, not a disruptive one
options.C: The claim is correct because smartphone cameras have already disrupted the dedicated camera market
options.D: The claim is incorrect because only software changes can be considered disruptive innovations

questions.explanation: Clayton Christensen's theory defines disruptive innovation as a process where a simpler, often cheaper product enters at the bottom of a market and eventually displaces incumbents — not an incremental improvement to an existing product for existing customers. A 20% camera upgrade serves current high-end users better, making it a sustaining innovation. The historical disruption of dedicated cameras by smartphones was already a past event and does not make every subsequent camera improvement disruptive.

questions.title: Material Properties: Hardness vs Toughness
questions.prompt: Compare hardness and toughness as material properties. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?

options.A: Hardness is the ability to absorb energy without fracturing; toughness is resistance to surface scratching
options.B: Hardness and toughness are interchangeable terms describing a material's resistance to deformation
options.C: Hardness is resistance to surface indentation or scratching; toughness is the ability to absorb energy and resist fracture
options.D: Hardness refers to a material's stiffness under compression; toughness refers to its flexibility under tension

questions.explanation: Hardness measures a material's resistance to localised surface deformation (assessed by tests like Vickers or Mohs), while toughness measures the total energy a material can absorb before fracturing — these can trade off against each other, as very hard materials (e.g., glass) are often brittle and low in toughness. Stiffness (Young's modulus) is a third, separate property describing resistance to elastic deformation.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Data Privacy by Design
questions.prompt: The principle of 'privacy by design' requires designers to embed data protection into a product from the outset. Which design decision best exemplifies this principle?

options.A: Adding a privacy policy page to an app after it has been developed and launched
options.B: Collecting all available user data during development and filtering out sensitive data before release
options.C: Designing the app to collect only the minimum data necessary for its function, with user consent controls built into the interface
options.D: Encrypting user data on the server after a security breach has been discovered

questions.explanation: Privacy by design, formalised by Ann Cavoukian and embedded in regulations like GDPR, requires data minimisation (collecting only what is needed) and proactive privacy controls built into the architecture from the start — not added later. Options A and D are reactive, adding privacy measures after the fact. Option B collects maximum data first, which itself creates risk and violates the data minimisation principle.

questions.title: Design Brief: Constraints vs Criteria
questions.prompt: A design brief states: 'The product must cost under $15 to manufacture' and 'The product should be comfortable to hold for extended periods.' Which statement correctly classifies these two requirements?

options.A: Both are constraints because they both set limits on the design solution
options.B: Both are criteria because they both describe desirable characteristics of the solution
options.C: The cost limit is a constraint (a non-negotiable limit); comfort is a criterion (a measurable quality standard the design should meet)
options.D: The cost limit is a criterion; comfort is a constraint because ergonomic requirements are legally mandated

questions.explanation: In design methodology, constraints are non-negotiable boundaries (budget, legal limits, physical size) that eliminate certain solutions entirely, while criteria are measurable standards of quality the solution should achieve. Cost under $15 is a hard constraint; comfort is a design criterion that can be tested and measured but allows design freedom in how it is achieved.

questions.title: Sustainability: Upcycling vs Recycling
questions.prompt: A designer takes discarded glass bottles and crafts them into decorative light fixtures that sell for more than the original bottles. This process is best described as:

options.A: Recycling, because the glass is being reprocessed into a new product
options.B: Downcycling, because the bottles lose their original function and value
options.C: Upcycling, because the waste material is transformed into a product of higher value
options.D: Remanufacturing, because the bottles are disassembled and rebuilt to original specifications

questions.explanation: Upcycling converts waste materials into products of greater value or quality without breaking the material down — the bottles retain their glass form but gain higher economic and aesthetic value as light fixtures. Recycling involves breaking materials down to raw form (melting glass); downcycling produces lower-value outputs (e.g., crushed glass for road aggregate); remanufacturing restores used products to original performance specifications.

questions.title: Systems Engineering: Subsystems
questions.prompt: What would happen if a designer failed to consider the interfaces between subsystems when engineering a complex product such as an electric vehicle?

options.A: Each subsystem would function perfectly, and the overall vehicle performance would be the sum of individual subsystem performances
options.B: Incompatibilities between subsystems could cause system-level failures even if each individual subsystem performs correctly in isolation
options.C: The vehicle would automatically adapt its subsystems to resolve any compatibility issues during operation
options.D: Only the most expensive subsystem would fail, while others continue to operate normally

questions.explanation: Systems engineering recognises that emergent failures often arise at interfaces between subsystems — for example, the battery management system and thermal management system of an EV must communicate precisely or thermal runaway can occur even if both are individually sound. This is why interface control documents are central to systems design; subsystems do not self-adapt to resolve incompatibilities without explicit design provision.

questions.title: UX Research: Quantitative Methods
questions.prompt: A design team wants to determine which of two app navigation layouts results in faster task completion across a large sample of 200 users. Which research method is most appropriate?

options.A: A focus group where users discuss which layout they prefer
options.B: A contextual inquiry where a researcher observes users in their home environments
options.C: A controlled A/B test measuring task-completion times for both layouts across the sample
options.D: An unstructured interview asking users to describe their navigation habits

questions.explanation: An A/B test is a controlled quantitative experiment that randomly assigns users to two conditions and measures objective performance metrics (e.g., task-completion time), making it ideal for comparing two design variants across a large sample. Focus groups and interviews yield qualitative preference data but cannot reliably measure performance differences; contextual inquiry is observational and not suited to controlled comparison.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Open Source
questions.prompt: A software company releases its product under an open-source licence. Which correctly describes the primary consequence of this decision?

options.A: The company permanently loses all intellectual property rights and cannot commercialise any derivative work
options.B: Any person or organisation may view, modify, and distribute the source code under the terms of the licence
options.C: Only academic institutions are permitted to access and modify the code without commercial use
options.D: The code enters the public domain, meaning no licence terms apply to its use or modification

questions.explanation: Open-source licences (such as MIT, Apache, or GPL) legally permit users to access, modify, and redistribute source code, subject to specific conditions that vary by licence — for example, the GPL requires derivative works to also be open-source (copyleft). The company retains copyright; open source does not mean public domain (which has no licence restrictions at all); access is not restricted to academic users.

questions.title: Material Selection: Life Cycle
questions.prompt: A student argues that aluminium is always a more sustainable material than plastic because it can be recycled indefinitely. Evaluate this argument.

options.A: The argument is fully correct; aluminium's infinite recyclability makes it sustainable in all applications
options.B: The argument is overstated; primary aluminium production is extremely energy-intensive, so sustainability depends on recycled content, energy source, and product lifespan
options.C: The argument is incorrect; aluminium cannot be recycled more than three times before its properties degrade significantly
options.D: The argument is correct only for food packaging, where aluminium's barrier properties justify its production energy cost

questions.explanation: While recycled aluminium requires only about 5% of the energy of primary smelting, producing virgin aluminium is one of the most energy-intensive industrial processes (approximately 15 kWh/kg), and sustainability claims must be assessed across the full lifecycle including extraction, use phase, and actual recycling rates in context. Aluminium does not degrade over recycling cycles (option C is a misconception more applicable to some polymers); restricting the argument to food packaging (option D) arbitrarily narrows the analysis.

questions.title: Ideation: SCAMPER Technique
questions.prompt: During ideation, a student applies the SCAMPER technique. The 'A' in SCAMPER stands for 'Adapt.' Which of the following correctly demonstrates this operation applied to a standard umbrella?

options.A: Removing the handle to make the umbrella lighter
options.B: Borrowing the aerodynamic canopy shape used in parachutes and applying it to the umbrella to resist wind inversion
options.C: Combining the umbrella with a backpack to create a hands-free solution
options.D: Replacing the metal frame with a shape-memory polymer that self-opens when wet

questions.explanation: The 'Adapt' operation in SCAMPER asks what ideas from other contexts can be borrowed and applied to the product — adapting the parachute canopy's aerodynamic geometry to reduce wind inversion is a textbook example. 'Combine' corresponds to the 'C' (combining umbrella with backpack); 'Eliminate' corresponds to 'E' (removing the handle); 'Substitute' corresponds to 'S' (replacing metal with polymer).

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Planned Obsolescence
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer intentionally releases a software update that slows down older models. Critically assess the ethical issue this raises.

options.A: There is no ethical issue; manufacturers have the right to optimise software for new hardware without obligation to older devices
options.B: The practice raises concerns about consumer deception and sustainability, as it can coerce users into premature purchases and increases electronic waste
options.C: The only issue is environmental, since slowing phones does not affect consumers financially
options.D: The practice is ethical because slower older devices benefit network performance for all users

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence through software throttling — as documented in Apple's 2017 'batterygate' case, which resulted in a $113 million settlement — raises dual concerns: it deceives consumers who may not know their device is being slowed, and it pressures premature replacement, generating e-waste. Dismissing financial harm (option C) ignores the coercive commercial outcome; claiming network benefits (option D) has not been established as a justification and deflects from consumer impact.

questions.title: Design Testing: Validity
questions.prompt: A student tests a new ergonomic keyboard by measuring typing speed of ten university professors over one day. A classmate says the results cannot be used to redesign a keyboard intended for secondary school students. Why is the classmate correct?

options.A: Because typing speed is not a valid measure of keyboard ergonomics under any circumstances
options.B: Because the test sample does not represent the target user group, reducing the external validity of the findings
options.C: Because one day of testing is too short for any ergonomic study to produce meaningful data
options.D: Because university professors type faster than students, so the keyboard would perform worse in school settings

questions.explanation: External validity refers to whether findings can be generalised to the intended population; testing professors for a student-targeted product violates this because hand size, typing habits, and skill levels differ significantly between the groups. While duration of testing is a separate validity concern, the primary flaw the classmate identifies is sample mismatch — a fundamental issue of ecological and population validity in design research.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Sympathy in Design
questions.prompt: A student conducting user research for a mobility aid says, 'I feel sorry for wheelchair users, so I know what they need.' A design teacher challenges this statement. Which response BEST explains why the student's reasoning is flawed?

options.A: Sympathy is sufficient because emotional connection automatically produces accurate user insights.
options.B: Empathy requires immersive observation and interaction; sympathy is a personal emotional reaction that does not reveal actual user needs or pain points.
options.C: The student should instead rely on secondary data such as sales figures rather than any form of emotional engagement.
options.D: Empathy and sympathy are interchangeable terms in the design thinking process, so neither leads to better research outcomes.

questions.explanation: Empathy in design thinking involves direct, immersive methods — interviews, observation, bodily experience — to uncover genuine user needs; sympathy is merely feeling pity without that investigative depth. The top distractor (A) is wrong because emotional reaction alone creates designer-centred assumptions rather than evidence-based insight.

questions.title: Material Fatigue Concepts
questions.prompt: An engineer notices that a metal bridge component fails after millions of low-stress load cycles, even though each individual load was far below the material's yield strength. Which concept BEST explains this failure?

options.A: Plastic deformation, because the metal permanently stretched under repeated stress.
options.B: Corrosion fatigue, because all metal failures under repeated loading must involve oxidation.
options.C: Material fatigue, because repeated cyclic stress causes microscopic cracks that propagate until sudden fracture occurs.
options.D: Elastic strain, because the component returned to its original shape each time and therefore accumulated no damage.

questions.explanation: Material fatigue describes crack initiation and propagation under cyclic loading well below yield strength — the Wöhler S-N curve models this quantitatively. Option D is a common misconception: elastic recovery does not mean no internal damage occurs, as micro-crack growth is irreversible even within the elastic range.

questions.title: UX Heuristic Evaluation
questions.prompt: A UX researcher uses Nielsen's heuristic evaluation rather than user testing to assess a new banking app. To what extent is this approach sufficient as a standalone usability method?

options.A: It is fully sufficient because expert evaluators can identify all usability problems without involving real users.
options.B: It is partially sufficient: heuristic evaluation efficiently identifies design-rule violations but may miss context-specific problems that only real users would encounter.
options.C: It is insufficient because heuristics only apply to mobile applications, not banking platforms.
options.D: It is fully sufficient because banking regulations require expert review rather than user participation.

questions.explanation: Heuristic evaluation is a discount usability method that catches structural design violations quickly, but research shows it misses approximately 50% of real-user problems because evaluators cannot replicate authentic user mental models and contexts. Option A is the top distractor — expert review is valuable but consistently misses emergent, context-driven usability failures.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secrets
questions.prompt: A company keeps its manufacturing process confidential rather than filing a patent. Which statement BEST evaluates the trade-off between trade secrets and patents as forms of intellectual property protection?

options.A: Trade secrets provide unlimited protection as long as secrecy is maintained, whereas patents expire after roughly 20 years but require public disclosure of the invention.
options.B: Patents provide unlimited protection, whereas trade secrets expire after 10 years.
options.C: Trade secrets and patents both require registration with an intellectual property office to be legally enforceable.
options.D: A patent is always preferable because trade secrets offer no legal protection if a competitor independently discovers the same process.

questions.explanation: A utility patent grants exclusive rights for approximately 20 years in exchange for full public disclosure; a trade secret can persist indefinitely (e.g., Coca-Cola's formula) but provides no protection if a competitor independently develops the same solution. Option D is wrong: trade secrets are legally protected through misappropriation law — the issue is independent discovery, not absence of protection.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Decisions
questions.prompt: Early in a design project, a team must decide whether to build a high-fidelity digital prototype or a low-fidelity paper prototype. Which reasoning BEST justifies choosing low-fidelity at this stage?

options.A: Low-fidelity prototypes should never be shown to clients because they undermine professional credibility.
options.B: Low-fidelity prototypes allow rapid, cheap iteration on core concepts before resources are committed, and users focus on function rather than aesthetic details.
options.C: High-fidelity prototypes are always preferred because they produce more statistically reliable usability data.
options.D: Low-fidelity prototypes are only appropriate for physical products, not digital interfaces.

questions.explanation: Paper and low-fidelity prototypes reduce sunk-cost bias and allow teams to pivot quickly; research by Snyder (2003) shows users critique function rather than aesthetics when fidelity is low, yielding more honest structural feedback. Option C is wrong because early high-fidelity prototypes often bias users toward commenting on surface aesthetics and discourage honest critique of fundamental flaws.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart thermostat system, the room temperature sensor detects that the temperature has risen above the set point and triggers the air conditioning to cool the room. This is an example of which type of system feedback?

options.A: Positive feedback, because the system amplifies the temperature deviation to create a stronger response.
options.B: Open-loop control, because the thermostat does not measure the actual room temperature.
options.C: Negative feedback, because the system detects the deviation from the set point and acts to reduce it, returning the system to equilibrium.
options.D: Feed-forward control, because the system anticipates future temperature changes before they occur.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback loops counteract deviations from a reference value — the thermostat is the canonical engineering example, correcting temperature back toward the set point. Option A is the top distractor: positive feedback amplifies deviation (e.g., a microphone near a speaker causing a squeal), which is the opposite of thermostat behaviour.

questions.title: Sustainability: Embodied Energy
questions.prompt: A designer argues that an aluminium water bottle is more sustainable than a single-use plastic bottle because aluminium is infinitely recyclable. Critically assess this claim.

options.A: The claim is fully valid: recyclability is the only metric that matters in a sustainability assessment.
options.B: The claim is partially valid: aluminium recycling saves up to 95% of production energy, but the high embodied energy in primary aluminium smelting means the bottle must be used many times before its lifecycle impact is lower than single-use plastic.
options.C: The claim is invalid because aluminium cannot actually be recycled more than three times before its properties degrade beyond use.
options.D: The claim is fully invalid because plastic production always has a lower carbon footprint than aluminium production, regardless of use frequency.

questions.explanation: Primary aluminium smelting is highly energy-intensive (approximately 14 kWh/kg), giving the bottle a large initial carbon debt; studies estimate an aluminium bottle must replace roughly 40–130 single-use plastic bottles to break even on lifecycle emissions. Option A ignores the embodied energy in manufacture, which is a critical stage in lifecycle assessment.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Anthropometric Data
questions.prompt: A school furniture designer uses the 50th-percentile student height as the standard for all chair and desk dimensions. Identify the flaw in this design approach.

options.A: Using the 50th percentile is flawed because the median student does not exist physically; designers should use the mean instead.
options.B: Designing for the 50th percentile excludes approximately half the population from an ergonomically suitable fit; adjustable designs or multiple sizes are needed to accommodate a broader range.
options.C: The 50th percentile is the correct standard in ergonomics because it minimises total production cost without any ergonomic disadvantage.
options.D: Anthropometric data should only be used for product categories involving physical safety, not school furniture.

questions.explanation: Ergonomics principles specify that designing for the 'average' user leaves roughly 50% of users either too large or too small for the product, causing discomfort or injury risk; best practice uses the 5th–95th percentile range or adjustability. Option C is a common student misconception that confuses cost optimisation with ergonomic adequacy.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A hiring algorithm trained on historical employee data systematically ranks female candidates lower than equally qualified male candidates. A student claims this is simply because 'the data is objective.' Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct: data collected from real hiring decisions is by definition objective and free from human bias.
options.B: The claim is partially correct: historical data is objective, but the algorithm's weighting system introduces bias during training.
options.C: The claim is incorrect: historical data can encode and perpetuate existing human biases, causing the algorithm to systematise past discrimination rather than eliminate it.
options.D: The claim is irrelevant because algorithms are not legally permitted to make hiring decisions in any country.

questions.explanation: Amazon's 2018 AI recruiting tool is a documented case where an algorithm trained on historical hiring data downgraded résumés containing the word 'women's,' demonstrating that biased historical patterns are amplified, not neutralised, by machine learning. Option B is a partial-credit distractor that incorrectly locates bias only in the weighting system rather than in the training data itself.
