questions.title: Innovation Economics: Disruptive vs Sustaining
questions.prompt: Christensen's theory distinguishes disruptive innovation from sustaining innovation. A car manufacturer introduces a new engine that improves fuel efficiency by 15% in its luxury range. Which category does this MOST likely represent, and why?

options.A: Disruptive innovation, because any improvement to an existing technology disrupts the market.
options.B: Sustaining innovation, because it improves the performance of an existing product for existing high-end customers rather than targeting new markets or non-consumers.
options.C: Disruptive innovation, because fuel efficiency changes challenge the dominant logic of luxury car performance.
options.D: Radical innovation, because a 15% efficiency gain exceeds the threshold required for market disruption.

questions.explanation: Christensen defines sustaining innovations as those that improve existing products along dimensions valued by current customers in established markets; disruptive innovations initially underperform for mainstream users but create new markets or target over-served segments. Option A is the top misconception — students conflate 'significant change' with 'disruption,' which has a specific theoretical meaning.

questions.title: Design Define Stage
questions.prompt: After empathising with users, a design team must write a Point of View (POV) statement. Which of the following BEST illustrates a well-formed POV statement for a hospital patient struggling to sleep during overnight stays?

options.A: 'We need to design a better hospital bed with built-in noise-cancelling technology.'
options.B: 'Hospital patients need more sleep aids because hospitals are noisy at night.'
options.C: 'An anxious adult patient needs to feel a sense of control over their sleep environment because helplessness in an unfamiliar, noisy space disrupts recovery.'
options.D: 'The problem is that hospitals are understaffed, leading to noise that keeps patients awake.'

questions.explanation: A well-formed POV statement frames the user, their need, and an insight — it avoids prescribing a solution and instead captures the human truth that drives the design challenge. Options A and B jump directly to solutions or restate the problem without the insight layer, which is the most common student error in the Define stage.

questions.title: Conductivity vs. Resistivity Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A student designing a portable electric heater element wants maximum heat output. She selects copper because it has one of the highest electrical conductivities of any metal. Identify the error in her reasoning.

options.A: There is no error; high conductivity maximises heat generation in a resistance heater element.
options.B: Copper's high conductivity means low resistivity, so it dissipates very little energy as heat; a high-resistivity alloy such as nichrome is needed to convert electrical energy efficiently into heat.
options.C: Copper is unsuitable only because it is too expensive, not because of its electrical properties.
options.D: Copper would overheat and melt instantly because it cannot withstand any current flow.

questions.explanation: Joule heating power is P = I²R; a heating element requires high resistance to maximise heat output at a given current. Nichrome (resistivity ~110 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) is standard for heater elements precisely because copper's very low resistivity (~1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) would produce negligible heat. Option A is the classic misconception linking 'electrical' performance to 'thermal' output without considering the direction of the relationship.

questions.title: Circular Economy Business Models
questions.prompt: A student claims that recycling alone is sufficient to achieve a circular economy. To what extent is this claim accurate?

options.A: Fully accurate: recycling closes material loops, which is the complete definition of a circular economy.
options.B: Largely accurate: recycling covers all but the final disposal stage of the circular economy model.
options.C: Partially accurate: recycling is the lowest-value loop in a circular economy; strategies such as reuse, repair, remanufacturing, and product-as-a-service models preserve more value and are prioritised above recycling.
options.D: Completely inaccurate: circular economy models explicitly exclude recycling as a strategy.

questions.explanation: The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's butterfly diagram places recycling as the outermost, lowest-value loop; inner loops (reuse, repair, remanufacture) retain more embodied energy and material value. Option A is the most common student error — conflating recycling with the full circular economy model because recycling is the most visible sustainability behaviour.

questions.title: Usability vs. Accessibility
questions.prompt: Compare usability and accessibility as design criteria. Which statement MOST accurately distinguishes the two concepts?

options.A: Usability and accessibility are synonymous: a product usable by the majority is automatically accessible to all.
options.B: Usability focuses on how effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily a defined user group can achieve goals; accessibility ensures the product can be used by people with a wider range of abilities, including disabilities.
options.C: Accessibility is a subset of usability; any product that scores highly on usability metrics automatically meets accessibility standards.
options.D: Usability applies only to digital products, whereas accessibility applies only to physical built environments.

questions.explanation: ISO 9241-11 defines usability in terms of effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction for a specified context; accessibility (e.g., WCAG 2.1) addresses the additional dimension of inclusion for users with sensory, motor, or cognitive disabilities — a product can be highly usable for most users yet completely inaccessible to others. Option C is wrong: high usability scores for a general population often mask specific barriers for users with disabilities.

questions.title: Ethics of Planned Obsolescence
questions.prompt: A smartphone manufacturer designs its battery so it cannot be replaced by the user, and stops providing software updates after three years. Critically assess the ethical dimensions of this design decision.

options.A: The design is ethically neutral because consumers choose freely to buy the product and can switch brands.
options.B: The design raises serious ethical concerns: it deliberately shortens product lifespan to drive repeat purchases, increases e-waste, disproportionately burdens lower-income consumers, and restricts the right to repair.
options.C: The design is ethically justified because shorter product cycles accelerate technological innovation that benefits society.
options.D: The design is unethical solely because of its environmental impact; consumer autonomy and economic factors are irrelevant to a design ethics analysis.

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence violates multiple ethical frameworks: it undermines consumer autonomy (right-to-repair movements), generates millions of tonnes of e-waste, and creates inequitable access since low-income users cannot afford frequent replacement. Option A employs a free-market fallacy that ignores asymmetric information and structural constraints on consumer choice.

questions.title: Tensile Strength vs. Hardness
questions.prompt: A student states that a material with high hardness will also have high tensile strength, and therefore the two properties can always be used interchangeably when selecting materials. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The claim is correct: hardness and tensile strength are linearly correlated for all engineering materials.
options.B: The claim is incorrect: hardness measures resistance to surface indentation, while tensile strength measures resistance to being pulled apart; a material such as glass is hard but has low tensile strength due to brittle fracture.
options.C: The claim is incorrect only for polymers; for metals, hardness and tensile strength are always interchangeable.
options.D: The claim is correct for ceramics but incorrect for metals, making it an unreliable general principle.

questions.explanation: Hardness (measured by Vickers or Brinell tests) and tensile strength are correlated empirically for steels but diverge significantly for other materials: glass scores ~5.5 on the Mohs scale yet fails catastrophically under tensile stress due to crack propagation from surface flaws. Option A is wrong because the correlation is empirical and material-class dependent, not a universal law.

questions.title: Human-Centred Design vs. User-Centred Design
questions.prompt: A design team is developing a water purification system for rural communities. They debate whether to use a human-centred design (HCD) approach or a purely technical engineering approach. Which argument BEST supports HCD in this context?

options.A: HCD is preferable because it guarantees a lower production cost than technical engineering approaches.
options.B: Technical engineering is always preferable for infrastructure projects because user preferences are secondary to functional performance.
options.C: HCD ensures the system is designed around the actual behaviours, cultural practices, and capacity of the community, increasing the likelihood of long-term adoption and maintenance.
options.D: HCD is preferable only when the target users have formal education in technology; otherwise technical engineering should lead.

questions.explanation: Numerous technically superior water projects have failed due to non-adoption — communities rejected systems that conflicted with cultural practices or that they could not maintain (documented in IDEO.org's HCD work in East Africa). Option B is a common techno-centric misconception that treats functional performance as independent of human adoption context.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright Duration
questions.prompt: A student wants to use a piece of music composed in 1940 for a school design presentation. She assumes it is in the public domain because it is old. What should she verify before using it?

options.A: Nothing — any work created before 1950 is automatically in the public domain in all countries.
options.B: Whether the composer died more than 70 years ago, as copyright typically lasts for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years in many jurisdictions, meaning some 1940s works are still protected.
options.C: Whether the work was registered with a national copyright office, since unregistered works are always public domain.
options.D: Whether the work is marked with a © symbol, since works without this symbol have no copyright protection.

questions.explanation: In most jurisdictions (including the EU and UK), copyright lasts for the author's life plus 70 years; a composer who died in 1990 would have works protected until 2060. Option A is factually wrong and is the most tempting error — students often assume 'old' equals 'public domain' without knowing the life-plus-70 calculation.

questions.title: Iterative Design: Test Stage
questions.prompt: During a test session, a designer observes that users complete all tasks successfully but report low satisfaction scores. Which action BEST reflects sound iterative design practice?

options.A: Conclude the design is successful because task completion rate is the primary usability metric.
options.B: Discard the prototype entirely and restart the design process from the empathise stage.
options.C: Investigate the gap between objective performance and subjective satisfaction using follow-up interviews, then iterate on the specific elements causing dissatisfaction.
options.D: Dismiss satisfaction scores as subjective and unreliable, prioritising only measurable task performance data.

questions.explanation: ISO 9241-11 defines usability as effectiveness, efficiency, AND satisfaction; a design that achieves task completion but scores poorly on satisfaction is incomplete. Follow-up qualitative methods (e.g., retrospective think-aloud) can pinpoint the causes before targeted iteration. Option A is wrong because satisfaction is an equally weighted usability dimension, not a secondary metric.

questions.title: Biomimicry in Material Design
questions.prompt: Engineers developed Velcro after studying how burdock burrs attached to clothing. This approach of drawing design solutions from biological systems is known as biomimicry. Which statement BEST evaluates biomimicry as a design strategy?

options.A: Biomimicry is a reliable strategy because natural selection has optimised biological systems over millions of years, though direct translation to manufactured materials requires engineering adaptation.
options.B: Biomimicry is unreliable because biological systems are too complex to provide actionable design principles for engineering.
options.C: Biomimicry is only applicable to adhesive or attachment systems; it cannot guide structural or aerodynamic design.
options.D: Biomimicry is always superior to conventional engineering because nature has already solved every design problem humans face.

questions.explanation: Biomimicry has produced innovations across fields — shark-skin riblets for drag reduction in swimwear (Speedo Fastskin), kingfisher-beak-inspired Shinkansen nose cones for aerodynamic efficiency — demonstrating broad applicability, but direct replication is rarely possible due to differences in scale and manufacturing constraints. Option D is wrong: natural systems are optimised for biological fitness, not necessarily for human engineering constraints such as cost, scalability, or non-biological loading conditions.

questions.title: Open Source vs. Proprietary Design
questions.prompt: A startup is deciding whether to release its medical device software as open source or keep it proprietary. Which argument MOST accurately reflects the trade-off between these models?

options.A: Open source is always riskier for medical devices because no one is legally responsible for errors in community-developed code.
options.B: Proprietary software is always safer because the company controls all code changes and bears full liability.
options.C: Open source enables broader peer review and faster identification of security vulnerabilities, but may reduce revenue and complicate liability; proprietary models protect competitive advantage but limit external scrutiny.
options.D: The choice is irrelevant to safety because medical device regulation requires identical certification regardless of software licensing model.

questions.explanation: Open-source medical software (e.g., OpenMRS, used in low-resource clinical settings) benefits from community-driven bug detection and transparency, but licensing models affect commercial viability and regulatory accountability. Option A is a misconception: open-source projects can have clearly defined maintainers and governance structures that assign responsibility.

questions.title: Lean Manufacturing Waste Types
questions.prompt: A factory manager notices that completed circuit boards sit on shelves for three weeks before being shipped because production runs faster than customer demand. According to lean manufacturing principles, which type of waste does this represent?

options.A: Motion waste, because workers are moving products from production to shelving unnecessarily.
options.B: Overproduction waste, because producing more than current demand creates inventory that ties up capital and space.
options.C: Defect waste, because any product not immediately shipped to a customer contains a latent quality problem.
options.D: Waiting waste, because the boards are waiting to be used by the next process in the value stream.

questions.explanation: Overproduction is identified in the Toyota Production System as the most serious of the seven wastes (muda) because it generates all other wastes: excess inventory consumes space, capital, and handling, and masks defects. Option D is a plausible distractor — waiting waste applies to people or machines idle within a process, not to finished goods accumulating ahead of demand.

questions.title: Design Criteria vs. Constraints
questions.prompt: A student lists 'the product must cost less than $20 to manufacture' and 'the product should be aesthetically appealing to teenagers' in their design specification. Which statement BEST distinguishes these two requirements?

options.A: Both are constraints because they limit what the designer can do.
options.B: Both are criteria because they describe qualities the design should have.
options.C: The cost limit is a constraint — a non-negotiable boundary — while aesthetic appeal is a criterion — a measurable quality that can be optimised and evaluated against a benchmark.
options.D: The cost limit is a criterion because it can be achieved to different degrees, while aesthetic appeal is a constraint because taste cannot be changed.

questions.explanation: In design methodology, constraints are fixed, non-negotiable limits (budget, size, regulatory requirements) that eliminate entire design directions, while criteria are evaluative qualities that solutions should maximise. The $20 limit is a hard boundary; aesthetic appeal is a graded, testable quality. Option D reverses the definitions — cost is binary (within/outside budget), while aesthetics admits of degree.

questions.title: Life Cycle Assessment: Hotspot Identification
questions.prompt: An LCA of a cotton T-shirt reveals that the cultivation and dyeing stages account for 87% of total water consumption across the product's lifecycle. What does this finding suggest about where sustainability improvements should be prioritised?

options.A: Improvements should focus on the retail and distribution stage because this is where the brand has the most direct control.
options.B: Improvements should be distributed equally across all lifecycle stages to ensure a balanced sustainability strategy.
options.C: Improvements should target the cultivation and dyeing hotspots — for example, switching to organic or recycled-fibre inputs and closed-loop dye systems — since these dominate total water impact.
options.D: The LCA finding is irrelevant because water consumption is less important than carbon emissions in sustainability assessment.

questions.explanation: LCA hotspot analysis directs designers toward high-impact stages; cotton cultivation requires approximately 10,000 litres of water per kilogram of fibre, and conventional dyeing contributes toxic effluent — addressing these two stages delivers the greatest environmental leverage. Option B ignores the 80/20 logic of hotspot prioritisation, which is a fundamental LCA application principle.

questions.title: Diffusion of Innovations Curve
questions.prompt: Rogers' diffusion of innovations model identifies five adopter categories. A new augmented reality textbook is enthusiastically adopted by 2.5% of students immediately after launch, while the majority wait to see reviews. Which adopter group does the initial 2.5% represent, and what implication does this have for the product's design testing phase?

options.A: Early adopters; their feedback should form the primary basis for final product decisions because they are most representative of all users.
options.B: Innovators; their enthusiasm and high tolerance for flaws means their feedback may not reflect the needs of the early and late majority, so testing must also include more risk-averse user groups.
options.C: Early majority; this group's cautious approach makes them the most reliable testers for identifying critical usability problems.
options.D: Laggards; this group's reluctance to adopt confirms the product has fundamental design flaws that must be corrected.

questions.explanation: Rogers defines innovators as the first 2.5% of adopters — technology enthusiasts with high risk tolerance who actively seek new products; their feedback over-represents technical curiosity and under-represents the pragmatic concerns of the early majority (34%), which is the key market for mainstream success. Option A mistakes innovators for early adopters and wrongly treats their feedback as representative.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Sympathy in Design
questions.prompt: A design team is developing a mobility aid for elderly users. One member suggests reading research papers about aging, while another insists on shadowing actual users through their daily routines. Evaluate which approach better fulfils the 'empathise' stage of design thinking, and why.

options.A: Reading research papers, because peer-reviewed data is more reliable than personal observation
options.B: Shadowing users, because it surfaces unarticulated needs that users themselves cannot always express
options.C: Both are equally valid since they provide complementary quantitative and qualitative data
options.D: Neither; the team should issue a survey so they can gather data from a larger sample

questions.explanation: The empathise stage prioritises direct immersive observation to uncover latent needs — things users feel but cannot articulate in a survey or paper, such as the awkward grip required to open a heavy door. Reading papers alone captures reported behaviour, not lived experience, missing the embodied insights that drive breakthrough design.

questions.title: Material Fatigue Under Stress
questions.prompt: A student claims that a metal bridge component should be replaced once it shows any visible cracks, but that a component with no visible cracks is safe indefinitely. Critically assess this claim using your knowledge of material properties.

options.A: The claim is fully correct; cracks are the definitive indicator of structural failure risk
options.B: The claim is partially correct: cracks do signal risk, but materials can fail below their elastic limit through fatigue even without visible cracks
options.C: The claim is fully incorrect; visible cracks do not indicate any increased failure risk in metals
options.D: The claim is partially correct: fatigue only occurs in polymers, not metals, so crack-free metals are always safe

questions.explanation: Metal fatigue occurs when cyclic stresses — even well below the ultimate tensile strength — cause microscopic internal cracks that grow invisibly over time; this is how the 1954 de Havilland Comet aircraft disasters occurred. The claim is therefore only half-right: cracks do matter, but the absence of visible cracks does not guarantee safety under repeated loading.

questions.title: Defining the Problem Statement
questions.prompt: In MYP Design, the 'define' stage produces a problem statement. A team writes: 'We want to design an app.' A mentor says this is inadequate. Which revised problem statement best exemplifies the 'define' stage?

options.A: 'We will build an app using React Native with push notifications and a dark mode interface'
options.B: 'Busy secondary students aged 14–17 need a way to track homework deadlines because they frequently miss submissions, leading to academic stress'
options.C: 'Students need a better app because current apps are not good enough'
options.D: 'We will design an app and test it with 30 users to measure its effectiveness'

questions.explanation: A valid 'define' stage problem statement specifies the user, their unmet need, and the root cause — it is human-centred and solution-agnostic. Option A jumps to solution specifications (a design error), Option C is vague with no measurable need, and Option D describes a testing protocol rather than a problem.

questions.title: UX Heuristics and Usability
questions.prompt: A user testing session reveals that participants repeatedly press a button expecting an immediate confirmation message, but none appears. According to Nielsen's usability heuristics, which principle is being violated?

options.A: Error prevention
options.B: Consistency and standards
options.C: Visibility of system status
options.D: Aesthetic and minimalist design

questions.explanation: Nielsen's 'visibility of system status' heuristic requires that users always be informed about what the system is doing through timely, appropriate feedback — such as a confirmation message or progress indicator. 'Error prevention' would apply if the system should stop a mistake before it happens, which is not the issue here.

questions.title: Innovation Economics and First-Mover
questions.prompt: To what extent does being the first company to launch a new product type guarantee long-term market dominance? Use economic reasoning to support your answer.

options.A: It guarantees dominance because patent law prevents competitors from entering the market for 20 years
options.B: It guarantees dominance because brand recognition built early creates permanent switching costs for consumers
options.C: It does not guarantee dominance; late entrants can exploit first-mover mistakes and enter with superior products at lower development costs
options.D: It guarantees dominance only in technology sectors, not in physical product markets

questions.explanation: First-mover advantage is real but not permanent; 'fast-follower' companies like Facebook (following MySpace) or Google (following earlier search engines) won markets by learning from pioneers' errors and reducing R&D costs through imitation. Patents protect specific implementations but not entire product categories, and brand loyalty can be eroded by superior alternatives.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secrets
questions.prompt: A company keeps its manufacturing process confidential rather than patenting it. A student claims this is always the worse strategy because patents provide stronger legal protection. Evaluate this claim.

options.A: The student is correct; patents always provide stronger protection than trade secrets in all circumstances
options.B: The student is incorrect; trade secrets can protect a process indefinitely, whereas patents expire after 20 years and require public disclosure
options.C: The student is correct; trade secrets offer no legal recourse if the information is stolen
options.D: The student is incorrect; trade secrets are legally superior to patents in all countries under TRIPS agreements

questions.explanation: A patent grants exclusivity for 20 years but requires full public disclosure of the invention, after which anyone can use it freely. A trade secret (such as the Coca-Cola formula) can last indefinitely as long as it remains confidential, and misappropriation is actionable under law — making it strategically superior when the process is hard to reverse-engineer.

questions.title: Ergonomics and Anthropometric Data
questions.prompt: A designer uses the average hand-span measurement from a national database to set the grip width of a new power tool. A colleague argues this will fail many users. Who is correct, and why?

options.A: The designer is correct; designing for the average ensures the largest number of people are accommodated
options.B: The colleague is correct; the average fits almost nobody perfectly, and extremes of the population — small or large hands — will find the tool unsafe
options.C: The designer is correct, provided the database sample size exceeds 1,000 participants
options.D: The colleague is correct; ergonomic tools must always be adjustable regardless of anthropometric data

questions.explanation: Designing for the average is a well-documented ergonomic fallacy — the US Air Force's 1950s study by Gilbert Daniels showed that virtually no pilot matched the average across ten physical dimensions simultaneously. Instead, designers use the 5th–95th percentile range or adjustable designs to accommodate the real population distribution.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A startup has limited time and budget before a pitch to investors. They must decide between a high-fidelity digital prototype and a low-fidelity paper prototype of their app. Which choice is most strategically justified at this early concept stage?

options.A: High-fidelity, because investors will only fund polished, realistic demonstrations
options.B: Low-fidelity, because paper prototypes can be created rapidly, tested with users, and iterated before significant resources are committed
options.C: High-fidelity, because low-fidelity prototypes cannot test any user interactions meaningfully
options.D: Low-fidelity, because investors are legally prohibited from viewing unreleased digital interfaces

questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototypes (e.g., paper wireframes) are explicitly designed for rapid, cheap iteration — they allow teams to surface fundamental usability problems before costly development begins. Research by IDEO and Stanford d.school consistently shows early-stage user testing with rough prototypes yields more actionable feedback than polished mockups that discourage honest criticism.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Hotspots
questions.prompt: An LCA of a rechargeable lithium-ion laptop battery reveals that 80% of its total carbon footprint occurs during the raw material extraction phase, not during use or disposal. What is the most strategically important implication for a designer?

options.A: Focus on designing a more energy-efficient charger to reduce emissions during the use phase
options.B: Focus on designing for recyclability so the battery materials can be reclaimed at end of life
options.C: Focus on reducing the quantity of virgin lithium and cobalt by designing for smaller battery capacity or using recycled materials
options.D: Focus on reducing packaging weight to lower transport emissions between factory and retailer

questions.explanation: LCA hotspot analysis directs design effort to the life-cycle stage with the greatest impact — here, raw material extraction. Reducing reliance on virgin lithium and cobalt (via recycled content or smaller, more efficient battery designs) directly targets that 80% hotspot. Improving charger efficiency addresses the use phase, which accounts for a much smaller share of the footprint.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart building's heating system, rising indoor temperature triggers the thermostat to reduce heat output, which lowers the temperature, which then triggers more heat. Identify the type of feedback loop present and its function.

options.A: A positive feedback loop that amplifies temperature change until the system overheats
options.B: A negative feedback loop that maintains the system near a target equilibrium
options.C: An open-loop system because the thermostat responds to an external signal
options.D: A positive feedback loop because the thermostat adds energy to the system when it acts

questions.explanation: A negative feedback loop counteracts deviation from a set point, stabilising the system — exactly what a thermostat does by reducing output when temperature exceeds the target. It is called 'negative' because the feedback signal opposes the change, not because its effect is harmful. A positive feedback loop would amplify deviations, leading to instability.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A hiring algorithm trained on a company's historical recruitment data consistently ranks female candidates lower than male candidates with equivalent qualifications. A student argues this is acceptable because the algorithm is only reflecting past data. Critically assess this view.

options.A: The view is correct; algorithms are objective by definition because they follow mathematical rules without human emotion
options.B: The view is correct, provided the historical data set contains more than 10,000 records, ensuring statistical validity
options.C: The view is incorrect; historical data encoding past discrimination perpetuates and scales that discrimination, causing measurable harm to protected groups
options.D: The view is partially correct; the bias is acceptable in private companies but not in public sector hiring

questions.explanation: Amazon's real-world hiring algorithm (scrapped in 2018) demonstrated exactly this problem: training on historically male-dominated hiring decisions caused the system to systematically penalise CVs mentioning women's colleges. Algorithms are not inherently objective — they encode the biases present in their training data, and deploying them at scale amplifies harm beyond what any individual human biased decision-maker could cause.

questions.title: Tensile Strength vs. Hardness
questions.prompt: A student confuses tensile strength and hardness when selecting a material for a drill bit. They choose a material with very high tensile strength, reasoning it will resist scratching rock. Identify the error in their reasoning.

options.A: There is no error; tensile strength and hardness are the same property measured in different units
options.B: The error is that drill bits require high compressive strength, not tensile strength, as they are pushed into material
options.C: The error is that scratch resistance requires hardness — the ability to resist surface indentation — not tensile strength, which measures resistance to being pulled apart
options.D: The error is that drill bits must be ductile, not hard, so they flex rather than break on contact with rock

questions.explanation: Hardness (measured on the Mohs or Vickers scale) describes resistance to surface deformation and scratching — which is why tungsten carbide (hardness ~9.5 Mohs) is used for drill bits, not high-tensile steel. Tensile strength measures the maximum stress a material can withstand while being stretched, a distinct property irrelevant to scratch resistance.

questions.title: Design for Disassembly
questions.prompt: A manufacturer designs a smartphone where the battery is glued in place to make the phone thinner. Evaluate this decision from a sustainability perspective, considering end-of-life impacts.

options.A: The decision is justified because a thinner phone requires fewer raw materials overall, reducing environmental impact
options.B: The decision is problematic because gluing prevents easy battery replacement, shortening product lifespan and making material recovery at end-of-life difficult
options.C: The decision is justified because modern recycling facilities can dissolve adhesives and recover all materials without design changes
options.D: The decision is neutral; battery disposal methods are standardised globally, so design for disassembly is irrelevant

questions.explanation: Design for disassembly is a core circular economy principle: products whose components cannot be separated end up in landfill or are recycled at low value because hazardous battery materials contaminate other streams. The EU's Right to Repair legislation (2023) specifically targets glued-in batteries as a sustainability barrier, requiring replaceable batteries in new devices by 2027.

questions.title: Evaluating Competing Prototypes
questions.prompt: Two teams prototype solutions to the same design problem. Team A's prototype scores 7/10 on user satisfaction but fails under stress testing. Team B's prototype scores 5/10 on satisfaction but passes all stress tests. Which prototype should move to development, and on what basis?

options.A: Team A's, because user satisfaction is always the primary criterion in design evaluation
options.B: Team B's, because passing safety and structural tests is a non-negotiable criterion that overrides satisfaction scores when safety is at stake
options.C: Team A's, because stress testing results can be improved in manufacturing without changing the prototype design
options.D: Neither; both prototypes must be discarded and the process restarted from ideation

questions.explanation: In design evaluation, criteria are weighted, and safety/structural integrity typically constitutes a threshold criterion — a minimum standard that must be met before other factors are considered. A product that fails under stress testing poses unacceptable risk to users regardless of satisfaction ratings; Team B's prototype provides a safe foundation on which satisfaction can be iteratively improved.

questions.title: Conductivity vs. Resistivity
questions.prompt: A student designing a wearable biosensor needs a material that conducts electricity across the sensor pad but insulates the wearer's skin beneath it. They incorrectly assume that low electrical resistivity and good insulation can be achieved by the same material. What would happen if they used a single low-resistivity material throughout?

options.A: The sensor would work correctly because low resistivity materials automatically switch between conducting and insulating based on applied voltage
options.B: Current would also flow through the wearer's skin, creating a potential electric shock hazard and inaccurate readings
options.C: The sensor would fail because low-resistivity materials cannot carry biosensor-level micro-currents
options.D: The wearer would experience increased sensitivity because electrical signals would be amplified by skin contact

questions.explanation: Electrical resistivity is a material property on a continuous spectrum — a low-resistivity (high-conductivity) material cannot simultaneously insulate the skin, as it allows current to pass freely in all directions. Using such a material throughout would create an unintended conductive path through the wearer's skin, risking micro-shock and producing signal noise that corrupts biometric readings.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Copyright Duration
questions.prompt: A student wants to use a famous song in a school design project video and assumes all music recorded before 1970 is in the public domain. Evaluate whether this assumption is reliable.

options.A: The assumption is reliable; all creative works produced before 1970 are now in the public domain worldwide
options.B: The assumption is unreliable; copyright duration varies by country and type of right — a song's composition and its sound recording may have different expiry dates
options.C: The assumption is reliable for educational use because all copyright restrictions are waived for non-commercial school projects
options.D: The assumption is reliable only for instrumental music; lyrics retain copyright indefinitely under international law

questions.explanation: Copyright law is jurisdiction-specific and distinguishes between the musical composition (melody and lyrics, typically life + 70 years) and the sound recording (in the US, recordings from before 1972 only entered public domain in 2022 under the Music Modernization Act). A pre-1970 song's underlying composition may be public domain while the specific 1968 recording remains protected.

questions.title: Biomimicry in Material Design
questions.prompt: Engineers designing a new adhesive that works on wet surfaces looked to the structural proteins of mussels, which anchor themselves to rocks in ocean waves. This approach to innovation is best described as:

options.A: Reverse engineering, because the team is deconstructing an existing product to copy its function
options.B: Biomimicry, because the design solution is inspired by a mechanism evolved in a biological organism
options.C: Incremental innovation, because mussel adhesion is a known phenomenon being applied to an existing product category
options.D: Systems engineering, because the team is modelling a biological system to optimise performance

questions.explanation: Biomimicry is the design philosophy of emulating strategies found in nature to solve human problems — mussel adhesion proteins (DOPA-containing proteins) inspired a family of wet-surface adhesives now used in medical and industrial applications. It is not reverse engineering (which deconstructs human-made products) nor simply systems engineering, which focuses on component integration rather than biological inspiration.

questions.title: User-Centred vs. Technology-Driven Design
questions.prompt: A tech company builds a voice-activated smart fridge because the technology is available and impressive. Sales are poor because most users find the feature unnecessary. Which design philosophy failure does this illustrate, and what should have been done differently?

options.A: The failure of incremental innovation; the company should have invested in a completely new product category instead
options.B: The failure of technology-push design; the company prioritised available technology over genuine user needs identified through research
options.C: The failure of market research; the company should have conducted larger surveys before choosing their technology stack
options.D: The failure of prototyping; a high-fidelity prototype would have revealed that voice activation was unnecessary

questions.explanation: Technology-push design begins with a technology and seeks applications for it, whereas demand-pull (user-centred) design begins with an identified user need and finds appropriate technology to address it. The former frequently produces features users did not request and will not pay for — the classic case being many 'smart home' features with very low adoption rates despite sophisticated engineering.

questions.title: Sustainability: Greenwashing
questions.prompt: A fashion brand labels its new clothing line 'eco-friendly' because the garments are made from recycled plastic bottles, but the dyeing process uses toxic chemicals that contaminate local waterways. A student says the brand's sustainability claim is valid because of the recycled content. Evaluate this view.

options.A: The view is correct; using recycled materials is the most important sustainability criterion for clothing
options.B: The view is correct, provided the brand publicly discloses all information about its dyeing process
options.C: The view is incorrect; a genuine sustainability assessment must consider the full production process, and toxic effluent constitutes significant environmental harm that invalidates the overall claim
options.D: The view is correct only if more than 50% of the garment by mass consists of recycled content

questions.explanation: Greenwashing occurs when a company highlights one environmental positive while concealing significant harms elsewhere in the value chain — a partial truth used to create a misleading overall impression. An LCA-informed sustainability claim must account for all life-cycle stages; textile dyeing is one of the largest sources of industrial water pollution globally, negating the benefit of recycled fibre content.

questions.title: Thermal Properties: Specific Heat Capacity
questions.prompt: A designer comparing two materials for a heat storage system finds that Material X has twice the specific heat capacity of Material Y, but both have the same mass. If both absorb the same amount of thermal energy, what is the relationship between their temperature rises?

options.A: Material X will show twice the temperature rise because it has twice the thermal capacity
options.B: Both materials will show the same temperature rise because they have equal mass
options.C: Material X will show half the temperature rise of Material Y because it requires more energy per degree of temperature change
options.D: Material Y will show half the temperature rise of Material X because lower specific heat means less energy is absorbed

questions.explanation: From Q = mcΔT, if Q and m are held constant, ΔT is inversely proportional to specific heat capacity c. With Material X having twice the c of Material Y, it experiences half the temperature rise for the same energy input — making it the superior choice for a heat storage system where stable, high-capacity storage (not rapid temperature change) is desired.

questions.title: Agile vs. Waterfall Development
questions.prompt: A software team uses a waterfall development model for a health app: they complete all design, then all coding, then all testing sequentially. Six months in, user research reveals the core feature is fundamentally wrong. Compare this to an agile approach and identify the key systemic weakness exposed.

options.A: The weakness is insufficient initial research; agile teams conduct more thorough upfront discovery so this error would never occur
options.B: The weakness is that waterfall delays user validation until after major investment, whereas agile's iterative sprints surface misalignment early at lower cost
options.C: The weakness is that waterfall teams cannot code and test simultaneously; agile solves this through parallel workstreams
options.D: There is no systemic weakness; the problem is individual team error that would occur in any methodology

questions.explanation: Waterfall's sequential, non-iterative structure means user feedback arrives only at the testing phase, after full design and development investment — making late-stage pivots extremely costly. Agile's two-week sprint cycles release working features to real users continuously, so fundamental product misalignments are discovered within weeks rather than months, dramatically reducing waste.

questions.title: TOK: Objectivity in Design Criteria
questions.prompt: A Theory of Knowledge student argues that design criteria are objective because they can be measured numerically (e.g., 'must withstand 500 N of force'). A classmate counters that all design criteria ultimately rest on value judgements. To what extent is the classmate's position defensible?

options.A: Not defensible; once criteria are expressed numerically they are purely objective and value-free
options.B: Fully defensible; the decision about which criteria to measure, and what threshold is 'good enough', reflects human priorities, cultural context, and value judgements
options.C: Partially defensible only for aesthetic criteria; structural criteria such as force thresholds are entirely value-free
options.D: Not defensible; design criteria are derived from physics and engineering principles that are universally objective

questions.explanation: Even a quantitative criterion like '500 N of force' encodes value judgements: why 500 N and not 400 or 600? The threshold was chosen based on assumptions about who will use the product, acceptable risk levels, cost trade-offs, and cultural standards of safety — all of which are value-laden. This is a classic TOK point: measurement can be precise without being value-free.

questions.title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary Innovation
questions.prompt: Synthesise the economic and ethical arguments to evaluate whether a pharmaceutical company should open-source the patent for a life-saving drug it developed at great expense.

options.A: The company should always open-source immediately because human life has absolute precedence over commercial interests under all ethical frameworks
options.B: The company should never open-source because patent protection is the sole mechanism incentivising pharmaceutical R&D investment
options.C: There is a genuine tension: open-sourcing enables equitable access and collaborative improvement, but may reduce future R&D investment if companies cannot recoup development costs; policy solutions like compulsory licensing attempt to balance both
options.D: The decision is irrelevant because the WTO automatically waives pharmaceutical patents for life-saving drugs under the TRIPS Agreement in all member states

questions.explanation: This is a genuine ethical and economic dilemma with defensible positions on both sides. The 2001 Doha Declaration and subsequent TRIPS flexibilities allow compulsory licensing — a compromise that permits generic production in developing nations while preserving some IP incentives. The COVID-19 mRNA vaccine patent waiver debate illustrates that neither absolute position is universally applied, and the trade-off between access and innovation incentives is real and unresolved.

questions.title: Empathy vs. Assumption in Design
questions.prompt: A design team skips the empathise phase and moves directly to defining the problem based on their own assumptions about users. Evaluate the most significant risk this introduces to the final outcome.

options.A: The prototype will take longer to manufacture because material choices were not researched.
options.B: The defined problem statement will reflect the designers' biases rather than genuine user needs, making all subsequent phases build on a flawed foundation.
options.C: The team will violate intellectual property law by using ideas that belong to existing products.
options.D: The ideation phase will generate too few ideas because the team lacks creative inspiration from user stories.

questions.explanation: In design thinking, the empathise phase exists specifically to ground the problem statement in observed, real user needs; skipping it means the 'define' output is shaped by designer assumptions, which corrupts every downstream phase. Option D is plausible but wrong: ideation quantity is limited by technique and time, not by whether empathy data was collected.

questions.title: Lifecycle Assessment Hotspot
questions.prompt: A lifecycle assessment of a lithium-ion smartphone battery reveals that 78% of its cumulative energy demand occurs at a single stage. Which stage is this most likely to be, and why?

options.A: End-of-life disposal, because landfill processing requires significant machinery.
options.B: Distribution, because global shipping of electronics consumes enormous fossil fuel energy.
options.C: Raw material extraction and processing, because mining and refining lithium, cobalt, and nickel are extremely energy-intensive.
options.D: Use phase, because consumers charge their devices daily over several years.

questions.explanation: LCA studies consistently identify raw material extraction — particularly the mining and smelting of cobalt and lithium — as the dominant energy hotspot for lithium-ion batteries, often exceeding 70% of lifetime energy demand. Option D is a common misconception: although charging is frequent, the low wattage of phone chargers makes the cumulative use-phase energy far smaller than extraction energy.

questions.title: Tensile Strength vs. Hardness
questions.prompt: A student claims that a material with high hardness will always have high tensile strength, and therefore the two properties can be used interchangeably when selecting materials for a load-bearing bracket. To what extent is this claim valid?

options.A: Fully valid, because hardness and tensile strength are both measures of how a material resists deformation under force.
options.B: Partially valid for metals only; in polymers, hardness and tensile strength are inversely related.
options.C: Not valid: hardness measures resistance to surface indentation while tensile strength measures resistance to pulling forces, and materials like cast iron are hard but brittle with relatively low tensile strength.
options.D: Not valid because tensile strength is a dynamic property and hardness is a static property, making them incomparable.

questions.explanation: Hardness (e.g., measured on the Vickers or Rockwell scale) specifically quantifies resistance to localised surface indentation, whereas tensile strength measures the maximum stress a material withstands before fracture under tension — these are distinct properties. Cast iron is a classic counterexample: it is very hard (≈200 HV) yet has low tensile strength (~150 MPa) because it is brittle. Option A conflates two separate mechanical properties that have different measurement methods and failure modes.

questions.title: UX Heuristic Evaluation
questions.prompt: A UX researcher conducts a heuristic evaluation of a hospital appointment app using Nielsen's ten usability heuristics. She identifies that clicking 'Cancel Appointment' immediately deletes the booking with no confirmation dialog. Which heuristic does this violate?

options.A: Visibility of system status
options.B: Error prevention
options.C: Consistency and standards
options.D: Recognition rather than recall

questions.explanation: Nielsen's 'error prevention' heuristic specifically requires that designs eliminate error-prone conditions or present confirmation dialogs before users commit to irreversible actions — exactly what a 'confirm cancellation?' prompt would provide. Option A ('visibility of system status') concerns whether the system keeps users informed of ongoing processes via feedback, not whether it prevents accidental destructive actions.

questions.title: Innovation Economics: Disruptive vs. Sustaining
questions.prompt: Christensen's theory distinguishes disruptive innovation from sustaining innovation. A company improves its premium electric car's range from 400 km to 520 km and adds a faster charging system. Critically assess whether this is best classified as disruptive or sustaining innovation.

options.A: Disruptive, because electric vehicles as a category disrupted the internal combustion engine market.
options.B: Disruptive, because the improvement changes the performance trajectory faster than competitors can respond.
options.C: Sustaining, because it improves an existing product along dimensions that current customers already value, targeting the same premium market segment.
options.D: Sustaining, because the innovation relies on already-established battery chemistry rather than a fundamentally new technology.

questions.explanation: Christensen defines sustaining innovation as improvements that make existing products perform better along metrics mainstream customers value — longer range and faster charging serve the same premium buyers more effectively, which is the hallmark of sustaining innovation. Option A confuses the historical category disruption of EVs (which is correct for the original introduction of EVs) with the incremental improvement being described here; an improvement to an already-successful product line is sustaining by definition.

questions.title: Ergonomics: Anthropometric Percentiles
questions.prompt: A designer is setting the adjustable height range for a factory workbench. She decides to design for the 5th-to-95th percentile standing elbow height of the adult worker population. A colleague suggests designing only for the 50th percentile to save cost. Evaluate why the colleague's approach is ergonomically inadequate.

options.A: Designing for the 50th percentile saves cost but violates international ISO anthropometry standards that mandate the 5th–95th range.
options.B: A 50th-percentile design would be comfortable for approximately half the workforce but would exclude workers at the extremes, increasing musculoskeletal injury risk for 50% of users.
options.C: The 50th percentile represents the median, which by definition fits no individual exactly, making the design useless.
options.D: Designing for the 50th percentile is only problematic in safety-critical environments; for factory workbenches it is an acceptable industry standard.

questions.explanation: Anthropometric design for the 50th percentile means the workstation is optimised for the median worker but progressively less suitable for those above or below that value — roughly half the workforce would work at non-optimal heights, increasing fatigue and musculoskeletal disorder risk. Option C is factually wrong: the 50th percentile is the median value and does represent real individuals; the error in option C misrepresents what a percentile means.

questions.title: Intellectual Property: Trade Secret vs. Patent
questions.prompt: A food technology company develops a novel fermentation process that gives its product a unique flavour. The legal team debates whether to patent the process or keep it as a trade secret. Identify the most significant strategic disadvantage of choosing a patent in this context.

options.A: A patent only lasts 20 years from the filing date, after which the process enters the public domain and competitors can legally use it.
options.B: Patents cannot be applied to food production processes under WTO TRIPS agreements.
options.C: Filing a patent requires paying a one-time fee that is typically prohibitive for food technology companies.
options.D: A patent grants exclusive rights only in the country of filing, whereas trade secrets offer automatic global protection.

questions.explanation: Patent protection expires 20 years from the priority filing date, placing the invention in the public domain — if the fermentation process would still be commercially valuable after 20 years, a trade secret (which can last indefinitely, as with Coca-Cola's formula) offers perpetual protection. Option B is incorrect: process patents for food production are explicitly permitted under the TRIPS Agreement, provided they meet novelty and inventive step criteria.

questions.title: Systems Thinking: Feedback Loops
questions.prompt: In a smart building's heating system, a thermostat detects that the room temperature exceeds the set point and signals the boiler to reduce heat output. A student classifies this as a positive feedback loop. Evaluate this classification.

options.A: Correct, because the system responds to a change (rising temperature) by producing an output, which is the definition of positive feedback.
options.B: Incorrect: this is a negative feedback loop because the system's response (reducing heat) counteracts the deviation from the set point, stabilising the system.
options.C: Incorrect: this is an open-loop system because the boiler does not continuously monitor its own output.
options.D: Correct, because the thermostat amplifies the signal by involving additional components (the boiler), which defines positive feedback.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback loops are characterised by a corrective response that reduces a deviation from a reference point — the thermostat signals the boiler to reduce heat when temperature rises above the set point, directly counteracting the change and restoring equilibrium. Option A reflects a common terminological confusion: 'positive' in feedback theory does not mean 'responds to a change' but rather that the response amplifies the original deviation, which does not happen here.

questions.title: Prototype Fidelity Trade-offs
questions.prompt: A startup developing a medical diagnostic device must decide between a low-fidelity paper prototype and a high-fidelity electronic prototype for initial user testing with clinicians. Synthesise the key trade-off that should determine the choice at this stage.

options.A: High-fidelity prototypes are always preferable for medical contexts because clinicians expect professional-grade equipment and will distrust paper models.
options.B: The key trade-off is between the speed and cost of learning about fundamental usability issues (favouring low-fidelity) versus the validity of testing fine interaction details that require real electronic responses (favouring high-fidelity).
options.C: Low-fidelity prototypes are always preferable at any stage because they reduce sunk cost and allow pivot without financial loss.
options.D: The choice depends entirely on regulatory approval timelines, not on user testing strategy.

questions.explanation: Prototype fidelity should match the question being tested: low-fidelity paper prototypes excel at revealing fundamental workflow and navigation problems cheaply and quickly, whereas high-fidelity prototypes are needed when testing response timing, error messages, or precise interactions that paper cannot simulate. Option A is a common misconception — research by IDEO and the Nielsen Norman Group consistently shows that users, including professionals, can provide valuable feedback on paper prototypes when the testing context is framed correctly.

questions.title: Tech Ethics: Algorithmic Bias
questions.prompt: A hiring algorithm trained on a company's historical employment data consistently ranks female candidates lower than male candidates with equivalent qualifications. A student argues this is not an ethical issue because the algorithm is simply reflecting real historical patterns. Critically assess this argument.

options.A: The argument is valid: algorithms that reproduce historical data are by definition objective, and objectivity is a prerequisite for ethical decision-making.
options.B: The argument is partially valid but only if the company can demonstrate that past hiring decisions were themselves free from discrimination.
options.C: The argument is flawed: encoding historical discrimination into an automated system perpetuates and scales injustice, and 'reflecting real patterns' does not confer ethical legitimacy if those patterns resulted from bias.
options.D: The argument is flawed only in jurisdictions with algorithmic accountability laws; in unregulated markets it is ethically acceptable to use historical data without adjustment.

questions.explanation: Training data encodes past human decisions, which may themselves reflect systemic discrimination — an algorithm that reproduces those decisions automates and scales the original bias, making it harder to detect and challenge, not more objective. Amazon's 2018 internal review of exactly this type of hiring tool found it penalised CVs containing the word 'women's' and was subsequently scrapped. Option A conflates mathematical reproducibility with ethical neutrality, a category error central to many AI ethics discussions.

questions.title: Material Sustainability: Bioplastics
questions.prompt: A student argues that replacing conventional polyethylene packaging with PLA (polylactic acid) bioplastic is straightforwardly more sustainable because PLA is made from plants. To what extent is this argument justified?

options.A: Fully justified: plant-based origin guarantees lower carbon emissions and complete biodegradability in all disposal environments.
options.B: Partially justified: PLA has a lower carbon footprint in production but degrades only in industrial composting conditions above 60°C, not in home compost or landfill, limiting real-world sustainability gains.
options.C: Not justified: PLA releases more CO₂ during production than polyethylene because fermentation is more energy-intensive than cracking petroleum.
options.D: Partially justified: PLA is more sustainable only when the corn or sugarcane feedstock is grown organically, otherwise pesticide use negates the environmental benefit.

questions.explanation: PLA does typically have a lower cradle-to-gate carbon footprint than polyethylene, but it requires industrial composting facilities (sustained temperatures ≥58–60°C) to degrade within months; in landfill or the ocean it persists similarly to conventional plastics and cannot be recycled in standard plastic streams. Option A overstates the case: 'plant-based' does not guarantee lower overall emissions when land use, agricultural inputs, and limited composting infrastructure are considered.

questions.title: Design Specification vs. Design Brief
questions.prompt: Identify the error in the following reasoning: 'A design brief and a design specification serve the same function. Once a brief is written, the specification adds no new information and is therefore redundant in a professional design project.'

options.A: The error is that a design brief is written after the specification, not before.
options.B: The error is conflating two distinct documents: the brief outlines the context, problem, and broad goals set by the client, while the specification provides measurable, testable criteria derived from research that the solution must meet.
options.C: The reasoning is correct; in MYP Design, the two terms are used interchangeably and refer to the same document.
options.D: The error is that the specification replaces the brief once testing begins, so both documents are needed at different stages for the same purpose.

questions.explanation: A design brief is a high-level document communicating the client's context, problem, and aspirations, whereas a design specification translates user research into precise, measurable constraints (e.g., 'must support ≥120 kg,' 'must operate between −10°C and 50°C') against which prototypes are tested — they serve fundamentally different functions. Option D partially captures that both documents exist at different stages but incorrectly implies they share the same purpose.

questions.title: TOK Link: Intuition vs. Data in Design
questions.prompt: A senior product designer argues: 'Decades of experience give me reliable intuition about what users want — large-scale UX surveys just confirm what I already know.' From a Theory of Knowledge perspective, evaluate the epistemic status of designer intuition compared to systematic user research.

options.A: Designer intuition is epistemically superior because tacit knowledge accumulated over decades cannot be captured by surveys, which measure only what users say, not what they do.
options.B: Designer intuition is a form of implicit knowledge that may contain genuine pattern recognition but is susceptible to confirmation bias and availability heuristics; systematic research provides intersubjective verification that intuition lacks.
options.C: Systematic user research is always epistemically superior because it produces quantitative data, and quantitative knowledge is more reliable than qualitative intuition in all knowledge domains.
options.D: Both forms of knowledge are equally valid but serve different purposes: intuition is used for ideation and research is used only for testing, so they never need to be compared.

questions.explanation: TOK distinguishes personal knowledge (tacit, experiential) from shared knowledge (intersubjective, methodologically verified); expert intuition can encode genuine pattern recognition but is vulnerable to cognitive biases such as confirmation bias and the representativeness heuristic, which systematic research with diverse samples can counteract. Option A is a nuanced but ultimately incomplete answer: it correctly identifies tacit knowledge but ignores the well-documented failure modes of expert intuition, including 'expert blind spot' where fluency prevents noticing novice difficulties.

questions.title: Cradle-to-Cradle Design Principle
questions.prompt: A manufacturer redesigns a washing machine so that all components are either fully recyclable technical nutrients or fully compostable biological nutrients, with no mixed-material composites. This approach is best described by which design philosophy, and what distinguishes it from standard 'green design'?

options.A: Eco-efficiency design, which differs from green design by prioritising cost reduction alongside environmental benefit.
options.B: Cradle-to-cradle (C2C) design, which differs from green design by aiming for waste elimination through continuous material cycles rather than merely reducing harm from linear throughput.
options.C: Biomimicry design, which models product lifecycles on natural ecosystem cycles where all outputs become inputs.
options.D: Cradle-to-grave design, which extends producer responsibility to include end-of-life management, unlike standard green design.

questions.explanation: Cradle-to-cradle, developed by McDonough and Braungart, explicitly categorises materials as either technical nutrients (infinitely recyclable in industrial cycles) or biological nutrients (safely compostable), aiming for zero waste by design rather than reduced waste — the key distinction from conventional 'green design,' which typically seeks to lessen environmental damage within a linear take-make-dispose model. Option C confuses C2C with biomimicry: biomimicry draws design inspiration from biological structures and processes, not specifically from material cycling classification.

questions.title: Failure Mode Analysis
questions.prompt: An engineer uses Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) and calculates a Risk Priority Number (RPN) of 210 for a brake sensor failure in an autonomous vehicle. The RPN is the product of Severity (S), Occurrence (O), and Detectability (D), each scored 1–10. A student suggests that to reduce the RPN most efficiently, the team should focus on whichever factor is currently scored highest. Evaluate this strategy.

options.A: The strategy is correct: reducing the highest-scored factor by one unit always produces the largest absolute RPN reduction.
options.B: The strategy is flawed: for safety-critical systems, Severity should be treated as non-negotiable first, and engineering effort should target Occurrence or Detectability regardless of their relative scores.
options.C: The strategy is correct because RPN is a linear product, so reducing any factor by the same proportion reduces RPN by the same proportion, making the highest factor irrelevant.
options.D: The strategy is flawed: since RPN is a multiplicative product, reducing the lowest-scored factor is mathematically optimal because small numbers have the greatest marginal impact per unit change.

questions.explanation: Industry guidance (e.g., SAE J1739) cautions against treating RPN alone as the sole prioritisation metric: in safety-critical applications, a Severity score of 10 (catastrophic) should trigger mandatory action regardless of Occurrence or Detectability scores, because even a rare, detectable failure with catastrophic consequences demands mitigation. Option A is mathematically incorrect — reducing the highest factor by one unit does not always yield the greatest RPN reduction when the other factors vary; and multiplicative products do not behave that simply across all combinations.

questions.title: UX: A/B Testing Validity
questions.prompt: A development team runs an A/B test on two versions of a checkout page. Version A uses a blue 'Buy Now' button and Version B uses a green one. They find a statistically significant increase in conversions for Version B (p = 0.03) and immediately redesign all buttons site-wide. Identify the most significant methodological error in their decision.

options.A: The p-value of 0.03 is above the conventional threshold of 0.01 required for UX research, so the result is not significant.
options.B: They changed only one variable (button colour), which means confounding variables such as user demographics were not controlled.
options.C: They generalised a result from a single isolated test on one page element to the entire site without considering whether colour preference context differs across page types and user segments.
options.D: A/B testing cannot establish causation because it is an observational method; they should have used a controlled laboratory experiment instead.

questions.explanation: A/B tests are contextually bounded: a result showing green outperforms blue on a checkout page may not hold on a homepage hero button, a mobile navigation element, or for different user demographics — site-wide generalisation from one test violates the principle of ecological validity. Option B is incorrect because changing only one variable is actually correct A/B test design methodology, not an error; proper A/B tests do isolate a single variable.

questions.title: Composite Materials: Properties
questions.prompt: Carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) is used in high-performance bicycle frames instead of steel. A student states: 'CFRP is superior to steel in all mechanical properties and should replace it in every structural application.' To what extent is this claim justified?

options.A: Fully justified: CFRP has higher specific strength, specific stiffness, and fatigue resistance than steel across all loading conditions.
options.B: Partially justified: CFRP outperforms steel in tensile strength-to-weight ratio, but steel is superior in compressive buckling resistance, impact toughness, repairability, and cost, making universal replacement unjustified.
options.C: Partially justified: CFRP is superior only in aerospace applications because its properties depend on temperature, and at room temperature steel remains stronger.
options.D: Not justified: steel has a higher ultimate tensile strength than CFRP when measured in absolute terms, making it strictly superior for structural use.

questions.explanation: CFRP has exceptional specific strength (~2400 MPa tensile strength at ~1.6 g/cm³) and specific stiffness, but it is brittle under impact, prone to delamination, difficult to inspect for internal damage, essentially non-repairable in the field, and far more expensive than structural steel; for applications requiring impact resilience, weldability, or low cost, steel is superior. Option D is factually wrong: high-modulus CFRP can achieve tensile strengths exceeding 3500 MPa, far above structural steels (~400–2000 MPa).

questions.title: Planned Obsolescence Ethics
questions.prompt: A consumer electronics company intentionally designs its smartphones so that software updates from year three onward significantly slow performance, encouraging users to purchase newer models. Critically assess this practice from both an innovation economics and an ethical standpoint.

options.A: Economically rational and ethically acceptable: planned obsolescence drives R&D investment by guaranteeing revenue cycles necessary for continued innovation.
options.B: Economically rational but ethically problematic: while it sustains revenue streams, it deliberately degrades a product the consumer already purchased without full disclosure, violating informed consent and generating unnecessary e-waste.
options.C: Economically irrational because it destroys brand loyalty and is also ethically unacceptable, so companies never engage in this practice in regulated markets.
options.D: Ethically acceptable under consequentialist ethics because the long-term innovation benefits to society outweigh the short-term inconvenience to individual consumers.

questions.explanation: Planned obsolescence through software throttling generates predictable upgrade revenue (economically rational from the firm's perspective) but involves degrading a product post-sale without informed consumer consent — Apple was fined €25 million by France's DGCCRF in 2020 specifically for this practice, establishing it as a consumer rights and transparency violation. Option D oversimplifies consequentialist analysis: the long-term benefits are speculative while the harms (financial burden on consumers, 50 million tonnes/year of e-waste) are concrete and measurable.

questions.title: Additive vs. Subtractive Manufacturing
questions.prompt: A company must produce 50,000 identical aluminium brackets per month. A student recommends switching from CNC milling (subtractive) to metal 3D printing (additive) to reduce material waste. Evaluate whether this recommendation is well-reasoned for this production context.

options.A: Well-reasoned: metal 3D printing always produces less waste than CNC milling regardless of batch size.
options.B: Partially reasoned: 3D printing does reduce material waste, but at 50,000 units per month it is significantly slower and more expensive per unit than CNC milling, making it economically unsuitable for high-volume identical parts.
options.C: Well-reasoned: material waste reduction is the only factor relevant to manufacturing process selection, so additive manufacturing is always preferable.
options.D: Poorly reasoned but for the wrong reason: CNC milling of aluminium produces no waste because all swarf is collected and remelted.

questions.explanation: Metal additive manufacturing (e.g., DMLS/SLM) does reduce buy-to-fly ratios compared to milling complex geometries, but cycle times for metal 3D printing are far slower (hours per part vs. minutes in CNC), and per-part costs at high volumes heavily favour CNC milling with its mature tooling and high throughput — 3D printing's advantages are most pronounced for low-volume, geometrically complex, or customised parts. Option D is misleading: CNC swarf is often recyclable, but 'no waste' overstates the case and ignores cutting fluid, energy, and tool wear as resource costs.

questions.title: User Persona Limitations
questions.prompt: A UX team creates three user personas for a banking app based on survey data from 200 respondents. A design critic argues that personas are 'fictional stereotypes that replace real user understanding.' To what extent does this critique identify a genuine methodological weakness?

options.A: The critique is entirely correct: personas have been abandoned by leading UX firms in favour of jobs-to-be-done frameworks.
options.B: The critique identifies a genuine risk — personas can create false specificity and encourage designing for an archetype rather than real diversity — but this is a misuse risk, not an inherent flaw, when personas are grounded in rigorous qualitative and quantitative data.
options.C: The critique is entirely wrong: personas are validated scientific instruments equivalent to sociological demographic profiles.
options.D: The critique is valid only if the personas are created without quantitative data; when based on surveys, personas are free from stereotype risk.

questions.explanation: Personas are synthesis tools that compress complex user data into memorable archetypes to guide design decisions; the legitimate critique is that poorly constructed personas can become stereotypes that marginalise edge-case users, a risk Alan Cooper himself acknowledged in later editions of 'The Inmates Are Running the Asylum.' However, when built from mixed-method research, they remain valuable decision aids — the critique describes a misuse risk, not a fatal methodological flaw. Option D is wrong because quantitative data alone does not prevent stereotyping; demographic segmentation can still obscure intra-group behavioural diversity.

questions.title: Design for Disassembly
questions.prompt: A laptop is designed with all internal components glued together and soldered to a single non-removable board. From a lifecycle assessment and circular economy perspective, what is the primary design principle being violated, and what is the consequence?

options.A: The principle of modularity is violated, which reduces aesthetic appeal and makes software updates more difficult.
options.B: The principle of design for disassembly is violated, preventing efficient repair, component reuse, and material recovery at end-of-life, thus forcing the entire device into e-waste streams prematurely.
options.C: The principle of ergonomic accessibility is violated because technicians cannot safely service the device.
options.D: The principle of standardisation is violated, which increases manufacturing costs and reduces compatibility with industry-standard components.

questions.explanation: Design for disassembly (DfD) requires that products be engineered to allow efficient separation of components for repair, reuse, or recycling — glued and soldered non-modular assemblies make this impossible, meaning functional components (screens, batteries, cameras) cannot be harvested and rare earth metals cannot be efficiently recovered, shortening product lifespan and maximising e-waste. Option A is partially related but 'modularity' in this context is a subset of DfD and 'aesthetic appeal' is irrelevant to the LCA critique.

questions.title: Trademarks vs. Copyright
questions.prompt: A student designs a logo for her school enterprise project using a distinctive hand-lettered font she created herself. She wants to protect both the font design and the logo as a brand identifier. Which statement correctly maps the appropriate intellectual property protection to each element?

options.A: Both the font and the logo should be protected by a single patent, as patents cover all novel creative works.
